n560144dd592.s: The Milindapanho records a dialogue between Menander and:
n560144dd592.x: The Milindapanho records the dialogue between the Indo-Greek king Menander and the monk Nagasena.
xa: **Andhranagari** is identified with **Dhanyakataka**; its river = **Krishna** (per **P. C. Ray**).
**Dipavamsa** and **Mahavamsa** = Sri Lankan Pali chronicles on Mauryan history and Andhra Buddhism.
Jain text **Nayadhammakahao** records the Ikshvaku ruler **Yashodhara** and his son **Dhanada**.
Other Buddhist sources: **Jatakas**, **Dighanikaya**, **Pitakas** (Tripitaka).

ndc2a11d1246.x: Gunadhya composed Brihatkatha in Paisachi; it is a source for the Satavahana age.
xa: ⚠ **Brihatkatha** = **Gunadhya**; **Brihatkatha Kosha** = **Harisena**.
**Gathasaptasati** by Satavahana king **Hala**, in **Maharashtri Prakrit**, describes Satavahana society.
**Harshacharita** of **Banabhatta** calls **Yajna Sri Satakarni** "**Trisamudradheesvara**".

n73e7e4b2794.s: Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam were written by:
n73e7e4b2794.x: Both plays were written by Vishakhadatta; Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita.
xa: ⚠ Vishakhadatta wrote both a **Mauryan** source (Mudrarakshasa) and a **Gupta** source (Devichandraguptam).
Other Mauryan-age sources: **Arthashastra** (Kautilya) and **Mahabhashya** (Patanjali).
**Harshacharita** is on **Harshavardhana**.

nc50b98533f9.x: Banabhatta's Harshacharita refers to Yajna Sri Satakarni as Trisamudradheesvara.
xa: **Hiuen Tsang** visited **Harsha** and **Pulakeshin II**.
The **Aihole** inscription by **Ravikirti** records **Pulakeshin II**'s defeat of Harsha.
Yajna Sri also issued **ship-motif** coins, showing maritime trade.

n60f22f5b571.s: Rajatarangini, a chronicle of the kings of Kashmir, was composed by
n60f22f5b571.x: Kalhana composed Rajatarangini in the 12th century on the kings of Kashmir. Banabhatta wrote Harshacharita, Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam, and Nayachandra Suri wrote Hammira-Mahakavya.
xs: **Rajatarangini** was composed by **Kalhana** in the **12th century** — option **(2)** (**APPSC 2025**).
**Banabhatta** wrote **Harshacharita**; **Vishakhadatta** wrote **Mudrarakshasa** and **Devichandraguptam**.
**Nayachandra Suri** wrote **Hammira-Mahakavya** on Hammira of Ranthambore.
xa: Exam angle: match the work with both its **author** and the **dynasty** it documents.
**Gathasaptasati** – King **Hala** (Satavahana); **Brihatkatha** – **Gunadhya** (Paisachi).
**Kashikhandam** – **Srinatha** – sea trade of the **Reddy** kingdom (**PYQ 2011**).

na8c402b3320.s: Gathasaptasati, an important source for Satavahana society, was composed by
na8c402b3320.x: Gathasaptasati is attributed to the Satavahana king Hala and is in Maharashtri Prakrit. Gunadhya wrote Brihatkatha in Paisachi, Srinatha wrote Kashikhandam, and Kautilya wrote the Arthashastra.
xs: **Gathasaptasati** was composed by Satavahana **King Hala** in **Maharashtri Prakrit** — option **(2)**.
**Gunadhya** wrote **Brihatkatha** in **Paisachi**.
**Srinatha** wrote **Kashikhandam**; **Kautilya** wrote the **Arthashastra**.
xa: Both Gathasaptasati and Brihatkatha are sources for the **Satavahana age**.
All **Satavahana inscriptions** are in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi** script.
The **Vishnu Purana** narrates the Satavahana story; the last Satavahana = **Pulomavi III**.

n592e10a9294.s: The first Telugu word, “Nagabu”, belongs to which period?
n592e10a9294.x: “Nagabu” is identified as the first Telugu word and belongs to the Satavahana period.
n592e10a9294.tq: Distinguish the period of the earliest word from the date of the first inscription.
xs: The first Telugu word "**Nagabu**" belongs to the **Satavahana period** — option **(4)**.
All **Satavahana inscriptions** are in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi** script.
xa: **First Telugu inscription** = **Kalamalla** (Renati Choda).
The **Telugu** script is traced to **Brahmi**.
Earliest literary reference to Andhras = **Aitareya Brahmana**.

ncf190595adb.s: Who wrote A Forgotten Empire, a work on Vijayanagara?
ncf190595adb.x: Robert Sewell wrote A Forgotten Empire on Vijayanagara.
ncf190595adb.tq: Match the historical work with its author while avoiding confusion with archaeologists of Andhra sites.
xs: **A Forgotten Empire** (on Vijayanagara) was written by **Robert Sewell** — option **(2)** (**PYQ 2011**).
**Mortimer Wheeler** excavated **Arikamedu**; **John Marshall** announced the Indus Civilization.
**James Burgess** studied stupas of **Amaravati and Jaggayyapeta**.
xa: Sewell's work is a source on **Vijayanagara**.
**Kashikhandam** (Srinatha) — sea trade of the **Reddy** kingdom (also **PYQ 2011**).
**Parvataneni Veeraiah Chaudhary** = "**Andhra Shivaji**".

nindian-history-90-16.s: Which is regarded as the earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript?
nindian-history-90-16.x: The Dastan-i-Amir Hamza (Hamzanama), painted under Akbar, is regarded as the earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript.
n: Dastan-i-Amir Hamza is the earliest Mughal illustrated manuscript. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #90 · pp 172-173]
xa: **Panchraksha** (**1105 CE**, **Ashutosh Museum**, Kolkata) is the **oldest paper evidence** in India.
**Dashpur inscription**: the **oldest advertisement tradition** in India.

nindian-history-13-1.s: Who wrote the grammatical work Ashtadhyayi?
nindian-history-13-1.x: Panini wrote the Ashtadhyayi, the classic Sanskrit grammar. Katyayana wrote the Varttika on it, Patanjali the Mahabhashya and Yaska the Nirukta on etymology.
nindian-history-13-1.tq: Discriminate the four grammarians by their works.
n: Panini wrote Ashtadhyayi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Ashtadhyayi deals with grammar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
xs: **Panini** wrote the **Ashtadhyayi** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is the **earliest known Sanskrit grammar**.
**Katyayana** wrote the **Varttika**, **Patanjali** the **Mahabhashya**, and **Yaska** the **Nirukta** (**etymology**).
xa: The **Mahabhashya** is a **grammar** and **commentary**, and a **Mauryan-age source**.
**Amarakosh** by **Amar Singh** is a **Sanskrit lexicon**.

nd8554cf6621.s: The Samarangana Sutradhara was written by:
nd8554cf6621.x: The Samarangana Sutradhara was written by King Bhoja, not Pravarasena II.
xa: The **Dashpur inscription** is the **oldest advertisement tradition** in India.
**Amarakosh** — **Amar Singh**; **Nirukta** — **Yaska**.
**Rajatarangini** (**Kalhana**) was asked in **APPSC 2025**.

nindian-history-97-19.x: Rajasekhara wrote Kavyamimamsa; Kalidasa was the great Sanskrit poet of the Gupta age.
n: Kautilya is also known as Chanakya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Kautilya is associated with the Arthashastra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Xuanzang, also known as Hieun Tsang, is associated with Si-Yu-Ki. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Kalidasa is associated with the Gupta period. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Kalidasa is associated with Sanskrit literature. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
Rajasekhara is associated with Kavyamimamsa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]
xa: **Amoghavarsha I** — **Kavirajamarga**.
Xuanzang is linked with **Harshavardhana** and **Nalanda**.
Kautilya is linked with **Chandragupta Maurya**.

nff799627d24.s: Which Buddhist text contains the earliest literary reference to the region of Andhra as “Andhrapatha”?
nff799627d24.x: Vinayavatthu contains the earliest Buddhist literary reference to Andhra as Andhrapatha.
nff799627d24.tq: Directly identify the text associated with the earliest reference.
xs: The earliest Buddhist reference to the region as "**Andhrapatha**" is in the **Vinayavatthu** — so option **(2)** is correct (asked in **PYQ 2019**).
**Milindapanho** is the dialogue of Indo-Greek **Menander (Milinda)** with monk **Nagasena**.
**Dipavamsa** is a **Sri Lankan Pali chronicle**; **Kathavatthu** mentions the **Andhakas** as a Buddhist branch.
xa: ⚠ "Andhrapatha" first in an **inscription** = **Maidavolu copper plates** of Pallava **Sivaskandavarma** (Prakrit, c. **300 CE**).
**Earliest literary reference** to the Andhras = **Aitareya Brahmana** (Sunahshepa story, Vishwamitra's disowned sons).
The Buddhist name for the region was "**Andhakaratta**".
First Telugu word = "**Nagabu**" (Satavahana period); first Telugu inscription = **Kalamalla** (Renati Choda).

n3fe3921c3d1.s: Andhranagari, mentioned in the Bhimasena and Serivanija Jatakas, is identified with:
n3fe3921c3d1.x: Andhranagari is identified with Dhanyakataka; P. C. Ray identified its river as the Krishna.
xa: Andhranagari is mentioned in the **Bhimasena**, **Serivanija** and other **Jatakas**, which describe Andhra settlements.
**Kathavatthu** refers to the **Andhakas** as an important Buddhist branch.
Buddhist name for the Andhra region: "**Andhakaratta**"; earliest Buddhist "**Andhrapatha**" = **Vinayavatthu**.

nc3914a64dc8.x: The Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa are Sri Lankan Pali chronicles that illuminate Mauryan history and Andhra Buddhism.
xa: The Sri Lankan chronicles also give the **Gajabahu-Senguttuvan synchronism** that dates the **Sangam age**.
Nayadhammakahao names the Ikshvaku ruler **Yashodhara** and his son **Dhanada**.
Buddhist sources: **Jatakas**, **Dighanikaya**, **Pitakas**, **Kathavatthu** (Andhakas), **Milindapanho**.

n3bfc2a7cad5.s: The earliest literary reference to the Andhras occurs in the:
n3bfc2a7cad5.x: The Aitareya Brahmana gives the earliest literary reference to the Andhras, in the story of Sunahshepa and Vishwamitra's disowned sons.
xa: Earliest Buddhist "**Andhrapatha**" = **Vinayavatthu** (**PYQ 2019**); first in an inscription = **Maidavolu** plates.
**First decipherable inscriptions** = Ashoka's edicts, **Prakrit** in **Brahmi** (**APPSC 2017**).
First definite coin references = **Pali texts** (kahapana, nikkha, kamsa, kakanika), corroborated by **punch-marked coins**.

n2bca626a6bb.s: According to the Puranas, the last Satavahana ruler was:
n2bca626a6bb.x: The Puranas name Pulomavi III, not Gautamiputra Satakarni, as the last Satavahana.
xa: The **Vayu Purana** refers to the **Andhra** people.
The **Myakadoni** (Bellary) inscription of **Pulumavi III** is the basis of the **Karnataka-homeland** theory.
**Nasik** Prashasti of **Gautami Balashri** records Gautamiputra Satakarni's achievements.

n7625951a33d.s: Sangam texts are dated to about:
n7625951a33d.x: Sangam texts are dated to about the 3rd century BCE - 3rd century CE and describe the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms.
xa: The **Gajabahu-Senguttuvan synchronism** from **Dipavamsa/Mahavamsa** dates the Sangam age.
**Tamil-Brahmi** (Tamizhi) is the earliest Tamil script, c. **3rd century BCE**.
The **Hathigumpha** inscription of **Kharavela** mentions the **Tamil kingdoms**.

n21b86b1f92c.s: Ashoka’s 13th Major Rock Edict lists the Andhras as part of the
n21b86b1f92c.x: The 13th Major Rock Edict of Ashoka lists the Andhras among the peoples within the Mauryan Empire.
n21b86b1f92c.tq: Use the edict number and the political entity together to avoid a dynasty swap.
xs: Ashoka's **13th Major Rock Edict** lists the **Andhras** in the **Mauryan Empire** — option **(3)**.
Ashoka was a **Mauryan** ruler; Satavahana, Kushana and Gupta came later.
xa: **Maski**: first edict naming "**Asoka**"; **Gulmika** = village headman.
**Erragudi** (Kurnool): teachers to inculcate **Dharma** in students.
**Megasthenes**, at Chandragupta Maurya's court, credited the Andhras with **30** forts.

n5af703eb640.s: Which Jain text refers to the Andhra traditions concerning the Ikshvaku ruler Yashodhara and his son Dhanada?
n5af703eb640.x: Nayadhammakahao contains the Andhra traditions concerning Yashodhara and his son Dhanada.
n5af703eb640.tq: Distinguish the specific Jain source from the broader Jain literary corpus.
xs: The Jain text on Ikshvaku ruler **Yashodhara** and his son **Dhanada** is **Nayadhammakahao** — option **(3)**.
It records **Andhra traditions**.
The other Jain text in the notes is the **Kalpasutra**, but it is not linked to Yashodhara.
xa: Buddhist counterparts: **Kathavatthu** (Andhakas), **Jatakas** (Andhranagari), **Vinayavatthu** (Andhrapatha).
**Smritis** (Narada, Vishnu, Brihaspati, Katyayana) → varna, law, inheritance in the **Gupta age**.
**Dipavamsa**, **Mahavamsa** → Sri Lankan Pali chronicles on Andhra Buddhism.

nfcdb07abf9e.s: Which inscription is associated with Kharavela of Kalinga and records his campaigns as well as references to Tamil kingdoms?
nfcdb07abf9e.x: The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela of Kalinga records his campaigns and mentions Tamil kingdoms.
nfcdb07abf9e.tq: Identify the issuer first, then match the inscription with its distinctive content.
xs: The **Hathigumpha** inscription (Odisha) of **Kharavela** of Kalinga records his campaigns and the **Tamil kingdoms** — option **(2)**.

**Bhitari** records the **repulse of the Hunas**.
**Sangam texts** describe the Tamil **Chera-Chola-Pandya** kingdoms.

nee7ec6395d2.s: The Nasik Prashasti, which hails Gautamiputra Satakarni as destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, was composed by:
nee7ec6395d2.x: The Nasik Prashasti was composed by Gautami Balashri, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
xa: ⚠ Composer vs king: **Harisena** → Samudragupta; **Ravikirti** → Pulakeshin II; **Gautami Balashri** → Gautamiputra Satakarni.
**Gautamiputra Satakarni** re-struck **Nahapana**'s coins.
**Naneghat** of Queen **Naganika** = early Satavahana history.

nd7f4d5080a3.s: Which inscription is particularly important for the early history of the Satavahana family?
nd7f4d5080a3.x: The Naneghat inscription, issued by Queen Naganika, is an important source for the early history of the Satavahana family.
nd7f4d5080a3.tq: Match the inscription with its specific historical use.
xs: The **Naneghat** (Nanaghat) inscription of Queen **Naganika** covers **early Satavahana history** — option **(3)**.
**Bhitari** = **Skandagupta** (Hunas); **Aihole** = **Pulakeshin II**; **Maski** = **Ashoka**.
xa: ⚠ **Rudradaman — Nanaghat** was the wrong pair in **APPSC 2012** (correct: **Junagadh**).
**Nasik** Prashasti of **Gautami Balashri** = achievements of Gautamiputra Satakarni.
**Myakadoni** (Bellary) of **Pulumavi III** = basis of the Karnataka-homeland theory.

n559deae064c.s: The Junagadh inscription was issued by:
n559deae064c.x: The Junagadh inscription of Rudradaman I is a long Sanskrit inscription recording the repair of the Sudarshana lake.

Other Sanskrit inscriptions: **Allahabad Pillar** (Harisena) and **Aihole** (Ravikirti).

n269d1742fa4.s: Which inscription provides a basis for the Karnataka-homeland theory of the Satavahanas?
n269d1742fa4.x: The Myakadoni inscription of Pulumavi III provides the basis for the Karnataka-homeland theory of the Satavahanas.
n269d1742fa4.tq: Match a regional inscription with the historical theory derived from it.
xs: The **Myakadoni** (Bellary) inscription of **Pulumavi III** is the basis of the **Karnataka-homeland** theory — option **(2)**.
**Nasik** = Gautami Balashri's praise of Gautamiputra Satakarni; **Hathigumpha** = Kharavela; **Erragudi** = Ashoka.
xa: **V. S. Sukthankar** held that Andhras and Satavahanas were **not the same people** (Karnataka theory).
The Puranas name **Pulomavi III** as the **last Satavahana**.
All Satavahana inscriptions are in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi** script.

n127bbde64a3.s: The Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela was composed in which language?
n127bbde64a3.x: The Hathigumpha inscription was composed in Prakrit using the Brahmi script.
xa: Hathigumpha records Kharavela's campaigns and mentions the **Tamil kingdoms**.
Junagadh = **first long Sanskrit inscription**.
Satavahana inscriptions too are in **Prakrit**, Brahmi script.

n06a57c6d1b0.s: The Alluru inscription is significant because it records
o: multiple donations to various communities and institutions
the thirty forts of the Andhras mentioned by Megasthenes
the first decipherable edict of Ashoka
n06a57c6d1b0.x: The Alluru inscription records multiple donations made to various communities and institutions.

**Amaravati** and **Nagarjunakonda** inscriptions and stupas are key Ikshvaku sources.
Satavahana inscriptions are in **Prakrit**, **Brahmi**.

nindian-history-1-12.s: The Ayodhya inscription is associated with:
nindian-history-1-12.x: The Ayodhya inscription is associated with Pushyamitra Shunga; Nashik is linked with Gautamiputra Satakarni and Hathigumpha with Kharavela.
n: The Hathigumpha Inscription is associated with Kharavela. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Ayodhya Inscription is associated with Pushyamitra Shunga. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

The Nashik Inscription is associated with Gautami Balashri and Gautamiputra Satakarni. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: The Nashik inscription gives Gautamiputra the title **Ekabrahmana** (**Unrivalled Brahmana**) and calls him destroyer of **Shakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas**.

nindian-history-1-13.s: The Sarnath Buddhist image inscription dated 81 AD is associated with:
nindian-history-1-13.x: The Sarnath Buddhist image inscription is dated to Kanishka's third year (81 AD).
n: The Sarnath Buddhist Image Inscription is associated with Kanishka. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

The Rabatak Inscription is written in Bactrian. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Rabatak Inscription uses the Greek script. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Sarnath inscription links Kanishka with 81 AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Rabatak Inscription links Kanishka with Bactrian and Greek script. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: The Rabatak Inscription was found in **Afghanistan**, **discovered 1993**.

nindian-history-1-29.s: Which inscription from Bengal deals with famine relief?

n: The Sohgaura Copper Plate concerns food-grain preservation. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

The Sohgaura Copper Plate is associated with grain preservation during famine. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Mahasthan Inscription concerns famine relief. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: Sohgaura is the **earliest known copper plate** and the **earliest royal famine-related order**.

nindian-history-1-32.s: The Rabatak inscription (discovered 1993) is in the Bactrian language written in which script?

n: The Rabatak Inscription was discovered in 1993. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Rabatak Inscription is written in Bactrian. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Rabatak Inscription uses the Greek script. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

The Rabatak Inscription links Kanishka with Bactrian and Greek script. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: Both Rabatak and the **Sarnath Buddhist Image Inscription** are associated with **Kanishka**.

nindian-history-1-58.s: The earliest long Sanskrit inscription and an early specimen of the Kavya style is the:
nindian-history-1-58.x: The Junagadh inscription is the earliest long Sanskrit inscription and an early Kavya-style work.
n: The Junagadh Inscription is the earliest perfect Sanskrit inscription. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

xa: It is located at **Girnar** or **Junagadh**, **Gujarat**; approximately **150 AD**, in **Sanskrit** in **Brahmi script**.

nindian-history-1-59.s: According to the Hathigumpha inscription, Kharavela followed which religion?
nindian-history-1-59.x: The Hathigumpha inscription opens with a salute to the Jinas, showing that Kharavela was a Jain.

The Hathigumpha Inscription mentions Mahapadmananda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

xa: Kharavela belonged to the **Chedi** or **Mahameghavahana dynasty** and **ruled Kalinga**.

nindian-history-1-62.s: Which title is associated with Gautamiputra Satakarni in the Nashik inscription?
nindian-history-1-62.x: The Nashik inscription of Gautami Balashri calls her son Gautamiputra Satakarni "Ekabrahmana" (unrivalled Brahmana). Sikandar-i-Sani, Param Saugat and Piyadasi Raja are titles of other rulers.
nindian-history-1-62.tq: Match each title to its ruler.
n: Gautamiputra Satakarni held the title Ekabrahmana. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Nashik Inscription associates Gautamiputra with the title Ekabrahmana. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xs: The **Nashik inscription** gives **Gautamiputra Satakarni** the title **Ekabrahmana** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Ekabrahmana** means **Unrivalled Brahmana**; the inscription is linked to his mother **Gautami Balashri**.
xa: It praises him as destroyer of the **Shakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas**.

nindian-history-1-95.s: Rudradaman repaired which lake without forced labour, as recorded in the Junagadh inscription?

nindian-history-1-37.s: According to the Aihole inscription, Pulakeshin II stopped Harsha's southward advance at the:

Harsha's southward expansion was stopped at the Narmada. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]

nindian-history-1-80.s: The Aihole inscription, written in Southern Brahmi, is in which language?

nindian-history-30-9.s: The earliest known copper plate in India is the:

nindian-history-30-15.s: Who is known as 'Padakavita Pitamaha', the earliest known Telugu song-composer?

nindian-history-54-19.s: Ibn Battuta served as qazi at Delhi under which Sultan?

nindian-history-97-1.s: Which ruler is associated with the Allahabad Pillar inscription and extensive conquests?

nfa57ab8e6f6.s: Megasthenes visited the court of which ruler as an envoy of Seleucus Nikator?

nf4128dcb99b.s: Which foreign work is regarded as the first foreign account to mention the Andhras?

n410557144a3.s: What economic issue concerning India did Pliny the Elder particularly complain about?
o: The shortage of Greek soldiers in India
The loss of Roman territory to the Satavahanas
The annual drain of Roman gold to India
The destruction of Roman ports by the Guptas

xs: **Pliny the Elder** complained of the drain of **Roman gold** to India — option **(3)**.

Rome paid for Indian **spices, pearls, muslin**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes (Jun 2026) put it at **55 million sesterces**.
Pliny wrote **Natural History** (Naturalis Historia), in **Latin**, **1st century CE**.
**Roman coins** have been found at **Bhattiprolu**.

n090643217f8.s: Masulia, mentioned by Ptolemy as an eastern trading centre, is identified with:

n4e0b0456fa8.s: Hiuen Tsang’s account of India is known as which of the following?

n481ef6d4bc7.s: I-Tsing is associated with which one of the following observations?

n36ceb6bfe7a.s: Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind in which language?

nindian-history-54-12.s: Which foreign visitor wrote about the Brahmins and Shramanas?

Hiuen-Tsang was associated with Nalanda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 128-129]

I-Tsing was associated with Buddhist pilgrimage. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 128-129]

nd104b576984.s: Ashokan inscriptions are significant as the first decipherable inscriptions of India. In which combination were they primarily written?

n40d2556cd0b.s: James Prinsep deciphered the Brahmi script in:

carried the names and portraits of rulers

xa: Nasik Prashasti praises him as destroyer of **Shakas, Yavanas, Pahlavas**.

Satavahana coin metals: **lead, copper, bronze, potin**.

n2be392430de.s: Ship-motif coins are associated with which Satavahana ruler?
n2be392430de.x: Ship-motif coins, evidence of maritime trade, are associated with Yajna Sri Satakarni (and Vasishthiputra Pulumavi); Gautamiputra is known for re-striking Nahapana's coins.

n12a9907b2e5.s: The first definite references to coins such as kahapana, nikkha, kamsa and kakanika occur in:

nf2b96e56b12.s: The Bhattiprolu inscription refers to which body?

Roman coins were found at Nagarjuna Konda. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 19-20]
Santamula-I was an Ikshvaku ruler who issued crores of gold coins. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 19-20]
xa: Satavahanas used **lead**, **copper**, **bronze** and **potin**.
**Punch-marked** coins, the earliest Indian coins, were recently found at **Balirajgarh** (Madhubani, Bihar).

n4ed652dab7f.s: Who was the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India?
n4ed652dab7f.x: Alexander Cunningham became the first Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India in 1861.

xs: **Alexander Cunningham** was the **first Director-General of the ASI** (**1861**) — option **(2)**.

**Mortimer Wheeler** excavated **Arikamedu**; **Alexander Rea** excavated **Bhattiprolu**.
xa: Cunningham is called the "**father of Indian archaeology**".
Marshall coined "**Indus Valley Civilisation**" and excavated **Mohenjodaro**.

n9292463d004.x: Mortimer Wheeler excavated Arikamedu in 1945; Marshall worked at Mohenjodaro, Rea at Bhattiprolu and Longhurst at Nagarjunakonda.

Arikamedu was a **Roman market** per the Periplus.

n39135fca53d.s: The Bhattiprolu stupa was excavated by:
n39135fca53d.x: Alexander Rea excavated the Bhattiprolu stupa; Robert Sewell wrote A Forgotten Empire.

Rea found **relic caskets** at Bhattiprolu.
**Bhattiprolu** inscription refers to the **Nigama-sabha**; Roman coins found there.

n3be8d544c78.s: The approximate half-life of carbon-14 used in radiocarbon dating is
n3be8d544c78.x: Carbon-14 has a half-life of approximately 5,730 years.

xs: The half-life of **carbon-14** is about **5,730 years** — option **(2)**.
Radiocarbon dating measures **C-14 decay** in **organic remains**.
xa: **Dendrochronology** = counting annual tree rings.
**Thermoluminescence** dates pottery or burnt material by radiation absorbed since last firing.
**Stratigraphy** follows **superposition**: lower layers are older.

neddd22a8405.s: In stratigraphy, the principle that lower layers are older than the layers above them is called:
neddd22a8405.x: This principle is superposition; counting annual tree rings is dendrochronology.
xa: **Radiocarbon (C-14)**: decay in organic remains; half-life about **5,730 years**.
**Thermoluminescence**: light released on heating **pottery**/burnt material.

ned68e5dc4fd.s: The first appearance of the term “Andhrapatha” in an inscription is associated with which record?
o: Kalamalla inscription of the Renati Chodas
Maidavolu copper plates of Pallava Sivaskandavarma
ned68e5dc4fd.x: Andhrapatha first appears epigraphically in the Maidavolu copper plates of Pallava Sivaskandavarma, composed in Prakrit and dated to about 300 CE.

xs: "**Andhrapatha**" first appears in an inscription in the **Maidavolu copper plates** of Pallava **Sivaskandavarma** — option **(4)**.

**Kalamalla** (Renati Choda) is the first **Telugu** inscription; **Mangulam** is a **Tamil-Brahmi** site.
**Shahbazgarhi** is an Ashokan **Kharosthi** edict.

Buddhist name for the region: "**Andhakaratta**".

n59431648c1a.s: Which inscription contains the first edict naming Ashoka as 'Asoka'?
n59431648c1a.x: The Maski inscription is the first edict that names Ashoka as 'Asoka'; it also uses the term Gulmika.

nc7fd32be5b6.s: The Boghaz-Koi inscription, which names Indra, Varuna, Mitra and Nasatya, belongs to the:

nindian-history-97-20.s: Kavirajamarga is attributed to which ruler?

Rajendra Chola I is associated with overseas expeditions. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]

Shivaji is associated with Ashtapradhan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #97 · pp 181-183]

**Aryabhata** — **Aryabhatiya**.

nap-history-1-29.s: The inscription in which the Kakatiyas were mentioned for the first time is the:

The first Muslim invasion of Warangal took place in 1303. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-5]
Alauddin Khilji led the first sultanate invasion of the Kakatiyas. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-5]
xa: **Kulottunga-I** was the **first Chalukya-Chola emperor**.

**Megasthenes** was the **earliest** to **mention forts** in Andhra.

nindian-history-6-47.x: Manusmriti, the law code attributed to Manu, is also called Manav Dharma Shastra. Muntakhab-ut-Tawarikh is Badauni's chronicle and Tahqiq-i-Hind is Al-Biruni's work.

**Samarangana Sutradhara** is by **King Bhoja**; **Tahqiq-i-Hind** (**Kitab-ul-Hind**) is **Al-Biruni**'s work.
xa: **Rajatarangini** — **Kalhana**, 12th century; history of the **kings of Kashmir**.
**Amarakosh** — **Amar Singh**, a **Sanskrit lexicon**.
**Nitivakyamrita** — **Somadeva Suri**.

n7ad61e5e789.s: According to the Matsya Purana, how many Satavahana kings ruled for 456 years?

nf35f002e255.s: Gathasaptasati, a Prakrit work of 700 verses, is attributed to:

**Matsya Purana**: **30** Satavahana kings, **456** years.

ncb50068f092.s: Which literary work or works reveal sea trade during the Reddi period?
ncb50068f092.x: Both Kashikhandam and Haravilasam, associated with Srinatha, reveal sea trade during the Reddi period.

n5bce5d8d0b9.s: The inscriptions that serve as a source for Satavahana history are written in:

n38909a39bf0.s: Which inscription records Santamula's foundation of the kingdom at Vijayapuri?

n9bf9552b8ef.s: The Manchikallu inscription records the conquest of Vijayapuri by Pallava:
n9bf9552b8ef.x: The Manchikallu inscription records Simhavarman's conquest of Vijayapuri.

nap-history-3-5.s: The only inscription about the Brihatpalayanas is the:

nap-history-3-16.s: Which inscription is the first to mention Vishnu temples in Andhra?

The Pedavegi inscription is the first to mention Vishnu temples in Andhra. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]

n9af0d0e0db2.s: The capital of the Brihatpalayana king Jayavarma was:

nfdd28b2b114.s: The Bhattiprolu relic caskets are associated with which pre-Satavahana local ruler?

n2620d20f01c.s: The Naneghat inscription was issued by:

nf800c4d45fd.s: Gautami Balasri's Nasik inscription belongs to the reign of:
nf800c4d45fd.x: The Nasik inscription was issued during Vasishthiputra Pulumavi's reign and records Gautamiputra Satakarni's victories.

nf586a6b7529.s: The Amaravati inscription is significant in Andhra history because it:
o: Is regarded as the first Satavahana inscription in Andhra and contains the word ‘Nagabu’
Records the defeat of Rudrapurushadatta by Simhavarman

n9105ba0f501.s: The last Ikshvaku ruler Rudrapurushadatta was defeated by:

o: Military orders from a village council

**Nigama-sabha** = town council (Bhattiprolu).

n5b83a946991.s: In Vishnukundin grants, land was measured in:

**Malkapuram** (Rudramadevi, **1261 CE**) names the Jalakaranda.

n2365c9029b2.s: Which of the following is NOT a stupa site listed among the archaeological sources of Andhra?

n90e7c8fee7b.s: Attirala, where a hoard of Roman gold coins was found, is in which district?

ndbd289c1549.s: The Middle Palaeolithic period in India is generally associated with:
o: Flake industry and prepared-core Levallois technique
Only large stone circles around burials
ndbd289c1549.x: The Middle Palaeolithic is characterized by flake tools, prepared cores such as the Levallois technique, scrapers, borers and points.
ndbd289c1549.tq: Identify the archaeological stage from its technological characteristics.
xs: The **Middle Palaeolithic** = **flake industry** with the prepared-core **Levallois** technique — option **(1)**.

**Iron** comes only in the Iron Age; **stone circles** around burials are **megalithic**.
xa: Middle Palaeolithic sites: **Nevasa**, **Bhimbetka**, Narmada, Godavari, Krishna valleys; **Sembur** (TN).
⚠ Trap: some notes call it the "microlithic stage" — microliths belong to the Upper Palaeolithic + Mesolithic.

n2d0b04a6aee.s: Which of the following sites is associated with the Upper Palaeolithic occurrence of blades and bone tools?

Upper Palaeolithic: c. **40,000-10,000 BCE**.

nde9ead6b340.s: The Middle Palaeolithic is principally a ____ stage.
nde9ead6b340.x: The Middle Palaeolithic is principally a flake-tool stage; microliths belong to the Upper Palaeolithic and Mesolithic.
xa: ⚠ Some notes wrongly call the Middle Palaeolithic the "microlithic stage".
The earliest human fossil is from **Hathnora**, Narmada valley ("**Narmada Man**").
**Mesolithic = Microlithic** period, end of the Ice Age.

n503889a9049.s: Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama are Mesolithic sites located in the:

n503889a9049.x: Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama are Mesolithic sites in the Ganga plain of Uttar Pradesh, particularly the Pratapgarh region.

xa: **Teri sites**: Thoothukudi (TN) and the Visakhapatnam coast.
**Paisra** = Bihar; **Birbhanpur** = West Bengal; **Langhnaj** = Gujarat.
Mesolithic = **Microlithic** period, end of the Ice Age.

ncb2dc4c8393.s: Yerragondapalem in Andhra Pradesh is known for:
ncb2dc4c8393.x: Yerragondapalem is known for well-made quartzite blades.
xa: Lower Palaeolithic by district: Chittoor (**Renigunta, Gudimallam**), Kurnool (**Veerapuram, Bethamcherla**), Guntur (**Karamapudi, Chebrolu**).
Prakasam: **Giddaluru**, **Dornala**; Visakhapatnam: **Paravada**.

n3c50022b20c.s: The microlith centres of Andhra Pradesh were discovered by:
n3c50022b20c.x: Robert Bruce Foote discovered the AP microlith centres; N. R. Banerji is the leading researcher of megaliths.
xa: Giddaluru (Prakasam) is the **microlithic centre** (**PYQ 2018, 2019**).
First microliths appear in the **Upper Palaeolithic**.

nfda2dbcfd93.s: Which one of the following Neolithic sites is associated with the sequence Neolithic–Chalcolithic–Iron?
nfda2dbcfd93.x: Koldihwa in Uttar Pradesh is associated with the Neolithic–Chalcolithic–Iron sequence and early rice.
nfda2dbcfd93.tq: Use the distinctive cultural sequence to identify the site.
xs: **Koldihwa** (UP) shows the **Neolithic-Chalcolithic-Iron** sequence — option **(4)**.
**Mehrgarh** = earliest farming; **Chirand** = bone and antler tools; **Gufkral** = pit dwellings.
xa: Koldihwa also has **early rice**, along with **Lehuradeva** (c. **6500 BCE**).
**Burzahom** (Kashmir): pit dwellings, **dog burials**.
**Utnoor** (Telangana): **ash mounds**.

nd060598b569.s: The Eastern Neolithic sites such as Birbhanpur, Chirand, Kuchai and Sankarjang are particularly associated with
o: polished stone rings and iron ploughshares
nd060598b569.x: Eastern Neolithic sites are associated with pointed-butt celts and shouldered axes, showing links with South-East Asia.
nd060598b569.tq: Identify the distinctive tool assemblage linked with a regional Neolithic tradition.
xs: **Eastern Neolithic** sites yield **pointed-butt celts** and **shouldered axes** — option **(1)**.
These show links to **South-East Asia**.
xa: The sites: **Birbhanpur, Chirand, Kuchai, Sankarjang**.
**Chirand** (Bihar) is also known for **bone and antler tools**.
**Birbhanpur** (West Bengal) is also listed as a Mesolithic site.

nb95854b87e1.s: Early rice cultivation at Lehuradeva is dated approximately to:
nb95854b87e1.x: Lehuradeva in Uttar Pradesh provides evidence of early rice cultivation dating to about 6500 BCE; Koldihwa is another associated site.
nb95854b87e1.tq: Match the distinctive date with the correct early rice site.
xs: Early rice at **Lehuradeva** dates to c. **6500 BCE** — option **(1)**.
**2172 BCE** is the AMS date for iron at **Mayiladumparai**.
**300 CE** is the end of the megalithic period.
xa: **Koldihwa** (UP) also has early rice.
Earliest **wheat, barley** = **Mehrgarh** (Baluchistan).

n2f99c1e8f52.s: At Karivalamvanthanallur in Tenkasi, Tamil Nadu, archaeological evidence indicates a transition from the Microlithic directly to the
o: Iron/Early Historic age, bypassing the Neolithic and Chalcolithic
Bronze Age, followed by the Megalithic
Gupta period, bypassing the Iron Age
n2f99c1e8f52.x: Karivalamvanthanallur shows occupation passing directly from the Microlithic to the Iron/Early Historic age, without a Neolithic or Chalcolithic phase.
n2f99c1e8f52.tq: Apply the sequence clue and identify the omitted cultural phases.
xs: At **Karivalamvanthanallur** (Tenkasi, TN) occupation passes from **Microlithic** straight to **Iron/Early Historic**, skipping **Neolithic + Chalcolithic** — option **(1)** (21 Jul **2026**).
So there is no Neolithic or Chalcolithic phase there, ruling out options (2), (3) and (4).
xa: Another recent find: megalithic **rock-cut burial chamber** at **Panayal** (Kasaragod, Kerala).
Earliest iron: **Mayiladumparai** (Krishnagiri, TN).
**Teri sites** (Thoothukudi, TN) are Mesolithic.

nindian-history-137-9.s: Ahar is the type site of which Chalcolithic culture?
nindian-history-137-9.x: Ahar is the type site of the Ahar/Banas culture; Inamgaon belongs to the Jorwe culture.
n: Daimabad is Chalcolithic. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Daimabad has a later Harappan-associated cultural horizon. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Inamgaon is associated with the Jorwe culture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Ahar is associated with the Ahar/Banas Chalcolithic culture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Kayatha is a Chalcolithic culture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
xa: Daimabad lies on the **Pravara River**; it yielded a **bronze chariot** and a **bronze buffalo**.
Inamgaon stands for **settlement archaeology**.
**Harappan contemporaries**: **Ahar** and **Kayatha**.

nindian-history-137-14.s: The Jorwe culture, known for village farming settlements, belongs to:
nindian-history-137-14.x: Jorwe belongs to Maharashtra, not Madhya Pradesh.
n: The Jorwe culture is located in Maharashtra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
The Jorwe culture is associated with village and agricultural settlements. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
xa: Jorwe dates c. **1400-700 BCE**; pottery: **painted red ware**.
Key Jorwe sites: **Inamgaon**, **Daimabad**.
**Malwa** and **Kayatha** cultures belong to **Madhya Pradesh**.

nindian-history-137-16.s: The Chalcolithic site of Kayatha is located in:
nindian-history-137-16.x: Kayatha is in Madhya Pradesh; Jorwe, Savalda and Inamgaon are in Maharashtra.
n: Inamgaon is located in Maharashtra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Kayatha is located in Madhya Pradesh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
The Jorwe culture is located in Maharashtra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
The Savalda culture is located in Maharashtra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
xa: **Daimabad** (Maharashtra) is the **southernmost Harappan** site.
**Ahar/Banas** culture belongs to south-east **Rajasthan** (**Balathal, Gilund**).

nindian-history-137-10.s: Navdatoli is identified as which of the following?
o: A Harappan urban site in Haryana
A Chalcolithic settlement in Madhya Pradesh
A port and dockyard in Gujarat
nindian-history-137-10.x: Navdatoli on the Narmada in Madhya Pradesh is a Chalcolithic settlement of the Malwa culture. Haryana, Gujarat and Rajasthan options describe Harappan sites.
nindian-history-137-10.tq: Recall the state and culture of Navdatoli.
n: Rakhigarhi is located in Haryana. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Rakhigarhi is a major Harappan urban site. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Lothal is located in Gujarat. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Lothal has a port and trade association. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Lothal has a dockyard association. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Navdatoli is located in Madhya Pradesh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
Navdatoli is a Chalcolithic settlement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #137 · pp 240-241]
xs: **Navdatoli** is **a Chalcolithic settlement in Madhya Pradesh** — option **(2)** is correct.
It belongs to the **Malwa culture**, a **pottery** and **cultural complex** of **MP**.
xa: The Malwa culture dates **1900-1400 BCE**; pottery: **coarse Malwa ware**; sites **Navdatoli**, **Eran**.
**Kayatha** (MP) has **chocolate-slipped ware**.
**Ahar** (Rajasthan) has **white-painted black-and-red ware**.

need7a8df4b4.s: V. S. Wakankar discovered Bhimbetka in:
need7a8df4b4.x: Bhimbetka was discovered by V. S. Wakankar in 1957 and became a UNESCO site in 2003.
xa: Upper Palaeolithic art in about **300** caves and shelters.
Mesolithic paintings: **hunting** and people **carrying baskets**.
Bhimbetka is also a **Middle Palaeolithic** site.

n3ae1ae2d301.s: Upper Palaeolithic cave art at Bhimbetka has been found in about how many caves and shelters?
n3ae1ae2d301.x: Bhimbetka has Upper Palaeolithic art in about 300 caves and shelters.
xa: Bhimbetka (near **Bhopal**) was found by **V. S. Wakankar** (**1957**); UNESCO **2003**.
AP rock art: **Borra Caves** (Visakhapatnam), **Kethavaram** (Kurnool).
**Malwa** culture: **1900-1400 BCE**, coarse Malwa ware.

n97b9bff4a05.s: The animal most commonly painted in rock art is the:
n97b9bff4a05.x: The deer, not the elephant, is the most commonly painted animal.
xa: **Petroglyphs** are **carved**, not painted; in India from the **Upper Palaeolithic-Mesolithic**.
**Bhimbetka** has Upper Palaeolithic art in about **300** caves.

n676ae653558.s: A fortified settlement yielding copper objects and regarded as the southernmost Harappan site is
n676ae653558.x: Daimabad had a fortified settlement and copper objects and is identified as the southernmost Harappan site.
n676ae653558.tq: Combine the settlement-type and material-find clues to identify the site.
xs: **Daimabad** had a **fortified settlement** and **copper objects** and is the **southernmost Harappan site** — option **(1)**.
**Ahar** and **Gilund** are Ahar-Banas sites; **Eran** is a Malwa site.
xa: Daimabad is a **Jorwe** culture site with **Inamgaon** (Maharashtra).
Jorwe: c. **1400-700 BCE**, **painted red ware**.
First metal used: **copper** (Chalcolithic).

ne9bb546e344.s: The Ahar and Kayatha Chalcolithic cultures were contemporaries of the:
ne9bb546e344.x: Ahar and Kayatha were Harappan contemporaries, though many Chalcolithic cultures were post-Harappan.
xa: **Daimabad** is the southernmost Harappan site.
Ahar-Banas began c. **2800 BCE**; Kayatha c. **2450 BCE**.

nb37f6f6bc8d.s: A table-like megalithic chamber made of large slabs is called a:
nb37f6f6bc8d.x: A dolmen is a table-like chamber; a cist is a stone-slab box, a menhir an upright stone and a sarcophagus a terracotta coffin.
xa: Menhirs are **2-6 m**, in **Krishna** district.
Sarcophagi: more in **Chittoor** and **Anantapur**.
**Anthropomorphic** = human-shaped stone, **Tirupati** region.

n36321423216.s: Billasurgam caves are significant in the prehistory of Andhra Pradesh because they have yielded:
o: Palaeolithic stone and rare bone tools with animal fossils
Neolithic ash mounds and iron objects
n36321423216.x: Billasurgam caves in Kurnool district belong to the Palaeolithic phase and have yielded stone tools, rare bone tools and animal fossils.
n36321423216.tq: Test the site–phase–find combination without confusing it with nearby Andhra sites.
xs: **Billasurgam caves** (Kurnool) are **Palaeolithic**, with **stone and rare bone tools** and **animal fossils** — option **(3)** (**PYQ 2017**).
**Anthropomorphic** megaliths are in the **Tirupati** region; **copper tools** are at **Keesarapalli**.
**Ash mounds** are Neolithic **Utnoor** (Telangana).
xa: **Robert Bruce Foote** pioneered AP prehistory at **Billasurgam** and the **Pennar**.
**Kurnool caves** and **Jwalapuram** are Upper Palaeolithic with bone tools.
**Patapadu** (Kurnool) = Chalcolithic painted pottery (**PYQ 2017**).

n02e858661c4.s: Megalithic burials in Andhra Pradesh are popularly known by which name?
n02e858661c4.x: Megalithic burials in Andhra Pradesh are popularly called Rakshasa Gullu; other names include Pandava Gullu, Kurambara Gullu and Morivara Gullu.
n02e858661c4.tq: Test the regional cultural name directly.
xs: AP megaliths are called "**Rakshasa Gullu**" — option **(2)**.
Other names: **Pandava Gullu**, **Kurambara Gullu**, **Morivara Gullu**.
xa: Megaliths = graves with weapons, tools, pottery, surrounded by big stones (**PYQ 2018**).
They are **Iron Age**, with **black-and-red ware**, c. **1500/1000 BCE to 300 CE**.
**Nagarjunakonda** is the AP megalithic centre.

ncd771fe3160.s: About how many types of megalithic burials have been identified in Andhra Pradesh?
ncd771fe3160.x: About twelve types of megalithic burials are noted in AP, studied by N. R. Banerji.
xa: Types include **cist, dolmen, sarcophagus, menhir, anthropomorphic, cairn circle, urn burial**.
**Anthropomorphic** megaliths: largest collection in the **Tirupati** region.

n189dc615718.s: In 1842 Meadows Taylor found a stone axe at:
n189dc615718.x: Meadows Taylor's 1842 stone axe was found at Lingasugur, not Jwalapuram.
xa: Foote also discovered the **AP microliths**.
**V. S. Wakankar** discovered **Bhimbetka** (**1957**).
**N. R. Banerji** = megaliths; **H. D. Sankalia** = rice in the Iron (Megalithic) age.

n53b1d4430f4.s: The earliest iron evidence in India, based on AMS dating, has been reported from which of the following sites?
n53b1d4430f4.x: Mayiladumparai in Krishnagiri district of Tamil Nadu has yielded the earliest AMS-dated iron evidence in India, dated to 2172 BCE.
n53b1d4430f4.tq: Use the site–date association to distinguish the earliest iron evidence from other metal-age sites.
xs: The earliest iron (AMS-dated **2172 BCE**) is from **Mayiladumparai** (**Krishnagiri**, TN) — option **(2)**.
**Patapadu** = painted pottery and **Keesarapalli** = copper tools (Chalcolithic).
**Brahmagiri** is listed as a megalithic site.
xa: Iron at **Sivagalai** is put at c. **2953 BCE**.
The first metal used was **copper** (Chalcolithic).
Megaliths belong to the **Iron Age**.

nf4bd5885343.s: Black-and-red ware was found at all Andhra megalithic sites except:
nf4bd5885343.x: Black-and-red ware was found at all Andhra megalithic sites except Visakhapatnam.
xa: ⚠ The APHQ book marks the **dolmen** statement instead; follow the **official key**.
Cists are common in AP but **not** numerous in Visakhapatnam.

n5dc5934978d.s: According to H. D. Sankalia, rice was first harvested in Andhra during which period?
n5dc5934978d.x: H. D. Sankalia associated the first harvesting of rice in Andhra with the Iron, or Megalithic, Age.
xs: **H. D. Sankalia** held that rice was first harvested in Andhra in the **Iron (Megalithic)** age — option **(4)**.
The notes link this first rice harvest to the megalithic burial culture, not to the Chalcolithic, Neolithic or Upper Palaeolithic.
xa: Elsewhere, early rice: **Lehuradeva** (c. **6500 BCE**) and **Koldihwa** (UP).
Megaliths: c. **1500/1000 BCE to 300 CE**, with black-and-red ware.
**N. R. Banerji** = leading megalith researcher.

n475b789e801.s: Palaeolithic tools from the Kadapa-Kurnool region were mainly made of:
n475b789e801.x: Quartzite was characteristic of Kadapa-Kurnool tools, while limestone was used north of the Krishna.
xa: Lower Palaeolithic tools: **handaxe, cleaver, chopper**.
Middle Palaeolithic raw material: **chert, jasper, chalcedony, quartz**.
Mesolithic weapons were of **dolomite**.

nd397c2ccaf1.s: Which of the following was NOT listed as a grave good in the Megalithic phase?
nd397c2ccaf1.x: The listed grave goods are pottery, beads, iron implements and gold ornaments. Glass mirrors were not included in the list.
nd397c2ccaf1.tq: Find the item outside the documented grave-good group rather than choosing a familiar artefact.
xs: **Glass mirrors** are not among the listed grave goods — option **(2)**.
Listed goods: **pottery**, **beads**, **iron implements**, **gold ornaments** (Brahmagiri).
xa: Megalithic = **Iron Age**, with **black-and-red ware**.
Centre of megalithic settlements: **Nagarjunakonda**.

nb448d1e3b20.s: Handaxes, cleavers and choppers of quartzite and limestone are typical of the:
nb448d1e3b20.x: Handaxes, cleavers and choppers are Lower Palaeolithic tools; flakes are Middle, blades Upper Palaeolithic and microliths Mesolithic.
xa: **Chalcolithic** = copper tools.
Kadapa-Kurnool used **quartzite**; north of the Krishna used **limestone**.

n18532a1a536.s: What has been reported from Manchirevula near Hyderabad in the context of Upper Palaeolithic evidence?
o: Neolithic ash mounds and painted pottery
n18532a1a536.x: Upper Palaeolithic quartz tools and petroglyphs have been reported from Manchirevula near Hyderabad.
n18532a1a536.tq: Match the recent site with its distinctive tool and art evidence.
xs: **Manchirevula** (Hyderabad) yielded an Upper Palaeolithic **quartz tool** and **petroglyphs** — option **(2)** (Mar **2026**).
**Copper and megalithic graves** = **Brahmagiri**; **ash mounds** = **Utnur**; **painted pottery** = **Patapadu**.
xa: Upper Palaeolithic tools: **blades**, **bone tools**.
Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites: **Kurnool caves**, **Muchatla Chintamani Gavi**; also **Jwalapuram**.

n9cb9876ca9a.s: The Billa Surgam caves are located in which district, and what kind of tools have been found there?
o: Kurnool, now Nandyal; stone and bone tools
n9cb9876ca9a.x: The Billa Surgam caves are in Kurnool district, now Nandyal, and have yielded stone and bone tools.
n9cb9876ca9a.tq: Separate the Billa Surgam location from the commonly confused Anantapur attribution.
xs: **Billa Surgam caves** are in **Kurnool (now Nandyal)**, with **stone and bone tools** — option **(3)** (**G2 2017**).
They are **not** in Anantapuramu.
xa: **Upper Palaeolithic bone tools**: Kurnool caves + **Muchatla Chintamani Gavi** = the only Indian sites.
**Jwalapuram** is also Upper Palaeolithic.
Discoverer of AP Palaeolithic sites: **Robert Bruce Foote**.

nd2e55e819ad.s: Which of the following correctly identifies the Indian Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites mentioned in relation to the Kurnool caves?
o: Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi
nd2e55e819ad.x: The Kurnool caves and Muchatla Chintamani Gavi are identified as the only Indian Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites in this context. Jwalapuram is also an Upper Palaeolithic site.
nd2e55e819ad.tq: Use the exclusive site-pair association while distinguishing it from other cave sites.
xs: The only Indian Upper Palaeolithic bone-tool sites are the **Kurnool caves** and **Muchatla Chintamani Gavi** — option **(3)**.
**Patapadu** is Chalcolithic (painted pottery); **Giddaluru** and **Nagarjunakonda** are microlithic centres.
xa: **Jwalapuram** is also an Upper Palaeolithic site.
Upper Palaeolithic tools: **blades, bone tools**, of silica-rich stone and bone.
**Billa Surgam** (Kurnool, now Nandyal) yielded stone and bone tools.

nf4a0b3ec6e3.s: Patapadu in Andhra Pradesh is known for:
nf4a0b3ec6e3.x: Patapadu has Chalcolithic painted pottery; Keesarapalli has copper tools.
xa: Standard answer for Chalcolithic evidence in Andhra = **Patapadu**.
Brahmagiri grave goods include **gold ornaments**.

n848e535fdd1.s: Who discovered the Palaeolithic tools associated with the Andhra region, and where else did he find such tools?
o: Robert Bruce Foote; Pallavaram near Chennai
n848e535fdd1.x: Robert Bruce Foote discovered the relevant Palaeolithic tools and also found Palaeolithic tools at Pallavaram near Chennai.
n848e535fdd1.tq: Apply the archaeologist–discovery–site association without swapping researchers.
xs: **Robert Bruce Foote** discovered AP's Palaeolithic sites and also found **Pallavaram** (Chennai) — option **(2)**.
**N. R. Banerji** is the megalith researcher; **Sankalia** linked first rice in Andhra to the Iron (Megalithic) age.
xa: Chittoor Lower Palaeolithic sites: **Renigunta**, Rallakalava, Vedurla Cheruvu, **Gudimallam**.
Kurnool: Veerapuram, Sangameswaram, Bethamcherla, K.K. Kottala.
Guntur (Krishna valley): **Nagarjunakonda**, Karamapudi, Chebrolu.

n3a30c5ef325.s: Mesolithic culture is also known as the __________ period, and its tools were made mainly by __________.
n3a30c5ef325.x: The Mesolithic is also called the Microlithic period, and its tools were produced by flaking and chipping.
n3a30c5ef325.tq: Distinguish the period name from the manufacturing process associated with it.
xs: The Mesolithic is the **Microlithic** period, with tools made by **flaking and chipping** — option **(2)**.
**Chalcolithic** = copper tools; **Megalithic** = Iron Age burials.
xa: Mesolithic raw material: **chert, jasper**; weapons of **dolomite**.
Key microlithic centre: **Giddaluru** (Prakasam) (G2 **2019**, GS **2018**).
Andhra microliths resemble **South Indian + Caspian** microliths.

na79cb04b78a.s: Giddaluru, the key microlithic centre of Andhra Pradesh, is in which district?
na79cb04b78a.x: Giddaluru in Prakasam district is the key microlithic centre, along with Nagarjunakonda, Kondapur and Khammam.
xa: Giddaluru was asked in G2 **2019** and GS **2018**.
**Mesolithic = Microlithic** period; tools made by flaking and chipping.

nf6ac9046456.s: Which of the following sites was identified as a centre among the Megalithic habitation settlements of Andhra Pradesh?
nf6ac9046456.x: Nagarjunakonda was identified as a centre among the Megalithic habitation sites. Other listed settlements include Jonnawada, Boodigapalli, Gudivada and Peddavadu.
nf6ac9046456.tq: Separate habitation centres of the Megalithic phase from burial and cave sites.
xs: **Nagarjunakonda** is the **centre** of Megalithic settlements — option **(2)**.
**Renigunta** is a Lower Palaeolithic site; **Utnur** a Neolithic ash mound; **Borra Caves** a rock art site.
xa: Other settlements: **Jonnawada**, **Boodigapalli**, **Gudivada**, **Peddavadu**.
Nagarjunakonda also has **Lower Palaeolithic** tools and **microliths**.
Megalithic pottery: **black-and-red ware**.

nebdb8934095.s: AMS dating at Mayiladumparai places the beginning of the Iron Age in South India at about:
nebdb8934095.x: Mayiladumparai AMS dating puts the start of the South Indian Iron Age at about 2100 BCE, earlier than the Gangetic Iron Age.
xa: An **Upper Palaeolithic** quartz tool and **petroglyphs** were found at **Manchirevula**, Hyderabad.
**Iron Age = Megalithic culture**, with typical **black-and-red ware**.
**Nagarjunakonda** was a megalithic **centre**.

n3dae48589b4.s: The main domesticated animals of the Neolithic phase of Baluchistan and the Indus plains were:
n3dae48589b4.x: The main domesticated animals were sheep and goats, not horses and camels.
xa: Villages had **mud houses** and **crafts**.
Mehrgarh Period I also had **cattle**.

n99ff209adc6.s: Mehrgarh, with the earliest evidence of agriculture in the subcontinent, lies near which pass?
n99ff209adc6.x: Mehrgarh lies in Baluchistan near the Bolan Pass; it begins c. 7000 BCE.
xa: Mehrgarh = **earliest settled life** (**PYQ UPPSC 2008**).
Remains run from **Stone Age to Harappan** times (**PYQ UPPSC 2009**).
Excavated by **J.-F. Jarrige** (**1974**).

nf6fb9afb123.s: Kili Gul Muhammad, an early farming village, lies in which valley?
nf6fb9afb123.x: Kili Gul Muhammad lies in the Quetta valley; Rana Ghundai is in the Zhob-Loralai valley.
xa: **Damb Sadaat** (Quetta valley) = Early Harappan-phase village.
Excavators: Rana Ghundai — **E. J. Ross**; Kili Gul Muhammad, Damb Sadaat — **W. A. Fairservis**.

nded5ae6ec83.s: At Mehrgarh, the dead were usually:
o: Buried under or near houses, flexed, with grave goods
Buried in public monuments without objects
nded5ae6ec83.x: At Mehrgarh the dead were buried under or near houses, often flexed, with ornaments, tools and sometimes goats.
xa: Mehrgarh: c. **7000 BCE**, earliest agriculture, domestication, pottery.
Period I: barley, wheat; sheep, goat, cattle.
Excavator: **J.-F. Jarrige** (**1974**).

n708fe4771b9.tq: Pair the excavation year with the correct archaeologist rather than a nearby site’s excavator.
xs: **J.-F. Jarrige** excavated **Mehrgarh** in **1974** — option **(4)**.
**R. S. Bisht** dug **Banawali** (also **1974**); **Fairservis** dug Kili Gul Muhammad and Damb Sadaat; **E. J. Ross** dug Rana Ghundai.
xa: ⚠ **1974** = Mehrgarh (**Jarrige**) and Banawali (**Bisht**).
Mehrgarh dates to c. **7000 BCE**.

n393b7de36f8.s: Which Early Harappan culture is particularly associated with a fortified settlement destroyed by fire and numerous stone implements?
n393b7de36f8.x: Kot Diji in Sindh was a fortified pre-Harappan settlement destroyed by fire and yielded many stone implements.
n393b7de36f8.tq: Link a distinctive archaeological description with its type site.
xs: **Kot Diji** (Sindh) was a **fortified** pre-Harappan settlement **destroyed by fire**, with many **stone implements** — option **(3)**.
**Amri** = transitional pre- to Mature Harappan, rhinoceros remains.
xa: Kot Diji: discovered by **Ghurye**; excavated by **F. A. Khan** (**1955**).
Kot Diji pottery and buildings **anticipate Mature Harappan** forms.
**Kot Diji ware** is a regional pottery tradition.

n8c2548f2860.s: Rhinoceros remains have been found at which Early Harappan site?
n8c2548f2860.x: Amri, which shows a transition from the pre-Harappan to the Mature Harappan phase, has yielded rhinoceros remains.
xa: **Mitathal** has Pre-, Mature + Late phases.
Amri excavated by **N. G. Majumdar** (**1929**), later **J.-M. Casal**.

**Early Harappan** (**3300-2600 BCE**) villages: **Kot Diji**, **Amri**, **Sothi-Siswal**.

na70867ed7cf.s: Which one of the following best supports the view that the Mature Harappan culture was non-Aryan or pre-Vedic?
o: Its settlements were exclusively temporary pastoral camps.

Its political system was based on medieval landlordism.
na70867ed7cf.x: The Mature Harappan culture was urban, whereas the Rigvedic culture was predominantly pastoral. The absence of horse, chariot and iron in the Mature Harappan context is also cited in this argument.
na70867ed7cf.tq: Use the urban–pastoral contrast to infer the cultural distinction.
xs: The **urban** Harappan culture contrasted with the **pastoral** Rigvedic culture — option **(3)**.

xa: **Continuity view**: **fire altars** and **pipal worship** link the two.
PYQ (**UPPSC 2020**): Indus — **urban**; Rigvedic — **pastoral**; Later Vedic — **agrarian**; Medieval — **landlordism**.

na2a4e656e20.s: Surkotada is particularly associated with which archaeological finding?

The earliest known gold coin hoard

nd269bc67b98.s: Which Harappan site is known for a dockyard regarded as the world's first tidal port?

n50c2fe92d1a.s: Which site is associated with the greatest number of wells in the developed stage of the Indus Civilization?

nee857822326.s: Which of the following best explains the significance of standardised bricks, grid planning and drainage in the Indus Valley Civilization?

n58ea77de544.x: The horse was not known to the Mature Harappans in the accepted view; the Surkotada claims are controversial.

"Which animal is not depicted on Harappan seals" → **Horse** (UPPSC **2009**).
⚠ **Cow** is not depicted; **lion** is absent from seals and figurines.
A **terracotta horse figure** is reported from **Lothal**.

ne52ab973376.s: Which metal was unknown to the Harappans?
ne52ab973376.x: Iron was unknown to the Harappans; copper, bronze, gold, silver and lead were used.
xa: Exam angle: "Which metal has not been found at Harappan sites" → **Iron** (CGPSC **2011**).
**Bronze = copper + tin**: tools, weapons, the **Dancing Girl**.
**Copper** came from **Khetri** and Oman.

n56fe49cd569.s: Which Harappan site is especially associated with trade with West Asia?
n56fe49cd569.x: Lothal is the site associated with trade with West Asia, supported by its dockyard and the Persian Gulf-type seal.
n56fe49cd569.tq: Use the site-specific trade clue rather than a general Harappan location.
xs: **Lothal** is the city that traded with **West Asia** — option **(3)** (BPSC **2024**).
Proof: its **tidal dockyard** and its **Persian Gulf-type seal** → direct contact with **Bahrain and Mesopotamia**.
**Ropar** = dog burial; **Amri** = rhinoceros remains; **Kalibangan** = ploughed field.
xa: Lothal also gave **boat models**, a **terracotta ship** and a **ship design on a seal**.
⚠ **Button seal** + **Persian Gulf seal** = **Lothal**.
Excavated by **S.R. Rao**, **1954**.

nc38866c0efb.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Harappan seals?
o: Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals were common at all sites.
Rectangular seals generally carry only an inscription.
Square seals generally carry an animal figure with an inscription.
Most seals were made of steatite.
nc38866c0efb.x: Mesopotamian-type cylinder seals were rare, not common, at Harappan sites.
xa: **Button seal** → **Lothal**.
Seals were mostly of **steatite**, easy to carve.
Seals helped **trade regulation** and **long-distance communication**.

n543378b98db.x: R. S. Bisht excavated Dholavira in 1990; it is the only Harappan site on the UNESCO list (2021).
xa: **Rakhigarhi** = on the **Tentative List**.
Dholavira's **signboard** has **10** large signs.
Dholavira had **reservoirs**.

n3500296503a.s: Harappan seals were mostly made of:
n3500296503a.x: Harappan seals were mostly of steatite and generally square.
xa: **Square** = animal + inscription; **rectangular** = inscription only.
**Button seal** → **Lothal**.
**Unicorn** is the most common motif.

n734b0b28c99.s: The seals of the Indus Valley Civilization were made mostly of which material?
n734b0b28c99.x: Most Indus seals were made of steatite, or soapstone, because it was easy to carve. Terracotta, copper and ivory were also used.
n734b0b28c99.tq: Use the material clue and distinguish the predominant material from occasional alternatives.
xs: Indus seals were mostly made of **steatite** (soapstone) — option **(2)**.
Steatite was chosen because it allows **easy carving**.
Other materials: **terracotta, copper, ivory**; iron was unknown.
xa: **Square** seals = animal + inscription; **rectangular** = inscription only.
Mesopotamian-type **cylinder** seals are **rare**; a **button seal** comes from **Lothal**.
Seals are the **most distinctive** IVC artefact (APPSC-GS **2024**).

n1248ea2237f.s: The presence of uniform seals and weights across the Harappan cultural region is the main evidence for:
n1248ea2237f.x: Uniform seals and weights indicate standardisation and regulated trade across the Harappan cultural region.
n1248ea2237f.tq: Infer the wider institutional meaning from archaeological uniformity.
xs: Uniform seals and weights are the main proof of **standardisation and regulated trade** — option **(3)**.
Similar weights across about **8,00,000 sq km** → **central regulation**.
The script is **undeciphered**, so option (2) is wrong.
xa: Weights: **binary** lower, **decimal** higher denominations.
**Rakhigarhi** gave **chert trade weights** (Jun **2026**).
Seals served **trade regulation + long-distance communication**.

na80530b51f9.s: Harappan weights, mostly of chert, were generally ____ in shape.
na80530b51f9.x: Harappan weights were generally cubical, not spherical.
xa: Lower denominations were **binary** (**1:2:4:8:16:32:64**); higher were **decimal**.
Similar weights across about **8,00,000 sq km** → **central regulation**.
**Chert trade weights** have been found at **Rakhigarhi**.

n2c349bd0de9.s: The numerical system of Harappan weights is best represented by:
o: A sexagesimal system without binary subdivisions
Only a decimal system from the smallest denomination onward
A random system varying from site to site
Binary values in lower denominations followed by decimal multiples
n2c349bd0de9.x: Lower denominations followed the binary sequence 1:2:4:8:16:32:64, after which decimal multiples such as 160, 320 and 640 were used.
n2c349bd0de9.tq: Separate the two successive numerical principles instead of treating the system as uniform.
xs: Weights were **binary in lower denominations**, then **decimal multiples** — option **(4)**.
Higher: **decimal** multiples — **160, 320, 640, 1600, 3200**.
xa: ⚠ Lower = **binary**; higher = **decimal**.
Weights were mostly **chert** and **cubical**.
Uniform across about **8,00,000 sq km** → central regulation.

n96287c57cae.s: The average Harappan inscription contains about how many signs?
n96287c57cae.x: The average inscription has about five signs; around 5,000 inscribed objects are known and the script is undeciphered.
xa: ⚠ Average **5** signs; longest **26**; signboard **10**; total signs about **400**.
Number of signs: estimates range **400-700**.
Most supported hypothesis: **Proto-Dravidian** (Mahadevan, Parpola).

n14456ec5b08.s: The usual direction of writing in the Harappan script is:
n14456ec5b08.x: Harappan inscriptions were generally written from right to left, as indicated partly by cramped spacing at the left end.
n14456ec5b08.tq: Use the directional clue associated with the spacing of signs.
xs: Harappan script was written **right to left** — option **(4)**.
Proof: **cramped spacing at the left end** of inscriptions.
Some texts are **boustrophedon** (alternate lines reversed), e.g. **Kalibangan**.
xa: The script is mostly **pictographic**; commonest sign = **fish**.
About **400** signs; about **5,000** inscribed objects.
**J. Fleet** first noticed seals with unknown symbols in **1912**.

n6601ab64da1.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Harappan script?
o: It is pictographic, contains about 40 signs and was deciphered through bilingual inscriptions.
It is alphabetic, contains about 40 signs and has been fully deciphered.
It is syllabic, contains about 4,000 signs and was written only vertically.
It is pictographic, contains about 400 signs and remains undeciphered.
n6601ab64da1.x: The Harappan script is pictographic, has approximately 400 signs and remains undeciphered.
n6601ab64da1.tq: Use the three-part combination of nature, number and decipherment status.
xs: The script is **pictographic**, has about **400 signs** and **remains undeciphered** — option **(4)**.
**No bilingual text** has been found, so options (1) and (2) are wrong.
It runs **right to left**, not only vertically.
xa: Estimates of signs range **400-700**.
Commonest sign = **fish**.
Inscriptions average about **5 signs**; longest **26**.

nf9345801cba.s: Long-distance communication in the Harappan context was carried out through:
nf9345801cba.x: Seals and sealings served as a means of long-distance communication, in addition to their commercial and identity-related functions.
nf9345801cba.tq: Recall the distinctive communication medium associated with seals.
xs: Long-distance communication used **seals and sealings** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2017**).
Seals served **trade regulation + long-distance communication**.
Sealed bags with an intact sealing proved **safe delivery + ownership**.
xa: Inscriptions may be **names or titles** → identity.
Seals are the **most distinctive** IVC artefact (APPSC-GS **2024**).
Seals were mostly of **steatite** (soapstone).

n6c361d80641.s: The Harappan script remains undeciphered mainly because:
o: No bilingual text has been found
The script was written only on perishable materials
All inscriptions are in a single long text
n6c361d80641.x: The Harappan script is still undeciphered because no bilingual text (like the Rosetta Stone) has been discovered.
n6c361d80641.tq: No Rosetta Stone for Harappa = no bilingual, no decipherment.
xs: The script is undeciphered because **no bilingual text** has been found — option **(2)**.
About **5,000** inscribed objects survive, so option (1) is wrong.
It is found on **seals, tablets, pottery, copper plates, tools**, not only perishable material.
xa: Inscriptions are short — average about **5 signs**, longest **26**.
Hypotheses: **Proto-Dravidian** (most supported), **Indo-Aryan**, **Proto-Munda**, **Isolate**.
The script is among the **world's earliest writing systems**.

n43395d0f15b.s: Which of the following is the strongest material indicator of social differentiation in Harappan society?
o: The absence of written royal genealogies
The existence of only one type of house
Variation in burial goods and ornament quality
n43395d0f15b.x: Differences in the quantity and quality of burial goods and ornaments suggest differentiation in social status. Uniformity in bricks is evidence mainly relevant to organisation and authority.
n43395d0f15b.tq: Identify the material evidence that directly reflects unequal status rather than administrative standardisation.
xs: **Variation in burial goods and ornament quality** is the strongest indicator of differentiation — option **(4)**.
The **quantity and quality of grave goods** reflect **status**.
Houses were of **three building types**, not one; uniform brick ratios point to **organisation and authority**, not stratification.
xa: Town layout: **citadel** on the **west** (elite, public buildings) vs **lower town** on the **east** (commoners).
**Single-roomed barracks** at **Harappa** suggest a working class.
The **four-fold division** (scholars, warriors, traders, labourers) is **speculative**.

n126f1eb48dd.s: Harappan maces, axes and spears were made of:
n126f1eb48dd.x: Harappan weapons were of copper and bronze, few and simple; no horse-drawn chariots are known.
xa: The **Mohenjodaro** "huddled" skeletons, once read as a **massacre**, are now **multiple burials**.
**No royal palaces** → power not personalised in a king.
⚠ "Great palaces and temples" is a **WRONG** statement (UPSC **2013**).

n2cb023ae9ed.s: The group of huddled skeletons at Mohenjodaro, once interpreted as evidence of a massacre, is now generally reinterpreted as:
o: A royal burial with grave goods
n2cb023ae9ed.x: The huddled skeletons at Mohenjodaro were once read as massacre victims but are now interpreted as representing multiple burials.
n2cb023ae9ed.tq: Track the change from an earlier interpretation to the current archaeological reading.
xs: The huddled **Mohenjodaro skeletons** are now read as **multiple burials** — option **(4)**.
They were once taken as evidence of a **massacre**.
Weapons were **few and simple**, suggesting a **relatively peaceful** society.
xa: **No horse-drawn chariots** existed.
Weapons: maces, axes, spears, bows and arrows of **copper and bronze**.
**Coffin burial** is from Harappa's **cemetery R-37**.

nf8ac20de100.s: Which one of the following views is associated with the interpretation of Harappan polity as a priestly rule?
o: The exclusive presence of horse-drawn chariots
The presence of citadels, the Great Bath and the steatite Priest-King
The use of hereditary Vedic assemblies
The absence of all public structures
nf8ac20de100.x: The priest-rule interpretation draws on the citadel, Great Bath and steatite Priest-King. These features have also been interpreted in other ways and do not conclusively prove priestly rule.
nf8ac20de100.tq: Match a political interpretation with the evidence used to support it.
xs: The **priest-rule** view rests on the **citadel, Great Bath and steatite Priest-King** — option **(2)**.
The citadel may have held **rulers or temples**.
There were **no horse-drawn chariots**, and hereditary assemblies belong to the **Later Vedic** polity.
xa: **Monarchy** view: fortified citadel (APP).
**Municipal governance** view: planned cities, advanced drainage.
Overall: **no clear-cut evidence** of political structure; polity "**appears corporate**".

ne580d88597f.s: The interpretation of Harappan polity as being dominated by merchant elites or civic administrators is based chiefly on:
o: The discovery of numerous royal inscriptions
Trade-driven uniformity and the absence of clear kings or palaces
The existence of hereditary monarchy in every city
The presence of large standing armies
ne580d88597f.x: Trade-driven uniformity, together with the absence of identifiable kings and palaces, has been used to argue for merchant elites or civic administrators.
ne580d88597f.tq: Link each political model to the evidence cited for it rather than to an unrelated feature.
xs: The merchant-elite / civic view rests on **trade-driven uniformity** and **no kings or palaces** — option **(2)**.
No royal inscriptions exist; the **script gives no names of rulers**.
Weapons were **few and simple**, so large armies (option 4) are not indicated.
xa: **Priest rule**: citadel, Great Bath, **Priest-King**.
**Monarchy**: fortified citadel.
**Municipal governance**: planned cities, advanced drainage.

nfbc4023cf2a.s: The centralised-state view of Harappan polity rests mainly on:
nfbc4023cf2a.x: The centralised-state view rests on uniformity over a huge area; no single capital has been identified.
xa: Uniformity: bricks in **1:2:4** ratio, **binary** weights, uniform seals.
Grid-plan towns across about **8,00,000 sq km**.
Polity "**appears corporate**".

n672e3135aeb.s: Standardised bricks, binary weights, uniform seals and grid-plan towns over a vast area suggest that the Harappans had:
o: A significant degree of central authority
n672e3135aeb.x: Widespread standardisation is the principal basis for inferring a significant degree of central authority.
xa: Counterpoint: the **city-state** argument — several large cities, no single capital.
Overall the polity "**appears corporate**", with **no clear-cut evidence**.
**Labour mobilisation** (walls, platforms, reservoirs) also supports central authority.

n759bc1417b1.s: The Harappan 'Priest-King' figure is depicted wearing a:
n759bc1417b1.x: The Priest-King is shown with a shawl; there is no evidence of stitching in Harappan clothing.
xa: Men had **trimmed beards** and **shaved upper lips**.
Cosmetics: **bronze mirrors, ivory combs, collyrium sticks**.
**Lipstick** → **Chanhudaro**.

n5a0030d5566.s: Lipstick is associated with which Harappan site?
n5a0030d5566.x: Chanhudaro is associated with lipstick; bronze mirrors, ivory combs and collyrium sticks were also used.
xa: Chanhudaro also had a **toy factory**.
Men had **trimmed beards + shaved upper lips**.
Clothing of **cotton and wool**, no evidence of stitching.

ne1a8ca45866.s: Grave goods such as pottery, ornaments and mirrors in Harappan graves indicate:
ne1a8ca45866.x: Such grave goods indicate belief in an afterlife and differences in status, not cremation.
xa: **Rakhigarhi** burials had **pots of provisions**.
**Cemetery R-37** (Harappa) = extended burials with grave goods.
Kalibangan has **circular pits with grave goods but no skeleton**.

neeb151edec6.s: How many burial types have been reported at Kalibangan?
neeb151edec6.x: Kalibangan has extended burials in rectangular pits, pot burials and circular pits with grave goods but no skeleton.
xa: **Harappa R-37**: extended burials, head generally to the **north**.
**Surkotada**: **four pot burials**.
Grave goods → **belief in afterlife**.

n89b84e257dc.s: The Harappan political structure, for which there is no clear-cut evidence, has been described as appearing:
o: A centralised empire with one capital
n89b84e257dc.x: The political structure is not clear-cut and has been described as appearing corporate.
xa: **City-state argument**: several large cities, no single capital.
**Centralised-state argument**: uniformity over a huge area.
Views include **priest rule**, **merchant elites**, **monarchy** and **municipal governance**.

nc60c74844d0.s: Which one of the following burial practices is associated with the R-37 cemetery at Harappa?
o: Extended burials with grave goods and coffin burial
North–south burials with jasper and agate ornaments
Dog buried with a human in an oval pit
nc60c74844d0.x: The R-37 cemetery at Harappa contains extended burials with goods and coffin burials. The other practices are associated with Ropar, Rakhigarhi and Surkotada respectively.
nc60c74844d0.tq: Match the burial type with the correct cemetery rather than with the site where another burial form occurs.
xs: Harappa's **cemetery R-37** has **extended burials with grave goods** and a **coffin burial** — option **(1)**.
**North-south** burials with **jasper and agate** beads → **Rakhigarhi**.
**Dog with human** → **Ropar**; **pot burials** with stone-covered grave → **Surkotada**.
xa: R-37 burials have the **head generally to the north**.
**Post-cremation** burials → Harappa's **Cemetery-H**.
**Fractional burial**: bones buried after exposure.

n53156c41910.s: Cemetery H at Harappa is particularly associated with:
o: Joint paired burials of the Mature Harappan phase
Post-cremation or fractional burials of the Late Harappan phase
n53156c41910.x: Cemetery H at Harappa is associated with post-cremation or fractional burials belonging to the Late Harappan phase.
n53156c41910.tq: Distinguish the cemetery name from the burial forms found at other sites.
xs: **Cemetery H** at Harappa is linked to **post-cremation** burials (ashes with pottery) — option **(3)**.
**Fractional** burials also occur at **Mohenjodaro** and **Harappa**.
**Dog burials** → **Ropar**; **joint burials** → **Lothal**; **pot burials** → **Surkotada**.
xa: Post-cremation burials also at **Mohenjodaro** and **Lothal**.
Harappa **R-37** = extended burials, **coffin burial**.
⚠ **Double burial** = Lothal; **dog with human** = Ropar; **pot burial** = Surkotada.

n98943488e2e.s: Fractional burial at Mohenjodaro and Harappa involved:
o: Placing ashes in an urn after cremation
Burying a human together with a dog
Burying the complete body in a coffin
Burying bones after exposure of the body
n98943488e2e.x: Fractional burial involved burying the bones after the body had been exposed.
xa: Fractional and extended burials both at **Mohenjodaro, Harappa**.
**Pot burial** → **Surkotada**.
Grave goods → **belief in afterlife**.

nf9d45b90997.s: Which one of the following sites is associated with joint or double burial in the Harappan context?
nf9d45b90997.x: Lothal is associated with joint or double burial. Ropar is noted for a dog buried with a human, while Surkotada is associated with pot burials.
nf9d45b90997.tq: Use the site-specific association and distinguish closely related burial practices.
xs: **Joint/double burial** is from **Lothal** — option **(4)** (UPPSC **2016**).
**Ropar** = **dog buried with a human**; **Surkotada** = **pot burial**.
**Kalibangan** = **three types** (extended, pot, circular pits).
xa: ⚠ **Double burial** = Lothal; **dog with human** = Ropar; **pot burial** = Surkotada.
Lothal also had **post-cremation** burials.
**Sanauli** → human burials (UPPSC **2004**).

n9d9d54c2e79.s: Reconstruction of Harappan social stratification and polity relies mainly on:
n9d9d54c2e79.x: Interpretations rely mainly on material remains, as the script gives no names of rulers.
xa: Evidence used: **town layout**, **house sizes**, **burial goods**.
**No textual evidence** of a rigid caste system.
Polity: **no clear-cut evidence**, "appears corporate".

n2b989e29f53.s: Which comparison between Harappan and Later Vedic polity is correct?
o: Harappan polity is described as corporate, whereas Later Vedic polity was a hereditary monarchy with declining Sabha and Samiti.
Harappan polity was a hereditary monarchy, whereas Later Vedic polity was fully corporate.
Later Vedic polity had no monarchy and no assemblies.
Both polities are known to have had identical assemblies and royal institutions.
n2b989e29f53.x: Harappan polity is characterised as corporate in comparison, while the Later Vedic polity is described as a hereditary monarchy with declining Sabha and Samiti.
n2b989e29f53.tq: Keep the direction of the comparison clear and avoid reversing the two political systems.
xs: Harappan polity was **corporate**; Later Vedic was a **hereditary monarchy** with **declining Sabha and Samiti** — option **(1)**.
The Harappan polity has **no clear-cut evidence** of kings or palaces.
Later Vedic polity did have monarchy and assemblies, so option (3) is wrong.
xa: **Caste crystallised** only in the **Later Vedic** period.
Harappan views: **priest rule**, **merchant elites**, **monarchy**, **municipal governance**.
**No single capital** identified (city-state argument).

naea801bc8e8.s: The lost-wax technique of metal casting is also known as:
naea801bc8e8.x: The lost-wax process, or cire perdue, coats a wax model with clay, melts out the wax and pours molten metal into the mould.
xa: Lost-wax objects: **Dancing Girl**, buffalo and goat figures.
Copper **dog and bird** of **Lothal**; **bronze bull** of **Kalibangan**.
Casting continued into **Late Harappan** and **Chalcolithic** cultures (**Daimabad** bronzes).
