ne2add6aad69.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of objects associated with the lost-wax technique?
o: Painted jar, perforated jar, faience bead
Steatite seal, silver vessel, terracotta whistle
Dancing Girl, copper dog and bird of Lothal, bronze bull of Kalibangan
ne2add6aad69.x: The Dancing Girl, the copper dog and bird of Lothal, and the bronze bull of Kalibangan are associated with the lost-wax technique.
ne2add6aad69.tq: Group the objects linked to one production technique and eliminate items made of unrelated materials.
xs: **Dancing Girl, copper dog and bird of Lothal, bronze bull of Kalibangan** were all lost-wax objects — option **(4)**.
**Buffalo and goat** figures were also lost-wax casts.
**Perforated jars**, **faience beads**, **steatite seals** and **terracotta whistles** are not cast objects.
xa: Lost-wax = **cire perdue**.
**Dog chasing a deer** (bronze) → **Harappa**.
**Daimabad**: chariot, bull, buffalo, rhinoceros, elephant.

ne961d7c9370.s: A Harappan gold foundry with an active furnace was found at:
ne961d7c9370.x: Rakhigarhi had a gold foundry with an active furnace; gold and silver necklaces were found at Allahdino.
xa: Rakhigarhi also had a **gemstone factory** with over **3,000** semi-precious stones.
⚠ **Chanhudaro** = bead + shell-ornament factory; **Rakhigarhi** = gemstone factory + gold foundry.
Tools: chisels, needles, fishhooks, razors, mirrors, axes, celts.

n85fdb15e826.s: Perforated jars of the Indus Civilization were characterised by:
o: A large hole at the base and small holes over the wall
A pointed base and a single hole in the lid
A small opening at the base and a large hole on the wall
A completely sealed body with no opening
n85fdb15e826.x: Perforated jars had a large hole at the base and several small holes over the wall, probably for straining liquor.
n85fdb15e826.tq: Pay attention to the reversed size and location of the holes, a common comparison trap.
xs: Perforated jars had a **large hole at the base** and **small holes over the wall** — option **(1)**.
They were **probably for straining liquor**.
The other descriptions do not match the notes.
xa: Pottery was **wheel-made**; red ware with **black painted** designs.
**Glazed pottery** (faience/mosaic glass) is described as the **world's first**.
**Lothal** gave a **painted jar**.

n56ab91358c4.s: Terracotta toy carts with seated drivers were found at:
n56ab91358c4.x: Toy carts with seated drivers come from Chanhudaro.
xa: Human figures: **lifelike bearded males** with **coiled hair**.
**Clay mask of a horned god** → **Gujarat, Kalibangan**.
Lost-wax objects include the **Dancing Girl**.

nb967023ce50.s: A gemstone factory with over 3,000 semi-precious stones was found at:
nb967023ce50.x: Rakhigarhi had the gemstone factory; Chanhudaro had a bead-making factory and Lothal bead workshops.
xa: Exam angle: bead industry → **Chanhudaro** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
Beads were exported to **Mesopotamia + Persian Gulf**.
Rakhigarhi also had a **gold foundry** with an active furnace.

nab7382e7855.s: Which animal motif was the most common on steatite seals of the Indus Civilization?
nab7382e7855.x: The unicorn was the most common animal motif on Indus steatite seals; bull, elephant, tiger and rhinoceros were also represented.
nab7382e7855.tq: Distinguish the most frequent motif from other genuine but less common seal animals.
xs: The **unicorn** was the most common seal motif — option **(2)**.
Other motifs: **bull, elephant, tiger, rhinoceros**.
Seals were of **steatite**.
xa: Seals also show the **Pashupati** figure and **short script lines**.
In terracotta, the great **humpless bull** is prominent.
**Seal carving** was listed as a **new technique** of the period.

n600ae096f7f.x: Carnelian came from Saurashtra, and carnelian beads were exported to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.
xa: **Kalibangan** = bead-making centre.
**Rakhigarhi** = gemstone factory, over **3,000** semi-precious stones (LENS, Jun **2026**).
**Carnelian working** was a **new technique** of the period.

n69cbac337f1.s: Which of the following products were made of faience in the Indus Civilization?
n69cbac337f1.x: Faience was used for beads, bangles and glazed ware, and its association with mosaic glass provides an early clue to glass-making.
n69cbac337f1.tq: Separate faience products from metal tools, stone sculpture and precious-metal ornaments.
xs: Faience was used for **beads, bangles and glazed ware** — option **(2)**.
**Copper, bronze, silver** were used for vessels; axes, celts and fishhooks were **metal tools**.
**Glazed pottery** (faience/mosaic glass) is described as the **world's first**.
xa: Faience/mosaic-glass link = **early clue to glass-making**.
⚠ "World's first glazed ware" = **faience**, not painted red ware.
Faience was also a **bead** material alongside carnelian and agate.

na28151811d6.s: The religious character of the Indus Valley Civilization is best described as:
o: Entirely atheistic, with no religious practices
Exclusively religious and completely controlled by temples
Predominantly secular, although religious elements were present
na28151811d6.x: The civilization is described as predominantly secular, with religious elements present but not dominant.
na28151811d6.tq: Choose the qualified description and reject absolute alternatives.
xs: The IVC was **predominantly secular**, though **religious elements were present** but not dominant — option **(4)**.
This was keyed correct in **UPSC 2011**.
Religion was not absent (idolatry, Great Bath), and there were **no temples** or Vedic sacrifices as its basis.
xa: **No temple** found; worship possibly **domestic or open-air**.
**Idolatry was practised** — the beginnings of idol worship.
**Yoga and meditation** were practised; belief in **spirits, ghosts and evil forces**.

n82fac714ba2.s: The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro is associated with:
n82fac714ba2.x: The Great Bath suggests ritual purification.
xa: **Amulets** show deities or persons in **yogic poses**.
**No temple** found.
**Fire altars** at **Kalibangan** and **Lothal**.

n1c39d0103ee.s: Differences in house size, burial goods and ornaments in the IVC indicate:
n1c39d0103ee.x: Differences in house size, burial goods and ornaments indicate social stratification; the four-fold division is speculative.
xa: **No palaces and no temples** (UPSC **2013**).
Planned cities + drains → **municipal governance**.
Citadel ruling group possibly **priestly or merchant** — debated.

n823dbcf6536.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the figure shown on the Pashupati seal?
o: A two-faced priest performing a fire sacrifice
A standing king holding a plough and surrounded by birds
A three-faced, horned figure seated in a yogic posture
A female deity seated in a chariot drawn by bulls
n823dbcf6536.x: The figure on the Pashupati seal is described as three-faced, horned and seated in a yogic posture.
n823dbcf6536.tq: Combine the figure’s posture, facial depiction and headdress to identify the correct description.
xs: The figure is **three-faced**, **horned** and seated in a **yogic posture** — option **(3)**.
It is surrounded by **elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo**, with **deer** below.
There were **no horse-drawn chariots**, and it is a **male** figure.
xa: Identified as **Proto-Shiva / Pashupati** (lord of animals) by **John Marshall**.
Some read it as a **deity of animals and fertility**, not Shiva.
Site: **Mohenjodaro**.

n183b181ce69.s: Who identified the figure on the Pashupati seal as Proto-Shiva?
n183b181ce69.x: John Marshall proposed the Proto-Shiva or Pashupati interpretation, which is debated.
xa: The Proto-Shiva reading is an **interpretation of an undeciphered culture**, not proven.
Exam angle: Indus people worshipped → **Shiva** (UKPSC **2006**).
The Pashupati figure later parallels **Shiva as Pashupati**.

ne027c59323c.s: The proto-Shiva reading of the Pashupati seal is treated cautiously mainly because:
o: The seal is made of gold
The seal was found outside India
The seal is a later forgery
ne027c59323c.x: The undeciphered script is a principal reason why the proto-Shiva interpretation remains debated.
xa: The Pashupati identification was named by **John Marshall**.
The figure is **three-faced**, in a **yogic posture**.
Exam angle: Indus people worshipped → **Shiva** (UKPSC **2006**).

n32454e139a4.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of animals regarded as sacred in the Indus Valley Civilization?
o: Humped bull, unicorn, elephant and tiger
n32454e139a4.x: The humped bull, mythical unicorn, elephant and tiger are identified as sacred animals in the Harappan religious tradition.
n32454e139a4.tq: Use the complete sacred-animal group and eliminate animals not associated with the stated Harappan evidence.
xs: **Humped bull, unicorn, elephant and tiger** were sacred animals — option **(2)**.
The **unicorn** is a **mythical** animal.
The **horse** and **lion** do not fit; the Rig Veda, not the IVC, lacks animal worship.
xa: **Pashupati animals** (elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo, deer) were probably also worshipped.
Sacred birds: **pigeons and doves**.
The **humped bull** motif first appears in the **Early Harappan** phase.

n46f4525b46a.s: Which tree is the most frequently depicted on Indus seals?
n46f4525b46a.x: The pipal is the most depicted tree on Indus seals and appears in ritual scenes with human figures.
n46f4525b46a.tq: Direct recall of the distinctive seal motif.
xs: The **pipal** is the most depicted tree on Indus seals — option **(2)**.
It appears in **ritual scenes with figures**.
Exam angle: tree shape on Indus seals → **Pipal** (MPPSC **2021**).
xa: The pipal motif goes back to the **Early Harappan** phase.
Pipal worship continues as the **sacred pipal tree**.
Harappan religion was **nature- and fertility-oriented**.

n819fdfb9a8b.s: The pipal motif in the Indus Valley Civilisation goes back to the:
n819fdfb9a8b.x: The pipal motif is traced to the Early Harappan phase and continued in later Indian religion.
xa: Pipal = most depicted tree on seals (MPPSC **2021**).
Other continuities: **Pashupati → Shiva**, **Mother Goddess → Shakti**, **linga-yoni → linga worship**.
**Swastika** → auspicious symbol today.

n2ea68ac7563.s: Terracotta female figurines found at Harappan sites are most commonly interpreted as evidence of:
n2ea68ac7563.x: The terracotta female figurines are associated with fertility symbolism and are interpreted as evidence of a fertility cult.
n2ea68ac7563.tq: Identify the religious interpretation attached to the figurines rather than their material form.
xs: Terracotta female figurines show a **fertility cult** — option **(3)**.
They carry **fertility symbolism** and are the **most important clay figures**.
They represent the **Mother Goddess**.
xa: Found at **Harappa**, **Kot Diji**, **Kalibangan**, Gujarat sites.
With the male **Pashupati** → worship of **both male and female deities** (UPSC **2013**).
Later parallel: **Shakti / mother-goddess cults**.

n2b8c40878b5.s: A row of seven fire altars has been found at:
n2b8c40878b5.x: Kalibangan yielded a row of seven fire altars. Fire altars have also been found at Lothal.
n2b8c40878b5.tq: Combine the distinctive number with its archaeological site.
xs: A row of **seven fire altars** is at **Kalibangan** — option **(3)**.
**Lothal** also has fire altars, but not the row of seven.
They suggest possible **fire worship or yajna**, a link that is **debated**.
xa: ⚠ **Lothal** = double burial + fire altars; **Kalibangan** = seven fire altars + horned deity on terracotta cake.
Fire altars (Kalibangan) → **Vedic yajna** (debated).
**Pits with animal remains** hint at **sacrificial rituals** (speculative).

n4b552638405.s: Which of the following correctly describes the evidence of phallic and yoni worship at Harappa?
o: The symbols were used exclusively as weapons.
Lingam and yoni symbols, including round and pierced stones, were possible fertility objects of worship.
Only metal images of fertility deities have been found.
Phallic symbols were absent from Harappan sites.
n4b552638405.x: Lingam and yoni symbols and round or pierced stones at Harappa are interpreted as fertility objects and possible early Shaivite elements.
n4b552638405.tq: Match the archaeological form with its cautious religious interpretation.
xs: **Lingam and yoni** symbols and **round, pierced stones** were possible **fertility objects of worship** — option **(2)**.
They were found at **Harappa** → possible **early Shaivite** elements.
So phallic symbols were present (option 4 wrong), and they were not weapons.
xa: Linga and yoni stones → later **linga worship**.
**AP angle**: **Gudimallam** (Satavahana era) = first **Shiva Lingam** in AP and India.
Mother Goddess → **fertility cult**.

nindian-history-42-16.s: The image of Lakshmi appears on the coins of:
nindian-history-42-16.x: Lakshmi appears on Muhammad Ghori's coins.
n: The Mother Goddess is associated with Harappan religion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 109-110]
Terracotta female figurines represent the Mother Goddess. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 109-110]
Saraswati is associated with Bhojshala Temple in Dhar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 109-110]
Lakshmi appears on Muhammad Ghori's coins. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 109-110]
Bharat Mata is depicted in Abanindranath Tagore's 1905 painting. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 109-110]
xa: Mother Goddess figurines were found at **Harappa**, **Kot Diji** and **Kalibangan**.
Saraswati is also linked with the **Veena**.
⚠ With the male **Pashupati** figure, they show worship of **both male and female deities** (UPSC **2013**).

n9715f4960ab.s: A horned deity represented on a terracotta cake has been associated particularly with which site?
n9715f4960ab.x: A horned deity on a terracotta cake was found at Kalibangan; a clay mask of a horned god is also associated with Kalibangan and Gujarat.
n9715f4960ab.tq: Link the archaeological object with its specific excavation site.
xs: The **horned deity on a terracotta cake** is from **Kalibangan** — option **(1)** (UPPSC **2008**).
A **clay mask** of a horned god is from **Kalibangan/Gujarat**.
**Ropar** is known for a dog burial, **Surkotada** for **pot burials**, **Lothal** for **double burial**.
xa: ⚠ **Kalibangan** = **seven fire altars** + horned deity on terracotta cake.
⚠ **Lothal** = **double burial** + **fire altars**.
Kalibangan's **bull figure** is bronze.

nf5e14453a93.s: Which one of the following features is associated with the Priest-King sculpture of Mohenjodaro?
o: A tribhanga posture with bangles covering both arms
A seated driver holding the reins of a toy cart
A clean-shaven face and a crown with animal horns
A beard, a forehead fillet and a shawl over one shoulder
nf5e14453a93.x: The Priest-King is represented as bearded, with a fillet on the forehead and a shawl over one shoulder.
nf5e14453a93.tq: Use the person–feature trap by separating the Priest-King’s attributes from those of the Dancing Girl and terracotta figures.
xs: The **Priest-King** has a **beard**, a **fillet on the forehead** and a **shawl over one shoulder** — option **(4)**.
The shawl has a **trefoil** pattern; it is of **steatite**, from **Mohenjodaro**.
**Bangles on the arm** belong to the **Dancing Girl**; the **seated driver** is a Chanhudaro toy cart.
xa: ⚠ **Dancing Girl** = **bronze**; **Priest-King** = **steatite**; nude male torso = **red sandstone**.
The "**priest-king**" label is an **interpretation**, not proven.
The Priest-King is cited in the **priest-rule** view of polity.

n343368fdaf8.s: The Harappan fire altars cannot be treated as conclusive evidence of:
n343368fdaf8.x: Their link with fire worship or yajna and resemblance to Vedic ritual spaces remain debated.
xa: The **fire-altar-yajna** link is an interpretation of an **undeciphered** culture, not proven.
Later Vedic religion was **sacrificial and ritualistic** (Indra, Agni, Varuna; yajna).
Harappan religion was **nature- and fertility-oriented**.

ne35f9f60d01.s: Which of the following was known to the Harappans?
ne35f9f60d01.x: Mirrors and combs were known to the Harappans.
xa: **Lipstick** → **Chanhudaro**.
**Dice** → **Harappa**.
Fashion in **hair and beard styles**.

n3ca805b68c7.x: Harappan religion was nature- and fertility-oriented; Later Vedic religion was sacrificial and ritualistic.
xa: Rig Vedic religion: **male nature gods**, open-air yajnas, **no temples or idols**, no animal worship.
Later Vedic religion was **priest-led**.
Harappan elements later entered **Hinduism**.

n5329ce0b51a.s: Harappan Mother Goddess worship has a later parallel in:
n5329ce0b51a.x: Mother Goddess worship has a later parallel in Shakti or mother-goddess cults.
xa: **Swastika** → auspicious symbol today.
**Linga and yoni stones** → **linga worship**.
**Pipal worship** → sacred pipal tree.

nbc07a5f59b3.s: Which of the following best expresses the historical significance of Harappan religious evidence?
o: It demonstrates that Harappan religion was exclusively based on Vedic sacrifice.
It provides early material evidence of cults involving a Shiva-like deity, a mother goddess and linga-related symbols that later show continuities.
It proves that the later Hindu religious system already existed in its complete form.
It establishes that all Harappan symbols had one fixed and universally accepted meaning.
nbc07a5f59b3.x: Harappan artefacts provide early material evidence of cultic elements that may have continued into later Hinduism. They do not prove that later Hinduism existed in a complete form or that every symbol has a certain interpretation.
nbc07a5f59b3.tq: Distinguish historical continuity from the claim of complete identity.
xs: Harappan evidence is the **earliest material evidence of cults** — a **Shiva-like deity**, **mother goddess**, **linga** — that later show **continuities** — option **(2)**.
These continuities: **Mother Goddess, Pashupati, linga-yoni, pipal, ritual bathing**.
The readings are **interpretations of an undeciphered culture**, so options (3) and (4) overstate.
xa: Harappan religion was **not Vedic**; it was nature- and fertility-oriented.
**AP angle**: **Gudimallam** = oldest Shaivite temple in AP.
**Swastika** survives as an auspicious symbol.

nindian-history-41-1.s: Which deity is identified with Pashupati and Harappan worship?
nindian-history-41-1.x: The Pashupati seal from Mohenjodaro shows a horned figure among animals, seen as a proto-Shiva. Shiva, called Rudra in the Vedas, is thus linked with Harappan worship.
nindian-history-41-1.tq: Recall the deity linked to the Pashupati seal.
n: Shiva or Rudra is associated with Pashupati. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Shiva or Rudra was worshipped in the Harappan culture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
xs: **Shiva / Rudra** is identified with **Pashupati** and Harappan worship — option **(2)** is correct.
**Shiva** (**Rudra**) as **Pashupati** (**Lord of Animals**) was **worshipped** in the **Harappan culture**.
**Agni** — **fire** and **sacrifice**; **Varuna** — **cosmic order**; **Indra** — **warfare**.
xa: The **Pashupati seal** from **Mohenjodaro** shows a figure in a **yogic posture**, surrounded by **elephant, tiger, rhinoceros, buffalo**.
The **Mother Goddess** was also worshipped, shown by **terracotta female figurines**.
Indus people worshipped **Shiva** (UKPSC **2006**).

n5abccccdfb8.s: Which of the following archaeological evidence most directly indicates a belief in an afterlife among the Harappans?
o: Grave goods such as pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads and food
The use of the pipal motif on seals
The presence of seals depicting animals
n5abccccdfb8.x: The placement of pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads and food with the dead indicates a belief in an afterlife and also reflects status differences.
n5abccccdfb8.tq: Identify the evidence that directly concerns funerary beliefs rather than general Harappan culture.
xs: **Grave goods** — **pottery, ornaments, mirrors, beads, food** — show **belief in afterlife** — option **(1)**.
They also reflect **status differences**.
Drains, pipal motifs and animal seals relate to civic life and worship, not the afterlife.
xa: **Cemetery-H**: **post-cremation** burials.
**Double burial** → **Lothal** (UPPSC **2016**).
**Pot burials** → **Surkotada** (four).

n1958af7741f.s: The bronze Dancing Girl was excavated in 1926 by:
n1958af7741f.x: Ernest Mackay excavated the Dancing Girl in 1926 under John Marshall.
xa: Material: **bronze**, **lost-wax** casting (UPSC **2025**).
Site: **Mohenjodaro**.
**Priest-King** from the same site is **steatite**.

n394e38d5312.s: Rig Vedic religion was centred on:
o: Male nature gods and open-air yajnas
n394e38d5312.x: Rig Vedic religion featured male nature gods like Indra, Agni and Varuna and open-air yajnas, with no temples or idols.
xa: Harappan focus: **Mother Goddess, pipal, animals**.
**Later Vedic** religion: **sacrificial, ritualistic, priest-led**.
Harappan **fire altars** → Vedic yajna link is **debated**.

n5477c5e13e4.s: Gudimallam, associated with the Satavahana era, is noted in Andhra Pradesh for:
o: The earliest known Buddhist stupa in India
The first Harappan fire altar in South India
The oldest Shaivite temple in Andhra Pradesh and a very early Shiva lingam
n5477c5e13e4.x: Gudimallam is described as having the oldest Shaivite temple in Andhra Pradesh and as representing the first Shiva lingam in Andhra Pradesh and India in the cited tradition.
n5477c5e13e4.tq: Use the AP-specific cultural association and distinguish it from Indus archaeological features.
xs: **Gudimallam** has the **oldest Shaivite temple in AP** and is called the **first Shiva Lingam** in AP and India — option **(4)**.
It belongs to the **Satavahana era**.
It represents the **linga tradition in historic form**.
xa: Harappan **lingam and yoni** symbols at **Harappa** → possible **early Shaivite** elements.
Linga and yoni stones → later **linga worship**.
Pashupati figure → **Shiva as Pashupati**.

nindian-history-41-8.s: The entire 9th Mandala of the Rigveda is devoted to:
nindian-history-41-8.x: Soma has the whole 9th Mandala of the Rigveda.
n: Indra is a Vedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Indra is associated with warfare. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Soma is associated with the ninth Mandala of the Rigveda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Vishnu is associated with the Chakra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Saraswati is associated with the Veena. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
xa: **Agni** — **fire**, **sacrifice**; **Varuna** — **cosmic order**.
Vishnu is the **supreme deity** of **Madhvacharya**.
Saraswati is the **presiding deity** of **Bhojshala** in **Dhar**.

nindian-history-41-14.s: In the Rigveda, Varuna is the upholder of:
nindian-history-41-14.x: Varuna is the upholder of cosmic order; Agni is the god of fire and sacrifice and Indra the warrior god.
n: Indra is a Vedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Indra is associated with warfare. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Agni is associated with fire. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Agni is associated with sacrifice. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Varuna is associated with cosmic order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
Saraswati is associated with the Veena. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-109]
xa: **Vishnu** — the **Chakra**, the **Varaha Avatar**.
**Shiva** (**Rudra**) — **Pashupati**, the **Lingam**, the **Trident**.

n543cc957353.s: The presence of both Mother Goddess figurines and the male Pashupati figure suggests that the Harappans:
o: Worshipped both male and female deities
n543cc957353.x: The Mother Goddess and Pashupati evidence together indicates the worship of both female and male deities.
n543cc957353.tq: Infer the broader religious pattern from two complementary archaeological symbols.
xs: The Harappans **worshipped both male and female deities** — option **(3)** (UPSC **2013**).
**Female**: Mother Goddess figurines; **male**: the **Pashupati** figure.
**Fertility symbolism** was central, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: ⚠ Of the UPSC **2013** claims, only "**worshipped both male and female deities**" is correct.
**No palaces, no temples**; **no horse-drawn chariots**.
Mother Goddess found at **Harappa, Kot Diji, Kalibangan**.

n6ff142bf917.s: The Dancing Girl of the Indus Valley Civilization was made of:
n6ff142bf917.x: The Dancing Girl from Mohenjodaro is a bronze figure produced by the lost-wax or cire perdue method.
n6ff142bf917.tq: Recall the distinctive material associated with the famous artefact.
xs: The **Dancing Girl** is **bronze** — option **(3)** (UPSC **2025**).
It was made by **lost-wax (cire perdue)** casting.
**Steatite** = Priest-King; **red sandstone** = nude male torso (Harappa); **terracotta** = Mother Goddess, toys.
xa: Found at **Mohenjodaro**; excavated **1926** by **Ernest Mackay**.
**Right hand on hip**; **left arm full of bangles**.
Mature Harappan, c. **2500 BCE**.

n8c95b0170bb.s: Mother Goddess figurines and the male Pashupati figure show that the Indus people worshipped:
n8c95b0170bb.x: These finds show worship of both female and male deities.
xa: ⚠ Of the three UPSC **2013** claims, only "**worshipped both male and female deities**" is correct.
Mother Goddess found at **Harappa, Kot Diji, Kalibangan**.
Pashupati seal → **Mohenjodaro**.

n64b024831bd.s: Who proposed the Aryan invasion theory of the decline of the Harappan civilisation in 1947?
n64b024831bd.x: Mortimer Wheeler proposed the Aryan invasion explanation in 1947; the theory is now generally rejected.
n64b024831bd.tq: Match the theory with its principal proponent and date.
xs: **Mortimer Wheeler** proposed the **Aryan invasion** theory in **1947** — option **(2)**; it is **now rejected**.
**Robert Raikes** = **tectonic damming**; **W.A. Fairservis** = **ecological imbalance**.
**H.T. Lambrick** = **shift of the Indus course**.
xa: **Gordon Childe** and **Stuart Piggott** are also linked to the invasion theory.
Wheeler cited **huddled skeletons at Mohenjodaro** and **Indra** as "fort-breaker" (**Purandara**).
Current consensus: decline was **multi-causal** and **gradual** (about **200 years**).

nfc3aba08290.s: The shift of the Indus course as a cause of the Harappan decline is associated with:
nfc3aba08290.x: H. T. Lambrick is linked with the Indus shift; Fairservis with ecological imbalance and Agrawal and Sood with Ghaggar-Hakra drying.
xa: ⚠ **M.R. Sahni** appears under both **floods** and **tectonic uplift**.
⚠ **Lambrick** = shift of Indus course, **not floods**.
**Floods** → **John Marshall, E. Mackay, S.R. Rao**.

n83d2eff27d6.s: The flood theory of the Harappan decline is associated with:
o: Marshall, Mackay and S. R. Rao
Aurel Stein and A. N. Ghosh
n83d2eff27d6.x: Marshall, Mackay and S. R. Rao are linked with floods; Wheeler, Childe and Piggott with invasion; Lambrick with the Indus shift.
xa: **IIT Kharagpur study**: **900 years** of low rainfall.
**Deoria Tal** pollen study (**2026**) backs the drought theory.
**Ecological imbalance** → **W.A. Fairservis**.

n474fa2538ae.s: The decline of Mesopotamian demand for Harappan goods around 1900 BCE is used to support which explanation?
n474fa2538ae.x: The fall in Mesopotamian demand around 1900 BCE is cited as an economic or trade-decline explanation.
n474fa2538ae.tq: Link the economic event to the corresponding decline theory.
xs: A fall in **Mesopotamian demand** (c. **1900 BCE**) supports the **trade decline** explanation — option **(3)**.
It is the **economic explanation** in the notes.
**Aryan invasion** = Wheeler; **ecological imbalance** = Fairservis; **tectonic damming** = Raikes.
xa: Long-distance trade **weakened** in the Late Harappan phase.
Weakening monsoon + rising aridity c. **1900 BCE** (palaeoclimate).
Decline is now seen as **multi-causal**.

n5b668b83b8d.s: The current consensus explains the Harappan decline as:
n5b668b83b8d.x: The consensus rejects a single sudden catastrophe and favours a gradual, multi-causal decline.
xa: Decline took about **200 years**, varying by region.
⚠ **900 years** = IIT Kharagpur low rainfall; **200 years** = pace of decline.
Debate: **climate as sole cause vs multi-causal**.

nde1f0b4b8cb.s: The IIT Kharagpur study associated the decline of the Harappan civilisation with continuous low rainfall for approximately:
nde1f0b4b8cb.x: The IIT Kharagpur study identified continuous weak monsoon or low rainfall for about 900 years as a major factor in the decline.
nde1f0b4b8cb.tq: Retain the exact duration attached to the climate study.
xs: The **IIT Kharagpur** study found **continuous low rainfall for about 900 years** — option **(3)** (BPSC **2018**).
It supports the **climate change / drought** theory.
**Aurel Stein** and **A.N. Ghosh** are the older names for this theory.
xa: ⚠ **900 years** = IIT Kharagpur; **4,200 years ago** = Deoria Tal **4.2 ka event**; **200 years** = pace of decline.
**Deoria Tal** pollen study (**30 Jul 2026**, PIB) also backs drought.
Palaeoclimate: weakening monsoon + rising aridity c. **1900 BCE**.

n7c6020097b0.s: Which of the following best represents the current debate regarding the decline of the Harappan civilisation?
o: The decline is considered entirely sudden and identical in every region.
Only drought is accepted, and all cultural continuity is rejected.
Invasion, migration, indigenous continuity, gradual internal decline and climatic factors continue to be debated, with multi-causal explanations receiving attention.
Only foreign invasion is accepted, while climate and internal factors are excluded.
n7c6020097b0.x: The debate includes invasion versus internal decline, migration versus continuity, and climate as a sole cause versus a multi-causal explanation. A gradual, regionally varied decline is widely emphasised.
n7c6020097b0.tq: Choose the option that captures the competing interpretations without using an exclusive or absolute explanation.
xs: **Invasion, migration, continuity, gradual decline and climate** are still debated, with **multi-causal** views prominent — option **(3)**.
Debates: **invasion vs internal decline**; **gradual vs sudden**; **climate as sole cause vs multi-causal**.
The Aryan invasion is **rejected**, but **migration and continuity** are still argued, so options (2) and (4) fail.
xa: Decline took about **200 years**, varying by region.
**Deoria Tal** pollen backs the drought theory.
**Rakhigarhi DNA** challenges invasion theories.

n34b8a3a2aa7.s: The invasion theory of the Harappan decline, now rejected, was put forward by:
n34b8a3a2aa7.x: Wheeler's invasion theory is rejected for lack of archaeological evidence and the reinterpretation of the skeletons.
xa: A fourth ground: decline was **gradual**.
Wheeler proposed the theory in **1947**.
**Rakhigarhi DNA** challenges invasion theories.

n1bb7ea60729.s: The absence of a ‘Steppe Pastoralist’ genetic component in the female DNA sample from Rakhigarhi is significant because it:
o: challenges invasion theories and suggests indigenous continuity
proves that the Harappan civilisation was founded by Steppe migrants
supports the theory of a sudden Aryan invasion
establishes that no population movement occurred in ancient India
n1bb7ea60729.x: The Rakhigarhi DNA finding challenges invasion theories and is used to support the possibility of indigenous continuity. It does not by itself prove that all population movement was absent.
n1bb7ea60729.tq: Apply a scientific finding to the historical theory it most directly supports without treating it as absolute proof.
xs: No "**Steppe Pastoralist**" gene in the **Rakhigarhi** female DNA **challenges invasion theories** and suggests **indigenous continuity** — option **(1)**.
It does not show Steppe founders or a sudden invasion.
The Aryan invasion theory is **rejected**, though **migration and continuity** are still argued.
xa: Rakhigarhi DNA + a new skeletal study by **AnSI** (Jun **2026**).
Wheeler's theory (**1947**) is rejected for **lack of archaeological evidence**.
Consensus: **limited folk continuity** + major shift with **Indo-Aryan speakers**.

n7f557f8a10e.s: Pollen evidence from Deoria Tal in Uttarakhand indicates that during the 4.2 ka event the monsoon:
n7f557f8a10e.x: The Deoria Tal evidence indicates a sharp weakening of the monsoon.
xa: This is the "**4.2 ka event**".
It cut water in the **Indus and Ghaggar-Hakra** → drought + **eastward migration**.
The **4.2 ka** event is also linked with the **fall of Akkad**.

n2c8034cf666.s: After the decline of the Harappan urban centres, settlement movement was mainly directed:
o: westward to Iran and northward to Central Asia
eastward towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and southward towards Gujarat and the Deccan
northward towards the Himalayan valleys only
n2c8034cf666.x: Post-urban settlement shifts were mainly eastward towards the Ganga-Yamuna Doab and southward towards Gujarat and the Deccan.
n2c8034cf666.tq: Remember the paired directional movement—eastward and southward—rather than a single-direction migration.
xs: Movement went **east** to the **Ganga-Yamuna Doab** and **south** to **Gujarat** and the **Deccan** — option **(2)**.
Cities gave way to **small rural settlements** and **regional cultures**.
The **4.2 ka** drought also drove **eastward migration**.
xa: Decline was **gradual** (about **200 years**).
**Daimabad** (Maharashtra) is a southern Late Harappan site.
**OCP** in the Doab (Haryana, western UP).

nc1ed30ad479.s: In the Late Harappan phase, pottery became:
nc1ed30ad479.x: Late Harappan cultures developed more regionally varied pottery, while stone and copper tools continued.
xa: **Seals, script, weights, bricks** lost uniformity.
**Long-distance trade** weakened.

nff24e48ee82.s: Which change occurred during the Late Harappan phase?
nff24e48ee82.x: In the Late Harappan phase seals, script and weights declined, long-distance trade weakened and bricks lost uniformity.
xa: Settlements became **smaller and rural** (**de-urbanisation**).
Pottery: **varied regional styles**.
Tools of **stone and copper**; no complicated casting.

n3b8176b018a.s: The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase of the Late Harappan culture is associated with which pottery tradition?
n3b8176b018a.x: The Ganga-Yamuna Doab phase is identified in the table with Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP).
n3b8176b018a.tq: Discriminate between closely associated archaeological pottery traditions.
xs: The **Ganga-Yamuna Doab** phase is linked to **Ochre Coloured Pottery (OCP)** — option **(2)**.
It covers **Haryana and western UP**.
**Painted Grey Ware** is a later culture that **overlaps the Late Harappan** at **Bhagwanpura**.
xa: **Copper Hoards** are often found with OCP in the Doab.
OCP is listed with **Cemetery-H** as a Late Harappan culture.
**Harappan legacy** may have shaped OCP.

n464b672c272.s: Copper Hoards are commonly linked with the Ochre Coloured Pottery culture because they are frequently found together in the:
n464b672c272.x: Copper Hoards are often found with OCP in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, forming the basis of their commonly proposed association.
n464b672c272.tq: Use the location clue to distinguish the OCP–Copper Hoard association from other archaeological regions.
xs: Copper Hoards and OCP are found together in the **Ganga-Yamuna Doab** — option **(4)**.
Hence they are **commonly linked**.
The Doab was a destination of the **eastward migration** after decline.
xa: OCP is a **Late Harappan** culture listed with **Cemetery-H**.
Ganga-Yamuna Doab (OCP) → **Haryana, western UP**.
**Alamgirpur** (UP) is a Late Harappan site.

na1c04381856.s: Bhagwanpura is significant in the debate on Harappan–Vedic continuity because it yielded:
o: only iron weapons and horse bones
a large Buddhist stupa over a Harappan citadel
a 13-roomed house with Late Harappan pottery and Painted Grey Ware
na1c04381856.x: Bhagwanpura provides evidence of overlap through a 13-roomed house containing Late Harappan pottery and Painted Grey Ware.
na1c04381856.tq: Use the distinctive archaeological feature and associated pottery to identify the site.
xs: **Bhagwanpura** yielded a **13-roomed house** with **Late Harappan pottery + PGW** — option **(4)**.
It shows **PGW sites overlap the Late Harappan** — a **continuity** argument.
Bhagwanpura is in **Haryana**.
xa: Continuity view also identifies Ghaggar-Hakra with the **Rigvedic Sarasvati**.
Discontinuity view: **horse, chariot, iron** absent in Mature Harappan.
Consensus: limited folk continuity + major shift.

n9907e3a12b2.s: The identification of the Ghaggar-Hakra river system with the Rigvedic Sarasvati represents the:
n9907e3a12b2.x: The identification of Ghaggar-Hakra with the Rigvedic Sarasvati is an argument used by scholars supporting continuity between Late Harappan and Vedic cultural traditions.
n9907e3a12b2.tq: Distinguish the continuity interpretation from theories that emphasise invasion or complete cultural replacement.
xs: Ghaggar-Hakra = **Rigvedic Sarasvati** is part of the **continuity view** — option **(3)**.
Another continuity argument: **PGW sites overlap the Late Harappan** (e.g. Bhagwanpura).
The **discontinuity view** stresses the **horse, chariot, iron** absent in the Mature Harappan.
xa: Consensus: **limited folk continuity** + **major shift** with Indo-Aryan speakers.
The Ghaggar-Hakra had the **densest cluster of settlements**.
Its drying → **D.P. Agrawal and Sood**.

n18822f8e532.s: Which of the following was absent in the Mature Harappan phase and became important only later?
n18822f8e532.x: Horse, chariot and iron were absent in the Mature Harappan phase; fire altars, pipal worship and burials are cited as continuities.
xa: Other continuities: **Mother Goddess**, **linga-yoni**, **ritual bathing**.
Material continuities: **bead-making in Gujarat**, **red ware with black designs**, **bullock carts**.
⚠ Continuity may reflect **similar functions** rather than direct survival.

n249afb1178c.s: The book *Rigvedic India*, associated with the Sapta Sindhu theory of the Aryan homeland, was written by
n249afb1178c.x: Avinash Chandra Das proposed Sapta Sindhu or India as the original home and wrote Rigvedic India.
n249afb1178c.tq: Use the author–work–theory linkage as a three-part recall question.
xs: **Rigvedic India** was written by **Avinash Chandra Das** — option **(4)**.
He placed the homeland in **Sapta Sindhu** (India).
**Dayananda Saraswati** = Tibet (**Satyarth Prakash**); **Max Muller** = Central Asia; **Asko Parpola** = migration theory.
xa: ⚠ **Tilak** = Arctic; **A.C. Das** = Sapta Sindhu; **Dayananda** = Tibet.
**Brahmarshi-desha** → **Ganganath Jha**.
Aryans entered via the **Khyber Pass** → spread to Sapta Sindhu.

ndd73861c963.s: Who located the original home of the Aryans in Tibet?
ndd73861c963.x: Dayananda Saraswati associated the homeland with Tibet in Satyarth Prakash.
xa: **Southern Russia** → **Nehring, Gordon Childe**.
Most plausible: **Southern Russia / Eurasia**.

nc11e1e023f1.s: The term 'Aryans' in the context of early Indian history is best understood as denoting:
nc11e1e023f1.x: 'Aryan' is primarily a linguistic label: the Vedic Aryans were speakers of Indo-Aryan (Indo-European) languages, so they form a speech group. It is not an ethnic or racial category, and 'superior race' reflects the rejected colonial racial misuse; 'nomadic people' describes a way of life, not what the term denotes.
xs: "Aryans" denotes a **speech group** — option **(3)**.
Vedic Aryans were **speakers of Indo-Aryan languages** — a **linguistic-cultural** label.
It is **not a race**; "**superior race**" reflects the rejected **colonial racial misuse**.
xa: **Max Muller** popularised the concept.
Vedic Sanskrit belongs to the **Indo-European** family.
Branches: **Iranian** (outside India), **Dardic** (J&K), **Indo-Aryan**.

nc84bb0686b2.s: According to Iranian literature, the Dasas were:
o: A branch of the early Aryans
nc84bb0686b2.x: The Dasas were regarded as a branch of the early Aryans, while the Dasyus were original inhabitants.
xa: Dasyus were possibly **phallus worshippers** and did not raise cattle for dairy.
**Panis** = non-Aryan **cattle-holders and traders**.
**Divodasa** (Bharata clan) defeated **Sambara**.
nc84bb0686b2.fixed: 'in the relevant interpretation' is unexamlike wording

nd4b9f1436c0.s: The Dardic branch of the Indo-European languages is associated with:
nd4b9f1436c0.x: Dardic is associated with Jammu and Kashmir; Iranian is found outside India.
xa: The Indo-European family = **~73%** of Indian speakers.
The **Avesta** (Iran) parallels the Rigveda — common **Indo-Iranian** stock.
Vedic Aryans = speakers of **Indo-Aryan** languages.

n605faa85713.s: The Boghazkoi inscription records a peace treaty between the Hittites and the rulers of:
n605faa85713.x: Boghazkoi records a Hittite-Mitanni treaty invoking Indra, Mitra, Varuna and the Nasatyas, c. 14th century BCE.
xa: It invokes **Indra, Mitra, Varuna and Nasatyas**.
It shows Vedic gods in **West Asia** → supports a **Central Asian homeland**.
Distractors in exams: **Mansehra, Shahbazgarhi, Junagadh, Ecbatana, Behistun**.

nf20112d7ae3.s: The oldest Iranian (Zoroastrian) text is the:
nf20112d7ae3.x: The Avesta is the oldest Iranian Zoroastrian text and closely parallels the Rigveda.
xa: Boghazkoi invokes **Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Nasatyas**.
Boghazkoi dates to c. **14th century BCE**.
**Iranian** is an Indo-European branch outside India.

ne0caf4b184d.s: The link between Painted Grey Ware archaeology and ____ remains an open question.
ne0caf4b184d.x: The relationship between Painted Grey Ware and Later Vedic textual geography remains an open question.
xa: **B.B. Lal** argued a **PGW-Vedic link** (indigenous school).
**Andronovo** and **Gandhara Grave** cultures are linked to the migration debate.
Migration arguments include changes in **pottery, burials, settlements**.

nb1d457ef135.s: The principal historical significance of the Boghazkoi inscription is that it:
o: Proves that Vedic culture originated exclusively in India
Records the establishment of the Mauryan Empire
Shows the presence of Vedic-speaking people or gods in West Asia
Describes the spread of Buddhism to Central Asia
nb1d457ef135.x: The inscription provides evidence of Vedic-speaking people or deities in West Asia and is used in support of a Central Asian homeland and movement towards Iran and India.
nb1d457ef135.tq: Choose the option expressing the evidentiary significance rather than an exaggerated conclusion.
xs: Boghazkoi shows **Vedic-speaking people or gods in West Asia** — option **(3)**.
This supports a **Central Asian homeland** and movement **towards Iran and India**.
It does not prove an exclusively Indian origin (option 1).
xa: It records a **Hittite–Mitanni** peace treaty, c. **1400 BCE**.
Gods named: **Indra, Mitra, Varuna, Nasatyas**.
Mainstream view: Indo-Aryan speakers came from **Central Asia c. 1500 BCE**.

n05464b4d5ba.s: Which scholar is a proponent of the indigenous or 'Out of India' theory?
n05464b4d5ba.x: S. R. Rao, B. B. Lal and Shrikant Talageri back the indigenous theory; Max Muller, Wheeler and Parpola back migration.
xa: It also uses **Harappan-script decipherment claims**.
**Mainstream**: migration from **Central Asia c. 1500 BCE** (Max Muller, Wheeler, Parpola).
**Synthesis**: **Romila Thapar, Upinder Singh**.

nc67430db23d.s: Which genetic haplogroup is discussed in relation to the Aryan migration theory?
nc67430db23d.x: The migration theory draws on linguistics, Rigvedic geography, horse and chariot archaeology and genetics, including the R1a haplogroup.
xa: Proponents: **Max Muller, Mortimer Wheeler, Asko Parpola**.
Mainstream: Indo-Aryan speakers came from **Central Asia c. 1500 BCE**, then **synthesis** with local people.
⚠ **Rakhigarhi DNA** is cited **against** invasion theories.

n0d38e5a6114.s: Romila Thapar and Upinder Singh are associated with which interpretation of the Aryan question?
o: An Arctic homeland based only on astronomical evidence
A synthesis involving migration, interaction and cultural assimilation
n0d38e5a6114.x: Romila Thapar and Upinder Singh represent a synthesis in which small groups migrated, achieved elite dominance and underwent cultural assimilation, without a simple invasion or replacement model.
n0d38e5a6114.tq: Match the scholars with the nuanced interpretation rather than an extreme theory.
xs: **Romila Thapar** and **Upinder Singh** hold the **synthesis** view — option **(3)**.
Small groups migrated; **elite dominance**; **cultural assimilation**; **no "invasion"**.
It is the **nuanced consensus**: migration + interaction, **not replacement**.
xa: **Migration** school: Max Muller, Wheeler, Parpola.
**Indigenous** school: S.R. Rao, B.B. Lal, Shrikant Talageri.
**Arctic** homeland = **Tilak**, not these historians.

nc1d864e8ccc.s: B. B. Lal linked which pottery with the Vedic tradition?
nc1d864e8ccc.x: B. B. Lal identified the Sarasvati with the Rigvedic river and linked Painted Grey Ware with the Vedic tradition.
xa: Other proponents: **S.R. Rao, Shrikant Talageri**.
Status: **marginal view**, weak linguistic and archaeological support.
The **PGW–Later Vedic** link remains an **open question**.

nccaebeafaf9.s: Which steppe culture, associated with horses and chariots, is linked to Indo-Iranian speakers?
nccaebeafaf9.x: Andronovo represents steppe pastoralists with horses and chariots linked to Indo-Iranian speakers.
xa: **BMAC** (Turkmenistan-Uzbekistan-north Afghanistan) = **contact zone** for migrants.
**Gandhara Grave** culture (**Swat valley**) = horse remains, new burials.
Migration theory also uses genetics (**R1a haplogroup**).

n7942db5de8a.s: The Swat valley culture known for horse remains and new burial practices is the:
n7942db5de8a.x: The Swat valley culture is the Gandhara Grave culture; BMAC lay in Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan and north Afghanistan.
xa: BMAC = **Bactria-Margiana Archaeological Complex**.
**Andronovo** = steppe pastoralists, horses and chariots.
Gandhara Grave culture is often correlated with **early Indo-Aryans**.

nf2c028951a9.x: Harappans used solid wheels; spoked-wheel chariots are part of the migration argument.
xa: Other migration arguments: changes in **pottery, burial practices, settlements** after Harappan decline.
**Andronovo**: steppe pastoralists with **horses and chariots**.
Rigvedic **horse** was **domesticated** and central to warfare.

n29881829ce8.s: Which animal was domesticated and central to Rigvedic warfare, but is not attested in the Harappan civilisation?
n29881829ce8.x: The Rigvedic horse was domesticated and central to warfare; no awareness of the horse is attributed to the Harappans.
xa: Rigvedic armour: **coat of mail and helmet**.
Harappans used **solid wheels**; migration argument = **spoked-wheel chariots**.
**Andronovo** steppe pastoralists had **horses and chariots**.

n8efada0cec3.s: The concept of 'Aryan' was popularised in modern scholarship by:
n8efada0cec3.x: Max Muller popularised the concept; it denotes a linguistic-cultural group, not a biologically superior race.
xa: "Aryan" as race = a **colonial idea**.
Arya originally meant **"noble"** / **high birth**.
Indo-European (Aryan) family = **~73%** of Indian speakers.

n4f28dac32de.s: The Rigvedic river Kubha is identified with the modern:
n4f28dac32de.x: Kubha, Krumu, Gomati and Suvastu are the Kabul, Kurram, Gomal and Swat rivers.
xa: **Mujavant** = a Hindu Kush mountain, source of **soma**.
**Sindhu (Indus)** = most mentioned river.
**Sarasvati** = holiest, "**naditama**".

n18c9ff757c7.s: The river mentioned most often in the Rigveda is the:
n18c9ff757c7.x: The Sindhu (Indus) is the most mentioned river; 'naditama' refers to the Sarasvati.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Yamuna** thrice vs **Ganga once** — not the other way round.
**Kubha (Kabul)** and **Krumu (Kurram)** show **Afghanistan** links.
**Samudra** in the Rigveda = a collection of water, **not necessarily the sea**.

nd6109bca762.s: The Early Vedic geographical core lay in:
nd6109bca762.x: The Early Vedic core lay in Punjab-Haryana; the Later Vedic core shifted east to the Doab, eastern UP and Bihar.
xa: Sapta Sindhu geography places the Early Vedic heartland in the **north-west**.
**Ganga** is mentioned only **once** in the Rigveda.
**Kurus + Panchalas** later ruled the **upper Gangetic basin**.

n4792797172a.x: Dhanva means desert land; Himavant is the Himalayas and Mujavant a Hindu Kush mountain associated with Soma.
xa: The later **Satapatha Brahmana** mentions **eastern and western seas**.
**Sarasvati** = "**naditama**".
**Ganga** mentioned **once** (**10th mandala**).

nindian-history-16-4.s: Madhya Desh was the region between the Himalayas and the:
nindian-history-16-4.x: Madhya Desh was the region between the Himalayas and the Vindhyas; Aryavarta was northern India.
n: Aryavarta referred to Northern India or the land occupied by Aryans. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
Madhya Desh was the region between the Himalayas and the Vindhyas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
Aryavarta was the name for the Aryan northern region. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
Madhya Desh was the name for the northern Indian region. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
xa: **Brahmarshi Desh** = the **Ganga-Yamuna Doab** and the **adjoining region**.
**Sapta-Sindhu** = the **land** of **seven rivers**, a **Rigvedic** region.
**Himavant** = Himalayas; **Mujavant** = Hindu Kush mountain, source of **soma**.

n4d056a0a937.s: Which tribe emerged dominant after the Battle of Ten Kings?
n4d056a0a937.x: The Bharatas emerged dominant; the defeated Purus later allied with them to form the Kurus.
xa: Site: banks of the **Parushni (Ravi)**.
Victor: **Sudas** (Tritsu family); priest **Vasishtha**.
Text: Rigveda, **Mandala VII**.

nf8930995c2b.s: By tradition, the Battle of Ten Kings arose from the rivalry between:
nf8930995c2b.x: Tradition traces the battle to the rivalry between the priests Vasishtha and Vishvamitra.
xa: The battle is in **Mandala VII**, on the **Parushni (Ravi)**.
The **Bharatas** under **Sudas** won; ⚠ **Vasishtha** = priest of **Sudas**, **Vishvamitra** = priest of the confederacy.
The defeated **Purus** later allied with the Bharatas to form the **Kurus**.

n229cb967aa7.s: In the Battle of Ten Kings, the Bharata chief Sudas was supported by:
n229cb967aa7.x: Sudas, Bharata chief of the Tritsu family, was supported by Vasishtha, not Vishvamitra.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Vasishtha** = priest of victor **Sudas**; **Vishvamitra** = priest of the losers.
Site: **Parushni (Ravi)**.
The confederacy had **10** tribes.

nf3202764300.s: The Dasarajna or Battle of Ten Kings described in the Rigveda was fought on the banks of the:
nf3202764300.x: The Battle of Ten Kings was fought on the banks of the Parushni, the Rigvedic name of the Ravi, where Sudas of the Bharatas defeated the confederacy. Vitasta is the Jhelum, Asikni the Chenab and Sutudri the Sutlej, none of which was the battle site.
nf3202764300.tq: Dasarajna = Parushni (Ravi), Mandala VII, Sudas + Vasishtha.
xs: The Dasarajna was fought on the **Parushni (Ravi)** — option **(2)**.
**Sudas** of the **Bharatas** defeated the confederacy of **10** tribes.
It is described in Rigveda **Mandala VII**.
xa: Priest of Sudas: **Vasishtha**; of the confederacy: **Vishvamitra**.
Defeated **Purus** later joined the Bharatas to form the **Kurus**.
**Kurus + Panchalas** later ruled the upper Gangetic basin.

na79c1047c34.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the early Vedic political hierarchy from the largest to the smallest unit?
na79c1047c34.x: The early Vedic hierarchy proceeded from Jana, the tribe, to Vis, the clan, Grama, the village, and Kula, the family.
na79c1047c34.tq: Test sequence by moving from the broadest kinship unit to the smallest.
xs: From largest to smallest, the hierarchy ran **Jana – Vis – Grama – Kula** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Jana** = tribe; **Vis** = clan under the **Vispati**; **Grama** = village under the **Gramani**; **Kula** = family under the **Kulapa**.
The other options jumble the order; the **Jana** always sits at the top.
xa: The term **Janapada** is **absent** from the Rigveda — the polity was tribal, not territorial.
The **Gramani** was also a military leader of the grama (leader of fighting groups).
⚠ Trap: **Kulapa / Kulapati** = head of the family; **Vrajapati** = officer in charge of **pasture land**.

n0f5956e1262.s: Which river was called 'Naditama' in the Rigveda?
n0f5956e1262.x: The Sarasvati was the most sacred river, called Naditama; the Sindhu was the most mentioned.
xa: **Sarasvati** is identified with the **Ghaggar-Hakra**.
The core region was **Sapta Sindhu**.
**Sadanira** (later Vedic) = **Gandak**.

n1cc7e41c8ac.s: The Samiti of the early Vedic period was primarily associated with:
o: General tribal participation and the choice of the chief
n1cc7e41c8ac.x: Samiti was the broader tribal assembly concerned with tribal business, legislative matters and the election or choice of the chief.
n1cc7e41c8ac.tq: Distinguish the broad folk assembly from the elite Sabha and military Gana.
xs: The **Samiti** stood for **general tribal participation and the choice of the chief** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was the folk assembly of general tribal members handling **tribal business**, **legislative** work and **election of the king**.
Pasture land was under the **Vrajapati**; chariot warriors were the **Rathins**.
xa: The Samiti is mentioned **9 times** in the Rig Veda; Sabha **8**; Vidatha **122**.
The **Atharvaveda** calls Sabha and Samiti the **twin daughters of Prajapati** and mentions women in the Samiti.
In the Later Vedic period the **Samiti weakened**.

nb9f98b49688.s: Women members of the early Vedic Sabha were called:
nb9f98b49688.x: Female members of the Sabha were called Sabhavati; women also attended the Vidatha.
xa: In the **Later Vedic** period **women were excluded** from the assemblies.
The **Vidatha** was the assembly of the **whole tribe** and the **earliest** one.
The Atharvaveda also calls the Sabha "**narishta**".

n61a6698096f.s: Which early Vedic assembly, composed mainly of elders and elites, is noted for exercising judicial functions in addition to advisory and social ones?
n61a6698096f.x: The Sabha was the assembly of elders and elites with advisory, social and judicial functions. The Samiti was the folk assembly that chose the chief, the Vidatha was the earliest assembly with secular, religious, economic and military roles, and the Gana was a troop of tribesmen with military functions.
n61a6698096f.tq: Judicial assembly = Sabha; earliest/most mentioned = Vidatha; king's election = Samiti.
xs: The **Sabha** — elders and elites — had **judicial** functions besides advisory and social ones — option **(3)**.
**Samiti** = folk assembly that **elected the king**; **Vidatha** = earliest assembly with **secular, religious, economic and military** roles.
**Gana** = troop of tribesmen with **military** functions.
xa: Exam angle: "judicial assembly" = **Sabha**; "earliest/most-mentioned assembly" = **Vidatha**.
There were **no officers for justice**; disputes were also settled by consensus or the **Madhyamasi** (mediator).
Women members of the Sabha = **Sabhavati**.

n131fc6397ac.s: Which one of the following was the earliest Vedic assembly and the first to disappear in the Later Vedic period?
n131fc6397ac.x: Vidatha was the earliest assembly and was also the first to disappear during the Later Vedic period.
n131fc6397ac.tq: Use the first-and-last clue to identify the assembly with the earliest chronological position and earliest disappearance.
xs: The **Vidatha** was the **earliest assembly** and the **first to disappear** in the Later Vedic period — option **(2)**.
It is also the most-mentioned assembly — **122 times** (Samiti 9, Sabha 8).
**Sabha and Samiti survived** into the Later Vedic period under chiefs and nobles.
xa: The Vidatha was an assembly of the **whole tribe**; **women attended**.
Its functions were **secular, religious, economic and military**.
**Gana** = troop of tribesmen, a military unit.

n2874ca425c0.s: The exceptional early Vedic ruler described as ‘ardhadeva’ was:
n2874ca425c0.x: Kingship was generally not considered divine, but the Puru king Trasadasyu was exceptionally described as ardhadeva, or demi-god.
n2874ca425c0.tq: Use the exception carefully rather than applying the general rule to every ruler.
xs: **Trasadasyu**, the **Puru** king, was called **ardhadeva** (demi-god) — so option **(3)** is correct.
He is the exception: Early Vedic kingship was otherwise **not linked to divinity**.
**Vispati** headed the Vis, **Gramani** the village and **Senani** the army — none bore this title.
xa: Other Rajan titles: **Gopati** (lord of cattle), **Gopa** (protector), **Gopajanasya**.
**Mahisi** = the chief queen.
The **Puru** were one of the **Panchajana** — Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa, Puru.

n9080223d028.s: The early Vedic Rajan was known by the title:
n9080223d028.x: The Rajan was called Gopati or Gopajanasya, protector of the tribe and its cattle.
xa: The Rajan was a **tribal chief**, not ruler of a fixed territory.
**Purohita** = chief priest and adviser; **Senani** = army commander.
**Mahisi** = chief queen; **ardhadeva** = title of Puru king **Trasadasyu**.

nfffec6ee3f2.s: In the early Vedic polity, the Vrajapati was the:
o: Officer in charge of pasture land
nfffec6ee3f2.x: Vrajapati was the pasture officer; Spasa was the spy, Senani the commander and Purohita the chief priest.
xa: **Gramani** = village head and military leader of the grama.
**Jivagribha / Ugra** = police officials; **Madhyamasi** = mediator in disputes.
There was **no formal bureaucracy** — governance was kinship-based.

n78477805c69.s: In the Rigvedic period, the head of the family was called:
n78477805c69.x: The family head was the Kulapa or Kulapati; Vrajapati was the pasture officer and Ugra and Jivagribha police officials.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Vrajapati** = pasture; **Gramani** = village head; **Madhyamasi** = mediator; **Spasa** = spies.
**Purohita** = chief priest and adviser; **Senani** = army chief.
Disputes were settled by **community consensus** or mediators — no officers for justice.

n38564989950.s: The temporary military force of the early Vedic polity was organised into units such as:
n38564989950.x: Sena was a temporary militia organised into units such as Sardha, Vrata and Gana.
n38564989950.tq: Separate military subdivisions from social units, revenues and assemblies.
xs: The militia was organised into **Sardha, Vrata and Gana** — option **(2)**.
The **Sena** was a **temporary militia** of able-bodied tribesmen — **no standing army**.
**Jana, Vis, Kula** are social units; **Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha** are assemblies.
xa: **Patti** = foot soldiers; **Rathins** = chariot warriors.
**Senani** = army commander.
**Gavishti** ("search for cows") — war often meant **cattle raids**.

n09866ffaf27.s: In the context of early Vedic warfare, the term ‘gavishti’ refers to:
n09866ffaf27.x: ‘Gavishti’ literally refers to the search for cows and denotes cattle raids, which were a common form of warfare in the Rig Vedic period.
n09866ffaf27.tq: Use the exact meaning of the specialised term rather than its literal military association.
xs: **Gavishti** means "**search for cows**" — option **(3)**.
War was often a **cattle raid**, since cattle were the main wealth.
The Rajan's titles reflect this: **Gopati** = lord of cattle.
xa: **Panis** hid cattle and were fought with **Indra's** help.
The **Sena** was a temporary militia — **no standing army**.
**Vrajapati** = officer in charge of **pasture land**.

ndd12c7521e3.s: The early Vedic Sena was a:
ndd12c7521e3.x: The Sena was a temporary militia of able-bodied tribesmen; there was no permanent standing army.
xa: Army units: **Sardha, Vrata, Gana**; **Senani** = army commander.
**Regular taxes** came only in the **Later Vedic** period.
There was **no formal bureaucracy** either.

nb7ce871ffd7.s: In the early Vedic period, ‘Bali’ was:
o: A military unit of chariot warriors
A compulsory land tax collected by appointed officials
A voluntary offering rather than a regular tax
nb7ce871ffd7.x: Bali was a voluntary offering. The early Vedic polity lacked a formal system of regular taxation and tax collection.
nb7ce871ffd7.tq: Distinguish a voluntary contribution from a regular and compulsory tax.
xs: **Bali** was a **voluntary offering rather than a regular tax** — option **(4)**.
There was **no regular tax** and **no tax-collecting machinery** in the Early Vedic polity.
Chariot warriors were **Rathins**; the judicial assembly was the **Sabha**.
xa: **Regular taxes** and **ratnins** are Later Vedic features.
The **Sena** was a temporary militia — no standing army.
Governance was kinship-based with **no formal bureaucracy**.

nb665ebaa36c.s: The Battle of Ten Kings, an intra-Aryan conflict of the early Vedic period, was fought on the banks of which river?
nb665ebaa36c.x: The Battle of Ten Kings was fought on the Parushni (modern Ravi). Asikni is the Chenab, Vitasta the Jhelum, and Sarasvati the sacred Naditama identified with the Ghaggar-Hakra; none of them was the battle site.
xs: The **Battle of Ten Kings** was fought on the **Parushni** — option **(2)**.
**Parushni** = modern **Ravi**.
**Asikni** = Chenab, **Vitasta** = Jhelum, **Sarasvati** = Ghaggar-Hakra — none was the battle site.
xa: It was an **intra-Aryan** war; wars were also fought against **Dasas/Dasyus**.
Bharata chief **Divodasa** defeated **Sambara**.
The **Bharatas** gave their name to **Bharatavarsha**.

n44df8153ed5.s: The Panchajana of the early Vedic period consisted of which five tribes?
o: Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa and Puru
Bharata, Tritsu, Krivi, Srinjaya and Puru
Anu, Bharata, Yadu, Panchala and Kuru
Druhyu, Turvasa, Kuru, Panchala and Matsya
n44df8153ed5.x: The five tribes of Panchajana were Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa and Puru.
n44df8153ed5.tq: Recall the complete named list and reject options containing later or additional tribes.
xs: **Panchajana** = **Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa and Puru** — option **(1)**.
**Bharata, Tritsu, Krivi, Srinjaya** are listed among the **other tribes**, not the Panchajana.
xa: The **Bharatas** gave their name to **Bharatavarsha**.
**Trasadasyu** of the **Purus** was called **ardhadeva**.
Bharata chief **Divodasa** defeated **Sambara**.

n6a0aecad305.x: Divodasa, the Bharata chief, defeated Sambara.
xa: **Panchajana**: **Anu, Druhyu, Yadu, Turvasa, Puru**.
The **Battle of Ten Kings** was fought on the **Parushni**.
**Horse-drawn chariots** gave a military edge.

naffcedd88a9.s: The ratnins and regular taxes are features of which period?
naffcedd88a9.x: The Later Vedic period saw hereditary territorial kingship, ratnins, regular taxes and royal sacrifices.
xa: Early Vedic had **Bali** (voluntary offering) — **no regular tax**.
The unit changed from **Jana** to **Janapada / Rashtra**.
The **Vidatha disappeared** and the **Samiti weakened**.

n996aaa18d7a.s: The basic character of the early Aryan administrative system was that of a:
n996aaa18d7a.x: Early Aryan administration was a tribal polity based on kinship, without a formal bureaucracy or fixed territorial organisation.
n996aaa18d7a.tq: Distinguish the exact constitutional character from nearby terms such as republic and autocracy.
xs: Early Aryan administration was a **kinship-based tribal polity** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It had **no formal bureaucracy** and **no fixed territory**, so it was neither a **bureaucratic republic** nor a **centralised territorial monarchy**.
APPSC (**2018**) keyed the nature as a **tribal polity** — not a republic or autocracy.
xa: The **Jana** (tribe) was the largest socio-political unit, mentioned **275 times** in the Rigveda.
Territorial units — **Janapada / Rashtra** — and the **hereditary king** belong to the **Later Vedic** period.
Assemblies **Sabha, Samiti, Vidatha** were powerful in the Early Vedic period; in the Later Vedic period **Vidatha disappeared** and the **Samiti weakened**.

ne86f566015a.s: The term ‘Janapada’ in the Rigveda is best described as:
o: A frequently used term for the territorial kingdom
The name of the smallest social unit
The title of the tribal chief
A term absent from the Rigveda
ne86f566015a.x: The term Janapada is absent in the Rigveda, reflecting the predominantly tribal rather than territorial character of early Vedic polity.
ne86f566015a.tq: Use the absence of a specific political term to distinguish tribal polity from later territorial states.
xs: **Janapada** is a **term absent from the Rigveda** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Its absence shows the Early Vedic polity was **tribal**, with **no fixed territory**.
The largest unit was the **Jana**, mentioned **275 times**; the chief was the **Rajan**, and the smallest unit the **Kula**.
xa: **Janapada / Rashtra** (territory) became the unit only in the **Later Vedic** period.
The Later Vedic chief was a **hereditary king**; the Early Vedic chief was **elective/limited**.
AP angle: the word **Andhra** also first appears later — in the **Aitareya Brahmana**, not the Rig Veda.

n255f5b093f1.s: Which assembly is mentioned most often in the Rigveda?
n255f5b093f1.x: Vidatha is mentioned 122 times, against 9 for the Samiti and 8 for the Sabha.
xa: The Vidatha was also the **earliest assembly** and the **first to disappear** in the Later Vedic period.
The Atharvaveda also mentions **women's participation in the Samiti**.
⚠ Exam trap: "daughters of Prajapati" = **Atharvaveda**, not Rigveda.

n41c594a2e77.s: Early Vedic weapons were made of:
n41c594a2e77.x: Early Vedic weapons were of bronze, not iron; warriors used a coat of mail and helmet.
xa: Rig Vedic Aryans knew the **horse** and **spoked-wheel chariot**; Harappans left little horse evidence.
War was often **gavishti** — cattle raids.
**Rathins** = chariot warriors; **Patti** = foot soldiers.

n2b06e08afe0.s: The Rigvedic river Parushni is the modern:
n2b06e08afe0.x: Parushni is the Ravi; Vitasta is the Jhelum and Asikni the Chenab.
xa: ⚠ UPSC trap: **Vitasta–Chenab** and **Asikni–Jhelum** are the classic wrong pairs.
**Vipas = Beas**; **Shutudri = Sutlej**.
**Sindhu** is the most mentioned river; **Sarasvati** the most sacred (**Naditama**).

n60ae09aa544.s: The Rigvedic river Vipas is the modern:
n60ae09aa544.x: Vipas is the Beas; Sutudri is the Sutlej and Drishadvati the Chautang.
xa: Drishadvati (Chautang) is a **Ghaggar tributary**.
**Sadanira** (later Vedic) = **Gandak**.
⚠ **Yavyavati** is **not** the Beas (UPSC trap).

nb40eb1b31a8.s: Which of the following is one of the seven rivers of Sapta Sindhu?
nb40eb1b31a8.x: The standard Sapta Sindhu list is Sindhu, Vitasta, Asikni, Parushni, Vipas, Sutudri and Sarasvati.
xa: Modern names: Indus, **Jhelum**, **Chenab**, **Ravi**, **Beas**, **Sutlej**, Ghaggar-Hakra.
**Yamuna** is mentioned thrice and **Ganga** once in the Rig Veda.
Extent: eastern **Afghanistan**, **NWFP**, **Punjab**, **Haryana**, fringes of western **UP**.

n7c1449b8577.x: Samudra means a collection or body of water and does not necessarily denote the sea.
xa: **Himvat** = snowy mountains; **Dhanva** = desert; **Mujavant** = source of soma.
The Rig Vedic region was **Sapta Sindhu** — eastern Afghanistan to fringes of western UP.
**Sindhu** was the most mentioned river.

nindian-history-16-14.x: Matetama means best of mothers; Devitama means best of goddesses and Naditama best of rivers.
n: The Saraswati River was called Matetama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
Matetama means “Best of all mothers.” [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
The Saraswati River was called Devitama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
Devitama means “Best of all goddesses.” [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 67-69]
xa: Saraswati was the **most sacred** river.
**Mahanadi** was **Chitrotpala** in the **Mahabharata** and **Matsya Purana**; **Nilotapala** in the **Vayu Purana**.
The **Sindhu** is the **most mentioned** river.

ne6381e9ac3e.s: The term ‘Aghanya’ in the Rigveda refers to the cow as:
o: The animal used in sacrifice only
The animal not to be killed
The animal that gives milk at dusk
ne6381e9ac3e.x: Aghanya literally means ‘not to be killed’ and is an epithet applied to the cow.
ne6381e9ac3e.tq: Discriminate between closely related cow-derived terms by their precise meanings.
xs: **Aghanya** means "**not to be killed**" — an epithet of the **cow** — option **(3)**.
Exam line: "Aghanya refers to — **cows**".
xa: ⚠ **Aghanya** = cow; **Gavishti** = war; **Gavyuti** = distance; **Godhuli** = time.
The cow was the **most valuable property** in the early Rigvedic period.
**Duhitri** (daughter) = "one who milks the cow".

n370049c66df.s: In the Rigveda, the term 'Godhuli' denoted:
o: The time of dusk, when cattle return
A wealthy man owning many cattle
n370049c66df.x: Godhuli was the dusk time-measure when cattle returned; Gavyuti was a measure of distance, Gomat a cattle-rich man and Duhitri a daughter.
xa: **Aghanya** = "not to be killed", epithet of the cow.
**Gopati / Gopa** = lord/protector of cattle — title of the chief.
**Gavishti** = "search for cows" = war.

n556ca065985.s: The economy of the Early Vedic people is best described as:
o: Mainly pastoral with agriculture as a secondary activity
Based entirely on hunting and gathering
n556ca065985.x: The Early Vedic economy was mainly pastoral, with cattle-keeping combined with secondary agriculture, constituting a mixed economy.
n556ca065985.tq: Use the broad economic description to distinguish the main activity from the supplementary one.
xs: The Early Vedic economy was **mainly pastoral with agriculture as a secondary activity** — option **(2)**.
It is called a **mixed economy**; the **cow** was the most valuable property.
With **no towns** and **no coinage**, it was not urban or commercial.
xa: **Gau** (cow) is mentioned **176 times** in the Rigveda.
**Gavishti** ("search for cows") = **war**.
Later Vedic = **agrarian**, rice/wheat, **iron**.

nc663d48f32f.s: In the early Rig Vedic period, which of the following was regarded as the most valuable property and is mentioned about 176 times in the Rigveda?
nc663d48f32f.x: The cow (gau) was the most valuable property and the standard unit of value, mentioned about 176 times in the Rigveda. Land was not yet the main form of wealth in this pastoral society; horses and gold were valued (priests received them) but did not hold the cow's central place.
nc663d48f32f.tq: Most valuable property in early Rig Vedic times = cow (gau, 176 mentions).
xs: The **cow** was the most valuable property, mentioned about **176 times** — option **(3)**.
It was also the **standard unit of value** and exchange.
**Horses and gold** were valued (priests got them) but did not hold the cow's central place.
xa: ⚠ **Jana** — **275 times** vs **Gau** — **176 times**.
Exam angle: "most valuable property in early Rigvedic period — **cow**".
**Aghanya** ("not to be killed") is the cow's epithet.

n1eeb92de665.s: In Rig Vedic irrigation, the term 'Kulya' referred to:
n1eeb92de665.x: Rig Vedic irrigation used wells (Avata) and canals (Kulya), with cattle-driven water lifts.
xa: Agriculture was **secondary** to pastoralism.
**Langala** = wooden ploughshare; **Sira** = plough drawn by bulls.

n96710161f28.s: Which of the following was regarded as the standard unit of value and exchange in the early Vedic period?
n96710161f28.x: The cow was the standard unit of value and exchange in the early Vedic economy.
n96710161f28.tq: Identify the standard of value rather than a later monetary unit.
xs: The **cow** was the standard unit of value and exchange — option **(3)**.
It was also the **most valuable property**; **Gau** occurs **176 times**.
The **nishka** was a gold ornament, only later a unit of value — not the standard unit in the Rig Veda.
xa: Trade was by **barter**; **no coinage**.
**Gomat** = rich man (owner of many cattle).
Priests were paid in **cows, horses, gold**.

n30b4bad6b89.s: In the Rigveda, the term 'nishka' denoted:
n30b4bad6b89.x: In the Rigveda nishka was a gold ornament or necklace; only later did it denote a unit of value. It was not a circulating coin then.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes call nishka a "**gold coin**" — it was not yet a coin.
Other units: krishnal, satmana, hiranyapindas, manas.

n47da7fabb6e.s: The Panis of the early Vedic period were primarily associated with which occupation?
n47da7fabb6e.x: The Panis were traders. They were described as wealthy in cattle, greedy and non-Aryan.
n47da7fabb6e.tq: Match the named social group with its principal occupation.
xs: The **Panis** were **traders**, so their occupation was **trade** — option **(1)** (**MPPSC 2019**).
They were rich in cattle, condemned for **greed** (hid cattle) and seen as **non-Aryan**.
xa: Trade was limited and by **barter**.
**Dana** (gifts) and **Dakshina** (priestly fees) circulated wealth.
**Samudra** = a mass of water, so sea trade is doubtful.

n65e46a32de9.s: In the Early Vedic period, bali was:
o: A tax collected by a regular tax department
The king's fixed share of the produce
A voluntary offering by tribesmen to the rajan
n65e46a32de9.x: Early Vedic bali was a voluntary offering or tribute by tribesmen to the rajan and could include war booty; there was no regular tax system.
xa: Later Vedic: bali became **compulsory**, with **bhaga** (**1/6** of produce) and **shulka**.
Collector in the Later Vedic period = **bhagadugha**.

n49938fa0d8a.s: In the Later Vedic period, bali, bhaga and shulka were collected by the:
n49938fa0d8a.x: The Bhagadugha collected bali, bhaga and shulka; bali had by then become compulsory.
xa: Rig Vedic bali had **no regular tax or collector**.
**Nishka** was a **gold ornament** in the Rigveda, later a **unit of value**.
⚠ No **coinage** in the Rig Vedic age.

n061c9d03b2f.s: Compared with the Early Vedic period, the position of women in the Later Vedic period:
o: Improved in assemblies but declined in rituals
n061c9d03b2f.x: Women's position declined in the Later Vedic period: they were excluded from Upanayana, rituals and assemblies.
xa: The **Aitareya Brahmana** calls daughters a source of **misery**.
Early Vedic women attended the **Sabha** and **Vidatha**.

nad8ac0c2c3d.s: The religious outlook of the Rig Vedic people is best described as:
o: Monotheism with exclusive worship of one god
Ancestor worship centred on royal tombs
Naturalistic polytheism with each god praised as supreme in turn
nad8ac0c2c3d.x: Rig Vedic religion was naturalistic polytheism. Its tendency to regard each god as supreme in turn is called Henotheism or Kathenotheism.
nad8ac0c2c3d.tq: Use the exact conceptual distinction between polytheism and Henotheism.
xs: Rig Vedic religion was **naturalistic polytheism**, with **each god praised as supreme in turn** — option **(4)**.
Gods personified **forces of nature**; praising each as supreme is **Henotheism / Kathenotheism**.
Many gods were worshipped, so it was not monotheism, and there were **no temples, no idols**.
xa: Worship: hymns and **yajnas in the open air**.
**Male gods dominate**; cult of the **domestic hearth**.
**Rita** = cosmic and moral order upheld by **Varuna**.

n4aa70c19a79.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Rig Vedic worship?
o: Temples and idols formed the normal basis of worship
Worship was conducted through hymns and yajnas in the open air
Its principal aims included cattle, sons and victory
The cult of the domestic hearth was significant
n4aa70c19a79.x: Temples and idols were absent in Rig Vedic worship, which used hymns and open-air yajnas for material ends such as cattle, sons and victory.
xa: Each god praised as supreme in turn = **Henotheism / Kathenotheism**.
**Male gods** dominate.

n32b08053084.s: Which Rig Vedic god was called Purandara, 'destroyer of forts'?
n32b08053084.x: Indra, called Purandara, is the most mentioned Rig Vedic god with about 250 hymns.
xa: Varuna is the **ethically highest** god.
**Vishnu** was minor — only **3 hymns**.

n2cbb6e815b4.s: The transition from a cattle-based tribal economy to a settled agrarian economy is significant because it helps explain the later rise of:
n2cbb6e815b4.x: The shift from a cattle-based tribal economy to an agrarian territorial society contributed to the emergence of territorial kingship and a more established varna hierarchy.
n2cbb6e815b4.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship between economic change and political-social formation.
xs: The shift to a settled agrarian economy explains the later rise of **territorial kingship and varna hierarchy** — option **(2)**.
It was a move from a **cattle-based tribal economy** to a **settled agrarian territorial** society.
xa: Later Vedic = **birth-based varna**, **iron**, rice/wheat.
Early Vedic: the cow was the **standard unit of value**.

nindian-history-51-3.s: Which Vedic god was called Ritasyagopa, the guardian of Rita (cosmic order)?
nindian-history-51-3.x: Varuna guards Rita, the cosmic and natural order, and is therefore called Ritasyagopa.
n: Varuna was a Rigvedic deity. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Varuna upheld Rita. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita was a Vedic concept. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita means cosmic order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Rita means natural order. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Varuna was called Ritasyagopa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: Varuna held **third place** and was the **ethically highest** god.
**Indra** (**250 hymns**) was the most important god; **Agni** (around **200 hymns**) second.
**Mitra**, a solar god, was Varuna's ally.

n13509549114.s: Which one of the following is the correct meaning of ‘Yava’ in the Rigvedic context?
n13509549114.x: Yava means barley, which was the chief grain known in the Rigveda.
n13509549114.tq: Avoid the look-alike crop trap by fixing the standard meaning of the Vedic term.
xs: **Yava** means **barley** — the chief grain of the Rigveda — option **(4)**.
**Godhuma** = wheat; **Vrihi** = rice; **Ikshu** = sugarcane.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **RPSC 2021** matched Yava to "**millet**" because barley was not an option.
Rice (**vrihi**) is prominent only in **Later Vedic** texts.
**Mudga** = mung bean (green gram).

n4866368e7ac.s: In Early Vedic agriculture, 'Langala' was a:
n4866368e7ac.x: Langala was a wooden ploughshare, while Sira was a plough drawn by bulls; iron was not used for the Langala.
xa: Irrigation: **Avata** (wells) and **Kulya** (canals).
⚠ **Sira** = plough; **Sita** = furrow; **Langala** = ploughshare.
Farming was probably **shifting**.

n8cd16fef712.s: In the Vedic period, a 'Hiranyakara' was a:
n8cd16fef712.x: Hiranyakara was a goldsmith; Takshan was a carpenter, Karmara a metal worker and Bhishak a physician.
xa: The Karmara worked **ayas** — **copper/bronze**, not iron.
**Kulala** = potter; **Rathakara** = chariot-maker; **vaya** = weaver.
**Vaptri / Charmamna** = barber / tanner.

n4c760a596fb.s: In the Rig Vedic context, the term ayas referred to:
n4c760a596fb.x: Ayas in the Rigveda referred to copper or bronze. Iron was designated as krishna ayas in a later context.
n4c760a596fb.tq: Distinguish the early meaning of ayas from the later expression for iron.
xs: **Ayas** in the Rig Veda meant **copper or bronze** — option **(4)**.
Iron was called **krishna ayas** — a later term.
xa: The **Karmara** (smith) worked ayas.
The **Langala** was a wooden ploughshare — **no iron**.
Early Vedic = **copper/bronze**; Later Vedic = **iron**.
