n0d6e2ffcc21.s: Which term for an inscription, used in Ashokan edicts, reflects the Darius (Persian) model?
n0d6e2ffcc21.x: The terms lipi/dipi, along with an opening in the third person shifting to the first person, show the Darius model in Ashokan edicts.
xa: Script: **Kharosthi** (right to left) derived from **Aramaic**; the **Kandahar edict** used Aramaic.
Pillars: **polished surface** and **animal capitals** resemble Persian ones.
Administration: the **satrapy system** was known in the north-west.

nf91c455e5a5.s: At the time of Alexander's invasion, the north-western part of India was politically characterised by which condition?
o: A single empire under the Nandas
A federation led by the Achaemenids
Small independent states such as Taxila, Porus's Punjab and Gandhara
nf91c455e5a5.x: The north-west was divided into small independent states, including Taxila, Porus's Punjab and Gandhara, rather than being united under one central power.
nf91c455e5a5.tq: Identify the broad political pattern instead of focusing on one ruler.
xs: The north-west was split into **small independent states** — **Taxila**, **Porus's Punjab**, **Gandhara** — option **(4)**.
This meant **no united resistance** to Alexander.
**Magadha** in the east was under the **Nanda dynasty** (Dhana Nanda), not the north-west.
xa: Causes of success (**UPPSC 2003** key "1, 2 and 3"): **no central power**, **superior army**, help from **traitorous Indian rulers**.
**Ambhi** of **Taxila** was the **first to surrender**.
The invasion later destroyed these small states, clearing the way for **Chandragupta**.

n8c3e0a106a1.s: After his defeat at the Hydaspes in 326 BC, Porus:
o: Had his kingdom restored and later enlarged
n8c3e0a106a1.x: Porus was defeated but not executed; Alexander restored and later enlarged his kingdom.
xa: Hydaspes = **Jhelum** = **Vitasta**; UPPSC 2013: king defeated on the Jhelum = **Porus**.
**Bucephala** and **Nicaea** were founded near the battlefield.
Porus (**Parvataka**) later allied with **Chandragupta** to expel the Greek satraps.

n137f80d1860.s: Alexander set up twelve large stone altars on the northern bank of the:
n137f80d1860.x: Alexander raised twelve altars on the northern bank of the Beas, then withdrew down the Indus while Nearchus led the fleet.
xa: He died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.
Entry via **Khyber Pass** in **326 BC**; **Hydaspes** battle the same year.
Nearchus, the **admiral**, left a first-hand account.

n206c84e8108.s: Alexander divided his conquered Indian territory into how many parts under Greek governors?
n206c84e8108.x: The conquered area was divided into three parts under Greek governors; most submitted states were returned to their rulers.
xa: Direct **Greece-India contact** and new **land and sea routes** opened.
**Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** recorded Indian geography and society.
Small NW states were destroyed → cleared the way for **Chandragupta**.

nindian-history-39-13.s: Which Indian ruler was an ally of Alexander?
nindian-history-39-13.x: Indian allies such as Ambhi, along with political disunity and a superior army, helped Alexander.
n: Political disunity contributed to Alexander's success in India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Alexander's superior army contributed to his success in India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Indian allies contributed to Alexander's success in India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Chandragupta did not defeat Alexander. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
xa: The north-west was split into small states (**Taxila**, Porus's Punjab, **Gandhara**) → **no united resistance**.
**Ambhi** of Taxila was the **first to surrender** and helped Alexander.
UPPSC **2003** causes: **no central power**, **superior army**, help from **traitorous Indian rulers**.
Magadha was then under **Dhana Nanda** of the **Nanda dynasty**, whose huge army deterred Alexander.

nindian-history-21-2.s: Which of the following about Alexander's Indian campaign is NOT correct?
o: Alexander fought Porus at the Hydaspes
The Hydaspes is identified with the Jhelum
Alexander's army refused to go beyond the Beas
Alexander's army was stopped at the Ravi
nindian-history-21-2.x: Alexander's army refused to go beyond the Beas, not the Ravi. He fought Porus at the Hydaspes, the Jhelum.
n: The Battle of Hydaspes was associated with Alexander’s invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Porus was involved in the Battle of Hydaspes. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Hydaspes is the ancient name associated with the Jhelum. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Alexander’s army was stopped at the Beas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: Causes of refusal at the Beas: **war weariness**, homesickness, disease, fear of the **Nanda army**.
**12 large stone altars** were set up on the Beas's northern bank.
⚠ **Hydaspes** = **Jhelum** = **Vitasta**.

n19e731ccb67.s: Which feature of the Nanda kingdom is said to have deterred Alexander from marching farther east?
n19e731ccb67.x: The huge army of the Nanda kingdom deterred Alexander from advancing east, though Dhana Nanda was unpopular for heavy taxation.
xa: The Nanda ruler was **Dhana Nanda**, Greek "**Agrammes/Xandrames**".
The Nandas were **unpopular** for **heavy taxation**.
Other causes of the Beas refusal: **war weariness**, **homesickness**, **disease**.

nb397b6dd606.s: Who was the first among the following Indian rulers to surrender to Alexander and subsequently assist him?
nb397b6dd606.x: Ambhi, also called Omphis, the king of Taxila, was the first to surrender and helped Alexander.
nb397b6dd606.tq: Test the precise response of a ruler, not merely his geographical association.
xs: **Ambhi** (Omphis), king of **Taxila**, was the **first to surrender** and helped Alexander — option **(3)**.
**Porus** resisted at the Hydaspes; **Abhisara** (Kashmir hills) submitted later; **Dhana Nanda** of Magadha was never reached.
xa: Exam angle: "first to submit" = **Ambhi**; "whose women fought" = **Massaga**.
The **Assakenoi** (capital **Massaga**, Swat valley) put up fierce resistance.
The **Malloi (Malavas)** fought him during the **retreat**.

n19dacbcec83.s: Which of the following groups fought Alexander during his retreat from the north-western region?
n19dacbcec83.x: The Malloi or Malavas and other gana-sanghas fought Alexander during his retreat.
n19dacbcec83.tq: Distinguish resistance during the retreat from submission or resistance at the initial advance.
xs: The **Malloi (Malavas)** and other **gana-sanghas** fought Alexander during his **retreat** — option **(4)**.
The **Nandas** of Magadha were never fought; their huge army only **deterred** his eastward march.
xa: On the retreat he withdrew down the **Indus**; **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.
Earlier resistance: the **Assakenoi** of **Massaga** and **Porus** at the Hydaspes.
He died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.

n9202d2e4ed4.s: During Alexander's invasion, the women of which people took up arms after their men suffered heavy losses?
o: The people of Taxila under Ambhi
The subjects of Porus on the Jhelum
n9202d2e4ed4.x: The Assakenoi (Ashvakas), with their capital at Massaga in the Swat valley, resisted fiercely, and their women took up arms after heavy losses (UPPSC 2013). Ambhi of Taxila surrendered first, Abhisara submitted, and Porus fought at the Hydaspes.
xs: The **Assakenoi (Ashvakas)** of **Massaga** — their **women took up arms** after heavy losses — option **(1)**.
Massaga lay in the **Swat valley** (**UPPSC 2013**).
**Ambhi** of Taxila **surrendered first**, **Abhisara** submitted, and **Porus** fought at the Hydaspes.
xa: Porus was defeated but Alexander **restored his kingdom** (later enlarged).
UPPSC 2013 also: king defeated on the **Jhelum** = **Porus**.
The **Malloi (Malavas)** fought him during the retreat.

nac7b7de0651.s: Besides war weariness and homesickness, Alexander's army refused to go beyond the Beas from fear of the army of the:
nac7b7de0651.x: War weariness, homesickness, disease and fear of the Nanda army caused the refusal.
xa: The army refused to go beyond the **Beas (Hyphasis)**, his furthest point.
He set up **12 large stone altars** on its northern bank.
He then withdrew down the **Indus**; **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.

nindian-history-39-14.s: The territory of Porus extended between the Jhelum and the:
nindian-history-39-14.x: Porus (Puru) ruled between the Jhelum and Chenab, and his kingdom was restored after his defeat.
n: Porus was also known as Puru. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Porus's territory lay between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Porus's kingdom was restored after his defeat. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Dhanananda was the contemporary ruler of Magadha. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
xa: Alexander fought Porus at the **Jhelum**, known as the **Hydaspes**, in **326 BC**.
UPPSC **2013**: the king defeated on the Jhelum = **Porus**.
Later **Chandragupta** expelled the Greek satraps with **Porus (Parvataka)** as ally.

n7d67c75f108.s: Alexander entered India in 326 BC through the:
n7d67c75f108.x: Alexander crossed the Hindu Kush in 327 BC and entered India through the Khyber Pass in 326 BC.
xa: **Battle of Hydaspes** with **Porus**: **326 BC**.
Campaign in India lasted about **19 months**.
Alexander died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.

nindian-history-39-15.s: Alexander's return point in India was:
nindian-history-39-15.x: Alexander invaded in 326 BC, left in 325 BC and returned via Patala (Paatal).
n: Alexander's Indian campaign took place in 326 BC. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Alexander left India in 325 BC. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Paatal was Alexander's return point. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Chandragupta did not defeat Alexander. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
xa: He crossed the **Hindu Kush** in **327 BC** and entered through the **Khyber Pass** in **326 BC**.
His army refused to go beyond the **Beas (Hyphasis)**.
The campaign in India lasted about **19 months**; he died at **Babylon** in **323 BCE**.
On return he withdrew down the **Indus**; **Nearchus** led the fleet by sea.

nc5a37817b37.s: Which pair of settlements was founded by Alexander near the battlefield of the Hydaspes?
nc5a37817b37.x: Alexander founded Bucephala, named after his horse, and Nicaea near the Hydaspes battlefield.
nc5a37817b37.tq: Start from the distinctive name linked with Alexander's horse and identify its associated settlement.
xs: **Bucephala** (named after his horse) and **Nicaea** were founded near the Hydaspes — option **(2)**.
**Taxila** was Ambhi's kingdom and **Massaga** the Assakenoi capital — not Alexander's foundations.
xa: The Hydaspes battle with **Porus**: **326 BC**.
Greek settlements such as **Alexandria** and **Bucephala** were an effect of the invasion.
⚠ **Hydaspes** = **Jhelum**; **Hyphasis** = **Beas**.

nd194c2fb026.s: A major commercial consequence of Alexander's invasion was:
o: Closure of the north-western land routes
Opening of direct contact and new land and sea routes between Greece and India
Persian control over Indian trade routes
The end of contact between Greece and India
nd194c2fb026.x: The invasion opened direct contact between Greece and India and encouraged new land and sea routes.
xa: **Onesicritus** and **Nearchus** recorded Indian **geography and society**.
The conquered area was split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.
Politically, it cleared the way for **Chandragupta**.

nf5370932b53.s: By destroying several small north-western states, Alexander's invasion cleared the way for the rise of:
nf5370932b53.x: The invasion weakened the small north-western states, helping Chandragupta, who expelled the Greek satraps with Porus (Parvataka) as an ally.
xa: Greeks name **Sandrokottas** (Chandragupta) as a contemporary — anchor of chronology (c. **322 BCE**).
The conquered area had been split into **three parts** under **Greek governors**.
Alexander had **restored Porus's kingdom** after the Hydaspes.

ne4757fa4c6f.s: The name 'Sandrokottas' in Greek accounts has been identified with which Indian ruler?
ne4757fa4c6f.x: Greek writers used the name Sandrokottas for Chandragupta Maurya, helping establish the chronology of the early Mauryas around 322 BCE.
ne4757fa4c6f.tq: Use the Greek–Indian name equivalence as a chronology anchor.
xs: **Sandrokottas** is **Chandragupta Maurya** — option **(3)**.
Greeks name him as a **contemporary**, the anchor of early Indian chronology (c. **322 BCE**).
xa: Chandragupta expelled the **Greek satraps** with **Porus (Parvataka)** as ally.
Alexander's invasion is the **first dated event** of Indian history.
**Dhana Nanda** was called **Agrammes/Xandrames** by the Greeks.

nad7e267408b.s: Alexander's invasion of India is regarded as:
o: The first Persian conquest of India
The first dated event of Indian history
The beginning of the Saka era
The end of the Nanda dynasty
nad7e267408b.x: Alexander's invasion is regarded as the first dated event of Indian history, and Greek accounts help fix Mauryan chronology.
xa: **Indian sources are silent** on Alexander.
Key dates: Hindu Kush **327 BC**; Khyber Pass and Hydaspes **326 BC**; death at **Babylon** **323 BCE**.
First-hand Greek writers: **Nearchus**, **Onesicritus**, **Aristobulus**.

nb35e154b35a.s: Who among the following accompanied Alexander and left a first-hand account of his campaign?
nb35e154b35a.x: Nearchus, Alexander's admiral, accompanied him and left a first-hand account. Arrian and Plutarch were later writers, while Deimachus was a later envoy.
nb35e154b35a.tq: Use the distinction between eyewitness companions and later reconstructive writers.
xs: **Nearchus**, Alexander's **admiral**, came with him and left a **first-hand account** — option **(2)**.
**Plutarch** and **Arrian** were **later** Roman-era writers.
**Deimachus** was a later envoy of **Antiochus I** to **Bindusara** — he did not come with Alexander (**UPPSC 2015**).
xa: Other first-hand writers: **Onesicritus** and **Aristobulus**.
Nearchus led the **fleet by sea** during the return.
**Indian sources are silent** on Alexander.

o: Alexander's admiral who sailed down the Indus
A later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara
nd0cde5cfb5a.x: Deimachus was a later envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara and did not accompany Alexander.
nd0cde5cfb5a.tq: Test the look-alike category of a Greek-associated name against the correct diplomatic role.
xs: **Deimachus** was a later **envoy of Antiochus I to Bindusara** — option **(3)**.
He **did not come with Alexander** (**UPPSC 2015**).
Alexander's **admiral** who led the fleet was **Nearchus**; the Nanda ruler was **Dhana Nanda**.
xa: First-hand writers: **Nearchus**, **Onesicritus**, **Aristobulus**.
Later writers: **Arrian**, **Curtius**, **Plutarch**.
**Bucephala** was founded by **Alexander**, after his horse.

nc448b31b3a0.s: The Battle of Hydaspes was fought on the bank of which river?
nc448b31b3a0.x: The Hydaspes was the Jhelum, called Vitasta in Sanskrit. The battle was fought there in 326 BC.
nc448b31b3a0.tq: Discriminate between the Greek and Indian names of the same river.
xs: The **Hydaspes** is the **Jhelum**, Sanskrit **Vitasta** — option **(4)**.
The battle with **Porus** was fought there in **326 BC**.
⚠ The **Beas** is the Greek **Hyphasis** — Alexander's furthest point, not the battle site.
xa: **Bucephala** (after his horse) and **Nicaea** were founded near the battlefield.
**12 large stone altars** stand on the **northern bank of the Beas**.
Porus's kingdom lay between the **Jhelum and Chenab**.

nindian-history-39-17.s: Massaga was the capital of the:
nindian-history-39-17.x: Massaga was the Ashvaka capital; Alexander fought Porus at the Jhelum.
n: Alexander fought Porus at the Jhelum River. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Porus's territory lay between the Jhelum and Chenab rivers. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Massaga was the capital of Ashvaka. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
Paatal was Alexander's return point. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 105-106]
xa: ⚠ **Hydaspes** = **Jhelum** = **Vitasta**; **Hyphasis** = **Beas**.
At **Massaga** (Swat valley) **women took up arms** during the resistance (UPPSC **2013**).
**Bucephala** and **Nicaea** were cities founded near the battlefield.
The **Beas** was the furthest point — **12 large stone altars** on its northern bank.

nindian-history-17-3.s: The Kalinga War, the turning point in Ashoka's life, was fought in:
nindian-history-17-3.x: The bloodshed of the Kalinga War (261 BC) turned Ashoka to Buddhism and the policy of Dhamma.
n: The Kalinga War was a turning point in Ashoka's life. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
The Kalinga War strengthened Ashoka's association with Buddhism and Dhamma. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
xa: The **Kalinga War** is dated **261 BC**.
Kalinga was **strategically important** for **eastern sea routes**, **overseas trade** and **Deccan routes**.
Other battles: **Hydaspes** (**326 BCE**, Alexander vs Porus); **Mauryan–Seleucid** conflict (**305 BC**).

nb26b0603797.s: The Arthashastra was rediscovered at Mysore in 1905 by:
nb26b0603797.x: R. Shamasastry rediscovered the Arthashastra in 1905 and it was published in 1909; it has 15 books called adhikaranas.
xa: ⚠ Found **1905**, published **1909** — both by **Shamasastry**.
Author: **Kautilya** = **Chanakya** = **Vishnugupta**.
Topics include **slavery rules**, the **Saptanga** state, revenue and courts.

n4d530757225.s: Which literary source is primarily associated with administration, economy, espionage and taxation?
n4d530757225.x: Kautilya's Arthashastra deals with administration, economy, espionage and taxation.
n4d530757225.tq: Match a work with its central subject rather than its author alone.
xs: The **Arthashastra** deals with **administration, economy, espionage and taxation** — option **(1)**.
**Mudrarakshasa** is a drama on the Nandas' overthrow; **Indica** is Megasthenes' Greek account; **Parishishtaparvan** is Jain, on Chandragupta's conversion.
xa: Arthashastra also covers **diplomacy** and **welfare**.
Compared with **Machiavelli's The Prince**.
It has **15 books (adhikaranas)**, rediscovered by **Shamasastry**.

na93491a2e09.s:
Kautilya is also known by which of the following names?
1. Chanakya
2. Pushyagupta
3. Vishnugupta
Which of the above is/are correct?
na93491a2e09.x: Kautilya is also called Chanakya and Vishnugupta; Pushyagupta was a governor associated with the Sudarshana lake.
xa: Kautilya wrote the **Arthashastra** on **statecraft** (APPSC-GS 2023 match).
It was rediscovered by **R. Shamasastry** (Mysore, **1905**; published **1909**).
It has **15 books (adhikaranas)**.

n6f64c4dc925.s: Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra by the name
n6f64c4dc925.x: Megasthenes referred to Pataliputra as Palibothra, also rendered in some accounts as Polibrotha.
n6f64c4dc925.tq: Discriminate between the Greek form of a place-name and Indian place-names from other contexts.
xs: Megasthenes called Pataliputra **Palibothra** — option **(1)**.
**UKPSC 2025** spelt it "**Polibrotha**".
xa: He described the **palace** (remains at **Kumrahar**) and the **city boards**.
The **80-pillared hall** at **Kumrahar** near Patna is part of the Pataliputra ruins.
Indica's fragments survive in **Diodorus, Strabo, Pliny, Arrian**.

nbd10708bf1d.s: Megasthenes described Indian society as divided into how many classes?
nbd10708bf1d.x: Megasthenes described seven classes and noted endogamy and hereditary occupations; this was not the fourfold varna scheme.
xa: The seven: **philosophers, farmers, soldiers, herdsmen, artisans, overseers, councillors**.
The seven "castes" and no-slavery claim are known **misreadings**.
He also wrongly claimed **no slavery**.

n886a87d16e8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Megasthenes' Indica?
o: It correctly reported that slavery was widespread in Mauryan India
It contains uncritical folklore such as the gold-digging ants
Strabo, following Megasthenes, said Indians did not know writing
Its claim of no slavery is contradicted by the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts
n886a87d16e8.x: Megasthenes claimed there was no slavery in India, a claim contradicted by the Arthashastra and Ashokan edicts that mention dasas.
xa: He also described **seven classes**, not the fourfold varna.
The original **Indica** is lost; known through **fragments**.
⚠ Despite errors, it is the **first foreign mention** of the **Andhras**.

n83d6f5297f3.s: Which foreign writer was the first to mention the Andhras, crediting them with 30 fortified towns and an army of 1,00,000 infantry?
n83d6f5297f3.x: Megasthenes' Indica is the first foreign work to mention the Andhras, with 30 fortified towns and 1,00,000 infantry besides cavalry and elephants. Deimachus was Antiochus I's envoy to Bindusara; Strabo and Arrian only preserved fragments of the Indica.
n83d6f5297f3.tq: First to mention Andhra forts = Megasthenes (APPSC G2 2002); 30 forts.
xs: **Megasthenes** in the **Indica** first mentioned the **Andhras** — option **(1)**.
He credited them with **30 fortified towns** and **1,00,000 infantry** (plus cavalry and elephants).
**Strabo** and **Arrian** only preserve fragments of the Indica.
xa: **APPSC G2 2002**: who first mentioned Andhra forts = **Megasthenes**.
⚠ Some notes print "**80 forts**" — a misprint; the correct figure is **30**.
⚠ **80** is the **pillared hall** at **Kumrahar**, not the forts.

ncb7b85ea5a9.s: Who wrote the Sanskrit drama Mudrarakshasa, which describes the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya?
ncb7b85ea5a9.x: Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa. The drama deals with the overthrow of the Nandas and the rise of Chandragupta Maurya.
ncb7b85ea5a9.tq: Use the author–work association and beware of swapping authors of related literary sources.
xs: **Vishakhadatta** wrote **Mudrarakshasa** — option **(3)**.
It is a Sanskrit drama on the **overthrow of the Nandas** and **rise of Chandragupta** (**APPSC-G1 2002**).
**Hemachandra** wrote **Parishishtaparvan**; **Dandin** **Dashakumaracharita**; **Patanjali** **Mahabhashya**.
xa: **Kathasaritsagara** — **Somadeva**; **Brihatkathamanjari** — **Kshemendra**.
**Rajatarangini** — **Kalhana**.
The **Puranas** (esp. **Vishnu Purana**) give Mauryan king lists.

n1e47623025c.s: Mamulanar, belonging to the Sangam tradition, is associated with references to the Mauryas'
n1e47623025c.x: Mamulanar's Sangam reference concerns the southward push of the Mauryas.
n1e47623025c.tq: Identify the distinctive event linked with the named literary source.
xs: Sangam poet **Mamulanar** refers to the Mauryas' **southward push** — option **(3)**.
**Conversion to Jainism** is Chandragupta's story in the Jain **Parishishtaparvan**.
xa: Tamil Sangam poems thus record **southern expansion** of the Mauryas.
Mauryan **punch-marked coins** and **NBPW** are found as far as **Andhra** and **Karnataka**.
**Mudrarakshasa** (Vishakhadatta) covers the rise of **Chandragupta**.

nca6644077ff.s: Which Purana is usually cited as an important source for Mauryan king lists and genealogies?
nca6644077ff.x: The Puranas provide Mauryan king lists and genealogies, with the Vishnu Purana being the one usually cited.
nca6644077ff.tq: Match the historical use of the Puranas with the specifically cited Purana.
xs: The **Vishnu Purana** is the one usually cited for **Mauryan king lists** — option **(3)**.
The **Puranas** give **genealogies** of Mauryan kings.
xa: **Mudrarakshasa** (**Vishakhadatta**) — overthrow of the Nandas.
**Dipavamsa** and **Mahavamsa** — Ashoka and Buddhism in Lanka.
**Parishishtaparvan** (**Hemachandra**) — Chandragupta's conversion to Jainism.

n6bf4182da2f.s: According to Rudradaman I's Junagadh inscription, the Sudarshana lake was built in Chandragupta Maurya's reign by the governor:
n6bf4182da2f.x: The Junagadh inscription (c. 150 CE) records that governor Pushyagupta built the Sudarshana lake under Chandragupta Maurya.
xa: The **Hathigumpha inscription** of **Kharavela** is also cited for Mauryan references.
Ashokan edicts were deciphered by **James Prinsep** in **1837**.
The **Greek-Aramaic** edict is at **Shar-i-Kuna (Kandahar)**.

nebb4199f7ed.s: The 80-pillared hall associated with Mauryan Pataliputra has been found at
nebb4199f7ed.x: The ruins of the 80-pillared hall of Pataliputra are located at Kumrahar near Patna.
nebb4199f7ed.tq: Match the archaeological structure with its excavation site.
xs: The **80-pillared hall** is at **Kumrahar near Patna** — option **(1)**.
It belongs to the **Pataliputra ruins**.
**Shravanabelagola** is Chandragupta's Jain death place; **Shar-i-Kuna** has the Greek-Aramaic edict; **Junagadh** the Rudradaman inscription.
xa: Megasthenes described the **palace** (remains at **Kumrahar**) and called the city **Palibothra**.
⚠ **80-pillared hall** vs "**80 forts**" misprint — Andhra forts = **30**.
Other finds: **punch-marked coins** and **NBPW**.

n7a87d5af437.s: Who first identified the Greek Sandrocottus with Chandragupta Maurya?
n7a87d5af437.x: Sir William Jones made the identification in 1793.
n7a87d5af437.tq: Distinguish the scholar who made the identification from later epigraphists.
xs: **Sir William Jones** first identified Sandrocottus with Chandragupta, in **1793** — option **(3)**.
This fixed early Indian chronology: Chandragupta was **Alexander's contemporary**, c. **322 BCE**.
xa: Greek writers using the name: **Justin, Plutarch, Arrian, Strabo**.
Bindusara's title **Amitraghata** = Greek **Amitrochates** (**UPSC**).
**Palibothra** is the Greek name for **Pataliputra**.

n5f91b9e106f.s: Chanakya, author of the Arthashastra, was also known as Kautilya and:
n5f91b9e106f.x: Chanakya was also called Kautilya and Vishnugupta; he guided Chandragupta and is associated with Taxila.
xa: Per **Taranath** and Jain legend, he also served as **Bindusara's** minister.
His story is told in **Mudrarakshasa**.
The **Vamsatthapakasini** (**10th c.**) records the Chanakya-Chandragupta legend.

nb73f66da42c.s: According to Taranath and Jain tradition, Chanakya also served as the minister of:
nb73f66da42c.x: Taranath and Jain traditions state that Chanakya continued to serve as Bindusara’s minister.
nb73f66da42c.tq: Avoid the common assumption that Chanakya’s service ended with Chandragupta.
xs: Per **Taranath** and **Jain** legend, Chanakya also served as minister of **Bindusara** — option **(4)**.
He had been **Chandragupta's chief minister/guide**.
xa: He taught at **Taxila**.
Bindusara's birth name: **Simhasena**; title **Amitraghata**.
Bindusara reigned **297-273 BCE**.

na61a1f42605.x: Bindusara, son of Chandragupta and Durdhara, was born Simhasena; Ashoka's mother was Subhadrangi.
xa: Title **Amitraghata** = Greek **Amitrochates**.
Standard religion answer: **Ajivika** patron.

n02d5cbfca8c.x: Amitraghata means ‘slayer of foes’ or ‘slayer of enemies’; the Greek form was Amitrochates.
n02d5cbfca8c.tq: Translate the title while distinguishing it from Ashoka’s religious epithet.
xs: **Amitraghata** means **"slayer of foes/enemies"** — option **(1)**.
The title is from the **Mahabhashya**; the Greek form is **Amitrochates** (**UPSC**).
xa: It is a title of **Bindusara**, whose birth name was **Simhasena**.
⚠ **Amitraghata** = **Amitrochates** = Bindusara; **Sandrocottus** = Chandragupta.
Bindusara received envoys **Deimachus** and **Dionysius**.

nc2600c64a2a.s: Chandragupta Maurya assumed the Magadhan throne in 321 BC after overthrowing:
nc2600c64a2a.x: Chandragupta Maurya took the Magadhan throne in 321 BC from Dhana Nanda, with the assistance of Chanakya.
nc2600c64a2a.tq: Connect a ruler with the predecessor he displaced.
xs: Chandragupta took the Magadhan throne c. **321 BC** from **Dhana Nanda** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **siege of Pataliputra**, with **Chanakya**'s guidance.
**Seleucus** was defeated later, c. **305 BCE**; **Susima** was Bindusara's eldest prince.
xa: First he eliminated the **Greek satraps** and allied with **Porus (Parvataka)**.
Story told in **Mudrarakshasa**.
Direction of conquest: from **Punjab** east to **Magadha**.

n4a299932c20.s: Who described Chandragupta Maurya's army as a 'gang of dacoits'?
n4a299932c20.x: The Roman historian Justin used the expression 'gang of dacoits' for Chandragupta's army.
n4a299932c20.tq: Match a distinctive quotation with its correct author.
xs: **Justin** called Chandragupta's army a **"gang of dacoits"** — option **(3)**.
It was recruited from **outlaws and frontier tribes**.
xa: Army size: **600,000 infantry, 30,000 cavalry**.
Justin is among the Greek writers who call Chandragupta **Sandrocottus**.
Chandragupta started from **Punjab** and moved east to **Magadha**.

n893d829a66a.s: According to classical (Greek and Latin) accounts, Chandragupta Maurya's army consisted of
n893d829a66a.x: Chandragupta's army is given as 6,00,000 infantry and 30,000 cavalry. 1,00,000 infantry is the Andhra army in Megasthenes; the reversed figures and the 80,000 figure are distractors.
n893d829a66a.tq: Chandragupta: 6 lakh infantry, 30,000 cavalry; Andhras: 1 lakh infantry, 30 forts.
xs: Chandragupta's army had **6,00,000 infantry and 30,000 cavalry** — option **(1)**.
**Justin** called it a **"dacoits' gang"**, recruited from outlaws and frontier tribes.
**1,00,000** infantry belongs to the **Andhras** in Megasthenes, not Chandragupta.
xa: Under the treaty, Chandragupta gave Seleucus **500 war elephants**.
Megasthenes credits the Andhras with **30 fortified towns**.
Conquest began in **Punjab** and moved east to **Magadha**.

nc3308d0fb48.s: Which one of the following was NOT among the territories ceded by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta Maurya?
nc3308d0fb48.x: The ceded territories were Aria, Arachosia, Paropanisadai and Gedrosia; Bactria was not among them.
xa: Paropanisadai is also spelt **Paropamisadae** (Kabul).
Chandragupta gave **500 war elephants**.
⚠ Egypt figures only through **Ptolemy II Philadelphus**, who sent **Dionysius** to Bindusara.

nea0336338fd.s: What did Chandragupta Maurya give to Seleucus I Nicator under the treaty?
nea0336338fd.x: Chandragupta gave Seleucus 500 war elephants as part of the treaty arrangement.
nea0336338fd.tq: Distinguish the specific military payment from territorial and matrimonial provisions.
xs: Chandragupta gave Seleucus **500 war elephants** — option **(3)**.
In return he received **Aria, Arachosia, Paropanisadai and Gedrosia**.
xa: Matrimonial alliance: Seleucus's daughter (**Helena** per CDI) married Chandragupta.
**Megasthenes** was sent as ambassador to Pataliputra.
Treaty date: c. **305 BCE**.

nd4b50f9a7c7.s: Which one of the following was NOT included among the seven classes described by Megasthenes?
nd4b50f9a7c7.x: Megasthenes listed philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors. Merchants were not included in this seven-class description.
nd4b50f9a7c7.tq: Find the outsider by comparing every option with the complete named list.
xs: **Merchants** are not among Megasthenes' seven classes — option **(1)**.
The seven: **philosophers, farmers, herdsmen, artisans, soldiers, overseers (spies), councillors**.
xa: **Philosophers** = **Brahmanas and Sramanas** (ascetics).
⚠ **Overseers** were in effect **spies**.
He also wrongly claimed there were **no slaves**.

n73671d1dddb.s: Who was the Jain teacher associated with Chandragupta Maurya?
n73671d1dddb.x: Chandragupta is described in Jain tradition as a disciple of Bhadrabahu, the sixth Jain Thera.
n73671d1dddb.tq: Distinguish the teacher who accompanied Chandragupta from the leader of the later Svetambara tradition.
xs: Chandragupta was a disciple of **Bhadrabahu**, the **sixth Jain Thera** — option **(3)**.
⚠ **APPSC G2 2003** key = **Bhadrabahu**, not **Sthulabhadra**.
**Hemachandra** wrote the **Parishishtaparvan**, the source of this story.
xa: A **12-year famine** in Magadha made Bhadrabahu migrate south; Chandragupta went with him.
He died by **Sallekhana** at **Shravanabelagola**.
The famine led to the **Digambara (Bhadrabahu) - Svetambara (Sthulabhadra)** split.

n4da70a507b9.s: The twelve-year famine in Chandragupta Maurya's time is traditionally linked with:
o: The split of Buddhism into Mahayana and Hinayana
The migration of the Ajivikas to the south
The division of Jains into Digambaras and Svetambaras
n4da70a507b9.x: The famine tradition is linked with the split between the Digambaras (Bhadrabahu) and the Svetambaras (Sthulabhadra).
xa: The **12-year famine** hit Magadha (South Bihar); Bhadrabahu migrated south with Chandragupta.
A **First Jain Council** was held at **Pataliputra**.
⚠ APPSC G2 2003 key for Chandragupta's guru = **Bhadrabahu**.

n946c2599792.s: Chandragupta Maurya’s reign is generally placed approximately between:
n946c2599792.x: Chandragupta’s reign is generally given as 324/321 to 297 BCE.
n946c2599792.tq: Distinguish Chandragupta’s regnal dates from those of Bindusara and Ashoka.
xs: Chandragupta reigned **324/321-297 BCE** — option **(3)**.
**297-273 BCE** is **Bindusara**'s reign, who succeeded in **297 BC**.
xa: Chandragupta took the Magadhan throne c. **321 BC** from **Dhana Nanda**.
He defeated **Seleucus** c. **305 BCE**.
**Samprati** ruled c. **230-215 BCE**.

n5698bc93689.x: Bindusara’s reign is generally placed between 297 and 273 BCE.
n5698bc93689.tq: Use the regnal sequence to distinguish Bindusara from Chandragupta and Ashoka.
xs: **Bindusara** ruled **297-273 BCE** — option **(1)**.
He succeeded in **297 BC**; **324/321-297 BCE** is Chandragupta's reign and **305-303 BCE** the Seleucus war.
xa: Parents: **Chandragupta** and **Durdhara**.
Birth name **Simhasena**; title **Amitraghata**.
Son: **Ashoka**, by queen **Subhadrangi (Dharma)**.

nb8d1a95f153.s: Of Bindusara's requests to Antiochus I, which one could not be met?
nb8d1a95f153.x: Antiochus sent sweet wine and dried figs, but a philosopher could not be sold or sent as a commodity.
xa: Envoys received by Bindusara: **Deimachus** (Antiochus I) and **Dionysius** (Ptolemy II Philadelphus).
Bindusara's title: **Amitraghata**.

ned09a126a8f.s: Who handled the later Taxila revolt during Ashoka's reign?
ned09a126a8f.x: Susima failed against the first Taxila revolt, Ashoka was then sent, and Kunala handled a later revolt during Ashoka's reign.
xa: Ashoka was Bindusara's son by queen **Subhadrangi (Dharma)**.
Bindusara reigned **297-273 BCE**.
Chanakya once **taught at Taxila**.

nb69818b143c.s: Which envoy was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to the court of Chandragupta Maurya?
nb69818b143c.x: Megasthenes was sent by Seleucus I Nicator to Chandragupta’s court and wrote Indica.
nb69818b143c.tq: Match the envoy with both the sending ruler and the receiving Mauryan ruler.
xs: **Megasthenes** was sent by **Seleucus Nicator** to **Chandragupta** — option **(2)**.
He came c. **302 BCE** and wrote the **Indica**.
**Deimachus** (from **Antiochus I**) and **Dionysius** (from **Ptolemy II Philadelphus**) went to **Bindusara**.
xa: Megasthenes = **first Greek envoy** to an Indian court.
Indica describes **Palibothra** at the **Ganga-Son** confluence.
Exam: "first mentioned Andhra forts?" = Megasthenes (**APPSC G2 2002**).

n7056e0b8cec.s: Deimachus was sent to Bindusara's court by:
n7056e0b8cec.x: Antiochus I sent Deimachus to Bindusara; Ptolemy II sent Dionysius, and Seleucus I sent Megasthenes to Chandragupta.
xa: Antiochus I was asked for **sweet wine, dried figs and a philosopher**.
Megasthenes = **first Greek envoy** to an Indian court (c. **302 BCE**).
Deimachus is also spelt **Daimachos**.

nc255f3f2589.s: Who is regarded as the first Greek envoy to an Indian court?
nc255f3f2589.x: Megasthenes was the first Greek envoy to an Indian court, at Chandragupta Maurya's court.
xa: FIRST/LAST: **Chandragupta** = first Mauryan ruler and first to rule a **pan-Indian empire**.
"Who first mentioned Andhra forts?" = Megasthenes (**APPSC G2 2002**).
Indica survives only in quotations (**Strabo, Arrian, Diodorus**).

n6da0b56b295.s: The Barabar caves in Bihar, the oldest surviving rock-cut caves, were dedicated by Ashoka and Dasharatha to the
n6da0b56b295.x: Ashoka and Dasharatha dedicated the Barabar caves to the Ajivikas, the sect also patronised by Bindusara. Jainism is linked with Chandragupta and Samprati, and Buddhism with Ashoka's Lanka mission, but the Barabar dedications were to the Ajivikas; Vedic Brahmanas were not the recipients.
n6da0b56b295.tq: Barabar and Nagarjuni caves = Ajivikas (Ashoka, Dasharatha).
xs: **Ashoka and Dasharatha** dedicated the **Barabar caves** to the **Ajivikas** — option **(1)**.
Barabar (**Bihar**) has the **oldest surviving rock-cut caves**, in **granite**.
**Jainism** is linked with Chandragupta and Samprati; the Barabar gifts were to the Ajivikas.
xa: **Dasharatha** was an Ajivika patron at **Nagarjuni**; personally counted a Buddhist (**CGPSC 2013** key).
**Bindusara** is the standard Ajivika patron.
**Ashoka** turned to **Buddhism** after Kalinga.

nindian-history-51-42.s: The Barabar and Nagarjuni caves were given to the monks of which sect?
nindian-history-51-42.x: The Barabar and Nagarjuni caves were given to the Ajivikas, patronised by Ashoka and Dasharatha.
n: Makkhali Gosala was associated with the Ajivika tradition. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Makkhali Gosala was a founder or leader of the Ajivikas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Niyativada was an Ajivika doctrine. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Niyativada means fate. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Niyativada means determinism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Ashoka patronised the Ajivikas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Dasharatha patronised the Ajivikas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Barabar Caves were associated with Ajivika monks. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Nagarjuni Caves were associated with Ajivika monks. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: **Barabar Caves** (Bihar) are Mauryan rock-cut caves containing **Ashokan inscriptions**.
**Lomas Rishi Cave** in the Barabar Hills is famous for its **rock-cut façade**.
**Bindusara** was a follower of the **Ajivikas**; **Chandragupta** — **Jainism**.

nindian-history-76-7.s: The Lomas Rishi cave, a Mauryan cave linked to the Ajivikas, is in the ____ Hills of Bihar.
nindian-history-76-7.x: Lomas Rishi is one of the Barabar Hill caves in Bihar, famous for its carved facade.
n: Lomas Rishi Cave is located in the Barabar Hills of Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 154-155]
Lomas Rishi Cave is associated with the Ajivika religion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 154-155]
Lomas Rishi Cave belongs to the Mauryan period. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #76 · pp 154-155]
xa: Lomas Rishi is famous for its **rock-cut façade**.
**Barabar Caves** contain **Ashokan inscriptions**; dedicated to Ajivikas by **Ashoka and Dasharatha**.
They are the **oldest surviving rock-cut caves**, carved in **granite**.

n7ce73233011.s: The municipal administration of Palibothra, according to Megasthenes, was conducted by:
o: A 40-member body divided into four boards
A 30-member body divided into six boards
A council of 12 members divided into three boards
A council of 64 members divided into eight boards
n7ce73233011.x: Megasthenes described a 30-member municipal body organised into six boards at Palibothra.
n7ce73233011.tq: Separate the exact institutional composition from nearby city statistics.
xs: Palibothra was run by a **30-member municipal body in six boards** — option **(2)**.
**64** is the number of **gates**, not council members.
xa: Palibothra = **Pataliputra**, at the **Ganga-Son confluence**.
It had a **wooden wall**, **64 gates** and **570 towers**.
Megasthenes was sent by **Seleucus Nicator** to Chandragupta.

n79e1f8878d7.s: Brahmagiri, Siddapura and Jatinga-Rameshwara, marking the southern reach of the Mauryan Empire, are in present-day:
n79e1f8878d7.x: The Mauryan southern reach extended into Karnataka, marked by these edict sites; the Tamil kingdoms lay outside the empire.
xa: Extent: **Afghanistan to Bengal**.
Andhra edicts: **Yerragudi** (major + minor) and **Rajula Mandagiri** (minor), **Kurnool** district.
**Rock Edict XIII** (c. **256 BCE**) names the **Andhras** within Ashoka's domain.

ncc48f35f98f.s: Which Ashokan site in Kurnool district has both major and minor edicts?
ncc48f35f98f.x: Yerragudi has both major and minor edicts; Rajula Mandagiri, also in Kurnool, has only a minor edict.
xa: **Rock Edict XIII** (c. **256 BCE**) names the **Andhras** among peoples following Ashoka's Dhamma.
Southern limit in **Karnataka**: **Brahmagiri**, **Siddapura**, **Jatinga-Rameshwara** minor edicts.
AP angle: Megasthenes on Andhra strength — **30 fortified towns**.

n23a619612de.s: Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among the peoples who:
o: Ruled the Mauryan capital at Pataliputra
Followed Ashoka's Dhamma within his domain
Served as Greek envoys at Bindusara's court
Defeated Ashoka in the Kalinga War
n23a619612de.x: Rock Edict XIII names the Andhras among peoples following Ashoka's Dhamma within his domain; the edict is dated approximately to 256 BCE.
n23a619612de.tq: Identify the action associated with a named people in an inscription.
xs: **Rock Edict XIII** names the **Andhras** among peoples **following Ashoka's Dhamma within his domain** — option **(2)**.
The edict is dated c. **256 BCE**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes place the Andhras "**on or beyond**" the limits of the empire.
The **Andhras** were already **Buddhist** by RE XIII.
Andhra edicts: **Yerragudi** (major + minor) and **Rajula Mandagiri** (minor), Kurnool district.

n115af3d4833.s: Which was the first empire to unite most of the Indian subcontinent?
n115af3d4833.x: The Mauryan Empire first united most of the subcontinent, covering present-day India, Pakistan, Bangladesh and parts of Afghanistan, and reached the Deccan.
xa: Extent: **Afghanistan to Bengal**; south to **Karnataka** (**Brahmagiri**, **Siddapura**, **Jatinga-Rameshwara**).
Outside: Tamil kingdoms — **Chola, Pandya, Satyaputra, Keralaputra**.
Mauryas = **first pan-Indian empire** (**BPSC 2020, 2024** keys).

n7018c53d15e.s: The Greek form ‘Sandrocottus’ refers to which Indian ruler?
n7018c53d15e.x: Sandrocottus or Sandrokottas, used by Greek writers, refers to Chandragupta Maurya.
n7018c53d15e.tq: Identify the Indian ruler behind the Greek transliteration.
xs: **Sandrocottus / Sandrokottas** is the Greek name of **Chandragupta Maurya** — option **(3)**.
It is used by **Justin, Plutarch, Arrian and Strabo**.
**Bindusara**'s Greek name was **Amitrochates** (from Sanskrit **Amitraghata**).
xa: The identification was first made by **Sir William Jones** (**1793**).
It fixes early Indian chronology: Chandragupta was a contemporary of **Alexander**, c. **322 BCE**.
⚠ **Sandrocottus** = Chandragupta; **Amitrochates** = Bindusara; **Palibothra** = Pataliputra.

nf8fd93f388f.s: Chandragupta Maurya is regarded as the founder of the first pan-Indian empire established by the:
nf8fd93f388f.x: The Mauryas under Chandragupta are regarded as the first pan-Indian empire, although some traditions also describe the Nandas as early empire-builders.
nf8fd93f388f.tq: Distinguish the first pan-Indian empire from earlier empire-building efforts.
xs: The **Mauryas** under Chandragupta formed the **first pan-Indian empire** — option **(3)**.
This is the key in **BPSC 2020, 2024**.
⚠ Some notes call the **Nandas** the first empire-builders, but the exam answer is still **Chandragupta Maurya**.
xa: The empire united most of the subcontinent — **India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, parts of Afghanistan**.
Extent: **Afghanistan to Bengal**, south to **Karnataka**.
Chandragupta = **first Mauryan ruler** (**324/321-297 BCE**).

nf7c7ca67042.s: In which two minor rock edicts does the personal name 'Ashoka' occur?
nf7c7ca67042.x: The name Ashoka appears in the Maski and Gujarra minor rock edicts.
nf7c7ca67042.tq: Recall the specific inscriptional locations of a personal name.
xs: The name "**Ashoka**" occurs in the **Maski** and **Gujarra** minor rock edicts — option **(4)**.
Maski calls him **"Buddhashakya Ashoka"**.
**Dhauli and Jaugada** carry the **Separate (Kalinga) Edicts**; **Rummindei** records the **Lumbini** visit; **Nigalisagar** the Kanakamuni stupa.
xa: Titles elsewhere: **Devanampiya** (beloved of the gods), **Piyadassi** (of pleasing appearance).
"**Dharmasoka**" occurs in the **Sarnath** inscription.
Ashoka was the **first Indian king** to address his people directly through inscriptions (**Prakrit**).

n842b9c98aa5.s: The Third Buddhist Council, after which Ashoka sent Buddhist missions to various regions, was held at
n842b9c98aa5.x: The Third Buddhist Council was held at Pataliputra under Ashoka, and missions such as Mahinda's to Sri Lanka and Mahadeva's to Mahishamandala followed. Rajagriha and Vaishali hosted the First and Second Councils, and Kashmir the Fourth under Kanishka.
n842b9c98aa5.tq: Third Council = Pataliputra, Ashoka; missions followed.
xs: The **Third Buddhist Council** was held at **Pataliputra** — option **(3)**.
After it, missions went out — **Mahinda and Sanghamitta** to Sri Lanka, **Mahadeva** to **Mahishamandala**.
xa: **Sona and Uttara** went to **Suvarnabhumi**.
**Majjhantika** went to **Kashmir-Gandhara**.
AP angle: Mahadeva's mission after the Third Council.

na5217054a13.s: With whom did Ashoka fight a succession struggle after Bindusara?
na5217054a13.x: Ashoka, son of Bindusara and Subhadrangi, faced a succession struggle with Susima before acceding around 273/272 BCE.
xa: Reign: **273-232 BC** or **268-232 BCE** (UPSC) — the gap = a **four-year succession struggle**.
Mahavamsa: he killed **99 brothers** — an exaggeration.
Before accession he was **Governor of Taxila** and **Viceroy of Ujjain**.

n3d3237f8396.s: Before his accession, Ashoka was sent as viceroy to quell a revolt at:
n3d3237f8396.x: Ashoka served as viceroy of Taxila, where he was sent to quell a revolt, and also of Ujjain or Avanti.
xa: **Kalinga** was not his governorship — it broke free in Bindusara's last years and was conquered c. **261 BC**.
Parents: **Bindusara** and **Subhadrangi (Dharma)**.
Succession war with **Susima**.

n6a723862670.s: Which one of the following sets is associated with the Ashokavadana or Divyavadana tradition?
o: Upagupta, Taxila campaign and the transformation of Chandashoka into Dharmashoka
Nigrodha, 99 brothers and the mission of Mahinda
Mahadeva, Mahishamandala and the Third Buddhist Council
Antiochus II, Magas and Antigonus Gonatas
n6a723862670.x: The Ashokavadana or Divyavadana, written in Sanskrit, associates Ashoka with Upagupta, the Taxila campaign and the legend of Chandashoka becoming Dharmashoka.
n6a723862670.tq: Identify the literary tradition through its distinctive cluster of associated names and episodes.
xs: The **Ashokavadana / Divyavadana** has **Upagupta**, the **Taxila campaign** and **Chandashoka** turned **Dharmashoka** — option **(1)**.
These are **Sanskrit** Buddhist legends.
**Nigrodha**, the **99 brothers** and **Mahinda's** mission belong to the Sri Lankan **Mahavamsa / Dipavamsa**.
xa: **Mahadeva** went to **Mahishamandala** after the **Third Council**.
**Antiochus II**, **Magas** and **Antigonus Gonatas** are Hellenistic kings named in **RE XIII**.
Divyavadana names **Upagupta** as the one who initiated Ashoka.

nbab4523b839.s: The Kalinga War was fought approximately in:
nbab4523b839.x: The Kalinga War took place around 261 BCE, in Ashoka's eighth regnal year.
nbab4523b839.tq: Pair the absolute date with the corresponding regnal year.
xs: The Kalinga War was c. **261 BCE**, Ashoka's **8th regnal year** — option **(4)**.
It was the **turning point** of the reign.
**272 BCE** is his accession and **269 BCE** his coronation; the **4th regnal year** is the **Nigrodha** initiation.
xa: **RE XIII**: **1,50,000 deported, 1,00,000 killed**.
After it, **Dhammavijaya** replaced conquest.
RE XIII is **absent at Dhauli and Jaugada**.

n8447690ed9e.s: Which Ashokan edict describes the Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse?
n8447690ed9e.x: Major Rock Edict XIII records the Kalinga War and Ashoka's remorse, with about 1,00,000 killed and 1,50,000 deported.
xa: RE XIII is **absent at Dhauli and Jaugada**, which carry **Separate Edicts**.
RE XIII also names the **Andhras** and Hellenistic contemporaries.

nd5110ba1535.s: Ashoka's post-Kalinga policy is symbolically expressed by the shift from:
nd5110ba1535.x: Ashoka described a shift from Bherighosha, the sound of the war drum, to Dhammaghosha, the proclamation of Dhamma. Dhammavijaya replaced military conquest.
nd5110ba1535.tq: Separate the paired terms by their direction of change and meaning.
xs: The shift was from **Bherighosha** (war drum) to **Dhammaghosha** — option **(2)**.
**Dhammavijaya** replaced conquest after the **Kalinga War**.
Option (1) reverses it; **Dhammayatra** replaced **viharayatra**, not samajas.
xa: Kalinga War: c. **261 BC**, **8th regnal year**.
RE XIII records Ashoka's **remorse**.
First **dhammayatra** to **Bodh Gaya** came in the **11th** year (RE VIII).

n9ba2a23c42c.s: Who is traditionally regarded as having initiated Ashoka into Buddhism in the fourth regnal year?
n9ba2a23c42c.x: According to the Sri Lankan tradition, the monk Nigrodha initiated Ashoka in his fourth regnal year. The Divyavadana associates the initiation with Upagupta.
n9ba2a23c42c.tq: Use the tradition-specific association instead of confusing different teachers.
xs: Sri Lankan tradition says monk **Nigrodha** initiated Ashoka in his **4th regnal year** — option **(1)**.
The **Divyavadana** names **Upagupta** instead; UPSC notes add the monk **Samudra**.
**Mahinda** was Ashoka's son, sent to **Sri Lanka**.
xa: First **dhammayatra** to **Bodh Gaya**: **11th** year (RE VIII).
Ashoka **followed Buddhism** (CGPSC 2013 key).
**Bhabru** edict: devotion to **Buddha, Dhamma, Sangha**.

n3e42c38b610.s: Ashoka's first Dhamma pilgrimage was made to Bodh Gaya in which regnal year?
n3e42c38b610.x: Ashoka visited Bodh Gaya, referred to as Sambodhi, in his 11th regnal year. This was regarded as his first dhammayatra.
xs: The first Dhamma pilgrimage to **Bodh Gaya** (Sambodhi) was in the **11th year** — option **(4)**.
It is recorded in **RE VIII**; dhammayatra **replaced viharayatra**.
The **8th** year is Kalinga; the **4th** the Nigrodha initiation; the **21st** the **Lumbini** visit.
xa: **12th** year: **quinquennial tours** (RE III).
**14th** year: **Dhamma Mahamatras** (RE V).
**26th** year: **rajukas** get judicial authority (PE IV).

ne3a557a1632.s: During his visit to Lumbini in his 21st regnal year, Ashoka reduced the village's tax to:
ne3a557a1632.x: Ashoka visited Lumbini in his 21st year, as recorded at Rummindei, and reduced its tax to one-eighth.
xa: Order: Bodh Gaya (**11th**) → quinquennial tours (**12th**) → Mahamatras (**14th**) → Lumbini (**21st**) → rajukas (**26th**).
Kanakamuni stupa site: **Nigalisagar**.
First dhammayatra = **Bodh Gaya** (RE VIII).

n9c3bd5f3d26.s: Which of the following was to be avoided under Ashoka's Dhamma?
o: Respect for elders, parents and teachers
n9c3bd5f3d26.x: Ashoka's Dhamma discouraged wasteful festive gatherings called samajas, while it encouraged respect for elders, courtesy to slaves and servants, and regard for Brahmanas and Shramanas.
xa: Killing of **animals** was also a vice to avoid.
**RE VII and XII** preach respect for **all sects**.
Dhamma rests on Buddhist **upasaka (lay) dhamma**.

n67f253e4503.s: Rajukas were given independent judicial authority by Ashoka in the:
o: 26th regnal year through Pillar Edict IV
11th regnal year through Rock Edict VIII
14th regnal year through Rock Edict V
12th regnal year through Rock Edict III
n67f253e4503.x: Ashoka granted independent judicial authority to the rajukas in the 26th regnal year. This measure is recorded in Pillar Edict IV.
n67f253e4503.tq: Link the administrative power with both its late regnal year and the correct pillar edict.
xs: **Rajukas** got **independent judicial authority** in the **26th** regnal year, via **Pillar Edict IV** — option **(1)**.
**11th**/RE VIII = Bodh Gaya; **14th**/RE V = Mahamatras; **12th**/RE III = quinquennial tours.
xa: **PE IV** also gave a **3-day respite** to condemned prisoners.
**PE V** (**26th** year): ban on killing specified animals, burning forests; **no branding of cattle**.
Rajukas also went on **quinquennial tours**.

n811c55417f0.s: Under Ashoka, the missionary Majjhantika was sent to:
n811c55417f0.x: Majjhantika went to Kashmir-Gandhara; Mahinda and Sanghamitta went to Sri Lanka, Sona and Uttara to Suvarnabhumi, and Mahadeva to Mahishamandala.
xa: The missions followed the **Third Buddhist Council** at **Pataliputra**.
**Rakkhita** — Vanavasi; **Yona Dhammarakkhita** — Aparantaka; **Majjhima** — Himavanta.
AP angle: **Mahadeva** went to Mahishamandala.

n6619d851ef0.s: After the Third Buddhist Council, the missionary Mahadeva was sent to which region?
n6619d851ef0.x: Mahadeva went to Mahishamandala after the Third Buddhist Council. Andhra tradition also links him with the Amaravati stupa, said to have been enlarged by Ashoka.
n6619d851ef0.tq: Match the missionary figure with the destination rather than with the monument alone.
xs: **Mahadeva** went to **Mahishamandala** after the **Third Buddhist Council** — option **(3)**.
Mahishamandala is **Mysore/Karnataka**.
xa: AP angle: **RE XIII names the Andhras**.
The Third Council was held at **Pataliputra**.
**Rakkhita** went to **Vanavasi** (Karnataka coast).
n6619d851ef0.fixed: Mahadeva is not linked to the Amaravati stupa; stem adds a dubious claim

n6dabfced459.s: Ashoka's Dhamma is best described as:
o: A sectarian doctrine exclusively for Buddhist monks
A moral code and social ethic aimed at discipline, harmony and welfare
A military doctrine for imperial expansion
n6dabfced459.x: Ashoka's Dhamma was a moral code or social ethic, not a religion or system of piety. It emphasised moral discipline, harmony among sects, social welfare and loyalty to the state.
n6dabfced459.tq: Distinguish the broad state ethic from a sectarian religious doctrine.
xs: Dhamma was a **moral code / social ethic** — option **(3)**.
Aims: **moral discipline**, **harmony among sects**, **social welfare**, loyalty to the state.
It was **not a religion or piety**, nor a sectarian code for monks.
xa: **Pillar Edict II**: Dhamma = **few faults, many good deeds**.
Central point: **non-violence and religious toleration together** (**BPSC 2017**).
Definition drawn from the **Rahulovada Sutta**.

n754fe839162.s: The definition of Dhamma associated with Ashoka is taken from which Buddhist text?
n754fe839162.x: The definition of Dhamma is identified with the Rahulovada-Sutta. It rests on the Buddhist upasaka or layperson's Dhamma.
xs: The definition of Dhamma is taken from the **Rahulovada-Sutta** — option **(1)**.
