n2c9d3897386.x: The Queen's edict on Karuvaki's gifts is on the Allahabad-Kosam pillar, which later also received Samudragupta's prashasti.
xa: **Delhi-Topra** is the **only pillar with PE VII**.
Allahabad-Kosam also has **PE I-VI** and a Schism edict.
The Sarnath lion capital is the **national emblem**.

ne19c8f10cb4.s: Ashoka's Pillar Edict VII is found only on which pillar?
ne19c8f10cb4.x: PE VII occurs only on the Delhi-Topra pillar; it says Dhamma spreads better by persuasion than by law.
xa: PE VII mentions **rajukas**, **Ajivikas** and **Nirgranthas** (Jainas).
The Topra pillar was moved from **Ambala** to Delhi (**Firozabad**) by **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**.
Delhi-Topra edicts were the **first Ashokan edicts read** (**Prinsep**, **1837**).

n2b36c32ff03.s: Who shifted the Topra pillar from Ambala to Delhi, where it was installed at Firozabad?
n2b36c32ff03.x: Firoz Shah Tughlaq shifted the Topra pillar from Ambala to Delhi and installed it at Firozabad.
n2b36c32ff03.tq: Use the ruler–action–place association to avoid a swapped patron trap.
xs: **Firoz Shah Tughlaq** moved the **Topra** pillar from **Ambala** to Delhi (**Firozabad**) — option **(1)**.
He also moved the **Meerut** pillar to the **Delhi Ridge**.
**Akbar** is linked with the **Kosam** pillar; **Jahangir** added his inscription to it.
xa: Topra pillar is the **only one with PE VII**.
Delhi-Topra edicts were the **first read** by **Prinsep**.
Delhi-Meerut pillar carries **PE I-VI**.

ne98f24310ac.s: The Maski edict, which confirmed that Devanampiya Piyadasi was Ashoka, was found in:
ne98f24310ac.x: The Maski edict, found in 1915, named Ashoka and so confirmed his identification with Devanampiya Piyadasi.
xa: Maski is in **Raichur, Karnataka**: "**Buddhashakya Ashoka**".
**Gujarra** (Madhya Pradesh) also names Ashoka.
**Brahmi** was deciphered by **James Prinsep** in **1837**.

n2a7506ea7b4.s: Which of the following is NOT named in any Ashokan edict?
n2a7506ea7b4.x: No Ashokan edict names the Eightfold Path, the Four Noble Truths or Nibbana; even the Greek and Aramaic versions carry Buddhist ideas without naming the Buddha.
xa: **Bhabru (Bairat)**: faith in the **Buddha, Dhamma and Sangha**.
**PE II** defines Dhamma: "few faults, many good deeds".
Dhamma was steeped in Buddhist ethics yet **not sectarian**.

nf50d01ba905.s: At which one of the following places has a Major Rock Edict of Ashoka been found?
nf50d01ba905.x: Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat carries the 14 Major Rock Edicts. Barabar has cave inscriptions, while Allahabad and Delhi-Topra are pillar edict sites.
nf50d01ba905.tq: Major Rock Edict = Girnar; Barabar = caves; Allahabad, Delhi = pillars.
xs: **Girnar** has the **Major Rock Edicts** — option **(3)**.
**Barabar** has **cave inscriptions**; **Allahabad** and **Delhi-Topra** are **pillar** sites.
xa: Girnar (Junagadh, Gujarat) has all **14 Major Rock Edicts**.
**Kalsi** (Uttarakhand) also has 14 Major Rock Edicts.
Allahabad-Kosam pillar later bears **Samudragupta's prashasti**.

na445d000bb9.s: Ashoka's Separate Kalinga Edicts were addressed to the officers of:
na445d000bb9.x: The Separate Kalinga Edicts address officers of Tosali and Samapa, telling them to stop unjust imprisonment and torture.
xa: They take the place of **RE XI-XIII** there.
Girnar and Kalsi carry the **14 Major Rock Edicts**.
RE XIII: **1,00,000 killed**, **1,50,000 captive**.

n1f109527723.s: Which of the following was NOT regarded as a vice in Ashoka's Dhamma?
n1f109527723.x: Dhamma promoted kindness and charity and condemned violence, cruelty, anger, pride and jealousy as vices.
xa: Dhamma was **not sectarian**.
**PE II** defines Dhamma.
Other virtues: **truthfulness**, **gratitude**, **respect for elders**.

n37ad46138ec.s: According to Major Rock Edict XIII, about how many people were taken captive in the Kalinga War?
n37ad46138ec.x: Major Rock Edict XIII records about 1,50,000 taken captive, about 1,00,000 killed, and many more deaths from famine and disease.
xa: The war was in **261 BC**, Ashoka's **8th regnal year**.
⚠ **1 lakh** killed; **1.5 lakh** captives — don't reverse them.
RE XIII also names **five Greek kings** and the **Andhras**.

na27c0cd1f86.s: Which of the following was NOT a consequence of the Kalinga War for Ashoka?
o: Adoption of Dhammavijaya in place of military conquest
Continuation of wars of conquest as the principal policy
na27c0cd1f86.x: D is the answer: after Kalinga Ashoka waged no more wars of conquest. The war's results were remorse, his conversion to Buddhism and Dhammavijaya replacing military conquest (A, B and C).
na27c0cd1f86.tq: Find the statement that reverses the documented policy change after Kalinga.
xs: **Continuation of wars of conquest** was not a consequence — option **(4)**.
After Kalinga, Ashoka waged **no more wars of conquest**.
Actual results: **remorse**, **conversion to Buddhism**, **Dhammavijaya** replacing military conquest.
xa: Policy shift: **Bherighosha** → **Dhammaghosha**.
**RE XIII** records it.
**Separate Kalinga edicts** urged just treatment of the people.

nfd09aea6430.s: Ashokan inscriptions in Andhra Pradesh were written in:
nfd09aea6430.x: The Andhra inscriptions of Ashoka were in Prakrit using the Brahmi script, and they show Mauryan administration extended into Rayalaseema.
xa: Sites: **Erragudi** and **Rajula Mandagiri**, Kurnool district.
Erragudi asks **teachers to instil Dhamma** (**APPSC 2019**).
**RE XIII** (c. **256 BCE**) lists the **Andhras** among peoples following Dhamma.

nea116c07506.s: The two important Ashokan rock-edict sites in the Kurnool-Nandyal region are:
nea116c07506.x: Erragudi and Rajula Mandagiri are the two important Ashokan rock-edict sites in the Kurnool-Nandyal region; Bhattiprolu is not an Ashokan edict site.
xa: ⚠ **Bhattiprolu** and **Dhanyakataka** are standard **distractors**.
Erragudi: **teachers** to instil Dhamma; Rajula Mandagiri: **guru-disciple** relation.
Both are in **Prakrit / Brahmi**.

nd60b2114a5e.s: Ashokan pillar edicts are concentrated in the Ganga plain mainly because:
o: River transport eased the movement of the heavy monoliths
Rock surfaces for edicts were absent there
Pillars were reserved for Buddhist monasteries
The pillars marked the route of the Kalinga campaign
nd60b2114a5e.x: The pillar edicts cluster in the Ganga plain because river transport made it easier to move the heavy monoliths.
xa: **Delhi-Topra** is the **only pillar with PE VII**.
**Lauriya Nandangarh** (Bihar) has **PE I-VI** and a **lion capital**.
**Sarnath** pillar: **Schism edict** and **lion capital** (national emblem).

na62da8a6d9f.s: The Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra, after which Ashoka's missions were sent, was held under:
na62da8a6d9f.x: Ashoka's Buddhist missions followed the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra held under Moggaliputta Tissa.
xa: Missions went to **Ceylon, Burma and South-East Asia**.
**Mahendra, Sanghamitra** — Sri Lanka; **Majjhantika** — Kashmir-Gandhara.
AP angle: **Mahadeva** — **Mahisha Mandala**.

nindian-history-1-1.s: Ashokan inscriptions are classified into which three groups?
nindian-history-1-1.x: Ashokan inscriptions are rock (major and minor rock edicts), pillar and cave (Barabar) inscriptions; copper-plates, seals and coin legends belong to later periods.
n: Ashokan inscriptions are classified into rock inscriptions, pillar inscriptions, and cave inscriptions. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: Major rock edict sites: **Shahbazgarhi**, **Mansehra**, **Kalsi**, **Girnar**, **Dhauli**, **Jaugada**, **Yerragudi**, **Sopara**.
"Where has a Major Rock Edict been found?" = **Girnar**; **Allahabad** and **Delhi** are pillar sites.
Edicts are found in **India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Pakistan, Afghanistan**.

n6d8ccd5665e.s: The sculptures of Dharanikota are described as:
o: Later than those of Sanchi and Bharhut
Older than those of Sanchi and Bharhut
n6d8ccd5665e.x: Dharanikota sculptures, in the Amaravati region, are described as older than those of Sanchi and Bharhut.
xa: Ashoka enlarged the **Amaravati** stupa; a **plaque** with his name was found.
**RE XIII** shows Buddhism already known in **Andhra**.
Andhras linked as "**Andhra-bhrityas**" — a **Puranic** term.

n4bdf2b3b693.s: Which council of ministers acted as a check on the authority of the Mauryan king?
n4bdf2b3b693.x: The Mantriparishad, along with paura-janapada assemblies and public opinion, checked the king's authority - a chariot cannot move on one wheel.
xa: Kautilya put it as "a **chariot cannot move on one wheel**" — a kingdom cannot run on one wheel.
Despite these checks the state is called a **"paternal despotism"** — the king headed executive, legislature and judiciary.
The **Mantriparishadadhyaksha** was the tirtha who headed the council.

n4615e2318d5.s: In Kautilya's Saptanga theory, which element comes first in the standard order?
n4615e2318d5.x: The standard order is Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala and Mitra, so Swami comes first.
xa: Meanings: **Swami** = king, **Amatya** = ministers, **Janapada** = territory and people, **Durga** = fort.
**Kosha** = treasury, **Danda/Bala** = army, force, justice, **Mitra** = ally.
⚠ Some notes list Durga 6th, Land 7th and add an 8th, **Shatru** (enemy) — learn the standard seven.
Later dynasties (**Eastern Chalukyas**, **Kakatiyas**) used the Saptanga and **18 Tirthas** model.

nf3af373eb33.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven standard elements in Kautilya's Saptanga theory?
nf3af373eb33.x: The standard seven elements do not include Shatru; some lists add it only as an eighth item.
xa: Standard order: **Swami, Amatya, Janapada, Durga, Kosha, Danda/Bala, Mitra**.
⚠ The non-standard lists also put **Durga 6th** and Land 7th — a common trap.
The Saptanga model was reused by the **Eastern Chalukyas** and **Kakatiyas**.

nf059149ec1a.s: What was the capital of the Mauryan province of Dakshinapatha?
nf059149ec1a.x: Suvarnagiri was the capital of Dakshinapatha; Pataliputra, Taxila and Ujjain were the capitals of Magadha, Uttarapatha and Avantirashtra.
xa: **Kalinga**, added under **Ashoka**, had its capital at **Tosali**.
**Suvarnagiri** was the southern capital governing the **Deccan**, with Andhra in its orbit (AP angle).
**Pataliputra** was founded by **Udayin**.
Chandragupta had **four** provinces, ruled by **Kumaras** helped by **Mahamatras**.

ne12cdf26a76.s: In Mauryan provincial administration, districts were known as:
ne12cdf26a76.x: Mauryan districts were called Vish or Ahara; Chandragupta's four provinces were ruled by Kumaras or governors.
xa: Kumaras were also called **Kumaramatyas**.
District-level officers: **Rajukas, Pradeshikas, Yuktas** (UPSC **2025** key).
Governors named in sources: **Pushyagupta Vaishya** (Saurashtra) and **Yavanaraja Tushaspa** (under Ashoka).

na9b265783dc.s: Which of the following Mauryan officials worked at the village level rather than the district level?
na9b265783dc.x: The Gramika was the village head, whereas Rajukas, Pradeshikas and Yuktas were district-level officials.
xa: **Pradeshika**: district head for revenue and police; toured every **5 years** (Rock Edict III).
**Rajuka**: land survey and assessment, with **judicial powers** (Pillar Edict IV).
**Yukta**: subordinate revenue/secretarial officer, touring with the pradeshikas.
Sub-district: **Sthanika** (tax collector), **Gopa** (accountant over **5-10 villages**).

n52270fad42c.s: Which Mauryan officials handled land survey and assessment and also possessed judicial powers?
n52270fad42c.x: Rajukas handled land survey and assessment and had judicial powers, while Yuktas were subordinate revenue or secretarial officers.
xa: Yuktas toured every **5 years** with the **pradeshikas** (Rock Edict III).
**Pradeshika** = district head for revenue and police.
⚠ **Agronomoi** (Megasthenes) were district officers for roads, irrigation and land measurement.

n373ae83dd4a.s: Which of the following did Megasthenes state about Mauryan law?
o: A fully codified penal code existed
Punishment was the same for all varnas
n373ae83dd4a.x: Megasthenes stated that there was no written code; Mauryan punishments included fines, mutilation and death, and their severity varied by varna.
xa: Civic offences like **dumping dirt** on streets drew fines.
Slave rules: selling a **pregnant slave** without arranging maternity was punished.
**Tax evasion on sales** was punishable by **death** (Megasthenes).

nd4d83e6ccac.s: Which Mauryan official was the Collector-General of Revenue and collected revenue in cash and kind with the assistance of the Bhagadhuk?
nd4d83e6ccac.x: Samaharta was the Collector-General of Revenue. He collected revenue in both cash and kind and was assisted by the Bhagadhuk.
nd4d83e6ccac.tq: Use the official–department association directly, while distinguishing the revenue collector from the treasurer.
xs: The **Samaharta** was the **Collector-General of Revenue**, collecting in **cash and kind** with the help of the **Bhagadhuk** — option **(2)**.
**Sannidhata** was the **treasurer** and keeper of state stores, not the collector.
**Pautavadhyaksha** handled **weights and measures**; **Sulkadhyaksha** handled **tolls and customs**.
xa: ⚠ **Samaharta** = revenue collector; **Sannidhata** = treasurer — do not swap.
Samaharta was an APPSC **2023** key (APPSC-GS 2023).
Each tirtha drew **12,000 panas** a year.
Land revenue was the main income; the king's share (**Bhaga**) was normally **1/6**.

n10d25b9685e.s: The Sannidhata in the Mauryan administration was primarily responsible for which of the following?
n10d25b9685e.x: Sannidhata was the treasurer and keeper of state stores. The Samaharta, in contrast, was the Collector-General of Revenue.
n10d25b9685e.tq: Discriminate between closely related revenue and treasury offices.
xs: The **Sannidhata** was the **treasurer and keeper of state stores** — option **(1)**.
**Crown lands and state agriculture** belonged to the **Sitadhyaksha**; **tolls and customs** to the **Sulkadhyaksha**.
**Markets** were under the **Samsthadhyaksha**.
xa: ⚠ The **Samaharta** was the **Collector-General of Revenue** — the classic swap with Sannidhata.
Other treasury-related officer: **Koshadhyaksha** (treasury); storehouses: **Koshthagaradhyaksha**.
Tirthas and Adhyakshas together ran about **26 departments**.

n1d2a4cf337b.s: In the Mauryan administrative system, Dandapala was the head of which department?
n1d2a4cf337b.x: Dandapala was the head of the army department in Kautilya’s Mauryan list of tirthas.
n1d2a4cf337b.tq: Use the Mauryan role rather than a similar title assigned to another administrative list.
xs: In Kautilya's list, the **Dandapala** headed the **army department** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2022** key).
**Criminal justice** was the **Pradeshtri**'s charge; the **treasury** was the **Sannidhata**'s.
The **palace household** was under the **Antarvamshika**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes call Dandapala **head of police** — from the Eastern Chalukya **Ashtadasha Tirthas** (Magallu inscription); for the Kautilya question the key is **army**.
The **Senapati** was the commander-in-chief.
Chandragupta's army: **6,00,000 foot** and **30,000 cavalry**, run by **six boards of five**.

nf35a187cbed.s: Among Kautilya's tirthas, the Vyavaharika was the:
nf35a187cbed.x: Vyavaharika was the civil judge; Prashasta looked after prisons, Nayaka was the city guard and Paura the capital's governor.
xa: **Durgapala** looked after forts and fort guards; **Antapala** the frontier.
**Pradeshtri** handled **criminal justice** (kantakashodhana courts).
**Mantriparishadadhyaksha** was the head of the council.

nf4df2d7850b.s: The Mauryan model of the Saptanga state and the 18 Tirthas was later adopted in Andhra by the
nf4df2d7850b.x: The Eastern Chalukyas (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and the Kakatiyas used the Saptanga and 18 Tirthas model. The Sungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas and Western Kshatrapas are not linked with it.
nf4df2d7850b.tq: 18 Tirthas in Andhra = Eastern Chalukyas (Ashtadasha Tirthas), Kakatiyas.
xs: The **Eastern Chalukyas** (Ashtadasha Tirthas) and the **Kakatiyas** used the Saptanga and **18 Tirthas** model — option **(1)**.
The notes do not link the Sungas, Kanvas, Indo-Greeks, Sakas, Kushanas or Kshatrapas with it.
xa: ⚠ The Eastern Chalukya list (**Magallu** inscription) makes **Dandapala** a police chief; Kautilya's Dandapala heads the **army**.
⚠ The same list makes **Antapala** an inner-palace guard; the Mauryan Antapala was a **frontier** officer.
Each Mauryan tirtha drew **12,000 panas** a year.

n6b0fe7e7f3c.s: In the Mauryan administration, the Pautavadhyaksha dealt with:
n6b0fe7e7f3c.x: Pautavadhyaksha handled weights and measures; Sitadhyaksha looked after crown lands and Panyadhyaksha state trade.
xa: ⚠ **Pautava** = weights and measures; **Panya** = commerce; **Sulka** = tolls.
**Sita** was also the revenue term for income from **crown (state) land**.
**Samsthadhyaksha** supervised markets; **Lavanadhyaksha** the salt monopoly.

n183f132ee1f.s: In the Mauryan administration, the Akaradhyaksha was in charge of:
n183f132ee1f.x: Akaradhyaksha supervised mines; Panyadhyaksha handled commerce, Koshadhyaksha the treasury and Lavanadhyaksha salt.
xa: Salt was a **state monopoly** under the Lavanadhyaksha.
**Lohadhyaksha** dealt with **iron**; **Lakshanadhyaksha** with the **mint and seals**.
⚠ **Panya** = commerce, **Pautava** = weights and measures, **Sulka** = tolls.

n2bc6037e0db.s: The province of Kalinga, added to the Mauryan Empire by Ashoka, had which capital?
n2bc6037e0db.x: Tosali was the provincial capital of Kalinga after its incorporation under Ashoka.
n2bc6037e0db.tq: Distinguish the added province from the original four provincial divisions.
xs: **Kalinga**, added to the empire under **Ashoka**, had its capital at **Tosali** — option **(4)**.
**Suvarnagiri** was the capital of **Dakshinapatha**, **Taxila** of **Uttarapatha**.
**Pataliputra** was the imperial centre (Magadha/Prachya).
xa: **Ujjain** was the capital of **Avantipatha (Avantirashtra)**.
Under **Chandragupta** there were only **four** provinces; Kalinga made a fifth under Ashoka.
Provinces were ruled by **Kumaras** (royal princes, also called Kumaramatyas).

neb3d27568b9.s: With reference to Mauryan administration, Suvarnagiri was:
o: The southern capital of the empire
The northern capital of the empire
The principal centre of the Paura-janapada
neb3d27568b9.x: Suvarnagiri was the southern capital of the Mauryan Empire. It was associated with the Dakshinapatha and the administration of the Deccan.
neb3d27568b9.tq: Test the location and regional association of an administrative centre.
xs: **Suvarnagiri** was the **southern capital** of the empire — option **(1)**.
It was the capital of **Dakshinapatha** and governed the **Deccan**, with Andhra in its orbit.
The northern province (**Uttarapatha**) had its capital at **Taxila**.
xa: **Ujjain** = capital of **Avantirashtra**; **Tosali** = capital of **Kalinga**.
**Pataliputra** was the centre, under the emperor.
**Paura-janapada** assemblies were a check on the king, not a place.

nda35e6f494c.s: The Mauryan official who acted as accountant over 5-10 villages was the:
nda35e6f494c.x: The Gopa was the accountant over 5-10 villages; the Sthanika collected taxes over a larger division and the Gramika was the village head.
xa: The **Gramika** was probably **elected** and worked with village elders.
Gopa and Sthanika were **sub-district** officers; above them were **Rajukas, Pradeshikas, Yuktas**.
The court ladder began at the **village** (Grama Sabha) and ended with the **king**.

neec6bdbf770.s: In the Mauryan system, spies who watched officials and provinces were called:
neec6bdbf770.x: Gudhapurushas were spies who watched officials and provinces; Samstha spies were stationary and Sanchara spies wandering.
xa: Samstha guises: **kapatika, udasthita, grihapatika, vaidehaka, tapasa**.
Sanchara guises: **satri, tikshna, rasada, parivrajika** (women).
Spies worked under the **mahamatyapasarpa**.

n64559476e02.s: In the Mauryan judicial hierarchy, which court stood just above the village court?
n64559476e02.x: The judicial ladder ran from the village court to Sangrahana, Dronamukha, Janapada and finally the king.
xa: Settlement units: **Sangrahana = 10** villages, **Dronamukha = 400**, **Sthaniya = 800**.
Main courts: **Dharmasthiya** (civil), **Kantakashodhana** (criminal).
**Rajukas** at the district level also had **judicial powers**.

n05d41b44ffb.s: In the Mauryan administration, the term 'Pradvivaka' is associated with the
n05d41b44ffb.x: Pradvivaka was the chief judicial adviser or judge (APPSC G2 2019: judicial system). Revenue was under the Samaharta, espionage under the gudhapurushas, and the municipal boards were the Astynomoi of Megasthenes.
xs: The **Pradvivaka** was the chief judicial adviser/judge — so it belongs to the **judicial system**, option **(2)** (APPSC G2 **2019**).
Revenue was under the **Samaharta**; espionage used **gudhapurushas**; municipal boards were Megasthenes' **Astynomoi**.
xa: Courts: **Dharmasthiya** (civil) and **Kantakashodhana** (criminal), each with three judges and three amatyas.
**Vyavaharika** = civil judge; **Pradeshtri** = criminal justice.
The **king** was the supreme judge.

n45177e9ddc1.s: Mauryan courts that tried civil cases such as marriage, contract and inheritance were called:
n45177e9ddc1.x: Dharmasthiya courts were civil courts, whereas Kantakashodhana ('removal of thorns') courts were criminal courts.
xa: Each court had **three judges and three amatyas**.
Kantakashodhana courts were presided over by **pradeshtris**.
⚠ **Dharmasthiya** = civil; **Kantakashodhana** = criminal.

n93e8add3097.s: The Mauryan Lakshanadhyaksha was associated with:
n93e8add3097.x: Lakshanadhyaksha was associated with the mint and seals; forest produce was under the Kupyadhyaksha and storehouses under the Koshthagaradhyaksha.
xa: **Akshapataladhyaksha** was effectively the **accountant-general**.
Other superintendents: **Navadhyaksha** (ships), **Ganikadhyaksha** (courtesans), **Suradhyaksha** (liquor).
**Akaradhyaksha / Lohadhyaksha** looked after **mines / iron**.

nbe9da1802f5.s: The highly centralised Mauryan government, with the king heading executive, legislature and judiciary, is described as:
nbe9da1802f5.x: Mauryan government was highly centralised under the king and has been described as paternal despotism.
xa: Checks on the king: the **Mantriparishad**, **paura-janapada** assemblies and **public opinion**.
Kautilya's maxim: "a **chariot cannot move on one wheel**".
The Mauryan state was the **first centralised bureaucratic empire**, with a census and standardised measures.

n9e4cb4e728e.s: Sita land in the Mauryan economy was:
o: Forest land reserved exclusively for hunting
Land donated permanently to Buddhist monasteries
Land owned collectively by village artisans
Crown land cultivated directly under state supervision
n9e4cb4e728e.x: Sita was crown land cultivated for the state, under the supervision of the Sitadhyaksha, often using slaves and hired labourers.
n9e4cb4e728e.tq: Directly identify the official economic meaning of a specialised term.
xs: **Sita** was **crown land cultivated directly for/under the state** — option **(4)**.
It was supervised by the **Sitadhyaksha** and worked often by **slaves and hired labourers**.
It was not forest, monastery or collective artisan land.
xa: The notes record **large-scale use of slaves** in farming on sita land.
**Dronavapa** = land sown with one **drona** of seed.
Revenue officials: **Samaharta**, **Gopa**, **Sthanika**.

n81ac325e3bd.s: In the Mauryan period, mining, forestry, salt, liquor, and arms and metallurgy were:
n81ac325e3bd.x: The Mauryan state exercised monopoly or strong control over mining, forestry, salt, liquor, arms and metallurgy.
xa: **Iron** deposits near Magadha were one basis of **Magadhan power**.
**Tax evasion** could mean **death**.
Sale of goods was **state-supervised**.

nb5c08cddbf6.s: Which pottery was typical of the Mauryan period?
nb5c08cddbf6.x: NBPW was the typical Mauryan pottery.
xa: The Arthashastra's interest rate: **15% a year**; students, poor and sick got **debt relief**.
**Mauryan polish** on pillars has a metallic shine like **NBPW** pottery.
Punch-marked coins and **NBPW** sherds reach **Bangladesh, Odisha, Andhra and Karnataka**.

n11214d958dc.s: The annual rate of interest mentioned in the Arthashastra was:
n11214d958dc.x: The Arthashastra mentions an annual interest rate of 15 percent.
n11214d958dc.tq: Recall the exact percentage rather than a commonly assumed round figure.
xs: The Arthashastra fixes interest at **15 percent (15%) a year** — option **(3)**.
**Usury** prevailed because there was **no banking**.
xa: **Students, the poor and the sick** got relief from debt.
Imperial currency: **punch-marked silver coins**.
Sale of goods was **state-supervised**.

n98788e9d3c7.s: In the Mauryan period, trade caravans were led by a:
n98788e9d3c7.x: Caravans were led by a Sarthavaha, and the state collected road tax in return for protecting them.
xa: Sale of goods was **state-supervised**.
The **royal highway** ran from the north-west to **Pataliputra**.
Interest: **15% a year** (Arthashastra).

nc4f0049e64d.s: Megasthenes reported that which of the following did NOT exist in India?
nc4f0049e64d.x: Megasthenes stated that India had no slavery, while describing hereditary occupations and endogamy.
xa: ⚠ Megasthenes: **no slaves**; Kautilya: **nine categories of slaves** — sources differ.
He also noted there was **no written law**.
On the **Andhras** he noted **30 walled towns** (some notes say 80).

nd0edf6f03e0.s: According to the Arthashastra, a person could become a slave through:
o: Birth, sale, capture in war and judicial punishment
nd0edf6f03e0.x: The Arthashastra recognised slavery arising through birth, sale, capture in war and judicial punishment.
xa: Kautilya lists **nine categories of slaves** (dasas); Ashokan inscriptions also mention dasas.
Freedom could be gained **by payment**.
A female slave who bore her master a **son** became **free**.

nf56cafabcad.s: In the Arthashastra, the divorce a wife deserted by her husband could seek was called:
nf56cafabcad.x: The Arthashastra recognised moksha for a deserted wife; anuloma and pratiloma refer to types of inter-varna marriage.
xa: Divorce was also allowed for **mutual enmity** in certain marriage forms.
**Stridhana** = a woman's own property (jewellery, maintenance).
⚠ Some notes say widow remarriage ceased.

nb1ff2e1e661.s: The religious policy of the Mauryan state was broadly:
o: Complete separation of religion from the state
Liberal and tolerant, while protecting varna and ashrama
nb1ff2e1e661.x: Mauryan religious conditions were liberal and tolerant, allowing freedom of faith, while the state protected varna and ashrama.
xa: **Chandragupta** followed **Bhadrabahu** (Jainism) to Shravanabelagola.
**Ashoka and Dasaratha** gave caves to the **Ajivikas**.
**Brahmanism** continued — Kautilya was a Brahmana, **'dvijarshabh'**.

ne975a253463.s: Kautilya, a Brahmana of the Mauryan period, was described as:
ne975a253463.x: Brahmanism continued under the Mauryas, and Kautilya was a Brahmana called 'dvijarshabh'.
xa: Policy was **liberal and tolerant**, with the state protecting **varna and ashrama**.
Tradition: Ashoka redistributed the relics into **84,000 stupas**.
**Chandragupta** followed **Bhadrabahu** (Jainism).

n4bc3dbe8814.s: Which untouchable groups grew in number during the Mauryan period?
n4bc3dbe8814.x: Chandalas and Shvapakas, untouchable groups, grew in number in the Mauryan period.
xa: The **Antyavasayins** were **five mixed castes** outside Aryan society.
The state still protected **varna and ashrama**.
**Shudras could own land** (Arthashastra).

nd65fdf51fac.s: Megasthenes compared Chandragupta's palace at Pataliputra with the palaces of:
nd65fdf51fac.x: Megasthenes compared the palace to Susa and Ecbatana; Fa-Hien admired it in the 5th century CE.
xa: **Kumrahar** yielded the **80-pillared hall** (8 rows x 10).
**Bulandibagh** yielded remains of the **wooden palisade**.
The city was built mainly of **timber**.

nd17b5058747.s: Balirajgarh fort, excavated by the ASI and yielding punch-marked coins, is in which district of Bihar?
nd17b5058747.x: Balirajgarh is in Madhubani district, Bihar; its habitation runs from the Mauryan to the Pala period.
xa: It was in the news in **Apr 2026**.
**Vaishya Tekri** (Ujjain) may hold a Mauryan stupa larger than Sanchi.
Punch-marked silver panas go back to the **Mahajanapada** age.

n16b95b6044c.s: Mauryan rainfall records predate Korea's Cheugugi rain gauge, which dates to:
n16b95b6044c.x: The Mauryan rainfall records are significant because they predate Korea's Cheugugi gauge of 1441 CE.
xa: A drona held about **13.2 kg** of water.
**Dronavapa** = land sown with one drona of seed.
The state gave **seed, cattle and tools** in famine.

nf044661da9a.s: The Uttarapatha connected which of the following routes?
o: Rajgir through Kalinga to Sri Lanka
nf044661da9a.x: Uttarapatha was the northern highway running from Taxila through Pataliputra to Tamralipti.
nf044661da9a.tq: Recall the route by identifying its north-western starting point and eastern terminus.
xs: **Uttarapatha** was the northern highway from **Taxila** through the Ganga valley / **Pataliputra** to **Tamralipti** — option **(2)**.
The southern route through Andhra was the **Dakshinapatha**.
xa: The **royal highway** ran from the north-west to Pataliputra.
Tamralipti was the **main port of the Ganga basin**.
Caravans were led by a **Sarthavaha**.

n86f8339c695.s: The Red Sea port associated with Mauryan trade with Egypt was:
n86f8339c695.x: The Egyptian connection through the Red Sea was linked with the port of Bernis, or Berenice.
n86f8339c695.tq: Distinguish the foreign Red Sea port from the Indian coastal ports.
xs: **Berenice (Bernis)** was the **Red Sea** port for trade with **Egypt** — option **(4)**.
**Sopara** and **Bharukachchha** were Indian **west**-coast ports; **Tamralipti** was on the **east** coast.
xa: Foreign partners: **Greece, Persia, Egypt, Syria, Sri Lanka, Java, Sumatra**.
Exports: **diamonds, pearls, muslin, fine textiles**.
Tamralipti was the **main port of the Ganga basin** (APPSC **2012**).

n0aabf1b9d31.s: Megasthenes divided Indian society into how many classes in the Indica?
n0aabf1b9d31.x: Megasthenes described seven classes: philosophers, farmers, herdsmen or hunters, artisans, soldiers, overseers and councillors.
n0aabf1b9d31.tq: Directly recall the distinctive numerical classification.
xs: Megasthenes' **Indica** divides society into **seven** classes — option **(1)** (BPSC **2017**).
They are **philosophers, farmers, herdsmen/hunters, artisans, soldiers, overseers, councillors**.
xa: ⚠ **Nine** is Kautilya's count of **slave categories**, not Megasthenes' classes.
Megasthenes noted **hereditary occupation** and **endogamy**.
He said India had **no slavery** and theft was **rare**.

ne0cc27100eb.s: In the Arthashastra, the five mixed castes outside Aryan society were called:
ne0cc27100eb.x: Kautilya referred to five mixed castes called Antyavasayins as outside Aryan society; learned men were called Sishtas.
xa: Centres of learning: **Taxila** (most famous), **Ujjain**, **Varanasi**.
**Chandalas** and **Shvapakas** (untouchables) grew in number.
Bhadrabahu's **Kalpasutra** belongs to this age.

n699f923309e.s: Which was the most famous centre of learning during the Mauryan period?
n699f923309e.x: Taxila was the most famous Mauryan-period centre of learning, ahead of Ujjain and Varanasi.
xa: Learned men were called **Sishtas**.
Bhadrabahu's **Kalpasutra** belongs to this age.
Taxila was the capital of **Uttarapatha** and the start of the northern highway.
n699f923309e.fixed: stem had a numbered list and 'code' wording that did not fit single-choice options; cf. PYQ y23c35a07fa7

nf52a1fff5dd.s: Stridhana in the Arthashastra referred to:
o: Property belonging exclusively to the king
A woman's own property, including jewellery and maintenance
Land held jointly by a village community
nf52a1fff5dd.x: Stridhana was a woman's own property, including jewellery and resources for maintenance.
nf52a1fff5dd.tq: Distinguish a personal property category from public and communal property.
xs: **Stridhana** was a **woman's own property** — **jewellery and maintenance** — option **(3)**.
It was not royal property, a tax on widows or village land.
xa: **Moksha** = divorce, allowed to a wife **deserted** by her husband.
**Widow remarriage** was permitted.
**Anuloma and pratiloma** inter-varna marriages occurred.

ndc00cbe1e4e.s: Yaksha worship was shared by which religious traditions?
ndc00cbe1e4e.x: Yakshas were revered in Jainism, Buddhism and Hinduism alike.
xa: Yaksha/yakshi statues are the **earliest large-scale human sculptures**.
The inscribed **Manibhadra Yaksha** is from **Parkham** (Mathura).
Yaksha from **Noh** (Bharatpur, Rajasthan).

n36a130866bc.s: Mauryan pillars are best described as:
o: Fluted wooden shafts with bronze capitals
Multi-block granite pillars with square bases
Monolithic circular shafts of Chunar sandstone with a lustrous polish
Composite brick pillars covered with lime plaster
n36a130866bc.x: Mauryan pillars were monolithic, free-standing and circular, generally made of Chunar sandstone and finished with the characteristic Mauryan polish.
n36a130866bc.tq: Use a compact material-and-construction description for direct identification.
xs: Mauryan pillars were **monolithic**, free-standing, **circular** shafts of **Chunar sandstone** with a **lustrous polish** — option **(3)**.
They were **smooth** (not fluted), stone (not wood or brick) and had **no base**.
xa: **"Mauryan polish"** gives a metallic shine, like **NBPW** pottery.
The sandstone is **buff/grey**.
Sequence: shaft → **inverted lotus (ghanta)** → abacus → **capital animal**.

n721b01aaea7.s: Which of the following were among the exports of the Mauryan period?
n721b01aaea7.x: Diamonds, pearls, muslin and fine textiles were among the exports of the period.
xa: Trade partners: **Greece, Persia, Egypt, Syria, Sri Lanka, Java, Sumatra**.
Ports: **Tamralipti** (east), **Bharukachchha** and **Sopara** (west).
Caravans were led by a **Sarthavaha**.

n60f7fa5da7a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the debate on Persian influence on Mauryan pillars?
o: Both traditions show polished surfaces and animal capitals
Mauryan pillars generally have bases like Persian pillars
Mauryan edicts resemble those of Darius in form and some expressions
Mauryan shafts are smooth, while Persian shafts are generally fluted
n60f7fa5da7a.x: Mauryan pillars generally lack the bases characteristic of Persian pillars; the other three statements are correct.
xa: The Mauryan **inverted lotus** bell and round abacus with free-standing animals are distinct.
Verdict: the differences point to an **Indian adaptation**.
Edicts in both shift from **third person** to **first person**.

ne01351c7657.s: The Sarnath capital has special significance in modern India because it is
ne01351c7657.x: The Sarnath capital has been adopted as the National Emblem of India.
ne01351c7657.tq: Distinguish the modern national significance of the capital from other Mauryan architectural distinctions.
xs: The **Sarnath** capital (four lions + Dharmachakra) is now India's **National Emblem** — option **(3)**.
The earliest stone ogee arch is **Lomas Rishi**; the largest brick stupa is **Kesariya**.
xa: Other capitals: **bull – Rampurva**, **single lion – Lauriya Nandangarh**, **elephant – Sankisa**.
Rainfall was measured in **drona** — the Mauryan rain gauge.
Pillars: **Chunar sandstone** with **Mauryan polish**.

n1d8f0c3f635.s: Ashoka and Dasaratha donated the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves to the:
n1d8f0c3f635.x: Ashoka and Dasaratha donated the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves to the Ajivikas, whom the edicts mention as distinct from the Nirgranthas.
xa: The Barabar caves are **India's oldest surviving rock-cut caves** (**3rd c. BCE**).
They lie in **Jehanabad district, Bihar** (near Gaya).
The caves were later used by **Buddhist, Jain and Hindu** worshippers.

n051c78a1bd0.s: Mauryan yaksha-yakshi statues and terracotta figurines belong to which category of art?
n051c78a1bd0.x: Yaksha-yakshi statues and terracotta figurines are folk art; palaces, pillars, stupas and caves are royal art.
xa: Yaksha/yakshi figures are the **earliest large-scale human sculptures** in Indian art.
Folk art arose from **folk worship**, not royal patronage.
Mauryan stone art **began Indian monumental architecture**.

nde2e259000f.s: The nude male torso of early Indian art was found at:
nde2e259000f.x: The nude male torso comes from Lohanipur, Patna; Kumrahar has the 80-pillared hall and Rampurva the bull capital.
xa: **Didarganj** (near Patna) gave the polished sandstone **chauri-bearer Yakshi**.
**Dhauli** (near Bhubaneswar) has the **rock-cut elephant**.
**Manibhadra Yaksha** (inscribed) is from **Parkham** (Mathura) — RPSC **2021** key.
nde2e259000f.fixed: Kanaganahalli Ashoka slab is a Satavahana-era work, not Mauryan art; stem reworded, key unchanged

n2cc15e40836.s: The polished chauri-bearer Didarganj Yakshi belongs to which period?
n2cc15e40836.x: The Didarganj Yakshi is a Mauryan work, like the Dhauli elephant, Ashoka's brick stupa at Sanchi and the Kumrahar hall.
xa: The Dhauli elephant (**3rd c. BCE**) is earlier than **Udayagiri Varaha**, Mahabalipuram and Lingaraja (UPSC **2015**).
Sanchi was later **stone-cased by the Sungas**; toranas added in the **Satavahana** period.
Kumrahar's hall had **8 rows x 10** polished pillars.

n9889349a1c0.s: According to tradition, Ashoka redistributed the Buddha's relics from eight stupas into how many stupas?
n9889349a1c0.x: Tradition states that Ashoka redistributed the relics from the original eight stupas into 84,000 stupas.
xa: **Sanchi (Great Stupa)** has Ashoka's **brick** stupa over relics.
**Dharmarajika** stupas are at **Sarnath** and **Taxila**.
**Kesariya** (Bihar) is the **largest brick stupa**.

n3e30ab62fea.s: Which stupa in Bihar is described as the largest brick stupa?
n3e30ab62fea.x: Kesariya in Bihar is described as the largest brick stupa.
xa: The **Sungas** stone-cased the Sanchi stupa.
⚠ **Sanchi** = India's largest stupa; **Kesariya** = largest brick stupa.
**Bharhut** has sculpted railings with **narrative scenes**.

n07fb34351ea.s: Which archaeological site yielded remains of the wooden palisade of Pataliputra?
n07fb34351ea.x: Bulandibagh yielded remains of the wooden palisade associated with the city of Pataliputra.
n07fb34351ea.tq: Associate the specific excavation site with the structural remains found there.
xs: **Bulandibagh** yielded the remains of a **wooden palisade** — option **(3)**.
**Kumrahar** gave the **80-pillared hall**; **Rampurva** the **bull** capital; **Sarnath** the four-lion capital.
xa: The city was mainly of **timber/wood**.
Megasthenes compared the palace to **Susa and Ecbatana**.
**Fa-Hien** (5th c. CE) admired the palace.

n1276dfcae5b.s: The seven caves located in the Barabar-Nagarjuni group are collectively known as:
n1276dfcae5b.x: The seven caves together are called Satghar, meaning ‘Seven Houses’.
n1276dfcae5b.tq: Direct recall of the collective name of a named group.
xs: The seven caves together are called **Satghar** ("**Seven Houses**") — option **(1)**.
They are **4** Barabar + **3** Nagarjuni caves.
xa: Carved from **granite** with a mirror polish; vaulted ceilings give an **echo**.
Barabar caves were **in the news** in **2026** as the "blueprint" of Indian rock-cut architecture.
Dedicated to the **Ajivikas**.

n72a65135f73.s: The Lomas Rishi cave belongs to which group of caves?
n72a65135f73.x: Lomas Rishi and Karna Chopar belong to Barabar, while Gopika and Vadathika are Nagarjuni caves.
xa: Other Barabar caves: **Sudama**, **Viswamitra**; other Nagarjuni cave: **Vahiyaka**.
**Lomas Rishi** has the **earliest stone ogee arch**.
**Gopika** is the largest Nagarjuni cave and has inscriptions.

nbaeec197b67.s: The dedicatory Brahmi inscriptions in the Barabar caves refer to Ashoka by which title?
nbaeec197b67.x: The dedicatory Brahmi inscriptions refer to Ashoka as ‘King Piyadasi’.
nbaeec197b67.tq: Test the exact royal title used in an inscription.
xs: The dedicatory **Brahmi** inscriptions call Ashoka **"King Piyadasi"** — option **(4)**.
**Three** Barabar caves carry Ashoka's inscriptions.
xa: ⚠ The inscriptions are **3rd c. BCE**, not 6th c. (UPPSC **2017**).
**Gopika** (Nagarjuni) also has inscriptions.
The caves were given to the **Ajivikas**.

nb1f9ecd0d7f.s: The Barabar and Nagarjuni caves are located in which district of Bihar?
nb1f9ecd0d7f.x: The caves are in Jehanabad district, near Gaya, and their dedicatory inscriptions are Mauryan, of the 3rd century BCE.
xa: ⚠ Some notes place the Nagarjuni caves in **Guntur, AP** — a mix-up with **Nagarjunakonda**.
The inscriptions are in **Brahmi** and call Ashoka **"King Piyadasi"**.
The caves were made by **Ashoka** and **Dasharatha**.

n4d3770b1d3c.s: Which feature of the Lomas Rishi cave is regarded as an early example in Indian rock-cut architecture?
o: A stone ogee-shaped arch at the entrance
n4d3770b1d3c.x: The Lomas Rishi entrance has the earliest known stone ogee, or horseshoe-shaped, arch. It imitates the form of a thatched wooden hut.
n4d3770b1d3c.tq: Associate a distinctive architectural feature with its monument.
xs: **Lomas Rishi**'s entrance is the **earliest stone ogee-shaped (horseshoe) arch** — option **(1)**.
It copies a **thatched wooden hut** (the **Parnashala** style).
xa: Lomas Rishi is a **Barabar** cave, with **Sudama**, **Viswamitra** and **Karna Chopar**.
The caves are carved from **granite** with a mirror polish.
FIRSTs: earliest rock-cut caves = **Barabar**; earliest stone ogee arch = **Lomas Rishi**.

nindian-history-66-16.s: The Ranabhar (Ramabhar) Stupa at Kushinagar, over the Buddha's cremation site, was built by the:
nindian-history-66-16.x: Ranabhar Stupa was built by the Mallas, unlike Sanchi, the original Dhamek Stupa and the Kanakamuni Stupa, which are associated with Ashoka.
n: Sanchi Stupa is associated with Ashoka. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
The original structure of Dhamek Stupa is associated with Ashoka. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Ashoka enlarged Kanakamuni Stupa 14 years after his coronation. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
xa: Tradition: Ashoka redistributed the relics into **84,000 stupas**.
**Dharmarajika** stupas stand at **Sarnath** and **Taxila**.
**Kesariya** (Bihar) is the largest brick stupa.

nindian-history-66-17.s: Which stupa was traced by Colin Mackenzie in 1797?
nindian-history-66-17.x: Amaravati was traced by Mackenzie in 1797; Bharhut was discovered by Cunningham, Sanchi is rated finest architecturally and Dhamek's present form is Gupta.
n: Sanchi Stupa is considered the best stupa architecturally. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Alexander Cunningham discovered Bharhut Stupa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Colin Mackenzie traced Amaravati Stupa in 1797. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
The present form of Dhamek Stupa belongs to the Gupta period. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
xa: Sanchi's stone **toranas** with Jataka scenes were added in the **Satavahana** period.
**Bharhut** has sculpted railings with narrative scenes (**Shunga** architecture).
**Dhamek**'s original structure was built by **Ashoka**.

nindian-history-66-18.s: The Kanakamuni Stupa is located at:
nindian-history-66-18.x: Kanakamuni Stupa is at Niglihawa in Nepal; Ranabhar is at Kushinagar and Dhamek at Sarnath.
n: Dhamek Stupa is located in Sarnath, Varanasi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Kanakamuni Stupa is located at Niglihawa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Ranabhar Stupa is associated with Kushinagar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
Ranabhar Stupa is located in Kushinagar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
xa: Ashoka enlarged the Kanakamuni Stupa **14 years** after coronation.
**Sanchi** is in **Raisen**, Madhya Pradesh.
**Amaravati** stands on the **right bank** of the **Krishna**.

nindian-history-66-20.s: Stupa No. 3 at Sanchi is associated with the remains of:
o: Monks of the Ashokan missionary era
nindian-history-66-20.x: Stupa No. 3 holds relics of the Buddha's disciples Sariputra and Mudgalayana; Stupa No. 2 holds relics of monks of the Ashokan missionary era.
n: Stupa No. 1 at Sanchi is the principal or primary stupa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
The remains at Stupa No. 2 at Sanchi are associated with Dhamma Mahamatras. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
The remains at Stupa No. 3 at Sanchi are of Sariputra and Mudgalayana. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #66 · pp 142-143]
xa: **Sanchi** (Raisen, MP) is considered the **best stupa architecturally**.
Ashoka's brick stupa was later **stone-cased by the Sungas**.
**Bharhut** (Satna, MP) was discovered by **Alexander Cunningham**.

nbaff3f6589b.s: The silver coin of the Mauryan period mentioned in the Arthashastra was called
nbaff3f6589b.x: The Arthashastra names the silver coin pana (karshapana). Kakani was a copper coin worth a quarter mashaka; Niska and Shatamana are not the Mauryan silver coin named in the Arthashastra.
nbaff3f6589b.tq: Mauryan silver = Pana (karshapana); copper = mashaka, kakani; gold = suvarna.
xs: The Arthashastra's silver coin was the **Pana (karshapana)** — option **(3)** (APPSC G2 **2011**).
**Kakani** was a **copper** coin worth **1/4 mashaka**; Niska and Shatamana are not the Mauryan silver coin.
xa: **Mashaka** = copper; **Suvarna** = gold.
Punch-marked silver coins bore **peacocks and hills** symbols.
They were minted in **state mints**, with barter continuing.

ne816c452eb1.s: The financial crisis theory of the decline of the Mauryan Empire was given by:
ne816c452eb1.x: Kosambi gave the financial crisis theory; H. P. Shastri gave the Brahmanical reaction theory, Raychaudhuri the pacifism theory and Romila Thapar stressed over-centralisation.
xa: Raychaudhuri: after **Kalinga**, non-violence **dulled the army's fighting spirit**.
Kosambi: army, bureaucracy and **Dhamma** spending emptied the treasury; **debased** coins.
**Divyavadana** evidence: revolts at **Taxila** against wicked officials.

nccf76b2f94f.s: The construction of the Great Wall of China around 220 BC affected the Mauryan north-west mainly because it
o: diverted Scythian tribes westward and southward towards India
forced the Indo-Greeks to migrate to Egypt
ended all contact between China and India
enabled the Mauryas to control Bactria
nccf76b2f94f.x: The Great Wall diverted Scythian tribes towards the west and south, increasing pressure on regions near India while Mauryan frontier defence weakened.
nccf76b2f94f.tq: Trace the stated cause–effect chain in an external-threat question.
xs: The **Great Wall of China** (c. **220 BC**) **diverted Scythian tribes westward and south towards India** — option **(1)**.
This added to the pressure on a north-west frontier the Mauryas had **neglected**.
xa: **Antiochus III** crossed the Hindu Kush c. **206 BC**.
**Bactrian (Indo-Greek)** invasions under **Demetrius** and **Menander**.
Indo-Greek raids **drained resources**.

nc737ca38ddf.s: Which of the following is cited as evidence of the financial crisis of the later Mauryas?
o: Increase in the purity of silver coins
Debasement of later punch-marked silver coins with more alloy
nc737ca38ddf.x: The higher alloy content of later punch-marked silver coins is read as evidence of fiscal strain and debasement.
xa: Other evidence: heavy spending on the **Dhamma mission** and donations to the **Sangha**.
**New taxes on everything**, even actors and prostitutes → revenue hunger.
Kosambi: a huge **army** and **bureaucracy** emptied the treasury.

n92238056657.s: Ashoka's expenditure on which of the following was regarded as a strain on the Mauryan treasury?
o: Dhamma missions and donations to the Sangha
n92238056657.x: Spending on Dhamma missions and donations to the Buddhist Sangha was considered a burden on the treasury.
xa: This supports **Kosambi**'s **financial crisis** theory.
Coins were **debased** — more alloy in the silver.
⚠ **Raychaudhuri** blamed Ashoka's **pacifism**, not his spending.

n43a86558cce.s: After the division of the later Mauryan Empire, the western part was associated with:
n43a86558cce.x: Kunala and later Samprati were associated with the western part, while Dasharatha through Brihadratha ruled the eastern part.
xa: The **Vishnu Purana** lists **seven successors** of Ashoka.
Usual list: **Kunala, Dasharatha, Samprati, Shalishuka, Devavarman, Shatadhanvan, Brihadratha**.
The **Indo-Greeks** virtually replaced the western rulers by **180 BC**.

na9750487c06.s: The western later Mauryan territories were virtually supplanted by the Indo-Greeks by about
na9750487c06.x: The Indo-Greeks had virtually replaced the western later Mauryas by about 180 BC.
na9750487c06.tq: Distinguish the date of western displacement from the dates of Mauryan succession.
xs: The **Indo-Greeks** virtually replaced the western later Mauryas by **180 BC** — option **(4)**.
**232 BC** is Ashoka's death; **187 BC** is the Sunga coup.
xa: The western rulers were **Kunala** and later **Samprati**.
Indo-Greek leaders: **Demetrius**, later **Menander**.
**Antiochus III** crossed the Hindu Kush c. **206 BC**.

nd2ad6141ed0.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a factor in the decline of the Mauryan Empire?
o: Weak and oppressive successors after Ashoka
A permanent alliance with the Indo-Greeks
nd2ad6141ed0.x: A permanent alliance with the Indo-Greeks was not a cause of Mauryan decline. Indo-Greek raids and pressure were among the external problems faced by the empire.
nd2ad6141ed0.tq: Find the option that reverses the recorded cause into an alliance.
xs: A **permanent alliance with the Indo-Greeks** was not a cause — option **(4)**; the Indo-Greeks were in fact **invaders**.
**Weak, oppressive successors**, **neglect of the north-west frontier** and **super-heavy taxation** are all listed causes (UPSC).
xa: Indo-Greek raids **drained resources**.
Financial strain: **Dhamma** spending, gifts to the **Sangha**, **debased** coins.
Taxes fell even on **actors and prostitutes** (Arthashastra).

na5c184790b2.s: Who founded the Sunga dynasty in Magadha?
na5c184790b2.x: Pushyamitra Sunga founded the Sunga dynasty after overthrowing the Mauryas.
xs: The Sunga dynasty was founded by **Pushyamitra Sunga**, the Mauryan **commander-in-chief (senani)** — option **(3)**.
**Brihadratha** was the last Maurya; **Vasudeva Kanva** founded the **Kanva** dynasty.
xa: The Sungas were the **immediate successors** of the Mauryas in Magadha (APPSC G2 **2003**).
Pushyamitra was a **Brahmana** of the **Bharadvaja gotra**.
He performed **two Ashvamedhas**.

ne4f6aa22b57.s: Pushyamitra Sunga seized power from the Mauryas by
o: defeating the Indo-Greeks in the north-west
obtaining the throne through a council of ministers
assassinating Brihadratha during an army review
marrying into the Mauryan royal family
ne4f6aa22b57.x: Pushyamitra, the Mauryan commander-in-chief, killed Brihadratha during a military review, thereby carrying out a military coup.
ne4f6aa22b57.tq: Identify the actor, occasion and manner of accession.
xs: Pushyamitra **assassinated Brihadratha at a military review** of the army — option **(3)** (APPSC **2023**; BPSC **2008**).
It was a **military coup** by the Mauryan **commander-in-chief**.
xa: The army-review detail comes from **Bana's Harshacharita**.
Year: **187 BC** (UPSC); some notes say c. **185 BCE**.
⚠ BPSC **2008** key — the king killed was **Brihadratha**.

n768b36c6197.s: The Sunga dynasty was founded approximately in
n768b36c6197.x: The Sunga dynasty is generally dated to 187 BC, though some accounts give approximately 185 BCE.
n768b36c6197.tq: Distinguish the close alternative dates by placing the key in the chronological sequence.
xs: The Sungas came to power in **187 BC** (UPSC) — option **(3)**.
Some notes and the AP History PYQ book give c. **185 BCE**.
**232 BC** is Ashoka's death; **206 BC** Antiochus III; **180 BC** the Indo-Greek takeover in the west.
xa: The coup: **Pushyamitra** killed **Brihadratha** at a military review.
Order in Magadha: **Mauryas → Sungas → Kanvas**.
The Kanvas ruled c. **73-28 BC**.

n0703d3a1837.s: Which Bactrian (Indo-Greek) rulers threatened the north-west of the Mauryan Empire after Ashoka?
n0703d3a1837.x: Bactrian or Indo-Greek invasions associated with Demetrius and later Menander threatened the north-west after Ashoka.
xa: **Antiochus III (Seleucid)** crossed the Hindu Kush c. **206 BC**.
The **Great Wall of China** (c. **220 BC**) diverted **Scythian** tribes towards India.
**Menander (Milinda)** had his capital at **Sakala (Sialkot)**.

n57611f47bc6.s: Antiochus III crossed the Hindu Kush around 206 BC and obtained tribute from
n57611f47bc6.x: Antiochus III crossed the Hindu Kush around 206 BC and took tribute from the local ruler Subhagasena.
n57611f47bc6.tq: Match the foreign ruler, approximate date and local ruler.
xs: **Antiochus III** took tribute from the local ruler **Subhagasena** — option **(4)**.
He was a **Seleucid** king who crossed the **Hindu Kush** c. **206 BC**.
**Demetrius** and **Menander** were Indo-Greek invaders; **Jalauka** ruled **Kashmir**.
xa: The **Great Wall** (c. **220 BC**) pushed **Scythian** tribes towards India.
The Mauryas **neglected frontier defence** (UPSC).
By **180 BC** the Indo-Greeks had virtually replaced the western Mauryas.

n9cf4ce1914e.s: The Andhra or Deccan region broke away from Mauryan control under the
o: Satavahanas, who had earlier been Mauryan feudatories
n9cf4ce1914e.x: The Satavahanas, earlier Mauryan feudatories, emerged as the breakaway power in the Andhra or Deccan region.
n9cf4ce1914e.tq: Distinguish the Deccan breakaway power from the powers of Kalinga and the north-west.
xs: **Andhra/Deccan** broke away under the **Satavahanas**, earlier **Mauryan feudatories** — option **(2)**.
**Kharavela** (Chedi) led **Kalinga**; the **Kanvas** ruled Magadha; **Menander** was Indo-Greek in the north-west.
xa: The Puranas call the Satavahanas **Andhra-bhrityas**.
Founder: **Simuka (Srimukha)**.
Ashokan edicts at **Erragudi** and **Rajula Mandagiri** (Kurnool) show Mauryan rule in Andhra.

na2525d0d82f.s: Yajnasena, mentioned in Malavikagnimitram, was associated with the breakaway of
na2525d0d82f.x: Yajnasena is associated with Vidarbha in the account of the regions that broke away after Ashoka.
xs: **Yajnasena** (Malavikagnimitram) is linked with the breakaway of **Vidarbha** — option **(2)** (UPSC).
**Kalinga** broke away under the **Chedis (Kharavela)**; **Kashmir** under **Jalauka**.
xa: **Malavikagnimitram** is by **Kalidasa**.
It also records **Vasumitra** defeating a **Yavana** army on the **Sindhu**.
The **north-west** fell to the **Indo-Greeks**.

neae65e4d2ee.s: The Puranas refer to the Satavahanas as:
neae65e4d2ee.x: The Satavahanas, earlier Mauryan feudatories, are called Andhra-bhrityas in the Puranas.
xa: Founder: **Simuka (Srimukha)**.
They **defeated the Sunga-Kanva line**, ending **Susharman**.
Other Deccan feudatory chiefs: **Bhojas, Maharathis, Rashtrikas**.

na5cc1154536.s: Pushyamitra Sunga belonged to which gotra and held which position before founding the Sunga dynasty?
na5cc1154536.x: Pushyamitra Sunga was a Brahmana of the Bharadvaja gotra and served as a senapati.
na5cc1154536.tq: Test the identity of a ruler through the paired details of lineage and office.
xs: Pushyamitra was a **Brahmana senapati** of the **Bharadvaja gotra** — option **(4)**.
He was the Mauryan **commander-in-chief (senani)** who killed Brihadratha.
xa: He led a strong **Brahmanical revival** with **two Ashvamedhas**.
**Patanjali** is linked with his court.
The Sunga core: **Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha, Narmada valley**.

ncfb68eda222.s: Which inscription refers to the two Ashvamedha sacrifices of Pushyamitra Sunga?
ncfb68eda222.x: Pushyamitra performed two Ashvamedhas, referred to in the Ayodhya inscription of Dhanadeva.
xa: He was a **Brahmana** of the **Bharadvaja gotra**.
⚠ **Divyavadana** calls him a **persecutor of Buddhists** — disputed.
His grandson **Vasumitra** beat a **Yavana** army on the **Sindhu**.

nf3535bd8513.s: According to Malavikagnimitram, who defeated a Yavana army on the Sindhu river?
nf3535bd8513.x: Malavikagnimitram records that Vasumitra, the grandson of Pushyamitra, defeated a Yavana army on the Sindhu river.
nf3535bd8513.tq: Distinguish the commander who won the battle from the ruler whose dynasty was involved.
xs: **Kalidasa's Malavikagnimitram** says **Vasumitra**, Pushyamitra's grandson, defeated a **Yavana** army on the **Sindhu** — option **(4)**.
**Menander** and **Demetrius** were the Indo-Greek (Yavana) side.
xa: The same play names **Yajnasena** of **Vidarbha**.
Pushyamitra held the Ganga heartland against **Demetrius** and **Menander**.
Menander debated **Nagasena** in the **Milindapanho**.

n225ca970c33.s: The Kanva dynasty was founded by Vasudeva Kanva after he killed the last Sunga ruler
n225ca970c33.x: Vasudeva Kanva, a Brahmana minister, killed Devabhuti, the last Sunga, and seized power. Vasumitra and Agnimitra were earlier Sungas, and Brihadratha was the last Maurya, killed by Pushyamitra.
n225ca970c33.tq: Devabhuti (last Sunga) killed by Vasudeva Kanva; Brihadratha (last Maurya) killed by Pushyamitra.
xs: **Vasudeva Kanva**, a Brahmana minister, killed the last Sunga **Devabhuti** — option **(3)** (UPSC **2003**).
**Vasumitra** was Pushyamitra's grandson; **Brihadratha** was the last Maurya, killed by **Pushyamitra**.
xa: The Kanvas ruled c. **73-28 BC**.
The last Kanva **Susharman** fell to the **Satavahanas**.
Order: **Mauryas → Sungas → Kanvas**.

n254da32bf80.s: The Hathigumpha inscription gives a year-by-year record of the reign of:
n254da32bf80.x: The Hathigumpha inscription in the Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves of Odisha records Kharavela's reign year by year; it belongs to the 2nd century BC.
xa: Kharavela was a **Jaina** king of the **Chedi (Mahameghavahana)** line.
He raided **Magadha** and brought back the **Jina image** the Nandas had taken.
⚠ **Nanaghat** is **Naganika**'s inscription, not Rudradaman's.

nf45b2d3506a.s: Who was regarded as the founder of the Satavahana dynasty?
nf45b2d3506a.x: Simuka, also known as Srimukha, is regarded as the founder of the Satavahana dynasty.
nf45b2d3506a.tq: Distinguish the dynasty's founder from rulers and founders of neighbouring post-Mauryan houses.
xs: The Satavahana founder was **Simuka (Srimukha)** — option **(3)**.
**Vasumitra** was a Sunga; **Vasudeva Kanva** founded the Kanvas; **Satakarni** was the king Kharavela ignored.
xa: The Puranas call the Satavahanas **Andhra-bhrityas**.
They were **feudatories of the Mauryas** before independence.
They were the **first to unite the Krishna-Godavari region**.

n0b6452dedaf.s: Which literary work contains the earliest reference to the Andhras as a people in the story of Sunahshepa?
n0b6452dedaf.x: The Aitareya Brahmana gives the earliest literary reference to the Andhras. In the Sunahshepa story, Vishwamitra cursed fifty of his sons to become Andhras, Pundras and Pulindas.
n0b6452dedaf.tq: Identify the earliest source by linking the text with its distinctive narrative.
xs: The **Aitareya Brahmana** gives the first mention of the Andhras as a people — option **(4)**.
In the **Sunahshepa** story, **Vishwamitra** cursed his **50 sons** to become **Andhras, Pundras, Pulindas**.
The **Mahabharata** and **Vayu Purana** mention the Andhras later; the **Mahavamsa** is a Buddhist chronicle.
xa: ⚠ **Aitareya Brahmana** = first mention; **Rigveda** = no mention.
The first **foreign** source to mention the Andhras is Megasthenes' **Indica**.
The **13th Major Rock Edict** lists the Andhras among peoples following Ashoka's Dhamma.

n82ffc12e1e9.s: According to the Mahabharata, the Andhras fought on the side of the:
n82ffc12e1e9.x: The Mahabharata states that the Andhras fought on the Kaurava side; the Rigveda does not mention them and the Vayu Purana places them in the Deccan.
xa: First mention: **Aitareya Brahmana** (Sunahshepa story).
**Anguttara Nikaya** names **Assaka**.
**Kathavatthu** names the **Andhakas** as a Buddhist school.

nab728fda15d.s: According to the Chulla-Kalinga Jataka, the king of Assaka (Asmaka) defeated the king of:
nab728fda15d.x: The Chulla-Kalinga Jataka records the Kalinga–Assaka conflict in which the king of Assaka defeated the king of Kalinga.
xa: **Assaka (Asmaka)** was a Mahajanapada on the **Godavari**, capital **Bodhan (Podana)**.
**Anguttara Nikaya** names Assaka.
⚠ Kharavela's own record is the **Hathigumpha** inscription.

n291d679196c.s: Which text refers to the 'Andhapatha' (Andhra Path)?
n291d679196c.x: The Vinayavatthu mentions Andhapatha (APPSC G2 2019). The Suttanipata has the Bavari story, the Kathavatthu mentions the Andhaka school, and the Mahavamsa is a Sri Lankan Buddhist chronicle.
n291d679196c.tq: Andhra Path = Vinayavatthu, not Suttanipata or the Jatakas.
xs: The **Vinayavatthu** mentions **"Andhapatha" (Andhra Path)** — option **(2)** (G2 **2019**).
The **Suttanipata** has the **Bavari** story; the **Kathavatthu** names the **Andhakas**; the **Mahavamsa** is a Buddhist chronicle.
xa: The **Bhimasena Jataka** marks out the region as **Andhrapatha**.
Exam angle: Andhra Path = Vinayavatthu, not Suttanipata or the Jatakas.
**Chulla-Kalinga Jataka**: Asmaka king **Satakarni** defeats **Kharavela**.

n614cc5739b5.s: According to the Bavari legend, how many disciples were sent to the Buddha?
n614cc5739b5.x: Bavari sent sixteen disciples to meet the Buddha. The episode is preserved in the Suttanipata, in the Parayana-vagga.
n614cc5739b5.tq: Fix the exact number associated with a narrative episode and distinguish it from nearby conventional numbers.
xs: **Bavari** sent **16 (sixteen) disciples** to the Buddha — option **(3)**.
The story is in the **Suttanipata (Parayana-vagga)**.
xa: Bavari was a Brahmin from **Kosala**, settled on the **Godavari** in Assaka.
It shows Buddhism reached the Godavari **before the Mauryas**.
⚠ "Andhra Path" is in the **Vinayavatthu**, not the Suttanipata.

n9c7f6de8c10.s: Bavari, who settled in Assaka territory on the Godavari, was originally a Brahmin teacher from:
n9c7f6de8c10.x: Bavari was a Brahmin teacher from Kosala who settled on the Godavari in Assaka territory.
n9c7f6de8c10.tq: Identify the person through the origin–settlement combination.
xs: **Bavari** was a Brahmin teacher from **Kosala** — option **(4)**.
He settled on the **Godavari** in **Assaka** territory.
xa: He sent **16 disciples** to the Buddha (Suttanipata, Parayana-vagga).
So Buddhist ideas reached the Godavari **before the Mauryan expansion**.
Assaka's capital was **Bodhan (Podana)**.

nc7c03ce785c.s: The Bavari legend suggests that Buddhist ideas reached the Godavari region:
nc7c03ce785c.x: The Bavari legend indicates that Buddhist ideas had reached the Godavari region before Mauryan expansion.
xa: He sent **16 disciples** to the Buddha.
Later, **Mahadeva Bhikshu** — sent by Ashoka — was the first Buddhist teacher in Andhra.
The **Mauryan phase** made Buddhism **institutional** in Andhra.

nd8540b277c0.s: Who is associated with the first Buddhist teaching mission to Andhra and the enshrinement of Buddha’s bone relics at Amaravati?
nd8540b277c0.x: Ashoka sent Mahadeva Bhikshu to Amaravati. He is regarded as the first Buddhist teacher in Andhra and is associated with enshrining Buddha’s bone relics there.
nd8540b277c0.tq: Identify the missionary figure by matching the person with the specific act and destination.
xs: **Mahadeva Bhikshu**, sent by Ashoka to **Amaravati** (Andhra tradition), was the **first Buddhist teacher in Andhra** and enshrined the Buddha's **bone relics** there — option **(4)**.
**Bavari** sent disciples to the Buddha; **Megasthenes** was a Greek ambassador.
xa: Amaravati also has a **fragment of an Ashokan pillar edict**.
Amaravati-Dharanikota = **Andhranagari / Dhanyakataka** on the **Krishna**.
**P.C. Ray** identified the river there as the Krishna.

nf6dc7c4fd4a.s: Andhranagari or Dhanyakataka is identified with:
nf6dc7c4fd4a.x: Andhranagari, also called Dhanyakataka, is identified with Amaravati-Dharanikota on the Krishna River. The river identification is associated with P. C. Ray.
nf6dc7c4fd4a.tq: Distinguish ancient place names by combining the modern site and river clues.
xs: **Andhranagari / Dhanyakataka** = **Amaravati-Dharanikota on the Krishna** — option **(1)**.
**P.C. Ray** identified the river there as the **Krishna**.
**Guntupalli** = Siddharthaka chaitya; **Bodhan** was Assaka's capital; **Nagarjunakonda** = Sriparvata.
xa: **Mahadeva Bhikshu** enshrined the Buddha's **bone relics** at Amaravati.
Amaravati has a fragment of an **Ashokan pillar edict**.
**Sriparvata / Vijayapuri** = Nagarjunakonda.

nfdbfe071b6d.s: Which early historic site in Krishna district shows continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times?
nfdbfe071b6d.x: Gudiwada Dibba in Krishna district is an early historic mound showing continuous occupation from Mauryan to Satavahana times.
nfdbfe071b6d.tq: Use the site–district–cultural sequence combination for archaeological identification.
xs: **Gudiwada Dibba** (Krishna district) shows continuous occupation from **Mauryan to Satavahana** times — option **(2)**.
**Adurru** was a Mahasanghika centre; **Rajula Mandagiri** has an Ashokan minor edict; **Nagarjunakonda** is ancient Sriparvata.
xa: The **Nagarjunasagar valley** digs give material proof of early Andhra settlement.
⚠ Some notes place **Siddharthaka chaitya** at Gudiwada; the key says **Guntupalli**.
Andhra was a distinct region **before the Satavahanas**.

n1480cab3918.s: Adurru, located in East Godavari district, was an important centre of the:
n1480cab3918.x: Adurru in East Godavari district was a Mahasanghika Buddhist centre.
n1480cab3918.tq: Match the archaeological site with its religious affiliation.
xs: **Adurru** (East Godavari) was a **Mahasanghika** Buddhist centre — option **(4)**.
The **Andhakas** were a separate Buddhist school (Kathavatthu, Third Council).
xa: **Gudiwada Dibba** shows Mauryan-to-Satavahana occupation.
**Nagarjunasagar valley** excavations prove early Andhra settlement.
The Mauryan phase made Buddhism **institutional** in Andhra.

n32e22da705f.s: Which Brahmana text refers to Andhra as a people before the Satavahana period?
n32e22da705f.x: Andhra appears as a people in the Aitareya Brahmana, as well as in Buddhist texts, Megasthenes' Indica and Ashoka's 13th Rock Edict, all before the Satavahanas.
xa: The **Mauryan phase** made Buddhism **institutional**.
Megasthenes counted **30 forts** of the Andhras.
Ashokan edicts in Andhra: **Erragudi**, **Rajula Mandagiri**, **Amaravati**.

o: The Satavahana conquest of the Deccan
n6b8869608ee.x: Mudrarakshasa concerns Chandragupta Maurya and the establishment of Mauryan power, so it is not used for the Yavana invasion in Pushyamitra's reign.
xa: Mudrarakshasa is by **Visakhadatta**.
Gargi Samhita: Yavanas advanced on **Saketa, Panchala, Mathura, Pataliputra**.
Mahabhashya: Yavana siege of **Saketa** and **Madhyamika**.

n7ec4ac5d30b.s: According to the Puranic tradition, which dynasties were defeated by the Satavahanas?
n7ec4ac5d30b.x: The Puranas state that the Satavahanas defeated the Sunga and Kanva dynasties.
n7ec4ac5d30b.tq: Identify the specific predecessor dynasties associated with a later dynastic conquest.
xs: The Puranas say the **Satavahanas defeated the Sungas and Kanvas** (Sunga and Kanva dynasties) — option **(3)**.
**Simuka (Srimukha)**, the Satavahana founder, overthrew the last Kanva **Susharman**.
xa: AP angle: **Satakarni I** is said to have defeated **Pushyamitra**.
The Sungas had already lost the **Deccan** to the Satavahanas.
Order: **Maurya → Sunga → Kanva → Kushana**.

ndc178d2fdc6.s: Which powerful feudatories rose during the Sunga period?
ndc178d2fdc6.x: Bhojas, Maharathis and Rastrikas rose as powerful feudatories, while the Sungas broadly kept Mauryan administrative institutions.
xa: Sunga heartland: **Magadha, Malwa-Vidisha, Narmada valley**.
The Sungas were **Brahmins**.
The north-west was lost to the **Yavanas**, the Deccan to the **Satavahanas**.

ne777b8edaef.s: The Manusmriti is said to have taken its early shape during the Sunga period and classified foreigners as:
ne777b8edaef.x: The Manusmriti took early shape in this period and classified foreigners as Vratya Kshatriyas.
ne777b8edaef.tq: Recall the exact technical social category instead of a broad caste label.
xs: The **Manusmriti**, taking shape in this period, classed foreigners as **"Vratya Kshatriyas"** — option **(4)**.
So foreigners were fitted into the varna order as Kshatriyas who had lapsed, not as Shudras or Brahmanas.
xa: Foreigners were also absorbed via **Bhagavatism** — e.g. **Heliodorus**.
The Sunga court revived **classical Sanskrit**.
The period is marked by a **Brahmanical revival**.

nindian-history-143-3.s: The Shunga dynasty ruled approximately during which period?
nindian-history-143-3.x: The Shungas ruled from about 185 BCE, when Brihadratha was killed, to about 73 BCE, when Vasudeva Kanva killed Devabhuti.
nindian-history-143-3.tq: Recall the start and end dates of Shunga rule.
n: The Shunga dynasty existed approximately from 185 BCE to 73 BCE. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #143 · pp 248-250]
xs: The **Shunga dynasty** ruled approximately **185 BCE to 73 BCE** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It began when **Pushyamitra Shunga** assassinated **Brihadratha**, the last Mauryan, in **185 BCE**.
It ended when **Devabhuti**, the last Shunga, was killed by his minister **Vasudeva Kanva**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes give **187-75 BC** (UPSC: **187-78 BC**).
⚠ APPSC GS **2023** key dates Brihadratha's killing to **187 BC**.
Sequence: **Maurya → Sunga → Kanva → Kushana** (BPSC **2025**).
The **Kanvas** ruled c. **73-28 BC**; their last king **Susharman** was overthrown by **Simuka**.

nindian-history-143-15.s: Who was the last ruler of the Shunga dynasty?
nindian-history-143-15.x: Devabhuti was the last Shunga ruler; he was killed by his minister Vasudeva Kanva.
n: Pushyamitra Shunga founded the Shunga dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #143 · pp 248-250]
Brihadratha was the last Mauryan ruler. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #143 · pp 248-250]
Devabhuti was the last ruler of the Shunga dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #143 · pp 248-250]
Devabhuti was killed by his minister, Amatya Vasudeva Kanva. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #143 · pp 248-250]
xa: **Pushyamitra** was Brihadratha's **commander**; he killed him in **185 BCE**.
**Harshacharita** says Pushyamitra killed Brihadratha while showing him the army.
Pushyamitra and the succeeding **Kanvas** were described as **Brahmins**.

nindian-history-29-12.s: In which year did the Tuluva dynasty begin its rule at Vijayanagara?
nindian-history-29-12.x: Vijayanagara was ruled by the Sangama (from 1336), Saluva (1485), Tuluva (1505) and Aravidu (1570) dynasties in turn.
n: The Saluva Dynasty succeeded the Sangama Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
The Tuluva Dynasty succeeded the Saluva Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
The Aravidu Dynasty succeeded the Tuluva Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
xa: Delhi Sultanate: **Slave → Khalji → Tughlaq → Sayyid → Lodi**.
**Nanda** succeeded **Shishunaga** in Magadha.
**Vasudeva Kanva** succeeded **Devabhuti** of the Shunga dynasty.

nindian-history-29-14.s: Which dynasty immediately preceded the Lodi dynasty in the Delhi Sultanate?
nindian-history-29-14.x: The sequence was Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, so the Sayyids preceded the Lodis.
n: The Khalji Dynasty succeeded the Slave Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
The Tughlaq Dynasty succeeded the Khalji Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
The Sayyid Dynasty succeeded the Tughlaq Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
The Lodi Dynasty succeeded the Sayyid Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
xa: Vijayanagara: **Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu**.
Magadha: **Shishunaga → Nanda**; later **Maurya → Shunga → Kanva**.
**Simuka** succeeded **Susharma** of the Kanva dynasty.

nindian-history-29-20.s: Which dynasty immediately preceded the Nanda Dynasty in Magadha?
nindian-history-29-20.x: The Nanda dynasty replaced the Shishunaga dynasty in Magadha, Mahapadma Nanda having overthrown the last Shishunaga king. The Haryankas came before the Shishunagas; the Mauryas and Shungas came after the Nandas.
nindian-history-29-20.tq: Recall the Magadhan sequence: Haryanka, Shishunaga, Nanda, Maurya.
n: The Nanda Dynasty succeeded the Shishunaga Dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 95-96]
xs: The **Shishunaga Dynasty** immediately preceded the **Nanda Dynasty** — so option **(1)** is correct.

nb025a24edff.s: Who united the five Yuezhi clans and took the Kabul valley and Kashmir?
nb025a24edff.x: Kujula Kadphises (Kadphises I) united the five clans; Vima Kadphises (Kadphises II) extended the empire to Mathura and Varanasi.
xa: **Kujula Kadphises** issued **copper** coins (c. **15-64 CE**).
**Vima Kadphises** was the first to issue **gold coins** on a **large scale**; title **Sarvalokeshvara**.
Rabatak genealogy: **Kujula → Vima Taktu → Vima Kadphises → Kanishka**.

na393dd5e026.s: Who was the last great Kushana ruler?
na393dd5e026.x: Vasudeva I was the last great Kushan; Kanishka represented the zenith and Huvishka was his successor.

Kanishka's capitals: **Purushapura (Peshawar)** and **Mathura**.

nee33dfb0419.s: The Kushana ruler who, as a devotee of Shiva, took the titles 'Maheshvara' and 'Sarvaloka Ishvara' was
nee33dfb0419.x: Vima Kadphises (Kadphises II), a Shiva devotee, called himself Maheshvara and Sarvaloka Ishvara (RPSC 2024). Kujula united the Yuezhi clans, Kanishka took Devaputra and the other titles, and Huvishka was Kanishka's successor.
xs: **Vima Kadphises** (Kadphises II), a **Shiva devotee**, took **Maheshvara** and **Sarvaloka Ishvara** — option **(2)** is correct (RPSC **2024**).

**Huvishka** was Kanishka's successor.

Shiva appears with **Nandi** on Kushana coins.

n4b193842d09.s: Which of the following sequences represents the genealogy given in the Rabatak inscription?
o: Kujula Kadphises → Vima Taktu → Vima Kadphises → Kanishka
Vima Taktu → Kujula Kadphises → Kanishka → Vima Kadphises
Kanishka → Vima Kadphises → Vima Taktu → Kujula Kadphises
Kujula Kadphises → Kanishka → Huvishka → Vima Taktu
n4b193842d09.x: The Rabatak inscription gives the succession as Kujula Kadphises, Vima Taktu, Vima Kadphises and Kanishka.
n4b193842d09.tq: Arrange the rulers using the inscriptional genealogy rather than general dynastic prominence.
xs: Rabatak genealogy: **Kujula Kadphises → Vima Taktu → Vima Kadphises → Kanishka** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Rabatak inscription** is in **Afghanistan**, written in **Bactrian**.
**Huvishka** was Kanishka's successor, so he cannot precede Vima Taktu.

**Sarnath** image inscription: Bodhisattva by **Friar Bala**, **year 3 of Kanishka**.
**Vasudeva I** was the **last great Kushan**.

n1c4ae7b1b06.s: Which ruler first issued gold coins on a large scale in India?
n1c4ae7b1b06.x: Vima Kadphises first issued gold coins on a large scale (BPSC 2018). The Indo-Greeks such as Menander issued the first gold coins but rarely, Kujula Kadphises issued copper coins, and Kanishka continued the gold issues.
n1c4ae7b1b06.tq: First gold = Indo-Greeks; first large-scale gold = Vima Kadphises.
xs: **Vima Kadphises** first issued **gold coins on a large scale** — option **(3)** is correct (BPSC **2018**).
**Kujula Kadphises** issued **copper** coins.
**Kanishka** came after Vima, so he was not first.
xa: ⚠ Copper = **Kujula**; large-scale gold = **Vima Kadphises**.
Gold dinara: about **8 g (120 grains)**, **22-23 carat**; Roman aurei probably melted down.
Daily trade used plentiful **copper and lead** coins.

n5cb3b8211cc.s: Kushana trade contributed to which development in India?

The decline of Mathura and Taxila

Kanishka's capitals: **Purushapura** and **Mathura**.

**Kanishka**'s gold and copper coins bear the **Buddha**.

n154f986361e.s: The Kushana royal title 'Devaputra' reflected influence from:
n154f986361e.x: Devaputra reflected Chinese influence, Shaonano Shao Persian, Kaisara Roman and Maharaja Indian traditions.
xa: These four titles belong to **Kanishka**.
**Vima Kadphises** took **"Sarvaloka Ishvara"** and **Maheshvara** as a Shiva devotee.
Kanishka's empire ran from the **Oxus** to the **Ganga**.

n6e3746f8533.s: The Kushanas played the role of middlemen in trade linking which of the following regions?
n6e3746f8533.x: The Kushanas acted as Silk Road intermediaries connecting Han China, Rome and India.

xs: The Kushanas were **Silk Road middlemen** between **Han China, Rome and India** — option **(1)** is correct.

xa: Urban centres: **Mathura, Taxila, Ujjain, Shravasti**.
Their **gold dinara** followed the **Roman weight** standard.
Kushana rule **led into the Gupta age** (UPSC).

nabfcbdb0b6d.x: Purushapura (Peshawar) was the main/winter capital; Mathura was another capital and Surkh Kotal only a provincial centre.
xa: **Mathura** was another capital.

Kanishka clashed in Central Asia with Chinese general **Pan Chao (Ban Chao)**.

n0ab87d7aafd.s: The era of 78 CE is usually credited to Kanishka, but some accounts credit which ruler with starting the Salivahana era?
n0ab87d7aafd.x: Some accounts credit Gautamiputra Satakarni with starting the Salivahana era, though the 78 CE era is commonly credited to Kanishka.
xa: It is called the **Saka era** because the **Western Kshatrapas (Sakas)** used it on records and coins.

n8a2e6e3a7e1.s: The era beginning in 78 CE came to be called the Saka era because it was used by:
o: The Western Kshatrapas in their records and coins
n8a2e6e3a7e1.x: The Western Kshatrapas, who were Sakas, used the era on their records and coins, so it became known as the Saka era.
xa: Some notes credit **Gautamiputra Satakarni** — the **Salivahana era (AD 78)**.
It became India's **national calendar in 1957**.
Also called **Salivahana Saka**.

n39423cd3d02.s: The era beginning in 78 CE is also called:
n39423cd3d02.x: The era of 78 CE is also called Salivahana Saka and became India's national calendar in 1957.
xa: Named **Saka era** because the **Western Kshatrapas** used it on records and coins.
It began in **78 CE**.

n824d8cfac81.s: Under the Kushanas, Buddhism shifted from Pali-Prakrit Hinayana to:
n824d8cfac81.x: The Kushana shift was to Sanskrit Mahayana, whose followers made images of the Buddha and worshipped him as a god.
xa: Mahayana developed after the **Fourth Council**.
First Buddha images: **1st century CE**, in **Gandhara and Mathura** styles.
Spread to **Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan**.

n21bfd32efd9.s: During the period associated with the Kushanas, Buddhism spread to:
o: Central Asia, China, Korea and Japan

Councils: **1st** Rajagriha, **2nd** Vaishali, **3rd** Pataliputra, **4th** Kashmir.

nindian-history-142-25.s:

Daily trade used plentiful **copper and lead** coins.

n480cd5c987f.s: Which of the following items of dress was introduced into India by the Shakas and Kushanas?

nd4b3e845fc3.s: Standing Buddha images became prominent in which phase of the Mathura school?
