Mathura is also the **Vaishnava** centre.
**Udayagiri** (MP): **1 Jain cave** among **20**.

n46c1d1c144d.s: The raised platform on which Gupta temples stood is called the:
n46c1d1c144d.x: Gupta temples established the square garbhagriha, pillared mandapa, pradakshina path and raised jagati platform.
xa: These mark the beginning of the **Nagara style**.
**Panchayatana** plan first at **Deogarh**.
No free-standing Hindu temple survives **before the Guptas**.

n37c6136d9cd.s: The earliest surviving free-standing Hindu temples belong to the period of the:
n37c6136d9cd.x: No free-standing Hindu temple survives from a period earlier than the Guptas.
xa: Stages: **Sanchi 17, Tigawa** → **Nachna, Bhumara** → **Deogarh, Bhitargaon**.
Gupta age = **Golden Age of art and architecture**.
Iconography of Brahmanical, Jain and Buddhist deities was **standardised**.

n3cdd42f2562.s: Compared with the Mauryan period, Gupta-age religious emphasis shifted from sacrifice to:
n3cdd42f2562.x: The Gupta shift was from sacrifice to temple worship and bhakti; the age is also called the Golden Age of art.
xa: Mauryan religion = **Vedic + Shramana**.
**Idol worship in temples** became common.
No free-standing Hindu temple survives **before the Guptas**.

n1f9a53cd701.s: Nandivarman II's Pedavegi inscription is regarded as the first inscription in Andhra Pradesh relating to:
n1f9a53cd701.x: The Pedavegi inscription of Nandivarman II is regarded as the first inscription in Andhra Pradesh concerning Vishnu temples.
xa: Salankayanas also used Shaiva **Parama Mahesvara** titles.
**Gudimallam's Parasurameswara** temple = oldest Shiva linga (APPSC G2 **2008**).
**Kapalikas**: **Bhairavakonda** caves.

nfe03e963530.s: The Pashupata sect, the oldest Shaiva sect, was founded by:
nfe03e963530.x: Pashupata, the oldest Shaiva sect, was founded by Lakulisha (Nakulisha); in it pashu is the individual soul and pati the Supreme soul.
xa: Lakulisha is placed in the **1st c. CE** per some notes.
**Kalamukhas** followed **Kalanana**, a disciple of Lakulisha.
Pashupata and Kalamukha later flourished under the **Kakatiyas**.

n825c9da3edd.s: Which pair of sects later flourished under the Kakatiyas?
n825c9da3edd.x: The Kalamukha and Pashupata sects later flourished under the Kakatiyas.
n825c9da3edd.tq: Start from the sure pair and reject combinations formed by mixing unrelated religious traditions.
xs: **Kalamukha and Pashupata** later flourished under the **Kakatiyas** — option **(2)**.
**Pashupata** = oldest Shaiva sect (founder **Lakulisha**); **Kalamukhas** followed **Kalanana**.
xa: Kalamukha: **Simha Parishat** (Andhra), **Shakti Parishat** (Karnataka).
**Kapalikas**: **Bhairavakonda** caves (AP).
**Gudimallam** (Tirupati district) = oldest Shiva linga.

nindian-history-51-32.s: The Lingayat sect followed the teachings of:
nindian-history-51-32.x: Lingayats followed Basava; Pashupata was founded by Lakulisha and the Nathpanth led by Matsyendranath and Gorakhnath.
n: Pashupata is associated with Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Lakulisha is associated with Pashupata. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Kapalika is associated with Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Kapalika is associated with Bhairava. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Kapalika is associated with skull symbolism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Kapalika is associated with cremation ashes. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Lingayat is associated with Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Basav is associated with Lingayat. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Nathpanth is associated with Shaivism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Matsyendranath was associated with Nathpanth. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
Gorakhnath was associated with Nathpanth. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 121-126]
xa: Pashupata is the **oldest Shaiva sect**; pashu = individual soul, pati = Supreme soul.
Nathpanthis regarded **Shiva** as **Adinath**.
**Kalamukha** — followers of **Kalanana**; **Simha Parishat** in Andhra, **Shakti Parishat** in Karnataka.
**Bhairavakonda** caves (AP) belong to the **Kapalikas**.

nca2e2cccc32.x: Buddhaghosa wrote the Visuddhimagga; Vasubandhu wrote the Abhidharmakosa and Dinnaga founded Buddhist logic.
xa: Asanga and Vasubandhu: **4th c.**; Dinnaga and Buddhaghosa: **5th c.**
Visuddhimagga is in **Pali** (**Theravada**).
**Kumaragupta I** founded **Nalanda**.

n29e97ada736.x: The Guptas patronised Bhagavatism, yet Samudragupta allowed Meghavarman to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya.
xa: **Sanchi**: Chandragupta II's officer **Amrakardava** granted to the Buddhist vihara.
**Kahaum pillar** (Skandagupta era) records **Jain images**.
Fa-Hien noted **cordial Hindu-Buddhist relations**.

n5d1e1a5511e.s: Who is associated with the foundation of Nalanda during the Gupta period?
n5d1e1a5511e.x: Kumaragupta I, also known as Shakraditya, is credited with founding Nalanda.
n5d1e1a5511e.tq: Use the founder–institution trap among Gupta rulers and Buddhist centres.
xs: **Kumaragupta I (Shakraditya)** founded **Nalanda** — option **(3)**.
**Mihirakula**, the Huna, **persecuted** Buddhism.
xa: **Mahayana** images flourished in Gupta art.
Buddhism **lost royal patronage and declined**.
Buddhist centres: **Nalanda, Sarnath**.

n68fb79f0cb1.s: Buddhism in the Gupta period was persecuted by the Huna ruler:
n68fb79f0cb1.x: Buddhism lost royal patronage and was persecuted by Mihirakula, though Mahayana images flourished in Gupta art.
xa: **Kumaragupta I** founded **Nalanda**.
Scholars: **Asanga, Vasubandhu, Dinnaga, Buddhaghosa**.
**Sanchi**: **Amrakardava's** grant to the Buddhist vihara.

nc538dce4ce4.s: The Vallabhi council of the fifth century CE is associated with:
o: The compilation and writing down of the Svetambara canon
The composition of the Tripitaka by Buddhist monks
The foundation of Nalanda by Kumaragupta I
The beginning of the Pashupata sect
nc538dce4ce4.x: The Vallabhi council, held under Devarddhi Kshamashramana, compiled and committed the Svetambara Jain canon to writing.
xs: The **Vallabhi council** (**5th c. CE**) compiled and wrote down the **Svetambara canon** — option **(1)**.
It was held under **Devarddhi Kshamashramana**.
**Tripitaka** is the Buddhist text; **Nalanda** was founded by **Kumaragupta I**; **Lakulisha** founded the Pashupatas.
xa: **Mathura** was a major centre of **Jain art**.
Jain centres: **Mathura, Vallabhi**.
Jain symbol: **Triratna** (APPSC G2 **2025**).

n90bbd429e0b.s: Amrakardava, who recorded a grant to a Buddhist vihara at Sanchi, was an officer of:
n90bbd429e0b.x: Amrakardava, an officer of Chandragupta II, recorded the Sanchi grant; the Kahaum pillar of Skandagupta's time records Jain images.
xa: **Samudragupta** allowed **Meghavarman**'s monastery at **Bodh Gaya**.
**Vallabhi council** (**5th c. CE**) under **Devarddhi Kshamashramana** wrote down the **Svetambara** canon.
**Mathura** was a major centre of **Jain art**.
**Ramagupta**'s Jain image inscriptions are at **Vidisha**.

n5a0abda1f04.s: Which temple belongs to the first stage of Gupta temple architecture, with a flat roof and shallow four-pillared portico?
n5a0abda1f04.x: First-stage temples such as Sanchi Temple 17 and Tigawa had a square sanctum, flat roof and shallow portico; Nachna is second stage and Deogarh and Bhitargaon third.
xa: ⚠ **Flat roof** = first stage; **shikhara** = third stage (Deogarh).
First stage also had a **low platform**.
Gupta temples mark the beginning of the **Nagara style**.

nddcc3a68a29.s: The Parasurameswara temple at Gudimallam (Tirupati district) is known for:
o: The earliest known Shiva linga, bearing a standing figure of Shiva
The earliest Buddhist stupa in Andhra
The earliest Jain cave shrine in Andhra
The earliest image of Vishnu as Varaha
nddcc3a68a29.x: Gudimallam near Renigunta has the oldest known Shiva linga, which carries a standing figure of Shiva.
xa: **Ekamukhalinga** (one face of Shiva) is a **Gupta** form — **Udayagiri Cave 4**, **Khoh**.
**Nandivarman II's Pedavegi** inscription = first in AP on **Vishnu temples**.
Saivism symbol: **Linga** (APPSC G2 **2025**).

na50fc56144a.s: Which of the following symbols appeared as sectarian symbols on Gupta coins and seals?
na50fc56144a.x: The linga, trident and bull appeared as sectarian symbols on Gupta coins and seals.
na50fc56144a.tq: Test a symbolic group by direct identification.
xs: **Linga, trident (trishula) and bull** appear on Gupta coins and seals — option **(4)**.
These are **Shaiva** sectarian symbols.
xa: **Gaja-Lakshmi** also appears on seals.
The Gupta emblem was **Garuda**; Skandagupta's coins show the **Garuda standard**.
Buddhism's principle: **Ashtanga Marga**.

n97cf2c68989.s: The earliest example of the Panchayatana plan is the:
n97cf2c68989.x: The Panchayatana plan (main shrine plus four corner shrines) first appears at the Deogarh Dashavatara temple; Bhumara has only two flanking shrines.
xa: Deogarh and **Bhitargaon** = third stage.
Third stage replaced the flat roof with a **low square shikhara**.
Basic elements: **garbhagriha, mandapa, pradakshina path, jagati**.

naba6b019105.s: The Kapalikas, an extremist skull-bearing sect, belonged to which tradition?
naba6b019105.x: Kapalikas were an extremist, skull-bearing Shaiva sect that emerged from the Misra Saivam (mixed Shaivism) school.
xa: ⚠ APPSC keys differ: **Pashupata Shaivism** (G2 **2019**) vs **Misra (mixed) Shaivism** (GS **2018**).
**Bhairavakonda caves** (AP) belong to the Kapalikas.
**Kalamukhas** were the other extreme sect.

n7df39cd9aa0.s: The Ajivika sect is associated with:
n7df39cd9aa0.x: Ajivika is associated with Makkhali Gosala; Jainism with Mahavira and Buddhism with Gautama Buddha.
xa: APPSC G2 **2025**: Jainism–**Triratna**, Buddhism–**Ashtanga Margam**, Saivism–**Linga**, Animism–**Nature Worship**.
Mahavira = **24th Tirthankara**; Ajivika principle = **Niyati (fate)**.
Vaishnavism: **Vasudeva-Krishna**, **Bhagavad Gita**, centre **Mathura**.

ncac5e319d69.s: The chakra, shankha and Garuda are symbols associated with:
ncac5e319d69.x: Chakra, shankha and Garuda belong to Vaishnavism; the linga to Saivism.
xa: APPSC G2 **2025** match also had **Animism → Nature Worship**.
Gupta dynastic emblem = **Garuda**, Vishnu's mount.
Saiva symbols on Gupta coins and seals: **linga, trident, bull**.

n30d05df590d.s: Which of the following Smritis is associated with the legal literature of the Gupta age?
n30d05df590d.x: Narada Smriti is one of the legal works associated with the age. Yajnavalkya, Katyayana and Brihaspati Smritis are also listed among such legal texts.
n30d05df590d.tq: Identify the legal text rather than a literary or scientific work.
xs: **Narada Smriti** is a Gupta-age law book — option **(2)**.
**Aryabhatiya** = maths/astronomy; **Panchasiddhantika** = Varahamihira's astronomy.
xa: Other Smritis: **Yajnavalkya, Katyayana, Brihaspati** (also **Vishnu**).
**Amarakosha** (Amarasimha) is the Sanskrit lexicon.
**Chandra Vyakarana** by **Chandragomin**, a Buddhist, **5th c.**

n94b35c144a4.s: In the traditional Navaratna list, Kshapanaka is associated with:
n94b35c144a4.x: Kshapanaka is linked with Jyotishyashastra; Shanku with architecture, Dhanvantari with Ayurveda and Amarasimha with the Amarakosha.
xa: ⚠ **Kshapanaka** = astrology; **Vetala Bhatta** = magic; **Vararuchi** = grammar.
**Kalidasa** = poet-dramatist.
**Shanku** shares sculpture and architecture with Ghatakarpara.
n94b35c144a4.fixed: Ghatakarpara is traditionally a poet, not sculptor; avoid a second wrong pair

n694807a30ee.s: Varahamihira, listed in the traditional Navaratna of Chandragupta II, actually belonged to which century?
n694807a30ee.x: The Navaratna list is traditional; Varahamihira belonged to the sixth century, later than Chandragupta II.
xa: Gems: **Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira, Dhanvantari, Kshapanaka, Vararuchi, Vetala Bhatta, Ghatakarpara, Shanku**.
**Dhanvantari** = "Father of Ayurveda".
**Vararuchi** = Prakrit Prakasha.

n8e2a14b1c8d.x: The Aryabhatiya was composed in 499 CE; it held the Earth spherical and rotating and gave an accurate value of pi.
xa: Aryabhata first treated **mathematics as a distinct subject** — **Ganitapada** (APPSC **2012**).
He **used zero and place value**.
Clear claim = Earth's **daily rotation**; some notes add the Sun is stationary.

ncf91a1ecc96.x: Hastyayurveda was written by Palakapya, not Dhanvantari.
xa: **Dhanvantari** = "Father of Ayurveda", a Navaratna.
Brahmagupta also wrote **Brahmasphutasiddhanta**.
Bhaskara II also wrote **Lilavati**.

n1f71440c5de.s: Which of the following is one of the five siddhantas summarised in Varahamihira's Panchasiddhantika?
n1f71440c5de.x: The five are Surya, Romaka, Paulisa, Vasishtha and Paitamaha.
xa: The **Panchasiddhantika** is **Varahamihira's** summary.
It shows **Greek/Roman influence** on Gupta astronomy.
**Charaka Samhita** = medicine (Kanishka's physician).

nd7ae9096186.s: The Romaka Siddhanta is primarily associated with which subject and influence?
nd7ae9096186.x: Romaka Siddhanta is an astronomical work summarised by Varahamihira and reflects Roman-Greek influence, comparable to the Paulisa tradition.
nd7ae9096186.tq: Separate the text's subject from the foreign cultural influence associated with it.
xs: **Romaka Siddhanta** = **astronomy** with **Roman/Greek influence** — option **(1)** (APPSC G2 **2025**).
Like **Paulisa**, it shows Greek input.
xa: Summarised in Varahamihira's **Panchasiddhantika** with **Surya, Paulisa, Vasishtha, Paitamaha**.
Debate: Greek input means "Indian science" was **not isolated**.
Varahamihira improved **Aryabhata's sine tables**.

nindian-history-48-10.s: Chandapradyota of Avanti was treated by the physician:
nindian-history-48-10.x: Jivaka, physician of Bimbisara, treated Chandapradyota of Avanti, not Sushruta.
n: Jivaka was the court physician of Bimbisara. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
Charaka was the court physician of Kanishka. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
Dhanvantari was associated with Chandragupta II. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
Jivaka was sent for medicinal service to Chandapradyota of Avanti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
Sushruta was associated with ancient India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
Sushruta was associated with Ayurveda and surgery. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #48 · pp 116-117]
xa: **Sushruta Samhita** — surgery; **Charaka Samhita** — medicine.
Physicians used **iron and mercury** preparations and performed **lithotomy**.
**Navanitakam** — medical manual of metallic preparations.
**Palakapya** — **Hastyayurveda** (elephant diseases).

n57c981196d5.s: Kalidasa was one of the Navaratnas in the court of which ruler?
n57c981196d5.x: Kalidasa is traditionally regarded as one of the Navaratnas in the court of Chandragupta II.
n57c981196d5.tq: Use the person–patron association to eliminate rulers from the same dynasty.
xs: **Kalidasa** was a **Navaratna** of **Chandragupta II** — option **(1)**.
He was the **greatest Sanskrit poet-dramatist**.
xa: Dramas: **Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram, Vikramorvashiyam**.
Mahakavyas: **Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava**; lyrics: **Meghaduta, Ritusamhara**.
⚠ The Navaratna list is **traditional** — members were not all contemporaries.

n629dd9c3776.s: The Katantra grammar was written by:
n629dd9c3776.x: Sharvavarman wrote the Katantra; Amarasimha the Amarakosha, Chandragomin the Chandra Vyakarana and Vararuchi the Prakrit Prakasha.
xa: **Chandragomin** was a **Buddhist**, **5th c.**
Amarasimha and Vararuchi were **Navaratnas**.
Satavahana-era Sanskrit works also include **Kamasutra** and Aryadeva's **Chittashuddhi Prakaranam**.

n76e54bc7ada.s: Malavikagnimitram centres on the love of Agnimitra and Malavika. Agnimitra was a
n76e54bc7ada.x: Malavikagnimitram portrays the love of Agnimitra, a Shunga king of Vidisha, and Malavika.
n76e54bc7ada.tq: Use the plot to identify the historical ruler and dynasty.
xs: **Agnimitra** was the **Shunga king of Vidisha** — option **(4)**.
**Malavikagnimitram** is Kalidasa's drama on his love for **Malavika**.
xa: Kalidasa's other dramas: **Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Vikramorvashiyam**.
Kalidasa was a **Navaratna** of **Chandragupta II**.
Usual "NOT by Kalidasa" distractors: **Mudrarakshasa, Mrichchhakatika, Kiratarjuniya**.

nindian-history-13-11.s: The Sanskrit drama Malavikagnimitram was written by:
nindian-history-13-11.x: Kalidasa wrote the drama Malavikagnimitram and the poems Meghaduta and Kumarasambhavam.
n: Vatsyayana wrote Kamasutra. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Kamasutra is a classical Sanskrit work. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Kalidasa wrote Meghaduta. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Meghaduta is Sanskrit poetry. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Kalidasa wrote Kumarasambhavam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Kumarasambhavam is Sanskrit poetry. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Kalidasa wrote Malavikagnimitram. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Malavikagnimitram is a Sanskrit drama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
xa: Kalidasa was a **Navaratna** of **Chandragupta II**.
His dramas: **Abhijnana Shakuntalam**, **Malavikagnimitram**, **Vikramorvashiyam**.
Lyric poems: **Meghaduta**, **Ritusamhara**.
Kamasutra: some notes place it in the **Gupta** period, others in the **later Satavahana** period.

n4ad6660b464.s: The work Devichandraguptam, which provides information about Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi, was written by
n4ad6660b464.x: Devichandraguptam is attributed to Vishakhadatta and deals with events connected with Ramagupta and Dhruvadevi.
n4ad6660b464.tq: Use the author–work–theme chain rather than relying on the name of the ruler alone.
xs: **Devichandraguptam** was written by **Vishakhadatta** — option **(1)**.
It gives Gupta court history (**Ramagupta–Dhruvadevi**) — a political source.
**Amarasimha** = Amarakosha; **Bhasa** = Charudatta; **Kamandaka** = Nitisara.
xa: Vishakhadatta also wrote **Mudrarakshasa** (**Chanakya vs Rakshasa**).
**Sudraka** wrote **Mrichchhakatika** ("Little Clay Cart").
**Harishena** wrote the **Prayaga (Allahabad) Prashasti**.

n10fd5c32a24.s: The Panchatantra, a collection of animal fables teaching statecraft, is a Gupta-period work composed by:
n10fd5c32a24.x: The Panchatantra is attributed to Vishnu Sharma and is placed in the Gupta period (APPSC 2012). Narayana Pandita wrote the later Hitopadesha, which was based on the Panchatantra; Kamandaka wrote the Nitisara on polity; Vishakhadatta wrote Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam.
n10fd5c32a24.tq: Panchatantra = Vishnu Sharma; Hitopadesha = Narayana Pandita
xs: The **Panchatantra** was composed by **Vishnu Sharma** — option **(2)** (APPSC **2012**; APPSC GS **2012**).
**Narayana Pandita** wrote the later **Hitopadesha**, based on the Panchatantra.
**Kamandaka** = **Nitisara**; **Vishakhadatta** = **Mudrarakshasa, Devichandraguptam**.
xa: Panchatantra = **animal fables on statecraft**.
Some notes credit Hitopadesha to Vishnu Sharma — a trap.
**Dandin** wrote **Dasakumaracharita**.

nindian-history-6-33.s: The Sanskrit drama Svapnavasavadattam was written by:
n: Svapnavasavadattam was written by Bhasa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Svapnavasavadattam deals with Sanskrit drama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: Bhasa wrote **13 plays** (APP; UPSC notes say **12**) and was **earlier than Kalidasa**.
**Mrichchhakatika** ("Little Clay Cart") — **Sudraka**, a social drama.
**Mudrarakshasa** and **Devichandraguptam** — **Vishakhadatta**.
**Dashakumaracharita** — **Dandin**, adventures of **ten princes**.

ndb760245d18.s: The inscription on the Mehrauli iron pillar refers to the king by which name?
ndb760245d18.x: The inscription refers to the ruler as ‘Chandra’, generally identified with Chandragupta II.
ndb760245d18.tq: Use the exact name in the inscription rather than the ruler’s full conventional name.
xs: The **Mehrauli iron pillar** names the king "**Chandra**" — option **(2)**.
He is identified with **Chandragupta II**.
xa: It claims authority over **North-West India and Bengal**.
Originally at **Udayagiri** near **Vidisha** (MP), now at **Mehrauli, Delhi**.
It has **not rusted for over fifteen centuries**.

n87ca0b2bbeb.s: The rust resistance of the Mehrauli iron pillar is attributed to its high content of:
n87ca0b2bbeb.x: The high-phosphorus iron forms a protective layer that has helped the pillar resist corrosion for over fifteen centuries.
xa: Inscription names king "**Chandra**" (**Chandragupta II**).
The **Sultanganj Buddha** (Bhagalpur), over **2 m** high, is the finest Gupta **bronze**.
Originally at **Udayagiri** near Vidisha.

neb3c6808db2.s: Sarnath school Gupta sculptures were made of polished:
neb3c6808db2.x: Sarnath sculpture used polished Chunar buff sandstone and avoided heavy ornamentation.
xa: Sarnath's seated Buddha is shown in the **Dharmachakra mudra**, with a thin clinging robe covering **both shoulders**.
The Sarnath halo carries **floral carving**; the school became a **model for Buddhist art across Asia**.
Gupta stone sculpture grew out of the **Mathura school**.
⚠ **Sarnath** = Chunar sandstone; **Sultanganj** = bronze; **Mehrauli** = iron.

n347ad7499e0.s: The Gupta-period Sultanganj Buddha, more than two metres high, is made of:
n347ad7499e0.x: The Sultanganj Buddha is a bronze image more than two metres high; Gupta stone sculpture grew out of the Mathura school.
xa: Sarnath used **Chunar (buff) sandstone**, polished, with little ornament; seated Buddha in **Dharmachakra mudra**.
The **Eran Varaha** shows **Vaishnava** presence; the **Bamiyan Buddhas** (Afghanistan) are of the Gupta period.
The **Mehrauli iron pillar** has not rusted for over **fifteen centuries**.

ndc1d245e495.s: An inscription of Virasena at Udayagiri records the conquests of:
ndc1d245e495.x: Virasena's inscription at Udayagiri records the conquests of Chandragupta II.
xa: Udayagiri (Vidisha, MP): **20** caves — **19** Hindu, **1** Jain.
Colossal **Varaha (boar) Vishnu** panel.
The **Mehrauli iron pillar** of Chandragupta II originally stood at **Udayagiri**.

nindian-history-13-12.s: The Buddhacharita and the Saundarananda were written by:
nindian-history-13-12.x: Ashvaghosha wrote the Buddhacharita, on the life of the Buddha, and the Saundarananda.
n: Buddhacharita deals with the life of Buddha. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Ashvaghosha wrote Saundarananda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
Saundarananda is Buddhist Sanskrit literature. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 57-60]
xa: Ashvaghosha also wrote **Buddhacharita**.
**Ratnavali, Priyadarshika, Nagananda** — **Harshavardhana**.
**Janaki-haranam** — **Kumaradasa**; **Ravanavadha** — **Bhatti**.
**Nitisara** — **Kamandaka**, Gupta treatise on polity.

ndc2a9ee6d7d.s: The Hitopadesha was a later work based on the:
ndc2a9ee6d7d.x: The Hitopadesha was composed later and was based on the Panchatantra.
xa: Bhasa wrote **13 plays** (UPSC notes say **12**), including **Svapnavasavadattam**.
Hitopadesha: **Narayana Pandita** (some notes credit Vishnu Sharma).
Panchatantra: **Vishnu Sharma**.
ndc2a9ee6d7d.fixed: Svapnavasavadattam (not Charudatta) is Bhasa's most famous play (ye1b643cb0ea); statement 3 false

n7613ee958fe.x: Shudraka wrote the Mrichchhakatika; Bhasa wrote Charudatta and Vishakhadatta the Devichandraguptam.
xa: ⚠ The **Harishena** of **Brihatkatha Kosha** is a different, later **Jain** author.
Mrichchhakatika = "**Little Clay Cart**", a social drama.
Vishakhadatta also wrote **Mudrarakshasa**.

nd61f819b8d0.s: Harishena's Prayaga Prashasti records the achievements of:
nd61f819b8d0.x: The Prayaga Prashasti records Samudragupta's achievements; the Harishena of the Brihatkatha Kosha was a different, later Jain author.
xa: Prayaga = **Allahabad** Prashasti.
⚠ Another pair: **Panchatantra** (Vishnu Sharma) vs **Hitopadesha** (Narayana Pandita).
Vishakhadatta's **Devichandraguptam** is another Gupta political source.

ne910800832a.s: Vetala Bhatta, of the Gupta age, is associated with:
ne910800832a.x: Vetala Bhatta is associated with Mantrashastra; Dhanvantari with Ayurveda and Vararuchi with Prakrit grammar.

nb18a27d9e9f.s: The Dashavatara Temple at Deogarh is associated with which combination?
o: Vishnu, stone construction, shikhara and panchayatana plan

nb18a27d9e9f.tq: Combine deity, material and architectural feature in one precise option.
xs: The Deogarh Dashavatara temple = **Vishnu**, **stone**, **shikhara** and **panchayatana** plan — option **(1)** is correct.

ne575a706372.s: The Bhitargaon temple in Kanpur district is noted as a:

n1a19e964f87.s: Which Gupta temple has two flanking shrines at the entrance?

rock-cut forms to free-standing structural temples

naea473f4643.s: Kannauj, to which Harsha later shifted his capital from Thanesar, was earlier the capital of the:

Some call **Prabhakaravardhana** the founder — he was the first great ruler.

n16e6c2c5117.s: Which one of the following works was NOT written by Harshavardhana?
n16e6c2c5117.x: Harshacharita, the semi-historical biography of Harsha, was written by his court poet Banabhatta (APPSC G2 2025). Ratnavali and Priyadarshika (romantic comedies) and Nagananda (a Buddhist play on self-sacrifice) are the three Sanskrit dramas written by Harsha himself.
n16e6c2c5117.tq: Harsha wrote 3 plays; Bana wrote Harshacharita and Kadambari
xs: **Harshacharita** was not written by Harsha — option **(4)** is the answer (APPSC G2 2025).
It was written by his court poet **Banabhatta**.
**Ratnavali**, **Priyadarshika** (romantic comedies) and **Nagananda** (Buddhist play) are Harsha's own.
xa: Bana also wrote **Kadambari**.
Bana is paired with **Harsha**, not the Guptas or Kanishka.
**Mayura** wrote **Suryashataka**.

n8da16121717.s: Under Harsha, the state revenue was divided into how many parts?
n8da16121717.x: Revenue was divided four ways: the king's use, public servants, scholars and religious activities.
xa: Land tax = **one-sixth** of produce.
Officials were paid in **land grants** → feudal trend.
Hiuen Tsang: taxation **light**, burden not heavy.

nd378ece1d1b.s: Harshavardhana is regarded as the last great Buddhist patron-king of northern India before the rise of which political order?
nd378ece1d1b.x: Harshavardhana is remembered as the last great Buddhist patron-king of northern India before the emergence of Rajput states.
nd378ece1d1b.tq: Use the distinctive historical transition associated with the ruler to eliminate unrelated dynasties.
xs: Harsha was the last great Buddhist patron-king of the north before the rise of the **Rajput states** — option **(1)** is correct.
His was the **last great empire** / unified north India of ancient times.
xa: His court at **Kannauj** was an **intellectual centre**.
It ended with his death in **647 CE** (no successor).
Like **Ashoka**, he turned to Buddhism and patronised **Nalanda**.

nindian-history-144-2.x: The Maukhari dynasty originated at Gaya in Bihar, where its earliest inscriptions are found. The family later ruled from Kannauj.
nindian-history-144-2.tq: Discriminate the place of origin from the later capital.
n: The Maukhari dynasty originated in Gaya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
xs: The Maukhari dynasty **originated** at **Gaya** — option **(1)**.
**Kannauj** was their later **capital** (CGPSC 2011), not their place of origin.
**Grahavarman**, the Maukhari husband of **Rajyashri**, was killed by **Devagupta of Malwa**.
xa: Maukhari rulers: **Harivarma**, **Adityavarma**, **Ishvaravarma**, **Sharvavarma**, **Grahavarma**.
Harsha freed his sister **Rajyashri** and drove **Shashanka** from Kannauj.
Harsha later shifted his capital from **Thanesar** to **Kannauj**.

n8df5486bb39.s: After Harsha, possession of Kannauj symbolised:
o: Control of the Deccan trade routes
Imperial sovereignty and the title of Samrat of North India
Command of the western sea ports
n8df5486bb39.x: After Harsha, Kannauj became a symbol of imperial sovereignty, associated with the title of Samrat of North India.
xa: Economic pull: **Gangetic-Doab agrarian wealth** and Arabian Sea trade via **Gujarat**.
Kannauj's primacy began under **Harsha** (Hiuen Tsang: Pataliputra lost its place).
Old names: **Mahodaya**, **Kanyakubja**.

ndd9f13a702a.s: Access to Arabian Sea trade through Gujarat let the masters of Kannauj bypass the Arab-held:
ndd9f13a702a.x: Kannauj commanded the Doab's agrarian wealth and Arabian Sea trade via Gujarat, bypassing the Arab-held Indus delta.
xa: Political value: the title of **Samrat** of North India.
The struggle lasted nearly **two centuries**, **8th-10th c.**
Outcome: shift of power to **regional kingdoms**.

n552e2069f2c.s: The struggle for Kannauj is historically significant because it illustrates which broader development in early medieval India?
o: The disappearance of dynastic competition in northern India
The complete centralisation of power under one pan-Indian emperor
The shift of political power towards regional kingdoms
The replacement of agriculture by maritime trade as the main economic base
n552e2069f2c.x: The struggle demonstrates the shift of power to regional kingdoms during early medieval India.
n552e2069f2c.tq: Identify the broad historical interpretation supported by the political pattern.
xs: The struggle shows the **shift of power to regional kingdoms** — option **(3)** is correct.
No power held Kannauj permanently, and all three ended **exhausted**.
xa: New Rajput states followed: **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
Kannauj stood for the title of **Samrat** of North India.
AP angle: Rashtrakuta pressure on the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** ran in parallel.

n17a8bc4c8d8.s: The capital of the Rashtrakutas during the tripartite struggle was:
n17a8bc4c8d8.x: The Rashtrakuta capital was Manyakheta (Malkhed) in the Deccan; the Pratiharas later held Kannauj.
xa: Pala base: **Gauda (Bengal)** and **Magadha (Bihar)**.
Rashtrakuta rulers: **Dhruva, Govinda III**, Amoghavarsha, **Indra III**.
Pratihara rulers: **Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja**, Mahendrapala I.

n1f16742a21c.s: The tripartite struggle for Kannauj began when which of the following rulers clashed with Dharmapala and Dhruva?
n1f16742a21c.x: The struggle began when Gurjara-Pratihara ruler Vatsaraja, around 780–800 CE, clashed with Dharmapala and Rashtrakuta ruler Dhruva.
n1f16742a21c.tq: Link the opening phase to the ruler who initiated the clash.
xs: **Vatsaraja** (c. **780-800 CE**) began the struggle by clashing with **Dharmapala** and **Dhruva** — option **(3)** is correct (UPSC).
**Nagabhata II** and **Mihira Bhoja** belong to later phases; **Indra III** sacked Kannauj c. **916 CE**.
xa: Phase I: Vatsaraja takes Kannauj, defeats Dharmapala; **Dhruva** defeats both and withdraws.
Dhruva ruled **780-793 CE**.
⚠ Dhruva's opponent was **Vatsaraja**, not Nagabhata II.

n228624951fd.s: Which Rashtrakuta ruler defeated both Vatsaraja and Dharmapala but returned south with booty?
n228624951fd.x: Dhruva defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala, took booty and returned south without retaining northern territory.
xa: APPSC GS 2023: Dhruva "**jumped into the fight**".
Dhruva ruled **780-793 CE**.
⚠ The **Sanjan plates** describe **Govinda III**, not Dhruva.

n550c3c502d7.s: Whom did Dharmapala install as ruler of Kannauj?
n550c3c502d7.x: Dharmapala installed Chakrayudha at Kannauj after Vatsaraja's occupation; Nagabhata II later ousted him.
xa: Under Bhoja the empire ran from the **Himalayas to the Narmada**.
**Govinda III** defeated both Nagabhata II and Dharmapala, then retreated.
Dharmapala held a **grand durbar** at Kannauj.

nc51aed713c9.s: During the second phase of the struggle for Kannauj, Dharmapala removed which ruler and installed Chakrayudha in his place?
nc51aed713c9.x: Dharmapala removed the Pratihara nominee Indrayudha and installed Chakrayudha as his puppet ruler at Kannauj.
nc51aed713c9.tq: Test the installed–removed ruler pair directly.
xs: Dharmapala removed **Indrayudha**, the Pratihara nominee — option **(2)** is correct.
He installed his puppet **Chakrayudha** and held a **grand durbar** at Kannauj.
xa: ⚠ **Indrayudha** = removed; **Chakrayudha** = installed.
The **Khalimpur plates** say Chakrayudha was installed with the **approval of northern kings**.
**Nagabhata II** later ousted Chakrayudha.

n862d5722adf.s: Indra III's campaign against Kannauj around 916 CE was directed against which Pratihara ruler?
n862d5722adf.x: Rashtrakuta ruler Indra III sacked Kannauj around 916 CE after defeating Pratihara ruler Mahipala I.
n862d5722adf.tq: Pair the date of the campaign with the ruler who was defeated.
xs: **Indra III** sacked Kannauj c. **916 CE** after defeating Pratihara **Mahipala I** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Nagabhata II** was beaten by **Govinda III**; **Mihira Bhoja** and **Mahendrapala I** held Kannauj earlier.
xa: After Indra III's raid the **Pratiharas declined**.
New Rajput states followed: **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
Rashtrakuta capital: **Manyakheta (Malkhed)**.

na4c08bc69d1.s: The Sanjan plates, dated to 871 CE and associated with Amoghavarsha I, provide information about which event?
o: Dharmapala's installation of Chakrayudha at Kannauj
na4c08bc69d1.x: The Sanjan plates, issued during the reign of Rashtrakuta ruler Amoghavarsha I in 871 CE, describe Govinda III's Himalayan campaign.
na4c08bc69d1.tq: Combine the source, date and dynasty clues before identifying the event.
xs: The Sanjan plates describe **Govinda III's Himalayan campaign** — option **(2)** is correct.
They are **Rashtrakuta** plates of **Amoghavarsha I** (**871 CE**).
**Chakrayudha's installation** is in the **Khalimpur plates**; **Indra III's sack** came c. **916 CE**.
xa: Quote: his horses "drank the icy waters of **Himalayan** streams, his elephants tasted the **Ganga**".
⚠ **Sanjan** = Rashtrakuta; **Gwalior** = Pratihara; **Khalimpur** = Pala.

nf47e31f6545.s: Which source records the victories of Nagabhata II over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala?
nf47e31f6545.x: The Gwalior prashasti of Mihira Bhoja records Nagabhata II's victories over Chakrayudha and Dharmapala.
nf47e31f6545.tq: Use the source–ruler–victory association rather than the dynasty name alone.
xs: The **Gwalior prashasti** records **Nagabhata II**'s victories over **Chakrayudha** and **Dharmapala** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **Pratihara** record of **Mihira Bhoja**.
**Sanjan plates** = Govinda III's campaign; **Khalimpur plates** = Chakrayudha's installation.
xa: ⚠ **Sanjan** = Rashtrakuta; **Gwalior** = Pratihara; **Khalimpur** = Pala.
Nagabhata II was in turn defeated by **Govinda III**.

nindian-history-1-91.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the tripartite struggle for Kannauj?
o: Govinda III was a Rashtrakuta king.
The Sanjan and Radhanpur plates record Govinda III's northern victories.
The Khalimpur inscription records the election of Gopala.
Nagabhata II, defeated by Govinda III, was a Pala king.
nindian-history-1-91.x: Nagabhata II was a Gurjara-Pratihara king, not a Pala; the other three statements are correct.
n: The Sanjan Copper Plates are associated with Govinda III. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
The Radhanpur Copper Plates are associated with Govinda III. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Govinda III belonged to the Rashtrakuta dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
Govinda III defeated the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-17]
xa: Sanjan plates: Govinda III's horses "drank the icy waters of Himalayan streams".
⚠ Dhruva's opponent was **Vatsaraja**; Govinda III's was **Nagabhata II**.
**Indra III** sacked **Kannauj** c. **916 CE**.
The **Gwalior prashasti** records Nagabhata II's victories over **Chakrayudha** and **Dharmapala**.

n71bb62073c9.s: Which power finally held Kannauj at the end of the tripartite struggle?
n71bb62073c9.x: Kannauj was finally held by the Pratiharas under Bhoja and Mahendrapala I, though no power retained it permanently for long.
xa: Duration: nearly **two centuries**, **8th-10th c.**
Pratihara decline after **Indra III**'s raid → **Chandelas**, **Chauhans**.
All three powers were **exhausted**.

n5b0ad25f2b4.s: What was one important consequence of the exhaustion of all three powers involved in the struggle for Kannauj?
o: The permanent Rashtrakuta annexation of Bengal
The abolition of regional kingdoms in northern India
The immediate restoration of Harsha's empire
The emergence of new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans
n5b0ad25f2b4.x: The exhaustion of the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas, along with Pratihara decline after Indra III's raid, opened the way for new Rajput states such as the Chandelas and Chauhans.
n5b0ad25f2b4.tq: Trace the political consequence of weakening major powers to the rise of regional states.
xs: Exhaustion of all three led to new Rajput states — **Chandelas** and **Chauhans** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Pratiharas** declined after **Indra III**'s raid.
xa: The overall significance: a shift of power to **regional kingdoms**.
Indra III defeated Pratihara **Mahipala I** c. **916 CE**.
**Chauhans** were not a party to the struggle itself.

naebf329aae2.s: Which of the following sets contains only dynasties listed as non-participants in the struggle for Kannauj?
naebf329aae2.x: Cholas, Pallavas and Kalyani Chalukyas were listed among the dynasties that did not participate. Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas were the contending powers.
naebf329aae2.tq: Check every member of the set rather than relying on one familiar dynasty.
xs: **Cholas, Pallavas and Kalyani Chalukyas** are all non-participants — option **(2)** is correct.
Every other set includes a contender — **Palas**, **Pratiharas** or **Rashtrakutas**.
Non-participants also include **Chauhans** and **Gahadavalas**.
xa: Cholas as non-participant: **UPPSC 2015**.
The **Chauhans** and **Chandelas** rose after the struggle exhausted all three.
The struggle lasted nearly **two centuries**.

nff60034cfe1.s: Gopala, founder of the Pala dynasty, came to power by:
o: Defeating the Sena ruler of Bengal
Inheritance from the later Guptas of Magadha
Election by notables to end matsyanyaya
nff60034cfe1.x: Gopala was elected by regional notables in the mid-eighth century to end matsyanyaya, a period of anarchy.
xa: UPPSC 2021: kings chosen by the people = **Gopala** and **Nandivarman II Pallavamalla**.
Gopala built **Odantapuri** (APPSC GS 2018).
He also displaced the **Khadgas** of east Bengal.

n08dec664b90.s: The Pala founder Gopala displaced the Khadgas of:
n08dec664b90.x: Gopala displaced the later Guptas in Magadha and the Khadgas in eastern Bengal, and built Odantapuri.
xa: Odantapuri is at **Bihar Sharif**, Nalanda district; about **12,000** monks.
Odantapuri was a **model for Tibetan monasteries**.
Gopala was **elected** c. mid-**8th c.**

n4b2e78af92f.s: Dharmapala was defeated by Nagabhata II near:
n4b2e78af92f.x: Dharmapala (c. 770-810) was defeated by Dhruva and by Nagabhata II near Monghyr.
xa: Dharmapala ruled c. **770-810**.
**Somapura** (Paharpur, Bangladesh) is also credited to Dharmapala.
Buddhist texts were compiled at **Nalanda** under Dharmapala; his **seal** was found there.

n57a108ee575.s: Which Pala ruler is associated with the revival of Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola?
n57a108ee575.x: Mahipala I, whose reign is placed around c. 977–1027, revived Pala power and was defeated by Rajendra Chola.
n57a108ee575.tq: Use the paired achievement to distinguish one ruler from the other Palas.
xs: **Mahipala I** (c. **977-1027**) revived Pala power and was defeated by **Rajendra Chola** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Gopala** was the elected founder; **Devapala** made the Nalanda grant; **Ramapala** was the last strong ruler.
xa: **Ramapala** (c. **1072-1126**): Kaivarta revolt, **Jagaddala**.
**Dharmapala** (c. **770-810**) founded **Vikramashila**.
The **Senas** succeeded the Palas in Bengal.

n2445a738333.s: The Kaivarta revolt took place in the reign of the Pala ruler:
n2445a738333.x: Ramapala (c. 1072-1126), the last strong Pala ruler, faced the Kaivarta revolt and is associated with Jagaddala.
xa: **Ramacharita** by **Sandhyakar Nandi** is about Ramapala and the Kaivarta revolt.
**Vikramashila** reached its **zenith under Ramapala**.
Jagaddala (Varendra, Bangladesh) **translated books into Tibetan**.

n2f83965fbd3.s: At the request of the envoy of the Shailendra ruler Balaputradeva, which Pala king granted five villages for the monastery at Nalanda?
n2f83965fbd3.x: Devapala granted five villages, as recorded in the Nalanda copper plate (BPSC 2018). Gopala was the elected founder, Dharmapala founded Vikramashila, and Mahipala I revived Pala power later.
n2f83965fbd3.tq: Balaputradeva + five villages = Devapala (Nalanda copper plate).
xs: **Devapala** granted **five villages** at Balaputradeva's envoy's request — option **(3)** is correct (BPSC 2018).
The grant is recorded in the **Nalanda copper plate**.
**Gopala** = elected founder; **Dharmapala** = Vikramashila; **Mahipala I** = later revival.
xa: **Balaputradeva** was a **Shailendra** ruler of **Suvarnadvipa/Suvarnabhumi**.
**Pala-style bronzes** in SE Asia show maritime exchange.

n08592ade6f0.s: Which Pala ruler founded both Vikramashila and Somapura?
n08592ade6f0.x: Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura; Gopala built Odantapuri and Nalanda was founded by Kumaragupta I.
xa: ⚠ Trap (BPSC 2023): Vikramashila is in **Bhagalpur (not Banka)**.
**Jagaddala** was founded by **Ramapala**.

n1eb8e44ceef.s: In the time of Harsha, Valabhi was known as a centre of:
n1eb8e44ceef.x: Valabhi was a Hinayana centre in Harsha's time, distinct from the Pala Mahaviharas.
xa: **Taxila** = ancient **Gandhara** centre — also not Pala-era.
Nalanda was the **Mahayana** counterpart.
**Balaputradeva** built a monastery at **Nalanda**, not Valabhi.

na0c30f11f9e.s: Under the Palas, which centre became associated with translating books into Tibetan?
na0c30f11f9e.x: Jagaddala was associated with translations into Tibetan, while Buddhist texts were compiled at Nalanda under Dharmapala.
xa: **Sakya Sri Bhadra** of Jagaddala took **Tantric Buddhism** to Tibet.
**Dharmapala's seal** was found at Nalanda.
Jagaddala was sacked in the early **13th c.**

nindian-history-14-11.s: Nalanda University in Bihar was founded in which century AD?
nindian-history-14-11.x: Nalanda was founded in the 5th century AD by the Gupta ruler Kumaragupta I.
n: Nalanda University was located in Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 60-64]
Nalanda University was founded in the 5th century AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 60-64]
Nalanda University had a Gupta foundation. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 60-64]
Nalanda University was a major Buddhist centre of learning. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 60-64]
xa: It **attracted students** from **China, Tibet, Greece, Persia** and other regions.
**Nava Nalanda Mahavihara** — **Bhikshu Jagadish Kashyap**; foundation stone laid on **20 November 1951**.
⚠ **Nalanda** is Gupta-founded; the other four mahaviharas are **Pala** foundations.
**Vikramashila** was founded by **Dharmapala**; **Odantapuri** by **Gopala**.

ncb520c34425.s: Vikramashila Mahavihara, at Antichak, lies in which district of Bihar?
ncb520c34425.x: Vikramashila is at Antichak in Bhagalpur district, not Banka (BPSC 2023 trap).
xa: It stood on the **Ganga**; its walls had **terracotta panels**.
**Atisha Dipankara Shrijnana** of Vikramashila revived Buddhism in Tibet.

n09357db0ff8.s: The destruction of major Pala-period centres of learning by Bakhtiyar Khilji is generally placed approximately in which period?
n09357db0ff8.x: The destruction is generally placed around 1193–1200. A separate chronological tradition gives 1194 specifically for the destruction of Nalanda, while Jagaddala was sacked in the early thirteenth century.
n09357db0ff8.tq: Use the approximate range rather than confusing it with a later event.
xs: **Bakhtiyar Khilji** destroyed the centres c. **1193-1200** — option **(4)** is correct.
Some notes give **1194** for Nalanda.
xa: **Jagaddala** was sacked in the early **13th c.**
Bakhtiyar Khilji also ousted the last Sena, **Lakshmanasena**.
The Palas were the **last great royal patrons of Buddhism** in India.

nad358049600.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out in the context of early-medieval Pala centres of learning?
nad358049600.x: Taxila was an ancient centre in Gandhara and does not belong to the early-medieval Pala group. Nalanda, Vikramashila and Somapura were important centres under Pala patronage.
nad358049600.tq: Separate the chronologically different institution from the Pala-period group.
xs: **Taxila** is the odd one out — option **(4)** is the answer.
Taxila was an ancient **Gandhara** centre, not Pala-era.
**Vikramashila**, **Somapura** (Dharmapala) and **Nalanda** (Pala patronage) are Pala-era centres.
xa: **Valabhi** was the **Hinayana** centre of Harsha's time.
Panchamahavihara: **Odantapuri, Vikramashila, Somapura, Jagaddala, Nalanda**.

n063eb94cb5d.s: Balaputradeva, who established a monastery at Nalanda, was the ruler of:
n063eb94cb5d.x: Balaputradeva was a Shailendra ruler of Suvarnadvipa or Suvarnabhumi. His envoy requested Devapala to grant five villages for maintaining the monastery at Nalanda.
n063eb94cb5d.tq: Match the foreign ruler with his geographical and dynastic identity.
xs: **Balaputradeva** was the **Shailendra** ruler of **Suvarnadvipa/Suvarnabhumi** — option **(2)** is correct.
He built a **monastery at Nalanda**.
xa: At his envoy's request **Devapala granted five villages** (BPSC 2018; **Nalanda copper plate**).
**Pala-style bronzes** in Southeast Asia show maritime cultural exchange (UPSC).
**Kamarupa** and **Kalinga** came under Pala influence under **Ramapala**.

n543271d8c2c.s: Illustrated Buddhist manuscripts of the Pala period were written on:
n543271d8c2c.x: Pala art includes bronze and black-stone sculpture and illustrated palm-leaf Buddhist manuscripts.
xa: Artists: **Dhiman** and his son **Vitapala** (per **Taranatha**).
**Pala-style bronzes** reached Southeast Asia.
Somapura: grand scale, rich **terracotta** ornamentation.

nd95c3d4a7b2.s: Dhiman and his son Vitapala, mentioned by Taranatha, were Pala-period:
nd95c3d4a7b2.x: Dhiman and his son Vitapala were noted artists of Pala art, as recorded by Taranatha.
xa: Pala sculpture: **bronze** and black-stone (**basalt**).
Manuscripts: **palm-leaf illustrated** Buddhist manuscripts.
Pala-style bronzes in **Southeast Asia** show maritime exchange.

nb6b936bf535.s: Who wrote Ramacharita, a work dealing with Ramapala and the Kaivarta peasant revolt?
nb6b936bf535.x: Ramacharita was written by Sandhyakar Nandi and deals with Ramapala and the Kaivarta peasant revolt.
nb6b936bf535.tq: Match the literary work with its author and subject.
xs: **Sandhyakar Nandi** wrote **Ramacharita** — option **(3)** is correct.
It deals with **Ramapala** and the **Kaivarta** peasant revolt.
**Jayadeva** was **Lakshmanasena**'s poet; **Taranatha** recorded the artists **Dhiman** and **Vitapala**.
xa: Ramapala (c. **1072-1126**) was the last strong Pala.
Ramapala founded **Jagaddala**.
**Atisha Dipankara** of Vikramashila revived Buddhism in Tibet.

na1acb0c8edb.s: The last Sena ruler, whose court poet was Jayadeva and who was ousted by Bakhtiyar Khilji, was:
na1acb0c8edb.x: Lakshmanasena was the last Sena ruler; Jayadeva was at his court and he was ousted by Bakhtiyar Khilji.
xa: Sena founders: **Samantasena** / **Vijayasena**, then **Ballalasena**.
Bakhtiyar Khilji also destroyed Pala-era centres c. **1193-1200**.

n77546d4746d.s: The term ‘Pratihara’ is traditionally interpreted as meaning:
n77546d4746d.x: Pratihara means door-keeper. The dynasty claimed descent from Lakshmana, who was regarded as Rama's door-keeper brother.
n77546d4746d.tq: Distinguish the literal meaning of the dynastic name from its origin legend.
xs: "Pratihara" means **door-keeper** — option **(1)** is correct.
The dynasty claimed descent from **Lakshmana**, Rama's door-keeper brother.
"Fire-born" refers to the separate **Agnikula legend** of **Mount Abu**.
xa: "**Gurjara**" is read as a tribe/people or as the region **Gurjaratra**.
Capitals: **Bhinmal → Ujjain/Avanti → Kannauj (Mahodaya)**.
Founder **Nagabhata I** (c. **730-760**) resisted the Arabs.

ne3d4dff4cc0.s: According to the Agnikula legend in Prithviraj Raso, which group of dynasties was born from the fire-pit at Mount Abu?
ne3d4dff4cc0.x: The Agnikula legend associates the Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras and Chauhans with birth from the fire-pit at Mount Abu.
ne3d4dff4cc0.tq: Recall the complete legendary group rather than a partial pair.
xs: The Agnikula clans are the **Pratiharas, Chaulukyas, Paramaras and Chauhans** — option **(1)** is correct.
The legend, from **Prithviraj Raso**, has them born from the fire-pit at **Mount Abu**.
xa: **Chauhans**, **Paramaras** and **Chaulukyas** later broke away from the Pratiharas as feudatories.
"Pratihara" = **door-keeper**.
Pratihara temple style peaked at **Khajuraho**.

nc5979cf1df8.s: Who among the following is regarded as the founder of the Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty and is known for resisting Arab expansion?
nc5979cf1df8.x: Nagabhata I is regarded as the founder of the dynasty and successfully resisted Arab expansion.
nc5979cf1df8.tq: Use the ruler–achievement association to identify the correct answer.
xs: **Nagabhata I** (c. **730-760**) was the founder and **resisted the Arabs** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Nagabhata II** made Kannauj capital; **Vatsaraja** began the tripartite struggle; **Mihira Bhoja** was the zenith.
xa: The Pratiharas kept Arab rule confined to **Sindh**.
⚠ Nagabhata I = founder, Arabs; Nagabhata II = Kannauj capital.
Sulaiman praised Pratihara cavalry as the **best in India**.

n813b56baa11.s: The Pratihara king Vatsaraja, after taking Kannauj and defeating Dharmapala, was defeated by which Rashtrakuta ruler?
n813b56baa11.x: Vatsaraja took Kannauj and defeated Dharmapala but was later defeated by the Rashtrakuta Dhruva, marking the beginning of the tripartite struggle.
xa: Vatsaraja ruled c. **780-800**.
Some notes say he made Kannauj capital; others say he only conquered it.

n65648679683.s: Near which place did the Pratihara king Nagabhata II defeat the Pala ruler Dharmapala?
n65648679683.x: Nagabhata II ousted Chakrayudha, defeated Dharmapala near Monghyr and made Kannauj the Pratihara capital.
xa: Govinda III's defeat of him came in a **Bundelkhand** campaign.
His grandson **Mihira Bhoja** was the son of **Ramabhadra**.
The **Gwalior prashasti** records his victories.

nc93b25d93ec.s: Which ruler of Kashmir checked the expansion of the Pratihara king Mihira Bhoja?
nc93b25d93ec.x: Mihira Bhoja's expansion was checked by Sankaravarman of Kashmir, along with the Rashtrakuta Krishna II and the Pala Devapala.
xa: Bhoja's title: **Adivaraha**.
Sulaiman called him "**Juzr**".

n1d54d233a97.s: Rajashekhara was associated with the courts of which of the following rulers?
n1d54d233a97.x: Rajashekhara was the court poet of Mahendrapala I and was also associated with the court of Mahipala I.
n1d54d233a97.tq: Match the court poet with both of his recorded patrons.
xs: Rajashekhara served **Mahendrapala I** and **Mahipala I** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Indra III** and **Krishna II** were Rashtrakutas, not his patrons.
xa: Works: **Kavyamimamsa**, **Karpuramanjari**, **Viddhasalabhanjika**.
Mahendrapala I ruled c. **890-910**.
Kannauj was sacked by **Indra III** under Mahipala I.

nf60bf80329b.s: Mihira Bhoja, grandson of Nagabhata II, was the son of:
nf60bf80329b.x: Mihira Bhoja was the son of Ramabhadra and therefore the grandson of Nagabhata II.
xa: Bhoja's capital: **Kannauj (Mahodaya)**.
Title **Adivaraha** — a devotee of Vishnu.
Bhoja ruled c. **836-890**, the dynasty's zenith.

n3f348646e2e.s: Which title of Mihira Bhoja reflects his devotion to Vishnu and also appears as a legend on his coins?
n3f348646e2e.x: Mihira Bhoja bore the title Adivaraha, reflecting his devotion to Vishnu; Adivaraha also appeared on his coins.
n3f348646e2e.tq: Match the ruler with the title and its numismatic association.
xs: **Adivaraha** reflects Bhoja's devotion to Vishnu and appears on his coins — option **(3)** is correct (UPPSC 2017).
**Juzr** was Sulaiman's name for him; **Aryavarta** is in Mahendrapala I's title; **Mahodaya** = Kannauj.
xa: Al-Masudi called him "**Baura**".
Bhoja built the **Teli-ka-Mandir**, Gwalior.

nindian-history-144-22.s: Mihir Bhoja captured Kannauj around which year?
nindian-history-144-22.x: Mihir Bhoja captured Kannauj around 836 AD and made it the Pratihara capital. 629 AD relates to Hiuen Tsang's journey.
nindian-history-144-22.tq: Place Mihir Bhoja in the early 9th century.
n: Mihir Bhoja captured Kannauj around 836 AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #144 · pp 250-252]
xs: **Mihir Bhoja** captured **Kannauj** around **836 AD** and made it his capital — option **(1)**.
His reign: c. **836-890**, the **zenith** of the dynasty.
**916** is when **Indra III** sacked Kannauj under **Mahipala I**.
xa: ⚠ Other notes say **Nagabhata II** made Kannauj the capital.
Titles: **Adivaraha** (UPPSC 2017) and **Prabhasa**; he followed **Vaishnavism**.
The **Barah copper plate** mentions a skandhavara at **Mahodaya**.
He built **Teli-ka-Mandir, Gwalior**.

n316d3efc50f.s: The Arab merchant Sulaiman (mid-9th century) referred to Mihira Bhoja as:
n316d3efc50f.x: Sulaiman called Mihira Bhoja 'Juzr' or 'Al-Juzr'; 'Baura' was Al-Masudi's name for him and Adivaraha was Bhoja's own title on his coins.
xa: Sulaiman came in the mid-**9th c.**, in **Bhoja I**'s reign (RPSC 2023).
Sulaiman named **Amoghavarsha** one of the four great kings of the world.

n6b188702ef8.s: Which of the following works was NOT written by Rajashekhara?
n6b188702ef8.x: Prabandhachintamani was written by Merutunga, whereas Kavyamimamsa, Karpuramanjari and Viddhasalabhanjika were works of Rajashekhara.
n6b188702ef8.tq: Use the author–work distinction to identify the wrongly attributed work.
xs: **Prabandhachintamani** is not Rajashekhara's — it is by **Merutunga** — option **(3)** is the answer (MPPSC 2025).
Rajashekhara wrote **Kavyamimamsa**, **Karpuramanjari** and **Viddhasalabhanjika**.
xa: **Kavyamimamsa** is on poetics; **Karpuramanjari** is a **Prakrit play**.
Rajashekhara was court poet of **Mahendrapala I** (and **Mahipala I**).

n6cadb2c1796.s: In which year did Mahmud of Ghazni attack Kannauj, hastening the decline of the Gurjara-Pratiharas?
n6cadb2c1796.x: Mahmud of Ghazni attacked Kannauj in 1018, one of the blows (with Indra III's raid and the secession of feudatories) that weakened Pratihara power.
xa: The **Chandelas** were based at **Khajuraho**.
Pratihara temple style peaked at **Khajuraho** (UNESCO site).
Indra III's sack is dated c. **916**.

n0379fc7a7a4.s: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were the main power that kept Arab rule confined to:
n0379fc7a7a4.x: The Gurjara-Pratiharas were the principal power that helped keep Arab rule confined to Sindh.
xa: Sulaiman praised Pratihara **cavalry** as the best in India.
He also praised their **army, wealth and security**.
Hiuen Tsang had described the **Sun temple of Multan**.

nindian-history-21-8.s: Which ruler of Sindh was defeated and killed by Muhammad bin Qasim?
nindian-history-21-8.x: Muhammad bin Qasim led the Arab invasion of Sindh, defeated and killed Raja Dahir, and his conquest stayed largely within Sindh and Multan.
n: Muhammad-bin-Qasim’s invasion was an Arab invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Dahir was defeated and killed by Muhammad-bin-Qasim. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Muhammad-bin-Qasim’s conquest was largely confined to Sindh and Multan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: The date is also given as **711–12 CE**.
The Pratiharas were the main power that kept Arab rule confined to **Sindh**.
Founder **Nagabhata I** (c. **730-760**) **resisted the Arabs**.
**Mahmud of Ghazni** attacked Kannauj in **1018**.

na5b2e6b5fe9.s: The Rashtrakuta ruler Krishna III defeated the Cholas at the Battle of:
na5b2e6b5fe9.x: Krishna III defeated the Cholas at Takkolam (949 CE).
xa: Takkolam (**949 CE**): Chola **Parantaka I** defeated, prince **Rajaditya** killed.
Krishna III patronised the poet **Ponna**.
The Kailasa is a **monolithic** temple.

n94ff060cb66.s: The first Rashtrakuta ruler to proceed towards northern India was:
n94ff060cb66.x: Dhruva was the first Rashtrakuta ruler to move north; he defeated Vatsaraja and Dharmapala.
xa: Against Vengi he acted through **Vemulavada Arikesari I**, beating **Vishnuvardhana IV**.
Vishnuvardhana IV gave his daughter **Shila Mahadevi** to Dhruva.
His successor **Govinda III** reached the **Himalayas**.

n70ded39450e.s: Which one of the following was a military achievement of Govinda III?
o: Sacking Kannauj in the reign of Indra III
Defeating Nagabhata II and Dharmapala and reaching the Himalayas
n70ded39450e.x: Govinda III defeated Nagabhata II and Dharmapala and is said in the Sanjan plates to have reached the Himalayas.
n70ded39450e.tq: Separate the military achievements of successive Rashtrakuta rulers instead of matching all northern campaigns together.
xs: **Govinda III** defeated **Nagabhata II** and **Dharmapala** and **reached the Himalayas** — option **(2)** is correct.
His Himalayan march is recorded in the **Sanjan plates**; defeat of Nagabhata II: UKPSC 2021.
**Takkolam** was **Krishna III**'s victory; **Tailapa II** overthrew the Rashtrakutas.
xa: Govinda III reigned **793-814**.
His title: **Prabhutavarsha**.
He was followed by **Amoghavarsha I** (**814-878**).

n7c76a04a27a.s: Amoghavarsha I is particularly associated with which of the following combinations?
n7c76a04a27a.x: Amoghavarsha I built Manyakheta, was associated with Kavirajamarga, and is described as a Jain ruler or patron.
n7c76a04a27a.tq: Use a cluster of contributions to identify the ruler rather than relying on a single isolated fact.
xs: Amoghavarsha I = **Manyakheta**, **Kavirajamarga** and **Jainism** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Kailasa** = Krishna I; **Takkolam** = Krishna III; **Gadayuddha** = **Ranna**; **Hiranyagarbha** = Dantidurga.
xa: Amoghavarsha won at **Vingavalli** (title **Viranarayana**); also titled **Nripatunga**.
He also wrote the Sanskrit Jain text **Prashnottara Ratnamalika**.
**Sulaiman** called him one of the **four great kings** of the world.

n284e76cab32.s: The Kannada poet Ponna was patronised by:
n284e76cab32.x: Ponna was patronised by the Rashtrakuta Krishna III; Pampa was patronised by Arikesari II and Ranna by Tailapa II.
xa: Pampa, Ponna and Ranna = the Kannada **Ratnatraya**.
Ranna wrote **Gadayuddha**; Ponna wrote **Santipurana**.
In Pampa's epic, **Arjuna** is modelled on his patron.

nindian-history-146-1.s: Who established the Rashtrakuta dynasty/Empire in 753 AD?
nindian-history-146-1.x: Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakuta empire in 753 CE by overthrowing the Badami Chalukya Kirtivarman II. Krishna I, Govinda III and Amoghavarsha I were later rulers.
nindian-history-146-1.tq: Recall the founder of the dynasty.
n: Dantidurga established the Rashtrakuta dynasty in 753 AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #146 · pp 255-256]
Dantidurga established the Rashtrakuta Empire in 753 AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #146 · pp 255-256]
xs: **Dantidurga** established the **Rashtrakuta dynasty** in **753 AD** — option **(1)**.
He overthrew the Badami Chalukya **Kirtivarman II** (UPSC 2006).
**Krishna I**, **Govinda III** and **Amoghavarsha I** were later rulers.
xa: Dantidurga performed the **Hiranyagarbha** ritual at **Ujjayini**.
He was a contemporary of Eastern Chalukya **Vijayaditya I**.
His inscription is in Ellora's **Dashavatara cave**.
⚠ **Manyakheta** was built by **Amoghavarsha I**, not Dantidurga.

n92a2acb08ec.s: The Rashtrakuta–Vengi conflict continued for approximately:
n92a2acb08ec.x: The Rashtrakuta–Vengi conflict lasted about 200 years, with repeated struggles against the Eastern Chalukyas.
xa: **Vijayaditya II** fought **108 battles**.
**Amoghavarsha** won at **Vingavalli**.
**Dhruva** won through **Vemulavada Arikesari I**.

ndbb2de0e165.s: Which Eastern Chalukya ruler is credited with fighting 108 battles against the Rashtrakuta forces?
ndbb2de0e165.x: Vijayaditya II of Vengi is credited with fighting 108 battles against the Rashtrakutas.
xa: Dhruva acted through **Vemulavada Arikesari I**.
Vijayaditya II built **108 Shiva temples** and named **Vijayawada**.

n290b05a2e7f.s: After his victory at Vingavalli, the Rashtrakuta Amoghavarsha I assumed the title:
n290b05a2e7f.x: Amoghavarsha I won at Vingavalli and took the title Viranarayana.
xa: Later **Gunaga Vijayaditya III** defeated **Krishna II**.
The conflict lasted about **200 years**.
Amoghavarsha's other title: **Nripatunga**.

n20106e8a513.s: Vijayaditya II of the Eastern Chalukyas is associated with which cultural and religious contribution?
o: Construction of 108 Shiva temples and the naming of Vijayawada
Construction of the Kailasa temple at Ellora
Establishment of Manyakheta as the Rashtrakuta capital
n20106e8a513.x: Vijayaditya II is associated with the construction of 108 Shiva temples and with the naming of Vijayawada.
n20106e8a513.tq: Match the regional contribution to the correct Eastern Chalukya ruler rather than to a Rashtrakuta monarch.
xs: **Vijayaditya II** built **108 Shiva temples** and named **Vijayawada** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Kailasa** = **Krishna I**; **Manyakheta** and **Kavirajamarga** = **Amoghavarsha I**.
xa: Vijayaditya II fought **108 battles** against the Rashtrakutas.
**Pampa** is hailed in AP as a **Telugu-born** poet.
The Rashtrakuta-Vengi war lasted about **200 years**.

n087b3f931ca.s: At the battle of Takkolam (949 CE), Krishna III defeated which Chola king?
n087b3f931ca.x: At Takkolam in 949 CE, Krishna III defeated the Cholas under Parantaka I, and the Chola prince Rajaditya was killed.
xa: Krishna III patronised **Ponna** (Santipurana).
⚠ The Ellora Kailasa is **Krishna I**'s, not Krishna III's.
**Tailapa II** ended the line c. **973**.

nindian-history-17-18.s: Who led the Chola side at the Battle of Takkolam (949 CE)?
nindian-history-17-18.x: Rajaditya led the Cholas at Takkolam, where the Western Gangas and Vaidumbas fought on the Rashtrakuta side.
n: The Battle of Takkolam belongs to the early medieval period. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
The Rashtrakuta-led confederacy included the Western Gangas and the Vaidumbas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
Rajaditya led the Cholas in the Battle of Takkolam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
xa: The **Rashtrakuta side won**; Chola prince **Rajaditya** was killed.
Krishna III defeated Chola **Parantaka I**.
The **Rajaditya Cholan RTC** at Thakkolam is named in his memory.
**Chola Gangam (Ponneri lake)** — **Rajendra Chola I**'s victory over the Ganga region.

n359ab708894.s: Kavirajamarga, the earliest work on Kannada poetics, is associated with which Rashtrakuta ruler?
n359ab708894.x: Kavirajamarga (c. 850) is associated with Amoghavarsha I and is the earliest work on Kannada poetics.
xa: Pampa wrote **Vikramarjuna Vijaya** (Pampa Bharata) in Kannada.
**Nalachampu** by **Trivikrama Bhatta** = first champu.

ne4f5766496b.x: Jinasena wrote a Sanskrit Adipurana, while Pampa wrote a Kannada Adipurana on the life of Rishabhadeva.
xa: Pampa also wrote **Vikramarjuna Vijaya** (Pampa Bharata).
His patron: **Arikesari II** of the **Vemulavada Chalukyas**.

n9607b3c1261.s: The Kannada ‘Ratnatraya’ traditionally refers to which group?
n9607b3c1261.x: The Kannada Ratnatraya consisted of Pampa, Ponna and Ranna, the three celebrated Kannada poets associated with major royal patrons.
n9607b3c1261.tq: Identify the complete literary triad rather than one poet or one patron.
xs: The Kannada **Ratnatraya** = **Pampa, Ponna and Ranna** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Trivikrama Bhatta**, **Halayudha** and **Jinasena** wrote in **Sanskrit**; **Swayambhu** wrote in Apabhramsha.
xa: Patrons: Pampa — **Arikesari II**; Ponna — **Krishna III**; Ranna — **Tailapa II**.
The Rashtrakuta age = **golden age of Kannada**.

nf0d13245ba4.s: Pampa's Kannada epic Vikramarjuna Vijaya is also known as:
nf0d13245ba4.x: Vikramarjuna Vijaya is also called Pampa Bharata; in it Pampa modelled Arjuna on his patron Arikesari II.
xa: Arikesari II was of the **Vemulavada Chalukyas**, a Rashtrakuta feudatory.
Pampa's **Adipurana** tells the life of **Rishabhadeva**.
⚠ Some notes make Pampa contemporary of **Vijayaditya I** — a slip.

n20a15a30545.s: 'Nripatunga' was a title of which Rashtrakuta ruler?
n20a15a30545.x: Nripatunga and Viranarayana were titles of Amoghavarsha I; Prabhutavarsha was associated with Govinda III.
xa: Balhara: contemporary of **Al-Masudi** (APPSC G1 2024).
Viranarayana came after the victory at **Vingavalli**.

nbb8735ee9ee.s: Manyakheta, the Rashtrakuta capital, was built by:
nbb8735ee9ee.x: Amoghavarsha I built Manyakheta; the early Rashtrakuta seat had been in the Elapura (Ellora) region.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes say **Dantidurga** made Manyakheta his capital — it was Amoghavarsha's work.
Manyakheta = **Malkhed, Karnataka**.
Paramara **Siyaka II** later sacked Manyakheta.

n7fc85140a77.s: Manyakheta, also known as Malkhed, is located in present-day:
n7fc85140a77.x: Manyakheta or Malkhed is in Karnataka and was built by Amoghavarsha I.
n7fc85140a77.tq: Use the present geographical location to resolve the historical capital question.
xs: **Manyakheta (Malkhed)** is in **Karnataka** — option **(4)** is correct.
It was built by **Amoghavarsha I** (UPSC).
xa: The earlier seat was the **Elapura (Ellora)** region.
Paramara **Siyaka II** sacked Manyakheta after defeating **Khottiga** on the **Narmada**.
**Tailapa II** of Kalyani overthrew the line c. **973**.

n95271ce8d66.s: Who overthrew the Rashtrakuta line around 973 CE?
n95271ce8d66.x: After Paramara Siyaka II defeated Khottiga and sacked Manyakheta, Tailapa II of the Kalyani Chalukyas overthrew the Rashtrakuta line around 973 CE.
xa: The Kannada poet **Ranna** was patronised by Western Chalukya **Tailapa II**.
Manyakheta was built by **Amoghavarsha I**.

n37da532bf6a.s: Arab writers used the term ‘Balhara’ for:
o: The Chola kings who ruled at Takkolam
n37da532bf6a.x: Balhara is the Arab form associated with Vallabharaja and was used generally for Rashtrakuta kings. Al-Masudi was a contemporary source for this usage.
n37da532bf6a.tq: Avoid the trap of assigning a dynastic title to one particular ruler when it had broader usage.
xs: Arab writers used "**Balhara**" for **Rashtrakuta kings generally** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is the Arab form of **Vallabharaja**; Al-Masudi was contemporary (APPSC G1 2024).
xa: **Sulaiman** called **Amoghavarsha I** one of the four great kings of the world.
Amoghavarsha's titles: **Nripatunga**, **Viranarayana**.
Govinda III's title: **Prabhutavarsha**.

n608d643d8aa.s: In Rashtrakuta administration, the Vishaya was headed by the:
n608d643d8aa.x: The Vishaya was headed by the Vishayapati; the Rashtra by the Rashtrapati, the Bhukti by the Bhogapati and the Grama by the Gramakuta or gavunda.
xa: **Nad-gavundas** were hereditary local officers of the **nadu**, helping in revenue collection.
Capital: **Manyakheta (Malkhed, Karnataka)**.
Learning centre: **Salotgi** (Bijapur).

n4384102779a.s: In Rashtrakuta administration, hereditary local officers of the nadu who assisted in revenue collection were called:
n4384102779a.x: Nad-gavundas were hereditary local officers of the nadu who assisted in revenue collection.
xa: Units: **Rashtra → Vishaya → Bhukti → Grama**.
Heads: **Rashtrapati**, **Vishayapati**, **Bhogapati**, **Gramakuta**.
Founder of the dynasty: **Dantidurga**.

nefc9433b7ec.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Rashtrakuta trade?
o: Horses were imported by sea from Arabia.
Cambay, Thana and Sopara were western ports connected with this trade.
Textiles were among the goods exported.
Arab merchants were barred from settling in the western ports.
nefc9433b7ec.x: Arab merchants settled peacefully in the western ports, so the statement that they were barred is false; the horse imports, textile exports and the listed ports are correct.
xa: Arab merchants could trade, worship and **build mosques** in port towns.
Prosperity came from **control of major trade routes**.
Al-Masudi noted the Balhara's **many Arab/Muslim subjects**.

na190fbd1cff.s: Who among the following travellers ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the four great kings of the world?
na190fbd1cff.x: Sulaiman, who visited during the reign of Amoghavarsha I, ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the four great kings along with the Caliph, the Chinese emperor and the Byzantine emperor.
na190fbd1cff.tq: Match the traveller with the distinctive description of his account.
xs: **Sulaiman** ranked the Rashtrakuta king among the **four great kings** of the world — option **(1)** is correct.
The others were the **Caliph**, the **Chinese** and **Byzantine** emperors; he came under **Amoghavarsha I**.
**Ibn Khurdadbeh** and **Al-Masudi** called the Balhara the **greatest king of India** — a different claim.
xa: ⚠ **Sulaiman** = Amoghavarsha I; **Al-Masudi** = **Indra III**.
"**Balhara**" = Arabic form of **Vallabha**.
Al-Masudi came c. **915-16 CE**.

ncb801eb9e7b.s: The Arab traveller Al-Masudi visited the Rashtrakuta kingdom (c. 915-16 CE) during the reign of:
ncb801eb9e7b.x: Al-Masudi came c. 915-16 CE under Indra III and described the Balhara as having many Arab/Muslim subjects.
xa: Balhara comes from **Vallabharaja**.
**Sulaiman** came under **Amoghavarsha I**.
Arab merchants could **build mosques** in port towns.

ne7aef4584f8.s: The decline of the Rashtrakutas occurred by the late tenth century primarily under pressure from which powers?
ne7aef4584f8.x: The Rashtrakutas declined by the late tenth century under Chalukya-Chola pressure.
ne7aef4584f8.tq: Use the dynasty-pair association rather than being distracted by other South Indian dynasties.
xs: The Rashtrakutas declined by the late **10th century** under pressure from **the Chalukyas and Cholas** — option **(3)** is correct.
The same late-**10th-century** period saw **Krishna III** still active in **Vengi** (**970 CE**) just before the decline.
xa: AP angle: **Krishna III** helped **Danarnava** seize **Vengi** (**970 CE**).
The era had raised **Kannada** to a classical medium.
It gave **Ellora** its Hindu peak.

n7b21133656c.s: Which faith reached its zenith of Rashtrakuta patronage under Amoghavarsha I?
n7b21133656c.x: Jainism reached a high point under Amoghavarsha I, who was a devout Jain and is described as having renounced the throne.
n7b21133656c.tq: Link the ruler with the specifically stated religious patronage.
xs: **Jainism** reached its zenith under **Amoghavarsha I** (**814-878**) — option **(3)** is correct.
He was a **devout Jain** who **renounced the throne**.
xa: His reign laid groundwork for **Gomateshvara (Shravanabelagola)**.
Early rulers were staunch **Shaivas**.
**Vaishnavism** and **Buddhism** had royal patronage, no persecution.

n5c61112c762.s: The early Rashtrakuta rulers were staunch followers of:
n5c61112c762.x: Early Rashtrakuta rulers were staunch Shaivas, though Vaishnavism and Buddhism also received patronage without persecution.
xa: **Jainism** peaked under **Amoghavarsha I**.
The **Kailasa** temple reflects the early Shaiva patronage.
Ellora shows **religious tolerance** — three faiths side by side.

nb12d32ba71f.s: The Ellora caves are carved in which hills of Aurangabad district, Maharashtra?
nb12d32ba71f.x: Ellora lies in the Charanandri hills near the Elaganga river, on the ancient Ujjain-Deccan route; the caves were carved c. 600-1000 CE.
xa: **34 caves** (APPSC-GS 2024): **12** Buddhist, **17** Hindu, **5** Jain.
Three faiths side by side = **religious tolerance**.
India-Jordan **Petra-Ellora** twinning agreement (**2026**).

nbf972414d8d.s: The Hindu caves (13-29) at Ellora are mainly the work of the:
nbf972414d8d.x: The Hindu caves at Ellora are mainly Rashtrakuta work; the Buddhist caves (c. 600-730 CE) are the earliest and the Jain caves the latest.
xa: Some notes credit later Jain additions to the **Yadavas**.
Some notes list the Buddhist caves as Rashtrakuta.
Ellora was carved c. **600-1000 CE**.

n3355a26535f.s: The Kailasa temple at Ellora is which cave of the Ellora group?
n3355a26535f.x: The monolithic Kailasa temple is Cave 16; Cave 10 is the Buddhist chaitya.
xa: Size: c. **200 ft long, 100 ft wide, 100 ft high**.
A **25-ft** plinth with elephants and lions.
Kailasa as Cave 16: **APPSC-GS 2025**.

ne25740aec80.s: The Kailasa temple at Ellora was carved during the reign of which Rashtrakuta ruler?
ne25740aec80.x: The Kailasa temple, with its three-tiered Dravida vimana, was carved under Krishna I (r. 756-773), not Dantidurga or Amoghavarsha.
xa: The Rashtrakutas shaped the **Vesara** synthesis (Nagara + Dravida).
⚠ APPSC G1 2024 wrong pair: **Krishna III** — Ellora Shiva temple.
It is **monolithic**, carved top-down from basalt.

n54615678355.s: The Vesara synthesis associated with the Rashtrakutas represents the combination of:
n54615678355.x: The Rashtrakutas contributed to the Vesara synthesis, which combined Nagara and Dravida architectural features and became associated with the Deccan style.
n54615678355.tq: Separate the two component traditions of a composite style.
xs: **Vesara** = **Nagara + Dravida** — option **(2)** is correct.
The Rashtrakutas shaped this synthesis into the **Deccan style**.
xa: The Kailasa has a **Dravida vimana** though in **Nagara** territory.
The era marks the **zenith of rock-cut art** (Kailasa, Elephanta).

n95a52c5de84.s: The Kailasa temple (Cave 16) at Ellora was carved during the reign of which Rashtrakuta ruler?
n95a52c5de84.x: It was carved under Krishna I (r. 756-773 CE). Dantidurga founded the dynasty, Amoghavarsha I built Manyakheta, and crediting Krishna III with it was the wrong pair in APPSC G1 2024.
xs: The Kailasa (Cave 16) was carved under **Krishna I** (r. **756-773 CE**) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Dantidurga** founded the dynasty; **Amoghavarsha I** built **Manyakheta**.
Crediting **Krishna III** was the **wrong pair** in APPSC G1 2024.
xa: Kailasa = **largest monolithic rock excavation** in the world.
Its size: c. **200 ft long**.
Exam angle: "carved during the reign of" — **Krishna I**.

n1c7ae444adc.s: The three-headed Shiva known as Trimurti or Maheshamurti is the principal masterpiece of:
n1c7ae444adc.x: The Trimurti (Maheshamurti) is the masterpiece of the Elephanta island caves near Mumbai, whose main cave many historians date to the sixth-century Kalachuris.
xa: MPPSC 2021 key: Ellora and Elephanta = **Rashtrakuta**.
Trimurti + Kailasa = Rashtrakuta **zenith of art**.

n7a015a03eba.s: The Badami cliff inscription records that Vatapi was fortified by Pulakesin I in
n7a015a03eba.x: Pulakesin I fortified Vatapi, as recorded in the Badami cliff inscription dated to 543 CE.
n7a015a03eba.tq: Distinguish the foundation-era date from the later reign and inscription dates.
xs: The **Badami cliff inscription** records that **Pulakesin I** fortified Vatapi in **543 CE** — option **(1)**.
**597** is the start of **Mangalesha**'s regency (597-609), **609** the accession of **Pulakesin II**, and **634** the date of the **Aihole inscription**.
xa: Pulakesin I is the **founder** of the independent kingdom with capital **Badami**, and performed the **Ashvamedha**.
Vatapi = modern **Badami**, **Bagalkot district, Karnataka**, among sandstone hills around **Agastya lake**.
⚠ The dynasty span **c. 543-757 CE** begins with this same year.

n4cddb7b501c.s: Why did Mangalesha become ruler after the death of Kirtivarman I?
o: He was the eldest son of Kirtivarman I.
He was appointed by the Pallava king.
He succeeded after defeating Vikramaditya II.
He ruled as regent because Kirtivarman I had left minor sons.
n4cddb7b501c.x: Kirtivarman I left minor sons, so his brother Mangalesha governed as regent.
n4cddb7b501c.tq: Use the succession circumstance to distinguish regency from hereditary succession.
xs: **Kirtivarman I** left **minor sons**, so his brother **Mangalesha** ruled as **regent** — option **(4)**.
Mangalesha was Kirtivarman I's **brother**, not his son; **Vikramaditya II** was a much later ruler.
He **refused to hand over power** and may have named his own son heir, which led to a succession war.
xa: Exiled **Pulakesin II** killed Mangalesha at **Elapattu-Simbige** (Bana territory, c. **609-10 CE**).
Mangalesha's regency: **597-609**; kingdom from **south Gujarat** to **Bellary-Kurnool**.
Mangalesha is credited with the **earliest rock-cut caves at Badami**.

nbca3b485b95.s: The description of Kirtivarman I as ‘the night of doom’ in the Aihole inscription refers particularly to his victories over the
nbca3b485b95.x: Kirtivarman I is described as the ‘night of doom’ to the Nalas, Mauryas and Kadambas.
nbca3b485b95.tq: Pair the distinctive epithet with the exact group of defeated powers.
xs: The Aihole inscription calls **Kirtivarman I** "the night of doom" to the **Nalas, Mauryas and Kadambas** — option **(4)**.
**Kosala, Kalinga, Alupas, Harsha, Pallavas, Gangas, Latas, Malavas, Gurjaras** are among **Pulakesin II**'s victories in the same record.
xa: Kirtivarman I is noted for **expansion** and the **Bahusuvarna-Agnishtoma** sacrifice (**Mahakuta pillar inscription**).
He left **minor sons**, so his brother **Mangalesha** became regent.
The inscription is by **Ravikirti**, Jain court poet of Pulakesin II.

nec81792fa3c.s: The last Badami Chalukya ruler, Kirtivarman II, was overthrown by:
nec81792fa3c.x: Dantidurga overthrew Kirtivarman II and founded the Rashtrakuta power around 753-757 CE.
xa: Dynasty span: c. **543-757 CE**.
Founder: **Pulakesin I** (c. **543**), who performed the **Ashvamedha**.
FIRST/LAST pair: first South Indian gold coins = **Pulakesin II**; last ruler = **Kirtivarman II**.

ndf91d1a3b2b.s: The earliest rock-cut caves at Badami are associated with
ndf91d1a3b2b.x: Mangalesha is associated with the earliest rock-cut caves at Badami.
ndf91d1a3b2b.tq: Use the ruler–monument association rather than the better-known founder association.
xs: The **earliest rock-cut caves at Badami** are associated with **Mangalesha** (597-609) — option **(4)**.
**Pulakesin I** is the founder who fortified Vatapi; **Kirtivarman I** is known for expansion; **Vikramaditya II** for Kanchi and the **Virupaksha temple** link.
xa: Mangalesha ruled as **regent** for Kirtivarman I's **minor sons**.
His kingdom ran from **south Gujarat** to **Bellary-Kurnool**.
He was killed by **Pulakesin II** at **Elapattu-Simbige** (c. 609-10 CE).

nbc4eee1152a.s: Which ruler took Kanchi three times but spared the city and is associated with the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal?
nbc4eee1152a.x: Vikramaditya II took Kanchi three times but spared it. His queen Lokamahadevi built the Virupaksha temple at Pattadakal.
nbc4eee1152a.tq: Link the repeated conquest and temple achievement to the same ruler.
xs: **Vikramaditya II** took **Kanchi** thrice but spared it — option **(2)**.
The **Virupaksha temple, Pattadakal** was built by his queen **Lokamahadevi**.
**Vikramaditya I** (655-680) restored Chalukya power after the Pallava occupation of Vatapi; **Kirtivarman II** was the last ruler.
xa: ⚠ Do not confuse the Virupaksha temple with the **Meguti Jain temple, Aihole**, site of the Aihole inscription.
