He is also called **Kaviraja Shikhamani**.
⚠ Nannechoda is **not** in the Kavitraya.

n02e362dd654.x: Bhimakhandam concerns Bhimeswara of Draksharama; Sringara Naishadham is on Nala and Damayanti and Palnati Veera Charitra on the battle of Palnadu.
xa: ⚠ CDI links **Bhimakhandam** to the **Bhima river**.
Palnati Veera Charitra mentions instruments such as **Sannai** and **Mukha Veena**.
⚠ The APPSC 2025 key treated **Palnati Vira Charitra** as **not** Srinatha's.

nd8cc6647eaa.x: Bhadraparinayamu is by Allamaraju Subrahmanya Kavi (APPSC-GS 2022). Madayagari Mallana wrote Rajasekhara Charitra, Ayyalaraju Ramabhadra Ramabhyudayam, and Nandi Timmana Parijatapaharanam.
xs: **Bhadraparinayamu** is by **Allamaraju Subrahmanya Kavi** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2022).
**Madayagari Mallana** wrote **Rajasekhara Charitra**; **Ayyalaraju Ramabhadra** wrote **Ramabhyudayam**.
**Nandi Timmana** wrote **Parijatapaharanam**.
xa: **Tenali Ramakrishna** wrote **Panduranga Mahatmyam**.
**Ramaraja Bhushana** wrote **Vasucharitra**.

nc3930c6f4f8.s: Which of the following is regarded as the first mathematics book in Telugu?
o: Sara Sangraha Ganitam of Pavuluri Mallana
nc3930c6f4f8.x: Pavuluri Mallana's Sara Sangraha Ganitam (Pavuluri Ganitam), from Mahaviracharya's Ganita Sara Sangraha, is the first mathematics book and first scientific kavya in Telugu (G2 2019 key). Andhra Shabda Chintamani is grammar, Kavijanasrayam prosody and Nitisara polity.
nc3930c6f4f8.tq: First Telugu maths book = Pavuluri Ganitam
xs: **Sara Sangraha Ganitam** of **Pavuluri Mallana** is the **first mathematics book** in Telugu — so option **(2)** is correct (G2 2019 key).
**Andhra Shabda Chintamani** is grammar; **Kavijanasrayam** is prosody (**Malliya Rechana**); **Nitisara** is polity (**Rudradeva**).
xa: It is also the first **scientific kavya** in Telugu.
It renders **Mahaviracharya's** Sanskrit **Ganita Sara Sangraha** (APPSC 2019).
It featured in the G2 2023 author list.

n24bcdf3cc77.s: Ketana earned the title 'Abhinava Dandi' for rendering into Telugu:
n24bcdf3cc77.x: His Dashakumara Charitra, from Dandin's Sanskrit work, is the first Telugu prose-story kavya and won him the title (APPSC G2 2019).
xa: Ketana's **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam** = **first grammar written in Telugu**.
His **Vijnaneshwariyam** = Telugu version of the **Mitakshara**.
He dedicated his work to **Tikkana** → first poet to receive a literary dedication.
Ketana was first to use the words **"Tenugu/Telugu"**.

n2f39987054e.s: Which work is regarded as the first Telugu grammar written in Telugu and contains 196 padyas?
n2f39987054e.x: Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam by Ketana is regarded as the first grammar written in Telugu and contains 196 padyas.
n2f39987054e.tq: Distinguish a work by combining its title, authorial field and numerical detail.
xs: **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam** of **Ketana** is the **first grammar written in Telugu**, with **196 padyas** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Andhra Shabda Chintamani** is a Telugu grammar **in Sanskrit** (Nannaya).
**Kavi Janasrayam** is on prosody; **Kavyalankara Chudamani** is the first alankara work (**Vinnakota Peddana**).
xa: Ketana — Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam was asked in **APPSC 2025**.
**Appakaviyam** is by **Kakunuri Appakavi** (17th c.).

n5e2ac6451a6.s: Who authored Kavijanasrayam, regarded as the first Telugu work on prosody?
n5e2ac6451a6.x: Kavijanasrayam, the first Telugu work on prosody, was authored by Malliya Rechana.
n5e2ac6451a6.tq: Match the specialised literary subject with its author.
xs: **Kavijanasrayam**, the first Telugu work on prosody, is by **Malliya Rechana** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Kakunuri Appakavi** wrote **Appakaviyam**; **Vinnakota Peddana** wrote **Kavyalankara Chudamani**.
**Ketana** wrote **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam**.
xa: ⚠ Do not confuse **Kavi Janasrayam** with **Kavijana Ranjanam**.
**Kavi Vakbandham** is by **Tikkana**.

n403d1ca8796.s: Who translated the Markandeya Puranam into Telugu?
n403d1ca8796.x: Marana translated Markandeya Puranam; Errana did Harivamsa and Ketana Dasakumara Charitra.
xa: **Viddhasalabhanjika** was rendered as **Keyurabahu Charitra** by **Manchena**.
Ramayana versions: **Gona Budda Reddy**, **Hulakki Bhaskara**, **Tikkana** (Nirvachanottara Ramayanam).

n87992af620c.s: Manchena's Keyurabahu Charitra is associated with the Telugu rendering of
n87992af620c.x: Manchena rendered Viddhasalabhanjika as Keyurabahu Charitra in Telugu.
n87992af620c.tq: Use the source-work to target-work association to distinguish similar classical titles.
xs: **Manchena's Keyurabahu Charitra** renders **Viddhasalabhanjika** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Viddhasalabhanjika is a work of **Rajasekhara**.
**Naishadha** → Srinatha; **Dasakumara Charita** → Ketana; **Markandeya Purana** → Marana.
xa: CDX spells the author **"Mallena"**.
**Manchena - Keyurabahu Charitra** appeared in APPSC G2 2023/2025 match lists.

na00a9c40a56.s: The first Telugu grammar, written in Sanskrit, is:
na00a9c40a56.x: Andhra Shabda Chintamani is the first Telugu grammar in Sanskrit; Ganita Sara Sangraha is the first Telugu mathematics book.
xa: First Telugu word: **Nagabu** (Amaravati); first inscription: **Kalamalla** (**575 CE**).
First poetic inscription: **Addanki**; first Ramayana: **Ranganatha Ramayanam**.
⚠ **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam** is also listed as first grammar (first **written in Telugu**).

n33ade6006fe.s: Tikkana Somayaji was the first Telugu poet to have a work dedicated to him. Which work was dedicated to him?
o: Ranganatha Ramayanam by Gona Budda Reddy
n33ade6006fe.x: Ketana dedicated Dasakumara Charitra to Tikkana Somayaji, making Tikkana the first Telugu poet to have a work dedicated to him.
n33ade6006fe.tq: Use the author–work–dedicatee relationship rather than confusing it with authorship of the major epics.
xs: Ketana dedicated **Dasakumara Charitra** to **Tikkana** — so option **(1)** is correct.
That makes Tikkana the **first poet to have a work dedicated to him**.
xa: Ketana was Tikkana's disciple and was called **Abhinava Dandi**.
Ketana was also the first to use the words **"Tenugu/Telugu"**.
Dasakumara Charitra is from **Dandin's** Sanskrit.

n650fd7de4cd.s: The Kesari Samudra tank was built by Kakatiya:
n650fd7de4cd.x: Rudradeva, author of Nitisara, is associated with building the Kesari Samudra tank.
xa: Other Kakatiya-court Sanskrit authors: **Vidyanatha**, **Jayapa Senani**, **Ekamranatha** (Pratapa Charitra).
**Ravipati Tripurantakudu** wrote the Sanskrit **Niroshthya Ramayanam**.

n8d87c4ee29d.s: Prataparudra Yashobhushanam, a Sanskrit work, was written by:
n8d87c4ee29d.x: Prataparudra Yashobhushanam is a Sanskrit work by Vidyanatha, not a Telugu work by Ketana.
xa: Jayapa also wrote **Geeta Ratnavali** and **Vadya Ratnavali**.
Kreedabhiramam calls Orugallu **"Andhra Nagari"**.

n22e7746c429.s: Kreedabhiramam is a Telugu rendering of Premabhiramam, a Sanskrit play by:
n22e7746c429.x: Kreedabhiramam renders Ravipati Tripurantakudu's Premabhiramam, hence the authorship debate with Vinukonda Vallabharaya.
xa: Author: **Vinukonda Vallabharaya (Vallabhamatya)**.
Form: **Veedhi natakam** on Orugallu.
Ravipati Tripurantakudu also wrote the Sanskrit **Niroshthya Ramayanam**.

n567e532c156.s: The line 'Desa Bhashalandu Telugu Lessa' is associated with:
n567e532c156.x: The line is associated with Krishnadevaraya, whose period with the Ashtadiggajas was the peak of Telugu literary culture.
xa: The Kakatiya era laid grammar, poetics and the **desi-metre** tradition.
**"Italian of the East"** was coined by **Niccolo de' Conti**.

nde838d31b45.s: Telugu belongs to which sub-branch of the Dravidian family?
nde838d31b45.x: Telugu is South-Central Dravidian with Gondi and Kui; Tamil and Malayalam are South Dravidian.
xa: Telugu is one of the **22 Eighth Schedule languages** and the official language of AP.
It grew out of the **Desi bhasha (Paisachi)** of Prakrit.
**Trilinga theory**: **Srisailam, Kaleshwaram, Draksharama** → "Telugu".
Telugu has been a **classical language since 2008**.

n3e4daffa033.s: Telugu, the official language of Andhra Pradesh, belongs to which language family?
n3e4daffa033.x: Telugu belongs to the Dravidian family and is one of the 22 Eighth Schedule languages.
xa: Telugu has been a **classical language since 2008**.
**Telugu Language Day**: **29 August** (Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy's birth anniversary).
AP holds a **Telugu Mahotsavam** every year.

nb44a787fa29.s: The Trilinga theory derives the name Andhra from the three Shaiva centres of:
nb44a787fa29.x: The Trilinga theory refers to Srisailam, Kaleshwaram and Draksharama as the three Shaiva centres of Trilinga desa.
nb44a787fa29.tq: Use a three-place association to distinguish the Trilinga theory from other regional lists.
xs: The **Trilinga theory** names **Srisailam, Kaleshwaram and Draksharama** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Andhra was called **Trilinga desa** after these three Shaiva centres, and "Telugu" is derived from **Trilinga**.
xa: Some derive **Tenugu** from **tene (honey)**.
**Andhra** / **Andhrika** are other names of the language.
**Draksharama Bhimeswara** is praised in **Srinatha's Bhimakhandam**.

n3951339ab54.s: The separate Telugu script with rounded letters and vowel signs emerged in the:
n3951339ab54.x: After the Bhattiprolu Brahmi variant and the common Old Kannada–Telugu script, the separate Telugu script came in the 11th–14th centuries.
xa: The Bhattiprolu stupa inscriptions are c. **400 BCE**, Guntur.
The separate script has **rounded letters** and vowel signs.
Telugu script derives from **Brahmi**.

n77237a6bab9.s: The Bhattiprolu stupa inscriptions are best described as:
o: Sanskrit inscriptions in the common Old Kannada script
Tamil inscriptions in the Grantha script
Prakrit inscriptions in a variant of Brahmi carrying early Telugu place and personal names
Telugu inscriptions in the fully developed medieval Telugu script
n77237a6bab9.x: The Bhattiprolu inscriptions, dated approximately to 400 BCE in Guntur, use a variant of Brahmi and contain early Telugu place and personal names.
n77237a6bab9.tq: Use the precise combination of date, place, script and linguistic evidence.
xs: The **Bhattiprolu stupa inscriptions** use a **Brahmi variant** carrying **early Telugu place and personal names** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They are dated c. **400 BCE**, in **Guntur**.
The fully developed Telugu script came only in the **11th-14th c.**
xa: Telugu script evolved from **Brahmi**.
Next stage: common **Old Kannada-Telugu** script (Kadamba-Chalukya).
The first Telugu word, **"Nagabu"**, is in the **Amaravati** inscription.

n5d64380e78f.s: In the Prakrit age of Andhra, whose golden age came under Hala, the royal language was:
n5d64380e78f.x: Prakrit was the royal language in this age (APPSC G2 2011 key), with its golden age under Hala. Sanskrit later became the official language of the Eastern Chalukyas; Telugu appears only as words in Prakrit records; Tamil is not the answer.
xs: The royal language of the Prakrit age was **Prakrit** (G2 2011 key) — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its golden age came under **Hala**.
Telugu then appears only as **words inside Prakrit records**.
xa: **Hala's Gatha Saptasati** has Telugu words like atta, addam, potta, pilla.
Later the official language was **Sanskrit** (G2 2008 key), with Telugu as the people's language.
**Mayidavolu** plates (Prakrit, c. **300 CE**) first record "Andhrapatha".

n7c6bb400422.s: The Gatha Saptasati, a Prakrit work containing early Telugu words, was compiled by:
n7c6bb400422.x: The Satavahana king Hala compiled the Gatha Saptasati, which holds words like atta, addam, potta and pilla.
xa: First Telugu word **"Nagabu"** — **Amaravati** inscription, identified by **Veturi Prabhakara Sastri**.
**"Vepuru"** occurs in the **Myakadoni** inscription.
The Gatha Saptasati **contained writing by women**.
Telugu script grew from **Brahmi**; **Bhattiprolu** inscriptions c. **400 BCE**.

nd1973acc230.s: In Eastern Chalukya inscriptions, the official language was:
nd1973acc230.x: Sanskrit was official while Telugu was the people's language; in bilingual records the eulogy was in Sanskrit and grant details in Telugu.
xa: **Nannaya** made Telugu a language for **high literature**.
**Chebrolu inscription** shows **Marga** and **Desi** forms.
**Addanki** = **first Telugu poetic inscription** (**Taruvoja** metre).

ndde5825cb0c.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of Nannaya's contribution to Telugu literature?
o: He established the desi-metre tradition during the Vijayanagara period.
He introduced Persian vocabulary into Telugu court literature.
He fixed the grammar and literary register of classical Telugu and initiated the Kavitrayam tradition.
He was the first poet to compose a Telugu satakam.
ndde5825cb0c.x: Nannaya's Bharatam helped fix the grammar and literary register of classical Telugu and began the tradition of the Kavitrayam.
ndde5825cb0c.tq: Select the option that combines the stated literary contributions without adding an unrelated claim.
xs: Nannaya's Bharatam **fixed the grammar and literary register of classical Telugu** and started the **Kavitrayam** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **desi-metre** tradition belongs to the **Kakatiya era**, not Vijayanagara.
The first satakam is credited to **Sivatattvasaram** or **Vrushadhipa Satakam**, not Nannaya.
xa: Nannaya is the **Adikavi**, at the court of **Rajaraja Narendra**.
He made Telugu a language for **high literature**.
**Andhra Mahabharatamu** is the **first book in Telugu**.

n6b2304de83a.s: Which of the following was a member of the Kavitraya?
n6b2304de83a.x: The Kavitraya consists of Nannaya, Tikkana and Errana.
xa: **Srinatha** (Kavi Sarvabhauma) bridges the Kavitraya and the **Prabandha** age.
**Nannechoda** wrote **Kumarasambhavam**; title **Kavirajasekhara**.
**Potana** bore the title **Sahaja Panditya**; **Veerabhadra Vijayam** is his.

ne8e8fad7098.s: The literary work associated with the rule that a woman's property passes to her daughter and granddaughter is:
ne8e8fad7098.x: Purushartha Saramu, composed by Sivadevayya, contains the stated rule regarding the succession of a woman's property.
ne8e8fad7098.tq: Use the distinctive content of the work to distinguish it from closely related literary and legal works.
xs: **Purushartha Saramu** of **Sivadevayya** gives the rule that a woman's property passes to her **daughter and granddaughter** — so option **(2)** is correct (G2 2019 key).
**Nitisara** is **Rudradeva's** polity work; **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam** is **Ketana's** grammar.
**Vijnaneswariyam** is **Ketana's** Telugu Mitakshara.
xa: Purushartha Saramu also deals with the **72 Niyogas**.
⚠ APPSC 2019 answer was **Purushartha Saramu**, not Ketana's Vignaneswaram.

nf4a552bb0b3.s: Ketana, known as Mula Ghatika, dedicated his work to:
nf4a552bb0b3.x: Ketana dedicated his work to Tikkana and was the first to use the words 'Tenugu' and 'Telugu'.
xa: Tikkana became the **first poet to receive a literary dedication**.
Ketana's title: **Abhinava Dandi** (APPSC G2 2019) for rendering **Dandin's Dashakumara Charitra**.
His **Andhra Bhasha Bhushanam** is the first Telugu grammar written in Telugu.

n6fb1fba2c23.s: Which one of the following works was NOT written by Srinatha?
n6fb1fba2c23.x: Veerabhadra Vijayam is by Bammera Potana, a common distractor. Haravilasam (dedicated to Tippayya Setti), Sivaratri Mahatmyam and Kashikhandam are Srinatha's works.
xs: **Veerabhadra Vijayam** is by **Bammera Potana**, not Srinatha — so option **(3)** is the answer.
**Haravilasam**, **Sivaratri Mahatmyam** and **Kashikhandam** are Srinatha's.
xa: Haravilasam is dedicated to merchant **Tippayya Setti**.
Potana's title: **Sahaja Panditya**.
⚠ The APPSC 2025 key treated **Palnati Vira Charitra** as not Srinatha's; **Madanavilasa Bhanam** was another option.

na29164baf26.s: Which of the following places was NOT among those captured by Muhammad bin Qasim?
na29164baf26.x: Muhammad bin Qasim captured Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad and Multan. Somnath was attacked much later by Mahmud of Ghazni.
na29164baf26.tq: Find the place belonging to a different invasion.
xs: **Somnath** was not taken by Muhammad bin Qasim — so option **(4)** is the answer.
He took **Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad and Multan** in **712 CE**.
Somnath was raided by **Mahmud of Ghazni** in **1025**.
xa: The Somnath loot is said to be **20 million dinars**.
Gujarat was then ruled by the Solanki **Bhima I**.
Raja Dahir's capital was **Alor (Aror)**.

n5cbfee8c3ee.s: The Chachnama, the chronicle of the Arab conquest of Sindh, was translated into Persian by:
o: Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi
n5cbfee8c3ee.x: The Chachnama, an Arabic chronicle of the conquest of Sindh, was rendered into Persian by Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi (BPSC 2024). Al-Biruni wrote Kitab-ul-Hind, Minhaj-us-Siraj Tabaqat-i-Nasiri and Hasan Nizami Taj-ul-Maasir.
xs: The **Chachnama** was translated into Persian by **Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi** (BPSC 2024) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Al-Biruni** wrote **Kitab-ul-Hind**.
xa: The Chachnama is an **Arabic chronicle** of the **conquest of Sindh**.
**Firdausi** wrote the **Shahnama**, commissioned by Mahmud.
**Utbi** wrote **Tarikh-i-Yamini**.

na6716a68ce5.s: The Ghaznavids declined after Mahmud chiefly under pressure from the:
na6716a68ce5.x: The Ghaznavid power declined after Mahmud under Seljuk pressure.
na6716a68ce5.tq: Identify the external power responsible for decline.
xs: The Ghaznavids declined after Mahmud under pressure from the **Seljuks** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Chaulukyas**, **Palas** and **Cholas** were Indian powers, not the cause named.
xa: Mahmud reigned **998-1030 CE**.
The line was founded by **Alptigin**; **Sabuktigin** was the real founder.
The Ghurids under **Muhammad Ghori** (**1173-1206**) came next.

n7cd9b777443.s: Which one of the following was the correct sequence of Muhammad Ghori's conquests in India?
o: Multan, Peshawar, Sindh, Punjab and Lahore
Peshawar, Multan, Punjab and Lahore, Sindh
Sindh, Multan, Peshawar, Punjab and Lahore
Punjab and Lahore, Sindh, Multan, Peshawar
n7cd9b777443.x: Ghori took Multan in 1175, Peshawar around 1179, Sindh around 1182, and Punjab and Lahore around 1190.
n7cd9b777443.tq: Arrange territorial conquests in chronological order.
xs: Order: **Multan → Peshawar → Sindh → Punjab and Lahore** — so option **(1)** is correct.
xa: Ghori entered through the **Gomal Pass**.
In between, he lost in Gujarat at **Kayadara (1178)**.
Then came **First Tarain (1191)**.

n499ae747a58.s: Which battle marked the turning point that opened North India to Muhammad Ghori?
n499ae747a58.x: The Second Battle of Tarain in 1192 was the turning point that opened North India to Ghori.
n499ae747a58.tq: Associate the turning-point description with the correct battle.
xs: **Second Tarain (1192)** was the turning point that opened North India — so option **(4)** is correct.
**First Tarain (1191)** was won by **Prithviraj**; **Kayadara (1178)** was a Ghori defeat.
**Chandawar (1194)** came after the turning point.
xa: After Tarain II, **Qutbuddin Aibak** was made Ghori's representative in India.
Ghori aimed at **permanent conquest**, unlike Mahmud.

na504bcee665.s: Who founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206 after the death of Muhammad Ghori?
na504bcee665.x: Qutbuddin Aibak, Ghori's slave and Master of Stables, founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.
xa: Aibak was Ghori's slave and **Master of Stables**.
The Delhi Sultanate lasted **1206-1526**: **Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi**.
He was made Ghori's representative in India after **Tarain II**.

nindian-history-19-8.s: Muhammad Ghori defeated Jayachandra (Jaichand) of Kannauj at the Battle of:
nindian-history-19-8.x: Ghori defeated Jayachandra at Chandawar (1194), near the Yamuna.
n: Muhammad Ghori defeated Jayachandra, also known as Jaichand, in the Battle of Chandawar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 74-76]
The Battle of Chandawar was fought near the Yamuna. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 74-76]
xa: ⚠ **1191** = Prithviraj won (First Tarain); **1192** = Ghori won (Second Tarain).
Jaichand belonged to the **Gahadavala** dynasty of **Kanauj**.
Ghori's invasion led to the **foundation** of the **Delhi Sultanate**.

nindian-history-21-9.s: How many times did Mahmud of Ghazni invade India between 1000 and 1027?
nindian-history-21-9.x: Mahmud raided India 17 times between 1000 and 1027.
n: Mahmud Ghazni invaded India during 1000–1027. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Mahmud Ghazni’s invasions were repeated invasions. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Mahmud Ghazni invaded India 17 times. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: His main objective: **wealth** and **plunder**.
**Somnath** campaign: **1025–1026**, under Solanki **Bhima I**.
Mahmud's reign: **998-1030 CE**.
⚠ **Alptigin** = founder; **Sabuktigin** = real founder.

n5179093be3f.s: The capital of Raja Dahir, defeated by Muhammad bin Qasim in 712 CE, was:
n5179093be3f.x: Dahir's capital was Alor (Aror); Brahmanabad was only one of the places taken.
xa: Places taken: **Debal, Nirun, Sehwan, Brahmanabad and Multan**.
The **Arabs** were the **first Muslim invaders**.
The **Chachnama** is the chronicle of this conquest.

naa9c0f7e317.s: Muhammad Ghori entered India through which pass?
naa9c0f7e317.x: Muhammad Ghori entered India through the Gomal Pass.
xa: His first conquest was **Multan (1175)**.
Then **Peshawar (c. 1179)**, **Sindh (c. 1182)**, Punjab and **Lahore (c. 1190)**.
He was beaten near **Mount Abu** (**Kayadara, 1178**).

n771118c9191.s: Who was the real founder of Turk rule in Bihar?
n771118c9191.x: Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji was the real founder of Turk rule in Bihar.
n771118c9191.tq: Distinguish the regional founder from the larger imperial conquerors.
xs: **Muhammad bin Bakhtiyar Khalji** was the real **founder of Turk rule in Bihar** (BPSC 2022) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Muhammad bin Qasim** conquered **Sindh**; **Qutbuddin Aibak** founded the **Delhi Sultanate**.
xa: He sacked **Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri** (c. **1193-1203**).
He drove **Lakshmana Sena** from **Nadia** (**1204**).
He ruled from **Lakhnauti**.

n0546884cf23.s: Which set of Buddhist centres was sacked by Bakhtiyar Khalji around 1193–1203?
n0546884cf23.x: Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked the Buddhist centres of Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri during approximately 1193–1203.
n0546884cf23.tq: Test a complete named list without substituting famous centres.
xs: Bakhtiyar Khalji sacked **Nalanda, Vikramashila and Odantapuri** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This happened c. **1193-1203**.
xa: He then attacked **Nadia** and drove out **Lakshmana Sena** (**1204**).
He was a general of **Ghori/Aibak**.
He is the real founder of **Turk rule in Bihar**.

n89f252bc822.s: Unlike Mahmud of Ghazni, who mainly raided for plunder, Muhammad Ghori aimed at:
n89f252bc822.x: Mahmud was mainly a plunder-seeking raider, while Ghori pursued conquest and a lasting political presence in North India.
xa: Ghori's win at **Second Tarain (1192)** opened North India.
**Qutbuddin Aibak** founded the Delhi Sultanate in **1206**.
Mahmud's motives included **temple wealth**, **Punjab** and **prestige**.

nindian-history-21-10.s: Mahmud Ghazni raided the Chakraswamin temple at Thanesar in:
nindian-history-21-10.x: Thanesar was raided in 1014; Mathura was sacked in 1018 and Somnath raided in 1025–26.
n: Mahmud Ghazni’s main objective was wealth and plunder. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Mahmud Ghazni attacked Mathura. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Mahmud Ghazni attacked Thanesar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Mahmud Ghazni attacked Somnath. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: Somnath loot was said to be **20 million dinars**.
**Nagarkot** (Kangra) was raided for temple treasure (**1009**).
The **Hindushahis** (**Jayapala, Anandapala**) were the first to resist.

nindian-history-20-9.s: Who entered Nadiya, drove Lakshman Sen to East Bengal and captured Lakhnauti?
nindian-history-20-9.x: Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bengal for the Ghurids after taking Bihar and destroying Nalanda and Vikramshila.
n: Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji’s Bihar campaign occurred during 1193–1203. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji’s Bihar campaign was part of Ghurid expansion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed Nalanda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed Vikramshila. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji captured Odantpur. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji conquered Bengal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji’s Bengal campaign occurred during 1198–1203. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji captured or entered Nadiya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Lakshman Sen fled to East Bengal during Bakhtiyar Khalji’s Bengal campaign. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
Bakhtiyar Khalji captured Lakhnauti. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 76-78]
xa: He was the real **founder of Turk rule in Bihar** (BPSC **2022**).
⚠ Other notes say Lakshmana Sena was driven out of Nadia in **1204**.
He ruled from **Lakhnauti**.

naa715ac7e89.s: Who among the following repelled the Arab forces and thereby helped prevent their expansion beyond Sindh?
naa715ac7e89.x: Nagabhata I repelled the Arabs. Arab writers also noted that the Pratiharas possessed the most formidable cavalry in India.
naa715ac7e89.tq: Match the resistance achievement with the correct Pratihara ruler.
xs: **Nagabhata I** (Pratihara) repelled the Arabs — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Mahmud of Ghazni** was a later raider, not a defender against the Arabs.
xa: Arab writers called the **Pratihara cavalry** the most formidable in India.
Arab rule stayed **confined to Sindh**, partly due to the strength of the **Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas**.
The **Thar** and **Aravallis** also blocked expansion.

nd86af684a07.s: Who resisted Mahmud of Ghazni among the following?
nd86af684a07.x: Chandela ruler Vidyadhara resisted Mahmud of Ghazni.
nd86af684a07.tq: Distinguish Mahmud's contemporary resister from rulers of other invasions.
xs: The **Chandela** ruler **Vidyadhara** resisted Mahmud (MPPSC 2021) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jaichand** fought **Ghori** at Chandawar; **Lakshmana Sena** was driven out by **Bakhtiyar Khalji**; **Raja Dahir** fought **Muhammad bin Qasim**.
xa: **Jayapala** and **Anandapala** (Hindushahis) were the first opponents to resist Mahmud.
**Bhima I** (Solanki) ruled Gujarat when **Somnath** was sacked.

n85ec40bc8ad.s: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind is an objective account of India in the:
n85ec40bc8ad.x: Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind is an objective account of eleventh-century India.
xa: Kitab-ul-Hind is also called **Tahqiq-i-Hind**.
All three — **Al-Biruni, Firdausi, Utbi** — were scholars in Mahmud's court.

nindian-history-6-3.s: Al-Biruni's Arabic translation of Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra is titled:
nindian-history-6-3.x: Al-Biruni translated the Yoga-Sutra into Arabic as Kitab Patanjal.
n: Kitab Patanjal was written by Al-Biruni. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Al-Biruni translated Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra into Arabic under the title Kitab Patanjal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: He also wrote **Kitab-ul-Hind** (**Tahqiq-i-Hind**) on Indian society and culture.
It was translated into English by **Edward Sachau** and into Hindi by **Rajnikant Sharma**.
Al-Biruni belonged to **Mahmud Ghaznavi's** period.

nindian-history-45-16.s: Who was the poet laureate (Malik-ush-Shuara) of Mahmud Ghaznavi's court?
nindian-history-45-16.x: Unsuri was poet laureate; Firdausi wrote the Shahnama and Utbi Kitab-ul-Yamini.
n: Firdausi wrote Shahnama. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Firdausi was known as the Homer of the East. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Unsuri was a Persian poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Uzari was a Persian poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
Asjadi was a court poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 112-113]
xa: **Baihaqi** wrote **Tarikh-i-Subuktigin**.
Other court poets: **Uzari**, **Asjadi**, **Farrukhi**.
The Shahnama was commissioned by **Mahmud**.

nindian-history-46-38.x: Baihaqi wrote Tarikh-i-Subuktigin; Utbi wrote Kitab-ul-Yamini and Al-Biruni Kitab-ul-Hind.
n: Asjadi was a court poet. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Asjadi was associated with Mahmud Ghaznavi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Al-Biruni was a scholar and historian. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Utbi was a historian and scholar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Utbi was associated with Mahmud Ghaznavi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Baihaqi was a historian and scholar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
Baihaqi was associated with Mahmud Ghaznavi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 113-115]
xa: **Firdausi** — **Shahnama**, "Homer of the East".
Al-Biruni's **Kitab Patanjal** = Arabic translation of Patanjali's Yoga-Sutra.
**Chachnama** (conquest of Sindh) — Persian translation by **Muhammad Ali bin Abu Bakr Kufi**.

n95fe8db2c01.s: Which of the following did NOT confine Arab rule to Sindh?
o: Complete political unity in North India
The strength of the Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas
n95fe8db2c01.x: North India was not completely united; geography, strong regional states and weak resources restricted the Arabs.
xa: ⚠ The **lack** of political unity later helped the **Turks** (UPPSC 2024).
**Nagabhata I** (Pratihara) repelled the Arabs.

n49b1a6bfedf.s: Which of the following was one of the important contributions transmitted from India to the Islamic world and subsequently to Europe?
n49b1a6bfedf.x: Indian mathematics, especially the decimal and place-value systems, along with astronomy and medicine, passed to the Islamic world and later to Europe.
n49b1a6bfedf.tq: Identify the cultural transmission rather than a political institution.
xs: India's **decimal and place-value systems** passed to the Islamic world and then Europe — so option **(3)** is correct.
Astronomy and medicine also travelled the same way.
xa: Arab contact from **712** is significant because **Indian science moved westward**.
⚠ **Feudal levies** belong to R.S. Sharma's "Indian feudalism" argument, not to knowledge transfer.
The Arab conquest led to **no mass Islamisation**.

na7b3daecb55.s: Which of the following is NOT among the features of Indian feudalism that R. S. Sharma linked to Turkish success?
o: Universal military participation across all castes
na7b3daecb55.x: Sharma linked feudal levies, sub-infeudation and a closed village economy; caste restricted fighting to a few groups.
xa: Political cause: **no political unity** after the Pratihara collapse.
Military cause: **superior war technique** (APPSC key).

n2708ba8df4b.s: The Second Battle of Tarain was fought in:
n2708ba8df4b.x: The Second Battle of Tarain was fought in 1192, the First in 1191, both against Prithviraj Chauhan.
xa: ⚠ **1191** = Prithviraj won; **1192** = Ghori won.
Tarain lies near **Karnal, Haryana**.
APPSC-G2 2011: Prithviraj defeated Ghori at the **first** Tarain.

nbfe23766428.s: The First Battle of Tarain (1191) arose over:
nbfe23766428.x: Tabarhinda (Bhatinda) was the cause; Prithviraj Chauhan won and Ghori barely escaped.
xa: Ghori returned to win **Second Tarain (1192)**.
Prithviraj was of the **Chahamana** dynasty.

n5b0649cb09b.s: Somnath Swabhiman Parv was launched in January 2026 to commemorate which historical event?
o: Muhammad Ghori's victory in the Battle of Chandawar
Mahmud of Ghazni's attack on Somnath, a thousand years earlier
The Arab conquest of Sindh by Muhammad bin Qasim
n5b0649cb09b.x: Somnath Swabhiman Parv was launched in January 2026 to mark 1,000 years since Mahmud of Ghazni's attack on Somnath.
n5b0649cb09b.tq: Use the distinctive event-year association and distinguish the commemoration from other invasions.
xs: **Somnath Swabhiman Parv** (Jan 2026) marks **1,000 years** since **Mahmud's attack on Somnath** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The raid was in **1025**, under the Solanki **Bhima I**.
xa: The loot is said to be **20 million dinars**.
It was one of Mahmud's **17 raids** (**1000-1027**).
⚠ Ghori, not Mahmud, was later beaten by **Bhimdev II**.

n6e5275547f0.s: The rise of the Chauhans of Ajmer, Chandelas of Bundelkhand and Paramaras of Malwa is principally associated with the
n6e5275547f0.x: These Rajput states rose after the collapse of the Pratihara Empire, which led to political fragmentation in North India.
xs: The Rajput states rose from the **collapse of the Pratihara Empire** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Out of that collapse came the **Chauhans of Ajmer**, the **Chandelas of Bundelkhand** and the **Paramaras of Malwa**.
With the Pratiharas gone, **North India became hyper-fragmented** into rival Rajput kingdoms.
xa: The **Agnikula** clans claimed birth from a sacrificial fire at **Mount Abu**: **Paramara, Pratihara, Chauhan, Solanki**.
The **Solankis** (Chalukyas of Gujarat) ruled from **Anahilapataka (Patan)**, c. **950-1300**.
The **Tomaras** held **Dhillika (Delhi)** until ousted by the **Chauhans** in the mid-12th century.

n737ab878f56.s: Khajuraho and Mahoba in Bundelkhand are associated with the:
n737ab878f56.x: The Chandelas held Bundelkhand with Khajuraho and Mahoba; the Paramaras held Malwa and the Gahadavalas Kanauj and Varanasi.
xa: Founders: Chauhan **Vasudeva**, Paramara **Upendra (Krishnaraja)**, Chandela **Nannuka**, Gahadavala **Chandradeva**, Solanki **Mularaja I**.
Key rulers: Chauhan **Prithviraj III**, Paramara **Bhoja**, Chandela **Dhanga** and **Vidyadhara**, Gahadavala **Jaichand**.
The **Kalachuris (Chedi)** ruled from **Tripuri (Jabalpur)**; founder **Kokalla I**.

n458056e7e5c.s: The Tomaras, whose coins carried a horseman-and-bull motif, ruled from:
n458056e7e5c.x: The Tomaras held Dhillika (Delhi); the Mehrauli Iron Pillar is a Gupta work only moved there.
xa: Tomara founder: **Anangapala**.
The Tomaras were ousted by the **Chauhans** in the mid-12th c.
Chauhan capital: Sakambhari → **Ajmer**; key ruler **Prithviraj III**.

nc7a8f256231.s: Bhojshala at Dhar, linked to Paramara Bhoja, is called by Muslims the:
nc7a8f256231.x: Muslims call Bhojshala the Kamal Maula Mosque; it became a mosque in the 14th century.
xa: The **Madhya Pradesh High Court** declared Bhojshala a **Hindu temple** on ASI findings (**May 2026**).
The ASI survey was ordered in **2024**; under a **2003** ASI arrangement both communities worshipped on separate days.

nc8f63a4c294.s: Which inscription gives the Paramara genealogy and praises Bhoja?
nc8f63a4c294.x: The Udaipur Prashasti gives the Paramara genealogy and praises Bhoja.
xa: ⚠ **Rani-ki-Vav** was built by queen **Udayamati** in memory of **Bhima I**.
**Bhojshala, Dhar** = Bhoja's Sanskrit learning centre, a **Saraswati (Vagdevi)** temple.
Paramara capital: **Dhara**.

na2ca11f2606.s: The Modhera Sun temple was built by the Solanki ruler:
na2ca11f2606.x: Bhima I built the Modhera Sun temple; Somnath was sacked in 1025 during his reign.
xa: Bhima I's queen **Udayamati** built **Rani-ki-Vav** (UNESCO) in his memory.
Later Solankis: **Jayasimha Siddharaja** (patron of **Hemachandra**), **Kumarapala** (Jainism).
The Solankis ruled c. **950-1300**.

n26ec924c65a.s: Kumarapala encouraged Jainism under the influence of:
n26ec924c65a.x: Kumarapala encouraged Jainism under Hemachandra's influence; he also rebuilt Somnath and curbed animal slaughter.
xa: **Jayasimha Siddharaja** was Hemachandra's earlier patron (**Siddha-Hema** grammar).
Somnath was sacked by **Mahmud** in **1025** under **Bhima I**.

nbbe497f7b73.s: Modhera, site of the Solanki Sun temple, is in the news because it:
o: Was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2022
Was fully solarised under an MNRE scheme, inaugurated on 9 October 2022
Was declared a Hindu temple by the Gujarat High Court
Became the site of the Somnath Swabhiman Parv
nbbe497f7b73.x: Modhera was fully solarised under an MNRE scheme (6 MW plant with 15 MWh storage), inaugurated on 9 October 2022. The court ruling on a temple concerned Bhojshala (MP High Court); Somnath Swabhiman Parv concerns Somnath; there was no 2022 UNESCO listing for Modhera.
xs: Modhera was **fully solarised under an MNRE scheme**, inaugurated **9 October 2022** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The project: a **6 MW** plant with **15 MWh** storage, costing **₹76.66 crore**.
The court ruling was on **Bhojshala** by the **Madhya Pradesh High Court**, not Gujarat.
xa: The **Modhera Sun temple** (Surya) was built by Solanki **Bhima I**, in Mehsana, Gujarat.
⚠ The Solanki UNESCO site in the notes is **Rani-ki-Vav**, built by queen **Udayamati**.

n7bb21166518.s: Rani-ki-Vav at Patan was built by Udayamati in memory of:
n7bb21166518.x: Rani-ki-Vav was built by Udayamati, queen of Bhima I, in his memory.
xa: Rani-ki-Vav is a **UNESCO** site.
⚠ **Vimal Vasahi** = Vimal Shah (Solanki, Rishabha); **Luna Vasahi** = Vastupala-Tejapala (Vaghela, Neminatha).
**Mahmud** sacked **Somnath** in **1025** during Bhima I's reign.

n641c16c2797.s: The Kandariya Mahadeva temple at Khajuraho is dedicated to:
n641c16c2797.x: Kandariya Mahadeva (by Vidyadhara) is a Shiva temple; the Lakshmana temple is Vishnu's.
xa: Khajuraho also has **Jain** temples.
Chandela region: **Bundelkhand** (**Jejakabhukti**), Khajuraho and Mahoba.
Chandela rulers to know: **Dhanga**, **Vidyadhara**, Kirtivarman, **Paramardi**.

n34af3a02b57.s: The Vijaya Stambha at Chittor was built by Rana Kumbha to commemorate his victory over
n34af3a02b57.x: Rana Kumbha built the Vijaya Stambha at Chittor to commemorate his victory over Mahmud Khalji of Malwa.
n34af3a02b57.tq: Separate the builder from the opponent associated with the monument.
xs: Rana Kumbha built the **Vijaya Stambha** at Chittor for his victory over **Mahmud Khalji of Malwa** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The builder Rana Kumbha is an APPSC G2 **2011** question.
⚠ **Alauddin Khalji** of Delhi is the **Rani Padmini** jauhar story, not this tower.
xa: ⚠ **Vijaya Stambha** = Rana Kumbha; **Kirti Stambha** = Jain merchant **Jijaji**.
Rana Kumbha also built **Kumbhalgarh** fort.

n21395f6174f.s: Who is the author of ‘Prithviraj Raso’?
n21395f6174f.x: ‘Prithviraj Raso’ was authored by Chand Bardai and is associated with Prithviraj Chauhan.
xs: **Prithviraj Raso** was written by **Chand Bardai** (APPSC 2018) — so option **(2)** is correct.
It celebrates **Prithviraj Chauhan** and carries the **Agnikula** origin story.
**Somadeva** wrote the play **Lalit Vigraharaja**, **Narapati** wrote **Bisaldeva Raso** and **Jagnik** wrote **Alha Khand**.
xa: ⚠ **Bisaldeva Raso** = Narapati (Nalha); **Prithviraj Raso** = Chand Bardai; **Alha Khand** = Jagnik.
**Khuman Raso** = **Dalpati Vijay**; **Shatrusal Raso** = **Dungar Singh** (RPSC 2024).

n1316c54bd54.s: Alha Khand, linked with the Chandela Paramardi, was written by:
n1316c54bd54.x: Alha Khand is by Jagnik; Chand Bardai wrote Prithviraj Raso and Narapati Nalha Bisaldeva Raso.
xa: **Khuman Raso** = **Dalpati Vijay**; **Shatrusal Raso** = **Dungar Singh**.
Bhoja wrote **Saraswati-Kanthabharana** and **Yuktikalpataru**.
Prithviraj Raso by Chand Bardai: APPSC **2018**.

ne1c02876abd.s: In R. S. Sharma's model of 'Indian feudalism', vishti means:
ne1c02876abd.x: Sharma's model includes sub-infeudation and vishti (forced labour), with closed village economies.
xa: The "Indian feudalism" thesis is one of the main **debates** on Rajput society, along with origin theories.
**Jauhar** (self-immolation to avoid capture) and **sati** were practised in Rajput society.

nb1973274c78.s: Which one of the following descriptions correctly refers to the Latina or Rekha-prasada type of Nagara temple tower?
o: A pyramidal tower with multiple terraces
nb1973274c78.x: Latina, also called Rekha-prasada, is characterised by a single curvilinear tower. Phamsana has a sloping, stepped roof, while Valabhi is barrel-vaulted.
nb1973274c78.tq: Separate the three Nagara tower forms by their distinctive roof profiles.
xs: **Latina / Rekha-prasada** is a **single curvilinear tower** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Phamsana** has a **sloping, stepped roof**; **Valabhi** is **barrel-vaulted**.
xa: Regional Nagara schools: **Khajuraho** (Chandela), **Odisha/Kalinga** (**rekha deul**), **Maru-Gurjara** (Solanki).
**Maru-Gurjara** often has a **Kirti-torana**.

n698130b455c.s: The Maru-Gurjara style of the 11th–13th centuries is associated with the:
n698130b455c.x: Maru-Gurjara is a Solanki-associated Nagara sub-style of Gujarat and Rajasthan, fusing Maha-Maru and Maha-Gurjara traditions.
xa: It often has a **Kirti-torana**.
**Somnath** is in **Maru-Gurjara** (Chaulukya) style: **Garbhagriha**, **Sabha Mandapa**, **Nritya Mandapa**.
Other schools: **Khajuraho** (Chandela) and **Odisha/Kalinga** (**rekha deul**).

n184b3dc1466.s: Which architectural feature is often associated with the Maru-Gurjara sub-style?
n184b3dc1466.x: The Maru-Gurjara style, associated with the Solanki tradition of Gujarat and Rajasthan, often includes a Kirti-torana.
n184b3dc1466.tq: Identify the specific architectural feature attached to the regional style, not merely its geographical location.
xs: The Maru-Gurjara sub-style often has a **Kirti-torana** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Rekha deul** belongs to the **Odisha/Kalinga** school; **Valabhi** is just a barrel-vaulted tower type.
xa: Maru-Gurjara = **Solanki**, **Gujarat-Rajasthan**, **11th-13th c.**, fusing **Maha-Maru** + **Maha-Gurjara**.
Shikhara types: **Latina** (single curvilinear), **Phamsana** (sloping, stepped), **Valabhi** (barrel-vaulted).

n625992a5a00.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the traditional four Agnikula Rajput clans?
n625992a5a00.x: The four Agnikula clans are Paramara, Pratihara, Chauhan and Solanki; the Chandelas are off the traditional list.
xa: The Chandelas, founded by **Nannuka**, ruled **Bundelkhand** from **Khajuraho** and **Mahoba**.
Chandela rulers: **Dhanga**, **Vidyadhara**, **Kirtivarman**, **Paramardi**.
The Agnikula story comes from **Chand Bardai's Prithviraj Raso**.

n4312ca8c04d.x: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri was dedicated to Nasiruddin Mahmud; Hasan Nizami's Taj-ul-Maasir was patronised by Aibak.
xa: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri covers the **Ghurids** and early **Delhi Sultans**.
Chronological order: **Kitab-ul-Hind** → **Taj-ul-Maasir** → **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** → **Futuh-us-Salatin** → **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi**.

n105f1237caa.s: The transition from trabeate to arcuate construction in Sultanate architecture is marked by the increasing use of:
o: Wooden pillars and flat roofs only
Timber frames and corbelled balconies only
True arches, domes and lime mortar
n105f1237caa.x: Sultanate buildings demonstrate the shift from trabeate construction to arcuate construction through the use of true arches, domes and lime mortar.
n105f1237caa.tq: Identify the architectural system from its characteristic structural elements.
xs: The **trabeate → arcuate** shift used **true arches, domes and lime mortar** — so option **(3)** is correct.
That change marks Sultanate buildings.
xa: **Naskh** script was used for Quranic verses, e.g. the **Jami Masjid mihrab**.
**Nastaliq** was used for **Persian** texts.

n33f9137f552.s: In Qutb Shahi calligraphy, Quranic verses were written in the script:
n33f9137f552.x: Naskh was used for Quranic verses, including those in the Jami Masjid mihrab; Nastaliq was used for Persian texts.
xa: Architecture shifted from **trabeate** to **arcuate** (true arch, dome, lime mortar).
The **Golconda school** of painting was founded by **Mir Hashimi**.

nindian-history-6-17.x: Tabqat-i-Nasiri is by Minhaj-us-Siraj; Khazain-ul-Futuh is by Amir Khusrau.
n: Tabqat-i-Nasiri was written by Minhaj-us-Siraj. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Khazain-ul-Futuh was written by Amir Khusrau. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Tarikh-i-Firuzshahi was written by Shams-i-Siraj Afif. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Rihla was written by Ibn Battuta. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: Tabaqat-i-Nasiri covers **Bengal** and **Bakhtiyar Khalji**, dedicated to **Nasiruddin Mahmud**.
**Futuhat-i-Firuz Shahi** is a **royal account** by **Firuz Shah Tughluq**.
**Tarikh-i-Mubarakshahi** — **Yahya bin Ahmad Sarhindi**.
⚠ **Tabaqat-i-Akbari** = **Nizamuddin Ahmad**, not Badauni.

nap-history-23-15.s: Itsing, who saw Indian students memorising Nagarjuna's Suhrllekha, was a pilgrim from:
n: Itsing was a Chinese traveller. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
Itsing saw students by-hearting “Sushrullekha” in India. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
xa: **Ibn Battuta** (Morocco) wrote the **Rihla** in Arabic.
**Mahmud Wali Balkhi** came from **Balkh (Afghanistan)**.
**Seydi Ali Reis** was a **Turkish** (Ottoman) admiral.

nf7403d36b1a.s: Fatawa-i-Jahandari is primarily a work on which subject?
o: The postal system of the Delhi Sultanate
nf7403d36b1a.x: Fatawa-i-Jahandari, written by Ziauddin Barani, deals with political theory and kingship.
nf7403d36b1a.tq: Identify the subject of a text rather than confusing it with the author’s historical chronicle.
xs: **Fatawa-i-Jahandari** deals with the **political theory of kingship** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Its author is **Ziauddin Barani**, who wrote from an **orthodox Sunni** viewpoint.
The postal system is in **Ibn Battuta's Rihla**; Golconda's conquest in **Khafi Khan's Muntakhab-ul-Lubab**; astronomy in **Al-Biruni**.
xa: Barani also wrote **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** (Balban to early Firoz Tughlaq).
Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi is the main account of **Alauddin's market regulations and ordinances**.

n2734b15d75c.s: Who wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh and accompanied Malik Kafur's 1310 invasion of Warangal?
n2734b15d75c.x: Amir Khusrau, court poet of Alauddin Khalji, wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh and accompanied the 1310 expedition.
xa: ⚠ As a court poet his history glorifies the patron — the **court bias** problem.
Muslim sources (**Amir Khusrau**, **Wassaf**) count **5** Warangal invasions; Telugu sources count **8**.

n7eda25720c8.s: Madhura Vijayam provides information chiefly about which of the following?
o: Kampana’s conquest of Madurai and conditions under Tughlaq rule
The conquest of Golconda by Aurangzeb
The life of Pala king Ramapala
n7eda25720c8.x: Madhura Vijayam, written by Gangadevi, describes Kampana’s conquest of Madurai and conditions under Tughlaq rule.
n7eda25720c8.tq: Associate the regional biography with its protagonist, campaign and political context.
xs: **Madhura Vijayam** describes **Kampana's conquest of Madurai and conditions under Tughlaq rule** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was written by **Gangadevi**.
Golconda's conquest is in **Muntakhab-ul-Lubab**; Ramapala in **Ramacharitam**; Kashmir in **Rajatarangini**.
xa: **Kumara Ramana Charitam** (Kannada) covers **South India after the fall of Warangal**.
**Siddhesvara Charitam** (Telugu, **Kase Siddhappa**) covers **Kakatiya-era society and religion**.

n48b498ae34d.x: Firishta, born at Astarabad in 1552, dedicated his work to Ibrahim Adil Shah of Bijapur, not to a Qutb Shahi ruler.
xa: Firishta calls **Telangana "Tilang"**.
⚠ His story of **Deva Raya kidnapping Nehal** is rejected by modern historians.
AP angle: **Isami** and **Firishta** → **Warangal**.

n5626e4d867a.s: Who founded the Golconda school of painting?
n5626e4d867a.x: The Golconda school of painting was founded by Mir Hashimi.
n5626e4d867a.tq: Test the founder of an artistic tradition against prominent literary figures.
xs: The Golconda school of painting was founded by **Mir Hashimi** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Amir Khusrau** was a court poet; **Abul Fazl** wrote the official history of **Akbar**.
xa: The **"Quliyat Quli"** manuscript has **14** miniatures.
Qutb Shahi calligraphy: **Naskh** (Quranic), **Nastaliq** (Persian).

n7e9ab2faa96.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Ziauddin Barani?
o: He wrote from an orthodox Sunni viewpoint and theorised kingship.
He was a Persian ambassador to Vijayanagara and described its markets.
He founded the Golconda school of painting.
He composed the royal memoirs of Jahangir.
n7e9ab2faa96.x: Ziauddin Barani wrote from an orthodox Sunni viewpoint and also theorised about kingship. The other descriptions belong to different figures or traditions.
n7e9ab2faa96.tq: Use the writer's viewpoint and intellectual contribution to identify him.
xs: Barani **wrote from an orthodox Sunni viewpoint and theorised kingship** — so option **(1)** is correct.
His kingship theory is in **Fatawa-i-Jahandari**.
The Persian envoy to Vijayanagara was **Abdur Razzaq**; the Golconda school was founded by **Mir Hashimi**.
xa: Barani's **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** covers **Balban** to early **Firoz Tughlaq**.
It is the main account of **Alauddin's market regulations** and Sultanate attacks on **south Indian kingdoms**.

nindian-history-6-4.x: Fawaid-ul-Fawad is by Amir Hasan Sijzi; Barani wrote Fatwa-i-Jahandari and Hasan Nizami Taj-ul-Masir.
n: Taj-ul-Masir was written by Hasan Nizami. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Fatwa-i-Jahandari was written by Ziauddin Barani. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Rihla was written by Ibn Battuta. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Fawaid-ul-Fawad was written by Amir Hasan Sijzi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: Hasan Nizami was patronised by **Qutbuddin Aibak**.
Fatwa-i-Jahandari is on the **political theory of kingship**.
**Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** — **Minhaj-us-Siraj**; **Khazain-ul-Futuh** — **Amir Khusrau**.

n77541c1a0c9.s: Rihla, the travel account of Ibn Battuta, was written in which language?
n77541c1a0c9.x: Ibn Battuta’s travel account, Rihla, was written in Arabic.
n77541c1a0c9.tq: Test the exact language of a source rather than its author’s place of origin.
xs: **Rihla** was written in **Arabic** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Ibn Battuta** was from **Morocco**, born at **Tangiers** in **1304**.
xa: He served **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**, who made him **qazi of Delhi** and sent him as **envoy to China**.
Rihla describes **espionage**, the **postal system**, **sati** and **slave markets**.
⚠ **Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind** is also in Arabic.

n2a69d4045b4.s: Which traveller is associated with observations on espionage, the postal system, sati and slave markets in the Delhi Sultanate?
n2a69d4045b4.x: Ibn Battuta’s account of Muhammad bin Tughlaq’s reign contains observations on espionage, the postal system, sati and slave markets.
n2a69d4045b4.tq: Match the distinctive subject described with the traveller who recorded it.
xs: **Ibn Battuta**, in his **Rihla**, describes **espionage**, the **postal system**, **sati** and **slave markets** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He served **Muhammad bin Tughlaq** as **qazi of Delhi**.
**Tavernier** wrote on **Golconda diamonds**; **Nicolo Conti** on **Diwali lamps** in Vijayanagara.
xa: Rihla is in **Arabic**; Ibn Battuta was born at **Tangiers** in **1304**.
⚠ "Who mentioned sati" at Vijayanagara = **Abdur Razzaq**.

nca6c61e1c11.s: Abdur Razzaq visited Vijayanagara in 1443–44 as an envoy sent by which ruler?
nca6c61e1c11.x: Abdur Razzaq was a Persian envoy of Shah Rukh and visited the court of Deva Raya II in 1443–44.
nca6c61e1c11.tq: Distinguish the envoy’s sending ruler from the ruler whose court he visited.
xs: **Abdur Razzaq** was the Timurid envoy of **Shah Rukh of Persia** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He visited **Deva Raya II** at Vijayanagara in **1443-44**.
**Ibrahim Adil Shah** was **Firishta's** patron; **Muhammad Qutb Shah** received **Mir Zainul Abidin** (**1614**).
xa: He called Vijayanagara among the **largest, richest cities**, with **diamonds sold in heaps**.
He mentions **sati** and **"300 ports"**.

n2c147bc0828.s: Afanasy Nikitin, a horse merchant who visited India during the reign of Virupaksha Raya II, belonged to which country?
n2c147bc0828.x: Afanasy Nikitin was a Russian traveller from Tver, situated on the Volga. He visited Vijayanagara during the reign of Virupaksha Raya II.
n2c147bc0828.tq: Test the traveller’s nationality through the associated ruler and occupation.
xs: **Afanasy Nikitin** was from **Russia** (**Tver**, on the **Volga**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
He was a **horse merchant** at Vijayanagara under **Virupaksha Raya II**.
**Persia** = Abdur Razzaq, **Afghanistan (Balkh)** = Mahmud Wali Balkhi, **Turkey** = Seydi Ali Reis.
xa: **Nicolo Conti** and **Marco Polo** were both from **Venice**.
**Tavernier** was from **France**.

n006ebfd9b15.s: Firishta's story that Deva Raya kidnapped Nehal is, by modern historians:
n006ebfd9b15.x: Modern historians reject Firishta's story that Deva Raya kidnapped Nehal, showing the need to evaluate chronicles critically.
xa: Tarikh-i-Firishta (**Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi**) was dedicated to **Ibrahim Adil Shah** of Bijapur.
Firishta was born at **Astarabad, Iran, 1552**; he calls Telangana **"Tilang"**.

necbfc12b3e6.s: Which traveller is associated with Motupalli?
necbfc12b3e6.x: Marco Polo is associated with Motupalli; Abdur Razzaq and Barbosa with Vijayanagara, and Tavernier with Golconda.
xa: Marco Polo landed at **Motupalli** and visited Kakatiya **Rudramadevi** (**1289-93**).
Tavernier wrote on **Golconda diamonds** under **Abdullah Qutb Shah**.
Abdur Razzaq visited **Deva Raya II** in **1443-44**.

nap-history-23-2.s: Marco Polo visited Andhra during the reign of:
nap-history-23-2.x: Marco Polo came in Rudramadevi's reign; Nicolo Conti came under Devaraya I.
n: Marco Polo visited Motupalli port during the Kakatiya period of Rudramadevi. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
Nicolo Conti visited South India during the reign of Devaraya I of Vijayanagara. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
Nuniz visited during the reign of Achyutadeva Raya of Vijayanagara. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
Tavernier lived in the 17th century. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
xa: ⚠ APPSC **2011** key placed **Nicolo Conti** in **Deva Raya II's** reign.
**Abdur Razzaq** (Persia) visited **Deva Raya II** in **1443-44**.
**Robert Sewell's** **A Forgotten Empire** used Paes, Nuniz and Abdur Razzaq.

nap-history-23-4.s: Tavernier, the 17th-century traveller, visited Andhra to see its:
nap-history-23-4.x: Tavernier, a 17th-century French jeweller, visited the Golconda-Andhra diamond mines for trade.
n: Tavernier lived in the 17th century. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
Tavernier visited the Andhra mines for precious stones and diamonds. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 32-33]
xa: He visited **Golconda** under **Abdullah Qutb Shah**.
**Marco Polo** visited **Motupalli** under **Rudramadevi**.
**Mir Zainul Abidin** (Persia) visited Golconda under **Muhammad Qutb Shah** (**1614**).

n2569a33c7e0.s: The Nizami Mosque inscription at Golconda is significant because it dates Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk's independence to:
n2569a33c7e0.x: The Nizami Mosque inscription at Golconda dates the independence of Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk to 1518.
n2569a33c7e0.tq: Test the precise date attached to a political event in an inscription.
xs: The **Nizami Mosque** inscription at Golconda dates **Quli Qutb-ul-Mulk's** independence to **1518** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1576** is the **Ghazinagar** inscription (Nalgonda, **Ibrahim Quli**, **1576-77**); **1595** is the **Daru-Shifa** inscription.
xa: **Badshahi Ashurkhana** inscription: **1592-96**.
These Qutb Shahi inscriptions are in **Persian**.

nec1231c4dd8.s: The Palam Baoli inscription of 1276, a Sanskrit record, praises:
nec1231c4dd8.x: The Palam Baoli inscription praises Balban; the Vilasa copper plate belongs to Musunuri Prolaya Nayaka.
xa: The Telugu sources **Vilasa**, **Kaluvacheru** and **Pratapa Charitra** count **8** Warangal invasions.
Muslim sources count **5**.

n4e3a79b00e8.s: Mahmud of Ghazni's Lahore dirhams are especially significant as medieval sources because they contain:
o: An Arabic legend and its Sanskrit translation in Sharada script
A Telugu inscription and an Arabic translation
A Sanskrit legend and its Persian translation in Devanagari script
Only a Persian inscription in Nastaliq script
n4e3a79b00e8.x: The Lahore dirhams of Mahmud of Ghazni carry an Arabic legend along with a Sanskrit translation written in Sharada script.
n4e3a79b00e8.tq: Use the script–language combination to distinguish bilingual numismatic evidence.
xs: Mahmud's **Lahore dirhams** carry **an Arabic legend and its Sanskrit translation in Sharada script** — so option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Mahmud's coins = Arabic + **Sanskrit**; **Iltutmish's** coins = purely **Arabic**.
xa: Iltutmish issued the silver **tanka** and copper **jital**.
The **Palam Baoli** inscription (**1276**) is another bilingual record, praising **Balban** in Sanskrit.

nf3fe19430b7.s: The Palam Baoli inscription of 1276 praises which ruler in Sanskrit?
nf3fe19430b7.x: The Palam Baoli inscription, dated 1276, praises Balban in Sanskrit.
nf3fe19430b7.tq: Link the inscription's date with the ruler praised in it.
xs: The **Palam Baoli** inscription of **1276** praises **Balban** in Sanskrit — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is a **bilingual** record.
**Mahmud of Ghazni** is linked with bilingual **Lahore dirhams**; **Iltutmish's** coins are purely **Arabic**.
xa: ⚠ Iltutmish: silver **tanka** and copper **jital**.
**Barani's Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi** covers **Balban** to early Firoz Tughlaq.

nf160a6ce95d.s: Foreign travellers' accounts of medieval India should generally be used by historians in which manner?
o: They should replace inscriptions and archaeological evidence.
They should be ignored because they were written outside India.
They should be accepted as accurate in every detail.
They should supplement Indian texts and be cross-verified with inscriptions and archaeology.
nf160a6ce95d.x: Foreign accounts supplement Indian textual evidence, but their statements must be cross-verified with inscriptions and archaeological evidence.
nf160a6ce95d.tq: Apply the principle of corroboration across different source types.
xs: Foreign accounts **supplement Indian texts** and must be **cross-verified with inscriptions and archaeology** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They neither replace other evidence nor are accurate in every detail; nor are they to be ignored.
xa: ⚠ Court histories have their own bias — they **glorify the patron**.
**Taj Mahal** case (**Jul 2026**): evidence that **Shah Jahan** built it includes **European travellers' accounts**.

nf5d7dba98de.s: Al-Biruni, who learned Sanskrit, wrote his account of India in:
nf5d7dba98de.x: Al-Biruni learned Sanskrit and wrote in Arabic on Indian religion, philosophy, astronomy and caste.
xa: He records **Diwali** on **Kartika Amavasya**.
He found Indians **unwilling to share learning with outsiders**.

n6cdc48c4fa9.s: According to Al-Biruni’s account, which of the following was observed on Kartika Amavasya?
o: The conquest of Madurai by Kampana
The coronation of Muhammad bin Tughlaq
The annual court of the Qutb Shahis
n6cdc48c4fa9.x: Al-Biruni recorded the celebration of Diwali on Kartika Amavasya.
n6cdc48c4fa9.tq: Match the festival and its calendrical occasion with the appropriate chronicler.
xs: Al-Biruni records **the celebration of Diwali** on **Kartika Amavasya** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Kampana's** Madurai conquest is in **Gangadevi's Madhura Vijayam**, not Al-Biruni.
xa: Vision PT365 cites **Al-Biruni**, **Nicolo Conti** and **Ain-i-Akbari** as early evidence of Diwali (UNESCO topic, **Apr 2026**).
**Nicolo Conti** described **"innumerable oil lamps"** at Diwali in Vijayanagara.

n03f1baff120.s: Al-Biruni, who came to India with Mahmud of Ghazni, was a native of:
n03f1baff120.x: Al-Biruni came from Khwarazm in Central Asia, in present Uzbekistan. Tangiers was Ibn Battuta's birthplace, Balkh was Mahmud Wali Balkhi's home, and Astarabad was Firishta's birthplace.
xs: Al-Biruni was from **Khwarazm in Central Asia (present Uzbekistan)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Tangiers (Morocco)** was **Ibn Battuta's** birthplace; **Balkh** was **Mahmud Wali Balkhi's** home; **Astarabad** was **Firishta's**.
xa: He came with **Mahmud of Ghazni** in the **11th century**.
Mahmud's other protégés: **Firdausi** and **Utbi**.

ndfd20709b62.s: According to Telugu sources such as Pratapa Charitra, how many times was Warangal invaded?
ndfd20709b62.x: Telugu sources (Pratapa Charitra, Vilasa, Kaluvacheru) record eight invasions; Muslim sources record five.
xa: Amir Khusrau went with **Malik Kafur's 1310** invasion of Warangal.
**Isami's Futuh-us-Salatin** covers the **Tughlaq campaigns against Warangal**.

ncccd5904e83.s: Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire is based principally on the accounts of which group?
o: Barbosa, Seydi Ali Reis and Mahmud Wali Balkhi
Marco Polo, Ibn Battuta and Tavernier
ncccd5904e83.x: Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire draws chiefly on the accounts of Paes, Nuniz and Abdur Razzaq.
ncccd5904e83.tq: Recognise the specific cluster of sources associated with a modern historical reconstruction.
xs: Sewell's **A Forgotten Empire** is built on the accounts of **Paes, Nuniz and Abdur Razzaq** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is a history of **Vijayanagara**, which all three described.
xa: **Abdur Razzaq** visited **Deva Raya II** in **1443-44**.
AP angle: **Abdur Razzaq** and **Barbosa** → **Vijayanagara**; **Tavernier** → **Golconda**.

nb0572734623.s: Which of the following does NOT belong to the Mamluk dynasty?
nb0572734623.x: Jalaluddin Khalji belonged to the Khalji dynasty. Alauddin Masud, Nasiruddin Mahmud and Ruknuddin Firuz were rulers of the Mamluk dynasty.
nb0572734623.tq: Identify the outsider from a list of rulers belonging to one dynasty.
xs: **Jalaluddin Khalji** was not a Mamluk — so option **(4)** is the answer.
He founded the **Khalji** dynasty at **Kilokhari** in **1290**.
**Ruknuddin Firuz** (**1236**), **Alauddin Masud** (**1242-46**) and **Nasiruddin Mahmud** (**1246-66**) were Mamluks.
xa: ⚠ Odd one out: **Jalaluddin Khalji** and the **Tughlaqs** are NOT Mamluks.
The last Mamluks after Balban: grandson **Kaiqubad**, then infant **Kaimurs**.

n3b16cffa947.s: Which Mamluk ruler immediately preceded Balban?
n3b16cffa947.x: Nasiruddin Mahmud (1246-66) was followed by Balban (1266-86).
xa: Between them: **Ruknuddin Firuz** (**1236**), **Bahram Shah** (**1240-42**), **Alauddin Masud** (**1242-46**).
Before Iltutmish: **Aibak**, then **Aram Shah**.

nf05db95fe21.x: Lakh Bakhsh means 'giver of lakhs'; 'shadow of God' (Zil-i-Ilahi) is Balban's idea of the Sultan.
xa: He was then a slave of **Muhammad Ghori** and rose to **Amir-i-Akhur** (Master of Stables).
His son **Aram Shah** ruled only about **8** months.

n1edf9bb9eef.s: Iltutmish shifted the capital of the Sultanate from:
n1edf9bb9eef.x: Iltutmish moved the capital from Lahore (Aibak's capital) to Delhi.
xa: His title was **Shamsuddin**.
He received investiture (**"mansur"**) from the **Abbasid Caliph of Baghdad** in **1229**.

n6c39fb722c7.s: During the reign of Nasiruddin Mahmud, Balban served as:
n6c39fb722c7.x: Balban was Nasiruddin Mahmud's principal minister, or naib, and leader of the Forty. He was briefly displaced by Imaduddin Raihan before returning to power.
n6c39fb722c7.tq: Test the exact office held by a powerful minister during a weak ruler's reign.
xs: Balban was Nasiruddin Mahmud's **principal minister and naib** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was also **leader of the Forty**.
He was briefly displaced by **Imaduddin Raihan**, then returned.
xa: **Altuniya** was governor of **Bhatinda**; **Amir-i-Akhur** was **Aibak's** post.
Balban became Sultan in **1266**.

n30cafa5509b.s: Balban broke the power of the Forty by:
n30cafa5509b.x: Balban broke the Forty's power by promoting junior Turks; he did not strengthen the Forty.
xa: ⚠ Iltutmish **created** the Forty; Balban **broke** it.
UPPSC **2024**: Balban centralised authority AND guarded the north-west, but the second is not the reason for the first.

n907e3360ffd.s: Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji crowned himself at which place in 1290?
n907e3360ffd.x: Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji crowned himself at Kilokhari in 1290, thereby ending Mamluk rule and beginning the Khalji dynasty.
n907e3360ffd.tq: Match the accession event with its precise location and year.
xs: Jalaluddin Firoz Khalji crowned himself at **Kilokhari** in **1290** — so option **(2)** is correct.
That ended **Mamluk** rule.
**Bhatinda** is linked with **Altuniya**, **Badaun** with Iltutmish's governorship and **Lahore** with **Aibak's** capital.
xa: The last Mamluks were **Kaiqubad** and the infant **Kaimurs**.
The **Khalji** dynasty ruled **1290-1320**.

n9d728284d59.s: Before becoming a general, Qutbuddin Aibak held the office of:
n9d728284d59.x: Aibak rose to the position of Amir-i-Akhur, or Master of Stables, and subsequently became a general.
n9d728284d59.tq: Test an earlier post through an official Persian title.
xs: Aibak rose to **Amir-i-Akhur** (**Master of Stables**) before becoming a general — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Diwan-i-Arz** is the military department later created by **Balban**, not an office of Aibak.
xa: After **Tarain II (1192)** Aibak was **Ghori's** representative in India.
He became Sultan on Ghori's death and ruled **1206-1210** from **Lahore**.

nd339289d907.s: Iltutmish refused shelter to which Khwarazmian prince, helping keep Chengiz Khan out of India?
nd339289d907.x: Iltutmish refused shelter to Jalaluddin Mangbarni of Khwarazm, which helped keep Chengiz Khan out of India.
xa: Balban later built **outposts and forts** against the **Mongols**.
Balban's son **Prince Muhammad** died fighting the Mongols (**1285**).

n26edac1aa65.s: Which of the following was a distinctive feature of Razia Sultan's rule?
o: She accepted the authority of Bahram Shah throughout her reign.
She maintained purdah and never appeared before the army.
She discarded purdah, wore male attire and led the army.
She ruled only through Balban as her regent.
n26edac1aa65.x: Razia discarded purdah, wore male attire and personally led the army. Her conduct challenged the expectations of the Turkish nobles.
n26edac1aa65.tq: Identify the correct application of a ruler's known social and military policy.
xs: Razia **discarded purdah, wore male attire and led the army** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Bahram Shah** was the noble's choice who replaced her; **Balban** was **naib** to Nasiruddin Mahmud, not her regent.
xa: Razia made Balban **Amir-i-Shikar**.
Turkish nobles resented her favour to **Yaqut** (Abyssinian).

ne9ced9ddf67.s: The Turkish nobles opposed Razia primarily because she favoured:
ne9ced9ddf67.x: The Turkish nobles resented Razia's favour towards Yaqut, an Abyssinian. Their opposition contributed to the revolt led by Altuniya.
ne9ced9ddf67.tq: Use the person–identity association to resolve a confusable court-politics question.
xs: The nobles resented her favour to **Yaqut, an Abyssinian** — so option **(4)** is correct.
In **1240** **Altuniya**, governor of **Bhatinda (Sirhind)**, revolted; Yaqut was killed and Razia imprisoned.
**Minhaj-us-Siraj** and **Hasan Nizami** were chroniclers; **Yildiz** was Iltutmish's rival.
xa: The nobles then enthroned **Bahram Shah**.
Razia married Altuniya, marched on Delhi, and was **defeated and killed** (**1240**).

na3710c84ca3.s: Which sequence correctly describes Balban's early rise?
o: Slave of Iltutmish → water-carrier → member of the Forty → Amir-i-Shikar
Water-carrier → slave of Aibak → Amir-i-Akhur → member of the Forty
Member of the Forty → slave of Iltutmish → water-carrier → governor of Bhatinda
na3710c84ca3.x: Balban was captured by the Mongols, bought by Iltutmish, rose from water-carrier to the Forty, and was made Amir-i-Shikar by Razia.
na3710c84ca3.tq: Arrange biographical stages rather than merely recalling an isolated title.
xs: **Slave of Iltutmish → water-carrier → member of the Forty → Amir-i-Shikar** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Balban was captured by the **Mongols** and **bought by Iltutmish**.
**Razia** made him **Amir-i-Shikar**; title **Ulugh Khan**.
xa: **Amir-i-Akhur** (Master of Stables) was **Aibak's** post, not Balban's.
Under Nasiruddin Mahmud he became **principal minister (naib)** and leader of the Forty.

n8058d4d1220.s: The military department reorganised by Balban was known as:
n8058d4d1220.x: Balban reorganised the army and created the military department Diwan-i-Arz. He also built outposts and forts against the Mongols.
n8058d4d1220.tq: Use the function of an institution to distinguish it from neighbouring departments.
xs: Balban created the military department **Diwan-i-Arz** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He reorganised the army and built **outposts and forts** against the **Mongols**.
xa: His son **Prince Muhammad** died fighting the Mongols (**1285**).
Diwan-i-Arz is one of the dynasty's **core institutions**, with iqta, the Forty and **tanka/jital**.

n8229e0876fe.x: Mamluk is an Arabic term meaning ‘owned’. In this context it denotes a military slave, distinct from a domestic slave.
n8229e0876fe.tq: Test the precise meaning of a technical historical term.
xs: **Mamluk** is Arabic for "owned" — **an owned military slave** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It means a **military** slave as opposed to a **domestic** slave.
xa: The **Slave / Mamluk** dynasty ruled **1206-1290**.
Aibak was a slave of **Muhammad Ghori** (APPSC G1 **2004**).
Balban was captured by the Mongols and **bought by Iltutmish**.

nc2799185918.x: Balban held the Sultan to be Zil-i-Ilahi (shadow of God) and required sijda and paibos.
xa: ⚠ **Sijda** = prostration; **paibos** = kissing the feet.
He created the military department **Diwan-i-Arz**.

n6acd7de6bbe.s: The Qutb Minar, begun by Qutbuddin Aibak, was completed by:
n6acd7de6bbe.x: Aibak began the Qutb Minar, but it was completed by Iltutmish.
xa: The Qutb Minar is dedicated to **Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki**.
The **Qutb complex** is now a **UNESCO** site.

n82dd4082b98.s: The Qutb Minar was dedicated to:
n82dd4082b98.x: Qutbuddin Aibak began the Qutb Minar and dedicated it to Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki.
n82dd4082b98.tq: Separate the dedicatee of a monument from other well-known Sufi figures.
xs: The Qutb Minar is dedicated to **Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** — so option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ It is named after the saint **Bakhtiyar Kaki**, not after Aibak.
xa: It was **begun by Aibak** and **completed by Iltutmish**.
Iltutmish's **Sultan Ghari** tomb made him the **"Father of tomb building"**.

nf03c888095f.s: Which monument led to Iltutmish being called the ‘Father of tomb building’?
nf03c888095f.x: Iltutmish built the Sultan Ghari tomb and is consequently called the Father of tomb building. He also completed the Qutb Minar.
nf03c888095f.tq: Match an architectural work with the historical epithet associated with its builder.
xs: The **Sultan Ghari tomb** made Iltutmish the **"Father of tomb building"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Arhai-din-ka-Jhonpra** at Ajmer was built by **Aibak** and is not a tomb.
xa: Iltutmish **completed** the **Qutb Minar** begun by Aibak.
Aibak's **Quwwat-ul-Islam** mosque, Delhi, is the **first mosque in India**.

n639e30cf484.s: Which one of the following correctly describes Jalaluddin Khalji's policy towards rebels and Hindus?
o: He imposed severe punishments on every rebel without exception.
He adopted a benevolent attitude and was lenient towards rebels such as Malik Chhajju.
He adopted a policy of complete exclusion of Hindus from administration.
He transferred the capital to Ranthambore to control Hindu chiefs.
n639e30cf484.x: Jalaluddin Khalji was the first Sultan described as having a benevolent attitude towards Hindus, and he was lenient towards rebels including Malik Chhajju.
n639e30cf484.tq: Identify the policy statement that combines the ruler's general approach with its specific example.
xs: Jalaluddin **adopted a benevolent attitude** and was **lenient towards rebels such as Malik Chhajju** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was the **first Sultan** with a benevolent attitude to **Hindus**.
His attack on **Ranthambore** failed; he never moved his capital there.
xa: He crowned himself at **Kilokhari** in **1290**, aged about **70**.
He was a **Khalji** from **Turkestan** who had fought the Mongols.

n8756a2d7b3e.s: Jalaluddin Khalji was murdered by Alauddin at:
n8756a2d7b3e.x: Jalaluddin, who crowned himself at Kilokhari, was murdered at Kara by Alauddin in 1296.
xa: Before the murder Alauddin raided **Devagiri** (**1294-96**) — the **first Turkish invasion of the south**.
Jalaluddin was lenient to rebels like **Malik Chhajju**.

nf4c8c26974b.s: Mongols who converted and settled in the Sultanate under Jalaluddin Khalji were called:
nf4c8c26974b.x: Settled converted Mongols were called New Mussalmans; Jalaluddin also married his daughter to Ulugh Khan, a descendant of Chengiz Khan.
xa: **Hammir Deva** of **Ranthambore** later sheltered the New Mussalmans — the cause of the **1301** campaign.
Alauddin met a Mongol **siege of Delhi** by sheltering in **Siri** fort.

n24453b59f70.s: Alauddin Khalji's raid on Devagiri is significant in the history of the Delhi Sultanate because it was:
o: The first expedition of the Tughlaqs into the south
The first Kakatiya invasion of Delhi
The first Turkish invasion of southern India
The first Mongol invasion of the Deccan
n24453b59f70.x: Alauddin Khalji's Devagiri raid of 1294–96 is described as the first Turkish invasion of the south.
n24453b59f70.tq: Use the FIRST/LAST marker to identify the historically defining event.
xs: Alauddin's Devagiri raid (**1294-96**) was **the first Turkish invasion of southern India** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was made under **Jalaluddin**, before Alauddin's accession — not by the Tughlaqs or Mongols.
xa: He later murdered Jalaluddin at **Kara (1296)**.
Devagiri (Yadava **Ramachandra**) was attacked again by **Malik Kafur** in **1307-08**.

n302711ccdf4.s: When the Mongols besieged Delhi, Alauddin Khalji took shelter in:
n302711ccdf4.x: Alauddin sheltered in Siri during the siege; Zafar Khan was killed at Kili.
xa: Alauddin built **Siri** as his new capital and kept a **large standing army**.
Ghazi Malik later killed **Khusrau Khan** in **1320** and founded the **Tughlaq** dynasty.

n0d94fd2915d.s: Before becoming Sultan, Alauddin Khalji was known as:
n0d94fd2915d.x: Alauddin Khalji's earlier name was Ali Gurshasp.
n0d94fd2915d.tq: Test the ruler’s earlier name directly against names of contemporaries.
xs: Alauddin's earlier name was **Ali Gurshasp** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Khizr Khan** was his son; **Ghazi Malik** and **Ain-ul-Mulk Multani** were his nobles.
xa: Under Jalaluddin he was **Amir-i-Tuzuk** (master of ceremonies) and **Ariz-i-Mumalik** (army minister).
He wished to be **Sikandar-i-Sani** — a second Alexander.

n8ad6802e8b8.s: Under Jalaluddin Khalji, Alauddin was Amir-i-Tuzuk, which means:
n8ad6802e8b8.x: Amir-i-Tuzuk was the master of ceremonies; the Ariz-i-Mumalik was the army minister.
xa: **Sikandar-i-Sani** = second Alexander, his world-conqueror ambition.
His court poet was **Amir Khusrau**.

n9c236e181c6.x: Sikandar-i-Sani means the second Alexander; Alauddin wished to be a world conqueror like Alexander.
xa: Alauddin ruled **without the ulema**, acting in the state's interest.
His nobles: **Ulugh Khan**, **Nusrat Khan**, **Zafar Khan**, **Ain-ul-Mulk Multani**, **Malik Kafur**, **Ghazi Malik**.

nc490708c932.s: Which pair of officials led Alauddin Khalji's Gujarat campaign of 1299?
o: Khwaja Haji and Malik Fakhruddin Juna
nc490708c932.x: Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan commanded the Gujarat campaign of 1299. Rai Karan, also known as Karnadeva II, was defeated, and Queen Kamala Devi was captured.
nc490708c932.tq: Use the commander–campaign association and reject swapped generals.
xs: **Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan** led the **1299** Gujarat campaign — so option **(3)** is correct.
They defeated **Rai Karan (Karnadeva II)** Vaghela; his queen **Kamala Devi** was captured.
**Malik Kafur** was acquired here; **Ain-ul-Mulk** led **Malwa** (**1305**).
xa: **1299** is the accepted date (APPSC **2023** key); older notes say **1297**.
**Nusrat Khan** was later killed at **Ranthambore** (**1301**).

nd7dc0d4cac5.x: After the conquest of Chittor in 1303, Alauddin Khalji renamed it Khizrabad after his son Prince Khizr Khan.
xs: Chittor was renamed **Khizrabad** after prince **Khizr Khan** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Alauddin took it in **1303** from **Rana Ratan Singh** of Mewar.
xa: **Rani Padmini's jauhar** is set at Chittor.
⚠ Prince **Khizr Khan** (set aside **1316**) ≠ Sayyid **Khizr Khan** (**1414-1421**).

nbe37d506f9b.s: Under Alauddin Khalji's southern policy, conquered rulers were generally:
o: allowed to keep their thrones on paying tribute
annexed and their kingdoms made provinces
nbe37d506f9b.x: In the south rulers kept their thrones and paid tribute, whereas northern kingdoms were generally annexed.
xa: **Ramachandra** of Devagiri agreed to **tribute** (**1307-08**).
Kakatiya **tribute stopped after 1316**.

n317d01f50e1.s: Which Vaghela ruler of Gujarat was defeated by Alauddin Khalji's forces?
n317d01f50e1.x: Gujarat's Rai Karan (Karnadeva II Vaghela) was defeated; Ratan Singh was of Chittor and Mahlak Deva of Malwa.
xa: **Ranthambore** — **Hammir Deva**; **Devagiri** — **Ramachandra**; **Dwarasamudra** — **Vira Ballala III**.
Warangal ended in a **treaty and annual tribute** (**1309-10**).
n317d01f50e1.fixed: Ain-ul-Mulk was the commander, not the Malwa ruler; pair list mixed rulers and commanders

n91019d77f34.s: Malik Kafur's first southern campaign (1307-08) was against:
n91019d77f34.x: The order was Devagiri (1307-08), Warangal (1309-10), Dwarasamudra (1310-11) and Madurai (1311).
xa: Some notes give **1307 / 1309 / 1310 / 1311**; others: Yadavas **1308**, Kakatiyas **1310**, Hoysalas **1311**.
Kakatiya troops aided Malik Kafur against Madurai.

nindian-history-21-16.s: Repeated Mongol invasions during Alauddin Khalji's reign led him to maintain:
o: a feudal levy of Rajput chiefs
nindian-history-21-16.x: The Mongol threat led Alauddin to keep a large standing army, with military reforms and revenue and market reforms to pay for it.
n: The Mongols repeatedly invaded during Alauddin Khalji’s reign. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Mongol invasions contributed to the creation of a large standing army. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Mongol invasions contributed to military reforms. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Mongol invasions contributed to revenue reforms. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: At the **Battle of Kili**, **Zafar Khan** was killed.
Alauddin built **Siri** as a new capital; **Ghazi Malik** was made governor of **Punjab**.
Ghazi Malik chased the Mongols **29 times**, later becoming **Ghiyasuddin Tughluq**.

nindian-history-67-10.s: Genghis Khan reached the Indus around 1221 during the reign of:
nindian-history-67-10.x: Genghis Khan reached the Indus under Iltutmish; the 1398 invasion was by Timur.
n: Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Timur, also known as Taimur, invaded India in 1398 CE. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
