ne150b433ccc.x: Roe obtained rights to trade and set up factories; the title English Khan belonged to William Hawkins.
xa: ⚠ **Hawkins** = "English Khan", no farman; **Roe** = ambassador, won trade rights.
**Captain Best's** win (**1612**) → English factory at **Surat (1613)**.

nbbe7340d2da.s: Kandahar, recovered by Shah Jahan in 1638, was finally lost to Persia in:
nbbe7340d2da.x: Kandahar was lost under Jahangir, recovered in 1638 and finally lost in 1649.
xa: Kandahar was surrendered in **1638** by Persian governor **Ali Mardan Khan** (some notes say **1639**).
Later sieges: **1649** and **1652** (Aurangzeb), **1653** (Dara Shikoh) — all failed.
Kandahar was lost in **1622** while **Khurram** was in revolt.

n1d481945c24.s: Shah Jahan defeated the Portuguese at Hughli in 1632 mainly because of their:
n1d481945c24.x: The Portuguese were defeated at Hughli in 1632 over their trading abuses.
n1d481945c24.tq: Link the military action with its stated immediate cause.
xs: At **Hughli (1632)**, Shah Jahan defeated the **Portuguese** over **trading abuses** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Kandahar** was a Persian, not Portuguese, issue; Ahmadnagar was isolated by winning over **Bijapur and the Marathas**.
xa: Early revolts: Bundelas under **Jujhar Singh**; **Khan Jahan Lodi** in the Deccan.
Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra c. **1628**, deposed **1658**.
Earlier, **Captain Best** beat the Portuguese off **Surat** (**1612**).

ne9cd089f6d1.s: The Peacock Throne, or Takht-i-Taus, was carried away from India by:
ne9cd089f6d1.x: Nadir Shah carried away the Peacock Throne from India in 1739. It had stood in the Diwan-i-Khas and was described by Tavernier.
ne9cd089f6d1.tq: Match the celebrated object with the invader who removed it.
xs: The **Peacock Throne** (Takht-i-Taus) was carried off by **Nadir Shah** in **1739** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It stood in the **Diwan-i-Khas** and was described by **Tavernier**.
**Ali Mardan Khan** surrendered Kandahar; **Mir Jumla** instigated the **1656** attack on Golconda.
xa: The throne is part of Shah Jahan's **"Golden Age"** with the **Taj Mahal**, **Red Fort** and **Jama Masjid**.
Court history of Shah Jahan: **Padshahnama** by **Abdul Hamid Lahori**.

nf78680fbff4.s: The Padshahnama of Shah Jahan's reign was written by:
nf78680fbff4.x: Abdul Hamid Lahori wrote the Padshahnama.
xa: **Adab-i-Alamgiri** = Aurangzeb's letters on the father-son money dispute.
The Peacock Throne was described by **Tavernier** and taken by **Nadir Shah** in **1739**.
**Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri** = Jahangir's memoir.

nef1e7604a4e.s: Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in:
nef1e7604a4e.x: Shah Jahan was crowned at Agra in 1628.
xa: He was **deposed in 1658** and confined in **Agra Fort** till **1666**.
**Hughli (1632)**: Portuguese defeated.
**Nadir Shah** carried off the Peacock Throne in **1739**.

n4df35b1acdf.s: Shah Jahan recovered Kandahar when its Persian governor surrendered it to the Mughal Empire. Who was that governor?
n4df35b1acdf.x: The Persian governor Ali Mardan Khan surrendered Kandahar to Shah Jahan. The recovery is generally dated 1638, though some accounts mention 1639.
n4df35b1acdf.tq: Match the captured or surrendered territory with the responsible official.
xs: Kandahar was surrendered by Persian governor **Ali Mardan Khan** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The recovery is dated **1638** (some notes say **1639**).
**Mir Jumla** instigated the Golconda attack; **Qamruddin Chin Qilich Khan** helped annex Golconda; **Khan Jahan Lodi** revolted in the Deccan.
xa: Kandahar was **lost again in 1649**.
Failed sieges: **1649**, **1652** (Aurangzeb) and **1653** (Dara Shikoh).
Kandahar was first lost to **Shah Abbas I** in **1622**.

n6cc6c505b4b.s: What was the result of the Mughal sieges of Kandahar in 1649, 1652 and 1653?
o: All three failed, and Kandahar was lost permanently.
All three succeeded in recovering Kandahar.
The first two failed but the third established Mughal control.
n6cc6c505b4b.x: Aurangzeb's sieges in 1649 and 1652 and Dara Shikoh's siege in 1653 all failed; Kandahar was thereafter lost for good.
n6cc6c505b4b.tq: Separate repeated unsuccessful campaigns from a successful territorial recovery.
xs: **All three sieges failed** and Kandahar was **lost for good** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1649** and **1652** were led by **Aurangzeb**; **1653** by **Dara Shikoh**.
xa: Kandahar had been recovered in **1638** (surrendered by **Ali Mardan Khan**) and lost again in **1649**.
The **Balkh-Badakhshan** campaign (**1646-47**) also ended in withdrawal.
Earlier loss: **1622**, under Jahangir, during **Khurram's** revolt.

n97a4c33be47.s: The letters relating to the dispute over money between Shah Jahan and his son are known as
n97a4c33be47.x: The letters concerning the father-son money dispute between Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb are known as the Adab-i-Alamgiri.
n97a4c33be47.tq: Identify the specific literary work from the subject matter associated with it.
xs: The letters on the father-son money dispute are the **Adab-i-Alamgiri** — so option **(1)** is correct.
They were written by **Aurangzeb**.
**Padshahnama** is **Abdul Hamid Lahori's** court history; **Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri** is Jahangir's memoir.
xa: Shah Jahan was confined in **Agra Fort** and nursed by **Jahanara** till **1666**.
Aurangzeb was crowned in **1658**.
The war of succession began with Shah Jahan's illness in **1657**.

n2d41548d63b.s: Which of the following correctly describes the later Maratha resistance to Aurangzeb?
o: Sambhaji – resisted from Jinji; Rajaram – executed in 1689
Sambhaji – released by Bahadur Shah I; Shahu – executed in 1689
Rajaram – released by Bahadur Shah I; Tarabai – surrendered at Jinji
Sambhaji – executed in 1689; Rajaram – resisted from Jinji; Shahu – released by Bahadur Shah I
n2d41548d63b.x: Sambhaji was executed in 1689, Rajaram continued resistance from Jinji, followed by Tarabai, and Shahu was later released by Bahadur Shah I.
xa: The **unwinnable** Maratha war drained the treasury; Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in **1707**.
Phase II of Aurangzeb's Deccan policy (**1668-84**): Marathas the main threat.
**Abul Hasan Tana Shah** of Golconda had helped **Shivaji**.

n2f28ab9eab5.s: The Nizam Shahi state of Ahmadnagar was annexed by the Mughals in:
n2f28ab9eab5.x: Ahmadnagar was annexed under Shah Jahan in 1636; 1687 is the annexation of Golconda.
xa: **Mahabat Khan** was then made Deccan governor.
⚠ **1636** = Ahmadnagar + treaties; **1686** = Bijapur; **1687** = Golconda.
The Deccan was organised into four subas: **Khandesh, Berar, Telangana, Daulatabad**.

n3a776db5694.s: The 1636 ahdnamas concluded with Bijapur and Golconda recognised:
n3a776db5694.x: The agreements recognised Mughal suzerainty, required tribute and provided for Mughal arbitration.
xa: Golconda's **Inqiyad Nama (1636)**: tribute of **2 lakh hun**; Shah Jahan's name on coins and in the **khutba**.
These treaties set up **Aurangzeb's** later annexations: Bijapur **1686**, Golconda **1687**.
Golconda's ruler then was **Abdullah Qutb Shah**.

n312b10b2cd8.s: Which of the following was one of the four subas into which the Mughal Deccan was reorganised?
n312b10b2cd8.x: The four subas were Khandesh, Berar, Telangana and Daulatabad.
xa: **Aurangzeb** was Deccan viceroy **1636-44** and **1652-57**.
**1656**: he attacked Golconda at **Mir Jumla's** instigation.
Ahmadnagar was annexed in **1636**.

n06bbe0770ae.s: In 1656, Aurangzeb attacked Golconda at the instigation of:
n06bbe0770ae.x: Aurangzeb attacked Golconda in 1656 at the instigation of Mir Jumla.
n06bbe0770ae.tq: Match the Deccan action with the person who prompted it.
xs: Aurangzeb attacked Golconda in **1656** at the instigation of **Mir Jumla** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Fath Khan** was Malik Ambar's son; **Ali Mardan Khan** surrendered Kandahar; **Sikandar Adil Shah** was Bijapur's last ruler.
xa: Aurangzeb was Deccan viceroy **1636-44** and **1652-57**.
Golconda was finally annexed in **1687**; last ruler **Abul Hasan Tana Shah**.
Aurangzeb's reign: first **25** years in the north, last **25** in the Deccan.

n29721e3835c.s: Abul Hasan Tana Shah, the last ruler of Golconda, was exiled to:
n29721e3835c.x: Tana Shah was exiled to Daulatabad and died in 1699; Gwalior was where Murad Bakhsh was imprisoned.
xa: Golconda was formally annexed on **3 Oct 1687**, bringing **Andhra** under the Mughals.
Tana Shah employed **Madanna and Akkanna** and helped **Shivaji**.
Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in **1707**.

na49f0e145b7.s: Which Maratha queen is associated with the resistance against Aurangzeb?
na49f0e145b7.x: Shivaji, Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai are all associated with the Maratha resistance against Aurangzeb.
xa: **Shahu** was released by **Bahadur Shah I**.
Golconda's **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** helped **Shivaji**.
Aurangzeb died in the Deccan in **1707**, the war unwon.

nb106999a9d7.s: After his deposition in 1658, Shah Jahan was kept under guard in:
nb106999a9d7.x: Shah Jahan was confined in Agra Fort and nursed by Jahanara.
xa: The war of succession began with his illness in **1657**.
**Adab-i-Alamgiri**: Aurangzeb's letters on the father-son money dispute.
He had been crowned at Agra c. **1628**.

na9433811f17.x: Jahangir sent Mir Makki; Mir Jumla is linked with Aurangzeb's 1656 attack on Golconda.
xa: Golconda paid Mughal tribute from **1636** (**2 lakh hun**).
Annexation of Golconda (**1687**) brought **Andhra** under the Mughals.
**Abul Hasan Tana Shah** employed **Madanna and Akkanna**.

n4a721a22a9b.s: Which of the following contributed to the decline of the Mughal Empire after Aurangzeb?
o: Loss of Bengal to the Marathas
n4a721a22a9b.x: The jagir crisis, along with the Deccan wars and Rajput alienation, contributed to the decline.
xa: The Deccan war **drained the treasury**; Aurangzeb died there in **1707**.
Rajput revolt: **Marwar and Mewar** under **Durgadas Rathore**.
Aurangzeb spent his last **25** years in the Deccan.

nb2f687c6cf4.s: At Samugarh (1658), Aurangzeb and Murad decisively defeated:
nb2f687c6cf4.x: Samugarh near Agra was the decisive defeat of Dara; Jaswant Singh was beaten at Dharmat and Shuja at Khajwa.
xa: **Deorai** (Mar **1659**, near **Ajmer**) was Dara's final defeat.
Dharmat was near **Ujjain**; Samugarh near **Agra**.
The war was triggered by Shah Jahan's illness in **1657**.

n4447377c74e.s: Dara Shikoh was the eldest son of:
n4447377c74e.x: Dara Shikoh was Shah Jahan's eldest son; Jahangir's son was Khusrau.
xa: Khusrau rebelled in **1606**.
Dara's title: **Shah-i-Buland Iqbal**; buried in **Humayun's Tomb**.
**Murad Bakhsh** governed **Malwa and Gujarat** and was executed in **1661**.

nc295675b859.s: Who among the following was the Hindu mother of Shah Jahan and the wife of Jahangir?
nc295675b859.x: Jagat Gosain was a Hindu wife of Jahangir and the mother of Shah Jahan.
nc295675b859.tq: Distinguish the emperor's mother from his wife and daughter.
xs: **Jagat Gosain**, Jahangir's Hindu wife, was **Shah Jahan's mother** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Mumtaz Mahal** was Shah Jahan's **wife**; **Nur Jahan** was Jahangir's empress; **Jahanara** was Shah Jahan's **daughter**.
xa: **Jahanara** nursed Shah Jahan in captivity at **Agra Fort**.
Mumtaz Mahal = **Arjumand Banu Begum**, **Asaf Khan's** daughter.
Emperor-queen: Jahangir — **Nur Jahan**; Shah Jahan — **Mumtaz Mahal**.

n01066716c95.s: Jahanara was honoured with the title:
n01066716c95.x: Jahanara was honoured as Sahibat-uz-Zamani (Mistress of the Age); Roshanara was made Padshah Begum.
xa: Roshanara **backed Aurangzeb** in the succession war.
Aurangzeb was also called **"Darvesh"**.
He was the first Mughal to fight the English (**Child's War, 1686-90**).

n2159dfc3e41.s: Aurangzeb's war with the English (1686–90), the first between a Mughal emperor and the English, is known as:
n2159dfc3e41.x: The Child's War of 1686–90 was the first conflict between the English and a Mughal emperor, fought under Aurangzeb.
xa: Regnal title **Alamgir**; popular titles **Zinda Pir** and **Darvesh**.
Golconda was annexed in the same period, **1687**.
He had a double coronation (**1658**, **1659**).

n7d32bd08c96.s: Aurangzeb ended music at the imperial court, yet he himself played the:
n7d32bd08c96.x: Aurangzeb banned court music, though Persian works on Indian music were written in his reign and he himself played the veena.
xa: ⚠ Yet Persian works on Indian music were written and he played the **veena**.
**1669** order: **Kashi Vishwanath** and **Keshava Rai** (Mathura) demolished.
**Muhtasibs** were appointed to enforce sharia.
Akbar had abolished jizya in **1564**.

n0b7f0a9b113.s: Which temple was named in Aurangzeb's temple-demolition order of 1669?
n0b7f0a9b113.x: The 1669 order included Kashi Vishwanath and Keshava Rai at Mathura.
xa: Policy: **newly built temples** were destroyed.
The same year, **Gokula** led the **Jat** revolt at **Mathura** (**1669**).
**Jizya** was reimposed in **1679**.

n5452b29e769.s: The officers Aurangzeb appointed to enforce the Sharia were called:
n5452b29e769.x: Aurangzeb appointed Muhtasibs to enforce the Sharia; he also banned Navroz and discontinued Jharokha darshan.
xa: **Tuladan** was also discontinued.
**Zawabit** = secular state regulations alongside sharia.
Court music was banned, yet he played the **veena**.

n8ed2193e64b.s: Under Aurangzeb's religious policy, newly built temples were:
n8ed2193e64b.x: Newly built temples were ordered to be destroyed, though court music bans coexisted with Persian works on Indian music.
xa: **1669** order: **Kashi Vishwanath** and **Keshava Rai** demolished.
**Navroz** was banned.
He was called **"Zinda Pir"**.

n4c1e3e0a64a.s: The Satnami revolt of 1672 was centred at:
n4c1e3e0a64a.x: The 1672 Satnami revolt of peasants and artisans was centred at Narnaul in Haryana.
xa: The Satnami revolt was **crushed**.
Narnaul is in **Haryana**.
Jat Rajaram plundered **Akbar's tomb at Sikandra**.

nc91faa50ffb.s: Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar, whose death led to the Rajput war of 1679-81, died in:
nc91faa50ffb.x: Jaswant Singh died in 1678; Durgadas Rathore then championed his posthumous heir Ajit Singh.
xa: After Jaswant Singh's death, Aurangzeb took **Marwar under direct control**.
Result: the **Rajput alliance** of Akbar's empire was broken.
Ajit Singh was a **posthumous heir**.

na8533a97b73.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Mughal conquest of Golconda?
o: Madanna and Akkanna were murdered in 1686.
Its last ruler, Abul Hasan Tana Shah, was exiled to Gwalior.
na8533a97b73.x: Tana Shah was exiled to Daulatabad, not Gwalior (where Murad Bakhsh was imprisoned).
xa: The fort fell on **3 Oct 1687** after **Abdullah Pani** opened the gates (**21 Sept 1687**).
**Abdur Razzaq Lari** defended it; honoured as **Mustafa Khan**.
**Bhakta Ramadasu** was the nephew of **Akkanna-Madanna**.

nf6d30eea9e6.s: Aurangzeb, who died at Ahmednagar in 1707, was buried in a simple grave at:
nf6d30eea9e6.x: He was buried in a simple grave at Khuldabad near Aurangabad, where Tana Shah was also buried.
xa: Tana Shah was imprisoned at **Bidar**, then **Daulatabad**, and died in **1699**.
Aurangzeb spent his last **25-27** years camped in the Deccan.
**Golconda** fell on **3 Oct 1687** and became the **21st suba**.

nd6f1726e3dd.s: The fall of Golconda to Aurangzeb in 1687 ended the rule of which dynasty over Andhra?
nd6f1726e3dd.x: Golconda fell in 1687 and Abul Hasan Qutb Shah (Tana Shah) was imprisoned, ending Qutb Shahi rule over Andhra; Golconda became a Mughal suba.
xa: **Bhakta Ramadasu** was the nephew of **Akkanna-Madanna**.
**Abdullah Pani** opened the gates; **Abdur Razzaq Lari** defended it.
Tana Shah died in **1699**; buried at **Khuldabad**.

n71411cb856e.s: Which event is associated with Shivaji's visit to Agra in 1666?
o: He was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad.
He began the campaign from Jinji.
He was insulted, placed under house arrest and escaped in fruit baskets.
He captured Sirhind from Wazir Khan.
n71411cb856e.x: During his 1666 visit to Agra, Shivaji was insulted and placed under house arrest, from which he escaped in fruit baskets.
n71411cb856e.tq: Identify the distinctive incident associated with a specific year and place.
xs: In **1666** at **Agra**, Shivaji was **insulted**, put under **house arrest**, and **escaped in fruit baskets** — so option **(3)** is correct.
His **Chhatrapati** coronation was at **Raigad** in **1674**.
**Sirhind** belongs to Banda Singh's story, not Shivaji's.
xa: **1700-07**: **Tarabai** (Rajaram's widow) raided Mughal territory in her son's name.
The Marathas split into the **Satara** line and Tarabai's **Kolhapur** line.
**Prince Akbar** fled to **Sambhaji**.

n7aa0e528da2.s: Under Akbar's Mansabdari system, a mansab denoted:
n7aa0e528da2.x: A mansab was a rank serving military and civil administration, not a hereditary office.
xa: "Mansab" is **Arabic** for **rank/position**; model from **Central Asia** (Mongol decimal grading).
The **Mir Bakhshi** ran the system (JPSC **2023**).
**Not all mansabdars were military officers**; high civil post-holders were graded the same way.

nd1722e42cd4.s: Under the Mansabdari system, ranks and jagirs normally:
o: Ended with the death of the holder
Passed to the holder's eldest son
nd1722e42cd4.x: Mansabs were not hereditary; ranks and jagirs normally ended with the holder's death.
xa: One grading served **both army and civil service** (BPSC **2019** "more than one").
The **Mir Bakhshi** ran the system.
Mansabdari was introduced by **Akbar**.

n41d1e177a57.s: In the Mughal Mansabdari system, 'sawar' denoted:
n41d1e177a57.x: Sawar indicated the number of cavalrymen to be maintained; zat was personal rank and status.
xa: Horse rule: every **10** sawars to bring **20** horses (**10-20-30** norm).
Class depends on the **sawar-zat** ratio (equal, half or more, less than half).
Jahangir's **du-aspa sih-aspa** raised sawar without raising zat.

n7f6b0caa1ac.s: Payment to a mansabdar in cash was known as:
n7f6b0caa1ac.x: Mansabdars were paid in cash (naqd) or by non-hereditary assignment of land revenue (jagir).
xa: A jagir was **not a property right**, only the right to collect revenue.
**Tankhwah** jagirs were **transferable**; **Watan** jagirs were hereditary and not transferred.
**Khalisa** = crown land whose revenue went to the treasury; not a jagir.

nf31ba08bb1a.s: The conditional increase in the sawar rank known as mashrut was associated with the reign of
nf31ba08bb1a.x: Aurangzeb introduced mashrut, a temporary increase in the sawar rank connected with a specific assignment.
nf31ba08bb1a.tq: Distinguish similar mansab innovations by linking each to its emperor.
xs: **Mashrut** (conditional) increase belongs to **Aurangzeb** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was a **temporary extra increase in sawar rank** tied to a specific assignment.
⚠ **Du-aspa sih-aspa** = **Jahangir**; **month-scale** = **Shah Jahan**.
xa: **Mashrut jagir** = jagir given on conditions of service.
Under Aurangzeb, mansabdars grew sharply while **paibaqi** shrank → **jagirdari crisis**.
Shah Jahan let mansabdars maintain only **1/5 to 1/3** of sawar strength.

ncd5e16d4a9d.s: Under Shah Jahan, a jagir yielding half its assessed revenue was termed:
ncd5e16d4a9d.x: A half-yield jagir was shashmaha and a quarter-yield jagir sihmaha.
xa: Pay was scaled down when the actual yield (**hasil**) fell below the estimate (**jama**).
⚠ **Du-aspa sih-aspa** = Jahangir; **mashrut** = Aurangzeb.
The **chakla** (group of parganas) also dates from Shah Jahan's time.

ne67442f930a.s: By the end of Akbar's reign, the number of subahs had risen to:
ne67442f930a.x: Akbar had 12 subahs in 1580 and 15 by the end of his reign; Aurangzeb had 21.
xa: The **Subahdar** handled law and order; the provincial **Diwan** handled revenue.
The subah also had a **Bakhshi**, **Sadr** and **Qazi**.
⚠ **Chakla** sits between pargana and sarkar.

ne6ea4b13c18.s: Gentlemen troopers recruited and paid directly by the Mughal emperor were called:
ne6ea4b13c18.x: Ahadis were recruited directly by the emperor; Tabinan were mansabdars' contingents, dakhili state-paid troops under mansabdars, Walashahi the bodyguard.
xa: Ahadis were paid by the state, under **their own bakhshi**.
The **bulk** of the army = **mansabdars' cavalry contingents**.
Head of the army: **Mir Bakhshi**.

n1fb04628c67.s: Under Akbar, the authority of the Wakil became largely
n1fb04628c67.x: Although the Wakil had traditionally been the chief adviser or regent, the office became largely symbolic under Akbar.
n1fb04628c67.tq: Test the change in the practical importance of a central office.
xs: Under Akbar the **Wakil's** authority became largely **symbolic** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Wakil (vakil-us-saltanat) was chief adviser/regent; **Bairam Khan** held it in the regency, after which Akbar reduced it.
xa: Real finance power passed to the **Wazir/Diwan**.
Military power lay with the **Mir Bakhshi**.
Sultanate ministries (**Wazir**, **Diwan-i-Arz**) fed the Mughal model.

n4eea97c12e9.s: In a Mughal province, revenue was managed by the ____, who acted as an independent check on the governor.
n4eea97c12e9.x: The provincial Diwan managed revenue and checked the Subahdar, who handled governance and law and order.
xa: Other subah officials: **Bakhshi**, **Sadr**, **Qazi**.
Pargana: **Shiqdar** (military/police).
Village: **Muqaddam**, **Patwari**.

neeed2dda9f4.s: Mughal intelligence, run through waqia-navis, khufia-navis and harkaras, came under the:
neeed2dda9f4.x: Intelligence was under the Mir Bakhshi.
xa: The Mir Bakhshi also ran **recruitment, pay and musters**.
**Muhtasib** = public morals.
**Mustaufi** = auditor.

o: Transferable assignments made to cavalrymen in lieu of salary
Crown lands reserved for the imperial treasury
Revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men under the Sadr
n28e24b809c5.x: Madad-i-maash consisted of revenue-free grants to scholars and religious men and was administered under the Sadr.
n28e24b809c5.tq: Identify the beneficiary and administrative authority associated with the grant.
xs: **Madad-i-maash** = **revenue-free grants** to scholars and religious men, under the **Sadr** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Grants in lieu of salary were **Tankhwah** jagirs; crown land was **Khalisa**; hereditary Rajput grants were **Watan** jagirs.
xa: The **Sadr-us-Sudur** handled religion, charity and religious endowments.
He also appointed **qazis**.
**Altamgha** = perpetual grant.

nf0fb27d4816.s: A perpetual Mughal jagir grant was called:
nf0fb27d4816.x: Altamgha was perpetual; Tankhwah was in lieu of salary, Watan hereditary in the homeland and Mashrut conditional.
xa: **In'am** jagir was free of any service obligation.
⚠ **Tankhwah** = transferable; **Watan** = hereditary, not transferred.
**Khalisa** was crown land, not a jagir.

o: The hereditary home territory of a zamindar or Rajput chief
A grant in lieu of salary
A grant subject to conditions of service
n2658374aa38.x: Watan jagirs were hereditary home territories and were not transferred by the state.
xa: **Tankhwah** (Tankha) jagirs were **transferable**, given in lieu of salary.
**Altamgha** = perpetual grant; **In'am** = free of service.
Transfers came about every **3-4** years.

n777cc6155b3.s: In the Mughal system, a jagir was an assignment of land revenue given to a mansabdar in lieu of:
o: judicial and police duties in the area
n777cc6155b3.x: Jagirs were revenue assignments in lieu of salary and military service; they carried no judicial or police duties (UPSC 2019 key: a statement linking jagirs to judicial/police duties is wrong). A jagir gave no ownership of land, and revenue-free grants for scholars and holy men were madad-i-maash.
n777cc6155b3.tq: Jagir = salary + military service, not police/judicial, not ownership.
xs: A jagir was given **in lieu of salary and military service** — so option **(2)** is correct.
UPSC **2019** key: jagirs carried **no judicial/police duties**.
A jagir gave **no ownership**; revenue-free grants for religious men were **madad-i-maash**.
xa: **Tankhwah** jagirs were **transferable**.
Transfers about every **3-4** years stopped mansabdars striking **local roots**.
⚠ Zamindars held **hereditary** rights; jagirdars did not.

ne8706c193a9.s: Why were Mughal jagirs frequently transferred, generally after about three to four years?
o: To convert all jagirs into Khalisa lands
To make them hereditary among local chiefs
To prevent mansabdars from developing local roots and becoming independent feudal lords
To ensure that peasants elected their revenue collectors
ne8706c193a9.x: Frequent transfers, usually every three to four years, were intended to prevent mansabdars from establishing local bases and becoming independent feudal lords.
ne8706c193a9.tq: Link the numerical interval with the administrative purpose rather than treating it as an isolated figure.
xs: Jagirs were transferred every **3-4** years to **stop mansabdars striking local roots** and becoming **independent feudal lords** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Transfers kept jagirs **non-hereditary**; they did not convert them to khalisa.
xa: Side effect: short-term jagirdars **squeezed peasants**.
**Bejagiri** (waiting without jagirs) bred discontent and faction.
The mansab-jagir system **bound the nobility to the emperor**.

n8cc54243280.s: The term ‘bejagiri’ refers to a situation in which:
o: Mansabdars were kept waiting without jagirs
Mansabdars were appointed as village accountants
Revenue was transferred directly to the imperial treasury
Jagirs became hereditary in the home territories of chiefs
n8cc54243280.x: Bejagiri meant that mansabdars remained without jagir assignments. It bred discontent and factionalism at the imperial court.
n8cc54243280.tq: Discriminate between a condition of non-assignment and the normal jagir arrangement.
xs: **Bejagiri** = mansabdars **kept waiting without jagirs** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It led to **discontent and faction** at court.
Revenue going straight to the treasury came from **khalisa**; hereditary homeland grants were **Watan** jagirs.
xa: Under **Aurangzeb**, mansabdars grew while **paibaqi** shrank.
**Satish Chandra**: shortage of jagirs relative to claimants.
**Athar Ali**: influx of **Deccani and Maratha** nobles.

n544915df4e8.s: Which combination best explains the jagirdari crisis under Aurangzeb?
o: Reduction of nobility through the exclusion of Deccani and Maratha nobles
Growth in mansabdars, shrinkage of good jagirs and increasing pressure on peasants
Decline in mansabdars, expansion of profitable land and relief to peasants
Abolition of jagirs and complete transfer of revenue collection to village panchayats
n544915df4e8.x: Under Aurangzeb, the number of mansabdars increased, profitable jagirs became scarce, and peasants were subjected to intensified extraction.
n544915df4e8.tq: Combine the linked causes and effects instead of treating them as isolated facts.
xs: **Growth in mansabdars**, **shrinkage of good jagirs** and **pressure on peasants** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Aurangzeb**, paying land for assignment (**paibaqi**) shrank as claimants grew.
Deccani and Maratha nobles were **added**, not excluded (**Athar Ali**).
xa: Result: ruthless extraction, **agrarian ruin**, decline.
⚠ **Irfan Habib** = agrarian crisis; **Satish Chandra** = jagir shortage.
The crisis is a **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

n2db376343c0.s: The Mughal central administration rested on the mansab, which was a:
n2db376343c0.x: Every officer held a mansab, a combined military-cum-civil rank, which is why the Mughal state was essentially military.
xa: The mansab fused **nobility, army and bureaucracy** into one graded service.
**Mir Bakhshi** was head of **military and intelligence**.
⚠ Contrast: the British **ICS** was purely civil with fixed cash salaries.

n323c7b3b685.s: In the Mughal provincial hierarchy, the correct ascending order was:
n323c7b3b685.x: The administrative order from the lowest to the highest level was village, pargana, sarkar and subah.
n323c7b3b685.tq: Arrange administrative units from the smallest to the largest.
xs: Ascending order: **village → pargana → sarkar → subah** — so option **(3)** is correct.
UPSC **2021** tested the order **Pargana-Sarkar-Suba**.
Option 4 is the descending order.
xa: **Chakla**: group of parganas between pargana and sarkar (from **Shah Jahan's** time).
Pargana officials: **Shiqdar**, **Amil**, **Qanungo**, **Chaudhari**.
Village: **Muqaddam**, **Patwari**, panchayat.

naefded2218e.s: Chakla in the Mughal administrative system was:
o: A group of villages below the pargana level
The imperial treasury attached to a subah
A military unit under the Mir Bakhshi
A group of parganas situated between the pargana and sarkar levels
naefded2218e.x: A Chakla was a group of parganas placed between the pargana and sarkar levels. This arrangement dates from the time of Shah Jahan.
naefded2218e.tq: Test the intermediate position of a lesser-known administrative unit.
xs: A **chakla** was a **group of parganas** between the **pargana** and **sarkar** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It dates from **Shah Jahan's** time.
xa: Ascending order: **village → pargana → sarkar → subah**.
Akbar had **12** subahs in **1580**; **15** by the end of his reign.
Under Tana Shah, Golconda had **37 sarkars and 517 parganas**.

nd7f89f695af.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a jagirdar from a zamindar?
o: A jagirdar held hereditary local rights, whereas a zamindar was frequently transferred
A jagirdar held a revenue assignment in lieu of salary, whereas a zamindar possessed hereditary local rights and acted as an intermediary
A zamindar was appointed only as a provincial governor, whereas a jagirdar was a village accountant
Both were hereditary proprietors of land with identical powers
nd7f89f695af.x: A mansabdar holding a jagir had a non-hereditary right to collect revenue in lieu of salary and was frequently transferred. A zamindar held hereditary rights over land revenue and local power and acted as an intermediary between the state and peasants.
nd7f89f695af.tq: Compare the basis of tenure, transferability and local role.
xs: A **jagirdar** held a **revenue assignment in lieu of salary**; a **zamindar** held **hereditary** rights and was a **local intermediary** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Jagirdars were **not hereditary** and **frequently transferred**; zamindars were **not transferred** by the state.
Neither was a governor or village accountant; their powers were not identical.
xa: A jagir was **not property in land**.
**Watan** jagirs of Rajput chiefs were hereditary and not transferred.
Sultanate **iqta** and Kakatiya **Nayankara** are compared with the jagir.

nc544b396e5e.s: Which historian explained the Mughal jagirdari crisis as a shortage of jagirs relative to claimants?
nc544b396e5e.x: Satish Chandra stressed the shortage of jagirs; Irfan Habib the agrarian crisis; Athar Ali the influx of Deccani and Maratha nobles.
xa: Revolts in Habib's view: **Jat**, **Satnami**, **Maratha**.
The crisis arose under **Aurangzeb** as **paibaqi** shrank.
The jagirdari breakdown is the **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

nfd8111704d0.s: Which of the following states retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration?
o: Qutb Shahi state of Golconda only
nfd8111704d0.x: The Asaf Jahi state of Hyderabad retained a Mughal-style jagirdari administration.
nfd8111704d0.tq: Use the regional application angle to identify the state associated with the administrative practice.
xs: The **Asaf Jahi** state of **Hyderabad** kept a Mughal-style **jagirdari** administration — so option **(1)** is correct.
The Kakatiya **Nayankara** is only compared with the jagir; Golconda's set-up was Qutb Shahi (Peshwa, Mir Jumla, Ain-ul-Mulk, Majumdar).
xa: Qutb Shahi officials: **Mir Jumla** (finance), **Ain-ul-Mulk** (military), **Majumdar** (auditor).
Under Tana Shah, Golconda had **37 sarkars and 517 parganas**.
The jagirdari breakdown is the **core explanation of Mughal decline**.

n397dbcee611.s: A Mughal Sarkar had the Faujdar and the ____ as its principal officials.
n397dbcee611.x: A Sarkar was run by the Faujdar and Amalguzar; a Suba by the Subedar and provincial Diwan.
xa: **Pargana** (tehsil): **Shiqdar** + amil, qanungo, chaudhari.
The Mughal **"district"** = **Sarkar**.
The **Diwan** was independent of the Subedar — a check on him.

n752366c469b.s: In Mughal provincial administration, the unit that corresponded to a 'district' was the:
n752366c469b.x: The Sarkar was the Mughal district, headed by the faujdar and amalguzar; in ascending order the units ran Pargana - Sarkar - Suba (UPSC 2021). The Suba was the province, the Pargana roughly a tehsil, and the Chakla an intermediate unit not identical with the Sarkar.
n752366c469b.tq: Suba = province, Sarkar = district, Pargana = tehsil.
xs: The Mughal **"district"** was the **Sarkar** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Suba** = province; **Pargana** = tehsil; **Chakla** = intermediate unit, **not identical** to the sarkar.
xa: Sarkar heads: **Faujdar** + **amalguzar**.
Ascending order: **Pargana - Sarkar - Suba** (UPSC **2021**).
Sarkar officials also included the **Bitikchi** (accountant) and **Potdar** (treasurer).

nd9d3a7e6c25.s: The official responsible for collecting revenue in charge of a district was the:
nd9d3a7e6c25.x: The amalguzar, also called amil, was the district-level revenue collector.
nd9d3a7e6c25.tq: Match the official with the level and function of revenue administration.
xs: The **Amalguzar** (amil) was the **revenue collector in charge of a district** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
**Karkun** = pargana clerk-writer; **Potdar** = treasurer; **Bitikchi** = accountant.
xa: ⚠ **Amalguzar** = collector; **Bitikchi** = accountant; **Potdar** = treasurer — all sarkar level.
**Karori** = collector of a circle yielding **one crore dams**.
**Chaudhari** = pargana revenue collector (local notable).

n390b8e6752d.s: The provincial Diwan in the Mughal administration was independent of the Subedar primarily because he
o: controlled the city police and markets
served as a check on the Subedar in revenue and finance
n390b8e6752d.x: The provincial Diwan handled revenue and finance independently of the Subedar, thereby acting as a check on the governor.
n390b8e6752d.tq: Ask which official performed the balancing or checking function rather than the executive function.
xs: The provincial **Diwan**, handling **revenue and finance**, was **independent of the subedar** — a **check** on him — so option **(3)** is correct.
Military command lay with the **Subedar**/**Faujdar**; city police with the **Kotwal**.
xa: The **Subedar** (sipahsalar/nazim) kept law and order and enforced imperial decrees.
Subedar-diwan separation + **zabti** = model for later revenue administration.
⚠ The British **district collector** combined powers the Mughals kept apart.

n06dce277629.s: A Mansabdar receiving payment through a tankhwah jagir was connected to revenue collection in which sequence?
o: Mansabdar — Tankhwah jagir — Jagirdar's agents — Zamindars — Peasant
n06dce277629.x: The Mansabdar got a rank and was paid by a tankhwah jagir; the jagirdar's agents collected the assessed revenue (jama) through the zamindars, who kept a hereditary share, and the peasant paid about one-third of the produce.
n06dce277629.tq: Trace the institutional flow from rank and assignment to local collection and peasant payment.
xs: **Mansabdar → tankhwah jagir → jagirdar's agents → zamindars → peasant** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The agents collected the assessed revenue (**jama**) through **zamindars**, who kept a **hereditary share**.
The peasant paid about **one-third** of produce.
xa: ⚠ Jagirdar = outsider, **not hereditary**; zamindar = local, **hereditary**.
Zamindars had armed retainers and helped **police and collection**.
Short-tenure jagirdars pressed for more → local face of the **jagirdari crisis**.

n62afe4e81b8.s: In the Mughal revenue system, the peasant generally paid approximately what share of the produce?
n62afe4e81b8.x: The peasant's payment was approximately one-third of the produce in the mansabdar-jagirdar-zamindar revenue linkage.
n62afe4e81b8.tq: Retain the approximate fraction and reject nearby conventional revenue shares.
xs: The peasant paid about **one-third** of produce — so option **(1)** is correct.
This sat at the end of the **mansabdar → jagirdar → zamindar** chain.
xa: Assessed revenue was called **jama**.
Zamindars kept a **hereditary share**.
Qutb Shahi Golconda instead **farmed out revenue by auction**.

nd549da215fd.s: Which of the following was a major local manifestation of the jagirdari crisis?
o: Zamindars became salaried imperial officials and peasants received remissions permanently.
The state abolished revenue collection through local intermediaries.
Short-tenure Jagirdars pressed for more revenue, zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants fled.
Jagirdars reduced demands and zamindars abandoned cultivation.
nd549da215fd.x: Short tenure encouraged Jagirdars to press for higher collections; Zamindars resisted or rebelled, and peasants sometimes fled, producing a local face of the jagirdari crisis.
nd549da215fd.tq: Identify the connected cause-and-effect chain rather than an isolated symptom.
xs: **Short-tenure jagirdars pressed for more**, **zamindars resisted or rebelled**, and **peasants fled** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This was the **local face of the jagirdari crisis**; jagirdars did not reduce demands.
xa: Jagirdars were transferred often and were **outsiders** to the area.
Zamindars had **armed retainers**.
UPSC **2019**: jagirs were neither for judicial/police duties nor hereditary.

n6064bc5fc7c.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the categories of zamindars in Mughal India?
o: Intermediary zamindars collected revenue from primary zamindars for the state for a commission.
Autonomous chiefs were Rajas ruling their own territories.
Autonomous chiefs paid tribute and served as mansabdars.
Primary zamindars held only temporary, non-hereditary rights over cultivated land.
n6064bc5fc7c.x: Primary zamindars did not hold merely temporary, non-hereditary rights; that statement is false, while the other three are correct.
xa: **Jagirdars** held revenue **in lieu of salary**; **not hereditary**, transferred often.
The peasant paid about **one-third** of produce.
⚠ UPSC **2019**: "jagirs hereditary" is **wrong**.

n82b030b5019.s: Under Tana Shah, Qutb Shahi Golconda was divided into how many Sarkars?
n82b030b5019.x: Golconda was organised into tarafs and simalu, with 37 Sarkars and 517 Parganas under Tana Shah.
xa: Officials: village **mukaddam**, accountant **kulkarni**, pargana accounts officer **desai**.
Revenue was **farmed out by auction**.
**Northern Circars** zamindars date from the Qutb Shahi era.

nd7cbc2ab051.s: Approximately what proportion of rural agricultural produce reached the market during the Mughal period?
nd7cbc2ab051.x: Approximately 15 percent of rural agricultural produce reached the market. The pressure to pay revenue in cash encouraged peasants to sell produce.
nd7cbc2ab051.tq: Recall the approximate quantitative share and reject inflated estimates.
xs: About **15 percent** of rural agricultural produce was marketed — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC G2 **2017** key).
The **cash revenue demand** pushed peasants to sell their produce.
xa: Under **zabt**, revenue was paid mainly in **cash**, tying peasants to the market.
Commercial crops (**jins-i-kamil**): **cotton, sugarcane, indigo**, oilseeds, opium.
Cash revenue under zabt **monetised the rural economy**.

n9f7095551e6.s: The Mughal term ‘jins-i-kamil’, meaning ‘perfect crops’, referred to
o: Crops reserved exclusively for royal kitchens
n9f7095551e6.x: Jins-i-kamil referred to commercial or superior cash crops such as cotton, sugarcane, indigo, oilseeds and opium.
n9f7095551e6.tq: Distinguish the technical term for commercial crops from land classifications and imported crops.
xs: **Jins-i-kamil** ("perfect crops") meant **commercial crops** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They were **cotton, sugarcane, indigo**, oilseeds and opium — not royal-kitchen or New World crops only.
xa: New World crops via the Portuguese: **tobacco**, **maize**, chillies.
Regional exports: Gujarat = **indigo** + food grains; Bengal = **sugar** + rice.
⚠ Fallow land classes were **Parauti**, **Chachar**, **Banjar** — unrelated to jins-i-kamil.

n2529bec91d4.s: Which of the following sets consists of crops that came to India through the Portuguese from the New World?
n2529bec91d4.x: Tobacco and maize (and also chillies) came from the New World via the Portuguese. Pepper, spices, oilseeds, cotton, indigo, opium, rice, wheat and sugarcane were established Indian crops.
n2529bec91d4.tq: Identify the complete set by separating introduced crops from established Indian crops.
xs: **Tobacco, maize and chillies** came from the New World via the **Portuguese** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Pepper, spices**, **cotton, indigo, opium**, **rice, wheat, sugarcane** were established Indian crops.
xa: Tobacco, **cocoa** and **rubber** were domesticated in the New World (UPSC **2019** PYQ).
AP is among the **top three tobacco producers**, about **25%** of India's output.
The **Tobacco Board** is in **Guntur**.

na54728703fc.s: The Shahab Nahr was built by restoring which earlier canal?
na54728703fc.x: The Shahab Nahr was constructed by restoring the Rajabwah canal of Firuz Shah.
na54728703fc.tq: Match a later irrigation work with the earlier canal it restored.
xs: The **Shahab Nahr** was built by restoring **Firuz Shah's Rajabwah** canal — so option **(4)** is correct (UPPSC **2020** key).
The notes give no "Ilahi Nahr" or Todarmal canal; **Ilahi Gaz** was Todarmal's measuring rod.
xa: By the **18th century**, agriculture was **stagnant** and technologically backward.
Peasants paid the state, **zamindars**, **jagirdars** and **revenue-farmers**.
About **15%** of produce was marketed.

n851af9d7d2b.s: Under the Zabt system, the state share was fixed at
o: One-half of the produce of the current year
One-third of the average produce of the past ten years
One-fourth of the average produce of the preceding five years
One-sixth of the average produce of the preceding twelve years
n851af9d7d2b.x: The state share was one-third of the average produce calculated over the past ten years.
n851af9d7d2b.tq: Keep the fraction and reference period together while eliminating altered figures.
xs: Under **Zabt**, the state took **one-third of the average produce of the past ten years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was devised by **Raja Todarmal**, Akbar's revenue minister.
xa: Payment was **mainly in cash** → cash crops, peasants tied to the market.
Four land classes: **Polaj, Parauti, Chachar, Banjar**.
Measurement: **Ilahi Gaz**.

na047c726521.x: The nobility consisted of high mansabdars, drawn from Turanis, Iranis, Hindustanis and Rajputs.
xa: Zamindars took a large share with **jagirdars** and **revenue-farmers**.
Peasants: **khud-kasht** (own village) and **pahi-kasht** (another village).
Artisans and merchants formed the **middle and lower urban strata**.

n4777d5f2eb9.s: Mughal karkhanas, continuing a Sultanate tradition, mainly produced:
n4777d5f2eb9.x: Karkhanas made court luxury goods such as gold and silver articles, fine textiles, arms and jewellery.
xa: Supervisor: **Mir Saman (Khan-i-Saman)**.
Artisans were often organised in **guilds**.
Artisans also worked in **private enterprises**.

nb9e5a12fcd8.s: The French traveller and physician who reached Surat in 1666 was:
nb9e5a12fcd8.x: Thevenot reached Surat in 1666; Manucci was Italian, Pelsaert Dutch and Mundy English.
xa: Manucci died in **Madras**; his work is called the "**Mirror of the 17th century**".
Thevenot visited **Machilipatnam** and **Golconda** and wrote **Travels of Thevenot into the Levant**.
Pelsaert's **Remonstrantie** described the **poverty of common people**.

n2c94585d076.s: What was one important economic consequence of collecting land revenue in cash under the zabt system?
o: It monetised the rural economy and linked peasants to markets.
It replaced agricultural production with pastoral activity.
It abolished all forms of rural credit.
It weakened the connection between peasants and markets.
n2c94585d076.x: Cash revenue under zabt monetised the rural economy and connected peasants with markets. The system did not abolish rural credit or replace agriculture with pastoralism.
n2c94585d076.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect relationship to the economic role of cash revenue.
xs: Cash revenue under **zabt** **monetised the rural economy** and **linked peasants to markets** — option **(1)**.
Payment mainly in **cash** pushed peasants towards **cash crops**, tying them to the market.
About **15%** of rural produce was marketed (APPSC G2 **2017** key).
xa: Zabt / Bandobast was framed by **Raja Todarmal**, Akbar's revenue minister.
State share = **one-third** of average produce of the **past ten years**.
Four land classes: **Polaj**, **Parauti**, **Chachar**, **Banjar**.

n4525cf3f6b7.s: Which European traveller held that there was no private property in land in Mughal India?
n4525cf3f6b7.x: Bernier held that private property in land did not exist, a view modern historians have contested.
xa: Bernier blamed this for **agrarian ruin** and peasant oppression.
He admitted the **inflow of precious metals** and that **merchants prospered**.
Bernier wrote **Travels in the Mogul Empire** (**1656-1668**).

n679a7c82e09.x: Banjaras transported grain in bullock caravans and played an important role in internal supply networks.
n679a7c82e09.tq: Identify the occupational function associated with the trading community.
xs: **Banjaras** carried **grain** in **bullock caravans** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They carried **bulk goods over long distances** (grain, salt) on **oxen** — the PYQ answer (APPSC G2 **2017**).
xa: ⚠ **Seths and Bohras** = long-distance trade; **Baniks** = local traders.
**Sarrafs** were money-changers and bankers who issued **hundis**.
Karkhanas were run under the **Mir Saman**, not traders.

ne34e861abcf.s: In the Mughal period, money-changers and bankers who issued hundis were called:
ne34e861abcf.x: Sarrafs were money-changers and bankers issuing hundis; Mahajans were moneylenders-cum-merchants and Baniks retail traders.
xa: **Banjaras** carried bulk goods over long distances on **oxen**.
**Beoparis** bought produce from villages for wholesale markets.
Sarrafs also underwrote **bima** (insurance) for a premium.

n549015ac2a5.s: Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals belonged to the ____ merchant community.
n549015ac2a5.x: The Marwaris comprised Oswals, Maheshwaris and Agarwals; Chettis were Coromandel merchants.
xa: Asian merchant groups also included **Bohras** and **Armenians**.
Sultanate overseas trade = **Multanis and Khurasanis**.
Community head: **nagarseth**.

n7aeab33655a.s: Who was the head of a merchant community and dealt with government officials?
n7aeab33655a.x: The nagarseth was the head of a merchant community and acted as its representative in dealings with officials.
n7aeab33655a.tq: Identify the institutional representative from a group of related administrative terms.
xs: The **nagarseth** headed a merchant community and dealt with officials — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Patwari** was a village accountant; **dalals** were brokers the EIC relied on.
xa: **Merchant strikes** are recorded, e.g. at **Ahmedabad**.
Trading communities were **organised and highly professional**.
Gujarati merchant communities **cut across religion**.

nf781e81c161.s: In the Sultanate period, before the Mughal pattern of trade took shape, overseas trade was largely in the hands of which merchants?
nf781e81c161.x: Under the Sultanate, overseas trade was dominated by Multanis and Khurasanis. Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra merchants handled inland trade, so option D is wrong. Chettis were later Coromandel merchants and Marwaris a Rajasthan inland group (B); Banjaras carried bulk goods overland and Baniks were local traders (C).
nf781e81c161.tq: Sultanate: overseas = Multanis + Khurasanis; inland = Gujaratis, Marwaris, Bohras.
xs: Sultanate **overseas** trade lay with the **Multanis and Khurasanis** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Inland** trade was with **Gujarati, Marwari and Muslim Bohra** merchants.
**Chettis** were Coromandel merchants; **Banjaras** carried bulk goods overland; **Baniks** were local traders.
xa: Mughal-era Asian merchant groups: **Gujaratis, Bohras, Chettis, Malabar Muslims, Armenians**.
European groups: **Portuguese, Dutch, English EIC (1600), French**.
**Muslim merchants** dominated **Malabar** trade.

n882492fba49.s: The first European trade centre in Andhra during the early modern period was established at
n882492fba49.x: Machilipatnam was the first European trade centre in Andhra, established by the Dutch in 1605. Guntur was associated with the Tobacco Board, while Nizampatnam (Petapoli) received European factories only later.
n882492fba49.tq: Distinguish the closely related names and match the place with its specific commercial role.
xs: **Machilipatnam** (Masulipatnam) was the first European trade centre in Andhra — option **(2)**.
The **Dutch** set up there in **1605**; it was the **Qutb Shahi** gateway.
**Guntur** is linked with the **Tobacco Board**; **Hyderabad** was Golconda's capital area.
xa: ⚠ Masulipatnam: **Dutch 1605** → **English 1611** → **French 1669**.
Exports: **Kalamkari/chintz** textiles and **saltpetre**.
Saltpetre centres in AP: **Machilipatnam**, **Narsapur**, **Pulicat**.

ne6f26ac6962.s: Which one of the following correctly describes bima in the Mughal commercial system?
o: Insurance of goods in transit against a premium
A cash receipt issued by a banik
A royal order issued by the emperor
A land deed issued under the Zabt system
ne6f26ac6962.x: Bima was insurance for goods in transit, underwritten by sarrafs for a premium.
ne6f26ac6962.tq: Distinguish insurance terminology from credit and revenue documents.
xs: **Bima** was **insurance of goods in transit**, underwritten by **sarrafs** for a **premium** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A royal order was a **farman**; land deeds were **patta** and **qabuliyat**.
xa: **Hundi** = letter of credit issued by sarrafs.
Sarrafs tested coins and took deposits.
The economy was **monetised and credit-backed**.

na5ca378a394.s: How many dams were equivalent to one rupee in the Mughal monetary system?
na5ca378a394.x: Forty copper dams were equivalent to one rupee. The dam was the copper denomination, while the rupiya was the silver coin.
na5ca378a394.tq: Identify the exact conversion figure rather than confusing it with the coin's metal or name.
xs: **40 dams = 1 rupee** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **dam** was **copper**; the **rupiya** was **silver**.
xa: ⚠ **Mohur – Rupiya – Dam** = **Gold – Silver – Copper**.
The rupiya was standardised by **Sher Shah** (**178 grains**) and continued by Akbar.
⚠ **Chalni** = current reign; **Khazana** = previous reign.

n0c2d16c7650.s: The silver rupiya that continued under Akbar had been standardised earlier by which ruler, and at what weight?
n0c2d16c7650.x: The silver rupiya was standardised by Sher Shah at 178 grains, and Akbar continued it. Option B gives the wrong weight (106 is the Koh-i-Noor's carats); option C names Tughlaq, known for token currency; option D confuses the 40 dams to a rupee.
n0c2d16c7650.tq: Rupiya = Sher Shah, 178 grains, silver; 40 dams = 1 rupee.
xs: The silver **rupiya** was standardised by **Sher Shah** at **178 grains** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Akbar** continued it.
**106** is the **Koh-i-Noor's** carats, and **40** is the number of **dams** to a rupee.
xa: ⚠ **Mohur – Rupiya – Dam** = **Gold – Silver – Copper**.
Silver inflow led to more **rupee** coinage and **rising prices**.
India was called the "**sink of precious metals**".

n8278b9cde02.s: Which Mughal port was known as the ‘Gate of Mecca’ or Bab-ul-Makka because of its association with the Haj pilgrimage?
n8278b9cde02.x: Surat was the chief Mughal port on the west coast and was known as the Gateway to Mecca or Bab-ul-Makka owing to its importance for Haj traffic.
xs: **Surat** was the "**Gate of Mecca**" (**Bab-ul-Makka**), the **Haj** port — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was the chief Mughal port on the **west coast**.
**Lahari Bandar** was at the Indus mouth; **Hugli** was a Bengal port; **Cambay** declined with silting.
xa: English ships arrived at Surat in **1608**; **Roe** (**1615**) secured the factory.
Hawkins got a firman in **1609**.
First English factory: **Hawkins**, **Captain Best**.

ncfe3adc95de.s: Masulipatnam, the Qutb Shahi port, was noted for which textile?
ncfe3adc95de.x: Masulipatnam was a Qutb Shahi (Golconda) port noted for Kalamkari, also called chintz, textiles.
xa: It was the **first European trade centre** in Andhra (Dutch **1605**).
The English came under **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah**.

n773407cdc64.s: Which of the following ports was a Portuguese base in Bengal until Shah Jahan expelled the Portuguese in 1632?
n773407cdc64.x: Hugli was the Portuguese settlement and base in Bengal; Shah Jahan expelled them in 1632.
xs: **Hugli (Hooghly)** was the **Portuguese** base in **Bengal** until **Shah Jahan** expelled them in **1632** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Surat** and **Cambay** were Gujarat ports; **Masulipatnam** was the **Qutb Shahi** port.
xa: Hugli later became an **English trading centre**.
Bengal exported **sugar, rice, muslin, silk**.
Shah Jahan granted the English duty exemptions in **1652**.

ndc64138876b.s: The term 'Sikka' in the Mughal monetary system denoted
o: the copper coin equal to one-fortieth of a rupee
the gold coin used for long-distance trade
coins of a previous reign accepted at a discount
the right of coinage in the ruler's name, signifying sovereignty along with the khutba
ndc64138876b.x: Sikka denoted the right of coinage in the ruler's name and, together with the khutba, symbolised sovereignty. The other options describe the dam, khazana and mohur respectively.
ndc64138876b.tq: Distinguish a political symbol of sovereignty from the names of actual coin denominations.
xs: **Sikka** = the **right of coinage in the ruler's name**, a mark of **sovereignty** with the **khutba** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The copper coin is the **dam**; previous-reign coins are **khazana**; the gold coin is the **mohur**.
xa: **40 dams = 1 rupee**.
**Chalni** = coins of the current reign in circulation.
Golconda minted only **copper**; Mughal silver circulated there.

n1fa84a190c2.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of goods exported from Mughal India?
o: War horses, silver, porcelain and wine
n1fa84a190c2.x: Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar were exports. The other groups contain goods listed as imports.
xs: **Muslin, saltpetre, indigo and sugar** were all exports — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Watches, tin, ivory, carpets, glass, copper, war horses, silver, porcelain, wine** were imports.
xa: Other exports: **calico**, **chintz**, opium, spices, raw silk.
European companies paid in **bullion**, drawing a large **silver inflow** (Bernier).
India was "the **largest producer of industrial goods**" in the 17th century.

n55c01ec082c.s: The expression ‘sink of precious metals’ in the context of early modern India refers to which of the following?
o: India’s export of all its silver coinage to Europe
India’s absorption of large quantities of imported gold and silver
The use of silver only in royal karkhanas
The replacement of silver by copper currency
n55c01ec082c.x: India became a ‘sink of precious metals’ because European companies paid for Indian goods with bullion, causing large inflows of gold and silver.
n55c01ec082c.tq: Translate the metaphor into its economic meaning.
xs: "Sink of precious metals" refers to **India's absorption of large quantities of imported gold and silver** — so option **(2)** is correct.
European companies paid for Indian goods in **bullion (gold and silver)**; India's **export surplus** drew a **large inflow of silver** (**Bernier**).
India did not export its silver away, nor did copper replace silver: the inflow led to **more silver rupee coinage**.
xa: In the **17th century** India was "the **largest producer of industrial goods** in the world".
**New World (Spanish American)** silver reached India via Europe and the Pacific; **Careri** (c.**1690**) traced its route.
Effects of the silver inflow: more **rupee** coinage and a **rise in prices**.
The trade balance favoured India until the **mid-18th century**.

ne448dfc2f24.s: The major source of the silver that reached India through European trade was the silver of which region?
ne448dfc2f24.x: Much of the silver came from Spanish America in the New World and reached India through Europe and the Pacific.
ne448dfc2f24.tq: Identify the source rather than the route.
xs: The silver reaching India came mainly from the **New World (Spanish America)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It travelled **via Europe and the Pacific** and finally reached India, as **Careri** (c.**1690**) described.
European companies paid for Indian goods in **bullion**, since India had an **export surplus**.
xa: India came to be called the "**sink of precious metals**".
Result of the inflow: more **silver rupee** coinage + **rise in prices**.
The **Rupiya** (silver) was standardised by **Sher Shah** at **178 grains** and continued by **Akbar**.
⚠ **Tobacco, cocoa and rubber** were also domesticated in the **New World** (UPSC **2019** PYQ).

ne812bdd35a3.s: One effect of the inflow of silver into Mughal India was:
o: The disappearance of bullion from markets
ne812bdd35a3.x: The silver influx increased silver rupee coinage and raised prices.
xa: The silver was **New World (Spanish American)** silver, reaching India via Europe and the Pacific.
**Rupiya** = **silver**; **Mohur** = **gold**; **Dam** = **copper** (**40 dams = 1 rupee**).
European companies paid in **bullion** because of India's **export surplus** (**Bernier**).

n88e6610a43b.s: The Golden Firman issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah granted trade rights to the:
n88e6610a43b.x: The Golden Firman issued by Abdullah Qutb Shah of Golconda granted trade rights to the English.
xa: Shah Jahan's exemptions: English (**1652**), Dutch (**1665**).
**Farrukhsiyar's firman** (**1716/1717**) cut English duties.
The English came to Masulipatnam in **1611**.

n0bf10d101b6.s: Who wrote *India at the Death of Akbar*?
n0bf10d101b6.x: *India at the Death of Akbar* was written by W. H. Moreland.
n0bf10d101b6.tq: Match the title with its historian-author.
xs: **India at the Death of Akbar** was written by **W.H. Moreland** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Irfan Habib** wrote **The Agrarian System of Mughal India, 1556-1707**; **Jadunath Sarkar** wrote **Fall of the Mughal Empire**.
xa: APPSC-G1 **2022** match: a-IV **Moreland**, b-I **Habib**, c-II **Bernier**, d-III **Foster**.
**William Foster** edited **Early Travels in India, 1583-1619**.
**Tapan Raychaudhuri** co-edited the **Cambridge Economic History of India, Vol. I** with Irfan Habib.

n90e9394654f.s: Francisco Pelsaert arrived in India in 1620, during the reign of:
n90e9394654f.x: Pelsaert came in Jahangir's time, in 1620.
xa: **Sir Thomas Roe** was at Jahangir's court in **1615**.
Pelsaert was a **Dutch (VOC)** factor; Mundy an **English** merchant who recorded a **famine**.
⚠ **Tavernier** = diamond merchant; **Manucci** = physician; **Pelsaert** = Dutch factor.

n5af5d066e76.s: Bernier's observations on the Mughal economy included which one of the following combinations?
o: Private ownership of all land, agrarian prosperity and outflow of precious metals
Imperial ownership of land, agrarian ruin, inflow of precious metals and prosperity of merchants
Village ownership of land, decline of trade and absence of merchants
Merchant ownership of land, peasant prosperity and exclusive use of copper currency
n5af5d066e76.x: Bernier believed that the emperor owned all land and blamed this arrangement for agrarian ruin. He nevertheless acknowledged that precious metals flowed into India and that merchants prospered.
n5af5d066e76.tq: Separate the traveller's criticism of landholding from his observations on trade and precious-metal inflow.
xs: Bernier noted **imperial ownership of land, agrarian ruin, inflow of precious metals and prosperity of merchants** — option **(2)**.
He held that the **emperor owned all land** (no **private property in land**) and blamed this for **agrarian ruin** and peasant oppression.
Yet he admitted the **inflow of precious metals** and that **merchants prospered**.
xa: Bernier wrote **Travels in the Mogul Empire** (**1656-1668**).
His "no private property in land" view is **contested by modern historians**.
He was physician of **Dara Shikoh**, patronised by **Danishmand Khan**.

n5c4dcdb7dc6.s: J.B. Tavernier was best known in the context of Mughal-period India as a
o: Dutch VOC merchant who spent seven years in Agra
English merchant who recorded a famine during Shah Jahan's reign
French diamond merchant who visited the diamond mines of Golconda
French physician who served Dara Shikoh
n5c4dcdb7dc6.x: Tavernier was a French gem and diamond merchant who made six visits to India and described the diamond mines of Golconda. The other descriptions relate to Bernier, Pelsaert and Peter Mundy.
n5c4dcdb7dc6.tq: Discriminate among European visitors by identifying profession and subject of observation.
xs: **Tavernier** was a **French diamond merchant** who visited the **diamond mines of Golconda** — option **(3)**.
The **Dutch VOC** merchant in Agra for **7 years** was **Pelsaert**; the English merchant who recorded a **famine** was **Peter Mundy**.
The French physician of **Dara Shikoh** was **Bernier**.
xa: Tavernier (**1605-1689**) made **6 visits** under Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb and wrote **Six Voyages**.
He recorded the **Koh-i-Noor (106 carats)** from **Kollur** (Guntur); also described the **Peacock Throne**.
"French trader who visited Andhra's mines" = Tavernier (APPSC G2 **2019** key).

naedc0521a01.s: Francois Bernier, who visited the Mughal Empire during 1656–1668, was associated with which of the following positions and patrons?
o: Physician of Shah Jahan and patronised by Mir Jumla
Physician of Dara Shikoh and patronised by Danishmand Khan
Physician of Aurangzeb and patronised by Shaista Khan
Physician of Jahangir and patronised by Asaf Khan
naedc0521a01.x: Francois Bernier was a French doctor who served as physician to Dara Shikoh and received the patronage of Danishmand Khan.
naedc0521a01.tq: Match the foreign traveller with his precise post and patron.
xs: Bernier was **physician of Dara Shikoh**, **patronised by Danishmand Khan** — option **(2)**.
He was a **French** physician in India **1656-1668**, under **Shah Jahan** and **Aurangzeb**.
xa: He wrote **Travels in the Mogul Empire**.
He noted the **absence of private property in land** and blamed it for agrarian ruin.
⚠ UPPSC **2008** key for "physician" = **Manucci**, though Bernier too served as a physician.

n7aa9ab5fd43.s: Who supervised the Mughal royal karkhanas?
n7aa9ab5fd43.x: The Mughal royal karkhanas were supervised by the Mir Saman, also known as Khan-i-Saman.
n7aa9ab5fd43.tq: Apply the ‘who would do this job?’ method.
xs: The royal **karkhanas** were supervised by the **Mir Saman (Khan-i-Saman)** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The other officials named are not linked to the karkhanas in the notes; the **Mir Saman** alone oversaw these royal workshops.
xa: Karkhanas made **gold and silver articles**, fine textiles, carpets, arms, jewellery and luxury goods for the court.
The tradition went back to **Sultanate karkhanas**.
Artisans, often in **guilds**, worked in state karkhanas or private enterprises.

n00962cf5210.s: Besides private enterprises, Mughal artisans worked in state workshops called:
n00962cf5210.x: Artisans worked in state karkhanas as well as private enterprises and were often organised in guilds.
xa: Artisans and merchants = **middle and lower urban strata**.
Karkhanas were supervised by the **Mir Saman**.
Coromandel was known for **textiles**; Bengal for **muslin** and silk.

nf0fbe2b1afa.s: A merchant deposits cash with a shroff and receives a document enabling the amount to be collected at another place after a journey. This document is known as
nf0fbe2b1afa.x: A hundi was a letter of credit issued by a shroff against cash deposited at one place and encashed later or elsewhere. A farman was a royal order and rokad denoted cash.
nf0fbe2b1afa.tq: Apply the functional definition to distinguish a credit instrument from nearby terms.
xs: The document is a **hundi**, a **letter of credit** issued by **sarrafs/shroffs** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS **2018** key).
Cash deposited at one place could be **encashed at another place** after a journey.
Distractors: **Farman** = royal order; **Rokad** = cash; **Parcha** is also a listed distractor.
xa: Hundis allowed **secure transactions over long distances**.
**Bima** = insurance of goods in transit.
The **EIC** fitted into this credit system.

nea9d799122a.s: Mughal nobles, drawn from Turanis, Iranis, Afghans, Hindustanis, Rajputs and Deccanis, remained dependent on:
nea9d799122a.x: The nobles were wealthy but wholly dependent on the emperor's favour.
xa: ⚠ **Turanis** = Central Asians; **Iranis** = Persians; **Hindustanis** = Indian Muslims.
**Akbar** added **Rajputs** and Hindustanis to balance the Turanis and Iranis.
Under **Aurangzeb**, Deccanis and **Marathas** swelled the nobility; Hindu share about **one-third** (**M. Athar Ali**).

n04767c21a61.s: Under Babur and Humayun, the Mughal nobility was dominated by:
n04767c21a61.x: Turanis and Iranis dominated under Babur and Humayun; Akbar added Rajputs and Hindustanis, and Deccanis and Marathas grew under Aurangzeb.
xa: Hindu share in Aurangzeb's nobility: about **one-third** (**M. Athar Ali**).
**Umara** = top mansabdars, wealthy but dependent on the emperor's favour.
⚠ **Turanis** = Central Asians; **Iranis** = Persians.

n571bf24a3a8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mughal court customs?
o: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Shah Jahan.
Jharokha darshan was begun by Akbar and ended by Aurangzeb.
Tuladan weighed the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday.
Nauroz was a Persian New Year festival adopted from the Zoroastrians.
n571bf24a3a8.x: Sijda and paibos were introduced by Akbar, not Shah Jahan.
xa: Tuladan was a **Hindu** custom adopted by Akbar; the goods were given to the poor.
Nauroz was **stopped by Aurangzeb** (UPPSC **2001** key for Zoroastrian origin).
**Qutb Shahi Golconda** also celebrated **Nauroz**.

n19ec77bfad0.s: The tomb of Itimad-ud-Daula at Agra was built by:
xa: ⚠ Pen name **Makhfi**: some notes give it for Nur Jahan, but it is best known as **Zeb-un-Nissa**'s.
**Jahanara** (Shah Jahan's daughter) was also **Padshah Begum**.
**Gulbadan Begum**, Babur's daughter, wrote the **Humayun-nama**.

n2416dd5b521.s: Jahanara, Shah Jahan's daughter and Padshah Begum, built:
o: The Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk
The Moti Masjid in Agra Fort
n2416dd5b521.x: Jahanara built the Jama Masjid at Agra and a sarai at Chandni Chowk. The Agra Fort Moti Masjid was Shah Jahan's and Itimad-ud-Daulah's tomb was built by Nur Jahan.
xa: Jahanara was **Shah Jahan's daughter** and **Padshah Begum**.
⚠ **Jahanara** = Jama Masjid, **Agra**; **Shah Jahan** = Jama Masjid, **Delhi**.
**Nur Jahan** married Jahangir in **1611**.

nda875090298.s: Bernier’s observation about the urban society of Delhi was that it
o: had no real middle class, with people tending to be either very rich or very poor
was dominated by peasants who had migrated from villages
had a large and prosperous middle class between the rich and poor
consisted entirely of artisans employed by the state
nda875090298.x: Bernier found no real middle class in Delhi and described a sharp contrast between the very rich and the very poor.
nda875090298.tq: Recall the traveller’s distinctive social observation.
xs: **Bernier** found **no real middle class** in Delhi — people were **very rich or very poor** — option **(1)**.
He also recorded **Sati**, **child marriage** and **polygamy**.
xa: His "bleak India" view reflects **European bias**, though he still conceded a **prosperous merchant class**.
**Pelsaert** contrasted **nobles' luxury** with the **misery of servants and workmen**.
Travellers' accounts = main source for Mughal social history, read against **Persian chronicles**.

n552f01850e1.s: Which measure did Akbar take in 1562?
o: Stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war
n552f01850e1.x: In 1562 Akbar stopped the enslavement of prisoners of war. Jizya was abolished in 1564, the pilgrimage tax in 1563, and the Ibadat Khana was built in 1575.
xa: Akbar also tried to stop **forced sati**.
Akbar began **Jharokha darshan** and introduced **sijda / paibos**.
Akbar added **Rajputs** and **Hindustanis** to the nobility.

nec5b9a8aca6.s: Bernier and Tavernier reported the prevalence of which practices in Mughal India?
o: Abolition of sati and widow remarriage
Widow remarriage, monogamy and late marriage
nec5b9a8aca6.x: Bernier and Tavernier referred to the prevalence of sati, child marriage and polygamy, though Akbar tried to stop forced sati.
xa: Muslim women had **inheritance shares** + **mehr** under sharia; Hindu women controlled **stridhana**.
**Purdah**: Muslim women strictly veiled; Hindu women moved freely (**John Fryer**).
Bernier's "bleak India" view is criticised as reflecting **European bias**.

nb60d92debd5.s: Who contrasted the strict veiling of Muslim women with the freer movement of Hindu women in A New Account of East India and Persia?
nb60d92debd5.x: John Fryer described this contrast for the Deccan in A New Account of East India and Persia.
xa: Social evils recorded: **Sati**, **child marriage**, **polygamy** (Bernier, Tavernier).
⚠ Property: **Mehr** = Muslim women; **stridhana** = Hindu women.
Akbar tried to stop **forced** sati.

nbf1014be513.s: In the Mughal period, property controlled by Hindu women was known as:
nbf1014be513.x: Hindu women controlled stridhana; Muslim women had inheritance shares and mehr under sharia.
xa: ⚠ **Mehr** = Muslim women; **stridhana** = Hindu women.
**Nur Jahan** held the title **Padshah Begum**; her name appeared on **coins** and **farmans**.
Social evils: **Sati**, **child marriage**, **polygamy** (Bernier, Tavernier).

n694d11e8e04.s: Firangi Mahal at Lucknow was noted for being a madrasa of
n694d11e8e04.x: Firangi Mahal in Lucknow was a madrasa associated with Muslim jurisprudence.
xs: **Firangi Mahal (Lucknow)** was a madrasa of **Muslim jurisprudence** — option **(2)**.
This was the UPPSC **2016** key.
xa: **Nauroz** = **Persian New Year**, adopted from the **Zoroastrians** (UPPSC **2001** key).
**Tuladan** = weighing the emperor against gold and goods on his birthday — a **Hindu** custom adopted by Akbar.

n45823559a49.s: In Qutb Shahi Golconda, Muharram was popularly known as:
n45823559a49.x: Muharram was known as Peerla Panduga in Golconda.
xa: **Abdullah Qutb Shah**'s Hyderabad had **20,000** registered prostitutes (Tavernier).
Golconda also shared the Mughal **Nauroz**.

na3d174bcf61.s: The Char Minar is located at:
na3d174bcf61.x: The Char Minar is in Hyderabad.
xa: APPSC G1 **2018** pairs: Charminar - **Hyderabad**; Akbar's Tomb - **Sikandara**; Humayun's Tomb - **Delhi**; Taj Mahal - **Agra**.
⚠ **Char Minar** (**1591**) is **Qutb Shahi**, not Mughal — a common distractor.
Jahangir's tomb is at **Shahdara, Lahore**; Aurangzeb's at **Khuldabad**.

n1a409f9c8b7.s: Char Minar at Hyderabad was built by:
n1a409f9c8b7.x: Char Minar was built at Hyderabad in 1591 by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah of the Qutb Shahi dynasty. It is not a Mughal monument.
n1a409f9c8b7.tq: Discriminate between rulers of the Qutb Shahi dynasty and Mughal builders.
xs: **Char Minar** at Hyderabad was built by **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah** in **1591** — option **(4)**.
It is a **Qutb Shahi**, not a Mughal, monument; it marked the **end of a plague**.
xa: Style: **Persian arches** + **Deccani stucco**.
**Golconda Fort**: acoustic warning system, piped water.
**Qutb Shahi tombs** at **Ibrahim Bagh**: onion domes on square bases, in gardens.

n99719e6b9d0.s: Fatehpur Sikri served as Akbar's planned capital during:
n99719e6b9d0.x: Fatehpur Sikri was Akbar's capital during 1571-1585 and shows Persian, Indian and Central Asian influences.
xa: Built in honour of **Sheikh Salim Chishti**, mainly in **red sandstone**.
**Jahangir Mahal at Orchha** (MP) continues Akbar's style.
UNESCO World Heritage Site (**1986**).

n9e8049d5bab.s: Agra Fort was begun by Akbar in:
n9e8049d5bab.x: Agra Fort was begun in 1565; Allahabad Fort was built in 1583.
xa: Agra Fort: **red sandstone**, on the **Yamuna**; has Diwan-i-Am and Diwan-i-Khas.
Agra Fort and Taj Mahal: UNESCO **1983**.

n98f60cbc17b.s: Which of the following is a Qutb Shahi monument rather than a Mughal one?
n98f60cbc17b.x: Golconda Fort is Qutb Shahi; the other three are listed UNESCO Mughal sites.
xa: Agra Fort and Taj Mahal were inscribed in **1983**.
**Qutb Shahi tombs** at Ibrahim Bagh: onion domes on square bases.

n0b5adc1f417.s: The architectural synthesis represented by Mughal monuments primarily blended which traditions?
n0b5adc1f417.x: Mughal architecture blended Persian, Timurid and Indian architectural elements.
n0b5adc1f417.tq: Test the exact components of a cultural synthesis without confusing them with general influences.
xs: Mughal architecture blended **Persian, Timurid and Indian** traditions — option **(3)**.
It is the **zenith of Indo-Islamic architecture**.
xa: **Persian-Indian synthesis**: arch and dome + trabeate, **chhatris**, Hindu motifs (Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's tomb).
Fatehpur Sikri: **Persian, Indian and Central Asian** blend.

n497a9f9093f.s: The Bahmani Jama Masjid at Gulbarga is noted for its:
n497a9f9093f.x: Its fully covered courtyard sets it apart from the open-court pattern of Mughal mosques.
xa: Shah Jahan's **Jama Masjid, Delhi** (**1650-1656**) is part of Shahjahanabad.
Akbar's **Jami Masjid, Fatehpur Sikri** (c. **1571-74**) has Buland Darwaza as its southern entrance.

nindian-history-86-12.s: The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque was built by:
nindian-history-86-12.x: The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque was built by Sher Shah Suri; Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal, Red Fort and Jama Masjid, Delhi.
n: Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque was constructed by Sher Shah Suri. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Taj Mahal was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Red Fort at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Jama Masjid at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
xa: Shah Jahan also built the **Moti Masjid** in **Agra Fort**.
⚠ The **Moti Masjid** in the **Red Fort** is **Aurangzeb's**.
The Red Fort's **Diwan-i-Khas** housed the **Peacock Throne**, taken by **Nadir Shah** in **1739**.

nindian-history-86-14.s: The Panch Mahal at Fatehpur Sikri was built by:
nindian-history-86-14.x: The Panch Mahal, Buland Darwaza and Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri are Akbar's.
n: Buland Darwaza was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Jama Masjid at Fatehpur Sikri was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Panch Mahal was constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
Red Fort at Delhi was constructed by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
The monuments at Fatehpur Sikri were constructed by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #86 · pp 168-169]
xa: **Panch Mahal**: five-storeyed pavilion influenced by **Persian wind towers**.
Akbar also built **Agra Fort**, begun **1565**.
APPSC-G1 **2024**: Salim Chishti's tomb, Buland Darwaza, Humayun's tomb and Jami Masjid all date to Akbar's reign.

n559b47fdd03.s: The Buland Darwaza at Fatehpur Sikri (c. 1575) commemorated Akbar's victory in:
n559b47fdd03.x: The Buland Darwaza was built for the Gujarat victory.
xa: APPSC-G1 **2024**: Salim Chishti's tomb, Buland Darwaza, Humayun's tomb and Jami Masjid (Fatehpur Sikri) — all Akbar's reign.
⚠ "Not built by Shah Jahan" = **Buland Darwaza** (APPSC GS **2019**).

nbe30c4518ee.s: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of which Sufi saint, after whom Prince Salim was named?
nbe30c4518ee.x: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of Sheikh Salim Chishti, after whom Prince Salim was named.
xs: Fatehpur Sikri was built in honour of **Sheikh Salim Chishti** — option **(2)**.
**Akbar** planned it as his capital, **1571-1585**.
xa: Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb lies in the **Jami Masjid** courtyard.
Main material: **red sandstone**; UNESCO site since **1986**.
Style: blend of **Persian, Indian and Central Asian**.

nc2c6332e1cc.x: Jahangir's tomb is at Shahdara, Lahore; Akbar's is at Sikandra and Aurangzeb's at Khuldabad.
xa: Babur — **Kabul** (Bagh-e-Babur), first buried at Agra.
Akbar's tomb was begun by Akbar and **completed by Jahangir**.

nindian-history-70-13.s: The Gommateshwara statue was built by:
n: The Gommateshwara statue at Shravanabelagola was built by Chamundraya. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
Bibi Ka Maqbara was built by Azam Shah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
Bibi Ka Maqbara was built for Azam Shah’s mother, Rabia-ud-Daurani. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
Construction of the Tomb of Akbar at Sikandra was started by Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
The Tomb of Akbar at Sikandra was completed under Jahangir. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
Jama Masjid in Delhi was built by Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 146-147]
xa: Bibi ka Maqbara is at **Aurangabad**, called the "**Taj of the Deccan**".
Shah Jahan also built the **Taj Mahal** and the **Red Fort at Delhi**.
**Jahangir's Tomb** at **Shahdara, Lahore** was built by **Nur Jahan**.

nindian-history-73-12.s: Nur Jahan built the marble tomb of her father Itmad-ud-Daula at Agra during:
nindian-history-73-12.x: The tomb of Itmad-ud-Daula (Mirza Ghiyas Beg) was built in 1622-1628.
n: Jahangir's Tomb was built by Nur Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Jahangir's Tomb was built by Jahangir's wife. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xa: Called the "**Baby Taj**"; first Mughal tomb in **white marble** with **pietra dura**.
**Pietra dura** began under **Jahangir** and peaked at the **Taj Mahal**.
Nur Jahan also built **Jahangir's Tomb** at **Shahdara, Lahore**.

nindian-history-73-15.s: Shaikh Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb stands in the Jama Masjid courtyard at:
nindian-history-73-15.x: Salim Chishti's white-marble tomb is in the Jama Masjid courtyard at Fatehpur Sikri.
n: Jahangir's Tomb was built by Jahangir's wife. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Itmad-ud-Daula's Tomb was built from 1622 to 1628. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Shaikh Salim Chishti's Tomb is a famous marble tomb. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Rabia Daurani's Tomb was built in memory of Azam Shah's mother. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xa: Humayun's Tomb: first **garden tomb**, introduced the **double dome**.
⚠ Some notes name **Hamida Banu Begum** as builder of Humayun's tomb.
"**Taj of the Deccan**" = Bibi ka Maqbara; "**Baby Taj**" = Itimad-ud-Daula.

nindian-history-73-18.s: Rabia-ud-Daurani, whose tomb is the Bibi ka Maqbara, was Aurangzeb's:
