nindian-history-73-18.x: Rabia-ud-Daurani was Aurangzeb's wife; their son Azam Shah built the tomb for his mother.
n: Rabia Daurani's Tomb is also called Bibi ka Maqbara. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Rabia Daurani's Tomb was built by Aurangzeb's son, Azam Shah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Rabia Daurani's Tomb was built in memory of Azam Shah's mother. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xa: It stands at **Aurangabad** and is called the "**Taj of the Deccan**".
It is a **late imitation** of the Taj Mahal.
⚠ "Baby Taj" = **Itimad-ud-Daula**, Agra.

nindian-history-73-19.s: At which place is Rabia Daurani's Tomb, also called Bibi ka Maqbara, located?
nindian-history-73-19.x: Bibi ka Maqbara, the tomb of Rabia-ud-Daurani, is at Aurangabad in Maharashtra and is often called the Taj of the Deccan.
nindian-history-73-19.tq: Recall the location of Bibi ka Maqbara.
n: Rabia Daurani's Tomb is also called Bibi ka Maqbara. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
Rabia Daurani's Tomb is located in Aurangabad. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #73 · pp 151-152]
xs: **Bibi ka Maqbara** is at **Aurangabad** — option **(2)**.
It was built by **Azam Shah** for his mother **Rabia-ud-Daurani**, in **Aurangzeb's** reign.
**Agra** has the Taj Mahal; **Sikandra** has **Akbar's tomb**; **Fatehpur Sikri** has **Salim Chishti's tomb**.
xa: Called the "**Taj of the Deccan**".
**Aurangzeb** himself lies at **Khuldabad** near Aurangabad.
It marks the last major imitation in the Mughal tomb tradition.

n3295d628f56.s: Humayun's tomb is notable as the subcontinent's first:
o: Octagonal tomb set in a tank
Tomb built entirely of white marble
n3295d628f56.x: Humayun's tomb was the first garden tomb in the subcontinent; it used red sandstone with white marble inlay and introduced the double dome.
xa: Its **jali (lattice)** work is a hallmark.
It inspired the **Taj Mahal** (garden tomb, double dome).
UNESCO World Heritage Site, inscribed **1993**.

n6961e5912d8.s: Which monument marked the transition from the Lodi tradition to the Mughal architectural tradition under the Sur rulers?
n6961e5912d8.x: Sher Shah's tomb at Sasaram marks the Sur transition in the evolution of Indo-Islamic tomb architecture.
n6961e5912d8.tq: Use the historical transition clue to connect the monument with the correct dynasty.
xs: **Sher Shah's tomb** marks the **Sur transition** — option **(1)**.
It is at **Sasaram**, Bihar, set in a tank; finished under **Islam Shah**.
The **Taj Mahal** is the climax and **Bibi ka Maqbara** the late imitation of the tradition.
xa: Sayyid-Lodi tombs: **Hindu-style gates**, plaster ornament, drip-stones.
**Itimad-ud-Daula** = first Mughal tomb in **white marble** with **pietra dura**.

n9591691e16b.s: The design of the Taj Mahal was particularly inspired by which earlier Mughal monument?
n9591691e16b.x: Humayun's Tomb provided an important design ancestry for the Taj Mahal, particularly through the garden-tomb form and use of a double dome.
n9591691e16b.tq: Trace architectural influence from an earlier monument rather than selecting a later or contemporary structure.
xs: **Humayun's Tomb** inspired the Taj Mahal's design — option **(1)**.
It gave the **garden tomb**, **double dome** and red sandstone with marble.
xa: Humayun's tomb = **first garden tomb** in the subcontinent.
The Taj stands at the **river end** of its **charbagh**, not the centre.
The Taj = **climax** of the tomb tradition; Bibi ka Maqbara = late imitation.

n6522b8f019f.s: Which comparison between the architectural phases of Akbar and Shah Jahan is correct?
o: Akbar is associated mainly with red sandstone, whereas Shah Jahan is associated mainly with white marble.
Akbar is associated mainly with white marble, whereas Shah Jahan is associated mainly with red sandstone.
Both rulers used only white marble.
Both rulers used only red sandstone.
n6522b8f019f.x: Akbar's phase is represented by red-sandstone structures such as Agra Fort and Fatehpur Sikri, while Shah Jahan's phase is dominated by white marble, as in the Taj Mahal.
n6522b8f019f.tq: Use the material contrast to distinguish the architectural phases of the two rulers.
xs: **Akbar** = mainly **red sandstone**; **Shah Jahan** = mainly **white marble** — option **(1)**.
Red sandstone: **Agra Fort**, **Fatehpur Sikri**; white marble: **Taj Mahal**.
The transition came under **Jahangir** (**Itimad-ud-Daula**).
xa: The **Red Fort** combines red sandstone structure with marble decoration.
Humayun's tomb: **red sandstone with white marble inlay**.

n2f8b3aa720e.s: Which of the following is regarded as the last major imitation in the Mughal garden-tomb tradition?
n2f8b3aa720e.x: Bibi ka Maqbara is regarded as the last major imitation in the Mughal garden-tomb tradition.
n2f8b3aa720e.tq: Distinguish the terminal example from the first example in an architectural sequence.
xs: **Bibi ka Maqbara** is the **last major imitation** — option **(4)**.
It is the "**Taj of the Deccan**" at Aurangabad, built by **Azam Shah**.
**Ram Bagh** = first Mughal garden; **Humayun's Tomb** = first garden tomb.
xa: FIRST/LAST: first Mughal garden = **Ram Bagh**; pietra dura first under **Jahangir**.
⚠ "**Baby Taj**" = Itimad-ud-Daula; "**Taj of the Deccan**" = Bibi ka Maqbara.

nindian-history-26-2-26.s: Pattadakal is a centre of ____ architecture.
nindian-history-26-2-26.x: Pattadakal is Chalukyan; Mahabalipuram is Pallava.
n: Mahabalipuram was associated with Pallava architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Pattadakal was associated with Chalukyan architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Ellora had the Kailasanatha Temple. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Ellora had Buddhist, Hindu, and Jain caves. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Elephanta had a Shaiva cave temple. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Elephanta was associated with Shiva. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xa: **Konark** has the **Sun Temple**.
**Thanjavur**: **Brihadeshwara Temple**, Chola architecture.
**Sikandra** has **Akbar's tomb**; **Fatehpur Sikri** has the **Buland Darwaza** and **Ibadat Khana**.

n10aac3a7abb.s: Who is identified as the chief architect of the Taj Mahal?
n10aac3a7abb.x: Ustad Ahmad Lahori is identified as the chief architect of the Taj Mahal.
n10aac3a7abb.tq: Test the specific architect associated with the monument rather than a general Mughal architect.
xs: The chief architect of the Taj Mahal was **Ustad Ahmad Lahori** — option **(2)**.
The Taj was built by **Shah Jahan** at **Agra**, **1632-1648**.
xa: Its marble came from **Makrana** (Rajasthan) (APPSC GS **2016**).
It is the mausoleum of **Mumtaz Mahal (Arjumand Banu Begum)**.
**V.A. Smith**: combination of **European and Asiatic genius**.

ne62b57f3300.s: The Taj Trapezium Zone (TTZ) rulings concerning protection of the Taj Mahal are associated with the case of:
ne62b57f3300.x: The Supreme Court's Taj Trapezium Zone rulings, including those concerning industrial pollution, were associated with the M.C. Mehta case in 1996.
ne62b57f3300.tq: Match an environmental protection measure with the relevant legal case.
xs: The **TTZ** rulings came in the **M.C. Mehta** case — option **(1)**.
The Supreme Court ruled in **1996** against pollution threatening the Taj.
xa: Threat: **marble cancer**, yellowing from **sulphur dioxide** (Mathura refinery, industries, traffic).
The Taj is a UNESCO site since **1983**.

nc628265906b.s: The white marble used in the construction of the Taj Mahal was obtained mainly from
nc628265906b.x: The Taj Mahal's marble came from Makrana in Rajasthan. Sasaram is the site of Sher Shah's tomb, Fatehpur Sikri was built mainly of red sandstone, and Kollur is known for diamond mines (the Koh-i-Noor).
xs: The Taj's marble came from **Makrana in Rajasthan** — option **(1)**.
This was the APPSC GS **2016** key.
**Sasaram** = Sher Shah's tomb; **Fatehpur Sikri** = red sandstone.
xa: Taj features: **pietra dura**, symmetry, white marble.
Architect: **Ustad Ahmad Lahori**.

n39823f8566d.s: Which historian described the Taj Mahal as the product of a combination of European and Asiatic genius?
n39823f8566d.x: V.A. Smith saw the Taj Mahal as a combination of European and Asiatic genius (APPSC-G1 2022 key). Fergusson and Percy Brown treated it as a product of the Indo-Persian tradition, and R.C. Majumdar is a distractor here.
xs: **V.A. Smith** saw the Taj as a combination of **European and Asiatic genius** — option **(3)**.
This is the APPSC-G1 **2022** key.
**James Fergusson** and **Percy Brown** saw it as a product of the **Indo-Persian tradition**.
xa: Chief architect: **Ustad Ahmad Lahori**; marble from **Makrana**.
Built **1632-1648** for **Mumtaz Mahal**.

nadd2cbf3094.s: Which building at Fatehpur Sikri served as a house of worship where scholars of different religions held philosophical debates?
nadd2cbf3094.x: The Ibadat Khana was the House of Worship used for philosophical debates among scholars of various religions.
nadd2cbf3094.tq: Match the building with its precise institutional purpose.
xs: The **Ibadat Khana** was the **House of Worship** for debates among scholars of various religions — option **(2)**.
It was built in **1575** and was part of the religious core of Fatehpur Sikri.
**Jodha Bai's palace** = trabeate + arcuate; **Diwan-i-Khas** = private audience; **Panch Mahal** = five-storeyed pavilion.
xa: The religious core also had the **Jama Masjid** and **Salim Chishti's tomb**.
**Buland Darwaza** was also built c. **1575**.

n4a8e6d423a7.s: Jodha Bai's palace at Fatehpur Sikri combines:
o: Hindu trabeate and Islamic arcuate styles
European Gothic and Islamic arcuate styles
n4a8e6d423a7.x: Jodha Bai's palace combines Hindu trabeate construction (beams and lintels) with Islamic arcuate construction (arches and domes).
xa: The **Persian-Indian synthesis**: arch and dome + trabeate, **chhatris**, **Hindu motifs** (Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's tomb).
**Panch Mahal** shows **Persian wind tower** influence.

nd8456492024.s: Shalimar Gardens at Lahore were built under which Mughal ruler?
nd8456492024.x: The Shalimar Gardens at Lahore were built under Shah Jahan. The Shalimar Bagh at Srinagar is associated with Jahangir.
nd8456492024.tq: Separate the similarly named Shalimar gardens by location and builder.
xs: The **Shalimar Gardens at Lahore** were built under **Shah Jahan** — option **(4)**.
The **Shalimar Bagh at Srinagar** is **Jahangir's**.
xa: ⚠ Shalimar: **Srinagar** = Jahangir; **Lahore** = Shah Jahan.
**Nishat Bagh** (Srinagar, Dal Lake) = **Asaf Khan**.
**Charbagh** introduced by **Babur** (Ram Bagh, Agra).

n6308539dfa9.s: The Moti Masjid in Agra Fort was built by:
n6308539dfa9.x: The Agra Fort Moti Masjid is Shah Jahan's; Aurangzeb built the one in the Red Fort, Delhi.
xa: Other Fatehpur Sikri buildings: **Buland Darwaza**, **Ibadat Khana**, **Diwan-i-Khas**, Salim Chishti's tomb.
⚠ Moti Masjid: **Red Fort** = Aurangzeb; **Agra Fort** = Shah Jahan.

n972a6a2eeec.s: The Peacock Throne in the Diwan-i-Khas of the Red Fort was taken by Nadir Shah in:
n972a6a2eeec.x: Nadir Shah took the Peacock Throne from the Diwan-i-Khas, the private audience hall, in 1739.
xa: The Red Fort's **Moti Masjid** was built by **Aurangzeb**.
**Sheesh Mahal** = mirror-work chambers.

n5bd81ae97a1.s: The charbagh garden tradition in Mughal architecture was introduced by:
n5bd81ae97a1.x: Babur introduced the charbagh, or four-quartered garden, tradition; Ram Bagh at Agra is an example.
n5bd81ae97a1.tq: Match the architectural innovation with the earliest Mughal ruler associated with it.
xs: **Babur** introduced the **charbagh** (four-quartered garden) — option **(4)**.
Example: **Ram Bagh**, Agra (c. **1528**), the **first Mughal garden**.
xa: Shalimar: **Srinagar** = **Jahangir**; **Lahore** = **Shah Jahan**.
**Nishat Bagh** (Srinagar) was built by **Asaf Khan**, Nur Jahan's brother.
**Pinjore garden** (Haryana): Fidai Khan, under Aurangzeb.

n5b15f7a546c.s: Pietra dura was first used on a large scale in Mughal architecture at:
n5b15f7a546c.x: Pietra dura began under Jahangir, appeared on a large scale at Itimad-ud-Daula and peaked at the Taj Mahal.
xa: Itimad-ud-Daula ("**Baby Taj**") = first Mughal tomb in white marble with pietra dura.
White marble: transition under **Jahangir**, dominant under **Shah Jahan**.

naf7afbd1dfd.s: The Red Fort Complex was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in:
naf7afbd1dfd.x: Red Fort Complex: 2007; Agra Fort and Taj Mahal: 1983; Fatehpur Sikri: 1986; Humayun's Tomb: 1993.
xa: The Taj was also named among the **New Seven Wonders** in **2007**.
Fatehpur Sikri: Akbar's capital, **1571-1585**.

nindian-history-26-2-13.s: The temples of Khajuraho belong to ____ architecture.
nindian-history-26-2-13.x: Khajuraho is Chandela; Thanjavur is Chola and Mahabalipuram Pallava.
n: Khajuraho was associated with Chandela architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Konark had the Sun Temple. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Thanjavur had the Brihadeshwara Temple. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Thanjavur was associated with Chola architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
Mahabalipuram was associated with Pallava architecture. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xa: **Pattadakal** — **Chalukyan architecture**.
**Ellora** — **Kailasanatha Temple** with Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves.
**Elephanta** — a **Shaiva cave temple**.

n91deeee1fee.s: Babur's final tomb is located at:
n91deeee1fee.x: Babur's tomb is at Bagh-e-Babur in Kabul, although he was first buried at Agra.
n91deeee1fee.tq: Watch the distinction between the first burial place and the final tomb location.
xs: Babur's final tomb is at **Kabul** (**Bagh-e-Babur**) — option **(1)**.
He was **first buried at Agra**.
xa: Humayun — **Delhi**; Akbar — **Sikandra**; Jahangir — **Shahdara, Lahore**.
Shah Jahan — **Taj Mahal, Agra**; Aurangzeb — **Khuldabad**.

n3e0fcf94311.x: Akbar's Tomb is at Sikandara near Agra.
xa: This is the APPSC G1 **2018** pairs question.
⚠ Charminar (**1591**) is **Qutb Shahi** — **Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah**.

nindian-history-10-5.s: The Bahmani Kingdom shifted its capital from Gulbarga to:
nindian-history-10-5.x: The Bahmanis moved their capital from Gulbarga to Bidar.
n: The initial Bahmani capital was Gulbarga. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 51-53]
The Bahmani capital was later shifted to Bidar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 51-53]
Vijayanagara was situated on the Tungabhadra River. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 51-53]
The Peshwas had Pune as their centre of power. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 51-53]
Peshwa power was centred at Pune. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 51-53]
xa: **Delhi** was the main political centre of the **Delhi Sultanate**.
Shivaji's Marathas had their capital at **Raigad**.
Akbar used **Agra**, **Fatehpur Sikri** and **Lahore**; Shah Jahan moved to **Shahjahanabad** (Delhi).

n8360e85f558.s: Which Persian master did Humayun bring to India to lay the foundation of the Mughal school of painting?
n8360e85f558.x: Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad; Basawan was Akbar-era and Mansur of Jahangir's court.
xa: Both masters supervised the **Hamzanama** in turn: first Mir Sayyid Ali, then Abdus Samad.
Abdus Samad's title = **Shirin Qalam**.
FIRST: **Humayun** first brought Persian painters.

n062760e4ca9.s: Akbar's painting atelier of more than 100 painters was known as the:
n062760e4ca9.x: The Tasvir Khana illustrated the Hamzanama, Tutinama, Akbarnama and Razmnama.
xa: Leading painters: **Daswant**, **Basawan**, **Mukand**.
**Hamzanama** = tales of **Amir Hamza**, supervised first by **Mir Sayyid Ali**, then **Abdus Samad**.

n098e2ad1ba5.s: The introduction of the halo or nimbus behind the emperor's head in Mughal painting is associated with the reign of:
n098e2ad1ba5.x: Jahangir's painters introduced the halo or nimbus behind the emperor's head, reflecting the period's refined and naturalistic style.
n098e2ad1ba5.tq: Test a distinctive visual innovation against neighbouring emperors.
xs: The **halo (nimbus)** behind the emperor's head was introduced under **Jahangir** — option **(4)**.
Jahangir's reign was the **zenith / golden age** of Mughal painting, with **portraits** and peak **naturalism**.
xa: Jahangir's painters: **Manohar**, **Bishandas**, **Mansur**, **Abul Hasan**.
European influence also marked his reign.

n65bf58134f2.s: Ustad Mansur is particularly associated with which aspect of Mughal painting?
n65bf58134f2.x: Ustad Mansur, a painter of Jahangir's court, was renowned for depicting flora and fauna.
n65bf58134f2.tq: Separate a painter's artistic speciality from literary and architectural activities.
xs: **Ustad Mansur** is known for **flora and fauna** — option **(1)**.
He was **Jahangir's** painter, titled **Nadir-ul-Asr**.
xa: ⚠ **Nadir-uz-Zaman** = **Abul Hasan**, Jahangir's court painter.
Jahangir's reign: peak of **naturalism** and precision.

n55c0e913b97.s: Kavindracharya Saraswati is associated with which one of the following achievements?
o: Persuading Shah Jahan to remit the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag
Writing the Persian translation of the Baburnama
n55c0e913b97.x: Kavindracharya Saraswati obtained Shah Jahan's remission of the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag and wrote Kavindra-kalpalata in Hindi.
n55c0e913b97.tq: Identify the patronage-related achievement rather than confusing it with translation work.
xs: **Kavindracharya Saraswati** got **Shah Jahan to remit the pilgrim tax at Banaras and Prayag** — option **(2)**.
He wrote the Hindi **Kavindra-kalpalata**.
**Atharvaveda** = Haji Ibrahim Sirhindi; **Baburnama** translation = Abdur Rahim; **Tappa** = Shori Miyan.
xa: **Keshavdas** = Bundela court of **Orchha**.
**Abdur Rahim Khan-i-Khana** was one of **Akbar's Navaratnas**.

nf67393ab6e9.s: Aurangzeb's Deccan wars drained the treasury as he campaigned there for about the last ____ years of his reign.
nf67393ab6e9.x: Aurangzeb spent roughly the last twenty-seven years of his reign campaigning in the Deccan against the Marathas, which drained the Mughal treasury.
xa: **Jizya** (**1679**) alienated Rajputs, Marathas and Sikhs.
**Be-jagiri**: too many mansabdars for too few revenue-yielding jagirs.

n01749b737e2.s: Aurangzeb's reimposition of jizya in 1679 particularly alienated the
n01749b737e2.x: The religious policy, including the reimposition of jizya in 1679, alienated important groups such as the Rajputs, Marathas and Sikhs.
n01749b737e2.tq: Link the dated policy with the affected social and political groups.
xs: **Jizya** (**1679**) alienated the **Rajputs, Marathas and Sikhs** — option **(1)**.
It was part of Aurangzeb's **religious policy**, a cause of Mughal decline.
xa: Other causes: **Deccan wars**, **jagirdari crisis**, **Sayyid brothers**.
**Kavindracharya** had earlier got Shah Jahan to remit the **pilgrim tax** at Banaras and Prayag.

nindian-history-71-6.s: The Dastan-i-Amir Hamza, begun under Humayun, comprised about how many paintings?
nindian-history-71-6.x: The Hamzanama took about 100 artists and about 1,400 paintings, supervised by Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad.
n: The Dastan-i-Amir Hamza was begun under Humayun and continued under Akbar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
Mir Sayyid Ali and Khwaja Abdus Samad supervised the Dastan-i-Amir Hamza. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
Approximately 100 artists worked on the Dastan-i-Amir Hamza. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
The Dastan-i-Amir Hamza contained approximately 1,400 paintings. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 147-150]
xa: **Razmnama** = illustrated Persian **Mahabharata** (Akbar).
**Padshahnama** = major illustrated manuscript of **Shah Jahan**.
**Tarikh-i-Alfi** = Akbar-era historical work.

n3a63229651a.s: The painter Basawan belonged to the atelier of:
n3a63229651a.x: Basawan belonged to Akbar's reign; Jahangir's painters included Manohar, Bishandas and Mansur.

**Bahadur Shah Zafar** was exiled to **Rangoon**, died **1862**.

ne2fc727085f.s: Who among the following was popularly known as ‘Rangeela’?
ne2fc727085f.x: Muhammad Shah, who ruled from 1719 to 1748, was known as Rangeela.
ne2fc727085f.tq: Directly identify the ruler associated with a well-known epithet.
xs: **Muhammad Shah** (**1719-1748**) was called "**Rangeela**" — option **(2)**.
**Nadir Shah** invaded in his reign (**1739**).
xa: He got rid of the Sayyids with **Nizam-ul-Mulk**'s help.
He gave Nizam-ul-Mulk the title **Asaf Jah** (**1725**).
Abdali's **first raid** came in **1748**.

nc9b8df51f82.s: Which event took place during the reign of Alamgir II?
nc9b8df51f82.x: The Battle of Plassey (1757) and repeated invasions by Ahmad Shah Abdali occurred during Alamgir II's reign.
xa: Alamgir II (**1754-59**) was **murdered by Imad-ul-Mulk**.
**Third Battle of Panipat**: **14 January 1761**.

nfd2ee8728b4.s: The first Mughal pensioner of the East India Company was:
nfd2ee8728b4.x: Shah Alam II became the Company's first Mughal pensioner.
xa: **Third Panipat (1761)** and **Buxar (1764)** came in his reign.
**Treaty of Allahabad (1765)**: he granted the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Blinded by **Ghulam Qadir Rohilla**, **1788**.

nb425a4dcf74.s: Shah Alam II returned to Delhi in 1771-72 under the protection of:
nb425a4dcf74.x: After living at Allahabad under Company protection, Shah Alam II returned to Delhi under Mahadji Scindia's protection.
xa: This was in **Madhav Rao I**'s time.
From **1772** **Warren Hastings** stopped his annual grant.

ne02fac11147.s: Punjab and Multan were ceded to Ahmad Shah Abdali, who invaded repeatedly during the reign of:
ne02fac11147.x: Abdali's repeated invasions occurred during Alamgir II's reign.
xa: Abdali raided from **1748** (first raid) to **1767**.
He defeated the Marathas at **Third Panipat** (**14 January 1761**).
Punjab and Multan were ceded under **Ahmad Shah**.

nf485fd19504.s: Safdar Jung, who succeeded Saadat Khan as Nawab of Awadh, was Saadat Khan's:
nf485fd19504.x: Safdar Jung was Saadat Khan's nephew and son-in-law and also became Wazir.
xa: **Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk** became Subedar of Awadh in **1722**.
**Buxar** (**1764**) came in **Shah Alam II**'s reign.

nindian-history-141-11.s: Who fought the battles of Tarain and Chandawar?
nindian-history-141-11.x: Muhammad Ghori fought at Tarain and Chandawar; Mahmud Ghazni made 17 raids.
n: Muhammad bin Qasim targeted Sindh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Muhammad bin Qasim's invasion resulted in the Arab conquest of Sindh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Mahmud Ghazni made 17 attacks. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Mahmud Ghazni's attacks involved plunder. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Muhammad Ghori fought at Tarain. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Muhammad Ghori fought at Chandawar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Timur invaded Delhi in 1398. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
xa: Ghori opposed **Prithviraj** and **Jayachandra**; his campaigns began approximately **1175 CE**.
Timur invaded in the reign of **Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah**.
Ghori **contributed** to the foundation of **Turkish power**.

nindian-history-11-13.s: Babur took the title 'Padshah' at Kabul in:
nindian-history-11-13.x: Babur became Padshah at Kabul in 1507 and took the title Ghazi after Khanwa in 1527.
n: Babur adopted the title Padshah at Kabul in 1504. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
The recall association for Babur's Padshah title is Kabul. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
Babur assumed the title Ghazi after his victory at Khanwa in 1527. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
The recall association for Babur's Ghazi title is Khanwa. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
xa: ⚠ The notes date Babur's Padshah title at Kabul to **1504**, not the question's 1507.
**Shah Jahan** (Prince Khurram) means **King of the World**.
**Bairam Khan** got the title **Khan-i-Khanan** from **Akbar**.

nindian-history-21-18.s: The Third Battle of Panipat was fought in:
nindian-history-21-18.x: Ahmad Shah Abdali (Durrani) defeated the Marathas at Third Panipat in 1761.
n: Ahmad Shah Abdali, also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani, invaded North India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Third Battle of Panipat occurred in 1761. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: Abdali had been **Nadir Shah's general**; his first raid came in **1748**.
**Punjab and Multan** were ceded to Abdali under **Ahmad Shah**.
Third Panipat was a **major setback** to Maratha expansion.

nindian-history-67-6.s: The Persian invasion of north-western India was led by:
nindian-history-67-6.x: Darius I led the Persian invasion; Alexander led the Greek one.
n: Darius I was associated with the Persian invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Alexander was associated with the Greek invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Muhammad bin Qasim was associated with the Arab invasion of Sindh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Genghis Khan reached the Indus during Iltutmish's reign. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
xa: Genghis Khan reached the **Indus** in **Iltutmish's reign**.
Muhammad bin Qasim opposed **Dahir** in **712 CE**.
Alexander opposed **Porus** at the **Jhelum**.

nindian-history-21-5.s: The First Battle of Tarain was fought in:
nindian-history-21-5.x: First Tarain was fought in 1191; Timur came in 1398, Panipat I was 1526 and Karnal 1739.
n: The First Battle of Tarain occurred in 1191. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Timur invaded Delhi in 1398. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The First Battle of Panipat occurred in 1526. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Battle of Karnal occurred in 1739. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: At Panipat **Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi**.
At Karnal **Nadir Shah** defeated the Mughals.
**Third Panipat** (**1761**): **Abdali** vs the **Marathas**.

nd38503e56ae.s: Ahmad Shah Abdali's raids into India began from:
nd38503e56ae.x: Abdali's raids began in 1748 and culminated at Panipat in 1761; Nadir Shah raided in 1739.
xa: Abdali's raids ended with **Panipat (1761)**.
Nadir Shah defeated **Muhammad Shah** at **Karnal**.
**Abdali** had been **Nadir Shah's general**.

nindian-history-11-14.s: What is the meaning of the title ‘Shah Jahan’?
nindian-history-11-14.x: Shah Jahan means King of the World, a title Prince Khurram took on his accession. Alamgir means Conqueror of the World, Sakari Saka-conqueror and Devanampiya Beloved of the Gods.
n: Shah Jahan means King of the World. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
Shah Jahan was called Shah Jahan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 53-55]
xs: **Shah Jahan** means **King of the World** — option **(1)**.
It was the title of **Prince Khurram**.
**Alamgir** (Aurangzeb) means **Conqueror of the World**.
xa: Aurangzeb was also called **Zinda Pir**.
Babur took **Padshah** at **Kabul** and **Ghazi** after **Khanwa** (**1527**).
**Shivaji**'s sovereign title **Chhatrapati** came with his **1674** coronation.

nindian-history-21-21.s: Along with Shah Jahan's Peacock Throne, Nadir Shah carried away the:
nindian-history-21-21.x: In 1739 Nadir Shah sacked Delhi and carried away the Koh-i-Noor and the Peacock Throne.
n: Nadir Shah sacked Delhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Nadir Shah took the Koh-i-Noor. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Nadir Shah took the Peacock Throne. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: He defeated **Muhammad Shah** at **Karnal** (**1739**).
⚠ Some notes wrongly say he was defeated at Karnal.
APPSC **2018**: the plunderer of Delhi who took the Koh-i-Noor = **Nadir Shah**.

nindian-history-67-13.s: Nadir Shah defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal in:
nindian-history-67-13.x: In 1739 Nadir Shah won at Karnal and then sacked Delhi.
n: Nadir Shah invaded India in 1739 CE. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Nadir Shah was associated with the Battle of Karnal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
Nadir Shah was associated with the sack of Delhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 143-144]
xa: The Mughal emperor then was **Muhammad Shah** ("Rangeela").
He took the **Koh-i-Noor** and the **Peacock Throne**.
The raid exposed Mughal military weakness and drained the treasury.

nindian-history-21-4.s: Muhammad Ghori first invaded India in:
nindian-history-21-4.x: Muhammad Ghori's first invasion was in 1175.
n: Muhammad-bin-Qasim targeted Sindh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Muhammad-bin-Qasim invaded Sindh in 712 AD. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Muhammad Ghori’s first invasion of India occurred in 1175. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Muhammad Ghori’s 1175 campaign was his first invasion of India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Timur invaded Delhi in 1398. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Timur’s 1398 campaign was known as Timur’s invasion. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
Nadir Shah defeated the Mughals at the Battle of Karnal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
The Battle of Karnal occurred in 1739. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 78-80]
xa: Ghori fought at **Tarain** and **Chandawar** against **Prithviraj** and **Jayachandra**.
Timur came in the reign of **Nasiruddin Mahmud Shah**.
**Babur** defeated **Ibrahim Lodi** at **Panipat** in **1526**.

nad1605da753.s: The Farman of 1717 issued by Farrukh Siyar is significant because it:
o: Granted chauth and sardeshmukhi to Shahu's agent
Exempted the English Company from customs duties in Bengal
Granted the Company Diwani rights in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa
Transferred Kora and Allahabad to the Company
nad1605da753.x: The Farman of 1717 exempted the Company from customs duties in Bengal and was called the Company's Magna Carta.
nad1605da753.tq: Distinguish the 1717 Farman from the 1765 Treaty of Allahabad.
xs: The **1717 farman** **exempted the Company from customs duties in Bengal** — option **(2)**.
It was called the Company's "**Magna Carta**".
Chauth to Shahu's agent = **1719**; Diwani = **1765**.
xa: ⚠ **1717** = customs exemption; **1719** = Marathas' chauth; **1765** = Company's Diwani.
It was issued by **Farrukh Siyar** (**1713-1719**).

nb0f7cab0676.s: The Mughal grant of 1719, issued through the Sayyids, granted to Balaji Vishwanath, as Shahu's agent:
o: Diwani rights in Bengal and Bihar
Kora and Allahabad with an annual payment
Chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan subas
nb0f7cab0676.x: The 1719 grant recognised Shahu's claim to chauth and sardeshmukhi from the six Deccan subas through his agent Balaji Vishwanath.
nb0f7cab0676.tq: Separate the content of the 1719 grant from the later Company concessions.
xs: The **1719** grant gave **chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan subas** — option **(3)**.
It went to Shahu's agent **Balaji Vishwanath**, issued through the **Sayyids**.
Diwani = **1765**; customs exemption = **1717**.
xa: **Shahu** had been released by **Bahadur Shah I**.
⚠ **1717** = Company; **1719** = Marathas; **1765** = Diwani.

n99b4f94a5fd.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Treaty of Allahabad of 1765?
o: The Sayyids granted the Company chauth of the Deccan subas.
Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Farrukh Siyar exempted the Company from customs duties in Bengal.
Akbar II granted the Company the title of Raja.
n99b4f94a5fd.x: Under the Treaty of Allahabad, Shah Alam II granted the Company the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The emperor received Kora and Allahabad and an annual payment of Rs 26 lakh.
n99b4f94a5fd.tq: Identify the correct grantor and the precise territorial content of the treaty.
xs: At the **Treaty of Allahabad (1765)** **Shah Alam II** granted the **Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa** — option **(2)**.
Chauth = Sayyids (**1719**); customs exemption = **Farrukh Siyar** (**1717**); "Raja" title = **Akbar II** to Ram Mohan Roy.
xa: The emperor got **Kora and Allahabad** and **Rs 26 lakh** a year.
Diwani (**1765**) = the Company's **legal foothold**.

n772f362a05b.s: Under the Treaty of Allahabad, Shah Alam II was entitled to an annual payment of:
n772f362a05b.x: Shah Alam II received Kora and Allahabad and Rs 26 lakh a year, which Warren Hastings stopped from 1772.
xa: The treaty gave the Company the **Diwani** of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
Shah Alam II returned to Delhi in **1771-72** under **Mahadji Scindia**.

n1d6f0fb9906.s: The Diwani granted in 1765 is regarded as the East India Company's:
o: First exemption from customs duties in Bengal
n1d6f0fb9906.x: The Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, obtained in 1765, provided the Company's legal foothold for territorial and fiscal power in India.
n1d6f0fb9906.tq: Link the constitutional-financial concession with its wider historical significance.
xs: The **1765 Diwani** was the Company's **legal foothold** — option **(1)**.
Granted by **Shah Alam II** at the **Treaty of Allahabad**: Diwani of **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**.
The customs exemption came in **1717** (Farrukh Siyar); the Raja title was **Akbar II**'s gift to Ram Mohan Roy.
xa: ⚠ **1717** = customs exemption; **1719** = Marathas' chauth; **1765** = Diwani.
The emperor got **Kora and Allahabad** and **Rs 26 lakh** a year.

n303b94677ce.s: Nadir Shah invaded India during the reign of:
n303b94677ce.x: Nadir Shah invaded in 1739, during Muhammad Shah's reign.
xa: Husain Ali was killed in **1720**.
Abdali's **first raid**: **1748**.

n1b78c595a6b.s: Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah held which Mughal offices before establishing the Asaf Jahi state?
o: Subedar of the Deccan and Wazir
Nawab of Carnatic and Mir Bakshi
Subedar of Bengal and Diwan of Awadh
Diwan of Bengal and Subedar of Gujarat
n1b78c595a6b.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk was Subedar of the Deccan and also served as Wazir in the Mughal administration.
n1b78c595a6b.tq: Distinguish the founder's Mughal offices from those of other successor-state founders.
xs: Nizam-ul-Mulk was **Subedar of the Deccan** and later **Wazir** — option **(1)**.
**Farrukh Siyar** made him Mughal Governor of the Deccan.
xa: Titles: **Chin Qilich Khan** (Aurangzeb), **Nizam-ul-Mulk** (Farrukh Siyar), **Asaf Jah** (Muhammad Shah, **1725**).
Bengal's **Murshid Quli Khan** was Diwan, then Nazim.

nbce5ba60c19.s: The founder of the Carnatic state of Arcot was
nbce5ba60c19.x: Saadatullah Khan, also rendered as Saadullah Khan, founded the Carnatic state of Arcot and named his nephew Dost Ali as successor.
nbce5ba60c19.tq: Use the founder-name and regional-state association.
xs: **Saadatullah Khan** founded the **Carnatic (Arcot)** — option **(1)**.
He was **Nawab under the Nizam** and named his nephew **Dost Ali** successor without the Nizam's approval.
**Daud Khan** governed the Deccan for Zulfiqar Khan; **Safdar Jung** = Awadh; **Puran Chand** = Nizam's Diwan.
xa: ⚠ **Saadat Khan** = Awadh; **Saadatullah Khan** = Carnatic.
The Nizam himself was **Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah**, Subedar of the **Deccan**.

nc03bdcccb42.s: Murshid Quli Khan held which offices in Bengal?
nc03bdcccb42.x: Murshid Quli Khan first served as Diwan and later became Nazim of Bengal. He ruled Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
nc03bdcccb42.tq: Test the exact office held by a regional founder rather than merely the state associated with him.
xs: **Murshid Quli Khan** was **Diwan, then Nazim** of Bengal — option **(4)**.
He ruled **Bengal, Bihar and Orissa**.
xa: He became autonomous under **Muhammad Shah**.
APPSC-G1 **2024** match: Murshid Quli Khan — **Bengal**.

n07d38ca7a39.s: The Carnatic state of Arcot was founded by:
n07d38ca7a39.x: Arcot was founded by Saadatullah Khan; Saadat Khan Burhan-ul-Mulk founded Awadh.
xa: ⚠ **Saadat Khan** = Awadh; **Saadatullah Khan** = Carnatic.
Successor: **Safdar Jung**.

n998f9151386.s: The revisionist interpretation of the eighteenth century views it chiefly as a period of:
o: Exclusive European control over the peasant surplus
Regional growth, with successor states controlling economic and law-and-order systems
Uninterrupted Mughal centralisation under weak successors
n998f9151386.x: The revisionist view treats the eighteenth century as a period of regional growth. The new states managed their own economic and law-and-order systems and controlled peasant surplus.
n998f9151386.tq: Contrast the revisionist regional-growth interpretation with the older collapse narrative.
xs: Revisionists see the 18th century as **regional growth**, with successor states running **economic and law-and-order systems** — option **(3)**.
The new states **controlled the peasant surplus** — not "complete collapse".
xa: Successor states: **Hyderabad**, **Bengal**, **Awadh**, **Carnatic**, **Rohilkhand**, **Farrukhabad**.
The decline's vacuum was filled by regional states, the **Marathas** and the **East India Company**.

n3bd027ff7b0.s: The decline of the Mughal Empire created a power vacuum that was successively filled by:
o: Regional states, the Marathas and finally the East India Company
The Rajputs, the Sikhs and the Portuguese
The Mughals, the Marathas and the Ottoman Empire
The Sayyids, the Afghans and the French alone
n3bd027ff7b0.x: The decline opened space for regional successor states, the Marathas and ultimately the East India Company.
n3bd027ff7b0.tq: Recall the broad political sequence following imperial decline.
xs: The vacuum was filled by **regional states, the Marathas and finally the East India Company** — option **(1)**.
**Diwani (1765)** gave the Company its **legal foothold**.
xa: Post-decline Hyderabad (**Asaf Jahi**) grew out of the **Mughal Deccan**.
Revisionist view: **regional growth**, not collapse.

n14e7e35a354.s: After helping overthrow the Sayyid brothers, Nizam-ul-Mulk appointed ____ as Diwan.
n14e7e35a354.x: Nizam-ul-Mulk helped overthrow the Sayyids and appointed Puran Chand as Diwan.
xa: He kept the **Marathas** out in his lifetime; after his death (**1748**) Hyderabad was vulnerable.
He defeated **Mubariz Khan** at **Shakar Kheda** (**1724**).

n6624d222e1d.s: Hyderabad State was integrated into the Indian Union in 1948 through:
n6624d222e1d.x: Operation Polo integrated Hyderabad in 1948; Mir Osman Ali Khan was the last Nizam.
xa: The dynasty ruled until **1948**.
First Nizam: **Asaf Jah I** (**1724-48**).

nda1a7351637.s: Who founded the Asaf Jahi state of Hyderabad in 1724?
nda1a7351637.x: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi founded the Asaf Jahi state and became its first Nizam.
nda1a7351637.tq: Identify the founder directly and distinguish him from the early successors.
xs: **Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi** founded the Asaf Jahi state — option **(1)**.
He was the **first Nizam** (APPSC **2018**, **2022**).
**Mubariz Khan** was the rival he defeated at **Shakar Kheda** (**1724**); **Nasir Jung** and **Nizam Ali Khan** were later Nizams.
xa: Titles: **Chin Qilich Khan**, **Nizam-ul-Mulk**, **Asaf Jah**.
**Puran Chand** was his Diwan.

n5c490c3b292.s: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan, founder of the Asaf Jahi state, defeated Mubariz Khan at:
n5c490c3b292.x: He defeated Mubariz Khan at Shakar Kheda; the state was founded in 1724.
xa: After **1748** Hyderabad became vulnerable to the **Marathas**.
**Muhammad Shah** gave him the title **Asaf Jah** (**1725**).

nb613cc86b03.s: Which one of the following was NOT a major cause of the decline of the Mughal Empire?
o: The invasions of Nadir Shah and Ahmad Shah Abdali
The long Deccan wars and the resulting drain on the treasury
The strengthening of central authority by independent nobles
nb613cc86b03.x: Independent nobles weakened, rather than strengthened, central authority. The Deccan wars, Maratha rise and invasions were among the major causes of decline.
nb613cc86b03.tq: Find the reversed effect in a cause-of-decline option.
xs: "**Strengthening of central authority by independent nobles**" is not a cause — option **(4)**.
Nobles **acted independently** and their rivalries **broke central authority**.
**Nadir Shah** and **Abdali**'s invasions, the **Maratha rise** and the long **Deccan wars** were real causes.
xa: **Jagirdari and agrarian crises** → peasant and zamindar revolts.
**European companies** also contributed.

n6642d98d8d4.s: At its greatest extent under Aurangzeb, the Mughal Empire extended approximately from:
o: Kashmir to Jinji and the Hindukush to Chittagong
Kabul to Bijapur and Sindh to Assam
Punjab to Madurai and the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal
Delhi to the Narmada and Gujarat to Bengal
n6642d98d8d4.x: Under Aurangzeb the empire reached from Kashmir to Jinji and from the Hindukush to Chittagong.
n6642d98d8d4.tq: Recall both geographical limits together instead of relying on one directional clue.
xs: The empire reached from **Kashmir to Jinji** and the **Hindukush to Chittagong** — option **(1)**.
This was its **greatest extent** under **Aurangzeb**.
xa: His intolerant policies and long **Deccan wars** weakened its foundations and drained the treasury.
Golconda became the **21st Mughal suba** after **1687**.

nindian-history-141-22.s: The Huna ruler Mihirakula was defeated by:
n: Mihirakula targeted India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Muhammad bin Qasim opposed Dahir. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Genghis Khan targeted the northwestern frontier. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
Nadir Shah targeted Mughal India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #141 · pp 244-246]
xa: Genghis Khan reached the **Indus** during **Iltutmish's reign** (**13th century**).
**Toramana** led the **second Huna attack**.
Nadir Shah fought at **Karnal** in **1739**.

nb8507d06c4b.s: Who wrote both History of Aurangzeb and Fall of the Mughal Empire?
nb8507d06c4b.x: Jadunath Sarkar authored both History of Aurangzeb and Fall of the Mughal Empire.
nb8507d06c4b.tq: Match the historian with the distinctive pair of works.
xs: **Jadunath Sarkar** wrote **History of Aurangzeb** and **Fall of the Mughal Empire** — option **(2)**.
He blamed Aurangzeb's **religious policy**, personal failings and **weak successors**.
**Irfan Habib** = **Agrarian System of Mughal India** (**1963**); **Satish Chandra** = **Parties and Politics at the Mughal Court**; **Moreland** = **India at the Death of Akbar**.
xa: **M. Athar Ali** (Mughal Nobility under Aurangzeb): enlarged nobility worsened the **jagir shortage**.
**Bernier**: no private property in land, so no incentive to improve.

n5264d61422e.s: The agrarian-crisis interpretation of Mughal decline, emphasising the over-exploitation of peasants and the resulting revolts, is associated with:
n5264d61422e.x: Irfan Habib explained the decline through an agrarian crisis in The Agrarian System of Mughal India (1963), arguing that over-exploitation of peasants provoked revolts.
n5264d61422e.tq: Link the interpretation to the historian rather than merely recalling the book title.
xs: The **agrarian-crisis** view is **Irfan Habib**'s — option **(4)**.
In **The Agrarian System of Mughal India** (**1963**) he argued that **over-exploitation of peasants** set off revolts.
**Jadunath Sarkar** blamed Aurangzeb's **religious policy**; **Athar Ali** the enlarged nobility; **Bernier** the absence of **private property in land**.
xa: ⚠ **Irfan Habib** = **agrarian crisis**; **Satish Chandra** = **jagirdari crisis**.
Jagirdari and agrarian crises shrank the **fiscal base** → **peasant and zamindar revolts**.

n7ba5c35264f.s: M. Athar Ali attributed the worsening of the jagir shortage primarily to:
o: The transfer of all jagirs to European companies
The enlargement of the nobility through the inclusion of Deccanis and Marathas
The abolition of the mansabdari system by Farrukh Siyar
The decline of agriculture caused by Nadir Shah's raid
n7ba5c35264f.x: Athar Ali argued that the enlarged nobility, including Deccanis and Marathas, intensified the shortage of jagirs.
n7ba5c35264f.tq: Apply the historian's specific causal argument rather than choosing a general cause of decline.
xs: Athar Ali blamed **the enlargement of the nobility** through **Deccanis and Marathas** — option **(2)**.
This worsened the **jagir shortage**.
xa: **Satish Chandra** = the **jagirdari crisis**: too few jagirs for too many nobles.
Nadir Shah's raid came in **1739**, well after the jagir crisis began.

nf7ae8ae9bc1.s: François Bernier traced Mughal decline mainly to:
o: The absence of private property in land
A shortage of nobles in imperial service
nf7ae8ae9bc1.x: Bernier held that the absence of private property in land removed the incentive to improve it and led towards ruin.
xa: Bernier's work: **Travels in the Mogul Empire**.
**Jadunath Sarkar** blamed Aurangzeb's **religious policy** and **weak successors**.

n67fa00cff3a.s: Among the Sayyid brothers, Husain Ali Khan held the post of:
n67fa00cff3a.x: Husain Ali Khan was Mir Bakhshi and Abdullah Khan the Wazir; they dominated Mughal politics from 1713 to 1720.
xa: They were overthrown with **Nizam-ul-Mulk's** help.
They made **Farrukh Siyar** emperor, then deposed and killed him (**1719**).

n4e4d24a4b8e.s: Shivaji captured Torna from Bijapur in
n4e4d24a4b8e.x: Shivaji seized Torna from Bijapur in 1646, and it was his first fort.
n4e4d24a4b8e.tq: Separate the first-fort date from the birth, battle and treaty dates.
xs: Shivaji seized **Torna** from declining **Bijapur** in **1646** — option **(2)**.
Torna was his **first fort**, taken at age **16**.
**1630** is his birth (Shivneri); **1659** the killing of Afzal Khan; **1665** the Treaty of Purandar.
xa: ⚠ **Shivneri** = birth (**1630**); **Torna** = first fort (**1646**); **Raigad** = coronation (**1674**).
**Raigad** was taken from the **Mores of Javli** in **1656**.
Torna is a **Giri Durg** (hill fort), like Raigad, Pratapgad, Rajgad, Sinhagad and Panhala.

nc4ddec5d3de.s: Dadaji Kondadev is best known in Shivaji’s early career as the
o: guardian of the Pune jagir and Shivaji’s tutor
commander of the Bijapur army at Panhala
Mughal envoy who negotiated the Treaty of Purandar
nc4ddec5d3de.x: Dadaji Kondadev served as guardian of the Pune jagir and acted as Shivaji’s tutor.
nc4ddec5d3de.tq: Match the individual with his specific early-career role.
xs: **Dadaji Kondadev** was **guardian of the Pune jagir** and Shivaji's **tutor** — option **(1)**.
**Sar Lashkar** of Golconda was **Akkanna**; the Purandar treaty was with **Raja Jai Singh**.
xa: With **Jijabai**, Dadaji Kondadev shaped Shivaji's early life.
⚠ **Akkanna = Sar Lashkar**; **Madanna = Mir Jumla** of Golconda.
**Niraj Pant** and **Prahlad Pant** were envoys to Golconda.

nc81043a3f9c.s: The Treaty of Purandar (1665) was concluded by Shivaji with:
nc81043a3f9c.x: Shivaji signed the Treaty of Purandar with Raja Jai Singh (Mirza Raja of Amber), surrendering 23 of his 35 forts.
xa: Exact date: **11 June 1665**; Jai Singh was the **Mirza Raja of Amber**.
⚠ Purandar was with the **Mughals**, not part of Shivaji's conflicts with Bijapur.
**1666**: Agra visit, house arrest, escape in **baskets of sweets and fruit**.

n4f45e3fc141.s: During his escape from house arrest at Agra in 1666, Shivaji was accompanied by:
n4f45e3fc141.x: Shivaji escaped together with Sambhaji, hidden in baskets of sweets and fruit.
xa: Sambhaji had gone to the Mughal court under the **Treaty of Purandar (1665)**.
**Diler Khan** served with **Jai Singh** at Purandar.

n6a6405e70d3.s: Shivaji's coronation at Raigad took place in:
n6a6405e70d3.x: Coronation 1674; second Surat raid 1670; treaty with Tana Shah 1677; death 1680.
xa: The 1677 treaty followed Shivaji's visit to **Hyderabad on 7 March 1677**, through **Akkanna and Madanna**.
Surat raids yielded nearly **one crore** rupees; religious places were spared.
**1677** conquests: **Ballari, Gingee, Vellore**.

n5173a666be7.s: In 1659 Shivaji killed the Bijapur general Afzal Khan at the foot of:
n5173a666be7.x: Shivaji killed Afzal Khan with a wagh nakh at the foot of Pratapgad.
xa: **Pratapgad** later served as a base for defence and expansion.
Wars with Bijapur began with seizing hill forts, starting with **Torna (1646)**.

n0a8142bea70.s: Under the treaty between Shivaji and Abul Hasan Tana Shah, Golconda agreed to provide money for the southern conquests and
o: send Sambhaji to the Mughal court
n0a8142bea70.x: The agreement provided financial support from Golconda for the southern conquests, with the spoils to be shared.
n0a8142bea70.tq: Identify the reciprocal terms of the alliance instead of confusing them with Purandar conditions.
xs: Golconda was to give money and **share the spoils** with Shivaji — option **(4)**.
The **1677** treaty with **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** was for aid in the southern campaign.
Sending **Sambhaji** to the Mughal court was a **Purandar** term, not a Golconda one.
xa: Shivaji afterwards **refused to share the spoils**.
Conquests: **Ballari, Gingee (Jinji), Vellore**.
Envoys to Golconda: **Niraj Pant** and **Prahlad Pant**.

n6d6775736e2.s: In his southern campaign, Shivaji took Gingee, Ballari and:
n6d6775736e2.x: Shivaji took Gingee, Vellore and Ballari and refused to share the spoils.
xa: **Vellore** was taken from step-brother **Venkoji/Ekoji**.
**1672** attack on Golconda took **2 lakh Honnu**.

n307e800c41d.s: Who officiated at Shivaji's coronation with Vedic rites?
n307e800c41d.x: Gaga Bhatt, a learned Brahmin from Banaras (Varanasi), officiated at the coronation with Vedic rites.
xa: Title taken: **"Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati"**.
The **Rajyabhisheka shaka** asserted sovereignty against the Mughals and Sultanates.

nade54945415.s: At his coronation, Shivaji adopted the title:
nade54945415.x: The coronation title was 'Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati'; he was also styled Haindava Dharmoddharak, not Hindavi Sultan.
xa: Coronation: **Raigad, 6 June 1674**, by **Gaga Bhatt**.
The new era: **Rajyabhisheka shaka**.

n07c0ff0a870.s: The era started by Shivaji to assert sovereignty against the Mughals and the Sultanates was known as the
n07c0ff0a870.x: Shivaji began the Rajabhisheka Shaka after his coronation to assert sovereign status.
n07c0ff0a870.tq: Match the political purpose with the precise name of the era.
xs: Shivaji's era was the **Rajabhisheka Shaka** (Rajyabhisheka shaka) — option **(3)**.
It began with the **1674** coronation and asserted **sovereignty** against the Mughals and Sultanates.
**Warna** is a **1731** treaty settling Tarabai's line at Kolhapur, not an era.
xa: Coronation title: **"Shri Raja Shiva Chhatrapati"**.
Priest: **Gaga Bhatt** of Banaras.

nbeab4487899.s: Which of the following groups contains only forts classified as Giri Durg?
nbeab4487899.x: Raigad, Pratapgad, Torna and Sinhagad are hill forts, or Giri Durg. Vishalgad is a land fort, while the others in the distractors include sea forts.
nbeab4487899.tq: Classify each example by fort type and eliminate groups containing a land or sea fort.
xs: **Raigad, Pratapgad, Torna and Sinhagad** are all **Giri Durg** (hill forts) — option **(1)**.
**Vishalgad** is a **Bhu Durg** (land fort); **Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg, Khanderi, Suvarnadurg** are **Jal Durg** (sea forts).
xa: **Rajgad** and **Panhala** are also Giri Durg.
Shivaji held over **300 forts**.
**Kolaba** was also a sea base guarding the Konkan.

nf4010a99d8e.x: Shivaji's coronation as Chhatrapati took place at Raigad in 1674. Agra is where he was placed under house arrest in 1666, Jinji was Rajaram's base, and Kolhapur was the seat of Tarabai's later line.
xs: Shivaji was crowned **Chhatrapati** at **Raigad** in **1674** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Agra** was his **1666** house arrest; **Kolhapur** was Tarabai's later line.
xa: He escaped from Agra in **fruit baskets**.
**Tarabai**, Rajaram's widow, raided Mughal lands **1700-07**.
The Maratha split: **Satara** line vs **Kolhapur** line.

n4dab091078f.s: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, the Nyayadhish was the:
o: Keeper of intelligence and the king's diary
n4dab091078f.x: The Nyayadhish was the chief justice; the Amatya handled finance, the Panditrao religion and the Mantri intelligence.
xa: ⚠ **Sachiv** = correspondence; **Sumant** = foreign affairs; **Mantri** = intelligence.
BPSC **2024**: Sachiv-correspondence, Peshwa-PM, Sumant-foreign, Amatya-finance.

nb0fd03b0e6d.s: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, every minister reported directly to the:
nb0fd03b0e6d.x: Each minister reported to the Chhatrapati; posts were not hereditary and ministers could be transferred or dismissed.
xa: All except **Panditrao and Nyayadhish** had to lead military campaigns.
Later the Peshwa post became **hereditary and supreme**.
Ashtapradhan was **advisory**, whereas the Mughal wazir system was hierarchical.

nbd3fe74b9c7.s: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, the Sumant (Dabir) was in charge of:
nbd3fe74b9c7.x: The Sumant or Dabir handled foreign affairs and received envoys as master of ceremonies; correspondence was the Sachiv's, grants the Panditrao's and accounts the Amatya's.
xa: PYQ: **Dabir = master of ceremonies** (APPSC-G1 **2024**).
⚠ **Sachiv** = correspondence; **Sumant** = foreign affairs; **Mantri** = intelligence.

naf31058019d.s: The combined effect of chauth and sardeshmukhi was to
o: finance military expansion and establish political hegemony without the cost of direct governance
confine Maratha authority to the fort of Raigad
replace the Ashtapradhan with a hereditary Mughal bureaucracy
end Maratha military expansion by restricting revenue collection
naf31058019d.x: Together, the levies financed military expansion and extended political hegemony without requiring the Marathas to administer every territory directly.
naf31058019d.tq: Infer the administrative consequence from the stated revenue mechanism.
xs: Chauth and sardeshmukhi **financed military expansion** and **political hegemony without the cost of direct governance** — option **(1)**.
They were collected from lands **outside the Maratha realm** — Mughal and Deccan Sultanate territory.
This let a **regional state become a pan-Indian power** without direct administration.
xa: ⚠ **Chauth = 25%** (protection); **Sardeshmukhi = 10%** (hereditary right).
Mughals formally conceded them in **1719**.
Peak extent later: **Attock to Cuttack**.

na2936b7dcce.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes chauth from sardeshmukhi?
o: Chauth: 25% protection levy; sardeshmukhi: additional 10% hereditary claim
Chauth: 25% hereditary claim; sardeshmukhi: 10% protection levy
Chauth: 10% hereditary claim; sardeshmukhi: 25% protection levy
Chauth: 10% protection levy; sardeshmukhi: additional 25% hereditary claim
na2936b7dcce.x: Chauth was generally one-fourth of land revenue as protection money; sardeshmukhi was an additional 10 per cent claimed as the king's hereditary right as Sardeshmukh.
xa: Both were collected from lands **outside the Maratha realm**.
Mughals formally conceded them in **1719** (Farrukhsiyar, six Deccan subas).
Exam angle: "Maratha revenue claim for protection" = **Chauth** (UPPSC **2018**).

o: territories under direct Maratha administration only
the personal estates of the Ashtapradhan ministers
n1f0444fc5cf.x: Chauth was levied on territories outside direct Maratha rule, including Mughal and Deccan Sultanate territories.
n1f0444fc5cf.tq: Apply the rule about the geographical scope of an external levy.
xs: Chauth was levied on **territories outside direct Maratha rule** — option **(4)**.
Chiefly **Mughal and Deccan Sultanate** territory.
It financed expansion **without the cost of direct governance**.
xa: Chauth = **25%** of land revenue.
Recognised by the **Nizam at Palkhed**; Nizam paid again after the **1795** war.
In **Rajputana** the Marathas took tribute and chauth but annexed no Rajput state.

nd09f0bfe492.s: The Mughal grants of 1719 gave the Marathas chauth and sardeshmukhi of how many Deccan subas?
nd09f0bfe492.x: The 1719 grants recognised Shahu, confirmed Swarajya lands and gave chauth and sardeshmukhi of the six Deccan subas.
xa: Granted by **Farrukhsiyar**; obtained by **Balaji Vishwanath**.
**Treaty of Warna (1731)**: Tarabai's line settled at **Kolhapur**.

n4d0964fb872.s: At its peak, the Maratha Empire extended from Attock to:
n4d0964fb872.x: The Maratha Empire ran from Attock to Cuttack and from the Gulf of Khambhat to beyond the Kaveri.
xa: This peak extent figures in the **NCERT map** row — a PIL in the **Bombay HC**.
**Chauth-sardeshmukhi** let a regional state become a pan-Indian power.

n4a550b094e3.s: Shivaji's revenue settlement, in which the state dealt directly with the cultivator, was of the ____ type.
n4a550b094e3.x: Shivaji dealt directly with cultivators in a ryotwari-type settlement and paid officials in cash.
xa: State share: **33%, later 40%** of gross produce.
Assessment was on **area cultivated and crop**.

n986ef709eb1.s: The service land grants that Shivaji abolished but which returned under Shahu and the Peshwas were called:
n986ef709eb1.x: Shivaji abolished jagirs and paid in cash; saranjam grants returned under Shahu and the Peshwas.
xa: The army too was **paid in cash**, so loyalty went directly to the state.
Comparison: Mughal mansabdari rested on **jagirs**.

nd112f754963.x: Bagayat was irrigated land, Jirayat dry land and Kathi a measuring rod.
xa: **Saranjam** = service land grants.
**Modi script** = cursive script for Marathi records.

n74749dbe0d5.s: The Rajvyavahar Kosh was associated with the replacement of
o: Persian official terms by Sanskrit terms
n74749dbe0d5.x: The Rajvyavahar Kosh replaced Persian official terminology with Sanskrit terminology.
n74749dbe0d5.tq: Test the direction of replacement in a language-policy reform.
xs: The **Rajvyavahar Kosh** replaced **Persian official terms by Sanskrit** ones — option **(1)**.
**Marathi and Sanskrit** replaced **Persian** as official languages.
xa: **Modi script** = cursive script for Marathi administrative records.
**Hindavi Swarajya** promoted Marathi and Sanskrit in administration over Persian.

n4548a846a4e.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies Shivaji’s coins?
n4548a846a4e.x: Shivaji issued the gold Hon and the copper Shivrai.
n4548a846a4e.tq: Discriminate between the names and metals of the two coins.
xs: Shivaji's coins were the **gold Hon** ("Shivrai hon") and the **copper Shivrai** — option **(1)**.
**Rupaya** and **Taka** were listed as silver, not gold or copper.
xa: ⚠ **Ruka** was the coin **not silver** (UPPSC **2016** key); Rupaya, Lari, Taka listed as silver.
**1672** attack on Golconda took **2 lakh Honnu**.

n257ebf1b2f7.s: Under Shivaji, Marathi administrative records were kept in the ____ script.
n257ebf1b2f7.x: Marathi and Sanskrit were promoted over Persian, and the cursive Modi script was used for Marathi records.
xa: **Rajvyavahar Kosh** replaced Persian official terms with Sanskrit ones.
**Ganimi Kava** = guerrilla hit-and-run warfare in the Sahyadri terrain.

nfdd4c42e546.s: At the Battle of Salher in 1672, the Marathas defeated in open battle the:
nfdd4c42e546.x: At Salher in 1672 the Marathas defeated the Mughals in open battle.
xa: Officials too were paid in cash — **jagirs abolished**.
Contrast: Mughal **mansabdari** rested on jagirs.

n24981d033f7.s: Which combination best describes the distinctive character of Shivaji’s state?
o: Mughal-style, mansab-based and paid only through jagirs
Decentralised, hereditary and entirely land-grant based
n24981d033f7.x: Shivaji built a centralised and non-hereditary state in which officials and forces were paid in cash.
n24981d033f7.tq: Compare the three defining features instead of selecting a single administrative characteristic.
xs: Shivaji's state was **centralised, non-hereditary and cash-paid** — option **(1)**.
**Jagirs abolished**; officials and army paid in **cash**; ministers could be **transferred or dismissed**.
xa: Mughal **mansabdari** rested on jagirs.
The **Ashtapradhan** was advisory, unlike the hierarchical Mughal wazir system.

nfe1acff2ca4.s: Shivaji's Ashtapradhan was ____, whereas the Mughal wazir system was hierarchical.
nfe1acff2ca4.x: The Ashtapradhan was advisory and the Mughal wazir system hierarchical; Shivaji also paid in cash rather than jagirs.
xa: The Ashtapradhan was modelled on the **Deccan Sultanates**.
Each minister reported directly to the **Chhatrapati**.

n1038d4f73a1.s: The burden of paying chauth after the 1795 war pushed the Nizam into the British Subsidiary Alliance in:
n1038d4f73a1.x: After the 1795 war the Nizam paid chauth to the Marathas, which contributed to his joining the Subsidiary Alliance in 1798.
xa: The Mughals had conceded chauth and sardeshmukhi in **1719**.
AP angle: Shivaji's **Golconda alliance (1677)** through Akkanna-Madanna.

n7344b808fd1.s: Ganimi Kava, associated with Shivaji's military tactics, refers to
o: A treaty-based system of revenue collection
Guerrilla hit-and-run warfare in the Sahyadri terrain
A system of permanent fortified cantonments in the Deccan
A naval blockade of Mughal ports
n7344b808fd1.x: Ganimi Kava was the guerrilla hit-and-run method used by Shivaji in the difficult Sahyadri terrain.
n7344b808fd1.tq: Translate the named tactic into its practical military application.
xs: **Ganimi Kava** was **guerrilla hit-and-run warfare** using the **Sahyadri terrain** — option **(2)**.
The **Sahyadri hills** and hill forts suited guerrilla war, a key cause of the Maratha rise.
xa: Shivaji held over **300 forts**; Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad were bases for defence and expansion.
**Mavali** infantry were the hill troops.
Yet at **Salher (1672)** the Mughals were beaten in **open battle**.
**Modi script** = cursive script for Marathi records; **Rajvyavahar Kosh** = Sanskrit official terms.

n6d68083370b.s: Each fort under Shivaji was placed under the charge of three officers of equal rank. Which set correctly identifies them?
n6d68083370b.x: The three officers were the Havaldar, Sabnis and Sarnobat. The Sabnis handled records, while the Havaldar and Sarnobat had garrison and military responsibilities.
n6d68083370b.tq: Distinguish the fort command structure from the Ashtapradhan and army categories.
xs: The three equal-rank fort officers were the **Havaldar, Sabnis and Sarnobat** — option **(2)**.
**Havaldar** = garrison commander; **Sabnis** = records; **Sarnobat** = military officer.
**Bargir, Shiledar, Mavali** are army troops; **Peshwa, Amatya, Dabir** belong to the Ashtapradhan.
xa: **Adnyapatra** of Ramachandrapant Amatya: "**forts are the core of the state**".
The army's smallest unit was led by a **havildar**.

nf2d069e0c8f.s: Maratha cavalrymen who were given horses and equipment by the state were called:
nf2d069e0c8f.x: Bargirs were state-equipped cavalry; Shiledars maintained their own horses.
xa: The standing army was **paid in cash**, no jagirs — loyalty direct to the state.
**Mavali** infantry were the hill troops.
**Battle of Salher (1672)**: Mughals beaten in open battle.

naa2a638dc6f.s: Shivaji's sea forts such as Sindhudurg, Kolaba and Vijaydurg guarded the ____ coast.
naa2a638dc6f.x: The sea forts guarded the Konkan coast; Shivaji is called the Father of the Indian Navy.
xa: Other Jal Durg: **Khanderi**, **Suvarnadurg**.
The "Father of the Indian Navy" title is a **Feb 2026** current-affairs row.

nb94d0d3952e.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the rise of the Marathas?
o: The Sahyadri hills and hill forts favoured guerrilla warfare.
Aurangzeb's Deccan campaign strengthened Mughal finances.
Bhakti saints promoted spiritual and regional unity.
Marathas had served in the armies and revenue offices of the Deccan Sultanates.
nb94d0d3952e.x: Aurangzeb's 27-year Deccan campaign drained the Mughal treasury rather than strengthening it.
xa: The **succession war after 1707** left a political vacuum that the Marathas filled.
Even the **Ashtapradhan** was modelled on the **Deccan Sultanate** councils.
Marathas' Deccan war, especially **Tarabai's raids**, broke Mughal finances.

nbcf7332d4e5.s: The Mughal weakness that created an opportunity for the Maratha rise was associated with
o: the Mughal conquest of Golconda in 1672 and the Treaty of Purandar
Aurangzeb’s short Deccan campaign and stable succession after 1707
the consolidation of Mughal finances through the Deccan revenues
Aurangzeb’s 27-year Deccan campaign and the succession war after 1707
nbcf7332d4e5.x: The prolonged Deccan campaign drained the treasury, while the succession war after 1707 created a political vacuum.
nbcf7332d4e5.tq: Select the option containing both linked causes without reversing their effects.
xs: The Mughal weakness was **Aurangzeb's 27-year Deccan campaign** and the **succession war after 1707** — option **(4)**.
The long campaign **drained the treasury**; the succession war left a **vacuum**.
So the campaign was not short, succession was not stable, and finances were not consolidated.
xa: **Aurangzeb** died in the Deccan in **1707** without subduing the Marathas.
**Shahu** was released by **Bahadur Shah I** in **1707** and beat Tarabai at **Khed**.
**Tarabai's raids** in particular broke Mughal finances.

n7d5118dc677.s: Samarth Ramdas, traditionally named as Shivaji's guru, wrote the:
n7d5118dc677.x: Samarth Ramdas wrote the Dasbodh; Shivaji's guardian was Dadaji Kondadev.
xa: ⚠ Ramdas as guru is **disputed**; APPSC **2012** dropped its key.
Father **Shahaji Bhonsle** was a Maratha general who served Bijapur and Ahmadnagar.
Step-brother **Venkoji/Ekoji** lost **Vellore** to Shivaji.

n95f0d26df1d.s: Rajaram, who created the post of Pratinidhi, directed Maratha resistance against Aurangzeb from:
n95f0d26df1d.x: Rajaram directed resistance from Gingee (Jinji) and drew Aurangzeb south.
xa: His widow **Tarabai** became regent for **Shivaji II**.
Gingee was among Shivaji's **1677** conquests.

n319e7f3f45d.s: Tarabai's line was later settled at Kolhapur under the Treaty of:
n319e7f3f45d.x: Tarabai's line was settled at Kolhapur under the Treaty of Warna.
xa: She led the Marathas at **Aurangzeb's death (1707)**.
**Shahu** beat Tarabai's forces at **Khed (1707)**.
Tarabai's raids especially **broke Mughal finances**.

n7684e7e93db.s: Balaji Vishwanath was appointed Peshwa in 1713 by:
n7684e7e93db.x: Shahu appointed Balaji Vishwanath (Peshwa 1713-20); real power then shifted from the Chhatrapati to the Peshwa.
xa: He **backed Shahu in the civil war** and rallied chiefs to him.
Under the later Peshwas the post became **hereditary and supreme**.

n937fb6add13.s: In Golconda, Akkanna held the post of:
n937fb6add13.x: Akkanna was Sar Lashkar and Madanna the Mir Jumla of Golconda.
xa: The **1677** treaty with **Abul Hasan Tana Shah** was made through Akkanna and Madanna.
Shivaji visited **Hyderabad** on **7 March 1677**.

n97132cc2e66.s: Balaji Baji Rao, Peshwa from 1740 to 1761, was also known as:
n97132cc2e66.x: Balaji Baji Rao was known as Nana Saheb; under him Maratha power reached its zenith, reaching Lahore and Peshawar.
xa: He ruled **1740-61**, took **Gujarat** (APPSC **2025**) and **lost Third Panipat (1761)**.
He died soon after Panipat, in **1761**.

n8e23bcb37d0.s: Which of the following best describes the achievement of Madhav Rao I after 1761?
o: He signed the Treaty of Bassein and became the last Peshwa.
He revived Maratha power after Panipat and defeated several regional opponents.
He founded Peshwa power and secured the 1719 Mughal grant.
He was removed by the Barabhai council immediately after his accession.
n8e23bcb37d0.x: Madhav Rao I revived Maratha power after Panipat and defeated the Nizam, Mysore under Haidar Ali, Rohillas, Rajputs and Jats.
n8e23bcb37d0.tq: Identify the recovery phase and reject contributions belonging to earlier or later Peshwas.
xs: **Madhav Rao I** (**1761-72**) **revived Maratha power after Panipat** — option **(2)**.
He defeated the **Nizam**, **Mysore (Haidar Ali)**, **Rohillas, Rajputs and Jats**.
**Bassein** and the last Peshwa = **Baji Rao II**; the **1719** grant = **Balaji Vishwanath**; ousted by the Barabhai = **Raghunath Rao**.
xa: In his time **Mahadji Scindia** restored **Shah Alam II** to Delhi (**1771**).
He beat the Nizam at **Rakshasbhuvan (1763)**.
Peshwa control over chiefs weakened after his death in **1772**.

n6211077ab0c.s: The infant Peshwa Madhav Rao II ruled through:
n6211077ab0c.x: Madhav Rao II, installed as an infant in 1774, ruled through Nana Phadnavis.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes say he was installed after Salbai — wrong.
He beat the Nizam at **Kharda (1795)**.

n5c8c391c0a0.s: Which Peshwa signed the Treaty of Bassein (1802)?
n5c8c391c0a0.x: Baji Rao II signed the Treaty of Bassein; he was the last Peshwa.
xa: He was pensioned off to **Bithur** near Kanpur; Peshwaship abolished in **1818**.
Bassein (**1802**) = **subsidiary subordination**.

n17a5943caf0.s: Which Peshwa was popularly known as Nana Saheb?
n17a5943caf0.x: Nana Saheb refers to Balaji Baji Rao, not Balaji Vishwanath.
xa: Balaji Baji Rao (**1740-61**) = **zenith** of Maratha power; lost **Third Panipat**.
Don't confuse with **Nana Phadnavis**, the "**Maratha Machiavelli**".

nb9e83a2404f.s: Gujarat was brought under Maratha control during the tenure of which Peshwa?
nb9e83a2404f.x: Gujarat was taken under Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb, 1740-61), during whose tenure Maratha power reached its zenith (APPSC 2025). Balaji Vishwanath secured the 1719 grant; Baji Rao I won Malwa and Bundelkhand; Madhav Rao I revived power after Panipat.
nb9e83a2404f.tq: APPSC 2025: Gujarat = Balaji Baji Rao (Nana Saheb).
xs: **Gujarat** was taken under **Balaji Baji Rao** (Nana Saheb) — option **(3)** (APPSC **2025**).
**Balaji Vishwanath** got the **1719** grant; **Baji Rao I** won **Malwa and Bundelkhand**; **Madhav Rao I** revived power after Panipat.
xa: Under Balaji Baji Rao (**1740-61**) the Marathas **reached Lahore and Peshawar**.
He lost the **Third Battle of Panipat (1761)**.

n58b2ee800c0.s: The phrase "strike the trunk, the branches will fall" is associated with:
n58b2ee800c0.x: The phrase is Baji Rao I's, about striking at the Mughal centre; his ideology is expressed as Hindu Pad Padshahi.
xa: Baji Rao I raided **Delhi** in **1737**.
He beat the Nizam at **Palkhed** and **Bhopal**.

nc80c0870be6.s: Which Peshwa died soon after the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761?
nc80c0870be6.x: Balaji Baji Rao died soon after the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.
xa: He was succeeded by **Madhav Rao I (1761-72)**.
His son **Vishwas Rao** died at Panipat.

n7c43ec83c51.s: The first Anglo-Maratha peace was the Treaty of:
n7c43ec83c51.x: The Treaty of Salbai (1782) was the first Anglo-Maratha peace; Bassein (1802) meant subsidiary subordination.
xa: Balaji Vishwanath was appointed in **1713** by **Shahu**.
Baji Rao II was **pensioned off to Bithur**.

n0ba896dec73.s: Who founded the Holkar house of the Maratha confederacy?
n0ba896dec73.x: The Holkar house was founded by Malhar Rao Holkar; Ranoji Scindia founded the Scindia house.
xa: Seats: Holkar — **Indore**; Scindia — **Gwalior**.
**Baji Rao I** built the confederacy.

nfa2bd5402fc.s: The Sangola agreement of 1750, which reduced the Chhatrapati to a nominal position, followed the death of:
nfa2bd5402fc.x: The Sangola agreement followed Shahu's death in 1749 and consolidated the Peshwa's position.
xa: The Peshwa's rise began in **1713** with **Balaji Vishwanath**.
Under the later Peshwas the office was **hereditary**.

n276fe96df81.s: Which Peshwa won Malwa and Bundelkhand and raided Delhi in 1737?
n276fe96df81.x: Baji Rao I won Malwa and Bundelkhand and raided Delhi in 1737.
xa: He beat the Nizam at **Palkhed (1728)** and **Bhopal**.
Ideology: **Hindu Pad Padshahi**.
The confederacy was built to **keep factions together** and satisfy older chiefs under **senapati Dabhade**.

n56bf87b2d45.s: Who among the following is regarded as the most charismatic Maratha leader after Shivaji?
n56bf87b2d45.x: Baji Rao I is regarded as the most charismatic Maratha leader after Shivaji.
n56bf87b2d45.tq: Use direct identification of the ruler associated with the stated historical reputation.
xs: **Baji Rao I** is the **most charismatic Maratha leader after Shivaji** — option **(2)**.
**Baji Rao II** was the **last Peshwa**; **Balaji Vishwanath** founded Peshwa power; **Madhav Rao I** revived it after Panipat.
xa: Ideology: **Hindu Pad Padshahi**; "**strike the trunk, the branches will fall**".
Conquests: **Malwa and Bundelkhand**; raided **Delhi (1737)**.

n5c2b3e4b32b.s: Which of the following was the principal weakness of the Maratha confederacy?
o: Internal rivalries and conflicting regional interests
Direct Mughal control over all Maratha territories
n5c2b3e4b32b.x: The confederacy was weakened by rivalries among semi-independent chiefs and their tendency to put regional interests before common Maratha interests.
n5c2b3e4b32b.tq: Identify the cause-effect link rather than a structural distractor.
xs: The main weakness was **internal rivalries** — semi-independent chiefs put **regional interest** first — option **(1)**.
This was the **main cause of decline**.
xa: Later decline: **corruption** + **slack** central and provincial government.
**Saranjam** land assignments for military service were the base of the confederacy.
After **Nana Phadnavis's death (1800)**, **Holkar and Scindia** fought over the weak Peshwa.

nf1c21d393d5.s: Baji Rao I organised the Maratha confederacy primarily in order to
o: keep the Maratha factions together and satisfy the older chiefs led by Senapati Dabhade
place the Maratha state under direct British protection
abolish the authority of Shahu immediately
transfer the capital from Poona to Nagpur
nf1c21d393d5.x: Baji Rao I built the confederacy to maintain unity among Maratha factions and to accommodate older chiefs led by Senapati Dabhade.
nf1c21d393d5.tq: Link the institutional arrangement with its stated political purpose.
xs: **Baji Rao I** built the confederacy to **keep the factions together** and satisfy the **older chiefs led by senapati Dabhade** — option **(1)**.
The chiefs still worked under the nominal authority of **Shahu**.
xa: UPSC spells Dabhade as "**Dabodi**".
The confederacy's base was **Saranjam** — land for military service.

nc252d18d01e.s: The Mungi-Shevgaon settlement between the Marathas and the Nizam came after the Battle of:
nc252d18d01e.x: Mungi-Shevgaon was a peace settlement between the Marathas and the Nizam after Palkhed.
xa: **Mahadji Scindia** recaptured Delhi in **1771**, unrelated to the Nizam.
**Udgir (1760)**: Nizam defeated by **Balaji Baji Rao**.

n4259d889820.s: Nana Phadnavis was popularly known as the
n4259d889820.x: Nana Phadnavis was called the “Maratha Machiavelli” because of his political skill in managing the confederacy.
n4259d889820.tq: Test the exact sobriquet rather than an approximate descriptive title.
xs: **Nana Phadnavis** was called the "**Maratha Machiavelli**" — option **(3)**.
He led the **Barabhai** (**12** chiefs) council and was regent for the infant **Madhav Rao II (1774-95)**.
xa: He held the confederacy together in the **First Anglo-Maratha War**, with **Mahadji Scindia** as northern arm.
After his death (**1800**), **Holkar and Scindia** fought over the weak Peshwa.
⚠ Don't confuse with **Nana Saheb = Balaji Baji Rao**.

n9e7fc198bb2.s: Who was the Peshwa at the time of the Third Battle of Panipat?
n9e7fc198bb2.x: Balaji Baji Rao, popularly known as Nana Saheb, was the Peshwa when the Third Battle of Panipat was fought.
n9e7fc198bb2.tq: Match the major event with the contemporary office-holder, not the battlefield commander.
xs: The Peshwa at Third Panipat was **Balaji Baji Rao** (Nana Saheb) — option **(3)**.
**Baji Rao I** died in **1740**; **Madhav Rao I** succeeded in **1761**; **Balaji Vishwanath** ruled **1713-20**.
xa: His son **Vishwas Rao** was killed in the battle.
He **died soon afterwards (1761)**.

nindian-history-17-47.s: In the Battle of Kharda (1795), the Marathas defeated:
nindian-history-17-47.x: At Kharda in 1795 the Marathas defeated the Nizam of Hyderabad.
n: The Battle of Kharda was fought between the Marathas and the Nizam. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
The Nizam was defeated in the Battle of Kharda. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #17 · pp 69-73]
xa: The Peshwa then was **Madhav Rao II**, ruling through **Nana Phadnavis**.
Earlier defeats of the Nizam: **Palkhed** (Baji Rao I) and **Udgir** (Balaji Baji Rao).
The defeat pushed the Nizam toward the **Subsidiary Alliance** (**1798**), blaming **Sir John Shore**'s neutrality.
**Mungi-Shevgaon** was a treaty between the **Marathas and the Nizam** (APPSC **2025**).

n7855bcd3e82.s: Who commanded the Maratha artillery at the Third Battle of Panipat?
n7855bcd3e82.x: Ibrahim Khan Gardi led the Maratha artillery, while Sadashiv Rao Bhau was the overall commander.
xa: Date: **14 January 1761**; opponent **Ahmad Shah Abdali**.
Peshwa at the time: **Balaji Baji Rao**.

n9eefdede06e.s: Who invited Ahmad Shah Abdali to intervene, leading to the Third Battle of Panipat?
n9eefdede06e.x: The Rohilla chief Najib-ud-Daula invited Abdali; Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh was an ally.
xa: The Maratha push into Punjab threatened Abdali's hold.
The Marathas had **almost no allies** — Jats (**Suraj Mal**) and Rajputs stayed away.

n00115105f44.s: Which of the following groups consisted of important allies of Ahmad Shah Abdali at Panipat?
o: Suraj Mal and the Rajput chiefs
n00115105f44.x: Abdali was supported by the Rohilla chief Najib-ud-Daula and Shuja-ud-Daula of Awadh.
n00115105f44.tq: Match the allied leaders with the correct side instead of assuming that all North Indian chiefs supported the Marathas.
xs: Abdali's allies were **Najib-ud-Daula** (Rohilla) and **Shuja-ud-Daula** of Awadh — option **(2)**.
**Suraj Mal** and the Rajputs **stayed away**; **Vishwas Rao** fought on the Maratha side.
xa: **Kashiraj Pandit**, Shuja-ud-Daula's official, wrote an eyewitness account.
**Ibrahim Khan Gardi** led the Maratha artillery.

n9242a9a99e7.s: Which of the following was NOT a major cause of the Maratha defeat at Panipat?
o: Alienation of some regional powers through earlier plunder
Heavy baggage and the presence of non-combatants
Strong and sustained support from the Jats and Rajputs
Collapse of supplies and starvation in the camp
n9242a9a99e7.x: The Marathas did not receive strong support from the Jats and Rajputs; their absence or neutrality contributed to the defeat. Supply failure, heavy baggage and alienation of regional powers were among the causes.
n9242a9a99e7.tq: Find the option that reverses the documented condition of the Maratha alliance system.
xs: Option **(3)** was NOT a cause: there was **no strong support from the Jats and Rajputs** — they stayed away.
Real causes: **no allies in the north**, **supply collapse and starvation**, **heavy baggage and non-combatants**, and earlier **plunder** that alienated Rajputs and Jats.
xa: Jat leader: **Suraj Mal**.
Consequence: northern ambitions halted, yet power recovered **within a decade**.

n1885108de50.s: The Third Battle of Panipat, fought on 14 January 1761, was fought between
o: the Marathas and the Mughals under Shah Alam II
the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali
the Mughals and Ahmad Shah Abdali
n1885108de50.x: The Third Battle of Panipat (14 January 1761) was fought between the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali (APPSC-G1 2018). Shah Alam II was the Mughal emperor of the time, not a combatant. Nadir Shah invaded in 1739. Abdali's opponents at Panipat were the Marathas, not the Mughals.
xs: Third Panipat (**14 January 1761**) was between **the Marathas and Ahmad Shah Abdali** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G1 **2018**).
**Shah Alam II** was the Mughal emperor, not a combatant.
