Reducing the cost of revenue collection
Securing an assured income for the Company
n4ad2371d45f.x: The rationale included assured income, lower collection costs, a loyal landlord class and the hope that zamindars would improve the land. A fixed demand actually prevented the Company from receiving additional revenue from later price increases.
n4ad2371d45f.tq: Find the option that contradicts the economic consequence of revenue fixity.
xs: Getting **every future increase in agricultural prices** was NOT a rationale — option **(2)**; a **fixed** demand gave the Company nothing extra.
Real rationales: **fixed, assured income**, **low collection cost** and a **loyal landlord class**.
xa: Another rationale: the hope that **zamindars would improve land**.
APPSC-GS **2022**: gains from agriculture went to the **zamindars**, not the Company.

n6756b66cff4.s: In Coastal Andhra, zamindars of the Zamindari areas paid the Company:
n6756b66cff4.x: Coastal lands were divided into Haveli (direct Company control) and Zamindari areas, whose zamindars paid peshkash.
xa: Old estates of **Vizianagaram, Bobbili and Pithapuram** came under peshkash.
Mootahs were held like proprietary estates after **1802**; many fell into arrears.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** confirmed valid **inam** titles on a **quit-rent**.

nc7f3079892e.s: The Madras Inam Commission, which investigated titles to rent-free inam lands, was constituted in:
nc7f3079892e.x: The Madras Inam Commission was constituted in 1858 to investigate rent-free inam titles.
xa: Valid titles were confirmed on payment of a **quit-rent**.
Full ryotwari conversion of estates came in **1948**.

n7a326e481b0.s: The three major British land-revenue settlements made land a:
n7a326e481b0.x: The settlements made land transferable, created a loyal landlord class and fed rural indebtedness and peasant revolts.
xa: They shaped agrarian class structure that land reforms after **1947** tried to undo.
All three were **extractive**, with revenue in **cash** regardless of harvest.

nfae1249ed64.s: The criticism that the State became the 'ultimate landlord' was directed at the:
nfae1249ed64.x: Critics held that under Ryotwari the state became the ultimate landlord and its revenue was as heavy as zamindari rent.
xa: Ryotwari revenue was often **50%+** of produce.
**Alice Thorner**: ryotwari **isolated farmers** from the government.

nindian-history-110-9.s: The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 dealt with which subject?
o: Auction of Zamindaris under the Sunset Clause
nindian-history-110-9.x: The Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885 dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants in Bengal and Bihar. Auction under the Sunset Clause belongs to the Permanent Settlement.
nindian-history-110-9.tq: Recall the subject of the 1885 Act.
n: The Sunset Clause required revenue payment by a prescribed sunset deadline. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Failure to pay revenue by the prescribed sunset deadline led to the auction of the zamindari. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Bengal Tenancy Act dealt with the rights of landlords and tenants. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Thomas Munro extended the Ryotwari Settlement to almost all parts of Madras except permanently settled areas. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
The Mahalwari revenue assessment was based on the village or community. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xs: The **Bengal Tenancy Act** of **1885** dealt with the **rights of landlords and tenants** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It applied to **Bengal** and **Bihar**.
Auction of zamindaris under the **Sunset Clause** belongs to the **Permanent Settlement**; village-community assessment is **Mahalwari**.
xa: **Sunset Law**: revenue due by **sunset** of the due date or the estate was **auctioned**.
Zamindari rights were **hereditary**, **transferable** or **saleable**.
The Permanent Settlement **strengthened landlords** and **increased pressure** on **peasants**.

nee8ba3058ab.s: In the Andhra region, Thomas Munro first introduced Ryotwari in 1802 in:
nee8ba3058ab.x: Munro brought Ryotwari to the Ceded Districts (Rayalaseema) in 1802; the Northern Circars were mainly zamindari.
xa: A **2018** PYQ stem gave the date as **1808**; the answer is still **Munro**.
From **1808** village-lease settlements replaced ryotwari in the Ceded Districts until restored around **1820**.

nab77370265b.s: Thomas Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was located at:
nab77370265b.x: Munro's headquarters as the first Collector of the Ceded Districts was at Anantapur.
nab77370265b.tq: Separate an official headquarters from the place of death and the wider regional headquarters.
xs: Munro's HQ as first **Collector of the Ceded Districts (1800)** was **Anantapur** — option **(2)**.
**Pattikonda** (Kurnool) is where he died of cholera in **1827**.
xa: He was **Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts** from **1800-07** (some notes say 1802 for the start).
He was buried at **Gooty**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

nb7c5548457d.s: Early in his career, Thomas Munro served in the Baramahal as assistant to:
nb7c5548457d.x: Munro was Assistant to Read in the Baramahal, then Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts, President of the Judicial Commission and Governor of Madras.
xa: He died at **Pattikonda** on **6 July 1827**, buried at **Gooty**.
As Governor he saw general Ryotwari adoption in Madras (**1820**).

naf98b4bc771.s: Sir Thomas Munro, who died of cholera at Pattikonda in 1827, was buried at:
naf98b4bc771.x: Munro died at Pattikonda (Kurnool) in 1827 and was buried at Gooty; Anantapur was his headquarters as Collector.
xa: UPSC notes give his governorship as **1819-26**.
He was born **27 May 1761** in **Glasgow**.

n9b41f74afc2.s: Who assisted Thomas Munro in suppressing the Palegars in the Ceded Districts before the introduction of Ryotwari settlement?
n9b41f74afc2.x: Munro suppressed the Palegars with the assistance of officer Campbell before bringing the Ceded Districts under Ryotwari settlement.
n9b41f74afc2.tq: Discriminate between persons associated with administration, resistance and nomenclature.
xs: Munro suppressed the Palegars with military officer **Campbell** — option **(2)**.
**Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** was a Kurnool Polygar who revolted in the **1840s**.
**Vijayarama Gajapati Raju** was the Vizianagaram zamindar defeated at **Padmanabham (1794)**.
**Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** proposed the name **Rayalaseema**.
xa: About **80** palegars resisted; suppression took **18** months.
Uyyalawada looted the treasury at **Kovela Kuntla**.

ncef7811e8ab.s: Which of the following correctly describes the land-revenue pattern in Andhra?
o: Ryotwari in the Circars, Zamindari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
Mahalwari in the Circars, Zamindari in Rayalaseema and Ryotwari in Nellore
Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and Mahalwari in Nellore
Ryotwari in the Circars, Mahalwari in Rayalaseema and Zamindari in Nellore
ncef7811e8ab.x: The Andhra pattern was Zamindari in the Circars, Ryotwari in the Ceded Districts and a Mahalwari-type arrangement in Nellore.
xa: Circar zamindaris: **Vizianagaram, Bobbili, Peddapuram, Pithapuram, Nuzvid**.
Ryotwari came to Rayalaseema in **1802**.
Some notes add **Chittoor** to Nellore for Mahalwari.

nceca1298e4b.s: Who was the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and established a direct ryot–state relationship there?
nceca1298e4b.x: Thomas Munro was the first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema and established the direct ryot–state relationship through ryotwari.
xa: HQ: **Anantapur**; died at **Pattikonda**, buried at **Gooty** (**1827**).
He spoke **Telugu** fluently and worked without interpreters.

n6a3a8e9d844.s: Under the Ryotwari system, which of the following rights was available to the ryot so long as the assessment was paid?
o: Only the right to cultivate, without transfer rights
The right to sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land
The right to remit all land revenue permanently
The right to collect revenue from other cultivators
n6a3a8e9d844.x: The ryot held proprietary rights and could sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land as long as the assessment was paid.
n6a3a8e9d844.tq: Identify the legal incidents of ryot ownership rather than confusing them with revenue-collection powers.
xs: The ryot could **sell, mortgage, gift or lease the land** as long as the assessment was paid — option **(2)**.
These were **proprietary rights**; he was not evicted while revenue was paid.
xa: Assessment was fixed on **land, not crop**.
On default the **land was auctioned**.
Problems: **over-assessment**, no proper records, corrupt subordinates → peasants to **moneylenders**.

nindian-history-110-15.s: Under the Ryotwari system, after a bad harvest:
o: an automatic general exemption from revenue was granted
occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible
nindian-history-110-15.x: Ryotwari gave no automatic exemption, but occasional remission or reduction was possible.
n: Ryotwari provided no automatic general exemption after a bad harvest. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
Occasional remission or reduction of revenue was possible under Ryotwari after a bad harvest. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #110 · pp 202-205]
xa: Ryotwari lacked famine remission, unlike the Mughal **zabt** (**one-third** share, **taccavi** loans).
Rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**.
Ryots were not evicted while revenue was paid; they could **sell, mortgage, gift** land.

n5196a79d4c6.s: Which regulations empowered zamindars to seize the property of tenants under the Permanent Settlement?
n5196a79d4c6.x: The regulations of 1799, known as Haftam, and 1812, known as Panjam, enabled zamindars to seize tenants' property.
n5196a79d4c6.tq: Pair the two regulations with their coercive effect rather than with settlement dates.
xs: The **Haftam (1799)** and **Panjam (1812)** regulations let zamindars seize tenants' property — option **(3)**.
**1822** and **1833** are Mahalwari regulations; **1793** made the settlement permanent.
xa: The result was **endless litigation** between zamindars and tenants.
Peasants were reduced to **tenants-at-will**.

nd975e1991af.s: Which of the following best represents Thomas Munro's administrative philosophy?
o: Exclusive reliance on village headmen and moneylenders
Direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries and communication in fluent Telugu
Permanent fixation of revenue irrespective of local conditions
Indirect rule through zamindars and complete absence of official contact with cultivators
nd975e1991af.x: Munro favoured direct contact with cultivators, avoided intermediaries and was fluent in Telugu. He was also particularly fond of Rayalaseema.
nd975e1991af.tq: Choose the option that combines the distinctive elements of a stated administrative philosophy.
xs: Munro stood for **direct contact with cultivators, no intermediaries**, and spoke **fluent Telugu** — option **(2)**.
He **distrusted Palegars** and big intermediaries, so indirect rule through zamindars is the opposite.
xa: He worked **without interpreters**.
Rayalaseema was chosen because it had **no strong zamindars**.
PYQ **2025**: Munro = **first Principal Collector of Rayalaseema**.

n5a7bf0fa211.s: Haveli lands were grouped into mootahs and auctioned to mootahdars after 1802. The mootahdars generally held them as—
n5a7bf0fa211.x: After 1802, mootahs were auctioned to mootahdars, who held them in the manner of proprietary estates. Many mootahdars later failed and fell into arrears.
n5a7bf0fa211.tq: Identify the legal-economic character of the holding created by a settlement arrangement.
xs: **Mootahdars** held the auctioned mootahs as **proprietary estates** after **1802** — option **(2)**.
Many failed and **fell into arrears**.
xa: **Haveli** lands were under direct Company control (vs **Zamindari**).
Haveli lands used auction, village or ryotwari methods.

n93ae354794f.s: In the Madras Presidency, the Northern Circars were mainly under the:
n93ae354794f.x: The Northern Circars were mainly zamindari; Haveli lands under direct British control later came under Ryotwari.
xa: Haveli lands were grouped into **mootahs** and auctioned to **mootahdars**; many fell into arrears.
The Northern Circars were obtained in **1765-66** (Mughal farman + Nizam treaty).

n7ee6633a7e2.s: Which legislation provided for the full conversion of Zamindari estates into Ryotwari holdings in the Madras Presidency?
o: Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948
n7ee6633a7e2.x: The Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 provided for the abolition of estates and their conversion into Ryotwari holdings.
n7ee6633a7e2.tq: Match the exact statute with its administrative purpose.
xs: Full conversion came with the **Madras Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948** — option **(3)**.
**1793** made the zamindari settlement permanent — it created, not abolished, zamindaris.
xa: Some notes date zamindari abolition to **1952** (First Plan).
APHQ **2025** order ends with zamindari abolition (**1948**) after **Guntur (1788)**, **Padmanabham (1794)**, **Ryotwari (1802)**.
The **Madras Inam Commission (1858)** dealt with **inam** (rent-free) titles.

n68b6e8f7902.s: The Permanent Settlement was applied in the Circars and Ryotwari introduced in Rayalaseema in:
n68b6e8f7902.x: These settlements came in 1802, after Guntur (1788), Padmanabham (1794) and the Ceded Districts (1800).
xa: The **Northern Circars** came earlier, in **1765-66**.
**Uyyalawada**'s revolt came in the **1840s**; zamindari abolition in **1948**.

nd14496778ba.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt in the 1840s is associated with which incident?
o: Defeating the Vizianagaram zamindar at Padmanabham
Introducing the Mahalwari system in Nellore
Obtaining the Northern Circars through a Mughal farman
Looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla
nd14496778ba.x: During the Kurnool Polygar revolt in the 1840s, Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy looted the treasury at Kovela Kuntla.
nd14496778ba.tq: Link the rebel with the specific action and place.
xs: **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy**'s **1840s** revolt is linked to **looting the treasury at Kovela Kuntla** — option **(4)**.
He was a **Kurnool Polygar**; Padmanabham (**1794**) was the Vizianagaram zamindar's defeat.
xa: Palegar resistance (**Uyyalawada**) followed **Munro**'s ryotwari in Rayalaseema.
Munro had suppressed about **80** palegars with **Campbell**.

nee2cb4818c0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the stages of colonialism in India?
o: The mercantilist stage (1757-1813) saw Company trade monopoly and direct plunder.
In the free-trade stage (1813-1858) India became a market for British goods and a source of raw materials.
The Charter Act of 1813 opened the free-trade stage.
nee2cb4818c0.x: The finance-capital stage began in 1858; 1813 opened the free-trade stage.
xa: The three stages were proposed by **R.P. Dutt** (**India Today**), drawing on **Karl Marx**.
The **Charter Act 1813** ended the Company's monopoly → **one-way free trade**.
Railways gave a **guaranteed 5% interest** to British investors.

nf4252807d91.s: The interpretation of colonialism in terms of mercantile, industrial-capital and finance-capital stages was proposed by:
o: Dadabhai Naoroji in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India
Richard Strachey in the Famine Code
Arthur Cotton in an irrigation report
nf4252807d91.x: R.P. Dutt proposed the three-stage interpretation in India Today, drawing on Karl Marx.
nf4252807d91.tq: Match the analytical framework with its author and work, not with other economic critics.
xs: The three-stage interpretation was proposed by **R.P. Dutt** in **India Today** — option **(1)**, drawing on **Karl Marx**.
**Naoroji**'s **Poverty and Un-British Rule** is the drain-theory text; **Strachey** is linked to the Famine Code; **Arthur Cotton** to the Godavari anicut.
xa: R.P. Dutt was a **later Marxist writer**, not an original drain theorist.
⚠ Do not confuse **R.P. Dutt** (India Today) with **R.C. Dutt** (**Economic History of India**).

n32fa03aa37b.s: Who popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory in colonial India?
n32fa03aa37b.x: Dadabhai Naoroji popularised the Drain of Wealth Theory and was known as the Grand Old Man and the father of Indian Nationalism.
n32fa03aa37b.tq: Direct identification of the proponent associated with a theory.
xs: The Drain of Wealth theory was popularised by **Dadabhai Naoroji** — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**R.C. Dutt**, **Ranade** and **Digby** developed or expanded it but did not popularise it.
xa: Naoroji's book: **"Poverty and Un-British Rule in India"** (**1901**).
He first stated it in **"England's Debt to India" (1867)** and coined **"moral drain"**.
He is called the **"Grand Old Man"** and **"father of Indian Nationalism"**.

nc207095a923.s: Dadabhai Naoroji first stated the drain argument in:
nc207095a923.x: Naoroji first stated the drain in 'England's Debt to India' (1867); 'Economic History of India' is R.C. Dutt's.
xa: **William Digby** wrote **"'Prosperous' British India"** (**1901**).
**M.G. Ranade** wrote **"Essays on Indian Economics"**.
The drain theory was **popularised by Naoroji** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
Naoroji was called the "**Grand Old Man**".

n8d37b4c05c8.s: Which newspaper and organisation are associated with Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti in the context of famine-related criticism in Andhra?
o: The Crescent and Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam
The Hindu and Madras Mahajana Sabha
Amrita Bazar Patrika and Indian Association
n8d37b4c05c8.x: Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti reported Andhra famines in his paper The Crescent and founded the Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam.
n8d37b4c05c8.tq: Match the individual with the publication and organisation associated with him.
xs: **Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti**: newspaper **"The Crescent"** and the **Chennapatnam Swadeshi Sangam (1852)** — option **(1)**.
He reported famines caused by **commercialisation of agriculture**.
xa: Andhra famines: **Guntur 1832-33** (**Dokkala / Nandana Karuvu**), **Kurnool 1866**.
Late **19th** century: **11** famines in Andhra; **1865-66** the most severe.

n4e7b3b0f456.s: The economic critique of colonialism made by the Moderates became an important base for:
o: The Swadeshi movement and early nationalism
The expansion of Company trade monopoly
n4e7b3b0f456.x: The drain theory and the wider economic critique were major contributions of the Moderates and helped provide the basis for Swadeshi and early nationalism.
n4e7b3b0f456.tq: Trace the political consequence of an economic critique rather than selecting an administrative reform.
xs: The Moderates' economic critique was a base for **Swadeshi** and **early nationalism** — option **(1)**.
Drain theory = the Moderates' **greatest contribution**.
xa: **Naoroji** popularised it; **R.C. Dutt** and **Ranade** expanded it.
The **Famine Code (1883)** came from the Strachey report, not from the Moderates.

n67f6186b138.s: Which of the following best describes the Drain of Wealth from India?
o: Transfer of Indian wealth to England without an adequate economic or material return
Movement of Indian capital from agriculture to indigenous industries
Exchange of Indian primary goods for British capital goods on equal terms
Import of British gold and silver into Indian markets
n67f6186b138.x: The Drain represented the transfer of India's wealth to England without a corresponding economic or material return.
n67f6186b138.tq: Apply the definition rather than selecting an associated but incorrect trade feature.
xs: The drain was **Indian wealth sent to England with no economic or material return** — option **(1)**.
India's **export surplus** brought **no gold or silver**; it paid British office and war expenses.
xa: The drain began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Components: **Home Charges**, interest, salaries and pensions, railway returns, military spending, profits.
**Unequal trade** was also a component.

n77a3da08cad.s: In response to the drain of wealth, the Moderates demanded:
n77a3da08cad.x: The Moderates demanded cuts in military spending, lower land revenue, abolition of the salt tax and protective tariffs.
xa: The drain also **shattered the myth of British benevolence**.
Drain meaning: wealth sent to England **with no economic or material return**; began with the **Diwani of Bengal (1765)**.
Naoroji's drain reason (APPSC-GS **2024**): **profits of British capitalists** — ⚠ NOT an excess of imports.

ned9072624ed.s: The interest component of the drain of wealth was interest on public debt raised in:
ned9072624ed.x: The interest was on public debt raised in Britain, not on loans from Indian peasants.
xa: **Guaranteed railway returns**: assured interest (**5%**) to British investors.
**Military expenditure** was the largest single budget head.
**Profits** of British capitalists, merchants and banks and **unequal trade** were also components.

n8d401edfa1f.s: British investors in Indian railways were guaranteed a return of:
n8d401edfa1f.x: Railway investors were guaranteed 5% whether or not the lines earned.
xa: **Home Charges**: India Office costs in London.
**Interest** on the public debt raised in Britain.
India's **export surplus** brought no gold or silver — it paid for British office and war expenses.

n20c00b36dd0.s: Which Act ended the Company's Indian trade monopoly and opened India to British machine-made goods?
n20c00b36dd0.x: The Charter Act of 1813 ended the Company's monopoly and opened India to British machine-made goods.
xa: Lancashire cloth was first offered in Bengal in **1786**; by **1793** Indian calicoes and muslins were displaced.
**Heavy duties** blocked Indian manufactures in Britain.
Causes per **B.D. Basu**: loss of patronage, free trade, raw-material export, internal **transit and customs duties**, railways.

nafc9f76bc09.s: The term “one-way free trade” in the context of Indian deindustrialisation refers to
o: Free export of Indian manufactures and prohibition of British imports
Low-duty entry of British goods into India while Indian goods faced heavy duties in Britain
Exclusive trade between Indian princely states
Equal tariff treatment for Indian and British manufactures
nafc9f76bc09.x: British goods entered India almost duty-free, whereas Indian manufactures faced heavy duties in Britain.
nafc9f76bc09.tq: Discriminate between equal free trade and an unequal tariff arrangement.
xs: **One-way free trade**: British goods entered India at **low duty** while Indian goods faced **heavy duties in Britain** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **Charter Act 1813**.
xa: By **1793** Indian calicoes and muslins were displaced.
Comparative note: IMF-World Bank **Structural Adjustment Programmes** caused deindustrialisation by the same logic.

na3bc0afea7d.s: Who said the British had 'inundated the very mother country of cotton with cottons'?
xa: Town handicrafts suffered a "**sudden and complete collapse**".
Famines also pushed weavers into agriculture or wage labour.
Artisans were even forced to divulge **trade secrets**.

n5eee719774a.s: What was the principal economic cause associated with the Ganjam famine of 1865–66?
o: The Company stopped collecting revenue in the Northern Circars.
Irrigation expansion caused rice prices to fall after the war.
Ryots shifted from cotton to paddy during the American Civil War.
Ryots shifted from paddy to cotton during the American Civil War, followed by a collapse in cotton prices.
n5eee719774a.x: During the American Civil War, ryots shifted from paddy to cotton. After the war, cotton prices collapsed and rice became scarce, contributing to the Ganjam famine.
n5eee719774a.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain instead of selecting an isolated crop or price statement.
xs: During the **American Civil War (1861-65)** Ganjam ryots switched **from paddy to cotton**, then **cotton prices collapsed** — option **(4)**.
Option 3 reverses the switch.
xa: After the war, rice was scarce — food shortage when demand ended (**1865**).
People migrated to **South Africa, Sri Lanka, Mauritius**.
In Ryotwari areas the cotton slump caused **defaults** and land loss to moneylenders.

nf48381f64e0.s: The Dutch set up their first factory in Andhra at:
nf48381f64e0.x: The Dutch set up their first Andhra factory at Machilipatnam, famous for chintz, dyed fabrics and muslins.
xa: ⚠ **Srikakulam** = muslin; **Eluru** = carpets; **Kurnool** = blankets; **Nellore** = towels.
**Uppada** = Jamdani silk; **Ponduru** = fine hand-spun **khadi**.
**Textiles** were the **second-largest employment after agriculture** in Andhra (APPSC-GS **2025**).

nd9fb807519c.s: India's export surplus under colonial rule was mainly used to:
o: bring gold and silver into India
meet British office and war expenses
nd9fb807519c.x: The export surplus did not bring matching gold or silver; it financed British office and war expenses.
xa: APPSC **2023** key: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
Colonial legacy: **deindustrialisation** + drain of wealth.

n2e3ca83a520.s: Which of the following was NOT a cause of deindustrialisation in India?
o: Railways carrying British goods into the interior
British traders being denied special privileges
Transit and customs duties hurting indigenous trade
Artisans being forced to reveal trade secrets
n2e3ca83a520.x: British traders actually received special privileges, so that statement is false.
xa: Causes are from **B.D. Basu**'s list.
Weavers were coerced by Company agents (**Bolt, 1772**).

n986c670963d.s: Under the Tinkathiya system, indigo had to be grown on ____ of each holding.
n986c670963d.x: Tinkathiya required indigo on 3/20 of each holding.
xa: Indigo regions: **Bengal**, **Bihar**; jute: **Bengal**; tea: **Assam**.
Peasants grew cash crops to pay the **cash revenue**, not by choice → **famines** frequent.
**Triangular trade:** Indian **opium to China** → Chinese **tea** to Britain → British **manufactures to India**.

n0fcacf7ad0d.s: In the triangular trade between India, China and Britain, India sent to China:
n0fcacf7ad0d.x: Indian opium went to China, Chinese tea and silver to Britain, and British manufactures to India.
xa: Opium regions: **Bengal-Bihar, Malwa**.
The **Suez Canal (1869)** tightened British control of trade.

nd01c5e50dca.s: Famines became frequent in areas of commercialised agriculture mainly because:
o: cash crops replaced food crops, reducing food security
nd01c5e50dca.x: Replacement of food crops by cash crops cut food security and made famines more frequent.
xa: **1854-1901**: **24** famines, about **29 million** deaths.
**Gajula Lakshmi Narasu Setti** reported famines from commercialisation in **"The Crescent"**.

nceb0c805d86.s: The Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) followed the:
nceb0c805d86.x: The Act, protecting peasants against moneylenders, followed the Deccan riots of 1875.
xa: The **cotton excise duty (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth is the classic "tariff policy" example.
The **Famine Code** of **1883** was based on the **Strachey** report.
Rigid cash demand drove ryots to **moneylenders (Mahajans)**.

nb3a7b510012.s: The Guntur famine of 1832-33 is known as:
nb3a7b510012.x: The Guntur famine of 1832-33 is called Dokkala or Nandana Karuvu.
xa: Missionary **John Clough**'s canal relief project = best-known relief effort.
⚠ Guntur famine = **1832-33**; **Kurnool** famine = **1866**.
**1876-78 Great Famine** devastated **Rayalaseema** and parts of coastal Andhra.

nd5c25ee0a57.s: Who fed the people during the Kurnool famine of 1866 and later received a gold medal from Queen Victoria?
nd5c25ee0a57.x: Budda Vengalareddy of Uyyalawada fed the people and received the medal on 1 January 1877.
xa: In the late 19th century Andhra had **11** famines; **1865-66** was the most severe.
**Ganjam**: ryots switched from paddy to **cotton** in the **American Civil War (1861-65)**; prices collapsed after it.
**Northern Coastal Famine (1945)**: **K.S. Gupta** formed a Famine Relief Committee.

n23e1ee9c2ad.s: Of the eleven famines Andhra suffered in the late 19th century, the most severe was that of:
n23e1ee9c2ad.x: Andhra suffered eleven famines in the late 19th century, 1865-66 being the most severe.
xa: The **Bengal famine 1943** killed about **3 million**.
The **1832-33 Guntur** famine (**Dokkala Karuvu**) killed about **2 lakh**.
**1876-78 Great Famine**: relief was **laissez-faire**.

ndd492febd42.s: The Famine Commission of 1880, whose report led to the Famine Code of 1883, was headed by:
ndd492febd42.x: Strachey's 1880 commission followed the 1876-78 famine and led to the 1883 Famine Code; Campbell was 1866, Lyall 1897-98, MacDonnell 1901.
xa: The **Famine Code** (**1883**) was based on the **Strachey** report.
Famine Commission chain: **Strachey** (Lytton) → **Lyall** (Elgin II) → **MacDonnell** (Curzon).
The **Hilton Young Commission (1926)** dealt with **currency**, not famine.

nc68ef6de5b4.s: The Famine Code, based on the report of the Richard Strachey Famine Commission, was issued in:
nc68ef6de5b4.x: The Famine Code was issued in 1883 on the basis of the Strachey Commission report (APPSC-G1 2022). 1866 is the Campbell Commission (Orissa famine), 1880 is when the Strachey Commission was appointed, and 1901 is the MacDonnell Commission.
xs: The **Famine Code** was issued in **1883**, based on the **Strachey** report — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
**1880** is the Strachey Commission itself; **1866** is Campbell; **1901** is MacDonnell.
xa: The Strachey Commission followed the Great Famine of **1876-78** (**Lytton**).

nf1c08f873c8.s: India's first jute mill was set up in 1855 at:
nf1c08f873c8.x: The first jute mill was set up at Rishra in Bengal in 1855.
xa: The first cotton mill was founded by **C.N. Davar** (**Cowasji Nanabhai Davar**).
**Nellore** district was the world leader in **manganese** (**1892-1929**); **mica** also from Nellore.
Andhra jute mills: **Chittivalasa and Nellimarla**; first Andhra railway **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.

n04d383e4d4e.s: The Hilton Young Commission (1926) fixed the rupee at:
n04d383e4d4e.x: It fixed the rupee at 1s 6d; Indian business wanted 1s 4d. Its central bank proposal led to the RBI (1935).
xa: **Purshottamdas Thakurdas** led Indian business opposition to the higher ratio.
The higher ratio made British imports cheaper and hurt Indian exporters.
⚠ Hilton Young = **1s 6d**; Indian demand = **1s 4d**.

n5cf285982b9.s: The higher rupee-sterling ratio (1s 6d) hurt Indian exporters because it:
o: made British imports dearer in India
n5cf285982b9.x: A higher ratio made Indian goods dearer abroad; it also made British imports cheaper, a separate effect.
xa: Hilton Young (**1926**) fixed **1s 6d**; Indian business wanted **1s 4d**.
The Commission also led to the **RBI (1935)**.

nb78e30cd9c8.s: Deindustrialisation in colonial India went along with an agriculture that remained:
nb78e30cd9c8.x: Indian industry declined through loss of markets while agriculture stayed stagnant with low productivity.
xa: India had a **strong industrial base** before British rule.
The economy was **agrarian**.

n59bc7d36f70.s: On the eve of independence, agriculture employed over 75% of the workforce but contributed about ____ of GDP.
n59bc7d36f70.x: Agriculture employed over 75% of workers but gave only about 50% of GDP, showing low productivity.
xa: Per-capita income: **Rs 265** a year (~**$60**).
Life expectancy **32 years**; literacy **under 16%** (female under **9%**).

n84f3a40053e.s: On the eve of independence, life expectancy in India was about:
n84f3a40053e.x: Per capita income was about Rs 265, life expectancy 32 years and literacy below 16%.
xa: Female literacy was under **9%**.
Per-capita income ~**$60** a year.

n7c09461bafb.s: Which of the following received top priority in the First Plan in response to the immediate economic challenges after independence?
o: Heavy engineering, automobiles and export subsidies
n7c09461bafb.x: Large foodgrain imports and inflation led the First Plan to give top priority to agriculture, irrigation and power. Post-partition stabilisation was another immediate challenge.
n7c09461bafb.tq: Link the policy priority with the immediate food and inflation problem.
xs: The **First Plan** gave top priority to **agriculture, irrigation, power** — option **(4)**.
This answered **large foodgrain imports and inflation**.
xa: Other challenge: **post-partition stabilisation**.
Agriculture had **over 75%** of the workforce but only about **50%** of GDP.

n57d79f55c2f.s: The cotton excise duty imposed during 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was intended to
o: promote the export of Indian handlooms to China
abolish all duties on Indian textiles
offset the import duty on British goods
n57d79f55c2f.x: The cotton excise duty of 1894–96 on Indian mill cloth was imposed to offset the import duty and is a classic example of tariff policy.
n57d79f55c2f.tq: Connect the date range with the purpose of the tariff measure.
xs: The **cotton excise duty (1894-96)** on Indian mill cloth was meant to **offset the import duty** on British goods — option **(3)**.
It is the classic example of colonial **tariff policy**.
xa: The Moderates demanded **protective tariffs** for Indian industry.
**Cotton mills** in Maharashtra and Gujarat were **Indian-owned**; jute mills were foreign-owned.

n50d72ee7e09.s: During the British period in Andhra, which sector provided the second-largest employment after agriculture?
n50d72ee7e09.x: Textiles provided the second-largest employment in Andhra after agriculture during the British period.
n50d72ee7e09.tq: Directly identify the sector associated with the stated employment rank.
xs: **Textiles** were Andhra's **second-largest employment after agriculture** in the British period — option **(4)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
**Machilipatnam** was the most famous handloom and textile port of the **16th-17th centuries**.
xa: Andhra products: **Srikakulam** muslin, **Uppada** jamdani silk, **Ponduru** khadi.
**Nellore** was the world leader in **manganese** (**1892-1929**).

n44b23e46b3e.s: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company, established in 1854, is associated with which person?
n44b23e46b3e.x: The Bombay Spinning and Weaving Company was established in 1854 by Cowasji Nanabhai Davar.
n44b23e46b3e.tq: Use the founder–enterprise association and reject names linked with other economic issues.
xs: The **Bombay Spinning and Weaving Co. (1854)** is linked to **Cowasji Nanabhai Davar** (C.N. Davar) — option **(3)**.
**Purshottamdas Thakurdas** argued for a **1s 4d** rupee; **Arthur Cotton** built anicuts.
xa: ⚠ First cotton mill = **Bombay 1854**; first jute mill = **Rishra 1855**.
Cotton mills were **Indian-owned** in **Maharashtra** and **Gujarat**.

n4b0204e7f69.s: The first railway in the Andhra region mentioned in the context of colonial industrial development was opened between:
n4b0204e7f69.x: The first railway was the Puttur-Renigunta line, opened in 1862.
n4b0204e7f69.tq: Use the exact terminal-pair distinction to avoid confusing railways with industrial centres.
xs: Andhra's first railway ran between **Puttur and Renigunta (1862)** — option **(3)**.
**Chittivalasa and Nellimarla** were jute mills, not a rail line.
xa: Railways guaranteed **5%** interest to British investors.
Railways carried raw materials out and British goods inland.

n824bc97912c.s: During 1892-1929, which district of the Andhra region was a world leader in the production of manganese?
n824bc97912c.x: Nellore district was the world leader in manganese during 1892-1929 (APHQ 2019 key; some sources credit Vizag). Kurnool, Anantapur and Guntur are associated with cotton ginning, not world-leading manganese output.
xs: **Nellore** district was the world leader in **manganese** in **1892-1929** — option **(3)** (APHQ **2019** key).
Some notes say **Vizag** district (world No.1 till **1929**).
xa: Nellore was also known for **mica**.
Nellore manganese + Andhra textiles = Andhra's examinable pair.
n824bc97912c.fixed: APPSC key: world-leading manganese district 1892-1929 = Visakhapatnam (y930a370c6da)

n44df11c95c6.s: On the eve of independence, foreign-owned jute mills were concentrated in:
n44df11c95c6.x: Indian-owned cotton mills were in Maharashtra and Gujarat, and foreign-owned jute mills in Bengal.
xa: In **1947**: per-capita income **Rs 265**; life expectancy **32 years**; literacy **under 16%**.
Over **75%** of the workforce was in agriculture, giving only about **50% of GDP**.
**Angus Maddison**: world income share fell from **27% (1700) to 3% (1950)** (APPSC-GS **2024**).

n6c10d54afb4.s: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the appointment of which commission?
n6c10d54afb4.x: The Orissa and Ganjam famine of 1865–66 led to the Campbell Commission.
n6c10d54afb4.tq: Link a famine directly with the commission appointed after it.
xs: The **Orissa and Ganjam famine (1865-66)** led to the **Campbell Commission** — option **(1)**.
Campbell (**1866**) was under Viceroy **John Lawrence** — the **first famine commission**.
xa: **MacDonnell** (**1901**, Curzon) followed the **1899-1900** famine.
**Lyall** followed the **1896-97** famine (**Elgin II**).
Last colonial commission: **Woodhead (1944)**.

n575b2458c61.s: The Great Famine of 1876-78, which affected Madras, Mysore, Hyderabad and Bombay, occurred under:
n575b2458c61.x: The Great Famine of 1876-78 occurred during Lytton's tenure.
xa: It devastated **Rayalaseema** and coastal Andhra.
The **Strachey Commission (1880)** followed, leading to the **Famine Code, 1883**.
**Sir Richard Temple** fixed the **Temple wage** in the **1877 Madras famine**.

n790a904265d.s: The Doji Bara famine occurred in:
n790a904265d.x: Doji Bara was in 1791-92, between the Great Bengal Famine (1770) and the Orissa-Ganjam famine (1865-66).
xa: **Chalisa** (**1783-84**) falls between the first two.
**Guntur** (**1832-33**) falls between Doji Bara and Orissa.

ne9f83459a6a.s: Which commission assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures against future famines?
ne9f83459a6a.x: The Lyall Commission assessed the causes of famine and recommended measures to prevent or mitigate future famines.
ne9f83459a6a.tq: Distinguish the commission’s function from its associated famine year.
xs: The **Lyall Commission** assessed the **causes** and recommended measures against **future famines** — option **(3)**.
It followed the **1896-97** famine under **Elgin II**.
**MacDonnell** stressed **early relief + more irrigation**; **Campbell** was the first (Orissa); **Woodhead** the last (Bengal **1943**).
xa: MacDonnell: **1901**, Curzon.
The **Famine Code (1883)** was framed on the **Strachey** Commission's recommendations.

nca03ee5db9e.s: What was the principal emphasis of the MacDonnell Commission?
nca03ee5db9e.x: The MacDonnell Commission stressed early relief and greater irrigation as measures against famine.
nca03ee5db9e.tq: Identify the policy recommendation rather than the commission’s name or date.
xs: The **MacDonnell Commission** stressed **early relief and more irrigation** — option **(1)**.
It came in **1901** under **Curzon**.
xa: R.C. Dutt wrote **"Open Letters to Lord Curzon"** (**1900**).
**Lyall** assessed causes and measures against future famines.

n2c127b263a4.s: During the Company period, famine policy was marked by:
o: a comprehensive famine code and extensive relief
no famine code and minimal relief
suspension of revenue in every famine
transfer of all relief to village councils
n2c127b263a4.x: The Company government never adopted a famine code and gave only minimal relief.
xa: The first Famine Code came only in **1883**.
Nationalists blamed **rigid revenue collection in drought** for famines.

ne8720ca321d.s: The last famine commission of the colonial period (1944) was the:
ne8720ca321d.x: The Woodhead Commission (1944) was the last; the Campbell Commission (1866) was the first.
xa: Campbell: Viceroy **John Lawrence**; Woodhead: **Wavell**.
In between: **Strachey (1880)**, **Lyall**, **MacDonnell (1901)**.

ndad2096b12c.s: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed primarily on the recommendations of which commission?
ndad2096b12c.x: The Famine Code of 1883 was framed on the recommendations of the Strachey Commission of 1880.
ndad2096b12c.tq: Link a policy code to the commission whose recommendations formed its basis.
xs: The **Famine Code, 1883** was framed on the **Strachey Commission (1880)** recommendations — option **(1)**.
**Campbell** (**1866**) came earlier; **Lyall** and **Woodhead** came later.
xa: Provisions: stages of scarcity and famine, **relief works**, **gratuitous relief**, revenue suspension or remission.
A **Famine Relief and Insurance Fund** was also set up.

n36af816fed6.s: Under the Famine Code, gratuitous relief was meant for:
n36af816fed6.x: The Code gave relief works for the able-bodied and gratuitous relief for the old and infirm.
xa: ⚠ **Relief works** = able-bodied; **gratuitous relief** = old and infirm.
It also created a **Famine Relief and Insurance Fund**.
The Code dates to **1883**, on the **Strachey** report.

ncc8cf750377.s: The Temple wage during the Madras famine of 1877 consisted approximately of which ration?
o: About 1 pound of grain a day on relief works
About 5 pounds of grain a day on relief works
One rupee a day without grain
A weekly ration of ten pounds of rice
ncc8cf750377.x: The Temple wage provided about 1 pound of grain per day on relief works and was criticised as a starvation wage.
ncc8cf750377.tq: Distinguish the exact quantitative ration from plausible but exaggerated alternatives.
xs: The **Temple wage** was **about 1 pound (1 lb) of grain a day** on relief works — option **(1)**.
**Sir Richard Temple** fixed it in the **1877 Madras famine**.
xa: It was criticised as a **starvation wage**.
Relief works gave employment on **roads and canals**.

nf45db32374c.s: The nationalist critique rejected the view that colonial famines were caused exclusively by:
nf45db32374c.x: Rigid revenue collection and grain exports were key causes; famines were not due to monsoon failure alone.
xa: Aggravators: **commercialisation** (cotton in **Ganjam**) + **laissez-faire** relief.
**Naoroji & R.C. Dutt** linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain**.

naa536113e0c.s: Who among the following linked Indian famines with high land revenue and the drain of wealth?
o: Dadabhai Naoroji and Sir Arthur Cotton
naa536113e0c.x: Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt connected famines with the burden of high land revenue and the drain of wealth.
naa536113e0c.tq: Use the thinker–argument association and reject combinations that mix a critic with an administrator or engineer.
xs: **Dadabhai Naoroji and R.C. Dutt** linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain** — option **(2)**.
**Arthur Cotton** was an irrigation engineer; **Curzon** was the Viceroy R.C. Dutt wrote to.
xa: R.C. Dutt wrote **"Open Letters to Lord Curzon"** (**1900**).
Nationalists blamed **export of food grains** too.

n204260e7749.s: 'Open Letters to Lord Curzon' (1900) was written by:
n204260e7749.x: R.C. Dutt's Open Letters to Lord Curzon dates to 1900.
xa: With **Naoroji** he linked famines to **high land revenue and the drain**.
The **MacDonnell Commission (1901)** came under **Curzon**.

nfd7768e1b52.s: Which Andhra official assisted Sir Arthur Cotton in building the Godavari anicut at Dowleswaram?
nfd7768e1b52.x: Veenam Veeranna was the Andhra official who helped Cotton build the Godavari dam (APPSC-G2 2019 key). Charles Orr supervised the Krishna anicut at Bezwada, Budda Vengalareddy fed people in the 1866 Kurnool famine and K.S. Gupta formed a relief committee in the 1945 famine.
xs: **Veenam Veeranna** helped Cotton build the Godavari dam — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2019** key).
**Charles Orr** supervised the **Krishna** anicut; **Budda Vengalareddy** fed people in the Kurnool famine; **K.S. Gupta** led **1945** relief.
xa: Cotton was born **15 May 1803**.
The Guntur famine convinced the Company irrigation was needed.

n010cdc92874.s: Which famine of 1833 gave the impetus for Cotton's Godavari anicut?
n010cdc92874.x: The Guntur famine of 1833 led to the construction of Cotton's Godavari anicut.

**Vedanta College** followed in **1825**.

nap-history-32-1.s: National College was established in which year and at which place?
nap-history-32-1.x: The National College, or Andhra Jatheeya Kalasala, was founded at Machilipatnam in 1910 to give nationalist and vocational education.
nap-history-32-1.tq: Recall the year and place of the National College.
n: National College was established in 1910. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
National College was located in Machilipatnam. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
xs: The **National College** (**Andhra Jatheeya Kalasala**) was set up in **1910** at **Machilipatnam** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Founders: **Hanumanta Rao**, **Krishna Rao** and **Pattabhi**; it gave **nationalist** and **vocational** education.
**1954, Tirupathi** is **Sri Venkateswara University**.
xa: The Machilipatnam National College was a centre of **Home Rule** protests (**1917**).
**Noble College** at Machilipatnam dates from **1843** (college in **1864**).
**Osmania University** (**1917**, also given as **1918**) used **Urdu** as medium.

nap-history-32-2.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly dated?
nap-history-32-2.x: Osmania University was founded by Mir Osman Ali Khan in 1917–18, not 1930; the other dates are correct.
n: Nizam College was established in 1887. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
Nizam College was located in Hyderabad. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
Osmania University was established in 1918. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
The school by Rev-Noble was established in 1843. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
The school by Rev-Noble was located in Machilipatnam. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
Madrasa-e-Aliya was established by Salarjung in 1873. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #32 · pp 43-44]
xa: Osmania was the **first Indian university** to use a **regional vernacular** — **Urdu** — for higher education.
Nizam College = merger of **Hyderabad School** and **Madrasa-i-Aliya**; linked with **Aghorenath Chattopadhyaya**.
**Andhra University** was inaugurated in **1926** at **Bezwada**.

nap-history-19-3.s: Andhra University, first started at Bezawada, was shifted to Waltair in:
nap-history-19-3.x: Constituted under the 1925 Act, it opened at Bezawada in 1926 and moved to Waltair in 1930.
n: The Andhra University Act was enacted in 1925. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Andhra University was inaugurated at Bezwada. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Andhra University was later located at Waltair. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
xa: Its **first Vice-Chancellor** was **C.R. Reddy**.
**Sri Venkateswara University** came in **1954** at **Tirupati**.
**Osmania University** was founded in **1917**.

nap-history-19-8.x: Kandukuri Veeresalingam founded the Vivekavardhini at Rajahmundry in 1874 to spread reform and women's education.
n: Kandukuri Veeresalingam founded Vivekavardhini Patasala/Sangham. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Vivekavardhini Patasala/Sangham was established in 1874. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Vivekavardhini Patasala/Sangham was located in Rajahmundry. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Kandukuri Veeresalingam** founded the **Vivekavardhini** (Patasala / Sangham) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was set up in **1874** at **Rajahmundry**.
It promoted **rationalism** and **female literacy** and **opposed** the **caste system**.
xa: Rajahmundry was the base of Veeresalingam's reform journalism.
Rajahmundry got a government second-grade college in **1873** and degree college in **1877**.
**Salar Jung I** founded the **Madrasa-e-Aliya** (**1873**).

nap-history-19-19.s: Sri Venkateswara University was established in which year at which place?
nap-history-19-19.x: Sri Venkateswara University was founded at Tirupati in 1954 by the Andhra State government under T. Prakasam to serve Rayalaseema.
nap-history-19-19.tq: Recall the year and place of SV University.
n: Sri Venkateswara University was established in 1954. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Sri Venkateswara University was located in Tirupati. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
T. Prakasam founded Sri Venkateswara University. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Sri Venkateswara University** was established in **1954** at **Tirupati** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was founded under **T. Prakasam** for **higher education** in **Rayalaseema**.
**1926 at Waltair**-type options refer to **Andhra University**; **1917 at Hyderabad** is **Osmania University**.
xa: **Andhra University Act** — **1925**; first VC **C.R. Reddy**.
**Nizam College** — **1887**, Hyderabad.
**Andhra Jatheeya Kalasala** — **1910**, Machilipatnam.

nap-history-19-28.s: Fergusson College (1885) was established by the:
nap-history-19-28.x: The Deccan Education Society, which promoted nationalist education, opened Fergusson College in 1885.
n: The Deccan Education Society promoted nationalist education. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
The Deccan Education Society established Fergusson College in 1885. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
CMS and Robert Turlington Noble founded Noble College/High School. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Noble College/High School provided early modern English education. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
xa: Deccan Education Society founders: **G.G. Agarkar** with **Tilak**, **Chiplunkar** and **Namjoshi**.
Noble's school became a college in **1864**.
⚠ **Noble** = Machilipatnam (**1843**); **G.N. Taylor** = Narsapur (**1852**).

nde0a11f1d62.s: Which missionary organisation was the first missionary body to spread Western education in Andhra?
nde0a11f1d62.x: The London Missionary Society was the first missionary body associated with the spread of Western education in Andhra. It began its work in 1805.
nde0a11f1d62.tq: Directly identify the earliest organisation from a group of closely related missionary bodies.
xs: The **London Missionary Society** was the first missionary body (**1805**) — option **(4)**.
**Kadapa** became its centre in **1824**.
xa: **North German Society**: Rajahmundry and Eluru (**1843**).
**Church Missionary Society**: **Machilipatnam** (**Rev. Robert Noble**).
**American Baptists**: Rayalaseema, **Ongole** and **Nellore**.

n49cd384c322.s: The London Missionary Society had its Andhra centre (1824) at:
n49cd384c322.x: The LMS centred on Kadapa (1824); Lutherans worked in Guntur, the North German Society in Rajahmundry-Eluru and the American Baptists in Ongole-Nellore.
xa: The **LMS** was the first missionary body (**1805**); Kadapa centre in **1824**.
The **Church Missionary Society** worked at **Machilipatnam**.
Mission schools admitted **Sudras and Panchamas**.

n0fba476c0a4.s: Who contributed most to the early spread of Western education in Andhra?
n0fba476c0a4.x: Western education in Andhra was first spread by Christian missionaries (APPSC key), beginning with the London Missionary Society in 1805 and followed by the CMS, North German, Lutheran and American Baptist missions. Zamindars, the Mahajana Sabha and karanams were not the pioneers.
n0fba476c0a4.tq: Western education in Andhra = missionaries first (LMS 1805).
xs: Western education in Andhra was first spread by **Christian missionaries** — option **(2)** (APPSC key for "who contributed most").
The **London Missionary Society (1805)** was the first missionary body.
xa: Mission schools admitted **Sudras and Panchamas**.
Wood's **grants-in-aid** encouraged largely **missionary** enterprise.

nba4c84a07d5.s: Which educational policy approach was criticised for neglecting mass literacy?
nba4c84a07d5.x: The downward filtration approach was criticised because it prioritised educating a limited section and neglected mass literacy.
nba4c84a07d5.tq: Match the criticism with the exact policy term rather than a general education objective.
xs: **Downward filtration** was criticised for **neglecting mass literacy** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It educated a small upper section in **English**, expecting knowledge to filter down to the masses, which left **primary education** weak.
**Compulsory primary education** was in fact a later demand: **Gokhale's** demand drew the **1913 Resolution on Education Policy**.
xa: **Hunter (1882)** and **Hartog (1929)** kept returning to **primary education** to correct this neglect.
**Sargent Plan (1944)** proposed **universal free compulsory education** for **6-14** years.
English education still created the **reformist middle class** of coastal Andhra, e.g. **Kandukuri Veeresalingam**.
⚠ **English Education Act 1835** (Bentinck + Macaulay) made **English** the medium of higher education.

nindian-history-124-2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Hunter Commission of 1882?
o: It was associated with W.W. Hunter.
nindian-history-124-2.x: Famine policy was the work of the Strachey Commission; the Hunter Commission under W.W. Hunter dealt with education.
n: The Hunter Commission was chaired by W.W. Hunter. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Hunter Commission was formed in 1882. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Hunter Commission focused on education. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Strachey Commission focused on famine policy. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
xa: Hunter focus: **primary and secondary education**; schools handed to **local boards and municipalities**.
⚠ The **Hunter Committee** (**1919**) = **Jallianwala Bagh** inquiry.
The **Campbell Commission** (**1866**) conducted the **Orissa famine** inquiry.

nindian-history-124-3.s: The Campbell Commission belongs to the era of:
nindian-history-124-3.x: The Campbell Commission belongs to the Sir John Lawrence era.
n: The Campbell Commission was associated with the era of Sir John Lawrence. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Hunter Commission was chaired by W.W. Hunter. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Strachey Commission was chaired by Sir Richard Strachey. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
The Raleigh University Commission was chaired by Thomas Raleigh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
xa: Campbell (**1866**) = famine inquiry, especially the **Orissa famine**.
Strachey (**1878**) = **famine policy**, basis for the **Famine Code**.
Raleigh (**1902**) was appointed by **Curzon**.

nindian-history-124-12.s: Who chaired the Royal Commission on Agriculture (1926)?
nindian-history-124-12.x: Lord Linlithgow chaired the Royal Commission on Agriculture in 1926; Butler, Hunter and Lee headed other inquiries.
n: The Royal Commission on Agriculture was chaired by Lord Linlithgow. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #124 · pp 226-227]
xa: **Lee Commission**: **1924**.
**Butler Committee**: **1927**, **paramountcy**.
**Whitley Commission** (**1929**): labour conditions.

nap-history-19-1.x: Salar Jung I, the reforming Diwan of Hyderabad, founded the Madrasa-e-Aliya in 1873. Mir Osman Ali Khan founded Osmania University.
nap-history-19-1.tq: Recall the founder of the Madrasa-e-Aliya.
n: Madrasa-e-Aliya was founded by Salar Jung I. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Madrasa-e-Aliya was established in 1873. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
Madrasa-e-Aliya was located in Hyderabad. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 27-29]
xs: **Salar Jung I** (**Salarjung**) founded the **Madrasa-e-Aliya** in **1873** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It served the **sons of nobility** and of **Paigah families** in **Hyderabad**.
**Mir Osman Ali Khan** founded **Osmania University**; **T. Prakasam** is linked with **Sri Venkateswara University**.
xa: In **1887** it merged with the **Hyderabad School** to form **Nizam College**.
**Aghorenath Chattopadhyaya** is associated with Nizam College.
Osmania (**1917**) used **Urdu** as the medium.

nc6d1942726b.s: The first railway line in Andhra (1862) was:
nc6d1942726b.x: Puttur-Renigunta (1862) was Andhra's first line; South India's first ran Royapuram-Wallajah Road in 1856.
xa: The first train ran on **16 April 1853**, covering **34 km** with a **14-coach train** and three steam locomotives.
**Dalhousie's Railway Minute (1853)** planned a trunk-line network.
Nine lines were laid in Andhra during **1871-1900**.
⚠ **Dalhousie** = railways, post and telegraph; **Mayo** = state railways.
nc6d1942726b.fixed: statement 1 'That line' had no referent; answer unchanged (Madras Railway ran it)

n996e5395cc0.s: Dalhousie's Railway Minute of 1853 primarily provided for:
o: Free railway travel for Indian cultivators
The transfer of railway ownership to municipalities
A network of trunk lines serving military, commercial and administrative purposes
The abolition of private railway companies
n996e5395cc0.x: Dalhousie's Railway Minute of 1853 set out a trunk-line network for military, commercial and administrative purposes.
n996e5395cc0.tq: Link a policy document with its stated administrative objectives.
xs: **Dalhousie's Railway Minute (1853)** planned a **network of trunk lines** for **military, commercial and administrative** ends — so option **(3)** is correct.
Lines were actually built by **private British companies** under a guarantee, so the Minute did not abolish them.
xa: The same year, the first passenger train ran **Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane** on **16 April 1853**.
Companies got a guaranteed **5%** return on capital from Indian revenues.
⚠ **Dalhousie** = railways, post and telegraph; **Mayo** = state railways.
**Post Office Act 1854** (Dalhousie): uniform low postage rates + postage stamps.

ne571b002dfb.s: An unintended effect of railways in colonial India was:
o: the creation of a national market
ne571b002dfb.x: Railways served colonial exploitation but unintentionally created a national market and sped nationalist mobilisation.
xa: Other unintended effects: **shared public travel across castes** and faster **pan-Indian** mobilisation.
British companies got a guaranteed **5%** return paid from Indian revenues.
Nationalists counted the guaranteed interest in the **"drain"** of wealth.

n7dd0349a9bb.s: The Post Office Act of 1854, which introduced uniform postage and stamps, is associated with:
n7dd0349a9bb.x: The 1854 Post Office Act is associated with Dalhousie.
xa: Dalhousie is credited with **railways, post and telegraph** together.
⚠ **1854** also = **Wood's Despatch** (Dalhousie); **1853** = Railway Minute.
**John Lawrence** opened telegraph communication with **Europe (1864-69)**.

nc2386f87a0d.s: India's first telegraph line (1851), under W.B. O'Shaughnessy, ran from Calcutta to:
nc2386f87a0d.x: The first line ran Calcutta-Diamond Harbour in 1851.
xa: Telegraph trunk lines linked **Calcutta, Peshawar, Bombay and Madras** by the mid-1850s.
**Post Office Act 1854** (Dalhousie): uniform low postage rates + **postage stamps**.
⚠ **1851** = first telegraph; **1853** = first passenger train; **1854** = Post Office Act.

nff1c3c8c988.s: Which journal was associated with Kandukuri Veeresalingam?
nff1c3c8c988.x: Veeresalingam ran Vivekavardhini, Hasyasanjivani and Sati Hitabodhini; Andhra Kesari was Gadicherla's.
xa: His other journals: **Satyasamvardhini (1891)** and **Zenana Patrika (1894)**.
Gadicherla's others: **Navayugam**, **Matru Seva**, **Panchayati Rajyam**.
**Chilakamarti** = **Desamata**.

n97d4d869e41.s: Desamata, which supported the Home Rule movement, was the paper of:
n97d4d869e41.x: Desamata of Chilakamarti supported Home Rule with Andhra Patrika and Krishna Patrika.
xa: **Gadicherla Harisarvottama Rao** ran **Andhra Kesari**, **Navayugam**, **Matru Seva**, **Panchayati Rajyam**.
**Andhra Prakasika** (**A.P. Parthasarathy Naidu**) was the **first political magazine of Andhra**.
**Hitavadi** (**1848**, **Masulipatnam**) was founded by **J. Edmund Sharky**.

n7b1ee8015b6.s: The Registration Act of 1867, dealing with printers and presses, is associated with:
n7b1ee8015b6.x: The 1867 Act on registration of printers and presses came under John Lawrence.
xa: It was replaced by the **Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023**, w.e.f. **1 March 2024**.
The RNI is now the **Press Registrar General of India**.
John Lawrence also opened telegraph links with **Europe (1864-69)**.

n2268f7ad2f9.s: Macaulay wrote his Minute (1835) as Law Member and President of the:
n2268f7ad2f9.x: Macaulay led the Anglicists and wrote the Minute as Law Member and GCPI President; Bentinck approved it.
xa: Bentinck is called the **"Father of Modern Western Education in India"**.
Orientalists: **H.T. Colebrooke**, **H.H. Wilson**; in Madras **Thomas Munro** backed vernacular schooling.
**Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education (1826)** found a wide network of village schools.

nd84cbd51fc9.s: Macaulay's Minute (1835) recommended that education funds be spent only on:
o: English-medium teaching of Western science and literature
nd84cbd51fc9.x: The Minute wanted funds spent only on English-medium Western science and literature.
xa: Famous remark: "a **single shelf** of a good European library was worth the whole native literature of India and Arabia" (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**Downward Filtration Theory**: educate a few upper-class Indians → knowledge filters to the masses.
The **1835** Resolution banned regional-language instruction in Madras district schools.

n7c239e93e01.s: The General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) was set up mainly to:
n7c239e93e01.x: The GCPI managed education funds; it was not a teacher-training body.
xa: The 1813 Act also **allowed missionaries**.
**Macaulay** was later President of the General Committee of Public Instruction.

n24165f52a3e.s: Which is called the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India'?
n24165f52a3e.x: Wood's Despatch (1854) is the Magna Carta; universities followed in 1857.
xa: Wood's Despatch introduced **grants-in-aid** and a vernacular primary → Anglo-vernacular → university ladder.
Wood's Despatch rejected **downward filtration**, asking for mass instruction.
**1882** under **Ripon** also saw the **repeal of the VPA** and the **Local Self-Government** Resolution.

n20b7d871a39.s: The statutory basis of the Press Council is the Press Council Act of:
n20b7d871a39.x: The Press Council rests on the Press Council Act, 1978, and still lacks punitive powers.
xa: India ranked **157th of 180** in the World Press Freedom Index **2026**.
RNI is now the **Press Registrar General of India**.

nd6fa6c556b7.s: Under the railway guarantee system, the 5% return to British companies was paid:
o: from Indian revenues whether or not the lines made a profit
only when the lines made a profit
nd6fa6c556b7.x: The guarantee was paid from Indian revenues regardless of profit, and nationalists counted it in the drain.
xa: Main motive of railways: **colonial exploitation** — troop movement, raw materials to ports, British manufactures inland.
Railways also moved grain for **famine relief**.
Unintended effects: a **national market**, shared travel across castes, faster **nationalist mobilisation**.

nindian-history-135-19.s: The colonial economic purpose of railways was to carry raw materials to the ports and:
nindian-history-135-19.x: Railways carried raw materials to ports for export and British goods into Indian markets.
n: The colonial economic purpose of railway development was to transport raw materials to ports. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #135 · pp 238-239]
The colonial economic purpose of railway development was to transport British goods to Indian markets. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #135 · pp 238-239]
xa: Officially railways were meant for **faster movement**, **communication**, **administration** and **troop movement**.
Guaranteed interest on railways was counted in the **"drain"** of wealth.
Unintended effect: an integrated **national market**.

nindian-history-8-13.s: Debendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh were associated with which journal?
nindian-history-8-13.x: Indian Mirror was started in Calcutta in 1861 by Debendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh. The Commonweal was Annie Besant's, Free Hindustan Tarak Nath Das's and The People Lala Lajpat Rai's.
nindian-history-8-13.tq: Recall the founders of Indian Mirror.
n: Devendranath Tagore and Manmohan Ghosh were associated with Indian Mirror. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
xs: **Indian Mirror** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was published in **Calcutta** from **1861** by **Devendranath Tagore** and **Manmohan Ghosh**.
xa: **Hindoo Patriot** (**1853**) and **The Bengalee** (**1862**) were started by **Girish Chandra Ghosh**.
**Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq** (**1870**, Urdu) — **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan**.
Annie Besant's **Commonweal** and **New India** paid security deposits under the Press Act.

ncfb5f5fc02f.s: Which newspaper is regarded as the first political magazine of Andhra?
ncfb5f5fc02f.x: Andhra Prakasika, associated with A.P. Parthasarathy Naidu, is identified as the first political magazine of Andhra.
ncfb5f5fc02f.tq: Distinguish a specific description from closely related newspaper names.
xs: **Andhra Prakasika**, of **A.P. Parthasarathy Naidu**, was the **first political magazine of Andhra** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Vivekavardhini (1874)** was **Veeresalingam's** reform journal; **Andhra Patrika** and **Krishna Patrika** were Home Rule-era supportive papers.
xa: ⚠ First newspaper of India = **Bengal Gazette (1780)**; first printing press = **Goa (1556)**.
Early Telugu journals: **Satyaduta (1835)**, **Vrittanti (1837-38)**, **Vartamana Tarangini (1842)**, **Hitavadi (1848)**.
Telugu journalism dates **from 1835**.

n4d74e9b1a43.s: Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by:
o: G. Subramania Iyer and M. Veeraraghavachariar
Sisir Kumar Ghosh and Motilal Ghosh
n4d74e9b1a43.x: Amrita Bazar Patrika was founded by the Ghosh brothers; The Hindu by Subramania Iyer and others; Kesari by Tilak.
xa: The Hindu: **Madras, 1878**, English.
Amrita Bazar Patrika became an **English** paper overnight (**1878**) to escape the **VPA**.
**Sambad Kaumudi** = **Ram Mohan Roy**; **Andhra Prakasika** = **A.P. Parthasarathy Naidu**.

na4063431023.s: India's first newspaper, the Bengal Gazette (Calcutta General Advertiser) of 1780, was started by:
na4063431023.x: James Augustus Hicky started the Bengal Gazette on 29 January 1780, India's first newspaper. Ram Mohan Roy ran Sambad Kaumudi, Surendranath Banerjea The Bengalee, and Sisir Kumar Ghosh (with Motilal Ghosh) the Amrita Bazar Patrika.
xs: **James Augustus Hicky** started the **Bengal Gazette**, India's first newspaper, on **29 January 1780** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Ram Mohan Roy** ran **Sambad Kaumudi**; **Surendranath Banerjea** ran **The Bengalee**; **Sisir Kumar Ghosh** (with Motilal) ran **Amrita Bazar Patrika**.
xa: It was also called the **Calcutta General Advertiser**.
⚠ First printing press = **Goa (1556)**, by **Portuguese Jesuits**.
First political magazine of Andhra = **Andhra Prakasika**.

n4c10f025162.x: Mirat-ul-Akhbar was in Persian; Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq was in Urdu and Sambad Kaumudi in Bengali.
xa: Roy shut **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** in protest against the **Licensing Regulations** of **1823**.
The first newspaper was **Hicky's Bengal Gazette** (**29 January 1780**).
**Samachar Chandrika** (**Bhavani Charan Bandyopadhyay**) opposed Rammohan Roy.

nce058eed195.s: In the education debate, the Orientalists favoured:
o: classical Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning
nce058eed195.x: Orientalists backed Sanskrit, Arabic and Persian learning; Anglicists backed Western science and English.
xa: Orientalists: **H.T. Colebrooke**, **H.H. Wilson**; in Madras **Thomas Munro**.
Anglicists: **T.B. Macaulay** (leader), **Bentinck**, **Charles Trevelyan**.
Macaulay's Minute (**1835**) settled the debate for English.

n49de7134296.s: Udant Martand of Jugal Kishore Shukla was the first ____ newspaper.
n49de7134296.x: Udant Martand was the first Hindi newspaper.
xa: Roy's **Sambad Kaumudi** (**1821**) was in Bengali; **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** (**1822**) in Persian.
**Hindoo Patriot** (**1853**) was associated with the **Indigo Movement**.
Som Prakash was a target of the **Vernacular Press Act**.

nindian-history-8-8.s: Hindoo Patriot was started in 1853 by:
nindian-history-8-8.x: Girish Chandra Ghosh started Hindoo Patriot in 1853; Harish Chandra Mukherjee later edited it.
n: Girish Chandra Ghosh started Hindoo Patriot. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Hindoo Patriot was started in 1853. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Girish Chandra Ghosh started The Bengalee. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
The Bengalee was started in 1862. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Harish Chandra Mukherjee was associated with Hindoo Patriot. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Harish Chandra Mukherjee was the editor of Hindoo Patriot. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Hindoo Patriot was associated with the Indigo Movement. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
Girish Chandra Ghosh was associated with The Bengalee. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 46-50]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say **The Bengalee** was founded by **Surendranath Banerjea**.
**Indian Mirror** (**1861**) — **Devendranath Tagore** and **Manmohan Ghosh**.
**The Pioneer** (**1865**, **Allahabad**) — **George Allen**.

nd2044d90d2e.s: The Licensing Regulations of 1823, which penalised printing without a licence, were issued by acting Governor-General:
nd2044d90d2e.x: Acting G-G John Adams issued them; Metcalfe repealed them in 1835 and became 'liberator of the Indian press'.
xa: **Ram Mohan Roy** shut **Mirat-ul-Akhbar** in protest.
Earlier: **Censorship of Press Act (1799)**, **Wellesley**.

n0fee0abef98.s: The Indian press enjoyed relative freedom after the 1835 measure of:
n0fee0abef98.x: Metcalfe's 1835 measure freed the press; Lytton's 1878 Act gagged it until Ripon's 1882 repeal.
xa: **Metcalfe** = "liberator of the Indian press".
**Lytton's** VPA = "**Gagging Act**"; **Ripon** repealed it.
**1908** = Newspapers (Incitement to Offences) Act; **1910** = Indian Press Act.

n69608565c76.s: Thomas Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education in 1826 found:
o: No organised system of village education in Madras
A complete absence of pathashalas in rural areas
Only English-medium colleges in the presidency towns
A wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency
n69608565c76.x: Munro's 1826 survey found a wide network of vernacular village schools in the Madras Presidency.
n69608565c76.tq: Use the survey's empirical finding to reject absolute claims about indigenous education.
xs: **Munro's Survey of Indigenous Education (1826)** found a **wide network of vernacular village schools** in the **Madras Presidency** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So options claiming no system or no pathashalas are wrong; Munro himself **backed pathashalas and vernacular schooling**.
xa: Munro is counted on the **Orientalist** side, in Madras.
Munro's collectorate and tahsildari schools (**2** in Kadapa, **1** Nellore, **2** Vizag by **1830**) were closed in **1836**.
The **1835 Resolution** banned regional-language instruction in Madras district schools.

n10f0b4fa169.s: The English newspaper Justice was edited by:
n10f0b4fa169.x: Justice was an English newspaper edited by T.M. Nair.
xa: **The Hindu** (Madras, **1878**, English) was founded by **G. Subramania Iyer** and **M. Veeraraghavachariar**.
**The Bengalee** (English) = **Surendranath Banerjea**; **Kesari** (Marathi) = **Tilak**.
**Sambad Kaumudi** (Bengali) = **Ram Mohan Roy**.

na80903ac3ef.s: The Vernacular Press Act of 1878 was introduced in the background of:
o: The Swadeshi movement and the First Factory Act
The famine of 1876–77 and the lavish Delhi Durbar of 1877
The Revolt of 1857 and the Ilbert Bill controversy
The Permanent Settlement and the Regulating Act
na80903ac3ef.x: The Act was passed by Lord Lytton amid public anger over the 1876–77 famine and the lavish Delhi Durbar held in 1877.
na80903ac3ef.tq: Connect a law with its immediate political and economic context.
xs: The VPA came amid anger over the **1876-77 famine** and the lavish **Delhi Durbar (1877)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was passed by **Lord Lytton**.
xa: It was nicknamed the **"Gagging Act"**.
It applied only to **Indian-language** papers, not English ones.
Repealed in **1882** by **Ripon**.

n0124525efc9.s: Under the Vernacular Press Act, 1878, a paper could obtain exemption by:
o: paying a fine to the magistrate
submitting proofs to a government censor before publication
n0124525efc9.x: Exemption came by submitting proofs to a censor; magistrates could demand bonds and there was no appeal to a court.
xa: Magistrates could also demand forfeitable **security deposits** and **seize presses** for repeat offences.
Targets: **Som Prakash, Bharat Mihir, Dacca Prakash, Samachar**.

n604cac3c82b.s: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the Vernacular Press Act, 1878?
o: Security deposits could be demanded and forfeited
There was no appeal to a court of law
Presses could be seized for repeated offences
English-language newspapers were subjected to the same restrictions
n604cac3c82b.x: The Act was discriminatory: it applied to Indian-language papers and not to English-language newspapers. The other three were provisions of the Act.
n604cac3c82b.tq: Find the exception by testing the discriminatory scope of the law.
xs: The VPA did **not** cover **English-language newspapers** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
It was **discriminatory**: it applied only to **Indian-language** papers.
**Security deposits**, **no appeal** and **seizure of presses** were all real provisions.
xa: **Amrita Bazar Patrika** turned **English** overnight to escape it.
Passed by **Lytton** (**1878**); repealed by **Ripon** (**1882**).

n7d3b3c7da47.s: Which paper turned itself into an English paper overnight to escape the Vernacular Press Act?
n7d3b3c7da47.x: Amrita Bazar Patrika became English overnight; The Hindu was already in English.
xa: The VPA was **Lord Lytton**'s **"Gagging Act"**, passed amid anger over the **1876-77 famine** and the **Delhi Durbar (1877)**.
It applied to Indian-language papers, **not English ones**; **no appeal** to a court of law.
**Som Prakash** was associated with **Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar**.

n16be836e2b9.s: After the Vernacular Press Act was repealed in 1882, the pre-censorship clause was dropped and ____ was appointed.
n16be836e2b9.x: Ripon's repeal dropped pre-censorship and a press commissioner was appointed.
xa: Under the VPA, **district magistrates** could demand **bonds** and **security deposits** and **seize presses**.
After the repeal came about **25 years** of relative freedom, until the **1908** and **1910** Acts.

nindian-history-7-17.s: Which English daily was founded by Swaminathan Sadanand in Bombay?
nindian-history-7-17.x: Swaminathan Sadanand founded the Free Press Journal, an English daily, in Bombay in 1930. Vande Matram was Bipin Pal and Aurobindo's Calcutta paper, Indian Nation came from Patna and Kesari was Tilak's Marathi paper.
nindian-history-7-17.tq: Use the founder and city in the stem to pick the paper.
n: Swaminathan Sadanand was associated with the Free Press Journal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 45-46]
The Free Press Journal was an English daily. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 45-46]
xs: **Swaminathan Sadanand** founded the **Free Press Journal**, an **English daily** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Kesari** (Marathi) was **Bal Gangadhar Tilak**'s paper.
xa: **Mook Nayak** — **B.R. Ambedkar** (**1920**).
**Qaumi Awaz** (**1945**, Lucknow) — **Nehru** and **Rafi Ahmed Kidwai**.
**Justice** (English, **1917**) was edited by **T.M. Nair**.

nindian-history-109-19.s: Which English weekly was started by Maulana Muhammad Ali in 1911?
nindian-history-109-19.x: Muhammad Ali started the English weekly Comrade in Calcutta in 1911. Sanjibani and Sandhya were Bengali papers, and Al-Hilal was Abul Kalam Azad's Urdu weekly.
nindian-history-109-19.tq: Match the founder and language given in the stem.
n: Comrade was associated with nationalist journalism. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #109 · pp 201-202]
xs: **Maulana Muhammad Ali** started **Comrade** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Comrade stood for **nationalist journalism**.
**Al-Hilal** (**1912**) was **Abul Kalam Azad**'s **Urdu** journal.
xa: **Dash Roja** — **Abdul Ghaffar Khan**.
**Qaumi Awaz** — **1945**, **Lucknow**.
**Tahzeeb-ul-Akhlaq** — **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** (**1870**).

n6e25d47c4b1.s: Telugu journalism is traced to the year:
n6e25d47c4b1.x: Telugu journalism dates from 1835, with Machilipatnam and Rajahmundry as early centres.
xa: AP angle: **Andhra Prakasika**, **Krishna Patrika**, **Andhra Patrika**; **Puttur-Renigunta (1862)**.
**Madras University** dates to **1857**.
**Hitavadi** came from **Masulipatnam (1848)**.

nc0bd4f11e7c.s: The first printing press in India was introduced by the:
nc0bd4f11e7c.x: Portuguese Jesuits introduced the first printing press in India at Goa in 1556.
nc0bd4f11e7c.tq: Identify the institution or group responsible for a historical introduction.
xs: The first printing press in India was set up at **Goa in 1556** by the **Portuguese Jesuits** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The first newspaper came much later: **Bengal Gazette**, **29 January 1780**, by **James Augustus Hicky**.
xa: ⚠ First printing press = **Goa (1556)**; first newspaper = **Bengal Gazette (1780)**.
First political magazine of Andhra = **Andhra Prakasika** (A.P. Parthasarathy Naidu).
First Telugu journal in the notes: **Satyaduta (1835)**.

nb6fb743c849.s: Which of the following best describes the Downward Filtration Theory?
o: A small upper class should first be educated so that learning would filter down to the masses
Education should begin with village schools and move upward to universities
Traditional learning should filter into English institutions through translation
Primary education should be universal before higher education is introduced
nb6fb743c849.x: The theory proposed educating a small upper class first, expecting knowledge to descend or filter down to the wider population.
nb6fb743c849.tq: Translate the policy theory into its practical educational sequence.
xs: **Downward Filtration**: educate a **few upper-class Indians** so knowledge **filters down to the masses** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Starting from village schools upward is the reverse — that was the ladder of **Wood's Despatch**, which **rejected** downward filtration.
xa: The theory relates to **education** (**APPSC-G2 2024**).
Wood's Despatch asked the Company to take up **mass instruction**.
It grew from **Macaulay's Minute (1835)**.

nd076dc4098e.s: Wood's Despatch rejected the ____ approach to education.
nd076dc4098e.x: Wood's Despatch recommended grants-in-aid and mass instruction and rejected downward filtration.
xa: Called the **"Magna Carta of English Education in India"**; dated **1854**, under **Dalhousie**.
Ladder: **vernacular primary** → **Anglo-vernacular high school** → **university**.
Universities of **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** followed in **1857**.

n9fb397c6b05.s: The Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023 replaced the Press and Registration of Books Act of:
n9fb397c6b05.x: The 2023 Act replaced the 1867 Act; the RNI is now the Press Registrar General of India.
xa: The **1867 Registration Act** came under **John Lawrence**.
