India ranked **157th of 180** in the **World Press Freedom Index 2026**.

nf3a58f6d8d0.s: The College of Fort William was established at Calcutta in 1800 primarily for which of the following purposes?
o: Administering the Provincial Public Service Commission
Conducting the first simultaneous ICS examination
Training only Indian judges in customary law
Training recruits of the Company's civil service
nf3a58f6d8d0.x: Wellesley established the College of Fort William at Calcutta in 1800 to train recruits of the Company's civil service.
nf3a58f6d8d0.tq: Match the institution with its specific administrative function and founder.
xs: **Wellesley** founded the **College of Fort William**, Calcutta (**1800**) for **training recruits** of the Company's civil service — so option **(4)** is correct.
Simultaneous ICS exams in India began only in **1922**; PSCs came under the **GoI Act 1935**.
xa: It was replaced by the **East India College, Haileybury** (England) by **1806**.
Haileybury taught **law, political economy** and **Indian languages**.
**Cornwallis** = "Father of Civil Services in India".

nf6aa26aca1c.s: The Macaulay Committee recommended that the civil service examination be held in:
nf6aa26aca1c.x: It recommended the examination in London and preference for Oxford and Cambridge graduates.
xa: The report is dated **1854** (some texts give **1855**).
**Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** backed the open competitive examination.
Patronage of the Company's **Directors** lasted **till 1853** (APPSC **2018**).

nf43de5441c1.s: The Indian Civil Services Act of 1861 allowed limited Indian entry mainly into:
nf43de5441c1.x: The 1861 Act allowed limited Indian entry, mainly into uncovenanted posts, subject to conditions such as seven years' residence and a local-language examination.
xa: Next step: **Statutory Civil Service** (**1878-79**, **Lytton**) — **1/6** of covenanted posts to Indians of "high families".
**Aitchison Commission (1886)** dropped covenanted/uncovenanted terms.
First Indian in the ICS: **Satyendranath Tagore (1864)**.

ne3d11ea1fd8.s: The reduction of the maximum age for the civil service examination to 19 years in 1878 was associated with the tenure of:
ne3d11ea1fd8.x: The maximum age was reduced to 19 in 1878 during the tenure of Lord Lytton, and this became an important Indian grievance.
ne3d11ea1fd8.tq: Link the numerical change to the Viceroy in office when it occurred.
xs: The maximum age was cut to **19** in **1878** under **Lord Lytton** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Dufferin** appointed the **Aitchison Commission (1886)**, which raised the limit to **23**; **Hardinge II** = **Islington**; **Reading** = **Lee**.
xa: It was a key **Indian grievance**; the INC demanded to **raise the age limit** from **1885**.
Lytton also set up the **Statutory Civil Service** (**1878-79**).

nda72de6e5a3.s: The patronage of the Company's Directors over civil service appointments was abolished, and open competitive examination introduced, by the:
nda72de6e5a3.x: Appointments were made by the Directors' patronage until 1853. The Charter Act of 1853 replaced patronage with open competition, with support from Trevelyan and Robert Lowe. The 1833 Act came before this change, the 1861 Act let Indians into mainly uncovenanted posts, and the 1858 Act transferred power to the Crown.
xs: The **Charter Act 1853** abolished **patronage** and brought **open competitive examination** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Patronage of the Company's **Directors** lasted **till 1853**; the **1861 Act** opened mainly **uncovenanted** posts to Indians.
xa: **Trevelyan** and **Robert Lowe** backed the open exam.
**Macaulay Committee (1854)**: exams in **London**, preference for Oxford/Cambridge graduates.
Patronage till **1853** was asked in **APPSC 2018**.

n3fe00162247.s: Who was the first Indian to enter the Indian Civil Service?
n3fe00162247.x: Satyendranath Tagore became the first Indian in the ICS in 1864 (many texts say 1863). Ram Mohan Roy, in 1832, was the first to demand Indians in higher posts. Surendranath Banerjea and Dadabhai Naoroji are not the 'first Indian ICS' answer.
xs: **Satyendranath Tagore** was the **first Indian in the ICS** (**1864**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Raja Ram Mohan Roy** (**1832**) was the first Indian to **demand** Indians in higher posts, not to enter the ICS.
xa: ⚠ Many texts give **1863** for Tagore.
The INC demanded **simultaneous examinations** from its first session (**1885**).
Exams were held in India from **1922** (Allahabad, later Delhi).

n44cd9d6a482.s: The demand for raising the age limit and holding the civil service examination simultaneously in India and England was taken up by the Indian National Congress from:
n44cd9d6a482.x: The INC began pressing these demands from its first session in 1885.
n44cd9d6a482.tq: Use the earliest stated organisational milestone rather than the later date of implementation.
xs: The INC took up these demands from its **first session (1885)** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Its demands were to **raise the age limit** and hold **simultaneous examinations** in India and England.
xa: The **GoI Act 1919 / Montford reforms** provided a separate ICS exam in India.
Exams were held in India from **1922** (Allahabad, later Delhi) alongside London.
Lytton had cut the maximum age to **19** in **1878**.

n7822c180484.s: Simultaneous ICS examinations in India and England, held from 1922, were provided for by the:
n7822c180484.x: The Government of India Act, 1919 provided for a separate ICS examination in India, held from 1922 alongside the London examination.
xa: Exams were held at **Allahabad, later Delhi**, alongside London.
This was an INC demand from its first session (**1885**).
UPPSC **2021** keyed both such statements correct.

n0459ead07b7.s: The codification of laws under the Law Commission headed by T.B. Macaulay was associated with which Act?
n0459ead07b7.x: The Law Commission under T.B. Macaulay and the codification of laws were associated with the Charter Act of 1833.
n0459ead07b7.tq: Match the law-making milestone with its enabling Act.
xs: The **Law Commission** under **T.B. Macaulay** (codification) came with the **Charter Act 1833** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Regulating Act 1773** set up the Supreme Court at Calcutta.
xa: The codes followed: **CPC 1859**, **IPC 1860**, **CrPC 1861**.
**Judicial Committee of the Privy Council** was formalised by the **Judicial Committee Act 1833**.

n51554d13299.s: The Federal Court in British India was provided for by the:
n51554d13299.x: The Federal Court was created under the Government of India Act, 1935. The 1861 Act set up High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, the 1833 Charter Act set up the Law Commission under Macaulay, and the 1919 Act brought dyarchy and an ICS exam in India.
xs: The **Federal Court** was provided by the **GoI Act 1935** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **1861 Act** set up **High Courts**; the **Charter Act 1833** the **Law Commission**; the **1919 Act** a separate ICS exam in India.
xa: The GoI Act 1935 also created the **Federal PSC** + provincial PSCs.
It made local self-government a **provincial subject**.

n6bf56a3abbf.s: The Aitchison Commission (1886) classified the services as:
n6bf56a3abbf.x: Aitchison (1886, Dufferin) replaced covenanted/uncovenanted with Imperial, Provincial and Subordinate.
xa: The three-tier plan was implemented under **Lansdowne**; the age limit was raised to **23**.
**Islington (1912-15)** = Indianisation of higher posts.

n6cc56a16915.s: The Lee Commission (1923-24), which proposed 50:50 parity in the ICS, was appointed under:
n6cc56a16915.x: The Lee Commission came under Reading; Hardinge II was Viceroy for the Islington Commission.
xa: **GoI Act 1935** created the **Federal PSC** + provincial PSCs.
**UPSC** replaced the Federal PSC from **1950**.
⚠ **Aitchison** = three-tier services (**1886**).

nd674667e8b6.s: Under Cornwallis's civil service reforms, promotion was based largely on:
nd674667e8b6.x: Cornwallis created a covenanted service, banned private trade and gifts, and based promotion on seniority.
xa: Cornwallis is the **"Father of Civil Services in India"**.
He also **separated revenue from justice**.
⚠ **Sardar Patel** called the ICS the **"Steel Frame"**.
**Wellesley** set up the **College of Fort William (1800)** to train recruits.

n192ff360118.s: Under Lytton's Statutory Civil Service (1878-79), the share of covenanted posts set aside for Indians of high families was:
n192ff360118.x: Lytton reserved one-sixth of covenanted posts for Indians of high families; the scheme was later abolished.
xa: Lytton also cut the maximum age to **19** (**1878**).
The **Aitchison Commission (1886)** followed, with **Imperial, Provincial, Subordinate** services.
Earlier, the **1861 Act** opened mainly **uncovenanted** posts.

nf4a04633c73.s: Who described the Indian Civil Service as the 'Steel Frame' of India?
nf4a04633c73.x: Sardar Patel described the Indian Civil Service as the 'Steel Frame' of India.
nf4a04633c73.tq: Match the distinctive phrase with the statesman associated with it.
xs: **Sardar Patel** called the ICS the **"Steel Frame"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Cornwallis** is the "Father of Civil Services"; **Ram Mohan Roy** first demanded Indians in higher posts (**1832**).
xa: Cornwallis, Wellesley and Macaulay built the "steel frame"; UPSC traces its roots to British-era bodies.
The ICS became the **IAS** in **1947**.

n6faa82e63d8.s: Who established the district Diwani and Faujdari Adalats in 1772?
n6faa82e63d8.x: Warren Hastings established the district Diwani Adalats for civil cases and Faujdari Adalats for criminal cases in 1772.
n6faa82e63d8.tq: Directly identify the Governor-General associated with a judicial reform.
xs: **Warren Hastings** set up district **diwani** (civil) and **faujdari** (criminal) adalats in **1772** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The civil adalat was **under the Collector**.
xa: He also set up the **Sadar Diwani** and **Sadar Nizamat Adalat** at Calcutta.
⚠ **Hastings** = Collector gets civil adalat; **Cornwallis** = Collector **loses judicial powers**.
**Regulating Act 1773** set up the **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)**.

n4e2b01f7b0e.s: Under Cornwallis, provincial courts of appeal were set up at Calcutta, Dacca, Murshidabad and:
n4e2b01f7b0e.x: The four provincial courts of appeal were at Calcutta, Dacca, Murshidabad and Patna.
xa: **Bentinck** later abolished these courts and gave their work to **Commissioners**.
Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats at Calcutta were presided over by the **G-G in Council**.

n7538d01efc7.s: Which of the following is NOT correctly associated with Bentinck's judicial reforms?
o: Abolition of Cornwallis's provincial courts of appeal
Creation of provincial courts of appeal at Dacca and Patna
Transfer of circuit courts' work to Commissioners
Establishment of separate Sadar courts at Allahabad
n7538d01efc7.x: The creation of provincial courts of appeal at Dacca and Patna was associated with Cornwallis. Bentinck abolished the provincial courts of appeal and circuit courts, transferred their work to Commissioners, and established separate Sadar courts at Allahabad.
n7538d01efc7.tq: Find the reform belonging to another Governor-General.
xs: **Creating provincial courts of appeal at Dacca and Patna** was **Cornwallis's**, not Bentinck's — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Bentinck** **abolished** those courts and circuit courts, gave their work to **Commissioners**, and set up separate Sadar courts at **Allahabad**.
xa: Bentinck also replaced **Persian** with vernacular/English in courts.
⚠ **Hastings** = Collector gets civil adalat; **Cornwallis** = Collector loses judicial powers; **Bentinck** = abolishes provincial courts.

na0293e5b700.s: The Supreme Court at Calcutta, set up in 1774 under the Regulating Act of 1773, had as its first Chief Justice:
na0293e5b700.x: The Regulating Act of 1773 created the Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774), with Sir Elijah Impey as its first Chief Justice. C.P. Ilbert was the Law Member behind the Ilbert Bill (1883), Macaulay headed the Law Commission under the 1833 Charter Act, and Sir John Shore was a Governor-General.
xs: The first Chief Justice of the **Supreme Court at Calcutta (1774)** was **Sir Elijah Impey** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**C.P. Ilbert** was the Law Member behind the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**; **Macaulay** headed the **Law Commission** (Charter Act **1833**).
xa: The Court was set up under the **Regulating Act 1773**.
The **Indian High Courts Act 1861** later replaced the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats.

n27d57f178fd.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of Cornwallis's police reorganisation?
o: The Royal Irish Constabulary model was adopted.
Indian darogas were placed in charge of thanas.
Zamindars were relieved of police duties.
n27d57f178fd.x: The Royal Irish Constabulary model was adopted for the Police Act of 1861, not for Cornwallis's reorganisation. Cornwallis introduced thanas under darogas and removed police duties from zamindars.
n27d57f178fd.tq: Separate the Cornwallis reorganisation from the later Police Act model.
xs: The **Royal Irish Constabulary** model belongs to the **Police Act 1861**, not Cornwallis — so option **(2)** is the answer.
**Cornwallis** divided districts into **thanas** under Indian **darogas** and **relieved zamindars of police duties**.
xa: The 1861 Act (**Canning**) created a colonial force meant to **suppress dissent**.
Under Cornwallis the **kotwal** ran the town police.

n36d33ec4585.s: The daroga was described as the local representative of the:
o: Aura and authority of Company Bahadur
n36d33ec4585.x: The daroga represented the “aura and authority of Company Bahadur” at the local level. Darogas also became notorious for abuse of power.
n36d33ec4585.tq: Recall the distinctive descriptive phrase associated with the office.
xs: The daroga was the local representative of the **"aura and authority of Company Bahadur"** — so option **(3)** is correct (UPPSC key).
He headed a **thana** under Cornwallis's system, assisted by constables.
xa: Darogas were notorious for **abuse of power**.
⚠ **Kotwal** = older Mughal chief of town police.
**Munro** wanted police supervision **under the Collector, not judges**.

n82326b3d245.s: The Police Act of 1861, passed under Canning, modelled the force on the:
n82326b3d245.x: The 1861 police was modelled on the Royal Irish Constabulary and meant to suppress dissent.
xa: Critique: colonial police were built **for control, not service**.
Canning also gave the **IPC (1860)** and **CrPC (1861)**.

nb30fe69ba7f.s: Munro's Judicial Commission recommended placing police supervision under the:
nb30fe69ba7f.x: Munro recommended police under the Collector and minor crimes tried by village officers.
xa: The Judicial Commission ran **1814-18**; report **April 1816**.
As Governor of Madras (**1820-27**) he extended the **Ryotwari** system.

n69207538a02.s: Which administrative measure is associated with Thomas Munro as Governor of Madras?
o: Creation of the Indian High Courts
Introduction of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal
Establishment of the Police Commission of 1902
n69207538a02.x: As Governor of Madras, Thomas Munro extended the Ryotwari system. The other measures belonged to different administrations and regions.
n69207538a02.tq: Match the administrator with the land-revenue measure linked to his Madras tenure.
xs: As **Governor of Madras (1820-27)**, Munro **extended the Ryotwari system** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**High Courts** came under the **1861** Act, long after Munro.
xa: Munro headed the **Judicial Commission (1814-18)**.
He recommended **village officers** try minor crimes at village level.
He wanted police supervision **under the Collector, not judges**.

n53826829725.s: The Indian Civil Service is the direct ancestor of the:
n53826829725.x: The ICS is the direct ancestor of the IAS.
xa: The ICS became the **IAS** in **1947**.
**Police Act 1861** was modelled on the **Royal Irish Constabulary**.
UPSC, CAG and Election Commission trace roots to British-era bodies.

nindian-history-134-12.s: The High Courts replaced the Supreme Courts and the Sadar Adalats under the:
nindian-history-134-12.x: The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 abolished the Supreme Courts and Sadar Adalats and set up High Courts.
n: The Indian High Courts Act was enacted in 1861. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Indian High Courts Act of 1861 laid the foundation of the High Court system. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The High Courts replaced the Supreme Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The High Courts replaced the Sadar Adalats. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The 1861 Act led to the establishment of the 1862 Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
xa: The first High Courts: **Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** (**1862**); **Allahabad** **1866**.
The High Courts were established through **Letters Patent** issued under **Crown authority**.
The **Federal Court** came under the **GoI Act 1935**.

nindian-history-134-15.s: The Allahabad High Court was set up in:
nindian-history-134-15.x: Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts were the first set (1862); Allahabad came in 1866.
n: The Calcutta High Court was part of the first set of High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Bombay High Court was part of the first set of High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Madras High Court was part of the first set of High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Allahabad High Court was established in 1866. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
xa: They were set up under the **Indian High Courts Act 1861**.
They replaced the **Supreme Courts** and **Sadar Adalats**.
The **Supreme Court at Calcutta** dated from **1774** (Regulating Act **1773**).

nindian-history-134-20.s: Under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861, the High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were set up in:
nindian-history-134-20.x: The High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were set up in 1862; Allahabad followed in 1866.
n: The Indian High Courts Act was enacted in 1861. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were the first High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Calcutta High Court was established in 1862. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Bombay High Court was established in 1862. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Madras High Court was established in 1862. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Allahabad High Court was established in 1866. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The 1861 Act led to the establishment of the 1862 Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
xa: The High Courts were set up by **Letters Patent** under Crown authority.
**Bentinck** had set up separate Sadar courts at **Allahabad** earlier.
**IPC** **1860**, **CrPC** **1861** — both under **Canning**.

n2153f23fae7.s: The principal aim of the Ilbert Bill was to empower Indian:
o: Collectors to try all revenue cases involving Europeans
Police officers to investigate cases against European officials
High Court judges to appoint European juries
District magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects
n2153f23fae7.x: The Ilbert Bill sought to allow Indian district magistrates and sessions judges to try European British subjects, removing the racial judicial privilege enjoyed by Europeans.
n2153f23fae7.tq: Identify the authority and jurisdiction targeted by the proposed legal change.
xs: The Bill let Indian **district magistrates and sessions judges try European British subjects** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Till then Europeans were tried **only by European judges**.
xa: Introduced in **1883** under **Lord Ripon**, drafted by Law Member **C.P. Ilbert**.
The European protest was called the **"White Mutiny"**.
Compromise (**1884**): a **jury** at least **half European**.

n7b273243196.s: Which of the following correctly describes the outcome of the Ilbert Bill controversy?
o: A compromise required a jury with at least half European members in cases involving Europeans.
The Bill was withdrawn and no compromise was made.
European subjects were placed under village courts.
The Bill was passed without modification.
n7b273243196.x: The Bill was diluted after European agitation. Europeans tried by an Indian judge could claim a jury containing at least half European members.
n7b273243196.tq: Distinguish the original objective from the diluted final arrangement.
xs: Ripon **watered the Bill down**: a European tried by an Indian judge could claim a **jury of which at least half were Europeans** — so option **(1)** is correct.
So it was neither withdrawn without compromise nor passed unchanged.
xa: The compromise came in **1884**.
The European protest was the **"White Mutiny"**.
It showed **racial discrimination** persisted.

nf4b1f8dd838.s: The European agitation against the Ilbert Bill is commonly described as the:
nf4b1f8dd838.x: The fierce European agitation against the Ilbert Bill was popularly described as the “white mutiny.”
nf4b1f8dd838.tq: Recall the distinctive contemporary label attached to the agitation.
xs: The fierce European agitation was called the **"White Mutiny"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It opposed Indian judges trying **European British subjects**.
xa: Ripon **diluted** the Bill: jury at least **half European** (**1884**).
It showed Indians the value of **organised agitation**.
⚠ The **Indian Association** **backed** the Bill; some notes wrongly say "opposed".

nb32f60764af.s: Which body supported the Ilbert Bill against European agitation?
nb32f60764af.x: The Indian Association supported the Bill; the controversy exposed British racial attitudes.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes wrongly say the Indian Association "opposed" it.
Bill: **1883**, **Ripon**, Law Member **C.P. Ilbert**.

n2d52f9f006c.s: The first municipal corporation in India was established at which place in 1688?
n2d52f9f006c.x: The first municipal corporation in India was established at Madras in 1688.
n2d52f9f006c.tq: Use the place-year association to distinguish the first corporation from the later corporations at Bombay and Calcutta.
xs: India's first municipal corporation was **Madras** (**1688**; **1687-88**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Bombay and Calcutta** got corporations later, in **1726**.
xa: The **Cantonments Act** came in **1924**.
APPSC-G2 **2025**: Cantonments Act 1924, Madras corporation 1688, Ripon as father of LSG — **all three correct**.
Madras was capital of the presidency governing **Coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema**.

n7aecd060d7d.s: The first step towards financial decentralisation was Lord Mayo's Resolution of:
n7aecd060d7d.x: Mayo's 1870 Resolution began financial decentralisation and divided central and provincial finances.
xa: Provinces got **fixed grants** and were told to raise **local taxes**.
Mayo (**1869-72**) also ran the first census (**1871**).
⚠ **Mayo** = financial decentralisation (**1870**); **Ripon** = "Magna Carta" of LSG (**1882**).

ndf12504a1a5.s: Lord Ripon's Resolution on local self-government was issued in:
ndf12504a1a5.x: Mayo 1870, Ripon 1882, GoI Act 1919 and GoI Act 1935.
xa: In between: **Royal Commission on Decentralisation, 1907** (report **1909**), chairman **C.E.H. Hobhouse**.
**Cantonments Act** passed by the Central legislature in **1924**.
⚠ **Mayo** = financial decentralisation; **Ripon** = "Magna Carta" of LSG.

n03c418a3415.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about local self-government in colonial India?
o: Local bodies after Ripon's Resolution were entirely free from official control.
Non-officials entered panchayats, municipal councils and district boards after 1882.
Local bodies were often starved of funds.
Village panchayats were set up in several provinces after the Government of India Act, 1919.
n03c418a3415.x: Local bodies remained controlled by colonial officials and short of funds.
xa: **Ripon's Resolution (1882)** gave local boards an **elected non-official majority**.
Ripon = **"Father of Local Self-Government in India"**.

n08b7756d1b6.s: Besides financial decentralisation, Lord Mayo's administration is associated with:
o: a statistical survey of India and the first census
the first municipal corporation at Madras
the transfer of local self-government to the provinces
n08b7756d1b6.x: Lord Mayo undertook a statistical survey of India and conducted the first census (1871).
xa: Mayo (**1869-72**): Resolution of **1870** on financial decentralisation.
All four **BPSC 2023** statements on his Resolution were true.
Mayo also introduced **state railways**.
n08b7756d1b6.fixed: first (non-synchronous) census under Mayo is dated 1872, not 1871

n858c80e5e90.s: Which one of the following features was associated with Lord Ripon’s Resolution of 1882?
o: Transfer of judicial supremacy to municipalities
Abolition of elected representation in local bodies
Exclusive control of local bodies by the Collector
n858c80e5e90.x: Lord Ripon’s Resolution provided for an elected non-official majority in local bodies.
n858c80e5e90.tq: Identify the institutional reform, avoiding extreme or unrelated powers.
xs: **Ripon's Resolution (1882)** provided an **elected non-official majority** in local boards — so option **(1)** is correct.
It stood for **local autonomy**, not Collector control.
xa: It is the **"Magna Carta" of local self-government**.
Ripon = **"Father of Local Self-Government in India"**.
Ripon also introduced the **Ilbert Bill (1883)**.

nad2b33355b8.s: Which is regarded as the 'Magna Carta of local self-government'?
nad2b33355b8.x: Ripon's Resolution is the Magna Carta; Mayo's dealt with financial decentralisation.
xa: **GoI Act 1935** made LSG a **provincial subject**.
Royal Commission chairman: **C.E.H. Hobhouse**.

nf25cd92454b.s: The Cantonments Act, 1924 was passed by the:
nf25cd92454b.x: The Cantonments Act of 1924 was passed by the Central legislature (an APPSC-G2 2025 statement). It was not a provincial council's Act or an Act of the British Parliament, and the Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907-09) only made recommendations.
xs: The **Cantonments Act, 1924** was passed by the **Central legislature** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Royal Commission on Decentralisation (1907-09)** only made recommendations.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2025** statement set: Cantonments Act 1924, Madras corporation 1688, Ripon as father of LSG — **all three correct**.
**GoI Act 1919**: LSG a **transferred subject**.

n1c174940d23.s: Who is known as the 'Father of Local Self-Government in India'?
n1c174940d23.x: Lord Ripon, whose 1882 Resolution is called the Magna Carta of local self-government, is the Father of Local Self-Government. Mayo's 1870 Resolution began financial decentralisation, and Hobhouse chaired the 1907 Royal Commission on Decentralisation. Curzon is not given this title.
n1c174940d23.tq: Ripon 1882 = Father of LSG; Mayo 1870 = financial decentralisation.
xs: **Lord Ripon** is the **"Father of Local Self-Government in India"** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His **1882 Resolution** is the **"Magna Carta" of local self-government**.
**Mayo's 1870 Resolution** began **financial decentralisation**; **C.E.H. Hobhouse** chaired the **1907** Royal Commission.
xa: After **1882**, unofficial members entered panchayats, municipal councils, local and **district boards**.
⚠ **Cornwallis** = "Father of Civil Services in India".

nindian-history-134-13.s: The High Courts in India were established through:
o: Letters Patent issued under Crown authority
a resolution of the Board of Control
nindian-history-134-13.x: The High Courts were set up by Letters Patent issued under the Crown's authority.
n: Letters Patent were the instruments of establishment of the High Courts. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
The Letters Patent were issued under Crown authority. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #134 · pp 237-238]
xa: The **Indian High Courts Act 1861** laid the foundation of the system.
**Calcutta, Bombay, Madras** — first set, **1862**.
Codes under **Canning**: **CPC 1859**, **IPC 1860**, **CrPC 1861**.

n467ddefe30b.s: Which one of the following was NOT a condition of the Subsidiary Alliance devised by Lord Wellesley?
o: The ruler had to maintain a British subsidiary force at his own cost
The ruler had to accept a British Resident
The ruler had to exclude other Europeans from his service
The ruler could freely conduct an independent foreign policy
n467ddefe30b.x: A subsidiary ally had to surrender independent foreign-policy control. The other conditions were part of the system devised by Wellesley.
n467ddefe30b.tq: Spot the option that reverses the central consequence of the alliance.
xs: A subsidiary ally could **not** run an **independent foreign policy** — so option **(4)** is the answer.
Real terms: keep a **British subsidiary force** at his cost, accept a **British Resident**, no other **Europeans** in service.
xa: The ruler also had to **disband his own army**; unpaid subsidy → **ceding territory**.
Devised by **Lord Wellesley, 1798**.
First to accept: **Nizam of Hyderabad** (**September 1798**).

n788ea5bbe7f.s: The 1800 treaty involving the Nizam resulted in the cession of the Rayalaseema districts, which came to be known as the
n788ea5bbe7f.x: The Nizam ceded the Rayalaseema districts in 1800 to meet the cost of the subsidiary force; these became known as the Ceded Districts.
n788ea5bbe7f.tq: Link the treaty, territorial transfer and historical regional name.
xs: The Rayalaseema districts ceded in **1800** became the **"Ceded Districts"** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They paid for the **subsidiary force** kept for the Nizam.
xa: The Nizam was the **first** subsidiary ally (**September 1798**), again **1800**.
AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.

n8a5590a2ab8.s: The first Indian ruler to accept Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance (September 1798) was the:
n8a5590a2ab8.x: The Nizam of Hyderabad was first, in September 1798 (and again in 1800). Mysore followed in 1799, Awadh in November 1801, and the Peshwa signed through the Treaty of Bassein.
xs: The **Nizam of Hyderabad** was first, in **September 1798** (again **1800**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Mysore** followed in **1799**, **Awadh** in **November 1801**, the **Peshwa** in **December 1802** (Treaty of Bassein).
xa: AP angle: asked in **APPSC G2 2002, 2008**.
The **1800** treaty created the **"Ceded Districts"** (Rayalaseema).

n630411a329a.s: After 1858, the British Crown guaranteed the princely states in return for their acceptance of
n630411a329a.x: After 1858, princely states were guaranteed in return for accepting British paramountcy.
n630411a329a.tq: Distinguish a guarantee under paramountcy from restoration of full sovereignty.
xs: After **1858** the Crown guaranteed princely states in return for **paramountcy** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Doctrine of Lapse** itself was **abolished** in **1858**, and adoption recognised.
xa: Canning called the princes **"breakwaters to the storm"**.
Proclamation read at the **Allahabad Durbar**, **1 November 1858**.

n2def91e710f.s: Lord Dalhousie announced the Doctrine of Lapse in
n2def91e710f.x: Lord Dalhousie formulated and applied the Doctrine of Lapse from 1848.
n2def91e710f.tq: Use the earliest date in the sequence of Dalhousie’s annexations and policies.
xs: Dalhousie applied the **Doctrine of Lapse** from **1848** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1853** = **Jhansi** lapsed; **1856** = **Awadh** annexed for misgovernment.
xa: First lapse annexation: **Satara (1848)**.
Dalhousie's term: **1848-56**.

n284f232b77e.s: The policy of annexation under the Doctrine of Lapse was formally abandoned after the Revolt of 1857 through
n284f232b77e.x: Queen Victoria’s Proclamation, read by Canning at the Allahabad Durbar on 1 November 1858, abolished the policy and recognised adoption.
n284f232b77e.tq: Connect the policy change with the correct proclamation, date and official occasion.
xs: **Queen Victoria's Proclamation** (**1 November 1858**) abandoned annexation — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was read by **Canning** at the **Allahabad Durbar**; the Treaty of Bassein was the Peshwa's subsidiary alliance.
xa: It **recognised adoption**.
Canning called the princes **"breakwaters to the storm"**.
After **1858** the Crown guaranteed princely states in return for **paramountcy**.

n16673a37fb4.s: Which of the following states was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse in spite of the presence of an adopted heir whose succession was refused?
n16673a37fb4.x: Rani Lakshmibai’s adopted son, Damodar Rao, was not recognised as heir and Jhansi was annexed in 1853.
n16673a37fb4.tq: Pair the adopted heir with the correct state rather than with another annexed territory.
xs: **Jhansi** lapsed (**1853**) after Rani Lakshmibai's **adopted son was denied the throne** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Awadh** was annexed for **misgovernment**, not lapse.
xa: First lapse annexation: **Satara (1848)**.
Lapse withdrawn by **Queen Victoria's Proclamation (1858)**, which **recognised adoption**.

nb05e0b0f85a.s: The first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse (1848) was:
nb05e0b0f85a.x: Satara (1848) was the first state annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse. Jhansi lapsed in 1853 and Nagpur later. Awadh (1856) was annexed for misgovernment, not under lapse.
nb05e0b0f85a.tq: Lapse: Satara first (1848); Awadh was NOT lapse.
xs: **Satara (1848)** was the first state annexed under lapse — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Jhansi** lapsed in **1853**; **Awadh (1856)** was annexed for **misgovernment**, not lapse.
xa: ⚠ First subsidiary ally = **Hyderabad (1798)**; last Maratha to sign = **Holkar (1818)**.
Lapse = ruler dying **without a natural male heir**; adopted son could not inherit the throne.

n12711e97aa9.s: Who among the following was deposed and exiled to Calcutta after the annexation of Awadh?
n12711e97aa9.x: Nawab Wajid Ali Shah was deposed after Awadh was annexed and was exiled to Calcutta.
n12711e97aa9.tq: Use the ruler–territory association to avoid swapping rulers of different annexed states.
xs: Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was deposed and exiled to **Calcutta** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Birjis Qadr** was **Begum Hazrat Mahal's** son, proclaimed ruler in **1857**; **Bahadur Shah Zafar** was at Delhi.
xa: Awadh was annexed in **1856** for **"misgovernment"**.
The **Summary Revenue Settlement (1856)** dispossessed the **taluqdars**.

n3539c777c75.s: The Summary Revenue Settlement introduced in Awadh in 1856 was made directly with:
n3539c777c75.x: The 1856 settlement was made directly with village proprietors, while the taluqdars lost their estates, were disarmed and had their forts demolished.
xa: It "deeply alienated the **sepoys** and the **landed aristocracy**".
The Bengal Army drew heavily from **Awadh**.

nbf9e982898b.s: The annexation of Awadh particularly alienated the Bengal Army sepoys because
o: most Bengal Army sepoys were recruited from Punjab alone
their families in Awadh were affected by the new revenue burden
their own regiments were immediately disbanded
they were denied promotion to the rank of Resident
nbf9e982898b.x: The Bengal Army drew heavily from Awadh, and the new revenue burden directly affected the families of its sepoys.
nbf9e982898b.tq: Link the social base of recruitment with the direct effect of annexation on soldiers’ families.
xs: The **Bengal Army** drew heavily from **Awadh**, and sepoys' **families bore the new revenue burden** — so option **(2)** is correct.
So the sepoys were **hurt directly** by the annexation; Awadh, not Punjab, was the recruiting ground.
xa: The Nawab's **lords, officials, retainers and soldiers** were thrown out of work.
Awadh became a **centre of unrest**.
Settlement: **Summary Revenue Settlement (1856)**.

na1e1e5bd63b.s: Begum Hazrat Mahal’s political grievance during the Revolt of 1857 was primarily connected with
o: the loss of the Red Fort by Mughal successors
the annexation of Awadh and the proclamation of her son Birjis Qadr as ruler
the confiscation of Kunwar Singh’s estates
the denial of Baji Rao II’s pension
na1e1e5bd63b.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal opposed the annexation of Awadh and had her son Birjis Qadr proclaimed ruler.
na1e1e5bd63b.tq: Match the leader with the specific grievance and associated claimant.
xs: **Begum Hazrat Mahal** (Lucknow) resented the **annexation of Awadh**; her son **Birjis Qadr** was proclaimed ruler — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Red Fort** grievance was **Bahadur Shah Zafar's**; the **pension** grievance **Nana Saheb's**.
xa: ⚠ **Kanpur** = Nana Saheb; **Lucknow** = Begum Hazrat Mahal; **Jagdishpur** = Kunwar Singh; **Bareilly** = Khan Bahadur Khan.
Awadh's Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was exiled to Calcutta.

n875f7e879b8.s: Which of the following grievances was associated with Nana Saheb?
o: Denial of the pension of his adoptive father, Baji Rao II
Refusal to recognise his adopted son as ruler of Jhansi
Removal from the Red Fort and loss of the imperial title
n875f7e879b8.x: Nana Saheb, the adopted son of Peshwa Baji Rao II, was denied the pension of his adoptive father.
n875f7e879b8.tq: Match the leader with his personal political grievance, avoiding swapped revolutionary leaders.
xs: **Nana Saheb** was denied the pension of his adoptive father **Baji Rao II** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jhansi** throne = **Rani Lakshmibai**; **Jagdishpur** estates = **Kunwar Singh**; Red Fort/title = **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
xa: Baji Rao II was the **last Peshwa**.
Nana Saheb led the revolt at **Kanpur**.

n9bd1b145581.s: Dalhousie announced that the successors of Bahadur Shah would have to leave the
o: Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli
Qutub at Mehrauli and move to Calcutta
Agra Fort and move to Delhi
Allahabad Fort and move to Lucknow
n9bd1b145581.x: Dalhousie declared that Bahadur Shah’s successors would have to leave the Red Fort and move to the Qutub at Mehrauli.
n9bd1b145581.tq: Use the place pair—Red Fort and Qutub, Mehrauli—to avoid confusing Mughal centres.
xs: **Dalhousie** said Bahadur Shah's successors must **leave the Red Fort** and move to the **Qutub, Mehrauli** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The move was from the **Red Fort** to the **Qutub**, not the reverse; Calcutta, Agra and Allahabad play no part.
xa: ⚠ **Dalhousie** = leave the **Red Fort**; **Canning (1856)** = lose the **imperial title**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's grievance: loss of **title and Red Fort** for his successors.

n404379e27f8.s: What did Canning announce in 1856 regarding the successors of Bahadur Shah Zafar?
o: They would receive pensions equal to those of the Peshwas
They would lose the imperial title and become mere princes
They would be recognised as governors of Awadh
They would inherit the imperial title and the Red Fort
n404379e27f8.x: Canning announced that after Bahadur Shah Zafar, his successors would lose the imperial title and would be treated merely as princes.
n404379e27f8.tq: Distinguish Canning’s announcement about imperial status from Dalhousie’s order about residence.
xs: **Canning (1856)** announced the successors would **lose the imperial title** and be **mere princes** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This would apply after **Bahadur Shah Zafar**; they would not inherit the title or the Red Fort.
xa: ⚠ **Dalhousie** had said they must **leave the Red Fort** for the **Qutub, Mehrauli**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar led the revolt at **Delhi**.

n4c96ffc3b71.s: Which of the following titles were abolished in 1855?
o: The titles of the Nizam and the Peshwa
The titles of the Raja of Satara and the ruler of Jhansi
The titles of the Mughal emperor and the Nawab of Awadh
The titles of the Carnatic Nawab and the Tanjore Raja
n4c96ffc3b71.x: The titles of the Carnatic Nawab and the Tanjore Raja were abolished in 1855.
n4c96ffc3b71.tq: Match the year with the two specific titles rather than with rulers affected by the Doctrine of Lapse.
xs: In **1855** the titles of the **Carnatic Nawab** and the **Tanjore Raja** were abolished — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Mughal** title was only threatened for Bahadur Shah's successors (Canning, **1856**), and **Awadh** was annexed in **1856** for misgovernment.
xa: **Nana Saheb** was denied his father's pension.
**Pindaris and irregular troops** were disbanded, adding to unemployment.
Mughal successors were to lose the **Red Fort** (Dalhousie) and the **imperial title** (Canning).

nindian-history-121-4.s: Who led the assault that recaptured Delhi from the rebels in 1857?
nindian-history-121-4.x: John Nicholson led the assault on Delhi; Hugh Rose took Jhansi, Colin Campbell relieved and recaptured Lucknow, and Henry Lawrence died defending the Lucknow Residency.
n: John Nicholson was associated with Delhi during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Hugh Rose was associated with Jhansi and Rani Lakshmibai during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Colin Campbell was associated with Lucknow during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Henry Lawrence was associated with Lucknow during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
xa: Other British names at Lucknow: **Havelock** and **Neil**.
Lucknow's rebel leader was **Begum Hazrat Mahal**, who proclaimed her son **Birjis Qadr** ruler.
Jhansi had **lapsed** in **1853** when the Rani's adopted son was denied the throne.

nindian-history-121-5.s: Who was the military commander who fought on behalf of Nana Sahib at Kanpur in 1857?
nindian-history-121-5.x: Tatya Tope was the military commander at Kanpur fighting for Nana Sahib, the political leader there.
n: Tatya Tope was the commander at Kanpur. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
xa: Tatya Tope also led in **Central India**.
Nana Sahib was the adopted son of **Peshwa Baji Rao II** and was denied his pension.
**Rani Lakshmibai** led at **Jhansi**.

nindian-history-121-11.s: Who led the Revolt of 1857 at Bareilly?
nindian-history-121-11.x: Khan Bahadur Khan led at Bareilly; Kunwar Singh led at Jagdishpur in Bihar, Ahmadullah Shah at Faizabad and Tatya Tope in Central India.
n: The 1857 Revolt was centred at Bareilly under Khan Bahadur Khan. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Khan Bahadur Khan was the leader at Bareilly during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred at Bihar and Jagdishpur under Kunwar Singh. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Kunwar Singh was the leader at Bihar and Jagdishpur during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred at Faizabad under Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah was the leader at Faizabad during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
The 1857 Revolt was centred in Central India under Tatya Tope. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
Tatya Tope was the leader in Central India during the 1857 Revolt. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #121 · pp 221-223]
xa: **Assam** — **Maniram Dutt**.
Khan Bahadur Khan was a **Rohilla** chief.
**Delhi** — **Bahadur Shah Zafar**, opposed by **John Nicholson**.

nd85f6b9a223.s: The fear of annexation among the princes contributed to the Revolt of 1857 by
o: turning a sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt
preventing the participation of Awadh’s landed aristocracy
making the revolt exclusively a movement of zamindars
nd85f6b9a223.x: Fear of further annexations encouraged princely and aristocratic participation and helped transform the sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt.
nd85f6b9a223.tq: Apply the political cause to the broader character and spread of the revolt.
xs: The princes' **fear of annexation** turned a **sepoy mutiny into a wider revolt** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Awadh's **landed aristocracy** was deeply alienated, not kept out.
xa: After **1858** the Crown guaranteed princely states in return for **paramountcy**.
**P.E. Roberts** called it "just a sepoy mutiny".

nindian-history-26-2-36.s: The Revolt of 1857 began at which place?
nindian-history-26-2-36.x: The Revolt of 1857 began at Meerut on 10 May 1857, when sepoys rose and marched to Delhi.
nindian-history-26-2-36.tq: Recall where the 1857 revolt broke out.
n: Meerut was associated with the beginning of the Revolt of 1857. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #26-2 · pp 90-93]
xs: The Revolt of **1857** began at **Meerut** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Delhi** (Bahadur Shah II), **Kanpur** (Nana Sahib) and **Lucknow** (Begum Hazrat Mahal) were later centres of the revolt.
xa: Delhi's leader faced British opponent **John Nicholson**.
**Rani Lakshmibai** of **Jhansi** was opposed by **Hugh Rose**.
Important leaders: **Bahadur Shah II**, **Rani Lakshmibai**, **Nana Sahib**, **Kunwar Singh**.

n12af53b3364.s: The annexation of princely states became a cause of discontent before the Revolt of 1857 because it—
o: ended the drain of wealth to Britain
created employment for thousands of court officials and soldiers
restored the authority of all displaced rulers
threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work
n12af53b3364.x: Annexations displaced thousands of officials, retainers and soldiers who had depended on princely courts for employment and patronage.
n12af53b3364.tq: Trace the administrative consequence of annexation.
xs: Annexations **threw officials, retainers and soldiers of princely courts out of work** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They did the opposite of creating jobs; and Company rule kept the **drain of wealth** going.
xa: In Awadh (**1856**), the deposition of **Wajid Ali Shah** cost lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
**Pindaris and irregular soldiers** were also disbanded.
Annexations also ended **princely/court patronage** of artisans.
n12af53b3364.fixed: stem said annexation hurt the colonial administration, which the answer does not support

nbcb93dca373.s: What was a major consequence of the high and rigid land revenue demand on peasants?
o: They became independent of moneylenders and traders
They were driven into debt and lost land to moneylenders and traders
They were exempted from commercial cultivation
nbcb93dca373.x: The heavy revenue burden pushed peasants into debt, often resulting in the loss of their land to moneylenders and traders.
nbcb93dca373.tq: Follow the economic cause to its immediate social consequence.
xs: **Heavy, rigid land revenue** drove peasants into **debt**, and they **lost land to moneylenders and traders** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Revenue was collected rigidly under **Permanent/Zamindari**, **Ryotwari** and **Mahalwari** settlements.
xa: **Commercialisation** forced **cash crops** under high taxes.
Sepoys were **"peasants in uniform"** — they carried these rural grievances into the army.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** + **drain of wealth**.

nee264d593f2.s: The Inam Commission of 1852, which confiscated about 20,000 estates whose owners could not show title, was set up in:
nee264d593f2.x: The Inam Commission (1852) worked in Bombay, not Madras, and confiscated some 20,000 estates lacking title.
xa: ⚠ **21,000** = taluqdars of Awadh (**1856**); **20,000** = Inam Commission estates (**1852**).
Result: a **fiercely anti-British landed class**.

nd8058bc9bd3.s: Which of the following best explains the ruin of Indian artisans and handicrafts before 1857?
o: The Industrial Revolution reduced the supply of British textiles
Indian handicrafts received increased princely patronage after annexations
British machine-made goods entered duty-free, while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs
British goods were excluded from Indian markets
nd8058bc9bd3.x: After the Industrial Revolution, cheap British machine-made goods, especially textiles, entered India duty-free while Indian goods faced heavy tariffs, causing deindustrialisation. A and D reverse this, and B is wrong because annexations ended princely patronage.
nd8058bc9bd3.tq: Compare unequal trade treatment rather than focusing on only one factor.
xs: **British machine-made goods entered duty-free**, while **Indian goods faced heavy tariffs** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This caused **deindustrialisation**; the Industrial Revolution **increased** cheap British goods, esp. **textiles**.
Annexations **ended** princely patronage, so option 2 is wrong.
xa: **Artisans were ruined** by cheap British goods.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** draining wealth to Britain.

na39a68ee4bb.s: The terms ‘absentee sovereignty’ and ‘drain of wealth’ in the context of the causes of 1857 refer primarily to—
o: the movement of peasants from villages to princely courts
the transfer of religious authority from temples to courts
the transfer of economic resources from India to Britain
the migration of British officials to Indian villages
na39a68ee4bb.x: Company rule was seen as 'absentee sovereignty', rule from distant Britain, under which India's wealth was drained to Britain. Both terms describe resources being transferred from India to Britain.
na39a68ee4bb.tq: Distinguish an economic concept from unrelated administrative or religious processes.
xs: Both terms describe **economic resources transferred from India to Britain** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Company rule was seen as **absentee sovereignty** (rule from distant Britain) plus a **drain of wealth** to Britain.
xa: Peasants faced **heavy land revenue** and lost land to **moneylenders**.
Artisans were ruined by **duty-free** British goods.

nfc3bc813e18.s: Which of the following social measures, resented by orthodox opinion before 1857, was enacted in 1856?
nfc3bc813e18.x: The Hindu Widow Remarriage Act was passed in 1856 and challenged orthodox norms. Sati was abolished in 1829, the Caste Disabilities Removal (Lex Loci) Act dates to 1850 (1856 is a trap date for it), and the Charter Act grant was 1813.
xs: The **Hindu Widow Remarriage Act** was passed in **1856** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Sati** was abolished in **1829**; the **Caste Disabilities Removal Act** is of **1850** (**1856** is the trap date).
xa: ⚠ Some notes date the Religious Disabilities Act to **1856**; the Act is of **1850**.
**1856** also = **General Service Enlistment Act** and the annexation of **Awadh**.

n1705e5439c3.s: Before 1857, the lower courts and judicial system in British India generally favoured:
n1705e5439c3.x: Justice was slow, costly and corrupt and generally favoured the rich over the poor.
xa: The administration was also **inefficient and prejudiced**.
Indians were **shut out of high administrative posts**.

n86c858b41c5.s: Which of the following was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse before 1857?
n86c858b41c5.x: Satara (along with Jhansi and Nagpur) was annexed under the Doctrine of Lapse; Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernance.
xa: **Rani Lakshmibai's** adopted son was refused the throne of Jhansi.
**Nana Saheb** was denied his pension.
Awadh's Nawab **Wajid Ali Shah** was deposed.

n5d73fe3cb2a.s: Which Nawab of Awadh was deposed when Awadh was annexed in 1856?
n5d73fe3cb2a.x: Wajid Ali Shah was deposed when Awadh was annexed in 1856 on the ground of misgovernance, costing lords, officials, retainers and soldiers their livelihoods.
xa: Awadh was the **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**, so its annexation angered high-caste sepoys.
About **21,000** taluqdars lost estates under the **Summary Settlement of 1856**.

n49e6fc86004.s: Which developments before 1857 generated fears of mass conversion among Indians?
o: Ending of the Company's trade monopoly
Western education, railways and the telegraph
n49e6fc86004.x: Western education, railways and the telegraph, along with missionaries preaching under police protection, created fears of mass conversion and loss of caste.
xa: Other grievances: **taxation of temple and mosque lands**; **racial arrogance** of officials.
After **1858** the Crown promised **religious neutrality** and withdrew state patronage from missionary work.

n758f58382b7.s: The General Service Enlistment Act, 1856 was passed under which Governor-General?
n758f58382b7.x: The Act was Canning's (1856); it required recruits to serve anywhere, including overseas, which orthodox Hindu sepoys feared would cost them caste.
xa: The order to travel by ship **was** a cause (BPSC key).
Earlier: **Barrackpore 1824** — refusal to go to **Burma by sea**.

n10cc2dc95e6.x: Bhatta was the foreign service allowance; it was withdrawn for service in Sindh and Punjab once they became British territory.
xa: **Bhatta mutinies** of the **1840s**: **34th NI 1844**, **66th NI 1849-50**.
Stopping of bhatta **was** a cause (BPSC **2018** key).

n57ff448cd2e.s: An Indian sepoy in the pre-1857 army could ordinarily rise no higher than:
n57ff448cd2e.x: Racial discrimination restricted the highest rank ordinarily attainable by an Indian soldier to Subedar.
n57ff448cd2e.tq: Test the exact promotion ceiling rather than general discrimination.
xs: An Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This was part of the **racial discrimination** in pay and promotion.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023** keyed the Subedar ceiling as correct.
Sepoys got **lower pay** than British soldiers and faced **racial contempt**.
Indians were also shut out of **high civil and military posts**.

n3124946017a.s: On the eve of the Revolt of 1857, the approximate ratio of Indian sepoys to European soldiers in India was:
n3124946017a.x: There were about 2.3 lakh Indian sepoys and 45,000 European soldiers, giving an approximate ratio of 5:1.
n3124946017a.tq: Convert the supplied troop figures into the approximate ratio.
xs: About **2.3 lakh sepoys to 45,000 Europeans** — roughly **5:1** — so option **(4)** is correct.
So sepoys far outnumbered Europeans; ratios like **2:1** or **3:1** understate the gap.
xa: Europeans had been drawn off for the **Crimean and Persian wars**.
**Awadh** was the **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

nf81814e702d.s: The expression “peasants in uniform” referred to the fact that the sepoys:
o: Were recruited only from European farming communities
Were trained exclusively in agricultural work
Received land grants instead of salaries
Carried rural and village grievances into the army
nf81814e702d.x: The sepoys were largely drawn from rural communities, so their grievances reflected those of the villages from which they came.
nf81814e702d.tq: Translate a descriptive phrase into its historical implication.
xs: **"Peasants in uniform"**: sepoys **carried rural and village grievances into the army** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Their grievances **mirrored the village's**.
xa: Peasants suffered **heavy land revenue**, **debt** and loss of land to **moneylenders**.
**Awadh** = **"nursery of the Bengal Army"**.

nb42d532d491.s: Before the Revolt of 1857, mysterious chapatis were passed from village to village across:
nb42d532d491.x: The chapatis passed village to village across North India, not South India.
xa: The **Enfield** cartridges were believed greased with **cow and pig fat**.
All read as a plot to **force conversion**.

nba78509b598.s: According to Sir Syed Ahmed Khan, one cause of the Revolt of 1857 was:
o: Complete equality between Indian and British soldiers
Lack of Indian representation in the Legislative Council
Excessive Indian representation in the Legislative Council
Too much British respect for Indian customs
nba78509b598.x: Sir Syed blamed the lack of Indian representation in the Legislative Council and the British misunderstanding of Indian customs; equality of soldiers was not a cause he identified.
xa: His **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** = "The Causes of the Indian Revolt" (**1859**).
He was the **first Indian** to write on the causes of 1857 in an **Indian language** (UPPSC **2009**).

n7d3bf87a7c1.s: After 1858, the British Crown's policy towards religion in India was one of:
n7d3bf87a7c1.x: After 1858 the Crown promised religious neutrality and withdrew state patronage from missionary work.
xa: Before 1857, missionaries **preached under police protection** and attacked Hindu and Islamic practice.
The **Lex Loci Act (1850)** let converts **inherit ancestral property**, seen as an incentive to convert.

nindian-history-6-10.x: India Divided was written by Rajendra Prasad; Gandhi wrote Hind Swaraj, My Experiments with Truth and Gokhale: My Political Guru.
n: Hind Swaraj was written by M.K. Gandhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
My Experiments with Truth was written by M.K. Gandhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Gokhale: My Political Guru was written by M.K. Gandhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
India Divided was written by Rajendra Prasad. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: **India Wins Freedom** — **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad**.
**The Indian Struggle** — **Subhas Chandra Bose**.
**Foundation of Indian Culture** — **Sri Aurobindo**.

na8a5e818a6f.s: The Vellore mutiny of 1806 was chiefly triggered by which of the following measures?
o: Introduction of a new dress code and prohibition of caste marks and earrings
Refusal to cross the sea to Burma
Refusal to use the new rifle cartridges
na8a5e818a6f.x: The new dress code, including a turban with a leather cockade and restrictions on caste marks and earrings, caused resentment among the sepoys at Vellore.
na8a5e818a6f.tq: Distinguish the cause attached to a specific mutiny.
xs: **Vellore (July 1806)** was triggered by a **new dress code** — turban with **leather cockade**, ban on **caste marks and earrings** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Burma by sea** = **Barrackpore 1824**; **bhatta** = **1840s**; cartridges = **1857**.
xa: **Tipu's sons** were lodged in the Vellore fort.
UPPSC match key: **Vellore = July 1806**; **Barrackpur = Nov 1824**; **Santhal = 1855-56**.

nd74db218032.s: The Barrackpore mutiny of November 1824 was caused by the sepoys’ refusal to—
nd74db218032.x: The 47th Native Infantry at Barrackpore refused to go to Burma by sea during the First Anglo-Burmese War.
xs: The **47th NI** at Barrackpore (**November 1824**) refused to **go to Burma by sea** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It came during the **First Anglo-Burmese War**.
xa: ⚠ **Barrackpore 1824** (47th NI, Burma) ≠ **Barrackpore 1857** (**Mangal Pandey**, 34th Bengal NI).
**38th NI (1852)** also refused to go to **Burma**.

n7a1ec04902e.s: Why did the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle offend both Hindu and Muslim sepoys?
o: They were believed to contain cow and pig fat, and had to be bitten open.
They required sepoys to cross the sea before use.
They were made exclusively from animal skin.
They were distributed only to European soldiers.
n7a1ec04902e.x: The greased-paper cartridges were believed to contain cow fat, offensive to Hindus, and pig fat, offensive to Muslims. Sepoys had to bite them open before loading.
n7a1ec04902e.tq: Identify the religious implication of the practical loading procedure.
xs: The cartridges were believed to contain **cow and pig fat** and had to be **bitten** open — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Cow** fat offended **Hindus**; **pig** fat offended **Muslims**.
xa: They were read as proof of a **colonial-missionary plot** to force conversion.
Rumours also spoke of **bone dust** in Company flour.

nae7ebb956e7.s: The Meerut rising of the Revolt of 1857 began on:
nae7ebb956e7.x: The Meerut rising began on 10 May 1857; Mangal Pandey's action at Barrackpore was on 29 March and the 19th Native Infantry refused at Berhampur in February 1857.
xa: Mangal Pandey was hanged on **8 April 1857**.
**9 May**: **85** sepoys of the **3rd Cavalry** sentenced to **10 years**.
**11-12 May**: rebels reach **Delhi**.

n2454abe7c0c.s: What immediately preceded the Meerut rising of 10 May 1857?
o: The proclamation of Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan
The sentencing of 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry to ten years’ imprisonment
The disbandment of Mangal Pandey’s regiment
The refusal of the 19th Native Infantry to use the rifle
n2454abe7c0c.x: On 9 May 1857, 85 sepoys of the 3rd Native Cavalry at Meerut were sentenced to ten years. The rising followed on 10 May, when officers were shot and imprisoned comrades were freed.
n2454abe7c0c.tq: Identify the immediately preceding event rather than the later consequence.
xs: On **9 May 1857**, **85** sepoys of the **3rd Native Cavalry** were sentenced to **10 years** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The rising followed on **10 May**: officers shot, comrades freed, **"Delhi Chalo"**.
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed only after it (**11-12 May**); the other events were earlier.
xa: Mangal Pandey's regiment was disbanded on **8 April 1857**.
**19th NI** refused the cartridges at **Berhampur** in **February 1857**.

ncceab30ad59.s: The rebels who reached Delhi on 11–12 May 1857 proclaimed whom as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan?
ncceab30ad59.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan on 11–12 May 1857.
ncceab30ad59.tq: Match the political title with the associated leader.
xs: Rebels reaching Delhi (**11-12 May 1857**) proclaimed **Bahadur Shah II** **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Kunwar Singh** was at Jagdishpur; **Wajid Ali Shah** had been deposed in **1856**; **Nana Sahib** was at Kanpur.
xa: They came from the **Meerut rising** (**10 May**) with the cry **"Delhi Chalo"**.
Bahadur Shah Zafar's successors were to lose the **Red Fort** and **royal title**.

ned4b909f551.s: Who is regarded as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857?
ned4b909f551.x: Mangal Pandey is identified as the first martyr of the Revolt of 1857.
ned4b909f551.tq: Test a first-in-sequence fact directly, while using other prominent figures as nearby distractors.
xs: **Mangal Pandey** is the **first martyr of 1857** — so option **(4)** is correct.
He attacked **Lt Baugh** and **Sergeant-Major Hewson** at **Barrackpore** on **29 March 1857**.
xa: He was hanged on **8 April 1857**; his regiment (**34th Bengal NI**) was disbanded.
On **21 July 2026** the PM paid tribute on his birth anniversary (born **19 July 1827**).
**Bahadur Shah II** was proclaimed **Shahenshah-e-Hindustan** on **11-12 May 1857**.

n3003615ee02.s: Which of the following was an administrative cause of resentment before the Revolt of 1857?
o: Exclusion of Indians from high civil and military posts
Rapid and inexpensive justice for all social groups
Abolition of corruption in lower courts
Admission of Indians to all high civil and military posts
n3003615ee02.x: Indians were excluded from high civil and military posts, producing resentment against the colonial administrative structure.
xs: Indians were **excluded from high civil and military posts** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Justice was in fact **slow and costly**, and **corruption** was rampant in lower courts, so options 2 and 3 are wrong.
xa: Corruption was rampant in **lower courts and police**; justice **favoured the rich**.
Annexations threw thousands of **officials, retainers and soldiers** of princely courts out of work.
In the army an Indian could rise **no higher than Subedar**.

nd32cd986361.s: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 is distinguished from the mutinies listed in the context of the 1857 uprising because it was—
o: the first mutiny of the 34th Native Infantry
a civil revolt rather than a sepoy revolt
an uprising caused by the new cartridges
a military revolt over sea service
nd32cd986361.x: The Santhal revolt of 1855–56 was a civil revolt and not a sepoy mutiny.
nd32cd986361.tq: Separate a civil revolt from a military mutiny.
xs: The **Santhal revolt (1855-56)** was a **civil revolt, not a sepoy revolt** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It had nothing to do with cartridges or sea service; those drove the sepoy outbreaks of **1824** and **1857**.
xa: UPPSC key: **Santhal revolt = 1855-56**; **Vellore = July 1806**; **Barrackpur = Nov 1824**.
Bhatta mutinies: **34th NI 1844**, **66th NI 1849-50**.

n72afcdda1a1.s: P.E. Roberts described the Revolt of 1857 as:
o: A religious war against the British
The First War of Indian Independence
n72afcdda1a1.x: P.E. Roberts characterized the revolt as “just a sepoy mutiny,” particularly in connection with the cartridge issue.
n72afcdda1a1.tq: Separate the British interpretive label from the nationalist interpretation.
xs: **P.E. Roberts** called it **"just a sepoy mutiny"** over the greased cartridges — so option **(2)** is correct.
**"First War of Independence"** is **V.D. Savarkar's** view.
xa: Savarkar: **The Indian War of Independence, 1857** (**1909**).
The revolt in fact combined **peasant, princely and sepoy** grievances.
**S.N. Sen**: **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**, centenary volume).

n72b40398953.s: Who wrote *Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind* on the causes of the Indian Revolt?
n72b40398953.x: Sir Syed Ahmed Khan wrote *Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind*, meaning “The Causes of the Indian Revolt.”
n72b40398953.tq: Match the author with the exact title of the work.
xs: **Sir Syed Ahmed Khan** wrote **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** ("The Causes of the Indian Revolt", **1859**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S.N. Sen** wrote **Eighteen Fifty-Seven**; **Vishnubhat Godse** wrote **Majha Pravas**; **Savarkar** wrote **The Indian War of Independence**.
xa: It was the **first Indian-language** work on the causes of 1857 (UPPSC **2009**).
He blamed lack of Indian representation in the **Legislative Council** and misunderstanding of Indian customs.
⚠ **The Great Rebellion** = **Ashok Mehta**; **The Great Mutiny** = **Christopher Hibbert**.

nindian-history-6-23.s: Who wrote 'The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857'?
nindian-history-6-23.x: R.C. Majumdar wrote The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857; Savarkar wrote The Indian War of Independence, 1857, Chaudhuri wrote Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies and Ashok Mehta wrote 1857: The Great Rebellion.
n: The Indian War of Independence, 1857 was written by V.D. Savarkar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857 was written by R.C. Majumdar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies (1857–1859) was written by S.B. Chaudhuri. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
1857: The Great Rebellion was written by Ashok Mehta. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xa: ⚠ **The Great Mutiny** = **Christopher Hibbert**; **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** = **S.N. Sen**.
**Sir Syed Ahmed Khan**'s **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** (**1859**) was the first Indian-language work on the causes.
**P.E. Roberts** called it "just a **sepoy mutiny**".

n8578ae9a83d.s: Which of the following was NOT a military grievance of the Indian sepoys mentioned in relation to the Revolt of 1857?
o: The ceiling of promotion at the rank of Subedar
n8578ae9a83d.x: Inefficiency of officers was identified as not being a cause of sepoy anger. Lower pay, racial contempt and the Subedar ceiling were genuine grievances.
n8578ae9a83d.tq: Find the one item expressly excluded from the list of grievances.
xs: **Inefficiency of officers** was **not** a cause — so option **(3)** is the answer (**BPSC 2018** key).
**Lower pay** than British soldiers, **racial contempt** and the **Subedar** ceiling were real grievances.
xa: **APPSC-GS 2023**: Subedar ceiling + greased cartridges both correct.
Missionary pressure, the order to travel by ship and stopping of **bhatta** **were** causes.

nindian-history-6-21.x: India for Indians was written by Chittaranjan Das (C.R. Das), the Swarajist leader. S.N. Banerjee wrote A Nation in Making and Subhas Chandra Bose wrote The Indian Struggle.
nindian-history-6-21.tq: Recall the author of each nationalist book.
n: India for Indians was written by C.R. Das. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 40-45]
xs: **India for Indians** was written by **C.R. Das** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S.N. Banerjee** wrote **A Nation in Making**; **Subhas Chandra Bose** wrote **The Indian Struggle**; **Jayaprakash Narayan** wrote **Towards Struggle**.
xa: **India Divided** — **Rajendra Prasad**.
**India Wins Freedom** — **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad**.
**Living an Era** — **D.P. Mishra**.

nfb23ef03344.s: The incident involving Mangal Pandey at Barrackpore occurred on:
nfb23ef03344.x: Mangal Pandey attacked British officers at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857.
nfb23ef03344.tq: Distinguish the date of the Barrackpore incident from the date of execution and the Meerut rising.
xs: **Mangal Pandey's** attack at **Barrackpore** came on **29 March 1857** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**8 April 1857** = his hanging; **10 May** = **Meerut**; **11 May** = rebels reach **Delhi**.
xa: He was of the **34th Bengal Native Infantry** and attacked **Lt Baugh** and **Sgt-Major Hewson**.
⚠ Some notes date the incident to **April**.
⚠ **Barrackpore** = first outbreak; **Meerut** = real **start** of the revolt.

n71c673bae4e.s: What was the slogan of the Meerut rebels when they marched in May 1857?
n71c673bae4e.x: After 85 sepoys of the 3rd (Light) Cavalry were jailed, the rebels freed the prisoners and marched to Delhi with the slogan 'Dilli Chalo'.
xa: **Meerut (10 May 1857)** = the **real start** of the revolt.
**APPSC-GS 2024** key: revolt began at **Meerut**, was widespread but failed.

n89c41cd6340.s: After entering the Red Fort in May 1857, the rebels at Delhi killed:
n89c41cd6340.x: After reaching Delhi, the rebels entered the Red Fort and killed Commissioner Simon Fraser.
xa: ⚠ Some notes write "**Simon Ripley**".
Bahadur Shah II was proclaimed **"Shahenshah-e-Hindustan"**.
Some notes say Delhi was seized on **12 May**.

n4d24e1326a5.s: After the fall of Delhi, Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to:
n4d24e1326a5.x: Bahadur Shah Zafar was captured after Delhi fell, tried and exiled to Rangoon.
xa: He died in **1862**.
Big states like **Hyderabad, Mysore**, **Scindia** and **Holkar** stayed loyal.

n41f5d2b79f7.s: The later use of the Hindu-Muslim unity displayed during the Revolt of 1857 was significant because it was cited against the
n41f5d2b79f7.x: The Hindu-Muslim unity associated with the revolt was later cited against the two-nation theory.
n41f5d2b79f7.tq: Match the historical experience with the later political theory it was used to challenge.
xs: The **Hindu-Muslim unity** of 1857 was later cited against the **two-nation theory** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The unity showed in practice: rebels of both faiths fought under a common symbolic leader, **Bahadur Shah Zafar**.
xa: Bahadur Shah's proclamations included a **ban on cow slaughter** and **joint commands**.
At Lucknow, **Hindus and Muslims shared offices**.

n82452d90537.s: General Bakht Khan, the real military leader of the rebels at Delhi, came to Delhi from:
n82452d90537.x: Bakht Khan came from Bareilly, reaching Delhi on 3 July 1857, and led a 10-member 'Court of Soldiers' there.
xa: **Delhi was recaptured** in **Sep 1857**.
Bareilly's own leader was **Khan Bahadur Khan**.

n7c173235d15.s: Begum Hazrat Mahal of Lucknow declared whom the ruler of Awadh in 1857?
n7c173235d15.x: Begum Hazrat Mahal led the revolt at Lucknow and proclaimed her son Birjis Qadr ruler of Awadh.
xa: Lucknow rose on **4 June 1857** and was recaptured in **Mar 1858**.
**Uda Devi** fought at **Sikandar Bagh**, Lucknow.

nindian-history-120-29.s: Tantia Tope led the Revolt of 1857 mainly in:
nindian-history-120-29.x: Tantia Tope operated in Central India; Kunwar Singh led in Bihar, Begum Hazrat Mahal in Awadh and Bakht Khan at Delhi.
n: Tantia Tope was associated with Central India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #120 · pp 218-221]
Kunwar Singh was associated with Bihar. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #120 · pp 218-221]
Begum Hazrat Mahal was associated with Awadh/Lucknow. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #120 · pp 218-221]
Bakht Khan was associated with Delhi. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #120 · pp 218-221]
xa: ⚠ In Delhi **Bahadur Shah** was the **nominal** leader; **Bakht Khan** the **real** one.
Bakht Khan led a **10-member "Court of Soldiers"** and reached Delhi on **3 July 1857**.
Begum Hazrat Mahal declared her son **Birjis Qadr** ruler of Awadh.

n3425ba6632b.s: Bareilly was recaptured by the British in:
n3425ba6632b.x: Bareilly was recaptured in May 1858, after Jhansi was retaken in April 1858.
xa: **Mar 1858**: **Lucknow** recaptured.
Kunwar Singh is linked with **Arrah**.

n2688f04b10c.x: Campbell retook Kanpur in December 1857 and Lucknow in March 1858; Hugh Rose took Jhansi in April and Gwalior in June 1858.
xa: **Delhi** had been recaptured earlier, in **Sep 1857**.
**Bareilly** was recaptured in **May 1858**.

n5ec415a5baf.s: Uda Devi fought against the British in 1857 at:
n5ec415a5baf.x: Uda Devi fought at Sikandar Bagh in Lucknow; Jhalkari Bai is linked with Jhansi and Azizun with Kanpur.
xa: Uda Devi was a **Pasi** woman; Azizun was a courtesan who **armed and rode with the sepoys**.
Jhalkari Bai commanded the Rani's **women's wing**.
**Shah Mal** mobilised the **chaurasee des (84 villages)** of Baraut.

n5f5b810b5ba.s: Shah Mal mobilised the headmen and cultivators of which area during the Revolt of 1857?
o: The chaurasee des of 84 villages in Baraut
n5f5b810b5ba.x: Shah Mal mobilised the chaurasee des, meaning the area of 84 villages, in the Baraut region of Uttar Pradesh.
n5f5b810b5ba.tq: Identify the distinctive local organisation and its numerical extent.
xs: **Shah Mal** mobilised headmen and cultivators of the **chaurasee des (84 villages)** of **Baraut** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jagdishpur** belongs to **Kunwar Singh**; **Rohilkhand** to **Khan Bahadur Khan**.
xa: Asked as the **APPSC-GS 2021** key.
Baraut is a pargana in **UP**.

n47e5bf5a05c.s: Which of the following regions formed the main zone of the Revolt of 1857?
o: The Doab, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bihar, Bundelkhand and Central India
Eastern, western and southern coastal India
n47e5bf5a05c.x: The main zone included the Doab, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bihar, Bundelkhand and Central India.
n47e5bf5a05c.tq: Select the complete geographical cluster instead of a partial region.
xs: The main zone was the **Doab, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bihar, Bundelkhand and Central India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Bengal, Punjab** and **eastern, western and southern India** were largely unaffected.
xa: The zone ran from near **Patna** to the **Rajasthan border**.
**Hyderabad** and **Mysore** stayed loyal.

n538ed6cb3b8.s: Which of the following regions was largely unaffected by the Revolt of 1857?
o: Bengal, Punjab, eastern, western and southern India
n538ed6cb3b8.x: Bengal, Punjab, and eastern, western and southern India were largely unaffected; British forces for suppression came from several of these regions.
n538ed6cb3b8.tq: Locate the unaffected regions by eliminating the principal revolt zone.
xs: **Bengal, Punjab, eastern, western and southern India** were largely unaffected — so option **(4)** is correct.
British power stayed intact there, and **suppression forces came from here**.
The other options list parts of the **main zone**.
xa: The revolt's **narrow territorial and social base** was a cause of failure.
**Martial groups of the north** mostly backed the British.

nfca0feedbb2.s: In 1857, Scindia of Gwalior, whose troops went over to the Rani, fled to:
nfca0feedbb2.x: Scindia stayed loyal to the British, but his troops defected to the Rani and he fled to Agra.
xa: The Nizam's loyalty **kept the Deccan quiet**.
**Mysore** and **Holkar** were also loyal.

nindian-history-136-14.s: The Revolt of 1857 was mainly centred in which region?
nindian-history-136-14.x: The Revolt of 1857 was centred in North and Central India. Bengal is linked to the Sanyasi-Fakir revolt, Chotanagpur to the Kol revolt and Andhra to the Rampa revolt.
nindian-history-136-14.tq: Recall the region of each revolt.
n: The Sanyasi-Fakir Rebellion occurred in Bengal. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #136 · pp 239-240]
The Kol Rebellion occurred in Chotanagpur. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #136 · pp 239-240]
The Revolt of 1857 occurred in North and Central India. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #136 · pp 239-240]
The Rampa Rebellion occurred in the Andhra region. [Indian History · ROCKET SHEET #136 · pp 239-240]
xs: The Revolt of **1857** occurred mainly in **North and Central India** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Bengal**, **Punjab**, eastern, western and southern India were **largely unaffected**.
In Andhra, the **Nizam** **Afzal-ud-Daula** stayed **pro-British**.
xa: Main zone: **Doab, Awadh, Rohilkhand, Bihar, Bundelkhand and Central India**.
Loyal rulers: **Hyderabad**, **Mysore**, **Scindia** of Gwalior, Holkar.
Local Andhra risings: **Dandasena** and **Korukonda Subba Reddy**, both in **August 1857**.

n74749b5474a.s: The revolt at Bareilly was led by Khan Bahadur Khan, who proclaimed himself:
n74749b5474a.x: Khan Bahadur Khan proclaimed himself Nawab Nizam at Bareilly and commanded an army of about 40,000.
n74749b5474a.tq: Test the exact title adopted by a regional leader.
xs: **Khan Bahadur Khan** proclaimed himself **Nawab Nizam** at Bareilly — so option **(3)** is correct.
**"Shahenshah-e-Hindustan"** was **Bahadur Shah II's** title.
xa: He led an army of **40,000** in **Rohilkhand**.
Bareilly rose in **May 1857** and was recaptured in **May 1858**.

n4f0de3e344d.s: Who among the following was the correspondent of The Times who reported on the Revolt of 1857 and British reprisals?
n4f0de3e344d.x: W. H. Russell, correspondent of The Times, reported on the revolt and British reprisals in My Diary in India.
n4f0de3e344d.tq: Distinguish the contemporary reporter from political advisers and military officers.
xs: **W.H. Russell**, correspondent of **The Times**, reported on the revolt and British reprisals — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Azimullah Khan** was **Nana Saheb's adviser**; **Afzal-ud-Daula** was the **Nizam**; **Captain Wilson** crushed **Dandasena**.
xa: Russell's account: **My Diary in India**.
Azimullah Khan went to **London** to plead Nana Saheb's **pension** case.

n7c185ed7c84.s: Dandasena, the Savara chief associated with the Revolt of 1857, rose at Paralakimidi after which development?
o: The ban on selling forest produce
The removal of the Nizam from Hyderabad
n7c185ed7c84.x: Dandasena rose at Paralakimidi on 9 August 1857 after the ban on selling forest produce.
n7c185ed7c84.tq: Link the local leader with the immediate cause rather than with a nearby Hyderabad event.
xs: **Dandasena** rose at **Paralakimidi** after the **ban on selling forest produce** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He rose on **9 August 1857**; **Mubariz-ud-Daula's** imprisonment belongs to **Hyderabad**.
xa: Dandasena was a **Savara chief**; Paralakimidi was then in **Ganjam** district.
He was crushed by **Captain Wilson** and **hanged**.

nbc3dcf6218e.s: Which Nizam of Hyderabad remained pro-British during the Revolt of 1857?
nbc3dcf6218e.x: Afzal-ud-Daula remained pro-British, and his loyalty helped keep the Deccan quiet.
xa: Dandasena = **Paralakimidi**; Subba Reddy = **Errannagudem**.
**APPSC-G1 2022**: **Mubariz-ud-Daula's** imprisonment in **Golconda** came before Turrebaz Khan's attack on the **Residency**.

n850d47bfecc.s: The two principal local risings in Andhra associated with the Revolt of 1857 occurred at which pair of places?
n850d47bfecc.x: Dandasena led the rising at Paralakimidi, while Korukonda Subba Reddy led the rebellion at Errannagudem; both occurred in August 1857.
