n850d47bfecc.tq: Separate the Andhra centres from the better-known northern and Hyderabad centres.
xs: The two Andhra risings were at **Paralakimidi** and **Errannagudem** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Dandasena** led at Paralakimidi; **Korukonda Subba Reddy** at Errannagudem — both in **August 1857**.
xa: In Hyderabad, **Turrebaz Khan** attacked the **Residency**.
**Bareilly** = Khan Bahadur Khan; **Meerut** and **Barrackpore** were the first outbreaks.

n1cc93a2dc3a.s: Azimullah Khan went to London primarily to plead which case?
o: The restoration of the Nizam’s authority
The pension case of Nana Saheb
The forest-produce rights of Savara chiefs
n1cc93a2dc3a.x: Azimullah Khan, Nana Saheb’s adviser, went to London to plead Nana Saheb’s pension case.
n1cc93a2dc3a.tq: Connect the adviser with the specific political mission he undertook.
xs: **Azimullah Khan** went to London to plead **Nana Saheb's pension** case — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was **Nana Saheb's adviser**.
xa: At **Kanpur** Nana Saheb led with **Tantia Tope** and **Azimullah Khan**.
Kanpur rose on **5 June 1857**; **Colin Campbell** retook it in **Dec 1857**.

n5291c75a545.s: Which one of the following was NOT a leader of the Revolt of 1857?
n5291c75a545.x: Bhagat Singh belongs to the later freedom movement and only drew on 1857's legacy (APPSC 2019 odd one out). Maulvi Ahmadullah led at Faizabad, Khan Bahadur Khan at Bareilly, and Maulvi Liyakat Ali at Allahabad and Banaras.
n5291c75a545.tq: Bhagat Singh = odd one out for 1857.
xs: **Bhagat Singh** was not part of 1857 — so option **(3)** is the answer.
He only **drew on its legacy** later (**APPSC 2019** odd one out).
**Maulvi Ahmadullah** = **Faizabad**; **Khan Bahadur Khan** = **Bareilly**; **Maulvi Liyakat Ali** = **Allahabad and Banaras**.
xa: 1857 heroes were invoked in the **Quit India** and **INA** phases.
⚠ At **Delhi**, **Bahadur Shah** was nominal leader; **Bakht Khan** the real one.

n0358fd35b79.s: Which of the following was a major limitation of the Revolt of 1857?
o: Participation of all major princes and urban elites
Superior arms in the hands of the rebels
Lack of coordination and central leadership
n0358fd35b79.x: The revolt suffered from lack of coordination and central leadership; many big princes and urban elites stayed away, and the rebels had inferior arms and no unified programme.
xa: Loyal big states: **Hyderabad, Mysore, Scindia, Holkar**.
**APPSC-GS 2024**: the revolt was widespread **but failed**.

n29b94b49963.s: Which British officer is associated with the recapture of Delhi in September 1857?
n29b94b49963.x: John Nicholson was associated with the recapture of Delhi in September 1857 and was killed in the assault.
n29b94b49963.tq: Match the British officer with the centre recaptured, avoiding the Campbell–Delhi trap.
xs: **Delhi** was recaptured in **September 1857** by forces under **John Nicholson** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Nicholson** was **killed in the assault** on Delhi; **Hodson** captured the emperor.
**William Taylor** retook **Bihar** (Kunwar Singh); **Colin Campbell** retook **Kanpur**, **Lucknow** and **Bareilly**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes credit "General **Campbell**" with Delhi — Delhi was retaken by **Nicholson** and others in **Sept 1857**.
Delhi's rebel leaders: **Bahadur Shah II** (nominal) and **Bakht Khan** (real commander).
Exam angle: "Which centre was recaptured by the English?" — **Delhi** (UPPSC **2015**).

n8010ec5edf8.s: Allahabad and Banaras were associated with the rebellion led by ______ and were recaptured by ______.
n8010ec5edf8.x: Maulvi Liyakat Ali led the rebellion at Allahabad and Banaras, which were recaptured by Colonel Neill.
n8010ec5edf8.tq: Match the rebel leader and British officer to the correct centres.
xs: **Allahabad** and **Banaras** were led by **Maulvi Liyakat Ali** and recaptured by **Colonel Neill** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Khan Bahadur Khan** led **Bareilly**; **Kunwar Singh** led **Bihar**; **Bakht Khan** led **Delhi**'s defence.
xa: **Neill** was later **killed at Lucknow**.
**Bihar** was retaken by **William Taylor**; **Delhi** by **John Nicholson** (**Sept 1857**).
**Bareilly** fell to **Colin Campbell** in **May 1858**.

nc6dc33b1ba6.s: Who among the following coordinated communication among rebel leaders while serving as an adviser to Nana Saheb?
nc6dc33b1ba6.x: Azimullah Khan served as Nana Saheb's adviser and coordinated communication among rebel leaders.
nc6dc33b1ba6.tq: Distinguish adviser, military associate and political successor roles.
xs: **Azimullah Khan** served **Nana Saheb** as adviser and **coordinated communication** among rebel leaders — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Tantia Tope** was Nana Saheb's military commander; **Havelock** was a British officer; **Birjis Qadir** was Begum Hazrat Mahal's son.
xa: **Nana Saheb** (Kanpur) **escaped to Nepal**.
Other leaders: **Khan Bahadur Khan** — Rohilkhand; **Maulvi Ahmadullah** — Faizabad/Awadh.
**Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and reached **Delhi on 3 July 1857**.

nc0540742bd7.s: Maulvi Ahmadullah led the Revolt of 1857 in:
nc0540742bd7.x: Ahmadullah operated in Faizabad; Khan Bahadur Khan was in Rohilkhand, Kunwar Singh in Bihar and Tantia Tope in Central India.
xa: Kunwar Singh was a **70-year-old zamindar** who waged guerrilla war; died April **1858**.
**Begum of Awadh** and **Maulvi Ahmadullah** quarrelled — an example of divided leadership.
**Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and commanded Delhi's defence.

nf4e8c5ff271.s: General Bakht Khan, who commanded the defence of Delhi in 1857, came to Delhi from:
nf4e8c5ff271.x: Bakht Khan came from Bareilly and reached Delhi on 3 July 1857 (APPSC-GS 2023 key). Lucknow was Begum Hazrat Mahal's centre, Kanpur Nana Saheb's, and Faizabad Maulvi Ahmadullah's.
nf4e8c5ff271.tq: Bakht Khan: Bareilly to Delhi, 3 July 1857.
xs: **Bakht Khan** came from **Bareilly** and reached **Delhi on 3 July 1857** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Lucknow** was **Begum Hazrat Mahal**'s centre, **Kanpur** Nana Saheb's, and **Faizabad** Maulvi Ahmadullah's.
xa: This is the APPSC-GS **2023** key.
Bakht Khan was the **real commander** at Delhi; **Bahadur Shah II** was nominal leader.
**Bareilly** itself was led by **Khan Bahadur Khan** and retaken by **Colin Campbell** (**May 1858**).

n939d8ea713c.s: The revolt of 1857 was chiefly a revolt of the:
n939d8ea713c.x: The revolt was chiefly of the Bengal Army; the Madras and Bombay armies largely remained loyal, while a Gorkha regiment assisted Campbell.
n939d8ea713c.tq: Distinguish the principal rebel army from the loyal presidency armies.
xs: The revolt was chiefly one of the **Bengal Army** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Madras** and **Bombay** armies stayed **largely loyal**.
A **Gorkha regiment** actually **helped Campbell's suppression**.
xa: It was confined mostly to **North and Central India** (Doab); Bengal, Madras, Bombay regions largely peaceful.
Lack of support from the "**martial races**" of the north was a cause of failure.

ncf5af0c9535.s: Bahadur Shah II, who was the nominal leader of the revolt at Delhi, was ultimately:
o: Killed in the assault on Delhi
Executed at Delhi after a public trial
Captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon
ncf5af0c9535.x: Bahadur Shah II was captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon in Burma, where he died in 1862.
ncf5af0c9535.tq: Directly distinguish the fate of the principal rebel leaders.
xs: **Bahadur Shah II** was **captured, tried and exiled to Rangoon** (Burma) — so option **(3)** is correct.
He died there in **1862**; he was neither killed in the assault nor sent to Nepal.
xa: His **sons were shot by Hodson** and the **Mughal line ended**.
Real commander at Delhi: Gen. **Bakht Khan**.
Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to — **Rangoon**" (APPSC-G1 **2018**).
⚠ **Nana Saheb** and **Hazrat Mahal** → **Nepal**; **Tantia Tope** → executed.

nc2b584263cc.s: Tantia Tope was captured and executed after being betrayed by:
nc2b584263cc.x: Tantia Tope was betrayed by Man Singh, captured and executed in April 1859.
nc2b584263cc.tq: Test the specific betrayer rather than the associated British officer.
xs: **Tantia Tope** was **betrayed by Man Singh**, captured and **executed** (April **1859**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Scindia** was loyal to the British and fled to **Agra**; **Hugh Rose** and **Colin Campbell** were British commanders.
xa: Tantia Tope fought at **Kanpur**, then **Central India**, and fought on after **Nana Saheb**'s escape.
He **captured Gwalior** with **Rani Lakshmibai**.
⚠ Fates: **Bahadur Shah** → Rangoon; **Nana Saheb**, **Hazrat Mahal** → Nepal; **Tantia Tope** → executed.

na75373af7d5.s: Rani Lakshmibai died fighting near Gwalior on 17 June 1858 against the force of:
na75373af7d5.x: After capturing Gwalior with Tantia Tope, the Rani died near Gwalior fighting Sir Hugh Rose's force, not defending Jhansi against Campbell.
xa: She was proclaimed head of state on **4 June 1858** at Gwalior.
**Scindia**'s troops deserted to the Rani, and he took refuge at **Agra**.
Her centres: **Jhansi**, then **Gwalior**.

ne77a9549566.s: After the recapture of Delhi, which of the following occurred?
o: Bahadur Shah was restored and his sons were pardoned.
Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, while his sons were shot by Hodson.
The Mughal line was strengthened under Birjis Qadir.
Bahadur Shah escaped to Nepal with Nana Saheb.
ne77a9549566.x: After Delhi was recaptured, Bahadur Shah was tried and deported, and his sons were shot by Hodson. The Mughal line consequently ended.
ne77a9549566.tq: Use the aftermath sequence to reject reversal and substitution traps.
xs: After Delhi's recapture, **Bahadur Shah** was **tried and deported**, and his **sons were shot by Hodson** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Mughal line ended**; Birjis Qadir was Begum Hazrat Mahal's son at **Lucknow**.
**Nana Saheb** escaped to **Nepal**; Bahadur Shah went to **Rangoon**.
xa: Delhi was retaken in **Sept 1857** by **John Nicholson**, who was killed in the assault.
Bahadur Shah died in Rangoon in **1862**.
Exam angle: "Bahadur Shah was exiled to — **Rangoon**" (APPSC-G1 **2018**).

n5b6023ab9ce.s: The loyal princes were described as “breakwaters to the storm” by:
n5b6023ab9ce.x: The phrase “breakwaters to the storm” is attributed to Lord Canning, although some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
n5b6023ab9ce.tq: Discriminate between two authorities associated with a memorable phrase.
xs: The loyal princes were called "**breakwaters to the storm**" by **Lord Canning** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Some notes credit **Lord Elgin**, but the standard key is Canning.
xa: Big **zamindars and moneylenders** also acted as "breakwaters" to protect class interests.
Loyal princes: **Scindia**, **Holkar**, Sikh chiefs, **Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula**.
Canning: Governor-General **1856-58**, first **Viceroy** **1858-62**.

n6a6fcd18f73.s: The educated middle class generally remained neutral during the revolt because it viewed it as:
o: A movement led by urban merchants
n6a6fcd18f73.x: The educated middle class generally saw the revolt as a backward-looking feudal reaction and therefore remained neutral.
n6a6fcd18f73.tq: Link a social class with its stated interpretation of the revolt.
xs: The **educated middle class** stayed **neutral**, seeing the revolt as a **backward-looking feudal reaction** — so option **(1)** is correct.
This is a UPSC **1998** angle.
xa: **Merchants** and the **urban elite** did not support the revolt.
Participants: **sepoys**, **peasants**, **artisans**, **dispossessed rulers**.
Failure factor: **no forward-looking programme** or modern nationalist vision.

n5ecbf068243.s: Which one of the following regions was largely peaceful during the revolt of 1857?
n5ecbf068243.x: The revolt was concentrated mainly in North and Central India, while Bengal, Madras and Bombay regions remained largely peaceful.
n5ecbf068243.tq: Find the region that falls outside the principal geographical base of the revolt.
xs: **Madras Presidency** stayed **largely peaceful** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The revolt was confined mostly to **North and Central India** (the **Doab**); Bengal, Madras and Bombay regions were peaceful.
xa: The **Madras** and **Bombay armies** were largely loyal; it was chiefly a **Bengal Army** revolt.
British power intact in **East, West and South** India let them send troops north.
**Nizam** and **Salar Jung I** kept the **Deccan** quiet.

n971bcad0514.s: The rebel attack on the Hyderabad Residency, which was repulsed, took place on:
n971bcad0514.x: The attack on the Hyderabad Residency on 17 July 1857 was repulsed, as the Nizam Afzal-ud-Daula and Salar Jung I stayed loyal.
xa: They **kept the Deccan quiet**.
Other large states that stayed out: **Mysore** and the **Rajput chiefs**.
**Scindia of Gwalior** was the most loyal (MPPSC **2010**).

n5a3cb52131f.s: The military disadvantage of the rebels during the revolt was mainly due to their dependence on:
n5a3cb52131f.x: The rebels generally used swords, spears and old muskets, whereas the British had Enfield rifles and the electric telegraph.
n5a3cb52131f.tq: Compare the weaponry and communication systems of the two sides.
xs: The rebels depended on **swords, spears and old muskets** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Enfield rifles** and the **electric telegraph** were **British** advantages, not the rebels'.
xa: Rebels also lacked **discipline** and **central coordination**.
British had **experienced generals** and troops sent north from East, West and South India.

ne997c1c7cde.s: The term 'Sepoy Mutiny' or 'Indian Mutiny' was predominantly used by which school of historians?
ne997c1c7cde.x: British or imperialist historians commonly used the labels Sepoy Mutiny or Indian Mutiny and denied the revolt a national character.
ne997c1c7cde.tq: Associate the label with the historiographical school that used it.
xs: **Sepoy Mutiny / Indian Mutiny** are the labels of **British / imperialist** historians — so option **(2)** is correct.
They blamed **religious fanaticism** and **administrative blunders** and denied a **national character**.
xa: Indian historians: **Great Rebellion**; **Savarkar**: **First War of Independence**.
Other names: **Revolt of 1857**, **Indian Insurrection**.
Imperialist names: **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**, **P.E. Roberts**.

na462bb7fef6.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a feudal reaction primarily emphasises the role of:
o: dispossessed princes and taluqdars attempting to restore their lost positions
urban middle classes demanding representative government
European merchants opposing the East India Company
na462bb7fef6.x: The feudal-reaction interpretation highlights dispossessed princes and taluqdars such as Nana Saheb, Lakshmibai and Begum Hazrat Mahal, who sought to recover lost positions.
na462bb7fef6.tq: Apply the interpretation to the social groups and motives it highlights.
xs: The **feudal reaction** view stresses **dispossessed princes and taluqdars** trying to **restore their lost positions** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Examples: **Nana Saheb**, **Lakshmibai**, **Begum Hazrat Mahal**.
The **educated middle class** stayed **aloof**, so it was no middle-class demand.
xa: **Nehru** (Discovery of India) called it essentially a **feudal rising**.
Verdict: a **traditional uprising**, not a modern nationalist movement.

nf1ee540aa92.s: “What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence” was the assessment of:
nf1ee540aa92.x: S.N. Sen concluded that the revolt began as a fight for religion but ultimately developed into a war of independence.
nf1ee540aa92.tq: Identify the historian from the famous concluding formulation.
xs: "What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence" is **S.N. Sen**'s verdict — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Savarkar** saw a planned **First War of Independence**; **Majumdar**: "neither first, nor national"; **Disraeli**: a **national rising**.
xa: Sen wrote **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**), the official centenary history.
Sen and Majumdar both judged mid-19th-century nationalism **embryonic** (MPPSC **2020**).

nf909c2852fb.s: R.C. Majumdar and S.N. Sen regarded Indian nationalism in the mid-nineteenth century as:
nf909c2852fb.x: Both Majumdar and Sen regarded Indian nationalism in the mid-nineteenth century as still embryonic.
xa: Majumdar: "**Neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**" (UPPSC **2017**).
Sen: began as a **fight for religion**, ended as a **war of independence**.
**Modern nationalism** had not yet emerged — a reason 1857 was not a "first war of independence".

n5385b1ba1f9.s: R.C. Majumdar, unlike the nationalist school, argued that the Revolt of 1857 was:
o: the first, national and completely successful war of independence
only a conflict between civilisation and barbarism
neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence
n5385b1ba1f9.x: R.C. Majumdar's own verdict was that the revolt was neither the first nor national nor a war of independence, despite some classifications placing him in a broader nationalist school.
n5385b1ba1f9.tq: Resolve the apparent contradiction by separating a school classification from the historian's own verdict.
xs: **R.C. Majumdar** argued 1857 was "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**" — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is his own verdict (UPPSC **2017**), though some tables put him in the nationalist "first war" school.
The **Hindu-Muslim conspiracy** view is **Outram**'s; **civilisation vs barbarism** is **T.R. Holmes**'.
xa: ⚠ Trap: learn Majumdar as the **sceptic**, opposite **Savarkar**.
He also judged mid-19th-century nationalism **embryonic** (with **S.N. Sen**).

n987adf86352.s: Which historian, emphasising local agrarian studies, viewed the Revolt of 1857 as a combination of several peasant and elite risings?
n987adf86352.x: Eric Stokes stressed local agrarian studies and saw the revolt as multiple peasant and elite risings, not one centrally directed movement.
xa: **Rudrangshu Mukherjee**: popular resistance of **peasants and taluqdars in Awadh** (**Awadh in Revolt**).
Peasants and artisans joined in **Awadh** and **western UP**, hit by revenue burden and ruin of crafts.

ned55099e1d8.s: Which one of the following was identified by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan as the main cause of the revolt of 1857?
o: The decline of the textile industry in Bengal
The annexation of Punjab by the British
The introduction of the Subsidiary Alliance
The absence of Indians in the Legislative Council
ned55099e1d8.x: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan argued that the absence of Indians in the Legislative Council caused the rulers to misunderstand the ruled.
ned55099e1d8.tq: Test the precise cause attributed by an identified contemporary observer.
xs: **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** held that the main cause was **no Indian in the Legislative Council** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Without Indians in the Council, the **rulers misunderstood the ruled**.
xa: His book: **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** (Causes of the Indian Revolt), **1859**.
Contemporaries: **Disraeli** — national rising; **Karl Marx** — national revolt.

nfce68d009fc.s: Which of the following historians characterised the uprising of 1857 as a purely military outbreak or a mere sepoy mutiny?
nfce68d009fc.x: Sir John Lawrence, along with J.R. Seeley and Charles Raikes, regarded the uprising primarily as a sepoy mutiny and denied it a popular or national character.
nfce68d009fc.tq: Match the historian with the distinctive verdict.
xs: **Sir John Lawrence** (with **J.R. Seeley** and **Charles Raikes**) saw it as a mere **Sepoy Mutiny** — a purely military outbreak — so option **(2)** is correct.
**S.N. Sen**: a fight for religion that became a **war of independence**; **Disraeli**: a **national rising**.
**T.R. Holmes**: a conflict between **civilisation and barbarism**.
xa: **P.E. Roberts**: "just a **sepoy mutiny**" over **greased cartridges**.
**L.E.R. Rees**: a war of **fanatic religionists against Christians**.
**Outram** and **W. Taylor**: a **Muslim/Hindu-Muslim conspiracy** exploiting Hindu grievances.

n08defbcc1a3.s: Who (with W. Taylor) described the Revolt of 1857 as a Muslim conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances?
n08defbcc1a3.x: Outram saw it as a Muslim conspiracy exploiting Hindu grievances; Rees called it a war of fanatic religionists against Christians and Holmes a conflict between civilisation and barbarism.
xa: The imperialist "Sepoy Mutiny" school also included **Sir John Lawrence**, **J.R. Seeley**, **Charles Raikes**.
The "**national rising**" view came from **Disraeli**; Marx called it a **national revolt**.

nc8c7041ffec.s: The interpretation of the Revolt of 1857 as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians is associated with:
nc8c7041ffec.x: L.E.R. Rees interpreted the revolt as a war of fanatic religionists against Christians.
nc8c7041ffec.tq: Discriminate between historians whose interpretations concern religion and mutiny.
xs: **L.E.R. Rees** called it a war of **fanatic religionists against Christians** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Charles Raikes** and **P.E. Roberts** saw a mere **Sepoy Mutiny**; **R.C. Majumdar**: "**neither first, nor national**".
xa: ⚠ Confusable: **T.R. Holmes** = conflict between **civilisation and barbarism**.
**Outram** and **W. Taylor**: a **Muslim/Hindu-Muslim conspiracy**.

nbb3bdc70b10.s: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels' articles on the uprising were compiled under which title?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859
nbb3bdc70b10.x: Karl Marx's and Friedrich Engels' articles were compiled as The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859.
nbb3bdc70b10.tq: Match the compilation title with the pair of writers associated with it.
xs: **Karl Marx** and **Engels**' articles were compiled as **The First Indian War of Independence 1857-1859** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857** is **R.C. Majumdar**'s book (**1957**).
xa: **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** — **S.N. Sen** (**1957**), the Government of India-commissioned centenary history.
**Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** — **Sir Syed Ahmad Khan** (**1859**).
**Awadh in Revolt** — **Rudrangshu Mukherjee**; **Discovery of India** — **Nehru**.

n30edf31c4b6.s: Who first described the Revolt of 1857 as the 'First War of Indian Independence'?
n30edf31c4b6.x: V.D. Savarkar called it the First War of Indian Independence, a planned rising and not a mere mutiny. Tilak is a common distractor. R.C. Majumdar held the opposite view: 'neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence'. S.N. Sen wrote the official centenary history Eighteen Fifty-Seven.
n30edf31c4b6.tq: First War of Independence = Savarkar; Majumdar is the sceptic.
xs: **V.D. Savarkar** first called it the **First War of Indian Independence** — a planned rising, not a mere mutiny — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Tilak** is a stock distractor; **R.C. Majumdar** said "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**".
**S.N. Sen** wrote the official centenary history **Eighteen Fifty-Seven** (**1957**).
xa: Exam angle: BPSC **2022**, **2024**.
**Sen**: "What began as a fight for religion ended as a war of independence".
Andhra nationalist writing too treated 1857 as India's first war of independence.

n3caadd62aeb.s: Who wrote 'Eighteen Fifty-Seven', the Government of India-commissioned centenary history of the revolt?
n3caadd62aeb.x: S.N. Sen's Eighteen Fifty-Seven was the official centenary history; R.C. Majumdar wrote his 1957 work independently after parting with the official project.
xa: Majumdar's book: **The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857**.
Majumdar's verdict: "**neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence**".
Sen's verdict: a fight for religion that ended as a **war of independence**.

n6728e55671e.s: Which one of the following books was written by R.C. Majumdar?
o: The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857
Civil Rebellion in the Indian Mutinies
n6728e55671e.x: R.C. Majumdar wrote The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857, published in 1957.
n6728e55671e.tq: Distinguish similar 1857 titles by their authors.
xs: **R.C. Majumdar** wrote **The Sepoy Mutiny and the Revolt of 1857** (**1957**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Eighteen Fifty-Seven** is **S.N. Sen**'s official centenary history.
xa: Majumdar wrote independently after **parting with the official project**.
Other books: **Awadh in Revolt** — Rudrangshu Mukherjee; **Asbab-e-Baghawat-e-Hind** — Sir Syed Ahmad Khan (**1859**).

nda817aa3618.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the limitations of calling the Revolt of 1857 the First War of Independence?
o: There was no common goal among all participants
The revolt spread evenly across the whole of India
Modern nationalism had not yet emerged
nda817aa3618.x: The revolt did not spread evenly; it was confined largely to North India while most of India remained neutral.
xa: It began as a **military mutiny** and became a **popular rebellion**.
It was a **traditional uprising** against a common foreign enemy.
Even so it **shook British rule**.

nefc8e69b264.s: The Revolt of 1857 began as a ____ and rapidly developed into a popular rebellion.
nefc8e69b264.x: It began among soldiers as a mutiny but quickly drew in rulers, peasants and common people.
xa: Sepoys spearheaded at **Meerut** (**10 May 1857**); Delhi seized **11-12 May**.
It was **not a modern nationalist movement**: the idea of one Indian nation-state had not emerged.

nc63c5f87093.s: The national character of the Revolt of 1857 is best described as:
o: A traditional uprising of different classes against a common foreign enemy
A modern nationalist movement with a common programme
nc63c5f87093.x: The idea of a single Indian nation-state had not yet emerged; different classes defended local, economic and religious interests against a common foreign enemy.
xa: **Majumdar** and **Sen**: mid-19th-century nationalism was only **embryonic**.
The revolt was confined largely to **North India**.

n658c82a49fa.s: Why did the educated middle class largely remain aloof from the revolt of 1857?
o: It considered British rule to be modernising.
It was led by the taluqdars of Awadh.
It had already established an independent national government.
It opposed all forms of education introduced by the British.
n658c82a49fa.x: The educated middle class generally remained aloof because it viewed British rule as modernising.
n658c82a49fa.tq: Identify the attitude of a social group rather than its formal position.
xs: The **educated middle class** **stayed aloof** because it saw British rule as **modernising** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **taluqdars of Awadh** were a separate group that joined the revolt.
xa: Elite and urban classes uninvolved — one reason 1857 is not called a "first war of independence".
Loyal too: **most princes**, **merchants and moneylenders**.

n57d3011929c.s: Which of the following groups stayed loyal to the British during the Revolt of 1857?
n57d3011929c.x: The big zamindars of Bengal stayed loyal, while Awadh taluqdars and zamindars, and peasants and artisans of Awadh and western UP, joined the revolt.
xa: **Merchants and moneylenders** were also loyal, as were **most princes**.
**Rudrangshu Mukherjee**'s **Awadh in Revolt** studies these peasants and taluqdars.

n0f2bd03b9f9.s: What was the significance of Bahadur Shah II during the revolt of 1857?
o: He led only the sepoys of the Bengal Army.
He was accepted as the symbolic head by Hindu and Muslim rebels.
He represented the educated middle class in the revolt.
He served as the principal British commander in Delhi.
n0f2bd03b9f9.x: Bahadur Shah II was accepted as the symbolic head by both Hindu and Muslim rebels.
n0f2bd03b9f9.tq: Distinguish symbolic leadership from direct military command.
xs: **Bahadur Shah II** was accepted as **symbolic head** by **Hindu and Muslim rebels** alike — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was no British commander, nor a middle-class leader — the **educated middle class** stayed aloof.
xa: The **greased cartridges** offended both communities.
After 1857 the British turned to **divide and rule**.

nd0d0c4fb404.s: Annapurnayya, known as ‘Andhra Netaji’, was sentenced to 18 months’ rigorous imprisonment for which of the following?
o: Writing the article *Chicharapidugu* on the revolt of 1857
Supporting the British policy of divide and rule
Organising the RIN revolt at Bombay
nd0d0c4fb404.x: Annapurnayya received 18 months’ rigorous imprisonment for his article *Chicharapidugu*, which dealt with the revolt of 1857.
nd0d0c4fb404.tq: Test the association between a regional nationalist figure and his specific written work.
xs: **Annapurnayya** ("**Andhra Netaji**") got **18 months RI** for his article "**Chicharapidugu**" on **1857** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He did not lead at **Meerut** (sepoys, **10 May 1857**) or organise the **RIN revolt** (**1946**).
xa: Andhra nationalist writing treated 1857 as India's **first war of independence**.
AP during 1857: Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daulah** stayed pro-British; **Turrebaz Khan** led a limited revolt in Hyderabad.

n8deb9b4fdc8.s: The Government of India Act, 1858 was officially titled as the:
o: Act for the Political Settlement of India
Act for the Better Administration of India
Act for the Good Government of India
Act for the Regulation of Crown Territories
n8deb9b4fdc8.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 was titled the Act for the Good Government of India.
n8deb9b4fdc8.tq: Directly identify the exact official title of the Act.
xs: The GoI Act, **1858** was titled the **Act for the Good Government of India** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was passed after the **1857 Revolt** and **abolished Company rule**.
xa: Government, territories and revenues of India passed to the **British Crown**.
It created the **Secretary of State for India** and the title **Viceroy**.
The **1858** answer appeared in APPSC-GS **2018**, **2019** and UPPSC **2010**.

n3419bcc2610.s: Which Act transferred the government, territories and revenues of India from the East India Company to the British Crown?
n3419bcc2610.x: The Government of India Act, 1858, passed after the Revolt, ended Company rule and vested India in the Crown. The Charter Act 1853 and Pitt's India Act 1784 left the Company in place, and the Indian Councils Act 1861 came after the transfer.
xs: The **Government of India Act, 1858** transferred the government, territories and revenues of India to the **British Crown** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Charter Act 1853** and **Pitt's Act** left the Company in place; the **Indian Councils Act 1861** came after the transfer.
xa: Exam angle: options mix Charter Acts **1833**/**1853**, Pitt's Act and ICA **1861** — only the **1858** Act transferred power.
The East India Company was finally **dissolved in 1874**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

nbba2517aaa5.s: The Charter Act of 1833 made the East India Company:
o: an agency of the Crown headed by the Secretary of State
a body subordinate to the Board of Control in commercial matters only
nbba2517aaa5.x: The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company’s remaining commercial functions and made it a purely administrative organisation.
nbba2517aaa5.tq: Use the change in the Company’s character to identify the correct Charter Act.
xs: The **Charter Act 1833** made the Company a **purely administrative** organisation — so option **(4)** is correct.
It also made the GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** (**Bentinck**).
The Company became no **agency of the Crown** under a SoS — that came only with the **1858** Act.
xa: APPSC G2 **2024** and G2 **2025** asked "GG of Bengal designated GG of India by?" — **Charter Act 1833**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

nf0cce5bfde3.s: Which Act changed the title to Governor-General of India?
nf0cce5bfde3.x: The Charter Act of 1833 changed the title to Governor-General of India, and William Bentinck was the first holder of that title.
nf0cce5bfde3.tq: Distinguish the Act changing the territorial scope of the title from the later Act creating the Viceroyship.
xs: The **Charter Act 1833** made the GG of Bengal the **Governor-General of India** — so option **(4)** is correct.
First holder: **Bentinck**.
The **1858** Act added the title **Viceroy**; it did not create "GG of India".
xa: APPSC G2 **2024** and G2 **2025** asked this — answer **Charter Act 1833**.
The 1833 Act also made the Company **purely administrative**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

n218ffc40f1e.s: The title ‘Viceroy and Governor-General’ was created by the:
n218ffc40f1e.x: The Government of India Act of 1858 created the title Viceroy and Governor-General. Lord Canning was its first holder.
n218ffc40f1e.tq: Match the constitutional title with the statutory change that followed the transfer of power.
xs: The title **Viceroy** was created by the **Government of India Act, 1858** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The GG (of India since **1833**) got the extra title **Viceroy**, the **Crown's representative**.
xa: First Viceroy: **Lord Canning**.
Viceroy → towards the **princely states**; Governor-General → for **British India**.
The same Act created the **Secretary of State for India** (first: **Lord Stanley**).

na6e2ec5ff6a.s: The East India Company, whose political rule ended under the Act of 1858, was formally dissolved in:
na6e2ec5ff6a.x: The Government of India Act, 1858 ended the Company's political rule, and the Company was formally dissolved in 1874.
xa: It had been chartered by **Elizabeth I** on **31 December 1600**.
The **1858** Act was titled the **Act for the Good Government of India**.

n81e5d3c7156.s: The rebels of 1857 proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as:
n81e5d3c7156.x: The rebels proclaimed him Shahenshah-e-Hindustan; he was later tried and exiled to Rangoon, formally ending Mughal rule.
xa: He died in Rangoon in **1862**.
LAST: **Bahadur Shah II** — last Mughal emperor.

o: The treaties made by the Company
nfa90aeefa71.x: The Proclamation disclaimed further annexation of Indian States and placed the administration of India under the Crown.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "regulating Company trade" is the planted wrong object.
The Proclamation was read by **Lord Canning** at **Allahabad**, **1 November 1858**.
It is called the "**Magna Carta of the Indian people**".

n92720d7cc5f.s: The Queen's Proclamation of 1858 was read out by Lord Canning at:
o: a Durbar at Delhi on 1 January 1858
a Durbar at Allahabad on 1 November 1858
a Durbar at Lucknow on 1 January 1859
n92720d7cc5f.x: Lord Canning read the Proclamation at a Durbar in Allahabad on 1 November 1858 (UPPSC 2009). Delhi is the venue of the 1877 Durbar that proclaimed Victoria Empress of India. Calcutta and Lucknow were not the venue, and the dates in A and D are wrong.
xs: **Lord Canning** read it at a **Durbar at Allahabad** on **1 November 1858** (UPPSC **2009**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Delhi** is the **1877** Durbar that proclaimed Victoria **Empress of India** (under **Lytton**).
xa: ⚠ **Allahabad 1858** = Proclamation (Canning); **Delhi 1877** = Empress of India (Lytton).
It is called the "**Magna Carta of the Indian people**".

n0f4e7fa172d.s: Queen Victoria, given the title 'Empress of India' by the Royal Titles Act 1876, was proclaimed so at the Delhi Durbar in:
n0f4e7fa172d.x: The title was proclaimed at the Delhi Durbar of 1 January 1877 under Lord Lytton.
xa: The Delhi Durbar was held on **1 Jan 1877**.
⚠ Some notes wrongly place the title at the **Allahabad Durbar** of **1858**.
⚠ **1833** = GG of India; **1858** = Viceroy + SoS; **1876** = Empress title.

n84e3d4e62a5.s: Under the Government of India Act, 1858, the powers of the British Crown in India were exercised through the:
o: President of the Board of Control
Chairman of the Court of Directors
n84e3d4e62a5.x: The Act created the office of the Secretary of State for India, through whom the British Crown exercised its powers in India.
n84e3d4e62a5.tq: Use the institutional-power clue to identify the authority concerned.
xs: The Crown's powers were exercised through the **Secretary of State for India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
He was a **British cabinet minister** and could **issue orders to the Viceroy**.
xa: First SoS: **Lord Stanley**.
He was assisted (advised) by a **15-member Council of India** in London.
The Council of India was abolished by the **1935** Act.

ndebae10ec7f.s: Who was the first Secretary of State for India under the Government of India Act, 1858?
ndebae10ec7f.x: Lord Stanley was the first Secretary of State for India under the new Crown administration.
ndebae10ec7f.tq: Distinguish the first office-holder from later Viceroys and Secretaries of State.
xs: The first **Secretary of State for India** was **Lord Stanley** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Lord Canning** was the first **Viceroy**; **Kimberley** was a later SoS; **Lytton** proclaimed Victoria **Empress** in **1877**.
xa: The SoS was a **British cabinet minister** exercising the Crown's powers.
SoS **Kimberley** said an adequate number of civil servants "**shall always be Europeans**".

nca62e26cd59.s: The Council of India created by the Government of India Act, 1858 to advise the Secretary of State had how many members?
nca62e26cd59.x: The Council of India consisted of 15 members and advised the Secretary of State for India.
xa: The SoS was a **British cabinet minister**; first SoS **Lord Stanley**.
nca62e26cd59.fixed: Council of India (15 members, advised SoS) was abolished by the 1935 Act, so all three statements are correct (notes 8#1)

n6ae2d3addfc.s: After 1858, the head of the Government of India was styled 'Viceroy' in relation to:
n6ae2d3addfc.x: The same office-holder was Viceroy in relation to the princely states and Governor-General in British India.
xa: First Viceroy: **Lord Canning** (**1858**).
The title GG of India dates from the **Charter Act 1833**.

n946c4631b95.s: The Indian princes, who stayed loyal in 1857, were described as 'breakwaters to the storm' by:
n946c4631b95.x: Lord Canning described the loyal princes as breakwaters to the storm, though some accounts credit Lord Elgin.
n946c4631b95.tq: Canning, the 1857 Viceroy, saw princes as breakwaters.
xs: **Lord Canning** called the loyal princes "**breakwaters to the storm**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
Some notes credit **Lord Elgin**; **Dalhousie** was the annexer whose policy was abandoned.
xa: Post-1857 princes became **subordinate allies** under **British paramountcy**.
Canning also withdrew the **Doctrine of Lapse**.

n82a127aa516.s: The Queen's Proclamation of 1858 promised that appointments to public service would be made on the basis of:
n82a127aa516.x: It promised appointment by merit and qualifications without discrimination of race or creed, and that Company treaties with the princes would be honoured.
xa: Other promises: **no further annexation**, Doctrine of Lapse abolished, **no interference in religion**.
Concluding line: "Their **satisfaction** is our **security**. Their **gratitude** is our **reward**."

n53afd81a76b.s: The period 1858-1885, when the Queen's Proclamation's promise of equal employment was not kept, is called the:
n53afd81a76b.x: 1858-1885 is the 'Era of Broken Promises': the ICS stayed European-dominated, Secretary of State Kimberley saying an adequate number 'shall always be Europeans'.
xa: SoS **Kimberley**: an adequate number of civil servants "**shall always be Europeans**".
Promises **kept**: no annexation, adoption, religious neutrality.
The **Madras Native Association** (**1852**) first petitioned over non-implementation of the Proclamation.

nc621d2e0e4f.s: The Queen’s Proclamation of 1858 is often regarded as the:
o: Magna Carta of the Indian people
Magna Carta of the East India Company
nc621d2e0e4f.x: The Queen’s Proclamation is often called the Magna Carta of the Indian people because of its wide-ranging assurances concerning rulers, religion, public service, property and land rights.
nc621d2e0e4f.tq: Recall the historically used descriptive title rather than the constitutional Act title.
xs: The Queen's Proclamation is called the "**Magna Carta of the Indian people**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
It promised the **princes**, **religious neutrality**, **equal public service** and **property** rights.
xa: **Gandhi** too cited Victoria's **1858** Proclamation as a "**Magna Carta**" (**12 May 2026**, on Magna Carta's legacy).
Read by **Lord Canning** at a **Durbar at Allahabad**, **1 November 1858**.

n73ddb83480b.s: Who withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised the right of adoption by childless Indian rulers?
n73ddb83480b.x: Lord Canning withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse and recognised adoption rights after 1857. This marked the abandonment of Dalhousie’s annexation policy.
n73ddb83480b.tq: Use the ruler-policy trap by separating the policy’s originator from the person who ended it.
xs: **Lord Canning** **withdrew the Doctrine of Lapse** and recognised the **right of adoption** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Dalhousie**'s annexation policy was thereby **abandoned**.
xa: Princes' territorial integrity was guaranteed if they accepted **British paramountcy**.
Canning also called the loyal princes "**breakwaters to the storm**" (some notes: **Lord Elgin**).
**Rani Avantibai Lodhi** of Ramgarh had fought the Doctrine of Lapse.

n1d08ba803ae.s: After 1857, Indian princes were assured their states would not ordinarily be annexed, provided they accepted:
o: Direct rule by the Board of Control
n1d08ba803ae.x: The princes kept their states subject to British paramountcy and became subordinate allies of the Crown.
xa: They had **stayed loyal in 1857**.
**Canning** withdrew the **Doctrine of Lapse**; adoption fully recognised.

nacefb9f80fd.s: After the reorganisation recommended by the Peel Commission, the ratio of European to Indian troops was:
o: 1:2 in the Bengal Army and 2:5 in the Madras and Bombay armies
2:5 in the Bengal Army and 1:2 in the Madras and Bombay armies
2:1 in the Bengal Army and 5:2 in the Madras and Bombay armies
nacefb9f80fd.x: The ratio of European to Indian troops was fixed at 1:2 in the Bengal Army and 2:5 in the Madras and Bombay armies.
nacefb9f80fd.tq: Read the ratios in the stated presidency order and watch for reversal of numerator and denominator.
xs: Ratios: **1:2** in the **Bengal Army** and **2:5** in **Madras and Bombay** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option 2 swaps them; option 4 inverts them.
xa: The Bengal Army ratio was earlier **1:5**.
⚠ Some notes give Madras and Bombay as **1:3**.
These came from the **Peel Commission** (**1859**).

n42a44308a6a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the reorganisation of the army after 1857?
o: Regiments were organised without regard to caste or region
Artillery and key positions were reserved for Europeans
Recruitment shifted towards groups described as martial races
Recruitment shifted from Awadh and Bihar towards Punjab, Gorkhas and the NWFP
n42a44308a6a.x: Under 'divide and counterpoise' regiments were deliberately mixed by caste and region, so those identities were not ignored.
xa: Aim: stop **cross-regional fraternising** — "**divide and counterpoise**".
The favoured groups had **stayed loyal in 1857**.

ne12b6e8512f.s: The policy of “divide and counterpoise” in the post-1857 army was reflected in the:
o: Abolition of all regional distinctions in recruitment
Mixing of regiments by caste and region
Replacement of Indian troops by police constables
ne12b6e8512f.x: The policy involved mixing regiments by caste and region to prevent unified opposition within the army.
ne12b6e8512f.tq: Apply the phrase to the organisational measure it describes.
xs: "**Divide and counterpoise**" meant **mixing regiments by caste and region** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It aimed to **prevent fraternisation** across regions.
xa: Exam angle: "**divide and rule**" inside the army — the counterpoise principle.
Regiments: **Sikh**, **Gurkha**, **Rajput**.
Recommended by the **Peel Commission** (**1859**).

nbefbbf14ff4.s: Which of the following best describes the change in British policy towards Muslims after 1857?
o: The British transferred all administrative posts exclusively to Muslims.
The British consistently treated Muslims as their principal allies from the beginning.
The British initially blamed and targeted Muslims, but later cultivated them against the educated Hindu middle class.
The British abandoned all communal distinctions and promoted joint political representation.
nbefbbf14ff4.x: The British initially held Muslims chiefly responsible for the revolt and adopted anti-Muslim measures, but later cultivated Muslim support against the rising educated Hindu middle class.
nbefbbf14ff4.tq: Follow the chronological shift rather than selecting an absolute statement.
xs: The British first held **Muslims chiefly responsible** (first **anti-Muslim policies**), then **cultivated them against the educated Hindu middle class** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This was **divide and rule**: Hindus and Muslims played against each other.
xa: **Bahadur Shah II** was exiled to **Rangoon**, ending Mughal rule.
English-educated "**Babus**" were viewed with suspicion.

nd59a0261c35.s: Who assassinated Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram in his camp after the fall of Bobbili?
nd59a0261c35.x: After Vijayarama Raju, with Bussy's support, took Bobbili from Ranga Rao, Tandra Paparayudu assassinated him in his camp.
xa: Date: **24 January 1757**; primary source: the play **Bobbili Yuddham**.
PYQ **2019**: the **French** helped Vizianagaram at Bobbili.
⚠ **Bobbili 1757** = Vizianagaram + French vs Bobbili; **Padmanabham 1794** = Company vs Vizianagaram.

n96eeb83a09f.s: The Treaty of Aurangabad of 1753, part of the background to the Battle of Bobbili, gave the Circars to the:
n96eeb83a09f.x: The Treaty of Aurangabad of 1753 gave the Circars to the French.
xa: The **Battle of Tummala** (**1757**) confirmed French control.
That is why **Bussy** backed **Vizianagaram** at **Bobbili** (**24 January 1757**).

n22df837518d.s: The primary source associated with the Battle of Bobbili is which of the following?
n22df837518d.x: The play Bobbili Yuddham is identified as the primary source associated with the Battle of Bobbili.
n22df837518d.tq: Discriminate between a literary source and administrative records.
xs: The primary source for Bobbili is the play **Bobbili Yuddham** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **Faujdari Adalat** record and **Kadapa Collector's** reports relate to **Uyyalawada** (**1846-47**); the **Queen's Proclamation** is **1858**.
xa: **Ranga Rao** and **Tandra Paparayudu** remain symbols of **Telugu valour**.
Battle date: **24 January 1757**.

n01195321c2e.s: The British officer associated with the command of the Company forces at the Battle of Padmanabham was
n01195321c2e.x: Colonel Pendergast commanded the English East India Company forces at the Battle of Padmanabham.
n01195321c2e.tq: Match the military commander with the correct battle, avoiding names from other suppressive operations.
xs: The Company's commander at **Padmanabham** was **Col. Pendergast** ("**Fender Gast**" in CDX's spelling) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**George Russell** was made **special officer over the forts** after the battle.
**Capt. Wilson** suppressed **Dandasena**; **Capt. Abbat** suppressed **Mir Fida Ali** at Aurangabad.
xa: Date: **10 July 1794** (CDI gives **8 July**).
The Raja and about **1,000** Kshatriya warriors were killed — compared to **Culloden**.

n204bc2db840.s: After the British seized the Vizianagaram fort on 2 August 1793, the Raja was ordered to live at:
n204bc2db840.x: The Raja was ordered to live in Machilipatnam, not Bobbili, after refusing the Rs 3 lakh tribute and disbanding of troops.
xa: Background: the Raja had removed his step-brother and Diwan **Sitarama Raju** for misrule (**1784**); Sitarama Raju bribed his way back.
Some notes say the estate was split into **three collectorates**.

n5e3b24fcd0d.s: The Battle of Padmanabham was fought between the English East India Company and
o: the Pusapati Vizianagaram zamindar Chinna Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II
the Munsubar of Rampachodavaram supported by the Rohillas
the Nizam's forces led by Turrebaz Khan
the Raja of Bobbili supported by Nana Saheb
n5e3b24fcd0d.x: The battle was fought between the English East India Company and Pusapati Chinna Vijayarama Gajapati Raju II, the Vizianagaram zamindar.
n5e3b24fcd0d.tq: Use the parties to the conflict to distinguish Padmanabham from other Andhra and Hyderabad episodes.
xs: **Padmanabham** was fought between the Company and **Pusapati (Chinna) Vijayarama Gajapati Raju (II)**, Vizianagaram zamindar — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Turrebaz Khan** belongs to **Hyderabad 1857**; Bobbili's **Ranga Rao** fell in **1757**.
xa: Site: between **Bhimunipatnam** and **Vizianagaram**; date **10 July 1794**.
Exam angle: "Padmanabham decided whose defeat?" — **Vijayarama Raju of Vizianagaram**, not Bobbili.

n4258ffa5e34.s: Before Vizianagaram was restored to him after the Battle of Padmanabham, the minor son Narayana Babu had hidden at:
n4258ffa5e34.x: Narayana Babu had hidden at Makkuva; the estate, reduced to an ordinary zamindari, was restored on accepting the Permanent Settlement (1802) and a Rs 6 lakh peshkash.
xa: **George Russell** was made special officer over the forts.
The battle (**10 July 1794**) was compared to **Culloden**.

n2137e6f4135.s: Which development adversely affected the traditional rights of the Poligars in the Carnatic and Tirunelveli region?
o: The introduction of Ryotwari settlement in 1847
The Subsidiary Alliance with the Nizam in 1798 alone
The recall of William Bentinck from Madras
The Company's 1781 arrangement allowing the Nawab of Arcot to manage revenue
n2137e6f4135.x: The Company's 1781 arrangement allowed the Nawab of Arcot to manage the revenues of Tirunelveli and the Carnatic, affecting the rights of the Poligars.
n2137e6f4135.tq: Link a policy arrangement with its institutional consequence.
xs: The Company's **1781** deal letting the **Nawab of Arcot** manage **Tirunelveli** and **Carnatic** revenue hit the poligars' rights — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Subsidiary Alliance** (**1798**) relates to the Nizam's **1800** cession; **Bentinck**'s recall followed **Vellore** (**1806**).
xa: **Kattabomman** (Panchalankurichi) was hanged **1799**.
**Marudu brothers** (Sivaganga) were executed **1801**.

n7d827719ac9.s: Alluri Sitarama Raju fought a direct battle with the British at which place during his Rampa rebellion?
n7d827719ac9.x: During the 1922–24 Rampa rebellion, Alluri Sitarama Raju fought the British directly at Panjerighat.
n7d827719ac9.tq: Test the place associated with a specific episode of the later Rampa rebellion.
xs: **Alluri Sitarama Raju** fought the British directly at **Panjerighat** (PYQ **2012**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rudravaram** and **Koilakuntla** belong to **Uyyalawada** (**1846**); **Errannagudem** to **Subba Reddy**.
xa: His rebellion: **1922-24**.
The earlier Rampa rebellion (**1879**) was **Tammandora**'s.

n602fc27b745.s: Ranga Rao and Tandra Paparayudu are remembered in Andhra history primarily as symbols of:
n602fc27b745.x: Ranga Rao and Tandra Paparayudu of Bobbili remain enduring symbols of Telugu valour.
n602fc27b745.tq: Match the historical personalities with the regional cultural significance attached to them.
xs: **Ranga Rao** and **Tandra Paparayudu** remain symbols of **Telugu valour**, from **Bobbili** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Bobbili (**24 January 1757**): Ranga Rao killed defending it; Paparayudu later killed **Vijayarama Raju**.
xa: The attackers were **Vizianagaram** + the **French (Bussy)**.
Primary source: the play **Bobbili Yuddham**.

nap-history-12-1.s: Who was the queen of Bobbili associated with the Battle of Bobbili (1757)?
nap-history-12-1.x: Mallamma Devi was the queen of Bobbili during the Battle of Bobbili in 1757. Nagamma belongs to the Battle of Palnadu, and Manmasiddhi II and Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I to the Muthukur Battle.
n: Mallamma Devi was the queen of Bobbili. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 17-18]
xs: **Mallamma Devi** was the **queen of Bobbili** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Nagamma** belongs to the **Battle of Palnadu** (**1182**).
**Manmasiddhi II** and **Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I** belong to the **Muthukur Battle** (**1263**).
xa: At Bobbili, **Vijayaramaraju** of Vizianagaram took **French help** (**Bussy**).
Bobbili was fought on **24 January 1757**; **Ranga Rao** was killed and the fort fell.
**Tandra Paparayudu** later assassinated Vijayarama Raju in his camp.

nap-history-12-22.s: The Battle of Chandurthi (1758), in which the English defeated the French, was fought for:
nap-history-12-22.x: The English beat the French at Chandurthi in 1758 in the struggle for the Northern Circars.
n: The English army defeated the French army in the Battle of Chandurthi. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 17-18]
The Battle of Chandurthi was associated with the Northern Circars. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 17-18]
xa: The **Treaty of Aurangabad** (**1753**) had given the Circars to the French.
The **Battle of Tummala** (**1757**) confirmed French control.
The French had helped **Vizianagaram** at **Bobbili** (PYQ **2019**).

n421d34384bf.x: Kattabomman was hanged in 1799; the Marudu brothers were executed in 1801.
xa: Kattabomman's seat: **Panchalankurichi** (Tirunelveli); Marudu brothers: **Sivaganga** (South Indian rebellion).
Velu Thampi was **Diwan of Travancore**; revolt **1808-09**.

n800bb3d9cad.s: Palegars in the Ceded Districts were best described as:
o: British civil servants appointed by the Madras Governor
Religious heads controlling the Wahabi Movement
Fortified military chiefs exercising autonomous power under the Nizam's nominal suzerainty
n800bb3d9cad.x: Palegars were fortified military chiefs who exercised autonomous power under the nominal suzerainty of the Nizam.
n800bb3d9cad.tq: Test the nature of the office through its political and military attributes.
xs: Palegars were **fortified military chiefs** with **autonomous power** under the **Nizam's nominal suzerainty** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They were not **village accountants** or **British civil servants**; the **Wahabi Movement** belongs to **Mubariz-ud-Daula** (**1839**).
xa: Dozens existed in **Kurnool**, **Cuddapah**, **Bellary** and **Anantapur**.
Collector **Thomas Munro** made them **disarm** and **pay peshkash**.

nfac2df10c50.s: Mutakuri Goudappa, who attacked the Sub-Collector's office at Taranikallu in 1801, was captured and hanged by:
nfac2df10c50.x: Goudappa was captured and hanged by Sub-Collector Dhakar, not by Collector Thomas Munro.
xa: Munro's suppression took **18 months** of military action.
The **Palakonda** poligars (Srikakulam) rebelled against heavy taxes.

n6b55c26e81a.s: Which of the following was NOT among the principal causes of resistance by Palegars and other local groups?
o: The Company's order to disarm the Palegars
The introduction of the Kundara Proclamation by Thomas Munro
Forfeiture of estates under the Permanent Settlement
n6b55c26e81a.x: Heavy revenue and peshkash demands, estate forfeiture and the order to disarm Palegars were causes of resistance. The Kundara Proclamation was associated with Velu Thampi, not Thomas Munro's Palegar policy.
n6b55c26e81a.tq: Find the wrongly attributed policy among several genuine causes.
xs: The **Kundara Proclamation** was **Velu Thampi Dalawa**'s (Travancore), not Munro's — so option **(3)** is the answer.
Real causes: the **disarm order**, heavy **revenue and peshkash**, **forfeiture of estates** under the Permanent Settlement.
xa: Territorial cessions: **Guntur** (**1788**) and the **Ceded Districts** (**1800**).
Munro was **Principal Collector** (PYQ **2011**).

ndcabf206756.s: The Nizam ceded Cuddapah, Kurnool, Anantapur and Bellary to the Company in:
ndcabf206756.x: The Ceded Districts were handed over in 1800 under the Subsidiary Alliance of 1798; Guntur had been taken in 1788 for Rs 7 lakh.
xa: The ceded area is **Rayalaseema** (Ceded Districts).
The cession bred **discontent**, behind the **1800** palegar rising.

n0e59fbeac32.s: Who was the principal officer responsible for suppressing the Palegar revolts in the Ceded Districts?
n0e59fbeac32.x: Thomas Munro, serving as Principal Collector, was chiefly responsible for suppressing the Palegar revolts.
n0e59fbeac32.tq: Identify the correct administrative officer rather than a military or neighbouring official.
xs: **Thomas Munro**, **Principal Collector** (PYQ **2011**), suppressed the palegars — so option **(2)** is correct.
He was helped by military officer **Campbell**.
**Bentinck** was Madras Governor at **Vellore** (**1806**); **Cochrane** was **Kadapa Collector** in **1846**.
xa: He introduced **Ryotwari** in the Ceded Districts.
Methods: proclamations, **18 months** of military action, **confiscation** of estates.

n82e0784e362.s: Military action to suppress the Palegars continued for about:
n82e0784e362.x: Suppression combined disarmament proclamations, eighteen months of military action, confiscation of rebel estates and small pensions for loyal heirs.
xa: Officers: **Thomas Munro** and **Campbell**.
Settlement that followed: **Ryotwari**.

ne2104a60a48.s: The settlement introduced in the Ceded Districts after the suppression of the Palegars was:
ne2104a60a48.x: The settlement introduced in the Ceded Districts was Ryotwari. Permanent Settlement is an incorrect attribution in this context.
ne2104a60a48.tq: Discriminate between closely associated revenue-settlement terms.
xs: The Ceded Districts got **Ryotwari** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ Some notes write "**Permanent Settlement**" here — an error; every other source gives Ryotwari.
xa: The Ryotwari was introduced by **Thomas Munro**.
Vizianagaram, by contrast, was restored under the **Permanent Settlement (1802)**.

n0c45d45d69f.s: What was the principal cause of the Vellore Mutiny?
o: The Company's takeover of Guntur from the Nizam
The introduction of Ryotwari settlement in the Ceded Districts
Confiscation of the estates of the Marudu brothers
New dress regulations that offended caste and religious sentiments
n0c45d45d69f.x: The new uniform regulations, including changes concerning the turban and a ban on caste marks, hurt the caste and religious sentiments of the sepoys.
n0c45d45d69f.tq: Identify the specific policy cause instead of confusing it with revenue grievances.
xs: **Vellore** (**1806**) broke out over **new dress/uniform regulations** hurting **caste and religious sentiment** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The turban change and the **ban on caste marks** offended sepoys.
xa: Second cause: **Tipu's family** lodged in the fort.
Vellore = **first major sepoy revolt**, half a century before **1857**.

n57653c011ff.s: Which consequence followed the Vellore Mutiny?
o: The Agency system was abolished immediately.
Thomas Munro was appointed Principal Collector of the Ceded Districts.
Mubariz-ud-Daula was released from Golconda Fort.
Madras Governor William Bentinck and Commander-in-Chief Cradock were recalled.
n57653c011ff.x: Following the mutiny, Madras Governor William Bentinck and the Commander-in-Chief Cradock were recalled.
n57653c011ff.tq: Match a revolt with its administrative consequence and avoid authority swaps.
xs: After Vellore, Madras Governor **William Bentinck** and C-in-C **Cradock** were **recalled** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Munro's Ceded Districts work came earlier (**1800-01**).
xa: Vellore (**1806**) = first major sepoy revolt.
Causes: **uniform regulations**; **Tipu's family** in the fort.

nc08b096e78d.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the immediate cause of Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt?
o: A ban on podu cultivation and toddy tapping
Takeover of his estate, reduction to a meagre pension, and the order to disarm and pay peshkash
Introduction of new military uniforms at Vellore
Forcible conversion of local chiefs to Christianity
nc08b096e78d.x: His estate was taken over under Munro, he was offered only a meagre pension, and he was ordered to lay down arms and pay peshkash.
nc08b096e78d.tq: Separate the specific revenue and disarmament cause from causes of other revolts.
xs: His grievance: the **estate taken over**, a **meagre pension** (**Rs 35**) and the order to **disarm and pay peshkash** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Podu** and **toddy** restrictions belong to **Rampa 1879**; uniforms belong to **Vellore 1806**.
xa: The disarm order dates from **1800-02** → read as the **root grievance** behind **1846**.
His grandfather's **Nosam** estate became government land by **1802** without a pension.

naf4cdac5d39.s: Which group formed the support base of Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy's revolt?
o: Only officials from the Godavari Agency
Farmers, Yanadis, tribal people and people of the Uyyalawada and Nosam estates
Only zamindars from Parlakimedi and Ghumsur
Sepoys of the Madras Army alone
naf4cdac5d39.x: The movement had about 5,000 followers, including farmers, Yanadis, tribal people and people from the Uyyalawada and Nosam estates.
xa: Comparison: the **1800-01** rising was **80 palegars** under Munro; **1846** was a single-leader guerrilla revolt with a peasant and tribal base.
It was the **last major palegar rising** in Rayalaseema, a decade before **1857**.

n90955a8e0c6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the palegar risings in Rayalaseema?
o: The 1846 rising was the last major palegar rising before 1857
Thomas Munro was associated with suppressing the 1800–01 rising
The 1846 rising was led jointly by about 80 palegars
n90955a8e0c6.x: About 80 palegars were involved in 1800–01; the 1846 rising was a single-leader guerrilla revolt with a peasant and tribal base.
xa: The 1846 leader was **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy**, with about **5,000 followers**.
Munro's suppression took **18 months** and ended in **Ryotwari** for the Ceded Districts.
In **1801** **Mutakuri Goudappa** attacked the Sub-Collector's office at **Taranikallu**.

n19ba888fac1.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy belonged to which district of present-day Andhra Pradesh?
n19ba888fac1.x: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy belonged to the Palegar family of Uyyalawada in Koilakuntla taluk of Kurnool district.
n19ba888fac1.tq: Use the direct place-based recall of the rebel leader.
xs: **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** was born in **Koilakuntla taluk, Kurnool district** — so option **(2)** is correct.
PYQ **2022**: "born in **Kurnool** district" is correct.
xa: Uyyalawada is now in **Nandyal district** after the **2022** reorganisation.
Father: **Pedda Mallareddy**, Palegar of Uyyalawada.

ne5ff4a76ae4.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy was the maternal grandson of:
ne5ff4a76ae4.x: He was the younger son of Pedda Mallareddy, Palegar of Uyyalawada, and the maternal grandson of Nosam Palegar Jayarama Reddy.
xa: The **three sons** got only **Rs 35** pension from the Uyyalawada estate.
Birthplace: **Koilakuntla taluk**, **Kurnool**.

nc26b03c9d69.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy was publicly hanged at Koilakuntla on:
nc26b03c9d69.x: Captured on 7 October 1846 and sentenced to death by the Faujdari Adalat in January 1847, he was publicly hanged near Koilakuntla on 22 February 1847. 22 February 1846 is a year too early (the revolt began only in July 1846), and 10 July 1806 is the Vellore Mutiny.
nc26b03c9d69.tq: Test the exact date through close year-and-day distractors.
xs: He was **publicly hanged near Koilakuntla** on **22 February 1847** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**1846** is too early — the revolt began only in **July 1846**; **10 July 1806** is **Vellore**.
xa: Captured **7 Oct 1846**; death sentence by the **Faujdari Adalat** in **January 1847**.
Memorial: **Orvakal airport** renamed **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy Airport**.

nbc699f9ab48.s: The leader of the 1846 revolt was captured on 7 October 1846 at:
nbc699f9ab48.x: He was captured at the Jagannatha Swamy temple, Pairamalla Konda; Mundlapadu was the ambush site and Rudravaram and Koilakuntla were looted.
xa: After the treasury raid he marched towards **Cumbum**.
In mid-**1846** he escaped to the **Nizam's dominions**, returning about **6 weeks** later.

n074776ff984.s: Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy was hanged on:
n074776ff984.x: The Faujdari Adalat sentenced him to death in January 1847 and he was hanged on 22 February 1847.
xa: Charges: **rebellion**, **murder**, **looting**.
Hanged on **22 February 1847** near Koilakuntla.

na1287bd13bd.s: Orvakal airport in Kurnool, operational from 25 March 2021, has been named after:
na1287bd13bd.x: Orvakal airport was renamed Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy Airport.
xa: Film: **Sye Raa Narasimha Reddy** (**2019**).
Uyyalawada is now in **Nandyal district** (**2022** reorganisation).

nf9a5d324eaf.s: After the 2022 district reorganisation, Uyyalawada is located in:
nf9a5d324eaf.x: After the 2022 reorganisation, Uyyalawada falls in Nandyal district.
xa: PYQ **2022**: "born in **Kurnool** district" is correct.
**Orvakal airport** (Kurnool) was renamed **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy Airport**.
**Bobbili** is linked with **Ranga Rao** and **Tandra Paparayudu**, symbols of Telugu valour.

nf3b7a2a4bea.s: The Nawabs of Kurnool, descended from Golconda nobles, were reduced and deposed in:
nf3b7a2a4bea.x: The Kurnool Nawabs were reduced and deposed in 1839.
xa: **Kurnool** was later the base of **Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy** (**1846**).
Kurnool was among the **Ceded Districts** (**1800**).

nf9fbb1051b5.s: Who succeeded Nizam Nasir-ud-Daula in Hyderabad in 1857?
nf9fbb1051b5.x: Afzal-ud-Daula succeeded Nasir-ud-Daula in 1857 and ruled until 1869.
xa: Nasir-ud-Daula died on **16 May 1857**.
APPSC G2 **2001**: Nizam of 1857 = **Afzal-ud-Daula**.
He was **pro-British** and later got the "**Star of India**".

nd2edde29cde.s: Mir Turab Ali Khan, the Diwan of Hyderabad during 1857, is better known as:
nd2edde29cde.x: Afzal-ud-Daula, who succeeded Nasir-ud-Daula on 16 May 1857, retained Mir Turab Ali Khan (Salar Jung I) as Diwan; both were pro-British.
xa: Their loyalty kept the revolt from spreading in the **Deccan**.
Rewards: **Star of India** for Afzal-ud-Daula; Salar Jung honoured.

nac6331d9898.s: Which unit of the Hyderabad Contingent came under suspicion and was disarmed at Aurangabad in June 1857?
nac6331d9898.x: The 1st Cavalry of the Hyderabad Contingent was suspected and disarmed at Aurangabad; Mir Fida Ali was hanged.
xa: Suppressor: **Capt. Abbot** (also spelt **Abbat**).
APPSC G1 **2023** chronology: Mubariz-ud-Daula's imprisonment → **Aurangabad** → **Turrebaz Khan**'s attack.

n988f76e6756.s: The immediate objective of Turrebaz Khan and Maulvi Allauddin in attacking the British Residency at Hyderabad was to
n988f76e6756.x: The attack was undertaken to free Jamedar Chida Khan, who had been arrested and held at Hyderabad.
n988f76e6756.tq: Identify the immediate purpose of an action rather than the broader background grievance.
xs: They attacked the Residency to **free Jamedar Chida Khan** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Chida Khan had been **arrested and held at Hyderabad**.
xa: Date: **17 July 1857**; repulsed by Resident **Davidson**.
**Capt. Abbot** was the suppressor at **Aurangabad**, not a target of the attack.
**Turrebaz Khan** was later caught and **shot near Toopran** (**1859**).

n091a954cb32.s: Turrebaz Khan, who led the attack on the Hyderabad Residency in 1857, was later caught and shot near:
n091a954cb32.x: After Resident Davidson repulsed the attack, Turrebaz Khan escaped but was caught and shot near Toopran (1859).
xa: Aim: to free **Jamedar Chida Khan**.
AP angle: Turrebaz Khan is the key **Hyderabad** leader of 1857.

n808896f7732.s: Mubariz-ud-Daula of Hyderabad was arrested in:
n808896f7732.x: Mubariz-ud-Daula was arrested in 1839, long before the Aurangabad outbreak and the Residency attack of 1857.
xa: The Residency attack was led by **Turrebaz Khan** and **Maulvi Allauddin**.
The new Nizam **Afzal-ud-Daula** had come in after **16 May 1857**.

n7f30e2ac755.s: The Wahabi Movement referred to in the context of anti-British resistance was organised in 1839 by:
n7f30e2ac755.x: The Wahabi Movement of 1839 was organised by Mubariz-ud-Daula, the brother of the Nizam, and was anti-British.
n7f30e2ac755.tq: Test the organiser of the movement while using nearby historical figures as traps.
xs: The **Wahabi Movement (1839)** was organised by **Mubariz-ud-Daula**, the Nizam's brother — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Munro** suppressed the **palegars**; **Velu Thampi** led **Travancore**; **Bentinck** was recalled after **Vellore**.
xa: It was **anti-British** (PYQ **2011**).
He was imprisoned in **Golconda Fort** — first item in the APPSC G1 **2023** chronology.

n9da5c279ce3.s: Which of the following sets contains the principal background grievances connected with discontent in Hyderabad State and Andhra before or during 1857?
o: The 1794 battle, the 1846–47 rising and the 1879 Rampa rebellion only
The Permanent Settlement, the Star of India and the restoration of Dharaseo
The 1800 cession, the 1839 Wahabi conspiracy and the 1853 Berar treaty
The 1857 Residency attack, the 1862 conspiracy and the 1801 hanging only
n9da5c279ce3.x: The major background grievances identified were the 1800 cession, the Wahabi conspiracy of 1839 and the 1853 Berar treaty, involving Berar, Raichur and Osmanabad/Dharashiv.
n9da5c279ce3.tq: Group the underlying grievances together rather than confusing them with later events or rewards.
xs: Background grievances: the **1800 cession**, the **Wahabi conspiracy of 1839** and the **1853 Berar treaty** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Berar treaty took **Berar**, **Raichur**, **Osmanabad/Dharashiv**.
xa: After 1857 **Raichur Doab** and **Dharashiv** were **restored** to Hyderabad.
The **1800** cession covered **Cuddapah, Kurnool, Anantapur, Bellary**.

ncb2676aa23c.s: Which loyalist received the Star of India after the revolt?
ncb2676aa23c.x: Afzal-ud-Daula received the Star of India, while Salar Jung was honoured separately.
ncb2676aa23c.tq: Distinguish the named award from the general statement of honour.
xs: **Afzal-ud-Daula** received the "**Star of India**" — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Salar Jung** (Mir Turab Ali Khan) was **honoured** separately; **Fida Ali** and **Dandasena** were **hanged**.
xa: Hyderabad also got **Raichur Doab** and **Dharashiv** back; its **debt written off**.
Afzal-ud-Daula ruled **1857-69**.

n34acddf84b0.s: As a reward for loyalty after 1857, which territories were restored to Hyderabad, along with the writing off of its debt?
n34acddf84b0.x: The Raichur Doab and Dharashiv were restored to Hyderabad and its debt was written off.
xa: **Afzal-ud-Daula** received the **Star of India**.
**Salar Jung** was honoured.

n0e1e9f1e21e.s: Which one of the following best explains the limited impact of the Revolt of 1857 in South India?
o: The British had withdrawn their forces from the Deccan before 1857
The rulers of all South Indian states openly supported the revolt
The revolts in South India were local and scattered, while the Nizam's loyalty kept the Deccan from joining the revolt
South India had already achieved complete independence from the East India Company
n0e1e9f1e21e.x: The revolts in South India were local and scattered. The Nizam's loyalty to the British also prevented the revolt from spreading across the Deccan.
n0e1e9f1e21e.tq: Identify the combined significance of two linked causes rather than selecting an absolute statement.
xs: South India's revolts were **local and scattered**, and the **Nizam's loyalty** kept the **Deccan** closed to 1857 — so option **(3)** is correct.
The British had not withdrawn, and southern rulers like the **Nizam** stayed **pro-British**.
xa: The revolt lacked **central leadership**, a **programme** and a **base in the south**.
It took the Company **50-60 years** to consolidate Andhra (coastal zamindars + Rayalaseema palegars).

n589a633f78c.s: Who raised the alarm regarding the revolt associated with Uyyalawada Narasimha Reddy?
n589a633f78c.x: Kadapa Collector J. H. Cockrane raised the alarm. Captain Nott, Captain Russell and Lieutenant Moore were deployed subsequently.
n589a633f78c.tq: Separate the civil official who raised the alarm from the military officers deployed.
xs: **Kadapa Collector J.H. Cockrane** raised the alarm and pursued him — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Captain Nott**, **Captain Russell** and **Lt. Moore** were the officers deployed.
xa: Some notes spell him **Cochrane**.
Main official record: the **Kadapa Collector's reports** and the **Faujdari Adalat** trial record.

n125fc2a034f.s: Who among the following was associated with the suppression of the uprising at Paralakimidi in the Ganjam region during the Revolt of 1857?
n125fc2a034f.x: Captain Wilson suppressed the uprising led by Radhakrishna Dandasena at Paralakimidi and Dandasena was subsequently hanged.
n125fc2a034f.tq: Match the person with the deed rather than with a nearby military name.
xs: **Capt. Wilson** (Wilson Nolt) suppressed **Dandasena**'s rising at **Paralakimidi** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**George Russell** was **special officer over the forts** after **Padmanabham**; **Capt. Abbat** suppressed **Aurangabad**.
xa: Dandasena was **hanged**.
Paralakimidi lies in **Ganjam** (now **Gajapati, Odisha**).

n99e30384772.s: Korukonda Subba Reddy's rising in the Godavari Agency was influenced by rumours about the army of:
n99e30384772.x: Subba Reddy, operating at Errannagudem, was influenced by rumours of Nana Saheb's army; he was captured and executed.
xa: He was village official of **Karaturu**; informer: **Musset Sunkaraswamy** of Buttayigudem.
His movement: **1857-58**, "in the spirit of **Nana Saheb**".

n5a01a3ecfcc.s: On 28 August 1857, Sheikh Peer Sahib of Cuddapah was reported to have
o: attacked the British Residency at Hyderabad
preached jihad and prayed for the success of the Mughal Emperor
raised a green flag at Machilipatnam
n5a01a3ecfcc.x: Sheikh Peer Sahib preached jihad at Cuddapah on 28 August 1857 and prayed for the success of the Mughal Emperor; he was later arrested.
n5a01a3ecfcc.tq: Combine the date with the precise action to separate closely related 1857 incidents.
xs: On **28 Aug 1857** **Sheikh Peer Sahib** of **Kadapa** **preached jihad** and **prayed for the Mughal Emperor's success** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Jaggayyapeta** — treasury looted; **Machilipatnam** — green flag; **Hyderabad Residency** — Turrebaz Khan.
xa: He was **arrested**.
A **2024** A/R on his jihad was keyed "**both true, R not the explanation**".

n90f19dd38d5.s: Korukonda Subba Reddy, leader of the Godavari Agency movement, was a village official of which place?
n90f19dd38d5.x: Korukonda Subba Reddy was the village official of Karaturu in Godavari district. Errannagudem was the centre of his movement.
n90f19dd38d5.tq: Distinguish the leader's official village from the movement's centre.
xs: **Korukonda Subba Reddy** was village official of **Karaturu**, Godavari district — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Errannagudem** was his movement's **centre**; **Buttayigudem** was the informer's home; **Nosam** is linked to **Uyyalawada**.
xa: He was **hanged** → movement ended.
It lasted **1857-58** in the **Godavari Agency**.

na73d5cdf80f.s: Which of the following explains the limited response to the Revolt of 1857 in Andhra?
o: Andhra had no local leaders at all
The Nizam had joined the revolt
Andhra was administered directly from London
Many preferred the stability of Company rule to the earlier anarchy
na73d5cdf80f.x: Many preferred Company stability to the earlier anarchy, and loyalty meetings were held at Visakhapatnam, Rajahmundry and Vijayawada; local leaders such as Korukonda Subba Reddy did exist.
xa: Other reasons: **Nizam and Salar Jung loyal**; **zamindars gained** from the Permanent Settlement.
APPSC-G2 **2025** key: "no local leaders" = **false**.

n1a227243de8.s: Who assisted the British in putting down the rising led by Korukonda Subba Reddy?
n1a227243de8.x: Buttaigudem Munsab Shankar Swamy helped the British suppress Korukonda Subba Reddy's rising in the Godavari Agency.
n1a227243de8.tq: Test the local collaborator associated with a particular uprising.
xs: **Buttaigudem Munsab Shankar Swamy** helped put down **Subba Reddy**'s rising — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Capt. Wilson** suppressed **Dandasena**; **George Russell** belongs to **Vizianagaram** (**1794**).
xa: Other notes name the informer **Musset Sunkaraswamy** of Buttayigudem.
Subba Reddy was **hanged** → the movement ended.

nb3b9f3b2604.s: The Rampa rebellion of 1879 in the East Godavari Agency was an uprising of the:
nb3b9f3b2604.x: The 1879 Rampa rising was a Koya uprising against forest and toddy restrictions affecting podu cultivation.
xa: Leader: **Tammandora**.
⚠ CDI wrongly names **Alluri** for **1879**.

n1b29830e607.s: Who led the Rampa rebellion of 1879?
n1b29830e607.x: The 1879 Rampa rebellion was led by Tammandora. Alluri Sitarama Raju led the later Rampa rebellion of 1922–24.
n1b29830e607.tq: Discriminate between two Rampa rebellions separated by several decades.
xs: The **1879** Rampa rebellion was led by **Tammandora** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Alluri Sitarama Raju** led the later Rampa rebellion of **1922-24**; **Korra Mallayya** — **1845-48**.
xa: ⚠ **Rampa 1879** = **Tammandora**; **Rampa 1922-24** = **Alluri**.
Exam angle: the year of the Rampa revolution is **1879**, not Alluri's **1922**.

nap-history-26-17.s: The Rampa Rebellion was associated with which tribe?
nap-history-26-17.x: The Rampa Rebellion of 1922–24 under Alluri Sitarama Raju was fought by the Koya and Konda Dora tribes of the Godavari hills. Khonds belong to Odisha, and Gonds and Santhals to central and eastern India.
nap-history-26-17.tq: Recall the hill tribes of the Rampa region.
n: The tribe associated with Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion was the Koyas and Konda Doras. [AP History · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 37-38]
xs: The **Rampa rebellion** was a **Koya** uprising (the **Koyas**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **1879** Rampa rebellion in the **East Godavari Agency** was led by **Tammandora** against forest and toddy restrictions on **podu** cultivation.
**Alluri Sitarama Raju**'s Rampa rebellion came in **1922-24**.
xa: **Koya rebellions** also broke out in the 1840s and 1860s in the **Godavari Agency**.
Alluri's **first face-to-face war** (**1922**) was at **Panjerighat** (PYQ **2012**).
⚠ **Rampa 1879** = **Tammandora**; **Rampa 1922-24** = Alluri Sitarama Raju.

n88e5c148878.s: The term ‘Poligars’ or ‘Palegars’ in the context of the early South Indian resistance referred primarily to:
o: Local military chiefs and long-time revenue farmers
n88e5c148878.x: Poligars were local military chiefs who had also functioned as long-time revenue farmers.
n88e5c148878.tq: Use the exact institutional meaning of a historical office.
xs: **Poligars** were **local military chiefs** and **long-time revenue farmers** — so option **(4)** is correct.
They were neither missionaries, judges nor merchants.
xa: In Rayalaseema they were **fortified military chiefs** under the **Nizam's nominal suzerainty**.
The Company's **1781** deal letting the **Nawab of Arcot** manage revenue hit their rights.
Leaders: **Veerapandya Kattabomman**, **Marudu brothers**.

nap-history-12-3.s: After the Battle of Tallikota (1565), the capital of Vijayanagara shifted to:
nap-history-12-3.x: Vijayanagara's defeat at Tallikota in 1565 led to the capital moving to Penugonda.
