nindian-polity-63-6.tq: Recall the five-year residence condition of Article 5.
n: Article 5 deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 5 requires domicile in India for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 5 recognizes birth in India as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 5 recognizes having either parent born in India as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 5 recognizes residence in India for at least five years before 1950 as a basis for citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
xs: **Article 5** includes **residence in India for at least 5 years** before **1950** — option **(1)**.
Art. 5 required **domicile** in India plus any one of: **birth** in India, **either parent** born in India, or **5 years'** ordinary residence.
**Two years**, Election Commission registration and **property** ownership are not Art. 5 conditions.
xa: ⚠ **Purchasing property** in India does **not** confer citizenship.
Domicile had to exist on **26 Jan 1950**.

nindian-polity-63-17.s: Under Article 6, the permit cut-off date for persons who migrated from Pakistan was:
nindian-polity-63-17.x: Article 6 turns on migration before or after 19 July 1948; 1 March 1947 is the date relevant to Article 7.
n: Article 6 distinguishes migration before and after the permit cut-off date. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
The permit cut-off date under Article 6 was 19 July 1948. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 7 deals with the rights of certain migrants to Pakistan. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 7 covers persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 7 covers migrants who later returned to India under a resettlement permit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 8 deals with the rights of Persons of Indian Origin residing abroad. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 8 provides for registration as a citizen by an Indian diplomatic or consular representative. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 10 deals with the continuance of the rights of citizenship. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Every citizen continues to be a citizen subject to laws made by Parliament under Article 10. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate citizenship by law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
Article 11 gives Parliament comprehensive power to legislate on all matters related to citizenship. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
xa: The resettlement permit required **6 months'** residence.
⚠ **Art. 6** = **from** Pakistan; **Art. 7** = **to** Pakistan.

n0a31934c78e.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about citizenship by birth?
o: Citizenship by birth is dealt with in Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955.
From 3 December 2004, one Indian-citizen parent suffices if the other is not an illegal migrant.
A person born between 1 July 1987 and 2 December 2004 needed at least one Indian-citizen parent.
For a person born in India on or after 3 December 2004, both parents must be Indian citizens.
n0a31934c78e.x: From 3 December 2004, one Indian-citizen parent is enough if the other is not an illegal migrant; both need not be Indian.
xa: Births **26 Jan 1950 - 30 Jun 1987**: citizen whatever the parents' nationality.
The **1986** amendment tightened the rule from **1 July 1987**; the **2003** amendment set the **3 Dec 2004** rule.
Excluded from birth: children of **foreign diplomats** and **enemy aliens**.

n9b168f478a3.s: Section 14A of the Citizenship Act, 1955, provides for:
o: The merger of PIO and OCI cards
The National Register of Indian Citizens and a national identity card
n9b168f478a3.x: Section 14A provides for the National Register of Indian Citizens and the issue of a national identity card.
n9b168f478a3.tq: Exact provision-to-section recall with nearby citizenship topics as distractors.
xs: **Sec. 14A** provides for the **National Register of Indian Citizens and national identity card** — option **(4)**.
It was added by the **2003** amendment.
Incorporation is **Sec. 7**, naturalisation **Sec. 6**, and the PIO-OCI merger came by the **2015** amendment — options (1)-(3) wrong.
xa: The **2003** amendment also introduced **OCI** registration and the birth rule from **3 Dec 2004**.
**NRC** (citizens only) is a **subset of NPR** (all usual residents).
**Sec. 7A** deals with registration of **OCI cardholders**.

n15a51cd1711.s: A Person of Indian Origin (PIO), as distinct from an NRI, is:
o: A foreign citizen of Indian origin
An Indian citizen of foreign origin
A stateless person of Indian origin
n15a51cd1711.x: A PIO is a foreign citizen whose ancestors were Indian nationals, whereas an NRI is an Indian citizen ordinarily residing abroad.
xa: Exam angle: **NRI = citizen abroad**; **PIO and OCI = foreign citizens**.
The PIO card was **merged into OCI in 2015**.
A **Commonwealth citizen** is a citizen of a member of the **Commonwealth of Nations**.

nb6f4a69ab31.s: Under Article 1, the 'Union of India' consists of:
o: States, Union Territories and acquired territories
nb6f4a69ab31.x: The Union of India consists of the States alone; the wider 'Territory of India' includes States, Union Territories and territories that may be acquired.
xa: The States are **the members of the federal system** — hence the Union means States only.
India can **acquire foreign territory** by cession, treaty, conquest — e.g. **Puducherry, Goa**.
Ceding territory needs an **Art. 368 amendment** (**9th Amendment 1960**).

nc1b32b0c6b1.s: The broad basis of Indian citizenship is said to have shifted:
o: From jus sanguinis to jus soli
From jus soli to jus sanguinis
nc1b32b0c6b1.x: India has moved from jus soli (citizenship by place of birth) towards jus sanguinis (citizenship by descent).
xa: The birth rule was tightened in steps: from **1 July 1987** one parent must be a citizen; from **3 Dec 2004** the other must not be an illegal migrant.
Before **1 July 1987**, birth in India gave citizenship whatever the parents' nationality.
**India does not allow dual citizenship** (**Art. 9**).

nb8b40264da0.s: The freedoms under Article 19 are available to:
nb8b40264da0.x: Article 19 freedoms, like Articles 15, 16, 29 and 30, are available only to citizens.
xa: Citizens alone can **vote and contest** elections.
Citizen-only offices: **President, VP, judges, Governor, AG**.
**OCI cardholders** are **not citizens** — they cannot vote, contest or hold constitutional offices.

o: Dual citizenship of the Union and the States
Single citizenship for the Union and the States
Separate citizenship for each Union Territory
n4c6c4aae584.x: India has one citizenship for the Union and the States; the Constitution does not recognise a separate State domicile.
xa: Single citizenship is borrowed from **Britain**; **Canada** also has it.
**USA and Switzerland** have **double citizenship**.
**India does not allow dual citizenship** — PYQ 2023 A-R: both true, R explains A.

n742b36d3e9d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about citizenship by naturalisation under the Citizenship Act, 1955?
o: Ordinary residence of 12 years is required.
The residence period includes the 12 months immediately before applying.
Residence conditions can be waived for distinguished service to science, art, literature or world peace.
No oath of allegiance is required.
n742b36d3e9d.x: Naturalisation does require an oath of allegiance.
xa: Naturalisation is **Sec. 6** of the Act; some notes say normally **11 years**.
**CAA 2019** cut the naturalisation residence to **5 years** for the specified migrants.
Citizens by **naturalisation** can be **deprived** of citizenship by the **Central Government** (**Sec. 10**).

n9b5eaa6e176.s: The current residence period for citizenship by registration of a person of Indian origin is:
n9b5eaa6e176.x: The current residence requirement for registration is 7 years; spouses of Indian citizens are also a registration category.
xa: Registration is **Sec. 5**; it covers **PIOs**, **spouses and minor children** of citizens.
**Sec. 7A** provides for registration of **OCI cardholders**.
⚠ Naturalisation (Sec. **6**) needs **12 years**; registration usually **7 years**.

nd30d3061e21.s: Deprivation of Indian citizenship by the Central Government applies only to citizens by:
nd30d3061e21.x: The Centre may deprive only citizens by naturalisation, registration or Art. 5(c), on grounds such as fraud, disloyalty or aiding an enemy.
xa: Deprivation is **Sec. 10**, ordered by the **Central Government**.
**Renunciation** (**Sec. 8**) is by **declaration**.
Citizens by **birth** or **descent** cannot be deprived — the section lists only the three categories.

na03dd171794.s: Minor children of a person who renounces Indian citizenship may resume citizenship within how long after attaining majority?
na03dd171794.x: Renunciation is by declaration; minor children also lose citizenship but may resume it within one year of attaining majority.
xa: Renunciation is **Sec. 8** of the Act.
**Termination** (**Sec. 9**) is automatic on voluntarily acquiring foreign citizenship.
**Deprivation** (**Sec. 10**) is by the **Central Government** for fraud, disloyalty, aiding an enemy.
The **2026 Rules** allow **online** application and renunciation for OCI (ociservices.gov.in).

ne52a36d71fd.s: Which community is NOT among the specified religious communities under the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019?
ne52a36d71fd.x: The specified communities are Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi and Christian; Muslims are not included.
xa: Countries: **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan**; cut-off: entered **on or before 31 Dec 2014**.
The challenge is under **Art. 14** (religion- and country-based classification) — **250+ petitions**.
Final SC hearing from **5 May 2026** before a Bench under **CJI Surya Kant**; still pending.

nf206d826036.s: The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 reduced the residence requirement for naturalisation to:
nf206d826036.x: The CAA 2019 reduced the naturalisation residence requirement to five years and gives citizenship effect from the date of entry.
xa: Cut-off: entered India **on or before 31 Dec 2014**.
Normal naturalisation needs **12 years** (**11 of the preceding 14 years + the last 12 months**).
Covered: **Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian** migrants from **Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Pakistan**.

nd439fe4095d.s: An Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) cardholder enjoys:
o: The right to vote in Indian elections
Eligibility to contest Lok Sabha elections
nd439fe4095d.x: OCI cardholders are foreign nationals of Indian origin with a lifelong visa facility; they cannot vote as OCI cardholders.
xa: Since **2016** the OCI card alone is enough to enter India.
Barred: those who are or were (or whose parents/grandparents were) citizens of **Pakistan or Bangladesh**, and **foreign military personnel**.
Also not available: **contesting elections, constitutional offices, public employment**.

n7f39eef10a9.s: A person is barred from an OCI card if the person or a parent or grandparent was a citizen of:
n7f39eef10a9.x: Those who are or were, or whose parents or grandparents were, citizens of Pakistan or Bangladesh are barred from OCI.
xa: OCI gives **lifelong, visa-free** entry; card alone suffices since **2016**.
OCI holders are **not citizens** — no voting or public employment as a rule.
OCI registration is under **Sec. 7A**; introduced by the **2003** amendment.

n268b189b254.s: Which of the following was introduced for OCI services by the Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026?
o: Merger of PIO and OCI cards
n268b189b254.x: The 2026 Rules introduced e-OCI cards, a central OCI database and online application and renunciation; the PIO-OCI merger was in 2015.
xa: Also: a **minor cannot hold another country's passport** alongside an Indian one.
The same Rules require CAA applicants to **surrender** Pakistani/Afghan/Bangladeshi passports **within 15 days**.
OCI card alone suffices to enter India since **2016**.

n5e37724927b.s: Mizoram became a State on 20 February 1987 under the:
n5e37724927b.x: Mizoram became a State under the State of Mizoram Act, 1986 and the 53rd Amendment, not the SR Act, 1956.
xa: The SR Act 1956 created **14 states and 6 UTs**.
**J&K and Ladakh UTs** came via the **J&K Reorganisation Act 2019** (**31 Oct 2019**).
⚠ APPSC G2 2025 key says **31 Oct 2020** for the J&K Act — correct is **31 Oct 2019**.

n3dc7cd96096.s: Puducherry and Goa are examples of territories that India:
n3dc7cd96096.x: As a sovereign State India may acquire foreign territory by cession, treaty or conquest; Puducherry and Goa are examples of acquired territories.
xa: The **Union of India** = **States only**, the members of the federal system.
Ceding territory needs an **Art. 368 amendment** (**Berubari**, **9th Amendment 1960**).

n3d26e68c430.s: Which Constitutional Amendment was enacted following the Berubari Union reference?
n3d26e68c430.x: Berubari held that territory could not be ceded under Article 3 and required an Article 368 amendment, which led to the 9th Amendment, 1960.
xa: This was the **Berubari Union reference (1960)**.
India can also **acquire** territory (cession, treaty, conquest) — e.g. **Puducherry, Goa**.

nb7b83c22b86.s: After the merger of Dadra and Nagar Haveli with Daman and Diu (26 January 2020), India has how many Union Territories?
nb7b83c22b86.x: India now has 8 Union Territories after the 2020 merger.
xa: UTs are administered by the **President through an administrator** (**Art. 239**).
**Lt Governor** in **Delhi, Puducherry, J&K, Ladakh, A&N**.
**J&K and Ladakh UTs** came on **31 Oct 2019**.

n15da1ca81c1.s: Aadhaar is not, by itself, proof of citizenship under which Section of the Aadhaar Act?
n15da1ca81c1.x: Aadhaar establishes identity, but under Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act it is not by itself proof of citizenship.
xa: A **passport** is a **travel document**, not conclusive proof of citizenship (**Sec. 20** Passports Act **1967**).
**Voter ID** and **ration card** are also not proof of citizenship (MEA, Jun **2026**).
**NRC** (citizens only) is a **subset of NPR** (all usual residents).

nindian-polity-63-31.s: A naturalised or registered citizen may be deprived of citizenship if imprisoned within five years of naturalisation or registration for at least:
nindian-polity-63-31.x: Under Section 10, two years' imprisonment within five years of naturalisation or registration is a ground, along with fraud, disloyalty and unlawful trade with an enemy.
n: Deprivation is governed by Section 10 of the Citizenship Act, 1955. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship on grounds of fraud. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship for disloyalty to the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship for unlawful trading with an enemy during war. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]

The Central Government may compulsorily terminate citizenship if the person is imprisoned for at least two years within five years of naturalization or registration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #63 · pp 167-170]
xa: Deprivation is a **compulsory** termination by the **Central Government**.
**Renunciation** (Sec. 8) is voluntary; **Termination** (Sec. 9) is automatic.

n5ae40c5f0b0.s: OCI registration and Section 14A were introduced by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act of:
n5ae40c5f0b0.x: The 2003 amendment introduced OCI and Sec. 14A; the 2005 amendment widened OCI and the 2015 amendment merged PIO and OCI.
xa: After these came **CAA 2019** — naturalisation residence cut to **5 years** for specified migrants.
**2008** had **no amendment** (APPSC GS 2023 key).
The **2003** amendment also set the birth rule from **3 Dec 2004**.

n5f2e5746f8a.s: The PIO and OCI cards were merged in:
n5f2e5746f8a.x: The PIO-OCI merger took place in 2015; the 2003 amendment introduced OCI registration.
xa: The **2003** amendment also added **Sec. 14A (NRC)**.
**2005:** OCI scheme widened.
**1986:** citizenship by birth from **1 July 1987** needs one Indian-citizen parent.

nfcce1ecdbb0.s: The Citizenship (Amendment) Rules under the CAA, 2019 became effective on:
nfcce1ecdbb0.x: The CAA was enacted on 12 December 2019, while its Rules became effective on 11 March 2024.
xa: The Act was passed by Parliament in **Dec 2019**.
The **Citizenship (Amendment) Rules 2026** require an affidavit on Pakistan/Afghanistan/Bangladesh passports.
Final SC hearing on the challenge from **5 May 2026**.

n7459941c3d5.s: Under the MHA order of 19 August 2026, CAA applications in the specified eight States and UTs are processed by:
n7459941c3d5.x: The 19 August 2026 order transferred processing in the eight States and UTs to District Collectors instead of Empowered Committees.
xa: CAA Rules were notified / effective on **11 Mar 2024**.
The **2026 Rules**: affidavit on Pakistan/Afghanistan/Bangladesh passports; **surrender within 15 days** of approval.
The **Union Home Ministry** frames citizenship rules.

nfb87ac0a08b.s: The constitutional validity of the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 has primarily been challenged with reference to:
nfb87ac0a08b.x: The challenge principally invokes Article 14, particularly concerning classification based on religion and country.
nfb87ac0a08b.tq: Match the constitutional challenge with the relevant Article.
xs: The CAA is challenged under **Article 14** — option **(2)**.
The issue is its **religion- and country-based classification**.
xa: **250+ petitions** are before a Bench under **CJI Surya Kant**.
Final hearing from **5 May 2026**; still pending before the SC.
The CAA covers **Hindu, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Parsi, Christian** migrants; **Muslims not covered**.

n6867bf49cdd.s: A CAA applicant holding a passport of Pakistan, Afghanistan or Bangladesh is required under the Citizenship (Amendment) Rules, 2026 to:
o: Retain the passport permanently after approval
Exchange the passport for an OCI card within seven years
File an affidavit concerning the passport and surrender it within 15 days of approval
Surrender the passport before entering India and file no affidavit
n6867bf49cdd.x: The applicant must file an affidavit concerning the relevant passport and surrender the passport within 15 days after approval.
n6867bf49cdd.tq: Apply the procedural sequence and the exact fifteen-day time limit.
xs: The applicant must **file an affidavit** on the passport and **surrender it within 15 days** of approval — option **(3)**.
This is under the **Citizenship (Amendment) Rules 2026**, for any **Pakistani, Afghan or Bangladeshi passport**.
Retaining it, exchanging it for an OCI card, or skipping the affidavit is not the rule — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: CAA work moved to **District Collectors** by the **19 Aug 2026** MHA order.
The original CAA Rules were effective **11 Mar 2024**.
The **2026 Rules** also brought **e-OCI cards** and a **central OCI database**.

n0b16ada7752.s: The Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh came into existence on:
n0b16ada7752.x: The Union Territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh came into existence on 31 October 2019 under the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019.
n0b16ada7752.tq: Reject the one-year-shift trap in a date-based question.
xs: The **J&K and Ladakh UTs** came into existence on **31 Oct 2019** — option **(1) 31 October 2019**.
They were created by the **J&K Reorganisation Act 2019**.
⚠ **31 Oct 2020** (option 2) is the error in the **APPSC G2 2025** key; **2 Jun 2014** is **Telangana** and **20 Feb 1987** is **Mizoram**.
xa: **Telangana** was formed under the **Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act 2014**.
**Mizoram** came via the **State of Mizoram Act 1986** and the **53rd Amendment**.
Of the UTs, only **Delhi, Puducherry, J&K** are represented in the **Rajya Sabha**.

ne4e20972588.s: The States Reorganisation of 1956 provided for:
ne4e20972588.x: The 1956 reorganisation created 14 States and 6 Union Territories and also set up Zonal Councils.
xa: **First linguistic state:** **Andhra State** (**1 Oct 1953**), under the **Andhra State Act 1953**.
Today there are **8 UTs**, after **Dadra & Nagar Haveli and Daman & Diu** merged on **26 Jan 2020**.
**Sikkim** became a full state in **1975** via the **36th** Amendment.

nc7dd7fd9fd9.s: Which of the following countries follow the principle of dual citizenship at the national and sub-national levels?
o: The United States of America and Switzerland
nc7dd7fd9fd9.x: The United States and Switzerland recognise national as well as state or cantonal citizenship. India follows single citizenship.
xs: **USA and Switzerland** have **double citizenship** (national + state) — option **(4)**.
**India** has **single citizenship** — allegiance only to the Union, no separate state citizenship.
**Britain** (source of India's model) and **Canada** both have **single citizenship** — option (3) wrong.
xa: **India does not allow dual citizenship** (**Art. 9**) — PYQ 2023.
India has only one **domicile** — the domicile of India; no state domicile in the constitutional sense.
India has shifted from **jus soli** to **jus sanguinis**.

n26f455aecfa.s: India's system of single citizenship was borrowed chiefly from the constitutional practice of:
n26f455aecfa.x: The Indian Constitution adopted the idea of single citizenship from Britain. Canada also follows single citizenship.
n26f455aecfa.tq: Test the source of a borrowed constitutional feature.
xs: India's **single citizenship** was borrowed from **Britain** — option **(3)**.
**Canada** also has single citizenship, while **USA and Switzerland** (options 1, 2) have **double citizenship**.
xa: Single citizenship = **allegiance only to the Union**; no separate state citizenship.
Only one **domicile** — the domicile of India.
**India does not allow dual citizenship** (**Art. 9**).

n64a4b2c08c9.s: Under Article 239, Union Territories are administered by the President through:
o: The Chief Minister of a neighbouring State
The Chief Justice of the High Court
n64a4b2c08c9.x: Article 239 provides that Union Territories are administered by the President through an Administrator.
xa: The administrator is a **Lt Governor** in **Delhi, Puducherry, J&K, Ladakh, A&N**.
India now has **8 UTs**.
Only **Delhi, Puducherry, J&K** are represented in the **Rajya Sabha**.

na34fc986038.s: In which of the following years was the Citizenship Act, 1955 NOT amended?
na34fc986038.x: The stated chronology identifies 1986, 2003 and 2019 amendments, while 2008 is specified as a year in which the Act was not amended.
na34fc986038.tq: Select the year that breaks the amendment sequence rather than the years linked to known changes.
xs: There was **no amendment in 2008** — option **(3) 2008**.
This is the **APPSC GS 2023** key (PYQ 2023).
**1986**, **2003** and **2019** are all amendment years.
xa: ⚠ UPSC notes list a "**1987** amendment for Tibetan refugees" — not in the standard list; the **1986** Act took effect on **1 July 1987**.
**2015** merged the **PIO and OCI cards**.
na34fc986038.fixed: drop odd 'stated legislative chronology' wording; APPSC GS 2023

nb357dfcf95d.s: Along with Inner Line Permit areas, which areas are exempted from the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019?
o: Sixth Schedule tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura
nb357dfcf95d.x: The Sixth Schedule tribal areas in Assam, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Tripura and the Inner Line Permit areas are exempt; West Bengal's districts are not.
xa: The **19 Aug 2026 MHA order** also covers **Assam, J&K, Ladakh**.
⚠ **Mizoram** appears in both lists — Sixth Schedule and Inner Line Permit.
CAA Rules effective **11 Mar 2024**.

nd5419221392.s: Sikkim became an associate State in 1974 and a full-fledged State in 1975 through, respectively:
nd5419221392.x: The 35th Amendment introduced Sikkim as an associate State, while the 36th Amendment made it a full State in 1975.
nd5419221392.tq: Discriminate between two consecutive constitutional amendments.
xs: Sikkim: **35th Amendment** (associate state, **1974**) then **36th Amendment** (full state, **1975**) — option **(2)**.
Option (4) reverses the order.
The **35th** Amendment inserted **Art. 2A** and the **Tenth Schedule** for the associate status.
xa: The **SR Act 1956** created **14 states and 6 UTs**.
**Mizoram** became a state on **20 Feb 1987** (**53rd** Amendment).
**Andhra State** — **first linguistic state** (**1 Oct 1953**).

n70472205d6f.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the present number and original number of groups of Fundamental Rights?
n70472205d6f.x: The Constitution originally contained seven groups of Fundamental Rights. The right to property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment, leaving six groups at present.
n70472205d6f.tq: Separate the original and present figures before examining the options.
xs: FRs were **originally seven**, and are **six** now — option **(3) Presently six; originally seven**.
The **Right to property (Art. 31)** was removed by the **44th Amendment 1978**.
xa: Property is now a legal right under **Art. 300A** (**Part XII**).
Exam angle: "How many FRs do citizens have?" → **Six** (APPSC **2018**).
The six: **equality, freedom, against exploitation, freedom of religion, cultural and educational, constitutional remedies**.

n42d8e5bc4cb.s: After the 44th Amendment, 1978, the right to property is protected under:
n42d8e5bc4cb.x: The 44th Amendment removed property from Part III; it is now a constitutional/legal right under Article 300A in Part XII.
xa: With property gone, FRs went from **seven** to **six**.
The **44th Amendment 1978** also bars suspension of **Arts. 20 and 21** under **Art. 359**.
The **1st Amendment (1951)** added **Art. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**.

n0095ea31a71.s: The Fundamental Rights, often described as the 'Magna Carta of India', are contained in:
n0095ea31a71.x: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12 to 35 (Art. 12 defines State, Art. 13 voids inconsistent laws, Arts. 33-35 cover limits and legislation). Part IV (Arts. 36-51) holds the Directive Principles and Part IVA (Art. 51A) the Fundamental Duties; Arts. 14-32 is only the span of the six groups, not the whole Part.
n0095ea31a71.tq: Part III = Arts 12-35; Magna Carta of India.
xs: FRs, the "**Magna Carta of India**", are in **Part III, Art. 12-35** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 12** defines "State", **Art. 13** voids inconsistent laws, and **Arts. 33-35** cover limits and legislation — so "14 to 32 only" (option 3) is too narrow.
xa: FRs are **justiciable** — an aggrieved person can move the **SC directly (Art. 32)**.
The model was the **US Bill of Rights**.
FRs are **qualified, not absolute**.

nc5324331ff7.s: Which case is associated with the widening of Article 21 through progressive interpretation?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India
Bhikaji Narain Dhakras v. State of MP
nc5324331ff7.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened the interpretation of Article 21 and is an important example of progressive constitutional interpretation.
nc5324331ff7.tq: Link the interpretive doctrine with its constitutional example.
xs: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** widened **Art. 21** — option **(1)**.
**Basheshar Nath** = **waiver**; **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras** = **eclipse** — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: **Progressive interpretation** treats the Constitution as a **living document**.
**Trauma care** was read into Art. 21 in **SaveLIFE Foundation v. UoI (2026)**.
Courts have also read **shelter** into **Art. 21**.

nc19b9987588.s: Unlike India, Britain protects rights largely through:
o: A codified chapter of Fundamental Rights
Conventions and the rule of law
nc19b9987588.x: Britain has no codified Fundamental Rights; protection rests largely on conventions and the rule of law.
xa: India's FRs are modelled on the **US Bill of Rights**.
FRs are called the "**Magna Carta of India**".
India's **single citizenship** is, however, borrowed from Britain.

n72588981b63.s: The right to freedom of religion is contained in Articles:
n72588981b63.x: Freedom of religion is in Articles 25-28; equality is 14-18, exploitation 23-24 and cultural and educational rights 29-30.
xa: **Right to freedom** = Arts. **19-22**; **Right to constitutional remedies** = Art. **32**.
FRs sit in **Part III, Art. 12-35** and are **justiciable**.
There are **six** groups now — the answer to "How many FRs do citizens have?" (APPSC **2018**).

nac53de68dc5.s: Which one of the following sets consists only of examples of positive Fundamental Rights?
nac53de68dc5.x: Articles 21A, 29 and 30 confer educational or cultural privileges and are treated as examples of positive rights. The other sets contain negative rights that primarily restrict State action.
nac53de68dc5.tq: Classify each option by the direction of the right rather than by its subject title.
xs: **Articles 21A, 29 and 30** are **positive** rights that confer privileges — option **(1)**.
**Negative** rights limit the State: Arts. **14, 15(1), 16(2), 18(1), 20, 22(1), 28(1)** — options (3) and (4).
Option (2) mixes **16(2)** (negative) with **17, 24** (absolute limits on legislative power).
xa: **Absolute limits on legislative power:** Arts. **15, 17, 18, 20, 24**.
Rights that also bind **private persons:** Arts. **15(2), 17, 23, 24**.
**Art. 21A** (education **6-14**) came via the **86th Amendment 2002**.

n02dfd0d1cec.s: Which one of the following Articles is available to both citizens and foreigners, subject to constitutional exceptions?
n02dfd0d1cec.x: Article 21 is available to all persons. Articles 19, 16 and 29 are included among the rights available only to citizens.
n02dfd0d1cec.tq: Discriminate between the closely placed citizen-only Articles 16, 19 and 29 and the all-persons Article 21.
xs: **Art. 21** is available to **all persons** — option **(1) Article 21**.
**Arts. 19, 16, 29** are **citizen-only** rights — options (2)-(4) wrong.
xa: Full citizen-only list: Arts. **15, 16, 19, 29, 30**.
Other all-persons rights: Arts. **14, 20, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28**.
**Companies** can claim the all-persons rights, but **not Art. 19**.

n3c91863b517.s: Parliament can amend a Fundamental Right:
o: Only by a constitutional amendment, subject to the basic structure
n3c91863b517.x: Fundamental Rights can be altered only by the amendment procedure, subject to the basic-structure doctrine of Kesavananda Bharati (1973); an ordinary law cannot amend the Constitution.
xa: Other limits on FRs: **Arts. 31A-31C**.
The **Ninth Schedule** protection is limited by **I.R. Coelho (2007)**.

n7b6419927f6.s: The Fundamental Rights chapter of the Indian Constitution was modelled principally on the:
n7b6419927f6.x: The model for the Fundamental Rights is the US Bill of Rights, not the Irish Constitution.
xa: **HCs** under **Art. 226** enforce FRs + other legal rights.
FRs are **qualified, not absolute** — restrictions by law, on named grounds only.
FRs **limit Parliament itself** (**Art. 13**).

o: Absolute and cannot be regulated by law
Qualified and subject to reasonable restrictions
n6cd3ac15e37.x: Fundamental Rights are qualified, not absolute; courts review restrictions for reasonableness.
xa: APPSC GS **2019**: "FRs are absolute" and "all FRs are suspended in an emergency" are **both false**.
**Art. 19** lists **11** restriction grounds in all.
Under **Art. 359**, enforcement of **Arts. 20 and 21** can never be suspended.

n5f06104fe66.s: Enemy aliens are excluded from the safeguards of Article 22 by its clause:
n5f06104fe66.x: Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens from the specified safeguards; Articles 23 and 24 are not denied to aliens.
xa: Citizens only: Arts. **15, 16, 19, 29, 30**.
⚠ APPSC G1 **2022** key: denied to aliens are **I, II and IV** — not Arts. 23-24.

n180c8d03fa4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about 'State' under Article 12?
o: It includes the Government and Parliament of India.
It includes the Government and Legislature of each State.
It includes other authorities in India or under the control of the Government of India.
n180c8d03fa4.x: Article 12 includes all local authorities within 'State'.
xa: **Rajasthan SEB v. Mohan Lal (1967)**: statutory bodies are "**other authorities**".
**Ajay Hasia (1981)**: the test is **how it was created and controlled**, not the form.
Writs do not ordinarily lie against **private bodies**, unless the State acts in collusion.

naee50e62ea5.s: Which of the following is included within the expression ‘law’ under Article 13(3)?
o: Ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage
Only a constitutional amendment made under Article 368
Only a judicial decision of the Supreme Court
Only an Act passed by Parliament
naee50e62ea5.x: Article 13(3) gives a broad meaning to law, including ordinances, orders, bye-laws, rules, regulations, notifications, customs and usages having the force of law.
naee50e62ea5.tq: Test the complete statutory list rather than one familiar item.
xs: Under **Art. 13(3)**, "law" includes **ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, regulation, notification, custom or usage** — option **(1)**.
Amendments under **Art. 368** are excluded by **Art. 13(4)** (**24th Amendment 1971**) — option (2) wrong.
xa: **13(1):** pre-constitution laws inconsistent with FRs are **void** to that extent.
**13(2):** the State shall not make a law **abridging FRs**.
**Art. 13** makes FRs **supreme over ordinary law**.

n7ad0cee72cf.s: Under Article 13(4), constitutional amendments made under Article 368 are:
o: Treated as ordinary laws under Article 13
Void if they abridge any Fundamental Right
n7ad0cee72cf.x: Article 13(4), inserted by the 24th Amendment, says Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368.
xa: The 24th Amendment answered **Golaknath (1967)**, which gave FRs a **transcendental** position.
**Golaknath** is also the case for **prospective overruling**.
FRs can be limited only by a **constitutional amendment**, not ordinary law.

n804cfd4f032.s: Under Article 33, the power to restrict the Fundamental Rights of members of the armed forces lies with:
n804cfd4f032.x: Article 33 gives the power exclusively to Parliament, and it may extend to non-combatant employees such as cooks and barbers.
xa: **Art. 34**: restrictions while **martial law** is in force; Parliament may pass an **indemnity** Act.
FRs can be limited only by a **constitutional amendment**, subject to the **basic structure**.

n00969d95e0e.s: 'Equal pay for equal work' is a constitutional goal under Article:
n00969d95e0e.x: Equal pay for equal work is under Article 39(d); property is protected under Article 300A.
xa: ⚠ APP says the right to vote comes from "RPA **1957**" — correct Act is **RPA 1951**.
Opposition demand to make the **right to vote a Fundamental Right** (Jul **2026**).
**Right to employment** is a DPSP (**Art. 41**).

nce850a41547.s: A prohibition imposed on an association can be treated as a restriction under Article 19(4) only when it is based on:
o: The grounds constitutionally permitted under Article 19(4)
Any reason considered desirable by the executive
An ordinance that is immune from judicial review
nce850a41547.x: Restrictions on freedom of association under Article 19(4) must be based on the constitutionally specified grounds and remain subject to constitutional scrutiny.
nce850a41547.tq: Ask whether the restriction fits the constitutional grounds rather than accepting executive discretion.
xs: A ban on an association is valid under **Art. 19(4)** only on **the grounds it permits** — option **(1)**.
FRs are **qualified, not absolute**: restrictions must be **by law**, on grounds the Constitution names, and **courts judge reasonableness**.
xa: **Art. 19** lists **11** restriction grounds in all.
⚠ "FRs are absolute" is **wrong** (PYQ **2019**).
Under **Art. 13(3)**, "law" includes an **ordinance** — so no ordinance escapes judicial review.

n57c1ae9d039.s: Which 2007 decision limited the protection given by the Ninth Schedule?
n57c1ae9d039.x: I.R. Coelho (2007) limited Ninth Schedule protection; the Schedule itself came with the 1st Amendment (1951).
xa: **2026** marks **75 years of the 1st Amendment (1951)**.
**Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)**: an eclipsed law **revived after the 1st Amendment**.
Other limits on FRs: **Arts. 31A-31C**.

n5491751c43a.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that Fundamental Rights occupy a transcendental position and that Parliament cannot abridge them, a position later countered by the 24th Amendment (1971)?
n5491751c43a.x: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a transcendental position and held Parliament could not abridge them; the 24th Amendment (1971) responded by adding Art. 13(4). Kesavananda Bharati (1973) came after and laid down the basic structure; Shankari Prasad had upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs; Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Art. 21.
xs: **Golaknath (1967)** gave FRs a **transcendental** position — Parliament **cannot** abridge them — option **(2)**.
The **24th Amendment (1971)** countered it by adding **Art. 13(4)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** came later and set the **basic structure** limit; **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** widened **Art. 21**.
xa: **Golaknath** also applied **prospective overruling** — the ruling operates only for the future.
⚠ **1967** twice: **Golaknath** (Art. 13) and **Rajasthan SEB** (Art. 12).
Limiting FRs now needs a **constitutional amendment**, subject to the **basic structure**.

na221c3d8295.s: Which case is associated with the doctrine of absolute liability for hazardous industries?
o: Motor General Traders v. State of Andhra Pradesh
M.C. Mehta, Oleum gas leak case
na221c3d8295.x: The absolute liability principle was evolved in M.C. Mehta’s 1987 Oleum gas leak case. It imposes liability on hazardous industries without the exceptions available under strict liability.
na221c3d8295.tq: Distinguish absolute liability from public trust and severability by the underlying subject.
xs: **Absolute liability** comes from **M.C. Mehta (1987)** — the **Oleum gas leak** case — option **(4)**.
A **hazardous industry** is liable without the exceptions of **strict liability**.
**Golaknath** = prospective overruling; **Motor General Traders** = severability (some notes).
xa: **Progressive interpretation**: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**.
**Waiver**: **Basheshar Nath v CIT (1959)**.
**Eclipse**: **Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955)**.

n9328d511fd3.s: Which doctrine is most directly applicable when a law enacted by one legislature appears to encroach upon a subject in another legislative List?
n9328d511fd3.x: Pith and substance is the relevant doctrine for examining Union-State List encroachment by looking at the true nature and character of the law.
n9328d511fd3.tq: Identify the doctrine from the federal legislative competence scenario.
xs: **Pith and substance** is the doctrine for **Union-State List encroachment** — option **(4)**.
Its variant is the **aspect doctrine**.
**Prospective overruling** and **absolute liability** are not federal doctrines.
xa: Other federal doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **territorial nexus**, incidental and ancillary powers, **repugnancy**.
**Territorial nexus**: a state law is valid outside the State if sufficient connection (**R.M.D.C., 1957**).
Exam angle: **doctrine-to-case matching**.

n327b6e97c61.s: During a National Emergency, the President's order under Article 359 cannot suspend the enforcement of which of the following Articles, as provided by the 44th Amendment, 1978?
n327b6e97c61.x: Since the 44th Amendment (1978), enforcement of Arts. 20 and 21 can never be suspended under Art. 359. Arts. 14, 19, 22 and the right to move courts under Art. 32 for other rights can be affected by such an order, so the other pairs are wrong.
xs: **Articles 20 and 21** can never be suspended — option **(2)**.
This is the **44th Amendment, 1978** limit on **Art. 359**.
xa: Under Art. 359 the **President** suspends **enforcement** of named FRs by order.
The **44th Amendment 1978** also removed the **Right to property (Art. 31)**.
⚠ "All FRs are suspended in an emergency" is **false** (APPSC GS **2019**).

n9b8b782da34.s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Right expressly included in Part III?
o: Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years
n9b8b782da34.x: The right to employment is a Directive Principle under Article 41, not a Fundamental Right. Education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
n9b8b782da34.tq: Distinguish claimed socio-economic rights from rights expressly placed in Part III.
xs: The **Right to employment** is **not an FR** — option **(2)**.
It is a **DPSP** under **Art. 41** (PYQ **2024**).
**Education (6-14 yrs)** **is an FR** under **Art. 21A** — option (4) is an FR.
xa: **Equal pay for equal work** is also **not an FR** — DPSP **Art. 39(d)**.
**Freedom of religion** = Arts. **25-28**; **constitutional remedies** = Art. **32**.
**Right to property** is a legal right under **Art. 300-A**.

ndb639d94b71.s: The right to education for children aged six to fourteen is a Fundamental Right under:
ndb639d94b71.x: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002; the RTE Act, 2009 gives effect to it.
xa: **Art. 21A** is a **positive** right, with **29** and **30**.
**Art. 21A** is available to **all persons**.
**Art. 24**: a child **below 14** may not work in a factory or mine.

nd05298c39ba.s: The right to vote in India is presently:
o: A right enforceable only under Article 32
A statutory right under Section 62 of the RP Act, 1951
nd05298c39ba.x: The right to vote is statutory under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, with a constitutional basis in Article 326; it is not a Fundamental Right.
xa: **Art. 326** = **adult suffrage**; **RPA 1950 (s.19)** is the other statutory base.
⚠ APP says "RPA **1957**" — correct Act is **RPA 1951**.
**Right to employment** is also not an FR — DPSP **Art. 41**.

n5256274c1e9.s: Paying labourers less than the minimum wage violates Article:
n5256274c1e9.x: Paying less than minimum wage is forced labour under Art. 23 (PUDR/Asiad, 1982); child labour in mines violates Art. 24.
xa: **Arts. 23 and 24** also bind **private persons**.

nfc993e6c5d0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about prohibited grounds of discrimination?
o: Descent is a prohibited ground under Article 15(1).
Caste and sex are prohibited grounds under Article 15(1).
Religion and race are prohibited grounds under Article 15(1).
Descent is a prohibited ground under Article 16(2).
nfc993e6c5d0.x: Article 15(1) covers only religion, race, caste, sex and place of birth; descent appears in Article 16(2).
xa: **Art. 15** is available to **citizens only** (PYQ **2018**).

nfb9558edce5.s: A private hotel refuses entry to a person solely on the ground of caste. Which constitutional provision is most directly attracted?
nfb9558edce5.x: Article 15(2) applies to access to places such as hotels and binds private persons as well as the State. It prohibits discrimination on the specified grounds in such access.
nfb9558edce5.tq: Apply the clause to a private-person situation rather than assuming that equality provisions bind only the State.
xs: **Article 15(2)** is attracted — it covers **hotels** and binds **private persons too** — option **(2)**.
15(2) covers **shops, restaurants, hotels, wells, tanks, bathing ghats**.
**Art. 16(2)** is about **public employment**, and **Art. 18(1)** about **titles** — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: Barred grounds under Art. 15: **religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth**.
**Art. 17** abolishes **untouchability**; enforcing any disability is an **offence**.
**Art. 14** applies to **any person**; **Art. 15** to **citizens only**.

n3a3e6d3fc96.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Articles 14 and 15?
o: Article 14 applies to all persons, whereas Article 15 is available only to citizens.
Article 14 applies only to citizens, whereas Article 15 applies to all persons.
Both Articles 14 and 15 are available only to citizens.
Both Articles 14 and 15 apply only to foreigners residing in India.
n3a3e6d3fc96.x: Article 14 applies to any person within the territory of India. Article 15 is a right available only to citizens.
n3a3e6d3fc96.tq: Discriminate between the beneficiaries of two neighbouring constitutional provisions.
xs: **Art. 14** applies to **all persons**; **Art. 15** to **citizens only** — option **(1)**.
Art. 14: "The State shall not deny to **any person** equality before the law or the equal protection of the laws".
xa: PYQ **2018**: "Art. 15 is available only to citizens" — correct.
APPSC **2025**: "Right to Equality" → **Art. 14**.
**Art. 16** (public employment) is also a citizen-only right.

na7e7f1815fa.s: Under Article 16(3), residence requirements for certain public employment may be prescribed by:
na7e7f1815fa.x: Article 16(3) permits Parliament to prescribe residence requirements; Article 16(2) lists descent and residence among prohibited grounds.

n972401a5b83.s: Article 17 of the Constitution deals with:
o: Prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion and race
Equality of opportunity in public employment
n972401a5b83.x: Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes enforcement of any disability arising from it an offence.
xa: Arts. **17-18** = **social equality** (PYQ **2017**).
Art. 17 also binds **private persons** (e.g. exclusion from a public well or shop).
**Art. 18** ends artificial distinctions, except **military and academic**.

na6da5a3e8f8.s: According to B. R. Ambedkar, liberty, equality and fraternity are best understood as:
o: Economic objectives confined to the Directive Principles
Three independent ideals applicable to separate institutions
Duties imposed only on public servants
na6da5a3e8f8.x: Ambedkar described liberty, equality and fraternity as an inseparable trinity.
na6da5a3e8f8.tq: Recall the precise formulation associated with the constitutional thinker.
xs: **Ambedkar** called liberty, equality, fraternity **an inseparable trinity** — option **(3)**.
They are not three separate ideals, nor confined to **DPSPs** or public servants — options (1), (2), (4) wrong.
xa: The **Preamble** promises "**equality of status and of opportunity**".
Arts. **14-18** lay the "**equality floor**" for fraternity.
Equality types: **social** (15, 17, 18), **economic** (39(b), (c), (d)), **political** (325, 326).

n5b48fc0b442.s: In which case did the Supreme Court state that ‘equality is antithetic to arbitrariness’ or that equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies?
o: M.R. Balaji v. State of Mysore
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu
n5b48fc0b442.x: E.P. Royappa v. State of Tamil Nadu (1974) established the close constitutional relationship between equality and non-arbitrariness.
n5b48fc0b442.tq: Match the distinctive judicial formulation with the case in which it was stated.
xs: **E.P. Royappa v. State of TN (1974)**: "**Equality and arbitrariness are sworn enemies**" — option **(4)**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** later held any **arbitrary action** violates Art. 14.
**M.R. Balaji** and **Indra Sawhney** are **reservation** cases — options (1) and (3) wrong.
xa: Royappa's other phrase: "**equality is antithetic to arbitrariness**".
Maneka Gandhi struck down **unguided discretionary power**.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.

n89fff6b0026.s: Article 16(5) permits a qualification relating to religion or denomination in respect of an office connected with:
o: Every public employment under a State
n89fff6b0026.x: Article 16(5) permits offices connected with religious or denominational institutions to be kept for persons professing that particular religion or belonging to that denomination.
n89fff6b0026.tq: Identify the institutional exception rather than applying the religious qualification to all public employment.
xs: **16(5)** allows a religious qualification for posts in **religious or denominational institutions** — option **(3)**.
Such posts may be kept for that religion.
xa: **16(3)**: **Parliament only** may prescribe **residence** for certain jobs.
**16(2)**: adds **descent and residence** as barred grounds.
**16(4)**: backward classes **not adequately represented** in services.

nedf09bcb71e.s: Article 18(1) bars the State from conferring titles except:
nedf09bcb71e.x: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring any title except military and academic distinctions.
xa: National awards must **not be used as prefix or suffix**; stopped in **1977**, revived in **1980**.

nindian-society-9-30.s: General equality of opportunity in public employment is guaranteed by Article:
nindian-society-9-30.x: Article 16(1) guarantees equality of opportunity in public jobs; 16(4) covers reservation and 15(5) educational advancement.
xa: **16(4A)**: reservation in **promotion** for SC/ST — **77th (1995)**, **85th (2001)**.

nindian-polity-75-10.s: The concept of 'equality before law' is of ____ origin.
nindian-polity-75-10.x: Equality before law is British and negative in nature; equal protection of the laws is American and positive.
n: Equality before law is of British origin. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before law is a negative concept. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before law means the absence of special privilege for any individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws is of American origin. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws is a positive concept. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws means equal treatment under equal circumstances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equal protection of the laws permits reasonable classification. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equality before law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Article 14 provides equal protection of the laws. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xa: ⚠ **British = negative**; **American = positive**.
Both are guaranteed by **Article 14** to **any person**.

nindian-polity-75-25.s: Dicey opposed the idea that executive officials should be subject only to:
o: The ordinary law of the land
nindian-polity-75-25.x: Dicey's second element puts everyone under the ordinary law and ordinary courts, so he opposed special tribunals for officials.
n: Dicey’s second classic element of the Rule of Law is equality before the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Equality before the law means equal subjection of all classes to the ordinary law of the land. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The ordinary law of the land must be administered by the ordinary law courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
No person is above the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The assertion that executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey opposed French *Droit Administratif*. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xa: ⚠ "Executive officials are subject only to special administrative tribunals" — **false** under Dicey.
Exceptions in India: **Art. 361** (President, Governors), **foreign diplomats**, **UN agencies**.

n28cb95a86fe.s: Which one of the following propositions is associated with Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) in the context of Article 14?
o: Class legislation is always valid if enacted by Parliament
Any arbitrary State action violates Article 14
Article 14 applies only to taxation laws
n28cb95a86fe.x: Maneka Gandhi reinforced the principle that arbitrary State action is inconsistent with Article 14. Unguided discretionary power may therefore be struck down.
n28cb95a86fe.tq: Use the case-law principle rather than confusing it with the classification test.
xs: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: **any arbitrary action violates Art. 14** — option **(2)**.
**Unguided discretionary power** was struck down — so option (3) is wrong.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation** — option (1) wrong.
xa: **E.P. Royappa (1974)**: "equality and arbitrariness are **sworn enemies**".
Twin test for classification: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus**.
Art. 14 applies to **any person**.

nce8dd4167be.s: A law creates two groups for different treatment. For the classification to be valid under Article 14, which combination is required?
o: Intelligible differentia and rational nexus with the object of the law
nce8dd4167be.x: The twin test of reasonable classification is an intelligible differentia distinguishing the grouped persons or things and a rational nexus between the differentia and the object sought to be achieved.
nce8dd4167be.tq: Apply the twin test to distinguish reasonable classification from class legislation.
xs: The twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus with the object** — option **(3)**.
Art. 14 forbids **class legislation**, not **reasonable classification**.
xa: Reiterated **Apr 2026**: the State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** (Kerala/KSRTC).
**Equal protection** (American, **positive**) permits reasonable classification.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: any **arbitrary action** violates Art. 14.

n91caf7b3797.s: The Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations in which case?
o: Pensioners Association v. Union of India
Mritunjay Tiwari v. State of Andhra Pradesh
Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India
Centre v. Scheduled Caste Employees Association
n91caf7b3797.x: The case in which the Supreme Court questioned the caste-discrimination clause of the UGC equity regulations was Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India.
n91caf7b3797.tq: Use the case-name discrimination method by matching the judicial issue with the exact parties.
xs: The SC questioned the **caste-discrimination clause** of the **UGC equity regulations** in **Mritunjay Tiwari v. Union of India** — option **(3)**.
The case was against the **Union of India** (UoI), not Andhra Pradesh — option (2) wrong.
xa: It came in Feb **2026**.
SC (**11** Apr **2026**): State **cannot treat pensioners differently from serving employees on DA** — Art. 14's **twin test**.
Twin test: **intelligible differentia** + **rational nexus** with the object.

n8983580b942.s: India borrowed the concept of the Rule of Law from:
n8983580b942.x: The Rule of Law, set out by the British jurist A.V. Dicey (1885), came from Britain, like the Cabinet System and Parliamentary Government.
xa: ⚠ **Equality before law** is **British** (negative); **equal protection of the laws** is **American** (positive).
Rule of law is a **basic feature** — **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975)**.

nindian-polity-75-17.s: Which of the following is NOT one of Dicey's three classic elements of the Rule of Law?
o: Primacy of the rights of the individual
nindian-polity-75-17.x: Dicey's elements are absence of arbitrary power, equality before law and primacy of individual rights; people's duty to government is not one.
n: Dicey’s first classic element of the Rule of Law is the absence of arbitrary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s second classic element of the Rule of Law is equality before the law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
Dicey’s third classic element of the Rule of Law is the primacy of the rights of the individual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
People’s responsibility to the Government is not a pillar of the Rule of Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law restrains the government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
The Rule of Law does not expand citizens’ obedience to authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #75 · pp 204-207]
xa: India accepts only the first two; it **reverses** the third — rights flow from the Constitution.
Dicey **opposed** the French **Droit Administratif**.

nindian-polity-75-20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Dicey's third principle and India?
o: In the UK, the Constitution is the result of judicial decisions on individual rights
It concerns the primacy of individual rights

n0a4b2f0e23c.s: The freedoms guaranteed under Article 19 are available to:
o: Citizens and companies as legal persons
n0a4b2f0e23c.x: Article 19 rights are available only to citizens; foreigners cannot claim them and a company as a legal person cannot itself claim them.
xa: Art. 19 operates against **State action only**; private violation → ordinary legal remedy.
**Kaushal Kishor (2023)**: Arts. **19/21** can also be enforced against **non-State actors**.

n8baba71ae8f.s: Which of the following is a ground for restricting the freedom of assembly under Article 19(3)?
n8baba71ae8f.x: Article 19(3) permits restrictions on assembly in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India and public order; morality and security of the State are not its grounds.
xa: Unlawful assembly of **five or more**: IPC s.**141** → **BNS s.189**.

ne93284f7c99.s: Which one of the following is NOT a ground for restricting the freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business under Article 19(6)?
o: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
ne93284f7c99.x: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes is a ground under Article 19(5), relating to movement and residence. Article 19(6) refers to general public interest, professional or technical qualifications, and State trade or monopoly.
ne93284f7c99.tq: Spot the ground borrowed from the neighbouring Article 19(5) provision.
xs: **Protection of Scheduled Tribes** is a **19(5)** ground (movement, residence), not 19(6) — option **(4)**.
**19(6)** grounds: **general public interest**, **professional or technical qualifications**, **State trade or monopoly**.
xa: 19(5) allows limiting outsiders' entry and settlement in **tribal/Inner Line areas**.
No right to carry on **dangerous or immoral** trades (e.g. trafficking).
The State-trade clause of 19(6) came by the **1st Amendment** and shielded **nationalisation**.

nebdd5375b9f.s: Which ground was added to Article 19(2) by the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963?
nebdd5375b9f.x: Sovereignty and integrity of India came with the Sixteenth Amendment, 1963; the other three grounds were added by the First Amendment, 1951.
xa: It followed **Romesh Thappar (1950)**, where "**public order**" was not then a ground.

nc4ec40ff40b.s: Telecast rights and the absence of a government monopoly over airwaves under Article 19(1)(a) are associated with:
nc4ec40ff40b.x: Cricket Association of Bengal concerned telecast and the absence of a government monopoly over airwaves; PUCL is associated with safeguards against phone tapping.
xa: Phone-tapping rulings of the **MP and Delhi HCs** revived the interception debate (Jun **2026**).
**Kameshwar Prasad (1962)**: demonstration protected, strike not.

n2bf4b480f49.s: Which of the following is excluded from the freedom of peaceful assembly under Article 19(1)(b)?
n2bf4b480f49.x: Meetings, demonstrations and processions are protected when peaceful and unarmed; armed gatherings are excluded.
xa: SC (**22 May 2026**): **peaceful protest** is everybody's right but must not occupy public space.
**Bandhs** are illegal (**CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar**).

n5df8ca76640.s: In India, the right to strike is:
n5df8ca76640.x: The right to strike is not a Fundamental Right; it is only a legal right. A gherao is also not protected as peaceful assembly.
xa: **T.K. Rangarajan (2003)**: government employees have no right to strike.
**Bandhs** are illegal (**CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar, 1997-98**).

ncb43640c2d6.s: Peaceful protest is recognised as a right of everybody, but a protest ____.
o: may occupy public space without restriction
is a Fundamental Right to strike
ncb43640c2d6.x: Peaceful protest is a right, but it cannot occupy public space without limitation or trouble other citizens.
xa: Assembly must be **peaceful and unarmed**.

n2ab13b67b76.s: The Centre has defended restrictions under the Foreign Contribution Regulation Act in relation to associations by invoking which provision?
n2ab13b67b76.x: The Centre has invoked Article 19(4), which concerns reasonable restrictions on the freedom to form associations or unions, in defending FCRA curbs.
n2ab13b67b76.tq: Match the restriction clause with the corresponding freedom under Article 19.
xs: The Centre defends **FCRA** curbs under **Article 19(4)** — option **(1)**.
19(4) is the restriction clause for **association** (sovereignty and integrity, public order, morality).
xa: **INSAF (2020)**: only associations in **active politics** barred from foreign funds.
**FCRA vs 19(1)(c)** debate (**25 Jun 2026**).
**19(3)** = assembly; **19(2)** = speech; **19(6)** = profession.

nc57d855a20c.s: Under Article 19(5), freedom of movement and residence may be restricted in the interests of the general public and:
o: Protection of the interests of Scheduled Tribes
nc57d855a20c.x: Article 19(5) permits restrictions on Articles 19(1)(d) and (e) in the interests of the general public and to protect Scheduled Tribes.
xa: e.g. limiting outsiders' entry and settlement in **tribal/Inner Line areas**.

n682c4603bca.s: Which clause permits the State to carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens, thereby allowing State monopolies?
n682c4603bca.x: Article 19(6) lets the State prescribe professional or technical qualifications and carry on a trade to the exclusion of citizens.
xa: The State-trade clause came by the **1st Amendment** — it shielded **nationalisation**.
No right to **dangerous or immoral** trades (e.g. trafficking).

n5430d94cb7c.s: Which one of the following is NOT protected as an occupation under the freedom of profession, trade or business?
o: A trade conducted under a State monopoly
A dangerous or immoral trade such as trafficking
A lawful profession subject to reasonable regulation
A trade requiring prescribed technical qualifications
n5430d94cb7c.x: There is no right to carry on dangerous or immoral trades, such as trafficking. Article 19(6) also permits qualifications and State monopolies.
n5430d94cb7c.tq: Find the exception that is inherently outside the protected field rather than merely regulated within it.
xs: A **dangerous or immoral trade** such as **trafficking** is not protected — option **(2)**.
State monopoly, qualifications and reasonable regulation are all valid under **19(6)**.
xa: 19(6) lets the State carry on trade **to the exclusion of citizens**.
**19(1)(g)** = any **profession, occupation, trade or business**.
**Anuradha Bhasin (2020)**: trade over the **internet** protected under **19(1)(g)**.

nindian-polity-16-7.s: Co-operative societies were added to Article 19(1)(c) by which Constitutional Amendment?
nindian-polity-16-7.x: The 97th Amendment (2011) added co-operative societies to Article 19(1)(c). The 44th deleted the Right to Property and the 86th added the Right to Education.
n: The 44th Amendment deleted the Right to Property. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 44th Amendment was enacted in 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 86th Amendment added the Right to Education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 86th Amendment was enacted in 2002. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 97th Amendment added cooperative societies to Article 19(1)(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 97th Amendment was enacted in 2011. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The Right to Property was removed from the list of Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment in 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 19(1)(c) provides freedom of association, union, and cooperative societies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
The 86th Amendment added the Right to Education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 19(1)(f) was deleted. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
xa: Article 19 originally had **seven** freedoms; now **six** after property was deleted.
⚠ **(c)** co-operative societies added by the **97th**; **(f)** property deleted by the **44th**.
Co-operative societies are also linked to **Art. 43B** and **Part IXB**.
Freedom of expression has been in force from **26 Jan 1950**.

nindian-society-51-18.s: The statutory Zero FIR is a provision of the:
nindian-society-51-18.x: The statutory Zero FIR is a BNSS provision, not a BNS one; BNS covers organised crime and mob lynching.
n: The offense under the Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act is non-bailable. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 103-103]
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) includes dedicated provisions on organized crime. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 103-103]
The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) includes dedicated provisions on mob lynching. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 103-103]
The Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) establishes digital forensics. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 103-103]
xa: **BNS** replaced the **IPC 1860**; **BNSS** replaced the **CrPC 1973**.
Both were enacted in **2023** and came into force on **July 1, 2024**.
**BNSS** mandates **video recording** of **searches and seizures**.
Hate speech is now **s.196 BNS**; unlawful assembly is **BNS s.189**.

n09f1a3739f7.s: Which of the following is correct about a detained person's Article 19 freedoms?
o: Freedom of expression is retained, subject to lawful restrictions
Freedom of movement is retained but expression is lost
They are converted into property rights
n09f1a3739f7.x: Detention curtails movement but does not by itself extinguish freedom of expression; a detainee may, subject to lawful restrictions, write or publish books.
xa: Freedom of expression in force from **26 Jan 1950** (APPSC **2018**).

n2ca1ce51c25.s: Under Article 19, freedom of speech and expression is protected:
o: Only for oral speech in public places
Only in printed newspapers and books
Irrespective of the medium of communication
n2ca1ce51c25.x: Article 19 protects expression irrespective of the medium, extended by courts to the press, television and the Internet, subject to lawful restrictions.
xa: **Naveen Jindal (2004)**: flying the **national flag** is expression.
**Films** can be pre-censored, unlike the press.

nb339f162d19.s: In Kaushal Kishor v State of Uttar Pradesh (2023), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Section 66A of the IT Act is valid subject to safeguards
Public order is not a ground under Article 19(2)
Flying the national flag is outside Article 19(1)(a)
The grounds in Article 19(2) are exhaustive
nb339f162d19.x: Kaushal Kishor held the Article 19(2) grounds exhaustive, so no extra restriction can be placed on ministers' speech; it also let Articles 19 and 21 be enforced against non-State actors.
xa: **Naveen Jindal (2004)**: flag-flying is expression.

nindian-polity-16-16.s: Protection in respect of conviction for offences is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-16-16.x: Article 20 gives protection in respect of conviction; Article 21 protects life and personal liberty, 22 protects against arrest and detention, and 19 lists the six freedoms.
n: Article 20 provides protection in respect of conviction for offences. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 21 provides protection of life and personal liberty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
Article 22 provides protection against arrest and detention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 40-42]
xa: Right to Freedom covers **Articles 19 to 22** (four Articles).
**Article 21-A** (Right to Education) was added by the **86th Amendment (2002)**.
Under Art. 22, preventive detention without an advisory board can last at most **three months**.

n07fd5ad2aab.s: The power of the State to prescribe professional or technical qualifications and to create a State monopoly under Article 19(6) was inserted by which Amendment?
n07fd5ad2aab.x: The First Amendment, 1951 rewrote Art. 19(6) and inserted the clause letting the State carry on any trade to the exclusion of citizens (State monopoly), shielding nationalisation. The 7th, 44th and 97th Amendments did not touch Art. 19(6); the 97th added co-operative societies to Art. 19(1)(c).
n07fd5ad2aab.tq: Match the Article 19 exception with the amendment that inserted it.
xs: These **19(6)** powers were inserted by the **First Amendment** (**1951**) — option **(4)**.
The **44th** deleted 19(1)(f); the **97th** added co-operative societies — options (2), (3) wrong.
xa: The 1st Amendment also added **public order, friendly relations, incitement** to 19(2).
The Act's **75**th year was in Jun **2026**.
19(6) shielded **nationalisation** (LENSD, **19 Jun 2026**).

n7ae4654f086.s: The right to silence (not singing the national anthem) was read into Article 19(1)(a) in:
n7ae4654f086.x: Bijoe Emmanuel recognised the right to silence. Tata Press concerned commercial speech, Naveen Jindal flag hoisting and Anuradha Bhasin internet speech.
xa: **Cricket Association of Bengal (1995)**: telecast; no govt monopoly on airwaves.
**PUCL (1997)**: safeguards against **phone tapping**.
Art. 19 protects speech "**irrespective of the medium**" (PYQ **2019**).

nc4c990389b3.s: The ban on the journal Cross Roads was struck down, as 'public order' was then not a ground under Article 19(2), in:
o: Aveek Sarkar v State of West Bengal
Bennett Coleman v Union of India
Kedar Nath Singh v State of Bihar
Romesh Thappar v State of Madras
nc4c990389b3.x: Romesh Thappar (1950) struck down the Cross Roads ban because public order was not then an Article 19(2) ground; it contributed to the First Amendment, 1951.
xa: Exam angle: **Romesh Thappar → 1st Amendment**.

n8ca6e0d2362.s: Which case recognised speech and trade over the internet as protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g)?
n8ca6e0d2362.x: Anuradha Bhasin protected speech and trade over the internet and required internet shutdowns to be proportionate, temporary and published.
xa: Sedition **s.124A IPC** was kept in abeyance by the SC in **2022**; now replaced by **s.152 BNS**.

n293f2aa4ef3.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that bandhs are illegal as they curb the freedoms of others?
n293f2aa4ef3.x: CPI(M) v. Bharat Kumar held bandhs illegal because they curb others' freedoms. Kameshwar Prasad protected demonstrations but not strikes, and T.K. Rangarajan denied government employees a right to strike.
xa: **All India Bank Employees' Assn (1962)**: strike only a **legal right**.
**Gherao** is not protected.

ndbfd774e2e8.s: Which of the following is not expressly listed in Article 19(1) but has been read into freedom of speech and expression?
ndbfd774e2e8.x: Courts have read freedom of the press into Article 19(1)(a); there is no fundamental right to strike, travel abroad falls under Article 21 and Article 19(1)(f) was deleted.
xa: PYQ **2019**: freedom of press is part of **Art. 19**.
Press freedom cases: **Romesh Thappar (1950)**, Sakal Papers (**1962**), Indian Express (**1985**).
The **right to protest** is also read in.

nfc83ee0df11.s: The Ninety-seventh Amendment, 2011, relating to co-operative societies, is also associated with which provisions?
nfc83ee0df11.x: The amendment relating to co-operative societies is also associated with Article 43B and Part IXB.
nfc83ee0df11.tq: Start with the sure amendment association and match the connected Article and Part.
xs: The **97th Amendment, 2011** is also linked with **Article 43B** and **Part IXB** — option **(1)**.
It added **"co-operative societies"** to **19(1)(c)**.
xa: Restrictions on association fall under **19(4)**: sovereignty and integrity, public order, morality.
⚠ **97th** added to (c); the **44th, 1978** deleted (f) property.
**FCRA** vs **19(1)(c)** is a current debate (**25 Jun 2026**).

n2404ddbe75e.s: Films may be pre-censored in a way the press cannot, mainly because films:
o: Are regulated only by the States
n2404ddbe75e.x: Films are considered capable of reaching larger audiences, so they may be pre-censored where the press cannot; neither enjoys absolute protection.
xa: Press freedom: **Romesh Thappar (1950)**; **Bennett Coleman (1972)** — newsprint policy violated it.
Debate: films pre-censored but the press cannot be.
**Aveek Sarkar (2014)**: **"community standards"** test for obscenity.

nf291171540a.s: The protection under Article 20(1) against a heavier penalty than that applicable when the offence was committed applies to:
nf291171540a.x: Article 20(1) applies to criminal laws; it bars conviction and a greater penalty, but does not necessarily bar the trial itself.
xa: Art. 20 is available to **citizens, foreigners and companies** and is **non-suspendable in emergency**.
⚠ Art. 20 does **not** cover **preventive detention**.

n3e8b24c7a3a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about protection against double jeopardy?
o: Article 20(2) bars prosecution and punishment more than once for the same offence
The protection covers prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal
Article 20(2) also bars departmental proceedings after a criminal conviction for the same act
Section 337 BNSS replaces Section 300 CrPC as the corresponding provision
n3e8b24c7a3a.x: Article 20(2) covers only prosecution and punishment by a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental proceedings.
xa: Rights of arrested persons moved from **CrPC 50, 57** to **Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS**.
Attempted suicide: **Sec. 309 IPC** → no general offence; only **Sec. 226 BNS**.

nbf95f3fc97b.s: The expression 'procedure established by law' is associated with the constitution of:
nbf95f3fc97b.x: 'Procedure established by law' is associated with Japan, while 'due process' is associated with the United States.
xa: "Procedure established by law" is **more definite** than "due process of law".
**A.K. Gopalan (1950):** no due process in India; **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** in effect introduced it.
After Maneka, Art. 21 protects against both **executive** and **legislative** action.

n01e7fecefbe.s: The protection under Article 21 is available to:
n01e7fecefbe.x: Article 21 protects citizens and non-citizens and has been read to include dignity, health and protection against solitary confinement.
xa: **Digital access** was also read into Art. 21 (SC ruling, Jun 2026).
**Privacy** — **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**.
⚠ Art. 20 goes further: also available to **companies**.

na4eb72f349c.s: In Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that which of the following, when conducted without consent, violates Article 20(3)?
o: Verification of age through official records
na4eb72f349c.x: Selvi (2010) held that narco-analysis, polygraph examination and brain-mapping without consent violate the protection against testimonial compulsion under Article 20(3).
na4eb72f349c.tq: Direct case-to-doctrine recall using physical-evidence distractors.
xs: **Selvi v State of Karnataka (2010)** held that **narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping** without consent violate **20(3)** — option **(2)**.
**Fingerprints** and physical specimens are **physical evidence**, not testimony — outside 20(3) (**Kathi Kalu Oghad 1961**).
xa: Art. 20(3) — **no self-incrimination** — applies only in **criminal proceedings** and covers **oral and documentary** testimony.
**20(1)** bars ex post facto criminal law; **20(2)** bars double jeopardy.
Art. 20 is available to **citizens, foreigners and companies**.

n13a3f6fa7dc.s: The protections under Article 20 are available to:
o: Citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies
Natural persons present in India only
n13a3f6fa7dc.x: Article 20 protections extend to citizens, foreigners and legal persons such as companies, subject to the nature of each protection.
xa: **Art. 21** is likewise available to **citizens and non-citizens**.
Art. 20 has three protections: **no ex post facto law**, **no double jeopardy**, **no self-incrimination**.
⚠ Art. 20 does not cover **preventive detention**.

nfb2a7d1686b.s: Which BNSS sections broadly correspond to CrPC Sections 50 and 57 on grounds of arrest and production before a magistrate?
nfb2a7d1686b.x: BNSS Sections 47 and 58 broadly correspond to CrPC Sections 50 and 57 on these arrest safeguards.
xa: Double jeopardy: **Sec. 337 BNSS** (earlier **Sec. 300 CrPC**).
Attempted suicide: **Sec. 309 IPC** → **Sec. 226 BNS** (only to compel a public servant).
The **BNS** replaced the IPC from **1 July 2024**.

n33fb1fce7d4.s: Compared with A.K. Gopalan, Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 also protects against:
n33fb1fce7d4.x: A.K. Gopalan read Article 21 narrowly without testing legislation for fairness; Maneka Gandhi extended protection against arbitrary legislative action.
xa: **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** overruled Gopalan; procedure must be **"fair, just and reasonable"**.
Gopalan (**1950**): "procedure established by law" = any procedure **enacted by the legislature**.
Maneka Gandhi also read the right to **travel abroad** into Art. 21.

nadd9e648cab.s: In Supriyo Chakraborty (2023), the Supreme Court held that:
o: There is an unqualified fundamental right to marry
The right to privacy is unconstitutional
Travel abroad is not protected under Article 21
There is no fundamental right to marry as such
nadd9e648cab.x: The Court held there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as such, while Article 21 protection for dignity, privacy and choice of partner remains.
xa: ⚠ **G2 2025** key: both "no FR to marry" and "travel abroad is an FR" were **right**.
Choice of partner: **Shafin Jahan (Hadiya case, 2018)** — PYQ 2019: Art. 21.
Recent additions to Art. 21: **mental health** and **digital access** (Jun 2026).

n857714796d3.s: Compensation for violation of human rights under Article 21 is associated with:
n857714796d3.x: Nilabati Behera (1993) is associated with compensation for human rights violations; Puttaswamy recognised privacy.
xa: **P. Rathinam (1994)** struck down **Sec. 309 IPC**; Gian Kaur restored it.
**Common Cause (2018)** — passive euthanasia an FR; **living will / advance directive** valid.
**Aruna Shanbaug (2011)** — **passive euthanasia** under **High Court** supervision.

nb9521a23645.s: The right to speedy trial was read into Article 21 in:
nb9521a23645.x: Hussainara Khatoon concerned speedy trial; Maneka Gandhi gave fair procedure, M.H. Hoskot free legal aid and Francis Coralie Mullin human dignity.
xa: Speedy trial was reaffirmed in **K.A. Najeeb (2021)**.
Maneka Gandhi **overruled A.K. Gopalan (1950)**.
**Emergency medical care** — **Paschim Banga Khet Mazdoor Samity (1996)**.

nindian-polity-41-8.s: The right to a clean environment and air was read into Article 21 in:
nindian-polity-41-8.x: Subhash Kumar recognised a clean environment; Parmanand Katara gave emergency medical aid, Olga Tellis shelter and livelihood, and Maneka Gandhi travel abroad.
n: Satwant Singh recognized the right to travel abroad under Article 21 in 1967. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Maneka Gandhi recognized the right to travel abroad under Article 21 in 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
