Parmanand Katara recognized the right to emergency medical aid under Article 21 in 1989. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Subhash Kumar recognized the right to a clean environment under Article 21 in 1991. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Subhash Kumar recognized the right to clean air under Article 21 in 1991. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Olga Tellis recognized the right to shelter under Article 21 in 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Olga Tellis recognized the right to livelihood under Article 21 in 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Chameli Singh recognized the right to shelter under Article 21 in 1995. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Chameli Singh recognized the right to livelihood under Article 21 in 1995. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Maneka Gandhi was linked to Article 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xa: **Privacy**: **Govind (1975)**, **Malak Singh (1980)**, **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**.
**Marry a person of choice**: **Lata Singh (2006)**; **Shafin Jahan (Hadiya case, 2018)**.
**Speedy trial**: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes date **Chameli Singh** to **1996**.

nc51f33f3bc5.s: In which year did the Supreme Court decide Common Cause, upholding the living will?
nc51f33f3bc5.x: Common Cause was decided in 2018, after P. Rathinam (1994), Gian Kaur (1996) and Aruna Shanbaug (2011).
xa: Earliest: **Maruti Shripati Dubal (Bombay HC, 1987)** — right to die part of Art. 21.
**Mental Healthcare Act, 2017** decriminalised attempted suicide in effect.
**Harish Rana** (PVS for **13** years) — parents sought withdrawal of life support (**16 Mar 2026**).

nd80c02ee40f.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Supreme Court rulings on the right to die?
o: P. Rathinam (1994) held Section 309 IPC unconstitutional
Aruna Shanbaug (2011) held the living will valid
Gian Kaur (1996) held there is no right to die and Section 309 IPC is valid
Common Cause (2018) upheld the living will / advance directive
nd80c02ee40f.x: Aruna Shanbaug allowed passive euthanasia under High Court supervision; it was Common Cause (2018) that upheld the living will.
xa: ⚠ Rathinam struck Sec. 309; Gian Kaur **restored** it.
Common Cause: right to die with dignity (passive euthanasia) is an **FR under Art. 21**.
Now **Sec. 309 IPC is history**: the BNS (from **1 July 2024**) has no general offence of attempted suicide.

n6fe6058b26e.s: Which of the following is correct about attempted suicide in India?
o: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 made it a general offence
The BNS retains Section 309 IPC unchanged
It was decriminalised in effect in 2017, and the BNS has no general offence for it
The BNS decriminalised every act intended to compel a public servant
n6fe6058b26e.x: The Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 decriminalised attempted suicide in effect, and the BNS (in force from 1 July 2024) has no general offence of attempted suicide.
xa: **BNS, 2023** in force **from 1 July 2024**.
**P. Rathinam (1994)** struck down Sec. 309; **Gian Kaur (1996)** upheld it.
**Common Cause (2018)** — **living will** valid.

na663a1ef192.s: Article 21A was inserted into the Constitution by the:
na663a1ef192.x: The 86th Amendment Act, 2002 inserted Article 21A; the RTE Act, 2009 only gives effect to it, since an Act of Parliament cannot add an Article.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** some notes loosely say the RTE Act "added" Art. 21A.
Act + Art. 21A came into force on **1 April 2010**.
Only **elementary education** is a Fundamental Right, not higher/professional education.

nacdafb6a13a.s: The RTE Act, 2009 reserves what share of entry-level seats in unaided private schools for children of weaker groups?
nacdafb6a13a.x: The Act provides 25 per cent entry-level seats in unaided private schools for weaker groups; the provision does not apply to minority schools.
xa: The **2019** amendment allowed assessment and **detention** at certain stages.
**Sec. 3:** right to education in a **neighbourhood school** till elementary education is complete.
Full name: **Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009**.

n10247d401d6.s: Section 3 of the Right to Education Act, 2009 gives free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school to every child aged:
n10247d401d6.x: Section 3 gives every child aged 6 to 14 years the right to free and compulsory education in a neighbourhood school until elementary education is completed.
xa: **25% entry-level seats** in unaided private schools for weaker groups (**not minority** schools).
Act and Art. 21A in force from **1 April 2010**.
**Art. 51A(k)**: parents/guardians to provide opportunities for education to children **6-14 years**.

n3f86065cce1.s: In which year was the right-to-education case Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka decided?
n3f86065cce1.x: Mohini Jain was decided in 1992, followed by Unnikrishnan in 1993, the 86th Amendment in 2002 and the RTE Act in 2009.
xa: **Unnikrishnan v State of AP (1993)** is the AP angle of the topic.
The RTE Act and Art. 21A came into force on **1 April 2010**.
Art. 21A is called an extension of the **Right to Life** (PYQ 2019).

n4825346bfeb.s: Which of the following is NOT a change made by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002?
o: Inserted Article 21A for free and compulsory education of children aged 6 to 14
Changed Article 45 to provide early childhood care and education below 6 years
Added Article 51A(k), a duty of parents to provide education to children aged 6 to 14
Deleted the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights
n4825346bfeb.x: The Right to Property was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978. The 86th Amendment changed Articles 21A, 45 and 51A(k).
xa: 51A(k) is the **11th duty** — the duty of parents.
⚠ Exam angle: Art. 21A vs Art. 45 vs Art. 51A(k) **age groups**.
The enabling law is the **RTE Act, 2009**.

n5b511b7c635.s: With reference to bail in cases under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, the Supreme Court has observed that delay alone is—
o: not a trump card for granting bail
sufficient to invalidate the detention order
n5b511b7c635.x: The Supreme Court observed on 6 January 2026 that delay alone is not a “trump card” for bail in UAPA cases.
n5b511b7c635.tq: Test the exact legal qualification instead of treating delay as an automatic remedy.
xs: The SC said delay alone is **not a "trump card" for bail** in **UAPA** cases (**6 Jan 2026**) — option **(3)**.
**UAPA 1967** is the **anti-terror and unlawful-associations** law.
xa: **Speedy trial** is part of Art. 21 — **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**, reaffirmed in **K.A. Najeeb (2021)**.
A letter to **CJI Surya Kant** on **Umar Khalid/Sharjeel Imam** cited K.A. Najeeb (**15 Aug 2026**).
**NSA 1980** allows detention up to **12 months** without charges.

n75e41a6a706.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the safeguards in Article 22(1) and 22(2)?
o: An arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours
The safeguards also cover a civil arrest and the deportation of an alien
The 24 hours exclude the time of journey
The safeguards are not available to an enemy alien or a preventive detainee
n75e41a6a706.x: Arrest under court orders, civil arrest and deportation of aliens fall outside these safeguards; Article 22(3) also excludes enemy aliens and preventive detainees.
xa: Arrested persons also have the right to be **informed of grounds** and to **consult a lawyer** of choice.
New code: **Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS** (earlier **CrPC 50, 57**).
**Vihaan Kumar (2025):** grounds of arrest must be **meaningfully communicated** to every arrestee.

nc487a752300.s: Under Article 22(1), a person arrested and detained in custody has the right to:
o: Be informed of the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice
Be released on bail as of right within 24 hours
Be tried only by a jury
Have the case reviewed by an Advisory Board within three months
nc487a752300.x: Art. 22(1) gives the right to be told the grounds of arrest and to consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice (now Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS for the procedure). Bail as of right and trial by jury are not guaranteed, and the Advisory Board review belongs to preventive detention under Art. 22(4).
xs: Under **Art. 22(1)** an arrestee must be **informed of the grounds** of arrest and may **consult and be defended by a lawyer of choice** — option **(1)**.
Bail as of right and jury trial are not guaranteed.
**Advisory Board** review within **3 months** belongs to **preventive detention** under **Art. 22(4)**.
xa: **Art. 22(2):** production before the **nearest magistrate within 24 hours**.
⚠ These rights are **not available** to **enemy aliens** or **preventive detainees**.
**Vihaan Kumar v State of Haryana (2025):** grounds must be **meaningfully communicated**.

ne1a6ccd1096.s: Preventive detention is best described as detention:
o: After conviction, to execute a sentence
Ordered by a criminal court after a finding of guilt
Only for non-payment of a civil debt
Without trial, on suspicion of future harmful acts
ne1a6ccd1096.x: Preventive detention is detention without trial based on apprehension of future harmful acts; punitive detention follows conviction.
xa: Preventive detention only for **'public order'**, not routine **'law and order'** (Jun 2026).
Roots: **Regulation III of 1818** and the **Rowlatt Act**.
NCRB: over **1.2 lakh** preventive detentions a year, about **50%** quashed by HCs.

n0b2c31eb03e.s: Under Article 22(7), who may prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention?
n0b2c31eb03e.x: Article 22(7) permits Parliament to prescribe the maximum period of preventive detention; Article 22(5) requires grounds and an opportunity of representation.
xa: **NSA 1980** allows detention up to **12 months** without charges.
Criticism: vague / misuse of "**public order**".

n62a94ef8236.s: The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 sought to cut the period of preventive detention without an Advisory Board report to:
n62a94ef8236.x: The 44th Amendment cut it from three to two months, but the clause was never notified, so three months still applies under Article 22(4).
xa: There are demands to **notify the 2-month limit** (**16 Jun 2026**).
**IYB** records the 2-month text.
The **Advisory Board** has **HC judges** or persons qualified to be.

n8aceebda10e.s: Parliament alone can make preventive detention laws on matters connected with:
o: Defence, foreign affairs and security of India
n8aceebda10e.x: Parliament alone legislates on preventive detention for defence, foreign affairs and security of India; Parliament and the States share public order, security of a State and essential supplies.
xa: State detention laws: **J&K PSA**, Kerala **KAPA**.
Central laws: **NSA 1980**, **COFEPOSA 1974**, **UAPA 1967**.
Preventive detention only for **public order**, not routine law and order.

n6676f3e86b5.s: Preventive detention is constitutionally justified under Article 22 in relation to which of the following?
o: Mere law and order in every local dispute
Any administrative inconvenience caused by an individual
Public order, but not merely routine law and order
Only a civil disagreement between private parties
n6676f3e86b5.x: The Supreme Court has distinguished public order from ordinary law and order. Preventive detention cannot be justified merely by routine law-and-order concerns.
n6676f3e86b5.tq: Use the higher-threshold comparison between public order and ordinary law and order.
xs: The SC held preventive detention valid only for **'public order'**, **not routine 'law and order'** — option **(3)**.
Detention is on **suspicion of future acts, without trial** — not for civil disputes or inconvenience.
xa: Allahabad HC criticised routine detentions in the **Chander Pal Singh** case.
NCRB: over **1.2 lakh** preventive detentions a year, about half (**50%**) quashed by HCs.
Criticism: vague / misuse of "public order"; **delayed Advisory Boards**.

n35cc2efc1c9.s: In which year was the National Security Act enacted?
n35cc2efc1c9.x: The National Security Act came in 1980, after the Preventive Detention Act (1950), MISA (1971) and COFEPOSA (1974).
xa: **UAPA 1967** — anti-terror and unlawful-associations law.
**MISA** was repealed in **1978**.
Roots: **Regulation III of 1818** and the **Rowlatt Act**.

n7b07a2f1562.s: In Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana (2025), the Supreme Court emphasised which of the following?
o: The grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee
The right to education is available only to citizens
Preventive detention can be ordered only after conviction
An Advisory Board must review every arrest within 24 hours
n7b07a2f1562.x: Vihaan Kumar v. State of Haryana emphasised that the grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee.
n7b07a2f1562.tq: Directly identify the precise legal requirement associated with a recent case.
xs: **Vihaan Kumar v State of Haryana (2025)** held that **grounds of arrest must be meaningfully communicated to every arrestee** — option **(1)** (reported **14 Aug 2026**).
It builds on **Art. 22(1)** — the right to be **informed of grounds** of arrest.
Advisory Boards concern **preventive detention** (beyond **3 months**), not ordinary arrest; preventive detention is **without trial**, not after conviction.
xa: An arrestee must be produced before the **nearest magistrate within 24 hours** (excluding journey time).
New code: **Secs. 47 and 58 BNSS** (earlier **CrPC 50, 57**).
⚠ These rights are **not available** to **enemy aliens** or **preventive detainees** (**Art. 22(3)**).
n7b07a2f1562.fixed: judgment is of 2025; stem's '14 August 2026' was a note date, not the ruling date

n57495642107.s: The Right to Freedom of Religion guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 of the Constitution is classified as a:
n57495642107.x: The freedoms guaranteed under Articles 25 to 28 constitute Fundamental Rights and are not merely legal rights or Directive Principles.
n57495642107.tq: Test the constitutional classification directly and distinguish a Fundamental Right from a legal right or DPSP.
xs: The right to religion (Arts 25-28) is a **Fundamental Right** — option **(1)** (PYQ 2019).
It is **not a legal right or DPSP**.
xa: Arts **25, 27, 28** are available to **all persons** — citizens and foreigners alike.
**Art. 26** is available to **religious denominations** or any section of them.
The right is subject to **public order, morality and health**.

n8a48e782051.s: Article 24 prohibits employment of children below fourteen years in:
o: Factories, mines and other hazardous employment
n8a48e782051.x: Article 24 bars employment of children below fourteen in factories, mines and other hazardous employment; harmless or innocent work is not covered.
xa: Related DPSP: **Art. 39(e)/(f)** — tender age of children not abused.
**Art. 21A** (education **6-14 years**) + **Art. 24** together protect children (APPSC G1 2022).
The **2016** amendment barred adolescents **14-18** from **hazardous work**.

nce8c3c0399d.s: Articles 23 and 24 of the Constitution together form the:
nce8c3c0399d.x: Articles 23–24 form the Right against Exploitation, and Articles 25–28 the Right to Freedom of Religion.
xa: **Art. 23** — traffic in human beings, **begar**, forced labour; **Art. 24** — child labour below **14**.
**Art. 23** protects **citizens and non-citizens** against **both the State and private persons**.
Arts **25, 27, 28** → **all persons**; Art. **26** → **religious denominations**.

n8527322a9d5.s: The protection against trafficking and forced labour under Article 23 is available:
o: Only to Indian citizens and only against the State
To citizens and non-citizens, and against both the State and private persons
Only to persons employed in government institutions
Only when the exploitation is committed by a public authority
n8527322a9d5.x: Article 23 protects both citizens and non-citizens and operates against the State as well as private persons.
n8527322a9d5.tq: Check the scope of a fundamental right by testing both beneficiaries and enforceability against private actors.
xs: **Art. 23** is available to **citizens and non-citizens** and protects against **both the State and private persons** — option **(2)**.
So it is not limited to citizens, public authorities or government employees.
xa: **Arts. 23 and 24** are both enforceable against **private individuals**.
Arts **25, 27, 28** → **all persons**; Art. **26** → **religious denominations**.
Right against exploitation = **Arts 23-24**.

nce20bc03113.s: Under the Child Labour Amendment Act, 2016, adolescents aged 14–18 years are:
o: Free to work in any occupation
Barred only from work in mines
nce20bc03113.x: The 2016 amendment bars adolescents aged 14–18 from hazardous work, and bars children below 14 from work except helping family after school.
xa: It renamed the law the **Child and Adolescent Labour Act**.
**Art. 24** does not bar **harmless/innocent work**.
DPSP **Art. 39(e)/(f)** protects children's tender age.

n2cde18bf5ba.s: "All persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and the right freely to profess, practise and propagate religion." This text is found in which Article of the Constitution?
n2cde18bf5ba.x: These words are Article 25(1), subject to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III. Article 19(1) lists the six freedoms of citizens. Article 26(1) gives religious denominations the right to manage their own affairs. Article 29(1) protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens.
n2cde18bf5ba.tq: Conscience + profess, practise, propagate = Art. 25(1). The usual wrong options are 19(1), 26(1) and 29(1).
xs: The quoted text is **Article 25(1)** — option **(2)**.
It is subject to **public order, morality and health** and other Part III provisions.
**Art. 19(1)** has the citizens' freedoms; **Art. 26(1)** is denominations managing affairs.
xa: ⚠ Exam angle: quoted text of 25(1) → identify the Article (asked **2018, 2023**).
Distractors used: **Arts 19(1), 26(1), 29(1)**.
"All persons" — Art. 25 is available to **citizens and non-citizens**.

nb22dd1537a8.s: The right under Article 27 is available to:
nb22dd1537a8.x: Article 27, like Articles 25 and 28, is available to all persons; Article 26 is available to religious denominations or any section of them.
xa: **Art. 23** protects **citizens and non-citizens**, against **State and private persons**.
Art. 27 **bars taxes, not fees**.

nc594c91c15e.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Article 26 – A religious denomination's right to manage its religious affairs
Article 27 – No compulsory tax for promotion of a particular religion
Article 28(1) – No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained out of State funds
Article 28(3) – Attendance at religious instruction can be made compulsory in State-aided institutions
nc594c91c15e.x: Article 28(3) protects freedom from compulsory attendance: no person can be compelled to attend religious instruction without consent.
xa: A **minor** needs the **guardian's consent**.
Art. 28 is an **individual right**.

n26d76dfccef.s: The Supreme Court has left it to the Ministry of Education to decide whether schools imparting religious instruction fall under:
n26d76dfccef.x: The question left to the Ministry of Education is whether such schools fall under Article 26(a), rather than under Articles 19(1)(g) or 30(1).
xa: **Art. 26(a):** denominations may **establish and maintain institutions** for religious and charitable purposes.
**Art. 343** is about the **official language** — Hindi — unrelated.

nc5bfcbb2f86.s: Which one of the following is a characteristic of a theocratic state?
o: The Constitution prohibits any relationship between religion and public policy
Religious practices are entirely outside constitutional regulation
The State has no religion and treats all religions equally
An official religion guides law and State policy
nc5bfcbb2f86.x: A theocratic or religious state has an official religion that guides its law and State policy. Such a system is not a feature of the Indian Constitution.
nc5bfcbb2f86.tq: Identify the defining feature of a theocratic state.
xs: A **theocratic state** is one where an **official religion guides law and state policy** — option **(4)**.
Option 3 describes India: **no state religion** and **equal respect for all religions**.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** "**Religious state**" is **not** a feature of the Indian Constitution (APPSC 2018).
Indian model: **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** — state neutrality + positive intervention.
The Constituent Assembly rejected adding **'God'** to the Preamble (**1949**).

n50ba9f5176b.s: Which of the following is NOT a component of Indian secularism?
o: Non-applicability of secular principles to irreligious persons
n50ba9f5176b.x: Secularism includes freedom of conscience, which protects believers as well as non-believers. Non-applicability to irreligious persons is not a component of secularism.
n50ba9f5176b.tq: Find the option that reverses the inclusive scope of freedom of conscience.
xs: "**Not applicable to irreligious persons**" is NOT a component — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2018).
**Freedom of conscience** covers **non-believers** too.
Components: **freedom of religion**, **equality of all religions**, state neutrality, **no religious tax**, **minority rights**.
xa: **Conscience** includes the freedom to follow **no religion**.
**Religious pluralism** = freedom to practise any religion **or none**.
Related Articles include **25, 26, 27** and **325**.

n87a02d0bd7b.s: Who among the following regarded religion as a form of collective worship of society and examined the distinction between the sacred and the profane?
n87a02d0bd7b.x: Emile Durkheim associated religion with collective worship of society and distinguished the sacred from the profane.
n87a02d0bd7b.tq: Match the distinctive conceptual pair—sacred and profane—with its sociologist.
xs: **Emile Durkheim**: **sacred vs profane**; religion as **collective worship of society** — option **(3)**.
**Tylor** — animism; **Weber** — The Religion of India; **Marx** — "opium of the people".
xa: Durkheim also studied **totemism** (**Elementary Forms of Religious Life, 1912**).
**Malinowski**: personal attachments and **death** are sources of religion.
**Frazer**: **magic → religion → science**.

n045a6f52879.s: In July 2026, which community renewed its demand for a separate religion code in the Census?
n045a6f52879.x: The Ravidassias renewed their demand for a separate religion code in the Census in July 2026. Jains, Parsis and Buddhists are already counted as separate religions in the Census, and all three are among the six notified minorities, so they have no such demand.
n045a6f52879.tq: Ravidassias = separate Census religion code demand (Jul 2026).
xs: The **Ravidassias** renewed the demand for a separate **religion code in the Census** (**15 Jul 2026**) — option **(2)**.
**Jains**, **Parsis** and **Buddhists** are already among the **six notified minorities**, so they make no such demand.
xa: The six notified minorities: **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains**.
Explanation II to Art. 25: "Hindus" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists** for **25(2)(b)**.
Other current issues: **Allahabad HC hijab ruling** (**26 Aug 2026**); Sabarimala **9-judge** reference.

nf2db3801176.s: Compulsory service for a public purpose is permitted as an exception under Article:
nf2db3801176.x: Article 23(1) prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; Article 23(2) is the exception for compulsory public service without discrimination.
xa: **Begar** = **forced unpaid labour** exacted by officials/**zamindars**.
Traffic covers buying/selling persons, **immoral traffic** incl. prostitution, **devadasi** system, slavery.
**Art. 21** (life with dignity) is the basis of **mandatory victim rehabilitation**.

n612c9a8a65e.s: ‘Begar’, as used in the context of Article 23, means:
o: Voluntary community service performed for religious purposes
Unpaid forced labour exacted by officials or zamindars
Paid labour performed under a written contract
Compulsory military service with regular remuneration
n612c9a8a65e.x: Begar refers to unpaid forced labour traditionally exacted by officials or zamindars.
n612c9a8a65e.tq: Test the exact meaning of an Indian constitutional term with a nearby but incorrect service concept.
xs: **Begar** = **forced unpaid labour** exacted by **officials/zamindars** — option **(2)**.
It is neither voluntary nor paid, so options 1, 3 and 4 fail.
xa: Begar is prohibited under **Art. 23(1)** with traffic in human beings and other forced labour.
**Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976** abolishes **debt bondage**.
**Art. 23(2):** compulsory **public service** (military/social) is allowed.

nac6e6f6708b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 23(2)?
o: The State may impose compulsory service for public purposes
Such service may include military or social service
The State cannot discriminate solely on grounds of religion, race, caste or class in imposing it
The State must pay remuneration in every case of compulsory service
nac6e6f6708b.x: Article 23(2) does not require payment in every case of compulsory public service.
xa: Art. 23 works against **both the State and private persons**.
**Art. 21** is the basis of **mandatory victim rehabilitation**.

nbc30871d236.s: Which pair most directly strengthens the constitutional protection of children against exploitation by combining education and child-labour safeguards?
nbc30871d236.x: Article 21A provides free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 years, while Article 24 prohibits their employment in factories, mines and hazardous work. Together they make the right against exploitation more meaningful for children.
nbc30871d236.tq: Link the complementary provisions instead of treating each Article in isolation.
xs: **Art. 21A** (free and compulsory education, **6-14 years**) + **Art. 24** (child labour) make the right against exploitation meaningful for children — option **(2)**.
PYQ answer: "**Articles 21A and 24**" (APPSC G1 2022).
**Arts 25-26** are freedom of religion, not child protection.
xa: Art. 21A came by the **86th Amendment 2002**.
Related DPSP: **Art. 39(e)/(f)** — tender age of children not abused.
**Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005** set up **NCPCR/SCPCR**.

n479e5adb5c1.s: Which Directive Principles direct the State to ensure that the tender age of children is not abused and that children are protected against exploitation?
n479e5adb5c1.x: Articles 39(e) and 39(f) protect children's tender age from abuse and ensure healthy development with protection against exploitation.
xa: **Art. 21A** + **Art. 24** together protect children (APPSC G1 2022).
**POCSO Act, 2012** is a linked child-protection law.
**Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986** became the **Child and Adolescent Labour Act** in **2016**.

n69a8d122ecb.s: The Bhakti movement, which rejected ritualism and caste, spans roughly the:
n69a8d122ecb.x: Bhakti spans the 6th to the 18th century, and its interaction with Sufi traditions built communal harmony and regional literatures.
xa: Andhra: **Vijayanagara** employed **Muslim officers** and protected **Jains**.
**Bammera Potana** offered the **Andhra Maha Bhagavatamu** to **Lord Rama**.
**Akbar** promoted tolerance and dialogue.

n0725fc2cc49.s: Which thinker linked karma, dharma and caste with the shaping of economic life in *The Religion of India*?
n0725fc2cc49.x: Max Weber examined the relationship of karma, dharma and caste to economic life in *The Religion of India*.
n0725fc2cc49.tq: Identify the thinker through the specific work and its analytical themes.
xs: **Max Weber** — **The Religion of India**: **karma, dharma, caste** shape economic life — option **(2)**.
He also wrote the **Protestant Ethic**.
xa: **Durkheim** — sacred vs profane.
**Marx** — "**opium of the people**".
⚠ **Tylor = animism; Frazer = magic → religion → science; Malinowski = death**.

n099aa16f6a6.s: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, which abolishes debt bondage, was enacted in:
n099aa16f6a6.x: The Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act is of 1976; ITPA is of 1956 and the Child Labour Act of 1986.
xa: Its **2016** amendment renamed it the **Child and Adolescent Labour Act**.
Trafficking is now **Sec. 143, BNS 2023**, which replaced **IPC Sec. 370**.
**POCSO Act, 2012** and the **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005** are linked laws.
**Article 23** bars **traffic in human beings** and **begar**; **Article 24** bars child labour below **14 years**.

nf2cf2355d2d.s: Trafficking is dealt with under which Section of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita?
nf2cf2355d2d.x: Section 143 of the BNS, which replaced the IPC from 1 July 2024, deals with trafficking; victim consent is immaterial.
xa: District **Anti-Human Trafficking Units** are **MHA-funded** (**2 Jun 2026**).
**ITPA 1956** penalises brothels and pimping.

n5dafd874045.s: The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (NCPCR) and the State Commissions (SCPCRs) are constituted under which law?
o: Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005
Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012
n5dafd874045.x: NCPCR and SCPCRs are set up under the Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005. POCSO 2012 deals with sexual offences against children, ITPA 1956 with brothels and immoral traffic, and the 1986 Act with child labour; none of them creates the commissions.
xs: **NCPCR/SCPCR** are set up under the **Commissions for Protection of Child Rights Act, 2005** — option **(1)**.
**POCSO 2012** — child sexual offences; **ITPA 1956** — brothels; **1986 Act** — child labour.
xa: District **Anti-Human Trafficking Units** are **MHA-funded**.
**Art. 24** bars children **below 14** from hazardous work.
**Art. 21A** gives free education for **6-14 years**.

ncb24c3e22b6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the terms in Article 25(1)?
o: Worship, rituals and ceremonies integral to the religion fall under 'practise'
The freedom to follow no religion falls under 'conscience'
Wearing a turban, crucifix or kirpan is an instance of 'profess'
'Propagate' means the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God
ncb24c3e22b6.x: Propagate means spreading one's beliefs to others; the inner freedom to mould one's relation with God is conscience.
xa: ⚠ Propagation does **NOT** include a right to **convert** another person.
**Stanislaus v. MP (1977):** no right to convert.

neb28b33c277.s: The freedoms in Article 25(1) are subject to public order, morality, health and:
o: The other provisions of Part III
neb28b33c277.x: Article 25(1) expressly subjects these freedoms to public order, morality, health and the other provisions of Part III.
xa: Art. 26 rights are subject to **public order, morality, health** only.
The State can intervene to root out **social evils**.

na0f45f3e201.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 25(2)?
o: 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate economic, financial, political or other secular activity associated with religion
25(2)(b) lets the State provide for social welfare and reform
25(2)(b) lets the State throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes of Hindus
25(2)(a) lets the State regulate only spiritual beliefs, not secular activities
na0f45f3e201.x: Article 25(2)(a) reaches secular activity associated with religion, not spiritual belief.
xa: **Explanation II:** "Hindus" includes **Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists**.
Indian secularism allows **positive intervention** for reform, e.g. **temple entry**.
**Church of God (2000):** loudspeakers subject to public order.

n8c22e8508c2.x: The explanation to Article 25 includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists within 'Hindus'; another explanation deems wearing kirpans part of the profession of Sikhism.
xa: ⚠ **Explanation I = kirpan (Sikh); Explanation II = "Hindus" includes Sikhs, Jains, Buddhists**.
**Profess** includes visible symbols like **turban, crucifix, kirpan**.
Hindu religious institutions are construed accordingly.

n87c606613fb.s: Where a religious practice involves a social evil, the State:
o: Can never intervene in religious matters
Must leave reform entirely to the religious denomination
May intervene to root it out, subject to constitutional limits
n87c606613fb.x: Freedom of religion is not absolute; the State can intervene to root out social evils while respecting constitutional restrictions.
xa: Indian model: **Sarva Dharma Sambhava** = state neutrality + **positive intervention** for reform.
Western model: **strict separation**; religion purely private.
**No forcible conversion** is another limit.

nd9c9fb5477a.s: The rights of religious denominations under Article 26 are subject to:
o: Security of the State and public order
nd9c9fb5477a.x: Article 26 lets a denomination set up institutions and own and administer property, all expressly subject to public order, morality and health.
xa: Holder: every **religious denomination** or section of it.
**Shirur Mutt (1954)** defined "religious denomination".
**Sabarimala (2018):** Ayyappa devotees **not a separate denomination**.

nf1f664f963a.s: Which of the following hinders religious pluralism?
o: Freedom to practise any religion or none
nf1f664f963a.x: Religious pluralism is the freedom and security to practise any religion or none, resting on freedom of religion and mutual respect; exclusivism hinders it.
xa: **S.R. Bhatt:** pluralism leads to secularism through the **unification of many religions**.
**Fundamentalism** rejects modern and plural readings.
**Bhakti-Sufi** interaction built communal harmony.

nindian-society-4-11.s: In Buddhism, the Tripitaka refers to:
nindian-society-4-11.x: The Tripitaka is the Buddhist sacred texts; the Sangha is the monastic order, the Dhamma the Buddha's teachings and Nirvana liberation.
n: Sangha is the Buddhist monastic order. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Tripitaka is the Buddhist sacred texts. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Dhamma is the teachings of Buddha. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Nirvana is liberation from birth and death. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
xa: A **Bodhisattva** is an **enlightened being**.
**Mahayana** = the **greater vehicle**; **Hinayana** (also **Theravada**) = an **older Buddhist school**.
⚠ Jain liberation is **Kaivalya**; Hindu liberation is **Moksha**.

nindian-society-4-13.x: Sallekhana is the Jain ritual fast unto death; Kaivalya is liberation, a Tirthankara a spiritual teacher and Ahimsa non-violence.
n: Kaivalya is liberation in Jainism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Tirthankara is a spiritual teacher in Jainism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Sallekhana is a Jain ritual fast unto death. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Ahimsa means non-violence. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
xa: Tirthankara means "**Ford-maker**": **24** teachers, **Rishabhanatha** first, **Mahavira** last.
⚠ Buddhist liberation = **Nirvana**; Hindu liberation = **Moksha**.
Buddhist monastic order = **Sangha**.

o: The law of action and consequence
nindian-society-4-27.x: Karma is the law of action and result; Dharma is duty, Samsara the cycle of rebirth and Moksha liberation.
n: Moksha is liberation in Hinduism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Dharma means duty or righteous conduct. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Karma is the law of action and consequence. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
Samsara is the cycle of rebirth. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 17-21]
xa: **Purusharthas**: **Dharma**, **Artha**, **Kama** and **Moksha**.
**Ashramas**: **Brahmacharya**, **Grihastha**, **Vanaprastha** and **Sannyasa**.
⚠ Jain liberation = **Kaivalya**; Buddhist = **Nirvana**.

nindian-society-4-34.s:
Which of the following are Ashramas?
1. Grihastha
2. Vanaprastha
3. Khalsa
nindian-society-4-34.x: Grihastha (householder) and Vanaprastha (forest-dweller) are Ashramas; the Khalsa is the Sikh brotherhood.
xa: The four Ashramas: **Brahmacharya**, **Grihastha**, **Vanaprastha**, **Sannyasa**.
The **Purusharthas** are **Dharma**, **Artha**, **Kama**, **Moksha**.
**Langar** = Sikh **community kitchen**.

n5cefa379290.s: The Essential Religious Practice test was formulated by the Supreme Court in:
n5cefa379290.x: The ERP test was formulated in 1954 to identify practices integral to a religion; the Constitution does not define 'essential'.
xa: Criticism: the ERP test makes **courts arbiters of religion** (e.g. **Sastri Yagnapurushadji, 1966**).
**Nine-judge Bench** under **CJI Surya Kant** heard ERP across faiths (**2026**).
Centre (SG **Tushar Mehta**): protection **not limited to ERP**.

nf49b0cbeaf3.s: The Essential Religious Practice doctrine is associated with the:
nf49b0cbeaf3.x: Shirur Mutt is associated with the ERP doctrine; Stanislaus concerned conversion, Bijoe Emmanuel the National Anthem and Shayara Bano instant triple talaq.
xa: **Ratilal (1954):** State cannot touch essential practices.
**Javed (2003):** **polygamy** not an ERP.
**Ramji Lal Modi** upheld **Sec. 295A IPC** (now **Sec. 299 BNS**).

n46f2a007d49.s: In the Sabarimala judgment (2018), the exclusion of women of a certain age group was held to be:
o: Protected because Ayyappa devotees are a separate denomination
n46f2a007d49.x: The 4:1 majority of the five-judge Bench held the exclusion was not an ERP and that Ayyappa devotees were not a separate denomination.
xa: An ERP claim **cannot restrict participation rights** of others; the **state cannot endorse a practice**.
⚠ **Sabarimala 2018 = 5-judge, 4:1; review reference = 9-judge Bench under CJI Surya Kant**.
Principle: "**Devotion cannot be subjected to gender discrimination**".

n559c6119a4d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State anti-conversion laws?
o: The Orissa Act, 1967 and the MP Act, 1968 arose from concern over missionary activity
Later amendments widened their scope to conversions to Islam
Stanislaus held that propagation does not include forcible conversion
In Stanislaus v. State of MP (1977), the Supreme Court struck down these laws
n559c6119a4d.x: Stanislaus upheld these laws, holding that the right to propagate does not include forcible conversion.
xa: Stanislaus held that **propagate** does not include a right to **convert**.
Debate: **anti-conversion laws vs freedom of conscience**.
Limits on Art. 25 include **no forcible conversion**.

neb916ace771.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Section 295A IPC (deliberate acts meant to outrage religious feelings)?
o: It was upheld on public-order grounds in Ramji Lal Modi v. State of UP
It was struck down in Rev. Stanislaus v. State of MP (1977)
It now corresponds to Section 299 of the BNS, 2023
Stanislaus dealt with propagation and anti-conversion laws
neb916ace771.x: Section 295A was upheld in Ramji Lal Modi; Stanislaus dealt with anti-conversion laws (upholding the Orissa and MP Acts), not Section 295A.
xa: **Stanislaus** upheld the **Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967** and **MP Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968**.
Punjab's **sacrilege Act** (assent **April 2026**) allows up to **life imprisonment**.
**Shirur Mutt (1954)** is the origin of the **ERP** test.

nfa65bf1e59f.s: Punjab's Jaagat Jot Sri Guru Granth Sahib Satkar (Amendment) Act provides punishment for sacrilege of up to:
nfa65bf1e59f.x: The Act, which got assent in April 2026, provides for punishment up to life imprisonment; it is challenged in the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
xa: Ground of challenge: it **protects only one faith** (**19-20 Aug 2026**).
It reopened the debate on **secularism vs faith protection**.
**Sec. 295A IPC** = now **Sec. 299 BNS** (upheld in **Ramji Lal Modi**).

n84aeb3f598a.s: The Arya Samaj's call 'Back to the Vedas', seeking to restore a golden past, is an example of:
n84aeb3f598a.x: Revivalism seeks to restore a golden past, as in 'Back to the Vedas'; fundamentalism is a return to literal scripture rejecting plural readings.
xa: Forms in India (since the **1970s**): **communalism**, separatism, fanaticism.
Threats: **hate speech** on social media + **illegal conversions**.
**Asghar Ali Engineer** wrote on communalism.

n72184b4675b.s: Which mutt is the hereditary Dharmakarta of the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD)?
n72184b4675b.x: The Sri Swamy Hathiramji Mutt at Tirupati is the hereditary Dharmakarta of the TTD; the AP Endowments Act, 1987 regulates Hindu temples and mutts.
xa: The AP Endowments Department administers **42,000+** temples (May **2026**).
AP HC/SC dealt with the Mutt's **interim management**.
**Art. 26** lets denominations **administer property in accordance with law**.

o: The official language of the Union
One of several equal official languages of the Union
The official language of every State
n6a85ccc125d.x: Article 343 makes Hindi the official language of the Union; India has no national language.
xa: The "no national language" point was noted in **Jul 2025**.
India has **no state religion**; secularism = **equal respect for all religions**.
**Art. 325**: no exclusion from electoral rolls on religion.

n63c1fb10175.s: Which one of the following most appropriately describes the constitutional meaning of secularism in India?
o: Complete exclusion of religion from public life
Preference to the religion followed by the majority
Establishment of one official religion by the State
Equal respect for all religions and absence of discrimination on religious grounds
n63c1fb10175.x: Indian secularism requires equal respect for all religions and prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion. It does not establish a state religion or demand complete exclusion of religion from public life.
n63c1fb10175.tq: Distinguish the Indian model of secularism from strict separation and majoritarian preference.
xs: Secularism means **equal respect for all religions** + **no discrimination on grounds of religion** — option **(4)** (APPSC 2019).
India has **no state religion** (UPPSC 2005) and does not exclude religion from public life.
xa: Indian model: **principled distance and equal respect**; Western: **strict separation**.
Components: freedom of religion, equality of all religions, state neutrality, **no religious tax**, **minority rights**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** secularism part of the **basic structure**.

nd5eebe23983.s: Indian secularism is best described as:
o: A state religion with tolerance of other faiths
A strict bar on all state aid to religious institutions
No state religion, with positive state intervention for reform
Complete non-interference by the State in religion
nd5eebe23983.x: India has no state religion and allows positive state intervention for social and religious reform; state aid to religious institutions is not necessarily barred.
xa: **Western (negative) secularism**: **no state aid** to religious institutions.
Indian model = **Sarva Dharma Sambhava**.
The State may aid **minority institutions**.

nc586dde692b.s: Unlike the Western model of strict separation, Indian secularism is based on:
o: A ban on state aid to religious institutions in all cases
Mutual exclusion of State and religion
nc586dde692b.x: The Western model rests on strict separation and mutual exclusion, while the Indian model adopts principled distance, equal respect and scope for reform.
xa: West: religion **purely private**; **no state aid**.
India: aid like **Amarnath Yatra, Haj** support.

ndd0a7491765.s: In 2022, the Karnataka High Court held that wearing the hijab is:
o: Identical to carrying a kirpan under Article 25
ndd0a7491765.x: The Karnataka High Court held in 2022 that hijab was not an Essential Religious Practice; the Allahabad High Court relied on this in August 2026.
xa: **Javed (2003):** **polygamy** is not an ERP.
The **Constitution does not define "essential"**.
ERP origin: **Shirur Mutt (1954)**.

nd43c73c599f.s: The Constituent Assembly, in 1949, rejected the proposal to include which word in the Preamble?
nd43c73c599f.x: The Constituent Assembly rejected the proposal to add the word “God” to the Preamble in 1949.
nd43c73c599f.tq: Test a specific rejected constitutional proposal rather than a word already present in the Preamble.
xs: The Constituent Assembly rejected adding **'God'** to the Preamble (**1949**) — option **(3)**.
This reflects India having **no state religion**.
xa: Roots of secularism: **Ashoka's Dhamma**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Karachi Resolution (1931)**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** secularism inherent **even before 1976**.
⚠ "Religious state" is **not** a feature of the Constitution.

n5e409395f9d.s:
Which of the following are regarded as roots of Indian secular thought?
1. Ashoka's Dhamma
2. Nehru Report, 1928
3. Karachi Resolution, 1931
n5e409395f9d.x: Ashoka's Dhamma, the Nehru Report (1928) and the Karachi Resolution (1931) are all identified as roots of Indian secular thought.
xa: The Constituent Assembly rejected **'God'** in the Preamble (**1949**).
**Mughal Akbar** promoted tolerance and dialogue.
**Bhakti (6th-18th c.)** rejected ritualism and caste.

n9857b09211a.s: Which Article prevents exclusion of a person from electoral rolls on grounds including religion?
n9857b09211a.x: Article 325 prevents exclusion from electoral rolls on grounds including religion; it does not authorise such exclusion.
xa: **Art. 25** — freedom of conscience; **26** — denominations; **27** — no tax for a religion.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed (**Art. 356**).
India has **no state religion**.

nae5280c31e6.s: Which case held secularism to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution?
nae5280c31e6.x: S.R. Bommai (1994) recognised secularism as basic structure, inherent even before the 42nd Amendment; Kesavananda Bharati set out the doctrine itself.
xa: Kesavananda counted secularism a **basic feature**.
The **Sabarimala case, 2026** reaffirmed secularism as **Basic Structure**.
Bommai: a State government acting against secularism can be dismissed (**Art. 356**).

n8b3184d9509.s:
Which of the following are identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India?
1. Communalism
2. Separatism
3. Fanaticism
n8b3184d9509.x: Communalism, separatism and fanaticism are all identified as forms of religious fundamentalism in India.
xa: Riots cited: **1984** anti-Sikh, **1992** Babri Masjid, **2002** Gujarat, **2023** Haryana.
Threats: **hate speech** on social media + **illegal conversions** eroding the "**Ganga-Jamuni tehzeeb**".
**Fundamentalism** = return to literal fundamentals of scripture.

nindian-society-47-6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about S.R. Bommai v. Union of India?
o: Governments acting against secularism can be dismissed under Article 356
It widened Section 123(3) of the RPA, 1951
It held secularism a basic feature of the Constitution
nindian-society-47-6.x: Section 123(3) of the RPA was widened by Abhiram Singh (2017), not Bommai; Bommai (1994) made secularism a basic feature enforceable via Article 356.
n: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India was decided in 1994. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 98-99]
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India established that secularism is a basic feature of the Constitution. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 98-99]
State governments acting against secularism can be dismissed under Article 356. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 98-99]
Abhiram Singh v. C.D. Commachen expanded Section 123(3) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 98-99]
xa: **Abhiram Singh**: appeals to **religion, race, caste, community or language** in campaigns are a **corrupt practice**.
Bommai: secularism was part of the **basic structure** **even before 1976**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** set out the **basic structure** doctrine.

n125a69e7596.s: Propagation under Article 25 does not include a right to convert another person, because that would affect the other person's:
n125a69e7596.x: Propagation means spreading one's beliefs; a right to convert another would impinge on that person's freedom of conscience.
xa: **Rev. Stanislaus v. State of MP (1977)** upheld the **Orissa and MP anti-conversion Acts**.
**Orissa Freedom of Religion Act, 1967**; **MP Dharma Swatantrya Adhiniyam, 1968**.
Limits on Art. 25 include **no forcible conversion**.

nbcbf2d5b3d0.s: The Supreme Court held in Javed (2003) that polygamy is:
o: Not an essential religious practice protected by Article 25
A practice protected only for religious denominations
An essential religious practice absolutely protected by Article 25
A secular activity regulated exclusively under Article 23
nbcbf2d5b3d0.x: In Javed (2003), polygamy was held not to be an essential religious practice protected by Article 25.
nbcbf2d5b3d0.tq: Use the case-law name to discriminate between an essential religious practice and a non-protected practice.
xs: **Javed (2003):** polygamy is **not an essential religious practice** protected by **Art. 25** — option **(1)**.
The **ERP test** decides which practices are integral to a religion.
xa: **Shayara Bano (2017)** invalidated **instant triple talaq**; **polygamy, nikah halala** left open.
The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).
**Karnataka HC 2022:** **hijab** not an ERP.

o: Any fee for the secular administration of religious institutions
Compelling payment of taxes whose proceeds promote a particular religion
Use of taxes to support all religions equally
nc2b7238e529.x: Article 27 bars taxes for promoting a particular religion; it does not bar fees, and taxes may support all religions equally.
xa: Indian secularism permits **aid** (e.g. **Amarnath Yatra, Haj** support).
Western secularism allows **no state aid** to religious institutions.

n34c56eaafd7.s: Who were the first women of the barred age group reported to have entered the Sabarimala temple in January 2019?
o: Kanaka Durga and Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar
n34c56eaafd7.x: Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga were reported as the first women of the barred age group to enter Sabarimala in January 2019.
n34c56eaafd7.tq: Recall the paired names associated with the immediate aftermath of a landmark judgment.
xs: **Bindu Ammini and Kanaka Durga** were the first women of the barred age group to enter (**Jan 2019**) — option **(4)** (PYQ G2 2025).
**Bijoe Emmanuel** is the National Anthem case; **Shayara Bano** the triple talaq case; **Lakshmindra Thirtha Swamiar** the Shirur Mutt case.
xa: The Sabarimala judgment came on **28 Sep 2018** (5-judge bench, **4:1**).
Women of **all ages** were allowed entry.
The review reference went to a **Nine-judge Bench** headed by **CJI Surya Kant** (**2026**).

n4260bdaec3c.s: The 2026 Sabarimala review reference on the Essential Religious Practice doctrine was heard by a nine-judge Bench headed by:
n4260bdaec3c.x: A nine-judge Bench headed by CJI Surya Kant heard the reference; the Centre argued the burden lies on the person challenging a practice.
xa: The Centre's argument was made on **14 May 2026**.
Criticism: the ERP test makes **courts arbiters of religion**; critics seek a **new test**.
The ERP test was formulated by the SC in **1954** (**Shirur Mutt**).

nf47bcd0c88e.s: In Zoroastrianism, Ahura Mazda refers to:
o: The highest grade of fire temple
nf47bcd0c88e.x: Ahura Mazda is the supreme god of good, while Angra Mainyu is the destructive or evil spirit.
xa: Guru Granth Sahib was compiled as the **Adi Granth** by **Guru Arjan**.
**Rishabhanatha** was the first Tirthankara, **Mahavira** the last.
Zoroastrianism is followed by the **Parsis**.

nca5a34eac34.s: Which thinker held that strong personal attachments and the fact of death are the main sources of religious belief?
nca5a34eac34.x: Malinowski traced religious belief mainly to strong personal attachments and to death; this was asked in APPSC Group 2, 2023. Tylor traced religion to animism, or belief in spirits. Durkheim saw religion as the collective worship of society, built on the sacred-profane divide. Frazer described a sequence of magic, then religion, then science.
nca5a34eac34.tq: Death and attachments = Malinowski; animism = Tylor; sacred-profane = Durkheim.
xs: **B. Malinowski**: **strong personal attachments** and **death** are the main sources of religious belief — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 2023).
**Tylor** — **animism**; **Durkheim** — **collective worship of society**, sacred vs profane; **Frazer** — **magic → religion → science**.
xa: ⚠ **Tylor = animism; Frazer = magic → religion → science; Malinowski = death**.
**Marx** — "**opium of the people**".
**Weber** — **The Religion of India** and the **Protestant Ethic**.

nb496d6e114c.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the six religious minorities notified for the purposes of the National Commission for Minorities?
o: Linguistic minorities as a general category
nb496d6e114c.x: The six notified religious minorities are Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains. “Linguistic minorities” is not one of the six notified religious categories.
nb496d6e114c.tq: Find the category that does not belong to the notified religious-minority list.
xs: "**Linguistic minorities as a general category**" is NOT one of the six — option **(3)**.
The **six notified minorities** are **Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis, Jains** (Apr **2026**).
xa: Linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise**.
The NCM's definition is **mainly religious**.
Notified under the **NCM Act, 1992**.

n0f1f7700a54.s: The constitutional provision relating to instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups is:
n0f1f7700a54.x: Article 350A deals with facilities for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for children belonging to linguistic minority groups.
n0f1f7700a54.tq: Discriminate between the closely numbered Articles 350, 350A and 350B by their functions.
xs: **Article 350A** — **mother-tongue instruction** at the **primary stage** for **linguistic minority** children — option **(2)**.
**Art. 350B** is another Article using "minority", but the mother-tongue clause is 350A.
xa: ⚠ **Trap:** **IYB 2026** (p.**290**) prints it as "**Article 360A**" — a misprint.
"Minority" is used in **Arts 29, 30, 350A, 350B** but **not defined**.
Kerala's **Malayalam Bhasha Bill** was contested for harming the **Kannada linguistic minority** in **Kasaragod**.

nafd9d71cb0c.s: Article 30(1A), inserted by the 44th Amendment, deals primarily with—
o: Exemption of minority institutions from all State regulation
Compulsory acquisition of property of minority educational institutions
Appointment of teachers in minority institutions
Reservation of seats in minority institutions
nafd9d71cb0c.x: Article 30(1A) concerns compulsory acquisition of the property of a minority educational institution. The amount fixed must not restrict or abrogate the right guaranteed by Article 30.
nafd9d71cb0c.tq: Link the sub-clause number with its specific subject instead of the general right under Article 30(1).
xs: **Art. 30(1A)** (**44th Amendment, 1978**) deals with **compulsory acquisition** of a **minority institution's property** — option **(2)**.
The amount fixed must **not restrict or abrogate** the Art. 30 right.
It does not exempt minority institutions from all regulation: the State may **regulate standards**.
xa: **30(1):** all minorities, **religious or linguistic**, may establish and administer institutions of their choice.
30(1) is called the **"Charter of Education Rights"**; **madrasas** run under it.
The same **44th Amendment** deleted the FR to property.

n3fd824ff514.s: Article 30(1) gives the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice to:
n3fd824ff514.x: Article 30(1) covers all minorities, religious or linguistic; the State may regulate standards but may not take away their minority character.
xa: **30(1A)** (**44th Amendment, 1978**): compensation must **not restrict or abrogate** the right.
**Pramati (2014):** RTE **25% quota** not for minority schools.

ndc840ad3293.s: What is the unit for determining a linguistic minority in India?
ndc840ad3293.x: The State is the unit for determining a linguistic minority; numerical inferiority and non-dominant status are relevant, and the Constitution does not define the term.
xa: Linguistic minorities are determined **State-wise**; religious minorities via the **NCM**, **Ministry of Minority Affairs**.
**Art. 350A:** **mother-tongue instruction** at the **primary stage** for linguistic minority children.
"Minority" appears in **Arts 29, 30, 350A, 350B** but is **not defined**.

ncd3fdd42d87.s: The term 'minority' in the Constitution of India is:
ncd3fdd42d87.x: The Constitution uses 'minority' in Articles 29, 30, 350A and 350B without defining it; the NCM Act, 1992 also does not define it.
xa: Test: **numerical inferiority**, non-dominant status, distinct identity; unit = **State** (**T.M.A. Pai**).
Types: **religious** (NCM) vs **linguistic** (State-wise).
The NCM's definition is **mainly religious**.

nb0e33c131f3.s: The 25 per cent quota under the Right to Education Act does not apply to minority schools in view of the decision in—
o: St. Stephen's College v. University of Delhi
T.M.A. Pai Foundation v. State of Karnataka
Pramati Educational and Cultural Trust v. Union of India
P.A. Inamdar v. State of Maharashtra
nb0e33c131f3.x: In Pramati, decided in 2014, the Supreme Court held that the RTE Act's 25 per cent quota does not apply to minority schools.
nb0e33c131f3.tq: Distinguish the case concerning RTE exemption from cases concerning autonomy, preference or reservation.
xs: The RTE Act's **25% quota** does not apply to minority schools — **Pramati, 2014** — option **(3)**.
**T.M.A. Pai** made the **State** the unit for deciding a minority.
xa: Critics: only **8.76%** disadvantaged enrolments in minority schools (**NCPCR, Sep 2025**).
Criticism: **misuse of minority status** to escape RTE obligations.
**Art. 30(1)** — the "**Charter of Education Rights**".

n3c199ac48fe.s: Which Amendment provided that land under personal cultivation could be acquired only on paying market value?
n3c199ac48fe.x: The 17th Amendment required market value for land under personal cultivation; Article 31 itself was deleted by the 44th Amendment, 1978.
xa: The 1st Amendment shielded **land reform laws**.
After 1978, property is in **Art. 300A**, **Part XII, Chapter IV**.
⚠ A-R pairs: "legal right under **300A** in **Part XII**" + "**44th Amendment, 1978**".

n34ca0b2d27c.s: The 44th Amendment, 1978 placed the Right to Property under:
n34ca0b2d27c.x: The 44th Amendment deleted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III and made property a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.
xa: Art. 300A sits in **Part XII, Chapter IV**.
The 44th also inserted **Art. 30(1A)** on minority institutions' property.
FR count: **six** now, **seven** originally.

o: No citizen shall be deprived of property except by executive order
No company shall be deprived of property under any circumstances
No person shall be deprived of property except with the consent of Parliament
No person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law
n865221399b7.x: Article 300A states that no person shall be deprived of his property save by authority of law.
n865221399b7.tq: Recall the exact constitutional wording and avoid replacing 'authority of law' with executive action.
xs: **Art. 300A:** "No person shall be deprived of his property save by **authority of law**" — option **(4)**.
It covers **all persons**, not only citizens, and requires **law**, not an executive order or Parliament's consent.
xa: Protects against **executive action**, not legislation.
Enforced via **Art. 226**/ordinary suit, **not Art. 32**.
⚠ **PYQ G1 2019** key said "Article 300"; the correct provision is **Art. 300A**.

n60cf77aab94.s: In GGR Housing v. State, the Andhra Pradesh High Court emphasised:
o: Strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A
The abolition of Article 300A as a legal right
The conversion of the right to property into a Fundamental Right
The exclusion of land acquisition from judicial review
n60cf77aab94.x: The Andhra Pradesh High Court insisted on strict statutory due process in land acquisition under Article 300A. Article 300A protects the right to property as a legal constitutional right.
n60cf77aab94.tq: Apply the case principle to the constitutional protection governing deprivation of property.
xs: **AP HC (GGR Housing v. State)** insisted on **strict statutory due process in land acquisition** under **Art. 300A** — option **(1)** (May **2026**).
Art. 300A: no deprivation of property **save by authority of law**.
xa: Art. 300A is a **legal (constitutional) right**, not an FR, after the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
It protects against **executive action**; enforced via **Art. 226**.
**LARR Act, 2013:** **SIA** mandatory; consent **70%** (PPP) / **80%** (private).

n53a1ba4e8bf.s: The Right to Property today is:
o: A constitutional legal right under Article 300A, available to all persons
A Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32
A statutory right under the RPA, 1951, available only to citizens
A constitutional legal right available only to citizens
n53a1ba4e8bf.x: Property is a constitutional legal right under Article 300A, available to citizens, non-citizens and companies, but not a Fundamental Right enforceable under Article 32.
xa: It protects against **executive action**, not legislation.
⚠ **Property = Art. 300A legal right; Vote = Art. 326 constitutional right; neither is an FR**.
AP angle: **GGR Housing v. State** — strict due process under Art. 300A.

ne1a98137a24.s: The Right to Work under Article 41 is a:
ne1a98137a24.x: Article 41 is a Directive Principle, not a Fundamental Right; the right to information, by contrast, is read into Article 19(1)(a).
xa: Rule: every **FR is a constitutional right**, but not every constitutional right is an FR.
**Art. 51A(k)** — parents' duty on education.
**Vote**: **Art. 326** — constitutional, not FR.

nd298a81be4d.s: The right to vote in India is classified as:
o: A Fundamental Right under Part III
A statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act
A Directive Principle of State Policy
A natural right beyond statutory regulation
nd298a81be4d.x: The right to vote is a statutory right under Section 62 of the Representation of the People Act, not a Fundamental Right.
nd298a81be4d.tq: Distinguish statutory rights from Fundamental Rights by identifying the governing provision.
xs: Voting is a **statutory right** under **Section 62 of the RPA 1951** — option **(2)**; it is **not an FR**.
It is also constitutional via **Art. 326** (adult suffrage, **18+**), but not in Part III.
xa: Registration: **Sec. 19, RPA 1950**.
**Voting paradox**: right to know candidates, **NOTA**, **ballot secrecy** recognised under **19(1)(a)**.
The Opposition sought **FR status** for the right to vote (**7 Jul 2026**).

nd11dc8078b7.s:
Although voting is a statutory right, which of the following have been recognised under Article 19(1)(a)?
1. Right to know the details of candidates
2. NOTA option
3. Secrecy of the ballot
nd11dc8078b7.x: Candidate details, NOTA and ballot secrecy have all been recognised under Article 19(1)(a), though voting itself is statutory (the 'voting paradox').
xa: The Opposition sought **FR status** for the right to vote (**7 Jul 2026**).
Voting: **Art. 326** (adult suffrage, **18+**); **Sec. 62, RPA 1951**.

n13dccfca009.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 32?
o: Clause (1) makes the right to move the Supreme Court for Part III rights itself a Fundamental Right
Under clause (2), the Supreme Court may issue directions, orders or writs
Under clause (4), the right may be suspended by an ordinary law of Parliament
Clause (4) says the right shall not be suspended except as the Constitution provides
n13dccfca009.x: Article 32(4) says the right cannot be suspended except as the Constitution provides, not by an ordinary law.
xa: Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.

n46cbbef365b.s: Which provision lets Parliament empower any other court to exercise the Supreme Court's powers under Article 32?
n46cbbef365b.x: Article 32(3) permits Parliament to empower other courts, though no such law has been made; High Courts issue writs under Article 226.
xa: Before **1950**, only the **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** HCs could issue writs.
HC writ power is **wider in scope**; SC's is **wider in territory**.
IYB counts **25 High Courts** (sanctioned strength **1,122**).

n9c98df14398.s: Which of the following is correct about Article 32?
o: It is a statutory remedy that Parliament may withdraw
It can be repealed by amendment as it is merely procedural
It is part of the basic structure and cannot be abridged by amendment
It applies only to rights created by ordinary law
n9c98df14398.x: Article 32 is part of the basic structure, so its essential guarantee cannot be abridged even by a constitutional amendment.
xa: Rationale: **a right without a remedy is worthless**.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** made **Art. 226** HC writ power basic structure too.
Dr. **Ambedkar** called Art. 32 "the **very soul**... and the **very heart**" of the Constitution.

n7f5ab8cdff3.s: The jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is best described as
n7f5ab8cdff3.x: Article 32 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights, but this jurisdiction is not exclusive because High Courts also exercise writ jurisdiction under Article 226.
n7f5ab8cdff3.tq: Split the paired descriptions—original and exclusive—instead of assuming that direct jurisdiction is exclusive.
xs: Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive** — option **(3)**.
It is **concurrent** with the HCs for FRs; the aggrieved person may choose either.
xa: HCs issue writs under **Art. 226**, which is **wider** — FRs and "**any other purpose**".
**Res judicata:** an HC dismissal **on merits** bars a fresh Art. 32 petition on the same plea.
The **Judiciary** is the **guardian of Fundamental Rights** (APPSC 2021).

n455cf140447.s: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described which constitutional provision as the ‘heart and soul’ of the Constitution?
n455cf140447.x: Dr. Ambedkar described Article 32 as the heart and soul of the Constitution because it provides the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
n455cf140447.tq: Associate the famous description with the exact Article, not merely with Part III generally.
xs: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called **Article 32** "the **very soul** of the Constitution and the **very heart** of it" — option **(2)**.
⚠ **Trap:** the **PYQ G2 2025** key gave **Art. 14**; the correct answer is **Art. 32**.
xa: **32(1)** — the right to move the SC — is itself a **Fundamental Right** (APPSC GS 2025).
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
**PIL** was developed by Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.

n5e1d4fc8a41.s: The writ of Habeas Corpus may be directed against:
o: Both public authorities and private individuals
n5e1d4fc8a41.x: Habeas Corpus lies against public authorities and private individuals for unlawful detention; it does not require release where detention is lawful.
xa: Habeas corpus = "**to have the body of**" — produce a detained person before court.
It is the "**bulwark of individual liberty**" against arbitrary detention.
Also not for **contempt of court/legislature** or detention **outside jurisdiction**.

nd9e03c7e3d5.s: The writ of Quo Warranto lies against the holder of:
o: A substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution
Any office in a private trust
nd9e03c7e3d5.x: Quo Warranto tests a claim to a substantive public office created by statute or the Constitution and may be sought by any interested person.
xa: Quo warranto = "**by what authority**".
It tests the **legality of a claim** to a **public office**.
**PYQ G2 2025** matched the literal meanings of writs.

n76f97380580.s: Before 1950, writ jurisdiction was exercised by the High Courts of:
n76f97380580.x: Before 1950 only the Calcutta, Bombay and Madras High Courts had writ jurisdiction; Article 226 now empowers all High Courts.
xa: HCs can issue writs beyond their territory if the **cause of action** arises within (**15th Amendment, 1963**).
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997):** Art. 226 is **basic structure**.
Art. 226 is **not suspendable as such**.

n2b188cdfea6.s: How many writs are specifically recognised for enforcement of Fundamental Rights under Article 32(2)?
n2b188cdfea6.x: Article 32(2) refers to five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto.
n2b188cdfea6.tq: Count the constitutionally named writs rather than adding other judicial remedies.
xs: **Five** writs — option **(4)**.
**Habeas corpus**, **mandamus**, **prohibition**, **certiorari**, **quo warranto**.
xa: Both the **SC** (Art. 32) and **HCs** (Art. 226) issue all **five**.
Writs come from **English** prerogative writs.
**Habeas corpus** is the only writ against **private persons**.

n24d89f46f32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the writ of mandamus?
o: It is not issued to enforce a discretionary duty
It is not issued to enforce a non-statutory departmental instruction
It is not issued to enforce a legislative function
As a general rule, it may be issued against a private individual or body
n24d89f46f32.x: Mandamus is not ordinarily issued against private bodies, nor for discretionary functions, legislative functions or non-statutory instructions.
xa: Also not for a **contractual obligation**.
Not against the **President, Governors** or a **HC Chief Justice** acting judicially.
Lies against **public officials**, **public corporations**, **inferior courts**, **tribunals**.

n13e49f797e4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about prohibition and certiorari?
o: Prohibition is issued while proceedings are pending
Certiorari can never be used in relation to a pending proceeding
Prohibition directs the lower body to stop the proceedings
Certiorari is generally issued after an order has been passed
n13e49f797e4.x: Certiorari is generally post-decision, but it may also be used to transfer a pending case.
xa: Prohibition directs **inactivity**; certiorari is **curative** after the order.
Both traditionally lie against **judicial/quasi-judicial** bodies.
Certiorari reaches certain **administrative** bodies since **1991**.

n8576d4137da.s: A High Court may issue a writ beyond its territorial limits under Article 226 when—
o: the cause of action, wholly or in part, arises within its territory
the Union Government transfers the proceeding to it
the Supreme Court authorises it in every individual case
the respondent is located anywhere in India, irrespective of cause of action
n8576d4137da.x: A High Court ordinarily exercises Article 226 jurisdiction within its territory, but may do so beyond that territory where the cause of action wholly or partly arises within its territorial jurisdiction. This position followed the Fifteenth Amendment of 1963.
n8576d4137da.tq: Apply the territorial-jurisdiction rule by focusing on the cause of action.
xs: An HC may issue writs beyond its territory if the **cause of action** arises within it — option **(1)**.
This came with the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
xa: The SC's Art. 32 power covers the **whole of India**.
HC writ power is **wider in scope**; SC's **wider in territory**.
Both issue all **five** writs.

n248aef544a0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 32 and Article 226?
o: The Supreme Court can issue five writs, whereas High Courts can issue only three
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right
A High Court under Article 226 can issue writs for 'any other purpose' too
The right under Article 32 can be suspended under Article 359
n248aef544a0.x: Both the Supreme Court and the High Courts can issue all five writs.
xa: Territory: SC — **whole of India**; HC — own territory (beyond it if cause of action arises within).
Extra-territorial reach came with the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Jurisdiction is **concurrent** for FRs.

n7c707296146.s: Public Interest Litigation primarily relaxes which traditional rule?
o: The rule that courts cannot issue writs against public authorities
The rule that Fundamental Rights are enforceable only by Parliament
The rule that judicial review is unavailable against administrative action
The rule that only the directly aggrieved person may approach the court
n7c707296146.x: PIL relaxes the traditional rule of locus standi by permitting a public-spirited person to approach the court on behalf of persons unable to do so themselves or for a larger public interest.
n7c707296146.tq: Identify the procedural rule changed by PIL rather than confusing it with a substantive right.
xs: **PIL** relaxes the rule that **only the aggrieved may sue** (**locus standi**) — option **(4)**.
**Any public-spirited person** can move the court for larger public interest or for those unable to.
xa: Pioneered by Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
Key case: **S.P. Gupta, 1981**.
PIL is **not itself a Fundamental Right**.

n3e48640b03f.s: Which 1981 case is associated with the development of Public Interest Litigation?
n3e48640b03f.x: S.P. Gupta (1981) is a key PIL case; Justices P.N. Bhagwati and V.R. Krishna Iyer are associated with PIL.
xa: **Epistolary jurisdiction:** letters/postcards treated as writ petitions.
**Sunil Batra** — a prisoner's letter.
Quo warranto also may be sought by **any interested person**.

ne358fd493b4.s: Under epistolary jurisdiction, a prisoner's letter was treated as a writ petition in:
ne358fd493b4.x: Epistolary jurisdiction treats letters or postcards as writ petitions; Sunil Batra, where a prisoner's letter was acted upon, is the example.
xa: PIL pioneers: **P.N. Bhagwati**, **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
**S.P. Gupta, 1981** — PIL.
PIL is **not itself a Fundamental Right**.

n176f347c449.s: Compared with the Supreme Court under Article 32, the writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 is wider in:
n176f347c449.x: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose', so their subject-matter scope is wider, while the Supreme Court's is wider territorially.
xa: Both issue **five** writs.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.
Jurisdiction is **concurrent** for FRs.

n52567b351e2.s: 'A right without a remedy is a worthless declaration' best explains the significance of:
n52567b351e2.x: Article 32 gives a direct constitutional remedy for enforcing Fundamental Rights, making Part III effective rather than merely declaratory.
xa: Ambedkar: "the **very soul**... and the **very heart**" of the Constitution.
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.

na29696a1ca8.s: The Supreme Court has examined an SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings under Articles 32 and 226 in matters involving:
na29696a1ca8.x: The proposed SOP for 24x7 urgent hearings concerns threats to life and liberty, strengthening access to remedies under Articles 32 and 226.
xa: **Habeas corpus** is the bulwark of liberty against arbitrary detention.
SC agreed (**20 Jan 2026**) to examine whether the **ED can invoke writ jurisdiction**.
ED-West Bengal: **Art. 32** petition vs **Art. 131** suit.

nindian-polity-42-2.s: Why did Dr. B.R. Ambedkar describe Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution”?
o: It empowers the President to issue constitutional writs
It guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies
It gives Parliament power to amend Fundamental Rights
It establishes the jurisdiction of High Courts over statutory rights
nindian-polity-42-2.x: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution because it makes the right to a remedy itself a Fundamental Right, giving direct access to the Supreme Court.
nindian-polity-42-2.tq: Link the description to the guaranteed remedy.
n: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar designated Article 32 as the “heart and soul of the Constitution.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Article 32 guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xs: Article 32 **guarantees a direct and effective Fundamental Right to constitutional remedies** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 32(1)**: the right to move the **Supreme Court directly** to enforce Part III rights is itself a **Fundamental Right**.
Writs are issued by the **SC and HCs**, not the **President**; amending FRs and HC statutory jurisdiction (**Art. 226**) are not Art. 32's role.
xa: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**: Art. 32 is "the **very soul** of the Constitution and the **very heart** of it".
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.
⚠ PYQ G2 **2025** key gave **Art. 14**; the correct answer is **Art. 32**.
Rationale: a right without a **remedy** is worthless.

nindian-polity-15-6.s: High Courts have wider writ jurisdiction than the Supreme Court because, under Article 226, they can issue writs for:
o: Legal rights only, not Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights only, but against private bodies
nindian-polity-15-6.x: Article 226 covers Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', while the Supreme Court under Article 32 acts only for Fundamental Rights.
n: The Supreme Court can be approached under Article 32 only for Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The High Courts can be approached under Article 226 for Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The High Courts can be approached under Article 226 for other purposes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The power of the High Courts under Article 226 is wider than the power of the Supreme Court under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xa: HC power is wider in **scope**; SC power is wider in **territory** (whole of India).
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**; both courts issue **five** writs.
SC jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive** — **concurrent** with HCs for FRs.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: Art. 226 HC writ power is **Basic Structure**.

nindian-polity-42-33.s: The writ remedies exercised by the Supreme Court and High Courts originated as prerogative remedies under:
nindian-polity-42-33.x: The writs come from the prerogative remedies of English common law and are exercised under Articles 32 and 226.
n: Prerogative remedies were borrowed from English common law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
The Supreme Court issues writs under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
High Courts issue writs under Article 226. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xa: Before **1950**, only the **Calcutta, Bombay and Madras** HCs could issue writs.
There are **five** writs: **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto**.

nfbe76654c49.s: Since 1991, the writ of Certiorari may also lie against
o: Certain administrative bodies when their actions affect rights
The President and Governor for their official acts
nfbe76654c49.x: The scope of Certiorari has been extended to certain administrative bodies whose decisions affect rights. It does not ordinarily lie against private persons or legislative bodies.
nfbe76654c49.tq: Use the date-linked expansion of jurisdiction to identify the precise category added.
xs: Since **1991**, certiorari also lies against **certain administrative bodies** affecting rights — option **(1)**.
It does not lie against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**.
