**Art. 361** shields the **President and Governors** from courts for official acts.
xa: Certiorari = "**to be certified**" / to be informed.
It **quashes an order** already passed or transfers a case.
Prohibition still lies only against **judicial and quasi-judicial** bodies.

n2a0d1a54fd9.s: Which writ is traditionally regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty?
n2a0d1a54fd9.x: Habeas Corpus is regarded as the bulwark of individual liberty because it provides a prompt judicial remedy against unlawful detention.
n2a0d1a54fd9.tq: Associate the liberty-protection function with the writ directed against unlawful detention.
xs: **Habeas corpus** is the "**bulwark of individual liberty** against arbitrary detention" — option **(3)**.
It means "**to have the body of**" — the detained person is produced before court and released if detention is illegal.
xa: It is the **only writ against private persons**.
Producing a person before court = habeas corpus (**APPSC 2021**).
Not for **lawful detention**.

nb2752ccd77d.s: Which writ directs a lower judicial body to stop continuing proceedings in excess of its jurisdiction?
nb2752ccd77d.x: Prohibition prevents continuation of proceedings, while certiorari quashes an order; both check jurisdictional excess by judicial or quasi-judicial bodies.
xa: Prohibition is **preventive only**; certiorari **preventive and curative**.
Certiorari can also **transfer a pending case**.
Since **1991** certiorari reaches certain **administrative** bodies.

nindian-polity-42-4.s: Which writ is primarily used to compel performance of a mandatory public or legal duty that has been refused or neglected?
nindian-polity-42-4.x: Mandamus ('we command') orders a public authority to perform a duty it has refused or neglected. Prohibition stops a court, Quo Warranto questions a title to office, Habeas Corpus frees a detainee.
n: Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus applies when a mandatory public or legal duty has been refused or neglected. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xs: The writ is **Mandamus** — option **(4)**.
**Mandamus** ("**we command**") compels performance of a **mandatory public or legal duty** refused or neglected.
**Quo-Warranto** tests title to a **public office**; **Habeas Corpus** frees from **illegal detention**; **Prohibition** stops a lower court **exceeding jurisdiction**.
xa: Mandamus does not lie against **private individuals/bodies**, the **President** or **Governors**.
It can lie against a **government company** or **statutory corporation** performing a public function.
Mandamus is **not issued to the Government to make a law**.

nindian-polity-42-7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Habeas Corpus?
o: It lies against public authorities and private individuals
It applies whenever detention is illegal
It cannot lie against private individuals
nindian-polity-42-7.x: Habeas Corpus lies against both public authorities and private individuals who detain a person illegally; it is the only writ available against private persons.
n: Habeas Corpus targets public authorities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus targets private individuals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus safeguards individual liberty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Habeas Corpus applies whenever detention is illegal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xa: It is the **only** writ directly against **private individuals** in cases of illegal confinement.
Literal meaning: "**to have the body**".
It is the "**bulwark of individual liberty** against arbitrary detention".
It does not lie against **lawful detention**.

nindian-polity-42-21.s: Which writ is directed against judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies to quash an illegal order suffering from lack or excess of jurisdiction or an error of law apparent on the face of the record?
nindian-polity-42-21.x: Certiorari quashes an order already passed by a judicial, quasi-judicial or administrative body for lack or excess of jurisdiction or error of law on the record. Prohibition acts earlier, while proceedings are pending.
n: Certiorari targets judicial bodies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari targets quasi-judicial bodies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari targets administrative bodies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari quashes an illegal order already passed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari applies when an order was passed due to lack of jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari applies when an order was passed due to excess of jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari applies when an order contains an error of law on the face of the record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari is issued after an order or decision is made. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari is issued to correct or quash an order. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari removes or quashes decisions suffering from jurisdictional error. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xs: The writ is **Certiorari** — option **(1)**.
**Certiorari** ("**to be certified**") **quashes** an order **already passed** for **lack or excess of jurisdiction** or **error of law** on the record.
It lies against **judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative** bodies.
**Prohibition** acts while proceedings are **pending**; **Habeas Corpus** ends **illegal detention**; **Mandamus** compels a **public duty**.
xa: Certiorari can also **transfer** a case from a lower court.
It is **curative and preventive**; Prohibition is **preventive** only.
It does not lie against **legislative bodies** or **private persons**.

nindian-polity-38-70.s: Which writ quashes an order already passed by an inferior court?
nindian-polity-38-70.x: Certiorari quashes an order already passed; prohibition prevents an order from being made.
n: Habeas Corpus means “To have the body.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Habeas Corpus quashes illegal or unlawful physical detention. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mandamus means “We Command.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mandamus directs a public official to perform a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mandamus directs an inferior court to perform a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mandamus directs a statutory authority to perform a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prohibition means “To Forbid.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A higher court issues Prohibition to prevent an inferior court from exceeding its jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A higher court issues Prohibition to prevent a tribunal from exceeding its jurisdiction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Prohibition is preventive. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Certiorari means “To be Certified.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A higher court issues Certiorari to quash an order already passed by an inferior court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Quo-Warranto means “By what warrant/authority.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Quo-Warranto inquires into the legality of a person's claim to a public office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Quo-Warranto prevents illegal usurpation of public office. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: Prohibition is **preventive**; Certiorari is **curative and preventive**.
Mandamus means "**we command**"; Quo-Warranto means "**by what authority?**".
Habeas Corpus is the only writ directly against **private individuals**.

nindian-polity-69-9.s: Which of the following writs is included in the Supreme Court's writ jurisdiction under Article 32?
nindian-polity-69-9.x: Under Article 32, the Court can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto. Review, advisory opinions and special leave are other kinds of jurisdiction.
nindian-polity-69-9.tq: Discriminate the five writs from other kinds of jurisdiction.
n: The Supreme Court has writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can issue the writ of Habeas Corpus under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: **Habeas Corpus** is among the writs under **Article 32** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 32(2)**: the SC may issue **five** writs — **Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo-Warranto**.
**Review**, **advisory opinion** and **Special Leave Petition** are not among these five writs.
xa: Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right** and part of the **basic structure**.
SC jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive**; HCs issue writs under **Art. 226**.
Writs come from **English common law** prerogative writs.

n1bb1ba431e8.s: Which of the following is correct about the writ of mandamus?
o: It can compel the Government to formulate a policy
It lies only against private individuals
It can direct the Government to enact a law it finds inadequate
It cannot compel law-making, but can enforce a policy once laid down
n1bb1ba431e8.x: Mandamus cannot compel the Government to make a law or policy, but the enforceable terms of a policy once laid down may be implemented through it.
xa: PYQ A-R **G2 2025**: both true, **R explains A**.
Mandamus = "**we command**" — perform a **public legal duty**.
Not against the **President or Governors**.

nindian-polity-42-8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Mandamus?
o: It compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty
It lies against the President and Governors
It may lie against a government company performing a public function
nindian-polity-42-8.x: Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors (or private bodies without public duties), though it can lie against government companies performing public functions.
n: Mandamus literally means “We command.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus compels performance of a mandatory public or legal duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus can lie against a government company performing a public function. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xa: It does **not** lie against purely **private bodies** unless they discharge a **public duty**.
Mandamus **cannot lie in the absence of a policy**; once laid down, a policy's terms can be enforced.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes say mandamus never lies against a **private individual/body**.

nindian-polity-42-26.s: Mandamus can lie against which of the following when it is performing a public function?
o: A purely private body discharging no public duty
A Governor acting in the discharge of office
A government company or statutory corporation
nindian-polity-42-26.x: Mandamus lies against a government company or statutory corporation performing a public function. It does not lie against the President, Governors or purely private bodies.
nindian-polity-42-26.tq: Look for the body that has a public duty.
n: Mandamus does not lie against purely private bodies unless they are discharging a public duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus does not lie against the President or Governors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus can lie against a government company performing a public function. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Mandamus can lie against a statutory corporation performing a public function. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xs: Mandamus can lie against **a government company or statutory corporation** performing a public function — option **(4)**.
It does **not** lie against purely **private bodies** discharging no **public duty**.
It does **not** lie against the **President** or **Governors** (**Art. 361**).
xa: Mandamus means "**we command**" — compels a **mandatory public or legal duty**.
It is **not issued to the Government to make a law**.
It does not lie against a **non-statutory departmental instruction**.

nindian-polity-42-37.s: Prohibition is called a ____ writ because it operates while the lower proceeding is still pending.
nindian-polity-42-37.x: Prohibition is preventive as it acts while the case is pending, while certiorari is curative as it acts after an order is made.
n: Certiorari is issued after an order or decision is made. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari provides postmortem review. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Prohibition operates while a judicial or quasi-judicial proceeding is pending. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
Certiorari operates after an order has been passed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 111-114]
xa: Certiorari is both **preventive and curative** — it can also transfer a pending case.
Both traditionally lie only against **judicial/quasi-judicial** bodies and check **excess of jurisdiction**.
Certiorari means "**to be certified**"; Prohibition means "**to forbid**".

n1c4ff63febe.s: Article 32A, which barred challenges to State laws under Article 32, was inserted by the:
n1c4ff63febe.x: The 42nd Amendment inserted Article 32A; the 43rd Amendment omitted Articles 32A, 131A, 144A, 226A and 228A.
xa: The **44th** also restored Art. 226.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997):** Art. 226 HC writ power is **basic structure**.
Art. 32 is also **basic structure**.

n346aea7fcda.s: The writ jurisdiction of High Courts under Article 226 was held to be part of the basic structure of the Constitution in—
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala, 1973
S.P. Gupta v. Union of India, 1981
L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India, 1997
n346aea7fcda.x: In L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997), the Supreme Court held that the power of judicial review under Articles 226 and 227 forms part of the basic structure.
n346aea7fcda.tq: Match the landmark case with the constitutional principle it established.
xs: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** held **Art. 226** HC writ power part of the **basic structure** — option **(4)**.
**Sunil Batra** — **epistolary jurisdiction**; **S.P. Gupta (1981)** — **PIL**.
xa: The **42nd Amendment** had curbed Art. 226; the **43rd** and **44th** restored it.
Art. 32 is also part of the **basic structure**.
HCs share the role of **guardian of FRs** under Art. 226.

nfe13b576376.s: In January 2026, the Supreme Court agreed to examine which question in appeals by Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling?
o: Whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction
Whether High Courts can issue writs of quo warranto against Ministers
Whether Article 32 can be suspended during a financial emergency
Whether Parliament can empower district courts to issue writs under Article 32(3)
nfe13b576376.x: On 20 January 2026, a Bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and S.C. Sharma agreed to examine whether the Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction. The appeals came from Kerala and Tamil Nadu against a Kerala High Court ruling. The other three options are not what was referred.
nfe13b576376.tq: ED itself filing a writ petition = Jan 2026 SC reference.
xs: The SC agreed to examine whether the **Enforcement Directorate can invoke writ jurisdiction** — option **(1)** (**20 Jan 2026**).
Bench: Justices **Dipankar Datta** and **S.C. Sharma**; appeals by **Kerala and Tamil Nadu** against a **Kerala HC** ruling.
xa: **32(3):** Parliament may empower other courts, but **no such law** has been made.
Art. 32 can be suspended under **Art. 359**.
ED-West Bengal matter: **Art. 32** vs **Art. 131**.

na18ffb1eae7.s: If a High Court dismisses a writ petition on merits, an Article 32 petition on the same plea is:
o: Maintainable, as Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right
Automatically converted into an Article 226 petition
Barred by res judicata; the remedy lies in appeal
Maintainable, as res judicata applies only to civil suits
na18ffb1eae7.x: After a dismissal on merits, the same plea ordinarily cannot be raised under Article 32; the remedy is an appeal. If the dismissal was not on merits, Article 32 may be invoked.
xa: Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive** — concurrent with HCs.
Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**; Art. 226 is a **discretionary** remedy.
Art. 226 is **wider** — FRs and "**any other purpose**".

n89febac1757.s: Which institution is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, with the Supreme Court acting as their protector and guarantor?
n89febac1757.x: The Judiciary is regarded as the guardian of Fundamental Rights, and the Supreme Court has the constitutional role of protecting and guaranteeing those rights.
n89febac1757.tq: Identify the constitutional institution associated with protection and enforcement of rights.
xs: The **Judiciary** is the **guardian of Fundamental Rights**, with the SC as "**protector and guarantor**" — option **(3)** (APPSC 2021).
**HCs share the role** under **Art. 226**.
xa: Art. 32 is itself a **Fundamental Right**.
Art. 32 jurisdiction is **original but not exclusive**.
Art. 32 is part of the **basic structure**.

n6988073029a.s: The immediate constitutional model for India's Directive Principles was the Constitution of:
n6988073029a.x: India took the idea from the Irish Constitution of 1937, which had itself copied it from the Spanish Constitution.
xa: Irish name: **Directive Principles of Social Policy**.
Indian antecedents: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Sapru Committee (1945)**.
**Ambedkar** called DPSPs a "**novel feature**" of the Constitution.

n629490bc26c.s: The Instrument of Instructions, an antecedent of the Directive Principles, was found under the:
n629490bc26c.x: The Instrument of Instructions under the 1935 Act and the Karachi Resolution (1931) are antecedents of the DPSPs.
xa: Other antecedents: the **Nehru Report (1928)** and **Gandhian ideals** (village self-sufficiency).
DPSPs were borrowed from the **Irish Constitution of 1937**, which took the idea from **Spain**.
DPSPs sit in **Part IV**, **Articles 36 to 51** (**16** articles).
They are called the **Instrument of Instructions** and the **Conscience of the Constitution**.

n9c8a7d5d8c4.s: The Directive Principles of State Policy are contained in which Part of the Constitution?
n9c8a7d5d8c4.x: The DPSPs are in Part IV (Articles 36–51); they are fundamental in governance but not enforceable by courts.
xa: It is the **duty of the State** to apply them in making laws.
Welfare state: "**The State is everywhere: it leaves hardly a gap**" (JPSC **2016**).

nindian-polity-19-19.s: The Directive Principles are referred to by which of the following expressions?
o: Instrument of Governance and Charter of the Constitution
Instrument of Instructions and Conscience of the Constitution
Instrument of Rights and Conscience of the Judiciary
Conscience of Parliament and Legal Instructions
nindian-polity-19-19.x: DPSP are called the 'Instrument of Instructions' (like those under the 1935 Act) and the 'conscience of the Constitution' (Granville Austin).
nindian-polity-19-19.tq: Recall the two names for DPSP.
n: The Directive Principles are called the Instrument of Instructions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
The Directive Principles are called the Conscience of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: DPSPs are called the **Instrument of Instructions** and the **Conscience of the Constitution** — option **(2)**.
The **Instrument of Instructions** under the **GoI Act 1935** is an antecedent of the DPSPs.
**Granville Austin** called FRs and DPSPs together the "**conscience of the Constitution**".
xa: **Ambedkar**: a "**novel feature**"; **K.C. Wheare**: "a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**".
**T.T. Krishnamachari**: "a **veritable dustbin of sentiments**".
DPSPs aim at **social and economic democracy** and a **welfare state**.

nindian-polity-20-6.s: The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish:
o: Social and economic democracy and a welfare state
nindian-polity-20-6.x: The DPSPs aim at social democracy, economic democracy and a welfare state; the idea was borrowed from Ireland.
n: The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from Ireland. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish social democracy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish economic democracy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
The Directive Principles of State Policy aim to establish a welfare state. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xa: Ireland copied the idea from the **Spanish Constitution**.
Indian antecedents: **Karachi Resolution (1931)**, **Nehru Report (1928)**, **Sapru Committee (1945)**.
FRs come from the **USA**; DPSPs from **Ireland**.

nindian-polity-20-11.s: Article 36 of the Constitution deals with which of the following?
o: Application of the Directive Principles of State Policy
Social order and minimisation of inequalities
nindian-polity-20-11.x: Article 36 defines 'State' for Part IV (as Article 12 does for Part III). Article 37 makes DPSP non-justiciable; 38 and 39 set the welfare and policy goals.
nindian-polity-20-11.tq: Link Article 36 to the definition of 'State'.
n: Article 36 defines the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xs: **Article 36** deals with the **definition of the State** — option **(1)**.
"State" in Part IV has the **same meaning as in Part III**.
**Article 37** is the **application** of DPSPs; **38** = **social order** and minimising inequalities; **39** = principles of policy incl. **livelihood**.
xa: **Art. 37**: DPSPs "**shall not be enforceable by any court**" but **fundamental in governance**.
Part IV spans **Articles 36 to 51**.
**Art. 38** was strengthened by the **44th Amendment** (added **38(2)**).

n7e0f092f46f.s: The sanction behind the Directive Principles is:
n7e0f092f46f.x: FRs carry a legal sanction enforced by courts, while DPSPs carry a moral and political sanction.
xa: FRs are **justiciable**; DPSPs are **non-justiciable**.
FRs are mostly **negative** obligations; DPSPs are **positive** obligations.
FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**; courts use **harmonious construction**.

n40ee9b2d117.s: The organisation of village panchayats is directed by Article:
n40ee9b2d117.x: Article 40 covers village panchayats; 39A is free legal aid, 43 living wage and cottage industries, and 44 the Uniform Civil Code.
xa: **39A** was added by the **42nd, 1976**; APPSC GS **2024** tested it.
Art. 40 → **73rd Amendment, 1992** (Panchayati Raj).
Art. 39A → **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.

n660177ad408.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of Articles generally classified as Gandhian principles?
n660177ad408.x: Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46 are generally included among Gandhian principles. The other sets contain Socialist or Liberal-intellectual principles.
n660177ad408.tq: Classify by the group as a whole and eliminate mixed sets.
xs: **Articles 40, 43, 43B and 46** are all **Gandhian** — option **(1)**.
**44, 45, 48A, 50** and **49, 50, 51** are **Liberal-intellectual**; **38, 39, 41, 42** are **Socialist**.
xa: 40 = panchayats; 43 = **cottage industries**; 43B = co-operatives; 46 = **SC/ST/weaker sections**.
47 (prohibition) and 48 (cow slaughter) are also Gandhian.

nindian-polity-19-8.s: Which of the following Directive Principles is a liberal-intellectual principle rather than a Gandhian one?
nindian-polity-19-8.x: Article 50 (separation of judiciary) is liberal-intellectual; Articles 40, 43B, 46 and 48 are Gandhian.
xa: The Gandhian group has **6** articles: **40, 43, 43B, 46, 47, 48**.
⚠ **43** and **47** are both Socialist and Gandhian; **48** is both Gandhian and Liberal-intellectual.
The Constitution itself does **not** classify DPSPs — the grouping is academic.

nindian-polity-20-13.s: A living wage and promotion of cottage industries are directed by Article:
nindian-polity-20-13.x: Article 43 covers living wage and cottage industries; 39A is free legal aid, 41 right to work and 42 humane work conditions.
n: Article 39A provides equal justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 39A provides free legal aid. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 41 concerns the right to work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 41 concerns the right to education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 41 concerns public assistance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 42 provides just and humane conditions of work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 42 provides maternity relief. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 43 concerns a living wage. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Article 43 concerns cottage industries. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xa: **39A** is implemented by the **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987** (in force **9 Nov 1995**).
**Art. 41** assistance covers **unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement**.
**43A** = **workers' participation in management** of industries.

n44f45fe336b.s: Courts have generally used the Directive Principles of State Policy in which of the following ways?
o: As independently enforceable rights replacing Fundamental Rights
As provisions applicable exclusively to local governments
As limitations that prevent all legislative action under Part III
As interpretive aids, including in reading certain principles into Article 21
n44f45fe336b.x: Although DPSPs are not independently enforceable, courts use them as interpretive aids and have read several welfare-oriented principles into the scope of Article 21.
n44f45fe336b.tq: Apply the distinction between non-justiciability and interpretive constitutional relevance.
xs: Courts use DPSPs as **interpretive aids**, reading many into **Art. 21** — option **(4)**.
Courts apply **harmonious construction** of Parts III and IV.
DPSPs are **not enforceable** by courts (**Art. 37**), so option (1) is wrong.
xa: **Minerva Mills (1980)**: the balance between Parts III and IV is **basic structure**.
FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**.

n6e94e87cae1.s: The Directive Principle relating to a social order based on social, economic and political justice and the minimisation of inequalities is contained in:
n6e94e87cae1.x: Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order informed by justice and to minimise inequalities of income, status, facilities and opportunities.
n6e94e87cae1.tq: Distinguish the general welfare-and-inequality provision from the specific objectives listed in Article 39.
xs: **Article 38**: social order of **social, economic, political justice** and **minimising inequalities** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 39** is livelihood, resources, equal pay; **Art. 41** is right to work; **Art. 46** is SC/ST/weaker sections.
xa: **38(2)** (minimise inequalities) was added by the **44th Amendment, 1978**.
Art. 38 is grouped as a **Socialist** principle.

n31f84062143.s: Article 39(a) of the Constitution directs the State to secure:
o: The right to work in every circumstance
Free legal aid to economically weaker citizens
Equal pay for equal work for men and women
Adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally
n31f84062143.x: Article 39(a) directs the State to secure adequate means of livelihood for men and women equally. Equal pay for equal work is contained in Article 39(d).
n31f84062143.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring clauses of the same Article.
xs: **39(a)**: **adequate means of livelihood** for men and women **equally** — option **(4)**.
**Equal pay** is **39(d)**; **free legal aid** is **39A**; **right to work** is **Art. 41**.
xa: **39(b)**: material resources for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth**.
Dignity of women links **39(a), (d), (e), 42** with FD **51A(e)**.

n05bbd46c6eb.s: The protection of children against exploitation and moral or material abandonment, along with development in freedom and dignity, is provided under:
n05bbd46c6eb.x: Article 39(f) directs that children should develop in a healthy manner and in conditions of freedom and dignity, and be protected against exploitation and abandonment. The present wording was introduced through the 42nd Amendment.
n05bbd46c6eb.tq: Identify the exact sub-clause by its distinctive subject matter.
xs: **Article 39(f)**: children to develop in **freedom and dignity**, protected from **exploitation** and **moral/material abandonment** — option **(4)**.
39(f) was added by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
**39(d)** = equal pay; **39(e)** = health of workers and children; **39(c)** = concentration of wealth.
xa: The 42nd also added **39A, 43A, 48A**.
Education of children: **Art. 45** (below 6), FR **21A**, FD **51A(k)**.

ncd10e0bdc37.s: Equal pay for equal work for men and women is provided in Article:
ncd10e0bdc37.x: Article 39(d) deals with equal pay; 39(e) protects the health and strength of workers and children from unsuited work.
xa: 39(e) also protects the **tender age of children** from abuse.
**39(f)**: children's development in freedom and dignity.

na8454c3f5cf.s: Which one of the following correctly states the subject matter of Articles 39(b) and 39(c)?
o: 39(b): distribution of community resources for the common good; 39(c): prevention of concentration of wealth and means of production
39(b): protection of monuments; 39(c): promotion of international peace
39(b): right to work; 39(c): free legal aid
na8454c3f5cf.x: Article 39(b) concerns distribution of material resources of the community to subserve the common good, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.
na8454c3f5cf.tq: Discriminate between neighbouring Directive Principles by their exact constitutional wording.
xs: **39(b)**: **material resources** distributed for the **common good**; **39(c)**: no **concentration of wealth** and means of production — option **(1)**.
APPSC G2 **2025**: both statements are in the Constitution.
xa: Implemented by **land reforms**, **zamindari abolition**, **ceiling laws**.
**Monuments** = **Art. 49**; **international peace** = **Art. 51**; **equal pay** = **39(d)**.

nbe698119cd3.s: Which of the following correctly describes Article 45 after the constitutional changes relating to education?
o: It provides for mother-tongue instruction to linguistic minorities.
It makes education from six to fourteen years a Fundamental Duty of the State.
It directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for children below six years of age.
It deals with free legal aid for all citizens.
nbe698119cd3.x: Article 45 directs the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years of age. Article 21A deals with the Fundamental Right to education for children aged six to fourteen years, while Article 51A(k) is the related Fundamental Duty.
nbe698119cd3.tq: Separate the age groups and distinguish DPSP, Fundamental Right and Fundamental Duty provisions.
xs: **Art. 45** now directs **early childhood care and education** for children **below six** — option **(3)**.
Since the **86th Amendment (2002)**, education for **6-14** is an FR under **Art. 21A**.
**Free legal aid** is **Art. 39A** — option (4) wrong.
xa: Education link: Art. 45, FR **21A**, FD **51A(k)**.
**RTE Act, 2009** Sec. **3**: free education **6-14** in a neighbourhood school.

nindian-polity-19-12.s: Just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief are directed by Article:
nindian-polity-19-12.x: Article 42 covers humane conditions of work and maternity relief; 38 is welfare of the people, 39 livelihood and equal pay, 41 right to work.
n: Article 38 directs the State to promote the welfare of the people. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for adequate means of livelihood. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for equal pay for equal work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 39 provides for the protection of children. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for the right to work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for the right to education. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 41 provides for public assistance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 42 provides for just and humane conditions of work. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Article 42 provides for maternity relief. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xa: **39A** = **equal justice** and **free legal aid** (42nd Amendment).
**Art. 43** = **living wage** and **cottage industries**.
**Art. 41** was given effect through **MGNREGA (2005)**.

n815fd01c290.s: Which Article provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities?
n815fd01c290.x: The Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities is under Article 350B; Article 350A concerns mother-tongue education.
xa: **Art. 1** describes India as a **Union of States**; **Art. 3** = **formation of new states**.
**371 Series** = **special provisions** for **states**.
**Art. 46** promotes **SC and ST interests**.

o: Early childhood care and education until six years
Free and compulsory education up to fourteen years
nc146f9b9d58.x: Article 45 now covers early childhood care and education until age six; education for ages 6–14 is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
xa: ⚠ IYB **2026** still gives the original Art. 45 ("free and compulsory education up to **14**").
First State UCC: **Uttarakhand**; second: **Gujarat**.

n0dc146946cb.s: Which of the following Directive Principles is grouped under the Gandhian, not the Socialist, principles?
n0dc146946cb.x: Article 43B (co-operative societies) is Gandhian; Articles 38, 39A and 47 are generally grouped under Socialist principles.
xa: Liberal-intellectual: **44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51**.

n39505132885.s: Which of the following was NOT added to the Directive Principles by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?
o: Article 39A – Equal justice and free legal aid
n39505132885.x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; the 42nd Amendment added Articles 39A, 43A, 48A and 39(f).
xa: The 42nd also added **39(f)** (children's development).
**43B** came by the **97th (2011)**; Art. 45 substituted by the **86th (2002)**.

n1a8aa7989eb.s: Article 38(2) of the Directive Principles was added by the:
n1a8aa7989eb.x: Article 38(2) was added by the 44th Amendment in 1978; Article 43B came by the 97th (2011) and the present Article 45 by the 86th (2002).
xa: 86th also linked to **Art. 21A** and **51A(k)**.

n1c9b9a6ac04.s: Heritage and monuments are covered by Article 49 and by Fundamental Duty:
n1c9b9a6ac04.x: Article 49 and Article 51A(f) relate to heritage; Article 45 pairs with 51A(k) on education, and Article 39 with 51A(e) on women's dignity.
xa: Environment — **48A** & FD **51A(g)**.
Education also links to FR **Art. 21A**.
Maternity relief — **Art. 42**.

n978dccaa78f.s: The Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 support which Directive Principle?
n978dccaa78f.x: Article 48A is supported by wildlife and environmental legislation; Article 47 is reflected in public health measures such as the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
xa: **44** → State UCCs: **Uttarakhand** (first), **Gujarat** (second).
**Art. 47** → prohibition laws.

n64f58eec506.s: The Ninth Schedule was introduced by the:
n64f58eec506.x: The First Amendment, 1951 introduced the Ninth Schedule and Articles 31A and 31B; the 73rd Amendment dealt with Panchayati Raj.
xa: Land reforms implement **39(b), (c)**: zamindari abolition, ceiling laws.
The 73rd gave panchayats **constitutional status** under **Art. 40**.

na6b42f733e1.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about recent developments on Article 44?
o: In Pavini Shukla v. Union of India (2026), the Supreme Court suggested a UCC to end gender discrimination
Article 44 is enforceable in court like a Fundamental Right
In March 2026 a three-judge Bench considered deferring to Parliament on Article 44
Article 44 is a Directive Principle with no legal force
na6b42f733e1.x: Article 44 is a DPSP with no legal force and is not enforceable like a Fundamental Right.
xa: **Art. 44** directs a **Uniform Civil Code** for citizens; it is classed as **liberal-intellectual**.
State UCCs: **Uttarakhand** first, **Gujarat** second (**UCC Bill 2026**).
Gujarat UCC Bill 2026: monogamy, equal inheritance, marriage registration in **60 days**, live-in in **30 days**, **STs exempted**.
**Goa** follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867**; the **22nd Law Commission** sought views in **2022**.

n7f33ebdebfe.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes Fundamental Rights from Directive Principles of State Policy?
o: Directive Principles are applicable only to private individuals, whereas Fundamental Rights apply only to the State.
Fundamental Rights are generally negative obligations, whereas Directive Principles are generally positive obligations on the State.
Fundamental Rights are positive obligations, whereas Directive Principles are enforceable by courts.
Both are negative obligations and both are directly enforceable by courts.
n7f33ebdebfe.x: Fundamental Rights mostly restrain the State from certain actions, while Directive Principles generally require the State to undertake measures for social and economic welfare.
n7f33ebdebfe.tq: Split the paired concepts by asking what each requires the State to do or not do.
xs: FRs are mostly **negative** obligations on the State; DPSPs are **positive** obligations — option **(2)**.
DPSPs are **not enforceable by any court** (**Art. 37**) — options (3) and (4) wrong.
xa: FRs and DPSPs are **complementary**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: balance between Part III and Part IV is **basic structure**.
**Granville Austin**: together they are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".

n95feb506ba2.s: Which Article, a directive outside Part IV, deals with the development of Hindi?
n95feb506ba2.x: Article 351 covers development of Hindi and Article 335 SC/ST claims to services; both are non-justiciable directives outside Part IV.
xa: DPSPs in Part IV span **Art. 36-51**.
**Art. 37** bars courts from enforcing Part IV.

n0afc721b082.s: The Legal Services Authorities Act, which implements Article 39A, came into force on 9 November of which year?
n0afc721b082.x: The Act of 1987 came into force on 9 November 1995, observed as National Legal Services Day; it sets up NALSA, SLSAs and DLSAs.
xa: Legal aid under 39A remains **underfunded** (Aug **2025**).

n41b41019dd8.s: MGNREGA, 2005, linked to Article 41, has since been replaced by the:
n41b41019dd8.x: MGNREGA was replaced by the VB-GRAM G Act; a sharp fall in employment under it has revived the right-to-work debate.
xa: **K.T. Shah** wanted the right to work as an FR; debate with **Ambedkar** in the CA.
Art. 41 also covers education and **public assistance**.

n619521a96ba.s: Which group is exempted from the Gujarat Uniform Civil Code Bill, 2026?
n619521a96ba.x: Scheduled Tribes are exempted. Gujarat is the second State after Uttarakhand to move a UCC, providing for monogamy and equal inheritance.
xa: Marriage registration in **60** days; live-in in **30** days.

n09fd5778e32.s: Which of the following descriptions of the Directive Principles is an approving one, not a criticism?
o: No better than New Year's resolutions
A novel feature of the Indian Constitution
n09fd5778e32.x: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution; the other remarks criticise their non-justiciable character.
xa: **K.T. Shah**: a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
**K.C. Wheare**: a **manifesto of aims and aspirations**.
**Granville Austin**: FRs and DPSPs together are the **conscience of the Constitution**.
**Art. 37**: Part IV **shall not be enforceable by any court**, yet the principles are **fundamental in the governance of the country**.

n26a27824e07.s: Who described the Directive Principles as 'a manifesto of aims and aspirations'?
n26a27824e07.x: K.C. Wheare called them a manifesto of aims and aspirations; Ivor Jennings called them 'pious aspirations' and T.T. Krishnamachari 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'.
xa: **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** called DPSPs a "**novel feature**" — the approving remark.
**Nasiruddin**: "no better than **New Year's resolutions**" broken on the second of January.
**Granville Austin**: FRs and DPSPs together are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".
**K.T. Shah** also wanted the **right to work** as an FR.

n0ccdd939556.s: The debate over the right to work as a Fundamental Right versus a Directive Principle was associated in the Constituent Assembly with which pair?
o: K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar
Rajendra Prasad and Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar
N. Rau and K. M. Munshi
n0ccdd939556.x: The Constituent Assembly debate on whether the right to work should be a Fundamental Right or remain a Directive Principle involved K. T. Shah and B. R. Ambedkar.
n0ccdd939556.tq: Match the constitutional debate with the specific participants named in it.
xs: The right-to-work debate (FR vs DPSP) in the Constituent Assembly was between **K.T. Shah** and **B.R. Ambedkar** — option **(1)**.
**K.T. Shah** wanted the **right to work** as an FR; it stayed a directive under **Art. 41**.
K.T. Shah also called the DPSPs a **cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank**.
xa: **Art. 41**: right to **work**, education, public assistance (unemployment, old age, sickness, disablement).
**MGNREGA (2005)** made the right to work a legal right; since replaced by the **VB-G RAM G Act**.
The fall in rural work under the **VB-GRAM G Act** revived the right-to-work debate (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ Ambedkar called the DPSPs a **novel feature**; Shah's remark was critical.

n37691c36cb9.s: According to the Minerva Mills case (1980), the relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is that:
o: Part IV is absolutely superior to Part III
A balance between Part III and Part IV is part of the Basic Structure
Part III is absolutely superior to Part IV
Both Part III and Part IV are outside judicial review
n37691c36cb9.x: The balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the Basic Structure; neither Part has unlimited supremacy.
xa: Courts use **harmonious construction**.
FRs = **negative** obligations; DPSPs = **positive** obligations.
Granville Austin: FRs and DPSPs together are the "**conscience of the Constitution**".

na0a37333f5d.s: Goa’s civil-law system is based on which of the following?
o: The Uniform Civil Code enacted by Parliament
na0a37333f5d.x: Goa follows the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867, making it a distinctive example in discussions concerning a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.
na0a37333f5d.tq: Use the jurisdiction–legal code association to distinguish Goa from proposed State UCCs.
xs: Goa follows the **Portuguese Civil Code of 1867** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Goa's code dates from **1867**; the first State UCC was **Uttarakhand**, then **Gujarat**.
xa: **Art. 44** directs a **Uniform Civil Code**.
⚠ State UCC: **Uttarakhand** first, **Gujarat** second.
**22nd Law Commission** sought views (**2022**).

nindian-polity-19-20.s: Environmental protection is provided under which provision as a Fundamental Duty?
nindian-polity-19-20.x: Protecting the environment is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(g). Article 48A makes it a Directive Principle, not a duty.
nindian-polity-19-20.tq: Separate the duty (51A(g)) from the directive (48A).
n: Environmental protection is provided under Article 51A(g) as a Fundamental Duty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xs: Environmental protection as a Fundamental Duty is **Article 51A(g)** — option **(4)**.
**Art. 48A** is the **Directive Principle** on environment, not a duty.
**Art. 45** = **early childhood care and education**; **Art. 49** = **monuments**.
xa: Both **48A** and **51A(g)** came with the **42nd Amendment**.
**51A(g)** covers **forests, lakes, rivers and wild life** and **compassion for living creatures**.
**48A** is in the **Liberal-Intellectual** group.

na7dfcab71f0.s: Fundamental Rights are mostly ____, while Directive Principles are positive directions to the State.
na7dfcab71f0.x: FRs are mostly negative and aim at political democracy; DPSPs are positive and aim at social and economic democracy.
xa: Justiciability: FRs (**Part III**, Arts **12-35**) are **justiciable**; DPSPs (**Part IV**, Arts **36-51**) are **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**).
Main difference (**UPSC 2009**): DPSPs are **not enforceable** in courts, FRs are.
Sources: FRs from the **USA**, DPSPs from **Ireland**.
Legal status: FRs are **superior**, but DPSPs are **fundamental in governance**.

n3529cc82b7b.s: A law violating a Fundamental Right and a law violating a Directive Principle have which respective legal consequences?
o: The former may be void under Article 13, while the latter cannot be struck down merely for violating a Directive Principle
The former cannot be examined by courts, while the latter is void under Article 37
Both laws are automatically void under Article 13
Both laws are immune from judicial review
n3529cc82b7b.x: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void to the extent of inconsistency. Courts cannot strike down a law solely because it violates a Directive Principle.
n3529cc82b7b.tq: Apply the constitutional consequence separately to an enforceable right and a non-justiciable directive.
xs: A law violating an FR may be **void under Article 13**, but a law **cannot be struck down** merely for violating a DPSP — option **(1)**.
DPSPs are **non-justiciable** under **Art. 37**, so (2) is wrong: Art. 37 does not make laws void.
(3) and (4) are wrong: only FR-violating laws are void; such laws are open to **judicial review**.
xa: FRs are mostly **negative** obligations; DPSPs **positive** directions to the State.
FRs aim at **political democracy**; DPSPs at **social and economic democracy**.
**Harmonious construction**: read Part III and Part IV **together** so both operate (**Kerala Education Bill, 1958**; **Minerva Mills, 1980**).

n5e7fc6d2646.s: Which was the first case of conflict between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles?
n5e7fc6d2646.x: Champakam Dorairajan (1951) was the first conflict case; I.R. Coelho (2007) was the last word on the Ninth Schedule.
xa: Champakam led to the **First Amendment** — the first amendment responding to a court.
Coelho: no blanket immunity for post-1973 Ninth Schedule entries.
FRs are **justiciable**; DPSPs **non-justiciable** (**Art. 37**).

n49b914ba570.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan (1951)?
o: It held that Fundamental Rights prevail and DPSPs run subsidiary to them
It struck down a Madras communal order on admissions under Article 29(2)
It led to the insertion of Article 15(4)
It adopted harmonious construction under which DPSPs prevail over Fundamental Rights
n49b914ba570.x: Harmonious construction came in In re Kerala Education Bill (1958), and even there Fundamental Rights still prevail.
xa: Champakam was the **first conflict case**; asked as "FR over DPSP in conflict" (**MPPSC 2024**).
Chronology: **Gopalan (1950) → Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva (1980)**.

n71e9f343453.s: In re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 is associated with which of the following approaches?
o: Harmonious construction, giving effect to both Fundamental Rights and DPSPs as far as possible
Parliament's inability to amend any Fundamental Right
Complete supremacy of DPSPs over Fundamental Rights
n71e9f343453.x: In re Kerala Education Bill adopted harmonious construction, requiring both Parts III and IV to be given effect as far as possible, while Fundamental Rights continued to prevail in case of direct conflict.
n71e9f343453.tq: Distinguish harmonious construction from either absolute rights supremacy or DPSP supremacy.
xs: **In re Kerala Education Bill (1958)** adopted **harmonious construction** — giving effect to both FRs and DPSPs as far as possible — option **(1)**.
FRs **still prevailed** in a conflict, so (4) is wrong.
"Parliament cannot amend FRs" (3) is **Golaknath (1967)**.
xa: **Champakam (1951)**, before it, held DPSPs **subsidiary** to FRs.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** later made **harmony and balance** part of the **Basic Structure**.
Harmonious construction treats FRs and DPSPs as **complementary, not competing**.

n06154e6b527.s: Which case denied Parliament the power to amend Fundamental Rights and applied the doctrine of prospective overruling?
n06154e6b527.x: Golaknath (1967) gave FRs a 'transcendental' position and applied prospective overruling; 'amendable but not the Basic Structure' is Kesavananda Bharati.
xa: The 24th also made the **President's assent** mandatory.
Chronology: **Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973)**.

n89096352804.s: In which year was Minerva Mills decided?
n89096352804.x: Minerva Mills (1980) came after Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and before Sanjeev Coke (1983).
xa: **Gopalan**: narrow reading of FRs; court checks only procedure.
**Champakam**: FRs prevail; **Golaknath**: Parliament cannot amend FRs.
**Kesavananda**: Basic Structure; **Minerva**: FR-DPSP **balance** is Basic Structure.
**RPSC 2018** asked this chronology.

nindian-polity-15-22.s: Which 1950 case gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21?
o: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
nindian-polity-15-22.x: A.K. Gopalan (1950) read Article 21 narrowly; Golaknath (1967) barred amendment of FRs and Kesavananda (1973) protected the basic structure.
n: The Indira Sawhney Case was decided in 1992. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Indira Sawhney Case concerned reservation under Article 16. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xa: **Golaknath** applied **prospective overruling**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** expanded **Art. 21** — **due process**.

nf95a3b6c15e.s: Article 15(4), inserted by the First Amendment Act, 1951, was a response to which judgment?
nf95a3b6c15e.x: Article 15(4) answered Champakam Dorairajan; Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule answered the land-reform judgments.
xa: ⚠ Some notes wrongly link 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to Champakam.
The Ninth Schedule grew to **over 280 entries**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity — post-1973 entries fall if they damage the **Basic Structure**.

nd6e0e21ff96.s: Article 31C was inserted into the Constitution by the:
nd6e0e21ff96.x: Article 31C came with the Twenty-fifth Amendment; the Seventeenth widened 'estate' in Article 31A and dealt with land under personal cultivation.
xa: **4th (1955)**: adequacy of compensation made **non-justiciable**.
**Art. 31A** came with the **1st Amendment (1951)**.
**26th (1971)**: abolished **privy purses**.

ncfa865647e4.s: The Twenty-fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 was enacted in response to Golaknath and provided that:
o: The adequacy of compensation could be examined by courts.
Parliament could amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
Only DPSPs could be amended by Parliament.
ncfa865647e4.x: The Twenty-fourth Amendment responded to Golaknath by affirming Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. It added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), and made presidential assent mandatory.
ncfa865647e4.tq: Link the amendment to the judgment it was intended to overcome and identify its broad power.
xs: The **24th Amendment (1971)** answered **Golaknath**: Parliament **can amend any part** of the Constitution, **including FRs** — option **(3)**.
It added Art. **13(4)** and **368(3)** and made the **President's assent** mandatory.
**Privy purses** (1) were abolished by the **26th Amendment (1971)**.
xa: **Golaknath (1967)** had held Parliament **cannot amend FRs** and applied **prospective overruling**.
**25th (1971)** answered **R.C. Cooper (1970)**: **amount** for compensation; **Art. 31C**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** then allowed amendment of FRs but not the **Basic Structure**.

n4b466524a92.s: Which Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all the Directive Principles?
n4b466524a92.x: The 42nd Amendment, not the 44th, attempted the extension, and it was struck down by the Supreme Court.
xa: ⚠ Trap (**RPSC 2013**): "the 44th Amendment gave all DPSPs primacy over 14 and 19" is **false**.
Only **39(b)-(c)** laws enjoy primacy, via the **25th (1971)**.
The 42nd also claimed **unlimited amending power** under **Art. 368**.

n9a49761de66.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 31C?
o: It was introduced by the 25th Amendment in 1971
It protects laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
Articles 39(b) and 39(c) are the only Directive Principles that override Fundamental Rights under it
Minerva Mills upheld the 42nd Amendment's extension of it to all Directive Principles
n9a49761de66.x: Minerva Mills struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C protection to all Directive Principles.
xa: **PYQ (UPPSC 2009)**: amendment protecting 39(b)-(c) laws from Arts 14/19 = **25th**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** struck down 31C's **second provision**.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: unamended 31C **continues in force**.

na62a866d728.s: In which year was I.R. Coelho, the last word on the Ninth Schedule, decided?
na62a866d728.x: I.R. Coelho came in 2007, after Champakam Dorairajan and the First Amendment (1951) and Minerva Mills.
xa: Champakam = **first conflict case**; 1st Amendment = first amendment responding to a court.
Coelho = **last word** on the Ninth Schedule.
Minerva made FR-DPSP balance part of the **Basic Structure** — the settled position.

nindian-polity-15-7.s: Which landmark case expanded the scope of Article 21 through due process?
nindian-polity-15-7.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 by requiring the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable (due process). A.K. Gopalan (1950) read it narrowly; Golaknath and Minerva Mills dealt with amending power.
nindian-polity-15-7.tq: Link the widening of Article 21 to Maneka Gandhi.
n: Gopalan versus State of Madras was decided in 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
Gopalan versus State of Madras gave a narrow interpretation of Article 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Golaknath Case was decided in 1967. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Golaknath Case held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Maneka Gandhi Case was decided in 1978. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Maneka Gandhi Case expanded the scope of Article 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Maneka Gandhi Case concerned due process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Minerva Mills Case was decided in 1980. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
The Minerva Mills Case concerned the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #15 · pp 38-40]
xs: Article 21 was expanded through due process in the **Maneka Gandhi Case** — option **(4)**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** **expanded** the scope of **Article 21** — **due process**.
**Gopalan (1950)** gave a **narrow** reading; **Golaknath (1967)** and **Minerva Mills (1980)** dealt with amending power and FR-DPSP balance.
xa: Chronology: **Gopalan (1950) → Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva (1980)**.
**Validity test** for DPSP laws uses the **golden triangle (Arts. 14, 19, 21)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** held FRs **superior** to DPSPs.

nindian-polity-51-14.s: The First Constitutional Amendment Act, which added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule, was enacted in:
nindian-polity-51-14.x: The 1st Amendment (1951) added Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule to protect land-reform and welfare laws from early court rulings.
n: The First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951 added Articles 31A and 31B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
The First Constitutional Amendment Act of 1951 added the Ninth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule were added to insulate agrarian laws from Judicial Review on Fundamental Rights grounds. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Articles 31A, 31B, and the Ninth Schedule were added to insulate land-reform laws from Judicial Review on Fundamental Rights grounds. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
The Ninth Schedule was enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare measures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
The Ninth Schedule was enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting land acquisition measures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: **Art. 31B** laws grew to **over 280 entries** in the Ninth Schedule.
**Waman Rao (1981)**: entries after **24 April 1973** open to challenge.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity — tested against the **Basic Structure**.
⚠ These answered the **land-reform** judgments, not **Champakam** itself.

n525bcb69410.s: The original Article 31C protected laws giving effect to Articles 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles:
n525bcb69410.x: The original Article 31C shielded such laws from Articles 14, 19 and 31, and put the declaration that they implemented the policy beyond judicial question.
xa: **Kesavananda (1973)** upheld the first provision and struck down the **second** (the declaration / bar on judicial review).
**42nd (1976)** extended 31C to **any DPSP**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck that down.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: original 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda, **continues in force**.

n9df29800fca.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Kesavananda Bharati relating to Article 31C?
o: The first provision was upheld and the second provision was struck down.
The first provision was struck down and the second provision was upheld.
Both provisions of Article 31C were struck down.
Both provisions were upheld without limitation.
n9df29800fca.x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down the second part, which excluded judicial review.
n9df29800fca.tq: Distinguish the first and second provisions rather than treating Article 31C as a single indivisible rule.
xs: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** upheld the **first provision** of Art. 31C and struck down the **second provision** — option **(1)**.
The second provision was the **bar on judicial review** — a law's **declaration** that it served 39(b)-(c) could not be questioned.
xa: ⚠ Trap (**APPSC G1 2024**): "first provision of 31C was invalidated in Kesavananda" is **wrong**.
Art. 31C was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)**.
The **42nd (1976)** extended 31C to **all DPSPs**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck it down.

n78e25c7501d.s: The continued operation of the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, was reaffirmed in which of the following decisions in 2024?
n78e25c7501d.x: The Property Owners Association decision of 2024 affirmed that the original Article 31C, as upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues in force.
n78e25c7501d.tq: Match the recent decision with the specific constitutional proposition it reaffirmed.
xs: **Property Owners Association (2024)** held the original **Art. 31C**, as upheld in Kesavananda, **continues in force** — option **(3)**.
**R.C. Cooper (1970)** was the **Bank Nationalisation** case; **Madhav Rao Scindia (1970)** the **Privy Purses** case.
**Sanjeev Coke (1983)** upheld coking coal nationalisation under **39(b)**.
xa: It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud** (**5 Nov 2024**).
It held **not every** privately owned resource is a 39(b) material resource.
It rejected **Justice Krishna Iyer**'s broad view (**Ranganatha Reddy, 1977**).

n47b507788c4.s: Which of the following correctly states the latest Supreme Court position on the expression “material resources of the community” in Article 39(b)?
o: No privately owned resource can ever be a material resource of the community
Only resources owned by the Union Government can be covered
Whether a privately owned resource is covered depends on factors such as its nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being and the consequences of concentration in private hands
Every privately owned resource is automatically a material resource of the community
n47b507788c4.x: In Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra, the Supreme Court held that private ownership alone does not automatically bring a resource within Article 39(b). The determination depends on the resource and its effects on the community and concentration of wealth.
n47b507788c4.tq: Apply the latest multi-factor judicial test instead of choosing an absolute public-versus-private rule.
xs: Whether a private resource is covered depends on its **nature, scarcity, effect on community well-being** and **consequences of concentration** in private hands — option **(3)**.
**Property Owners Association (2024)**: **not every** privately owned resource is a "material resource of the community", so (4) is wrong.
Private resources are not excluded either — the test decides — so (1) is wrong.
xa: It was a **9-judge** Bench, **7:2**, majority by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.
⚠ **Krishna Iyer** (**1977**, minority) = all private resources; Property Owners Association = not every private resource.
The broad view had been followed in **Sanjeev Coke (1983)**.

n288b5f1f75b.s: The 7:2 majority opinion in Property Owners Association v. State of Maharashtra (2024) was written by:
n288b5f1f75b.x: CJI D.Y. Chandrachud wrote the nine-judge Bench's majority; it rejected Justice Krishna Iyer's 1977 Ranganatha Reddy minority view.
xa: It held **not every** privately owned resource falls under **39(b)**.
It held unamended **31C** survives for 39(b)-(c) laws.
Krishna Iyer's view came in **State of Karnataka v. Ranganatha Reddy (1977)**.

nb5809b8d63f.s: The Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 inserted which of the following?
o: Part IVB containing Article 51B and clauses (a) to (k)
Part IVA containing Article 51A and clauses (a) to (j)
nb5809b8d63f.x: The Forty-Second Amendment inserted Part IVA, containing the single Article 51A with clauses (a) to (j).
nb5809b8d63f.tq: Match the amendment with the exact Part, Article and initial clause range.
xs: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** inserted **Part IVA** with **Art. 51A**, clauses **(a)-(j)** — option **(4)**.
Part IVA has a **single Article, 51A**, placed after Part IV (DPSP).
Clause **(k)** was added later by the **86th Amendment (2002)**, so (3) is wrong.
xa: The 42nd is called the "**Mini Constitution**".
Part IVA is one of the **4 Parts added** since 1950 — with **IXA, IXB, XIVA**.
Count: **10 in 1976 → 11 now**.

nd3d688848a1.s: The Fundamental Duties are contained in which Part, one of the four Parts added to the Constitution after 1950?
nd3d688848a1.x: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA; Parts IVA, IXA, IXB and XIVA are the four Parts added after 1950.
xa: Part IVA is a **single Article, 51A**, placed after Part IV (DPSP).

n9f88a8c1788.s: Article 48A, relating to the environment, is a:
o: Directive Principle addressed to the State
n9f88a8c1788.x: Article 48A is a Directive Principle addressed to the State; the citizens' duty is in Article 51A(g), and Article 21 is read to include a clean environment.
xa: Environmental FD = **51A(g)** (**APPSC 2025**), not 48A.
Both 51A(g) and 48A came with the **42nd Amendment, 1976**, after the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.
**Art. 253** is the basis of the **Environment Protection Act, 1986**.

n7eff2c08c56.s: Which Fundamental Duty is specifically addressed to parents or guardians?
n7eff2c08c56.x: Only Article 51A(k) addresses parents or guardians; clauses (b), (f), (h) and (j) are generally regarded as moral duties.
xa: Example: civic duty **(a)** (respect Flag, Anthem), moral duty **(b)** (ideals of the freedom struggle).
Count: **10 in 1976 → 11 now**.

nb75c6b45374.s: Which of the following categories is covered by the Fundamental Duties under Article 51A?
o: Only public servants and elected representatives
Citizens and all foreign nationals residing in India
All persons, whether citizens or foreigners
nb75c6b45374.x: Fundamental Duties are addressed to every citizen of India and do not extend to foreigners. This differs from certain Fundamental Rights, such as those under Articles 14, 20, 21 and 25, which are available to non-citizens as well.
nb75c6b45374.tq: Discriminate between citizens-only duties and rights available to all persons.
xs: FDs apply to **citizens of India only** — option **(3)**.
Art. 51A says "it shall be the duty of **every citizen** of India" — not foreigners.
Unlike several FRs (Arts **14, 20, 21, 25**) that cover non-citizens.
xa: **51A(k)** is addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**.
Source: the former **USSR**; **Japan** is the only major democracy with a comparable list.

n1645b822760.s: Among the major democratic constitutions, which country is noted for having a comparable list of citizens' duties?
n1645b822760.x: Japan's Constitution is identified as the only major democratic Constitution with a comparable list of citizens' duties. Socialist States generally give Fundamental Rights and duties relatively equal weight.
n1645b822760.tq: Use a country-comparison fact rather than confusing democratic and socialist constitutional models.
xs: **Japan** is the only major democracy with a comparable list of citizens' duties — option **(4)**.
The FD idea itself came from the former **USSR**.
xa: **Socialist States** give FRs and duties **equal weight**.
India's FDs apply to **every citizen** — not foreigners.

na76edbb2e75.s: Which amendment simultaneously inserted Article 51A(g), added Article 48A and transferred forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List?
na76edbb2e75.x: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted the environmental duty in Article 51A(g), added DPSP Article 48A and moved forests and protection of wild animals and birds to the Concurrent List through Entries 17A and 17B.
na76edbb2e75.tq: Recognise a cluster of linked constitutional changes instead of relying on the amendment number alone.
xs: The **42nd Amendment, 1976** did all three — option **(1)**.
It inserted **51A(g)**, added DPSP **Art. 48A**, and moved **Entry 17A/17B** (forests; wild animals and birds) to the **Concurrent List**.
The **86th (2002)** added **51A(k)**, not (g).
xa: These changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.
Environmental FD = **51A(g)**; 48A is a DPSP for the State.

n172f136e72e.s: The environmental changes associated with Article 51A(g) were introduced after which international development?
n172f136e72e.x: The insertion of Article 51A(g), Article 48A and the related legislative-list changes followed the 1972 Stockholm Conference.
n172f136e72e.tq: Use the date and causal sequence linking an international conference with constitutional change.
xs: The changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference** — option **(1)**.
**51A(g)** and **Art. 48A** came through the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
xa: **Entry 17A/17B** (forests; wild animals and birds) moved to the **Concurrent List**.
**Art. 253** lets Parliament implement international agreements → **Environment Protection Act, 1986**.

n2625cec22b4.s: The number of Fundamental Duties immediately after the Forty-Second Amendment and the number at present are, respectively:
n2625cec22b4.x: The Forty-Second Amendment introduced ten Fundamental Duties. The Eighty-Sixth Amendment later added clause (k), taking the total to eleven.
n2625cec22b4.tq: Track the numerical change caused by the later amendment.
xs: **10** duties after the 42nd Amendment and **11** now — option **(2)**.
The **42nd (1976)** added clauses **(a)-(j)**; the **86th (2002)** added **(k)**.
**8** was the number suggested by the **Swaran Singh Committee**, so (1) is a trap.
xa: ⚠ **8 – 10 – 11** = suggested – added in 1976 – total after 2002.
**51A(k)**: parent/guardian to provide education to a child aged **6-14**.

n5dfc78ada08.s: The Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 is associated with which combination?
o: Insertion of Article 21A, substitution of Article 45 and addition of Article 51A(k)
Insertion of Article 32A, substitution of Article 44 and deletion of Article 51A
Insertion of Part IXA and addition of Article 51A(a)
Substitution of Article 48A and insertion of Article 51A(j)
n5dfc78ada08.x: The Eighty-Sixth Amendment inserted Article 21A, substituted Article 45 and added the eleventh Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(k).
n5dfc78ada08.tq: Use the common education theme to match the amendment’s three provisions.
xs: The **86th Amendment (2002)** — **insertion** of **Article 21A**, **substitution** of Art. 45 and **addition** of 51A(k) — option **(1)**.
The **86th** is the Act that added the **11th** duty; the **42nd (1976)** had added **10**.
**51A(a)** and **(j)** came with the **42nd (1976)**, so (3) and (4) are wrong.
xa: 51A(k): parent/guardian to provide **opportunities for education** to a child aged **6-14**.
51A(k) is the only duty addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**; it is a **civic** duty.
⚠ Answer is **86th, 2002** — options often mix 86th/96th and 2001/2002.

n97d71115259.s: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee of 1999 was primarily concerned with which of the following?
o: Drafting a new Preamble to the Constitution
Operationalising Fundamental Duties by identifying existing legal provisions
Reviewing the federal distribution of legislative powers
Recommending the abolition of Fundamental Rights
n97d71115259.x: The Justice J.S. Verma Committee examined ways to operationalise Fundamental Duties and identified existing laws that already gave effect to several of them.
n97d71115259.tq: Identify the precise mandate of a committee instead of its broad constitutional context.
xs: The **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)** worked on **operationalising Fundamental Duties** — option **(2)**.
It found **existing laws** already give effect to some duties.
xa: ⚠ **Swaran Singh** = **1976**, suggested duties; **J.S. Verma** = 1999, operationalising them.
Example: **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** → **51A(a)**.

n493e2bdab7f.s: Renouncing practices derogatory to the dignity of women is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A clause:
n493e2bdab7f.x: Article 51A(e) covers harmony, common brotherhood and renouncing practices derogatory to women; 51A(d) covers defending the country.
xa: The Preamble look-alike for 51A(e) is **Fraternity**.
The **Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** serves 51A(e).
Both (d) and (e) are classed as **civic** duties.

n0cf3d2f02c9.s: The duty of a parent or guardian to provide opportunities for education to a child or ward between six and fourteen years of age is contained in:
n0cf3d2f02c9.x: Article 51A(k) places this duty on a parent or guardian in respect of a child or ward aged six to fourteen years.
n0cf3d2f02c9.tq: Use the age range to identify the specific educational duty.
xs: **Article 51A(k)**: parent or guardian to provide **opportunities for education** to a child or ward aged **6-14** — option **(2)**.
Added by the **86th Amendment, 2002** — the **11th** duty.
**51A(g)** = environment; **(h)** = scientific temper; **(j)** = excellence.
xa: The same Act inserted **Art. 21A** and substituted **Art. 45**.
51A(k) is the only duty addressed specifically to **parents or guardians**.

n0b0c2f24e1e.s: The Supreme Court has recognised that corporations, as legal persons, may also carry which duty under Article 51A(g)?
o: To protect and improve the natural environment
To provide free and compulsory education
To preserve the composite culture of India
To promote international peace and security
n0b0c2f24e1e.x: Corporations, being legal persons, have also been held capable of carrying the duty under Article 51A(g) to protect and improve the natural environment.
n0b0c2f24e1e.tq: Apply the constitutional duty to a non-natural legal person in a practical situation.
xs: Corporations, as **legal persons**, carry the **51A(g)** duty to **protect and improve the natural environment** — option **(1)**.
SC (**Mar 2026**) linked this to **CSR** — at least **2%** of average net profit, **Sec. 135 Companies Act, 2013**.
Education is **51A(k)**; composite culture is **51A(f)**.
xa: **M.K. Ranjitsinh v. UoI**: **CSR includes environmental protection**, linked to 51A(g).
SC (**Aug 2025**) linked **PCB enforcement** to 51A(g).
The **NGT** was formed to secure the environmental right.

nb0d98369ff0.s: Freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) is presented as being correlative with which Fundamental Duty?
o: The duty to develop scientific temper
The duty to provide educational opportunities to children
The duty to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
The duty to preserve the rich heritage of composite culture
nb0d98369ff0.x: Rights and duties are treated as complementary. Freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is linked with the duty under Article 51A(c) to uphold and protect India's sovereignty, unity and integrity.
nb0d98369ff0.tq: Apply the idea of reciprocal rights and duties to a constitutional freedom.
xs: **Art. 19(1)(a)** is correlative with **51A(c)** — uphold and protect the **sovereignty, unity and integrity** of India — option **(3)**.
Scientific temper is **51A(h)**; education is **51A(k)**; composite culture is **51A(f)**.
xa: **AIIMS Students' Union (2002)**: rights and duties are **correlative**.
Rights are to be exercised with **restraint** and respect for others' rights.

nindian-polity-18-4.s: Developing scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A clause:
nindian-polity-18-4.x: Clause (h) is scientific temper; (e) is harmony and dignity of women, (f) composite culture and (g) the natural environment.
n: The duty under Article 51-A(e) requires citizens to promote harmony. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(e) requires citizens to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(f) requires citizens to value the rich heritage of India’s composite culture. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(f) requires citizens to preserve the rich heritage of India’s composite culture. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(g) requires citizens to protect the natural environment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(g) requires citizens to improve the natural environment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(h) requires citizens to develop scientific temper. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(h) requires citizens to develop humanism. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(h) requires citizens to develop the spirit of inquiry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
xa: **(i)** = **safeguard public property** and **abjure violence**.
**(j)** = **strive towards excellence**.
**(k)** = parent or guardian to provide education for child aged **6 to 14 years**.

nindian-polity-18-7.s: Which clause of Article 51A asks citizens to cherish the noble ideals that inspired the freedom struggle?
nindian-polity-18-7.x: Clause (b) covers the ideals of the freedom struggle; (a) respect for Constitution, Flag and Anthem, (c) sovereignty and integrity, (d) defence of the country.
n: The duty under Article 51-A(a) requires citizens to abide by the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(a) requires citizens to respect the National Flag. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(a) requires citizens to respect the National Anthem. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(b) requires citizens to cherish the noble ideals that inspired the freedom struggle. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(c) requires citizens to uphold the sovereignty of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(c) requires citizens to uphold the unity of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(c) requires citizens to uphold the integrity of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(d) requires citizens to defend the country. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(d) requires citizens to render national service when called upon to do so. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
xa: Civic duties: **(a), (c), (d), (g), (i)**; moral duties: **(b), (f), (h), (j)**.
**Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** serves **51A(a)**.
**Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967** serves **51A(c)**.

nindian-polity-18-8.s:
Which of the following are duties under Article 51A(i)?
1. To safeguard public property
2. To abjure violence
3. To strive towards excellence
nindian-polity-18-8.x: Article 51A(i) asks citizens to safeguard public property and abjure violence. Striving towards excellence is clause (j).
n: The duty under Article 51-A(i) requires citizens to safeguard public property. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(i) requires citizens to abjure violence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
The duty under Article 51-A(j) requires citizens to strive towards excellence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 44-45]
xa: **51-A(j)**: excellence in **individual and collective activity** so the nation rises to higher levels of **endeavour and achievement**.
**51-A(h)**: **scientific temper, humanism** and **spirit of inquiry and reform**.
Not duties: **pay taxes**, **cast a vote**, family planning.

nfe86a54e034.s: Which one of the following was NOT accepted as a recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee?
o: The broad idea of incorporating duties of citizens
The formulation of a constitutional list of duties
The inclusion of Fundamental Duties in the Constitution
Parliament’s power to prescribe punishment for non-compliance with duties
nfe86a54e034.x: The proposal that Parliament could prescribe penalties for non-compliance was not accepted. The constitutional list of Fundamental Duties was incorporated in a modified form.
nfe86a54e034.tq: Identify the rejected enforcement proposal rather than the accepted constitutional idea.
xs: **Parliament's power to prescribe punishment** for non-compliance with duties was **not accepted** — option **(4)**.
The idea of a list of duties was accepted: the **42nd Amendment, 1976** inserted **Part IVA** (**Art. 51A**) — so (1), (2), (3) were accepted.
