Also rejected: that such penalty laws **not be challenged in court** for violating FRs.
xa: Also rejected: the **duty to pay taxes** as a Fundamental Duty.
The Committee suggested **8** duties; **10** were added.
FDs today are **non-justiciable** — no legal sanction or penalty in the Constitution.

n1a4ba3ce922.s: Which Fundamental Duty proposed by the Swaran Singh Committee was not included in the Constitution?
n1a4ba3ce922.x: The committee suggested payment of taxes as a Fundamental Duty, but the proposal was not accepted.
xa: Paying taxes, **casting a vote** and **family planning** are common "not a duty" distractors.
Criticism: the list is **not exhaustive** — omits voting, paying taxes, family planning.
The penalty proposal for non-observance was also rejected.

n44a0571f895.s: The constitutional provision on Fundamental Duties was inspired primarily by the Constitution of which country?
o: Former Union of Soviet Socialist Republics
n44a0571f895.x: The Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR. The provisions on Fundamental Rights, in contrast, drew inspiration substantially from the United States Constitution.
n44a0571f895.tq: Distinguish the foreign source of one constitutional feature from sources of other features.
xs: FDs were inspired by the Constitution of the former **USSR** — option **(4)**.
**Socialist States** give FRs and duties equal weight.
xa: Among major democracies only **Japan** has a comparable list of citizens' duties.
Inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee**'s advice.

n49069d2a991.s: Which environmental law draws on Parliament's power under Article 253 to implement international agreements?
o: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
n49069d2a991.x: Article 253 lets Parliament legislate to implement international agreements, and it forms the constitutional basis of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
xa: **Art. 21** includes a clean, healthy, pollution-free environment (**Subhash Kumar, 1991**).
Changes followed the **1972 Stockholm Conference**.

nd0214c2ff52.s: In M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India, CSR including environmental protection was linked to:
nd0214c2ff52.x: The case held that CSR includes environmental protection and linked the principle to the Fundamental Duty in Article 51A(g).
xa: CSR: at least **2%** of average net profit (**Sec. 135, Companies Act, 2013**).
SC (**Mar 2026**): corporations, as **legal persons**, carry the 51A(g) duty.

nf82746856cb.s: Which one of the following laws is most directly associated with giving effect to the duty to respect the National Flag, the National Anthem and the Constitution?
o: Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971
nf82746856cb.x: The Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 gives statutory effect to aspects of Article 51A(a), concerning respect for the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem.
nf82746856cb.tq: Match a duty with the legislation that operationalises it.
xs: The **Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971** gives effect to **51A(a)** — option **(1)**.
**Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955** → **51A(e)**; **UAPA 1967** → **51A(c)**; **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980** → **51A(g)**.
xa: These links were noted by the **Justice J.S. Verma Committee (1999)**.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: respect for national symbols needs only respectful conduct.

nfe3fcd8d9a7.s: Which case held that Fundamental Duties cannot override Fundamental Rights and that respect for national symbols does not require compelled participation?
o: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala
Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
nfe3fcd8d9a7.x: In Bijoe Emmanuel (1986), the Court held Fundamental Duties cannot override Part III rights and respect for symbols needs no compelled participation.
xa: **Vande Mataram** recitation debate: 51A duties cannot cut down **Arts. 25-26** rights (**24 Aug 2026**).
**AIIMS Students' Union (2002)**: rights and duties are **correlative**.

n97514fa63a3.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that rights and duties are correlative and that Fundamental Duties are as important as Fundamental Rights?
o: Bijoe Emmanuel v. State of Kerala (1986)
Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980)
M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India
n97514fa63a3.x: In AIIMS Students' Union (2002), the Court held that rights and duties are correlative and that duties are as important as rights. Bijoe Emmanuel held that duties cannot override Fundamental Rights. Minerva Mills concerns the FR-DPSP balance. M.K. Ranjitsinh linked CSR to the environmental duty in 51A(g).
n97514fa63a3.tq: Correlative = AIIMS Students' Union, 2002. Duties cannot override rights = Bijoe Emmanuel.
xs: **AIIMS Students' Union (2002)** held rights and duties are **correlative** — FDs as important as FRs — option **(1)**.
**Bijoe Emmanuel (1986)**: duties **cannot override FRs**.
**Minerva Mills** concerns FR-DPSP balance; **M.K. Ranjitsinh** linked **CSR** to **51A(g)**.
xa: Courts use FDs to judge the **reasonableness** of laws.
FDs aim at a **code of conduct** for citizens.

n5d65f95ade6.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a criticism of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They are directly enforceable by courts without legislation
They are not exhaustive and omit matters such as voting and payment of taxes
Their placement as an appendage to Part IV is said to reduce their value
They are vague and ambiguous in several expressions
n5d65f95ade6.x: A is the odd one out: direct court enforcement without legislation is not a criticism, and it is not even true, because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable. Being not exhaustive (voting, taxes left out), placed as an appendage to Part IV, and vague are all recognised criticisms.
n5d65f95ade6.tq: Separate criticism of content and placement from the actual constitutional status of duties.
xs: Being **directly enforceable by courts** is not a criticism — and is untrue, since FDs are **non-justiciable** — option **(1)**.
Real criticisms: **not exhaustive** (omits **voting**, **paying taxes**, family planning).
**Placement** as an **appendage to Part IV** instead of after Part III reduces their value.
**Vague and ambiguous** terms: "noble ideals", "scientific temper", "composite culture".
xa: FDs are also called a "**code of moral precepts**" and **superfluous**.
**Parliament may enforce them by law**; courts use them to interpret laws.
The **Swaran Singh Committee** had proposed a **duty to pay taxes**, which was not accepted.

nbf85ca6a175.s: The description of Fundamental Duties as a ‘code of moral precepts’ is primarily related to their being:
o: Enforceable only during a National Emergency
Placed within Part III as enforceable rights
Non-justiciable and lacking direct constitutional sanctions
nbf85ca6a175.x: Because Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable and do not carry direct constitutional sanctions, they have been described as a code of moral precepts and, by critics, as superfluous.
nbf85ca6a175.tq: Connect a descriptive criticism with the constitutional feature that produces it.
xs: The "**code of moral precepts**" label stems from FDs being **non-justiciable**, with **no direct constitutional sanction** — option **(4)**.
FDs sit in **Part IVA** (**Art. 51A**), not Part III, and bind **every citizen** — so (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Critics also call them **superfluous**.
There is **no legal sanction or penalty** in the Constitution; the Swaran Singh idea of penalties was **not accepted**.
Still, courts may look to FDs when judging the **reasonableness** of a law restricting an FR.

ne1b8cae1202.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised significance of the Fundamental Duties?
o: They help in promoting action against anti-national activities.
They provide an independent constitutional basis for suspending all Fundamental Rights.
They help courts assess the reasonableness of laws.
They remind citizens of their obligations towards the nation.
ne1b8cae1202.x: Fundamental Duties remind citizens of their obligations, assist courts in judging the reasonableness of laws and support action against anti-national activities. They do not provide an independent basis for suspending all Fundamental Rights.
ne1b8cae1202.tq: Find the option that exaggerates the legal effect of Fundamental Duties by using an absolute constitutional claim.
xs: FDs do **not** provide a basis for **suspending all Fundamental Rights** — option **(2)**.
Their recognised significance: they **remind citizens** of obligations, help courts judge **reasonableness** of laws, and act against **anti-national activity**.
Duties **cannot override FRs** (**Bijoe Emmanuel, 1986**).
xa: Aim: a **code of conduct** for citizens, civic virtue and patriotism.
**Parliament may enforce them by law**.
Example: **UAPA 1967** serves **51A(c)** (sovereignty and integrity).

n8a784ea0770.s: Which one of the following is NOT a component of the Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(h)?
o: Protection of monuments of national importance
n8a784ea0770.x: Article 51A(h) covers scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. Protection of monuments is associated with Article 49, a Directive Principle.
n8a784ea0770.tq: Find the look-alike provision placed outside the Fundamental Duties.
xs: **Protection of monuments** is not part of 51A(h) — option **(2)**.
**51A(h)** covers **scientific temper, humanism** and the **spirit of inquiry and reform**.
Protection of **monuments** is DPSP **Art. 49**.
xa: Scientific temper is **only an FD** — no look-alike elsewhere.
51A(h) is a **moral** duty.
Critics call "**scientific temper**" vague.

n29dd29a52eb.s: Environmental protection appears in the Directive Principle Article 48A and in Fundamental Duty:
n29dd29a52eb.x: Environment is in Article 48A and 51A(g); education links Article 45, 21A and 51A(k); heritage links Article 49 and 51A(f).
xa: Sovereignty: **51A(c)** ↔ Preamble "**unity and integrity of the Nation**".
Scientific temper (**51A(h)**) and public property (**51A(i)**) are **only FDs**.

n916cd9ba1da.s: Critics say the Fundamental Duties are not exhaustive because they omit which of the following?
n916cd9ba1da.x: The list does not include duties such as voting, paying taxes and family planning; the flag, environment and scientific temper are already covered.
xa: Other "not a duty" distractor: protecting the **elderly, differently abled and children** (**APPSC G2 2025**, asked twice).
Exam tip: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" — check the list **word for word**.

n10b6bf4f524.s: Which one of the following is NOT a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A?
o: To develop the scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform
To protect the elderly, the differently abled and children
To strive towards excellence in all spheres of individual and collective activity
To safeguard public property and to abjure violence
n10b6bf4f524.x: Protecting the elderly, the differently abled and children is not in Article 51A; APPSC Group 2, 2025 used it twice as the distractor. Scientific temper is 51A(h), striving towards excellence is 51A(j), and safeguarding public property is 51A(i).
n10b6bf4f524.tq: Check the 51A list word for word. Elderly/children, paying taxes, voting and family planning are NOT duties.
xs: Protecting the **elderly, the differently abled and children** is not in Art. 51A — option **(2)**.
**APPSC G2 2025** used this distractor **twice**.
Scientific temper = **51A(h)**; excellence = **51A(j)**; public property = **51A(i)**.
xa: Other distractors: **pay taxes**, **cast a vote**, **family planning**.
Exam tip: "which is not a Fundamental Duty" — check the list **word for word**.

nfcf1f126ae8.s: The constitutional amendment procedure in India was borrowed from which country?
nfcf1f126ae8.x: India borrowed the amendment procedure from South Africa. The method of electing members of the Rajya Sabha was also borrowed from South Africa.
nfcf1f126ae8.tq: Test the source of a constitutional feature while avoiding confusion with countries associated with other federal provisions.
xs: The amendment procedure was borrowed from **South Africa** — option **(2)**.
South Africa also gave the **election of Rajya Sabha members**.
⚠ Not the **US**, whose Constitution is **very rigid**.
xa: India's procedure is partly rigid, partly flexible — unlike the flexible **British** one.
**Granville Austin**: "one of the **most ably conceived aspects**" of the Constitution.
Location: **Part XX, Article 368**.

n3e234057829.s: Which of the following expressions is used in Article 368 to describe Parliament’s constituent power to amend the Constitution?
o: May, in exercise of its judicial power, interpret or repeal any provision
Shall, in exercise of its constituent power, amend every provision by referendum
May, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal any provision
May, in exercise of its legislative power, repeal only those provisions approved by the States
n3e234057829.x: Article 368 states that Parliament may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend the Constitution by way of addition, variation or repeal of any provision, subject to the basic-structure limitation.
n3e234057829.tq: Select the precise constitutional wording and reject substitutions of legislative or judicial power.
xs: Art. 368: Parliament "**may, in exercise of its constituent power, amend by way of addition, variation or repeal** any provision" — option **(3)**.
The power lies with **Parliament** alone — no referendum and no prior State approval, so (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: Limit: Parliament **cannot alter the basic structure** (**Kesavananda Bharati, 1973**).
The amending power includes **Fundamental Rights**, by special majority.
Art. 368 is the **sole Article** of **Part XX**.

n35c09846cb6.s: Who described the constitutional amendment process as appearing 'complicated' but being 'merely diverse'?
n35c09846cb6.x: Granville Austin said the process appears complicated but is merely diverse, calling it one of the most ably conceived aspects of the Constitution.
xa: The procedure is a **synthesis** of rigidity and flexibility.
Three routes: **simple majority**, **special majority**, **special majority + State ratification**.

n3882f8e805c.s: As of 2026, which is the latest constitutional amendment to have been enacted in India?
n3882f8e805c.x: The 106th Amendment (2023) is the latest enacted amendment. The 101st (2016, GST) and 104th (2020) are earlier enactments, and the 131st was only a Bill that failed in the Lok Sabha in April 2026.
n3882f8e805c.tq: Latest enacted = 106th (2023); 129th and 131st are Bills only.
xs: The latest enacted amendment is the **106th Amendment (2023)** — option **(3)**.
The **101st (2016)** is older — it added the **GST Council (Art. 279A)** to the federal list.
The **131st (2026)** was only a **Bill**, negatived in the Lok Sabha on **17 April 2026**.
xa: The **129th Bill, 2024** (simultaneous elections, **Art. 82A**) is with a **Joint Committee**.
The **24th (1971)** made the President's **assent** to amendment bills obligatory.

nindian-polity-23-1.s: Which Article and Part of the Constitution govern the amendment powers and procedure?
nindian-polity-23-1.x: Article 368, in Part XX, gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and sets the procedure. Article 356 is President's Rule and 280 the Finance Commission.
n: Article 368 in Part XX governs the amendment power and procedure of the Indian Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xs: Amendment powers and procedure are in **Article 368 in Part XX** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 368** is the **sole Article** of **Part XX**; Parliament amends "**by way of addition, variation or repeal**".
**Articles 280, 324, 356** are not amendment provisions.
xa: The procedure was borrowed from **South Africa**.
The Constitution is **neither rigid nor flexible but a synthesis of both**.
**Granville Austin**: the process "appears complicated" but "**is merely diverse**".

nda4e335045c.s: Which one of the following best characterises the nature of the Indian constitutional amendment procedure?
o: It is entirely flexible because every provision can be changed by ordinary law.
It is rigid only in matters relating to Fundamental Rights.
It is a synthesis of rigidity and flexibility.
It is entirely rigid because every provision requires State ratification.
nda4e335045c.x: The Indian Constitution combines different methods of amendment and is therefore neither purely rigid nor purely flexible; it is a synthesis of both.
nda4e335045c.tq: Compare the constitutional system as a whole instead of applying one amendment method to every provision.
xs: The procedure is a **synthesis of rigidity and flexibility** — option **(3)**.
It is **neither purely rigid nor purely flexible**: some provisions change by **simple majority**, others by **special majority**, some also need **State ratification**.
Only **federal provisions** need ratification by **half the States** — so (4) is wrong.
xa: Unlike the **very rigid US** Constitution and the **flexible British** one.
**Granville Austin**: the process "**appears complicated**" but "**is merely diverse**".
Source of the procedure: **South Africa**.

n0ea64af1ceb.s: A Bill for amendment of the Constitution may be introduced:
o: By a minister or a private member, without the President's prior permission
Only by a minister, with the President's prior permission
Only after ratification by the States
n0ea64af1ceb.x: An amendment Bill needs no prior presidential permission and may be moved by a private member; Article 108 joint sittings do not apply to it.
xa: Exam angle: "prior permission", "joint sitting" and "President may return" are all **false** for amendment bills.
The President's assent is **obligatory** (**24th Amendment, 1971**).

nf59e7489592.s: The requirement that the President must give assent to a constitutional amendment bill was made obligatory by the:
nf59e7489592.x: The 24th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971 made the President's assent to a constitutional amendment bill obligatory.
nf59e7489592.tq: Match the precise amendment with the specific procedural change rather than the more famous 42nd or 44th Amendments.
xs: The **24th Amendment Act, 1971** made the President's **assent** to amendment bills obligatory — option **(1)**.
The 24th answered **Golaknath (1967)** and restored Parliament's power to amend FRs.
xa: It amended **Arts. 13 and 368** and inserted **Art. 13(4)**: an Art. 368 amendment is not "law" under Art. 13.
The **42nd (1976)** later inserted **368(4) and (5)**, struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

nd444aa1ee89.s: What time limit is prescribed for State ratification of an amendment affecting specified federal provisions?
nd444aa1ee89.x: State ratification is needed only for specified federal provisions, not every amendment, and no time limit is prescribed for it.
xa: Ratification by **simple majority** of each State Legislature.
**FRs** need only special majority — no ratification.

nd7ff850e660.s: Which of the following is NOT a criticism commonly made of the constitutional amendment procedure in India?
o: A joint sitting is available to resolve a deadlock between the two Houses on an amendment Bill.
There is no time limit for State ratification.
There is no special constitutional body or referendum for amendments.
nd7ff850e660.x: The Constitution provides no joint sitting mechanism for resolving a deadlock between the Houses on an amendment Bill. The other three are recognised criticisms of the procedure.
nd7ff850e660.tq: Look for the proposition that reverses an actual criticism by asserting that a safeguard exists.
xs: The claim that a **joint sitting is available** for a deadlock on an amendment bill is false — option **(2)**.
In fact the criticism is that there is **no joint sitting** to resolve such a deadlock.
Real criticisms: States **cannot initiate**, **no time limit** for ratification, **no special body** or referendum.
xa: Ratification is needed only for a **few provisions**.
2026 vote: special majority protects against a **slim majority**.

nindian-polity-21-12.s: A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed by a special majority in:
o: A joint sitting of both Houses
The Lok Sabha, with recommendations from the Rajya Sabha
nindian-polity-21-12.x: An amendment Bill can start in either House without the President's recommendation and needs a special majority in each House separately; there is no joint sitting.
n: A Constitution Amendment Bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill must be passed separately by each House by a special majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill cannot be passed through a Joint Sitting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Constitution Amendment Bill does not require the President’s prior recommendation for introduction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting under Article 108 is not applicable to a Constitution Amendment Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: Special majority = majority of **total membership** + **two-thirds** present and voting.
A **private member** may move it; a **State Legislature** cannot introduce one.
The President **must** give assent — made mandatory by the **24th Amendment (1971)**.

nindian-polity-21-15.s: In case of a deadlock between the two Houses over an Ordinary Bill, the Constitution provides for:
o: Passage by the Lok Sabha alone
A final decision by the President
nindian-polity-21-15.x: An ordinary Bill needs a simple majority, both Houses have equal powers over it, and a deadlock can go to a joint sitting.
n: The Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha have equal legislative powers over an Ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
An Ordinary Bill is passed by a simple majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Joint Sitting is possible for an Ordinary Bill in case of a deadlock. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider an Ordinary Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: A **Money Bill** originates in the **Lok Sabha only**; Rajya Sabha gives only **recommendations** within **14 days**.
A **Money Bill** has **no joint sitting**.
An **Amendment Bill** needs a **special** majority and has **no joint sitting**.

nindian-polity-23-6.s: Amendments to specified federal provisions require ratification by:
o: At least one-half of the State Legislatures
nindian-polity-23-6.x: Federal provisions need ratification by at least half the States; the President's qualifications and tenure need no ratification.
n: Federal provisions require a special majority and ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Federal ratification requires a simple majority of at least half of the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Federal ratification does not require ratification by all States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The qualifications of the President do not require State ratification. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The conditions of the President’s office do not require State ratification. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The tenure of the President does not require State ratification. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: Ratification is by **simple majority** in each State Legislature, with **no time limit**.
Federal provisions include **election of the President**, **Seventh Schedule** Lists, **Supreme Court and High Courts**, **Article 368** itself.
States **cannot initiate** constitutional amendments.

n30bd6911c7b.s: A special majority for amending the Constitution means:
o: Three-fourths of the members present and voting in each House
Two-thirds of the total membership of each House
A majority of the total membership of each House and two-thirds of members present and voting
A majority of members present and voting in a joint sitting
n30bd6911c7b.x: Special majority combines two requirements in each House: a majority of the total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting.
n30bd6911c7b.tq: Do not substitute two-thirds of total membership or a joint sitting for the two-part constitutional formula.
xs: Special majority = a **majority of the total membership** of each House + **two-thirds of members present and voting** — option **(3)**.
It applies in **each House separately**; there is **no joint sitting** — so (4) is wrong.
**Two-thirds of total membership** (2) is the **Art. 61** type — impeachment of the President.
xa: Art. 368 type also used for removal of **SC/HC judges** (**124, 217**), **CAG (148)**, **CEC (324)**, **SEC (243K)**, approval of **National Emergency (352)**.
**Art. 249/312** type: two-thirds present and voting in the **Rajya Sabha only**.

n7b2ce984996.s: Which of the following requires a special majority of Parliament along with ratification by at least half of the State Legislatures?
n7b2ce984996.x: The Seventh Schedule, the President's election and representation of States need State ratification; Fundamental Rights need only a special majority.
xa: Other federal items: **executive power** (**73, 162**), **Supreme Court and High Courts**, **Art. 368 itself**.
**GST Council (Art. 279A)** was added by the **101st Amendment (2016)**.
Ratification: **not less than half of the States**, by **simple majority**, **no time limit**.

nf74552fc78b.s: Which one of the following subjects is amended by a simple majority of Parliament outside the procedure of Article 368?
nf74552fc78b.x: Quorum is among the matters that can be altered by a simple majority outside Article 368. Fundamental Rights and DPSPs require the special majority procedure, while the election of the President also requires State ratification.
nf74552fc78b.tq: Use the amendment-method classification to identify the simple-majority exception.
xs: **Quorum in Parliament** is changed by **simple majority**, outside Art. 368 — option **(4)**.
**FRs** and **DPSPs** need a **special majority** under Art. 368.
**Election of the President** also needs **State ratification**.
xa: Other simple-majority items: **salaries of MPs**, **privileges**, **citizenship (11)**, **official language (343)**, **Fifth and Sixth Schedules**.
Such changes are **not deemed amendments** under Art. 368.

n0041f387500.s: Creation or abolition of a State Legislative Council under Article 169 requires:
o: A simple majority of Parliament, outside Article 368
A special majority plus ratification by half of the States
A special majority of the State Legislature only
n0041f387500.x: Legislative Councils are dealt with by simple majority outside Article 368; the President's election needs special majority plus State ratification.
xa: States can only pass a **resolution** asking Parliament to create/abolish a Council.

n195d712c8b3.s: Which of the following can NOT be changed by Parliament by a simple majority outside Article 368?
o: Formation of new States and alteration of their boundaries
Creation or abolition of Legislative Councils in States
The basic structure of the Constitution
Change in the official language under Article 343
n195d712c8b3.x: The basic structure cannot be amended even by the special procedure; the other three are simple-majority matters outside Article 368.
xa: Also simple majority: **use of English in Parliament**, **Fifth and Sixth Schedules**, **Union Territories**.

ne8d8b542ac9.s: Which one of the following is NOT a provision that may be amended by a simple majority outside Article 368?
o: The distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States
The number of puisne judges of the Supreme Court
ne8d8b542ac9.x: The distribution of legislative powers, including the Seventh Schedule, is a federal provision requiring the prescribed State ratification. Citizenship, the Fifth and Sixth Schedules and the number of puisne judges of the Supreme Court are amendable by simple majority.
ne8d8b542ac9.tq: Find the federal provision that does not belong to the ordinary-law category.
xs: The **distribution of legislative powers** is not a simple-majority item — option **(1)**.
It is a **federal provision** (**any List of the Seventh Schedule**) needing **State ratification**.
**Citizenship (11)**, **puisne judges of the SC**, **Fifth and Sixth Schedules** change by **simple majority**.
xa: Other federal items: **election of the President** (**54, 55**), **executive power** (**73, 162**), **Fourth Schedule**.
Ratification: **one-half of the States**, **simple majority**, **no time limit**.

n61bff1f62c6.s: Which of the following can be changed by Parliament by a simple majority outside Article 368?
n61bff1f62c6.x: Quorum, MPs' salaries and parliamentary privileges are simple-majority matters outside Article 368; the others need a special majority.
xa: **Emoluments**: **Second Schedule**.
**Number of puisne judges of the SC** also changes by simple majority.

ne9c372a3a36.s: Which one of the following was added to the category of provisions requiring State ratification by the Constitution (101st Amendment) Act, 2016?
ne9c372a3a36.x: The 101st Amendment Act, 2016 added Article 279A relating to the GST Council to the federal provisions requiring State ratification.
ne9c372a3a36.tq: Use the amendment-year association and distinguish the GST Council from other constitutional bodies.
xs: The **101st Amendment (2016)** added the **GST Council (Art. 279A)** to the ratification list — option **(2)**.
It did so by amending **Art. 368**.
xa: Other federal items: **election of the President** (**54, 55**), **executive power** (**73, 162**), **Seventh Schedule**.
Latest enacted amendment = **106th (2023)**.

n45469783125.s: The majority required for the impeachment of the President of India is
o: Two-thirds of the total membership of the House concerned
Two-thirds of the members present and voting in both Houses
Majority of the total membership and two-thirds of members present and voting in both Houses
Three-fourths of the total membership of Parliament
n45469783125.x: Under the Article 61 type of majority, impeachment of the President requires two-thirds of the total membership of the House concerned.
n45469783125.tq: Watch for the distinction between total membership and members present and voting.
xs: Impeachment of the President needs **two-thirds of the total membership** of the House — option **(1)**.
This **Art. 61** type is the **strongest majority**.
xa: ⚠ **61** = two-thirds of total membership; **249/312** = two-thirds present and voting, **Rajya Sabha only**; **368** = both Houses, total + two-thirds.
Art. 368 type is used for removal of **SC/HC judges**, **CAG**, **CEC**, and approval of a **National Emergency (352)**.

nfe7f719f672.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the constitutional amendment procedure?
o: Ratification by the States is required for every amendment
No outside convention or special body is required
Parliament alone can amend most provisions
States cannot initiate an amendment under Article 368
nfe7f719f672.x: State ratification is required only for a limited group of federal provisions, not for every amendment.
xa: Other criticisms: **no joint sitting**; **no time limit** for ratification.
Critics say **simple-majority** routes are too easy.

nb607dccdae5.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the President's role after a constitutional amendment bill has been duly passed?
o: The President must give assent and can neither withhold nor return the bill.
The President may refer the bill to a joint sitting of Parliament.
The President may return the bill once for reconsideration.
The President may withhold assent on grounds of public interest.
nb607dccdae5.x: The President's assent to a duly passed constitutional amendment bill is obligatory. The President can neither withhold assent nor return the bill for reconsideration; this position was made mandatory by the 24th Amendment Act, 1971.
nb607dccdae5.tq: Use the constitutional-assent distinction: amendment bills are not subject to the ordinary return or withholding choice.
xs: The President **must give assent** and can **neither withhold nor return** the bill — option **(1)**.
Assent was made obligatory by the **24th Amendment, 1971**.
There is **no joint sitting** for amendment bills — so (2) is wrong.
xa: No **prior presidential sanction** is needed to introduce the bill either.
The bill passes each House **separately** by **special majority**.
Federal provisions also need ratification by **half the States**.

nindian-polity-21-24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about presidential action on Bills?
o: The President may return a Money Bill once for reconsideration
The President may return an Ordinary Bill once
The President may withhold assent to an Ordinary Bill
The President may withhold assent to a Money Bill
nindian-polity-21-24.x: A Money Bill can be assented to or withheld but never returned; only an ordinary Bill can be returned once.
n: The President may assent to, withhold assent from, or return an Ordinary Bill once. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President may assent to or withhold assent from a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The President cannot return a Money Bill. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: **Amendment Bill**: the President **must give assent** — **no veto**, no power to return.
Mandatory assent was added by the **24th Amendment (1971)**.
A Money Bill needs the President's **prior recommendation**; an Amendment Bill does **not**.

nindian-polity-21-33.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the passage of Bills?
o: A Money Bill originates only in the Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha may only make recommendations
An Ordinary Bill may originate in either House, with equal powers for the Rajya Sabha
A Financial Bill (I) can only be recommended on, not rejected or amended, by the Rajya Sabha
A Constitution Amendment Bill may originate in either House and must pass each House separately
nindian-polity-21-33.x: A Financial Bill (I) originates only in the Lok Sabha, but the Rajya Sabha has full power to reject or amend it.
n: A Financial Bill (I) may be introduced only in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has full power to reject a Financial Bill (I). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has full power to amend a Financial Bill (I). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for an Ordinary Bill may be the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for a Money Bill is the Lok Sabha only. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The House of origin for a Constitution Amendment Bill may be the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has equal powers over an Ordinary Bill and may amend or reject it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on a Money Bill, and its consideration is limited to 14 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
The Rajya Sabha has equal powers over a Constitution Amendment Bill, which must be passed separately by both Houses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
An Ordinary Bill may originate in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: Money Bills: **Arts. 109 and 110**; Ordinary: **107 and 108**; Amendment: **368**.
Rajya Sabha has **14 days** for a Money Bill; **no fixed time limit** for an Ordinary Bill.
**Joint sitting** (**Art. 108**) only for Ordinary Bills.

o: A special majority plus ratification by half the States
A special majority of Parliament without State ratification
No procedure, as it cannot be amended at all
n8edc0e72267.x: Article 32 may be amended by special majority without State ratification, though the Supreme Court's power under it is part of the basic structure.
xa: **PYQ G2 2017** key: Art. 32 needs a "**two-thirds majority**".
All **FRs** (incl. Art. 32) and **DPSPs** fall in the special-majority route.

n0b9f4ce8a6e.s: The Supreme Court’s decision in Rajendra N. Shah (2021) is associated with which of the following?
o: Striking down Part IXB in its entirety for violating the federal structure without any further qualification
Invalidating the GST Council under Article 279A
Declaring the 24th Amendment unconstitutional for abridging Fundamental Rights
Striking down the provisions relating to State co-operative societies in Part IXB for want of ratification by the States
n0b9f4ce8a6e.x: In Rajendra N. Shah (2021), the provisions of Part IXB relating to State co-operative societies were struck down for want of ratification by the required number of States.
n0b9f4ce8a6e.tq: Match the judgment with the precise constitutional defect rather than the broad subject of federalism.
xs: **Rajendra N. Shah (2021)** struck down the **State co-operative** provisions of **Part IXB** for **want of ratification** — option **(4)**.
Part IXB came with the **97th Amendment**.
The **GST Council (Art. 279A)** was added to the federal list by the **101st (2016)** — not invalidated.
xa: Federal provisions need ratification by **half the States**, by simple majority.
Limits chain: **Shankari Prasad (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → 24th (1971) → Kesavananda (1973)**.

n75d04b498e8.s: What was the effect of the Constitution (24th Amendment) Act, 1971 on Articles 13 and 368?
o: It declared every constitutional amendment to be ordinary law under Article 13.
It empowered Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), excluding an Article 368 amendment from the term ‘law’ in Article 13.
It prohibited Parliament from amending Fundamental Rights and removed Article 368.
It made all constitutional amendments subject to approval by a national referendum.
n75d04b498e8.x: The 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368, empowered Parliament to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights and inserted Article 13(4), under which an amendment made under Article 368 is not ‘law’ for Article 13.
n75d04b498e8.tq: Test the paired effects of one amendment instead of confusing it with the later basic-structure judgments.
xs: The 24th **empowered Parliament to amend FRs** and inserted **Art. 13(4)** — option **(2)**.
It amended **Arts. 13 and 368** → Parliament can **abridge or take away** any FR.
Art. 13(4): an Art. 368 amendment is **not "law"** under Art. 13 — so (1) is wrong.
xa: It answered **Golaknath (1967)**.
It made the President's assent **obligatory**.

nbb03dbb32ba.s: The Kesavananda Bharati judgment upheld which Constitutional Amendment?
nbb03dbb32ba.x: Kesavananda Bharati upheld the 24th Amendment and held that FRs and the Preamble are amendable but the basic structure cannot be altered.
xa: ⚠ **Kesavananda** propounded the limit; **Indira Gandhi (1975)** first applied it.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: **limited amending power** is itself a basic feature.

n88ba159f901.s: Which case first applied the basic-structure doctrine?
n88ba159f901.x: Kesavananda Bharati first propounded the doctrine and Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain first applied it; Golaknath first limited the amending power over FRs.
xa: **Shankari Prasad (1951)** had held FRs amendable.
The **24th (1971)** restored the power after Golaknath.

nf6ad1caf0e7.s: The amendment procedure of the Constitution of India is:
o: A combination of rigidity and flexibility
Wholly flexible, with every provision amendable by simple majority
nf6ad1caf0e7.x: The procedure combines rigidity and flexibility, and the basic-structure limitation permits judicial review of amendments.
xa: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**: Parliament **cannot alter the basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)**: **limited amending power** is itself a basic feature.
**Granville Austin**: the process "**appears complicated**" but "**is merely diverse**".

nindian-polity-67-12.s: Which case(s) held that constitutional amendments are not 'law' under Article 13(2)?
nindian-polity-67-12.x: Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh held so; Golaknath barred abridging FRs, Kesavananda allowed amendment within the basic structure, and Minerva Mills held limited amending power basic.
n: Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh held that ordinary law under Article 13(2) does not include constitutional amendments made under Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Golaknath held that a constitutional amendment is law under Article 13(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Golaknath held that Parliament cannot abridge or take away any Fundamental Right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Kesavananda Bharati held that Parliament cannot damage or destroy the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Minerva Mills (1980) reaffirmed that a limited amending power is itself a Basic Feature of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
The statement that Fundamental Rights can never be amended after Kesavananda is false. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Chain: **Shankari Prasad 1951** = yes; **Golaknath 1967** = no; **Kesavananda 1973** = yes, but not the basic structure.
The **24th Amendment (1971)** restored the power after Golaknath.
**Indira Gandhi (1975)** first applied the doctrine.

n08ca829b75b.s: If either House of Parliament rejects a Constitutional Amendment Bill:
o: A joint sitting is summoned to resolve it
n08ca829b75b.x: There is no joint sitting for a Constitutional Amendment Bill, so rejection by either House causes failure; once duly passed, assent is obligatory under the 24th Amendment.
xa: Criticism: there is no mechanism to resolve a **deadlock** between Houses on an amendment.
The President can neither **withhold** nor **return** the bill.

neb94fcbdb15.s: Changes relating to Articles 2, 3 and 169 of the Constitution can be made by:
o: A special majority plus ratification by half the States
A simple majority, without being deemed amendments under Article 368
neb94fcbdb15.x: Changes under Articles 2, 3 and 169 are made by simple majority and are not deemed amendments under Article 368; the Constitution has both flexible and rigid methods.
xa: Other simple-majority items: **citizenship (11)**, **official language (343)**, **delimitation (327)**.
⚠ Exam: "Which is NOT amended by special majority?" — official language, citizenship, **Fifth/Sixth Schedule**.

n349f795d7ee.s: The Article 368 type of special majority is relevant to which one of the following sets of provisions?
n349f795d7ee.x: The Article 368 type of majority is used for removal of Supreme Court and High Court judges, the CAG, the CEC and State Election Commissioners, constitutional amendment, and approval of a National Emergency. The relevant provisions include Articles 124, 217, 148, 324, 243K and 352.
n349f795d7ee.tq: Use the provision-number cluster to distinguish the Article 368 category from Articles 249, 312 and 61.
xs: **Articles 124, 217, 148, 324, 243K and 352** use the Art. 368 type — option **(3)**.
Removal of **SC/HC judges** (124, 217), **CAG** (148), **CEC** (324), **SEC** (243K); **National Emergency** approval (352).
**249, 312** need Rajya Sabha two-thirds only; **61** needs two-thirds of total membership — so (1), (2), (4) are wrong.
xa: Art. 368 type = majority of **total membership** + **2/3 present and voting**, each House.
Art. 61 type (**two-thirds of total membership**) is for **impeachment of the President**.

n3feb16e2d69.s: A constitutional amendment bill received 298 votes in favour and 230 against out of 528 members present and voting. What is the correct conclusion, assuming the other requirement of special majority is satisfied?
o: It failed because two-thirds of 528 is 352.
It passed because it secured more than half of the votes cast.
It must be referred to a joint sitting for final approval.
It passed because 298 is more than two-thirds of the total membership.
n3feb16e2d69.x: Two-thirds of 528 is 352. Since the bill received only 298 votes in favour, it did not secure the required two-thirds majority of members present and voting and therefore failed.
n3feb16e2d69.tq: Calculate two-thirds of members present and voting; a simple majority is insufficient for a constitutional amendment.
xs: The bill **failed** because two-thirds of **528** is **352** — option **(1)**.
It got only **298** votes — short of two-thirds of members **present and voting**.
A simple majority is not enough, so (2) is wrong; there is **no joint sitting** for amendment bills, so (3) is wrong.
xa: This was the **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** (Lok Sabha **550 → 850**), **negatived** on **17 April 2026**.
⚠ **298** for vs **352** needed = two-thirds of **528** present and voting.
The **129th Bill, 2024** (simultaneous elections, **Art. 82A**) was referred to a **Joint Committee**.

n462cd78a69e.s: The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024, which proposes a new Article 82A, relates to which of the following?
o: Simultaneous elections to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies
Reservation of one-third seats for women in the Lok Sabha
Increase in the strength of the Lok Sabha to 850
Removal of the Prime Minister and Chief Ministers on arrest
n462cd78a69e.x: The 129th Amendment Bill, 2024 concerns simultaneous elections and proposes a new Article 82A; it was referred to a Joint Committee. Women's reservation is the 106th Amendment (2023); raising Lok Sabha strength to 850 was the 131st Bill, 2026; removal of PM/CMs on arrest is a separate pending proposal.
n462cd78a69e.tq: 129th = One Nation One Election, Art. 82A, Joint Committee.
xs: The **129th Amendment Bill, 2024** proposes a new **Art. 82A** for **simultaneous elections** to the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies — option **(1)**.
It was referred to a **Joint Committee** (**2026**).
Raising Lok Sabha strength to **850** was the **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** — so (3) is wrong.
xa: The 131st Bill (**550 → 850**, delimitation) was **negatived** in the Lok Sabha on **17 April 2026**.
The **Delimitation Bill, 2026** was **withdrawn** on **20 Apr 2026**.
Latest enacted amendment = **106th (2023)**.

n81893dddc5d.s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 proposed raising the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to:
n81893dddc5d.x: It sought 850 seats with delimitation but failed in the Lok Sabha on 17 April 2026 (298 for, short of the 352 needed); there is no joint sitting for amendment Bills.
xa: Failure in **either House** makes an amendment bill **lapse**.
Special majority = majority of **total membership** + **two-thirds present and voting**, in each House **separately**.
The **Delimitation Bill, 2026** was **withdrawn** on **20 Apr 2026**.

n4c0400548b8.s: The provisions relating to Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule were introduced into the Constitution by which Constitutional Amendment?
n4c0400548b8.x: The First Amendment Act, 1951 introduced Articles 31A and 31B and added the Ninth Schedule. It also amended the grounds of restriction under Article 19(2) and inserted Article 15(4).
n4c0400548b8.tq: Use the amendment-to-subject association rather than relying on the sequence of amendment numbers.
xs: **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule** came with the **1st Amendment, 1951** — option **(2)**.
The **25th (1971)** brought **Art. 31C**; the **24th (1971)** let Parliament amend FRs; the **7th (1956)** reorganised States.
xa: The 1st also added **Art. 19(2)** grounds, **Art. 15(4)** and protected State monopoly under **Art. 19(6)**.
It was enacted by the **Provisional Parliament** under PM **Nehru**.
Its validity was upheld in **Shankari Prasad (1951)**.

n5334ebc5023.s: Which one of the following was a major feature of the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956?
o: Creation of the National Capital Territory of Delhi
Reorganisation of States and abolition of the former Part A, Part B, Part C and Part D classification
n5334ebc5023.x: The Seventh Amendment, 1956 accompanied the reorganisation of States, abolished the Part A, B, C and D classification, repealed Part VII and dealt with Union Territories.
n5334ebc5023.tq: Match the amendment with its distinctive structural change and reject provisions belonging to later amendments.
xs: The **7th Amendment (1956)** carried out **States reorganisation** and abolished the **Part A/B/C/D** classification — option **(4)**.
It also **repealed Part VII**.
The Ninth Schedule is the **1st (1951)**; anti-defection the **52nd (1985)**; Delhi as NCT the **69th (1991)**.
xa: Other notes describe it as **Schedule VII repealed**.
Delhi's NCT status: **Arts. 239AA, 239AB**.

n15fc3c7cb3a.x: The 24th Amendment inserted Article 13(4), clarified Parliament's power to amend FRs and made presidential assent to amendment Bills obligatory.
xa: The **25th (1971)** replaced "compensation" with "**amount**" and inserted **Art. 31C**.
Both came in **1971**; the **42nd (1976)** followed as the "**Mini-Constitution**".

n78a00dd6e79.s: Articles 239AA and 239AB, providing Delhi's special constitutional framework, were inserted by the:
n78a00dd6e79.x: The 69th Amendment gave Delhi its framework; the 52nd introduced the Tenth Schedule and the 86th inserted Article 21A.
xa: The 86th also gave a new **Art. 45** and duty **51A(k)**.
The 52nd touched **Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191**.

n154d993bfb9.s: Which Constitutional Amendment substituted the word 'amount' for 'compensation' in Article 31 and inserted Article 31C?
n154d993bfb9.x: The 25th Amendment (1971), after the Bank Nationalisation case, replaced 'compensation' with 'amount' in Article 31 and inserted Article 31C. The 24th (1971) dealt with Parliament's power to amend FRs and Art. 13(4); the 42nd widened Art. 31C; the 44th removed property from Part III.
xs: The **25th Amendment (1971)** put "**amount**" for "compensation" in **Art. 31** and inserted **Art. 31C** — option **(2)**.
It followed the **Bank Nationalisation** case.
The **24th** let Parliament amend FRs (**Art. 13(4)**); the **44th** took property out of Part III.
xa: The **42nd (1976)** widened 31C — **DPSPs given primacy over FRs**.
The **44th (1978)** made property a **legal right** under **Art. 300A, Part XII**.

n2980b801e9b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the rulings overcome by the First Amendment?
o: Kameshwar Singh v. State of Bihar concerned zamindari abolition / land reform
Articles 31A and 31B were the direct response to Champakam Dorairajan
Romesh Thappar (1950) concerned freedom of speech
Champakam Dorairajan concerned a communal order in admissions, leading to Article 15(4)
n2980b801e9b.x: Champakam Dorairajan led to Article 15(4); Articles 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule answered the land-reform judgments.
xa: The 1st Amendment answered land-reform rulings with **Arts. 31A, 31B** and the **Ninth Schedule**.

n17bc40348dc.s:
Which of the following words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment?
1. Socialist
2. Justice
3. Integrity
n17bc40348dc.x: The 42nd Amendment added 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'Integrity'. 'Justice' was already in the original Preamble.
xa: "Socialist" and "secular" are still contested; the SC holds **secularism was always basic** (**Jul 2025**).
The 42nd also inserted **Part IVA, Art. 51A** (**10** duties).

n6b40b503480.s: Which of the following was transferred from the State List to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment?
n6b40b503480.x: The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice to the Concurrent List.
xa: The 42nd also changed the **Seventh Schedule** as part of the "Mini-Constitution".
It gave **DPSPs primacy over FRs** through a wider **Art. 31C**.

n0c0682de4c5.s: The constitutional provisions relating to the Six-Point Formula and the Central University in Andhra Pradesh (Articles 371D and 371E) were inserted by which amendment?
n0c0682de4c5.x: The AP-specific reference identifies the 32nd Amendment Act of 1973 as having inserted Articles 371D and 371E relating to the Six-Point Formula and the Central University. A conflicting reference to the 33rd Amendment is ambiguous and is not the applicable identification here.
n0c0682de4c5.tq: Match the amendment number with the Articles and the regional constitutional subject.
xs: The **32nd Amendment (1973)** inserted **Arts. 371D and 371E** — option **(1)**.
371D: **Six-Point Formula**; 371E: **Central University**.
⚠ Trap: CDX AP History says "**33rd**" — some notes follow it.
xa: The **36th (1975)** dealt with **Sikkim**.
The **35th (1974)** gave Sikkim **associate status**.
n0c0682de4c5.fixed: drop meta phrase 'as identified in the AP-specific reference'

nindian-polity-23-9.s: Privy purses were abolished by the:
nindian-polity-23-9.x: The 26th abolished privy purses; the 24th made presidential assent compulsory, the 44th removed property from FRs and the 52nd added anti-defection law.
n: The 24th Amendment of 1971 made Presidential assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill mandatory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 26th Amendment abolished the privy purses of former princely state rulers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 44th Amendment removed the Right to Property from the Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 52nd Amendment introduced the Anti-Defection Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **24th (1971)** also affirmed Parliament's power to **amend Fundamental Rights**.
Property is now a legal right under **Article 300A**.
The **25th (1971)** substituted "**amount**" for "compensation" and inserted **Art. 31C**.

nindian-polity-23-20.s: Which provision added by the First Amendment, 1951 validates Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule?
nindian-polity-23-20.x: Article 31B validates Ninth Schedule Acts; Article 31A saves estate-acquisition laws and Article 15(4) permits special provisions for backward classes, SCs and STs.
n: The 1st Amendment added the 9th Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 1st Amendment added Articles 31A and 31B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 1st Amendment added Article 15(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 1st Amendment protected agrarian and land reforms from judicial review. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **1st Amendment** received assent on **18 June 1951** from President **Rajendra Prasad**.
It was enacted by the **Provisional Parliament** under PM **Nehru**.
It overcame **Kameshwar Singh**, **Champakam Dorairajan** and **Romesh Thappar**; upheld in **Shankari Prasad (1951)**.

n8a6328c8a06.s: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act was introduced in the Lok Sabha in:
n8a6328c8a06.x: The Constitution (Forty-second Amendment) Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in September 1976 during the Emergency period.
n8a6328c8a06.tq: Read the question as a precise date-recall item rather than confusing introduction with enactment.
xs: The 42nd Amendment Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha in **September 1976** — option **(4)** (**PYQ 2019**).
It was passed during the **Emergency**, under PM **Indira Gandhi**.
xa: Called the "**Mini-Constitution**" — changed the Preamble, Seventh Schedule and **54** articles.
The **44th (1978)** undid many of its changes.

nc961e0d527b.s: Which one of the following was a change made by the Forty-second Constitutional Amendment?
o: Extension of the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from five to six years
Abolition of tribunals under Part XIVA
Reduction of the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies to four years
Removal of Article 368 from the Constitution
nc961e0d527b.x: The 42nd Amendment extended the term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies from five to six years. It also inserted Part XIVA relating to tribunals and froze delimitation on the basis of the 1971 Census.
nc961e0d527b.tq: Use the reversed-term trap: the 42nd extended, rather than reduced, legislative terms.
xs: The 42nd **extended the term** of the Lok Sabha and Assemblies **from five to six years** — option **(1)**.
It **created** (not abolished) **Part XIVA** tribunals (**323A, 323B**).
It made Art. 368 amendments **non-justiciable** via **368(4)-(5)** — it did not remove Art. 368.
xa: It froze delimitation on the **1971 Census**.
⚠ **42nd** term = **6 years**; the **44th** restored **5-year** terms.

n082338dc19e.s: Which Constitutional Amendment restored the five-year term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies after the Forty-second Amendment had extended it to six years?
n082338dc19e.x: The Forty-fourth Amendment, 1978 restored the normal five-year term of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies and restored judicial review in important respects.
n082338dc19e.tq: Distinguish the two post-Emergency amendments by the specific excess each addressed.
xs: The **44th Amendment (1978)** restored the **five-year** term — option **(3)**.
It also restored **judicial review**.
xa: It was enacted by the **Janata government** (PM **Morarji Desai**).
It was a corrective to the **38th**, **39th** and **42nd**.
The 44th is called the "**saviour**" of Emergency safeguards.

n1426054c0c8.s: Which Amendment enabled a National Emergency to be proclaimed in only a part of India?
n1426054c0c8.x: The 42nd Amendment enabled Emergency in a part of India; it also inserted Part IVA (Fundamental Duties) and Part XIVA (tribunals).
xa: It also raised LS/Assembly terms to **6 years**.

n6d70cec1356.s: Who can disapprove or revoke a Proclamation of Emergency under the safeguard associated with the Forty-fourth Amendment?
n6d70cec1356.x: The Forty-fourth Amendment strengthened the power of the Lok Sabha to disapprove or revoke a Proclamation of Emergency.
n6d70cec1356.tq: Identify the institution specifically empowered to check executive continuation of Emergency.
xs: The **Lok Sabha** can **disapprove or revoke** an Emergency — option **(1)**.
This was a **44th Amendment** safeguard.
xa: Proclamation needs a **written Cabinet recommendation** (**PYQ 2025**).
Approval within **one month** by **special majority** of each House.
**Arts. 20 and 21** cannot be suspended.

n07a36cd13b2.s: With reference to the right to property after the Forty-fourth Amendment, which one of the following is correct?
o: It remains a Fundamental Right under Article 31.
It became a legal right under Article 300A.
It was made a Directive Principle under Article 39.
It was abolished completely from the Constitution.
n07a36cd13b2.x: Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 were deleted, and the right to property was retained as a legal right under Article 300A in Part XII.
n07a36cd13b2.tq: Separate Fundamental Rights from legal rights by checking the Article number.
xs: Property became a **legal right under Article 300A** — option **(2)**.
The **44th (1978)** deleted **Arts. 19(1)(f) and 31** from the FRs.
Art. 300A sits in **Part XII** — the right was not abolished.
xa: **APPSC-G2 2025** A-R on this: both true, R explains A.
The **25th (1971)** had earlier replaced "compensation" with "**amount**" in Art. 31.

n0ad0d3d1f3a.s: The Forty-fourth Amendment restored the power of courts to hear election disputes relating to which set of offices?
o: President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker of the Lok Sabha
President, Governor, Prime Minister and Chief Justice of India
Vice-President, Chief Minister, Speaker and Attorney-General
President, Vice-President, Governors and Chief Ministers
n0ad0d3d1f3a.x: It reversed the bar created by the Thirty-ninth Amendment and restored judicial consideration of election disputes concerning the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker.
n0ad0d3d1f3a.tq: Use the office-combination to distinguish the Forty-fourth Amendment from the Thirty-ninth Amendment.
xs: Courts could again hear election disputes of the **President, Vice-President, Prime Minister and Speaker** — option **(1)**.
The **44th** reversed the **39th Amendment**'s bar on courts hearing these disputes.
xa: The 44th was a corrective to the **38th**, **39th** and **42nd**.
**38th, 39th, 42nd** are called the **most controversial** amendments.

nd4e7dddef78.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Emergency safeguards of the 44th Amendment Act, 1978?
o: A National Emergency can be proclaimed only on the written recommendation of the Union Cabinet
'Armed rebellion' replaced 'internal disturbance' as a ground
The Proclamation must be approved by Parliament within one month
Rights under Articles 20 and 21 can be suspended during an Emergency by Presidential order
nd4e7dddef78.x: After the 44th Amendment, Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during an Emergency.
xa: Approval within **one month** by **special majority** of each House.
The **Lok Sabha** can disapprove/revoke the Proclamation.

nindian-polity-22-8.s: Which Constitutional Amendment is known as the 'Mini-Constitution'?
nindian-polity-22-8.x: The 42nd Amendment made sweeping changes, such as adding Fundamental Duties and 'Socialist, Secular and Integrity' to the Preamble.
n: The 42nd Amendment is known as the Mini-Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The 42nd Amendment inserted Fundamental Duties. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Fundamental Duties were inserted as Part IVA. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The Fundamental Duties were inserted under Article 51A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The 42nd Amendment added Socialist to the Preamble. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The 42nd Amendment added Secular to the Preamble. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
The 42nd Amendment added Integrity to the Preamble. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 52-55]
xa: PYQ **2025** key: A and R both true, R explains A.
It moved **Education, Forests, Weights and measures** to the **Concurrent List**.
It made **Council of Ministers'** advice **completely binding** on the President.
⚠ **42nd** term = **6 years**; **44th** restored the **5-year** term.

nindian-polity-23-11.s: Which Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground for National Emergency?
nindian-polity-23-11.x: The 44th Amendment made this change and also let the President return ministerial advice once.
n: The 44th Amendment replaced the expression “internal disturbance” with “armed rebellion.” [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 44th Amendment allowed the President to return the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **44th (1978)** was enacted by the **Janata government** (PM **Morarji Desai**).
Emergency now needs a **written recommendation of the Union Cabinet**.
**Arts. 20 and 21** cannot be suspended during an Emergency.

nindian-polity-23-24.s: Part XIV-A, added by the 42nd Amendment, deals with:
nindian-polity-23-24.x: The 42nd Amendment added Part XIV-A on tribunals, listed Fundamental Duties in Article 51A and shifted education to the Concurrent List.
n: The 42nd Amendment added ten Fundamental Duties. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 42nd Amendment added Directive Principles of State Policy under Articles 39A and 43A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 42nd Amendment shifted Education to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 42nd Amendment added Part XIV-A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The 42nd added **Socialist, Secular** and **Integrity** to the Preamble.
**Forests**, **Weights and measures** and **Wild animals and birds** also went to the Concurrent List.

n12e1b14fdfd.s: The 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988, brought about which of the following changes?
o: Reduction of the voting age from 21 years to 18 years
Introduction of Electors' Photo Identity Cards
Linking of electoral rolls with Aadhaar
n12e1b14fdfd.x: The 61st Amendment reduced the voting age from 21 to 18 years; the change came into force in 1989.
n12e1b14fdfd.tq: Match the constitutional amendment with its distinctive electoral reform.
xs: The **61st Amendment (1988)** reduced the **voting age from 21 to 18** — option **(2)**.
It amended **Art. 326** and came into force in **1989**.
xa: The **52nd (1985)** came just before: anti-defection **Tenth Schedule**.
The **69th (1991)** gave Delhi **NCT** status.

n469b2870ce5.s: Which one of the following correctly gives the sequence of the First, Forty-second, Fifty-second, Eighty-sixth and Ninety-sixth Amendments with their years?
n469b2870ce5.tq: Match each amendment number with its exact enactment year.
xa: 96th: "Oriya" renamed "**Odia**" in the Eighth Schedule.
86th: **Art. 21A**; 52nd: **Tenth Schedule**.

n9056052c547.s: The delimitation freeze was extended up to 2026 by which Amendment?
n9056052c547.x: The 84th Amendment extended the freeze to 2026; the issue is now linked to the 2027 Census, and the 131st Bill failed in April 2026.
xa: The 42nd froze delimitation on the **1971 Census**.
The 131st Bill also aimed to **fast-track** the 106th's women's quota.

nindian-polity-23-27.s: Which of the following was NOT a provision of the 73rd Amendment?
nindian-polity-23-27.x: Constitutional status to Municipalities came with the 74th Amendment; the other three belong to the 73rd.
n: The 73rd Amendment gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 73rd Amendment added Part IX. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX contains Articles 243 to 243O. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 73rd Amendment added the 11th Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 11th Schedule contains 29 subjects. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 73rd Amendment provided at least one-third reservation for women. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 73rd Amendment provided for State Finance Commissions under Article 243I. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 73rd Amendment provided for State Election Commissions under Article 243K. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 74th Amendment gave constitutional status to Municipalities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 11th Schedule was added by the 73rd Amendment in 1992. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **73rd** set up a **three-tier** system, enforced **24 April 1993**.
The **74th** added **Part IX-A** (**243P to 243ZG**) and the **12th Schedule** (**18** subjects).
The **83rd (2000)** exempted **Arunachal Pradesh** from SC reservation in **Panchayats**.

nindian-polity-23-28.s: The 12th Schedule, added by the 74th Amendment, contains how many subjects?
nindian-polity-23-28.x: The 74th Amendment (1992) added Part IX-A and the 12th Schedule with 18 subjects; the 11th Schedule of the 73rd has 29.
n: The 74th Amendment was enacted in 1992. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 74th Amendment gave constitutional status to Municipalities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 74th Amendment added Part IX-A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX-A contains Articles 243P to 243ZG. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 74th Amendment added the 12th Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 12th Schedule contains 18 subjects. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **74th** was enforced on **1 June 1993**.
⚠ **73rd** = Part IX, **11th Schedule** (**29** subjects).
The **97th (2011)** added **Part IX-B** for co-operatives.

n51c287a0b2d.s: Anti-defection provisions were introduced for the first time by the:
n51c287a0b2d.x: The 52nd Amendment introduced anti-defection provisions; the 91st later modified them.
xa: The 106th is the **Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam**.
⚠ Trap: the **62nd (1989)** extended **SC/ST seats** to **2000**, not anti-defection.

nb9ca90d8b0c.s: Which of the following was NOT a provision associated with the First Constitutional Amendment?
o: Reservation of one-third seats for women in State Assemblies
nb9ca90d8b0c.x: Reservation of one-third seats for women in State Assemblies is associated with the 106th Amendment, not the First Amendment. The First Amendment dealt with Article 15(4), Article 19(2), and the Ninth Schedule.
nb9ca90d8b0c.tq: Eliminate provisions belonging to later amendments and retain the First Amendment cluster.
xs: **One-third seats for women** was not part of the 1st Amendment — option **(1)**.
**Women's reservation** came with the **106th (2023)**.
The 1st did insert **Art. 15(4)**, the **Ninth Schedule**, and amended **Art. 19(2)**.
xa: It also added **Arts. 31A, 31B** and protected State monopoly via **Art. 19(6)**.
Assent: **18 June 1951**.

nindian-polity-23-32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: 97th Amendment (2011) – Part IX-B, permitting a maximum of 31 directors under Article 243ZJ
91st Amendment (2003) – Barred defectors from ministerial posts (Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A))
101st Amendment (2016) – GST and the GST Council under Article 279A
nindian-polity-23-32.x: Article 243ZJ, added by the 97th Amendment, permits a maximum of 21 directors, not 31.
n: The 91st Amendment was enacted in 2003. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 91st Amendment inserted Articles 75(1A) and 164(1A). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 91st Amendment barred defectors from ministerial posts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment was enacted in 2011. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment added Directive Principle Article 43B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 97th Amendment added Part IX-B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX-B contains Articles 243ZH to 243ZT. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Article 243ZJ provides for a maximum of 21 directors. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 100th Amendment was enacted in 2015. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]

The India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement involved the exchange of 111 Indian enclaves and 51 Bangladeshi enclaves. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment was enacted in 2016. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment introduced the Goods and Services Tax. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Goods and Services Tax became effective on 1 July 2017. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 101st Amendment created the GST Council. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The GST Council is provided under Article 279A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
Part IX-B was added by the 97th Amendment in 2011. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The **91st** enforced the **15%** ceiling on the **Council of Ministers**.
GST became effective on **1 July 2017**.

nindian-polity-23-33.s: The National Judicial Appointments Commission was created by which Amendment?
nindian-polity-23-33.x: The 99th Amendment (2014) created the NJAC, which the Supreme Court struck down in 2015 for violating judicial independence.
n: The 99th Amendment was enacted in 2014. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The 99th Amendment created the National Judicial Appointments Commission. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission as unconstitutional in 2015. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
The Supreme Court struck down the National Judicial Appointments Commission for violating judicial independence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 55-59]
xa: The NJAC case (**SC Advocates-on-Record Assn.**) was decided **4:1**.
**Independent judiciary** is part of the **basic structure**.
The **100th (2015)** = **India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement**.

n9be81f52a61.s: Goa became a State of India under which Constitutional Amendment?
n9be81f52a61.x: The Fifty-sixth Amendment of 1987 dealt with Goa’s statehood and inserted Article 371I.
n9be81f52a61.tq: Match the statehood event with the adjacent amendment numbers without confusing Goa with Arunachal Pradesh.
xs: **Goa** became a State under the **56th Amendment (1987)** — option **(4)**.
It inserted **Art. 371I**.
The **53rd (1986)** was **Mizoram**; the **55th (1986)** was **Arunachal Pradesh**.
xa: The **12th (1962)** had earlier made **Goa, Daman and Diu** a UT.

n7dbb6c6d1f2.s: Which Amendment made Sikkim a full State?
n7dbb6c6d1f2.x: The 36th (1975) made Sikkim a full State; the 13th (1962) dealt with Nagaland and the 55th (1986) gave Arunachal Pradesh statehood.
xa: The 36th omitted **Art. 2A** and its Schedule.

n0abc1185af8.s: The constitutional validity of the First Amendment was upheld in which case?
n0abc1185af8.x: The First Amendment was upheld by the Supreme Court in Shankari Prasad (1951).
n0abc1185af8.tq: Use the case connected with the early judicial recognition of Parliament’s amending power.
xs: The 1st Amendment was upheld in **Shankari Prasad (1951)** — option **(4)**.
**Golaknath**, **Kesavananda** and **Minerva Mills** came later and dealt with limits on amending power.
xa: The 1st was enacted by the **Provisional Parliament** under **Nehru**.
Assent by President **Rajendra Prasad** on **18 June 1951**.

n7b5bd7d89b6.s: The Ninety-sixth Constitutional Amendment changed the name ‘Oriya’ to which name?
n7b5bd7d89b6.x: The Ninety-sixth Amendment, enacted in 2011, changed the constitutional reference from ‘Oriya’ to ‘Odia’.
n7b5bd7d89b6.tq: Test the exact official word in a look-alike language-name pair.
xs: The **96th Amendment (2011)** changed "Oriya" to "**Odia**" — option **(4)**.
The change was in the **Eighth Schedule**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the 11th FD came via the **86th**, not "96th".

nc1fb70eb404.s: The earlier Tenth Schedule added by the 35th Amendment, 1974 dealt with:
nc1fb70eb404.x: The 35th Amendment (1974) added a Tenth Schedule on Sikkim's associate status; the anti-defection Tenth Schedule came with the 52nd Amendment (1985).
xa: The **36th (1975)** made Sikkim a **full State**, omitting **Art. 2A** and that Schedule.
⚠ The anti-defection Tenth Schedule covers Arts. **101, 102, 190, 191**; later modified by the **91st (2003)**.

n466e118f5b6.s: Which Constitutional Amendment extended the reservation of seats under Article 334 up to 2030 and also ended the nomination of Anglo-Indians to legislatures?
n466e118f5b6.x: The 104th Constitutional Amendment, 2019, extended the reservation of seats for SCs and STs up to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.
n466e118f5b6.tq: Use the paired consequence—extension plus ending Anglo-Indian nomination—to identify the amendment.
xs: The **104th Amendment (2019)** extended **SC/ST seats to 2030** and **ended Anglo-Indian nomination** — option **(1)**.
The **101st** was **GST** — option (4) wrong.
xa: ⚠ The **103rd** (also **2019**) gave **10% EWS** reservation.
The **106th (2023)**: **one-third seats for women**.

n90fb2a04865.s: Implementation of the women's reservation under the 2023 law has been linked to the completion of:
n90fb2a04865.x: The women's reservation remains unimplemented because its implementation is linked to the completion of delimitation.
xa: A **revised delimitation bill** is expected.
The **131st Bill, 2026** on delimitation was **defeated** (**17 Apr 2026**).
Southern States fear a **smaller share** after delimitation.

n908d7e168cb.s: Which of the following is the latest enacted Constitutional Amendment Act?
n908d7e168cb.x: The 106th Constitutional Amendment, enacted in 2023, is the latest enacted amendment in the sequence. The 105th Amendment of 2021 is therefore not the latest.
n908d7e168cb.tq: Avoid the stale-current-affairs trap by identifying the highest enacted amendment number and year.
xs: The **106th Amendment, 2023** is the **latest enacted** amendment — option **(4)**.
⚠ UPSC notes calling the **105th** "the most recent" are **stale**.
xa: The 106th gives **one-third seats for women**.
⚠ **103rd and 104th** are both **2019** — EWS and SC/ST seats to **2030**.
Pending: **129th** (ONOE), **130th** (detained ministers); the **131st** was **defeated**.
n908d7e168cb.fixed: oddly worded 'referred to in the current constitutional amendment sequence'

n5ef9a9f4d68.s: In which case did the Supreme Court strike down Part IXB insofar as it applied to State co-operative societies?
o: Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021)
n5ef9a9f4d68.x: In Rajendra N. Shah (2021), Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT, added by the 97th Amendment) was struck down for State co-operatives as State ratification was absent.
xa: India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives (**2026**).

n3a76a4f1b75.s: Which Article was inserted into the Directive Principles of State Policy by the 97th Constitutional Amendment?
n3a76a4f1b75.x: Article 43B was inserted to promote the voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control and professional management of co-operative societies.
n3a76a4f1b75.tq: Use the exact Article number rather than confusing it with the adjacent Article 43A.
xs: The **97th** inserted **Article 43B** into the DPSPs — option **(2)**.
43B: **voluntary formation, autonomy, democratic control, professional management** of co-operatives.
xa: The 97th also made forming **co-operative societies** a Fundamental Right under **Art. 19(1)(c)**.
New **Part IXB** (**Arts. 243ZH-243ZT**).
Board: **maximum 21** directors; **5-year** term.

n4d44153c900.s: Under the constitutional provisions on co-operative societies, the term of the board is:
n4d44153c900.x: The board has a five-year term; the provisions also fix a maximum of 21 directors, one SC/ST seat, two women seats and audit within six months.
xa: Elections must be held **before the term expires**.
**Rajendra N. Shah (2021)**: Part IXB survives only for **multi-State** co-operatives.

ndd3cf65d115.s: In Rajendra N. Shah v. Union of India (2021), Part IXB was held inapplicable to State co-operative societies mainly because
o: It dealt exclusively with municipal bodies
It had been repealed by the 105th Amendment
It had not been ratified by the States as required
ndd3cf65d115.x: The Supreme Court struck down Part IXB in its application to State co-operative societies because the required ratification by the States had not been obtained. It continues to operate for multi-State co-operative societies.
ndd3cf65d115.tq: Connect the judicial outcome with the precise constitutional procedural defect.
xs: Part IXB fell for **State** co-operatives as it had **not been ratified by the States** as required — option **(4)** (**Rajendra N. Shah, 2021**).
It **survives** for **multi-State** co-operatives.
xa: Part IXB came by the **97th Amendment, 2011**.
The 97th also amended **Art. 19(1)(c)** and added **Art. 43B**.
India has **8.5 lakh+** registered co-operatives.

nce7cbfd4c27.s: Which of the following Articles is proposed to be inserted by the 129th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2024?
nce7cbfd4c27.x: The 129th Amendment Bill proposes insertion of Article 82A and amendments to Articles 83, 172 and 327 in connection with simultaneous elections.
