nce7cbfd4c27.tq: Identify the newly proposed Article while separating it from Articles inserted by enacted amendments.
xs: The **129th Bill, 2024** proposes **Article 82A** (One Nation, One Election) — option **(2)**.
It also amends Arts. **83, 172, 327**.
xa: It came with a **UT Laws Bill**; introduced **17 Dec 2024**.
JPC chair: **P.P. Chaudhary**.

nb6453fb1f6a.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill, 2025?
o: It provides one-third reservation for women in the Rajya Sabha.
It implements the India-Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement.
It concerns removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges.
It increases the Lok Sabha strength to 850 members.
nb6453fb1f6a.x: The 130th Amendment Bill proposes provisions concerning the removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Ministers and Ministers detained for 30 consecutive days on serious charges. It also involves Articles 75, 164 and 239AA, including Delhi.
nb6453fb1f6a.tq: Identify the Bill by its distinctive consequence and detention-duration condition.
xs: The **130th Bill, 2025** concerns removal of the **PM, CMs and Ministers** detained **30 consecutive days** on serious charges — option **(3)**.
It amends **Arts. 75, 164, 239AA** (CMs incl. **Delhi**).
Lok Sabha **850** is the **131st** (defeated **17 Apr 2026**) — option (4) wrong.
xa: The 130th is **with a JPC**; deadline extended (**1 Aug 2026**).
Women's **one-third** seats came by the **106th (2023)**.

n569f1afe9fe.s: Who argued in India in 1965 that the amending power has implied limitations, drawing upon Germany's Basic Law?
n569f1afe9fe.x: German jurist Dietrich Conrad argued in India in 1965 that constitutional amending power is subject to implied limitations, drawing on the experience of Germany's Basic Law.
n569f1afe9fe.tq: Pair the jurist with both the year and the country from which the idea was drawn.
xs: **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India in **1965** that the amending power has **implied limits** — option **(3)**.
His argument drew on **Germany**'s **Basic Law** and is treated as the **origin of the idea** of basic structure.
xa: **Justice Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**".
CJI **S.M. Sikri** headed the **13-judge bench** in Kesavananda Bharati.
The doctrine was **first propounded** in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

n00ea42c34b4.s: The dissent of Justice Mudholkar in which case first referred to the idea of ‘basic features’ of the Constitution?
n00ea42c34b4.x: Justice Mudholkar’s dissent in Sajjan Singh (1965) is noted as the first judicial reference to the idea of basic features.
n00ea42c34b4.tq: Test the precursor observation rather than the later case that formally propounded the doctrine.
xs: Justice **Mudholkar**'s dissent in **Sajjan Singh (1965)** first spoke of "**basic features**" — option **(3)**.
**Sajjan Singh** upheld the **17th Amendment** and reaffirmed **Shankari Prasad**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** came later and **first propounded** the doctrine itself.
xa: Jurist **Dietrich Conrad** argued in India (**1965**) that the amending power has **implied limits**.
**Golaknath (1967)** overruled both Shankari Prasad and Sajjan Singh.
First application of the doctrine: **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.

n6bb40a197c0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Golaknath case (1967)?
o: It arose from a challenge to the 24th Amendment
It was decided by an 11-judge Bench by a 6:5 majority
It held that Fundamental Rights are 'transcendental and immutable'
It held that a constitutional amendment is 'law' under Article 13
n6bb40a197c0.x: Golaknath challenged the 17th Amendment, not the 24th.
xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Golaknath 11 judges, 6:5**; **Kesavananda 13 judges, 7:6**; **NJAC 4:1**.
**Prospective overruling** originated in **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** overruled Golaknath.

n92656eb5c25.s: Which case first propounded the basic structure doctrine and overruled Golaknath?
n92656eb5c25.x: Kesavananda Bharati propounded the doctrine, overruled Golaknath and upheld the 24th Amendment.
xa: Bench: **13 judges** (largest ever), CJI **S.M. Sikri**, **7:6**, on **24 Apr 1973**.
⚠ Exam angle: first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati**, not Golaknath or Shankari Prasad (**MPPSC 2025**).
Elements held basic: **secularism**, **federalism**, **separation of powers**, **supremacy of Constitution**.

n698b513a18c.s: In which case was the basic structure doctrine applied for the first time, with free and fair elections treated as a basic feature?
n698b513a18c.x: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) marked the first application of the basic structure doctrine, and the relevant clause of the 39th Amendment was struck down; free and fair elections were recognised as a basic feature.
n698b513a18c.tq: Distinguish the formal propounding of a doctrine from its first subsequent application.
xs: The doctrine was first applied in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)** — option **(2)**.
The **39th Amendment** clause putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts (**Art. 329A(4)**) was struck down; **free and fair elections** held basic.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** concerned the **42nd Amendment**; **Waman Rao (1981)** the cut-off date; **Golaknath (1967)** predates the doctrine.
xa: The case also held **democracy, rule of law, judicial review** basic.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also tied **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
In **2026**, free and fair elections as basic structure were cited in the debate on making **voting** a fundamental right.

nd720dcd640b.s: Which of the following provisions introduced or widened by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment was struck down in Minerva Mills?
o: Articles 368(4) and 368(5), and the widened Article 31C
nd720dcd640b.x: Minerva Mills struck down Articles 368(4) and 368(5), which sought to make Parliament's amending power unlimited and amendments non-justiciable, along with the widened form of Article 31C.
nd720dcd640b.tq: Use the specific amendment-provision pairing rather than identifying the case by name alone.
xs: **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)** and the **widened Art. 31C** — option **(2)**.
These **42nd Amendment (1976)** clauses excluded **judicial review** and claimed unlimited amending power.
**Art. 329A(4)** fell in **Raj Narain (1975)**; the **NJAC** fell in **2015**; the Ninth Schedule was never struck down as a whole.
xa: Minerva Mills held **judicial review**, **limited amending power** and **FR-DPSP harmony** basic.
**Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** and widened by the **42nd**.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: no blanket immunity for Ninth Schedule laws.

nab590e88653.s: The Supreme Court struck down the 99th Amendment and the NJAC Act in 2015 by a majority of:
nab590e88653.x: The NJAC case was decided 4:1, treating judicial independence as part of the basic structure.
xa: ⚠ Bench splits: **Golaknath 6:5**, **Kesavananda 7:6**, **NJAC 4:1**.
**Independent judiciary** was earlier held basic in **All India Judges Association (2002)**.
**Judicial review** is basic — **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

n63459f0b82c.s: Which of the following was NOT associated with the First Amendment Act, 1951?
o: Addition of public order, friendly relations with foreign States and incitement as grounds under Article 19(2)
n63459f0b82c.x: Article 31C was inserted by the Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971.
xa: **2026 = 75 years** of the 1st Amendment (18 June 2026); assent by President **Rajendra Prasad**.
The Ninth Schedule began with **13** Acts; now **282**.
**I.R. Coelho** limit was restated on the 1st Amendment's **75th** year.

n36c255c2e01.s: Laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are:
o: Open to review on the basis of the basic structure
n36c255c2e01.x: Waman Rao used 24 April 1973 as the cut-off; post-cut-off entries are open to basic-structure review rather than enjoying immunity.
xa: **24 April 1973** is the date of the **Kesavananda Bharati** judgment.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**, a **nine-judge bench**, rejected **blanket immunity**.
Waman Rao applied the cut-off to **Ninth Schedule/Art. 31A** laws.

ndc5a84d618a.s: Which one of the following sets was associated with the basic structure in Kesavananda Bharati?
o: Secularism, federalism and separation of powers
Preventive detention, reservation and emergency powers
Property taxation, trade regulation and local government
Official language, citizenship and electoral rolls
ndc5a84d618a.x: Kesavananda Bharati associated secularism, federalism and separation of powers, among other constitutional principles, with the basic structure.
ndc5a84d618a.tq: Recognise the cluster of foundational constitutional principles rather than isolated ordinary provisions.
xs: **Secularism, federalism and separation of powers** were linked to basic structure in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** — option **(1)**.
Kesavananda's list also includes **supremacy of Constitution**, **sovereign democratic republic**, **parliamentary system**, **welfare state**, **individual dignity**.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** **reaffirmed secularism** and federalism.
**Free and fair elections**: **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**.
⚠ Secularism was basic **even before** the **42nd Amendment (1976)** put the word in the Preamble.

n7c2d8ccda00.s: The principle of secularism was reaffirmed as part of the basic structure in which case?
o: Kuldip Nayar v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Indira Sawhney v. Union of India
n7c2d8ccda00.x: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), decided by a nine-judge Bench, reaffirmed secularism and federalism as basic-structure principles.
n7c2d8ccda00.tq: Link secularism and federalism with S.R. Bommai rather than with the earlier Kesavananda ruling.
xs: **Secularism** was reaffirmed in **S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994)** — option **(3)**.
Bommai, a **nine-judge bench**, also held **federalism** basic in the context of **Art. 356**.
**All India Judges Association (2002)** = independent judiciary; **Kuldip Nayar (2006)** = free and fair elections; **Indra Sawhney** = equality.
xa: Secularism was basic even before the **42nd Amendment (1976)** added the word to the Preamble.
Bommai is an **APPSC-G2 2008** key.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** first listed secularism and federalism.

na0f1bf5157d.s: Which case is associated with the basic-structure status of the powers of the High Courts under Articles 226 and 227?
o: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India
Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
P. Sambamurthy v. Union of India
Bhim Singhji v. Union of India
na0f1bf5157d.x: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) is associated with the basic-structure status of the High Courts’ powers under Articles 226 and 227.
na0f1bf5157d.tq: Match the specific constitutional Articles with the case dealing with judicial review powers.
xs: **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** made the **HC powers under Arts. 226, 227** basic — option **(1)**.
**Indra Sawhney** = equality and rule of law; **P. Sambamurthy (1987)** = rule of law; **Bhim Singhji (1981)** = welfare state.
xa: SC powers under **Arts. 32, 136, 141, 142**: **Delhi Judicial Service Assn. (1991)**.
**High Courts can** declare central laws invalid: the **42nd Amendment** bar was removed by the **43rd (1977)**.
**Judicial review** is basic: **Raj Narain**, **Minerva Mills**.

n61a10caa9e1.s: The argument that voting should be elevated beyond a statutory right is linked in the contemporary basic-structure debate primarily with:
o: Democracy and free and fair elections as basic features
The primacy of Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights
The basic feature of judicial independence alone
The immunity of all election disputes from judicial review
n61a10caa9e1.x: The argument is based on the view that democracy and free and fair elections are basic features of the Constitution, and therefore voting deserves stronger constitutional protection.
n61a10caa9e1.tq: Connect the proposed legal change with the basic constitutional features invoked to support it.
xs: The argument rests on **democracy and free and fair elections as basic features** — option **(1)**.
In the **2026** debate on making **voting a fundamental right**, it was argued voting should be **more than a statutory right**.
xa: **Free and fair elections** were held basic in **Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)**, the **first application** of the doctrine.
**Kuldip Nayar (2006)** also linked **free and fair elections, democracy** to basic structure.
Raj Narain struck down the **39th Amendment** clause (**Art. 329A(4)**) putting the PM's election disputes beyond courts.

nc5fe32b98f7.s: A law can be placed in the Ninth Schedule only by:
o: A State Legislature by ordinary law
nc5fe32b98f7.x: Inclusion needs a constitutional amendment by Parliament; the Schedule covers Central and State laws and was created mainly for land-reform laws.
xa: Created by the **1st Amendment (1951)** with **Art. 31B**.
Size: **13** Acts at start → **282** now.
**I.R. Coelho (2007)**: post-1973 entries can be tested on basic structure.

n1937cf86092.s: Tamil Nadu's law providing 69 per cent reservation was placed in the Ninth Schedule by which Constitutional Amendment?
n1937cf86092.x: The Tamil Nadu 69 per cent reservation law was placed in the Ninth Schedule through the 76th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1994.
n1937cf86092.tq: Link the famous law with its specific amendment number and year.
xs: The **76th Amendment Act, 1994** placed Tamil Nadu's **69%** reservation Act in the Ninth Schedule — option **(1)**.
It shows that laws enter the Ninth Schedule **only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment**.
xa: Since such an entry came after **24 April 1973**, it is open to basic-structure review (**Waman Rao**, **I.R. Coelho**).
**I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007)**: post-1973 laws invalid if they abrogate the essence of **Arts. 14, 19, 21**.
The Schedule covers **both Central and State laws**.

nb9d0aa994d0.s: The I.R. Coelho case applied the ‘rights test’ or ‘direct impact test’ primarily with reference to the essence of which Articles?
nb9d0aa994d0.x: Under the rights or direct-impact test, a post-1973 Ninth Schedule law may be invalid if it abrogates the essence of the rights protected under Articles 14, 19 and 21.
nb9d0aa994d0.tq: Separate the three Articles in the direct-impact test from other Fundamental Rights provisions.
xs: The **rights / direct-impact test** looks at the essence of **Arts. 14, 19 and 21** — option **(1)**.
Under **I.R. Coelho (2007)**, post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws are invalid if they damage the basic structure or abrogate the essence of these Articles.
xa: Coelho was decided by a **nine-judge bench**.
**Arts. 31A, 31C** save certain laws from **Arts. 14, 19**.
**No blanket immunity**, because **judicial review is basic**.

n94a54a5c9c0.s: In which year was the Waman Rao judgment on the Ninth Schedule delivered?
n94a54a5c9c0.x: Waman Rao came in 1981, after the First Amendment (1951) and Kesavananda Bharati (1973), and before I.R. Coelho (2007).
xa: Waman Rao's cut-off date (**24 April 1973**) is the date of Kesavananda.
In between: **Golaknath (1967)**, **24th Amendment (1971)**, **Raj Narain (1975)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)**.
Later: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**; **NJAC case (2015)**.

nc68f4ff7570.x: The doctrine is not expressly defined in the Constitution; it was developed by the Supreme Court and its content has evolved through case law.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "incorporated by an **Act of Parliament**" is false (PYQ **APPSC-G1 2024**, statement I false).
Origin of the idea: jurist **Dietrich Conrad** (1965) argued that the amending power has **implied limits**.
Critics say the **list is open-ended**, so its content is uncertain.

n923d3a8172f.s: With reference to the present position on constitutional amendments, which one of the following is correct?
o: Fundamental Rights may be amended only by an executive order
Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged
Fundamental Rights cannot be amended under any circumstances
Fundamental Rights are outside the scope of Article 368
n923d3a8172f.x: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368, but the amendment remains subject to the basic structure limitation.
n923d3a8172f.tq: Apply the rule to a specific constitutional component rather than recalling an isolated case name.
xs: Today, **Fundamental Rights may be amended, provided the basic structure is not damaged** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 368** lets Parliament amend any part, **including FRs and the Preamble**; the only limit is the **basic structure**.
So FRs are neither outside Art. 368 nor unamendable; and amendment is by **Parliament**, never by executive order.
xa: **Golaknath (1967)** once held Parliament **cannot abridge FRs**; **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** overruled it.
**Shankari Prasad (1951)**: Art. 368 **includes the power to amend FRs**.
Exam angle: "can Parliament amend FRs today" — **yes, subject to basic structure**.

n635001b80ff.s: Which of the following sets consists entirely of doctrines evolved by the Supreme Court?
o: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance
Article 31C primacy, prospective overruling and colourable legislation
Unlimited amending power, territorial nexus and harmonious construction
n635001b80ff.x: Eclipse, severability and pith and substance are all Supreme Court-evolved interpretive doctrines. Article 31C primacy, Article 13(4) and unlimited amending power were created through constitutional amendments, while prospective overruling originated in Golaknath.
n635001b80ff.tq: Eliminate sets containing a Parliament-created amendment rule or a separately identified doctrine.
xs: **Eclipse, severability and pith and substance** are all Supreme Court-made doctrines — option **(1)**.
**Art. 31C primacy** came from Parliament's **25th Amendment (1971)**; **unlimited amending power** from the **42nd Amendment**.
So options 2, 3 and 4 each mix in a **Parliament**-made rule.
xa: Other judge-made doctrines: **colourable legislation**, **harmonious construction**, **territorial nexus**.
**Prospective overruling**: Supreme Court — **Golaknath (1967)**.
**Basic structure**: Supreme Court — **Kesavananda (1973)**.

nb524f8a3443.s: In Kesavananda Bharati, which part of Article 31C was struck down as violating the basic structure?
o: The provision giving effect to any Directive Principle an absolute priority over the Constitution
The provision creating the Ninth Schedule
The provision enabling Parliament to amend Fundamental Rights
The provision barring courts from questioning whether a law gives effect to the Directive Principles
nb524f8a3443.x: Kesavananda Bharati struck down the part of Article 31C that barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to a Directive Principle. Judicial review was held to be part of the basic structure.
nb524f8a3443.tq: Identify the precise judicial-review restriction rather than confusing it with the general objective of Article 31C.
xs: Kesavananda struck down the part **barring courts from questioning** whether a law gives effect to the **Directive Principles** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **judicial review is basic**.
The **Ninth Schedule** came from the **1st Amendment** with **Art. 31B**, not Art. 31C; the power to amend FRs was **upheld** (24th Amendment).
xa: **Art. 31C** was inserted by the **25th Amendment (1971)** for **Art. 39(b), (c)** laws.
The **42nd** widened it; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck the widened form down.
Art. 31C = DPSP primacy — a **Parliament**-made rule, not a judge-made doctrine.

ncf94b69e0f9.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court of India in which case?
ncf94b69e0f9.x: Prospective overruling is a judge-made doctrine that the Supreme Court first applied in Golaknath (1967). Kesavananda (1973) propounded the basic structure; Minerva Mills (1980) struck down Art. 368(4),(5); Shankari Prasad (1951) upheld Parliament's power to amend FRs.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied by the Supreme Court in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(2)**.
It is a **judge-made** doctrine, like eclipse, severability and pith and substance.
**Kesavananda (1973)** propounded the **basic structure**; **Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down **Art. 368(4), (5)**; **Shankari Prasad (1951)** held Art. 368 includes power to amend FRs.
xa: Golaknath: FRs **"transcendental and immutable"**; an amendment **is** "law" under **Art. 13**.
Bench: **11 judges, 6:5**; it challenged the **17th Amendment**.
Parliament's reply: the **24th Amendment (1971)**, amending **Arts. 13 and 368**.

nf8f06964020.s: The basic structure doctrine primarily rests on which constitutional principle?
o: Supremacy of Parliament over the Constitution
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
Supremacy of conventions over written provisions
Supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts
nf8f06964020.x: The doctrine rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the power of courts to review constitutional amendments against its basic features.
nf8f06964020.tq: Test the underlying constitutional principle rather than the name of the doctrine.
xs: The doctrine rests on the **supremacy of the Constitution and judicial review by the courts** — option **(4)**.
The judicial review principle **accepts the theory of supremacy of Courts** = supremacy of the **Constitution and the courts** over Parliament (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
As a limit, basic structure means supremacy of the **Constitution**, not of **Parliament** — so option 1 is the reverse.
xa: Indian Parliament is **not sovereign in the British sense**.
**Judicial review** is itself basic, so it **cannot be removed even by amendment**.
The doctrine keeps **Art. 368** limited.

n84fb9eab237.s: The restriction imposed by the 42nd Amendment on High Courts’ power to review central laws was removed by the:
n84fb9eab237.x: The 42nd Amendment attempted to bar High Courts from reviewing central laws, and the 43rd Amendment Act, 1977 removed that restriction.
n84fb9eab237.tq: Use the amendment sequence to identify the restoring constitutional change.
xs: The **43rd Amendment Act, 1977** removed the bar — option **(2)**.
The **42nd Amendment (1976)** had barred High Courts from declaring central laws invalid; after the 43rd, **High Courts can** do so.
xa: **Constitutional amendments can** also be challenged on **basic structure** grounds.
⚠ Trap: both "cannot" statements are false (**UPSC 2019**).
The **42nd Amendment**'s Art. 368(4), (5) and widened Art. 31C were struck down in **Minerva Mills (1980)**.

nc13122c8969.s: Which one of the following most accurately describes the basic structure doctrine?
o: The Supreme Court alone may amend the Constitution when required
Only the Preamble can be amended subject to judicial approval
Parliament may amend every constitutional provision without limitation
Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features
nc13122c8969.x: The doctrine permits amendment of any part of the Constitution under Article 368, but prohibits alteration, damage or destruction of features that give the Constitution its identity.
nc13122c8969.tq: Choose the precise statement distinguishing the amending power from its constitutional limitation.
xs: Under the basic structure doctrine, **Parliament may amend the Constitution, but cannot damage or destroy its core features** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 368** lets Parliament amend any part, including **Fundamental Rights** and the **Preamble**, so "every provision without limitation" (option 3) ignores the limit.
The power to amend lies with **Parliament**, not the Supreme Court; and the doctrine is not about "the Preamble alone".
xa: Basic structure = what **cannot be amended in exercise of the power under Art. 368** (APPSC-G1 2018 key).
The idea was borrowed from **Germany** (Basic Law) and propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)**.
⚠ PYQ 2024 key: "**core features cannot be amended or altered by Parliament**".

n8de89b726e0.s: Which of the following best describes the present position on the Preamble?
o: It is part of the Constitution and amendable, subject to the basic structure
It is not a part of the Constitution
It is part of the Constitution but cannot be amended at all
It alone constitutes the basic structure
n8de89b726e0.x: The Preamble is part of the Constitution and amendable subject to the basic structure doctrine, which is not confined to the Preamble.
xa: **PYQ G1 2018**: the Preamble's objectives embody the basic structure, so they "**cannot be amended**" under Art. 368.
The word **'secular'** entered the Preamble by the **42nd Amendment (1976)**, yet secularism was basic even before.
Basic structure is **judge-made**, first propounded in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**.

ned440a9f440.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about secularism and the basic structure?
o: Secularism was recognised as a basic feature even before the word was put in the Preamble
The word 'secular' was inserted into the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
Secularism became a basic feature only because of its textual insertion in 1976
S.R. Bommai held secularism to be part of the basic structure
ned440a9f440.x: Secularism was treated as a basic feature even before the 42nd Amendment added the word 'secular' to the Preamble.
xa: **S.R. Bommai (1994)** reaffirmed **secularism**, with **federalism**.
Bommai was a **nine-judge bench** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).

na095699ff93.s: Which one of the following propositions was laid down in Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India?
o: Procedure established by law need not satisfy standards of fairness.
The right to life includes a life with dignity and the procedure under Article 21 must be just, fair and reasonable.
The right to travel abroad is exclusively a statutory right.
na095699ff93.x: Maneka Gandhi held that Article 21 protects more than mere existence, includes dignity and travel abroad, and requires a procedure that is just, fair and reasonable. This interpretation also binds the legislature.
na095699ff93.tq: Distinguish the expanded constitutional meaning from the narrow pre-Maneka interpretation of Article 21.
xs: Maneka Gandhi held the right to life includes a life **with dignity** and Art. 21 procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable** — option **(3)**.
Art. 21 is **not mere existence** (option 1 wrong), and it covers the **right to travel abroad** (option 4 wrong).
The fairness standard **now binds the legislature too** — so option 2 is wrong.
xa: The case arose from **passport impounding** in **1978**.
Decided by a **7-judge** bench.
⚠ **ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. Art. 21 **unenforceable in Emergency** — the "darkest day", effectively overruled.

n56f04ba135b.s: Which one of the following cases is associated with the compulsory registration of marriages?
o: Shayara Bano v. Union of India
Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
n56f04ba135b.x: In Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006), the Supreme Court directed compulsory registration of marriages.
n56f04ba135b.tq: Match the social reform direction with the correct judgment.
xs: **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)** directed **compulsory registration of marriages** — option **(1)**.
**Vishaka** = workplace harassment; **Shayara Bano** = triple talaq; **Prem Shankar Shukla** = handcuffing.
xa: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments like **Vishaka, Seema** fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts.
**D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.

nc6a75e400a1.s: The Supreme Court judgment concerning handcuffing only in exceptional cases is associated with:
o: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India
nc6a75e400a1.x: Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980) held that handcuffing should be confined to exceptional cases.
nc6a75e400a1.tq: Recall the specific liberty-related holding attached to the case.
xs: **Prem Shankar Shukla v. Delhi Administration (1980)** — **handcuffing only in exceptional cases** — option **(2)**.
**Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** is about **bail** being the rule under the **UAPA**.
xa: **D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: FIR mandatory (**Sec. 173 BNSS**).
**Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**: compulsory registration of marriages.

nindian-polity-24-6.s: Which case established the ‘golden triangle’ involving Articles 14, 19 and 21?
o: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
nindian-polity-24-6.x: Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that Articles 14, 19 and 21 work together, the 'golden triangle', so any law affecting liberty must satisfy all three.
nindian-polity-24-6.tq: Recall the case behind the golden triangle.
n: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India established the golden triangle of Articles 14, 19, and 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Articles 14, 19, and 21 are mutually inclusive under the golden triangle doctrine. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The **golden triangle** comes from **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India** — option **(1)**.
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)** linked **Articles 14, 19 and 21** as mutually inclusive.
Procedure must be **just, fair and reasonable**; it **widened** Article 21 incl. the **right to travel abroad**.
**A.K. Gopalan** read Art. 21 **narrowly**; **S.R. Bommai** dealt with **Article 356**.
xa: Maneka was about **passport impounding** and a life **with human dignity**.
Maneka was a **7 judges** bench.
**ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. Art. 21 unenforceable in Emergency — the "darkest day".

nindian-polity-24-10.s: Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain is linked to which Constitutional Amendment?
nindian-polity-24-10.x: Raj Narain concerned the 39th Amendment; Sambamurthy the 32nd, Kihoto Hollohan the 52nd and Champakam led to the 1st.
n: Champakam Dorairajan directly led to the First Constitutional Amendment, 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 32nd Amendment was associated with special provisions for Andhra Pradesh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 52nd Amendment was associated with the Anti-Defection Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
The 39th Amendment was associated with Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: The **39th** was later nullified by the **44th**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992–93)**: the **Speaker's** ruling is subject to **judicial review**.

nindian-polity-24-11.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cases on the Preamble?
o: Kesavananda Bharati held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution
The Berubari Union case held that the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution
S.R. Bommai held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution
Golaknath was about the amending power
nindian-polity-24-11.x: Berubari held the opposite, that the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
n: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala recognized the Preamble as part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case held that the Preamble is not an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India reaffirmed the Preamble as an integral part of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: **Berubari** is linked to **Article 3**.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** also held **secularism** and **federalism** basic features.
**Bommai** was a **Nine-judge** bench.

nindian-polity-24-29.s: In which year was the Berubari Union case decided?
nindian-polity-24-29.x: Berubari was 1960, after A.K. Gopalan (1950) and Shankari Prasad (1951) and before Sajjan Singh (1965).
n: Shankari Prasad v. Union of India was decided in 1951. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan was decided in 1965. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras was decided in 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case was decided in 1960. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras preceded Shankari Prasad v. Union of India chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Shankari Prasad v. Union of India preceded Champakam Dorairajan chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Champakam Dorairajan preceded Berubari Union Case chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
Berubari Union Case preceded Sajjan Singh v. State of Rajasthan chronologically. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xa: After Sajjan Singh: **Golaknath** → **Kesavananda Bharati** → **Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain**.
Then **Maneka Gandhi (1978)** → **Minerva Mills (1980)** → **Kihoto Hollohan** → **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
**Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** sits between **Shankari Prasad** and **Berubari**.

nindian-polity-24-34.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment was nullified by which Amendment?
nindian-polity-24-34.x: The 44th Amendment (1978) undid the 39th Amendment's changes. The 42nd (1976) was the Emergency-era amendment, and the 52nd added the anti-defection law.
nindian-polity-24-34.tq: Recall that the 44th Amendment undid the Emergency amendments.
n: The 39th Amendment was nullified by the 44th Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 59-62]
xs: The **39th Amendment** was nullified by the **44th Amendment** — option **(4)**.
The 39th had barred judicial review of election disputes of the **Prime Minister** and **Speaker** (**Article 329A**).
**Raj Narain (1975)** struck down parts of it; the **32nd** concerned **Andhra Pradesh**, the **52nd** the **Tenth Schedule**.
xa: **Raj Narain** held **free and fair elections** part of the **Basic Structure**.
The **42nd Amendment**'s clauses were struck down in **Minerva Mills**.
**P. Sambamurthy (1987)** struck down portions of the **32nd Amendment**.

nindian-polity-41-22.s: The Berubari Union case dealt with:
nindian-polity-41-22.x: Berubari dealt with Article 3 and the Preamble; Shankari Prasad weighed Article 13 against 368, Raj Narain the 39th and Minerva Mills the 42nd.
n: Shankari Prasad concerned the relationship between Article 13 and Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Berubari Union was decided in 1960. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Berubari Union was linked to Article 3. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Berubari Union was linked to the Preamble. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Indira Nehru Gandhi was decided in 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Indira Nehru Gandhi was linked to the 39th Constitutional Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Indira Nehru Gandhi was linked to Article 329A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Minerva Mills was decided in 1980. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Minerva Mills was linked to the 42nd Constitutional Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Minerva Mills was linked to the Article 368 clauses. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xa: **Berubari (1960)** held the Preamble **not** integral.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** struck down the 42nd's **unlimited-power** clauses.
**Shankari Prasad** preceded **Champakam** in the chronology.

n27a55480891.s: Which case made President's Rule under Article 356 subject to judicial review and emphasised the floor test?
n27a55480891.x: The nine-judge S.R. Bommai judgment made Article 356 reviewable, stressed the floor test and recognised secularism as basic structure.
xa: Bench: **9 judges** (PYQ G2 2008; **APPSC-G2 2008** key).
Bommai was revived by **Tamil Nadu** government formation **2026** — majority tested on the **floor of the House**.
Other nine-judge cases: **Indra Sawhney (1992)**, **Puttaswamy (2017)**.

n8169161ad52.s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued primarily because workplace sexual harassment was held to violate which combination of constitutional guarantees?
o: Freedom of religion and cultural rights
Rights against exploitation and freedom of conscience
n8169161ad52.x: The Vishaka judgment treated workplace sexual harassment as a violation of the constitutional guarantees of equality and life. The Guidelines operated until Parliament enacted a law on the subject.
n8169161ad52.tq: Test the rights affected rather than merely recalling the name of the case.
xs: **Vishaka (1997)** held workplace sexual harassment violates **equality and life** — option **(1)**.
So the Court issued binding **Vishaka Guidelines** on sexual harassment at the workplace, to last **till Parliament's law**.
xa: The Guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Bench: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**.
⚠ **Vishaka** and **D.K. Basu** are both **1997** — workplace harassment vs arrest/custody.

n81a47ea0e34.s: In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), the Supreme Court held that:
o: Privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21.
Article 21 does not include decisional autonomy.
Privacy is a statutory right but not a fundamental right.
Privacy is available only to citizens during an Emergency.
n81a47ea0e34.x: The Puttaswamy judgment recognised the right to privacy as a fundamental right under Article 21. It also rejected the reasoning adopted in ADM Jabalpur.
n81a47ea0e34.tq: Test the exact constitutional status and Article attached to the right.
xs: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)** held **privacy is a fundamental right under Art. 21** — option **(1)**.
It rejected the **ADM Jabalpur** reasoning that Art. 21 is unenforceable in Emergency.
xa: Bench: **nine judges**, CJI **J.S. Khehar**.
⚠ **Shreya Singhal** = **Sec. 66A IT Act** (speech); **Puttaswamy** = privacy under **Art. 21**.
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the **Aadhaar Act 4:1** with limits; Puttaswamy has also been applied to **DNA paternity tests**.

n5cdaa36490d.s: Which one of the following was NOT a holding associated with Indra Sawhney?
o: A 50 per cent ceiling on reservation in ordinary circumstances
No reservation in promotion under Article 16(4)
Recognition of secularism as a basic feature
n5cdaa36490d.x: Recognition of secularism as a basic feature was associated with S.R. Bommai, not Indra Sawhney. Indra Sawhney dealt with the reservation ceiling, creamy layer exclusion and reservation in promotion under Article 16(4).
n5cdaa36490d.tq: Use a nearby landmark judgment as the distractor while isolating the actual subject of the case.
xs: **Recognition of secularism as a basic feature** was not an Indra Sawhney holding — option **(4)**; that was **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)** held: **50% ceiling**, **creamy layer** excluded, **no reservation in promotion under Art. 16(4)**.
xa: Indra Sawhney was a **nine-judge** bench.
**Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: States may **sub-classify SCs**.
Bommai: **Art. 356** reviewable; **floor test**.

n7fb0fdc0eca.s: In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015), the Supreme Court struck down which provision as violating Article 19(1)(a)?
o: Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000
Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code
Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act
n7fb0fdc0eca.x: Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down Sec. 66A of the IT Act, 2000 under the freedom of speech, Art. 19(1)(a). Sec. 377 was read down in Navtej Johar (2018); Sec. 497 was struck down in Joseph Shine (2018); Sec. 8(4) RPA was struck down in Lily Thomas (2013).
n7fb0fdc0eca.tq: Shreya Singhal = 66A IT Act = free speech.
xs: **Shreya Singhal (2015)** struck down **Section 66A of the Information Technology Act, 2000** under **Art. 19(1)(a)** — option **(1)**.
**Sec. 377** was read down in **Navtej (2018)**; **Sec. 497** struck in **Joseph Shine (2018)**; **Sec. 8(4) RPA** struck in **Lily Thomas (2013)**.
xa: ⚠ **Shreya Singhal** = Sec. 66A (speech); **Puttaswamy** = privacy under Art. 21.
Shreya Singhal came between **Vishaka (1997)** and **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)** rested on **voters' right to information**.

ne1be3511485.s: Which one of the following developments is associated with the application of the privacy principle in Puttaswamy?
o: Selection of Election Commissioners by a committee
ne1be3511485.x: Puttaswamy's privacy principle was reported as having been applied to DNA paternity tests.
ne1be3511485.tq: Apply a broad constitutional right to the specific modern factual context.
xs: The **Puttaswamy** privacy principle has been **applied to DNA paternity tests** — option **(3)**.
**NOTA** came from **PUCL (2013)**; EC selection by committee from **Anoop Baranwal (2023)**; **compulsory registration of marriages** from **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**.
xa: **K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)**: **privacy** is a fundamental right under **Art. 21**; **nine-judge** bench.
It **rejected the ADM Jabalpur** reasoning.
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the **Aadhaar Act 4:1** with limits.

nindian-polity-41-3.s: The Champakam Dorairajan case led to which Constitutional Amendment?
nindian-polity-41-3.x: Champakam held that FRs prevail over DPSPs, striking down caste-based quotas, so Parliament passed the 1st Amendment adding Article 15(4).
n: Champakam Dorairajan held that Fundamental Rights prevail over Directive Principles of State Policy in a conflict. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Champakam Dorairajan led to the First Constitutional Amendment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Champakam Dorairajan was linked to Article 15. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xa: Champakam is linked to **Articles 15, 29, 37, 46**.
**Minerva Mills (1980)** later held FRs and DPSP **complementary**.

nindian-polity-41-10.s: Which case validated reservation in promotions subject to quantifiable backwardness and efficiency data under Article 335?
nindian-polity-41-10.x: M. Nagaraj (2006) allowed reservation in promotions only on data showing backwardness and inadequate representation, without harming efficiency (Article 335).
nindian-polity-41-10.tq: Discriminate M. Nagaraj (promotions) from Indra Sawhney (the OBC quota).
n: M. Nagaraj was decided in 2006. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
M. Nagaraj validated reservation in promotions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
M. Nagaraj made reservation in promotions subject to quantifiable backwardness data. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
M. Nagaraj made reservation in promotions subject to efficiency data. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
M. Nagaraj was linked to Article 335. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xs: The case is **M. Nagaraj** — option **(3)**.
**M. Nagaraj (2006)** validated **reservation in promotions** subject to **quantifiable backwardness** and **efficiency** data under **Article 335**.
**Indra Sawhney** held **no reservation in promotion** under Art. 16(4); **Champakam** and **Randhir Singh** dealt with other issues.
xa: **Indra Sawhney (1992)** set the **50% ceiling**.
**Randhir Singh (1982)** = **equal pay for equal work**.
**Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: States may **sub-classify SCs** (**6:1**).

nindian-polity-41-17.s: Guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace were laid down in:
nindian-polity-41-17.x: Vishaka laid down the guidelines; Kihoto Hollohan made Speaker's defection rulings reviewable and Minerva Mills balanced Parts III and IV.
n: Free and fair elections are part of the Basic Structure according to Indira Nehru Gandhi. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Minerva Mills restored the balance between Part III and Part IV. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Kihoto Hollohan held that the Speaker’s ruling on defection is subject to judicial review. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
Vishaka formulated guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xa: **Vishaka (1997)** guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
⚠ **Vishaka** and **D.K. Basu** both **1997** = workplace harassment vs arrest/custody.
**Vishaka** was decided by **3 judges** under CJI **J.S. Verma**.

nfb93bcd6003.s: Which case was the first to read down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code?
nfb93bcd6003.x: The Naz Foundation case before the Delhi High Court in 2009 was the first to read down Section 377. Navtej Singh Johar subsequently gave the Supreme Court ruling in 2018.
nfb93bcd6003.tq: Separate the earlier initiating judgment from the later Supreme Court judgment.
xs: **Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down **Sec. 377** — option **(2)**.
The Supreme Court's **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** came later, overruling **Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013)**.
**Shreya Singhal (2015)** was about **Sec. 66A IT Act**; **Puttaswamy (2017)** about **privacy**.
xa: ⚠ **Sec. 377** = Navtej (read down); **Sec. 497** = Joseph Shine (struck down); both **2018**.
Navtej was a **five-judge bench**.
**Supriyo (Oct 2023)**: no fundamental right to marry; same-sex marriage left to **Parliament**.

nde60e57bc53.s: The Supreme Court in Shayara Bano v. Union of India held that:
o: Instant triple talaq was valid as an essential religious practice.
Article 25 completely excludes personal law from judicial review.
Polygamy and halala were both declared unconstitutional in the same judgment.
Instant triple talaq was invalid and was not an essential religious practice.
nde60e57bc53.x: Shayara Bano declared instant triple talaq invalid and held that it was not an essential religious practice under Articles 25 and 26. The questions of polygamy and halala were left open.
nde60e57bc53.tq: Find the precisely limited holding and reject the overbroad extension of the judgment.
xs: **Shayara Bano (2017)** held **instant triple talaq invalid** and **not an essential religious practice** — option **(4)**.
**Polygamy and nikah halala were left open** — so option 3 is wrong.
It examined **Arts. 25-26** — personal law was not kept out of review.
xa: Instant triple talaq = **Talaq-e-biddat**.
Bench: **five judges**, split **3:2**.
⚠ SC issued notice (**Aug 2026**) on a PIL to **ban polygamy**; **Javed (2003)**: polygamy not an essential religious practice.

n25b385fa378.s: Which 2018 judgment struck down Section 497 of the IPC dealing with adultery?
n25b385fa378.x: Joseph Shine (2018) struck down Section 497 IPC; the BNS, in force from 1 July 2024, has no adultery offence and no Section 377 equivalent.
xa: ⚠ **Sec. 377** = **Navtej** (read down); **Sec. 497** = **Joseph Shine** (struck down); both **2018**.
**Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down Sec. 377.
**Sarla Mudgal (1995)** and **Lily Thomas (2000)**: conversion to Islam cannot evade bigamy law.

nca4f1524970.s: In Supriyo v. Union of India (October 2023), the issue of same-sex marriage was:
nca4f1524970.x: Supriyo held there is no fundamental right to marry and left same-sex marriage to Parliament; transgender persons in heterosexual relationships can marry under existing law.
xa: **Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** decriminalised consensual same-sex acts between adults.
**Naz Foundation (Delhi HC, 2009)** first read down **Sec. 377**.
**Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**: **compulsory registration of marriages**.

n89e32462c30.s: Which case made registration of an FIR mandatory for cognizable offences?
n89e32462c30.x: Lalita Kumari made FIR registration mandatory under Section 154 CrPC (now Section 173 BNSS); arrest memos and medical checks are D.K. Basu guidelines.
xa: **Handcuffing** only in exceptional cases: **Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)**.
**Compulsory registration of marriages**: **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)**.
Shah Bano's **Sec. 125 CrPC** = **Sec. 144 BNSS**.

n356c1c6ebe3.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the decision in Shah Bano (1985)?
o: It held that instant triple talaq was constitutionally valid.
It struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act.
It prescribed the composition of the Election Commission.
It concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code.
n356c1c6ebe3.x: The Shah Bano case concerned maintenance under Section 125 of the CrPC and called for a Uniform Civil Code. Section 125 CrPC is now reflected in Section 144 of the BNSS, 2023.
n356c1c6ebe3.tq: Use the provision-and-principle combination to identify the correct case.
xs: **Shah Bano (1985)** concerned **maintenance under Sec. 125 CrPC** and **called for a UCC** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 125 CrPC** is now **Sec. 144 BNSS, 2023**.
**Sec. 8(4) RPA** fell in **Lily Thomas (2013)**; the EC selection committee came in **Anoop Baranwal (2023)**.
xa: **Sarla Mudgal (1995)** + **Lily Thomas (2000)**: conversion to Islam cannot evade **bigamy** law.
**Shayara Bano (2017)**: instant triple talaq invalid.
Bigamy = **Sec. 82 BNS**.

n6d627e8c3ab.s: Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act was struck down in:
n6d627e8c3ab.x: Lily Thomas (2013) concerned disqualification of convicted legislators; Sarla Mudgal and Lily Thomas (2000) dealt with conversion and bigamy.
xa: Bigamy = **Sec. 82 BNS**.

n6f4b0f3c76f.s: In Union of India v. ADR (2002), the Supreme Court required election candidates to disclose:
o: Criminal record, assets and educational qualifications
n6f4b0f3c76f.x: The ADR judgment required disclosure of criminal record, assets and educational qualifications.
xa: **PUCL (2013)**: **NOTA** option on EVMs.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: scheme struck down on **voters' right to information**.

n6e93e615dd5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the selection of the CEC and Election Commissioners?
o: Anoop Baranwal (2023) provided for a committee of the PM, the Leader of Opposition and the CJI
Parliament's 2023 Act replaced the CJI with a Union Minister in the committee
The Anoop Baranwal arrangement was permanent and could not be changed by Parliament
The Court's committee was to operate only till Parliament made a law
n6e93e615dd5.x: The Court's committee was to operate only until Parliament made a law, which Parliament did in 2023.
xa: **ADR (2002)**: disclosure of criminal record, assets, education.
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: voters' **right to information**.

n5a8f2259456.s: In the December 2023 Article 370 judgment, the Supreme Court treated Article 370 as:
o: Inoperable except by a constitutional amendment
n5a8f2259456.x: The Court treated Article 370 as temporary, upheld the President's power to make it inoperative and directed elections.
xa: Bench: **5 judges, unanimous**, CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; abrogation **upheld**.
J&K **statehood to be restored**; Assembly polls by **30 Sep 2024**.
Also in **Dec 2023**'s year: **Demonetisation (Jan 2023)** upheld **4:1**.

n705c8b5df3c.s: Which of the following correctly describes the recent legal position regarding the capital of Andhra Pradesh?
o: Kurnool became the sole capital under the 2022 Andhra Pradesh High Court judgment.
Visakhapatnam became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and the Supreme Court approved three capitals.
Amaravati became the sole capital with effect from 2 June 2024, and Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
The Andhra Pradesh High Court upheld the three-capital proposal in 2022 without legislative action thereafter.
n705c8b5df3c.x: After the Andhra Pradesh High Court’s 2022 ruling against three capitals, Amaravati became the sole capital from 2 June 2024. Parliament passed the AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026, in April 2026.
n705c8b5df3c.tq: Track the sequence of court ruling, effective date and subsequent parliamentary action.
xs: **Amaravati** became the **sole capital w.e.f. 2 June 2024**, and Parliament passed the **AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill, 2026** — option **(3)**.
The **AP HC (2022)** ruled **against three capitals** — so options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong.
xa: The Bill passed **LS on 1 Apr** and **RS on 2 Apr 2026**.
**E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)**: AP's **SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000** struck down.
**Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)**: **100% ST quota** struck down.

n39c6baa6b73.s: Which case held that polygamy is not an essential religious practice?
n39c6baa6b73.x: Javed (2003) held polygamy not an essential religious practice; the SC has issued notice on a PIL to ban polygamy, and bigamy is an offence under Section 82 BNS.
xa: **Shayara Bano (2017)** left **polygamy and nikah halala** open.
**Sarla Mudgal (1995)** + **Lily Thomas (2000)**: conversion cannot evade bigamy law.
**Shah Bano (1985)** called for a **UCC**.

nfc55a09c77a.s: Articles 32, 141 and 142 are significant in the context of Vishaka and Seema because they enable the Supreme Court to:
o: Fill legislative gaps temporarily until Parliament acts
Dissolve State Legislatures whenever legislation is absent
Exercise only advisory jurisdiction in social matters
nfc55a09c77a.x: Articles 32, 141 and 142 provide the constitutional basis through which judicial decisions can fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts, as illustrated by Vishaka and Seema.
nfc55a09c77a.tq: Connect constitutional provisions with the institutional function they collectively support.
xs: **Arts. 32, 141, 142** let judgments **fill legislative gaps until Parliament acts** — option **(1)**.
Examples: **Vishaka (1997)** guidelines and **Seema v. Ashwani Kumar (2006)** on **compulsory registration of marriages**.
xa: Vishaka's guidelines were replaced by the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Criticism: such **guideline-making** is seen as **judicial legislation**.
**Lalita Kumari (2013)**: **FIR mandatory** for cognizable offences.

nindian-society-46-4.s: Which judgement recognised transgender individuals as the Third Gender?
o: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
Bachpan Bachao Andolan v. Union of India
X v. Principal Secretary, H&FW, GNCTD
nindian-society-46-4.x: NALSA v. Union of India (2014) recognised transgender people as a third gender, with the right to self-identify their gender. Navtej Johar (2018) was about Section 377.
n: NALSA v. Union of India was decided in 2014. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
NALSA v. Union of India recognized transgender individuals as the Third Gender. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
NALSA v. Union of India affirmed the fundamental right of transgender individuals to self-identify their gender identity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 96-98]
xs: The judgement is **NALSA v. Union of India** — option **(1)**.
**NALSA (2014)** **recognized transgender individuals** as the **Third Gender** and their right to **self-identify** their **gender identity**.
**Navtej Singh Johar (2018)** dealt with **Sec. 377 IPC**, not third-gender status.
xa: **Supriyo (Oct 2023)**: **no fundamental right to marry**; same-sex marriage left to Parliament.
Supriyo: **transgender persons** in heterosexual relationships can marry under existing law.
**Shayara Bano (2017)**: instant **Triple Talaq** unconstitutional.

nindian-polity-41-45.s: Which case struck down the IMDT Act for breaching the Union's duty under Article 355?
nindian-polity-41-45.x: In Sarbananda Sonowal (2005), the IMDT Act was held to hamper detection of illegal migrants, breaching Article 355.
n: S.R. Bommai was linked to Article 355. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xa: IMDT = **Illegal Migrants (Determination by Tribunals) Act**.
**S.R. Bommai** is also linked to **Articles 356, 355**.
**Coal Allocation Scam Case (2013)** = "**Caged Parrot**".

n665eb4cc388.s: Aadhaar was held mandatory for which of the following purposes?
o: Subsidies or benefits charged to the Consolidated Fund and PAN or income-tax returns
Private insurance contracts and employment applications
Opening every bank account and obtaining every SIM card
n665eb4cc388.x: Aadhaar was held mandatory for specified subsidies and benefits funded from the Consolidated Fund, and for PAN and income-tax return requirements. It was not made mandatory for bank accounts, SIMs, school admissions or examinations.
n665eb4cc388.tq: Separate constitutionally permitted mandatory uses from services for which Aadhaar was not compulsory.
xs: Aadhaar is mandatory for **subsidies from the Consolidated Fund** and **PAN/ITR** — option **(1)**.
It is **not** mandatory for **bank accounts**, **SIMs / mobiles**, **school admissions**, **exams** — options 3 and 4 wrong.
**Private entities** cannot demand it (**Sec. 57** struck down) — option 2 wrong.
xa: ⚠ UPSC 2020 key: statements 2 and 4 correct; the **3-month retention** and **insurance** statements are wrong.
Act upheld **4:1** by a bench of **5 judges**.
Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth**.

n4c7acfd54be.s: Under the Aadhaar judgment, Aadhaar was held NOT mandatory for:
n4c7acfd54be.x: The judgment held Aadhaar not mandatory for bank accounts, SIM cards or school admissions, and did not permit unrestricted data-sharing contracts with private corporations.
xa: Mandatory only for **Consolidated Fund** benefits and **PAN/ITR**.
Records kept **6 months** at most.
Bench: **5 judges**, **4:1**.

n6c2f84d0377.s: Aadhaar, by itself, does NOT establish which of the following?
o: Eligibility for a specified benefit when legally required
Citizenship, domicile or date of birth
n6c2f84d0377.x: Section 9 of the Aadhaar Act provides that Aadhaar does not by itself prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth.
n6c2f84d0377.tq: Identify the legal limitation that prevents an identity document from becoming proof of unrelated status.
xs: Aadhaar does **not prove citizenship, domicile or date of birth** — option **(3)**.
This is stated in **Sec. 9, Aadhaar Act**.
xa: Aadhaar is **mandatory** for **Consolidated Fund** subsidies and **PAN/ITR**.
**Private entities cannot use Aadhaar data** (Sec. 57 struck down).
**Puttaswamy II (2018)** upheld the Act **4:1** with limits.

n2e8052921a8.s: The nine-judge Puttaswamy (privacy) Bench was associated with which Chief Justice?
n2e8052921a8.x: Puttaswamy was a nine-judge case associated with CJI J.S. Khehar; Bommai was also nine judges, while Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh were seven.
xa: **5 judges**: Shayara Bano (**3:2**); Navtej, Joseph Shine, Aadhaar (CJI **Dipak Misra**).
**3 judges**: Vishaka (CJI **J.S. Verma**).
**Indra Sawhney** was also a **nine-judge** bench.

n796bf250d49.s: Which group of cases was associated with a five-judge Bench headed by CJI Dipak Misra?
o: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar
Bommai, Maneka Gandhi and Davinder Singh
Vishaka, Shayara Bano and D.K. Basu
n796bf250d49.x: Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar were five-judge Bench cases associated with CJI Dipak Misra.
n796bf250d49.tq: Recognise the correct case cluster instead of matching a single isolated case.
xs: **Navtej Johar, Joseph Shine and Aadhaar** — **5 judges** under CJI **Dipak Misra** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 370** and **Electoral Bonds** were under CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**; **Puttaswamy** and **Bommai** had **9 judges**.
xa: **Vishaka**: **3 judges**, CJI **J.S. Verma**.
**Maneka Gandhi**, **Davinder Singh**: **7 judges**.
**Shayara Bano**: **5 judges**, **3:2**.

n0eb73ccba8e.s: The judgment in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (August 2024) held that:
o: States cannot classify Scheduled Castes internally under any circumstances.
Sub-classification applies only to Other Backward Classes.
Only Parliament may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and E.V. Chinnaiah was reaffirmed.
States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes, and it overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
n0eb73ccba8e.x: The seven-judge Bench in State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh, by a 6:1 majority, held that States may sub-classify Scheduled Castes and overruled E.V. Chinnaiah (2004).
n0eb73ccba8e.tq: Test the precise direction of the later judgment and the precedent it overruled.
xs: **Davinder Singh (Aug 2024)**: **States may sub-classify SCs**, overruling **E.V. Chinnaiah (2004)** — option **(4)**.
Bench: **7 judges**, **6:1**.
So options 1 and 3 (no State sub-classification, Chinnaiah reaffirmed) are wrong.
xa: **E.V. Chinnaiah v State of AP (2004)** had struck down AP's **SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000**.
**Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020)**: struck down **100% ST quota** for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
**Indra Sawhney (1992)**: **50% ceiling**, creamy layer excluded.

n867d79d9af0.s: The Supreme Court upheld demonetisation in January 2023 by what majority and under which provision?
o: 3:2 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
4:1 under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act
n867d79d9af0.x: The demonetisation decision was upheld by a 4:1 majority under Section 26(2) of the RBI Act.
n867d79d9af0.tq: Combine the majority figure with the exact statutory provision.
xs: Demonetisation was upheld **4:1** under **Section 26(2) of the RBI Act** — option **(4)**.
**Sec. 173 BNSS** is the FIR provision; **3:2** was **Shayara Bano**; **Art. 370** was a separate case.
xa: Decided in **Jan 2023**.
The **Aadhaar Act** was also upheld **4:1** (Puttaswamy II, **2018**).
**Electoral Bonds (Feb 2024)**: struck down unanimously by **5 judges**.

n3339ec8c8d7.s: The Supreme Court struck down the electoral bonds scheme primarily in relation to which constitutional right?
n3339ec8c8d7.x: In February 2024, the Court unanimously struck down the electoral bonds scheme in the context of voters’ right to information.
n3339ec8c8d7.tq: Connect the scheme with the constitutional transparency right identified in the judgment.
xs: The **Electoral Bonds** scheme was struck down on **voters' right to information** — option **(4)**.
Decided **Feb 2024** by **5 judges**, **unanimously** (ADR (Electoral Bonds)).
xa: **Union of India v. ADR (2002)**: candidates must disclose criminal record, assets, education.
**PUCL (2013)**: **NOTA** on EVMs.
Bench headed by CJI **D.Y. Chandrachud**.

nc3af4b70bcd.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about judgments on Andhra Pradesh reservation matters?
o: Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao (2020) upheld a 100% ST quota for teachers in Scheduled Areas
E.V. Chinnaiah was overruled by State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)
E.V. Chinnaiah (2004) struck down AP's SC sub-categorisation Act, 2000
Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao was decided in 2020
nc3af4b70bcd.x: Chebrolu Leela Prasad Rao struck down, not upheld, the 100% ST quota for teachers in Scheduled Areas.
xa: Davinder Singh: **7 judges, 6:1**; States may **sub-classify SCs**.
**AP HC (2022)** ruled against **three capitals**.
**Amaravati** = **sole capital w.e.f. 2 June 2024**.

nindian-polity-41-12.s: What was the ruling in Bachan Singh concerning capital punishment under Article 21?
o: Death penalty is subject to Article 356 review.
Death penalty is permissible only in the “rarest of rare cases.”
Death penalty is governed by the 10th Schedule.
Death penalty is unconstitutional in every case.
nindian-polity-41-12.x: Bachan Singh (1980) held that the death penalty is valid under Article 21, but only in the 'rarest of rare' cases.
n: Bachan Singh held that the death penalty in the “rarest of rare cases” is not unconstitutional under Article 21. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
The “rarest of rare” capital-punishment principle is associated with Bachan Singh. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xs: **Bachan Singh** held the death penalty permissible **only in the "rarest of rare cases"** — option **(2)**.
Death penalty in the "**rarest of rare cases**" is **not unconstitutional** under **Article 21**.
So it is not unconstitutional **in every case**; **Article 356** and the **10th Schedule** are unrelated.
xa: **Randhir Singh (1982)** = **equal pay for equal work**.
**Coal Allocation Scam Case (2013)**: SC coined "**Caged Parrot**".
**Sarbananda Sonowal (2005)** struck down the **IMDT Act**.

nindian-polity-41-18.s: In which context did the Supreme Court use the expression “Caged Parrot”?
nindian-polity-41-18.x: The Supreme Court called the CBI a 'caged parrot' in the coal allocation scam case of 2013, criticising government interference.
nindian-polity-41-18.tq: Recall the coal scam remark of 2013.
n: The Supreme Court coined the expression “Caged Parrot” during the Coal Allocation Scam Case in 2013. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 108-111]
xs: "Caged Parrot" was used in the **Coal Allocation Scam Case, 2013** — option **(1)**.
The SC coined "**Caged Parrot**" in the **Coal Allocation Scam Case (2013)**.
**IMDT Act** case (**2005**) = **Article 355**; **Vishaka (1997)** = **workplace harassment**; **Kesavananda (1973)** = basic structure.
xa: **Sarbananda Sonowal (2005)** struck down the **IMDT Act**.
**Bachan Singh**: death penalty only in the "**rarest of rare cases**".
**Randhir Singh (1982)**: **equal pay for equal work**.

n2a9db8831a3.s: The proposition that “bail is the rule even under the UAPA” was associated with:
o: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab
n2a9db8831a3.x: Andrabi v. NIA, reported on 18 May 2026, was associated with the proposition that bail is the rule even under the UAPA.
n2a9db8831a3.tq: Identify the case from the precise bail principle attributed to it.
xs: **Andrabi v NIA (18 May 2026)** held that **bail is the rule even under the UAPA** — option **(1)**.
**S.R. Bommai** concerned **Art. 356** and the floor test; **Vishaka** concerned workplace sexual harassment.
xa: **ADM Jabalpur (1976)**: FRs incl. **Art. 21** unenforceable in Emergency — the "darkest day".
**Maneka Gandhi (1978)**: Art. 21 procedure must be **fair, just and reasonable**.
**D.K. Basu (1997)**: arrest memo, informing kin, medical checks.

n2cb4f5e4de0.s: Which one of the following best describes the doctrine of colourable legislation?
o: A law operating outside a State is always unconstitutional
A State law automatically prevails over a Parliamentary law
A law may be invalidated because its political motive is improper
A legislature cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly
n2cb4f5e4de0.x: Colourable legislation embodies the principle that what cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly. It is concerned with legislative competence, not with the motive of the legislature.
n2cb4f5e4de0.tq: Distinguish legislative competence from legislative motive.
xs: **Colourable legislation**: a legislature **cannot do indirectly what it cannot do directly** — option **(4)**.
It is called a "**fraud on the Constitution**" and concerns **competence, not motive** — so option 3 is wrong.
Laws operating outside a State can be valid under **territorial nexus** — so option 1 is wrong.
xa: Field: **legislative competence**.
**Pith and substance**: incidental trespass is fine if the law's **true nature** is within the list.
Entries get the **widest meaning**.

n7d21c137d17.s: The doctrine of harmonious construction requires courts to:
o: Prefer Fundamental Rights over every Directive Principle in all cases
Read apparently conflicting provisions so that both can operate
Treat all constitutional provisions as legally unenforceable
n7d21c137d17.x: Harmonious construction seeks an interpretation under which apparently conflicting provisions, including Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles, can operate together.
n7d21c137d17.tq: Select the interpretation that preserves both apparently conflicting provisions.
xs: **Harmonious construction**: read conflicting provisions so **both operate** — option **(2)**.
Its field: **FR vs DPSP**; provision vs provision — so it does not make one side automatically win.
xa: Case: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** — temple entry (**Art. 25(2)(b)**) reconciled with **Art. 26(b)**.
**Minerva Mills**: **FR-DPSP harmony** — "FRs are means, DPSPs the ends".
**Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry covers matters incidental to it.

na21a1142627.s: The doctrine of incidental and ancillary powers implies that:
o: An incidental matter must always be placed in the Residuary List
Parliament has no power over matters not expressly listed
A legislative entry covers matters incidental to the subject expressly assigned to it
A State legislature can legislate on every subject connected with public order
na21a1142627.x: A legislative power over a subject includes powers over matters incidental and ancillary to that subject. Legislative entries are given a wide meaning for this purpose.
na21a1142627.tq: Apply the main-entry rule to an ancillary matter.
xs: **Incidental and ancillary**: power over an entry **covers matters incidental to it** — option **(3)**.
Entries get the **widest meaning**.
xa: Cases: **R.D. Joshi v Ajit Mills**; **Calcutta Gas**.
Residuary power is with Parliament (**Art. 248**).
**Pith and substance**: incidental trespass is fine.

n63d0da89385.s: Constitutional morality is best understood as:
o: Following the opinion of the numerical majority in every case
Giving priority to customary morality over constitutional text
Fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality
Applying only the personal morality of judges
n63d0da89385.x: Constitutional morality requires fidelity to constitutional values, even where those values conflict with prevailing or popular morality. The phrase is associated with Ambedkar, drawing on Grote.
n63d0da89385.tq: Distinguish constitutional values from popular or customary morality.
xs: **Constitutional morality** = **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality** — option **(3)**.
It is not the majority's opinion or customary morality.
xa: The phrase is **Ambedkar's, after Grote**.
Applied in **Navtej Johar (2018)**, **Sabarimala (2018)**, **NCT Delhi (2018)**.
Criticism: attacked as **subjective** → route to **judicial overreach**.

nde464588fa6.s: The phrase “constitutional morality” is associated with B.R. Ambedkar’s reference to:
nde464588fa6.x: Ambedkar used the phrase constitutional morality after Grote.
nde464588fa6.tq: Recall the thinker linked to the phrase through Ambedkar.
xs: Ambedkar used "**constitutional morality**" **after Grote** — option **(4)**.
**Montesquieu** is linked with **separation of powers**, not this phrase.
xa: Meaning: **fidelity to constitutional values over popular morality**.
Cases: **Navtej Johar**, **Sabarimala**, **NCT Delhi** (all **2018**).
⚠ Criticised as **subjective**.

n1caa09903f5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951)?
o: It is associated with the doctrine of pith and substance
The Act only incidentally touched imports
The Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure
The Prohibition Act was struck down because it touched imports
n1caa09903f5.x: The Prohibition Act was upheld as a public-health measure even though it incidentally touched imports.
xa: ⚠ **1951** = **Balsara** (pith and substance); **1957** = **R.M.D.C.** and **A.S. Krishna**.
Pith and substance is borrowed from **Canada**.
It is the APPSC answer for reconciling **Central & Provincial laws** (PYQ G2 2017).

nc191a8db89b.s: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) is associated with harmonious construction in the context of reconciling:
nc191a8db89b.x: Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958) reconciled temple-entry provisions under Article 25(2)(b) with the rights of religious denominations under Article 26(b).
nc191a8db89b.tq: Start from the sure case-article pairing.
xs: **Sri Venkataramana Devaru (1958)** reconciled **Articles 25(2)(b) and 26(b)** — option **(1)**.
Temple entry under **Art. 25(2)(b)** was read with **Art. 26(b)** by **harmonious construction**.
xa: Harmonious construction: read conflicting provisions so **both operate**.
**Minerva Mills** applied it to **FR-DPSP harmony**.
Order of lists: **Union > Concurrent > State**.

ne51be22cec7.s: The basic structure doctrine is commonly traced to the constitutional jurisprudence of which country?
ne51be22cec7.x: The basic structure doctrine is identified with Germany as its foreign origin in the given constitutional comparison.
ne51be22cec7.tq: Distinguish the origin of basic structure from the origin of separation of powers.
xs: **Basic structure** = **Germany** — option **(2)**.
**Japan** = "procedure established by law"; **Canada** = pith and substance; **France** = separation of powers.
xa: **Separation of powers** is part of the basic structure (**Kesavananda**).
**Public trust** = **Roman law**.
**Pleasure** = **England**; **prospective overruling** = **USA**.

ncd22538d79e.s: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied in India in:
ncd22538d79e.x: The doctrine of prospective overruling was first applied by the Supreme Court in Golaknath (1967).
ncd22538d79e.tq: Use the chronology of leading constitutional cases to identify the anchor case.
xs: **Prospective overruling** was first applied in **Golaknath (1967)** — option **(3)**.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)** concerns **separation of powers**; **Kesavananda** the basic structure.
xa: Origin: **USA**.
**Stare decisis**: **Art. 141** — SC's law binds all courts.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.

n0df3dfd48d4.s: The doctrine of pleasure in relation to civil services is primarily contained in:
o: Article 310, subject to safeguards under Article 311
n0df3dfd48d4.x: Article 310 embodies the pleasure doctrine, while Article 311 provides safeguards for civil servants against arbitrary dismissal, removal or reduction in rank.
n0df3dfd48d4.tq: Pair the principal Article with its constitutional safeguard.
xs: The **pleasure** doctrine is in **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards — option **(1)**.
Art. 311 protects **civil servants**.
xa: Origin of the pleasure doctrine: **England**.
**Stare decisis** = **Art. 141**.
**Prospective overruling** = **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.

nf70e1748ea1.s: Article 141 embodies the principle of stare decisis by providing that:
o: The law declared by every High Court binds all courts in India
Only advisory opinions of the Supreme Court are binding
Parliament must approve every Supreme Court judgment
The law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts within India
nf70e1748ea1.x: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding on all courts within India, reflecting the principle of stare decisis.
nf70e1748ea1.tq: Link the doctrine to the exact constitutional effect of Article 141.
xs: **Art. 141**: the **law declared by the Supreme Court binds all courts** — option **(4)**.
This is **stare decisis**; it is the SC's law, not a High Court's.
xa: **Prospective overruling**: first in **Golaknath (1967)**, origin **USA**.
**Pleasure**: **Art. 310**, with **Art. 311** safeguards.
**Separation of powers**: functional, not rigid (**Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955**).

n1fbab16b296.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 254(2)?
o: A State law on a Concurrent List matter may prevail in that State if it receives the President's assent
President's assent makes the State law permanently immune from Parliamentary legislation
It concerns matters in the Concurrent List
Parliament may subsequently override such a State law
n1fbab16b296.x: Parliament may later override a State law even after it has received the President's assent.
xa: General rule (**Art. 254**): Parliament's law **prevails** over a repugnant State law.
Order: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
Residuary power: **Art. 248**.

nd19c3aa3e7c.s: According to Montesquieu, the most effective means of protecting liberty is:
nd19c3aa3e7c.x: Montesquieu held that division of powers was the most effective way to protect liberty.
xa: His work: **"The Spirit of Laws" (1748)**; he drew on the **British constitution**.
UPSC 2021 key: best safeguard of liberty = **separation of powers**.
Separation of powers is a **presidential (USA)** principle; India and the UK follow **fusion**.

n25172113540.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about parliamentary and presidential systems?
o: In India the President is the real executive and the Council of Ministers the nominal executive
The principal checks in the US system are checks and balances among the three organs
The parliamentary system rests on fusion of powers
In the USA the President is independent of Congress
n25172113540.x: In India the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers the real executive.
xa: Parliamentary checks: **questions**, **confidence/no-confidence votes**.
The USA has a **single real executive**.
⚠ Ambedkar preferred **responsibility over stability**.

nb41132b512b.s: Article 50 of the Constitution directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in
o: the public services of the State
nb41132b512b.x: Article 50, a Directive Principle, directs separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
nb41132b512b.tq: Read the exact constitutional scope of Article 50 instead of expanding it to all institutions.
xs: **Art. 50 (DPSP)**: State shall **separate the judiciary from the executive** in the **public services of the State** — option **(1)**.
It is a Directive Principle, not about Governors, elections or Parliament.
xa: **Judiciary insulated**: Arts. **50, 121, 211, 235** (control of subordinate courts).
**AP angle**: Madras Presidency separated the **Collector's judicial powers** in **1816**.
India has **no rigid separation**; it is **implicit**, not absolute.

n81700615a23.s: Separation of powers in India is:
o: Implicit, not absolute, with overlapping functions creating checks and balances
Absolute, as in a pure presidential system
n81700615a23.x: India has no rigid separation; it is implicit, and overlapping functions create checks and balances.
xa: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: the Constitution does **not** recognise a rigid separation of powers.
**Legislature-executive fusion** under the parliamentary system; **judiciary insulated**.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.

n1fed3a37180.s: Collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is provided under
n1fed3a37180.x: Article 75(3) provides for the collective responsibility of the Union Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha.
n1fed3a37180.tq: Match the constitutional provision with the Union-level responsibility rule.
xs: **Article 75(3)** makes the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the **Lok Sabha** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Art. 164(2)** is the State parallel (Assembly); **Art. 85** = summon/prorogue; **Art. 61** = President's impeachment.
xa: Council stays only with **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
**No-confidence motion** — Lok Sabha only.

n772471a9fde.s: A no-confidence motion for removal of the government can be moved only in:
n772471a9fde.x: A no-confidence motion lies only in the Lok Sabha; Question Hour and Zero Hour give day-to-day watch over administration.
xa: **Adjournment** motions also draw attention to lapses.
Financial control: **Budget**, **cut motions**, **PAC** and **Estimates Committees**.
BPSC 2001 key: **executive subordinate to the legislature**.

ncda73232024.s: The Governor summons and prorogues the State Legislature under Article:
ncda73232024.x: The Governor acts under Article 174 (the President under Article 85); Article 175 is the Governor's address and messages. The gap between sessions cannot exceed six months.
xa: Ordinances: **Art. 123** (Union), **Art. 213** (State).

nd55f8a9e1fe.s: An ordinance, including one used to alter the legal basis of a judgment, can be issued when:
o: The legislature is not in session
A National Emergency is in force
nd55f8a9e1fe.x: An ordinance is issued when the legislature is not in session; it is subject to judicial review and must be laid before the House.
