xa: Criticism: the **ordinance** route is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Union ordinance **Art. 123**; State **Art. 213**.
Other route: **review / curative petition** (**Art. 137**).

n53adccca0ad.s: The Governor's ordinance-making power is contained in Article:
n53adccca0ad.x: Article 213 covers State ordinances; Article 123 Union ordinances, Article 175 the Governor's addresses and Article 86 the President's addresses.
xa: President's messages also = **Art. 87**; Governor's = **Art. 176**.
Assent: **Art. 111** (President), **Art. 200** (Governor); reservation for President **Art. 201**.
Summon/prorogue: **85 - 174**.

n58d40919d69.s: Which one of the following correctly states the constitutional provisions relating to assent and reservation of Bills?
n58d40919d69.x: Article 111 concerns presidential assent, Article 200 concerns the Governor's assent, and Article 201 concerns Bills reserved for the President.
n58d40919d69.tq: Separate the Union and State assent provisions from ordinance and reference Articles.
xs: **President — Art. 111; Governor — Art. 200; reservation for President — Art. 201** — option **(2)**.
**Art. 123 / 213** are the ordinance pair; **Art. 143** is the Presidential reference to the SC.
xa: **Art. 143** advice is **not binding** on the President.
Ordinances are subject to **judicial review** and must be **laid before the House**.

n625e519b002.s: A law declared ultra vires by the courts in exercise of judicial review is:
n625e519b002.x: Judicial review covers laws and executive action, rests on Articles 13, 32 and 226, and an ultra vires law is void.
xa: **Art. 142** "complete justice" fills gaps — risk of overreach.
**Arts. 122, 212**: courts cannot question legislative proceedings on irregular procedure.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.

ne548d1308b7.s: Which Article bars discussion in Parliament on the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court judge, except on a motion for removal?
ne548d1308b7.x: Article 121 bars it in Parliament and Article 211 in State Legislatures; Articles 122 and 212 stop courts inquiring into legislative proceedings for irregular procedure.
xa: ⚠ **121 / 211** = legislature cannot discuss judges; **122 / 212** = courts cannot question legislative procedure.
**Art. 235**: control of subordinate courts.
**Art. 50**: separation of judiciary from executive.

n286f3c1cbf6.s: Article 142 enables the Supreme Court to do which of the following?
o: Prevent all legislative proceedings from judicial scrutiny
Issue ordinances when Parliament is not in session
Remove a High Court judge without parliamentary procedure
Do complete justice and fill legal gaps in appropriate cases
n286f3c1cbf6.x: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to do complete justice and may allow it to fill legal gaps. Its use can raise concerns about judicial overreach, and its scope is not precisely defined.
n286f3c1cbf6.tq: Apply the constitutional power to a legal-gap situation rather than confusing it with ordinance or removal powers.
xs: **Art. 142** lets the SC do **"complete justice"** and **fill gaps** — option **(4)**.
Example: **Vishaka** guidelines before the **POSH Act, 2013**.
Ordinances are issued by the executive (**Art. 123/213**), not the Court.
xa: Risk: **overreach**; scope **undefined**.
Frequent **Art. 142** use is said to erode **separation of powers**.
Judicial review rests on Arts. **13, 32, 226**.

n751ca37f2ca.s: Which one of the following correctly reflects the ruling in Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab (1955)?
o: The executive can exercise power only after receiving prior approval from the judiciary.
The Indian Constitution does not recognise a rigid separation of powers, and executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
The Indian Constitution establishes a rigid separation of powers among the three organs of government.
The legislature may decide disputes arising from judicial proceedings.
n751ca37f2ca.x: In Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, the Supreme Court held that the Indian Constitution does not provide for a rigid separation of powers. It also recognised that executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws.
n751ca37f2ca.tq: Test the precise holding of a constitutional case rather than accepting the extreme phrase ‘rigid separation’.
xs: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: **no rigid separation of powers**; **executive power extends to matters on which the legislature can make laws** — option **(2)**.
So option 3 (rigid separation) is the reverse of the holding.
Deciding disputes is a **judicial function** (Raj Narain) — so option 4 is wrong.
xa: **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**: separation of powers among the **basic features**.
In India separation is **implicit**, not absolute.
Overlapping functions create **checks and balances**.

n4c692c78602.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about separation of powers in India?
o: Kesavananda Bharati recognised separation of powers as a basic feature
Raj Narain held that the legislature could finally decide an election dispute
Raj Narain was connected with the challenge to the 39th Amendment
Deciding an election dispute is a judicial function
n4c692c78602.x: Raj Narain held the legislature cannot decide an election dispute because it is a judicial function.
xa: **Minerva Mills**: the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review struck down.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)**: no rigid separation of powers.

n34b7b926707.s: Which Amendment placed Tamil Nadu's 69 per cent reservation law in the Ninth Schedule?
n34b7b926707.x: The 76th Amendment did so; after I.R. Coelho, such post-24 April 1973 entries can be reviewed if they damage the basic structure.
xa: Override routes are all tested against the **basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills** struck down the **42nd Amendment**'s bar on review.
**24th Amendment** overrode **Golaknath**.

n5785de44a85.s: The 42nd Amendment's bar on judicial review was struck down in:
o: Indira Nehru Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975)
n5785de44a85.x: Minerva Mills struck down the bar; Raj Narain struck down the 39th Amendment's validation of the PM's election, and Golaknath predates the 42nd Amendment.
xa: Raj Narain: the legislature **cannot decide an election dispute** — a judicial function.
**I.R. Coelho**: Ninth Schedule entries after **24 Apr 1973** reviewable.
**Kesavananda (1973)**: separation of powers a **basic feature**.

ne5fdfac8597.s: The 77th Constitutional Amendment (promotion quota) followed which judgment?
ne5fdfac8597.x: The 77th followed Indra Sawhney; the 24th followed Golaknath, the 26th Madhav Rao and the 1st Champakam Dorairajan.
xa: **Limit**: every override is tested against the **basic structure**.
Exam angle: Parliament **cannot** overrule a judgment by a **simple resolution**.
**76th Amdt** placed the TN **69%** quota in the Ninth Schedule.

n3c8898ace06.s: The system of proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote used in the election of the President was borrowed from the Constitution of
n3c8898ace06.x: The Presidential election method of proportional representation by single transferable vote was borrowed from Ireland.
n3c8898ace06.tq: Use the source-country association for a distinctive constitutional device.
xs: The **single transferable vote** system for the President's election was borrowed from **Ireland** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It works by **proportional representation** with a **secret ballot** (**Art. 55(3)**).
xa: ⚠ **Impeachment** of the President is borrowed from the **USA**; the election method from **Ireland**.
Disputes over the election are decided **only by the Supreme Court** (**Art. 71**).

nca5a33daaea.s: In the Presidential election, the value of an MLA's vote = (population of the State / number of elected MLAs) × ____.
nca5a33daaea.x: An MLA's vote value is State population divided by elected MLAs, multiplied by 1/1000, so it varies with the State's population.
xa: Population base: **1971 Census**, frozen till the first Census after **2026**.

n858d7e933d4.s: The population base for calculating the value of votes in the Presidential election is the Census of:
n858d7e933d4.x: The 1971 Census is the base, frozen under the 84th Amendment till the first Census after 2026.
xa: **MLA vote** = (State population / elected MLAs) x **1/1000**.
**MP vote** = total value of all MLAs' votes / total elected MPs.

nf0c2f846c2b.s: Disputes connected with the election of the President under Article 71 are decided by:
o: The Supreme Court or the High Courts
nf0c2f846c2b.x: Only the Supreme Court decides them; acts done before an election is declared void remain valid, and a vacancy in the electoral college is no ground for challenge.
xa: An election **declared void** is a cause of vacancy; the new election must be held **within 6 months** (**Art. 62**).
The new President gets a **full 5-year term**.

nindian-polity-8-16.s: In the Presidential election, the value of an MP's vote is calculated to ensure:
o: Equality between the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
Parity between the Union and the States
nindian-polity-8-16.x: MP vote values ensure parity between the Union and the States, while MLA vote values ensure uniformity among States.
n: The value of an MLA’s vote is calculated to ensure uniformity among the states. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The value of an MP’s vote is calculated to ensure parity between the Union and the states. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: MLA vote = (State population / elected MLAs) x **1/1000**.
MP vote = total value of all MLAs' votes / total elected MPs.

nindian-polity-9-6.s: The electoral college for the election of the Vice-President consists of:
o: All MPs and the State Legislative Assemblies
All members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
nindian-polity-9-6.x: All MPs, elected and nominated, vote by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot; State Assemblies do not take part.
n: The Electoral College for the Vice-Presidential election consists of members of both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Elected Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Nominated Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected by proportional representation by means of the Single Transferable Vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-Presidential election is conducted by secret ballot. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Only Members of Parliament participate in the Vice-Presidential Electoral College. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Nominated Members of Parliament vote in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
State Legislative Assembly members do not vote in the Vice-Presidential election. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected indirectly. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-Presidential election differs from the Presidential election because State Legislative Assemblies do not participate in it. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is elected and is not appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: The **11th Amdt, 1961** ended the joint-meeting method for VP election.
The President's college includes **elected** MLAs, incl. **Delhi and Puducherry**.
VP qualification is linked to the **Rajya Sabha**.

nd689e4b9b55.s: The emoluments of the President of India are:
o: Fixed by the Union Cabinet and listed in the First Schedule
Fixed by the Finance Commission and listed in the Fourth Schedule
Fixed by Parliament by law and listed in the Second Schedule
Fixed by the Supreme Court and listed in the Third Schedule
nd689e4b9b55.x: Parliament fixes the President's emoluments by law; they are listed in the Second Schedule and cannot be reduced during the term.
xa: **Art. 59:** official residence **rent-free**; the President cannot be a member of any legislature.
Conditions of office (no office of profit, emoluments) are in **Art. 59**.

n3c19913544e.s: The President of India addresses his resignation to the:
n3c19913544e.x: The President resigns in writing to the Vice-President, who informs the Speaker; the CJI administers the oath under Article 60.
xa: The President swears to "**preserve, protect and defend the Constitution** and the law".
Emoluments are **charged** on the **Consolidated Fund of India** and cannot be diminished during the term.
⚠ The **Vice-President** resigns to the **President**.

n0f1d8f2349a.s: The Eleventh Constitutional Amendment of 1961 is associated with which of the following changes?
o: Removal of nominated members from the Vice-Presidential electoral college
Providing for election of the Vice-President by State Legislatures
Ending the joint-meeting method for the election of the Vice-President
Introduction of direct election to the office of Vice-President
n0f1d8f2349a.x: The Eleventh Amendment ended the earlier joint-meeting method and provided for election of the Vice-President by the members of both Houses of Parliament.
n0f1d8f2349a.tq: Test the amendment by identifying the precise institutional procedure it altered, not the broader office concerned.
xs: The **11th Amendment, 1961** **ended the joint-meeting method** of electing the Vice-President — so option **(3)** is correct.
The VP's electoral college is **all MPs, elected and nominated**, with **no MLAs** — so nominated members were not removed and States play no part.
xa: ⚠ The President's electoral college **excludes nominated MPs** but includes **elected MLAs**.
A **VP vacancy** (**Art. 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.

nindian-polity-8-17.s: Under Article 58, the minimum age for election as President of India is:
nindian-polity-8-17.x: A candidate must be an Indian citizen, have completed 35 years, be qualified for the Lok Sabha and hold no office of profit.
n: A Presidential candidate must be a citizen of India under Article 58. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A Presidential candidate must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A Presidential candidate must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A Presidential candidate must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: **Term**: **five years** (**Article 56**); re-election any number of times (**Article 57**).
⚠ The **Vice-President**'s qualification is linked to the **Rajya Sabha**.
**Art. 59**: not a member of any legislature; rent-free residence.

nindian-polity-8-29.s: The term of office of the President of India is prescribed as five years under which Article of the Constitution?
nindian-polity-8-29.x: Article 56 fixes the President's term at five years. Article 57 is re-election, 61 impeachment and 65 the Vice-President acting as President.
nindian-polity-8-29.tq: Link the term of office to Article 56.
n: The term of the President is five years under Article 56. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xs: The President's five-year term is under **Article 56** — option **(1)**.
**Article 56** fixes the term at **five years**; the outgoing President continues until the successor enters office.
**Article 57** = **re-election**; **Article 61** = **impeachment**; **Article 65** = VP **acts as President**.
xa: **Article 58** = **qualifications**; **Article 60** = **oath**.
**Article 62** = time of election to fill a vacancy.
**Article 71** = election disputes.

nindian-polity-9-8.s: A candidate for Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the:
nindian-polity-9-8.x: A Vice-President must be qualified for the Rajya Sabha, besides being an Indian citizen aged 35 holding no office of profit.
n: A Vice-President must be a citizen of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must have completed 35 years of age. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must be qualified for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
A Vice-President must not hold any office of profit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The qualification for election as Vice-President is linked to eligibility for the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: The **President**'s qualification is linked to the **Lok Sabha**.
The VP resigns to the **President**.
The VP is **not** part of Parliament; the President is.

ned1775a559c.s: How many terms may a person serve as President of India?
ned1775a559c.x: The President holds office for five years and may be re-elected; the Constitution prescribes no limit on terms.
xa: Only **Rajendra Prasad** served two full terms (elected **1952**, **1957**).
⚠ Contrast: **US 22nd Amendment** = two terms; **South Korea** = single 5-year term.

n7fedecdc144.s: The emoluments of the President of India:
o: May be diminished by Parliament during the term
Are decided afresh by each Finance Commission
Cannot be diminished during the term
Can be cut by the Council of Ministers
n7fedecdc144.x: The President's emoluments cannot be diminished during the term; the President also gets a rent-free residence and cannot be a member of any legislature.
xa: Emoluments are listed in the **Second Schedule**.
**Art. 58**: no **office of profit** under the Union, a State or any local/other authority.

nd450a8ad9b2.s: The impeachment resolution against the President must be signed by at least ____ of the members of the House, after 14 days' notice.
nd450a8ad9b2.x: One-fourth of the members must sign after 14 days' notice; the charge may start in either House, and no President has been impeached so far.
xa: Passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of the initiating House; the other House investigates.
⚠ **Nominated MPs take part**; **elected MLAs do not**.

n3697af0c1ac.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the impeachment of the President under Article 61?
o: The other House investigates the charge
The initiating House may pass the charge by a simple majority
The President has the right to appear and be represented during the investigation
The other House must pass the charge by two-thirds of its total membership
n3697af0c1ac.x: Both Houses must pass the charge by a two-thirds majority of their total membership; a simple majority is not enough.
xa: Charges need a resolution signed by **one-fourth** of members after **14 days'** notice.
Ground: **"violation of the Constitution"** only (**Art. 61**).

nb90eb9944be.s: Who among the following does NOT take part in the impeachment of the President?
o: Elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
Elected members of the Lok Sabha
nb90eb9944be.x: Elected and nominated members of both Houses of Parliament take part; elected MLAs of the States, Delhi and Puducherry do not.
xa: ⚠ Election: **elected MLAs vote, nominated MPs do not**; impeachment: the reverse.
The VP's electoral college is also **all MPs, elected and nominated**, with no MLAs.

na6f65b81d98.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about filling a vacancy in the office of the President?
o: On expiry of the term, the election must be completed before the term expires
A person elected to fill a vacancy holds office only for the predecessor's unexpired term
A vacancy by death, resignation or removal must be filled within six months
The rule on vacancy by expiry of term is in Article 62(1)
na6f65b81d98.x: A President elected to fill a vacancy gets a full five-year term, not the unexpired part.
xa: The outgoing President **continues until the successor enters office** (**Art. 56**).
⚠ A **VP vacancy** (**Art. 68**) has **no** 6-month deadline.

n8908748b6e4.s: While the Vice-President acts as President under Article 65, the Rajya Sabha is presided over by the:
o: Senior-most member of the Rajya Sabha
n8908748b6e4.x: The Vice-President stops functioning as Chairman while acting as President, and the Deputy Chairman presides.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (July 2025)** → **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected — a mid-term VP vacancy.
**B.D. Jatti** acted after **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed** died in office.

n11d7db690aa.s: Under Article 240, the President may make regulations for Puducherry:
o: Only with the consent of the Lieutenant Governor
When its Legislative Assembly is suspended or dissolved
n11d7db690aa.x: Article 240 covers UTs such as Andaman and Nicobar, Lakshadweep and DNH-DD, and Puducherry when its Assembly is suspended or dissolved.
xa: The President administers **UTs** through **administrators**.
Ordinances are under **Art. 123**.

n54c39ed69d3.s: The Comptroller and Auditor General is appointed under Article:
n54c39ed69d3.x: Article 148 concerns the CAG; Article 76 the Attorney General, 155 Governors and 324 the Election Commission.
xa: CAG, Governors and AG are appointed **on the advice of the PM / Council of Ministers** (**Art. 74**).

na2e26578c7c.s: In the formal sense under Article 74, the CJI, judges, the Attorney General and Governors are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the:
na2e26578c7c.x: Under Article 74 the President acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM, so these appointments are formally on the PM's recommendation.
xa: In practice judges are chosen by the **collegium** (**CJI + 4** senior-most, **Third Judges Case 1998**).

n10950664378.s: A joint sitting of Parliament is summoned by the ____ and presided over by the ____.
o: President; Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
President; Speaker of the Lok Sabha
n10950664378.x: Summoning a joint sitting is a legislative function of the President, and the Speaker of the Lok Sabha presides over it.
xa: A **joint sitting** is presided over by the **Speaker**.
He also **nominates 12 to the RS** and issues **ordinances** (**Art. 123**).

n7462f6a1821.s: How many members does the President nominate to the Rajya Sabha?
n7462f6a1821.x: The President nominates twelve members to the Rajya Sabha; under Article 79 the President is part of Parliament.
xa: The President can **summon/prorogue** both Houses, **dissolve Lok Sabha** and summon a **joint sitting**.
Prior recommendation is needed for **Art. 3** and **money bills**.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123**.

n36f052783fa.s: The President's prior recommendation is required for the introduction of:
o: An Ordinary Bill in the Rajya Sabha
n36f052783fa.x: Prior recommendation is needed for a Money Bill and a Bill under Article 3, not for every Private Member's Bill.
xa: **Demands for grants** also need his recommendation.
⚠ For a **Money Bill** he can only **assent or withhold** — no suspensive veto.

n3c0faaa496b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pardoning powers of the President and Governor?
o: The President may pardon a death sentence
The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence but may suspend, remit or commute it
The President may exercise pardoning power in court-martial cases
The Governor may grant pardon in a court-martial case
n3c0faaa496b.x: The Governor has no power to pardon a court-martial sentence; only the President has.
xa: President: offences against **Union laws**; Governor (**Art. 161**): **State laws**.
**Kehar Singh (1989):** no right of oral hearing; **Epuru Sudhakar (2006)**: limited judicial review.

n217368aa0f1.s: Under Article 72, the President's power of pardon does NOT necessarily cover which of the following?
o: Sentences imposed under State laws, in every case
Offences against laws within the Union's executive power
All cases involving a death sentence
n217368aa0f1.x: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, Union-law offences and all death sentences, but not sentences under State laws in every case.
xa: Forms: **pardon, commutation, remission, respite, reprieve**.
**Amnesty** lies outside **Art. 72**.

n07e8959987f.s: The suspensive veto of the President is NOT available in respect of:
n07e8959987f.x: A suspensive veto returns an Ordinary Bill once for reconsideration, with assent mandatory if passed again; it does not apply to Money Bills.
xa: ⚠ "Suspensive veto on Money Bills" is a **trap** (**APPSC-G1 2024**).
The President's veto is under **Article 111**.

n96610521688.s: Who is the only Chief Justice of India to have acted as President?
n96610521688.x: M. Hidayatullah acted as President in 1969; V.V. Giri won on second-preference votes, and S. Radhakrishnan was the first President from South India.
xa: **N. Sanjiva Reddy**: only President elected **unopposed**; from **AP**; first CM of AP (**1956**).
**Rajendra Prasad**: only President **elected twice** (**1952, 1957**).
⚠ Died in office: **Zakir Husain** and **Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed**; acted: **M. Hidayatullah** and **B.D. Jatti**.

nf23efcaebce.s: Who was the only President of India elected unopposed?
nf23efcaebce.x: N. Sanjiva Reddy (President 1977–82), from Andhra Pradesh, was elected unopposed; he was earlier Lok Sabha Speaker and AP's first Chief Minister.
xa: He came from **Anantapur / Nandyala**.
⚠ Elected President in **1977** (some notes say **1978**).
He was the **6th** President.

n53c8be7fce5.s: The electoral college for the election of the President is provided in Article:
n53c8be7fce5.x: Article 54 covers the electoral college; Article 52 creates the office, 60 is the oath and 71 election disputes.
xa: **Art. 55** = manner of election (value of votes, **STV**).
**Art. 61** = impeachment; **Art. 62** = time of election to fill a vacancy.

n4b5d3bdb851.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Article 60 deals with the President's eligibility for re-election
Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President
Article 56 deals with the President's term and resignation to the Vice-President
Article 58 lays down the qualifications for election as President
n4b5d3bdb851.x: Article 60 concerns the President's oath or affirmation; eligibility for re-election is in Article 57.
xa: **Art. 59** = conditions of office (no office of profit, emoluments).
**Art. 65** = VP to act as President.

nindian-polity-8-19.s: The impeachment of the President for violation of the Constitution is dealt with in Article:
nindian-polity-8-19.x: Article 61 governs impeachment; either House can prefer the charge and each must pass it by a special majority.
n: The President can be removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The impeachment procedure is provided under Article 61. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
A charge for impeachment of the President can be preferred by either House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
Impeachment of the President requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: Resolution signed by **one-fourth** of members after **14 days'** notice.
Passed by **two-thirds of the total membership** of each House.
**No President has ever been impeached**.

nindian-polity-8-31.s: Which of the following is exercised by the President on ministerial advice and is NOT a situational discretionary power?
o: Appointing a PM in a hung Parliament
Dismissing a government that has lost its majority
nindian-polity-8-31.x: Appointing Ambassadors is done on ministerial advice; the other three are listed as situational discretion.
n: The President may appoint a Prime Minister in case of a hung Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may dismiss a government that has lost its majority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
The President may dissolve the Lok Sabha as a limited discretionary power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 22-25]
xa: The **pocket veto** is another limited discretion.
The **44th Amendment** let the President **return advice** **once** for reconsideration.
⚠ **42nd** = advice binding; **44th** = one reconsideration, then binding.

nf50fde5b9b5.s: Jagdeep Dhankhar’s resignation as Vice-President in July 2025 and the subsequent election of C. P. Radhakrishnan are relevant primarily to which constitutional provisions?
nf50fde5b9b5.x: Articles 65 and 68 deal respectively with the Vice-President acting as President and the filling of a vacancy in the office of Vice-President. The July 2025 resignation therefore invoked these provisions.
nf50fde5b9b5.tq: Use the office-function pairing: identify the Articles dealing with acting arrangements and a Vice-Presidential vacancy.
xs: The resignation tested the arrangements of **Articles 65 and 68** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned (July 2025)** → **C.P. Radhakrishnan** elected — the **third** mid-term VP vacancy.
**Art. 61** = impeachment, **Art. 72** = pardon, **Art. 74** = aid and advice, **Arts. 52-53** = the President and executive power.
xa: **Art. 65:** VP acts as President; meanwhile the **Deputy Chairman** presides over the Rajya Sabha.
⚠ Unlike a Presidential vacancy, **Art. 68** has **no** 6-month deadline.

n976b086a951.s: Which of the following correctly states the comparison concerning presidential term limits?
o: The United States permits only one presidential term, whereas South Korea permits two five-year terms.
The United States limits a President to two terms, whereas South Korea provides for a single five-year term.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe two presidential terms.
Both the United States and South Korea prescribe a single five-year presidential term.
n976b086a951.x: The Twenty-Second Amendment of the United States limits a President to two terms. South Korea follows a single five-year presidential term.
n976b086a951.tq: Handle comparison questions by checking both parts of the pair rather than recognising only one correct country.
xs: The **US** limits a President to **two terms** and **South Korea** has a **single 5-year term** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The US limit comes from its **22nd Amendment**.
xa: India has **no term limit** (**Art. 57**: re-election allowed).
India borrowed **impeachment** from the **USA**.

nc61f998edd3.s: The advice tendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 is:
o: Binding only during a financial emergency
Binding after approval by the Rajya Sabha
nc61f998edd3.x: Under Article 143, the President may consult the Supreme Court, but the advice given by the Court is not binding.
nc61f998edd3.tq: Discriminate between consultation and compulsory compliance by focusing on the legal effect of the advice.
xs: Advice given under **Art. 143** is **not binding** on the President — so option **(3)** is correct.
The President **consults the SC**; the advice is advisory only.
xa: Other judicial power: **pardons** under **Art. 72**.
⚠ Contrast **Art. 74**: Council of Ministers' advice **is binding** (**42nd Amendment**).

n7d585a7dbbe.s: Financial Emergency is provided under Article:
n7d585a7dbbe.x: Financial Emergency is Article 360; Article 352 is National Emergency, 356 failure of constitutional machinery in a State and 143 advisory jurisdiction.
xa: Emergency powers of the President: **Arts. 352, 356, 360**.
**Art. 143** advice is **not binding**.

n5148cc15fab.s: Which one of the following is a financial power of the President of India?
o: Fixing the repo rate for the Reserve Bank of India
Advancing money from the Contingency Fund of India
n5148cc15fab.x: The President can authorise advances from the Contingency Fund of India. The Budget is laid before Parliament in the President's name, and recommendations are required for Money Bills and demands for grants.
n5148cc15fab.tq: Identify the function that belongs to the President's constitutional financial role without assigning executive or monetary-policy powers to that office.
xs: Advances from the **Contingency Fund** of India are a **financial power** of the President — so option **(3)** is correct.
Other financial powers: the **budget** is laid in his name; **money bills** and **demands for grants** need his recommendation.
No tax can be imposed without Parliament; repo rate and audits are not his powers.
xa: The **CAG** is appointed by the President (**Art. 148**).
The **Finance Commission** is also appointed by the President.

n21e29ffbcdf.s: Articles 52 to 78 of the Constitution of India constitute
o: Part V, Chapter I dealing with the Union Executive
Part VI, Chapter I dealing with the State Executive
Part III dealing with Fundamental Rights
Part V, Chapter II dealing with Parliament
n21e29ffbcdf.x: Articles 52 to 78 fall under Part V, Chapter I, which deals with the Union Executive.
n21e29ffbcdf.tq: Distinguish the Part and Chapter classification from the adjacent chapter on Parliament.
xs: **Arts. 52-78** form **Part V, Chapter I** — **The Executive** (Union) — so option **(1)** is correct.
It opens with **Art. 52** (there shall be a President) and ends with **Art. 78** (PM's duty to inform the President).
xa: **Art. 74** = Council of Ministers to aid and advise; **Art. 76** = Attorney General.
**Art. 53**: executive power of the Union vested in the President.

na06f67d4db1.s: President Droupadi Murmu promulgated the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026. What change did the Ordinance provide?
o: Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 37 to 40, excluding the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, including the CJI
Increase in the number of Supreme Court judges from 31 to 33, excluding the CJI
na06f67d4db1.x: The 2026 Ordinance increased the number of Supreme Court judges from 33 to 37, with the Chief Justice of India excluded from this count.
na06f67d4db1.tq: Separate the numerical change from the counting exception relating to the Chief Justice of India.
xs: The Ordinance raised SC judges from **33 to 37, excluding the CJI** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Promulgated by **Droupadi Murmu**; gazette dated **16 May 2026**.
xa: It was **criticised as ordinance misuse**.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123**.

n6ef8daae0a2.s: The pardoning power of the President under Article 72 and of the Governor under Article 161 respectively relates primarily to offences against:
n6ef8daae0a2.x: The President deals with offences against Union laws, while the Governor deals with offences against State laws.
n6ef8daae0a2.tq: Use the Union–State jurisdiction contrast to avoid reversing the two constitutional provisions.
xs: The President's power covers offences against **Union laws** and the Governor's against **State laws** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 72** (President) → **Union** law; **Art. 161** (Governor) → **State** law; option (2) reverses them.
xa: The Governor **cannot pardon a death sentence** but can **suspend, remit or commute** it.
The Governor has **no power** over **court-martial** sentences.
**Madras HC** Full Bench (**Apr 2026**): Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **remission**.

nindian-polity-38-16.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the forms of the pardoning power?
o: Pardon – Removal of both sentence and conviction
Reprieve – Permanent cancellation of the sentence
Commutation – Substitution of a heavier punishment with a lighter one
Remission – Reduction in duration without changing the sentence's character
nindian-polity-38-16.x: A reprieve is only a temporary postponement of execution; removal of sentence and conviction is a pardon.
n: Pardon completely removes the sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pardon completely removes the conviction. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Commutation substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission reduces the period or duration of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission does not change the fundamental character of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a postponement of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xa: **Respite**: a **lesser sentence** due to **pregnancy**, **mental** or **physical disability**.
⚠ **Commutation** = lighter **form**; **remission** = shorter **period**.
**Article 72** covers **court-martial**, **Union law** offences and **death sentence**.

nindian-polity-38-51.s: Which pardoning power awards a lesser sentence because of special personal circumstances such as pregnancy or physical disability?
nindian-polity-38-51.x: A respite gives a lesser sentence because of special circumstances such as pregnancy or disability. Remission shortens a sentence without changing its nature.
n: Commutation substitutes a heavier form of punishment with a lighter form. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Remission reduces the period or duration of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite awards a lesser sentence in place of the original penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Respite is granted due to special personal circumstances. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Pregnancy is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Mental disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Physical disability is an example of a special personal circumstance for Respite. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve grants a postponement of the execution of a sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
Reprieve especially applies to the death penalty. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The power is **Respite** — option **(4)**.
**Respite** awards a **lesser sentence** due to **special personal circumstances** — **pregnancy**, **mental** or **physical disability**.
**Commutation** changes the **form**; **Remission** cuts the **period**; **Reprieve** **postpones** execution.
xa: **Pardon** makes it as if the offence had **never been committed**.
**Article 72** vs **Article 161**: President covers **Union laws**; Governor **State laws**.
Judicial review of pardons is **limited** — **mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant** grounds.

nindian-polity-38-80.s: Which form of executive pardon may substitute a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment?
nindian-polity-38-80.x: Commutation replaces a punishment with a lighter one, such as a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. Remission only shortens the term.
n: Commutation may substitute a death sentence with rigorous life imprisonment. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: The pardon is **Commutation** — option **(1)**.
**Commutation** substitutes a **lighter** form of punishment — e.g. **death sentence → rigorous life imprisonment**.
**Pardon** wipes out sentence and conviction; **Respite** is due to personal circumstances; **Remission** only shortens the **period**.
xa: ⚠ **Commutation** = lighter **form**; **remission** = shorter **period**, same character.
The Governor cannot pardon a **death sentence** but can **commute** it.
**Maru Ram (1980)**: exercised on **Council of Ministers' advice**.

n203eeedb826.s: In respect of which of the following must the President give assent, so that the absolute veto cannot apply?
o: A Government Bill when the Cabinet resigned before assent
n203eeedb826.x: A Constitutional Amendment Bill must receive assent; absolute veto may apply to a private member's Bill or a Government Bill after the Cabinet resigns.
xa: **Pocket veto**: Bill kept pending — **no time limit** in the Constitution.
**Suspensive veto**: return **once**; then must assent.

nindian-polity-2-40.s: The 15% size limit on the Council of Ministers is contained in Article:
nindian-polity-2-40.x: Article 75(1A) sets the size limit; Article 74 is aid and advice, 75(3) collective responsibility and 76 the Attorney-General.
n: Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 75(3) provides for collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 75(1A) concerns the size limit of the Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 76 concerns the Attorney-General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 77** = **conduct of business** of the Government of India.
**Article 78** = PM's duty to inform the President.

n7f1316ec5e9.s: Which one of the following best describes the constitutional position of the President and the Prime Minister?
o: The President is the real executive and the Prime Minister is the nominal executive.
The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister is the real or de facto executive.
The Prime Minister is the constitutional head and the President is only a ceremonial officer without executive status.
Both are independent real executives with equal authority in all matters.
n7f1316ec5e9.x: The President is the nominal or de jure executive, while the Prime Minister, heading the Council of Ministers, functions as the real or de facto executive.
n7f1316ec5e9.tq: Use the nominal-versus-real executive distinction and reject the reversal of roles.
xs: The President is the **nominal / de jure** executive and the PM the **real / de facto** executive — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Council of Ministers headed by the PM** aids and advises the President (**Art. 74**).
xa: All executive action is taken **in his name**.
⚠ **42nd** = advice binding; **44th** = one reconsideration, then binding.

n631c73a2aaa.s: Under Article 74(2), which of the following is correct regarding the advice tendered by the Council of Ministers?
o: The advice tendered to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.
The advice becomes public automatically after being tendered.
Any court may inquire into the advice if the President requests it.
Only the Supreme Court may inquire into the advice.
n631c73a2aaa.x: Article 74(2) provides that the question, if any, and what advice was tendered by Ministers to the President cannot be inquired into by any court.
n631c73a2aaa.tq: Identify the constitutional bar on judicial inquiry and reject options that create exceptions not provided here.
xs: Under **Art. 74(2)** the advice **cannot be inquired into by any court** — so option **(1)** is correct.
No court, not even the Supreme Court, may inquire into it.
xa: **Art. 74(1):** Council of Ministers aids and advises; advice binding since the **42nd Amendment (1976)**.
**Maru Ram (1980):** even the pardoning power is exercised on the **Council of Ministers' advice**.

n343dcb6aa32.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cases on the pardoning power?
o: Maru Ram (1980) held that the power is exercised on the advice of the Council of Ministers
Kehar Singh (1989) held that the President may examine the evidence afresh
Epuru Sudhakar (2006) allowed limited judicial review on mala fide, arbitrary or irrelevant grounds
Kehar Singh held that a convict has a right to an oral hearing before the President
n343dcb6aa32.x: Kehar Singh held that the President may examine evidence afresh but the convict has no right to an oral hearing.
xa: **Epuru Sudhakar** arose from **AP**.
**Madras HC** Full Bench (**Apr 2026**): Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **remission**.
⚠ The Governor (**Art. 161**) cannot pardon a **death sentence** and has no power over **court-martial**.

n4cdbdb387eb.s: A Chief Minister who is a member of the Legislative Council of a State, rather than its Legislative Assembly, is entitled to
o: not vote in the election of the President
vote only if nominated by the Governor
vote in the election of the President by virtue of being the Chief Minister
vote only in the election of the Vice-President
n4cdbdb387eb.x: Only elected members of State Legislative Assemblies form part of the Presidential electoral college. Membership of a Legislative Council does not confer this right, even on a Chief Minister.
n4cdbdb387eb.tq: Apply the precise constitutional distinction between the Legislative Assembly and Legislative Council.
xs: A CM who sits in the **Legislative Council** does **not vote in the election of the President** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Only **elected members of State Legislative Assemblies** (and elected MPs) form the electoral college; **all members of Legislative Councils**, elected or nominated, are excluded.
Being **Chief Minister** gives no vote, and the Governor nominates no one into the electoral college.
xa: This exact point was an **APPSC-GS 2025** key.
**Elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry** vote, added by the **70th Amendment, 1992**.
⚠ The **VP's electoral college** is **all MPs, elected and nominated**, and has **no MLAs**.

ndf6b7cff9fb.s: Which of the following correctly describes the President's power over a Money Bill passed by Parliament?
o: The President must reject it if it was introduced on prior recommendation.
The President may return it for reconsideration but cannot reject it.
The President has no role after passage by Parliament.
The President may ratify or reject it, but cannot return it for reconsideration.
ndf6b7cff9fb.x: In relation to a Money Bill, the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration. Such Bills are generally introduced with prior recommendation.
ndf6b7cff9fb.tq: Use the Money Bill exception to the general return power under Article 111.
xs: On a **Money Bill** the President may **ratify or reject** it but **cannot return** it for reconsideration — so option **(4)** is correct.
He usually **assents**, since a Money Bill is introduced with his **prior recommendation** — he is not bound to reject it.
Returning a Bill is possible only for **Ordinary Bills** (and Financial Bills I and II).
xa: ⚠ **Money Bill** = cannot return; **Constitutional Amendment Bill** = must assent; **Ordinary Bill** = return once.
The same applies at the State level: Money Bill — **ratify or reject; cannot return**.

n55d7a182653.s: With reference to a Constitutional Amendment Bill passed by Parliament, which one of the following is correct?
o: The President may reject it by absolute veto.
The President may return it once for reconsideration.
The President must give assent under the 24th Amendment, 1971.
The President may refer it to the Governor for advice.
n55d7a182653.x: The 24th Amendment, 1971 made presidential assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill mandatory; the President cannot reject or return it.
n55d7a182653.tq: Remember the special constitutional-amendment exception to presidential veto powers.
xs: The President **must assent** to a **Constitutional Amendment Bill** under the **24th Amendment, 1971** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He **cannot reject or return** it, so absolute veto and return for reconsideration are both ruled out.
xa: For **Ordinary Bills** he may **ratify, reject or return**.
The Constitutional Amendment Bill row is **not applicable** to State legislation.

nded3ca79b37.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the pocket veto of the President of India?
o: As in the USA, the President must decide within 10 days, failing which the Bill becomes law.
It is possible because Article 111 prescribes no time limit for the President's decision on a Bill.
Under it, the President neither assents to, nor rejects, nor returns the Bill.
President Giani Zail Singh used it on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
nded3ca79b37.x: The 10-day limit is a US feature; Article 111 sets no time limit in India, which is what makes the pocket veto possible.
xa: Only Union instance: **Zail Singh (1986)**, **Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill**.
The **Governor** has **no** pocket veto.

n777da22b250.s: The Governor’s power corresponding to the President’s power to promulgate Ordinances under Article 123 is provided under:
n777da22b250.x: Article 213 confers the parallel Ordinance-making power on the Governor of a State.
n777da22b250.tq: Discriminate between the Governor’s pardoning provision and the Governor’s Ordinance provision.
xs: The Governor's parallel ordinance power is in **Article 213** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 161** is the Governor's **pardoning** power, not ordinances.
xa: **AP** used an **Art. 213** ordinance on **organ-transplant committees**.
The **38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable.

n743db328900.s: The ordinance-making power of the President under Article 123 is regarded as a relic of which earlier enactment?
n743db328900.x: The President's ordinance-making power under Article 123 is a relic of the Government of India Act, 1935, which gave the Governor-General power to issue ordinances. The 1909 Act brought Morley-Minto reforms, the 1919 Act introduced dyarchy, and the 1947 Act ended British rule; none is the stated source of Article 123.
n743db328900.tq: Ordinance = 1935 Act legacy, like the Governor-General's ordinances.
xs: The ordinance power is a **relic of the Government of India Act, 1935** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The notes trace **Art. 123** to this Act, not to the 1909, 1919 or 1947 Acts.
xa: Governor's parallel power: **Art. 213**.
Criticism: frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation**.

nindian-polity-74-3.s: An ordinance can be promulgated only when:
o: a Proclamation of Emergency is in force
the Lok Sabha passes a resolution permitting it
both Houses are in full session
nindian-polity-74-3.x: An ordinance can be issued only when the legislature is in recess and the Head of State is satisfied that immediate action is needed; none can be issued while both Houses are sitting.
n: An ordinance can be promulgated only when the Legislature is in recess. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Head of State must be satisfied that circumstances exist requiring immediate action before promulgating an ordinance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance cannot be issued when both Houses are in active session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate an ordinance when either or both Houses of the State Legislature are not in session. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: President's power: **Article 123** (**Part V**); Governor's: **Article 213** (**Part VI**).
An ordinance is a **legislative** power of the **Executive**.
It is a relic of the **GoI Act, 1935**.

nindian-polity-74-6.s: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limitations as which of the following?
o: An Act of Parliament or State Legislature
A judicial decree of the Supreme Court
An executive or administrative order only
nindian-polity-74-6.x: An ordinance has the same force, effect and limits as an Act of Parliament or the State Legislature. It is legislative, not executive, and cannot amend the Constitution.
nindian-polity-74-6.tq: Treat an ordinance as a temporary Act.
n: The ordinance-making power is not an executive or administrative function. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance has the same effect as an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance is subject to the same limitations as an Act of Parliament or a State Legislature. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance cannot amend the Constitution under Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xs: An ordinance has the force of **an Act of Parliament or State Legislature** — option **(2)**.
It has the **same force and effect** as an Act and the **same limitations**.
It **cannot amend the Constitution** (**Article 368**), is not a **judicial decree**, and is **not** an executive or administrative function.
xa: It can be **retrospective** and can **amend or repeal** an Act.
It is void if beyond Parliament's competence or violating **Fundamental Rights**.
Re-promulgation without ratification is a **subversion of the Constitution**.

nindian-polity-74-26.s: Under which Article is an ordinance treated as 'law', so that it is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights?
nindian-polity-74-26.x: An ordinance is 'law' under Article 13(2) and is void if it abridges Fundamental Rights, though it can make or change tax provisions within legislative power.
n: An ordinance can introduce tax provisions within legislative power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance can amend tax provisions within legislative power. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance cannot violate Fundamental Rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance is subject to Article 13(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
An ordinance is void if it takes away or abridges Part III rights. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: It **cannot amend the Constitution** under **Article 368**.
It can operate **retrospectively** like an ordinary statute.
Its scope is **co-extensive** with Parliament's power.

nindian-polity-74-28.s: Which Article fixes the maximum gap of six months between two sessions of Parliament?
nindian-polity-74-28.x: Article 85 sets the six-month limit for Parliament; Article 174 does the same for State Legislatures.
n: Article 123 is in Part V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
Article 213 is in Part VI of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The maximum gap between legislative sessions is six months under Articles 85 and 174. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: The maximum gap between sessions is **six months**.
Maximum ordinance life = **six months** + **six weeks**.
An ordinance lapses **six weeks** after reassembly.

n6cf268d5d64.s: Which Constitutional Amendment made the President’s satisfaction in promulgating an Ordinance final, and which Amendment reversed that position?
o: 38th Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
39th Amendment made it final; 42nd Amendment reversed it
42nd Amendment made it final; 44th Amendment reversed it
44th Amendment made it final; 38th Amendment reversed it
n6cf268d5d64.x: The 38th Amendment of 1975 made the President’s satisfaction final, while the 44th Amendment reversed that position.
n6cf268d5d64.tq: Pair the two Amendments with opposite effects and check their chronological order.
xs: The **38th Amendment made it final** (**1975**) and the **44th Amendment reversed it** (**1978**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
The 38th made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** **non-justiciable**.
xa: ⚠ **38th** = non-justiciable; **44th** = reversed; **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)** = **justiciable**.
**IYB 2026** p.**699** prints "would be called in question" — read "**would not**".

nbd94f25f9e2.s: The Supreme Court in D.C. Wadhwa v. State of Bihar (1987) held that:
o: Every Ordinance automatically becomes a constitutional amendment
Routine re-promulgation of Ordinances without placing them before the legislature is a fraud on the Constitution
The President’s satisfaction is never subject to review
An Ordinance must remain in force for at least six months
nbd94f25f9e2.x: D.C. Wadhwa held that routine re-promulgation without placing the Ordinance before the legislature amounts to a fraud on the Constitution.
nbd94f25f9e2.tq: Match the case with its distinctive holding and avoid importing the later case’s broader formulation.
xs: **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)**: **repeated re-promulgation** without placing before the legislature is a **fraud on the Constitution** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The case is about re-promulgation; it did not make satisfaction unreviewable or fix a minimum life.
xa: **Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)**, a **7-judge** bench: **laying before the legislature is mandatory**.
Satisfaction is **open to judicial review** (Krishna Kumar Singh).

ndd3eb77d5fd.s: In which case (2017) did the Supreme Court hold that re-promulgation of an Ordinance may be a fraud on the Constitution?
o: Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar
S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
A.K. Roy v. Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
ndd3eb77d5fd.x: Krishna Kumar Singh (2017) held that re-promulgation can be a fraud on the Constitution and that laying the Ordinance before the legislature is mandatory.
xa: It was a **7-judge** bench, **Krishna Kumar Singh v. State of Bihar (2017)**.
**D.C. Wadhwa (1987)** first called repeated re-promulgation a fraud on the Constitution.

n5d432101f5d.s: Which recent development revived the debate on the possible misuse of the ordinance-making power and executive overreach?
o: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026
The Inter-State Water Disputes Amendment Ordinance, 2026
n5d432101f5d.x: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 revived the debate on ordinance misuse and executive overreach.
n5d432101f5d.tq: Identify the precise recent development instead of being misled by similarly worded legislative titles.
xs: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** revived the debate on **ordinance misuse** and **executive overreach** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Ordinances are issued under **Art. 123** while Parliament is **not in session**.
xa: Criticism: frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation**.
**Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**: **re-promulgation** is a fraud on the Constitution.

ncd3b5a5d6d5.s: What is the principal criticism of the frequent promulgation of ordinances?
o: They can be issued only during a financial emergency.
They require prior approval from the Supreme Court.
They transfer all legislative powers to the States.
ncd3b5a5d6d5.x: Frequent ordinances are criticised because they bypass parliamentary deliberation.
ncd3b5a5d6d5.tq: Link the institutional criticism to the constitutional function being bypassed.
xs: Frequent ordinances **bypass parliamentary deliberation** — so option **(3)** is correct.
They need no Supreme Court approval, are not limited to emergencies, and do not shift power to the States.
xa: **D.C. Wadhwa (1987)**: repeated **re-promulgation** = fraud on the Constitution.
The **2026** Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Ordinance revived this debate.

nindian-polity-74-19.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ordinances?
o: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
The ordinance-making power is beyond judicial review.
Re-promulgation without legislative ratification may subvert the Constitution.
The Governor can withdraw an ordinance at any time.
nindian-polity-74-19.x: Ordinances are subject to judicial review; the other three statements are correct.
n: The President can withdraw an ordinance at any time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can withdraw an ordinance at any time. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The ordinance-making power is subject to judicial review. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
Re-promulgation of ordinances without legislative ratification is a subversion of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: The **38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction **non-justiciable**; the **44th (1978)** reversed it.
**Krishna Kumar Singh** was a **7-judge** bench.
⚠ "The President cannot repeal or withdraw an ordinance" is **false**.

nd7d19c8cde7.s: The Vice-President of India is elected by an electoral college consisting of:
o: elected members of both Houses of Parliament only
elected MPs and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
all members of both Houses of Parliament, elected and nominated
all MPs and elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies
nd7d19c8cde7.x: All MPs, elected and nominated, vote by PR-STV and secret ballot; State legislatures have no role in the Vice-President's election.
xa: Size of the electoral college = all MPs, **788** (**543 LS + 245 RS**) when both Houses are full.
The election is conducted by the **ECI** under the **Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952**.
⚠ Nominated MPs **vote** for the VP; State MLAs do **not**.
A removal resolution against the VP can first be moved **only in the Rajya Sabha**.

n300bd4d9888.s: Which one of the following is NOT a qualification for election as Vice-President of India?
o: Qualification for election as a member of the Lok Sabha
Qualification for election as a member of the Rajya Sabha
n300bd4d9888.x: The Vice-President must be a citizen of India, at least 35 years old and qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha. Qualification for election to the Lok Sabha is not the prescribed condition.
n300bd4d9888.tq: Find the one swapped constitutional qualification among closely related House requirements.
xs: Qualification for election to the **Lok Sabha** is NOT a VP qualification — so option **(2)** is correct.
The VP must be a **citizen**, aged **35 years**, and eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha** — options (1), (3), (4) are real qualifications.
⚠ Lok Sabha eligibility is the **President's** qualification; the VP's is **Rajya Sabha** eligibility.
xa: **Art. 64:** the VP is **ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** but is **not a member** of the RS.
The VP holds **no other office of profit**.
**Art. 63** simply says there shall be a Vice-President.

na2ac0548034.s: The 39th Constitutional Amendment and the 44th Constitutional Amendment had what effect on Presidential election disputes?
o: The 39th Amendment vested the disputes in Parliament and the 44th retained that arrangement
The 39th Amendment removed the Supreme Court’s power and the 44th Amendment restored it
The 39th Amendment created the power and the 44th Amendment abolished it
Both Amendments transferred the power to the Election Commission
na2ac0548034.x: The 39th Amendment of 1975 took away the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction over these disputes, while the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored it.
na2ac0548034.tq: Link each Amendment to its opposite constitutional effect instead of relying on the later amendment alone.
xs: The **39th Amendment (1975)** removed the **Supreme Court's** power over these election disputes and the **44th Amendment (1978)** restored it — so option **(2)** is correct.
The power was never vested in the **Election Commission**, and the 44th did not abolish or retain a parliamentary forum.
xa: The 39th Amendment covered disputes on elections of the **President, VP, PM and Speaker**.
Today the forum is the **Supreme Court** under **Art 71**.
**Acts done before** the SC voids an election remain valid.

n84fcf1afbfc.s: The Vice-President of India may resign his office by writing under his hand addressed to the
n84fcf1afbfc.x: Under Article 67(a) the Vice-President resigns by writing to the President, and the resignation takes effect immediately. The President resigns to the Vice-President; the CJI administers the President's oath; the Speaker is informed of the President's resignation; the Prime Minister receives no constitutional resignation of either office.
n84fcf1afbfc.tq: President resigns to VP; VP resigns to President.
xs: The VP resigns by writing to the **President of India** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The **President** resigns to the **Vice-President** — the reverse pair is a common trap.
xa: The VP's **oath** is administered by the **President** (**Art 69**).
**Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned on health grounds under **Art 67(a)** in **July 2025**.
Term: **5 years**, re-eligible **any number of times**.

nindian-polity-9-5.s: Which Article makes the Vice-President the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
nindian-polity-9-5.x: Article 64 makes the Vice-President ex-officio Chairman; 63 creates the office, 66 covers election and 67 the term.
n: Article 63 provides for a Vice-President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha under Article 64. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The term of office of the Vice-President is five years under Article 67. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Article 69:** VP's **oath**, administered by the **President**.
**Article 71:** election disputes decided by the **Supreme Court** — final.
**Article 65:** VP **acts as President** during a vacancy, for at most **six months**.
⚠ **Article 68:** vacancy election "as soon as possible", **no deadline** — unlike the President's **6 months** (Art 62).

nindian-polity-9-10.s: The office of the Vice-President of India is modelled on that of the:
o: Deputy Prime Minister of the UK
nindian-polity-9-10.x: The Indian Vice-President's office is modelled on the American Vice-President.
n: The Vice-President holds the second-highest constitutional office after the President in the Order of Precedence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The office of the Vice-President is modelled on the American Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
The Vice-President is eligible for re-election any number of times. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
Dr. S. Radhakrishnan was the first Vice-President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Dr. S. Radhakrishnan** was also the **longest-serving** VP — **two** terms (**1952-62**).
**Mohammad Hamid Ansari:** only VP to serve **two full terms** (**2007-17**).
⚠ **S. Radhakrishnan** = first VP; **C.P. Radhakrishnan** = present VP (**2025**).

nindian-polity-46-6.s: Who is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
nindian-polity-46-6.x: The Vice-President is ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
n: The President appoints the Prime Minister under Article 75(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President appoints other Union Ministers on the advice of the Prime Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President is the Head of State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The Prime Minister is the Head of Government. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xa: Executive power is constitutionally vested in the **President** — **Article 53**.
The VP holds the **second-highest** office in the Order of Precedence.

nd2685d9f94f.s: Who administers the oath of office to the Vice-President of India?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The senior-most judge of the Supreme Court
nd2685d9f94f.x: Under Article 69 the President administers the Vice-President's oath; the CJI administers the President's oath.
xa: The VP is **re-eligible any number of times**.
Removal resolution: **only in the RS**, by **effective majority**; LS agrees by **simple majority**; **no grounds** stated.
Resignation is addressed to the **President** (**Art 67(a)**), effective immediately.

ne23ba46f88b.s: Which of the following is NOT a duty of the Prime Minister under Article 78?
o: Furnishing information relating to administration when called for by the President
Submitting for the consideration of the Council any matter decided by an individual Minister when the President requires it
Communicating to the President decisions of the Council of Ministers relating to administration and legislative proposals
Administering the oath of office and secrecy to all Union Ministers
ne23ba46f88b.x: Options A, B and C are duties of the Prime Minister under Article 78 (communicating Council decisions, furnishing information, and placing a minister's individual decision before the Council when the President requires). Administering the oaths of office and secrecy to Union Ministers is done by the President, not the PM.
ne23ba46f88b.tq: Find the one function belonging to the President rather than the Prime Minister.
xs: **Administering the oath** to Union Ministers is NOT a PM duty under Art 78 — the **President** administers it — so option **(4)** is correct.

**Art 78** duties: **communicate all decisions** of the CoM and legislative proposals; **furnish information** called for; submit a minister's sole decision to the **CoM** if the President requires — options (1)-(3).
xa: **Art 77(1):** all executive action is **expressed in the President's name**.
**Art 74(2):** ministerial advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
The PM's own oath is also administered by the **President**.

ne026ef296d1.s: Who was the first Deputy Prime Minister of India?
ne026ef296d1.x: Sardar Patel was the first Deputy PM; the office is not mentioned in the Constitution and its holder takes oath as an ordinary Minister.
xa: Table of Precedence: **President 1, VP 2, PM 3**.
The **PMO** is also not mentioned in the Constitution — an **extra-constitutional staff agency**.
**Leader of the House (LS)** is likewise **not a constitutional office**.

nindian-polity-46-4.s: Who administers the Oath of Office and the Oath of Secrecy to a Union Minister?
o: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
nindian-polity-46-4.x: The President administers the oath of office and the oath of secrecy to Union Ministers, in the forms given in the Third Schedule.
nindian-polity-46-4.tq: Recall who swears in Union Ministers.
n: The President administers the Oath of Office to Union Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The President administers the Oath of Secrecy to Union Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
The Oath of Office and Oath of Secrecy are provided under the Third Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 123-125]
xs: The **President** administers the Oath of Office and Secrecy to Union Ministers — option **(1)**.
The oath forms for Ministers are in the **Third Schedule**; the oath is under **Article 75(4)**.
The **Vice-President** takes his oath before the President but administers none to Ministers.
xa: The **President's** own oath (**Article 60**) is given by the **Chief Justice of India**.
The **Governor's** oath (**Article 159**) is given by the **Chief Justice** of the **High Court**.
⚠ Oaths of the **President**, **VP** and **Governor** are codified in their **Articles**, **not** in the **Third Schedule**.

nindian-polity-56-2.s: To whom does the Governor of a State address his resignation?
o: The Chief Justice of the High Court
nindian-polity-56-2.x: The Governor resigns to the President; the High Court's Chief Justice administers his oath.
n: The oath of the Governor of a State is administered by the Chief Justice of the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The oath of the Governor of a State may be administered by the senior-most High Court Judge if the Chief Justice is unavailable. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor of a State addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor takes oath from the Chief Justice of the State High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor resigns to the President of India under Article 156(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xa: The Governor is removed by the **President** **at pleasure** — **Article 156** — **without impeachment**.
The **VP** resigns to the **President**; his oath (**Article 69**) is given by the **President**.

nindian-polity-56-9.s: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha addresses his resignation to the:
o: Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha
nindian-polity-56-9.x: Under Article 94 the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker.
n: The Vice-President communicates the President’s resignation to the Lok Sabha Speaker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Vice-President of India addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor of a State addresses resignation to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Chief Minister and State Ministers address resignation to the Governor of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The Governor resigns to the President of India under Article 156(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xa: The VP **communicates** the President's resignation to the **Lok Sabha Speaker**.
Union Ministers **route** resignations **through** the **Prime Minister**; State Ministers **through** the **Chief Minister**.

n05ebacfbccd.s: The Vice-President of India is ex officio President of which of the following bodies?
n05ebacfbccd.x: The Vice-President is also the ex-officio President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA).
n05ebacfbccd.tq: Use the exact institutional title to distinguish ICWA from other national bodies.
xs: The VP is ex officio **President of the Indian Council of World Affairs (ICWA)** — so option **(2)** is correct.
His other ex-officio role is **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha** (**Art. 64**).
xa: VP qualifications: **citizen**, **35 years**, eligible for election to the **Rajya Sabha**.
Electoral college: **members of both Houses**, elected **and nominated**, by **PR-STV**.
⚠ The VP holds **no other office of profit**, but ex-officio posts like these are part of the office.

n0f5644271b3.s: A vacancy in the office of the Vice-President of India is to be filled
o: Within six months of the vacancy in every case
As soon as possible, without a constitutionally prescribed six-month deadline
Within one year, after approval by the Supreme Court
Only at the next general election to the Lok Sabha
n0f5644271b3.x: Article 68 requires an election to fill a vacancy in the office of Vice-President as soon as possible. Unlike the vacancy in the office of President, no six-month deadline is prescribed for this election.
n0f5644271b3.tq: Compare the vacancy rules for President and Vice-President, especially the presence or absence of a fixed deadline.
xs: A VP vacancy is filled **"as soon as possible"**, with **no deadline** (**Art 68**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **six-month** limit applies to a **President's** vacancy (**Art 62**), not the VP's.
xa: **Jagdeep Dhankhar** resigned in **July 2025** — the **third mid-term vacancy** after **V.V. Giri (1969)** and **Krishan Kant (2002)**.
**C.P. Radhakrishnan** was elected after that vacancy (**September 2025**).
The VP continues in office till the successor takes charge (**Art 67(c)**).

n2893622d113.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tenure of the Prime Minister?
o: The Prime Minister can be removed only by the Supreme Court.
The Prime Minister holds office for life unless removed by impeachment.
The Prime Minister continues in office while commanding the confidence of the Lok Sabha, subject to the President's pleasure in the constitutional sense.
The Prime Minister has a fixed tenure of five years irrespective of legislative support.
n2893622d113.x: The Prime Minister has no fixed tenure and ordinarily continues while enjoying the confidence of the Lok Sabha. The Constitution formally states that Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure.
n2893622d113.tq: Reject the fixed-term trap and connect tenure with legislative confidence.
xs: The PM has **no fixed tenure**: he holds office during the **President's pleasure**, in practice while he commands a **Lok Sabha** majority — so option **(3)** is correct.
There is **no five-year fixed term**, no **impeachment**, and no removal by the **Supreme Court** for the PM.
xa: **Art. 75(2):** ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**, who removes a minister only **on the PM's advice**.
**No term limit for the PM:** **Ambedkar** preferred daily parliamentary accountability to fixed terms.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

n59d62d3918f.s: Which one of the following correctly states the ruling in S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)?
o: A non-member cannot be repeatedly reappointed as Minister without getting elected.
Only a member of the Lok Sabha can be appointed as a Minister.
A non-member may be reappointed as Minister indefinitely without election.
A non-member cannot be appointed as Prime Minister under any circumstances.
n59d62d3918f.x: The Supreme Court held that the constitutional provision for a non-member Minister cannot be used for repeated reappointments without the person securing election to the legislature.
n59d62d3918f.tq: Discriminate the judicial limitation from the general six-month rule.
xs: In **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001)**, a non-member **cannot be re-appointed** repeatedly as minister **without getting elected** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Art 75(5)** lets **any person** be a minister for **six months**, so options (2), (3) and (4) are wrong — a non-member can even be **PM** for six months.
xa: The six-month rule is **six consecutive months** and **applies to the PM** too.
UPSC notes spell the case name **"S.R. Chauhan"**.
The PM **may belong to either House** of Parliament.

n92b6c7abbe5.s: A non-member appointed as a Union Minister must become a member of either House of Parliament within:
n92b6c7abbe5.x: The six-month rule applies to every non-member Minister, including the Prime Minister.
xa: **S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab (2001):** no repeated **re-appointment** without election.
**P.V. Narasimha Rao (1991)** became PM without being an MP and later entered the LS from **Nandyal**.
Ministers are appointed by the President on the **PM's advice**.

n5354ba6e487.s: During a National Emergency, the President of India
o: acquires unrestricted discretion to disregard the advice of the Council of Ministers
continues to be bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers
becomes the real executive in place of the Prime Minister
may dismiss the entire Council without following constitutional advice
n5354ba6e487.x: A National Emergency does not confer discretionary power on the President to disregard the binding advice of the Council of Ministers. The parliamentary executive relationship continues.
n5354ba6e487.tq: Guard against the emergency-powers trap by checking whether the constitutional advice requirement has been altered.
xs: During a **National Emergency** the President **continues to be bound** by the CoM's advice — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ The President does **not** acquire **discretionary powers** in an emergency — a PYQ trap; options (1), (3), (4) assume such powers.
xa: **Art 74(1):** advice is binding **after one reconsideration**.
**Art 74(2):** advice is **not inquired into** by any court.
PM = **de facto** head of government; President = **de jure** head of State.

n0bdc0557043.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the position of the Prime Minister in the United Kingdom from that in India?
o: The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Lords, whereas the Indian Prime Minister must belong to the Lok Sabha.
The UK Prime Minister must belong to the House of Commons, whereas the Indian Prime Minister may belong to either House of Parliament.
