nindian-polity-21-6.s: On dissolution of the Lok Sabha, a Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that the Lok Sabha has never passed:
o: goes automatically to a joint sitting
nindian-polity-21-6.x: Such a Bill survives dissolution, while Bills pending in the Lok Sabha or passed by it and pending in the Rajya Sabha lapse; prorogation ends no Bill.
n: A Bill pending in the Lok Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Bill passed by the Lok Sabha but pending in the Rajya Sabha lapses on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
A Bill pending in the Rajya Sabha that has not been passed by the Lok Sabha does not lapse on the dissolution of the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
Prorogation does not cause a Bill to lapse. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 49-52]
xa: A Bill for which a **joint sitting** was notified before dissolution does **not** lapse.
A Bill **passed by RS, pending in LS** lapses.
⚠ "Passed by LS but not yet taken up in RS does not lapse" is **false**.

n9ef79b1e4fb.s: The Constitution refers to the Union Budget as the:
n9ef79b1e4fb.x: Article 112 uses 'Annual Financial Statement'; the word 'Budget' does not occur in the Constitution.
xa: The financial year runs **1 April - 31 March**.
It is presented in the Lok Sabha by the **Finance Minister**.
First Union budget: **26 Nov 1947**, by **R.K. Shanmukham Chetty**.

n958561072cb.s: The Budget process begins with the issue of the Budget Circular, generally in:
n958561072cb.x: The Budget Circular is generally issued in September, and printing of Budget documents is marked by the Halwa ceremony.
xa: "Budget" comes from **"bougette"** (French, "little bag").
Prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**, Ministry of Finance.
First Union budget: **26 Nov 1947** (APPSC-GS 2018).

n73ee35a96ca.s: The Union Budget is prepared by the Budget Division of the
o: Department of Expenditure, Ministry of Finance
Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
n73ee35a96ca.x: The Budget is prepared by the Budget Division in the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance.
n73ee35a96ca.tq: Apply the “which department does this job?” authority-identification method.
xs: The budget is prepared by the **Budget Division, Department of Economic Affairs**, Ministry of Finance — so option **(2)** is correct.
Not the Departments of Expenditure or Revenue, nor Parliamentary Affairs.
xa: The **Contingency Fund** is held by the **Finance Secretary (DEA)**.
The **Budget Circular** starts the process (**September**).
The **Halwa ceremony** at North Block marks printing.

n60ed084cc29.s: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on:
n60ed084cc29.x: R.K. Shanmukham Chetty presented the first Union Budget of independent India on 26 November 1947.
xa: The Budget = **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112**.
Union Budget 2023-24: **Nirmala Sitharaman** (APPSC-GS 2023).
Union Budget 2026-27: **1 Feb 2026**.

n69aedb76c4a.s: Who presented the Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27 on 14 February 2026?

xa: Union Budget **2026-27** was presented on **1 Feb 2026**.
The FM proposed an **Economic Stabilisation Fund** of **₹1 lakh crore**.
The LS approved the **second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants (2025-26)** (**Art. 115**).

n1526c023abe.s: The second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants for 2025-26 approved by the Lok Sabha is associated with
n1526c023abe.x: Supplementary, additional or excess grants are provided for under Article 115. The second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants for 2025-26 was approved by the Lok Sabha.
n1526c023abe.tq: Use the Article-function association and distinguish supplementary grants from the Annual Financial Statement.
xs: Supplementary Demands for Grants are under **Article 115** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 112** = AFS; **Art. 117** = financial bills.
xa: Art. 115 also covers **additional** and **excess** grants.
**Art. 116** = vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional grant.
Supplementary grant = sanctioned amount **insufficient**.

nindian-polity-61-34.s: Which Article provides for the vote on account, votes of credit and exceptional grants?
nindian-polity-61-34.x: Article 116 covers these; 112 is the Annual Financial Statement, 113 the estimates procedure and 115 supplementary, additional or excess grants.
n: Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement, or Union Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 113 deals with the procedure in Parliament regarding estimates. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 115 deals with supplementary grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 115 deals with additional grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 115 deals with excess grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 116 deals with the Vote on Account. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 116 deals with Votes of Credit. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 116 deals with Exceptional Grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
xa: **Article 114:** **Appropriation Bills**.
**Supplementary grant:** sanctioned amount insufficient; **additional grant:** new service not in the budget.
Since the **1 Feb** budget (**2017**), vote on account is usually needed only in **interim-budget** years.

n47d67ba747a.s: The Union Budget is presented in two parts, namely the:
n47d67ba747a.x: The Budget covers the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account and is presented in Revenue and Capital parts.
xa: The **CAG** audits all three funds of the Union and states.
The word **"budget"** is not used in the Constitution.

n000130c706b.s: Which of the following forms part of the Consolidated Fund of India?
o: Treasury Bills raised by the Union Government
n000130c706b.x: The CFI comprises Union revenues, loans raised (including Treasury Bills) and loan repayments; provident funds, small savings and remittances go to the Public Account.
xa: **Contingency Fund** (**Art. 267**): unforeseen expenditure, at the **President's** disposal.

ncca12304447.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Public Account of India?
o: Provident funds held in a fiduciary capacity are credited to it.
Small savings are credited to it.
Deposits and remittances are included in it.
Every withdrawal from it requires an appropriation law.
ncca12304447.x: Withdrawal from the Public Account does not need appropriation the way withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund does.
xa: The **CAG** audits all three funds.

n572917a8966.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Contingency Fund of India?
o: It is provided for under Article 267.
It was established by the Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950.
It is held by the Finance Secretary in the Department of Expenditure.
It is at the President's disposal for unforeseen expenditure pending Parliament's approval.
n572917a8966.x: The Fund is held by the Finance Secretary in the Department of Economic Affairs, not the Department of Expenditure.
xa: Corpus: **₹30,000 crore** from FY **2021-22**.
Earlier ₹**500 crore** from **2005**, raised from ₹**50 crore**.

n9cc44d2fc3c.s: Cut motions are moved in the Lok Sabha during:

n9cc44d2fc3c.x: Cut motions are moved only in the Lok Sabha during voting on Demands for Grants; if passed, they signal loss of confidence.

Supplementary, additional and excess grants are under **Art. 115**.
A **token grant** (re-appropriation) must also be voted by the LS.

ndda57110f03.s: An amendment to the Appropriation Bill that varies the amount of expenditure charged on the CFI is:
o: permitted in the Lok Sabha only
ndda57110f03.x: No amendment may vary a voted grant or charged expenditure; the Appropriation Bill also carries an automatic repeal clause.
xa: ⚠ APPSC-G1 2024 key: statements **I and IV** valid.
It covers voted grants + charged expenditure, within the **AFS** amount.

n9b5ea742f87.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a vote on account?
o: It is an advance for part of the year, generally about two months, until the Appropriation Act is passed.
In election years it may cover three to five months.

n9b5ea742f87.x: Since the 1 February Budget, a vote on account is usually needed only in interim-Budget years.

**Exceptional grant** (Art. 116): not part of the current service of any year.
⚠ **115** = supplementary, additional, excess; **116** = vote on account, credit, exceptional.

n18b73995d4e.s: An excess grant becomes relevant when:
o: The expenditure is not part of the current service of any year
A new service is proposed in the current Budget
The sanctioned amount is insufficient before expenditure is incurred
Expenditure has exceeded the amount originally granted and prior approval of the Public Accounts Committee is required
n18b73995d4e.x: An excess grant is required when expenditure has exceeded the amount granted. It requires prior scrutiny and approval by the Public Accounts Committee.
n18b73995d4e.tq: Distinguish an excess already incurred from a supplementary requirement anticipated during the year.
xs: An excess grant is for spending **more than granted**, needing **PAC approval first** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Not current service = **exceptional**; new service = **additional**; insufficient amount = **supplementary**.
xa: It falls under **Art. 115**.
The **PAC** examines **CAG** audit reports.
**Token grant** (re-appropriation) must also be voted by the LS.

n28963fa8368.s: A token grant is associated with:
o: An emergency demand of indefinite magnitude
A fresh withdrawal from the Public Account without parliamentary approval
A reduction of a Demand for Grant to Re 1
Re-appropriation and approval by the Lok Sabha
n28963fa8368.x: A token grant relates to re-appropriation and must also be voted by the Lok Sabha.
n28963fa8368.tq: Distinguish the budgetary token grant from the token cut motion.
xs: A token grant is for **re-appropriation** and must be **voted by the Lok Sabha** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Reducing a demand to **Re 1** is a **policy cut**; indefinite demand = **vote of credit**.
xa: ⚠ A **token cut** (cut motion) reduces a demand by **Rs 100** — not the same as a token grant.
**Excess grant** needs PAC approval first.
The **Public Account** needs no appropriation at all.

nindian-polity-61-8.s: Money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India only on the authority of:
o: an appropriation law passed by Parliament
nindian-polity-61-8.x: The President cannot withdraw money alone; Article 114 requires a law of Parliament (the Appropriation Act).
n: No money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under appropriation made by a law passed by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 114 provides the appropriation authority for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
The President cannot authorize withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India on the President’s own authority. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
The Parliament of India controls the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Parliamentary approval through an Appropriation Act under Article 114 is mandatory for withdrawals from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Appropriation Bills provide authority for withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
xa: The CFI is controlled by **Parliament**.
The **Contingency Fund** is at the **disposal of the President**, with **ex-post facto** approval.
The **Public Account** needs **no prior** parliamentary vote.

nindian-polity-61-9.s: Executive disbursements from the Public Account of India:
o: need no prior vote of Parliament
need the approval of the Rajya Sabha
need a joint sitting of Parliament
nindian-polity-61-9.x: The government runs the Public Account as a banker for money held in trust, so payments need no prior vote of Parliament.
n: The Executive or Government controls the Public Account of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
The Public Account of India operates as a banker. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Prior parliamentary voting is not required for executive disbursements from the Public Account of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
xa: It holds **provident funds**, **judicial deposits**, **savings bank deposits**.
The **CAG** audits all three funds.

nindian-polity-61-11.s: Under which Article is the Public Account of India constituted?
nindian-polity-61-11.x: The Public Account is under Article 266(2); the Consolidated Fund is under 266(1) and the Contingency Fund under 267(1).
n: The Consolidated Fund of India is constituted under Article 266(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
The Public Account of India is constituted under Article 266(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
The Contingency Fund of India is constituted under Article 267(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Article 112 deals with the Annual Financial Statement, or Union Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
xa: Contingency Fund corpus: **₹30,000 crore** from FY **2021-22**.
Contingency Fund is held by the **Finance Secretary (DEA)** on the President's behalf.

nindian-polity-61-40.s: Savings bank deposits held by the Government in trust are credited to the:
nindian-polity-61-40.x: Savings bank deposits are held in trust in the Public Account; treasury bills, market loans and foreign loans go to the CFI.
n: Government loans include treasury bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Government loans include market loans. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Government loans include foreign loans. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
Savings bank deposits are held in the Public Account of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]
xa: Public Account also holds **provident funds** and **judicial deposits**.
CFI is the dynamic **main treasury** account.
Withdrawal from the CFI only under an **Appropriation Act** (**Article 114**).

nindian-polity-79-37.s: Which provision requires an Appropriation Act for every withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India, even for charged expenditure?
nindian-polity-79-37.x: Article 114(3) requires an Appropriation Act for every withdrawal, so even charged expenditure, which is not voted, needs one.
n: Charged expenditure is not submitted to a vote. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
Any withdrawal from the Consolidated Fund of India requires an Appropriation Act under Article 114(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
xa: The Appropriation Bill covers **grants voted by Lok Sabha + charged expenditure**.
Charged expenditure is **not submitted to the vote** but can be **discussed**.
No amendment may **vary charged expenditure**.

nindian-polity-55-13.s: A Token Cut Motion seeks to reduce a demand for grant by:
nindian-polity-55-13.x: A token cut reduces a demand by ₹100 to air a specific grievance. A policy cut reduces it to ₹1, and an economy cut by a specified amount.
nindian-polity-55-13.tq: Discriminate the three cut motions: ₹1, ₹100 and a specified amount.
n: A Token Cut Motion proposes reducing a demand for grant by ₹100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
A Token Cut Motion ventilates a specific grievance within government responsibility. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #55 · pp 146-150]
xs: A **Token Cut** reduces a demand by **₹100** — option **(1)**.
It ventilates a **specific grievance** within government responsibility.
A **Policy Cut** reduces it to **₹1**; an **Economy Cut** by a **specified amount**.
xa: Cut motions are moved only in the **Lok Sabha** during voting on demands.
⚠ **Re 1** = policy cut; **Rs 100** = token cut.

nindian-polity-38-11.s: A token cut reduces a demand for grant by:
nindian-polity-38-11.x: A token cut reduces a demand by ₹100; a policy cut reduces it to ₹1 and an economy cut by a specified amount.
n: Charged Expenditure is non-votable expenditure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Policy Cut moves to reduce a demand to ₹1. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
An Economy Cut moves to reduce a demand by a specified amount. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]

nindian-polity-61-15.s: The pensions of High Court Judges are charged on the:

Debt charges for which the Government of India is liable are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #61 · pp 161-164]

xa: HC judges' **pensions** are charged on the **CFI**.

nindian-polity-79-19.s: The Third Schedule of the Constitution deals with:

nindian-polity-79-14.s: Under which Article does Parliament fix by law the salaries of the Speaker and the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha?

nindian-polity-79-18.s: Whose salary, pension and office expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India?

The expenditure on the Election Commission is not charged. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
The office of the Vice-President carries no separate charged salary. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers are completely votable through annual Demands for Grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
The salaries and administrative expenses of the Election Commission are not listed under the charged items of Article 112(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]

Article 148(3) deals with the salary, pension, and administrative expenses of the Comptroller and Auditor General being charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
The salary and allowances of the Comptroller and Auditor General are paid from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
The pension of the Comptroller and Auditor General is paid from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #79 · pp 215-218]
xa: The VP is paid as **Chairman of the Rajya Sabha**, which is charged.

n18fa780ed10.s: An exceptional grant is one which:
o: Provides an advance for the first two months of the year
Is not part of the current service of any year
Is sanctioned after expenditure has exceeded the grant
Meets a new service not included in the Budget
n18fa780ed10.x: An exceptional grant is made for a purpose that is not part of the current service of any financial year.
n18fa780ed10.tq: Separate the exact meanings of exceptional, additional and excess grants.
xs: An exceptional grant is **not part of the current service of any year** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Advance for **two months** = vote on account; spending beyond the grant = **excess grant**; new service = **additional grant**.
xa: It is under **Art. 116**.
**Vote of credit** (Art. 116): unexpected demand of **indefinite magnitude/character**.
**Supplementary grant** (**Art. 115**): sanctioned amount insufficient.

nindian-polity-38-38.s: A Vote of Credit is best described as:
o: An advance grant for part of the financial year pending budget passage
A statutory authorization to withdraw voted grants from the Consolidated Fund
An unexpected, blank-check grant for an emergency or an indefinite demand
A grant reduced to ₹100 to ventilate a specific grievance
nindian-polity-38-38.x: A vote of credit is an emergency grant, like a blank cheque, for a need whose details cannot be stated in the budget. Option A describes a vote on account.
nindian-polity-38-38.tq: Discriminate the vote of credit from the vote on account.
n: The Appropriation Bill authorizes withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
The Appropriation Bill authorizes withdrawal for voted grants. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote on Account is an advance grant given by the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote on Account covers estimated expenditure for part of the financial year. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote on Account operates pending passage of the budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote of Credit is an unexpected financial grant. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote of Credit is a blank-check financial grant. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote of Credit is used for an emergency or indefinite demand. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Vote of Credit is used when the details cannot be stated in a budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Token Cut moves to reduce a demand by ₹100. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
A Token Cut ventilates a specific grievance within the Government's sphere of responsibility. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 97-101]
xs: A **Vote of Credit** is an **unexpected, blank-check grant** for an **emergency** or **indefinite** demand — option **(3)**.
It is for a demand whose details **cannot be stated** in a budget (**Article 116**).
An **advance grant** for part of the year is a **Vote on Account**; **₹100** is a **token cut**.
xa: **Vote on Account:** about **two months** (one-sixth); **3-5 months** in election years.
**Exceptional grant:** not part of the current service of any year.
⚠ **115** = supplementary, additional, excess; **116** = vote on account, vote of credit, exceptional.

n5c614d8596e.s: What is the corpus of the Contingency Fund of India stated for the financial year 2021-22 onwards?
n5c614d8596e.x: The corpus of the Contingency Fund of India was raised to ₹30,000 crore from the financial year 2021-22.
n5c614d8596e.tq: Distinguish the present corpus from the earlier corpus and from larger budgetary figures.
xs: The Contingency Fund corpus is **₹30,000 crore** from FY **2021-22** — so option **(2)** is correct.
₹**500 crore** was the earlier corpus (from **2005**); ⚠ ₹**1 lakh crore** is the proposed **Economic Stabilisation Fund**.
xa: Before 2005 it was ₹**50 crore** (some notes say ₹**5 crore**).
It is held by the **Finance Secretary (DEA)** and is at the **President's** disposal.
Established by the **Contingency Fund of India Act, 1950** under **Art. 267(1)**.

n26e6d976adc.s: The Union Budget for 2026-27 was presented on
n26e6d976adc.x: The Union Budget 2026-27 was presented on 1 February 2026. The date 14 February 2026 relates to the presentation of the Andhra Pradesh Budget 2026-27.
n26e6d976adc.tq: Separate closely placed Union and State budget dates.
xs: Union Budget 2026-27 was presented on **1 February 2026** — so option **(3)** is correct.
⚠ **14 Feb 2026** is the **AP Budget** date.
xa: BUD 2026-27 lists **Arts. 109-117, 265-267** as budget provisions.
The FM proposed an **Economic Stabilisation Fund** of **₹1 lakh crore**.
The **1 Feb** budget date dates from **2017**.

n3980ddf3cec.s: The Economic Stabilisation Fund proposed in the Union Budget 2026-27 has a proposed size of:
n3980ddf3cec.x: The proposed Economic Stabilisation Fund is Rs 1 lakh crore; Rs 30,000 crore is the corpus of the Contingency Fund of India.
xa: It is meant for **global shocks** and **supply-chain disruptions**.
Proposed in Union Budget 2026-27 (**1 Feb 2026**).
The LS approved the **second batch of Supplementary Demands for Grants (2025-26)** under **Art. 115**.

na0b2165ed65.s: Which of the following committees is chaired by the Speaker of the Lok Sabha?
na0b2165ed65.x: The Speaker chairs the Lok Sabha Business Advisory Committee, which allots time for government and other business.
na0b2165ed65.tq: Use the authority–function relationship to identify the committee chaired by the Speaker.
xs: The Speaker chairs the **Business Advisory Committee** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It allots time for **government and other business**.
xa: It has **15** members in the Lok Sabha.
Privileges: **LS 15** members, **nominated by the Speaker**.
**Petitions** = "Ombudsman"; **Subordinate Legislation** = delegated rule-making.

nab202dba8b4.s: Which of the following is an ad hoc committee of Parliament?
nab202dba8b4.x: Ad hoc committees are of two kinds: inquiry committees on a particular subject, and Select or Joint Committees constituted to examine Bills.
xa: Inquiry examples: **MPLADS**, **Security in Parliament Complex**, **Railway Convention**.
**Select Committee** = one House; **Joint Committee** = both Houses.
Financial standing committees: **Estimates, PAC, COPU**.

ned084736c7a.s: A Bill is referred to a Select Committee or a Joint Committee by:
o: A recommendation of the Business Advisory Committee
A decision of the Union Cabinet
ned084736c7a.x: Referral of a Bill to a Select or Joint Committee takes place through a motion in the House.
xa: JPC examples: **Bofors** (**1987**), **2G spectrum** (**2011**).
Currently before JPCs: **129th Amendment** (ONOE), **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
Ad hoc committees **cease once they report**.

n3854722eb1a.s: Which of the following is NOT part of the parliamentary 'watchdog' group of committees?
n3854722eb1a.x: The watchdog group comprises the Committees on Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances, the Estimates Committee, PAC, COPU and DRSCs; the Business Advisory Committee only allots time for business.
xa: ⚠ The PAC alone is often called the **"Watchdog"**.
Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**.
These committees keep an **"unremitting vigil"** on the executive's spending.

nindian-polity-35-3.s: How many Department-Related Standing Committees are there in Parliament?
nindian-polity-35-3.x: There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha. 22 is the strength of the PAC.
n: There are 24 Department-Related Standing Committees. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
The Lok Sabha has 16 Department-Related Standing Committees. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
The Rajya Sabha has 8 Department-Related Standing Committees. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
The standard joint ratio of Department-Related Standing Committees is approximately 2:1. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #35 · pp 87-91]
xa: Each DRSC has **31 members: 21 LS + 10 RS**; quorum **11**.
DRSCs came in **1993** (**17** committees); **24** since **2004**.
**Ministers are ineligible** to be DRSC members.

n24a19799320.s: The Estimates Committee, the largest financial committee of Parliament, consists of:
o: 22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members, all from the Lok Sabha
n24a19799320.x: The Estimates Committee has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, with a chairman from the ruling party; the PAC has 22 (15 LS + 7 RS).
xa: ⚠ The **Opposition chairman** convention (since **1967**) belongs to the **PAC**, not the Estimates Committee.
**COPU** also has **22** members (**15 LS + 7 RS**).
Members are elected annually by **proportional representation (STV)** for a **1 year** term; **Ministers are ineligible**.
Financial committees act **after** expenditure, while the budget acts **before** it — the two are **complementary**.

n7faa99c6739.s: Which parliamentary committee is described as a 'continuous economy committee'?
n7faa99c6739.x: The Estimates Committee is called a 'continuous economy committee' because it suggests economies and alternative policies. The PAC is the 'watchdog' on expenditure; the Petitions Committee is the 'Ombudsman'; the Business Advisory Committee allots time.
n7faa99c6739.tq: Estimates = economy; PAC = watchdog; Petitions = Ombudsman.
xs: The **Estimates Committee** is the **"Continuous economy committee"** — so option **(3)** is correct.
PAC = **"Watchdog"**; Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**; Business Advisory = **allots time**.
xa: It suggests **economies and alternative policies**.
**30** members, all LS; chairman from the **ruling party**.
Present form in **1950** (John Mathai).

n38410815d54.s: Ethics Committees were constituted in the two Houses of Parliament in which order?
o: Lok Sabha in 1997, Rajya Sabha in 2000
Rajya Sabha on 4 March 1997, Lok Sabha on 16 May 2000
Both Houses on the same day in 2000
Rajya Sabha in 2000, Lok Sabha in 2004
n38410815d54.x: The Rajya Sabha set up its Ethics Committee first, on 4 March 1997; the Lok Sabha followed on 16 May 2000. The other options reverse or misstate the dates.
xs: Ethics Committees: **Rajya Sabha on 4 March 1997**, **Lok Sabha on 16 May 2000** — so option **(2)** is correct.
⚠ **RS first**, LS later — option (1) reverses it.
xa: The Ethics Committee deals with **members' conduct**.
Source: **IYB 2026**.
⚠ Privileges (not Ethics) handles **questions of privilege**.

n271afb2831b.s: The term of office of members of the financial committees of Parliament is:
n271afb2831b.x: Members are elected annually by PR-STV for a one-year term; Ministers are ineligible.
xa: Financial committees: **Estimates**, **PAC**, **COPU**.
Their role: keep **"an unremitting vigil"** over expenditure and performance.
Their control is **after** expenditure; the budget's is **before** — complementary.

n2f05595ebe9.s: The Public Accounts Committee primarily examines:
o: Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and CAG audit reports
n2f05595ebe9.x: The PAC examines the Appropriation Accounts, Finance Accounts and the audit reports of the Comptroller and Auditor-General.
xa: It checks money spent **"within the scope of the demand"**.
It flags **waste, extravagance, loss, nugatory expenditure**.
It reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.

n95be8cec87d.s: The Public Accounts Committee checks whether government expenditure remained within the scope of the:
o: Demand for grant approved by Parliament
n95be8cec87d.x: The PAC checks whether money was spent within the scope of the demand for grant approved by Parliament.
xa: It scrutinises **appropriation accounts**, **finance accounts** and **CAG audit reports**.
It tests **efficiency, economy and propriety**, not only legality.
Its recommendations are **not binding**.

n6863c4e6097.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Public Accounts Committee?
o: It may take up certain matters on its own.
It tests efficiency, economy and propriety, not merely legality.
It examines the audit reports of the CAG.
It can examine the formulation of policy itself.
n6863c4e6097.x: The PAC examines only the execution of policy, not policy as such; its recommendations are also not binding.
xa: It reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.
Criticism: a **post-mortem** check.
It is the **"Watchdog"** on departmental expenditure (APPSC-G2 2017).

n2f9ad0c0388.s: Who is the Chairman of the Public Accounts Committee for 2026-27?
n2f9ad0c0388.x: K.C. Venugopal, an Opposition member, chairs the PAC for 2026-27, in line with the convention of an Opposition chairman. Jairam Ramesh is linked to a privilege notice; Om Birla is the Speaker; Dharmendra Pradhan is the Education Minister.
n2f9ad0c0388.tq: PAC chair = Opposition by convention; 2026-27 K.C. Venugopal.
xs: The PAC chairman for **2026-27** is **K.C. Venugopal** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Jairam Ramesh** gave a privilege notice; **Dharmendra Pradhan** is the Education Minister.
xa: The PAC chairman is from the **Opposition** by **convention** since **1967**.
Average MP attendance at **16** DRSCs and the PAC was only **53%** since the September reconstitution.
The PAC reports to the **Lok Sabha (Speaker)**.

n0f795b0ba9d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Departmentally Related Standing Committees (DRSCs)?
o: Each DRSC has 31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
There are 24 DRSCs: 16 under the Lok Sabha and 8 under the Rajya Sabha.
The quorum of a DRSC is 15.
Ministers are ineligible to be members.
n0f795b0ba9d.x: The quorum of a DRSC is 11, not 15.
xa: DRSCs scrutinise **demands for grants**, **bills referred**, **annual reports** and **long-term policy** of their ministries.
⚠ **31** (21 LS + 10 RS) = each DRSC; **30** (20 LS + 10 RS) = **SC/ST Welfare Committee**; **30** all-LS = **Estimates**.
DRSCs date from **1993**, on the **Rules Committee** recommendation.

naf46605db41.s:
Departmentally Related Standing Committees scrutinise:
1. Demands for grants
2. Bills referred to them
3. Annual reports of ministries
Which of the above are correct?
naf46605db41.x: DRSCs scrutinise demands for grants, referred Bills, annual reports and long-term policy of the ministries under them.
xa: **24** DRSCs, each with **31** members.
Origin: **1993**, Rules Committee recommendation.
Low attendance: only **53%** since the September reconstitution.

n24daf1ebf86.s: Which parliamentary committee examines the reports of the National Commissions for SCs and STs?
o: Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs
n24daf1ebf86.x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs examines welfare programmes and the National Commissions' reports; Ministers cannot serve on it.
xa: It also examines implementation of **constitutional safeguards**.
Strength: **30** = **20 LS + 10 RS**.
It is a **standing** committee.

neb0db7223d7.s: Which of the following committees exist only in the Lok Sabha?
o: Committee on Petitions and Committee of Privileges
Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and Committee on Absence of Members
Rules Committee and Committee on Papers Laid on the Table
Committee on Subordinate Legislation and Committee on Government Assurances
neb0db7223d7.x: The Committee on Private Members' Bills and Resolutions and the Committee on Absence of Members are Lok Sabha-only. Petitions, Privileges, Rules, Papers Laid, Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances committees exist in both Houses.
neb0db7223d7.tq: LS-only: Private Members' Bills; Absence of Members.
xs: **Private Members' Bills and Resolutions** and **Absence of Members** are **LS-only** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Petitions, Privileges, Subordinate Legislation and Government Assurances exist in **both Houses** (separate LS and RS strengths).
xa: Also standing: **Papers Laid on the Table**, **Rules Committee**.
Petitions: **LS 15, RS 10**; Government Assurances: **LS 15, RS 10**.
Subordinate Legislation: **LS 15, RS 15**.

nfc060b58296.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Bills before parliamentary committees?
o: The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 on One Nation, One Election is before a JPC.
The FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026 is before a JPC.
The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025 is before a Select Committee of the Rajya Sabha alone.
The Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill, 2024 proposes a new Article 82A.
nfc060b58296.x: The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhisthan Bill, 2025 is also before a JPC (a joint committee of both Houses), not a single-House Select Committee.
xa: A JPC = members of **both Houses**; a Select Committee = **one House**.
Past JPCs: **Bofors 1987**, **Harshad Mehta 1992**, **2G 2011**.
Referral is **by motion in the House**.

nea72838b731.s: Which parliamentary committee suggests economies and alternative policies?
nea72838b731.x: The Estimates Committee suggests economies and alternative policies; the PAC is the watchdog on departmental expenditure and irregularities.
xa: Estimates Committee: **financial control reforms** (APPSC-G1 2018).
Petitions = **"Ombudsman"**.
Estimates = **"Continuous economy committee"**.

n2cfddd73217.s: The Committee on Welfare of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes consists of:
o: 31 members: 21 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha
22 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha
30 members: 15 from the Lok Sabha and 15 from the Rajya Sabha
n2cfddd73217.x: The Committee on Welfare of SCs and STs has 30 members, comprising 20 from the Lok Sabha and 10 from the Rajya Sabha.
n2cfddd73217.tq: Compare the committee’s 20–10 composition with the similar 21–10 DRSC figure.
xs: The SC/ST Welfare Committee has **30 members: 20 LS + 10 RS** — so option **(2)** is correct.
xa: A **minister is ineligible**.
It examines reports of the **National Commissions for SCs and STs**.
⚠ **30** all-LS = Estimates — same number, different make-up.

n75f3fe49813.s: Which committee is popularly described as the ‘Ombudsman’ of Parliament?
n75f3fe49813.x: The Committee on Petitions is popularly described as the Ombudsman of Parliament because it considers petitions on bills and matters of public interest.
n75f3fe49813.tq: Match the distinctive nickname with the committee’s grievance-related function.
xs: The **Committee on Petitions** is the **"Ombudsman"** of Parliament — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025).
**Government Assurances** tracks promises; **Privileges** handles privilege; **Ethics** handles conduct.
xa: It examines petitions on **bills** and **public-interest** matters.
⚠ "Watchdog" = **PAC**; "Continuous economy" = **Estimates**.
Strength: **LS 15, RS 10**.

n79de1662fbb.s: In Raja Ram Pal (2007), the Supreme Court held that decisions of a House in matters of privilege are:
o: Reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality
Reviewable on every ground of procedural irregularity
Subject to approval by the President
n79de1662fbb.x: Raja Ram Pal (2007) held that privilege decisions can be reviewed, but only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality. They are not wholly immune; mere procedural irregularity is protected by Art. 122/212; the President has no approving role.
n79de1662fbb.tq: Raja Ram Pal 2007 = limited review of privilege decisions.
xs: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions are **reviewable only for gross illegality or unconstitutionality** — option **(2)**.
So they are not wholly immune (option 1 wrong).
Mere **procedural irregularity** is shielded by **Art. 122/212**, so option (3) is wrong; the President has no approving role.
xa: **Sita Soren (2024)**: **7-judge Bench**, **no immunity for bribery** to speak or vote.
Final say on a privilege notice lies with the **House**, after the **Privileges Committee** recommends.
Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.

n73cbcf5d2d0.s: A Member of Parliament wishing to allege breach of privilege or contempt by a minister, another member or an outsider generally raises the matter under
o: Lok Sabha Rule 187 or Rajya Sabha Rule 222
Lok Sabha Rule 222 or Rajya Sabha Rule 187
n73cbcf5d2d0.x: Privilege notices are raised under Rule 222 in the Lok Sabha and Rule 187 in the Rajya Sabha, usually after Question Hour.
n73cbcf5d2d0.tq: Test the paired procedural rules while guarding against a deliberate reversal of the two Houses.
xs: A privilege notice is raised under **Lok Sabha Rule 222 / Rajya Sabha Rule 187** — option **(3)**.
It is usually raised **after Question Hour**; any MP can allege breach by a **minister, member or outsider**.
Option (1) swaps the rules; **Arts 103/192** deal with other disqualifications; **Para 6** of the Tenth Schedule is about defection.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS**.
Presiding Officer grants/denies consent → House decides or refers to **Privileges Committee**.
**RS Privileges Committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.

na90291b157e.s: In a breach of privilege case, the final decision on action against the offender is taken by the:
na90291b157e.x: The Committee of Privileges examines and recommends, but the House takes the final decision.
xa: Notice is raised under **LS Rule 222 / RS Rule 187**, usually after **Question Hour**.
**RS committee**: **10** members, usually chaired by the **Deputy Chairman**.
**Contempt** is wider than breach: any act **obstructing the House** or its members.

n008b92c6b65.s: Which of the following best distinguishes contempt of the House from breach of privilege?
o: Contempt is wider and includes any act obstructing the House or its members in their functions
Contempt is narrower and concerns only members of the House
Breach of privilege applies only to ministers, whereas contempt applies only to outsiders
There is no distinction between the two expressions
n008b92c6b65.x: Contempt has a wider scope and includes acts that obstruct the House or its members in the discharge of their functions. A breach concerns infringement of a specific privilege.
n008b92c6b65.tq: Discriminate between the broader concept and the specific infringement instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: **Contempt is wider** — any act **obstructing the House or its members in their functions** — option **(1)**.
So contempt is not narrower (option 2), and the two terms are distinct (option 4 wrong).
A privilege notice can allege breach or contempt by a **minister, member or outsider**, so option (3)'s split is wrong.
xa: Punishments: **admonition**, **reprimand**, **imprisonment**, **suspension/expulsion**.
**Maharashtra**: the **Legislative Council's Privileges Committee** summoned **Kunal Kamra** on a breach notice.
Privileges rest on **conventions**, rules, statutes and judicial rulings — **never codified**.

n8ac5eb5b9e4.s: The Committee of Privileges of the Rajya Sabha consists of:
o: 10 members usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman
22 members chaired by the Leader of the Opposition
31 members chaired by a member of the ruling party
n8ac5eb5b9e4.x: The Rajya Sabha Privileges Committee has 10 members and is usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman. Fifteen members is the Lok Sabha committee's strength; 22 and 31 are PAC/COPU and DRSC sizes.
xs: The **Rajya Sabha** Privileges Committee has **10 members**, **usually chaired by the Deputy Chairman** — option **(2)**.
It examines witnesses and **recommends**; the **House decides**.
xa: ⚠ **Rule 222 = LS**, **Rule 187 = RS** for privilege notices.
The Presiding Officer may let the House decide or refer the matter to the **Privileges Committee**.
**Maharashtra Legislative Council's** committee summoned **Kunal Kamra**.

n932fa57a540.s: In July 2026, the Bench of Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe, while hearing the challenge to Paragraph 4, stated that shortcomings in the provision were:
o: Outside the jurisdiction of every constitutional authority
Matters for the Election Commission alone
n932fa57a540.x: The Bench sought the Centre’s reply but observed that any shortcomings in Paragraph 4 were matters for Parliament.
n932fa57a540.tq: Distinguish a judicial observation about legislative remedy from a transfer of jurisdiction.
xs: The Bench said any shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"** — option **(1)**.
**Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** sought the **Centre's reply** on a plea against "**deemed merger**" under **Para 4**.
xa: **Subhash Desai (2023)**: two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a **deemed merger**.
Para 4 has **two tests**: the **original political party** must merge and **two-thirds** of the legislature party must agree.
Timeline: Telangana contempt warning (Feb **2026**) → AAP and TMC "merger" cases (Apr-Jul **2026**).

n068e7187b8d.s: Which one of the following is a major criticism of the anti-defection law mentioned in the context of Indian parliamentary practice?
o: It stifles intra-party dissent and legislators’ free expression without necessarily stopping mass defections.
It has abolished the Speaker’s authority over the House.
It prevents all coalition governments from being formed.
It applies exclusively to nominated Members of Parliament.
n068e7187b8d.x: Critics argue that the law suppresses intra-party dissent and free expression, while failing to prevent mass defections effectively. The other statements do not describe the criticism.
n068e7187b8d.tq: Find the option that captures both sides of the criticism rather than an absolute consequence.
xs: The law **stifles intra-party dissent and free expression** without stopping **mass defections** — option **(1)**.
The Speaker still decides disqualification (**Para 6**); the law covers party, independent and nominated members, not only nominated.
xa: Critics say the law has been left "**impotent**".
**Speaker not neutral**: Indian Speakers **do not resign from their party**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.

n5e0a45f8f8d.s: The principal objective of the anti-defection law is to:
o: Ensure internal democracy within political parties
Limit the size of the Council of Ministers
Curb defections for office and promote stable governments
n5e0a45f8f8d.x: The law was meant to curb horse-trading and defections for office, promoting party discipline and stable governments.
xa: Background: defections toppled governments in the **1960s-70s** ("**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**", Haryana **1967**).
**Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)** studied defections; Bills of **1973 and 1978** lapsed.
Enacted by the **52nd Amendment, 1985** (**Tenth Schedule**).
Criticism: muzzles **dissent** without stopping **mass defections**.

n2d89753a432.s: The expression 'Aaya Ram Gaya Ram' became associated with defections in which State in 1967?
n2d89753a432.x: The phrase comes from Haryana, 1967; the Y.B. Chavan Committee studied defections in 1967-69, and the law came with the 52nd Amendment, 1985.
xa: The law finally came through the **52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985**, adding the **Tenth Schedule**.
**Jammu and Kashmir** enacted its **own state** anti-defection law in **1979**.
Aim: curb defections "**induced by the lure of office**" and horse-trading; ensure **party discipline** and stable governments.

n484d06eedf6.s: The 1984 defection led by Nadendla Bhaskara Rao toppled the Andhra Pradesh government of:
n484d06eedf6.x: Nadendla Bhaskara Rao's defection toppled N.T. Rama Rao's government in 1984; NTR was restored after a month, strengthening the demand for the 1985 law.
xa: The 1985 law = **52nd Amendment**, inserting the **Tenth Schedule**.
Earlier: "**Aaya Ram Gaya Ram**" (Haryana **1967**); **Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)**.
AP **June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP** RS MPs merged with BJP.

nindian-polity-54-14.s: The recognition of political parties in the constitutional framework through the anti-defection provisions was introduced by which amendment and Schedule?
o: 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976 and Seventh Schedule
91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 and Eleventh Schedule
44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978 and Ninth Schedule
52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 and Tenth Schedule
nindian-polity-54-14.x: Political parties entered the Constitution through the 52nd Amendment (1985), which added the Tenth Schedule on anti-defection. They were not in the original text.
nindian-polity-54-14.tq: Recall the 52nd Amendment and the Tenth Schedule.
n: Political parties were not included in the original 1950 constitutional text. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
Political parties were introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 introduced the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
Anti-defection provisions are contained in the Tenth Schedule. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: Political parties were recognised through the **52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 and Tenth Schedule** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Political parties were **not** in the **original 1950** text; the **52nd Amendment** mentioned them **for the first time**.
The **91st Amendment (2003)** only **strengthened** the anti-defection law; it did not introduce it.
xa: The 52nd Amendment also amended **Articles 101, 102, 190 and 191**.
Bill passed **15 February 1985**; in force **1 March 1985**.
⚠ The old Sikkim "Tenth Schedule" came by the **35th Amendment (1974)** and was deleted by the **36th (1975)** — a different schedule.

nindian-polity-77-4.s: Which Article deals with disqualifications for membership of a State Legislature?
nindian-polity-77-4.x: Article 191 covers State disqualifications and 190 State vacation of seats; Articles 101 and 102 are the Parliament counterparts.
n: The 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 amended Articles 101, 102, 190, and 191. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: The **52nd Amendment, 1985** amended all four Articles while inserting the **Tenth Schedule**.
General disqualification is decided by the **President** (**Art. 103**) or **Governor** (**Art. 192**) on the **EC's binding opinion**.

nindian-polity-77-5.s: Jammu & Kashmir enacted its own State anti-defection law in:
nindian-polity-77-5.x: Jammu and Kashmir passed its own anti-defection law in 1979, before the national law of 1985.
n: The Anti-Defection Law was introduced through the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Anti-Defection Law came into force on 1 March 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
Jammu and Kashmir enacted its own state Anti-Defection legislation in 1979. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: The Bill was passed on **15 February 1985**.
The **91st Amendment, 2003** later **strengthened** the law.
Earlier Bills of **1973 and 1978** **lapsed**.

nindian-polity-77-12.s: The Anti-Defection Law (52nd Amendment) came into force on:
nindian-polity-77-12.x: The 52nd Amendment received assent on 15 February 1985 and took effect on 1 March 1985.
n: The Anti-Defection Bill was passed on 15 February 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Anti-Defection Law came into force on 1 March 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
Jammu and Kashmir enacted its own state Anti-Defection legislation in 1979. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003 strengthened the Anti-Defection Law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: The **Y.B. Chavan Committee (1967-69)** studied defections earlier.
Bills of **1973 and 1978** lapsed before the 1985 law.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** upheld the Tenth Schedule but struck down **Para 7**.

n338d6f543d9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about anti-defection case law?
o: G. Viswanathan: an expelled member continues to belong to the original party for Tenth Schedule purposes.
G. Viswanathan: expulsion automatically protects a member from disqualification for joining another party.
G. Viswanathan: an expelled member who joins another party may be treated as having voluntarily given up membership.
Ravi S. Naik: voluntarily giving up membership may be inferred from conduct.
n338d6f543d9.x: Expulsion gives no such protection; an expelled member who joins another party may be disqualified for voluntarily giving up membership.
xa: **Ravi S. Naik (1994)**: giving up membership is **not the same as resigning**; inferred from **conduct**.
**Subhash Desai (2023)**: **political party** appoints the whip and leader in the House.
⚠ **Kihoto** (1992) = validity + review; **Keisham** (2020) = **three months**.

n3b201d518b1.s: The 'one-third split' exception under the Tenth Schedule was deleted by the:
n3b201d518b1.x: The 91st Amendment (2003) deleted the split exception; only the Para 4 merger exception remains.
xa: Per **IYB 2026**, the deletion brought **splits within the purview of disqualification**.
Merger needs the **original political party** to merge **and** two-thirds of the legislature party.
Presiding officers (**Para 5**) may leave their party on election and rejoin later.

n3c79e030eba.s: Under Para 4 of the Tenth Schedule, protection from disqualification on the ground of merger requires that
o: two-thirds of the legislature party agrees to merge and the original political party also merges
all members of the legislature party join another party
one-half of the legislature party joins another party
the Speaker alone approves the merger
n3c79e030eba.x: A valid merger requires two conditions: the original political party must merge with another party, and at least two-thirds of the legislature party must agree to the merger.
n3c79e030eba.tq: Apply both cumulative tests for a valid merger instead of relying only on the numerical threshold.
xs: A valid merger needs **two-thirds of the legislature party** to agree **and** the **original political party** to merge — option **(1)**.
These are the **two tests** in **Para 4**.
Two-thirds of legislators cannot by themselves create a "**deemed merger**" (**Subhash Desai**, 2023).
xa: Neither those who merge nor those who stay are disqualified.
⚠ **Merger = two-thirds** (Para 4, in force); **Split = one-third** (Para 3, deleted **2003**).
**June 2019**: **4 of 6 TDP Rajya Sabha MPs** "merged" with BJP under Para 4.
Misuse: Para 4 used as a **defence for mass defection** (AAP, TMC cases, **2026**).

nd7a359c563f.s: In the Karnataka defection case (2019), the Supreme Court upheld the disqualification of how many rebel MLAs?
nd7a359c563f.x: The Court upheld the disqualification of 17 rebel MLAs but held the Speaker could not bar them from contesting till the end of the term.
xa: **Karnataka 2019** is also an example of the **resignation route**.
**Telangana**: SC gave the Speaker a **final 3 weeks** (Feb **2026**).
Speaker decisions reviewable for **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice**.

nindian-polity-77-28.s: Which Articles govern defection disqualification of Members of Parliament and State Legislatures, respectively?
nindian-polity-77-28.x: Defection disqualification comes under Article 102(2) for MPs and 191(2) for State legislators, read with the Tenth Schedule. Clauses (1) are the general grounds.
n: Defection disqualification is governed by the 10th Schedule and Articles 102(2) and 191(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xs: Defection disqualification is governed by **Articles 102(2) and 191(2)** — so option **(3)** is correct.
These Articles, read with the **10th Schedule**, cover MPs and State legislators respectively.
**Articles 102(1) and 191(1)** are the **general** disqualification grounds; **Articles 103 and 192** give the President/Governor's decision on them.
xa: **Articles 101 and 190** deal with **vacation of seats** in Parliament and State Legislatures.
General disqualifications: **President** (MP) or **Governor** (MLA/MLC), with **ECI opinion** **mandatory and binding**.
Defection matters: **Speaker or Chairman alone**, acting as a **tribunal**; subject to **judicial review** (**Kihoto Hollohan, 1992**).

nindian-polity-77-36.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about general (non-defection) disqualification of legislators?
o: The President decides the question for a Union MP.
The Governor decides the question for a State MLA or MLC.
The ECI's opinion is non-binding in the case of a State legislator.
The ECI's opinion is mandatory and binding in the case of an MP.
nindian-polity-77-36.x: For both MPs and State legislators the ECI's opinion is compulsory and binding.
n: The President of India must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a Union MP is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Governor must obtain the Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
The Election Commission of India’s opinion on general disqualification of a State MLA or MLC is mandatory and binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: ⚠ In **defection** cases the **ECI is not consulted** — the **Speaker or Chairman** decides.
The **Election Commission** and **Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990)** proposed that defection cases too be decided by the **President or Governor on the EC's advice**.
**NCRWC (2002)**: defectors to be barred from **public or remunerative political office** for the rest of the term.

n9856f799cc7.s: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), the Supreme Court held that legislative privilege
o: gives no immunity for bribery connected with speaking or voting
gives complete immunity for accepting a bribe to speak or vote
applies only to proceedings of State Legislatures
overrides the power of courts to investigate corruption
n9856f799cc7.x: The seven-judge Bench held that privilege does not protect bribery to speak or vote, thereby overruling the contrary position in P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998).
n9856f799cc7.tq: Use the later larger-Bench decision to identify the overruling of an earlier precedent.
xs: **Sita Soren (2024)** held privilege **gives no immunity for bribery** connected with speaking or voting — option **(1)**.
A **7-judge Bench** gave the ruling and **overruled P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998)**, which had allowed such immunity.
So option (2) states the overruled position; the ruling is not limited to State Legislatures.
xa: **Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.
Privilege source: **Art. 105** (Parliament) and **Art. 194** (states).
⚠ **P.V. Narasimha Rao** = **1998** (overruled); **Sita Soren** = **2024**.

n056842331cd.s: While deciding a disqualification question under the Tenth Schedule, the Speaker or Chairman acts as a:
n056842331cd.x: The presiding officer acts as a tribunal, subject to limited judicial review; the ECI gives no opinion here (that applies under Articles 103 and 192).
xa: ⚠ Contrast: **other** disqualifications (**Arts 103 and 192**) → President/Governor decides on the **EC's opinion**.
Review grounds: **mala fides**, **perversity**, violation of **natural justice** or constitutional mandate.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.

nc1c63fcb102.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu (1992)?
o: It was decided by a Constitution Bench.
It upheld the constitutional validity of the Tenth Schedule.
It struck down Paragraph 7 of the Schedule.
It held that the Tenth Schedule violates the basic structure by restricting legislators' freedom of speech.
nc1c63fcb102.x: The Court held that the law did not violate legislators' freedom of speech or the basic structure.
xa: Decided by a **Constitution Bench**.
Speaker's decision reviewable only **after** it is made.

n7316f68f071.s: Why was Paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule struck down in Kihoto Hollohan v. Zachillhu?
o: It barred judicial review without the required ratification by the States under Article 368(2)
It transferred disqualification powers to the Election Commission
It permitted nominated members to vote in all elections
It abolished the office of the Speaker
n7316f68f071.x: Paragraph 7 attempted to oust the jurisdiction of courts. Its provisions were held invalid because the amendment had not been ratified by the States as required under Article 368(2).
n7316f68f071.tq: Match the constitutional defect with the provision that attempted to exclude court jurisdiction.
xs: **Para 7** barred courts but was **not ratified by the States under Art. 368(2)** — option **(1)**.
**Kihoto Hollohan (1992)** struck it down; the ruling on Para 7 was **3:2**.
EC has no role under the Tenth Schedule; the Speaker remains the deciding authority (**Para 6**).
xa: The Tenth Schedule itself was **upheld as valid**.
Decision now **subject to judicial review**, but only **after** the decision.
⚠ **Kihoto** (1992) = validity + review; **Keisham** (2020) = **three months**; **Subhash Desai** (2023) = whip.

ncc3f5bf9a20.s: Judicial review of a decision of the Speaker or Chairman under the Tenth Schedule is generally available
o: under no circumstances, because the decision is final
before the decision is made, on every question of fact
only after the decision, and on limited grounds such as mala fides or perversity
only when the Election Commission grants permission
ncc3f5bf9a20.x: Kihoto Hollohan preserved judicial review after the decision, but limited it to grounds such as mala fides, perversity, violation of natural justice and constitutional mandate.
ncc3f5bf9a20.tq: Reject the absolute-finality trap and identify both the timing and limited grounds of review.
xs: Review is available **only after the decision**, on limited grounds like **mala fides or perversity** — option **(3)**.
Other grounds: violation of **natural justice** or of a **constitutional mandate**.
**Para 7**, which barred courts, was **struck down** in **Kihoto Hollohan**, so option (1) is wrong; the EC has no role.
xa: Deciding authority: **Speaker/Chairman** acting as a **tribunal** (**Para 6**).
No time limit in the Schedule; **Keisham (2020)** set **three months**.
**Raja Ram Pal (2007)**: privilege decisions reviewable only for **gross illegality or unconstitutionality**.

n057de95e924.s: In Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur, the Supreme Court indicated that disqualification petitions should ordinarily be decided within:
n057de95e924.x: The Supreme Court indicated that the Speaker should decide disqualification petitions within three months, except in extraordinary circumstances.
n057de95e924.tq: Recall the specific judicially indicated time period.
xs: **Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020)**: decide within **three months** — option **(2)**.
Exception: **extraordinary cases**.
xa: The Court also asked **Parliament** to consider a **permanent independent tribunal** instead of the Speaker.
The Schedule itself prescribes **no time limit**.
⚠ **Keisham** = time; **Kihoto** = review; **Subhash Desai** = party over legislature party.

n9d162d1c145.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Keisham Meghachandra Singh v. Speaker, Manipur?
o: Disqualification petitions are ordinarily to be decided within three months.
The three-month period admits exceptions in extraordinary cases.
The judgment transferred all Tenth Schedule decisions to the Election Commission.
The Court asked Parliament to consider replacing the Speaker with a permanent independent tribunal.
n9d162d1c145.x: The Court did not transfer Tenth Schedule decisions to the Election Commission; it only suggested considering an independent tribunal.
xa: Case date: **Jan 2020**, Speaker of **Manipur**.
**Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and the **EC** had urged decisions by the **President or Governor** on EC advice.
**Telangana**: SC gave a **final 3 weeks** with a **contempt** warning (Feb **2026**).

n19bb1a739ec.s: According to the Subhash Desai judgment, the whip of a party in the House is appointed by the:
n19bb1a739ec.x: The legislature party cannot be conflated with the political party, and it is the political party that appoints the whip.
xa: Context: the **Shiv Sena** case, May **2023**.
**SC Bench (Jul 2026)** — **Justices P.S. Narasimha and Alok Aradhe** — sought the Centre's reply on "deemed merger" under **Para 4**.
**AIADMK** Palaniswami camp cited the ruling (May **2026**) to claim the whip.

n83614563267.s: The Palaniswami camp of the AIADMK cited the Subhash Desai ruling in May 2026 in relation to control over the:
n83614563267.x: The Palaniswami camp cited the ruling to claim control of the whip under Paragraph 2(1)(b).
n83614563267.tq: Link the contemporary application to the precise constitutional provision mentioned.
xs: The Palaniswami camp claimed control of the **whip under Para 2(1)(b)** — option **(2)**.
It relied on **Subhash Desai (2023)**: the **political party** appoints the whip.
xa: Para **2(1)(b)** is the whip clause: vote/abstain against it, not condoned within **15 days** → disqualified.
Legislature party **cannot be conflated** with the political party.
Valid merger needs two-thirds of the legislature party **of the original party**.

n0c3b794ab23.s: Which of the following is a newer proposal concerning the anti-defection law?
o: Exempting independent members from the law
Fixed timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal
n0c3b794ab23.x: Newer proposals include fixed constitutional timelines for Speakers and an independent tribunal, the latter suggested for consideration by the Supreme Court in 2020.
xa: **Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
Reform: limit whips to **confidence votes and Money Bills**.
**Telangana**: SC gave a **final 3 weeks** with a **contempt** warning (Feb **2026**).

nee67bcb3f8d.s: The proposal to limit the operation of the whip and disqualification under the anti-defection law primarily to confidence and money votes seeks to ensure that legislators may:
o: Vote against every money bill without party discipline
Avoid all party whips during the entire legislative term
Dissent even on a confidence motion without consequences
Dissent freely on matters that do not threaten the government's survival
nee67bcb3f8d.x: The proposal would retain party discipline for votes threatening government survival, such as confidence, no-confidence and money bills, while allowing dissent on other matters.
nee67bcb3f8d.tq: Apply the reform principle to distinguish survival votes from ordinary legislative votes.
xs: Legislators could **dissent freely on votes that do not threaten the government's survival** — option **(4)**.
The whip would apply only to **confidence and no-confidence motions and money bills**.
So discipline stays on confidence and money votes — options (1), (2) and (3) are wrong.
xa: Backers: **Dinesh Goswami (1990)** and **Law Commission (1999)**.
**Manish Tewari's private member's Bill (2010)** proposed the same.
Criticism it answers: the law **muzzles dissent** without stopping mass defections.

n643cf6afb57.s: In the Telangana Speaker matter, how much time did the Supreme Court later allow for deciding the last two of ten BRS disqualification petitions?
n643cf6afb57.x: After a time-bound direction, the Supreme Court gave three weeks for the last two of ten BRS petitions, warning of contempt.
xa: The **10 BRS MLAs** had moved to **Congress**.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months** limit.
AP precedent: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (2014-19), petitions **never decided**.

n316c05d1442.s: “Resort politics” in the context of anti-defection and floor tests refers to:
o: Sending legislators abroad for parliamentary training
Dissolving the legislature before a confidence motion
Sequestering legislators before a floor test to prevent poaching
Suspending legislators who abstain from voting
n316c05d1442.x: Resort politics involves keeping legislators together or sequestered before a floor test to prevent rival parties from poaching them.
n316c05d1442.tq: Decode the political practice from its purpose rather than from its literal name.
xs: Resort politics = **sequestering legislators before a floor test** to stop **poaching** — option **(3)**.
It is one of the **ways around the law**, along with the **resignation route** and **merger misuse**.
xa: **Resignation route**: MLAs **resign** to cut the majority mark (Karnataka **2019**, MP **2020**).
**Merger misuse**: Para 4 **two-thirds** rule as a defence for mass defection.
**AAP**: **7 of 10** Rajya Sabha MPs claimed a "merger" with the BJP (Apr **2026**).

n5301ea4de2d.s: In the 'resignation route' used to avoid disqualification proceedings, legislators:
o: Seek prior permission from the Election Commission before switching parties
Resign, lowering the majority mark, and later re-contest on the new party's ticket
Abstain from every vote until the next election
Merge into the new party without resigning
n5301ea4de2d.x: In the resignation route, MLAs resign instead of defecting, reducing the majority mark without disqualification, and may re-contest on the new party's ticket.
xa: Examples: **Karnataka 2019**, **MP 2020**.
**Karnataka 2019**: SC upheld disqualification of **17** rebel MLAs.
**Resort politics**: legislators **sequestered** before a floor test.

n09f787e59a7.s: Delay by Speakers in deciding disqualification petitions is a concern mainly because:
o: Speakers need the Governor's approval to decide
The Election Commission must concur in every decision
Petitions must first be heard by the High Court
There is no fixed time limit and Speakers remain members of their parties
n09f787e59a7.x: There is no fixed time limit, and Speakers, who do not resign from their parties, decide petitions in a partisan context.
xa: Examples: **AP 2014-19** (**23 YSRCP MLAs**, petitions undecided); **Telangana 2024-26**.
**Keisham (2020)**: **three months**; asked Parliament to consider an **independent tribunal**.
Newer proposal: **fixed constitutional timelines** (Jul **2026**).

nb14c435f09d.s: In April 2026, seven Rajya Sabha MPs of which party joined the BJP, an episode cited as misuse of the merger exception?
nb14c435f09d.x: Seven AAP Rajya Sabha MPs joined the BJP in April 2026; twenty TMC MPs joining the NPCI in June 2026 was the other example cited.
xa: NPCI = **Nationalist Citizens Party of India**; another source calls it "**National People's Congress of India**".
These show **merger misuse** — Para 4 used as a defence for mass defection.
**SC Bench (Jul 2026)** said shortcomings are **"matters for Parliament"**.

n4a77ead8527.s: The disqualification petitions against 23 YSRCP MLAs who moved to the TDP between 2014 and 2019 were:
o: Upheld, and the MLAs disqualified immediately
Decided by the Supreme Court in 2014
n4a77ead8527.x: The petitions were never decided, a standard example of delay by the Speaker in anti-defection proceedings.
xa: Speakers are partisan as they **do not resign from their party**; the Schedule sets **no time limit**.
**Keisham (2020)**: decide within **three months**.
Other example: **Telangana 2024-26** (**10 BRS MLAs** to Congress).

ne582c8cab59.s: What was the constitutional significance of the June 2019 event involving four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs?
o: They were disqualified by the Rajya Sabha Chairman for voting against the party
They were nominated to the Rajya Sabha by the President
They merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger
They formed an independent party without invoking the Tenth Schedule
ne582c8cab59.x: In June 2019, four of the six TDP Rajya Sabha MPs were treated as having merged with the BJP under Paragraph 4, and the Rajya Sabha Chairman accepted the merger.
ne582c8cab59.tq: Identify the relevant Tenth Schedule provision and distinguish a merger from disqualification.
xs: **4 of 6 TDP Rajya Sabha MPs** "merged" with the **BJP** under **Para 4**; the **RS Chairman accepted** it — option **(3)**.
In the Rajya Sabha the **Chairman** decides Tenth Schedule questions (**Para 6**).
They were not disqualified, nor nominated; Para 4 is the Tenth Schedule merger exception.
xa: Para 4 needs **two-thirds** of the legislature party to agree.
AP **1984**: **Nadendla Bhaskara Rao** toppled **NTR's** government.
AP **2014-19**: **23 YSRCP MLAs** moved to TDP; petitions never decided.

nindian-polity-77-15.s: The time limit prescribed in the Tenth Schedule for the Presiding Officer to decide a defection petition is:
nindian-polity-77-15.x: The Tenth Schedule sets no time limit for deciding a defection petition, which is often criticised.
n: The 10th Schedule prescribes no statutory time limit for the Presiding Officer to decide a defection petition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #77 · pp 210-212]
xa: **Keisham Meghachandra Singh (Jan 2020)**: Speakers to decide **within three months**, except in extraordinary cases.
Keisham also asked **Parliament** to consider a **permanent independent tribunal** in place of the Speaker.
Speaker delay example: **23 YSRCP MLAs** (AP **2014-19**) — petitions **never decided**.
**Telangana**: SC gave the Speaker a **final 3 weeks** and warned of **contempt** (Feb **2026**).

nca34fa8cf81.s: The original Tenth Schedule, concerning Sikkim's association with India, was added by the:
nca34fa8cf81.x: The 35th Amendment introduced a Sikkim-related Tenth Schedule, which the 36th Amendment omitted; it was not the anti-defection Schedule.
xa: ⚠ Trap: Sikkim schedule = **35th**, **1974**; anti-defection schedule = **52nd**, **1985**.
The 52nd Amendment also amended **Arts. 101, 102, 190, 191**.
**91st Amendment (2003)** tightened the law.

n2c738e4a350.s: Under Article 164(1A), the Council of Ministers in a State cannot exceed 15 per cent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, subject to a minimum of
n2c738e4a350.x: The State Council of Ministers is capped at 15 per cent of the Assembly strength, but it cannot consist of fewer than 12 ministers.
n2c738e4a350.tq: Recall both parts of a compound numerical rule: the percentage ceiling and the statutory minimum.
xs: Minimum is **12 ministers** — option **(1)**.
**Art. 164(1A)** caps a State Council of Ministers at **15%** of Assembly strength, with a minimum of **12**.
xa: **Art. 75(1A)**: Union Council capped at **15%** of Lok Sabha strength.
Both added by the **91st Amendment, 2003**, which also deleted the **split** exception.
**Arts 75(1B), 164(1B), 361B**: defector cannot be a Minister until **re-elected**.

n52bf8d7204c.s: A person disqualified under the anti-defection provisions is barred from becoming a Minister or holding a remunerative political post until re-elected under
n52bf8d7204c.x: Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B impose these restrictions on a disqualified defector until re-election.
n52bf8d7204c.tq: Match the consequence of disqualification with the specific provisions introduced by the 91st Amendment.
xs: The bar is in **Articles 75(1B), 164(1B) and 361B** — option **(1)**.
A disqualified defector cannot be a **Minister** or hold a **remunerative political post** until **re-elected**.
**Arts 101, 102, 190, 191** were amended by the **52nd** Amendment for vacation of seats; **105/194** are privileges.
xa: These came with the **91st Amendment, 2003**.
Same Amendment: **15%** cap under **Art. 75(1A)** and **Art. 164(1A)**.
**NCRWC (2002)** had urged barring defectors from any **public or remunerative political office**.

n27c12c52826.s: The average number of sitting days per year declined from approximately how many in the First Lok Sabha to approximately how many in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha (2019–24)?
n27c12c52826.x: The average sittings declined from about 135 days per year in the First Lok Sabha to about 55 days per year in the Seventeenth Lok Sabha.
n27c12c52826.tq: Use the paired historical figures and eliminate reversed or rounded alternatives.
xs: Sittings fell from about **135 days/year** (**1st Lok Sabha**) to about **55** (**17th Lok Sabha, 2019-24**) — option **(2)**.
That is a decline of well over half across the Lok Sabhas.
xa: Lok Sabha now sits **60-70 days a year** vs **150+** sittings of the **UK House of Commons**.
**Art. 85(1)** only bars a gap of more than **six months** between sessions; **no minimum** sitting days.
**NCRWC (2000-02)** proposed a minimum of **120** days (LS) and **100** (RS).

n279bcada197.s: The Lok Sabha generally sits for about how many days in a year?
n279bcada197.x: The Lok Sabha sits around 60–70 days a year, whereas the UK House of Commons has more than 150 sittings.
xa: Trend: **135** days/year (**1st LS**) → about **55** (**17th LS**).
Proposal: a **fixed parliamentary calendar**.

n40dd36cbb74.s: Article 85(1) of the Constitution provides that:
o: The Rajya Sabha must sit for at least 100 days every year
There cannot be a gap of more than six months between two sessions of Parliament
The Lok Sabha must hold three sessions every year
Parliament must sit for at least 120 days every year
n40dd36cbb74.x: Article 85(1) bars a gap of more than six months between sessions but prescribes no minimum number of sitting days.
n40dd36cbb74.tq: Distinguish a constitutional maximum gap from a minimum sitting requirement.
xs: **Art. 85(1)** bars a **gap of more than six months** between sessions — option **(2)**.
It sets **no minimum** sitting days, so options (1), (3) and (4) are wrong.
The **120 / 100** figures are **NCRWC** proposals, not constitutional rules.
xa: ⚠ **Art. 85(1)** = Parliament's six-month gap; **Art. 174** = States' **6**-month gap.
State Assemblies met on average **24 days** (PRS **2025**), many only to satisfy **Art. 174**.
**Art. 123** = Ordinances.

nec2cf682295.s: In the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for approximately what proportion of its scheduled time?
nec2cf682295.x: During the Seventeenth Lok Sabha, Question Hour ran for only 60 per cent of its scheduled time.
nec2cf682295.tq: Distinguish the long-term Lok Sabha figure from the much lower Monsoon Session 2026 figure.
xs: In the **17th Lok Sabha**, Question Hour ran only **60 per cent** of scheduled time — option **(3)**.
So about two-fifths of the hour meant for **questions to ministers** was lost to disruption or adjournment.
xa: ⚠ **60%** is also the share of Bills referred to committees in the **14th LS**.
Monsoon **2026**: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS), **12%** (RS); only **2** (LS) and **16** (RS) questions answered orally.
Proposal: **strengthen Question Hour** and protect opposition debate time.

na7331ed8064.s: The NCRWC recommended minimum annual sitting days of:
o: 150 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
120 for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha
100 for Lok Sabha and 120 for Rajya Sabha
na7331ed8064.x: The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution recommended 120 sitting days for Lok Sabha and 100 for Rajya Sabha.
na7331ed8064.tq: Keep the House-wise figures in their stated order.
xs: **NCRWC (2000-02)**: minimum **120 days for Lok Sabha** and **100 for Rajya Sabha** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) swaps the Houses.
xa: **Art. 85(1)** prescribes **no minimum** sitting days.
Actual: about **55** days/year in the **17th LS**.

n87da6f58db8.s: During the Monsoon Session of 2026, which of the following correctly describes the productivity of the two Houses?
o: Lok Sabha 25 per cent and Rajya Sabha 16 per cent
Lok Sabha 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha 39 per cent
Lok Sabha 60 per cent and Rajya Sabha 53 per cent
Lok Sabha 39 per cent and Rajya Sabha 19 per cent
n87da6f58db8.x: PRS data placed Lok Sabha productivity at 19 per cent and Rajya Sabha productivity at 39 per cent during the Monsoon Session of 2026.
n87da6f58db8.tq: Read the House-wise figures without reversing the pair.
xs: Monsoon Session **2026**: **Lok Sabha 19%**, **Rajya Sabha 39%** — option **(2)**.
LS productivity was **among the lowest in 22 years** (PRS).
Option (4) swaps the Houses; **25%/16%** are Bill-referral shares of the **16th/17th** LS.
xa: Question Hour ran **1%** (LS) and **12%** (RS) of scheduled time.
Estimated loss: **₹175 crore**; **12** Bills passed, only one debated in detail.

n86418f36683.s: In which Lok Sabha was the highest share of Bills referred to parliamentary committees?
n86418f36683.x: The 15th Lok Sabha referred 71% of Bills to committees, against 60% in the 14th, 25% in the 16th and only 16% in the 17th.
xs: The **15th Lok Sabha** referred the highest share — **71%** — option **(2)**.
xa: ⚠ **60%** = Bills referred (**14th**) and Question Hour run (**17th**).
**17th LS**: **58%** of Bills passed within **two weeks**; **35%** debated under **one hour**.
UK: every Bill examined by committees of both Houses.

nec82be0973b.s: The systematic system of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committees was introduced in India in:
nec82be0973b.x: The systematic committee system, including Department-related Standing Committees, began in 1993.
nec82be0973b.tq: Distinguish the institutional starting year from later reform proposals.
xs: The systematic **DRSC** committee system began in **1993** — option **(3)**.
