Before that India had no **systematic** committee scrutiny of departments; even now **less than a fifth** of Bills go to committees.
xa: **1977** = **LoP Salary and Allowances Act**; **1967** = PAC chaired by Opposition.
Average attendance at **DRSC** meetings: **53%**.
Referral share fell to **16%** in the **17th LS**.

na1d637607f2.s: Which of the following was NOT among the proposals concerning the use of ordinances?
o: Judicial examination of urgency in light of Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)
Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval
na1d637607f2.x: The proposals were to define immediate necessity, permit courts to test urgency, and publish reasons for ordinances. Permanent operation without legislative approval was not proposed.
na1d637607f2.tq: Identify the extreme proposal that goes beyond the stated reform measures.
xs: **Making every ordinance permanent without legislative approval** was not proposed — option **(2)**.
Real proposals: define "**immediate necessity**" by law, test urgency per **Krishna Kumar Singh (2017)**, **publish reasons**.
xa: Ordinances = **Art. 123**.
Ordinances and delegated legislation grow as **legislative engagement falls**.
Other bypass: **Money Bill route** under **Art. 110**.

n8fcb119b9d6.s: The principal constitutional concern regarding the use of the Money Bill route is that it:
o: Requires the approval of every State Legislature
Can bypass the Rajya Sabha for measures that may not strictly fall within Article 110
Can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha
Prevents the Lok Sabha from considering financial legislation
n8fcb119b9d6.x: The Money Bill route may bypass the Rajya Sabha for laws whose provisions may not strictly fit within Article 110. The Aadhaar Act, 2016, is cited as an example.
n8fcb119b9d6.tq: Identify the institutional consequence of the classification rather than the subject of the Bill.
xs: The Money Bill route can **bypass the Rajya Sabha** for laws that may not strictly fit **Art. 110** — option **(2)**.
Example: **Aadhaar Act, 2016**.
xa: Notes: the **RS only returned it**.
Other bypass: heavy use of **ordinances (Art. 123)**.
Criticism of weak control: **executive dominance**, **guillotine**, delegated legislation.

nb9bbb4d15b5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about suspension-related rules in the Lok Sabha?
o: Rule 373 – Automatic suspension for five sittings for grave disorder
Rule 373 – Member directed to withdraw for the day
Rule 374 – Suspension by a House motion up to the remainder of the session
Rule 374A – Automatic suspension for grave disorder
nb9bbb4d15b5.x: Automatic suspension for grave disorder is under Rule 374A; Rule 373 only directs a member to withdraw for the day.
xa: Rajya Sabha: **Rule 255** = withdrawal for the day (Chairman); **Rule 256** = suspension by House motion.
⚠ **373 / 255** = withdraw for the day; **374 / 256** = House motion; **374A** = automatic.

n314047542b6.s: The statutory status of the Leader of the Opposition is provided under the:
o: Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977
n314047542b6.x: The Leader of the Opposition has statutory status under the Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977.
n314047542b6.tq: Match the office with the statute specifically dealing with its salary and allowances.
xs: The LoP's statutory status comes from the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977** — option **(1)**.
The other Acts named do not give the LoP statutory status in the notes.
xa: Recognised by the **Speaker** if the party has **one-tenth** of the House (**55** in LS).
**PAC** chaired by the Opposition since **1967**.
Monsoon **2026**: united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a **JPC**.

n7a0026e3bc5.s: Since which year has the Public Accounts Committee generally been chaired by a member of the Opposition?
n7a0026e3bc5.x: The Public Accounts Committee has been chaired by a member of the Opposition since 1967.
n7a0026e3bc5.tq: Retain the institutional convention’s specific starting year.
xs: The **PAC** has been chaired by the Opposition since **1967** — option **(2)**.
Committees are one of the Opposition's tools, along with **Question Hour** and **motions**.
xa: LoP recognition needs **one-tenth** of the House (**55** in LS).
Opposition tools: **Question Hour**, **motions**, **committees**.

nd746abbe1dc.s: Which of the following is NOT a proposal for improving parliamentary functioning?
o: Restricting all opposition debate to confidence motions alone
Making committee scrutiny mandatory before passage of Bills
nd746abbe1dc.x: The proposals include a fixed calendar, stronger Question Hour, mandatory committee scrutiny, and protection of opposition debate time. The proposal is to limit whips, not all opposition debate, to confidence votes and Money Bills.
nd746abbe1dc.tq: Separate a proposal concerning whips from the broader protection of opposition debate.
xs: **Restricting all opposition debate to confidence motions** is not a proposal — option **(2)**.
Proposals: **fixed calendar**, **stronger Question Hour**, **protect opposition debate time**, **mandatory committee scrutiny**.
What is limited to **confidence votes and Money Bills** is the **whip**, not debate.
xa: **National Legislative Index** announced by the **LS Speaker**.

nindian-polity-54-12.s: In which year was the Leader of Opposition first formally recognized?
nindian-polity-54-12.x: The Leader of the Opposition was first formally recognised in 1969.
nindian-polity-54-12.tq: Recall the year the post was formally recognised.
n: The Leader of Opposition was first formally recognized in 1969. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: The Leader of Opposition was first formally recognized in **1969** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The statutory status came later through the **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.
**1964** is the year **COPU** was set up, not LoP recognition.
xa: Threshold: the **largest opposition party** must hold at least **10%** (**one-tenth**) of the House — about **55 seats** in the Lok Sabha.
Opposition tools: **Question Hour**, motions, committees — **PAC chaired by Opposition since 1967**.
**Monsoon 2026**: the united opposition pushed the **FCRA (Amendment) Bill, 2026** to a **JPC**.

nindian-polity-54-13.s: What numerical threshold must the largest opposition party meet for recognition as the Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha?
o: At least 5% of the total House strength
At least 15% of the total House strength
At least 10% of the total House strength
At least 20% of the total House strength
nindian-polity-54-13.x: To be recognised as Leader of the Opposition, the largest opposition party needs at least 10% of the House, about 55 Lok Sabha seats.
n: The largest opposition party must hold at least 10% of the total House strength to receive recognition as the Leader of Opposition. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
The 10% Leader of Opposition threshold is approximately 55 seats in the Lok Sabha. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 144-146]
xs: The largest opposition party needs **at least 10% of the total House strength** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is **one-tenth** of the House — approximately **55 seats** in the **Lok Sabha** (quorum-size).
Recognition is by the **Speaker**.
xa: The LoP was **first formally recognized** in **1969**.
Statutory status: **Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977**.
The **PAC** has been chaired by the **Opposition since 1967** by convention.

n40154b355f6.s: The proposed National Legislative Index is intended to provide a data-driven assessment of:
o: Only the attendance of Members of Parliament
Sittings, legislative business, disruptions, committee use and grievance redressal
The performance of State courts and tribunals
Only the financial expenditure of Parliament
n40154b355f6.x: The National Legislative Index covers sittings, business, disruptions, use of committees and grievance redressal.
n40154b355f6.tq: Choose the option that covers the complete range of functions named for the index.
xs: It assesses **sittings, business, disruptions, committee use and grievance redressal** — option **(2)**.
It was announced by the **LS Speaker** as a **data-driven** index.
xa: **PRS Legislative Research** compiles productivity and Bill-scrutiny data.
**Digital Sansad** gives official attendance/sitting data.
**86th AIPOC** at **Lucknow**: theme "**Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation**".

n9ca34cfa958.s: In the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, the agenda for the Budget Session 2026 was fixed by the Business Advisory Committee chaired by:
n9ca34cfa958.x: The Business Advisory Committee fixing the agenda was chaired by Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu.
n9ca34cfa958.tq: Apply the authority test: identify who presides over the relevant legislative committee.
xs: The **BAC** was chaired by **Speaker Chintakayala Ayyanna Patrudu** — option **(2)**.
It fixed the agenda of the AP **Budget Session 2026** (TH **12** Feb **2026**).
xa: Session ran **11 Feb to 7 Mar 2026**.
PRS **2025**: State Assemblies met on average **24 days**.

n96dc82d0885.s: The proposed enlargement of the Lok Sabha would raise its strength from 550 to how many seats?
n96dc82d0885.x: The proposal increases the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850 seats, raising the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha ratio from 2.2:1 to 3.3:1.
xa: Joint sittings used only **3 times** so far.
**86th AIPOC** at **Lucknow**; AIPOC dates to **1921**.

nefa4f2a6182.s: Joint sittings of the Parliament have been used, so far, on how many occasions?
nefa4f2a6182.x: Joint sittings of Parliament have been used only three times so far.
nefa4f2a6182.tq: Distinguish the exact numerical count from nearby plausible figures.
xs: Joint sittings have been used only **three times** — option **(1)**.
The notes put it as **3 times** so far.
xa: Context: the **131st Amendment Bill** (**550 → 850** LS seats) would raise the LS:RS ratio to **3.3:1**.
A larger LS would weigh more in a joint sitting.
Current ratio: **2.2:1**.

nf1453fe213a.s: The 86th All India Presiding Officers' Conference (AIPOC) was held at:
nf1453fe213a.x: The 86th AIPOC was held at Lucknow with the theme 'Strong Legislature - Prosperous Nation'.
xa: **National Legislative Index** announced by the **LS Speaker**.
**131st Amendment Bill**: **550 → 850** LS seats.

n320351f5639.s: Under Article 74(1) of the Constitution of India, the President ordinarily acts on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers because:
o: the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Rajya Sabha
the advice of the Council of Ministers is constitutionally binding
the Prime Minister is directly elected by the people
the President is the de facto executive
n320351f5639.x: Article 74(1) provides for a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, and the President is bound by that advice.
n320351f5639.tq: Distinguish the nominal head from the real executive and identify the constitutional provision.
xs: Under **Art. 74(1)** the ministers **aid and advise** the President, and **the advice of the Council of Ministers is constitutionally binding** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The President is the **de jure** (nominal) head; the **PM + Council of Ministers** form the **de facto** executive, so option (4) reverses the roles.
The PM is the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha**, not directly elected by the people — option (3) is wrong.
xa: India adopted the British **parliamentary system**, based on **cooperation and co-ordination** of legislature and executive.
⚠ **Trap:** the President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
**Dual membership:** ministers must be MPs; a non-member must be elected within **six months**.

nc9f9b6632ab.s: A person who is appointed as a Union Minister without being a member of either House of Parliament must secure election or nomination to Parliament within:
nc9f9b6632ab.x: A non-member may become a minister, but must become a member of either House of Parliament within six months.
nc9f9b6632ab.tq: Test the precise constitutional time limit using closely spaced numerical options.
xs: A non-member appointed minister must become a member of either House within **six months** — so option **(2)** is correct.
This flows from the parliamentary feature of **dual membership**: ministers must be **MPs**.
xa: **Britain** is stricter: ministers must be MPs; India allows **six months** as a non-member.
**Majority party rule:** the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM.
Other features: **nominal and real executive**, **leadership of the PM/CM**, and possible **dissolution** of the lower House.

n2e561830fe3.s: In the Indian parliamentary system, who provides central leadership to the Council of Ministers?
n2e561830fe3.x: The Prime Minister leads the Council of Ministers; the President is only the nominal head of the executive.
xa: ⚠ The "President is not the real head" point was the **APPSC-G2 2017** key.
The PM's role has grown so much that scholars call it **"Prime Ministerial Government"** in both India and Britain.

nce2040de9c7.s: The Westminster model of parliamentary government originated in:
nce2040de9c7.x: The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is commonly called the Westminster model.
nce2040de9c7.tq: Recall the origin country without confusing it with countries that later adopted the system.
xs: The **Westminster model** of parliamentary government originated in **Britain** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **USA** is the origin of the **presidential** system, so option (2) is wrong.
**India** and **Japan** follow the parliamentary model but did not originate it.
xa: ⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.
Parliamentary examples: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil** and most of **Latin America**.
Semi-presidential: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.

nba59bc0bf03.s: Which of the following is a feature of the presidential system?
o: A plural executive headed by a Prime Minister
Executive accountable to the legislature as in a parliamentary system
A fixed term for the executive
Fusion of executive and legislative powers
nba59bc0bf03.x: A presidential system generally has a single, directly elected executive with a fixed term, not accountable to the legislature in the parliamentary sense.
xa: ⚠ **APPSC-G2 2025** key: "Accountable to the legislature" is the **wrong** feature.
The President is **both Head of State and Head of Government**.
Cabinet members **may or may not** sit in the legislature (US secretaries do not).

nbecc18cd08f.s: Which of the following features is associated with Britain but not with India in the same form?
o: Collective responsibility to the lower House
nbecc18cd08f.x: Britain has an institutionalised shadow cabinet, legal ministerial responsibility and ministers who must be MPs; India lacks these in the same form.
xa: Common to both: the PM's role is so large it is called **"Prime Ministerial Government"**.
Britain: **hereditary** monarch, **unitary** state, **sovereignty of Parliament**.
India: **indirectly elected** President, **federal** state, **constitutional supremacy**.

na3bed572fd2.s: Which one of the following correctly compares the removal of the Prime Minister in the UK and India?
o: In the UK, the ruling party can replace the PM; in India, removal is linked to loss of Lok Sabha confidence
In India, the ruling party can replace the PM regardless of Lok Sabha confidence, but not in the UK
In both countries, the PM can be removed only after losing the confidence of the lower House
In neither country can the ruling party replace the PM
na3bed572fd2.x: The ruling party in the UK can replace its Prime Minister, whereas in India removal of the government is linked to losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
xa: In a parliamentary system the executive can be removed by **no-confidence**.
Britain's PM comes from the **House of Commons**; India's from **either House**.
The **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM in India.

n99c18ceaa8b.s: Who is the Leader of the Lok Sabha (Leader of the House) and the chief spokesperson of the Government?
n99c18ceaa8b.x: The Prime Minister leads the majority in the Lok Sabha, is Leader of the House and the Government's chief spokesperson; the President is Head of State.
xa: The PM **heads the Council of Ministers**.
⚠ The President is **not** the real head of the executive (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
A non-member minister must be elected within **six months** (**dual membership**).

nb6115a406a8.s: The parliamentary system of government is based on:
o: Fusion of executive and legislative powers
nb6115a406a8.x: The parliamentary system rests on fusion of executive and legislative powers, while the presidential system rests on separation of powers.
xa: India's parliamentary system rests on **cooperation and co-ordination** of legislature and executive.
Parliamentary: **collective executive (cabinet)**; presidential: **single executive (President)**.
Parliamentary: **nominal head + real head (PM)**; presidential: **one person is both heads**.

n29abf27c6ed.s: Which one of the following sets contains only examples of parliamentary systems?
o: United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India
United States, Brazil, India and Canada
United Kingdom, United States, Brazil and Japan
Brazil, United States, Canada and India
n29abf27c6ed.x: The United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India are examples of parliamentary systems. The United States and Brazil are presidential systems.
n29abf27c6ed.tq: Classify every country in the option before accepting an all-correct grouping.
xs: **United Kingdom, Japan, Canada and India** are all parliamentary systems — option **(1)** is correct.
The **United States** (origin) and **Brazil** are **presidential** systems, which rules out options (2), (3) and (4).
xa: The parliamentary system originated in **Britain** — the **Westminster model**.
Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka** — President and PM coexist.
**France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** and **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)** have a **directly elected President** with real powers.

n39ad02c1665.s: Which one of the following best describes a semi-presidential system?
o: A system in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist, with the Prime Minister responsible to the legislature
A system in which the legislature alone performs both executive and ceremonial functions
A system in which the President is only a nominal head and no Prime Minister exists
A system in which the Prime Minister is directly elected and the President has no constitutional role
n39ad02c1665.x: In a semi-presidential system, a President and a Prime Minister coexist. The President may possess real powers, while the Prime Minister is responsible to the legislature.
n39ad02c1665.tq: Identify the defining institutional combination rather than focusing on only one executive office.
xs: In a semi-presidential system a **President and a Prime Minister coexist**, with the **PM responsible to the legislature** — option **(1)** is correct.
They may even come from **different parties**; the President has **real powers**.
xa: Examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.
**France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** and **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution)** have a **directly elected President**.
⚠ India differs: its President is **indirectly elected and nominal**.

n1cb1ebae81e.s: Which of the following countries are associated with semi-presidential systems in which a President and a Prime Minister coexist?
o: Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom and the United States
Russia, India and the United States
India, the United Kingdom and France
n1cb1ebae81e.x: France, Russia and Sri Lanka are identified as examples of countries where a President and a Prime Minister coexist under a semi-presidential arrangement.
n1cb1ebae81e.tq: Use the complete country group and reject groups containing parliamentary or presidential examples outside the stated set.
xs: **France, Russia and Sri Lanka** are semi-presidential — option **(3)** is correct.
The **UK** and **India** are parliamentary; the **United States** is presidential — so the other options fail.
xa: **France (Fifth Republic, 1958)** + **Sri Lanka (1978 Constitution):** **directly elected President** with real powers + PM responsible to the legislature.
Parliamentary: **UK, Japan, Canada, India**; presidential: **Brazil**, most of Latin America.
⚠ **Westminster** = Britain; presidential origin = **USA**.

n1a6a23d5e60.s: France's Fifth Republic was established in:
xa: Semi-presidential examples: **France, Russia, Sri Lanka**.
In India the President is **de jure** head; PM + Council of Ministers = **de facto** executive.
India's President is **indirectly elected** for a **5-year term**; Britain's head is a **hereditary** monarch.

n4bbab1ab32e.s: Regarding the Prime Minister's position in India and Britain, which one of the following is correct?
o: The Prime Minister may be from either House in India, but must be from the House of Commons in Britain
The Prime Minister is directly elected in both countries
The Prime Minister must be from the upper House in India and the House of Lords in Britain
The Prime Minister must belong to the lower House in both countries
n4bbab1ab32e.x: In India, the Prime Minister may belong to either House of Parliament. In Britain, the Prime Minister is drawn from the House of Commons.
n4bbab1ab32e.tq: Focus on the precise membership rule rather than the general similarity of parliamentary government.
xs: In India the PM may come from **either House**; in Britain from the **House of Commons** — option **(1)** is correct.
The PM is **not directly elected** in India: the **leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha** becomes PM — (2) is wrong.
xa: Britain: ministers **must be MPs**; India allows **six months** as a non-member.
In both, the PM's role is so large that scholars call it **"Prime Ministerial Government"**.
UK: the **ruling party** can replace the PM; India: removal needs **loss of Lok Sabha confidence**.

nbace7c9d1f9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct regarding the Indian and British parliamentary systems?
o: The Indian Parliament is bound by a written Constitution and judicial review
Britain has a hereditary monarch as head of state
India has an elected head of state
The British Parliament is subject to the basic structure doctrine
nbace7c9d1f9.x: The basic structure doctrine belongs to the Indian constitutional framework and does not govern the British Parliament.
xa: British courts **cannot question Acts of Parliament**.
India's President has a **5-year term**.
Britain is **unitary**; India is **federal**.

n4c55d698727.s: In India, the residuary powers of legislation are vested in:
o: Both Parliament and the States concurrently
n4c55d698727.x: India vests residuary powers in Parliament, whereas the United States leaves the remaining powers to the States.
xa: India's three lists make for a **strong centre**.
Common to both: **written Constitution**, **federal structure**, **independent judiciary** with judicial review.
India: **parliamentary** executive; USA: **presidential**.

nb7b3417d9a4.s: Judicial review in India and in the USA is based, respectively, on:
o: Due process of law; procedure established by law
Procedure established by law; due process of law
Due process of law in both
Procedure established by law in both
nb7b3417d9a4.x: India follows the narrower 'procedure established by law', while the USA follows the wider 'due process of law' standard.
xa: Because of its wide review, the US Supreme Court is called a **"third chamber"**.
Both countries have an **independent judiciary with judicial review**.
Britain: courts **cannot question Acts of Parliament**.

n82255221a5f.s: In which year did the United States adopt the 22nd Amendment, associated with limiting presidential tenure?
n82255221a5f.x: The US adopted the 22nd Amendment in 1951; India has no term limit for its Prime Minister.
xa: He passed **Pawan Kumar Chamling** (**8,930** days).
A **fixed term** is a feature of the **presidential** executive.
**Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.

nc583603c290.s: Which of the following is a merit of the parliamentary system?
o: A fixed tenure for the executive
Continuous accountability of the executive to the legislature
nc583603c290.x: Continuous accountability of the executive to the legislature is a merit of the parliamentary system; fixed tenure is not its feature.
xa: Parliamentary demerits: **unstable coalitions**, ministers not always specialists, **cabinet dictatorship** when the majority is large.
Presidential merit: a **stable, fixed-term executive**.
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar**: India chose **responsibility** over guaranteed tenure.

n86e875a1583.s: Which of the following is a demerit of the presidential system?
o: Frequent fall of governments through no-confidence motions
n86e875a1583.x: Executive-legislature deadlock (and a personality cult around a single executive) are demerits of the presidential system; it has a fixed tenure.
xa: Avoiding **US-style executive-legislature conflict** was a reason the Constituent Assembly chose the parliamentary form.
The risk of a **personality cult** under a single executive was another reason.
Parliamentary demerit: **cabinet dictatorship** when the majority is large.

nb79acb240cd.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar's observation on democratic government, the choice made by India involved giving greater weight to:
o: Responsibility and continuous accountability over guaranteed tenure
nb79acb240cd.x: Dr B.R. Ambedkar observed that a democracy cannot maximise both stability and responsibility. India chose responsibility, meaning continuous accountability, over guaranteed tenure.
nb79acb240cd.tq: Distinguish the two competing values identified by Ambedkar and identify the one preferred by India.
xs: India chose **responsibility** — **continuous accountability** — **over guaranteed tenure** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Dr B.R. Ambedkar** held that a democracy cannot maximise **both stability and responsibility**.
Options (3) and (4) describe the **presidential** choice (fixed tenure, executive independence).
xa: **Vasant Sathe** made early proposals for a presidential system in the **1970s-80s**.
**NCRWC (Venkatachaliah, 2000-02)** advised keeping the **parliamentary system**.
Parliamentary merit: the executive is **continuously accountable** to the legislature.

n26e18fb20f4.s: Under Article 153 of the Constitution, which of the following is permissible?
o: A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States
A State may function without a Governor for an indefinite period
Only Union Territories can have a common Governor
A Governor may be elected jointly by two State Legislatures
n26e18fb20f4.x: Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State, while the Seventh Amendment Act, 1956 enables one person to serve as Governor of two or more States.
n26e18fb20f4.tq: Test the constitutional exception to the general rule instead of choosing the broad statement.
xs: **A single Governor may be appointed for two or more States** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 153** provides a Governor for each state; the **7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956** lets **one person be Governor of 2 or more states**.
The Governor is **neither directly nor indirectly elected** — he is appointed by the **President** (Art. 155), so option (4) is wrong.
xa: With a **common Governor**, the cost is **shared among the states** as the President decides.
**E.S.L. Narasimhan** was the common Governor for **AP and Telangana**, **2014 to July 2019**.
The 7th Amendment point was asked in **APPSC-GS 2025** and **2021**.

n0da450d9bf5.s: Which one of the following correctly states the constitutional position regarding the tenure of a Governor?
o: The Governor holds office for six years unless removed by the State Legislature.
The Governor holds office for five years and may continue until the successor enters office.
The Governor necessarily vacates office on completion of five years, even if no successor has entered office.
The Governor has a fixed tenure which cannot be interrupted by transfer.
n0da450d9bf5.x: The normal term is five years, but the Governor continues in office until the successor enters office. The Governor may also be transferred before completion of the term.
n0da450d9bf5.tq: Focus on the distinction between the normal term and automatic cessation of office.
xs: Normal term is **five years**, but the Governor **continues until his successor enters office** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (3) is the classic trap: "quits office immediately after the term expires" is **wrong** (**APPSC-G1 2019**).
He may be **transferred** and **reappointed**, so tenure is not fixed — (4) is wrong.
xa: **Art. 156:** holds office **during the pleasure of the President**.
**No grounds for removal** are stated in the Constitution; limits set by **B.P. Singhal (2010)**.
**Punchhi** Commission recommended a **fixed tenure** to insulate the Governor from the Centre.

n72ca9480c4b.s: The emoluments of a Governor are determined by:
n72ca9480c4b.x: Under Article 158, a Governor's emoluments are fixed by Parliament by law, not by the State Legislature.
xa: Emoluments **cannot be reduced** during the term.
A **common Governor's** cost is shared among states as the **President** decides.

n9203ebd3232.s: By convention, before a Governor is appointed, who is consulted?
o: The Chief Minister of the State
The Chief Justice of the High Court
n9203ebd3232.x: By convention the Governor is generally an outsider and the State's Chief Minister is consulted; the Constitution does not mandate this.
xa: **Sarkaria** recommended a politically neutral **outsider**, chosen **after consulting the CM**.
**First ARC**: persons of long experience in public life with a **non-partisan** attitude.
**NCRWC**: appointment by a committee of **PM, Union Home Minister, Lok Sabha Speaker and the state CM**.

n8ad26b65fbd.s: The qualifications of a Governor are laid down in Article:
n8ad26b65fbd.x: Article 157 deals with qualifications; 155 with appointment, 156 with tenure and 158 with conditions of office.
xa: **Art. 153:** a Governor for each state.
**Art. 159:** oath by the **Chief Justice of the High Court** (else senior-most judge).
**Art. 161:** **pardon**, reprieve, remission for offences under state law.

nd4d5d93cb78.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Governor's immunity under Article 361?
o: The Governor is not answerable to any court for official acts
The Governor cannot be arrested or imprisoned during the term of office
Civil proceedings concerning personal acts require two months' notice
Criminal proceedings can be instituted during the term with prior permission of the High Court
nd4d5d93cb78.x: No criminal proceedings can be instituted against the Governor during the term, even with a court's prior permission.
xa: These immunities are under **Art. 361**.
The Governor is also not answerable to the **state legislature** or **Council of Ministers**.

nb32fc5edd19.s: Under Article 174, not more than ____ may intervene between two sessions of a State Legislature.
nb32fc5edd19.x: Article 174 bars a gap of more than six months between two sessions.
xa: **Nabam Rebia (2016):** summoning, proroguing and dissolving are **not discretionary**; done on **aid and advice**.
He **nominates 1/6th** of the Legislative Council (**Art. 171**).

nbccd4fa86e5.s: If a Chief Minister loses majority in the Legislative Assembly, he:
o: Continues in office until the next general election
Can be removed only by impeachment
Must resign or may be dismissed
nbccd4fa86e5.x: A Chief Minister who loses majority must resign or may be dismissed; once a new Chief Minister is sworn in, the former ceases to hold office.
xa: Dismissing a ministry that has lost majority is **situational discretion**.
**West Bengal:** **Mamata Banerjee** refused to resign after losing (**5 May 2026**); the **Art. 164 "pleasure"** clause lets the Governor dismiss her.
**S.R. Bommai (1994):** majority to be tested **on the floor**.

n4a28104e450.s: Under the 91st Amendment Act, 2003, a State Council of Ministers including the CM cannot exceed what share of the Assembly's total strength?
n4a28104e450.x: The ceiling is 15% of the Legislative Assembly's total strength, with a minimum of 12 (Art. 164(1A)).
xa: ⚠ **91st** (2003) = **15%** cap and minimum **12**; **94th** (2006) = Bihar dropped from the tribal-minister list.

nc5d29b7cc16.s: According to the recommendations of the First Administrative Reforms Commission’s Centre-State study team, deployment of central armed forces in States could take place:
o: On the request of the States or otherwise
Only with the prior approval of the State Legislature
Only on the direction of the Inter-State Council
nc5d29b7cc16.x: The study team recommended deployment of central armed forces in States on their request or otherwise.
nc5d29b7cc16.tq: Focus on the qualifying phrase that distinguishes a conditional power from an exclusively State-initiated measure.
xs: **Central armed forces** could be deployed in States **on their request or otherwise** — option **(2)** is correct.
This was a recommendation of the **First ARC**'s study team on **Centre-State relations**.
xa: Other recommendations: **Inter-State Council under Art. 263**, maximum delegation, more **financial resources** for States.
The study team was headed by **Setalvad** (**1969**).
⚠ The **Rajamannar Committee** (**1969**) was a separate **TN Govt** body.

n165db570c87.s: The reported 2026 proposal for automatic removal of the Prime Minister, Chief Minister or a Minister concerns detention for
o: 30 consecutive days on charges carrying five or more years of imprisonment
60 consecutive days on charges carrying ten or more years of imprisonment
n165db570c87.x: The 130th Constitutional Amendment Bill proposes automatic removal after detention for 30 consecutive days on charges carrying a possible sentence of five or more years.
n165db570c87.tq: Match the exact duration and punishment threshold rather than combining figures from distractors.
xs: The **130th Constitutional Amendment Bill** proposes automatic removal after detention for **30 consecutive days** on charges carrying **5+ years** — option **(3)** is correct.
It covers the **PM, CM or a minister**.
xa: It amends **Arts 75, 164, 239AA**.
**Art. 164** governs the CM and state ministers.
A CM who loses majority must **resign or be dismissed**.

nindian-polity-10-1.s: Which of the following correctly describes the constitutional position of the Chief Minister in a State?
o: The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head
The Chief Minister is the nominal head, while the Governor is the real executive head
The Chief Minister and Governor are jointly the real executive heads
The Governor is the head of the Council of Ministers, while the Chief Minister is its nominal head
nindian-polity-10-1.x: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State and heads the Council of Ministers. The Governor is the nominal or constitutional head, like the President at the Centre.
nindian-polity-10-1.tq: Discriminate the nominal head from the real executive.
n: The Chief Minister is the real executive head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Governor is the nominal and constitutional head of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
The Chief Minister is the head of the State Council of Ministers. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 27-29]
xs: **The Chief Minister is the real executive head, while the Governor is the nominal or constitutional head** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The **CM** and **Council of Ministers** are the **real executive**; the CM **heads** the Council.
The Governor is the **nominal / constitutional head**, so options (2), (3), (4) misplace the roles.
xa: The CM is the **leader** of the majority in the **Legislative Assembly** and **chief spokesperson** of the State Government.
**Article 154**: executive power of the State is vested in the **Governor** — exercised on ministerial advice.
**Art. 167**: the CM is the **chief link** between Governor and Council.

n199b3d16168.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the State Council of Ministers?
o: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Chief Minister
A non-member may be a Minister but must become an MLA or MLC within six months
The Governor appoints the Chief Minister, normally the Assembly majority leader
Article 164 deals with the State Council of Ministers
n199b3d16168.x: State Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor, not the Chief Minister.
xa: Union parallel: ministers hold office at the **President's** pleasure, not the PM's.
**91st Amendment (2003)**: ministers ≤ **15%** of the Assembly; **minimum 12** (**Art. 164(1A)**).
A **Minister for Tribal Welfare** is mandatory in **Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha**; Bihar dropped by the **94th Amendment, 2006**.

n47c44ad14db.s: The Governor's special address at the first session after each general election and at the first session of each year is under Article:
n47c44ad14db.x: The special address under Article 176 is mandatory on both occasions and is delivered on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.
xa: ⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.
In **Jan 2026**, Governors walked out of or skipped the **Art. 176** address in Opposition-ruled states.
Under **Nabam Rebia**, the address must reflect **Cabinet policy**.

n0655efb9ede.s: When a Governor is appointed administrator of an adjoining Union Territory under Article 239(2), he acts:
o: On the aid and advice of his own State Council of Ministers
Independently of his own State Council of Ministers
Only on the advice of the State Legislature
Only with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court
n0655efb9ede.x: Under Article 239(2), the Governor administering an adjoining UT acts independently of his State's Council of Ministers; it is an express discretion. He is not bound by State ministers, the legislature or the High Court in this role.
n0655efb9ede.tq: Art. 239(2) = express discretion, independent of State ministry.
xs: Under **Art. 239(2)**, as administrator of an adjoining UT, the Governor acts **independently of his own state Council of Ministers** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is an **express discretion** (UPSC).
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 200** reservation, **Art. 356** report, **Art. 167** information.
The Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.
**Art. 163(2):** his decision on what is discretionary is **final**.

n7f52c3d1b43.s: A State Bill imposing restrictions on inter-State trade requires the previous sanction of the President before introduction under:
n7f52c3d1b43.x: Article 304(b) requires previous Presidential sanction before a Bill restricting inter-State trade is introduced. Article 288 concerns taxes on water/electricity in inter-State river projects, Article 254(2) Concurrent List repugnancy, and Article 31C property-related protection.
n7f52c3d1b43.tq: Inter-State trade restriction = Art. 304(b), prior sanction (PYQ 2018).
xs: **Article 304(b)** requires **previous sanction of the President** before introducing a bill restricting inter-state trade — option **(3)** is correct (PYQ **2018**).
**Art. 288** = taxes on water/electricity in inter-state river projects; **Art. 254(2)** = Concurrent-List repugnancy; **Art. 31C** = property acquisition.
xa: ⚠ **304(b)** = prior sanction, **not** reservation after passage.
Other protective reservations: money bills during a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
Such controls show the **Centre's control over state legislation**.

n39da7a624fe.s: During President's Rule, the State Legislative Assembly may be:
n39da7a624fe.x: During President's Rule the Assembly may be suspended or dissolved, while Parliament legislates for the State.
xa: **Bommai:** Assembly **not dissolved before Parliament approves**; ministry can be **restored**.
Example: the **Water Amendment Act** extended to **Manipur** (**Dec 2025**).

nf771f2c0d74.s: Parliamentary legislation for a State under President's Rule is enabled by which Article?
nf771f2c0d74.x: Article 357 provides for the exercise of legislative powers under a proclamation issued under Article 356.
nf771f2c0d74.tq: Match the emergency provision with the related legislative-power provision.
xs: **Article 357** lets **Parliament legislate** for a state under President's Rule — option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 164** concerns the CM and ministers; **Art. 153** a Governor for each state.
xa: Central laws reach the state only through an **Art 357(1)(a)** resolution.
Example: **Water Amendment Act**, extended to **Manipur** (**Dec 2025**).
The Assembly is **suspended or dissolved** during President's Rule.

n6365772f642.s: The Governor nominates what proportion of the members of the Legislative Council?
n6365772f642.x: Under Article 171, the Governor nominates one-sixth of the members of a State Legislative Council from persons having special knowledge or practical experience in specified fields.
n6365772f642.tq: Test the constitutional fraction directly against nearby Legislative Council proportions.
xs: The Governor **nominates one-sixth** (**1/6th**) of the Legislative Council — option **(2)** is correct.
This is under **Art. 171**.
xa: **Art. 174:** summons, prorogues and **dissolves** the Assembly.
⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.
He places reports of the **CAG**, **SPSC** and **State Finance Commission** before the legislature.

n4342052c672.s: In January 2026, Governors in Opposition-ruled States drew controversy by walking out of or skipping the mandatory address under:
n4342052c672.x: The controversy concerned the mandatory Governor's address under Article 176; under Nabam Rebia, the address must reflect Cabinet policy.
xa: **Art. 176:** special address at the first session after each general election + first session of each year.
⚠ **175** = optional; **176** = mandatory.
**Shamsher Singh (1974):** public criticism of Cabinet policy is an "**unconstitutional faux pas**".

n65eb6f3a506.s: In May 2026, after Mamata Banerjee refused to resign despite losing the election, which provision was cited as allowing the Governor to dismiss a Chief Minister who has lost majority?
n65eb6f3a506.x: Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure under Article 164, which allows dismissal of a CM who has lost majority. Article 356 is President's Rule, Article 163(3) bars inquiry into ministerial advice, and Article 361 grants the Governor immunity.
n65eb6f3a506.tq: CM who lost majority → Art. 164 pleasure.
xs: The **Art. 164 "pleasure" clause** lets the Governor dismiss a CM who has lost majority — option **(1)** is correct.
**Mamata Banerjee** refused to resign after losing (**5 May 2026**).
**Art. 356** is President's Rule, **Art. 163(3)** bars inquiry into advice, **Art. 361** gives immunity.
xa: Dismissing a ministry that has lost majority is **situational discretion**.
**Art. 164(1):** ministers hold office during the **Governor's pleasure**.
Once a new CM is sworn in, the old one **ceases**.

nindian-polity-45-20.s: Which Article provides for the State Council of Ministers aiding and advising the Governor?
nindian-polity-45-20.x: Article 163 provides for a State Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor, like Article 74 for the President. Article 164 deals with appointment of Ministers.
nindian-polity-45-20.tq: Discriminate the Union and State parallels: 74 with 163, 75 with 164.
n: The constitutional basis of the State Council of Ministers is Article 163. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The State Council of Ministers aids and advises the Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
The Council of Ministers is an executive body aiding and advising the President or Governor. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 120-123]
xs: **Article 163** provides for the State Council of Ministers to **aid and advise** the **Governor** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Article 74** is the Union counterpart (aid and advice to the **President**).
**Article 164** deals with **appointment** of the CM and ministers; **Article 171** relates to the **Legislative Council** (Governor nominates **one-sixth**).
xa: **Art. 163(2)**: the Governor's own decision on whether a matter is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
Collective responsibility: Union — **Article 75(3)** to the **Lok Sabha**; State — **Article 164(2)** to the **Legislative Assembly**.

nf236332fd23.s: Compared with the President, the constitutional discretion of the Governor is:
nf236332fd23.x: The Governor's discretion is wider than the President's; the Constitution confers no comparable general discretion on the President.
xa: Constitutional discretion: reserving a bill (**Art. 200**), **Art. 356** report, seeking information (**Art. 167**), adjoining UT (**Art. 239**).
Situational discretion: appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly**, dismissing a ministry that lost majority.

na53b34a49f5.s: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (1994), the Supreme Court held that a proclamation under Article 356 is
o: reviewable only after approval by the State Legislature
subject to judicial review, and the Union must disclose relevant material
beyond judicial review in all circumstances
reviewable only by the Governor of the concerned State
na53b34a49f5.x: The nine-judge Bench in S.R. Bommai held that an Article 356 proclamation is subject to judicial review and that the Centre must show relevant material supporting it.
na53b34a49f5.tq: Test the constitutional safeguard against an extreme claim of complete immunity from judicial review.
xs: **S.R. Bommai (1994)**: an **Art. 356** proclamation is **subject to judicial review** and the Centre **must show relevant material** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is not beyond review, and review is by **courts**, not the Governor.
xa: Majority tested by a **floor test**, not in **Raj Bhavan**.
Assembly **not dissolved before Parliament approves**; ministry can be **restored**.
**Secularism** is a basic feature; a government violating it can be dismissed.

n04aedda05be.s: The Governor of a State is the Chancellor of
o: the State universities, as provided by the applicable university laws
all Central universities located in that State
n04aedda05be.x: The Governor is also the Chancellor of State universities under the applicable State university laws. This role does not extend to all Central or private universities.
n04aedda05be.tq: Distinguish the Governor's State-level university role from Union-level higher-education institutions.
xs: The Governor is **Chancellor** of the **State universities** and appoints their **VCs** as Chancellor — option **(1)** is correct.
The role does not extend to **all Central** or **private** universities, or to the UGC.
xa: He does **not appoint HC judges** — the **President** does.
He appoints the **Advocate-General** (**Art. 165**) and **SPSC** members (**Art. 316**).
All executive action is taken in the Governor's name (**Art. 166**).

n092b44307b0.s: Which one of the following can the Governor of a State NOT do?
o: Appoint the Chairman of the State Public Service Commission
Remove a member of the State Public Service Commission
n092b44307b0.x: Although the Governor appoints SPSC members, only the President can remove them. The Governor does appoint the Advocate-General (Art. 165), the SPSC Chairman (Art. 316) and the State Election Commissioner (Art. 243K).
n092b44307b0.tq: Governor appoints SPSC, but only the President removes.
xs: The Governor **cannot remove a member of the State Public Service Commission** — only the **President** can — option **(3)**.
He does appoint the **Advocate-General** (**Art. 165**), the **SPSC** Chairman (**Art. 316**) and the **State Election Commissioner** (**Art. 243K**).
xa: ⚠ **SPSC**: Governor appoints (**316**), only the **President** removes.
He also does **not appoint HC judges**.
He **fixes the Advocate-General's pay**.

n00dd0a9b377.s: Which one of the following is associated with the Tamil Nadu Kurian Joseph Committee of 2026?
o: A proposal to replace Governors with elected Chief Ministers
A proposal for a new Schedule codifying the Governor’s discretion
A proposal to transfer all State finances to local bodies
n00dd0a9b377.x: The Kurian Joseph Committee was reported to have proposed a new Schedule to codify the Governor’s discretion.
n00dd0a9b377.tq: Match the committee with its specific institutional proposal.
xs: The **Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026)** proposes a **new Schedule** to **codify the Governor's discretion** — option **(2)** is correct.
It also revisits Rameshwar Prasad's **"cooling-off" period** before a politician becomes Governor.
xa: **Art. 163(2):** the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Discretion is subject to judicial review** (Rameshwar Prasad, Nabam Rebia).
Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

nindian-polity-74-4.s: The Governor's ordinance-making power is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-74-4.x: The Governor's ordinances are under Article 213 (State and Concurrent subjects); the President's under Article 123.
n: The ordinance-making power of the President is governed by Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The ordinance-making power of a State Governor is governed by Article 213. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The President can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
The Governor can promulgate ordinances on matters in the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #74 · pp 201-204]
xa: Both can be issued only when the legislature (or either House) is **not in session**.
Both **lapse six weeks** after the legislature **reassembles**, unless approved earlier.
The Governor needs **prior Presidential instructions** in **three** cases: Bills needing **prior sanction**, **reservation** or **Presidential assent**.

nindian-polity-11-18.s: The Governor's pardoning power, limited to offences against State laws, is under Article:
nindian-polity-11-18.x: The Governor pardons under Article 161 (State laws only); the President under Article 72 (all cases).
n: The President makes Ordinances under Article 123. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
The President has pardoning power under Article 72 in all cases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xa: Governor's pardoning covers **pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions**, and he may **suspend** or **commute** sentences.
**Perarivalan (2022)**: the Governor is **bound by Cabinet advice** on pardon/remission under **Art. 161**.
President's discretion is **very limited**; the Governor's is **comparatively more**.

n32d847d20a6.s: Which of the following is a constitutional or express discretionary power of the Governor?
o: Dissolving the Assembly after a ministry loses its majority
Dismissing a ministry that has lost its majority
Reserving a Bill for the consideration of the President
Appointing a Chief Minister in a hung Assembly
n32d847d20a6.x: Reserving a Bill for the President under Article 200 is an express constitutional discretion. The other options describe situational discretion.
n32d847d20a6.tq: Distinguish express constitutional discretion from discretion arising out of political circumstances.
xs: **Reserving a Bill for the President** (**Art. 200**) is a **constitutional (express) discretion** — option **(3)** is correct.
Dissolving the Assembly or dismissing a ministry after loss of majority, and appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly**, are **situational** discretion.
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 356** report, **Art. 167** information, **Art. 239** adjoining UT.
⚠ **Hung Assembly** = situational; **Art. 200** reservation = constitutional.
Reservation is **an example of central control over states** (**APPSC 2025** key).

n8d50ca5d235.s: Which one of the following is the correct constitutional method for determining whether a State ministry enjoys majority support?
o: Assessment by the Governor in Raj Bhavan
A report of the State Election Commission
A floor test in the Legislative Assembly
n8d50ca5d235.x: S.R. Bommai established that majority must ordinarily be tested on the floor of the House, not in Raj Bhavan.
n8d50ca5d235.tq: Ask who should perform the majority test instead of accepting the Governor's personal assessment.
xs: Majority is tested by a **floor test in the Legislative Assembly** — option **(3)** is correct.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: **on the floor**, **not in Raj Bhavan**.
xa: **Sarkaria** recommended a mandatory **floor test**.
In a hung Assembly, an **early floor test** follows the invitation.
**Tamil Nadu (May 2026):** **C. Joseph Vijay** invited with an early floor test.

n91d0a761e29.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a State Bill reserved for the President under Article 201?
o: A returned Bill must be reconsidered by the State Legislature within six months
Article 201 prescribes no fixed time limit for the President's decision
The President is not bound to assent even after the Bill is passed again
The President may direct the Governor to return even a Money Bill for reconsideration
n91d0a761e29.x: Only a non-Money Bill can be returned to the State Legislature for reconsideration.
xa: **No time limit** is prescribed for the President (**Apr 2025**: assent withheld to TN's **anti-NEET Bill**).
Nov 2025 Reference: the President **need not seek SC advice** on each reserved bill.
Under **Art. 200**, a re-passed bill must get the **Governor's** assent.

n5bbf6914e7c.s: Under Article 200 of the Constitution, which one of the following is NOT an option available to the Governor in respect of a Bill passed by the State Legislature?
o: To withhold assent to the Bill
To reserve the Bill for the consideration of the President
To return a Money Bill for reconsideration
n5bbf6914e7c.x: The Governor may return a Bill for reconsideration only if it is not a Money Bill. The other three are options available under Article 200.
n5bbf6914e7c.tq: Identify the exception by applying the special constitutional rule for Money Bills.
xs: The Governor **cannot return a Money Bill** for reconsideration — option **(4)** is correct.
**Art. 200** gives four options: **assent**, **withhold**, **return** once (not a Money Bill), or **reserve** for the President.
xa: A **re-passed** bill must get the Governor's **assent**.
Mandatory reservation: a bill **derogating from the powers of the High Court**.
Nov 2025 Reference: Governor **not bound by advice** in choosing among Art. 200 options.

n6e43a5e1ae8.s: When a Bill returned by the Governor is passed again by the State Legislature, which one of the following is constitutionally correct?
o: The Governor must assent to the Bill and cannot withhold assent again.
The Bill automatically becomes law without any further action.
The Bill must necessarily be reserved for the President.
The Governor may withhold assent again at his discretion.
n6e43a5e1ae8.x: If the Legislature re-passes a Bill that was returned for reconsideration, the Governor must assent to it and cannot withhold assent again.
n6e43a5e1ae8.tq: Test the effect of re-passage rather than the Governor's initial alternatives.
xs: If a returned bill is re-passed, the Governor **must assent** and **cannot withhold assent again** — option **(1)** is correct (**APPCA 2026**).
**Punjab (2023)** also held **a re-passed bill must get assent**.
xa: A bill may be **reserved only once**; a re-enacted bill cannot be reserved again unless **materially altered**.
**TN v. Governor (8 April 2025):** **1 month** for assent after re-passage.
⚠ The Nov 2025 **Art. 143** opinion rejected **deemed assent** and court-imposed timelines.

n8dcee2f54d7.s: Reservation by the Governor for the President is mandatory for a Bill that:
o: Derogates from the powers of the High Court
n8dcee2f54d7.x: A Bill derogating from the High Court's powers must be reserved; not every Bill affecting State finances needs mandatory reservation.
xa: Money bills during a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)** may be reserved.
**Art. 304(b):** **previous sanction** of the President for bills restricting inter-state trade (PYQ **2018**).

nindian-polity-11-16.s: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with which of the following?
nindian-polity-11-16.x: Under Article 233, the Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court.
n: The Governor appoints District Judges in consultation with the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 29-32]
xs: The Governor appoints **District Judges** in consultation with **the High Court** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **State PSC** chair and members are themselves appointed by the Governor (**316**); the **State Election Commissioner** is also his appointee.
The **Chief Minister** advises on appointing **ministers**, not district judges.
xa: The Governor does **not** appoint **HC judges** — the **President** does.
He **cannot remove** SPSC members — only the **President** can.
He appoints the **Advocate-General** (**165**) and acts as **Chancellor** of state universities.

n70f1be5ef4a.s: Under Article 163(1) of the Constitution, the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister aids and advises the Governor
o: Except in matters where the Governor is required to act in his discretion
Only when the Legislative Assembly is in session
n70f1be5ef4a.x: Article 163(1) provides for aid and advice by the Council of Ministers except where the Governor is required to exercise discretion.
n70f1be5ef4a.tq: Test the constitutional exception rather than the general rule.
xs: Under **Art. 163(1)**, the Council of Ministers headed by the CM advises the Governor **except where he must act in his discretion** — option **(1)** is correct.
So aid and advice is not "in all matters without exception" — (3) is wrong.
xa: **Art. 163(2):** the Governor's decision on what is discretionary is **final**.
**Art. 163(3):** ministers' advice **cannot be inquired into in any court**.
The Governor's discretion is **wider than the President's**.

n43434021f2d.s: Which provision bars courts from inquiring into the advice tendered by Ministers to the Governor?
n43434021f2d.x: Article 163(3) bars courts from inquiring into ministers' advice; Article 163(2) makes the Governor's decision on discretion final.
xa: Even so, **discretion is subject to judicial review** (Rameshwar Prasad, Nabam Rebia).
**Nabam Rebia (2016):** **no general discretion** for the Governor.
**Art. 167:** the CM must **communicate** Cabinet decisions to the Governor.

nf37df593ac1.s: The Governor's special responsibility for law and order in Arunachal Pradesh is provided under Article:
nf37df593ac1.x: Article 371H gives the Governor of Arunachal Pradesh law and order responsibility; Article 371A does so for Nagaland.
xa: Other express discretion: **Art. 200**, **Art. 356**, **Art. 167**, **Art. 239**.
**AP Reorganisation Act 2014 (Sec. 8):** special responsibility for **law and order** and government buildings, mainly in **Hyderabad**.
That Sec. 8 role lapsed on **2 June 2024**.

n5a06b250359.s: The Supreme Court's decision in State of Punjab v. Principal Secretary to Governor (2023) held that the Governor:
o: Could reserve every State Bill for the President without giving reasons
Could keep Bills pending indefinitely if no time limit was expressly stated
Must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely
Could reject a Bill permanently after returning it once
n5a06b250359.x: The 2023 Punjab case held that the Governor must act as soon as possible and cannot keep Bills pending indefinitely. It also affirmed the consequence of re-passage of a returned Bill.
n5a06b250359.tq: Test the operative judicial direction using the precise phrase “as soon as possible”.
xs: **Punjab (2023)**: the Governor **must act "as soon as possible"** and **cannot keep bills pending indefinitely** — option **(3)** is correct.
It also held that **a re-passed bill must get assent**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: **TN v. Governor (8 April 2025)** went further and read **time limits** into **Art. 200**.
The **Nov 2025** Reference: no court-imposed timelines, but prolonged inaction invites **limited mandamus**.
**Longest delays:** **Kerala** and TN.

n1a60d261b98.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion?
o: The President need not seek the Supreme Court's advice on each reserved Bill
Judicial review is limited to issues such as mala fides and procedure
Courts may impose a fixed deadline for every Bill pending before a Governor
n1a60d261b98.x: The opinion rejected court-imposed timelines, permitting only limited intervention in cases of prolonged unexplained inaction.
xa: Prolonged, unexplained inaction → **limited mandamus**.
The Governor was called the "**guide, philosopher and friend**" of the government.
The **April 2025** timelines and deemed assent **do not survive** this opinion.

n0181964c642.s: In the context of the 16th Presidential Reference, the Governor was described as the:
o: Permanent representative of the Union Cabinet in the State
Final constitutional sovereign of the State
Judicial guardian of the State Legislature
Guide, philosopher and friend of the government
n0181964c642.x: The November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion described the Governor as a “guide, philosopher and friend” of the government.
n0181964c642.tq: Direct recall of the distinctive constitutional phrase used in the opinion.
xs: The **Nov 2025** Reference called the Governor the "**guide, philosopher and friend**" of the government — option **(4)** is correct.
The same opinion held the Governor **not bound by advice** in choosing among the **Art. 200** options.
xa: It was the **16th Presidential Reference** under **Art. 143**, a **5-judge** bench.
It rejected **deemed assent** and **court-imposed timelines**.
Inaction can still attract a **limited mandamus**.

n1e1ab18e63c.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes the Presidential Reference opinion of November 2025 from the ruling in State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu dated 8 April 2025?
o: The ruling concerned Article 248, whereas the Reference concerned Article 254.
The Reference rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent, whereas the ruling prescribed timelines including deemed assent.
The Reference accepted deemed assent, whereas the ruling rejected it.
Both decisions prescribed identical rigid deadlines.
n1e1ab18e63c.x: The 8 April 2025 ruling prescribed timelines and recognised deemed assent, while the November 2025 Presidential Reference opinion rejected rigid deadlines and deemed assent.
n1e1ab18e63c.tq: Discriminate between two closely dated decisions by comparing their holdings.
xs: The **Nov 2025 Reference** rejected rigid deadlines and **deemed assent**, while the **8 April 2025** ruling prescribed **timelines** including deemed assent — option **(2)** is correct.
The ruling set **1 month** (withheld on advice), **3 months** (against advice), **1 month** after re-passage.
xa: ⚠ **Art 142** = deemed assent granted (Apr 2025); **Art 143** Reference = deemed assent rejected (Nov 2025).
⚠ Some notes (**APPCA 2026**) date the TN case to **2023** and treat deemed assent as good law.
The Reference allowed only a **limited mandamus** for prolonged inaction.

n6124cda372e.s: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu, decided on 8 April 2025, which timeline was associated with the Governor's action on Bills?
o: Two months, three months and two months on re-passage
Three months, six months and three months on re-passage
One month, three months and one month on re-passage
One month, six months and one month on re-passage
n6124cda372e.x: The ruling referred to timelines of one month, three months and one month on re-passage, along with the concept of deemed assent.
n6124cda372e.tq: Retain the three-part timeline as a numerical sequence rather than relying on general impressions.
xs: **TN v. Governor (8 April 2025)**: **one month** if withheld on advice, **three months** against advice, **one month** after re-passage — option **(3)** is correct.
The Court **read time limits into Art. 200**.
xa: It granted **"deemed assent"** to **10 bills** using **Art 142**.
**NCRWC 2002** had suggested assent within about **4 months**.
These timelines **do not survive** the **Nov 2025** Reference opinion.

ne74da67d57b.s: In State of Tamil Nadu v. Governor of Tamil Nadu (April 2025), the Supreme Court held that the referral of ten re-enacted Bills to the President was:
o: Valid because the Governor has absolute discretion under Article 200
Invalid only because the Bills were Money Bills
Unconstitutional, and the Court declared the Bills assented to by invoking Article 142
Valid because a re-enacted Bill must always be reserved for the President
ne74da67d57b.x: The Supreme Court held that the referral of the ten re-enacted Bills was unconstitutional and used Article 142 to declare them assented to.
ne74da67d57b.tq: Link the case with its number of Bills, constitutional conclusion and remedy.
xs: Referring **10 re-enacted bills** was **unconstitutional**, and the Court **declared them assented** using **Art 142** — option **(3)** is correct.
A bill may be **reserved only once**; a re-enacted bill cannot be reserved again unless **materially altered**.
xa: A re-passed bill must get the Governor's **assent**; he **cannot withhold** again.
⚠ The **Nov 2025** **Art 143** Reference held **deemed assent** unconstitutional.
The judgment was dated **8 April 2025**.

n5748ee23c88.s: Under Section 8 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014, the Governor was given special responsibility mainly in relation to which area?
o: Law and order and allocation of government buildings in Hyderabad
Conduct of elections to all local bodies in both States
Appointment of judges to the Telangana High Court
n5748ee23c88.x: Section 8 assigned special responsibility to the Governor for law and order and allocation of government buildings, mainly in Hyderabad as the common capital.
n5748ee23c88.tq: Identify the specific statutory responsibilities instead of broad constitutional powers.
xs: **Sec. 8** of the **AP Reorganisation Act 2014** gave the Governor special responsibility for **law and order and allocation of government buildings**, mainly in **Hyderabad** — option **(2)** is correct.
Hyderabad was the **common capital**.
xa: It lapsed when the **10-year** common-capital period ended on **2 June 2024**.
The common Governor then was **E.S.L. Narasimhan** (**2014 to July 2019**).
Compare special responsibilities under **Art. 371A** (Nagaland) and **371H** (Arunachal).

nb0498cbb2eb.s: The special responsibility assigned to the Governor under Section 8 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 ceased with the expiry of the common-capital period on:
nb0498cbb2eb.x: The ten-year common-capital period ended on 2 June 2024, after which the special responsibility under Section 8 lapsed.
nb0498cbb2eb.tq: Distinguish the statutory ten-year endpoint from the dates of gubernatorial appointments.
xs: The **10-year** common-capital period ended on **2 June 2024**, and **Sec. 8** lapsed — option **(1)** is correct.
**17 August 2026** is the Monsoon Session date, not a lapse date.
xa: Sec. 8 covered **law and order** and **government buildings** in **Hyderabad**.
**N. Chandrababu Naidu** became CM again from **June 2024**.
**S. Abdul Nazeer** is Governor from **Feb 2023**.

nd642996f408.s: The Supreme Court's decision in B.P. Singhal v. Union of India (2010) established that
o: the Governor's office is completely independent of the President's pleasure
a Governor cannot be removed arbitrarily or merely because the Centre's Government has changed
a Governor can be removed only after impeachment by Parliament
a Governor can be removed whenever the Union Government changes
nd642996f408.x: The pleasure doctrine is not unfettered: removal cannot be arbitrary or based merely on a change in the Government at the Centre. Such removal is open to limited judicial review.
nd642996f408.tq: Use the case-law principle to reject both absolute executive power and the invented impeachment procedure.
xs: **B.P. Singhal (2010)**: a Governor **cannot be removed arbitrarily** or **merely because the Centre's government changes** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **pleasure doctrine is not unfettered**, so (1) and (4) are wrong; there is **no impeachment** route, so (3) is wrong.
xa: Reasons for removal **need not be given**, but removal must not be **arbitrary**.
Being **out of tune with the Centre** is not a ground; **limited judicial review** applies.
The Constitution states **no grounds for removal** of a Governor.

n5d8671a88f2.s: According to the November 2025 opinion in the 16th Presidential Reference, the Governor, while choosing among the options under Article 200, is:
o: Required to refer every Bill to the Supreme Court
Bound in every case by the advice of the State Council of Ministers
Not bound by such advice in choosing among the Article 200 options
Required to follow the advice of the President alone
n5d8671a88f2.x: The Presidential Reference opinion stated that the Governor is not bound by the advice of the State Council of Ministers while choosing among the options available under Article 200.
n5d8671a88f2.tq: Test the distinction between constitutional discretion under Article 200 and ordinary aid-and-advice situations.
xs: The Governor is **not bound by advice** in choosing among the **Art. 200** options — option **(3)** is correct.
No reference to the **Supreme Court** is required; the President **need not seek SC advice** on each reserved bill either.
xa: Art. 200 options: **assent**, **withhold**, **return** once (not a Money Bill), **reserve**.
Courts **cannot fix timelines** or declare **deemed assent**.
Contrast: **Perarivalan (2022)** held the Governor bound by Cabinet advice on **pardon** under **Art. 161**.

n89236b60992.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that summoning, proroguing and dissolving the Assembly under Article 174 are not discretionary powers of the Governor?
n89236b60992.x: Nabam Rebia held these powers and the address under Articles 175–176 are exercised on aid and advice, rejecting a general discretion.
xa: Under Nabam Rebia, the **Art. 176** address must reflect **Cabinet policy**.
In **Jan 2026**, Governors walked out of or skipped the **Art. 176** address in Opposition-ruled states.
⚠ **175** = optional address; **176** = mandatory special address.

n59325ba57f6.s: The judgment that reaffirmed that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice regarding pardon or remission under Article 161 is:
n59325ba57f6.x: The Perarivalan judgment of 2022 held that the Governor is bound by Cabinet advice on pardon or remission under Article 161; this position was reaffirmed subsequently.
n59325ba57f6.tq: Use the subject of the power—pardon or remission—to identify the relevant case.
xs: **Perarivalan (2022)** held the Governor bound by **Cabinet advice** on **pardon/remission** under **Art. 161** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was **reaffirmed in 2026**.
**Rameshwar Prasad** concerns Assembly dissolution; **Bommai** the floor test; **Nabam Rebia** summoning the House.
xa: **Art. 161:** **pardon**, reprieve, remission for offences under **state law**.
**Shamsher Singh (1974)** first held the Governor bound by **aid and advice**.

n6b5fe203c7f.s: Which case rejected the dissolution of an Assembly based on unproven fears of horse-trading?
n6b5fe203c7f.x: Rameshwar Prasad (2006) rejected dissolution on unproven fears of horse-trading.
xa: Rameshwar Prasad struck down the **Bihar** Assembly dissolution.
**Perarivalan (2022):** bound by advice on **pardon** under **Art. 161**.
**Bommai (1994):** majority tested **on the floor**.

nafdb25d8ee9.s: After the Ayodhya events of December 1992, BJP governments of Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and ____ were dismissed.
nafdb25d8ee9.x: The BJP governments of UP, MP, Rajasthan and Himachal Pradesh were removed; Bommai upheld the dismissals of MP, Rajasthan and HP.
xa: **Bommai:** **secularism** is a basic feature; a government violating it can be dismissed.
Bommai also held proclamations **judicially reviewable**.
Majority to be tested by a **floor test**, not in Raj Bhavan.

n1d3be7bd60f.s: Rameshwar Prasad referred to the Sarkaria Commission in connection with which issue?
o: Misuse of reports under Article 356 and a cooling-off period before politicians become Governors
The procedure for electing the Governor
The Governor's power to appoint judges of the High Court
The distribution of royalty under the Sixth Schedule
n1d3be7bd60f.x: Rameshwar Prasad cited Sarkaria regarding misuse of Article 356 reports and urged a cooling-off period before politicians are appointed as Governors.
n1d3be7bd60f.tq: Link the later judicial observation to the precise commission recommendation or concern it invoked.
xs: **Rameshwar Prasad** cited **Sarkaria** on **misuse of Art. 356 reports** and urged a **cooling-off period** before politicians become Governors — option **(1)** is correct.
The Governor is **appointed**, not elected; HC judges are appointed by the **President**, not the Governor.
xa: **Rameshwar Prasad (2006)** struck down the **Bihar Assembly dissolution**.
The **Kurian Joseph Committee (TN, 2026)** is revisiting the **"cooling-off" period**.
**Sarkaria:** the Governor should **not be a recent active politician**.

n62958ecacee.s: A Governor holds office during the pleasure of the:
n62958ecacee.x: Article 156 incorporates the President's pleasure, though B.P. Singhal held it cannot be exercised arbitrarily.
xa: Reasons for removal **need not be given**; limited **judicial review** applies.
A change of government at the **Centre** is not, by itself, a ground.
**Punchhi** urged a **fixed tenure** for Governors.

n986d6791b7e.s: The CAG's report relating to a State is placed before the State Legislature by the:
n986d6791b7e.x: The Governor places the CAG report on the State, along with the State PSC and State Finance Commission reports, before the Legislature.
xa: He appoints the **State Election Commissioner** and constitutes the **State Finance Commission** (**243K, 243I**).
He appoints the **SPSC** chair and members (**316**); only the **President** removes them.
He **nominates 1/6th** of the Legislative Council.

n9315a4c3060.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the ordinance-making powers of the Governor and the President?
o: The Governor's ordinance power extends to the State and Concurrent Lists
The Governor may promulgate an ordinance when the State Legislature is not in session
Ordinances cease six weeks after the Legislature or Parliament reassembles
The President's ordinance power extends only to the Union List
n9315a4c3060.x: The President's ordinance power is co-extensive with Parliament's legislative power, including the Concurrent List.
xa: The Governor needs **President's instructions** where the bill would need prior sanction or reservation; the President needs none.
**Art. 161:** Governor's **pardon** power for offences under state law.
**Art. 174:** max **6 months** between sessions.

nf92413064d2.s: In a hung State Assembly, the Sarkaria and Punchhi approach gives first preference for forming the government to:
o: A post-poll alliance with outside support
nf92413064d2.x: The order is pre-poll alliance, largest party with support, post-poll coalition, then post-poll alliance with outside support.
xa: Appointing a CM in a **hung Assembly** is **situational discretion**.
**Tamil Nadu (May 2026):** **TVK** won **108** seats (10 short); Governor invited **C. Joseph Vijay** on **120** letters of support.
**Sarkaria** made the **floor test** mandatory.

nc5860f14226.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Article 201?
o: Even after reconsideration, the President is not bound to assent
The President may direct the Governor to return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration
The President may withhold assent to a Bill reserved by the Governor
The Constitution fixes a period within which the President must decide every reserved Bill
nc5860f14226.x: Article 201 prescribes no fixed time limit for the President's decision on a reserved Bill.
xa: This gives the President an **absolute veto** over reserved bills.
**Apr 2025:** the President withheld assent to Tamil Nadu's **anti-NEET Bill**.
The legislature must reconsider a returned bill within **6 months**.

n6f1a51a86fb.s: The maximum period for which President's Rule can ordinarily continue is:
n6f1a51a86fb.x: President's Rule continues six months at a time with parliamentary approval, up to a maximum of three years.
xa: The **44th Amendment** set the conditions for going **beyond 1 year**: a **National Emergency** + an **EC** certificate.
**Punjab** was also the **first** state under President's Rule, in **1951**.
Parliament legislates for the state under **Art 357**.

n34bbfc53d32.s: To extend President's Rule beyond one year, a National Emergency must be in operation and elections must be certified as impossible by the:
n34bbfc53d32.x: Beyond one year, a National Emergency must be in force and the Election Commission must certify that elections cannot be held.
xa: Maximum duration: **3 years**, in spells of **6 months**.
The **68th Amendment** stretched Punjab's **1987** proclamation to **5 years**.
**Punchhi** suggested a **localised emergency** (a district, up to **3 months**).

n2dfafe3e926.s: President's Rule under Article 356 was first imposed in 1951 in:
n2dfafe3e926.x: President's Rule was first imposed in Punjab in 1951; Kerala (1959) saw the first dismissal of an elected government.
xa: ⚠ **Punjab** = first use (**1951**); **Kerala** = first dismissal (**1959**).
Art. 356 has been used **over 125 times**; most often in **Manipur** — **2025** was its **11th** time.
Manipur's spell from **13 Feb 2025** was **revoked on 4 Feb 2026**; **Y. Khemchand Singh** became CM.
AP instance: **Andhra State** had President's Rule in **1954-55**.

n5d8c597b38d.s: The latest spell of President's Rule in Manipur began on:
n5d8c597b38d.x: The latest spell began on 13 February 2025 (Manipur's 11th) and was revoked on 4 February 2026.
xa: Manipur was the **APPSC 2024** key for **Art 356**.
President's Rule overall: used **over 125 times**.

n51793dfb32e.s: Under the former Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, Governor’s Rule could continue for a maximum period of
o: 6 months under Section 92 of the J&K Constitution
n51793dfb32e.x: In the former Jammu and Kashmir constitutional arrangement, Governor’s Rule was imposed under Section 92 of the J&K Constitution for six months, after which Article 356 could apply.
n51793dfb32e.tq: Discriminate between the special provision, its duration and the later Article 356 stage.
xs: In former J&K, **Governor's Rule** ran **6 months** under **Sec 92 of the J&K Constitution**, then **Art 356** — option **(2)** is correct.
Example: **2018**.
