n5b6edbaa785.tq: Distinguish the enabling Act from the year in which revival actually occurred.
xs: Revival in **2007** came under the **AP Legislative Council Act, 2005** — option **(3)**.
⚠ Trap: the Act is of **2005**; the revival took effect in **2007**.
The **2014** Reorganisation Act and **104th Amendment (2020)** are unrelated to the revival.
xa: Abolished in **1985** (NTR); created in **1958**.
**2015** amendment: raised to **58**.

nda20091d8f4.s: The Repeal Act of November 2021 relating to the three-capitals law resulted in:
o: designation of Visakhapatnam as the sole capital
withdrawal of the three-capitals and CRDA repeal, with Amaravati restored
designation of Kurnool as the sole capital
nda20091d8f4.x: The November 2021 Repeal Act withdrew the three-capitals law and the CRDA repeal, thereby restoring Amaravati.
nda20091d8f4.tq: Use the reversal trap: identify the legal effect of the repeal rather than the original three-capitals proposal.
xs: It **withdrew the three-capitals law and the CRDA repeal**, restoring **Amaravati** — option **(3)**.
No single capital at **Visakhapatnam** or **Kurnool** resulted.
xa: Same month (**Nov 2021**): the Council-abolition resolution was **withdrawn**.
Assembly sits at **Velagapudi** (Amaravati) since **2017**.

n51bff8fe423.s: Who is the present Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
n51bff8fe423.x: Ch. Ayyanna Patrudu is the present Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly.
n51bff8fe423.tq: Use the current office-holder carefully and distinguish it from the first woman Speaker.
xs: **Ch. Ayyanna Patrudu** is the present Speaker — option **(3)**.
**K. Pratibha Bharati** was the **first woman Speaker**, not the present one.
xa: Present **Deputy Speaker (2026)**: **K. Raghu Ramakrishna Raju**.
**Kodela Siva Prasada Rao**: first Speaker of residual AP (**2014-19**); **Tammineni Sitaram**: **2019-24**.
First Speaker (**1956**): **Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao**.

n6392160b4c5.s: Who was the first Leader of Opposition in the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
n6392160b4c5.x: Puchalapalli Sundarayya was the first Leader of Opposition; Kaleswara Rao was the first Speaker and Madapati Hanumantha Rao the first Council Chairman.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Kaleswara Rao** / **Kalluri Subbarao** / **Madapati Hanumantha Rao** = Speaker / Deputy / Council Chairman.
First woman Speaker: **K. Pratibha Bharati**.

nb91d91d1c61.s: Who was the first woman Speaker of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
nb91d91d1c61.x: K. Pratibha Bharati was the first woman Speaker of the AP Assembly. Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the first Speaker (1956), Kodela Siva Prasada Rao the first Speaker of residual AP (2014-19), and Ch. Ayyanna Patrudu is the present Speaker.
nb91d91d1c61.tq: First Speaker = Kaleswara Rao; first woman Speaker = Pratibha Bharati.
xs: **K. Pratibha Bharati** was the **first woman Speaker** — option **(1)** (APPSC-GS **2019** key).
**Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao** was the first Speaker (**1956**); **Kodela** first of residual AP; **Ayyanna Patrudu** is present.
xa: First Council Chairman: **Madapati Hanumantha Rao**.
First Leader of Opposition: **Puchalapalli Sundarayya**.

nfb8bd033837.s: After bifurcation, under Section 25 of the AP Reorganisation Act, the Chairman of the united AP Legislative Council:
o: Became Deputy Chairman of the AP Council
Continued as Chairman of the AP Council
Was replaced through a fresh election
nfb8bd033837.x: The Chairman continued as Chairman of the AP Council, while the Deputy Chairman went to Telangana's Council.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **Sec. 21** sends the **Deputy Speaker**, **Sec. 25** the **Deputy Chairman**, to Telangana.
**Sec. 22**: Councils — AP **50** (now **58**), Telangana **40**.
First Council Chairman: **Madapati Hanumantha Rao**.

na2411345a7d.s: How many seats in the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly are reserved for the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes respectively?
na2411345a7d.x: The Andhra Pradesh Assembly has 29 seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and 7 seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes.
na2411345a7d.tq: Test paired figures in the same order as stated, avoiding reversal of the categories.
xs: AP reserves **29 SC** and **7 ST** seats — option **(2)**.
So the other pairs (**29/9**, **30/7**, **28/8**) misstate one or both figures.
xa: Total elected strength: **175** (**Sec. 17**).
Anglo-Indian nomination ended with the **104th Amendment (2020)**.
Constituencies follow the **Delimitation Order 2008**.

n8c10d3f38f8.s: The nomination of an Anglo-Indian member to the Legislative Assembly under Article 333 and Section 18 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act ended with the:
n8c10d3f38f8.x: The Anglo-Indian nomination provision under Article 333 ended with the 104th Constitutional Amendment in 2020.
n8c10d3f38f8.tq: Use the amendment-number trap by distinguishing the constitutional change from nearby amendment numbers.
xs: It ended with the **104th Constitutional Amendment** (**2020**) — option **(2)**.
The nomination was under **Sec. 18** of the AP Reorganisation Act and **Art. 333**.
xa: **Sec. 18** gave **one Anglo-Indian nominee each** to AP and Telangana — now **lapsed**.
**Sec. 19**: sitting MLAs continue for their allotted constituencies.

n4142145e3ba.s: Why did the YSRCP not obtain official Opposition status in the 16th Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly?
o: It declined to claim the position.
It did not win any reserved seat.
It won fewer than one-tenth of the total Assembly seats.
n4142145e3ba.x: The YSRCP won 11 of the 175 seats, which was below the one-tenth threshold required for official Opposition status.
n4142145e3ba.tq: Apply the numerical threshold to the election result rather than relying on the party's name or vote share.
xs: The YSRCP won **11**, **fewer than one-tenth** of the **175** seats — option **(4)**.
**One-tenth** of the House is needed for **official Opposition** status.
xa: PAC chair goes to the **Opposition** by convention.
First Leader of Opposition: **Puchalapalli Sundarayya**.

n4978208a864.s: Which Section of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 relates to orders on Legislative Council constituencies?
n4978208a864.x: Section 24 concerns Council constituencies; Section 18 provided an Anglo-Indian nominee and Section 20 the five-year term.
xa: Anglo-Indian nomination ended with the **104th Amendment (2020)**.

n0f8b440a47a.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the composition of the 58-member Andhra Pradesh Legislative Council?
o: Local authorities 20, MLAs 20, graduates 5, teachers 5, Governor's nominees 8
Local authorities 18, MLAs 20, graduates 6, teachers 6, Governor's nominees 8
Local authorities 20, MLAs 18, graduates 8, teachers 5, Governor's nominees 7
Local authorities 22, MLAs 18, graduates 5, teachers 5, Governor's nominees 8
n0f8b440a47a.x: The Council comprises 20 members elected by local authorities, 20 elected by MLAs, 5 by graduates, 5 by teachers and 8 nominated by the Governor.
n0f8b440a47a.tq: Start from the sure pair and verify that all component figures add up to the total.
xs: **Local authorities 20, MLAs 20, graduates 5, teachers 5, Governor's nominees 8** — option **(1)**.
These follow the **Art. 171** fractions for a **58**-member Council.
xa: Governor's **8** nominees came under the **2015** amendment (APPSC-GS **2018**).
⚠ The printed key "**78**" is garbled.
Original cap under **Sec. 22(1)**: **50**.

ne0e8a491185.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the proposed increase in Assembly seats under Section 26 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014?
o: The proposed strength for Telangana is 153
The increase is subject to Article 170
The proposed strength for Andhra Pradesh is 225
The increase has already been implemented
ne0e8a491185.x: Section 26 contemplates 225 seats for AP and 153 for Telangana subject to Article 170, but the increase has not yet been implemented.
xa: An earlier increase needs a **constitutional amendment**.
**131st Amendment Bill, 2026** was **negatived** in the Lok Sabha (Apr **2026**).

ne8b25625f30.s: Article 170(3) of the Constitution freezes the number of Assembly seats until:
ne8b25625f30.x: Article 170(3) freezes Assembly numbers until the first Census after 2026. An earlier increase would require a constitutional amendment.
ne8b25625f30.tq: Focus on the exact constitutional time reference.
xs: **Art. 170(3)** freezes seats until the **first census after 2026** — option **(1)**.
An earlier increase needs a **constitutional amendment**.
xa: So **Sec. 26** (AP **225**, Telangana **153**) is not yet implemented.
The **131st Amendment Bill, 2026** was **negatived**; the **84th Amendment** freeze stays.

na2ae6a17719.s: The present elected strength of the Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly, as provided under Section 17 of the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, is:
na2ae6a17719.x: Section 17 provides 175 elected Assembly seats for Andhra Pradesh; Telangana has 119 seats.
na2ae6a17719.tq: Separate the Andhra Pradesh figure from the corresponding Telangana figure.
xs: **Sec. 17** of the AP Reorganisation Act gives AP **175** elected seats — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2019** key).
**119** is **Telangana**; **225** is the proposed Sec. **26** increase; **301** was the **1956** Assembly.
xa: Reserved: **29 SC** + **7 ST**.
**Sec. 26** increase not yet made: **Art. 170(3)** ties it to the census after **2026**.

na8e079bb6e0.s: Which Section of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 deals with continuance of the AP Speaker and transfer of the Deputy Speaker?
na8e079bb6e0.x: Section 21 deals with the presiding officers; Sections 17, 19 and 20 deal with seats, sitting MLAs and the five-year term.
xa: **Sec. 18** = Anglo-Indian nominee (now lapsed); **Sec. 22** = Councils.
**Sec. 26**: raising seats to **225** (AP) and **153** (Telangana).

n8d0a1be89ee.s: Under the 2008 delimitation, which of the following AP districts has the highest number of Assembly constituencies?
n8d0a1be89ee.x: East Godavari has 19 Assembly constituencies, the highest among these districts.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "**Guntur - 13**" is wrong; Guntur has **17** (APPSC-GS **2019**).
Fewest: **Vizianagaram 9**.
Total across **13** districts: **175**.

ne90060401cb.s: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966 made which language the official language of Andhra Pradesh?
ne90060401cb.x: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966 provided for Telugu as the official language.
ne90060401cb.tq: Match the Act with its specific linguistic subject.
xs: The **AP Official Language Act, 1966** made **Telugu** the official language — option **(4)**.
It is listed among the notable **Bills passed in the AP Assembly**.
xa: Jan **2014**: the united Assembly **rejected** the Draft Reorganisation Bill by voice vote.
Nov **2021**: Repeal Act restored **Amaravati**.

n85bdd40c5a1.s: What was the response of the united Andhra Pradesh Legislative Assembly to the Draft Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Bill in January 2014?
o: It amended the Bill and enacted it as State law.
It referred the Bill to the Legislative Council for final approval.
It approved the Bill unanimously by secret ballot.
It rejected the Bill by resolution through voice vote, but Parliament's law prevailed.
n85bdd40c5a1.x: The united Assembly rejected the Draft Reorganisation Bill by a resolution through voice vote; nevertheless, the law enacted by Parliament prevailed.
n85bdd40c5a1.tq: Distinguish a State Assembly resolution from the final law-making authority in the reorganisation process.
xs: The Assembly **rejected** the Draft Bill by resolution (**voice vote**), but **Parliament's law prevailed** — option **(4)**.
This was in **Jan 2014**.
xa: The resulting **AP Reorganisation Act, 2014** fixed **175** seats (**Sec. 17**).
**Sec. 21**: the **Deputy Speaker** went to Telangana.

ncded906ef19.s: In which year did the Supreme Court shift to its building on Tilak Marg?
ncded906ef19.x: The Federal Court was set up in 1937, the Supreme Court was inaugurated in 1950 and shifted to Tilak Marg in 1958.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **26 Jan 1950** = SC replaces the Federal Court; **28 Jan 1950** = first sitting of the SC.
Constitutional basis of the SC: **Arts 124-147**, **Part V, Chapter IV**.
**H.J. Kania** was the **first CJI**; **M. Fathima Beevi** the **first woman SC judge** (**1989**).

n2c6291b605c.s: The Supreme Court of India is dealt with in which Part and Chapter of the Constitution?
n2c6291b605c.x: The Supreme Court is in Part V, Chapter IV (Articles 124–147).
xa: **Seat (Art. 130):** the SC sits in **Delhi** or other places the **CJI** appoints with the **President's approval**.
**Bench size:** usually **2 or 3** judges; **5+** judges for constitutional matters.
The SC replaced the **Federal Court** (**1937**) on **26 Jan 1950**; first sitting on **28 Jan 1950**.

n24102c2d7ed.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the sanctioned strength of the Supreme Court, including the Chief Justice of India, in the years indicated?
n24102c2d7ed.x: The strength was 8 in 1950, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986 and 31 from 2009. These figures include the Chief Justice of India.
n24102c2d7ed.tq: Use the complete numerical sequence rather than relying on a single familiar figure.
xs: Strength including the CJI: **1950—8; 1977—18; 1986—26; 2009—31** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) and (3) misplace **26/31/34**; option (4) wrongly gives **7** for 1950 — 1950 was **8** (CJI + **7**).
The figure of **31** held for **2009-2019**.
xa: **2019** (Amendment Act **37 of 2019**, assent **10 Aug 2019**) raised it to **34** (CJI + **33**).
**May 2026**: raised to **38** (CJI + **37**) by ordinance.
⚠ Trap: older notes giving **34** (2019) as current strength are out of date.

n62114caf431.s: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026 raised the number of judges other than the CJI from thirty-three to:
n62114caf431.x: The Ordinance, notified on 16 May 2026 under Article 123, replaced 'thirty-three' with 'thirty-seven', making total strength 38.
xa: On **6 May 2026** the Union Cabinet approved **four more judges**; sanctioned strength stayed **34** until enacted.
The ordinance came as the **backlog neared six figures**.
The **2019** amendment (assent **10 Aug 2019**) had fixed the strength at **34**.

n2630d2c8821.s: A person may be appointed a Supreme Court judge as a distinguished jurist if he is one in the opinion of the:
n2630d2c8821.x: The President's opinion governs the distinguished-jurist route, which has never been used; the person must be a citizen of India.
xa: Other routes: **5 years** as an HC judge or **10 years** as an HC advocate.
Justice **Ujjal Bhuyan** revived the transparency debate on appointments (**26 Aug 2026**).
Retirement at **65**; resignation addressed to the **President**.

n67249382eee.s: Who was to be the Chairperson of the National Judicial Appointments Commission?
o: The senior-most Supreme Court judge after the CJI
n67249382eee.x: The CJI was to chair the six-member NJAC; the Attorney-General was not a member.
xa: Eminent persons were picked by a panel of **PM, CJI and Leader of Opposition** / largest opposition party in LS.
Basis: **99th Amendment, 2014** (Art. **124A**) + **NJAC Act, 2014**.
The idea came from the **Venkatachaliah Commission** (**2000**).

n2cff86e86f6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about a retired judge sitting in the Supreme Court under Article 128?
o: The consent of the retired judge is required
Such a judge is deemed a regular judge of the Court for all purposes
The CJI requires the President's previous consent
Such a judge exercises all the powers of a Supreme Court judge
n2cff86e86f6.x: Such a judge has the powers of a Supreme Court judge but is not deemed a regular judge of the Court.
xa: Art. **128** covers a **retired SC, Federal Court or HC judge** (a qualified retired HC judge).
**Art. 127** = ad hoc judges when quorum is lacking; **Art. 126** = acting CJI.

n547b98e227e.s: With reference to a Judge of the Supreme Court, which one of the following is correct?
o: He holds office until 62 years and resigns by writing to the CJI
He holds office until 65 years and resigns by writing to the President
He holds office until 65 years and resigns by writing to the Vice-President
He holds office until 70 years and resigns by writing to the President
n547b98e227e.x: A Supreme Court judge retires at 65 and addresses his resignation to the President. 62 is the High Court retirement age, the CJI does not receive resignations, and the Vice-President has no role; 70 is not a constitutional limit.
n547b98e227e.tq: SC 65, HC 62; both resign to the President.
xs: An SC judge holds office until **65 years** and **resigns by writing to the President** — option **(2)** is correct.
Resignations do not go to the **CJI** or the **Vice-President**; **62** and **70** are not the SC age.
The age is determined as **Parliament** provides by law (**Art. 124(2A)**, **15th Amendment 1963**).
xa: Removal is only for **proved misbehaviour or incapacity** (**Art. 124(4)**).
**Art. 128**: retired judges may sit with the **President's previous consent** and the **judge's consent**.
**Art. 124(7)**: a retired SC judge **cannot plead in any court** in India.

ne6d7f663731.s: The pension of High Court Judges is charged on the:
ne6d7f663731.x: High Court salaries are charged on the State fund, but the pension is charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
xa: Salaries cannot be cut except in a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
**Art. 129** also makes the SC a **court of record**.
Contempt is defined by the **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** (**H.N. Sanyal Committee**), not the Constitution.

nf98fe3b488a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about recommendations on judicial appointments?
o: A 2023 Standing Committee sought MoP changes for women and marginalised candidates
The Law Commission's 214th Report was submitted in 1998
The 14th Report favoured appointing members of the Bar directly to the Supreme Court
The Law Commission's 14th Report was submitted in 1958
nf98fe3b488a.x: The 214th Report was submitted in 2008, not 1998.
xa: **Venkatachaliah Commission (NCRWC, 2000)**: report **2002** recommending a **National Judicial Commission**.
**P. Wilson's** Bill (**19 Feb 2026**): **diversity**, **90-day** limit, **regional benches**.

n07f7252894a.s: The Justice M.N. Venkatachaliah Commission (NCRWC), set up in 2000, submitted its report in:
n07f7252894a.x: The NCRWC submitted its report in 2002 and recommended a National Judicial Commission.
xa: LENS calls it a **National Judicial Appointments Commission**.
The NJAC came via the **99th Amendment, 2014** and was struck down in **2015**.
Law Commission **214th Report (2008)**: urgent review of the appointment procedure.

n62778e7394d.s: The High Court of Andhra Pradesh has been functioning at Amaravati since
n62778e7394d.x: The Andhra Pradesh High Court has sat at Amaravati since 1 January 2019.
n62778e7394d.tq: Distinguish the exact commencement date from nearby constitutional and administrative dates.
xs: The AP High Court has functioned at **Amaravati** since **1 January 2019** — option **(1)** is correct.
Other dates are distractors not in the notes.
xa: CJIs from AP: **K. Subba Rao** (**1966-67**) and **N.V. Ramana** (**2021-22**).
HC proposals are initiated by the **HC Chief Justice** + **2** senior-most HC judges.
HC judges are removed in the same way as SC judges, under **Art. 218**.

nindian-polity-30-11.s: Under which Article is the Supreme Court a Court of Record?
nindian-polity-30-11.x: Article 129 makes it a Court of Record with power to punish contempt; Article 130 fixes its seat at Delhi.
n: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Supreme Court has the power to punish for contempt of itself under Article 129. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 130 provides for the seat of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The seat of the Supreme Court is Delhi. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Chief Justice may decide on other places for Supreme Court sittings with the approval of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: HCs are **Courts of Record** under **Article 215**.
**Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** (**H.N. Sanyal Committee**) defines civil and criminal contempt.
No **regional benches** yet; **P. Wilson's** private member's Bill (**19 Feb 2026**) seeks them.

nindian-polity-69-2.s: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on:
nindian-polity-69-2.x: The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, two days after the Constitution came into force on 26 January.
n: The Supreme Court of India was inaugurated on 28 January 1950. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: The Supreme Court was inaugurated on **28 January 1950** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It replaced the **Federal Court** on **26 Jan 1950**, but its **first sitting** was on **28 January 1950**.
It was inaugurated in part of the **old Parliament House**.
xa: ⚠ **1937** Federal Court; **1949** Privy Council appeals end; **1958** move to **Tilak Marg**.
First CJI: **H.J. Kania**.
The SC is in **Part V, Chapter IV**: **Articles 124 to 147**.

nindian-polity-69-33.s: The Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-69-33.x: Article 145(3) provides for the Constitution Bench.
n: Article 142 empowers the Supreme Court to pass any decree or order necessary for doing complete justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A Constitution Bench requires a minimum of five judges under Article 145(3). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court is a Court of Record under Article 129. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The High Court is a Court of Record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Art. 142 was used to declare **10 TN bills assented** (**Apr 2025**).
HCs have **no equivalent** of Art. 142 (**Anil Kumar Jain v. Maya Jain**).
**Article 141**: law declared by the SC is **binding on all courts**.

nindian-polity-69-14.s: Under Article 145(3), a reference under Article 143 must be heard by a bench of at least:
nindian-polity-69-14.x: Article 145(3) requires at least five judges; the Article 143 opinion does not bind the President.
n: The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Opinions rendered by the Supreme Court to the President under Article 143 are strictly advisory. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 143 opinions are not binding on the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Constitution Benches also hear cases with a **substantial question of law** on interpreting the Constitution.
The US Supreme Court has **no** advisory jurisdiction.

n5a1d0dcbff0.s: The collegium system of judicial appointments arises from:
n5a1d0dcbff0.x: The collegium is a judicial creation of the Three Judges Cases, with no express constitutional mention.
xa: SC collegium: **CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges** (**5** members) — handles SC appointments and HC transfers.
HC collegium: **HC Chief Justice + 2 senior-most HC judges** — initiates HC appointments.
The Government can **return a name once**; if the Collegium **reiterates**, it is bound to appoint.

n332efa53761.s: The transfer of a High Court Chief Justice is linked with Article:
n332efa53761.x: Transfer is under Article 222, while appointment is linked with Article 217(1).
xa: After recommendation → **Union Law Minister** → **State consulted** → **President** appoints after consulting **CJI and Governor**.
Collegium picks CJs for **Patna, Calcutta, Bombay, Punjab & Haryana** HCs (**10 Aug 2026**).
The Centre notified **30 HC judges** in **Aug 2026**.

n35bb577dd10.s: The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 inserted which provision in the Constitution in connection with the NJAC?
n35bb577dd10.x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment inserted Article 124A, among related provisions, to provide for the National Judicial Appointments Commission.
n35bb577dd10.tq: Test the exact Article number associated with a constitutional amendment.
xs: The **99th Amendment Act, 2014** inserted **Article 124A** for the NJAC — option **(3)** is correct.
It came with the **NJAC Act, 2014** (APPSC-GS **2022**); some notes say Art. **124(2A)**.
Articles 143A, 222A and 368A are not part of the NJAC scheme in the notes.
xa: Origin: the **Venkatachaliah Commission** (set up **2000** under PM **Vajpayee**) recommended an NJAC.
Timeline: LS **13 Aug 2014**, RS **14 Aug 2014**, ratified by **16** states, assent **31 Dec 2014**, in force **13 Apr 2015**.
Struck down in **2015** (Fourth Judges Case, **16 Oct 2015**).

n693fb314ef8.s: The 99th Constitutional Amendment (NJAC) received Presidential assent on:
n693fb314ef8.x: It was ratified by 16 States and assented to on 31 December 2014; the framework came into force on 13 April 2015.
xa: Passed **Lok Sabha 13 Aug 2014**, **Rajya Sabha 14 Aug 2014**.
It inserted **Art. 124A** along with the **NJAC Act, 2014**.
Struck down by **4:1** on **16 Oct 2015** for violating **judicial independence**.

n2830c9f65ad.s: In the Fourth Judges Case (2015), which judge was the lone dissent upholding the NJAC?
n2830c9f65ad.x: Justice J. Chelameswar dissented in the 4:1 verdict; the Bench was led by Justice J.S. Khehar.
xa: Ground: violation of **judicial independence (Basic Structure)**; the **collegium was restored**.
Date: **16 Oct 2015** (**SCAORA v Union of India**).
⚠ Trap: **Khehar** led the bench; **Chelameswar** dissented.

nf881e0f5aa8.s: Which constitutional amendment sought to replace the collegium system but was struck down in 2015?
nf881e0f5aa8.x: The 99th Constitutional Amendment sought to replace the collegium system. It was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.
nf881e0f5aa8.tq: Discriminate among nearby amendment numbers using the subject associated with each.
xs: The **99th Amendment** (**2014**) sought to replace the collegium and was struck down in **2015** — option **(4)** is correct.
It set up the **NJAC** by inserting **Art. 124A**, with the **NJAC Act, 2014**.
xa: Exam angle: "Which amendment was declared void in **2015**?" → **99th**; "Who upheld NJAC?" → **Chelameswar**.
It came into force on **13 April 2015**, ratified by **16** states.
NJAC = CJI (chair) + **2** senior-most SC judges + **Union Law Minister** + **2** eminent persons.

n76159bb54e7.s: The In-House Procedure (1999) for lesser misconduct in the higher judiciary followed which case?
n76159bb54e7.x: The In-House Procedure came after C. Ravichandran Iyer (1995) to handle misconduct not warranting removal.
xa: Its international counterpart: the **Bangalore Principles** (**8 Sep 2026**).
Reform ideas: **Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill**, **asset disclosure**, a **permanent disciplinary authority**.

n75a51370b4d.s: A retired High Court judge may plead only in:
o: The Supreme Court and other High Courts
n75a51370b4d.x: Article 220 permits practice only in the Supreme Court and other High Courts; Article 124(7) bars a retired SC judge altogether.
xa: Salaries fixed by **Parliament** (Art. **125**, **221**; **54th Amendment 1986**) and not varied to their disadvantage.
Conduct not discussed in Parliament (**Art. 121**) or State Legislature (**Art. 211**) except on a removal motion.
**Art. 128**: a retired judge may still sit in the SC at the **CJI's** request with consents.

n1da6b9fa944.s: Which of the following disputes does NOT fall within the Supreme Court's exclusive original jurisdiction under Article 131?
o: Between the Government of India and one or more States
Between the Union and some States on one side and other States on the other
Between two private companies incorporated in different States
n1da6b9fa944.x: Article 131 covers federal disputes only; a dispute between private companies is outside it.
xa: Excluded: **inter-state river waters (Art. 262)**, **Finance Commission** matters (**Art. 280**), **Art. 290** expense adjustments, pre-Constitution treaties.
**Election disputes** of Parliament and state legislatures go to **High Courts** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
**Art. 32** writ jurisdiction is also original but **not exclusive** (HCs have **Art. 226**).

n6607d0f9d6d.s: Which of the following falls outside the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court?
o: A dispute between two or more States
A dispute between the Union and some States against other States
A dispute between the Union and one or more States
n6607d0f9d6d.x: Election disputes concerning Parliament and State Legislatures go to the High Courts; federal disputes fall under Article 131.
xa: Other exclusions: **inter-state river waters (Art. 262)**, **Finance Commission** (**Art. 280**), **Art. 290**, pre-Constitution treaties.
President/VP election disputes are **original, exclusive and final** in the SC (**Art. 71**).

n10715e67ba3.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the reform ideas associated with judicial appointments and accountability?
o: Abolition of the Collegium system by executive notification
RTI coverage of the administrative side of the judiciary
n10715e67ba3.x: The listed reform ideas include judicial standards and accountability legislation, a permanent disciplinary authority, asset disclosure, RTI on the administrative side and transparent appointments. Abolition of the Collegium system by executive notification is not included.
n10715e67ba3.tq: Find the option that introduces a reform not contained in the stated set.
xs: **Abolition of the Collegium by executive notification** is NOT among the reform ideas — option **(1)** is the answer.
Listed ideas: **Judicial Standards and Accountability Bill**, **permanent disciplinary authority**, **asset disclosure**, **RTI on administrative side**, **transparent appointments**.
xa: Transparency gaps: **no notification of vacancies**, no **eligibility matrix**, no methodology.
Justice **Ujjal Bhuyan** revived this debate (**26 Aug 2026**).
Criticisms: "**imperium in imperio**", "**judges selecting judges**".

n1c1e7106a4c.s: The expression 'procedure established by law' in India, contrasted with 'due process of law' in the United States, indicates that
o: Indian courts cannot review any law enacted by Parliament
Indian judicial review is generally narrower than the substantive and procedural review in the United States
US courts conduct only procedural review
Both expressions have exactly the same constitutional meaning
n1c1e7106a4c.x: The Indian formulation is associated with a narrower review standard, while due process in the United States permits substantive as well as procedural review. The US Court has consequently been described as a 'third chamber'.
n1c1e7106a4c.tq: Discriminate between two similar constitutional phrases by their scope of review.
xs: "**Procedure established by law**" means **Indian judicial review is generally narrower** than US **substantive and procedural** review — option **(2)** is correct.
Indian courts do review laws; US courts are not limited to procedural review; the two phrases do not mean the same.
US "**due process of law**" review has led the Court to be called a "**third chamber**".
xa: India blends **American judicial supremacy** with **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
India has **advisory** jurisdiction (**Art. 143**); the US does not.

nindian-polity-30-6.s: The Second Judges Case was decided in:
nindian-polity-30-6.x: The First Judges Case was 1981, the Second 1993 and the Third 1998, before the NJAC (2014–15).
n: The First Judges Case was decided in 1981. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Second Judges Case was decided in 1993. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The Third Judges Case was decided in 1998. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The 99th Constitutional Amendment and the National Judicial Appointments Commission occurred in 2014–15. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: Some notes date the First Judges Case to **1982**.
The **Fourth Judges Case** (**16 Oct 2015**) struck down NJAC by **4:1**.
The Third Judges Case expanded the Collegium to **CJI + four**.

nindian-polity-47-32.s: The Second Judges Case was decided in which case?
o: S.P. Gupta v. Union of India
nindian-polity-47-32.x: The Second Judges Case (1993) was Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association (SCAORA) v. Union of India. S.P. Gupta was the First.
nindian-polity-47-32.tq: Recall the name of each Judges Case.
n: The Second Judges Case was SCAORA v. Union of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
xs: The Second Judges Case was **SCAORA v. Union of India** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was decided in **1993** by the **Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association** case.
**S.P. Gupta** is the **First** Judges Case; the **Presidential Reference** is the **Third**.
xa: **Fourth Judges Case** — also **SCAORA** — the **NJAC case** (**2015**).
Second Judges Case: consultation **means concurrence**; Collegium born.
⚠ **Khehar** led the NJAC bench; **Chelameswar** dissented.

n7f0b10a0f2c.s: If the collegium reiterates a recommendation returned by the Government, the Government:
o: May refer it to the President
Is bound to appoint the person
n7f0b10a0f2c.x: The Government may return a name once, but is bound to appoint if the collegium reiterates it.
xa: The collegium is a **judicial creation** (Second Judges Case, **1993**), in present form since **1998**.
Criticisms: "**imperium in imperio**", "**judges selecting judges**", opacity vs **executive delays** in notifying names.
**P. Wilson's** Bill proposes a **90-day** limit for the Centre to notify collegium names.

nindian-polity-47-15.s: Recommendations for High Court appointments are initiated by:
o: The High Court Chief Justice and two senior-most HC judges
nindian-polity-47-15.x: The proposal starts with the HC Chief Justice and two senior judges and goes to the CJI and two senior SC judges.
n: The NJAC included the Union Law Minister. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Union Law Minister was a permanent member of the NJAC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
High Court appointment recommendations are initiated by the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court and two senior-most High Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
High Court appointment recommendations are forwarded to the Supreme Court Collegium. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Supreme Court Collegium for High Court appointments consists of the Chief Justice of India and two senior-most Supreme Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Collegium System covers appointments to the High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
xa: Under the MoP, names go to the **Union Law Minister** → State consulted → **President** appoints.
HC Chief Justices are chosen **from outside their parent High Court**.
**HC transfers** go through **CJI + four** senior-most SC judges.

nindian-polity-47-31.s: The Supreme Court Collegium for Supreme Court appointments consists of the CJI and:
o: Four senior-most judges and the Law Minister
nindian-polity-47-31.x: The collegium has five members, the CJI and four senior-most judges, with no executive member.
n: The Collegium System had zero executive representation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Union Law Minister was a permanent member of the NJAC. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Supreme Court Collegium for appointments and elevations consists of the Chief Justice of India and four senior-most Supreme Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The total membership of the Supreme Court Collegium for appointments and elevations is five. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Collegium System covers appointments to the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
The Collegium System has a total strength of five members for Supreme Court appointments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 125-127]
xa: The Collegium is **judicially evolved**, with **no mention in the Constitution**.
The government does **IB background checks** and can **return a name once**.
NJAC had **six members**, chaired by the **CJI**.

n0762c04a0cf.s: The Chief Justice of India is appointed by—
o: The Collegium of the Supreme Court
n0762c04a0cf.x: Under Article 124(2) the President appoints the CJI (and other judges); by convention the senior-most judge is appointed. The Collegium only recommends, the Prime Minister/Cabinet advises, and Parliament has no role in appointment.
n0762c04a0cf.tq: Appoints = President; recommends = Collegium; convention = senior-most judge.
xs: The **CJI** is appointed by **the President of India** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS **2025** key).
By convention, upheld by the Court, the **senior-most judge** becomes CJI.
The **Collegium** only recommends; **Parliament** has no appointing role — it only takes part in **removal**.
xa: The convention was broken in **1973 (A.N. Ray)** and **1977 (M.H. Beg)**.
**Art. 126**: the President appoints an **acting CJI** when the office is vacant.
Present CJI: **Surya Kant**, who succeeded **B.R. Gavai** (retired November **2025**).

nda859ef90ea.s: As of June 2026, which one of the following was NOT a member of the Supreme Court collegium?
nda859ef90ea.x: The Supreme Court collegium in June 2026 comprised CJI Surya Kant and Justices Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh and P.S. Narasimha. Justice J.K. Maheshwari had retired before that composition was reported.
nda859ef90ea.tq: Use the current-membership list to identify the excluded name.
xs: **Justice J.K. Maheshwari** was NOT in the June 2026 collegium — option **(4)** is the answer.
The collegium was **CJI Surya Kant**, **Vikram Nath**, **B.V. Nagarathna**, **M.M. Sundresh** and **P.S. Narasimha**.
**Narasimha** joined after **Maheshwari retired** (**29 Jun 2026**).
xa: The SC collegium has **5** members: **CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges**.
Vacancies: Justice **Rajesh Bindal** retired April **2026**; **Pankaj Mithal** due June **2026**; **Sanjay Karol** due August **2026**.
**Surya Kant** succeeded **B.R. Gavai** (retired November **2025**).

n15e3a5e2b59.s: Under Article 222 of the Constitution, a Judge of a High Court may be transferred by the President after consultation with the
o: Chief Minister of the concerned State
n15e3a5e2b59.x: Article 222 provides for transfer of a High Court judge by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
n15e3a5e2b59.tq: Apply the “who would do this job?” test to identify the constitutionally relevant authority.
xs: Under **Art. 222**, the President transfers HC judges after consulting the **Chief Justice of India** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **Union Law Minister**, **Chief Minister** and **Speaker** are not the consultees under Art. 222.
xa: HC Chief Justices: appointment under **Art. 217(1)**, transfer under **Art. 222**.
HC transfers are handled by the SC collegium of **CJI + 4 senior-most judges**.
**Punjab** objected that the State was bypassed in appointing the **Punjab and Haryana HC** Chief Justice (**9 Sep 2026**).

ne3ccf87555b.s: The Punjab Cabinet's objection in September 2026 related to the allegation that
o: the Collegium had recommended only retired judges for Punjab
the Supreme Court had abolished the Punjab and Haryana High Court
the Union had transferred all Punjab judges to the Supreme Court
the State was bypassed in appointing the Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court
ne3ccf87555b.x: The Punjab Cabinet objected that the State had been bypassed in the appointment of the Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court.
ne3ccf87555b.tq: Identify the precise administrative grievance rather than the broader issue of judicial appointments.
xs: Punjab's objection: the **State was bypassed** in appointing the **Chief Justice of the Punjab and Haryana High Court** — option **(4)** is correct.
The MoP requires the **concerned State** to be consulted after the **Union Law Minister** stage.
No HC was abolished and no judges were moved en masse — the dispute was about **consultation**.
xa: Final step: the **President** appoints after consulting the **CJI and Governor** (**9 Sep 2026**).
The collegium had picked CJs for **Patna, Calcutta, Bombay, Punjab & Haryana** HCs (**10 Aug 2026**).
HC CJs are recommended by **CJI + 2 senior-most judges**, from outside their **parent High Court**.

nfa4a820fa64.s: The jurisdiction to decide disputes relating to the election of the President and Vice-President of India is
o: appellate jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 136
original jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226
original, exclusive and final jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 71
advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 143
nfa4a820fa64.x: Article 71 vests the Supreme Court with original, exclusive and final jurisdiction over disputes concerning the election of the President and Vice-President.
nfa4a820fa64.tq: Link the special election jurisdiction with its distinctive constitutional features.
xs: Disputes over the election of the **President and Vice-President** fall under the **original, exclusive and final** jurisdiction of the SC under **Article 71** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Art. 136** is SLP, **Art. 226** is HC writs, **Art. 143** is advisory — none covers these elections.
xa: By contrast, **election disputes of Parliament and state legislatures** go to **High Courts**.
**Art. 131** original jurisdiction covers **federal disputes** only.
**Art. 143**: the **16th Presidential Reference** (Nov **2025**) answered questions on bill timelines.

n88105d66042.s: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments?
n88105d66042.x: Article 137 provides review; Article 141 makes SC law binding and Article 142 allows orders for complete justice.
xa: Art. 142 uses: declared **10 TN bills assented** (Apr **2025**); **Right to Safe Travel** (**27 May 2026**).
HCs have **no equivalent power** (**Anil Kumar Jain v. Maya Jain**).
**Curative petition**: **Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)**.

n6f677db2d54.s: Which Article empowers the Supreme Court to pass orders necessary for doing complete justice?
n6f677db2d54.x: Article 142 is a power specific to the Supreme Court; High Courts have no equivalent under it.
xa: **Art. 141**: SC's law binds all courts.
**Art. 143** advisory: the **16th Presidential Reference** (Nov **2025**) on bill timelines.
**Art. 129**: court of record with **contempt** power.

o: A registry for appointments through the collegium system
A free digital database of the Supreme Court’s reported judgments launched in 2023
An online system for filing presidential references under Article 143
An electronic voting system for Supreme Court proceedings
n82506858a1b.x: e-SCR means electronic Supreme Court Reports. It is a free digital database of the Court’s reported judgments, launched in 2023.
n82506858a1b.tq: Decode the official abbreviation and match it with its function and launch year.
xs: **e-SCR** is **a free digital database of the Supreme Court's reported judgments launched in 2023** — option **(2)** is correct.
It has nothing to do with collegium registries, **Art. 143** references or voting.
xa: **Curative petition**: created in **Rupa Ashok Hurra (2002)**.
**Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** defines civil and criminal contempt.
**Art. 141**: law declared by the SC binds all courts.

n6b7bb74a59f.s: The expression “imperium in imperio” is used in the debate on the Collegium system to indicate criticism that it is
o: a forum exclusively for resolving Centre-State disputes
a self-contained authority operating within the State
a body subordinate to State legislatures
a constitutional body headed by the Union Law Minister
n6b7bb74a59f.x: “Imperium in imperio” literally conveys the criticism that the Collegium functions like an authority within an authority, reflecting concerns about opacity and judges selecting judges.
n6b7bb74a59f.tq: Translate the Latin expression into the institutional criticism it represents.
xs: "**Imperium in imperio**" criticises the Collegium as **a self-contained authority operating within the State** — option **(2)** is correct.
It goes with charges that the Collegium is **opaque** and amounts to "**judges selecting judges**".
The collegium is not a Centre-State forum, not under State legislatures, and not headed by the Law Minister.
xa: The collegium has **no mention in the Constitution**.
The other side of the debate: **executive delays** in notifying names.
Transparency debate revived by Justice **Ujjal Bhuyan** (**26 Aug 2026**).

n94d40a02655.s: Which one of the following proposals was associated with the private member's Bill concerning judicial appointments?
o: Abolition of Article 222 and direct election of High Court judges
A 90-day limit for the Centre to notify Collegium recommendations, along with social diversity and regional Supreme Court benches
Appointment of all Supreme Court judges by State legislatures
Replacement of the Collegium by the Finance Commission
n94d40a02655.x: The private member's Bill proposed social diversity in appointments, a 90-day period for the Centre to notify Collegium names and regional benches of the Supreme Court.
n94d40a02655.tq: Separate the specific contents of a proposal from unrelated constitutional mechanisms.
xs: The Bill proposed **a 90-day limit** for the Centre to notify Collegium names, **social diversity** and **regional SC benches** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was DMK MP **P. Wilson's** private member's Bill (**19 Feb 2026**).
Other options (direct election, State legislatures, Finance Commission) do not appear in it.
xa: **Art. 130** allows other seats by the **CJI's** decision with the Centre's approval.
There are **no regional benches yet**.
Standing Committee (**2023**) sought **women and marginalised** candidates via the MoP.

nebb79a568c2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct when comparing the Supreme Court of India with the US Supreme Court?
o: India's Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143
India's appellate jurisdiction includes special leave under Article 136
The US Supreme Court lacks advisory jurisdiction
The US Supreme Court has a writ jurisdiction equivalent to Article 32
nebb79a568c2.x: The key marks the claim of an Article 32-equivalent writ jurisdiction in the US Supreme Court as false.
xa: India: "**procedure established by law**" — narrower review; US: "**due process of law**".
The US Court has been called a "**third chamber**".
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.

nab4868647d1.s: India's constitutional system is described as synthesising
o: American parliamentary sovereignty with British judicial supremacy
American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty
French judicial supremacy with American parliamentary sovereignty
British federalism with American unitary government
nab4868647d1.x: The Indian system combines the American principle of judicial supremacy with the British principle of parliamentary sovereignty.
nab4868647d1.tq: Avoid reversing the two comparative constitutional influences.
xs: India synthesises **American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary sovereignty** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the sources — the classic trap.
France and federal/unitary pairings are not part of the synthesis.
xa: US review = "**due process of law**"; Indian = "**procedure established by law**".
The US Supreme Court has been called a "**third chamber**".
India's SC has **advisory** (**Art. 143**) and **Art. 32** writ powers that the US Court lacks.

nindian-polity-69-6.s: The writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-69-6.x: Writs are under Article 32; original jurisdiction 131, review 137 and advisory 143.
n: The Supreme Court has original and exclusive jurisdiction under Article 131. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has writ jurisdiction under Article 32. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has advisory jurisdiction under Article 143. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: ⚠ **131** = original (exclusive); **32** = writ (not exclusive, HCs **Art. 226**); **136** = SLP; **143** = advisory (not binding).
Disputes on **President and Vice-President elections** (**71**): original, exclusive and final.
Appeals: **132 / 133 / 134** = constitutional / civil / criminal.

nindian-polity-69-11.s: Civil appeals to the Supreme Court are governed by Article:
nindian-polity-69-11.x: Civil appeals are under Article 133; constitutional appeals 132, criminal 134 and special leave 136.
n: The Supreme Court has constitutional appellate jurisdiction under Article 132. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has civil appellate jurisdiction under Article 133. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Arts 132 and 133 need an HC **certificate** under **Article 134A**.
Art. 134 appeals where an HC **reversed an acquittal into a death sentence** lie **as of right**.
Art. 136 is **not** available against **Military Tribunals**.

nindian-polity-69-12.s: Under Article 136, the Supreme Court's power to grant Special Leave to Appeal is:
o: Discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, subject to the stated exception
Mandatory and limited to High Court judgments
Advisory and limited to presidential references
Available only in civil proceedings involving a constitutional question
nindian-polity-69-12.x: Under Article 136, the Court may, at its discretion, grant special leave to appeal against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal, except military tribunals (Article 136(2)).
nindian-polity-69-12.tq: Recall Article 136 and its military exception.
n: The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The power under Article 136 is plenary and residual. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136(2) does not apply to Military Tribunals or Armed Forces Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xs: Art. 136 power is **discretionary and available against any judgment or order of any court or tribunal**, subject to the exception — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is a **plenary and residual** power.
Exception: **Article 136(2)** — **not** against **courts-martial / Military Tribunals / Armed Forces Courts**.
xa: Advisory jurisdiction is a separate power — **Article 143**.
Constitutional / civil / criminal appeals: **132 / 133 / 134**.
India's appellate scope is **very wide** compared with the US Supreme Court.

nindian-polity-69-13.s: The review jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 137 refers to its power to:
o: Review its own judgments or orders
Review High Court judgments on appeal
nindian-polity-69-13.x: Article 137 concerns review of the Court's own judgments, which differs from judicial review of statutes.
n: The Supreme Court has review jurisdiction under Article 137. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments or orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Review jurisdiction under Article 137 is distinct from judicial review of statutes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Review is subject to **Parliamentary law** and **court rules**.
After a review petition is **dismissed**, a **curative petition** may follow (**Rupa Ashok Hurra, 2002**).
**Article 141**: SC's law is **binding on all courts**.

nindian-polity-69-26.s: An appeal under Article 134 where a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death:
o: Lies only to a larger High Court bench
Lies without a High Court certificate
nindian-polity-69-26.x: Such an appeal lies as of right and needs no High Court certificate.
n: Article 132 covers appeals from High Court judgments involving a substantial question of law concerning the interpretation of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 133 covers appeals in civil proceedings involving a substantial question of law of general importance. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
HC certificates are issued under **Article 134A**.
**Article 136** SLP is **discretionary**.

nindian-polity-69-40.s: The curative petition rests on the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article:
nindian-polity-69-40.x: The curative petition, filed after dismissal of a review under Article 137, rests on inherent powers under Article 142.
n: The curative petition was evolved under the Supreme Court's inherent powers anchored in Article 142. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition prevents abuse of process. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition cures gross miscarriages of justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
A curative petition is available after a review petition under Article 137 has been dismissed. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: It was evolved in **Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002)**.
**Article 142**: any decree or order for **complete justice**.
**e-SCR**: free digital database of reported judgments, launched **2023**.

nindian-polity-69-52.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about appeals to the Supreme Court?
o: Civil appeals under Article 133 need a High Court certificate
Special leave under Article 136 needs a High Court certificate
Constitutional appeals under Article 132 need a High Court certificate
An appeal under Article 134(1)(a) after a death sentence on reversal of acquittal lies as of right
nindian-polity-69-52.x: Special leave under Article 136 is granted at the Supreme Court's discretion and needs no High Court certificate.
n: An appeal under Article 132 requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The High Court must certify under Article 134A that the question in a civil appeal needs determination by the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has criminal appellate jurisdiction under Article 134. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has reversed an acquittal into a death sentence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 134 covers criminal appeals where a High Court has withdrawn a trial to itself. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Capital-punishment reversals under Article 134 are appealable as of right without a High Court certificate. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court has discretionary appellate power under Article 136 to grant special leave to appeal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 136 permits special leave to appeal from any judgment or order of any court or tribunal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Special Leave Petitions do not lie against judgments or sentences passed by courts-martial or military tribunals under Article 136(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Art. 136 covers **any judgment or order** of **any court or tribunal**, except military ones.
Art. 134 also covers cases where an HC **withdrew a trial** to itself.
SC's appellate scope is **very wide** — constitutional, civil, criminal, special leave.

nindian-polity-39-1.s: Who was the longest-serving Chief Justice of India?
nindian-polity-39-1.x: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud, the 16th CJI, was the longest-serving, from 22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985, over seven years.
nindian-polity-39-1.tq: Recall the longest and shortest CJI tenures.
n: Justice Y.V. Chandrachud was the 16th Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud was the longest-serving Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud served from 22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
Justice Y.V. Chandrachud served for over seven years as Chief Justice of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 101-104]
xs: The longest-serving CJI was **Justice Y.V. Chandrachud** — so option **(3)** is correct.
He was the **16th Chief Justice of India**, from **22 February 1978 to 11 July 1985** — over **seven years**.
**Kamal Narain Singh** was the **shortest-serving**; **M. Fathima Beevi** was the first woman SC judge, not a CJI.
xa: Kamal Narain Singh served **18 days** (**25 November 1991 to 12 December 1991**).
First CJI: **H.J. Kania**.
CJIs from AP: **K. Subba Rao** and **N.V. Ramana**.

nindian-polity-2-47.s: The advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court on a Presidential reference is under Article:
nindian-polity-2-47.x: Article 143 provides advisory jurisdiction; Article 141 makes the Supreme Court's law binding.
n: Article 141 makes the law declared by the Supreme Court binding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 143 concerns the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 143 concerns Presidential reference. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Articles 148 to 151 concern the Comptroller and Auditor-General. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 214 provides for High Courts for States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 129**: SC a **Court of Record**; **215**: HCs Courts of Record.
**Article 216**: **constitution** of High Courts; **217**: appointment of HC judges.
CAG is removed in the **same manner** as an SC judge (**Art. 148**).

nindian-polity-69-35.s:
Which of the following are excluded from the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court under Article 131?
1. Inter-State water disputes
2. Finance Commission matters
3. Disputes between States involving a legal right
nindian-polity-69-35.x: Inter-State water disputes (Article 262) and Finance Commission matters (Article 280) are excluded; disputes between States about legal rights are the core of Article 131.
n: Article 131 covers direct federal disputes involving a legal right. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The Supreme Court can hear under Article 131 disputes between one State and another State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 excludes inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover inter-State water disputes under Article 262. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover Finance Commission matters under Article 280. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Article 131 does not cover recovery of damages by a private party against the Union. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Also excluded: **political questions**, **pre-Constitution treaties**, **Art. 290** expense adjustments.
**Election disputes** of Parliament and state legislatures go to **High Courts**.
Art. 131 also covers **Centre and some states vs other states**.

nindian-polity-30-5.s: The appointment of ad hoc judges in the Supreme Court is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-30-5.x: Article 127 covers ad hoc judges; 126 the Acting CJI, 128 retired judges and 129 the Court of Record.
n: Article 126 provides for the appointment of an Acting Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 127 provides for the appointment of ad hoc judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 128 concerns the attendance of retired judges at Supreme Court sittings. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
Article 129 declares the Supreme Court to be a Court of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed under Article 127 by the Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: ⚠ **126** = acting CJI (President); **127** = ad hoc (CJI, HC judge); **128** = retired judges (both consents).
A retired judge under Art. 128 has full powers but is **not deemed a judge** of the court.
There are **no additional judges in the SC** — only in **High Courts** (**Art. 224**).

nf07b48adca4.s: The Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956 was enacted under which constitutional provision relating to the composition of the Supreme Court?
nf07b48adca4.x: Article 124(1) provides the constitutional basis for determining the number of judges of the Supreme Court. Parliament may increase the number by law, and such an amendment requires only a simple majority.
nf07b48adca4.tq: Match the statutory mechanism with the correct constitutional provision.
xs: The **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Act, 1956** was enacted under **Article 124(1)** — option **(1)** is correct.
Under **Art. 124(1)**, **Parliament** increases the number of judges by law, by a **simple-majority** amendment of the 1956 Act.
**Art. 126** = acting CJI; **Art. 128** = retired judges sitting; **Art. 137** = review of its own judgments.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2025** key: the number of SC judges is increased by **Parliament**.
The **2026** increase came through the **Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Ordinance, 2026** (Art. **123**).

nebd97d2b15e.s: The process of appointing a High Court Chief Justice begins with a recommendation by:
o: The CJI and two senior-most Supreme Court judges
nebd97d2b15e.x: The CJI and two senior-most judges recommend first, followed by the Law Minister, the State, and appointment by the President.
xa: Candidates are chosen **from outside their parent High Court**.
**Punjab** Cabinet objected that the State was **bypassed** for the Punjab and Haryana HC Chief Justice (**9 Sep 2026**).

n989c0a29fc2.s: Which one of the following combinations correctly states the constitutional provisions relating to removal of judges?
o: Supreme Court judge—Article 124(4); High Court judge—Article 218
Supreme Court judge—Article 148; High Court judge—Article 324(5)
Supreme Court judge—Article 218; High Court judge—Article 124(4)
Supreme Court judge—Article 67(b); High Court judge—Article 61
n989c0a29fc2.x: Article 124(4) deals with removal of a Supreme Court judge, while Article 218 applies the relevant provisions to High Court judges.
n989c0a29fc2.tq: Use exact Article–office matching and reject swapped constitutional authorities.
xs: Removal: SC judge — **Article 124(4)**; HC judge — **Article 218** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Art. 148** and **Art. 324(5)** are for the **CAG** and **CEC**, removed in the same manner as an SC judge.
**Art. 61** is **impeachment of the President**, not judges.
xa: Address by each House: **majority of total membership** + **two-thirds of present and voting**.
Grounds: only **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
⚠ The Constitution says "**removal**" for judges; "impeachment" only for the President.

nc5a893a445d.s: The Comptroller and Auditor-General and the Chief Election Commissioner are removed from office in the same manner as:
nc5a893a445d.x: Under Articles 148 and 324(5), the CAG and the CEC have removal protection comparable to that of a Supreme Court judge.
nc5a893a445d.tq: Identify the constitutional office whose removal procedure is expressly borrowed rather than guessing from seniority.
xs: The **CAG** (**Art. 148**) and **CEC** (**Art. 324(5)**) are removed in the same manner as **a Supreme Court judge** — option **(1)** is correct.
An SC judge is removed by the President after an address by **both Houses** on **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
xa: Special majority: **majority of total membership** + **two-thirds of present and voting**.
HC judges are removed the same way under **Art. 218**.
⚠ "Impeachment" is used only for the **President** (Art. **61**).

nindian-polity-30-20.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about an ad hoc judge of the Supreme Court?
o: The previous consent of the President is required
Such a judge is appointed by the President on the collegium's advice
Such a judge is appointed to meet a lack of quorum
The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is consulted
nindian-polity-30-20.x: The CJI appoints an ad hoc judge with the President's consent; appointment by the President on collegium advice applies to regular judges.
n: An ad hoc judge is appointed with the previous consent of the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed after consultation with the concerned High Court Chief Justice. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
An ad hoc judge is appointed to meet a lack of quorum. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
The President appoints Supreme Court judges in consultation with the prescribed collegium concurrence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 75-78]
xa: The **SC Collegium** = **CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges** (**5 members**).
The Collegium is **judicially evolved** — **no mention in the Constitution**.
The government can **return a name once**; if the Collegium **reiterates**, it must appoint.

nindian-polity-69-51.s: The removal of a Supreme Court judge is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-69-51.x: Article 124(4) covers removal; 124(1) the number of judges, 124(2) retirement and 134A certificates for appeal.
n: Parliament has exclusive power to increase the number of Supreme Court judges by law under Article 124(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Supreme Court judges retire at 65 years of age under Article 124(2). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
The President removes Supreme Court judges after an Address supported by a Special Majority in each House of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Proved misbehaviour is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
Incapacity is a ground for removing a Supreme Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
An appeal under Article 132 requires a certificate from the High Court under Article 134A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #69 · pp 185-189]
xa: Strength rose to **38** (CJI + **37**) by ordinance in **May 2026**.
In **1950** the strength was **8** (CJI + 7).
**Art. 124(2A)** (**15th Amendment 1963**): age determined as **Parliament** provides by law.

nindian-polity-71-21.s: A High Court judge retires at the age of:
nindian-polity-71-21.x: A High Court judge retires at 62 and a Supreme Court judge at 65.
n: The retirement age of a Supreme Court Judge is 65 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The retirement age of a High Court Judge is 62 years. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
Supreme Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
High Court Judges address their written resignations to the President of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The resignation of a High Court Judge is addressed to the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A Supreme Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 124(2)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A High Court Judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xa: HC salary is on the **State Fund**, pension on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
SC salary and pension are both on the **Consolidated Fund of India**.

nindian-polity-70-57.s: The salary and pension of a Supreme Court judge are charged on which fund?
o: The Consolidated Fund of the State
The State Fund for both salary and pension
The State Fund for salary and the Consolidated Fund of India for pension
nindian-polity-70-57.x: A Supreme Court judge's salary and pension are both charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. Option C describes a High Court judge.
nindian-polity-70-57.tq: Discriminate the Supreme Court (both Union) from the High Courts (salary from the State).
n: The salary and pension of a Supreme Court judge are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: Both are charged on **the Consolidated Fund of India** — so option **(4)** is correct.
SC salaries and expenses are **charged on the Consolidated Fund of India** — **non-votable**.
Option (3) describes an **HC judge** (salary on **State Fund**, pension on **CFI**).
xa: Salaries are fixed by **Parliament** by law (**Art. 125**).
Salaries cannot be reduced except in a **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
A retired SC judge **cannot plead** in any court in India (**Art. 124(7)**).

nindian-polity-2-13.s: The power of superintendence of High Courts is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-2-13.x: Article 227 gives superintendence; Article 226 is the High Court writ power.
n: Article 124 concerns the establishment and constitution of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 137 concerns the review of judgments of the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue writs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 227 concerns the power of superintendence of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 125**: **salaries** of SC judges; **Article 127**: **ad hoc judges**.
**Article 131**: **original jurisdiction**; **132 to 136**: appellate.
**Article 233**: appointment of **District Judges**.

nindian-polity-2-48.s: The appointment of District Judges is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-2-48.x: Article 233 covers District Judges; 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record, 216 constitutes them and 217 covers HC judges.
n: Article 215 makes High Courts Courts of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 216 concerns the constitution of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 217 concerns the appointment and conditions of service of High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
Article 233 concerns the appointment of District Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 6-12]
xa: **Article 226**: HC **writs**; **Article 227**: **superintendence**.
**Article 214**: High Courts for States.
HC strength is fixed by the **President** (**Article 216**).

n33e5221e224.s: A motion for the removal of a judge must be signed by at least how many Lok Sabha members?
n33e5221e224.x: The motion needs 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members.
xa: The **Speaker/Chairman may admit or refuse** the motion.
Attempts: **V. Ramaswami (1993)** failed in the Lok Sabha; **Soumitra Sen (2011)** resigned before the LS vote.
**No judge has been removed so far**.

nf13078a4890.s: For taking judges out of office, the Constitution uses the term:
nf13078a4890.x: The Constitution uses 'removal', not 'impeachment', for judges.
xa: Signatures: **100 LS** or **50 RS** members.
Lesser misconduct: **In-House Procedure (1999)** after **C. Ravichandran Iyer, 1995**.
**Restatement of Values of Judicial Life (1997)**: a **16**-point code.

n42bdd7917f7.s: The conduct of a Judge of the Supreme Court may be discussed in Parliament only during:
o: A motion for the removal of the Judge
A discussion initiated by the Law Minister
A debate on the annual budget
n42bdd7917f7.x: Under Article 121, the conduct of a Supreme Court or High Court Judge cannot be discussed in Parliament except upon a motion for the Judge’s removal.
n42bdd7917f7.tq: Use the constitutional exception rather than the broad prohibition alone.
xs: A judge's conduct can be discussed in Parliament only on **a motion for the removal of the Judge** (**Art. 121**) — option **(1)** is correct.
No amendment procedure, Law Minister's discussion or budget debate permits it.
For State Legislatures the same bar is in **Art. 211**.
xa: Other safeguards: **contempt power** — **Art. 129** (SC), **Art. 215** (HC).
The SC controls its **own staff** (**Art. 146**).
Post-office bar on employment: **Art. 319**.

n808a9a5de0e.s: As of the period referred to, the Chief Justice of India who succeeded B.R. Gavai was
n808a9a5de0e.x: Justice Surya Kant succeeded Justice B.R. Gavai as Chief Justice of India. B.R. Gavai retired in November 2025.
n808a9a5de0e.tq: Track succession rather than confusing the current CJI with other senior Judges listed for retirement.
xs: **Surya Kant** succeeded **B.R. Gavai** (retired November **2025**) as CJI — option **(3)** is correct.
**Sanjay Karol** and **J.K. Maheshwari** are SC judges due to retire in **2026**, not CJIs.
xa: **CJI Surya Kant** heads the SC collegium with **Vikram Nath, B.V. Nagarathna, M.M. Sundresh, P.S. Narasimha** (June **2026**).
The CJI is **appointed by the President**; by convention the **senior-most judge**.
Vacancy: Justice **Rajesh Bindal** retired April **2026**.

n6c42a0f8f9a.s: Who was the first Chief Justice of India?
n6c42a0f8f9a.x: H.J. Kania was the first Chief Justice of India. K. Subba Rao was a CJI from Andhra Pradesh (1966-67), Y.V. Chandrachud was the longest-serving CJI (1978-85), and M. Patanjali Sastri came after Kania, so he was not the first.
n6c42a0f8f9a.tq: First CJI Kania; longest Y.V. Chandrachud; first woman SC judge Fathima Beevi.
xs: The first CJI was **H.J. Kania** (APPSC-GS **2022** key) — option **(1)** is correct.
**K. Subba Rao** was a CJI from AP (**1966-67**); **Y.V. Chandrachud** the longest-serving (**1978-85**).
xa: The SC's first sitting: **28 Jan 1950**.
**M. Fathima Beevi**: first woman SC judge (**1989**).
Seniority convention broken in **1973 (A.N. Ray)** and **1977 (M.H. Beg)**.

n9d86f183399.s:
Which of the following were Chief Justices of India from Andhra Pradesh?
1. K. Subba Rao
2. N.V. Ramana
3. P. Wilson
n9d86f183399.x: K. Subba Rao and N.V. Ramana were Chief Justices of India from Andhra Pradesh; P. Wilson is associated with a private member's Bill on judicial diversity, not the office of CJI.
xa: Subba Rao served **1966-67**; Ramana **2021-22**.
AP High Court at **Amaravati** since **1 January 2019**.
First CJI: **H.J. Kania**.

n0e825887d5a.s: A new High Court established under a law made by Parliament comes into being through:
o: A resolution of the concerned State Legislative Assembly
An order of the Chief Justice of India
A notification issued by the Governor alone
A notification issued by the President
n0e825887d5a.x: A new High Court is created under a law made by Parliament and brought into being through a Presidential notification. The Andhra Pradesh High Court was notified by the President under the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act.
n0e825887d5a.tq: Distinguish the law-making authority from the authority bringing the institution into effect.
xs: A new HC created under a Parliament law comes into being through **a notification issued by the President** — option **(4)** is correct.
Not a State Assembly resolution, the **CJI's** order, or the **Governor** alone.
Example: the **AP High Court** was notified by the **President** under the **AP Reorganisation Act**.
xa: The AP HC began functioning at **Amaravati** on **1 Jan 2019** — India's **25th** HC.
**Sec. 31** of the AP Reorganisation Act **2014** provides the **separate AP HC**.
**Art. 231**: Parliament may set up a **common High Court**.

n5925fa9d0e0.s: A High Court consists of a Chief Justice and such other judges as may be deemed necessary by the:
n5925fa9d0e0.x: Article 216 leaves the number to the President; it fixes no uniform strength.
xa: Sanctioned strength (**18 Sep 2025**): **1,122** for all HCs, of which **804** filled.
**30** HC judges appointed on **8 Aug 2026** (Madras **15**, Karnataka **6**).

ncd00f6e782c.s: In which country can courts not invalidate Acts of Parliament as in the US, because of parliamentary sovereignty?
ncd00f6e782c.x: Parliamentary sovereignty in the UK prevents US-style judicial review; Canada and Australia have judicial review.
xa: Origin: **USA**, **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.
India blends **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
Roots: **Sir Edward Coke** vs **King James I**.

n1991f14c813.s: The decisions taken by the President or Governor may be subjected to judicial review when they are challenged on grounds such as:
o: The personal popularity of the office-holder
Mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds
The absence of legislative approval for every executive act
n1991f14c813.x: Although constitutional protection applies to the office-holder in the manner specified by Article 361, the decisions themselves may be reviewed on grounds such as mala fides or irrelevant considerations. The review of President’s Rule in S.R. Bommai illustrates this principle.
n1991f14c813.tq: Distinguish reviewable grounds of invalidity from mere political disagreement.
xs: Decisions can be reviewed for **mala fides or reliance on irrelevant grounds** — option **(3)** is correct.
Example: President's Rule reviewed in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.
Popularity or mere policy disagreement are not grounds.
xa: **Art. 361**: the **President/Governor** personally are **not answerable** to courts.
**Art. 74(2)** / **163(3)**: ministerial advice **cannot be inquired into**.
**44th Amendment (1978)** reversed the **38th**'s non-justiciability bar.

ne1353746c75.s: Which Article bars courts from inquiring into the advice of Ministers to the President?
ne1353746c75.x: Article 74(2) is the bar for advice to the President; Article 163(3) for advice to the Governor.
xa: **No mandamus** lies against the President/Governor (TH, **29 Jan 2026**).
Their decisions may still be reviewed for **mala fides** — **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

nf868dea6ea4.s: Which one of the following is NOT an evolution genuinely attributed to the Supreme Court?
o: Exemptions to Fundamental Rights expressly written in Articles 31A to 31C and Article 33
nf868dea6ea4.x: Exemptions and restrictions relating to Fundamental Rights in Articles 31A–31C and 33 are constitutional provisions, not judicial evolutions created by the Supreme Court.
nf868dea6ea4.tq: Distinguish a court-created doctrine from provisions expressly embedded in the Constitution.
xs: **Exemptions to Fundamental Rights** in **Arts. 31A-31C and 33** are written in the Constitution itself, not evolved by the Supreme Court — option **(3)**.
