**Basic Structure** was evolved in **Kesavananda (1973)**; **continuing mandamus** and **expansion of Art. 21** are also genuine SC evolutions.
This exact point was asked in **APPSC 2017**.
xa: Other genuine SC evolutions: **PIL** and **removal of handcuffs** (prisoners' dignity).
**Continuing mandamus**: the case is kept open to **monitor compliance**.
Art. 21 expansion covered **livelihood (Olga Tellis)**, education, health and clean environment.

nf211182d1ea.s: The Ninth Schedule was added to the Constitution of India by the—
nf211182d1ea.x: The First Amendment (assent 18 June 1951) created the Ninth Schedule, following early land-reform rulings. The Fourth Amendment dealt with property compensation, the Seventh with reorganisation of States, and the 42nd was the 1976 omnibus amendment.
xs: The **1st Amendment (1951)** created the **Ninth Schedule** (assent **18 June 1951**) — option **(1)**.
It followed early **land-reform** and reservation rulings (e.g. **Kameshwar Singh**).
xa: The 1st Amendment marked **75 years** in 2026.
**38th Amendment (1975)** made satisfaction under **Arts. 123, 213, 352** non-justiciable; **44th (1978)** reversed it.
⚠ **42nd (1976)** barred HCs from reviewing central laws → **43rd (1977)** restored the power.

nindian-polity-70-1.s: The constitutional provisions relating to High Courts are contained in which Part, Chapter and range of Articles?
nindian-polity-70-1.x: High Courts are in Part VI (the States), Chapter V, Articles 214–231. The Supreme Court is in Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124–147.
nindian-polity-70-1.tq: Discriminate the Supreme Court's Articles (124–147) from the High Courts' (214–231).
n: The constitutional framework for High Courts is governed by Part VI, Chapter V of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Articles 214 to 231 deal with High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
High Courts are governed by Articles 214 to 231 in Part VI. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Supreme Court is governed by Articles 124 to 147 in Part V. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: High Courts are in **Part VI, Chapter V, Articles 214–231** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The Supreme Court is in **Part V, Chapter IV, Articles 124 to 147** — option (2).
**Article 214** provides **a High Court for each State**.
xa: **Art. 231**: **common High Court** for two or more States/UTs, established by **Parliament**.
**Art. 230**: Parliament can extend an HC's jurisdiction to a **UT** (**7th Amendment Act, 1956**).
**Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute a High Court for a **UT**.

nindian-polity-70-41.s: The strength of the Supreme Court is determined by:
nindian-polity-70-41.x: Under Article 124(1) Parliament fixes the Supreme Court's strength by law; under Article 216 the President fixes a High Court's.
n: The President of India decides and fixes the strength of judges for each High Court under Article 216. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Parliament decides the strength of the Supreme Court by law under Article 124(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 216 concerns the composition of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: ⚠ HC strength is **not** fixed by **Parliament**, the **Governor** or the **Chief Minister**.
HC strength is **not uniform** — set per workload.
Sanctioned HC strength (**18 Sep 2025**): **1,122**, of which **804** filled.

nindian-polity-70-52.s: The oath or affirmation by High Court judges is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-70-52.x: Article 219 covers the oath; Article 220 restricts practice after retirement.
n: The oath of a High Court judge is administered by the Governor of the State under Article 219. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge addresses a resignation to the President of India under Article 217(1)(a). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 220 restricts practice after a person has been a permanent High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
A High Court judge may be removed only on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The removal mechanism for High Court judges is provided under Article 217(1)(b) read with Article 124(4). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 217 concerns the appointment and conditions of office of a High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: A retired HC judge may plead only in the **Supreme Court** and **other High Courts**.
**Article 218** applies SC removal provisions to HCs.
Removal needs a **special majority** in **each House** — at least **50%** of total strength and **two-thirds** present and voting.

nindian-polity-71-24.s: Which of the following is a qualification specifically available for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge but not provided for appointment as a High Court Judge?
o: Taking an oath before a constitutional authority
Holding office until the prescribed retirement age
nindian-polity-71-24.x: Under Article 124(3)(c), a distinguished jurist can be made a Supreme Court judge. No such route exists for High Courts.
nindian-polity-71-24.tq: Recall the extra route to the Supreme Court.
n: A distinguished jurist is eligible for appointment as a Supreme Court Judge under Article 124(3)(c). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
A distinguished jurist is not eligible for appointment as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Constitution has no provision for appointing a distinguished jurist as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for Supreme Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The President of India is the appointing authority for High Court Judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **Being a distinguished jurist** is available only for the SC — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Article 124(3)(c)** makes a distinguished jurist eligible for the SC; there is **no such provision** for HCs.
Oath, retirement age and **appointment by the President** apply to both courts.
xa: HC qualification: **10 years** in **judicial office** or **10 years** as an **HC advocate**.
HC oath before the **Governor**; SC oath before the **President**.
Transfer (**Article 222**) applies only to HC judges.

nindian-polity-56-16.s: What is the method of removal of a High Court Judge?
o: Removal by a resolution of the Rajya Sabha alone
Removal by the Governor at pleasure
An order of the President following an address by Parliament
nindian-polity-56-16.x: Like a Supreme Court judge, a High Court judge is removed by the President's order after an address by Parliament (Article 217(1)). The Governor cannot remove judges.
nindian-polity-56-16.tq: Recall that both courts' judges are removed the same way.
n: A High Court Judge is removed by an order of the President following an address by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
The removal of a High Court Judge is governed by Article 217(1). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: An HC judge is removed by **an order of the President following an address by Parliament** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **address** must pass **each House** by **special majority** — at least **50%** of the **total strength** and **two-thirds** present and voting.
Grounds: **proved misbehaviour** or **incapacity**; the **Governor** has no removal power, and **Article 61** impeachment is for the **President**.
xa: Removal under **Article 217(1)(b)** read with **Article 124(4)** and **Art. 218**.
Procedure: **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.
Justice **Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the Rajya Sabha voted for removal.

nindian-polity-56-37.s: Who administers the oath of office to a Supreme Court Judge?
o: The Chief Justice of India or the senior-most Supreme Court Judge
The President of India or a person appointed by the President
nindian-polity-56-37.x: A Supreme Court judge is sworn in by the President or someone the President appoints (Article 124(6)).
n: The oath of a Supreme Court Judge is administered by the President of India or a person appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #56 · pp 150-153]
xs: The oath to an SC judge is administered by **the President of India or a person appointed by the President** — so option **(3)** is correct.
This is under **Article 124(6)**.
The **Governor** administers the oath to **HC judges** (**Article 219**), not SC judges.
xa: SC judges' **resignation** is addressed to the **President** (**Article 124(2)(a)**).
SC judges retire at **65**.
SC judges are removed by the **President's** order after Parliament's address (**Article 124(4)**).

nc8723b21816.s: The seat of the common High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh is at:
o: Leh in summer and Jammu in winter
Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer
nc8723b21816.x: The common High Court sits at Jammu in winter and Srinagar in summer.
xa: **Puducherry** → Madras HC; **Lakshadweep** → Kerala HC.
**Delhi** is a UT with its **own HC**.
**Art. 241**: Parliament may constitute an HC for a **UT**.

neff3d00b841.s: Under Article 241, a High Court for a Union Territory may be constituted by:
neff3d00b841.x: Article 241 authorises Parliament by law to constitute a High Court for a UT; the President alone has no such power.
xa: **Art. 230**: Parliament may **extend or exclude** an HC's jurisdiction over a UT (**7th Amendment, 1956**).
A new HC is created by a **Parliament law** and brought into being by **Presidential notification**.
**Delhi** has its own HC; **J&K and Ladakh** a common HC.

nf1d25a7e205.s: The Guwahati High Court has jurisdiction over Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and:
nf1d25a7e205.x: Guwahati covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh; Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura got their own HCs in 2013.
xa: Guwahati covered seven states until **23 March 2013**, when **Manipur, Meghalaya and Tripura** got own HCs.
The Telangana HC stays at **Hyderabad**.
Bifurcation took India's HC count from **24 to 25**.

nf19351ac695.s: The appointment of an acting Chief Justice of a High Court is provided under Article:
nf19351ac695.x: Article 223 covers an acting Chief Justice; 224(1) additional judges, 224(2) acting judges and 224A retired judges.
xa: Additional judges are appointed for up to **2 years**, usually made permanent in about **two years**.
**Art. 224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Retired judges sit with prior consent of the **President** and the judge.

nf58017536c3.s: Article 224A, on retired judges sitting in High Courts, was inserted by the:
nf58017536c3.x: Article 224A was inserted by the 15th Amendment, 1963; additional judges fall under Article 224(1).
xa: Additional judges are usually made permanent in about **two years** (TH, **9 Aug 2026**).

neb4725acb0b.s: Under Article 217, a Judge of a High Court is appointed by the:
o: Chief Justice of the High Court
neb4725acb0b.x: The President appoints after consulting the CJI, the Governor and, for a puisne judge, the HC Chief Justice.
xa: For a common HC, the **Governors of all states concerned** are consulted.
Proposal starts with the **HC collegium** (CJ + **2**) → SC collegium (CJI + **2**).
Qualifications: citizen + **10 years** judicial office or HC advocate.

n721c9092471.s: The procedure for removal of a High Court judge is governed by the:
n721c9092471.x: Article 218 and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 govern removal; a Governor cannot remove a judge by executive order.
xa: Grounds: **proved misbehaviour or incapacity**.
**Soumitra Sen** (Calcutta HC) resigned in **2011** after the RS voted for removal.
Motion against **G.R. Swaminathan** noticed by **107** MPs (Dec **2025**).

ne52a627041d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about proceedings against High Court judges?
o: Justice Soumitra Sen was a judge of the Calcutta High Court
Soumitra Sen resigned in 2011 after the Rajya Sabha voted for his removal
A motion against Justice G.R. Swaminathan was noticed by 107 MPs in December 2025
Yashwant Varma was formerly a judge of the Madras High Court
ne52a627041d.x: Yashwant Varma was formerly of the Allahabad High Court.
xa: Varma's inquiry report was to be tabled **despite his resignation** (LENSD **11 Jul 2026**).
Ethics codes: **1997 Restatement of Values** (**16** points) + **1999 in-house procedure**.
Removal procedure: **Art. 218** + **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.

n96a7b43a84b.s: Which one of the following best describes the scope of writ jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226?
o: It extends only to disputes arising within the physical territory of the High Court
It is confined exclusively to enforcement of Fundamental Rights
It extends to Fundamental Rights and other legal rights, including where the cause of action arises within its territory
It can be exercised only on a reference from the Supreme Court
n96a7b43a84b.x: Article 226 enables High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose. A High Court may act even when the respondent is outside its territory if the cause of action arises within it.
n96a7b43a84b.tq: Contrast the wider wording of Article 226 with the narrower purpose traditionally associated with Article 32.
xs: **Art. 226** covers **Fundamental Rights and other legal rights**, even beyond its territory **where the cause of action arises within** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not confined to its physical territory or to FRs alone, and needs no SC reference.
Writs "**for any other purpose**" make it **wider than Art. 32**.
xa: **Art. 227**: superintendence over all courts and tribunals **except military tribunals**.
PIL may be filed under **Art. 32 (SC)** or **Art. 226 (HC)**.
HCs are primarily **courts of appeal**.

n98aa272cc87.s: The High Court's superintendence under Article 227 covers:
n98aa272cc87.x: Article 227 covers administrative and judicial superintendence and may be exercised suo motu.
xa: Art. 227 excludes **military tribunals**.
It is also **revisional** in nature.
**Art. 235** vests **control** over district and subordinate courts in the **HC**.

nc8524fa1864.s: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 was enacted pursuant to the recommendations of the:
nc8524fa1864.x: The Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the report of the H.N. Sanyal Committee.
nc8524fa1864.tq: Associate the statute with the committee that directly preceded it.
xs: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee** — option **(4)** is correct.
No link to the ARC or **Sarkaria** in the notes.
xa: **Civil contempt** = wilful disobedience; **criminal contempt** = scandalising or obstructing justice.
Exceptions: **fair criticism** + **accurate reporting**.
Contempt powers: **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).

n2bef84e52a0.s: Under the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, wilful disobedience of a court's judgment or order is:
n2bef84e52a0.x: Civil contempt is wilful disobedience; criminal contempt covers scandalising or obstructing justice.
xa: The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** followed the **H.N. Sanyal Committee**.
Contempt power flows from **Court of Record** status — **Art. 129** (SC) and **Art. 215** (HC).
An HC punishes contempt of itself **and subordinate courts** (**Art. 215**).

nce59d77ce2c.s: Which State has the first fully paperless district court?
nce59d77ce2c.x: Kerala has the first fully paperless district court.
xs: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the **digitisation** push with **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **NJDG**.
xa: More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.
The **Department of Justice** web portal tracks district vacancies monthly.
Infrastructure scheme outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**.

n3b0508012e9.s: Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme for court infrastructure, the normal Centre-State funding ratio is:
n3b0508012e9.x: The normal ratio is 60:40, 90:10 for NE and Himalayan States, and 100% for UTs; it is monitored on the Nyaya Vikas Portal.
xa: It is a **Centrally Sponsored Scheme**.
Outlay: **₹5,357 crore** for **2021-26**, incl. **₹50 crore** for **Gram Nyayalayas**.
Digitisation runs through **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)**.

na9e2302abd7.s: Which Article makes legislative power subject to the provisions of the Constitution?
na9e2302abd7.x: Article 245 makes legislative power subject to the Constitution; Articles 251 and 254 deal with repugnancy.
xa: **Lack of legislative competence** is one of the **three grounds** of review.
**Art. 13**: laws inconsistent with FRs are **void**.

n16ac91f3dda.s: Which 2024 case held that delimitation decisions can be reviewed if capricious?
n16ac91f3dda.x: Kishorchandra Chhanganlal Rathod (2024) held delimitation review limited but possible if the decision is capricious.
xa: **State of Rajasthan (1977)**: SC declined a political question.
Review is **narrower than the USA** under **Art. 21**.
**Aravali Golf Club (2007)**: judges told not to encroach on other branches.

nfe1ddc8d673.s: Judicial intervention that enters the executive or legislative domain and strains separation of powers is called:
nfe1ddc8d673.x: Judicial overreach occurs when courts enter the executive or legislative domain.
xa: **Upendra Baxi**: ideal = **judicial prudence** — fill the vacuum, don't replace institutions.
Overreach concerns: "**judicial adventurism**", weak enforcement of PIL orders.

n6b7f9fb2b7c.x: Judicial dynamism is another term for judicial activism, the antithesis of judicial restraint.
xa: Restraint cases: **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** + **State of Rajasthan (1977)**.
Activism cases: **Vishaka**, **Olga Tellis**, **M.C. Mehta**.

nf81f093e256.s: A Public Interest Litigation before a High Court may be filed under Article:
nf81f093e256.x: PIL lies under Article 226 in High Courts and Article 32 in the Supreme Court.
xa: **S.P. Gupta (1981)** dealt with **locus standi**.
**Epistolary jurisdiction**: letters and postcards treated as petitions.
PIL = **SAL**, an outcome of **judicial activism**.

n524850eb381.s: Under which instrument of judicial activism does a court keep a case open to monitor compliance?
n524850eb381.x: Continuing mandamus keeps a case open to monitor compliance.
xa: **Guidelines** fill a legislative vacuum — **Vishaka (1997)** before the **POSH Act 2013**.
**Art. 142 "complete justice"**: interim remedy for legislative delay; resolves deadlocks between branches.
Judicial activism is also called **judicial dynamism**; its antithesis is **judicial restraint**.

n666479f9257.s: According to Upendra Baxi’s view, the proper role of courts in a democratic system is to:
o: Exercise executive power whenever a PIL is filed
Avoid intervention even where constitutional rights are violated
Replace democratic institutions whenever they act slowly
Fill a constitutional or institutional vacuum without replacing democratic institutions
n666479f9257.x: Upendra Baxi argued that courts should fill a vacuum rather than replace democratic institutions. Judicial prudence represents the ideal approach.
n666479f9257.tq: Identify the middle position between judicial passivity and judicial substitution.
xs: **Upendra Baxi**: courts must **fill the vacuum**, **not replace democratic institutions** — option **(4)**.
His ideal for the judiciary is **judicial prudence**.
xa: **Overreach** = courts entering the executive or legislative domain, straining **separation of powers**.
Restraint: **Aravali Golf Club (2007)** told judges not to encroach on legislative and executive functions.
Pioneers of PIL: Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.

nf0b798bbad1.s: The separate High Court of Andhra Pradesh began functioning at Amaravati on:
nf0b798bbad1.x: It began on 1 January 2019 as India's 25th High Court; the Telangana High Court stayed at Hyderabad.
xa: India has **25 High Courts**; **AP (1 Jan 2019)** is the newest.
Oldest: **Calcutta** (**2 July 1862**); Madras HC also 1862.
AP Reorganisation Act: **Sec. 30** common HC, **Sec. 31** separate AP HC, **Sec. 32** judges.

nc2da1a37c81.s: Which of the following is a criticism of judicial activism?
o: It may blur the separation of powers
It has no effect on court workload
nc2da1a37c81.x: Activism can blur separation of powers and overburden courts; wider access and executive accountability are its merits.
xa: Pendency: over **4.7 crore** cases, about **87%** in subordinate courts (as of May 2022).
Other concerns: weak enforcement of PIL orders, **flood of letter petitions**, "**judicial adventurism**".
PIL negatives: overburdened courts; increasingly **misused**.

n945684323c6.s: Which of the following is NOT a concern raised in the recent debate on revisiting PIL jurisdiction?
o: Complete abolition of access to justice
n945684323c6.x: The debate concerns misuse, overreach and weak enforcement, not abolition of access to justice.
xa: PIL misuse: **publicity**, political or personal motives.
PIL is also called **Social Action Litigation (SAL)** — an outcome of judicial activism.
**Epistolary jurisdiction**: letters, postcards and newspaper reports treated as petitions.

nindian-polity-70-3.s: The first three High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay and Madras were established in:
nindian-polity-70-3.x: The presidency High Courts came in 1862, then Agra (1866), which moved to Allahabad in 1869.
n: The first three High Courts were established in 1862. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Calcutta High Court was established in 1862. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Bombay High Court was established in 1862. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Madras High Court was established in 1862. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The High Court for the North-Western Provinces was established at Agra in 1866. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The High Court for the North-Western Provinces was shifted from Agra to Allahabad in 1869. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: **Calcutta** is the oldest (**2 July 1862**).
Oldest four: **Calcutta, Madras, Bombay, Allahabad**.
Newest: **Andhra Pradesh (1 Jan 2019)** — India now has **25 High Courts**.

nindian-polity-70-5.s: A common High Court for two or more States is provided under Article:
nindian-polity-70-5.x: Article 231 provides a common High Court; 222 covers transfer of judges.
n: A High Court is a Court of Record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 216 concerns the composition of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 222 provides for the transfer of a High Court judge from one High Court to another by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 231 concerns the establishment of a Common High Court for two or more States or Union Territories. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: Under **216** the **President** fixes each HC's strength.
Transfers are by the **President** **after consulting the CJI**.
⚠ **214** = HC for each State; **230** = UT jurisdiction; **241** = HC for a UT.

nindian-polity-70-14.s: Which Article applies certain Supreme Court removal provisions to High Court judges?
nindian-polity-70-14.x: Article 218 applies the Supreme Court's removal rules to High Court judges.
n: A High Court can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and ordinary legal rights under Article 226. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 218 applies certain Supreme Court removal provisions to High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 224 concerns the appointment of Additional Judges and Acting Judges of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 224A concerns the attendance of retired judges of High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 230 concerns the extension of High Court jurisdiction to Union Territories. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: **224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Removal of HC judges follows the **Judges (Inquiry) Act 1968**.
Bombay HC covers **Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu**; Calcutta covers **Andaman and Nicobar Islands**.

nindian-polity-70-18.s: Which High Court has jurisdiction over Puducherry?
nindian-polity-70-18.x: The Madras High Court covers Tamil Nadu and Puducherry; Kerala covers Lakshadweep.
n: The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over Maharashtra. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over Goa. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Bombay High Court has jurisdiction over Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Calcutta High Court has jurisdiction over West Bengal. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Calcutta High Court has jurisdiction over the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Kerala High Court has jurisdiction over Kerala. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Kerala High Court has jurisdiction over Lakshadweep. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Madras High Court has jurisdiction over Tamil Nadu. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Madras High Court has jurisdiction over Puducherry. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: ⚠ A&N Islands → **Calcutta HC**, not Madras (circuit bench at **Port Blair**).
**Punjab and Haryana** HC: **Punjab, Haryana, Chandigarh**.
**J&K and Ladakh** share a common HC (Jammu in winter, Srinagar in summer).

nbe1abf015ba.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the appellate jurisdiction of a High Court mentioned in the constitutional scheme?
o: The High Court is primarily a court of appeal
A death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court requires High Court confirmation
Second civil appeals are confined to questions of law
Every factual finding of a subordinate court must be reconsidered in every second appeal
nbe1abf015ba.x: A second civil appeal is limited to a substantial question of law; there is no requirement that every factual finding be reconsidered. The other three describe features of High Court appellate work.
nbe1abf015ba.tq: Find the statement that exaggerates a limited appellate power into an absolute one.
xs: "**Every factual finding** must be reconsidered in **every second appeal**" is NOT a feature — option **(4)** is the answer.
**Second civil appeals** are on **questions of law only**.
The HC is **primarily a court of appeal**, and **death sentences** of Sessions Courts need **HC confirmation**.
xa: Death-sentence confirmation is now under **BNSS 2023**, which replaced CrPC from **1 July 2024**.
**Art. 227** superintendence is also **revisional**.

n411299d2474.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about District Judges under Article 233?
o: The Governor appoints them in consultation with the High Court
A direct recruit needs seven years' standing as an advocate or pleader
Article 233 deals with the appointment of District Judges
A person already in Union or State service qualifies merely on seven years as an advocate
n411299d2474.x: Article 233 requires a direct recruit not to be already in the service of the Union or the State.
xa: **Art. 233A**: validation of certain appointments (**20th Amendment, 1966**).
**Art. 234**: other judicial officers — Governor's rules after consulting the **SPSC and HC**.
**Art. 235**: **control** over subordinate courts vests in the **HC**.

n75fb07c64da.s: Which of the following is included within the constitutional meaning of ‘District Judge’ under Article 236?
o: City civil court judges and additional, joint and assistant district judges
All members of the Supreme Court
n75fb07c64da.x: Article 236 includes judges of a city civil court and additional, joint and assistant district judges within the expression ‘District Judge’.
n75fb07c64da.tq: Test the inclusive constitutional definition rather than the ordinary administrative meaning.
xs: **Art. 236** includes **city civil court judges** and **additional, joint and assistant district judges** — option **(2)** is correct.
Magistrates come in only if the Governor applies the provisions (**Art. 237**); SC judges and the District Magistrate are outside it.
xa: The **District Judge** is the highest civil court and also **Sessions Judge**.
Appeals: **District Court → High Court**.
**Art. 233**: 7 years' standing as advocate/pleader for direct recruits.

nbfcbcada80f.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the position of a District Judge in the district judicial hierarchy?
o: The District Judge is subordinate to the District Magistrate in judicial matters
The District Judge hears only constitutional writ petitions
The District Judge is the highest civil court of the district and also functions as Sessions Judge in criminal matters
The District Judge is the lowest criminal court of the district
nbfcbcada80f.x: The District Judge is the highest civil court in the district and also exercises the powers of a Sessions Judge in criminal matters.
nbfcbcada80f.tq: Combine the civil and criminal roles instead of treating the District Judge as belonging to only one jurisdiction.
xs: The District Judge is **the highest civil court** of the district and also **Sessions Judge** in criminal matters — option **(3)** is correct.
He is not under the District Magistrate, does not hear only writs, and is not the lowest court.
Appeals go **District Court → High Court**.
xa: District Judges are appointed by the **Governor in consultation with the HC** (**Art. 233**).
**National Judicial Academy**: **Bhopal**.
More than **4 crore cases** are pending in lower courts.

ndea87e6465a.s: The National Judicial Academy is located at:
ndea87e6465a.x: The National Judicial Academy is at Bhopal; the AIJS (Article 312) has not yet been created.
xa: AIJS debate: **uniform merit-based recruitment** vs **state/HC control** + **local language** needs.
Control of subordinate courts lies with the **HC** (**Art. 235**).

ndedd09f039c.s: Which of the following correctly describes a Gram Nyayalaya?
o: It is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level
It is presided over by a High Court Judge and hears only constitutional cases
It is a permanent bench of the Supreme Court in every village
It is presided over by the District Magistrate and hears only revenue disputes
ndedd09f039c.x: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari of Judicial Magistrate First Class rank and functions as a mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level.
ndedd09f039c.tq: Identify the institution through its presiding officer, level and mobile character.
xs: A Gram Nyayalaya is presided by a **Nyayadhikari of JMFC rank** and is a **mobile court at the intermediate Panchayat level** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is not an HC/SC bench and not run by the District Magistrate.
xa: Act: **Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008** (in force **2 Oct 2009**).
First mobile court: **Punhana (Haryana), 2007**.
Funding: **₹50 crore** within the **₹5,357 crore** court-infrastructure outlay.

nfdbd80f1d02.s: The first mobile court in India was established at Punhana in:
nfdbd80f1d02.x: The first mobile court was established at Punhana in Haryana in 2007.
nfdbd80f1d02.tq: Combine the place, State and year instead of selecting a familiar judicial institution.
xs: The first mobile court was at **Punhana**, **Haryana in 2007** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Gujarat 1982** is the first **Lok Adalat** camp; **Delhi 1985** an alternative Lok Adalat date; **Bhopal** hosts the **National Judicial Academy**.
xa: Gram Nyayalayas also function as **mobile courts**.
**Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008**.

n24de7ff182e.s: The first Lok Adalat camp was held in 1982 in:
n24de7ff182e.x: The first camp was in Gujarat in 1982; a Lok Adalat award is deemed a civil court decree and is final.
xa: Basis: **Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987**.
Some notes say the first camp was in **Delhi 1985**.
**CGIT-cum-Labour Courts** also hold Lok Adalats.

nindian-polity-70-50.s: The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President after consultation with the:
o: CJI and the Union Law Minister
nindian-polity-70-50.x: For a HC Chief Justice the President consults the CJI and the Governor; for other judges also the HC Chief Justice.
n: High Court judges are appointed by the President of India by warrant under Article 217. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The Chief Justice of a High Court is appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the State. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]

Other High Court judges are appointed by the President after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor, and the Chief Justice of that High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
The composition of a High Court includes a Chief Justice and other judges appointed by the President. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 217 concerns the appointment and conditions of office of a High Court judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xa: The Governor only administers the **oath** (**Article 219**).
HC collegium: **CJ + 2**; SC side: **CJI + 2** senior-most judges.
Common HC: the **Governors of all states** concerned are consulted.

n9b902124fc2.s: The expression 'judicial review' in the Indian Constitution is:
o: Not used, though the power flows from several Articles
n9b902124fc2.x: The term is not used in the Constitution; the power flows from several Articles and is part of the basic structure.
xa: Meaning: courts test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and declare them **ultra vires / void**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.

n177bc467071.s: Judicial review in India is based on which combination of constitutional features?
o: Collective responsibility, adult suffrage and emergency powers
A written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights
An unwritten constitution, unitary government and parliamentary privilege
n177bc467071.x: Judicial review follows from India’s written Constitution, federal structure and protection of Fundamental Rights.
n177bc467071.tq: Select the combination of structural features that supports the power under examination.
xs: Judicial review rests on **a written Constitution, federalism and Fundamental Rights** — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire** of the Centre-State division and guardian of a **written, supreme Constitution**.
The other combinations (DPSPs, conventions, unwritten constitution) are not the basis in the notes.
xa: It is a **symbol of federal government** (APPSC key).
**Britain** has no review of Acts of Parliament (**parliamentary sovereignty**).
Origin: **USA** — **Marbury v. Madison (1803)**.

nc2ce5d5a03b.s: The Supreme Court’s recognition of judicial review as part of the basic structure is associated particularly with
o: Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and L. Chandra Kumar, 1997
nc2ce5d5a03b.x: The basic-structure status of judicial review is associated with Kesavananda Bharati, 1973, and was reaffirmed in the context of judicial review of tribunals in L. Chandra Kumar, 1997. Golaknath and Sajjan Singh predate the basic-structure doctrine (Minerva Mills, 1980, later reaffirmed it).
nc2ce5d5a03b.tq: Match the constitutional doctrine with its landmark cases and years.
xs: Judicial review as **basic structure** is tied to **Kesavananda Bharati, 1973** and **L. Chandra Kumar, 1997** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hussainara Khatoon (1979)** = first PIL (speedy trial); **Vishaka (1997)** = workplace harassment guidelines.
**S.P. Gupta (1981)** = locus standi; **M.C. Mehta** = environment cases.
xa: **Kesavananda (1973)** also laid down the **Basic Structure** doctrine itself.
**Madras Bar Association (2025)** struck down re-enacted tribunal conditions of the **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**.
Amendments overcoming judgments remain subject to the **basic structure**.

n6c9b61ce4e7.s: The constitutional theory underlying judicial review in India is principally the theory of:
o: Supremacy of the Constitution and limited government
Supremacy of the executive over the legislature
n6c9b61ce4e7.x: Judicial review rests on the supremacy of the Constitution and the idea of limited government. India combines elements of American judicial supremacy with British parliamentary supremacy, while Parliament remains subject to the Constitution.
n6c9b61ce4e7.tq: Reject absolute formulations and identify the constitutional limitation underlying review.
xs: The theory behind judicial review is **supremacy of the Constitution and limited government** — option **(3)** is correct.
Not unlimited judicial supremacy, absolute parliamentary sovereignty, or executive supremacy.
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
xa: ⚠ Judicial review = symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key); theory = **supremacy of the Constitution**.
Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + FRs.
SC (**17 May 2026**): **majoritarianism cannot override constitutionalism**.

n02a22c0e537.s: Judicial review in India is regarded as a symbol of which of the following?
n02a22c0e537.x: Judicial review is a symbol of federal government: courts act as umpire of the Centre-State division under a written, supreme Constitution. Parliamentary, unitary and presidential forms do not by themselves require such an umpire.
n02a22c0e537.tq: Judicial review = symbol of federalism; theory = supremacy of the Constitution.
xs: Judicial review is a symbol of **federal government** (APPSC key) — option **(2)** is correct.
Courts act as **umpire of the Centre-State division** under a **written, supreme Constitution**.
Parliamentary, unitary or presidential forms do not by themselves need such an umpire.
xa: Basis: **written constitution** + **federalism** + Fundamental Rights.
Theory: **supremacy of the Constitution / limited government**.
**Art. 131**: SC original jurisdiction in **Centre-State** disputes.

n2f73f6f03e4.s: Article 372(1) is relevant to judicial review because it concerns
o: the appointment of High Court judges
the advisory jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
n2f73f6f03e4.x: Article 372(1) provides the constitutional basis for continuing pre-Constitution laws subject to their consistency with the Constitution and judicial review.
n2f73f6f03e4.tq: Identify the historical category of laws linked to the Article.
xs: **Art. 372(1)** concerns **the review of pre-Constitution laws** — option **(1)** is correct.
HC appointments = **Art. 217**; advisory = **Art. 143**.
xa: **Art. 13** also voids pre-Constitution laws inconsistent with FRs.
**Arts. 251, 254**: **repugnancy**.
APPSC **2023** matched **137**-review, **226**-HC writs, **13**-void laws, **32**-SC writs.

n3786ed20ea0.s: Which one of the following is NOT a recognised ground of judicial review in India?
o: Contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure
Disagreement with the policy preference of the majority party
n3786ed20ea0.x: The recognised grounds include violation of Fundamental Rights, lack of legislative competence and contravention of constitutional provisions or the basic structure. Mere disagreement with political policy is not by itself a ground.
n3786ed20ea0.tq: Exclude a political preference that is not a constitutional ground of review.
xs: **Disagreement with the majority party's policy** is NOT a ground of review — option **(2)** is the answer.
The three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of constitutional provisions / Basic Structure**.
xa: Courts **avoid policy/political questions**.
**State of Rajasthan v. Union of India (1977)**: SC declined a political question → **restraint**.
Writs are **discretionary** — refused where an effective alternative remedy exists.

nc5087cd91ad.s: Article 21 of the Indian Constitution uses the expression:
nc5087cd91ad.x: Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law', while the US Constitution uses 'due process of law'.
xa: The US Supreme Court is called a "**third chamber**".
Courts in India **avoid political questions**.
Writs are **discretionary**.

n51d7f259b14.s: When a legislature responds to a judicial judgment, which of the following is constitutionally permissible?
o: Overruling the Constitution through an ordinary statute
Removing the basis of the judgment through an amendment to law, including retrospectively where valid, or amending the Constitution subject to the basic structure
Directing the judiciary to reconsider every concluded case through an executive order
Simply declaring the judgment void without changing the legal basis
n51d7f259b14.x: The legislature cannot simply overrule a judgment. It may remove the legal basis through a valid amendment, including a retrospective validating Act where appropriate, or amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure doctrine.
n51d7f259b14.tq: Distinguish changing the legal basis of a judgment from directly nullifying judicial power.
xs: The legislature may **remove the basis of the judgment** by amending the law (retrospectively if valid) or **amend the Constitution subject to the basic structure** — option **(2)** is correct.
It **cannot simply overrule** a judgment or declare it void; an executive order cannot reopen cases.
An ordinary statute cannot override the Constitution.
xa: The judicial route: **review petition** under **Art. 137**; **curative petition** as last resort.
Example: **Tribunals Reforms Act 2021** re-enacted struck-down conditions → struck down again in **Madras Bar Association (2025)**.

nac972cce836.s: The First Amendment to the Constitution in 1951 was associated with the legislative response to early rulings concerning:
o: Emergency powers and preventive detention only
nac972cce836.x: The First Amendment, enacted in 1951, followed early judicial rulings relating to land reform and reservation.
nac972cce836.tq: Link a constitutional amendment with the subjects that prompted it.
xs: The **1st Amendment (1951)** followed early rulings on **land reform and reservation** — option **(4)** is correct.
Example: **Kameshwar Singh** on land reform.
xa: Assent on **18 June 1951**; it created the **Ninth Schedule**.
Its **75 years** were marked in **2026**.
⚠ Later: **42nd** barred HC review of central laws → **43rd** restored.

nf6643842113.s: The re-enacted provisions of the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021 were struck down in 2025 in:
nf6643842113.x: The Act re-enacted conditions struck down earlier, and these were struck down again in Madras Bar Association (2025).
xa: Core rule: the legislature **cannot simply overrule** a judgment.
Valid route: **remove the basis** of the judgment via a **validating Act**.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: judicial review is **part of the basic structure**.

nindian-polity-51-1.s: What does Judicial Review primarily empower the higher judiciary to do?
o: Examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders
Hear only ordinary appeals from lower courts
Review the political wisdom of every legislative policy
Grant automatic pre-assent to all Bills
nindian-polity-51-1.x: Judicial review is the higher judiciary's power to test laws and executive orders against the Constitution and strike them down if they conflict with it. It does not judge whether a policy is wise, and it is not an ordinary appeal.
nindian-polity-51-1.tq: Discriminate testing constitutionality from judging political wisdom.
n: Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of executive orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review permits the higher judiciary to declare legislative enactments void when they contravene constitutional provisions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review permits the higher judiciary to declare executive orders void when they contravene constitutional provisions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the political wisdom of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not an ordinary appellate proceeding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the policy merits of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xs: Judicial review empowers the higher judiciary to **examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Laws or actions that contravene the Constitution are declared **void** (**ultra vires**).
Courts avoid **policy/political questions**, so it does not test political wisdom; it is not ordinary appeal.
xa: "Judicial review" is **not used** in the Constitution — it flows from **Articles 13, 32, 136, 137, 226 and 227**.
Three grounds: **violation of FRs**, **lack of legislative competence**, **contravention of constitutional provisions / Basic Structure**.
It is **part of the basic structure** (**Kesavananda 1973**; **L. Chandra Kumar 1997**).

nindian-polity-67-35.s: The doctrine of judicial review originated in which case?
o: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
Prafulla Kumar v. Bank of Commerce
nindian-polity-67-35.x: Judicial review began in Marbury v. Madison (1803), decided by Chief Justice John Marshall of the USA.
n: The Judicial Review Doctrine originated in Marbury v. Madison (1803). [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
Chief Justice John Marshall of the USA was associated with Marbury v. Madison. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 178-181]
xa: Roots: **Sir Edward Coke's** resistance to **King James I** (17th century England).
India's model is a **synthesis** of **American judicial supremacy** + **British parliamentary sovereignty**.
⚠ **UK**: **parliamentary sovereignty** — primary statutes **cannot be struck down**.

n5c99fce80ce.s: The High Courts' power to review Central laws, barred by the 42nd Amendment, was restored by the:
n5c99fce80ce.x: The 43rd Amendment (1977) restored it; the 44th (1978) reversed the 38th Amendment's non-justiciability clauses.
xa: ⚠ **42nd** barred → **43rd** restored; **38th** barred → **44th** reversed.
The **1st Amendment (1951)** followed early land-reform rulings (e.g. **Kameshwar Singh**).
Still reviewable: decisions on **mala fides** — e.g. President's Rule in **S.R. Bommai (1994)**.

n3be1c92fab5.s: Article 139A deals with the power of the Supreme Court to:
o: Issue writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights
n3be1c92fab5.x: Article 139A empowers the Supreme Court to transfer certain cases to itself.
xa: The **44th Amendment** also reversed the **38th Amendment**'s non-justiciability bar.
**Art. 137**: review of its own judgments.
**Art. 141**: SC law binding on all courts.
n3be1c92fab5.fixed: 139A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976), not the 44th

n9670337aa57.s: The description of the United States Supreme Court as a ‘third chamber’ primarily indicates its extensive role in
o: Reviewing and shaping governmental policy through constitutional adjudication
n9670337aa57.x: The expression reflects the extensive policy impact of the United States Supreme Court’s constitutional review and interpretation.
n9670337aa57.tq: Interpret the institutional metaphor rather than treating it as a literal constitutional body.
xs: "**Third chamber**" points to the US Court **reviewing and shaping governmental policy** through constitutional adjudication — option **(2)** is correct.
It flows from US "**due process of law**" review (procedural + **substantive** fairness).
The US Court does not run elections, appoint governors or prepare budgets.
xa: Indian review under "**procedure established by law**" is **narrower**.
Judicial activism also **began and developed in the USA** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).

nindian-polity-70-23.s: Which of the following is a consequence of a High Court being a Court of Record under Article 215?
o: It can exercise general advisory jurisdiction
It can appoint all subordinate court judges
It has evidentiary value and the power to punish for contempt
nindian-polity-70-23.x: As Courts of Record under Article 215, High Courts' records count as evidence, and they can punish contempt of themselves.
nindian-polity-70-23.tq: Recall what being a Court of Record means.
n: A High Court is a Court of Record under Article 215. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 215 gives High Courts evidentiary value as Courts of Record. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
Article 215 gives High Courts the power to punish for contempt. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #70 · pp 189-193]
xs: As a Court of Record, an HC's judgments have **evidentiary value and the power to punish for contempt** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Its records **cannot be questioned** when produced before a subordinate court.
HCs have **no** advisory jurisdiction and **cannot amend the Constitution**; **district judges** are appointed by the **Governor in consultation with the HC** (**233**).
xa: **Art. 215**: HC punishes contempt of itself and **subordinate courts**.
**Contempt of Courts Act, 1971**: **civil** = wilful disobedience; **criminal** = scandalising or obstructing justice.
**Art. 235**: **control** over subordinate courts vests in the **High Court**.

n12a03fb7982.s: The term 'judicial activism' was coined in 1947 by:
n12a03fb7982.x: Arthur Schlesinger Jr. coined the term in 1947; in India activism took root post-Emergency.
xa: Judicial **restraint**, its antithesis, also developed in the USA.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.
PIL era: CJI **Y.V. Chandrachud**'s tenure (**1978-85**).

neb827e7b0cc.s: In which year was privacy recognised as a fundamental right in Puttaswamy?
neb827e7b0cc.x: Puttaswamy (2017) came after post-Emergency activism, the expansion of Article 21 and governance cases like 2G.
xa: Mid-1970s: **Krishna Iyer** and **Bhagwati** opened access.
1990s cases also include the **CVC case**, **Jharkhand Assembly** case and the **Affidavit case**.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**.

n335e6a3aa7e.s: Who filed the first Public Interest Litigation case, Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, in 1979?
n335e6a3aa7e.x: Kapila Hingorani filed Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, the first major PIL case, concerning the rights of undertrial prisoners.
n335e6a3aa7e.tq: Match the landmark case with the person who initiated it.
xs: **Kapila Hingorani** filed **Hussainara Khatoon** (**1979**) — option **(2)** is correct; she is the "**Mother of PILs**".
**P.N. Bhagwati** was a **pioneer** judge of PIL; **O. Chinnappa Reddy** and **D.A. Desai** laid the base of activism — none filed the case.
xa: The case secured undertrials' right to **speedy trial**.
⚠ "Mother of PILs" = **Hingorani** (petitioner); pioneers = **Bhagwati** + **Krishna Iyer** (judges).
Bhagwati became CJI in **1985**.

n2a63bd4adf7.s: The expression ‘epistolary jurisdiction’ in the context of PIL refers to the practice of treating which of the following as petitions?
o: Only affidavits filed by government departments
Police charge sheets and audit reports
n2a63bd4adf7.x: Under epistolary jurisdiction, courts treated letters and postcards as writ petitions and also acted on newspaper reports indicating violations of rights.
n2a63bd4adf7.tq: Identify the exact forms of informal communication accepted by courts.
xs: **Epistolary jurisdiction** treats **letters, postcards and newspaper reports** as petitions — option **(3)** is correct.
It goes with relaxed **locus standi** — any public-spirited citizen can move court for others.
xa: A downside: a **flood of letter petitions** is listed among overreach concerns.
PIL = **Social Action Litigation (SAL)**.
PIL definition (APPSC **2019**): action for **public or general interest**.

na0c67ea3eae.s: Which of the following judges, apart from Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati, helped lay the foundation for judicial activism?
o: O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai
na0c67ea3eae.x: Justices O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai are identified as having laid the base of judicial activism along with the better-known PIL pioneers.
na0c67ea3eae.tq: Distinguish judicial contributors from cases and litigants.
xs: **O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai** laid the base of activism — option **(1)** is correct.
**Kapila Hingorani** was a petitioner; **M.C. Mehta**, **Hussainara Khatoon**, **S.P. Gupta** and **Vishaka** are case names.
xa: PIL pioneers: Justices **P.N. Bhagwati** and **V.R. Krishna Iyer**.
**Y.V. Chandrachud**: PIL era was his tenure (**1978-85**).
**Upendra Baxi**: ideal = **judicial prudence**.

n9097ecd0267.s: The Vishaka Guidelines were issued by the Supreme Court primarily to
o: fill a legislative vacuum relating to workplace sexual harassment
abolish the writ jurisdiction of High Courts
n9097ecd0267.x: The Vishaka Guidelines of 1997 addressed workplace sexual harassment in the absence of legislation and operated until the POSH Act, 2013.
n9097ecd0267.tq: Identify the subject of the guidelines and distinguish them from other activism cases.
xs: **Vishaka Guidelines (1997)** filled a **legislative vacuum** on **workplace sexual harassment** — option **(1)**.
They operated until Parliament passed the **POSH Act 2013**.
xa: Guidelines are one of the **instruments of activism**, along with suo motu cognisance and **continuing mandamus**.
**Coal block cancellation** and **2G** belong to the 1990s-onward governance stage of activism.
⚠ Activism cases = **Vishaka**, **Olga Tellis**, **M.C. Mehta**; restraint cases = **Aravali Golf Club (2007)**, **State of Rajasthan (1977)**.

nf9b3188457d.s: The concern relating to Article 142 in the context of judicial activism arises mainly because of which combination?
o: Its undefined expression ‘complete justice’ and the possibility of bypassing democratic scrutiny
Its complete prohibition of judicial remedies and legislative review
Its exclusive application to criminal appeals and election disputes
Its transfer of all executive powers to the Supreme Court
nf9b3188457d.x: The broad and undefined expression ‘complete justice’ under Article 142 is viewed as capable of bypassing democratic scrutiny when used expansively.
nf9b3188457d.tq: Link a constitutional provision with the specific institutional concern attached to it.
xs: The worry about **Art. 142** is its **undefined "complete justice"** and that it **bypasses democratic scrutiny** — option **(1)**.
Art. 142 is an instrument of activism: interim remedy for **legislative delay** and resolving deadlocks between branches.
xa: Other concerns of activism: **separation of powers**, weak enforcement of PIL orders, "**judicial adventurism**".
LENSD (**27 May 2026**) carried the Art. 142 debate.
**Upendra Baxi**'s ideal = **judicial prudence**.

n877c17dcb1d.s: Which of the following is generally described as creative, proactive and reform-oriented?
n877c17dcb1d.x: Judicial activism is creative and reform-oriented, while judicial review is generally interpretative and legalistic.
xa: Review asks "**Is the law valid?**"; activism asks "**Is the law just and adequate for today?**"
Instruments: **suo motu cognisance**, **continuing mandamus**, **guidelines**, **Art. 142**.

n251b6d37d55.s: The decision in Olga Tellis is primarily associated with the proposition that
o: workplace harassment guidelines are constitutionally mandatory
the right to livelihood is included within Article 21
police officers must have fixed tenure
n251b6d37d55.x: Olga Tellis (1985) recognised the right to livelihood of pavement dwellers as part of the protection afforded by Article 21.
n251b6d37d55.tq: Match the case with its specific Article 21 expansion.
xs: **Olga Tellis (1985)** brought the **right to livelihood** of pavement dwellers within **Art. 21** — option **(2)**.
Workplace harassment guidelines = **Vishaka (1997)**; privacy as a fundamental right = **Puttaswamy (2017)**.
xa: Stage **1979 to 1980s**: PIL/SAL era; Art. 21 expanded to livelihood, **education**, **health**, **clean environment**.
**S.P. Gupta (1981)**: **locus standi** relaxed.
**M.C. Mehta** cases (1980s onward): wide environmental directives.

nf7973db43bb.s: Which of the following is NOT commonly identified as a concern associated with judicial activism?
o: Weak enforcement of orders passed in public interest litigation
Reduction of delays in all other pending cases as an automatic consequence
nf7973db43bb.x: Judicial activism has been associated with concerns such as violation of separation of powers, courts doing executive work, weak enforcement of PIL orders, letter petitions and delays in other cases. Reduction of all other delays is not such a concern.
nf7973db43bb.tq: Locate the option that does not fit the established list of concerns.
xs: **Reduction of delays** in other cases is not a concern — activism actually causes **delays in other cases** — option **(2)**.
Listed concerns: violation of **separation of powers**, **courts doing executive work**, **weak enforcement** of PIL orders, flood of letter petitions.
xa: Critics also call it "**judicial adventurism**".
**PIL misuse**: publicity, political or personal motives.
**Art. 142** worry: undefined "**complete justice**" bypasses democratic scrutiny.

nd0d5d6b9b3b.s: In the case of a common High Court for two or more States, the appointment consultation involves the Governors of:
o: All States in the region, whether or not they share the court
Only the State where the principal seat is located
nd0d5d6b9b3b.x: For a common High Court, the Governors of all the States concerned are included in the consultation process.
nd0d5d6b9b3b.tq: Focus on the phrase ‘all States concerned’ and reject the location-based limitation.
xs: For a common HC, the **Governors of all the States concerned** are consulted — option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Art. 217**, the President consults the **CJI and Governor** for the CJ; for other judges, also the **CJ of that HC**.
xa: Common HCs: **Bombay**, **Punjab & Haryana**, **Guwahati**.
**Art. 231** lets Parliament set up a **common High Court**.
**Three** HCs have jurisdiction over more than one State.

n574f495309b.s: The High Court collegium that initiates appointment proposals consists of the Chief Justice and the ____ senior-most judges of that High Court.
n574f495309b.x: The HC collegium is the Chief Justice plus two senior-most judges; the SC side is the CJI plus two senior-most judges.
xa: HC Chief Justice is appointed after consulting the **CJI** and the **Governor**.
Other HC judges: after consulting the **CJI**, the **Governor** and the **Chief Justice of that High Court**.
For a common HC, the **Governors of all states** concerned are consulted.

n62348029668.s: In March 2026, the Supreme Court’s action concerning an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption was criticised by opponents as:
o: Delegated legislation by the Election Commission
A violation of Article 32 by Parliament
n62348029668.x: The Supreme Court’s ban on the NCERT chapter was criticised as censorship under Article 19. The criticism formed part of the debate on judicial overreach.
n62348029668.tq: Identify the constitutional criticism associated with a contemporary judicial action.
xs: Critics called the SC's **Mar 2026** ban on an NCERT chapter on judicial delay and corruption **censorship under Art. 19** — option **(2)**.
It is cited as a **debate example** of judicial overreach.
xa: **Overreach** strains **separation of powers**.
**Art. 142** worries: undefined "complete justice", bypassing **democratic scrutiny**.
**Upendra Baxi**: courts fill the vacuum but must not replace democratic institutions.

n43604a947e6.s: The Andhra State High Court was originally established at:
n43604a947e6.x: It was established at Guntur and shifted to Hyderabad on 1 November 1956.
xa: First CJ of the Andhra State HC: **Koka Subba Rao**.
Journey: Guntur (**1954**) → Hyderabad (**1956**) → common HC (**2014**) → **Amaravati** (**2019**).
Separate AP HC at Amaravati from **1 Jan 2019** — India's **25th** High Court.

nindian-polity-71-15.s: Who may request a retired High Court or Supreme Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge, subject to the President’s prior consent?
o: The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court
nindian-polity-71-15.x: Under Article 224A, a High Court's Chief Justice may ask a retired High Court or Supreme Court judge to sit, with the President's prior consent.
nindian-polity-71-15.tq: Recall who makes the request under Article 224A.
n: The Chief Justice of a High Court may request a retired High Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Chief Justice of a High Court may request a retired Supreme Court Judge to sit and act as a High Court Judge. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
The Chief Justice of a High Court requires the President’s prior consent for such a request. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #71 · pp 193-196]
xs: **The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court** may make the request — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under **Article 224A**, the HC **Chief Justice** may ask a **retired HC or SC judge** to sit and act as an HC judge, with the **President's prior consent**.
The judge's own consent is also needed.
xa: **224A** was inserted by the **15th Amendment, 1963**.
Additional judges (**224(1)**) serve up to **two years**, not beyond **62**.
⚠ **223** = Acting CJ; **224(1)** = Additional; **224(2)** = Acting; **224A** = Retired.

n30b40a9540a.s: The requirement that a death sentence awarded by a Sessions Court must be confirmed by the High Court is presently governed in the criminal procedural framework by the:
n30b40a9540a.x: Confirmation of Sessions Court death sentences by the High Court is now governed by the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, which replaced the CrPC from 1 July 2024. The CPC is civil procedure, the IPC is substantive criminal law, and the Contempt of Courts Act deals with contempt.
n30b40a9540a.tq: Use the current statutory replacement rather than the repealed procedural code.
xs: HC confirmation of death sentences is now governed by the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023** — option **(1)** is correct.
**BNSS 2023** replaced the CrPC from **1 July 2024**.
The **Contempt of Courts Act, 1971** deals only with contempt.
xa: HCs are primarily courts of **appeal**; second civil appeals are on **questions of law only**.
The **District Judge** also sits as **Sessions Judge** in criminal matters.

n66f5bf93a99.s: More than ____ cases are pending in the lower courts.
n66f5bf93a99.x: More than four crore cases are pending in the lower courts.
xa: Reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** and the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**.
**Kerala**: first **fully paperless district court**.
The **Department of Justice** portal tracks district vacancies monthly.

nf0fbff64d17.s: Which of the following correctly describes e-Courts Phase III?
o: It is limited to Gram Nyayalayas and excludes district courts.
It is a scheme for appointing judges to the Supreme Court.
It covers only the period 2014–2019 and replaces all High Courts.
It covers the period 2023–2027 and functions alongside the National Judicial Data Grid as a reform tool.
nf0fbff64d17.x: e-Courts Phase III covers 2023–2027 and, together with the National Judicial Data Grid, is intended to improve judicial administration and access to case information.
nf0fbff64d17.tq: Combine the duration of a programme with its institutional purpose.
xs: **e-Courts Phase III** covers **2023-27** and works alongside the **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)** as a reform tool — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **digitisation** tool — not limited to Gram Nyayalayas, not an appointment scheme, and it replaces no court.
xa: **Kerala** has the first **fully paperless district court**.
**Fast-track courts** handle paper-leak cases under the **Public Examinations (Prevention of Unfair Means) Act, 2024**.
Court infrastructure is monitored on the **Nyaya Vikas Portal**.

n1fe9c8a5b8f.s: Public Interest Litigation in India is also known as—
n1fe9c8a5b8f.x: PIL is also called Social Action Litigation (SAL); it is an outcome of judicial activism, not restraint. Class-action arbitration is a different private remedy, and 'epistolary' describes the letter-petition jurisdiction, not the name of PIL.
n1fe9c8a5b8f.tq: PIL = SAL; via Art 32/226; relaxed locus standi.
xs: PIL is also called **Social Action Litigation (SAL)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
SAL is an outcome of **judicial activism**, not judicial restraint.
"**Epistolary**" describes letter-petition jurisdiction, not PIL's name.
xa: PIL definition (APPSC **2019**): legal action for **public or general interest**.
First PIL: **Hussainara Khatoon (1979)**, filed by **Kapila Hingorani**.
Filed under **Art. 32** or **Art. 226**.

nd0e780ed880.s: As of May 2022, approximately what proportion of the more than 4.7 crore pending cases was reported to be in subordinate courts?
nd0e780ed880.x: More than 4.7 crore cases were pending, with approximately 87% reported to be in subordinate courts.
nd0e780ed880.tq: Use the magnitude and percentage together to identify the correct pendency figure.
xs: About **87%** of the **4.7 crore** pending cases were in **subordinate courts** (May 2022) — option **(1)**.
This was an **APPSC 2022 PYQ** figure.
xa: **Lower courts** have more than **4 crore** cases pending.
Reform tools: **e-Courts Phase III (2023-27)** + **National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG)**.
**Kerala**: first **fully paperless district court**.

n0b141062a6e.s: Chairpersons of tribunals are generally given the status of a:
o: Secretary to the Government of India
n0b141062a6e.x: Tribunal chairpersons get High Court judge status. They are not equated with Supreme Court judges, district judges or Secretaries to the Government of India.
xs: Tribunal Chairpersons get **High Court judge** status — option **(1)**.
It is listed among the **merits** of tribunals, with expertise, speed and low cost.
xa: CAT **Judicial members** must be qualified as **HC judges**.
CAT **Administrative members**: **Additional Secretary** level or above.
NTC (Bill 2026) Chairperson: **former SC judge** or **former HC Chief Justice**.

nea239d12679.s: Articles 323A and 323B (Part XIV-A) were inserted by the:
nea239d12679.x: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 inserted them, following the Swaran Singh Committee; the 75th Amendment added the rent and tenancy clause.
xa: **323A** = service matters; **323B** = taxation, foreign exchange, land reforms, elections and more.
**CAT (1985)** was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A.
**32nd Amendment (1973)** gave the AP Administrative Tribunal authority under **Art. 371D**.
nea239d12679.fixed: Constitution (75th Amendment) Act is of 1994, not 1993

nec9d43baa4b.s: What principle was laid down in R. Gandhi (2010) regarding tribunal members performing judicial functions?
o: They must be nominated by consumer commissions.
They must be appointed exclusively by the executive.
They must be independent of the executive.
nec9d43baa4b.x: R. Gandhi (2010) held that tribunal members performing judicial functions must remain independent of the executive.
nec9d43baa4b.tq: Identify the constitutional principle from the case rather than the appointing authority.
xs: **R. Gandhi (2010)**: tribunal members performing judicial functions must be **independent of the executive** — option **(3)**.
This fits the criticism that parent ministries administer the tribunals they litigate before.
xa: **Rojer Mathew (2019)**: first recommended the **NTC**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down **equating members with civil servants**.
Executive control via **Finance Act 2017** + the **2021 Ordinance**.

nindian-polity-72-1.s: Tribunals are governed under which Part of the Constitution?
nindian-polity-72-1.x: Tribunals are in Part XIV-A, Articles 323-A and 323-B. Part XIV covers services and Part XI Centre-State relations.
nindian-polity-72-1.tq: Discriminate Part XIV (services) from Part XIV-A (tribunals).
n: Tribunals are governed under Part XIV-A of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part XIV deals with services under the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part XIV-A deals with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tribunals are not placed in Part XI. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tribunals are not placed in Part X. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Articles 323-A and 323-B deal with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xs: Tribunals are dealt with in **Part XIV-A** (**Articles 323-A and 323-B**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Part XIV-A was inserted by the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee's** recommendations.
**Part XIV** covers **Services** (**308 to 323**); **Part XI** covers **Union–State relations**; **Part X** covers **Scheduled and Tribal Areas**.
xa: **Part IX** = Panchayats (**243 to 243-O**); **Part IX-A** = Municipalities (**243-P to 243-ZG**); **Part IX-B** = Co-operative Societies (**243-ZH to 243-ZT**).
The **75th Amendment, 1993** added the **rent/tenancy** clause (h) to Art. 323-B.
⚠ **42nd (1976)** inserted Part XIV-A; **75th (1993)** added rent/tenancy.

nindian-polity-72-41.s: Part XIV-A of the Constitution deals with:
o: Services under the Union and the States
nindian-polity-72-41.x: Part XIV-A covers tribunals; services are in Part XIV, co-operatives in IX-B and Municipalities in IX-A.
n: Part IX deals with the Panchayats. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part IX-A deals with the Municipalities. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part IX-B deals with the Co-operative Societies. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part XIV deals with services under the Union and the States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Part XIV-A deals with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xa: Part IX = **243 to 243-O**; Part IX-A = **243-P to 243-ZG**; Part IX-B = **243-ZH to 243-ZT**.
Part XIV-A was inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976** on the **Swaran Singh Committee's** advice.

n3329c29d41b.s: Which one of the following subjects is associated with Article 323B but NOT with Article 323A?
o: Service conditions in public sector undertakings
Conditions of service of State employees
n3329c29d41b.x: Land reforms are among the subjects listed under Article 323B. Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants.
n3329c29d41b.tq: Discriminate between the service-matter jurisdiction of Article 323A and the broader subject list of Article 323B.
xs: **Land reforms** is an **Art. 323B** subject — option **(2)**.
**Art. 323A** covers only **recruitment and service conditions** of public servants (Centre, states, local bodies, **PSUs**).
xa: Other 323B subjects: taxation, foreign exchange, industrial and labour disputes, urban land ceiling, **elections**, foodstuffs, **rent and tenancy**.
⚠ **323A** = **Parliament only**, no hierarchy; **323B** = **Parliament and state legislatures**, hierarchy allowed.
Both in **Part XIV-A**, inserted by the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.

n23d451c5fa5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Articles 323A and 323B?
o: Article 323B permits a hierarchy of tribunals
Article 323A deals with recruitment and service conditions of public servants
Article 323B covers subjects such as taxation, foreign exchange and industrial disputes
Article 323A permits Parliament and State Legislatures to legislate equally
n23d451c5fa5.x: Under Article 323A, Parliament alone can legislate.
xa: 323B tribunals may be set up by **Parliament and state legislatures** within their competence.
**75th Amendment, 1993** added rent and tenancy to 323B.

nindian-polity-72-14.s: Cyber appellate orders of TDSAT lie before the:
nindian-polity-72-14.x: TDSAT decides telecom, broadcasting and airport tariff disputes; its cyber appellate orders go to the High Court.
n: TDSAT adjudicates disputes in telecommunications. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
TDSAT adjudicates disputes in broadcasting. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
TDSAT adjudicates disputes in airport tariffs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Telecom appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Broadcasting appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tariff appeals lie directly to the Supreme Court on substantial questions of law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Cyber appellate orders route to the High Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xa: TDSAT was set up by the **TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000**; parent Act **TRAI Act, 1997**.
**NGT** appeals go **directly to the Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
**CAT** appeals go to a **High Court Division Bench**, not directly to the SC.

nindian-polity-72-28.s: Tribunals under Article 323A can be established by:
nindian-polity-72-28.x: Only Parliament can act under Article 323A; both Parliament and States can act under 323B.
n: Article 323-A deals with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B deals with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-A exclusively covers public service matters. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers taxation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers foreign exchange. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers industrial disputes. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers land reforms. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers ceiling on property. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers foodstuffs. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers elections to Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Article 323-B covers elections to State Legislatures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tribunals under Article 323-B can be created by Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tribunals under Article 323-B can be created by State Legislatures. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
State Legislatures can create tribunals under Article 323-B only within their respective legislative competence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
State Legislatures have no power to enact laws under Article 323-A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Parliament has exclusive power to enact laws under Article 323-A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
State Legislatures can enact tribunal laws under Article 323-B. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
State Legislatures can enact Article 323-B tribunal laws on subjects within their legislative competence. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Tribunals under Article 323-A are created only by Parliament by law. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Articles 323-A and 323-B deal with tribunals. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xa: 323-B subjects: **taxation**, **foreign exchange**, **industrial disputes**, **land reforms**, **ceiling on property**, **foodstuffs**, **elections**, **rent and tenancy**.
⚠ **323A** allows **no hierarchy**; **323B** allows a **hierarchy** (original + appellate).
Parliament used Art. 323-A to pass the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**; **State Legislatures have no power** under it.

nfb3ae0a96c5.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal (CAT) derives its legal basis from which of the following provisions?
o: Article 262 and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
Article 315 and the Central Civil Services Act, 1985
Article 323A and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
Article 323B and the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021
nfb3ae0a96c5.x: CAT is empowered by Article 323A and was established under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985. It is a statutory and quasi-judicial body.
nfb3ae0a96c5.tq: Link the constitutional enabling provision with the parent statute instead of confusing Articles 323A and 323B.
xs: CAT is empowered by **Art. 323A** and set up under the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** — option **(3)**.
**Art. 323B** covers other subjects; **Art. 262** is about **water tribunals**.
xa: CAT is a **statutory**, quasi-judicial body set up by the **Central Government**.
Set up in **1985** under PM **Rajiv Gandhi**.
Main bench at **New Delhi** + **18** outlying benches; disposal rate **92.9%**.

ne90ab1b4516.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal was set up in 1985 during the Prime Ministership of:
ne90ab1b4516.x: The CAT was set up in 1985 under Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi. It was not established during Lal Bahadur Shastri's tenure.
ne90ab1b4516.tq: Use the year–office-holder association and guard against a swapped Prime Minister trap.
xs: CAT was set up in **1985** under PM **Rajiv Gandhi** — option **(4)**.
⚠ Trap: **not Lal Bahadur Shastri** (UPSC 2009).
xa: Members from **both judicial and administrative** streams (APPSC-G1 2022).
**10th All India Conference** of CAT held in New Delhi (Sep 2025).
CAT strength: **69 Members** — **35 Judicial** + **34 Administrative**.

nf33918363cd.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the eligibility of members of the Central Administrative Tribunal?
o: Judicial Members must be district judges, while Administrative Members must have served at the level of Joint Secretary only.
Judicial Members must be serving Supreme Court judges, while Administrative Members must be serving Cabinet Secretaries.
Judicial Members must be qualified as High Court judges, while Administrative Members must have served at the level of Additional Secretary or above.
Both categories of Members must be serving members of the Union Public Service Commission.
nf33918363cd.x: Judicial Members must possess qualifications equivalent to those of High Court judges. Administrative Members require service at the level of Additional Secretary or above.
nf33918363cd.tq: Separate the judicial and administrative eligibility streams rather than applying one qualification to both.
xs: **Judicial members** qualified as **HC judges**; **Administrative members** at **Additional Secretary** level or above — option **(3)**.
They come from **both judicial and administrative** streams, not from UPSC or serving SC judges.
xa: Strength: **69 Members — 35 Judicial** (incl. Chairperson) + **34 Administrative**.
Main bench at **New Delhi** + **18** outlying benches.
Appeals lie to the **High Court (Division Bench)**, not directly to SC.
