ncd67e73df9a.s: Which one of the following correctly states the composition and bench structure of the Central Administrative Tribunal?
o: Main Bench at New Delhi, 18 benches and 69 members comprising 35 Judicial and 34 Administrative Members
Main Bench at Mumbai, 16 benches and 69 members comprising 34 Judicial and 35 Administrative Members
Main Bench at New Delhi, 18 benches and 69 members comprising 34 Judicial and 35 Administrative Members
Main Bench at New Delhi, 20 benches and 69 members comprising 35 Judicial and 34 Administrative Members
ncd67e73df9a.x: CAT has its main bench at New Delhi and 18 benches. It has 69 members: 35 Judicial Members, including the Chairperson, and 34 Administrative Members.
ncd67e73df9a.tq: Check the location, number of benches, total strength and category-wise split together.
xs: CAT: **main bench at New Delhi**, **18** benches, **69 Members** — **35 Judicial** + **34 Administrative** — option **(1)**.
⚠ The Chairperson is counted among the **35 Judicial** members.
xa: Disposal rate: **92.9%**.
Judicial members qualify as **HC judges**; administrative members are **Additional Secretary** or above.
**10th All India Conference**: New Delhi (Sep 2025).

nf2b4161bb97.s: State Administrative Tribunals are established by the Central Government:
o: Only on the recommendation of the Supreme Court
Only through a resolution of the State Legislative Council
At the request of the concerned State Government
Automatically in every State under Article 323B
nf2b4161bb97.x: A State Administrative Tribunal is set up by the Central Government at the request of the concerned State Government.
nf2b4161bb97.tq: Test the correct initiating authority and avoid swapping the Central and State roles.
xs: **SATs** are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state** — option **(3)**.
They come under **Art. 323A**, not 323B, and are not automatic in every state.
xa: **Joint** tribunals are possible for **two or more states**.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: **32nd Amendment (1973)**, **Art. 371D**.
CAT is set up by the Central Government under the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985**.

nc8502c4892a.s: The 32nd Constitutional Amendment, 1973 provided constitutional authority for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh under:
nc8502c4892a.x: The 32nd Amendment inserted the constitutional basis under Article 371D for an Administrative Tribunal for Andhra Pradesh to deal with public-service grievances.
nc8502c4892a.tq: Avoid the Article-number swap by linking the amendment with its specific regional provision.
xs: The **32nd Amendment (1973)** gave constitutional authority under **Article 371D** for the **AP Administrative Tribunal** — option **(3)**.
It handles **public-service grievances**; **Art. 323A** is the general base for CAT/SATs, **Art. 262** for water tribunals.
xa: **Water tribunals (Art. 262)**: AP in Godavari (**1969**), Krishna-II (**2004**), Vansadhara (**2010**).
**CAT (1985)** was the first tribunal under Art. 323A.
SATs are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state**.

nff5dd3bc5ef.s: The Principal Bench of the Armed Forces Tribunal is located at:
nff5dd3bc5ef.x: The Principal Bench is at New Delhi; Jaipur, Jabalpur and Guwahati have Regional Benches.
xa: Other regional benches: **Chandigarh, Lucknow, Kolkata, Chennai, Kochi, Mumbai, Srinagar**.
Parent Act: **AFT Act, 2007**; asked in **APPSC-GS 2024**.
CAT covers **civilian defence employees**, not armed forces personnel.

n3bf70acfefe.s: The National Company Law Tribunal and the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal were set up in:
n3bf70acfefe.x: NCLT and NCLAT were set up in 2016 under the framework of the Companies Act, 2013.
n3bf70acfefe.tq: Distinguish the year of the parent Act from the later year in which the tribunals were set up.
xs: **NCLT and NCLAT** were set up in **2016** — option **(3)**.
Their parent Act is the **Companies Act, 2013** — ⚠ do not confuse the Act year with the set-up year.
xa: NCLAT hears appeals from **NCLT**, plus **IBC** and **CCI** appeals.
⚠ **2007** = AFT Act; **1962** = Customs Act (CESTAT); **1993** = DRT Act.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended a **National Tribunals Commission**.

ndff699fc856.s: Which of the following functions is associated with the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT)?
o: It hears only customs and excise appeals.
It hears appeals from NCLT and also appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and from the Competition Commission of India.
It hears only income-tax appeals under Article 323A.
It hears appeals exclusively from Debt Recovery Tribunals.
ndff699fc856.x: NCLAT hears appeals from NCLT and also deals with appeals under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code and appeals from the Competition Commission of India.
ndff699fc856.tq: Identify the appellate body's wider subject jurisdiction instead of limiting it to company-law appeals alone.
xs: **NCLAT** hears appeals from **NCLT**, and also **IBC** and **CCI** appeals — option **(2)**.
Customs and excise appeals go to **CESTAT**; DRT appeals go to the **DRAT**.
xa: NCLT/NCLAT: **Companies Act, 2013**, set up **2016**.
**ITAT** hears income tax appeals, under the **Law Ministry**.
CGIT-cum-Labour Courts: **Industrial Disputes Act, 1947**; **22** courts.

n102ed6b2845.s: Appeals from the Debt Recovery Tribunals lie to the:
o: Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal
n102ed6b2845.x: Appeals from Debt Recovery Tribunals lie to the Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal (DRAT).
n102ed6b2845.tq: Use the corresponding appellate-body name and avoid swapping DRAT with other specialised appellate tribunals.
xs: Appeals from **Debt Recovery Tribunals** go to the **DRAT** (Debt Recovery Appellate Tribunal) — option **(3)**.
NCLAT hears **NCLT**, IBC and CCI appeals; CESTAT customs/excise; CAT service matters.
xa: DRT parent Act: **Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993** (Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act, 1993).
Art. 323B allows a **hierarchy** (original + appellate) of tribunals.
NCLT/NCLAT set up **2016** under the **Companies Act, 2013**.

nde2e524430e.s: The National Sports Tribunal, notified under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, provides for appeals to the:
nde2e524430e.x: Appeals from the National Sports Tribunal lie to the Supreme Court.
nde2e524430e.tq: Test the appellate forum and avoid confusing it with the High Court review route generally applicable to tribunals.
xs: Appeals from the **National Sports Tribunal** lie to the **Supreme Court** — option **(2)**.
It is notified under the **National Sports Governance Act, 2025**.
xa: **West Bengal**: EC set up **19 Appellate Tribunals** under retired HC judges for roll disputes after the **SIR**.
**Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026**: passed **10-11 Aug 2026**; creates the **NTC**.
Tribunals remain **subject to HC judicial review**.

nindian-polity-72-13.s: The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal was established under which enactment?
nindian-polity-72-13.x: TDSAT was set up by the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000, which amended the original TRAI Act of 1997.
nindian-polity-72-13.tq: Discriminate the 1997 TRAI Act from the 2000 amendment.
n: The Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal was established under the TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
The original parent legislation of TDSAT was the TRAI Act, 1997. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xs: **TDSAT** was set up by the **TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **TRAI Act, 1997** is only the parent Act that the 2000 amendment changed.
**NGT Act, 2010** created the **National Green Tribunal**; the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** created the **CAT**.
xa: TDSAT decides disputes in **telecommunications**, **broadcasting** and **airport tariffs**.
Telecom, broadcasting and tariff appeals go **directly to the Supreme Court** on substantial questions of law.
⚠ TDSAT's **cyber** appellate orders go to the **High Court**.

nindian-polity-72-16.s: The National Green Tribunal was established under which Act?
nindian-polity-72-16.x: The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body set up under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
nindian-polity-72-16.tq: Recall the NGT's Act and year.
n: The National Green Tribunal is a statutory body. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
The National Green Tribunal was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xs: The **National Green Tribunal** was set up under the **National Green Tribunal Act, 2010** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is a **statutory** body; the **Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007** created the AFT, the **Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985** the CAT, and the **TRAI (Amendment) Act, 2000** the TDSAT.
xa: NGT is guided by **natural justice** and **not bound** by the **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908**.
Appeals against NGT orders go **directly to the Supreme Court** within **90 days**.
⚠ AFT has benches at **Jaipur, Jabalpur, Guwahati** but **no bench at Bhopal** (APPSC-GS 2024).

nindian-polity-72-18.s: Appeals against orders of the National Green Tribunal lie directly to the Supreme Court within:
nindian-polity-72-18.x: Appeals against NGT orders go straight to the Supreme Court, within 90 days.
n: Appeals against National Green Tribunal orders lie directly to the Supreme Court. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
Appeals against National Green Tribunal orders must be filed within 90 days. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xs: Appeals against **NGT** orders lie **directly to the Supreme Court** within **90 days** — option **(1)** is correct.
The NGT is a **statutory** body under the **NGT Act, 2010**.
xa: NGT is **not bound** by the **Code of Civil Procedure, 1908**; it follows **natural justice**.
**TDSAT** telecom, broadcasting and tariff appeals also go **directly to the Supreme Court**.
⚠ **CAT** appeals go first to a **High Court Division Bench**, not directly to the SC.

n8fb1ec8781f.s: Which of the following is NOT a merit of administrative tribunals?
o: Compulsory application of the full Civil Procedure Code
n8fb1ec8781f.x: Tribunals follow natural justice rather than the full Civil Procedure Code; expertise, speed and lower cost are their merits.
xa: CAT procedure: **not bound by the CPC**, nominal filing fee, parties can appear **in person**.
Chairpersons get **HC judge** status.
Nature: **quasi-judicial** — between an executive body and a court.

nc149e0c30fb.s: Tribunals for elections and foodstuffs are associated with Article:
nc149e0c30fb.x: Elections and foodstuffs fall under Article 323B; Article 323A covers service matters with one tribunal for the Centre and each State.
xa: 323B allows a **hierarchy** (original + appellate).
**SATs** are set up by the **Central Government** at the **request of the state**; **joint** tribunals for two or more states.
CAT was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A (**1985**).

n2be13c67128.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal has no original jurisdiction over service disputes of:
n2be13c67128.x: CAT covers Central civil servants, AIS officers and civilian defence employees, not private-sector employees.
xa: ⚠ CAT covers civilian defence employees, **not armed forces personnel** — they go to the **Armed Forces Tribunal**.
AFT parent Act: **AFT Act, 2007**; principal bench **New Delhi**.
CAT appeals lie to the **High Court (Division Bench)**.

n7cbdb5fadd1.s: Which of the following constitutional provisions were struck down in L. Chandra Kumar as exclusion clauses?
n7cbdb5fadd1.x: The Supreme Court struck down the exclusion clauses contained in Article 323A(2)(d) and Article 323B(3)(d).
n7cbdb5fadd1.tq: Check both the Article numbers and their sub-clauses, since a nearby provision is a likely trap.
xs: SC struck down exclusion clauses in **Articles 323A(2)(d)** and **323B(3)(d)** — option **(1)**.
These clauses had excluded the courts' jurisdiction over tribunal matters.
xa: Holding: judicial review under **Arts. 32 and 226** = **basic structure**.
Route: tribunal → **High Court (Division Bench)** → SC.
⚠ **Sampath Kumar (1987)**: tribunals may replace HCs; **Chandra Kumar (1997)**: only **supplement**.

n91cdc04c1f7.s: In relation to the High Courts, tribunals:
o: Supplement them but do not replace them
n91cdc04c1f7.x: Because judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 is basic structure, tribunals supplement but cannot replace the High Courts.
xa: Tribunal decisions go to the **High Court (Division Bench)**, not directly to SC.
Significance: faster, expert adjudication, but **subject to HC judicial review**.

n2882d1a47c1.s: The National Tribunals Commission was first recommended in which case?
n2882d1a47c1.x: The National Tribunals Commission was first recommended in the Rojer Mathew case of 2019.
n2882d1a47c1.tq: Link the recommendation to the correct case and year instead of the later implementation discussion.
xs: **Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended an independent **National Tribunals Commission (NTC)** — option **(2)**.
**R. Gandhi (2010)** dealt with **independence** of members; **Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** ordered an NTC within four months.
xa: NTC under **Bill 2026**: HQ **New Delhi**; **5** members.
NTC tenure: **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier.
NTC role: tribunal **appointments**, **performance review**, **disciplinary inquiries**.

n8689fc24153.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Supreme Court's Madras Bar Association ruling of November 2025?
o: It struck down the four-year tenure for tribunal members
It ordered a National Tribunals Commission within four months
It required the Search-cum-Selection Committee to send two names per vacancy
It struck down the minimum appointment age of 50 for tribunal members
n8689fc24153.x: The two-name arrangement was struck down; it is now one name per vacancy.
xa: It also struck down **equating members with civil servants** and **restored the earlier framework**.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended the NTC.
**Bill 2026** NTC: HQ **New Delhi**; tenure **5 years or age 70**.

nd3124fd7c6a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about tribunals?
o: They are intended to provide faster adjudication
They bring specialised expertise into dispute resolution
Parent ministries may face a conflict of interest in administering them
They are completely outside the supervisory jurisdiction of constitutional courts
nd3124fd7c6a.x: Tribunals remain subject to judicial review by the High Courts.
xa: Other criticism: **vacancies**; **tenure fights** with the SC.
**CDI** proposes the **Law Ministry** administer tribunals.
**L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**: judicial review under **Arts. 32 and 226** = basic structure.

nindian-polity-72-5.s: Which case held that judicial review by High Courts (Articles 226/227) and the Supreme Court (Article 32) is part of the Basic Structure?
nindian-polity-72-5.x: L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India (1997) so held.
n: The Supreme Court decided L. Chandra Kumar v. Union of India in 1997. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
The power of judicial review of High Courts under Article 226 is an integral part of the Basic Structure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
The power of judicial review of High Courts under Article 227 is an integral part of the Basic Structure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
The power of judicial review of the Supreme Court under Article 32 is an integral part of the Basic Structure. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #72 · pp 196-199]
xa: Tribunals **supplement** HCs and do not replace them.
⚠ **S.P. Sampath Kumar (1987)** said tribunals may replace HCs if an equally effective substitute; **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)** reversed this.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** and **Minerva Mills (1980)** also treat judicial review as an inviolable part of the Basic Structure.

nindian-polity-51-10.s: Judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 cannot be abrogated by Parliament even through Article:
nindian-polity-51-10.x: Being part of the basic structure, judicial review cannot be removed even by amendment under Article 368.
n: In Kesavananda Bharati in 1973, Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Minerva Mills in 1980 reaffirmed that Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 is an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Parliament cannot abrogate Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 even through Article 368. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not vested in the Supreme Court alone. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: This was held in **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)**, **Minerva Mills (1980)** and **L. Chandra Kumar (1997)**.
Constitutional amendments themselves are subject to judicial review on the **Basic Structure** touchstone.

n92e5700194f.s: After the abolition of the Film Certification Appellate Tribunal, the Intellectual Property Appellate Board and the Airport Appellate Tribunal, their functions were primarily shifted to the:
n92e5700194f.x: The functions of the dissolved appellate tribunals were moved to the High Courts.
n92e5700194f.tq: Test the institutional destination of transferred functions.
xs: Functions of the abolished tribunals moved to the **High Courts** — option **(4)**.
Abolished: **Film Certification Appellate Tribunal**, **IPAB**, **Airport Appellate Tribunal** (**Tribunals Reforms Act 2021**).
xa: Also abolished: **Authority for Advance Rulings (Customs)** and **Plant Varieties Protection Appellate Tribunal**.
2021 Act: Chairperson up to **70**; members up to **67**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down its re-enacted conditions.

n145cb828627.s: The Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026 was passed by the Lok Sabha on 10 August 2026 and by the Rajya Sabha on:
n145cb828627.x: It passed the Rajya Sabha on 11 August 2026; it repeals the 2021 Act and creates a National Tribunals Commission.
xa: Moved by Law Minister **Arjun Ram Meghwal**.
**Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** had ordered an NTC within **four months**.
NTC: HQ **New Delhi**, **5** members, tenure **5 years or age 70**.

nfce3926ee73.s: In March 2026, the Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals headed by retired High Court judges to hear disputes relating to the electoral rolls of which State after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR)?
nfce3926ee73.x: The Election Commission set up 19 Appellate Tribunals under retired High Court judges for West Bengal roll disputes after the SIR. Bihar, Assam and Kerala are not linked to these tribunals.
xs: The EC set up **19 Appellate Tribunals** under **retired HC judges** for **West Bengal** roll disputes after the **SIR** — option **(3)**.
Reported in TH, **22 Mar 2026**.
xa: **National Sports Tribunal**: **National Sports Governance Act, 2025**; appeals to the **SC**.
Proposal: universal **"Zero FIR"-style filing** for tribunals.
**Tribunals Reforms Bill 2026** creates the **NTC**.

n164c3ac7af3.s: Under the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2021, which one of the following correctly describes the tenure and age framework?
o: Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; all members up to 70 years
Tenure of four years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; Chairperson up to 70 years and members up to 67 years
Tenure of five years; minimum appointment age of 45 years; Chairperson up to 67 years
Tenure of three years; minimum appointment age of 50 years; members up to 65 years
n164c3ac7af3.x: The 2021 framework prescribed a four-year tenure, a minimum appointment age of 50 years, a maximum age of 70 years for the Chairperson and 67 years for members.
n164c3ac7af3.tq: Split the option into tenure, minimum age and maximum-age components.
xs: 2021 Act: **4 years** tenure; minimum age **50**; Chairperson up to **70**, members up to **67** — option **(2)**.
⚠ Tenure was 4 years, not 5 or 3, and minimum age 50, not 45.
xa: **Madras Bar Association (Nov 2025)** struck down **minimum age 50** and **4-year tenure** (made **5 years**).
**Bill 2026 NTC** members: **5 years or age 70**.
Search-cum-Selection Committee now sends **one name** per vacancy.

ndd6f3f5b501.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the National Tribunals Commission proposed in the Tribunals Reforms Bill, 2026?
o: Its headquarters is proposed at New Delhi
Its Chairperson must be a serving judge of the Supreme Court
Its functions include appointments, performance review and disciplinary inquiries
It is to have two judicial and two technical members besides the Chairperson
ndd6f3f5b501.x: The Chairperson may be a former Supreme Court judge or a former High Court Chief Justice, not necessarily a serving SC judge.
xa: Technical members need **25+ years'** experience.
Tenure: **5 years or age 70**, whichever is earlier.
**Rojer Mathew (2019)** first recommended an NTC.

n27674c5fd84.s: The Central Administrative Tribunal was established in:
xa: CAT (**1985**) was the **first** tribunal under Art. 323A.
**AP Administrative Tribunal**: **Art. 371D** (**32nd Amendment**).
CAT was set up under PM **Rajiv Gandhi**.

nba9530bc70d.s: Which one of the following is correct about the United Kingdom's constitutional system?
o: Parliament holds all law-making power, reflecting its unitary character.
It was formed by a compact among States.
Residual powers are divided between the centre and the provinces.
The judiciary distributes legislative subjects among the units.
nba9530bc70d.x: The United Kingdom is a unitary country in which Parliament holds all law-making power.
xa: Unitary: one supreme central government; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
**Britain** has no judicial review over Acts of Parliament (parliamentary sovereignty).
India's parliamentary form follows the **British model**: nominal head = **President**.

n16b09795732.s: Which one of the following is NOT a characteristic of a unitary form of government?
o: Local units being creations of the central government
Local units exercising powers delegated by the Centre
A constitutional division of powers between the Centre and the local units
n16b09795732.x: A unitary government does not constitutionally divide sovereign powers between the Centre and local units. Local units derive their authority from the central government.
n16b09795732.tq: Find the statement that belongs to federalism rather than unitary government.
xs: A **constitutional division of powers** is **not** a unitary feature — it marks a federation — option **(4)**.
Unitary: **one supreme central government**; local units are its **creations** with **delegated powers**.
xa: Federalism: **sharing of power** between Union and States, each supreme in its sphere, with an **independent umpire**.
**Confederation**: loose league of sovereign States that keep the **right to secede**.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

n33c0cee800e.s: Which of the following is NOT a merit of a unitary government?
o: Maximum accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments
n33c0cee800e.x: Uniform laws, quick decisions and a strong response to crises are merits of a unitary system. Accommodation of regional diversity through autonomous governments is more characteristic of federalism.
n33c0cee800e.tq: Separate the advantages of centralisation from the advantages of regional autonomy.
xs: **Accommodating regional diversity** through autonomous governments is not a unitary merit — option **(3)**.
Unitary merits: **uniform laws and policy**, **quick decisions**, **strong crisis response**.
xa: Demerits: **over-centralisation**; local needs neglected; poorly suited to **large, diverse countries**.
**Holding-together** federations divide power to hold **diversity** together — e.g. **India**, Spain, Belgium.
India = "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

nd90a2c44e7a.s: Federalism is a system in which:
o: all power is concentrated in one central authority
the Union and States share power, each supreme in its own sphere under a written Constitution
sovereign States form a loose league with a right to secede
local units exercise only powers delegated by the Centre
nd90a2c44e7a.x: Federalism divides powers constitutionally between the Union and the States, each supreme in its own sphere, with an independent umpire to settle disputes.
xa: This was the answer in **APPSC-GS 2018**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Essential federal feature: **independence of the judiciary** to settle Centre-State disputes (UPSC 2021).

n8bff995a277.s: The States and Union Territories of India are specified in which constitutional Schedule?
n8bff995a277.x: The First Schedule specifies the States and Union Territories of India. The Fourth Schedule deals with allocation of seats in the Council of States.
n8bff995a277.tq: Discriminate between the First Schedule’s territorial listing and nearby Schedule numbers with different subjects.
xs: States and UTs are specified in the **First Schedule** — option **(1)**.
The **Fourth Schedule** allots Rajya Sabha seats; the **Seventh** has the three Lists.
xa: **Art. 1(1)**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules** (**Art. 4**).
Rajya Sabha seats by population: **Uttar Pradesh 31**, small States **1**.

n275857c08d5.s: In the Indian constitutional scheme, the federal system can become unitary during an emergency
o: only with the consent of every State Legislature
only after a formal amendment of the Constitution
only after abolition of the Rajya Sabha
without a formal amendment of the Constitution
n275857c08d5.x: An emergency can substantially centralise the constitutional system and make it operate in a unitary manner without a formal constitutional amendment.
n275857c08d5.tq: Distinguish an operational change during emergency from a formal constitutional amendment.
xs: In an **Emergency** the federation becomes **unitary without a formal amendment** — option **(4)**.
This is a **unique feature** of **Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360)**.
xa: Ambedkar: "**federal in normal times and unitary in emergencies**".
National Emergency: Parliament may legislate on **State List** matters (**Art. 250**).
Financial Emergency (**Art. 360**): **never declared**.

nb742f99943d.s: Which of the following is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution?
nb742f99943d.x: Single citizenship is a unitary feature; dual polity and bicameralism are federal features.
xa: Emergency (**Arts. 352-360**) turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.
USA has **dual** citizenship; India **single**.
**Rajya Sabha** = Upper House for States, but seats are **by population** (unequal representation).

nde492e6e8a0.s: An independent judiciary acting as umpire in Union-State disputes is regarded as:
o: a unitary feature of the Constitution
a Directive Principle of State Policy
nde492e6e8a0.x: An independent judiciary can act as an impartial umpire in Centre-State disputes, which is regarded as an essential feature of federalism.
xa: Federalism needs an **independent umpire** under a written constitution.
The **Supreme Court** acts as **guardian** of the Constitution.
**S.R. Bommai (1994)**: federalism is part of the **basic structure**.

n60e5b0bd12b.s: K.C. Wheare gave which fuller description of the Indian constitutional system?
o: A unitary state with subsidiary federal features
A presidential state with subsidiary federal features
A confederation with subsidiary unitary features
A federal state with subsidiary unitary features
n60e5b0bd12b.x: Wheare described India as a unitary state with subsidiary federal features rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features.
n60e5b0bd12b.tq: Discriminate between the reversed federal–unitary formulations.
xs: **K.C. Wheare**: India is "**a unitary state with subsidiary federal features**" rather than a federal state with subsidiary unitary features — option **(1)**.
He is the standard answer for "**quasi-federal**".
xa: Wheare was a **British constitutional expert**.
Distractors in PYQs: **Ambedkar**, **Austin**, **Appleby**, **Morris-Jones**, **Sachchidananda Sinha**.
**Ivor Jennings**: "federation with a **strong centralising tendency**" (APPSC-G2 2025).

n69d7795d372.s: 'Federal in structure with unitary features' best describes the constitutional system of:
n69d7795d372.x: India is described as federal in structure with unitary features and as a Union of States.
xa: Debate labels: **"quasi-federal"** / federal system with **unitary bias**.
Media label: "**federal in structure, unitary in spirit**" (TH, 26 Mar 2026).
India is a **holding-together** federation (with Spain, Belgium); **USA**, Switzerland, Australia are **coming-together**.
Supreme Court: "**fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements**".

n406a8e51237.s: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973), the federal character of the Constitution was held to be:
o: one of the basic features of the Constitution
n406a8e51237.x: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) listed the federal character among the basic features of the Constitution.
xa: **State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962)**: Constitution **not truly federal**.
**Bommai (1994)**: federalism part of the **basic structure**; **floor test**.
**Minerva Mills** reopened judicial review barred by the **38th Amendment**.

n39f6ebd2306.s: The Supreme Court has described the Indian Constitution as:
o: purely federal with no unitary features
fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements
purely unitary with a nominal federal distribution
n39f6ebd2306.x: The Constitution has been described as fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements, reflecting a federal distribution alongside strong centralising provisions.
xa: **State of West Bengal (1962)**: **not truly federal**; States **not sovereign**.
**Kesavananda (1973)** and **Bommai (1994)**: federal character is a **basic feature**.
Official label: **"federal in structure with unitary features"** (IYB 2026).

n3d7b9a918d7.s: Which Article enables Parliament to legislate on a subject in the State List when the Rajya Sabha declares that it is necessary in the national interest?
n3d7b9a918d7.x: Article 249 empowers Parliament to legislate on a State List subject following a Rajya Sabha resolution in the national interest.
n3d7b9a918d7.tq: Identify the Article from the specific constitutional trigger.
xs: **Article 249** lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject after a **Rajya Sabha** resolution in the national interest — option **(4)**.
The resolution needs **2/3 of members present and voting** and is valid **1 year**, renewable.
**Art. 250** = State List law during **National Emergency**; **Art. 356** = **President's Rule**.
xa: Laws under **Art. 250** lapse **6 months** after the emergency ends.
**Part XVIII (Arts. 352-360)** makes the federation **unitary without a formal amendment**.
Under Art. 356, Parliament/President exercise the **State's powers**.

nce2f77a71bf.s: Which of the following conditions is required for continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year?
o: A special majority in the Rajya Sabha alone
A National Emergency in operation and certification by the Election Commission
A resolution of the Inter-State Council
nce2f77a71bf.x: Continuation of President’s Rule beyond one year requires that a National Emergency is in operation and that the Election Commission certifies the difficulty of holding elections in the State.
nce2f77a71bf.tq: Identify the additional safeguards attached to extension beyond the normal period.
xs: President's Rule beyond **1 year** needs a **National Emergency** in operation plus **ECI certification** (**Art. 356(5)**) — option **(3)**.
Approval is within **2 months** by **simple majority**; maximum **3 years**.
xa: Ground: **failure of constitutional machinery** in a State; also **Art. 365**.
**One Nation, One Election** deferrals could clash with **Art. 356(5)** limits (TH 9 Mar 2026).
**S.R. Bommai (1994)** made Art. 356 proclamations **open to judicial review**.
AP under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).

n417e7fe408c.s: The resolution authorising Parliament to legislate on a State List matter in the national interest is passed by:
o: the Rajya Sabha by two-thirds of members present and voting
the Rajya Sabha by a majority of the total membership
the Lok Sabha by a simple majority
both Houses by a special majority
n417e7fe408c.x: Article 249 requires a resolution of the Rajya Sabha supported by two-thirds of the members present and voting. The Lok Sabha does not participate in passing this resolution.
n417e7fe408c.tq: Separate the required House from the exact form of majority.
xs: The **Art. 249** resolution is passed by the **Rajya Sabha** by **2/3 of members present and voting** — option **(1)**.
It lets Parliament legislate on a **State List** subject in the **national interest**.
The resolution is valid **1 year**, renewable.
xa: **Art. 250**: Parliament legislates on State List during **National Emergency**; laws lapse **6 months** after it ends.
**Rajya Sabha** represents States — **bicameralism** is a federal feature.
These provisions turn the federation **unitary without a formal amendment**.

n45d0250aaaf.s: As part of asymmetric federalism, the administration of Scheduled Areas is provided for in which Schedule of the Constitution?
n45d0250aaaf.x: The Fifth Schedule deals with the administration of Scheduled Areas. The Fourth Schedule allocates Rajya Sabha seats, the Seventh Schedule holds the three legislative Lists, and the Tenth Schedule deals with anti-defection.
xs: Administration of **Scheduled Areas** is in the **Fifth Schedule** — option **(2)**.
The **Fourth Schedule** allots **Rajya Sabha** seats; the **Seventh Schedule** has the three legislative lists.
xa: Other asymmetric provisions: **Art. 370** (J&K) and **Arts. 371 to 371J**.
**Art. 371D**: Andhra Pradesh.
**First Schedule** lists States and UTs (**Art. 1**).

n49e17c0ce54.s: The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, which was defeated in the Lok Sabha, proposed to increase the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to:
n49e17c0ce54.x: The Bill proposed increasing the maximum strength of the Lok Sabha from 550 to 850.
n49e17c0ce54.tq: Test the exact numerical change rather than the related seat-freeze debate.
xs: The **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026** proposed raising the Lok Sabha maximum from **550 to 850** — option **(4)**.
The **Lok Sabha defeated** the Bill (LENSD 20 May 2026).
It proposed **+50% seats for every State**.
xa: The debate was framed around the **1971** seat freeze and **southern States**.
AP's seats would have risen **25 to 38**.

n5e63333dd7a.s: Under the proposed formula in the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026, the number of Lok Sabha seats for Andhra Pradesh was to rise from 25 to:
n5e63333dd7a.x: The proposed 50 per cent increase would have raised Andhra Pradesh’s Lok Sabha seats from 25 to 38.
n5e63333dd7a.tq: Apply the stated percentage formula to the State-specific figures.
xs: AP's Lok Sabha seats were to rise from **25** to **thirty-eight** (**38**) under the **+50%** formula — option **(4)**.
Source: TH **17 Apr 2026**, on the **Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026**.
xa: The Bill proposed Lok Sabha max **550 to 850**; it was **defeated** in the Lok Sabha.
Debate: the **1971** seat freeze and southern States.
**Art. 371D**: AP's special provisions.

nindian-polity-50-1.s: Under which Part of the Constitution are the Emergency Provisions contained?
nindian-polity-50-1.x: The emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352–360. Part XX is amendment and Part XVI covers reservations for SCs, STs and others.
nindian-polity-50-1.tq: Recall Part XVIII and its Articles 352 to 360.
n: Emergency provisions are governed under Part XVIII of the Constitution. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Emergency provisions are covered by Articles 352 to 360. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xs: Emergency provisions are in **Part XVIII** (**Articles 352 to 360**) — option **(4)** is correct.
Their unique feature: the federation becomes **unitary without a formal amendment**.
xa: Three types: **National Emergency (Art. 352)**, **President's Rule (Art. 356)**, **Financial Emergency (Art. 360)**.
**K.M. Nambiar** called the President's emergency powers a "**fraud on the Constitution**".
⚠ "Art. 311 - Financial Emergency" is a mismatch; Financial Emergency is **Art. 360**.

ndb89749542d.s: The expression “Elephantine size” in relation to the Indian Constitution was used by
ndb89749542d.x: H.V. Kamath referred to the Indian Constitution as having an “Elephantine size.”
ndb89749542d.tq: Match the distinctive quotation with its author.
xs: **H.V. Kamath** used "**Elephantine size**" for the Constitution — option **(4)**.
This was asked in **APPSC GS 2018**.
xa: **Carl Friedrich**: India is "not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope" (APPSC-G1 2022).
**K.C. Wheare**: "**quasi-federal**".
**Ambedkar**: "**not in a tight mould of federalism**".

n81feb1ce771.s: Who described the Indian Constitution as 'quasi-federal'?
n81feb1ce771.x: K.C. Wheare called it quasi-federal; Morris Jones used 'bargaining federalism' and Austin 'cooperative federalism'.
xa: ⚠ **Wheare – Jennings – Austin – Morris-Jones – Appleby** = **quasi-federal – centralising tendency – cooperative – bargaining – extremely federal**.
**Paul Appleby** called India **"extremely federal"**.
**H.V. Kamath** spoke of the Constitution's **"elephantine size"** (APPSC GS 2018).
**Harold Laski** has no India-specific label in the notes — treat him as a distractor.

nc35d5076d4b.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a confederation from a federation?
o: A confederation is made of sovereign States that retain the right to secede.
A federation is a temporary league of sovereign States.
A confederation always has a stronger centre than a federation.
A federation needs no written division of powers.
nc35d5076d4b.x: A confederation is a loose league of sovereign States that generally keep the right to secede, while a federation creates a constitutional division of powers.
xa: **Ambedkar**: in India **no State has the right to secede** → Union is **indestructible**.
**Unitary**: units draw power from the Centre.
Coming-together federations: **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.

n04284562aea.s: How does the origin of Indian federalism differ from that of the USA?
o: The USA was first unitary; India was formed by an agreement among States
The USA was formed by integration of States; India moved from a unitary colonial system to a federal one
Both arose from the break-up of unitary systems
Both were created by amendments made by their central governments
n04284562aea.x: The US federation was formed by agreement and integration of States, while India converted a unitary colonial set-up into a federal one, giving it a centripetal bias.
xa: ⚠ **Integration** = USA (**coming together**); **disintegration** = India (**holding together**).
Framed after Partition + integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**.
USA = "indestructible Union of **indestructible** states"; India = of **destructible** States.

nf990f7ae2b2.s: Which historical circumstances particularly encouraged the framers of the Constitution to adopt a strong centralising design?
o: The prior existence of a fully developed confederation
The aftermath of Partition and the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States
The peaceful integration of only a few provinces before Independence
The absence of linguistic and cultural diversity
nf990f7ae2b2.x: The Constitution was framed after Partition and during the integration of 14 provinces and more than 500 princely States. In that context, centralisation was viewed as indispensable for national integration.
nf990f7ae2b2.tq: Link constitutional design to the historical context in which it was adopted.
xs: Framed after **Partition** and integration of **14 provinces and 500+ princely States**, centralisation looked **indispensable** — option **(2)**.
This is the **national-integration design** (TH 17 Feb 2026).
xa: India = **holding-together** federation with a **stronger Centre**.
**K. Santhanam**: Union's strength lies in refusing functions that do not belong to it.
Official label: "**federal in structure with unitary features**" (IYB 2026).

n5ec1ffc166e.s: Which of the following countries represents a coming-together federation?
n5ec1ffc166e.x: Switzerland is a coming-together federation in which independent States or units pool sovereignty while retaining equal power. India, Spain and Belgium are examples of holding-together federations.
n5ec1ffc166e.tq: Separate examples of the two federation types rather than relying only on their definitions.
xs: **Switzerland** is a **coming-together** federation — option **(4)**.
**India**, **Spain** and **Belgium** are **holding-together** federations.
xa: Coming-together: independent States **pool sovereignty**, keep **equal power** — **USA**, Switzerland, Australia.
Holding-together: large country divides power to hold **diversity** together; **stronger Centre**.
⚠ USA = **integration**; India = **disintegration** (CDI view).

ncfa3b19b0e1.s: Which of the following subjects is dealt with by Article 2 of the Constitution?
o: Admission or establishment of new States not part of India
Formation of new States and alteration of existing State boundaries
Amendment of the Constitution through the special procedure
ncfa3b19b0e1.x: Article 2 concerns the admission or establishment of new States into the Union, particularly territories not already part of India.
ncfa3b19b0e1.tq: Separate Article 2, concerning admission or establishment, from Article 3, concerning existing States.
xs: **Art. 2** = **admission or establishment of new states** not part of India (e.g. **Sikkim**) — option **(1)**.
Forming new States / altering boundaries is **Art. 3**.
xa: **Art. 1**: "**India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States**".
**Art. 4**: Art. 3 laws amend the **First and Fourth Schedules**; **not** Art. 368 amendments.
States and UTs are listed in the **First Schedule**.

n1d8763a0142.s: A law made under Articles 3 and 4 that alters the First and Fourth Schedules is:
o: valid only if passed by a special majority
not deemed an amendment under Article 368
valid only after ratification by half the States
n1d8763a0142.x: Article 4 permits consequential changes in the First and Fourth Schedules, and such a law is not deemed an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
xa: **First Schedule** = States and UTs; **Fourth Schedule** = Rajya Sabha seats **by population**.
Art. 3 Bill needs the **President's recommendation**; the state legislature's views are **not binding**.
No territorial guarantee → India = indestructible Union of **destructible** States.

o: A destructible Union of destructible States
An indestructible Union of destructible States
An indestructible Union of indestructible States
A destructible Union of indestructible States
n4f8502dc5af.x: India is an indestructible Union of destructible States; the US is an indestructible Union of indestructible States.
xa: Art. 3 laws pass by **simple majority**.
**Ambedkar**: Union is **indestructible**; no State has the **right to secede**.
The word "**Federation**" is **not used** anywhere in the Constitution.

n4c7a2b9f002.s: The Constitution describes India as a:
n4c7a2b9f002.x: India is a 'Union of States'; the Constitution does not use 'Federation of States'.
xa: Residuary powers: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.
USA: each State has its **own constitution**; in India the former **J&K** was the exception.
⚠ Residue: **Canada** = Centre (India's model); **USA and Australia** = states.

n979d66e4161.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about amendment of the Indian Constitution?
o: The Constitution is neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible
Most provisions can be amended by Parliament without State ratification
Certain federal provisions need ratification by at least half the State Legislatures
n979d66e4161.x: The Constitution is neither wholly rigid nor wholly flexible.
xa: **Rigid** amendment for federal provisions is a **federal** feature.
**Flexibility** — power to amend vests in Parliament — is a **unitary** feature.
Emergency turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.

n3da7fbb4952.s: Officers of the All India Services are recruited through the:
n3da7fbb4952.x: AIS officers are recruited through the UPSC and serve both the Union and the States under central control.
xa: Provided under **Art. 312**: **IAS, IPS, IFoS**.
PYQ 2025: Governor, Central Services, **CAG** and Emergency powers all "**violate federal principles**".
Other integrated machinery: **CAG** and **Election Commission**.

n6c2d20204e2.s: Which single authority audits both Union and State accounts, regarded as a unitary feature?
n6c2d20204e2.x: A single CAG auditing Union and State accounts, central appointment of Governors, AIS control and emergency powers are unitary features.
xa: **Office of the Governor** was the "not a federal feature" answer (APPSC-G1 2018); **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).
CAG audits **both Union and State accounts**.
Emergency turns the system unitary **without a formal amendment**.

n1f188e26b7a.s: According to Dr B.R. Ambedkar, the use of the word 'Union' shows that:
o: the Union was formed by a compact of sovereign States
the Constitution is set in a tight mould of federalism
the States retain a right to secede
India is not the result of an agreement among States, and States cannot secede
n1f188e26b7a.x: Ambedkar stressed that India was not formed by an agreement among States, that States had no right to secede, and that the system could be unitary or federal as circumstances required.
xa: Ambedkar's two reasons for "Union": federation **not the result of an agreement** (unlike **USA**) and **no State can secede** → **centripetal bias**.
**K.C. Wheare** called India **"quasi-federal"**; **Ivor Jennings** — a federation with a **strong centralising tendency**.
Official label (IYB 2026): **"federal in structure with unitary features"**.

nf9272df3ac7.s: In which case did the Supreme Court hold that the Constitution is not truly federal and that the States are not sovereign?
o: State of West Bengal v Union of India
Kesavananda Bharati v State of Kerala
S. R. Bommai v Union of India
Minerva Mills v Union of India
nf9272df3ac7.x: In State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962), the Supreme Court held that the Constitution was not truly federal and that States were not sovereign. The case also concerned Parliament’s power to acquire State property.
nf9272df3ac7.tq: Match the case with its specific judicial characterisation of federalism.
xs: **State of West Bengal v Union of India (1962)** held the Constitution **not truly federal** and the States **not sovereign** — option **(1)**.
Parliament's law could **acquire State property** in that case.
**Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** listed **federal character** among basic features; **S.R. Bommai (1994)** made federalism part of the **basic structure**.
**Minerva Mills** reopened judicial review of Emergency barred by the **38th Amendment**.
xa: SC in several rulings: "**fundamentally federal with pronounced unitary elements**".
**Bommai** limited misuse of **Art. 356** — proclamation open to **judicial review**; **floor test**.
**Mineral Area Development Authority v SAIL (July 2024, 9 judges, 8:1)**: royalty is **not a tax**; States can tax mineral rights.

n22733395cc3.s: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on:
n22733395cc3.x: The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam came into force on 1 July 2024, replacing the IPC, CrPC and Evidence Act respectively.
n22733395cc3.tq: Recall the precise commencement date while distinguishing it from other major constitutional and legal dates.
xs: **BNS, BNSS and BSA** came into force on **1 July 2024** — option **(2)**.
They replaced the **IPC**, **CrPC** and **Evidence Act**.
Criminal law, procedure and evidence are **Concurrent** subjects (Entries 1, 2, 12).
xa: **Public order**, **police**, **prisons** are **State** subjects (Entries 1, 2, 4).
Concurrent **Entry 33**: trade and commerce in foodstuffs (used for Farm Laws).
In the Concurrent List, a **Union law prevails**.

n97e788ef497.s: Which one of the following is correct regarding State constitutions in India and the USA?
o: Every Indian State has its own constitution; no US State has one
Both Indian and US States have their own constitutions
Neither Indian nor US States have separate constitutions
Indian States generally have no separate constitutions; each US State has its own
n97e788ef497.x: Indian States generally do not have separate constitutions (the former Jammu and Kashmir was an exception), while each US State has its own.
xa: India: **single citizenship**; USA: **dual**.
Upper House: India by **population**; USA **2 seats** per State.
J&K's separate constitution ended when **Art. 370** was made inoperative in **August 2019**.

nf5592fac2de.s: Which constitutional provision provides special treatment to Andhra Pradesh in respect of equal opportunities in public employment and education?
nf5592fac2de.x: Article 371D provides special provisions for Andhra Pradesh concerning equal opportunities in public employment and education.
nf5592fac2de.tq: Use the exact Article-number and subject pairing.
xs: **Article 371D** gives **Andhra Pradesh** special provisions for **equal opportunities in public employment and education** — option **(2)**.
AP is one of the States with special treatment under **Arts. 371 to 371J**.
xa: AP was under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).
Delimitation proposal: AP Lok Sabha seats **25 to 38** under the **+50%** formula (TH 17 Apr 2026).
Other 371-series States: **Maharashtra**, **Gujarat**, **Nagaland**, **Sikkim**, **Goa**, **Karnataka**.

nindian-polity-68-42.s: Stock exchanges and futures markets fall in the:
nindian-polity-68-42.x: Stock exchanges, banking, foreign affairs and inter-State migration are all Union List subjects.
n: Foreign affairs are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Treaties are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Banking is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Insurance is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Inter-State migration is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Quarantine is a Union List subject under Entry 81. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Stock exchanges are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Futures markets are a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Other Union subjects: **defence**, **railways**, **census**, **corporation tax**, **atomic energy**, **radio and television**.
The Union List had **97** entries originally and has **98** now.
**Residuary powers** lie with Parliament under **Article 248** and **Entry 97, List I**.

nindian-polity-51-13.s: Which of the following is part of judicial review?
o: Questioning the political wisdom of legislation
Examining the constitutionality of executive orders
nindian-polity-51-13.x: Testing executive orders is part of judicial review; it does not question political wisdom, pre-screen Bills or act as an appeal.
n: Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is the inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of executive orders. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the political wisdom of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review is not an ordinary appellate proceeding. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
Judicial Review does not involve the court questioning the policy merits of legislation. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 135-137]
xa: Judicial review reinforces the **federal principle** and preserves the **distribution of powers**.
It is **not** a **unitary** element; unitary elements include **All India Services**, the **Governor's appointment** and **Emergency provisions**.
It also does not question the **policy merits** or **advisability** of legislation.

n08fb487dcac.s: Under the Seventh Schedule, the order of precedence in case of overlapping legislative fields is:
o: State List, Concurrent List, Union List
Concurrent List, State List, Union List
Union List, Concurrent List, State List
Union List, State List, Concurrent List
n08fb487dcac.x: The order of precedence is Union List over Concurrent List over State List. In the Concurrent List, a valid Union law generally prevails over a State law in case of inconsistency.
n08fb487dcac.tq: Remember the hierarchy as Union, Concurrent, State and reject the tempting placement of the State List above the Concurrent List.
xs: Precedence under the Seventh Schedule is **Union List > Concurrent List > State List** — option **(3)**.
In the **Concurrent List**, a **Union law prevails** over a State law.
The Seventh Schedule operates through **Article 246**.
xa: Entries: **Union 97 → 98**, **State 66 → 59**, **Concurrent 47 → 52** (original → now).
Union List = **national importance**, uniform law; State List = **local/regional importance**.
**Strong Centre** borrowed from **Canada**; **Concurrent List** from **Australia**.
Residuary powers: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.

nca9456a0743.s: Entry 92A in the Seventh Schedule was inserted by the:
nca9456a0743.x: Entry 92A was inserted by the Sixth Amendment, 1956; inserted entries make counts differ from last entry numbers.
xa: Some notes give counts as **100/61/52**.
⚠ Entry **97** = residuary entry of List I and also the original Union List count **97**.
Original counts: Union **97**, State **66**, Concurrent **47**.

n347f8fff4c5.s: The distribution of legislative subjects among the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule operates through which Article?
n347f8fff4c5.x: Article 246 gives effect to the three Lists of the Seventh Schedule. Article 245 deals with the territorial extent of laws, Article 248 with residuary powers, and Article 254 with repugnancy.
xs: The Seventh Schedule's three lists operate through **Article 246** — option **(2)**.
**Article 248** is the **residuary powers** Article (Part XI, Chapter I).
Precedence under it: **Union > Concurrent > State**.
xa: Three lists: **I - Union**, **II - State**, **III - Concurrent**.
**Art. 249**: Rajya Sabha resolution (**2/3 present and voting**) lets Parliament legislate on a State subject.
**Art. 250**: Parliament legislates on State List during **National Emergency**.
**101st CAA, 2016**: Art. 248 now "subject to **Article 246A**".

n33ea934685c.s: The constitution and organisation of High Courts is a subject in the:
n33ea934685c.x: It is a Union subject; defence is Union, taxes on mineral rights State, and social security Concurrent.
xa: APPSC 2025 key matched HC organisation → **Union**, mineral-right taxes → **State**, education → **Concurrent**.
**Mineral Area Development Authority v SAIL (July 2024)**: royalty is **not a tax**; States can tax mineral rights.
**Economic and social planning** — **Concurrent** (Entry 20).
**Opium** (export) — **Union** (Entry 59).

nindian-polity-68-17.s: Price control is a subject in the:
nindian-polity-68-17.x: Price control and economic and social planning are Concurrent subjects; census is Union and railway police is State.
n: Railway Police is included under the State List subject of police. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Economic planning is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Social planning is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

Economic and Social Planning belongs to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Census belongs to the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: ⚠ **Railways** → Union, but **Railway Police** → State.

nindian-polity-68-20.s: Corporation Tax is placed in the Union List at Entry:

Inter-State Trade and Commerce is a Union List subject under Entry 42. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Public health is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Sanitation is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

The Code of Criminal Procedure is a Concurrent List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Corporation tax belongs to the Union List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Inter-State Trade and Commerce belongs to the Union List under Entry 42. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

xa: **Trade and Commerce within a State** = State **Entry 26**, subject to Concurrent **Entry 33**.

nindian-polity-68-29.s: Which of the following was NOT transferred to the Concurrent List by the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976?

nindian-polity-68-29.x: Public order remained in the State List (Entry 1). The 42nd Amendment moved education, forests, weights and measures, protection of wild animals and birds, and administration of justice.
n: Public order is a State List subject under Entry 1. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Public order belongs to the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act was enacted in 1976. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred education from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred forests from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred weights and measures from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
The 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act transferred protection of wild animals and birds from the State List to the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

xa: Administration of justice covers all courts **except** the **Supreme Court and High Courts**.

nindian-polity-68-36.s: Radio and television broadcasting is a subject in the:
nindian-polity-68-36.x: Broadcasting is a Union subject, while agriculture, land and fisheries are State subjects.
n: Radio broadcasting is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Television broadcasting is a Union List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Agriculture is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Agricultural education is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Land is a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Land reforms are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Fisheries are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Markets and fairs are a State List subject. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Other State subjects: **public order**, **police**, **prisons**, **public health and sanitation**, **tolls**, **capitation taxes**.
**Agriculture**, **water** and **land** = State **Entries 14, 17, 18**.

nindian-polity-50-9.s: Which of the following can happen during a Financial Emergency?
o: Financial directions are given and salaries may be reduced
Parliament legislates on State List subjects
nindian-polity-50-9.x: In a Financial Emergency, financial directions can be given and pay cut; State Budgets are passed by Parliament under President's Rule.
n: During a National Emergency, Parliament can make laws on subjects in the State List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During President’s Rule, the State Assembly may be dissolved or suspended. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During President’s Rule, Parliament passes the State Budget. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During a Financial Emergency, the executive gives financial directions. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
During a Financial Emergency, salaries may be reduced, including the salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: In National Emergency, **Articles 358 and 359** operate.
Financial Emergency: State **money bills** can be **reserved** for the President.
⚠ Only **352** directly affects Fundamental Rights; **Articles 20 and 21** can never be suspended.

nindian-polity-50-28.s: If the Lok Sabha is dissolved before approving an Emergency proclamation already approved by the Rajya Sabha, it survives until ____ from the new Lok Sabha's first sitting.
nindian-polity-50-28.x: The 30-day rule applies to National Emergency, President's Rule and Financial Emergency alike.
n: A National Emergency survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency survives for 30 days from the first sitting of a new Lok Sabha after the Lok Sabha is dissolved. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: Approval: **352** = **1 month** (**special** majority); **356** and **360** = **2 months** (**simple** majority).
**Special sitting:** notice by **1/10th of Lok Sabha** members → sitting within **14 days** to consider disapproval of a National Emergency.
Financial Emergency has **never** been declared.

nindian-polity-50-13.s: Parliament's laws on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate ____ after it is revoked.
nindian-polity-50-13.x: Such laws lapse six months after the Emergency ends.
n: Parliament can extend the terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies by law during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies can be extended by 1 year at a time during a National Emergency. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
The terms of the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies can be extended up to a maximum of 6 months after the Emergency ceases. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Laws made by Parliament on State List subjects during a National Emergency cease to operate 6 months after the Emergency is revoked. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: **Article 354:** the President may **modify** Centre-State **revenue** distribution, valid until the end of the **financial year** in which the proclamation ceases.
The Union's executive power extends to directing **any State** on how to use its executive power.
Proclamation is only on the **written advice** of the **Union Cabinet**.

nd46c48a0658.s: Which one of the following about the use of Concurrent List entries is correct?
o: Entry 33 concerns only the organisation of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
The Union has used them for farm laws (Entry 33) and education measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.
Only State Legislatures can legislate on Concurrent subjects.
The Concurrent List bars Union laws on education.
nd46c48a0658.x: Concurrent List entries permit Union legislation; cited examples include farm laws through Entry 33 and education measures such as the NEP and NMC Act.
xa: **Education** is Concurrent **Entry 25**, moved by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
Suggested fix: a **narrower/tighter Concurrent List** and stronger **Inter-State Council** (TH, 2 Mar 2026).
**Constitution and organisation of High Courts** is Union **Entry 78**.

n006fbb29bf8.s: Institutions for scientific or technical education financed by the Government of India and declared by Parliament to be of national importance fall under:
n006fbb29bf8.x: Such institutions are under Union List Entry 64. Union Entry 66 covers coordination and standards in higher education, and Concurrent Entry 25 covers education generally. State Entry 32 is not the entry for these institutions.
n006fbb29bf8.tq: National-importance S&T institutions = Union 64; HE standards = Union 66
xs: **Institutions for scientific or technical education** financed by GoI and of **national importance** — **Union List, Entry 64** — option **(3)**.
**Union Entry 66** is **coordination and standards in higher education**.
**Concurrent Entry 25** is **education** in general.
xa: Education was moved to the Concurrent List by the **42nd CAA, 1976**.
Union List now has **98** entries.
⚠ **64** = institutions; **66** = standards.

n4a3a5fb059e.s: Which Article of the Constitution confers on Parliament exclusive power to legislate on matters not enumerated in the State List or the Concurrent List?
n4a3a5fb059e.x: Article 248 deals with residuary legislative powers and gives Parliament exclusive power over matters not included in the State or Concurrent Lists, including residuary taxes.
n4a3a5fb059e.tq: Separate the specific residuary-power Article from the general distribution-of-powers Article.
xs: **Article 248** gives **Parliament alone** power over matters not in the State or Concurrent List — option **(1)**.
It works with **Entry 97, List I** and includes **residuary taxes** (gift tax, wealth tax, expenditure tax).
**Art. 249** = Rajya Sabha resolution; **Art. 250** = State subjects during National Emergency; **Art. 246** = the three lists.
xa: Art. 248 is in **Part XI, Chapter I**.
**101st CAA, 2016**: Art. 248 now "subject to **Article 246A**" (GST).
PYQ 2025: "Art. 248 = residuary" and "Parliament has exclusive power over items in no list" → **both correct**.
Residue with the Centre follows **Canada**; **USA and Australia** leave it with the states.

ncc6136258f3.s: Article 248 was made subject to Article 246A by which Constitutional Amendment Act?
o: One hundred and third Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019
One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016
ncc6136258f3.x: The One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016, inserted the GST-related constitutional provisions, including the qualification of Article 248 by Article 246A.
ncc6136258f3.tq: Distinguish the GST amendment from the major structural amendment dealing with transferred subjects.
xs: The **One hundred and first Constitutional Amendment Act, 2016** (**101st CAA**) made Art. 248 "**subject to Article 246A**" (GST) — option **(4)**.
The **42nd CAA, 1976** moved **5 subjects** to the Concurrent List.
xa: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I** = residuary power with **Parliament alone**.
**GST** arrived in **2017**, under the "cooperative-competitive" label.
Residuary taxes include **gift tax**, **wealth tax**, **expenditure tax**.

n1ed4fbc1391.s: Which of the following correctly states where residuary powers lie?
o: India and Canada – States; USA – Centre
India, Canada, USA and Australia – all with the Centre
India and Canada – Centre; USA and Australia – States
n1ed4fbc1391.x: Residuary powers lie with the Centre in India and Canada, and with the States in the USA and Australia; under the 1935 Act they were vested in the Governor-General.
xa: Residuary power: **Article 248** + **Entry 97, List I**.
**Strong Centre** borrowed from **Canada**; **Concurrent List** from **Australia**.
India vs USA: India has **three lists**; USA enumerates only **federal** powers.

n797fe3dcb58.s: Residuary legislative matters are associated with which entry of the Union List?
n797fe3dcb58.x: Union List Entry 97, read with Article 248, covers matters not enumerated in the State List or Concurrent List, including residuary taxation.
n797fe3dcb58.tq: Use the exact entry number to distinguish residuary power from neighbouring Union List entries.
xs: Residuary matters are **Entry 97** of the Union List — option **(1)**.
Read with **Article 248**, Parliament alone legislates on matters not in the State or Concurrent List.
xa: ⚠ **97** is also the **original** count of the Union List.
Residuary taxes: **gift tax**, **wealth tax**, **expenditure tax**.
**Entry 92A** (inter-state sales tax) added by the **6th CAA, 1956**.

nindian-polity-68-28.s: Trade and commerce within a State is placed in which List, subject to the relevant Concurrent List entry?
nindian-polity-68-28.x: Trade and commerce within a State is State List Entry 26, subject to Concurrent List Entry 33. Inter-State trade is Union Entry 42, and Entry 5 is local government.
n: Trade and Commerce within a State belongs to the State List under Entry 26. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Trade and Commerce within a State is subject to List III, Entry 33. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xs: **Trade and commerce within a State** is **State List, Entry 26**, subject to Concurrent List **Entry 33** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Union List Entry 42** is **Inter-State** trade and commerce; **State Entry 5** is **local government**.
**Concurrent Entry 20** is **economic and social planning**.
xa: Concurrent **Entry 33** = trade and commerce in **foodstuffs**; the **Farm Laws** were made via Entry 33.
**Public order** = State **Entry 1**; **police** and **prisons** = State Entries 2 and 4.
**Population control and family planning** = Concurrent **Entry 20A**.

n95c60d6c521.s: Elections to State Legislatures and elections conducted by the Election Commission fall respectively under:
n95c60d6c521.x: Elections to the State Legislature are State List Entry 37 (subject to parliamentary law); elections conducted by the Election Commission are Union List Entry 72.

⚠ "Not a federal feature" answers: **Office of the Governor** (APPSC-G1 2018) and **CAG** (APPSC-G2 2017).

nindian-polity-68-50.s: Population control and family planning was inserted in the Concurrent List as Entry:

Administration of justice includes the constitution and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and High Courts. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A was inserted into the Concurrent List. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
Entry 20A concerns population control and family planning. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]

Family planning is a Concurrent List subject under Entry 20A. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 181-185]
xa: Other transfers: **education**, **forests**, **weights and measures**, **protection of wild animals and birds**.
Constitution and organisation of **High Courts** = **Union** (Entry 78).
The Centre uses Concurrent entries for sweeping laws — e.g. **NEP** and **NMC Act** in education.

na15213077f6.s: The expression 'Union of India' refers to:
na15213077f6.x: The Union of India refers to the States; the Territory of India also includes UTs and acquired territories.
xa: ⚠ Territory is the **wider** term; Union = members of the federal system.

nd7e50b9fff7.s: A law under Article 3 to form a new State is passed by:
o: A special majority with State ratification
nd7e50b9fff7.x: Article 3 laws need only a simple majority.
xa: The Bill needs the **President's recommendation** + reference to the state legislature (views **not binding**).
**Art. 4**: such laws are **not** Art. 368 amendments.
Result: "**an indestructible Union of destructible States**".

n9a8a0f3c5c8.s: A Bill under Article 3 to alter the boundaries of a State can be introduced only on the recommendation of the:
n9a8a0f3c5c8.x: An Article 3 Bill needs the President's recommendation and is referred to the State legislature, whose views do not bind Parliament.
xa: It passes by **simple majority**.
Such a law is **not** an **Art. 368** amendment (**Art. 4**).
Parliament altering state boundaries is counted a **unitary** feature.

ndb170477b45.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Indian federal structure?
o: The Constitution provides completely separate judicial and administrative machinery for every State
The Supreme Court is an independent adjudicator in Centre-State disputes
The Constitution provides for two sets of governments
The Constitution is written and supreme
ndb170477b45.x: India has an integrated judicial and administrative framework, not separate machinery for every State.
xa: Essential federal feature: **independence of the judiciary** (UPSC 2021).
The **Centre appoints High Court judges** — a unitary feature.
Other federal features: **Seventh Schedule** division, **rigid** amendment, **bicameral** legislature.

nfcdb2f8395d.s: The Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister is collectively responsible to the:
nfcdb2f8395d.x: Under Articles 74(1) and 75 the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; the President is the nominal head.
xa: Parliamentary form follows the **British model**.
The **real executive** = Council of Ministers under the **PM**.
India = "federal system with **unitary bias**".

n77f1a7bc937.s: Which case recognised federalism as part of the basic structure and opened Article 356 proclamations to judicial review?
n77f1a7bc937.x: S.R. Bommai (1994) recognised federalism as basic structure and limited misuse of Article 356.
xa: In the **coalition era (1989-2014)**, the **ISC** was set up (**1990**) and **Bommai (1994)** limited Art. 356.
**TH (23 Mar 2026)**: Bommai recalled against earlier misuse of Art. 356 amid a "hollowing federal spirit".
President's Rule: approval within **2 months**, **simple majority**, maximum **3 years**.
AP came under President's Rule in **1973** (**Jai Andhra** agitation).

na3478e659a8.s: Article 19 is suspended during a National Emergency only when the emergency is proclaimed on the ground of:
o: Failure of constitutional machinery in a State
External emergency involving war or external aggression
na3478e659a8.x: Article 19 is automatically suspended only when the National Emergency is based on war or external aggression. Article 20 and Article 21 cannot be suspended under Article 359 orders.
na3478e659a8.tq: Discriminate between the grounds of emergency for the limited suspension of Fundamental Rights.
xs: **Art. 19** is suspended only in an **external** emergency — **war or external aggression** — option **(2)** (**Art. 358**).
Other rights are suspended by order under **Art. 359**, **except Arts. 20 and 21**.
"**Internal disturbance**" is no longer a ground; it was replaced by **"armed rebellion"** by the **44th Amendment**.
Failure of constitutional machinery is the ground for **Art. 356**, not a National Emergency.
xa: National Emergency grounds: **war, external aggression, armed rebellion**.
National Emergencies: **1962, 1971, 1975**.
⚠ Trap: "internal disturbance" is no longer a ground (APPSC-GS 2018).

n40200d56161.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Forty-fourth Amendment?
o: Emergency must be proclaimed on the Union Cabinet's written advice
It retained 'internal disturbance' as a ground for Emergency
It reduced the approval period for National Emergency to one month
One-tenth of Lok Sabha members can require a special sitting within 14 days to consider disapproval
n40200d56161.x: The 44th Amendment replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
xa: Parliament approval within **1 month**.
**Arts 20-21** made non-suspendable by the **44th Amendment (1978)**.
**38th Amendment** barred judicial review of Emergency; **Minerva Mills** reopened it.

n26a3e3f9e84.s: A proclamation of National Emergency under Article 352 must be approved by Parliament within:
n26a3e3f9e84.x: Article 352 needs approval within one month; Articles 356 and 360 within two months by simple majority.
xa: National Emergency is renewable every **6 months**.
President's Rule: maximum **3 years**; beyond **1 year** only with a National Emergency + **ECI certification**.

n3183497027c.s: Financial Emergency is provided for under Article:
n3183497027c.x: Financial Emergency is under Article 360, not Article 311.
xa: State Assembly terms can also be extended during a National Emergency.
**Art. 250** laws on State subjects lapse **6 months** after the emergency.
The **44th Amendment (1978)** replaced "internal disturbance" with **"armed rebellion"**.

n80a7b8847bf.s: The Inter-State Council was set up in:
n80a7b8847bf.x: The Inter-State Council was set up in 1990, during the 1989–2014 coalition era.
xa: **Morris Jones** called Indian federalism **"bargaining federalism"**.
Preceding phase **1977-89**: Janata interlude; **Sarkaria Commission (1983)**.
Next phase **2014 onward**: **NITI Aayog** (2015), **GST** (2017).

ndef78c0cd29.s: The allocation of Rajya Sabha seats to States is provided in the:
ndef78c0cd29.x: Seats are allotted broadly by population in the Fourth Schedule, unlike equal representation in the US Senate.
xa: **Unequal representation** in Rajya Sabha is counted as a **unitary feature**.
Rajya Sabha for States = **bicameral** legislature, a federal feature.
India vs USA: **single** vs **dual** citizenship; **single integrated** vs dual judiciary.

nda5c88caf02.s: In Mineral Area Development Authority v. SAIL, the nine-judge Bench held by majority that royalty:
o: Is a fee under the Union List
Can be levied only by the Union
nda5c88caf02.x: The 8:1 majority held royalty is not a tax and recognised that States can tax mineral rights.
xa: **Taxes on mineral rights** are in the **State List (Entry 50)**, subject to limits set by Parliament.
APPSC 2025 key: mineral-right taxes → **State**.

nindian-polity-50-8.s: How many times has a National Emergency been proclaimed in India?
nindian-polity-50-8.x: National Emergencies were declared in 1962, 1971 and 1975; a Financial Emergency has never been declared.
n: National Emergency has been invoked 3 times in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
National Emergencies were invoked in 1962, 1971, and 1975. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule has been invoked over 100 times across various States. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
Financial Emergency has never been invoked in India. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
xa: The **1975** Emergency was proclaimed on **25 June 1975** on the ground of **Internal Disturbance**; withdrawn **21 March 1977**.
**AP** came under President's Rule in **1973** (Jai Andhra agitation).
**Samvidhan Hatya Diwas:** **25 June**.

nindian-polity-50-19.s: Parliamentary approval of a National Emergency requires:
o: A special majority in both Houses
A special majority in the Lok Sabha only
A simple majority in both Houses
nindian-polity-50-19.x: A National Emergency needs a special majority; President's Rule and Financial Emergency need simple majorities.
n: A National Emergency requires a special majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
President’s Rule requires a simple majority in both Houses of Parliament. [Indian Polity · ROCKET SHEET #50 · pp 131-135]
