n61e85e90355.x: RMK follows a quasi-wholesale model: it lends to intermediary NGOs and microfinance bodies, which lend onward to poor women and SHGs.
xa: RMK was set up in **1993** under the **Ministry of Women and Child Development**.
RMK is a society under the **Societies Registration Act, 1860**.
**SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** (**NABARD**) was piloted in **1992**.

n4d6217714eb.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the community resource-person roles associated with DAY-NRLM?
n4d6217714eb.x: The listed roles are Pashu Sakhi, Krishi Sakhi, Bank Sakhi, Bima Sakhi and Poshan Sakhi. Nyaya Sakhi is not included in the stated list.
n4d6217714eb.tq: Identify the odd term by recalling the complete set of community resource-person roles.
xs: **Nyaya Sakhi** is not among DAY-NRLM's community resource persons — option **(3)** is correct.
The listed roles are **Pashu Sakhi, Krishi Sakhi, Bank Sakhi, Bima Sakhi, Poshan Sakhi**.
xa: **DAY-NRLM** is **community-driven**.
It runs the **SVEP** umbrella for village enterprises.

n50cc4bd6238.s: Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, which provides microcredit to poor women through intermediary organisations, was set up in:
o: 1993 under the Ministry of Women and Child Development
2011 under the Ministry of Rural Development
1982 under the Reserve Bank of India
n50cc4bd6238.x: Rashtriya Mahila Kosh was set up in 1993 under the Ministry of Women and Child Development as a society. 1992 is when NABARD piloted the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme; the Ministry of Rural Development runs DAY-NRLM; and 1982 is NABARD's year, not RMK's, and RMK is not under the RBI.
xs: **Rashtriya Mahila Kosh** was set up in **1993** under the **Ministry of Women and Child Development** — option **(1)** is correct.
**1992** is when NABARD's **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** was piloted, not RMK's year.
xa: RMK is a **society** under the **Societies Registration Act, 1860**.
RMK lends to **intermediary NGOs/microfinance bodies**, which lend to poor women and SHGs.
NABARD has been **fully owned by GoI** since **2019**.

n1179c9328b0.s: The Press Council of India was first set up in 1966 under which legislation?
o: Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
n1179c9328b0.x: The Press Council was first set up in 1966 under the Press Council Act, 1965. Its present statutory framework is associated with the Press Council Act, 1978.
n1179c9328b0.tq: Separate the original establishment year and Act from the later statutory framework.
xs: The PCI was first set up in **1966** under the **Press Council Act, 1965** — option **(2)** is correct.
The present Act is the **Press Council Act, 1978** — option (4) is the current law, not the first.
xa: ⚠ PCI: **1965 Act** → set up **1966**; present Act **1978**.
PCI is a **statutory, quasi-judicial** body with a **Chairman + 28 members**.
It covers **print only** and **lacks punitive powers**.

naf455062f41.s: The Press Council of India is a statutory, quasi-judicial body under the:
o: Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867
naf455062f41.x: The PCI functions under the Press Council Act, 1978 (first set up in 1966 under the 1965 Act); its Chairman is by convention a retired SC judge.
xa: ⚠ First set up in **1966** under the **1965 Act**.
Composition: **Chairman + 28 members**; covers **print only**.

n7fe73d6a0d9.s: Almond and Powell classify pressure groups into which of the following categories?
o: State, market, civil society and electoral
n7fe73d6a0d9.x: Almond and Powell classify pressure groups as institutional, associational, non-associational and anomic.
n7fe73d6a0d9.tq: Recall the exact classification associated with the named scholars.
xs: **Almond and Powell** classify pressure groups as **institutional, associational, non-associational and anomic** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) lists **Indian types** (business, professional, peasant, religious), not Almond and Powell's categories.
xa: **Anomic** groups: spontaneous **riots, demonstrations, agitations**.
Pressure groups are called the **"Anonymous Empire"**.

n0160ee1364f.s: Which one of the following best describes acculturation?
o: Absorption of a minority culture into the dominant culture with loss of its identity
Convergence of all cultures towards a single global pattern
Mixing of global and local elements into a new blended form
Exchange of cultural traits between two cultures in contact, with both changing while remaining distinct
n0160ee1364f.x: Acculturation involves mutual exchange of traits between cultures in contact. Both cultures change, but each retains its distinct identity.
n0160ee1364f.tq: Distinguish closely related cultural-change terms by checking whether identities are retained.
xs: **Acculturation**: two cultures in contact **exchange traits**; **both change, but each stays distinct** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (1) is **assimilation**; (2) is **homogenisation**; (3) is **hybridisation**.
xa: ⚠ **Acculturation** = both change, stay distinct; **Assimilation** = minority loses identity.
**Diffusion** = spread of cultural traits from one society to another.
**Glocalisation** = global products adapted to local tastes, e.g. local menus of global food chains.

n7593eb941a6.s: A minority culture is absorbed into the dominant culture and loses its distinct identity. This process is known as:
n7593eb941a6.x: Assimilation occurs when a minority culture is absorbed into the dominant culture and loses its distinct identity.
n7593eb941a6.tq: Use the identity-loss clue to distinguish assimilation from acculturation.
xs: A minority culture absorbed into the dominant one, **losing its identity**, is **assimilation** — option **(1)** is correct.
In **acculturation** both cultures change but **stay distinct** — the key trap.
**Glocalisation** is local adaptation; **hybridisation** is blending into new forms.
xa: ⚠ **Acculturation** = both change, stay distinct; **Assimilation** = minority loses identity.
**Homogenisation** = cultures converge towards one global pattern.

n83774687691.s: The spread of cultural traits from one society to another is known as:
n83774687691.x: Diffusion is the spread of cultural traits from one society to another. Assimilation is absorption into a dominant culture, homogenisation is convergence to one pattern, and glocalisation is local adaptation of global products.
n83774687691.tq: Diffusion: traits spread like ink in water.
xs: Spread of cultural traits from one society to another is **diffusion** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Assimilation** = minority absorbed; **homogenisation** = convergence to one pattern; **glocalisation** = local adaptation of global products.
xa: **Acculturation**: two cultures exchange traits, both change but stay distinct.
**Hybridisation**: global and local mix into new, blended forms.

n0ebc100241d.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as an effect of global integration on consumption and media?
o: Complete elimination of local cultural influences
n0ebc100241d.x: Global integration is associated with wider consumer choice, global brands, media expansion and cultural fusion. It does not imply the complete elimination of local cultural influences.
n0ebc100241d.tq: Find the absolute statement that goes beyond the stated effects.
xs: **Complete elimination of local cultural influences** is not listed — option **(4)** is correct.
Listed effects of **consumerism**: **wider consumer choice**, **global brands + media**, and the risk of **cultural fusion**.
xa: Another risk: **"mindless aping of Western lifestyle"** and **loss of traditional identity**.
**Glocalisation** and **hybridisation** show local culture adapting and blending, not vanishing.

n71c3dfa5920.s: The concept of the 'space of flows' is associated with:
n71c3dfa5920.x: 'Space of flows' and the network society are Castells's; Robertson gave glocalisation, Giddens time-space distanciation.
xa: **Ritzer** — McDonaldisation; **Appadurai** — five "scapes".
**Wallerstein** — **world-systems theory**: core, semi-periphery, periphery.

nf7806585ea6.s: Which of the following is NOT one of Arjun Appadurai’s five ‘scapes’?
nf7806585ea6.x: Appadurai’s five scapes are ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes and ideoscapes. ‘Politiscapes’ is not included in this list.
nf7806585ea6.tq: Find the item outside the memorised five-member list.
xs: **Politiscapes** is not one of Appadurai's scapes — option **(3)** is correct.
**Arjun Appadurai**'s five scapes: **ethnoscapes, mediascapes, technoscapes, financescapes, ideoscapes**.
xa: **Castells**: **network society**, "space of flows".
**Giddens**: time-space distanciation; **"runaway world"**.

n47dee2cfdea.s: Immanuel Wallerstein’s world-systems theory classifies the global system into:
o: Developed, developing and least developed regions only
n47dee2cfdea.x: Wallerstein’s world-systems theory divides the global system into core, semi-periphery and periphery.
n47dee2cfdea.tq: Recall the exact three-part classification and reject near-synonymous substitutions.
xs: **Immanuel Wallerstein**'s **world-systems theory** divides the world into **core, semi-periphery and periphery** — option **(3)** is correct.
Centre-hinterland or North-South-East divisions are not Wallerstein's terms.
xa: **Appadurai**: five "scapes"; **Castells**: network society.
**World Inequality Report 2026**: **Global South** transfers more than **1%** of world GDP to the **Global North** each year.

n5cb2cad5429.s: Who coined the term ‘informal sector’ during 1971–73?
n5cb2cad5429.x: Keith Hart coined the term ‘informal sector’ during 1971–73.
n5cb2cad5429.tq: Match the specific terminology and period with the associated scholar.
xs: **Keith Hart** coined **"informal sector"** (**1971-73**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Jan Breman** = **footloose labour**; **Castells** = network society; **Ritzer** = McDonaldisation.
xa: Breman's **Footloose Labour** appeared in **1996**: circular and casual labour.
New **Labour Codes** raise concerns for informal workers.

n2ca1b81ffc7.s: Jan Breman is associated with which of the following concepts?
n2ca1b81ffc7.x: Jan Breman is associated with footloose labour and the concepts of circular and casual labour. His work Footloose Labour was published in 1996.
n2ca1b81ffc7.tq: Use the labour-mobility cluster to distinguish Breman from Hart and globalisation theorists.
xs: **Jan Breman** is associated with **footloose, circular and casual labour** — option **(3)** is correct.
His book **Footloose Labour** came out in **1996**.
**Informal sector** was coined by **Keith Hart**; **time-space distanciation** is **Giddens**; **world-systems** is **Wallerstein**.
xa: Keith Hart coined "informal sector" in **1971-73**.
**NITI Aayog (2022)**: gig workers **77 lakh** in **2020-21**.

n58fc911b34a.s: Remittances and services exports help keep India’s current account deficit stable despite the:
n58fc911b34a.x: Remittances and services exports offset pressures arising from the trade deficit and help keep the current account deficit stable.
n58fc911b34a.tq: Identify the cause-effect relationship rather than confusing the current and capital accounts.
xs: Remittances plus **services exports** keep the **current account deficit** stable despite the **trade deficit** — option **(2)** is correct.
This is an **ES 2025-26** observation.
xa: Gulf labour = "the backbone of India's **remittance economy**".
**ES 2025-26**: shift to **"geostrategic globalisation"**.

nfa853d0dad2.s: According to the World Migration Report 2026, the number of international migrants and their share in world population are approximately:
nfa853d0dad2.x: The IOM's World Migration Report 2026 counts 304 million international migrants, or 3.7 per cent of the world population. Options B and D pair 3.7 per cent with the wrong number, and option C pairs 304 million with the wrong share.
nfa853d0dad2.tq: Match the current population figure with its corresponding percentage rather than the outdated estimate.
xs: **WMR 2026**: **304 million** international migrants, **3.7%** of world population — option **(1)** is correct.
Options (2) and (4) pair **3.7%** with the wrong count; option (3) pairs **304 million** with the wrong share.
xa: Published by the **IOM**, biennially since **2000**.
India = **largest diaspora**; corridors **India-UAE** (5th), **India-US** (6th).

n404b628e26d.s: A key criticism of globalisation is that it:
o: Narrows the gap between rich and poor nations
Widens the gap between rich and poor nations
n404b628e26d.x: A key criticism is that globalisation widens rich-poor and inter-nation gaps.
xa: Globalisation can become **"commercial imperialism"**.
Farmer suicides (debt + crop failure) were marked in **Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh**.

n52a220fd8fd.s: Competition from multinational corporations for artisans and domestic firms can lead to:
o: Guaranteed expansion of all domestic firms
Transfer of all unskilled labour to MNCs
Shutdowns and layoffs, with skilled labour moving to MNCs and unskilled labour left behind
End of competition between domestic firms and MNCs
n52a220fd8fd.x: MNC competition can cause shutdowns and layoffs; skilled labour may move to MNCs while unskilled labour remains behind.
xa: **Youth**: **29%** of tertiary-educated youth unemployed in **2023-24** (skills-job mismatch).
**Small growers**: **98%** of coffee growers are small farmers facing price swings.

o: Liberalisation of trade in goods alone, with restrictions on capital flows
Free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, ideas and people across borders
Nationalisation of foreign enterprises to protect domestic industry
Free movement of people while restricting trade in goods and services
n4cad929df40.x: Globalisation means the free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, ideas and people across national borders.
n4cad929df40.tq: Globalisation lets everything flow: goods, money, ideas and people.
xs: **Globalisation** = **free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, ideas, people** — option **(2)** is correct.
Options (1) and (4) restrict some flows; (3) nationalisation is the opposite of globalisation.
xa: **Anthony Giddens**: globalisation as **time-space distanciation**; "runaway world".
**ES 2025-26**: shift from **"hyper-globalisation"** to **"geostrategic globalisation"**.
Criticism: widens rich-poor gaps; can become **"commercial imperialism"**.

n539b9dd069d.s: The World Social Forum was first held at:
n539b9dd069d.x: The first World Social Forum was held in Porto Alegre, Brazil, in 2001. Mumbai hosted the Forum in 2004.
n539b9dd069d.tq: Use the place-year pair rather than confusing the first venue with a later host city.
xs: The first **World Social Forum** was held at **Porto Alegre** (Brazil) in **2001** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Mumbai** hosted it in **2004**; **Seattle 1999** was the "Battle of Seattle" against the **WTO Ministerial**.
xa: WSF slogan: **"Another world is possible"**.
**Stiglitz**: **Globalization and Its Discontents** (**2002**).

n95f446fb0a3.s: The Economic Survey 2025–26 describes the shift from:
n95f446fb0a3.x: The Economic Survey 2025–26 describes a shift from ‘hyper-globalisation’ to ‘geostrategic globalisation’.
n95f446fb0a3.tq: Test the exact paired terminology and avoid replacing a qualified shift with an extreme one.
xs: **ES 2025-26** describes a shift from **"hyper-globalisation"** to **"geostrategic globalisation"** — option **(4)** is correct.
It does not describe complete **deglobalisation** or a return to protectionism.
xa: ES 2025-26: remittances and services exports keep the **CAD** stable despite the **trade deficit**.
Globalisation = free flow of goods, services, capital, technology, ideas, people.

n8d525b80338.s: Which of the following best captures a major criticism of globalisation?
o: It narrows all income differences between countries
It prevents the movement of capital and labour across borders
It widens gaps between rich and poor and may become a form of commercial imperialism
It affects only cultural life and not economic relations
n8d525b80338.x: A major criticism is that globalisation can widen disparities between rich and poor people and between nations, and can develop into ‘commercial imperialism’.
n8d525b80338.tq: Select the option containing both linked elements of the criticism without accepting an absolute claim.
xs: Globalisation **widens rich-poor + inter-nation gaps** and can become **"commercial imperialism"** — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) states the opposite of this criticism.
xa: **World Inequality Report 2026**: India's **top 10%** hold about **65%** of wealth.
**Global South** transfers more than **1%** of world GDP to the **Global North**.
**Stiglitz** critiqued **IMF** policy conditions.

nd6d0d6d2bbc.s: The Gulf labour force is described as the backbone of India’s:
nd6d0d6d2bbc.x: Gulf labour is described as the backbone of India’s remittance economy.
nd6d0d6d2bbc.tq: Identify the economic channel directly associated with overseas Gulf employment.
xs: Gulf labour is "the backbone of India's **remittance economy**" — option **(1)** is correct.
The **war on Iran** brought job uncertainty for Gulf migrants and families.
xa: Remittances, with **services exports**, keep the **current account deficit** stable despite the **trade deficit** (ES 2025-26).
AP angle: Gulf-dependent households face uncertainty from the **2026 West Asia war**.

n94039254080.s: Which one of the following is NOT a salient feature of Indian society?
n94039254080.x: Indian society is multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, multi-class and broadly patriarchal. The absence of patriarchal institutions is not a salient feature.
n94039254080.tq: Find the option that reverses a stated social characteristic.
xs: **Absence of patriarchal institutions** is not a feature — Indian society is **patriarchal** — option **(1)** is correct.
Salient features: **multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, multi-class, patriarchal** — options (2), (3), (4) are features.
xa: ⚠ Matrilineal exceptions to patriarchy: **Khasi, Jaintia, Garo**.
Social life historically centred on **castes, ethnic groups, extended families**.
**UPPSC 2014** listed **excess population in villages, various religions, various castes** as main features.

n1bcaa5e5c2e.s: Which form of stratification is birth-based, closed and associated with cumulative inequality?
n1bcaa5e5c2e.x: Caste is birth-based, closed and cumulative; class is relatively open, permits mobility and reflects dispersed inequality.
xa: **André Béteille**: traditional **cumulative** inequality → **dispersed** inequality.
Indian society is **multi-class** as well as multi-ethnic and multi-lingual.

n718eb46364a.s: Which of the following communities is a matrilineal exception to the broadly patriarchal pattern of Indian society?
n718eb46364a.x: The Khasi, Jaintia and Garo are cited as matrilineal exceptions.
xa: Indian society is otherwise **patriarchal**, with multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, multi-class features.
Social life historically centred on **castes, ethnic groups, extended families**.

nce797fba9e7.s: Which of the following is an economic condition rather than a main feature of Indian social structure?
nce797fba9e7.x: A large village population, many religions and many castes are features of social structure; poverty is an economic condition.
xa: Salient features: **multi-ethnic, multi-lingual, multi-class, patriarchal**.
Religion (Census 2011): **Hindu 79.8%**, **Muslim 14.2%**.

n99a9393b1f3.s: Which sociologist described the change in Indian stratification as a shift from 'cumulative' to 'dispersed' inequality?
n99a9393b1f3.x: Andre Beteille described traditional caste-based cumulative inequality giving way to dispersed, class-type inequality. Ghurye wrote Caste and Race in India, Dumont wrote Homo Hierarchicus on purity and pollution, and Yogendra Singh wrote on orthogenetic and heterogenetic change.
xs: **Andre Beteille** (André Béteille) described the shift from **cumulative** to **dispersed** inequality — option **(2)** is correct.
**Ghurye** wrote **Caste and Race in India** (**1932**); **Dumont** stressed **purity-pollution**; **Yogendra Singh** gave **orthogenetic vs heterogenetic** change.
xa: Caste = birth-based, closed, **cumulative inequality**; class = open, **dispersed inequality**.
**M.N. Srinivas**: Sanskritisation, Westernisation, **dominant caste**.

nec4b69805c8.s: Census 2011 recorded about how many languages in India?
nec4b69805c8.x: Census 2011 recorded about 122 languages; the Constitution recognises 22.
xa: ⚠ **122** languages (Census 2011) vs **22** in the Constitution.
Religious diversity: **6** major religions; Hindus are a minority in **8** States/UTs.
Racial classifications: **S.S. Sarkar** (cephalic index) and **B.S. Guha** (Negrito, Proto-Australoid etc.).
Census 2011: Hindu **79.8%**, Muslim **14.2%**, Christian **2.3%**, Sikh **1.7%**.

n99bded8a852.s: Hindus are a minority in how many States/UTs of India?
n99bded8a852.x: Hindus are a minority in eight States/UTs; six major religions underlie India's religious diversity.
xa: Racial diversity: **S.S. Sarkar** (cephalic index) and **B.S. Guha** (Negrito, Proto-Australoid).
Census 2011: **Hindu 79.8%**, **Muslim 14.2%**, **Christian 2.3%**.

n2fd9f3db03c.s: Which of the following is NOT a bond of unity in Indian society?
o: Festivals such as Onam shared by all communities
n2fd9f3db03c.x: Shared festivals, Bhakti-Sufi syncretism and Khanqahs are bonds of unity; India is not linguistically homogeneous.
xa: **Shankaracharya** sent priests between southern and northern temples.
Remedies: **National Integration Council**, **SRA 1956**, **Zonal Councils**, **Art. 350-B**.

n277f96a34b5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about national integration in India?
o: Communalism and casteism are threats to national integration
Regionalism and linguism are threats to national integration
The National Integration Council and Zonal Councils are listed as remedies
Article 350-B provides for a Finance Commission for linguistic minorities
n277f96a34b5.x: Article 350-B provides for a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities, not a Finance Commission.
xa: **UPPSC 2025** A-R: national integration has **political, economic, social, cultural and psychological** dimensions.
Bonds of unity: **Onam**, **Bhakti-Sufi syncretism**, **Khanqahs**.

n45f0a85e96b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about continuity from Harappan times?
o: Zebu cattle and binary weights are cited as continuity
Double cropping and the plough at Kalibangan are cited as continuity
The deciphered Harappan script strengthens the evidence of continuity
Courtyard houses and bangles are cited as continuity
n45f0a85e96b.x: The Harappan script remains undeciphered, which, with the urban collapse around 1900 BCE, limits the evidence.
xa: **Milton Singer**: continuity within change — **When a Great Tradition Modernizes** (Madras).
**A.M. Shah**: joint family continues **in function**.

n0103312015d.x: Article 350-B provides for the Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities; Article 17, the Caste Disabilities Removal Act and the Hindu Code Acts drove caste and family change.
xa: **Technology** as a force: digital citizenship, **DPDP Act 2023**.
**Education**: individualism, privacy and rights.
**Henry Maine**: societies move **"from status to contract"**.

n73c99bca443.s: Universalisation, the upward movement of Little Tradition elements into the Great Tradition, is associated with:
n73c99bca443.x: McKim Marriott used universalisation for local elements rising into the Great Tradition, e.g. local Jagannath integrated with Vishnu.
xa: **Parochialisation**: Great-Tradition elements localised **downwards**.
Great/Little Tradition originated with **Robert Redfield**.

n7be9e45ee06.s: G.S. Ghurye, founder of the Bombay School, wrote 'Caste and Race in India' in:
n7be9e45ee06.x: Ghurye wrote 'Caste and Race in India' in 1932 and saw caste as a product of Indo-Aryan culture.
xa: ⚠ **Ghurye 1932** – **Karve 1953** – **Marriott 1955** – **Dumont 1966**.
Ghurye used the **Indological** (textual) approach.

n983224aaac1.s: Orthogenetic and heterogenetic sources of change are associated with:
n983224aaac1.x: These sources of change are Yogendra Singh's; Srinivas gave Sanskritisation, Westernisation and dominant caste.
xa: Srinivas: the **joint family is modified, not eliminated**.
His works: **Religion and Society among the Coorgs**; **The Remembered Village**.

nefa45b8db9b.s: The concept of 'collective conscience' is associated with:
nefa45b8db9b.x: Durkheim gave social facts, collective conscience and the sacred-profane distinction; ideal bureaucracy is Weber's.
xa: Durkheim also gave **mechanical/organic solidarity** and **anomie**.
Durkheim's works: **Division of Labour** (**1893**), **Suicide** (**1897**), **Elementary Forms of Religious Life** (**1912**).

nindian-society-24-20.s:
Which of the following are identified as groups among whom power is concentrated?
1. Military leaders
2. Sociologists
3. Corporate elites
Select the correct answer:
nindian-society-24-20.x: The power elite comprises political, military and corporate leaders; sociologists are not part of it.
xa: Mills highlighted the **concentration of power** in modern society.
He is famous for the **sociological imagination** (**1959**).
He was an **American sociologist** (**1916 to 1962**).

nindian-society-13-3.s: Marx's theory that economic conditions shape society, politics and culture is called:
nindian-society-13-3.x: Historical materialism holds that the economic base shapes society, politics and culture.
n: Historical materialism states that economic conditions shape society. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 45-46]
Historical materialism states that economic conditions shape politics. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 45-46]
Historical materialism states that economic conditions shape culture. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 45-46]
xa: Marx: history is the history of **class conflicts**.
⚠ Other notes say class struggle works through **dialectical materialism**.
**Alienation**: from the **product**, the **production process**, **society** and **themselves**.
Marx is the **Father of Scientific Socialism**.

nindian-society-15-15.s: In Comte's Theological Stage, rain is explained as resulting from:
nindian-society-15-15.x: The theological stage explains events by supernatural forces (God's will); nature's force is the metaphysical explanation.
xa: **Positive Stage**: rain from **atmospheric processes**.
The Law of Three Stages was proposed by **Auguste Comte**.
Comte's motto: "**Order and Progress**".

nindian-society-3-21.s: Who held that tribes should develop according to their own culture and opposed their rapid assimilation into Hindu society?
nindian-society-3-21.x: Elwin opposed quick assimilation of tribes because he believed they should develop according to their own culture, unlike Ghurye.
xa: **G. S. Ghurye** wrote **Backward Hindus** and saw caste as a product of **Indo-Aryan** culture.
**N. K. Bose**: change in India comes through **adjustment rather than conflict**.
**D. P. Mukerji**: **tradition** is essential to understand Indian society.

ncb28d0970dd.s: The concept of 'class-status-power' is associated with:
ncb28d0970dd.x: Weber gave class-status-power; Durkheim social facts, Marx alienation and Comte positivism.
xa: **Comte** coined **"sociology"** and gave the **law of three stages**.
**Durkheim** also gave **collective conscience**, **sacred vs profane**, **anomie**.
**Weber**: **verstehen**, **ideal type**, ideal bureaucracy, life chances.

n73c2ca7ceb1.s: 'The Religion of India' was written by:
n73c2ca7ceb1.x: Weber wrote 'The Religion of India' and gave class-status-power, life chances and ideal bureaucracy.
xa: Weber also gave **verstehen** (interpretive understanding) and **ideal type**.
Durkheim's concepts: **social facts**, **collective conscience**.

ncc49a6c20b8.s: The concept of 'Verstehen' is associated with:
ncc49a6c20b8.x: Verstehen is Weber's; social facts are Durkheim's, sociological imagination Mills's and network society Castells's.
xa: Castells wrote **The Rise of the Network Society** (**1996**).
Verstehen means **interpretive understanding**.

nindian-society-13-1.s: Karl Marx is known as the Father of which of the following?
nindian-society-13-1.x: Karl Marx is called the father of scientific socialism. Class struggle, surplus value and historical materialism are his ideas, not titles given to him.
nindian-society-13-1.tq: Discriminate Marx's title from the concepts he developed.
n: Karl Marx is known as the Father of Scientific Socialism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #13 · pp 45-46]
xs: **Karl Marx** is the **Father of Scientific Socialism** — option **(1)**.
**Class struggle**, **surplus value** and **historical materialism** are his ideas, not titles given to him.
xa: Marx (**1818**-**1883**) is one of the most influential sociologists in **conflict theory**.
Works: **Das Kapital** (**1867**); **Communist Manifesto** with **Friedrich Engels** (**1848**).
He predicted workers would **overthrow capitalism** and establish a **classless society**.
⚠ **Comte** = Father of Sociology; **Durkheim** = Father of Modern Sociology; **Weber** = Father of Interpretative Sociology.

nindian-society-13-8.s: Karl Marx is regarded as one of the most influential sociologists in which of the following theories?
nindian-society-13-8.x: Marx is one of the most influential conflict theorists. Surplus value, historical materialism and scientific socialism are ideas within his work, not the theory he is placed in.
nindian-society-13-8.tq: Discriminate the school (conflict theory) from the concepts inside it.
xs: Marx is one of the most influential sociologists in **conflict theory** — option **(4)**.
**Surplus value**, **historical materialism** and **scientific socialism** are ideas within his work.
xa: Marx is called the **Father of Scientific Socialism**.
**C. Wright Mills** also highlighted **inequality** and the **concentration of power** (Power Elite Theory).

nindian-society-14-1.s: Emile Durkheim is regarded as the:
nindian-society-14-1.x: Emile Durkheim is called the father of modern sociology. Collective conscience, social facts and anomie are his concepts.
nindian-society-14-1.tq: Discriminate Durkheim's title from his concepts.
n: Emile Durkheim is regarded as the Father of Modern Sociology. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 46-47]
xs: **Emile Durkheim** is the **Father of Modern Sociology** — option **(3)**.
**Collective conscience**, **social facts** and **anomie** are his concepts, not titles.
xa: Works: **The Division of Labour in Society**, **Suicide**, **Rules of Sociological Method**.
For Durkheim, **society** is a **reality sui generis**.
He defined **religion** as beliefs and practices concerning **sacred things**.
⚠ **Auguste Comte** = Father of Sociology.

nindian-society-14-4.s: A condition of normlessness caused by rapid social change, associated with crime and suicide, is called:
nindian-society-14-4.x: Anomie is normlessness caused by rapid social change, which shows up as crime, suicide and unrest.
n: Anomie is a condition of normlessness caused by rapid social change. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 46-47]
Crime is an example of anomie. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 46-47]
Suicide is an example of anomie. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 46-47]
Social unrest is an example of anomie. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 46-47]
xa: **Collective conscience**: shared beliefs and values that unite society.
**Social facts**: external forces such as **laws** and **customs**.
Durkheim's book **Suicide** is among his important works.

nindian-society-14-17.s:
Which of the following are examples of social facts?
1. Laws
2. Customs
3. Religion and traditions
Select the correct answer:
nindian-society-14-17.x: Laws, customs, religion and traditions are all social facts, as they exist outside the individual and shape behaviour.
xa: Durkheim **developed** the concept of social facts.
**Collective conscience**: shared beliefs and values that unite society.
For Durkheim, society is a **reality sui generis**.

nindian-society-14-18.s: Which of the following is NOT a book by Emile Durkheim?
o: The Division of Labour in Society
nindian-society-14-18.x: Collective conscience is a Durkheimian concept, not a book; the other three are his works.
xa: Another Durkheim work: **Elementary Forms of Religious Life**.
His other concepts: **social facts**, **anomie**.
Weber's work: **The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism**.

nindian-society-16-4.s: In Weber's typology of social action, action guided by values and ethics is:
nindian-society-16-4.x: Value-rational action follows values; instrumentally rational action is goal-oriented, traditional follows custom, affective follows emotion.
n: Instrumentally rational action is goal-oriented behaviour. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Value-rational action is guided by values and ethics. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Traditional action is based on customs and traditions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Affective action is based on emotions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
xa: Authority types: **traditional** (customs), **charismatic** (personality and leadership), **legal-rational** (laws and rules).
Bureaucracy: **hierarchy**, **rules and regulations**, **specialization**, **merit system**, **impersonality**.
Weber also gave class-status-power and **life chances**.

nindian-society-16-5.s:
Which of the following are characteristics of Weber's bureaucracy?
1. Hierarchy
2. Impersonality
3. Charismatic leadership
Select the correct answer:
nindian-society-16-5.x: Weber's bureaucracy has hierarchy, specialisation and impersonality; charisma belongs to charismatic authority, not bureaucracy.
n: Bureaucracy is characterized by hierarchy. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Bureaucracy is characterized by specialization. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Bureaucracy is characterized by impersonality. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
Charismatic authority is based on personality and leadership. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 48-50]
xa: Other bureaucracy features: **rules and regulations** and a **merit system**.
**Charismatic** authority rests on **personality and leadership**.
**Legal-rational** authority rests on **laws and rules**.

nindian-society-3-14.s: Who is known as the Father of Sociology?
nindian-society-3-14.x: Auguste Comte, who coined the word, is called the father of sociology. Durkheim is called the father of modern sociology.
nindian-society-3-14.tq: Discriminate 'father of sociology' (Comte) from 'father of modern sociology' (Durkheim).
n: Auguste Comte is known as the Father of Sociology. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
xs: **Auguste Comte** is the **Father of Sociology** — option **(3)**.
He **coined** the term **Sociology** and founded **Positivism**.
**Emile Durkheim** is the **Father of Modern Sociology**; **Max Weber** of **Interpretative Sociology**; **Karl Marx** of **Scientific Socialism**.
xa: **G. S. Ghurye**: the **Father of Indian Sociology**, the first Indian sociologist.
**M. N. Srinivas**: the **Father of Modern Indian Sociology**.
First Sociology Department in India: **University of Bombay**, **1919**.

nindian-society-24-1.s: Who wrote The Sociological Imagination, published in 1959?
nindian-society-24-1.x: C. Wright Mills, an American sociologist, wrote 'The Sociological Imagination' (1959).
nindian-society-24-1.tq: Recall the author of 'The Sociological Imagination'.
n: C. Wright Mills wrote The Sociological Imagination. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 58-59]
The Sociological Imagination was published in 1959. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 58-59]
C. Wright Mills was famous for the concept of sociological imagination. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #24 · pp 58-59]
xs: **C. Wright Mills** wrote **The Sociological Imagination** (**1959**) — option **(1)**.
Mills (**1916 to 1962**) was an **American sociologist**.
xa: Sociological imagination: understanding the relationship between **biography**, **history** and **society**.
**Power Elite Theory**: power concentrated among **political**, **military** and **corporate** elites.
Personal trouble (being **unemployed**) vs public issue (**large-scale unemployment** from an economic slowdown).

nindian-society-24-19.s: In the sociological imagination, 'biography' refers to:
o: The wider sweep of past events and eras
The individual's own life and personal troubles
The social structure surrounding the individual
A group among whom power is concentrated
nindian-society-24-19.x: Biography is the individual's own life; history is the sweep of past eras and society the surrounding structure.
xa: Sociological imagination: connecting **personal experiences** with **larger social forces** and **historical processes**.
The power elite: **political leaders**, **military leaders**, **corporate elites**.
Mills: **The Sociological Imagination** (**1959**).

nindian-society-25-1.s: George Simmel was known for studying which of the following?
nindian-society-25-1.x: Georg Simmel, a German sociologist, studied social interaction and city life. Caste, welfare and national income belong to other fields.
n: George Simmel studied social interaction. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
George Simmel studied urban life. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
xs: **George Simmel** studied **social interaction** and **urban life** — option **(2)**.
He was a **German sociologist** (**1858 to 1918**).
xa: **Formal sociology**: studies **patterns of social interaction** — society exists because individuals interact.
**Dyad** = two people (husband and wife); **triad** = three (teacher, parent, student).
**Urbanization** increases **individualism**, **competition** and **social distance**.

nindian-society-25-4.s: In Simmel's formal sociology, a 'triad' is a group of:
nindian-society-25-4.x: A dyad is a group of two and a triad a group of three; formal sociology studies patterns of interaction.
n: Formal sociology studies patterns of social interaction. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
A dyad is a group of two people. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
A triad is a group of three people. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
Urbanization increases individualism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
Urbanization increases competition. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
Urbanization increases social distance. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 59-60]
xa: Simmel lived **1858 to 1918**.
Society exists because **individuals interact**.
⚠ **Mills** = sociological imagination; **Simmel** = formal sociology.

nindian-society-23-1.s: Sociological Imagination is best defined as the ability to:
o: Study competitive education without relating it to students
Connect personal experiences with larger social forces and historical processes
Explain large-scale unemployment only through personal choices
Treat public issues as unrelated to personal troubles
nindian-society-23-1.x: The sociological imagination is the ability to connect personal experience with wider social forces and history. It sees personal troubles as linked to public issues.
n: Sociological imagination is the ability to connect personal experiences with larger social forces. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 57-58]
Sociological imagination is the ability to connect personal experiences with historical processes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 57-58]
Individual problems are often reflections of wider social issues. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 57-58]
Large-scale unemployment due to economic slowdown is a public issue. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #23 · pp 57-58]
xs: The sociological imagination is the ability to **connect personal experiences** with **larger social forces and historical processes** — option **(2)**.
It treats **individual problems** as **reflections** of **wider social issues**, not as unrelated to them.
xa: It links **biography**, **history** and **society**.
Given by **C. Wright Mills** in **The Sociological Imagination** (**1959**).
Personal trouble: **being unemployed**; public issue: **large-scale unemployment** due to **economic slowdown**.

nindian-society-12-1.s: Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains which of the following despite social changes?
o: Religious tolerance, democratic institutions and welfare schemes only
Social cohesion, constitutional values and inclusive development only
Peace, order, harmony, continuity and effective functioning of institutions
Economic security, political stability and regional equality only
nindian-society-12-1.x: Social stability means society keeps peace, order, harmony, continuity and working institutions even as it changes. The other options list only some of these or name factors that support it.
nindian-society-12-1.tq: Recall the definition of social stability.
n: Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains peace. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains order. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains harmony. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains continuity. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
Social stability refers to a condition in which society maintains the effective functioning of institutions. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
Social stability persists despite social changes. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 44-45]
xs: **Social stability** is a condition where society maintains **peace, order, harmony, continuity** and the **effective functioning of institutions** despite social change — option **(3)**.
The other options list only some **features** (social cohesion, inclusive development) or **promoting factors** (tolerance, welfare schemes).
xa: Key features: **social cohesion**, **social harmony**, **rule of law**, **economic security**, **political stability**, **inclusive development**.
Promoted by the **family**, **education**, **constitutional values**, **democratic institutions**.
Threatened by **poverty and unemployment**, **casteism**, **communalism**, **regionalism**.

nindian-society-12-17.s:
Which of the following promote social stability?
1. Religious and cultural tolerance
2. Regionalism
3. Democratic institutions
Select the correct answer:
nindian-society-12-17.x: Tolerance and democratic institutions (with education and values) promote stability; regionalism threatens it.
xa: The **family** — the primary agent of socialization — also promotes stability.
**Welfare schemes** and **constitutional values** promote stability too.
Threats also include **poverty and unemployment** and **extremism and terrorism**.

n8316376afb0.s: The shift towards nuclear families in India indicates that:
o: The joint-family ideal may continue despite structural change
The joint-family ideal has been completely rejected
Caste has disappeared from social life
Rural society has ceased to exist
n8316376afb0.x: The movement towards nuclear households does not mean rejection of the joint-family ideal. Structural change may coexist with continuity in values and functions.
n8316376afb0.tq: Separate a change in family structure from a complete change in family ideal.
xs: The shift to nuclear families **≠ rejecting the joint-family ideal**; the ideal may continue — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) wrongly treats structural change as complete rejection.
xa: **A.M. Shah**: joint family **changes in structure but continues in function**.
**M.N. Srinivas**: the joint family is **modified, not eliminated**.
**Urbanisation/industrialisation** produce **nuclear households**; family becomes a **consumption unit**.

n9f85a4f3b50.s: The Indological approach to the study of Indian society primarily relies on:
o: Textual sources to explain Indian institutions
n9f85a4f3b50.x: The Indological approach uses textual sources to explain Indian social institutions.
n9f85a4f3b50.tq: Identify the defining method of an approach rather than its subject matter alone.
xs: The **Indological approach** uses **textual sources** to explain Indian institutions — option **(4)** is correct.
Its exponents include **Ghurye, Dumont, Maine**.
xa: **Ghurye**: "Father of Indian Sociology"; founded the **Bombay School**.
**Maine** wrote **Ancient Law** (**1861**).

nbc1c86b7001.s: Louis Dumont's Homo Hierarchicus, published in 1966, is associated with the study of:
o: The four kinship zones of India
Purity-pollution and the encompassing power of the Brahmin
The social background of Indian nationalism
The movement from status to contract
nbc1c86b7001.x: Homo Hierarchicus, published in 1966, discusses hierarchy through purity-pollution and the encompassing power of the Brahmin.
nbc1c86b7001.tq: Connect a title and year with its distinctive conceptual theme.
xs: **Homo Hierarchicus** (**1966**) deals with **purity-pollution** and the **Brahmin's encompassing power** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Four kinship zones** = **Karve**; **Indian nationalism** = **A.R. Desai**; **status to contract** = **Maine**.
xa: **Dumont** was a **French structuralist**.
With **D. Pocock** he founded **Contributions to Indian Sociology** (**1957**).

n6a9d3fec285.s: Who founded Contributions to Indian Sociology with D. Pocock?
n6a9d3fec285.x: Louis Dumont and D. Pocock founded Contributions to Indian Sociology in 1957.
n6a9d3fec285.tq: Identify the correct collaborator pair and avoid swapping scholars across traditions.
xs: **Louis Dumont** founded **Contributions to Indian Sociology** with **D. Pocock** (**1957**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ghurye** founded the **Bombay School**; **Maine** wrote **Ancient Law**.
xa: Dumont's **Homo Hierarchicus** (**1966**): purity-pollution.
Dumont is a **French structuralist** in the **Indological** tradition.

n074e987f193.s: Henry Maine's thesis on the movement of societies is expressed as a movement from:
n074e987f193.x: Maine's well-known thesis describes the movement of societies from status to contract.
n074e987f193.tq: Discriminate between the two reversed terms in a famous sociological formulation.
xs: **Henry Maine**: societies move **"from status to contract"** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses the direction.
xa: Maine wrote **Ancient Law** (**1861**) and **Village Communities in the East and West** (**1871**).
He is grouped in the **Indological** approach.

n5c14c4915c8.s: Which one of the following works was written by M.N. Srinivas?
o: Religion and Society among the Coorgs
n5c14c4915c8.x: Religion and Society among the Coorgs was written by M.N. Srinivas. The other works are associated respectively with Yogendra Singh, A.R. Desai and Iravati Karve.
n5c14c4915c8.tq: Match each sociologist with the distinctive title of the work.
xs: **Religion and Society among the Coorgs** is by **M.N. Srinivas** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Modernization of Indian Tradition** = **Yogendra Singh**; **Social Background of Indian Nationalism** = **A.R. Desai**; **Kinship Organization in India** = **Karve**.
xa: Srinivas also wrote **The Remembered Village**.
Srinivas gave **Sanskritisation**, **Westernisation**, **dominant caste**.

n86984721cd8.s: According to M.N. Srinivas, the joint family in India is:
o: A purely religious institution without social functions
Eliminated by every process of modernisation
n86984721cd8.x: Srinivas viewed the joint family as modified rather than eliminated by social change.
n86984721cd8.tq: Distinguish a qualified sociological observation from an absolute statement.
xs: **M.N. Srinivas**: the joint family is **modified but not eliminated** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) contradicts this view.
xa: ⚠ **A.M. Shah** = changes in structure but **continues in function**.
Shift to nuclear ≠ rejecting the **joint-family ideal**.

n77b8786dc49.s: Who was the first to systematically study Indian kinship?
n77b8786dc49.x: Irawati Karve was the first to systematically study Indian kinship.
xa: Karve wrote **Kinship Organization in India** (**1953**) and identified **four kinship zones**.
She also wrote **Hindu Society: An Interpretation**.

nindian-society-3-6.s: 'Caste, Class and Power' was written by:
nindian-society-3-6.x: 'Caste, Class and Power' is Beteille's; A.R. Desai wrote 'Social Background of Indian Nationalism'.
n: A. R. Desai is associated with Social Background of Indian Nationalism. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
Andre Beteille is associated with Caste, Class and Power. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
Verrier Elwin is associated with Tribal Isolation. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
B. R. Ambedkar is associated with Division of Labourers. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
Andre Beteille studied the relationship among caste, class and power. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
xa: Ambedkar: caste is **not merely** a division of labour but a **division of labourers**.
Beteille: traditional **cumulative** inequality → **dispersed** inequality.
Desai: nationalism emerged from **socio-economic changes** under **colonialism**.

nindian-society-3-9.s: Who stated that kinship is the backbone of Indian social organization?
nindian-society-3-9.x: Irawati Karve called kinship the backbone of Indian social organisation ('Kinship Organisation in India').
n: Irawati Karve stated that kinship is the backbone of Indian social organization. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
xs: **Irawati Karve** said **kinship** is the **backbone** of Indian social organization — option **(2)**.
Her work: **Kinship Organization in India** (**1953**), describing **four kinship zones**.
xa: Karve was the **first** to systematically study Indian kinship.
She also wrote **Hindu Society: An Interpretation**.
**A. M. Shah**: the joint family is **changing, not disappearing**.
**Yogendra Singh**: **Modernization of Indian Tradition**.

nindian-society-3-12.s: 'Kinship Organization in India' was written by:
nindian-society-3-12.x: Karve wrote 'Kinship Organization in India'; Ghurye 'Caste and Race in India', Yogendra Singh 'Modernization of Indian Tradition'.
n: G. S. Ghurye is associated with Caste and Race in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
Irawati Karve is associated with Kinship Organization in India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
Yogendra Singh is associated with Modernization of Indian Tradition. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
G. S. Ghurye is associated with Backward Hindus. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 15-17]
xa: ⚠ **Ghurye 1932** – **Karve 1953** – **Marriott 1955** – **Dumont 1966**.
Yogendra Singh's book is dated **1973**; Desai's **1948**.
**McKim Marriott**: **Village India** (**1955**) — universalisation and parochialisation.

nindian-society-1-9.s: Who is called the 'Father of Modern Indian Sociology'?
nindian-society-1-9.x: M.N. Srinivas is the father of modern Indian sociology; Ghurye is the father of Indian sociology and Karve India's first woman sociologist.
n: Auguste Comte was the father of Sociology. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
G. S. Ghurye was the father of Indian Sociology. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
M. N. Srinivas was the father of Modern Indian Sociology. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
Irawati Karve was the first woman sociologist of India. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-13]
xa: Karve was the **first** to systematically study Indian **kinship**.
Ghurye was also the **first Indian sociologist** and founded the **Bombay School**.
First Sociology Department in India: **University of Bombay**, **1919**.
Durkheim = **Father of Modern Sociology**.

nd882e160d19.s: Which of the following correctly describes Milton Singer's contribution to the study of continuity and change?
o: He wrote When a Great Tradition Modernizes, concerning Madras
He formulated the theory of status to contract
nd882e160d19.x: Milton Singer wrote When a Great Tradition Modernizes, a work concerning Madras. The other descriptions belong to Ghurye, Karve and Maine respectively.
nd882e160d19.tq: Match the scholar with the exact title and regional reference.
xs: **Milton Singer** wrote **When a Great Tradition Modernizes**, on **Madras** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Bombay School** = **Ghurye**; **four kinship zones** = **Karve**; **status to contract** = **Maine**.
xa: Singer's theme: **continuity within change**.
Singer and **McKim Marriott** applied **Great/Little Tradition** to India.

n4fb58685321.s: The Great Tradition and the Little Tradition respectively refer to
n4fb58685321.x: The Great Tradition denotes the elite-Sanskritic tradition, whereas the Little Tradition denotes local-folk traditions.
n4fb58685321.tq: Discriminate between two paired sociological terms by their precise meanings.
xs: **Great Tradition** = **elite-Sanskritic**; **Little Tradition** = **local-folk** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Material vs non-material** culture belongs to **Ogburn**'s **cultural lag**, not to this pair.
xa: Originated by **Robert Redfield**; applied to India by **Milton Singer** and **McKim Marriott**.
⚠ **Universalisation** = upward; **Parochialisation** = downward (both **Marriott**).

nf98aa7908b1.s: Parochialisation denotes the process by which
o: class divisions disappear through social mobility
local traditions move into the Great Tradition
material culture falls behind non-material culture
nf98aa7908b1.x: Parochialisation is the downward localisation of elements from the Great Tradition into local contexts. Universalisation is the reverse upward movement of Little Tradition elements.
nf98aa7908b1.tq: Use the direction of cultural movement to distinguish parochialisation from universalisation.
xs: **Parochialisation**: **Great-Tradition elements are localised downward** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (3) describes **universalisation**; option (4) is a reversed **cultural lag**.
xa: ⚠ **Universalisation** = upward; **Parochialisation** = downward (both **McKim Marriott**).
Marriott's **Village India** appeared in **1955**.

n6ec67adf58d.s: Cultural lag refers to the situation in which
o: local culture replaces the Great Tradition
non-material culture lags behind material change
material culture lags behind non-material change
n6ec67adf58d.x: Cultural lag describes the delay in the adaptation of non-material culture to changes in material culture. Ogburn discussed the concept in Social Change (1922).
n6ec67adf58d.tq: Apply the material–non-material distinction to identify the direction of the lag.
xs: **Cultural lag**: **non-material culture lags behind material change** — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses it; the concept is **W.F. Ogburn**'s (**Social Change, 1922**).
xa: **Durkheim**: **social facts**, collective conscience.
**Universalisation** and **parochialisation**: **McKim Marriott**.

n42c774ea61e.s: The Great and Little Tradition was applied to the Indian context by:
n42c774ea61e.x: Robert Redfield originated the concept, and Milton Singer and McKim Marriott applied it to India.
n42c774ea61e.tq: Distinguish the originator of a concept from the scholars who applied it to India.
xs: **Milton Singer and McKim Marriott** applied the **Great/Little Tradition** to India — option **(1)** is correct.
The concept was originated by **Robert Redfield**.
xa: **Singer**: **When a Great Tradition Modernizes** (Madras).
**Marriott**: **Village India** (**1955**); universalisation and parochialisation.
**Ogburn** is linked with **cultural lag**, not this concept.

o: the upward movement of local traditions
nf0eed4d8781.x: Verstehen, associated with Max Weber, means interpretive understanding of social action.
nf0eed4d8781.tq: Translate the technical term into its precise meaning before considering the options.
xs: **Verstehen** means **interpretive understanding** (**Max Weber**) — option **(1)** is correct.
Upward movement of local traditions is **universalisation**; delay of non-material culture is **cultural lag**.
xa: Weber also gave **ideal type** and **ideal bureaucracy**.
**Durkheim**: social facts; **Marx**: alienation; **Comte**: positivism.

nindian-society-22-19.s: An approach to Indian society that relies on interpretation through culture is called:
nindian-society-22-19.x: Cultural interpretation reads society through culture; the text-based approach rests on texts and the historical perspective on history.
xa: Indology studies society through **ancient texts**, **scriptures**, **epics** and **religious literature**.
Indological approach scholars: **Ghurye**, **Dumont**, **Maine**.
**Henry Maine**: societies move "**from status to contract**" (**Ancient Law**, **1861**).

n53be32d338a.s: Which historical practice is associated with Shankaracharya as a bond of unity?
o: Sending priests from southern temples to the north and vice versa
n53be32d338a.x: Shankaracharya is associated with sending priests from the south to temples in the north and vice versa, thereby strengthening cultural links.
n53be32d338a.tq: Match the historical personality with the institution-building practice attributed to him.
xs: **Shankaracharya** **sent priests from south to northern temples and vice versa** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Zonal Councils** and linguistic States are modern **remedies**, not Shankaracharya's work; **Hindu Code Acts** are legal change.
xa: Other bonds: **Onam** shared by all communities; **Bhakti-Sufi syncretism**; **Khanqahs**.
Threats: **communalism, casteism, regionalism, linguism, ethnic conflict**.

n4d8abdae32b.s: Linguistic reorganisation of States was described as a safety valve because it:
o: Ended the need for national integration
Accommodated linguistic aspirations within the Union
n4d8abdae32b.x: Linguistic reorganisation acted as a safety valve by accommodating linguistic aspirations. It made India a State-Nation rather than a homogeneous nation-state.
n4d8abdae32b.tq: Infer the institutional effect of accommodating diversity without assuming its elimination.
xs: Linguistic reorganisation was a **"safety valve"** that **accommodated linguistic aspirations** — option **(3)** is correct.
It made India a **"State-Nation"**, **not a homogeneous nation-state** — option (1) is wrong.
xa: Andhra (**1953**) = **first State formed on linguistic lines**, the start of "safety-valve" reorganisation.
**SRA 1956** is listed as a remedy for national integration.
⚠ **Linguism** is still listed as a **threat** to integration.

n5891855dd91.s: The technological force of change associated with digital citizenship is the:
n5891855dd91.x: Digital citizenship is associated with technology and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023.
n5891855dd91.tq: Use the year and policy-domain clue to identify the technology-related law.
xs: **Technology** → **digital citizenship**, linked to the **DPDP Act 2023** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hindu Code Acts** and **Caste Disabilities Removal Act 1850** are **legal** forces; **SRA 1956** is a national-integration remedy.
xa: Education → **individualism, privacy and rights**.
Urbanisation → **nuclear households**; family a **consumption unit**.

n26a6b42ecb0.s: On which occasion was a report proposing a National Mission for Mother-Tongue-Based Multilingual Education mentioned?
n26a6b42ecb0.x: The report proposing a National Mission for Mother-Tongue-Based Multilingual Education was mentioned on Mother Language Day, 21 February 2026.
n26a6b42ecb0.tq: Distinguish the exact observance associated with the policy proposal.
xs: The report was linked to **Mother Language Day** (**Feb 2026**) — option **(1)** is correct.
It proposed a **National Mission for Mother-Tongue-Based Multilingual Education**.
xa: **Jan 2026**: **55 volumes** of classical-literature translations released.
⚠ **122** languages (Census 2011) vs **22** in the Constitution.

n63461356e62.s: The formation of Andhra in 1953 is associated with the beginning of
o: the three-stage theory of social development
n63461356e62.x: The formation of Andhra in 1953 as the first State on linguistic lines marked the beginning of the safety-valve reorganisation of States.
n63461356e62.tq: Link the event to its specific constitutional and political significance.
xs: **Andhra** (**1953**) was the **first State formed on linguistic lines**, starting the **"safety-valve" reorganisation** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Universalisation** is Marriott's concept; the **three-stage** law is Comte's; **network society** is Castells'.
xa: Linguistic reorganisation made India a **"State-Nation"**, not a homogeneous nation-state.
**SRA 1956** is listed as a remedy for national integration.

nindian-society-10-1.s: Which Act was enacted in 1850 to remove legal disabilities arising from caste conversion?
nindian-society-10-1.x: The Caste Disabilities Removal Act, 1850, removed the legal disabilities, such as loss of inheritance, that came from changing religion or caste.
n: The Caste Disabilities Removal Act was enacted in 1850. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 39-42]
The Caste Disabilities Removal Act removed legal disabilities due to caste conversion. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 39-42]
xs: The **Caste Disabilities Removal Act** (**1850**) removed legal disabilities due to **caste conversion** — option **(1)**.
It is listed among **law** as a force of social change.
xa: Other legal forces of change: **Art. 17** and the **Hindu Code** Acts.
Education as a force of change: **individualism**, **privacy** and **rights**.
Technology: **digital citizenship**; **DPDP Act 2023**.

nindian-society-11-16.s: The National Integration Council, chaired by the Prime Minister, was set up mainly to combat which problems?
nindian-society-11-16.x: The National Integration Council works against communalism, casteism and regionalism to promote national integration. Poverty, women's status and exams belong to other bodies.
nindian-society-11-16.tq: Recall the divisive forces the Council targets.
n: The purpose of the National Integration Council is national integration. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 42-44]
xs: The **National Integration Council** combats **communalism, casteism and regionalism** — option **(2)**.
These are listed **threats** to unity; the Council is one of the **remedies**.
xa: Other remedies: **SRA 1956**, **Zonal Councils**, **Art. 350-B** (Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities).
Other threats: **linguism** and **ethnic conflict**.
Andhra (**1953**) was the first State formed on linguistic lines — the "**safety-valve**" reorganisation.
⚠ UPPSC 2025 A-R: national integration has **political, economic, social, cultural and psychological** dimensions.

n6683352cb60.s: National integration in India is best described as having which dimensions?
o: Political, economic, social, cultural and psychological dimensions
n6683352cb60.x: National integration has political, economic, social, cultural and psychological dimensions (the true Assertion in a UPPSC 2025 question). The other options each leave out most of these dimensions.
xs: National integration has **political, economic, social, cultural and psychological** dimensions — option **(2)** is correct.
The other options keep only one or two of these dimensions.
xa: This was the Assertion in **UPPSC 2025** (keyed: **A true, R false**).
Remedies: **National Integration Council**, **SRA 1956**, **Zonal Councils**, **Art. 350-B**.

nda6a736a8eb.s: A.M. Shah's interpretation of the joint family is that it:
o: Is eliminated by all forms of education
Continues in structure but disappears in function
Changes in structure but continues in function
nda6a736a8eb.x: A.M. Shah argued that the joint family changes in structure but continues in function.
nda6a736a8eb.tq: Distinguish structural change from functional continuity.
xs: **A.M. Shah**: the joint family **changes in structure but continues in function** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses structure and function.
xa: ⚠ **A.M. Shah** = continues in function; **Srinivas** = **modified, not eliminated**.
Shift to nuclear ≠ rejecting the **joint-family ideal**.

nd7d3800a070.s: A family in which a married couple establishes a separate residence away from both sets of parents is described as:
nd7d3800a070.x: A neo-local family residence is established independently by the married couple.
nd7d3800a070.tq: Distinguish residence-based classifications by identifying the location created after marriage.
xs: A couple setting up a **new home** away from both sets of parents is **neo-local** residence — option **(1)** is correct.
**Patrilocal**, **matrilocal** and **bilocal** all involve living with a natal family.
xa: ⚠ **Duo-local** = spouses stay with their **own natal families**; **neo-local** = new home.
Other bases of family type: **descent** (patrilineal/matrilineal) and **authority** (patriarchal/matriarchal).
**Lakshadweep Muslims** are **duolocal** ("Taravad").

nb957fe1e54c.s: A person’s family consisting of the family into which he or she is born is called the:
nb957fe1e54c.x: The family of orientation is the family into which a person is born, whereas the family of procreation is established after marriage.
nb957fe1e54c.tq: Discriminate between two closely related sociological terms by their time of formation.
xs: The family one is **born into** is the **family of orientation** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **family of procreation** is the one **set up after marriage** — option (4) is the trap.
xa: **Murdock**: family = **common residence, economic co-operation, reproduction**.
**MacIver**: group defined by sex relationships precise + enduring enough for **procreation and upbringing**.

n13ed454f696.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a factor contributing to the rise of single-parent and female-headed households?
n13ed454f696.x: Widowhood, marital instability and male migration are identified as causes of rising single-parent and female-headed households. Expansion of joint-family residence is not listed as a cause.
n13ed454f696.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated causes rather than merely naming a related family feature.
xs: **Expansion of joint-family residence** is not a cause — option **(2)** is correct.
Single-parent / **female-headed households** rise due to **widowhood, marital instability, male migration** — options (1), (3), (4).
xa: **Dual-income** urban households: pressure on **child care + caregiving** (UPSC).
**Women's employment** also raises female-headed households.

n610cb1fe775.s: Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has recently advocated:
o: Replacing joint families with nuclear households
A return to the joint family and incentives for families with two or more children
A two-child limit with penalties for larger families
n610cb1fe775.x: In the context of declining fertility, Naidu urged a return to the joint family and incentives for having two or more children.
xa: **NFHS-6** TFR **2.0**; NFHS-5 urban TFR **1.6**.
AP's **1985** succession amendment preceded the central **2005** amendment by **20 years**.

nindian-society-8-1.s: Which of the following is described as a basic and primary social institution?
nindian-society-8-1.x: The family is the basic, primary social institution, the first place where a person is socialised.
nindian-society-8-1.tq: Recall the family as the primary institution.
n: Family is a basic and primary social institution. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
xs: The **family** is a **basic** and **primary social institution** — option **(3)**.
Its functions: **reproduction**, **socialization**, **emotional support**, **economic security**, **cultural transmission**.
xa: Scholars of family: **George Peter Murdock**, **Talcott Parsons**, **Irawati Karve**.
⚠ Family of **orientation** = born into; family of **procreation** = set up after marriage.
Census 2011: over half of all households were **nuclear**.

nindian-society-6-1.s: Which of the following is described as the first school of the child?
nindian-society-6-1.x: The family is the child's first school, teaching language, customs, values, traditions and norms before any formal schooling.
nindian-society-6-1.tq: Recall why the family is the first school.
n: Family is the first school of the child. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: The **family** is the **first school** of the child — option **(2)**.
It teaches **language**, **customs**, **values**, **traditions** and **norms**, and basic education **before school**.
xa: It **develops discipline** and **moral values** and encourages learning habits.
A child learns **manners** and **respect for elders** in the family.
Murdock's **educational** function = **socialization of children**.

naa782f4c396.s: According to Talcott Parsons, the two irreducible functions of the family are:
o: Primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of adult personality
naa782f4c396.x: Parsons identified primary socialisation of children and stabilisation of the adult personality as the family's two irreducible functions.
xa: **Murdock**: 4 universal functions; **Ogburn**: 7 functions.
General functions: **biological, economic, socialisation, psychological**.

n455f2f0ba00.s: Persistent failure of family functions, for example through abuse or alcoholism, is termed:
n455f2f0ba00.x: Dysfunction is the persistent failure of the family's biological, economic, socialisation or psychological functions, e.g. through abuse or alcoholism.
xa: **Ogburn**: "**loss of functions**" — only affection stays.
**High-risk families**: single-parent / **female-headed**, **dual-income** urban, elderly-care strain.

nindian-society-6-20.s: Who identified the four universal functions of the family?
nindian-society-6-20.x: George Peter Murdock named four universal functions of the family: sexual regulation, reproduction, economic cooperation and education.
n: George Peter Murdock identified four universal functions of the family. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 24-28]
xs: **George Peter Murdock** identified the **four universal functions** of the family — option **(2)**.
They are **sexual regulation**, **reproductive**, **economic** and **educational**.
xa: **Ogburn**: **7** functions, all except affection passing to outside agencies ("**loss of functions**").
**Talcott Parsons**: **2** — primary socialisation and stabilisation of adult personality.
Murdock's definition: **common residence, economic co-operation, reproduction**.

nindian-society-31-1.s: High-risk families are best described as families facing:
o: Only economic difficulties such as poverty and unemployment
Only health-related challenges and chronic illness
Only the problems of single-parent households
Severe social, economic, health, psychological or environmental challenges harming members' well-being
nindian-society-31-1.x: High-risk families face serious social, economic, health, psychological or environmental problems that harm their members; they are not limited to one kind of problem.
n: High-risk families are families facing severe social, economic, health, psychological, or environmental challenges. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 65-67]
xa: Characteristics: **poverty**, **unemployment**, **domestic violence**, **substance abuse**, **single-parent households**.
Also: **chronic illness** or **disability**, **child neglect and abuse**, **family conflicts**.
Types in India: **female-headed** households, **dual-income urban** households, families needing **elderly care**.

na445dba8fab.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the tharawad among Tiyans, some Moplas and Bants?
o: A patrilocal household in which the eldest son inherits
A duolocal household of Lakshadweep Muslims called Taravad
A household headed by the heiress’s husband called nokma
A household consisting of a woman, her siblings and her sisters’ children, without the husband in the unit
na445dba8fab.x: Among Tiyans, some Moplas and Bants, the tharawad consists of a woman, her siblings and her sisters’ children; the husband is not part of the unit.
na445dba8fab.tq: Use the membership details to distinguish similar matrilineal systems.
xs: Among **Tiyans, some Moplas, Bants**, the **tharawad** = **a woman, her siblings and her sisters' children**, **no husband in the unit** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (2) is the **Lakshadweep** Taravad; option (3) is the **Garo nokma** household.
xa: These communities are in **Malabar / Kanara**.
**Nair tharavad** (Kerala): **Marumakkathayam**, abolished in **1975**.

n0859786b7f4.s: Which category of urban family is associated with a joint family form and strong elder-male authority?
n0859786b7f4.x: The proprietary class is described as having joint families and strong elder-male authority.
n0859786b7f4.tq: Match the urban income category with its authority structure.
xs: The **proprietary class** has **joint** families and **strong elder-male authority** — option **(3)** is correct.
The other urban categories by income are **entrepreneurial-cum-professional** and **service**.
xa: **T.K. Oommen** reads urban families by **livelihood, income, authority structure, social milieu, value pattern**.
**UPPSC 2014** asked how Oommen distinguished urban families.

n7dc270fac55.s: In the Khasi matrilineal system, the youngest daughter inherits. This practice is known as:
n7dc270fac55.x: Inheritance by the youngest daughter is called ultimogeniture and is associated with the Khasi of Meghalaya.
n7dc270fac55.tq: Distinguish inheritance by the youngest child from inheritance by the eldest child.
xs: Inheritance by the **youngest daughter** among the **Khasi** is **ultimogeniture** — option **(1)** is correct.
Khasi families are also **matrilocal** (Meghalaya).
xa: ⚠ **Khasi** = youngest daughter; **Garo** = **Machong**.
**Garo**: the heiress's husband (**nokma**) heads the household.

nea58b3d6e77.s: The Marumakkathayam system of the Nair tharavad in Kerala was abolished by which of the following?

n029285a93ed.s: The Mitakshara school of Hindu law is based on Vijnaneshwara’s commentary on the:
n029285a93ed.x: Mitakshara is Vijnaneshwara’s commentary on the Yajnavalkya Smriti, composed in the Kalyani Chalukya court.

⚠ Do not confuse with **Dayabhaga**, which is **Jimutavahana**'s work.

n40ff854cafc.s: The 2005 amendment to the Hindu Succession Act made daughters:

n17e71663a7f.s: In Vineeta Sharma (2020), the Supreme Court held that daughters' coparcenary rights by birth apply:

na5f77a63f3e.s: Who was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, of which the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 formed a part?
na5f77a63f3e.x: B.R. Ambedkar was the main advocate of the Hindu Code, which included the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara and Jimutavahana the Dayabhaga, the two classical schools of inheritance; Irawati Karve was a sociologist of the joint family and kinship.

**Vijnaneshwara** wrote the **Mitakshara**; **Jimutavahana** the **Dayabhaga**; **Karve** studied jointness.
xa: **2005** amendment: daughters = **coparceners by birth**.

nc096732de74.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about studies on the persistence of the joint family?

nfa2c62c1b18.s: Which one of the following changes is associated with industrialisation and its impact on the family?

n75c557a5450.s: Which one of the following trends is associated with the Later Vedic period?

xs: In the **Later Vedic** period, **child marriage emerged**, **Swayamvara declined** and **widow remarriage was discouraged** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the trend: Swayamvara declined and widow remarriage was discouraged, not encouraged.

Polygyny is a type of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
Polyandry is a type of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
Endogamy is a type of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
Exogamy is a type of marriage. [Indian Society · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-36]
xa: Marriage is a **socially approved union** that **legitimizes children** and **creates kinship ties**.
Other marriage terms: **Anuloma**, **Pratiloma**, **Levirate**, **Sororate**.
Kinship rests on **blood** (**consanguineal**) and **marriage** (**affinal**) ties.

na4b67c1a7bc.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Dumont's observations on South Indian kinship?
o: Kin are clustered in a narrow area
There is a sharp consanguine-affine division
na4b67c1a7bc.x: Dumont observed no sharp line between consanguines and affines in the South.
xa: The South prefers **cross-cousin** marriage; parallel cousins barred.
**Kolenda** (**1968**) built on **Karve**.
AP: **menarikam** (cross-cousin and uncle-niece marriage).

nfdc09cfa3a8.s: Irawati Karve is known as the ‘Mother of Indian Kinship Studies’ mainly because she
o: introduced the concept of fictive kinship
nfdc09cfa3a8.x: Karve is regarded as the ‘Mother of Indian Kinship Studies’ because she was the first to map Indian kinship systematically.
nfdc09cfa3a8.tq: Use the ‘first’ clue to identify the scholar’s distinctive contribution.
xs: **Karve** is the "**Mother of Indian Kinship Studies**" as the **first to map Indian kinship systematically** — option **(1)**.
The **classificatory-descriptive distinction** is **L.H. Morgan**'s, not Karve's.
xa: Her **Kinship Organization in India (1953)** divided India into **4 zones**.
**Kolenda** (**1968**) built on Karve.
Karve also analysed **sapinda** and **gotra**.

n66072030d50.s: Which of the following elements formed part of H.H. Risley’s definition of caste?
o: Only a common geographical residence and a common language
A group defined exclusively by political office
A common name, a claimed mythical ancestor and a common hereditary calling
A purely voluntary association based on individual choice
n66072030d50.x: Risley described caste in terms of families sharing a common name, claiming descent from a mythical ancestor and following the same hereditary calling.
n66072030d50.tq: Select the complete cluster of defining elements associated with Risley.
xs: **H.H. Risley** defined caste as families with **a common name**, **a claimed mythical ancestor** and **the same hereditary calling** — option **(3)**.
Caste is fixed by birth, so a **voluntary association** (option 4) contradicts every definition in the notes.
xa: Risley also gave the **racial theory** of caste origin.
**Ketkar** (**1909**): membership by birth + a ban on marrying outside.
**Martindale and Monachesi**: obligations and privileges fixed by birth, sanctioned by religion.

n1a9c7aca283.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Traditional or Divine theory of the origin of caste?
o: The four varnas originated from the body of Purusha as described in the Purusha Sukta
Caste developed through restrictions on commensality to preserve culture
Caste was a device created by Brahmins to preserve superiority and purity
Caste originated from hereditary occupations becoming guilds
n1a9c7aca283.x: The Traditional or Divine theory is associated with the Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda, which describes Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas and Shudras as emerging from different parts of Purusha.
n1a9c7aca283.tq: Match the theory with its distinctive core idea and source.
xs: The **Traditional / Divine** theory traces the four varnas to the body of **Purusha** in the **Purusha Sukta** (RV **10.90**) — option **(1)**.
