xs: **Odisha** is not among the seven — option **(3)** is the answer.
The **7** States: **MP, UP, Bihar, Assam, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Rajasthan**.
xa: Target: TFR **2.1 by 2025**.
Outreach teams in **146 districts**.
**ASHA** birth-spacing scheme: **2**-year gap after marriage, **3**-year spacing after first child.

n8ea8bb4f8a2.s: Which scheme provides maternity benefits for pregnant and lactating women?
n8ea8bb4f8a2.x: PM Matru Vandana Yojana 2.0 is a maternity-benefit scheme for pregnant and lactating women.
n8ea8bb4f8a2.tq: Match the scheme with its specific target group.
xs: **PM Matru Vandana Yojana 2.0** gives **maternity benefit** to **pregnant and lactating women** — option **(4)** is correct.
**JSY** gives a cash incentive for **institutional delivery**; **Mission Parivar Vikas** targets TFR in **7** States.
xa: NFHS-6 lists PMMVY under **maternal-health drivers**.
**JSY** launched **2005** under **NRHM**.
NFHS-6: institutional deliveries **90.6%**.

n98391aaa894.s: The main objective of the Janani Suraksha Yojana is to:
o: reduce maternal and neonatal mortality by promoting institutional delivery through a cash incentive
provide a pension to elderly women
bring the TFR to 2.1 in seven high-fertility States
give maternity benefit to all lactating women in the organised sector
n98391aaa894.x: JSY (2005, NRHM) gives a cash incentive for institutional delivery to cut maternal and neonatal mortality (APPSC 2018 key). Option C is Mission Parivar Vikas; option D resembles PMMVY; JSY is not a pension scheme.
n98391aaa894.tq: JSY = cash for institutional delivery; MPV = TFR 2.1 in 7 States; PMMVY = maternity benefit.
xs: **JSY** aims to **reduce maternal and neonatal mortality** by a **cash incentive** for **institutional delivery** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC **2018** key).
TFR **2.1** in **7** States is **Mission Parivar Vikas**; maternity benefit for lactating women is **PMMVY**.
xa: JSY launched **2005** under **NRHM**.
NFHS-6: institutional deliveries **88.6% → 90.6%**.
**ASHA** birth-spacing: **2**-year gap after marriage.

n2dd31b8b0d3.s: The 42nd Constitutional Amendment froze Lok Sabha and State Assembly seats on the basis of the 1971 Census until:
n2dd31b8b0d3.x: The 42nd Amendment of 1976 froze the allocation of seats based on the 1971 Census until 2000.
n2dd31b8b0d3.tq: Separate the original freeze period from its later extension.
xs: The **42nd Amendment** (**1976**) froze seats on the **1971 Census** until **2000** — option **(2)** is correct.
**2026** relates to the **84th Amendment** extension.
xa: **84th Amendment** (**2001**): freeze **until the first Census after 2026**.
**87th Amendment** (**2003**): boundary readjustment on **2001 Census**.
Seats allotted on population under **Art. 82 and 170**.

n72b3b899b81.s: Which amendment extended the freeze on seat allocation until the first Census after 2026?
n72b3b899b81.x: The 84th Amendment of 2001 extended the freeze until the first Census after 2026.
n72b3b899b81.tq: Distinguish the amendment that created the freeze from the amendment that extended it.
xs: The **84th Amendment** (**2001**) extended the freeze **until the first Census after 2026** — option **(2)** is correct.
**42nd** froze seats until **2000**; **87th** readjusted boundaries on the **2001 Census**.
xa: It was a **motivational measure** under NPP strategy.
It allowed boundary readjustment on the **1991** Census.
Southern States fear losing **8-10 Lok Sabha seats** at delimitation.

ncffa6a4d397.s: Seats in the Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assemblies are allotted on the basis of population under which Articles?
ncffa6a4d397.x: Articles 82 and 170 relate to the allocation and readjustment of seats on the basis of population.
ncffa6a4d397.tq: Use Article-number discrimination between parliamentary and local-government provisions.
xs: Seats are allotted on population under **Articles 82 and 170** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seat counts themselves were **frozen** — on the **1971 Census** by the **42nd Amendment**, extended by the **84th**.
xa: **42nd Amendment** (**1976**) froze seats on the **1971 Census** until **2000**.
**84th Amendment** (**2001**) extended the freeze until the first Census after **2026**.
**Boundary readjustment** = no change in seat numbers.

nd184c4b3b58.s: Which Constitutional Amendment allowed readjustment of constituency boundaries on the basis of the 2001 Census, without changing the number of seats?
nd184c4b3b58.x: The 87th Amendment (2003) allowed boundary readjustment on the 2001 Census; the 84th extended the seat freeze and the 42nd froze seats on the 1971 Census.
xa: **84th Amendment**: **2001**.
**42nd Amendment**: **1976**, freeze till **2000**.
Southern fear: loss of **8-10** Lok Sabha seats.

nc2adb7261ce.s: According to Census 2011, migration was recorded using which two bases?
o: Place of birth and place of last residence
nc2adb7261ce.x: The Census recorded migration by place of birth and by place of last residence.
nc2adb7261ce.tq: Recall the two official migration bases as a paired concept.
xs: Census records migration by **place of birth** and **place of last residence** — option **(1)** is correct.
Female inter-state streams (**2011**) are reported by **last residence**.
xa: **141.2 million** moved during **2001-2011**.
Largest stream overall: **rural→rural**, driven by **marriage**.
Reasons: **marriage** for women; **work** for men.

nbf060523d5f.s: Which one of the following was the order of inter-State female migration streams by place of last residence in 2011, from highest to lowest?
nbf060523d5f.x: The order was Urban-Urban, Rural-Urban, Rural-Rural and Urban-Rural.
nbf060523d5f.tq: Read the ranking carefully instead of applying the general rural-rural migration pattern.
xs: **Urban-Urban > Rural-Urban > Rural-Rural > Urban-Rural** — option **(4)** is correct (JPSC **2023** key).
This is **inter-state female** migration by **last residence** (**2011**).
xa: ⚠ Overall, the largest stream is **rural→rural**, driven by marriage.
**141.2 million** moved during **2001-2011**.
Census bases: **place of birth** + **place of last residence**.

na085d3ecc0d.s: The National Policy on Older Persons, 1999 contains how many areas of intervention?
na085d3ecc0d.x: The policy, associated with the Ministry of Social Justice, has 14 areas of intervention including health care and nutrition.
xa: **Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007**.
**NPHCE** launched **2010-11**.
**NCOP** = highest advisory body.

n69a59096ed2.s: The National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE) was launched in
n69a59096ed2.x: NPHCE was launched in 2010–11 to provide health care for persons aged 60 years and above.
n69a59096ed2.tq: Distinguish the launch year of the health programme from the years of the policy and legislation.
xs: **NPHCE** was launched in **2010–11** — option **(4)** is correct.
It covers **60+** health care.
xa: **1999** = National Policy on Older Persons; **2007** = Maintenance Act.
**NCOP** (National Council for Senior Citizens) = highest advisory body.
Elderly share **9.7%** (SRS **2024**).

ne0010968e85.s: Under the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007, maintenance of parents and senior citizens is
o: a legal duty of children and relatives
a responsibility of the Union Government alone
a duty imposed exclusively on local bodies
ne0010968e85.x: The Act makes the maintenance of parents and senior citizens a legal duty of children and relatives.
ne0010968e85.tq: Ask who bears the legal responsibility rather than relying on the general welfare objective.
xs: Under the **2007 Act**, maintenance is a **legal duty of children and relatives** — option **(1)** is correct.

xa: **National Policy on Older Persons 1999**: **14 areas** of intervention.
AP pillar **Kshema** = elderly care.

n32eac6fd41c.s: With reference to pension coverage among the elderly, which one of the following is correct?
o: About 40% of both elderly women and men have no formal pension.
Nearly 70% of both elderly women and men have no formal pension.

Nearly 70% of elderly women have no formal pension, compared with about 40% of elderly men.
n32eac6fd41c.x: Nearly 70% of elderly women have no formal pension, whereas the corresponding proportion among elderly men is about 40%.
n32eac6fd41c.tq: Preserve the direction of the gender comparison while checking both percentages.
xs: Nearly **70%** of elderly **women** lack a formal pension vs about **40%** of elderly **men** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option (3) reverses the two.
xa: Elderly = **9.7%** of population (SRS **2024**).
Elderly projected **230 mn** by **2036**.
IMF: ageing could cut growth by **70 basis points** a year.

n3655a663af5.s: Which change is associated with Andhra Pradesh’s draft population policy of March 2026?
o: Introduction of a three-child norm for local elections
Removal of the two-child norm for local body elections
n3655a663af5.x: The Andhra Pradesh draft policy proposed removing the two-child norm for local body elections.
n3655a663af5.tq: Identify the policy change by spotting the reversal of the existing norm.
xs: AP's March 2026 draft **Population Management Policy** proposes the **removal of the two-child norm for local body elections** — so option **(4)** is correct.

It offers a **₹25,000** incentive for a **second or third child**.
xa: Its package is called **"Poshana-Shiksha-Suraksha"**.
Five pillars: **Matrutva**, **Shakti**, **Kshema**, **Naipunyam**, **Sanjeevani**.
Health Minister **Satya Kumar Yadav** warned of "**shrinconomics**"; AP's TFR is **1.50**.
**Gram Sabhas** were held in all districts to gather feedback on the draft.

nb0d23e752d1.s: The relatively low impact of family planning programmes in rural areas has been attributed primarily to:
nb0d23e752d1.x: Social orthodoxy and psychological factors were identified as important causes of the low rural impact of family planning programmes.
nb0d23e752d1.tq: Match the social outcome with its stated behavioural and cultural causes.
xs: Low rural impact is due to **social orthodoxy and psychological factors** — option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 **2008** key).
Option (3) is wrong: the barriers are **early marriage** and **low female literacy**, not late marriage.
xa: Other rural factors: **son preference**; children seen as **old-age "insurance"**.
**Early marriage**; **low female literacy**.
Distrust after **1976-77** coercion.

n4a5f3b3cb35.s: Which of the following is associated with weak rural acceptance of family planning?
n4a5f3b3cb35.x: Son preference, children as old-age insurance, early marriage and low female literacy are all barriers.
xa: Primary cause: **social orthodoxy and psychological factors** (APPSC-G2 **2008**).
Reluctance to **sterilisation**, men especially.
Female sterilisation **37.9%** (NFHS-5).

n377b1026247.s: The Couple Protection Rate refers to the percentage of eligible couples who are:
o: Married before the legal age and protected from early marriage
Eligible for maternity benefits under PMMVY
Effectively protected against childbirth by an approved contraceptive method
n377b1026247.x: The Couple Protection Rate is the percentage of eligible couples effectively protected against childbirth by an approved contraceptive method.
n377b1026247.tq: Distinguish a technical demographic indicator from related welfare measures.
xs: **Couple Protection Rate** = % of eligible couples **effectively protected against childbirth** by an **approved contraceptive method** — option **(3)** is correct.
It measures contraceptive protection — not maternity benefits (**PMMVY**) or institutional delivery (**JSY**).
xa: NPP 2000's immediate objective: meet **unmet need for contraception**.
**Contraception access** is a determinant of birth rate.

n888d714bd04.s: The United Nations defined absolute poverty at the:
o: World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995
n888d714bd04.x: Absolute poverty was defined by the United Nations at the World Summit for Social Development held at Copenhagen in 1995.
n888d714bd04.tq: Match the definition with the correct international summit and year.
xs: The UN defined absolute poverty at the **World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Absolute poverty** = lack of the **minimum resources for survival**, set by a fixed consumption/calorie norm.
xa: Absolute poverty is **India's focus**; **relative** poverty is used in developed economies.
APSES 2024-25 measures absolute poverty by the **World Bank line**.
The first **UN Decade for the Eradication of Poverty** ran **1997-2006**.
**SDG 1**: "End poverty in all its forms everywhere" by **2030**.

nadf64cf9a1d.s: Relative poverty is primarily concerned with:
o: The inability to obtain the minimum resources required for physical survival
An individual's personal feeling about his or her social position
Income being well below the median income of a society
Temporary poverty caused by seasonal employment
nadf64cf9a1d.x: Relative poverty compares a person's income with the income distribution of society, particularly the median. Absolute poverty concerns minimum survival resources, while subjective poverty concerns personal perception.
nadf64cf9a1d.tq: Separate relative poverty from absolute, transient and subjective poverty by its comparison standard.
xs: **Relative poverty** means **income well below the society's median** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Minimum resources for survival = **absolute** poverty; personal feeling about position = **subjective** poverty; temporary seasonal poverty = **transient/cyclical** poverty.
xa: Relative poverty compares **fractile groups** and persists even in the **USA** and **UK**.
⚠ **Absolute** = India's focus; **relative** = developed economies.
**Chronic** poverty lasts over long periods or **generations**.

ne8172f4e40a.s: Poverty that persists over long periods or across generations is known as:
ne8172f4e40a.x: Chronic poverty lasts for long periods or is transmitted across generations. Transient or cyclical poverty is temporary and generally arises from shocks, seasons or economic cycles.
ne8172f4e40a.tq: Use duration as the deciding clue when distinguishing chronic from transient poverty.
xs: Poverty lasting over long periods or across **generations** is **chronic poverty** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Transient** poverty is temporary (shocks, seasons, cycles); **relative** compares income with the **median**; **subjective** rests on a person's own sense of position.
xa: **Culture of poverty** (**Oscar Lewis**): poverty passed on as a **way of life**.
**Absolute** poverty: fixed consumption/**calorie norm** — India's focus.
UN defined absolute poverty at **Copenhagen, 1995**.

nbcc23754e6a.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about poverty measurement?
o: Absolute poverty can be measured against a fixed line such as the World Bank line.
A fixed calorie norm is associated with absolute poverty.
Relative poverty is widely used in developed economies.
Relative poverty is defined exclusively by a fixed calorie norm.
nbcc23754e6a.x: A fixed calorie norm belongs to absolute, not relative, poverty.
xa: Relative poverty = income well below the society's **median**; compares **fractile groups**.
India's calorie norm: **2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban**.
Absolute poverty was defined at the **World Summit for Social Development, Copenhagen, 1995**.
nbcc23754e6a.fixed: statement 1 as worded implied absolute poverty is only measured by the World Bank line

na1e1f29063b.s: The concept of the 'culture of poverty', in which poverty is passed on as a way of life, is associated with:
na1e1f29063b.x: Oscar Lewis described the culture of poverty, where poverty is transmitted as a way of life. Amartya Sen is known for the capability approach; Ravenstein and Todaro are migration theorists.
xs: The **culture of poverty** — poverty passed on as a way of life — is associated with **Oscar Lewis** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Amartya Sen**, **E.G. Ravenstein** and **Michael Todaro** are not linked to this concept in the notes; Lewis alone describes poverty as a transmitted **way of life**.
xa: **Transient** poverty is temporary — from shocks, seasons or cycles.
**Chronic** poverty persists over long periods or **generations**.
**Subjective** poverty = a person's own sense of relative position.

nd6f43a40e54.s: The Head Count Ratio, Poverty Gap Index and Squared Poverty Gap belong to the:
nd6f43a40e54.x: HCR, PGI and the squared poverty gap are measures belonging to the Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT) family.
nd6f43a40e54.tq: Identify the common methodological family rather than confusing it with related inequality indices.
xs: **HCR**, **PGI** and the **Squared Poverty Gap** belong to the **Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT)** family — so option **(1)** is correct.
They measure **incidence**, **depth** and **severity** of poverty respectively.
xa: HCR formula: **HC = Nq / N**.
PGI: **(1/n) Σ (Z − yi)/Z**; the squared gap squares this shortfall.
**Engel's Law**: as family income rises, the **share spent on food falls**.

n96cd0a7ce55.s: If the poor become poorer while the number of poor people remains unchanged, which one of the following measures will remain unchanged?
n96cd0a7ce55.x: The Head Count Ratio depends only on the number or share of people below the poverty line, so it does not change when existing poor people become poorer. The Poverty Gap Index changes with the depth of poverty.
n96cd0a7ce55.tq: Apply the incidence-depth distinction to a change in the condition of existing poor persons.
xs: The **Head Count Ratio** stays unchanged when the poor get poorer, because it counts only the **share below the line** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Poverty Gap Index** (average shortfall) and **Squared Poverty Gap** (severity) both rise as the poor get poorer.
xa: HCR = **incidence**; PGI = **depth**; squared gap = **severity**.
All three form the **Foster-Greer-Thorbecke (FGT)** family.
HCR formula: **HC = Nq / N**.

n436fd568221.s: According to Engel's Law, as family income rises, the share of income spent on food:
n436fd568221.x: Engel's Law: the proportion of income spent on food declines as income rises, though the absolute amount may increase.
xa: **HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24** (MoSPI) were the first full **MPCE** update in over a decade.
India's poverty line is based on **consumption expenditure**, not income.
The **FGT** family: HCR, PGI, squared poverty gap.

n276b525de4b.s: A Poverty Line Basket (PLB) is best described as:
o: A basket based only on the income tax records of households
A socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs purchased in the market
A basket containing only food grains supplied through the Public Distribution System
A basket consisting exclusively of services provided free by the government
n276b525de4b.x: The Poverty Line Basket is a socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs bought in the market. It is not confined to food grains or government-provided services.
n276b525de4b.tq: Choose the precise official meaning rather than a narrower everyday interpretation.
xs: A **Poverty Line Basket** is a **socially accepted minimum basket of basic needs** bought in the **market** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not limited to **PDS food grains**, tax records or free government services.
xa: Poverty lines differ across **time** and **countries** because basic needs vary (UPPSC 2025 key: A and R true, R explains A).
RBI updated the **Rangarajan line** with HCES 2022-23 using a **PLB-weighted price index**.
Calorie norm: **2,400 kcal rural / 2,100 kcal urban**.

n9402bea93c1.s: According to the Tendulkar Committee estimates for 2011-12, the monthly poverty line was fixed at:
o: ₹816 in rural areas and ₹1,000 in urban areas
₹1,000 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
₹816 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
₹972 in rural areas and ₹1,407 in urban areas
n9402bea93c1.x: For 2011-12, the Tendulkar poverty line was ₹816 per month for rural areas and ₹1,000 per month for urban areas, approximately ₹27 and ₹33 per day respectively.
n9402bea93c1.tq: Separate the committee-specific figures from the later revised poverty-line values.
xs: The **Tendulkar** line for **2011-12** was **₹816 rural and ₹1,000 urban** per month — so option **(1)** is correct.
**₹972 rural / ₹1,407 urban** is the **Rangarajan** line; options 2 and 3 mix the two.
That is about **₹27/day rural** and **₹33/day urban**; it was criticised as **too low**.
xa: Tendulkar all-India poverty: **21.9%** (rural **25.7**, urban **13.7**).
⚠ Trap: some notes list ₹816/₹1,000 under "2010-11" — they are **2011-12** figures.

n1f94f6c878c.s: Under the Rangarajan Expert Group (2011-12), the rural poverty line per person was about:
n1f94f6c878c.x: Rangarajan's rural line was Rs 972 a month, about Rs 32 a day (APPSC-GS 2025 key). Rs 27 and Rs 33 a day are Tendulkar's rural and urban lines; Rs 47 a day is Rangarajan's urban line.
n1f94f6c878c.tq: Rangarajan 32/47 a day; Tendulkar 27/33 a day.
xs: **Rangarajan's rural line** (2011-12) was **₹972 a month**, about **Rs 32 a day** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
**Rs 27** and **Rs 33** a day are **Tendulkar's** rural and urban lines; **Rs 47** a day is Rangarajan's **urban** line.
xa: Rangarajan all-India poverty: **29.5%**.
**MMRP** (7-day recall) was first used by **Rangarajan**.
⚠ Trap: some notes list **₹972/₹1,407** as Tendulkar's — a mix-up.

n94c4e86caa1.s: The international poverty line of $1.90 per person per day was based on which Purchasing Power Parity (PPP) base year?
n94c4e86caa1.x: The World Bank revised the international poverty line to $1.90 per person per day in October 2015, using 2011 PPP.
n94c4e86caa1.tq: Discriminate between closely spaced monetary thresholds and their PPP base years.
xs: The **$1.90** line (October **2015**) was based on **2011 PPP** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
xa: The latest line (June **2025**) is **$3.00** at **2021 PPP**.
⚠ Trap: the **$2.15** line was the **2022** revision; **$3** came in 2025.
Global extreme poverty at $2.15: about **9.2%** (over **700 mn**).

n1833fbc5e62.s: The international poverty line revised by the World Bank in June 2025 is:
n1833fbc5e62.x: In June 2025, the latest international poverty line was stated as $3.00 per person per day at 2021 PPP.
n1833fbc5e62.tq: Match the latest figure with its corresponding PPP base year rather than an earlier revision.
xs: The latest World Bank line (June **2025**) is **$3.00 at 2021 PPP** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**$4.20** is the lower-middle-income line; **$1.90** (2011 PPP) and **$2.15** (2017 PPP) are older lines.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some notes say $3 came "in 2022" — 2022 was the **$2.15** revision.
Upper-middle-income line: **$8.30**.

n303aaf31923.s: Tendulkar-line poverty was estimated at approximately what percentages in 2022-23 and 2023-24 respectively?
n303aaf31923.x: Tendulkar-line poverty was estimated at 4.7 per cent in 2022-23 and 2.3 per cent in 2023-24.
n303aaf31923.tq: Read the years in sequence and avoid reversing the two reported estimates.
xs: **Tendulkar-line poverty** was **4.7 per cent in 2022-23** and **2.3 per cent in 2023-24** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option 4 reverses the order; **9.20 / 21.92** are AP and India HCRs for **2011-12**; **23.9 / 24.2** are from the UNDP West Asia simulation.
xa: Data from **HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24** (MoSPI).
Critique: subsistence lines **hide vulnerability** just above the threshold.
Share below the World Bank lower-middle-income line fell from over **50%** to about **30%**.

n6c85e84c109.s: Sustainable Development Goal 1 aims to end poverty in all its forms everywhere by:
n6c85e84c109.x: SDG 1 is to end poverty in all its forms everywhere by 2030.
xa: Third **UN Decade for Eradication of Poverty**: **2018-2027**.
About **9.2%** of the world (over **700 mn**) is in extreme poverty at the $2.15 line.
Latest World Bank line: **$3.00** at **2021 PPP**.

n1810357faf4.s: Who among the following authored the study titled ‘Poverty in India’ published in 1971?
o: Suresh D. Tendulkar and C. Rangarajan
n1810357faf4.x: The 1971 study ‘Poverty in India’ was authored by V.M. Dandekar and N. Rath.
xs: The **1971** study "**Poverty in India**" was written by **V.M. Dandekar and N. Rath** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was the **FIRST systematic poverty assessment on nutritional norms**, using **1960-61 NSS data** and **2,250 kcal** a day for rural and urban.
**Alagh** chaired the **1979** Task Force; **Lakdawala** (1993), **Tendulkar** (2005) and **Rangarajan** (2012) headed later Expert Groups; **Panagariya** led the 2015 NITI Task Force.
xa: Order to remember: **1971 – 1979 – 1993 – 2005 – 2012** = **Dandekar-Rath – Alagh – Lakdawala – Tendulkar – Rangarajan**.
APPSC-GS 2022 matched **Alagh (1979)** with the nutrition norm and **Dandekar-Rath (1971)** with the first systematic study.
**N.C. Saxena** dealt with the **rural BPL Census**, not poverty estimation.

nc34e4fe31b3.s: The NITI Aayog Task Force on Elimination of Poverty, constituted in 2015, was chaired by:
nc34e4fe31b3.x: The 2015 NITI Aayog Task Force on Elimination of Poverty was chaired by Arvind Panagariya.
xs: The **2015** NITI Aayog **Task Force on Elimination of Poverty** was chaired by **Arvind Panagariya** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**N.C. Saxena** worked on the rural **BPL Census**; **Rangarajan** chaired the **2012** Expert Group; **Alagh** the **1979** Task Force.
xa: Rangarajan's group was set up in **2012** and reported in **2014**.
Tendulkar: set up **Dec 2005**, reported **Dec 2009**.
AP angle: AP's **MPI** fell **0.053 to 0.025**; ranks **9th**.

ndd789cd5376.s: The Dandekar-Rath study (1971) used a calorie norm of:
o: 2,100 kcal for both rural and urban
2,250 kcal for both rural and urban
ndd789cd5376.x: Dandekar-Rath used 2,250 kcal for both; 2,400/2,100 was Alagh and 2,155/2,090 Rangarajan.
xa: Rangarajan treated **food and non-food** needs separately and used **MMRP** data.
⚠ **Tendulkar** moved away from the calorie anchor altogether.
**Lakdawala** kept the calorie basis with **State-specific lines**.

nc716d494763.s: Which of the following was a significant change introduced by the Tendulkar methodology?
o: Replacement of MRP by URP for all items
Use of one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas
Removal of private health expenditure from consumption
nc716d494763.x: The Tendulkar methodology used one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas. It moved away from an exclusive calorie anchor, included private health and education expenditure, and used MRP in place of URP.
nc716d494763.tq: Identify the methodological reform and reject reversed or extreme alternatives.
xs: **Tendulkar** used **one urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It used **MRP in place of URP** (not the reverse), moved **away from the calorie anchor**, and **added** private **health and education** spending.
xa: **MRP** = **365-day recall** for five low-frequency items.
Tendulkar Expert Group: set up **Dec 2005**, report **Dec 2009**.
Tendulkar 2011-12 poverty: **21.9%**.

nindian-economy-3-5.s: The Tendulkar Committee, set up in 2005, published its report in:
nindian-economy-3-5.x: The Tendulkar Committee (2005) reported in 2009; Dandekar-Rath was 1971 and Lakdawala 1989.
n: Dandekar and Rath conducted the first study of the concept of the poverty line in 1971. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Lakdawala Committee was established in 1989. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Tendulkar Committee was established in 2005. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
The Tendulkar Report was published in 2009. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 4-5]
xa: **Alagh Committee** (**1979**) = **nutrition/calorie-based poverty line**.
**Rangarajan Committee** (**2014**) = separate rural/urban consumption basket.
Dandekar-Rath line: **2,250 kcal** per day on **1960-61** NSS data.

nindian-economy-34-1.s: The Alagh Task Force, which set the first calorie-based poverty line, was constituted in:
nindian-economy-34-1.x: The Alagh Task Force (1979) set the first poverty line based on calorie needs: 2,400 kcal rural and 2,100 kcal urban.
n: The Alagh Committee was established in 1979. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
The Alagh Committee is associated with a nutrition/calorie-based poverty line. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 51-52]
xa: Alagh headed the **Task Force on Minimum Needs** — **Y.K. Alagh**.
**Lakdawala** introduced **State-specific lines**, updated by **CPI-AL (rural)** and **CPI-IW (urban)**.
⚠ **1971 – 1979 – 1993 – 2005 – 2012** = **Dandekar-Rath – Alagh – Lakdawala – Tendulkar – Rangarajan**.

n74e8f7b0eb7.s: For urban areas, the Lakdawala methodology updated poverty lines using:
n74e8f7b0eb7.x: Lakdawala used CPI-AL for rural and CPI-IW for urban areas, with State-specific lines, and stopped scaling to National Accounts.
xa: Lakdawala reported in **1993**; accepted in **1997**.
⚠ Tendulkar later used one **urban PLB** for both areas instead of State-wise calorie lines.

nf1cef30505c.s: The Uniform Reference Period (URP) and the Mixed Reference Period (MRP) are both used to measure the:
nf1cef30505c.x: URP and MRP are recall methods for consumption data, and both are used to measure the incidence of poverty (APPSC 2018 key). They are not measures of inflation, unemployment or inequality.
nf1cef30505c.tq: URP/MRP = consumption recall periods -> poverty incidence.
xs: **URP** and **MRP** are recall methods that both measure the **incidence of poverty** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
They gather **consumption** data; they do not measure inflation, unemployment or inequality.
xa: **URP**: **30-day** recall for all items; used up to **1993-94**.
**MRP**: **365-day** recall for clothing, footwear, durables, education, institutional medical care.
**Tendulkar** replaced URP with **MRP**.

n544b644e69c.s: Which one of the following is NOT a feature of the Rangarajan poverty estimation methodology?
o: Use of calorie, protein and fat norms
Use of a single urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas
Separate treatment of food and non-food requirements
n544b644e69c.x: The single urban poverty line basket for both rural and urban areas was associated with Tendulkar. Rangarajan used separate food and non-food requirements, nutritional norms and MMRP data.
n544b644e69c.tq: Identify the method belonging to the neighbouring committee.
xs: A **single urban poverty line basket** for rural and urban areas was **Tendulkar's** feature, not Rangarajan's — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rangarajan** treated **food and non-food** needs separately, used calories **2,155 rural / 2,090 urban** plus **protein and fat** norms, and used **MMRP** data.
xa: Rangarajan group: set up **2012**, report **2014**; poverty **29.5%** (2011-12).
**RBI (2025)** updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23** using PLB food + non-food weights.
Updated line: rural poverty highest in **Chhattisgarh (25.1%)**, lowest in **HP (0.4%)**.

n8957664315c.s: N.C. Saxena’s report of August 2009 was primarily concerned with:
o: Preparing the rural BPL Census methodology
n8957664315c.x: N.C. Saxena’s report, prepared for the Ministry of Rural Development, dealt with the method for the rural BPL Census rather than poverty estimation itself.
n8957664315c.tq: Separate BPL identification from poverty-line estimation.
xs: **N.C. Saxena's** report (Ministry of Rural Development, **Aug 2009**) gave the method for the **rural BPL Census** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was **not** about poverty estimation; the **urban BPL** method came from **S.R. Hashim**.
xa: Automatic **exclusion**: e.g. **income-tax payers**.
Automatic **inclusion**: **PVTGs**, single-woman-headed, destitute + homeless households, **bonded labourers**.
⚠ **Saxena** = rural BPL; **Hashim** = urban BPL.

n2963a36a59a.s: Which of the following was proposed as an example of automatic inclusion in the rural BPL identification approach associated with N.C. Saxena?
n2963a36a59a.x: The proposed automatic-inclusion categories included PVTGs, single-woman-headed households, destitute and homeless households, and bonded labourers. Income-tax payers were examples of automatic exclusion.
n2963a36a59a.tq: Distinguish automatic inclusion from automatic exclusion categories.
xs: **PVTGs** were an **automatic inclusion** category in **N.C. Saxena's** rural BPL approach — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Income-tax payers** were an example of **automatic exclusion**.
xa: Other automatic-inclusion groups: **single-woman-headed**, **destitute + homeless** households, **bonded labourers**.
Saxena's report: Ministry of Rural Development, **Aug 2009**.
⚠ **Hashim** = urban BPL identification.

n67abaa20cfe.s: The Planning Commission working group associated with the identification of urban BPL families was chaired by:
n67abaa20cfe.x: S.R. Hashim headed the Planning Commission working group concerned with identifying urban BPL families.
n67abaa20cfe.tq: Match the expert with the specific BPL-identification task.
xs: The Planning Commission working group to **identify urban BPL** families was chaired by **S.R. Hashim** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**N.C. Saxena** handled the **rural BPL Census**; **Alagh** and **Lakdawala** worked on poverty estimation, not BPL identification.
xa: ⚠ **Saxena** = rural BPL; **Hashim** = urban BPL.
Saxena's report came in **Aug 2009** for the Ministry of Rural Development.
Saxena's automatic inclusion: **PVTGs**, bonded labourers, destitute households.

n9db6a7deb98.s: For 1993-94, the poverty ratio under the Tendulkar methodology was:
xa: Source: **Annexure 9.1** (2024-25).

n905c019fb74.s: For 2011-12, the poverty ratio under the Rangarajan estimate was:
xa: Rangarajan used **MMRP** data, which records higher consumption.
Rangarajan group: set up **2012**, report **2014**.
**RBI (2025)** updated the Rangarajan line with **HCES 2022-23**.

n1e00aad5307.s: Under the Tendulkar methodology, India's poverty ratio for 2004-05 was:
n1e00aad5307.x: Tendulkar put 2004-05 poverty at 37.2% (rural 41.8, urban 25.7). 27.5% is the Lakdawala estimate for 2004-05 (and a mistaken Tendulkar urban figure in some tables); 29.8% is Tendulkar for 2009-10; 45.3% is Tendulkar for 1993-94.
xs: **Tendulkar** put **2004-05** poverty at **37.2%** (rural **41.8**, urban **25.7**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**27.5%** is **Lakdawala's** 2004-05 estimate; **29.8%** is Tendulkar 2009-10; **45.3%** is Tendulkar 1993-94.
xa: ⚠ Trap: some tables show Tendulkar urban 2004-05 as **27.5**; correct = **25.7**.
Lakdawala 2004-05: rural **28.3**, urban **25.7**.

ne42482e578b.s: According to the Tendulkar methodology, the rural poverty ratio in India in 2011-12 was:
ne42482e578b.x: Rural poverty was 25.7% in 2011-12 (APPSC-GS 2018 key). 13.7% was urban poverty, 21.9% the all-India ratio, and 33.8% the rural ratio in 2009-10.
xs: Tendulkar **rural** poverty in **2011-12** was **25.7%** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2018 key).

n2f17f7f11a1.s: The World Bank extreme-poverty estimate using the $3-a-day line declined from 27.1 percent in 2011–12 to
n2f17f7f11a1.x: The World Bank extreme-poverty estimate using the $3-a-day line declined to 5.3 percent in 2022–23.
n2f17f7f11a1.tq: Keep the dollar threshold and reference year attached to the correct estimate.
xs: World Bank **$3-a-day** poverty fell from **27.1%** (2011-12) to **5.3 percent in 2022-23** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**11.28%** is the **NITI MPI** (2022-23); **2.3%** is the **Tendulkar** line (2023-24); **6.06%** is AP's MPI headcount (2019-21).
xa: Sources: **ES 2025-26** and **LENS Jun 2025**.

ne2cd895ff1a.s: Approximately how many people in India were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2015, as cited in APPSC-GS 2025?
ne2cd895ff1a.x: More than 90 million people were lifted out of poverty between 2011 and 2015 (APPSC-GS 2025 key). The other figures are either too small or far larger than the cited estimate.
xs: **More than 90 million** people were lifted out of poverty between **2011 and 2015** — so option **(2)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2025 key).
The MDG target was to halve poverty to **23.9% by 2015**.

n013f310b15f.s: According to NITI Aayog's National MPI, India's multidimensional poverty headcount fell from 55.3% in 2005-06 to:
n013f310b15f.x: The NITI MPI headcount fell from 55.3% (2005-06) to 14.96% (2019-21) and 11.28% (2022-23). Option B mixes Tendulkar-line figures, option C is the World Bank $3/day series, and option D gives Tendulkar estimates.
xs: Option 2 mixes **Tendulkar** figures; option 3 is the **World Bank $3/day** series; option 4 is **Tendulkar** 2009-10 and 2011-12.
xa: AP's MPI headcount (2019-21): **6.06%**, rank **9th**.

n336baac87de.s: The Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana, a graduation-approach livelihood model, belongs to:
n336baac87de.x: Satat Jeevikoparjan Yojana is Bihar's; Kerala has its poverty-eradication model and the Centre the Samaveshi Aajeevika Yojana.
xa: **VB-G RAM G Bill, 2025**: rural job guarantee raised to **125 days**.
Social protection coverage: **22% (2016) to 64.3% (2025)**.
Kerala has the **lowest MPI** (**0.002**).

ncabf6cdee3d.s: Which of the following is NOT among the BIMARU and eastern belt States with concentrated poverty?
ncabf6cdee3d.x: The belt is Bihar, UP, MP, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh; Kerala is not in it.
xa: **Convergence**: high-poverty States fell fastest.
MPI exits: **UP 5.94 crore**, Bihar **3.77**, MP **2.30**, Rajasthan **1.87**.
Rural Odisha fell **47.8% to 8.6%**; urban Bihar **50.8% to 9.1%** (2011-12 to 2022-23).

n9d97e1f8c60.s: According to the National MPI 2023 (NFHS-5, 2019-21), the States with the highest and lowest multidimensional poverty were respectively:
n9d97e1f8c60.x: Bihar had the highest MPI (0.16, ranked 28th) and Kerala the lowest (0.002), followed by Goa and TN. UP and Jharkhand are also near the bottom but below Bihar; Chhattisgarh was highest under the Tendulkar 2011-12 ratio, not the MPI.
n9d97e1f8c60.tq: MPI: Bihar worst, Kerala best. Tendulkar 2011-12: Chhattisgarh worst, Goa best.
xs: National MPI 2023 (2019-21): **Bihar** highest (MPI **0.16**, ranked **28th**) and **Kerala** lowest (**0.002**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**UP (0.103)** and **Jharkhand (0.131)** are near the bottom but below Bihar; **Chhattisgarh** topped the **Tendulkar 2011-12** ratio, not the MPI.
xa: After Kerala, the lowest MPI States are **Goa** and **TN**.
⚠ Highest ratio = **Chhattisgarh** (Tendulkar); highest MPI = **Bihar**; largest number = **UP**.
India's MPI score: **0.066**; AP's **0.025**.

n335af25a49f.s: Which social group has the highest poverty ratio in India according to the Tendulkar estimates for 2011-12?
n335af25a49f.x: Scheduled Tribes had the highest poverty ratio among social groups; rural ST poverty was about 45%, followed by Scheduled Castes.
n335af25a49f.tq: Use the social-group ranking rather than the overall rural or urban ranking.
xs: **Scheduled Tribes** have the highest poverty (Tendulkar 2011-12: **rural ST about 45%**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Scheduled Castes** come **next**.
xa: In AP, districts with **large tribal populations** have higher poverty.
Education gap: **35.1%** of those with no formal education are poor vs **14.9%** with post-secondary education.
North Coastal Andhra's poverty is linked to **tribal/ITDA agency tracts**.

n8877226cf58.s: Under the Tendulkar method (2011-12), Andhra Pradesh's total poverty ratio was:
n8877226cf58.x: AP's ratio was 9.20% (rural 10.96%, urban 5.81%) against India's 21.92%.
xa: AP MPI headcount (2019-21): **6.06%** vs India **14.96%**.
AP MPI score **0.025** vs India **0.066**.

ne9e8e155c5d.s: Higher agricultural poverty in Rayalaseema, compared with the delta districts, is mainly attributed to its greater dependence on:
ne9e8e155c5d.x: Delta districts benefit from better irrigation and higher productivity, while rain-fed Rayalaseema faces greater agricultural vulnerability and poverty.
xa: Rayalaseema's **Kurnool** (**12.84%**) is AP's poorest district by MPI.
**West Godavari** (delta) is the least poor (**2.42%**).
Other causes: **seasonal unemployment**, **climate vulnerability**, rural-urban divide.

n2c32b1efc72.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about regional poverty differences in Andhra Pradesh?
o: A skill mismatch arises as the economy shifts towards technology.
Remoteness of tribal areas contributes to poverty.
Rayalaseema is the rain-fed and poorer region.
Delta districts are poorer than Rayalaseema because of rain-fed agriculture.
n2c32b1efc72.x: Rayalaseema is the rain-fed, poorer region; the irrigated delta districts are the least poor.
xa: Least poor: **West Godavari** (**2.42%**); poorest: **Kurnool** (**12.84%**).
**Social transfers** (PMGKAY, MGNREGA, PMAY-G) helped cut poverty.

n34596ac016a.s: Which district had the highest MPI poverty headcount ratio among the districts listed for Andhra Pradesh?
n34596ac016a.x: Kurnool had the highest listed MPI poverty headcount ratio at 12.84%, with an MPI of 0.054.
n34596ac016a.tq: Identify the maximum value while separating it from other high-poverty districts.
xs: **Kurnool** had the highest MPI headcount among AP districts — **12.84%** (MPI **0.054**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Vizianagaram (8.66%)**, **Visakhapatnam (7.60%)** and **Anantapur (6.74%)** follow.
xa: ⚠ **West Godavari** = least poor (**2.42%**); **Kurnool** = poorest.
Also higher-poverty: **Prakasam (6.28%)**, **East Godavari (6.13%)**.
Poorer belts: **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal Andhra**.

n0d9718c4af1.s: Which district of Andhra Pradesh had the lowest MPI poverty headcount ratio among the districts listed?
n0d9718c4af1.x: West Godavari had the lowest headcount ratio (2.42%, MPI 0.010). YSR Kadapa (3.34%), Guntur (4.36%) and Krishna (4.38%) followed it.
xs: **West Godavari** had the lowest MPI headcount — **2.42%** (MPI **0.010**) — so option **(4)** is correct.
**YSR Kadapa (3.34%)**, **Guntur (4.36%)** and **Krishna (4.38%)** follow.
xa: ⚠ **West Godavari** = least poor; **Kurnool** = poorest (**12.84%**).
Least poor are **delta districts**.
Poorer belts: **Rayalaseema** + **North Coastal Andhra**.

n7e23e96e538.s: In Andhra Pradesh, SERP stands for, and is primarily concerned with:
o: Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty: mobilising the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods
State Employment and Relief Programme: wage employment in urban areas
Scheme for Elimination of Rural Poverty: cash transfers to farmers
Society for Economic Reforms and Planning: drafting the State budget
n7e23e96e538.x: SERP is the Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (2000), which mobilises the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods (APPSC 2021 key). The other expansions are invented and describe roles SERP does not play.
n7e23e96e538.tq: SERP = rural SHGs; MEPMA = urban; Velugu -> IKP.
xs: **SERP** = **Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty**: **mobilising the rural poor into women's SHGs and livelihoods** — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2021 key).
It is not a wage-employment, cash-transfer or budget body.
xa: SERP was set up in **2000** and ran **Velugu**.
**MoUs**: SERP + MEPMA with **ISB, XLRI, IIM-Visakhapatnam**.

nedb77f9edf3.s: APMSS, an Andhra Pradesh poverty-alleviation body for rural and urban poor households, stands for:
o: Andhra Pradesh Mission for Social Security
nedb77f9edf3.x: APMSS is the Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha, working on poverty alleviation for rural and urban poor households (APPSC 2018 key). The other expansions are made up.
xs: **APMSS** = **Andhra Pradesh Mahila Sadhikara Samstha**, for **rural and urban poor** households — so option **(1)** is correct (APPSC 2018 key).
Its role is **poverty alleviation**; the other expansions do not appear among AP's poverty bodies.
xa: **SERP** = Society for Elimination of Rural Poverty (**2000**).
**IKP** = **Indira Kranthi Patham**, Velugu renamed (**2004-05**).
SHG loans **Mar 2026**: **₹10,100 crore** under SERP, MEPMA, Stree Nidhi, PMEGP.

n348b3863aab.s: Who proposed the Gini coefficient in 1912 in the work titled “Variability and Mutability”?
n348b3863aab.x: Corrado Gini proposed the coefficient in 1912 in “Variability and Mutability”.
n348b3863aab.tq: Use the author–year–work combination to distinguish the Gini coefficient from the Lorenz curve.
xs: The **Gini coefficient** was proposed by **Corrado Gini** in **1912** in "**Variability and Mutability**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Max Lorenz** gave the **Lorenz curve (1906)**; **Simon Kuznets** the inverted-U **Kuznets curve (1955)**; **Amartya Sen** wrote **Inequality Reexamined**.
xa: Gini range: **0 to 1**; **Gini index** = value × **100**.
**Higher value means more inequality** (JPSC 2023 key).
The Gini is derived from the **Lorenz curve**.

n93f354ccafa.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Lorenz curve?
o: The X-axis shows the cumulative percentage of population, poorest first.
The Y-axis shows the cumulative percentage of income.
The Gini coefficient, not the curve, gives a single number for inequality.
The farther the curve bows from the 45-degree line, the lower the inequality.
n93f354ccafa.x: The 45-degree line is perfect equality, so bowing farther away means greater inequality.
xa: Lorenz curve: **Max Lorenz**, **1906**.
Gini = area between curve and equality line ÷ whole area under that line.
Gini range: **0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything)**.

n2017c040337.s: The Gini coefficient is derived from the Lorenz curve as:
o: Area under the Lorenz curve ÷ whole area under the equality line
Area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line ÷ area under the Lorenz curve
Area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line ÷ whole area under the equality line
Slope of the Lorenz curve at the median
n2017c040337.x: The Gini coefficient is the area between the Lorenz curve and the equality line divided by the whole area under the equality line.
xa: Range: **0 (perfect equality)** to **1 (one person has everything)**.
The **equality line** is the **45° diagonal**.
Gini index = coefficient × **100**.

n8a3698288f3.s: The district-level Multidimensional Poverty Index gaps are used in Andhra Pradesh primarily as a measure of:
n8a3698288f3.x: In Andhra Pradesh, district-level MPI gaps serve as a measure of inequality within the State. They capture disparities among districts rather than merely measuring urbanisation or agricultural productivity.
n8a3698288f3.tq: Apply the indicator to the level of analysis at which it is used.
xs: In AP, district-level **MPI** gaps serve as the State's measure of **intra-State inequality** in **APSES** — so option **(2)** is correct.
They compare districts, not urbanisation, inter-State income or farm productivity alone.
xa: Range: **West Godavari 2.42%** to **Kurnool 12.84%** (Table **9.4**).
Lagging: **Rayalaseema** and **North Coastal** districts.
Inter-State MPI: **Kerala 0.002** to **Bihar 0.16**.

n6325310e448.s: The Environmental Kuznets Curve, with per-capita income on the X-axis and environmental degradation on the Y-axis, is:
n6325310e448.x: Degradation first rises with income, peaks and then falls, giving an inverted-U shape.
xa: Degradation **rises** in early growth, **peaks**, then **falls** as income rises.
Message: "**the solution to pollution is economic growth**".
It is borrowed from the **Kuznets Curve** (inequality vs income).

n78a2c0621d7.s: The Kuznets hypothesis describes the relationship between inequality and growth as:
n78a2c0621d7.x: Inequality first rises and then falls as the economy grows - an inverted U.
xa: **Simon Kuznets** proposed it in **1955**.
The **Environmental Kuznets curve** borrows the same inverted-U shape for pollution.
⚠ **1906 – 1912 – 1955** = Lorenz – Gini – Kuznets.

n84f37e6073e.s: The indicator used in NSSO/NSO household surveys for measuring household inequality is generally:
n84f37e6073e.x: Household inequality in these surveys is assessed through consumption expenditure, particularly monthly per capita consumption expenditure (MPCE), rather than income or wealth.
n84f37e6073e.tq: Distinguish the survey indicator from the two commonly confused concepts of income and wealth.
xs: **NSSO/NSO** surveys measure inequality through **consumption expenditure (MPCE)**, not income or wealth — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2017 key).
India has **no official income survey**; **wealth** is measured by the **All India Debt and Investment Survey**.
xa: **HCES** (MoSPI) gives rural + urban MPCE every **five** years.
Consumption data make inequality **look lower** than other measures.
Critique: consumption data **understate top-end incomes**.

n1c00c823888.s: In India, consumption inequality is measured mainly using data from:
o: the All India Debt and Investment Survey
n1c00c823888.x: Consumption inequality rests on NSS/HCES; income inequality uses PLFS wages, tax data and WID; wealth uses AIDIS.
xa: WID: income inequality **rising**; top 10% median earnings = **13 times** bottom 10% (**2023-24**).
Top 10% hold about **77%** of national wealth (older Oxfam figure).
Land: about **46%** of rural households are **landless**.

ne631c5ae213.s: Which one of the following is identified as a limitation of consumption-based inequality estimates?
o: They may understate the incomes of the highest-income groups.
They measure only inter-State per capita income gaps.
They necessarily show that inequality is falling.
They exclude all information about poverty.
ne631c5ae213.x: Consumption data may understate the incomes of the top end, thereby affecting the assessment of inequality. Such data do not necessarily measure only inter-State gaps or prove that inequality is declining.
ne631c5ae213.tq: Find the specific limitation and reject absolute claims about what the data necessarily show.
xs: Consumption-based estimates may **understate the incomes of the top end** (highest-income groups) — so option **(1)** is correct.
They do not necessarily show falling inequality; they are household data, not inter-State income gaps.
xa: Official estimates rest on **consumption** (NSS/HCES), so inequality **looks lower** than on other measures.
India has **no official income survey**; estimates use **PLFS** wages, tax data and **WID**.
Debate: **poverty falls while inequality rises**.

nf74cc4d675d.s: A Gini coefficient value of 0 indicates:
o: one person holds all the income
half the population holds all the income
nf74cc4d675d.x: The Gini runs from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has everything).
xa: **Gini index** = coefficient × **100**.
The Gini is derived from the **Lorenz curve**.
**Corrado Gini** proposed it in **1912**.

nea666f33a17.s: According to the NSS 2011–12 figures, the rural and urban MPCE were respectively:
nea666f33a17.x: The NSS 2011–12 figures were ₹1,430 for rural MPCE and ₹2,630 for urban MPCE.
nea666f33a17.tq: Compare the survey-year labels before matching the numerical pair.
xs: **NSS 2011-12**: rural MPCE **₹1,430**, urban **₹2,630** — so option **(3)** is correct (gap about **₹1,200**, APPSC-GS 2018 key).
xa: Urban MPCE was about **84%** above rural in **2011-12**.
HCES (MoSPI) is the official consumption source.

nc3fccb78f79.s: Which of the following is a DIRECT measure for reducing inequality?
nc3fccb78f79.x: A ceiling on land holdings directly redistributes assets. Taxes such as wealth tax, capital gains tax and progressive income tax are indirect measures.
nc3fccb78f79.tq: Classify asset redistribution as direct and taxation-based intervention as indirect.
xs: A **ceiling on land holdings** is a **direct** measure that **redistributes assets** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2008 key).
**Capital gains tax**, **progressive income tax** and **wealth tax** are **indirect** measures (through taxes and policy).
xa: Other direct measures: **land reforms**, **tenancy laws**.
Other indirect measures: **estate duty** (introduced **1953**, abolished **1985**).
**Art. 39(c)**: prevents concentration of wealth.

nf3de12d13c7.s: Wealth tax in India was abolished with effect from:
nf3de12d13c7.x: Wealth tax was abolished from 1 April 2016 for low yield and high compliance cost; estate duty went in 1985.
xa: The rich are now taxed through **income-tax surcharges**.
Wealth tax, estate duty, capital gains tax are **indirect** measures against inequality.

ne9fbe89c86f.s: Which Articles of the Constitution respectively direct the State to minimise inequalities in income and prevent concentration of wealth?
ne9fbe89c86f.x: Article 38(2) concerns minimising inequalities in income, while Article 39(c) seeks to prevent concentration of wealth.
ne9fbe89c86f.tq: Match each constitutional provision with its specific directive rather than relying on the general theme.
xs: **Articles 38(2)** and **39(c)**: Art. 38(2) directs the State to **minimise inequalities in income**; Art. 39(c) to **prevent concentration of wealth** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are cited as UPSC facts on reducing inequality.
xa: ⚠ Do not swap them: **38(2)** = income; **39(c)** = wealth.
Direct measure: **ceiling on land holdings** (APPSC-G2 2008 key).
**Wealth tax** abolished from **1 April 2016**.

nindian-economy-36-1.s: Who authored the book *The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money*?
nindian-economy-36-1.x: J.M. Keynes wrote 'The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money' (1936), which founded Keynesian economics. Adam Smith wrote 'The Wealth of Nations'.
nindian-economy-36-1.tq: Match each book to its author.
n: The author of The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money is J.M. Keynes. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
J.M. Keynes is associated with General Theory. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
xs: **J.M. Keynes** wrote **The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Adam Smith** wrote **The Wealth of Nations**; **David Ricardo** wrote **Principles of Political Economy & Taxation**.
**R.C. Dutt** wrote **The Economic History of India**.
xa: **Dadabhai Naoroji**: **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India** — the **Drain of Wealth**.
**J.S. Mill**: **Principles of Political Economy**; **Joan Robinson**: **The Accumulation of Capital**.
**Thomas Piketty**: **The Economics of Inequality**; **Amartya Sen**: **Inequality Reexamined**.

nindian-economy-36-2.s: 'The Economic History of India' was written by:
nindian-economy-36-2.x: R.C. Dutt wrote The Economic History of India; Smith, Ricardo and Stiglitz wrote the other listed works.
n: The author of The Wealth of Nations is Adam Smith. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation is David Ricardo. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of The Economic History of India is R.C. Dutt. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
The author of The Price of Inequality is Joseph E. Stiglitz. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
David Ricardo is associated with Principles of Political Economy & Taxation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 53-54]
xa: **The General Theory** = **J.M. Keynes**.
**Inequality: What Can Be Done** = **Anthony B. Atkinson**.
World Inequality Report / Database = **World Inequality Lab** (Paris School of Economics).

n3b05b60161c.s: Which organisation is associated with inequality reports released in contexts such as Davos?
n3b05b60161c.x: Oxfam International is associated with inequality reports released in contexts such as Davos.
n3b05b60161c.tq: Use the report theme and organisation pairing rather than confusing it with wealth databases.
xs: Inequality reports released at **Davos** are by **Oxfam International** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Credit Suisse** published the **Global Wealth Report**; the **World Inequality Lab** (Paris School of Economics) publishes the **World Inequality Report**.
xa: Oxfam's older figure: top 10% hold about **77%** of India's wealth.
**Credit Suisse** is now **UBS**.
**Joseph Stiglitz** — **The Price of Inequality (2012)**.

nbdac4e89ff7.s: Which regions of Andhra Pradesh are identified as lagging in intra-State disparities?
nbdac4e89ff7.x: Rayalaseema and North Coastal districts lag; district MPI headcount ranges from 2.42% to 12.84%.
xa: District-level **MPI** gaps are AP's inequality measure in **APSES**.
Inter-State MPI range: **Kerala 0.002** to **Bihar 0.16**.

n50b6088bd1f.s: Which type of unemployment is predominantly found in Indian agriculture, where more family members work on a farm than are actually needed?
n50b6088bd1f.x: Disguised unemployment is predominant in agriculture (family farms): output stays unchanged if some workers are withdrawn. Educated unemployment is mainly urban, cyclical arises in industry and services during recession, and technological unemployment occurs in manufacturing and routine services.
n50b6088bd1f.tq: Agriculture: disguised first; seasonal if disguised is not an option.
xs: More family members on a farm than needed = **disguised unemployment**, predominant in **agriculture** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Educated** is mainly **urban**; **cyclical** arises in industry and services during **recession**; **technological** in **manufacturing and routine services**.
xa: Test: withdrawing some workers leaves **total output unchanged** (**MPL = 0**).
⚠ APPSC 2025 asked "predominant in agriculture" twice: **Disguised** in GS, **Seasonal** in G2 (when disguised was not an option).
It is **hidden**, not open, unemployment.

n2267142dc4e.s: Which one of the following is the defining test for identifying disguised unemployment?
o: Workers remain unemployed throughout the business cycle
Withdrawal of some workers leaves total output unchanged
Workers change jobs frequently in search of higher wages
Withdrawal of some workers reduces total output proportionately
n2267142dc4e.x: In disguised unemployment, removing some workers does not reduce total output, implying zero marginal productivity.
xa: It is common among **family members in agriculture**.
It is **hidden** unemployment; **PLFS** headline rates do not capture it.
Rural areas = **seasonal + disguised** unemployment (NCERT).

o: The seasonal closure of agricultural activities
A fall in aggregate demand for goods and services
The time taken to search for a new job
A mismatch between acquired skills and available jobs
nbc36d6e5dc4.x: Cyclical unemployment results from deficient aggregate demand during recession or depression, leading firms to reduce employment.
nbc36d6e5dc4.tq: Match the unemployment type with its immediate macroeconomic cause.
xs: **Cyclical** unemployment comes from a **fall in aggregate demand** for goods and services during **recession/depression** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Agricultural closure = **seasonal**; job-search time = **frictional**; skills mismatch = **structural**.
xa: Firms **lay off workers to cut costs** in the downturn.
⚠ "Unemployment caused by depression" = **Cyclical** (APPSC 2019).
**Keynes**: unemployment in developed economies = **deficiency in effective demand**.

nc5e8b8ec241.s: Educated unemployment in India is predominantly found in:
nc5e8b8ec241.x: Educated unemployment is an urban phenomenon: qualified persons fail to find jobs matching their education and industry's needs.
xa: Only **46%** of graduates employable (**India Skills Report 2024**).
PLFS 2025: **secondary schooling and above = 6.5%** (more than double the national rate).
**40.1%** of tertiary-educated youth are **NEET**.

nindian-economy-33-3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Frictional unemployment is associated with transition between jobs.
Structural unemployment involves a mismatch of skills or geography.
Institutional unemployment can arise from regulatory and policy barriers.
Underemployment refers to surplus labour with zero marginal output.
nindian-economy-33-3.x: Surplus labour adding nothing to output is disguised unemployment; underemployment means workers not using their full skills or hours.
n: Frictional unemployment is caused by transitions between jobs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Structural unemployment is caused by a mismatch of skills or geography. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Disguised unemployment is caused by surplus labour with zero marginal productivity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Underemployment is caused by the underutilization of worker capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Institutional unemployment is caused by regulatory and policy barriers. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Underemployment involves working below one’s skill level or being forced into involuntary part-time work. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
Institutional unemployment arises from labour laws, high minimum wages, or union rules. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 49-51]
xa: Underemployment example: an **engineer working part-time as a cashier**.
**Invisible underemployment**: full-time work at very low income, e.g. an **MBA** working as a driver.
**Visible underemployment**: working fewer than normal hours.

n78042d3ab85.s: Technological unemployment, caused by changes in technology, is treated as a subtype of:
n78042d3ab85.x: Technological unemployment results from technological change and is a subtype of structural unemployment.
xa: Drivers: **automation in manufacturing** and **AI in services**.
It hits **low-skilled, routine** jobs.
Predominant in **manufacturing** and **routine services**.

n2975923f449.s: Why is disguised unemployment generally not captured in PLFS headline unemployment rates?
o: It occurs only in urban areas
The persons concerned appear to be employed
It lasts for less than one week
n2975923f449.x: People in disguised unemployment appear employed, so this hidden form is not captured by headline rates like open unemployment.
xa: The surplus workers add no productive value: **MPL = 0** or negative.
It is common on **family farms** in agriculture.
Criticism: a falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**.

n480d4431a61.s: An MBA graduate working full-time as a driver at a very low income is an example of
n480d4431a61.x: Invisible underemployment exists when a person works full-time but earns very little or works below their ability, as in the example of an MBA working as a driver.
n480d4431a61.tq: Look beyond the number of hours and identify underutilisation of skills or income.
xs: An **MBA** working full-time as a driver at low income is **invisible underemployment** — full-time work **below one's ability** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Visible** underemployment means fewer than normal hours; **seasonal** and **frictional** involve no job at all for a time.
xa: **Educated** unemployment: qualified persons unable to find matching jobs (**urban**).
Only **46%** of graduates employable.
Criticism: falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**.

n40292cb6b80.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about voluntary and involuntary unemployment?
o: Voluntary unemployment means unwillingness to work at the prevailing wage.
Involuntary unemployment means being willing to work at the prevailing wage but finding no job.
The labour force counts only voluntary unemployment.
The labour force counts only involuntary unemployment.
n40292cb6b80.x: The labour force counts only involuntary, not voluntary, unemployment.
xa: Causes of voluntary unemployment: **high benefits**, **high marginal tax**, **waiting for a better job**.
Involuntary unemployment comes from **market structure/aggregate demand**.
**Unemployment trap**: benefits discourage work.

nc0810de4234.s: The natural rate of unemployment is composed of:
nc0810de4234.x: The natural rate is the combination of frictional and structural unemployment existing at full employment.
nc0810de4234.tq: Recall the exact components of a standard composite concept.
xs: The **natural rate of unemployment** = **frictional + structural** at full employment — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Cyclical** and **seasonal**, **open** and **disguised**, and **voluntary/involuntary** are other classifications.
xa: Associated with **Milton Friedman**.
Friedman-Phelps: long-run Phillips curve **vertical** at the natural rate.
**Okun's law**: unemployment above the natural rate cuts output.

naf877d72c4b.s: A decline in the measured unemployment rate may fail to indicate genuine job creation when it results from:
o: A rise in potential GDP caused by technology
A permanent reduction in the labour force due to higher wages
naf877d72c4b.x: A falling unemployment rate may reflect people entering low-productivity work under distress rather than the creation of good or adequate jobs.
naf877d72c4b.tq: Distinguish an apparently favourable indicator from its possible underlying labour-market condition.
xs: A falling UR may reflect **distress entry into low-productivity work**, not real job creation — so option **(1)** is correct.
Expansion of high-productivity jobs would be genuine job creation.
xa: **Disguised** unemployment is hidden and not captured by **PLFS** headline rates.
**Invisible underemployment**: full-time work at very low income (e.g. **MBA** as driver).
~**90%** of the workforce is informal.

nea8a01bc53c.s: According to Keynes, unemployment in developed economies primarily results from
o: A mismatch caused only by technological change
nea8a01bc53c.x: Keynes explained unemployment in developed economies mainly through deficiency in effective demand, which is associated with demand-deficient or cyclical unemployment.
nea8a01bc53c.tq: Associate the economist with the precise explanation rather than a related unemployment type.
xs: **Keynes**: unemployment in developed economies stems from a **deficiency in effective demand** — so option **(4)** is correct.
This is **cyclical/demand-deficient** unemployment; a farm-labour surplus describes India's **disguised** unemployment instead.
xa: India differs: its unemployment is basically **structural**, plus **disguised** and seasonal.
**Milton Friedman** — **natural rate of unemployment**.
**A.W. Phillips (1958)** — inverse unemployment–inflation link.

n5941c93b0c3.s: The concept of the natural rate of unemployment is particularly associated with:
n5941c93b0c3.x: The concept of the natural rate of unemployment is associated with Milton Friedman.
n5941c93b0c3.tq: Link the named economist with the specific concept rather than a related curve or law.
xs: The **natural rate of unemployment** is associated with **Milton Friedman** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**A.W. Phillips** gave the **Phillips curve (1958)**; **Keynes** linked unemployment to **deficient effective demand**; **Arthur Okun** gave **Okun's law**.
xa: **Friedman-Phelps**: long-run Phillips curve is **vertical** at the natural rate.
Natural rate = **frictional + structural**.
⚠ **Phillips** = unemployment vs inflation; **Okun** = unemployment vs output.

n252dd0e6fbf.s: The traditional trade-off between inflation and unemployment breaks down in a situation of:
o: Stable prices with potential output growth
Stagflation, characterised by high inflation and high unemployment
n252dd0e6fbf.x: Stagflation combines high inflation with high unemployment and therefore breaks down the traditional Phillips-curve trade-off.
n252dd0e6fbf.tq: Identify the unusual combination that contradicts the traditional inverse relationship.
xs: The Phillips trade-off **breaks down** in **stagflation** — **high inflation and high unemployment** together — so option **(3)** is correct.
The curve normally pairs **lower unemployment** with **higher inflation**.
xa: Friedman-Phelps: long-run curve **vertical** at the natural rate.
**Milton Friedman** — natural rate of unemployment.

n527110e9a13.s: According to Okun's law, a one percentage point rise in unemployment above the natural rate is associated approximately with:
o: A 2% rise in output above potential GDP
A 1% rise in output above potential GDP
A 2% fall in output below potential GDP
A 5% fall in output below potential GDP
n527110e9a13.x: Okun's law states that a one percentage point increase in unemployment above the natural rate is associated with roughly a 2% reduction in output below potential GDP.
n527110e9a13.tq: Track both parts of the quantitative relationship: the unemployment point and the output percentage.
xs: **Okun's law**: a **1 percentage point** rise in unemployment above the natural rate → roughly a **2% fall in output below potential GDP** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Output **falls**, not rises; the figure is about **2%**, not 1% or 5%.
xa: Implication: an **inverse link between growth and unemployment**.
⚠ **Okun** = unemployment vs output; **Phillips** = unemployment vs inflation.
Given by **Arthur Okun**.

nb12ae703a39.s: According to PLFS 2025, the unemployment rate among youth aged 18-29 was about 14.8%. What was it for tertiary-educated youth in that age group?
nb12ae703a39.x: Tertiary-educated youth recorded an unemployment rate of 29.4%, about double the overall youth rate of 14.8%. 6.5% is the rate for persons with secondary schooling and above, 11.9% is the Gen Z (15-26) rate, and 40.1% is the share of tertiary-educated youth who are NEET.
xs: PLFS 2025: youth (18-29) UR **14.8%**, rising to **29.4%** for **tertiary-educated** youth — so option **(3)** is correct.
**6.5%** = secondary and above; **11.9%** = **Gen Z** (15-26); **40.1%** = share of tertiary-educated youth who are **NEET**.
xa: Female Gen Z graduates UR **36.9%**; male **29%** (**22 Jul 2026**).
AP youth (15-29) UR **17.5%**; urban female youth **29.1%**.
Cause: **curriculum mismatch** with industry needs.

n7ac9539b596.s: Which of the following may still exist at full employment?
o: Involuntary unemployment of those willing at the prevailing wage
n7ac9539b596.x: Full employment means everyone willing at the prevailing wage finds work, but frictional and structural unemployment may persist.
xa: **Natural rate of unemployment** = frictional + structural at full employment.
**Milton Friedman** is linked to the natural rate.
Friedman-Phelps: long-run **Phillips curve vertical** at the natural rate.

nd6a6ec2251c.s: India's basic unemployment problem is mainly:
nd6a6ec2251c.x: India's problem is structural, with seasonal, disguised and underemployment, unlike the demand-deficient unemployment Keynes stressed for developed economies.
xa: Core nature: Indian unemployment is basically **structural**.
Causes: **rapid population growth**, **labour immobility**, shift to **capital-intensive** production.
~**90%** of the workforce is informal.

ne36d4068c14.s: Which situation best illustrates structural unemployment?
o: A firm laying off workers during a recession
A worker changing jobs after voluntarily quitting
A farm worker remaining idle during the agricultural off-season
A labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production
ne36d4068c14.x: A shift from labour-intensive to capital-intensive production changes the demand for labour and creates a long-term structural mismatch.
ne36d4068c14.tq: Match the example to long-term structural change rather than a temporary interruption.
xs: A **labour-intensive economy shifting towards capital-intensive production** illustrates **structural** unemployment — so option **(4)** is correct.
Recession layoffs = **cyclical**; voluntary job change = **frictional**; idle in the off-season = **seasonal**.
xa: Structural unemployment is **long-run** and needs **reskilling**.
**Technological** unemployment is a sub-type of structural.
**Indian unemployment is basically structural** — labour demand < supply.

n10189e20ffb.s: Which combination best explains the structural nature of unemployment in India?
o: Only seasonal rainfall variations and tourism cycles
High labour mobility, labour-intensive production and low population growth
Rapid population growth, labour immobility and a shift towards capital-intensive production
Short job-search periods and temporary workplace transfers
n10189e20ffb.x: Rapid population growth, labour immobility and the shift towards capital-intensive production contribute to a long-run shortfall of labour demand relative to supply.
n10189e20ffb.tq: Select the option containing the structural causes rather than temporary causes.
xs: India's unemployment is basically **structural** due to **rapid population growth**, **labour immobility** and a **shift to capital-intensive production** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Labour **demand < supply** in the **long run**; option 2 lists the opposites.
xa: Also high **seasonal** + **disguised** unemployment and underemployment.
It differs from the **Keynesian** demand-deficient unemployment of developed countries.
**Jobless growth**: growth driven by **IT, finance**.

n02cde4e96f0.s: Which one of the following is NOT a structural cause of unemployment in India identified in the context of the secondary sector?
o: Jobless growth and inadequate focus on MSMEs
Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing generating abundant jobs
Slow infrastructure and delays in official paperwork
Neglected structural transformation of the secondary sector
n02cde4e96f0.x: Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing generating abundant jobs would reduce, rather than cause, structural unemployment. The other factors are identified structural impediments.
n02cde4e96f0.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of a stated structural cause.
xs: **Rapid expansion of labour-intensive manufacturing** creating jobs is NOT a cause — it would cut unemployment — so option **(2)** is correct.
Real structural causes: **neglected structural transformation** of the secondary sector, **jobless growth**, less focus on **MSMEs**, **slow infrastructure** and paperwork delays.
xa: Also: **stringent labour laws** and an **import-oriented** rather than export-led economy.
Exam angle: odd-one-out questions slip in "**high growth of labour-intensive manufacturing**" as a non-cause.
Other causes: skill-curriculum mismatch, ~**90%** informal workforce, low female **LFPR**.

n91fa1af78a5.s: Under the Usual Principal Status (UPS) approach, a person is treated as employed if he or she worked for at least how many days in the 365-day reference period?
n91fa1af78a5.x: UPS uses a 365-day reference period; working for the major part of it, generally 183 days or more, counts as employed.
xa: UPS captures **chronic** (long-term) unemployment.
⚠ **183** days is also the Census **main worker** line — but Census is **not** an NSS approach.
Memory: **365 days – 7 days – half day** = **UPS – CWS – CDS**.

n6c297b64cbd.s: Under the UPSS approach, a person is also counted as employed if he or she did subsidiary work for at least ____ in the 365-day reference period.
n6c297b64cbd.x: UPSS includes principal-status workers and those who did subsidiary work for at least 30 days during the year.
xa: UPSS gives the **broadest count of workers**.
Reference period: **365 days**.

na250b3f05c9.s: In the Current Daily Status approach, the basic time unit used for recording employment is:
na250b3f05c9.x: CDS uses a half-day as the unit of measurement. Four or more hours of work are treated as employment for that day.
na250b3f05c9.tq: Test the precise quantitative unit used in a statistical approach.
xs: **CDS** records employment in units of **half a day**; **4+ hours** = employed for the day — so option **(4)** is correct.
It covers **each day of the 7 days** of the reference week.
xa: CDS is the **most inclusive**, capturing **daily/intermittent** unemployment.
CDS gives the **highest** rate: NSS 68th CDS **5.6%**.

n2c47a7d91ab.s: Why does the Current Daily Status approach generally produce the highest unemployment rate?
o: It counts days of unemployment even for persons treated as employed under CWS.
It uses a reference period of 365 days.
It includes only persons who are not seeking work.
It excludes all seasonal workers from employment.
n2c47a7d91ab.x: CDS records unemployment separately for each day and therefore captures intermittent unemployment that may not be reflected when a person is counted as employed under CWS.
n2c47a7d91ab.tq: Identify the cause behind a comparison in measured unemployment rates.
xs: **CDS** gives the highest rate because it **counts days of unemployment even for persons "employed" under CWS** — so option **(1)** is correct.
A **365-day** period is UPS, not CDS.
xa: CDS unit = **half day**; **4+ hours** = employed for the day.
It captures **daily/intermittent** unemployment.

n67acd5786c8.s: The Unemployment Rate (UR) is unemployed persons as a percentage of the:
n67acd5786c8.x: UR uses the labour force as base; the proportion unemployed (PU) uses the population.
xa: ⚠ UR divides by **labour force**; PU divides by **population**.
UR measures only the **unutilised part** of the labour force.
**WPR = LFPR × (1 − UR)**.

n5e09b2741b6.s: The percentage of employed persons in the total population is known as the
n5e09b2741b6.x: Worker Population Ratio (WPR) is employed persons as a share of population, and WPR = LFPR x (1 - UR). LFPR counts employed plus unemployed per 100 persons, UR is unemployed as a share of the labour force, and Proportion Unemployed is unemployed as a share of population.
xs: Employed persons as a % of population = **Worker Population Ratio** — so option **(3)** is correct (APPSC 2023).
**LFPR** includes the unemployed too; **UR** divides by the labour force; **PU** = unemployed / population.
xa: Identity: **WPR = LFPR × (1 − UR)**.

n32ebc1ff9c6.s: The Periodic Labour Force Survey is conducted by:
o: The Census of India under the Ministry of Home Affairs
The National Statistical Office under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation
The Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy under NITI Aayog
The Labour Bureau under the Ministry of Labour and Employment
n32ebc1ff9c6.x: PLFS is conducted by the National Statistical Office, which functions under the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation.
n32ebc1ff9c6.tq: Apply the 'who conducts the survey?' agency test.
xs: The **PLFS** is conducted by the **National Statistical Office (NSO)** under the **Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation** (MoSPI) — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **Labour Bureau (MoLE)** runs EUS/QES; **CMIE** is private; the **Census** gives decennial worker data.
xa: Designed by the **SCLFS**, set up on the **National Statistical Commission's** advice.
Launched **April 2017**; first report (**2017-18**) in **May 2019**.
Now the standard NSO mechanism for India's UR (APPSC G2 2025).

nindian-economy-48-2-5.x: WPR is employed over total population; LFPR is labour force over working-age population.
n: WPR is employed population divided by total population. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #48-2 · pp 72-73]
LFPR is the labour force divided by the working-age population. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #48-2 · pp 72-73]
The real sector consists of goods and services. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #48-2 · pp 72-73]
The financial sector consists of money and financial assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #48-2 · pp 72-73]
Microfinance provides financial services to low-income groups. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #48-2 · pp 72-73]
xa: Identity: **WPR = LFPR x (1 - UR)**.
⚠ UR divides by **labour force**; Proportion Unemployed divides by **population**.
"Percentage of employed persons in the population" = **Worker Population Ratio** (APPSC 2023).
