xa: **J-curve**: the trade balance first worsens after depreciation.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.
**Terms of trade** (NTT) = export price index / import price index × **100**.

nindian-economy-52-2-7.s: A closed economy is one which has:
nindian-economy-52-2-7.x: A closed economy has no foreign trade, neither exports nor imports. An open economy has both.
nindian-economy-52-2-7.tq: Recall the definition of a closed economy.
n: A closed economy has neither exports nor imports. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #52-2 · pp 78-79]
xs: A **closed economy** has **neither exports nor imports** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Exports** are goods and services **sold** to the rest of the world; **imports** are **purchased** from it.
xa: **Net exports** = **X − M**; positive = **trade surplus**, negative = **trade deficit**.
Merchandise exports 2024-25: **$437.70 bn** vs imports **$721.20 bn**.
Services exports 2024-25: **$387.54 bn**.

n329d0effa56.s: Which of the following was the largest export item of India in 2024-25 by share?
n329d0effa56.x: Petroleum products constituted the largest listed export item in 2024-25, with a share of 14.48 percent.
n329d0effa56.tq: Identify the leading item from a ranked composition list.
xs: **Petroleum products** were India's largest export in **2024-25**, with a **14.48%** share — option **(1)**.
**Telecom instruments** came second (**5.96%**), **drug formulations, biologicals** third (**5.52%**).
**Electric machinery and equipment** had only **3.29%**.
xa: ⚠ **Petroleum products** = largest export; **crude petroleum** = largest import (**19.84%**).
**Electronics** exports rose **32.46%** to **$38.56 bn** in 2024-25; **smartphones = 62.5%** of them.
**Non-petroleum exports**: **$374.32 bn** (**+6.07%**).

neadf7ccc43c.s: Which of the following groups accounted for approximately one-third of India’s imports in 2024-25?
o: Crude petroleum, gold and petroleum products
neadf7ccc43c.x: Crude petroleum, gold and petroleum products together accounted for approximately one-third of India’s imports.
neadf7ccc43c.tq: Combine the leading categories rather than selecting only the single largest item.
xs: **Crude, gold and petroleum products** make up about **one-third** of India's imports (ES 2025-26) — option **(3)**.
Their **2024-25** shares: crude **19.84%**, gold **8.04%**, petroleum products **5.92%**.
xa: **Coal, coke, briquettes** had **4.31%**; **electronic components** **5.1%**.
**Oil and gold** are named among the factors widening the trade deficit since 1991.
The FY26 Q4 deficit alone was **$83.4 bn**, driven by oil and gold.

nff9dd422ced.s: Which one of the following was India’s largest source of imports in 2024-25?
nff9dd422ced.x: China was India’s largest import source in 2024-25, accounting for 15.73 percent of imports.
nff9dd422ced.tq: Distinguish the largest import source from the largest export destination.
xs: **China** was India's largest import source in **2024-25**, at **15.73%** — option **(2)**.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**, overtaking the USA.
Imports from China: **APIs**, **solar PV cells**, semiconductor chips, telecom machinery.
**H1 2026** imports from China: a record **$79.41 bn**.

n7849201c10a.s: On the basis of the 2024-25 direction-of-trade data, India ran a trade surplus with which of the following groups?
n7849201c10a.x: India ran a surplus with the United States and the Netherlands. It ran deficits with China, Russia, the UAE and Saudi Arabia because imports exceeded exports with those partners.
n7849201c10a.tq: Infer surplus or deficit by comparing the relative export and import positions.
xs: India runs a **surplus with the United States and Netherlands** — option **(2)**.
It runs **deficits** with **China, Russia, UAE and Saudi Arabia**, where oil and goods imports exceed exports.
xa: USA took **19.77%** of exports; Netherlands **5.2%**.
Saudi Arabia supplied **4.18%** of imports.
With China, the goods deficit was **over $100 bn** (Jun 2026).

n15aa710acef.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's trade with China?
o: China supplies about 16% of India's imports.
India imports iron ore from China as a major item.
China supplies APIs and solar cells to India.
India exports iron ore, cotton and marine products to China.
n15aa710acef.x: India does not import iron ore; it exports iron ore, including to China.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**; trade **$151.1 bn**.
**Calendar 2025** (Chinese data): trade **$155.62 bn**, deficit **$116.12 bn**.
China dependence for APIs, solar cells, chips → responses: **QCOs**, **NTBs**, **PLI**.

naaef348414b.s: In FY 2025–26, India's largest overall trading partner was:
naaef348414b.x: China became India's largest overall trading partner, while the United States remained its largest export market.
xa: ⚠ **USA** = top export destination (surplus); **China** = top import source and largest partner (deficit).
India–China trade: **$151.1 bn**; goods deficit **over $100 bn** (Jun 2026).
USA's export share in 2024-25: **19.77%**.

ncb7abbb849d.s: The twin deficit hypothesis states that:
o: A services surplus always causes a merchandise surplus
A current account surplus necessarily causes a fiscal deficit
A rising trade surplus is associated with a rising fiscal surplus
A rising fiscal deficit is associated with a rising trade deficit
ncb7abbb849d.x: The twin deficit hypothesis links a rising fiscal deficit with a rising trade deficit.
ncb7abbb849d.tq: Translate the economic hypothesis into its direct cause-and-association relationship.
xs: **Twin deficit hypothesis**: a **rising fiscal deficit** goes with a **rising trade deficit** — option **(4)**.
It links two deficits, not surpluses, so options (1)–(3) are wrong.
xa: Current deficit drivers: **oil and gold**, electronics components, rising imports from China/FTA partners.
A **services surplus** offsets the goods deficit.
**Marshall-Lerner condition**: devaluation helps only if elasticities sum to **greater than 1**.

nfed975e7a30.s: Which of the following is NOT listed as a response to India's dependence on China for APIs, solar cells and chips?
nfed975e7a30.x: The listed responses are QCOs, NTBs and PLI. Abolition of all import regulations is not listed as a response.
nfed975e7a30.tq: Find the policy measure that contradicts the stated strategic response.
xs: **Abolition of all import regulations** is not a listed response — option **(3)**.
Responses to China dependence for **APIs**, **solar cells**, **chips** are **QCOs**, **NTBs** and **PLI**.
xa: China became India's **largest trading partner in FY 2025-26**; goods deficit **over $100 bn**.
**H1 2026** imports from China: a record **$79.41 bn**.
China was the top import source in 2024-25 (**15.73%**).

necca3ba4038.s: India's merchandise exports in 2024-25 were about:
necca3ba4038.x: Merchandise exports were US$ 437.70 billion and merchandise imports US$ 721.20 billion; the higher figures include services.
xa: **Services** exports: **$387.54 bn**; services imports **$198.72 bn**.
FY25 merchandise deficit: **$283.5 bn** (ES 2025-26).

n3c3489eb5c0.s: The merchandise trade deficit of India in FY25, according to the Economic Survey 2025–26, was:
n3c3489eb5c0.x: The merchandise trade deficit in FY25 was $283.5 billion, representing an increase of 17.6%. RBI balance-of-payments data placed it at $286.9 billion.
n3c3489eb5c0.tq: Distinguish the Economic Survey estimate from the separate RBI balance-of-payments estimate.
xs: The **ES 2025-26** puts the FY25 merchandise deficit at **$283.5 billion** (**+17.6%**) — option **(2)**.
**$337.3 bn** is **FY26**; **$198.72 bn** is services imports; **$437.70 bn** is merchandise exports.
xa: ⚠ The **RBI BoP basis** puts FY25 at **$286.9 bn** — quote the source.
FY26 Q4 alone: **$83.4 bn** (oil, gold).
The **services surplus** hit a record **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.

n834b0688691.s: Which of the following factors has NOT contributed to the widening of India's trade deficit since 1991?
o: Non-tariff barriers imposed by trading partners
Import liberalisation of capital goods and electronic components
n834b0688691.x: Services performed well and generated a surplus; therefore, lacklustre services performance was not a cause of the widening trade deficit. Oil, gold, import liberalisation and external competition were among the contributing factors.
n834b0688691.tq: Find the exception by separating causes of the goods deficit from the performance of services.
xs: **Lacklustre services** is **NOT** a factor — services did well (PYQ 2017) — option **(1)**.
**Non-tariff barriers** of partners, **competition from China** and **import liberalisation** are all listed factors since 1991.
xa: Other factors: the **South-East Asian crisis 1997-98**, **oil and gold**.
**Services surplus**: record **$188.8 bn** in FY25.
**Twin deficit hypothesis**: rising fiscal deficit goes with rising trade deficit.

na8646ce3ad9.s: India recorded a trade surplus after independence only in which of the following years?
na8646ce3ad9.x: Since independence India has run a trade surplus in only two years, 1972-73 and 1976-77; in every other year imports exceeded exports.
na8646ce3ad9.tq: Use the paired-year recall method for an exceptional historical record.
xs: India recorded a trade surplus only in **1972-73 and 1976-77** since independence — option **(1)**.
In every other year imports exceeded exports.
xa: FY26 merchandise deficit: **$337.3 bn**.
**Aug 2026**: first time merchandise exports grew more than imports in absolute value.
Deficit causes since 1991 include the **South-East Asian crisis 1997-98**.

nb6d17386a3f.s: The 1991 New Trade Policy shifted India from import substitution and quantitative restrictions to:
nb6d17386a3f.x: The 1991 policy moved to a price-based regime, alongside a two-step rupee devaluation in July 1991.
xa: **Import substitution** = inward-looking; **export promotion** = outward-looking.
**Devaluation** makes exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home.
**J-curve**: after depreciation the trade balance first **worsens**, then improves.

n77d2d8f635e.s: The principal purpose of India's rupee trade settlement framework is to:
o: Replace the WTO dispute settlement system
Encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade
n77d2d8f635e.x: The framework is intended to encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade; it does not prohibit all foreign-currency transactions.
n77d2d8f635e.tq: Apply the stated purpose of a financial mechanism to a practical trade situation.
xs: The **RBI rupee trade settlement framework** aims to **encourage the use of the Indian rupee in cross-border trade** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
It works through **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts**; it does not ban foreign-currency transactions.
xa: FTP 2023 is framed by the **Department of Commerce**.
**EXIM Bank** gives **Lines of Credit** to foreign governments and buyer's/seller's credit.
Depreciation makes **exports cheaper abroad and imports dearer at home**.

nindian-economy-54-1.s: Which of the following best describes Anti-dumping measures?
o: Determination of country of origin for trade-policy purposes
Protection against goods exported below normal value
nindian-economy-54-1.x: Anti-dumping duties protect against imports sold below their normal value. A quota limits quantity, and licensing is an administrative control.
nindian-economy-54-1.tq: Match each trade tool to its meaning.
n: Anti-dumping measures protect against goods exported below normal value. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #54 · pp 80-81]
xs: **Anti-dumping measures** protect against **goods exported below normal value** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Rules of origin** determine country of origin; **import licensing** = administrative restriction; **import quota** = quantity restriction.
xa: **Dumping** = exporting below home-market price or cost.
**Countervailing duty** offsets foreign subsidies.
**Tariff** = a **tax on imports**.

nc158fb17f23.s: Which one of the following is classified as a non-bulk import?
nc158fb17f23.x: Capital goods are included among non-bulk imports. Crude and petroleum products, cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertiliser, metals and ores are listed as bulk imports.
nc158fb17f23.tq: Discriminate between two classifications by recalling the category membership.
xs: **Capital goods** are a **non-bulk import** — option **(2)**.
**Edible oils**, **pulses** and **fertiliser** are all **bulk imports**.
xa: Bulk imports: crude and products, cereals, pulses, edible oils, sugar, fertiliser, **metals and ores**.
Non-bulk imports: **capital goods**, **precious products**, **chemicals**.
Import liberalisation of capital goods, APIs and electronic components is a deficit factor since **1991**.

nad8da75aa94.s: Which of the following best explains how India's services sector cushions the merchandise trade deficit?
o: Remittances are recorded as merchandise exports
Services imports exceed services exports and increase the deficit
The services surplus, particularly from IT and IT-enabled services, along with remittances, offsets the merchandise deficit
The services sector eliminates the need for merchandise imports
nad8da75aa94.x: The services surplus, especially from IT and IT-enabled services, together with remittances, offsets a substantial part of the merchandise deficit.
nad8da75aa94.tq: Link the surplus-generating sector with the deficit it helps to offset.
xs: The **services surplus** (**IT/ITeS**) plus **remittances** offsets the merchandise deficit — option **(3)**.
Services exports exceed services imports (**$387.54 bn** vs **$198.72 bn** in 2024-25), so option (2) is wrong.
xa: Record services surplus: **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.
**Services surplus** vs structural **merchandise deficit** → Ricardian comparative advantage in services.
Services share of total exports: about **49%**.

na59f5428aea.s: In foreign trade, 'direction' of trade refers to:
o: The money value of exports and imports
The country-wise or region-wise pattern of trade
The balance between exports and imports
na59f5428aea.x: Direction is the country-wise or region-wise pattern; composition is the items traded and volume the money value.
xa: Top export destination 2024-25: **USA** (**19.77%**); top import source: **China** (**15.73%**).
⚠ **Petroleum products** = largest export; **crude petroleum** = largest import.
**China** became India's largest trading partner in **FY 2025-26**.

n2b2054e38d9.s: According to the WTO (April 2025), India's rank among world commercial services exporters in 2024 was:
n2b2054e38d9.x: India was 8th in commercial services exports; 18th is its rank as a merchandise exporter. Its services share rose from 2% (2005) to 4.3% (2024).
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: the **Economic Survey** calls India the **7th-largest** services exporter.
**Services surplus**: record **$188.8 bn** in **FY25**.
Services share of total exports about **49%**, up from **39%** in **2014**.

nd2a1a3f68b2.s: The Foreign Trade Policy target for India's share in world services exports by 2022 was:
nd2a1a3f68b2.x: The Foreign Trade Policy had set a target of 4.2% for India's share in world services exports by 2022.
nd2a1a3f68b2.tq: Distinguish a policy target from the later achieved share.
xs: The **FTP** target was a **4.2%** share in world services exports **by 2022** (PYQ 2019) — option **(3)**.
**4.3%** is the actual **2024** share; **2%** the **2005** share.
xa: **FTP 2023** targets **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
**WTO**: India **8th** services exporter (2024); ES says **7th**.
Record **services surplus**: **$188.8 bn** in FY25.

n34d314ac4ba.s: In 2024, with a 2.8% share, India was the world's ____ largest merchandise importer.
n34d314ac4ba.x: India was the 9th largest importer (2.8%) and the 18th exporter, with its export share rising from 1% (2005) to 1.8% (2024).
xa: India was the **18th** merchandise exporter (**1.8%**) in 2024.
⚠ Merchandise exporter rank **18th** vs services exporter rank **8th**.
India ran a trade surplus only in **1972-73** and **1976-77** since independence.

n0c5f577b176.s: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 targets India's exports by 2030 at:
n0c5f577b176.x: FTP 2023, in effect from 1 April 2023 with no fixed end date, targets US$ 2 trillion of exports by 2030.
xa: Framed and monitored by the **Department of Commerce**.
Pillars: duty-free input schemes, **Districts as Export Hubs**, logistics, better FTA use.
**RoDTEP** replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20**.
**RBI** rupee trade settlement uses **Special Rupee Vostro Accounts**.

n1feb445a3cb.s: RoDTEP replaced which WTO-challenged scheme of FTP 2015–20?
n1feb445a3cb.x: RoDTEP replaced the WTO-challenged Merchandise Exports from India Scheme (MEIS) of FTP 2015–20.
n1feb445a3cb.tq: Match the successor scheme with the scheme it replaced.
xs: **RoDTEP** replaced the WTO-challenged **MEIS** of **FTP 2015-20** — option **(4)**.
RoDTEP = **Remission of Duties and Taxes on Export Products**.
xa: **FTP 2023**: from **1 April 2023**, target **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
A **countervailing duty** offsets foreign subsidies — the risk export incentives face abroad.
e.g. US preliminary **CVD of 125.87%** on an Indian product (**Mar 2026**).

n02c5fca0a39.s: The nodal agency for Agri Export Zones in India is:
n02c5fca0a39.x: The Agricultural and Processed Food Products Export Development Authority (APEDA) is the nodal agency for Agri Export Zones.
n02c5fca0a39.tq: Identify the institution assigned the specific export-promotion function.
xs: **APEDA** is the nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones** — option **(1)** (PYQ key).
APEDA works under the **Department of Commerce**; **EXIM Bank** is a finance body, not the nodal agency.
xa: ⚠ **APEDA** = agri exports; **MPEDA** = marine products.
**Agriculture Export Policy 2018** aimed to double agri exports.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.

n05209fada06.s: Export promotion of marine products is handled by:
n05209fada06.x: MPEDA handles marine products; APEDA (under the Department of Commerce) handles agricultural exports.
xa: APEDA is the nodal agency for **Agri Export Zones**.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.
**Marine products** are among India's exports to **China**.

n8cac2dc03a2.s: India's first Export Processing Zone was set up in 1965 at:
n8cac2dc03a2.x: Kandla (Gujarat) got India's first EPZ in 1965. Santacruz (Mumbai), Falta (West Bengal) and Visakhapatnam got EPZs later, and these were converted into SEZs after the 2000 SEZ policy.
xs: India's first **Export Processing Zone** came up at **Kandla** in **1965** — option **(2)**.
Kandla's EPZ came decades before the **SEZ** framework of **April 2000**.
xa: The **SEZ** policy followed in **April 2000**; the **SEZ Act** in **2005**.
SEZs are treated as **foreign territory** for trade and tariff purposes.
First **Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre**: **Pune, May 2021**.

n2538eb058e0.s: India's FTAs have been criticised mainly for:
o: Widening deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea, and weak utilisation
Eliminating the merchandise deficit with all Asian partners
n2538eb058e0.x: The criticism is that FTAs widened deficits with ASEAN, Japan and Korea and have been poorly utilised.
xa: India has **14 FTAs and 6 PTAs** (**Apr 2026**).
**Rules of origin** decide which goods qualify for FTA concessions.
FTP 2023 pillars include **better FTA use**.

nindian-economy-39-6.s: India's SEZ Policy, aimed at export competitiveness and FDI, was announced on:
nindian-economy-39-6.x: The SEZ Policy was announced on 1 April 2000 to make exports competitive and attract FDI.
n: The Special Economic Zone Policy was announced on 1 April 2000. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy was announced under the Globalisation framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The primary objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy was to boost export competitiveness. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy aimed to attract foreign direct investment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
The Special Economic Zone Policy aimed to create an internationally competitive trade environment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 58-60]
xa: SEZ concept proposed in the **EXIM Policy 1997-2002**; PYQ key: **EXIM Policy 2000-01**.
SEZ Act **2005**; first EPZ **Kandla, 1965**.
First Agriculture Export Facilitation Centre: **Pune, May 2021**.

nindian-economy-37-10.s: What was the objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy in relation to the business environment?
o: To establish a mixed economic model
To provide an internationally competitive environment
To create a long-term fiscal policy
nindian-economy-37-10.x: One SEZ objective was an internationally competitive business environment. Licensing and the mixed economy belong to older policies.
n: The objective of the Special Economic Zone Policy was to provide an internationally competitive environment. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #37 · pp 54-56]
xs: The SEZ Policy aimed to **provide an internationally competitive environment** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Its objectives: **promote exports**, **attract FDI**, an **internationally competitive trade environment** and a **level playing field** for exports.
A **mixed economic model** and **industrial licensing** belong to older policies.
xa: SEZs offer **simplified procedures** and a **business-friendly environment**.
**FTP 2023** targets **$2 trillion** exports by **2030**.
**RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS** of FTP 2015-20.

nc2dd30799c0.s: Under the partial current-account convertibility introduced in 1992, foreign exchange transactions were divided as follows:
o: 60% at the official rate and 40% at the market rate
50% at the official rate and 50% at the market rate
20% at the official rate and 80% at the market rate
40% at the official rate and 60% at the market rate
nc2dd30799c0.x: In 1992, partial current-account convertibility provided for 40% of foreign exchange at the official rate and 60% at the market rate.
nc2dd30799c0.tq: Watch for the reversal of the two percentages in quantitative reform questions.
xs: Under **1992** partial current-account convertibility, **40%** of forex went at the **official rate** and **60%** at the **market rate** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the split.
xa: Raw materials and capital goods were placed under **OGL**.
It followed the **1991 Trade Policy** shift from **QRs** to a price-based regime.
**FTP** replaced EXIM policies from **2004**.

n245eeb28ebf.s: Foreign Trade Policy 2023 came into force on:
n245eeb28ebf.x: FTP 2023 came into force on 1 April 2023 and has no fixed end date.
xa: ⚠ FTP target **$2 trillion** vs **Piyush Goyal's $1 trillion** exports goal (Board of Trade, **Jul 2026**).
Approach: shift from **incentives to remission** and entitlement-based support.
**Districts as Export Hubs** brings a district-level export focus.

n601a554aef2.s: The Foreign Trade Policy is administered through the Directorate General of Foreign Trade under the:
o: Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises
n601a554aef2.x: The Foreign Trade Policy is administered by the Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, through the DGFT.
n601a554aef2.tq: Use the ‘which ministry’ trap to separate the Department of Commerce from neighbouring ministries.
xs: FTP is administered by the **Department of Commerce, Ministry of Commerce and Industry**, through **DGFT** — option **(3)**.
Finance, MSME or External Affairs ministries do not administer the FTP.
xa: **DGFT** is an attached office of the Dept of Commerce, HQ **Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi**.
DGFT issues FTP authorisations and runs **Districts as Export Hubs** and the **Export Promotion Mission**.
EXIM policies gave way to the **Foreign Trade Policy from 2004**.

nba62e4999bd.s: Which one of the following is a feature of the Foreign Trade Policy 2023?
o: A shift from remission and entitlement support to only quantitative restrictions
A shift from incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support
A complete withdrawal of electronic initiatives
nba62e4999bd.x: FTP 2023 shifts the emphasis from conventional incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support, while also promoting e-initiatives and merchanting trade.
nba62e4999bd.tq: Reject the options that reverse the direction of policy change.
xs: **FTP 2023** shifts **from incentives towards remission and entitlement-based support** — option **(3)**.
It also promotes **e-initiatives** and **merchanting trade**, so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: One-time **amnesty scheme** for **EPCG/Advance Authorisation** export-obligation defaults.
New **Towns of Export Excellence** added.
**EPCG green list** widened to **BEVs**, vertical farming, green hydrogen.

n8b2cd611afa.s: FTP 2023 offers a one-time amnesty for export-obligation defaults under:
n8b2cd611afa.x: FTP 2023 includes a one-time amnesty for EPCG and Advance Authorisation export-obligation defaults, along with rupee trade settlement and new Towns of Export Excellence.
xa: **EPCG green list** widened to **BEVs**, vertical farming, wastewater recycling, rainwater harvesting, green hydrogen.
**Districts as Export Hubs**: district-level export focus.
Export target: **$2 trillion by 2030**.

na6c2cd977c0.s: EOUs, EHTPs and STPs are units that:
o: Export at least half of their output
Pay full customs duty on inputs
Must be located only in SEZs
na6c2cd977c0.x: These units export all their output, may be located anywhere and get duty-free inputs.
xa: ⚠ SEZ = enclave treated as **foreign territory**; EOU/EHTP/STP = located anywhere.
SEZs: **100% FDI** automatic for most manufacturing.
SEZ law = **SEZ Act 2005**.

n0fb866cf8aa.s: Export credit insurance in India is provided by:
n0fb866cf8aa.x: ECGC provides export credit insurance; DGFT issues FTP authorisations and runs Districts as Export Hubs and the Export Promotion Mission.
xa: DGFT HQ: **Vanijya Bhavan, New Delhi**.
FTP is administered by the **Department of Commerce** through DGFT.
**NIRVIK (2019)**: bigger ECGC insurance cover for export credit.

n96ad20639d4.s: Under the Foreign Trade Policy 2015-20, MEIS and SEIS respectively related to:
n96ad20639d4.x: MEIS provided support for exports of goods, while SEIS related to exports of services under FTP 2015-20.
n96ad20639d4.tq: Separate the two similar-sounding schemes by their covered sectors.
xs: Under **FTP 2015-20**, **MEIS** covered **goods exports** and **SEIS** **services exports** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the pair.
xa: **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS**; **SEIS** was discontinued.
⚠ **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL** (apparel and made-ups).
**EPCG** = capital goods; **Advance Authorisation** = inputs.

na052781a9ec.s: RoDTEP replaced which scheme and seeks to refund which category of burden?
o: SEIS; only income tax paid by exporters
MEIS; unrebated central, state and local taxes
RoSL; only customs duties on imported inputs
na052781a9ec.x: RoDTEP replaced MEIS and refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes, including electricity duty and VAT on transport fuel.
na052781a9ec.tq: Separate the replaced scheme from the similar RoSCTL and RoSL schemes.
xs: **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS** and refunds **unrebated central, state and local taxes** — option **(3)**.
Examples: **electricity duty**, **VAT on transport fuel**.
**RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL**; **SEIS** was a services scheme — so options (1), (2), (4) mismatch.
xa: RoDTEP is run online by **CBIC** (IYB 2026).
**Duty drawback** refunds **customs duty** on imported inputs used in exports.
⚠ RoDTEP = replaced MEIS; RoSCTL = replaced RoSL.

na07be354c85.s: RoSCTL replaced RoSL and provides a rebate mainly for:
na07be354c85.x: RoSCTL replaced RoSL and provides a rebate for apparel and made-ups.
na07be354c85.tq: Match the scheme with its specific product category.
xs: **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL** and gives a rebate for **apparel and made-ups** — option **(3)**.
Services exports were covered by **SEIS**; capital goods imports by **EPCG**.
xa: ⚠ **RoDTEP** replaced **MEIS**; **RoSCTL** replaced **RoSL**.
**Budget 2026-27** extended the Advance Authorisation export period for leather/textile garments and footwear from **6 months to 1 year**.
**SEIS** was the services exports reward under **FTP 2015-20**.

o: Customs duty on imported inputs used in exports
n53acaf9d6b0.x: Duty drawback refunds customs duty on imported inputs used in exports, not income tax on export profits.
xa: ⚠ **EPCG** = capital goods; **Advance Authorisation** = inputs.
One-time **amnesty** in FTP 2023 for **EPCG/Advance Authorisation** obligation defaults.
**RoDTEP** refunds unrebated central, state and local taxes.

n4034eb6f7b8.s: The Export Promotion Mission, aimed at MSMEs and first-time exporters, is run by:
n4034eb6f7b8.x: DGFT runs the Export Promotion Mission, which merges Interest Equalisation and the Market Access Initiative.
xa: Niryat Disha tools: **TRACE**, **FLOW**, **LIFT**, **INSIGHT**.
**RELIEF Scheme 2026**: **₹497 crore** under EPM via ECGC.

n2afdf418cdf.s: The RELIEF Scheme 2026, implemented through ECGC, provides support mainly for:
o: Interest subsidy on domestic housing loans
War-risk and logistics costs in West Asia
n2afdf418cdf.x: RELIEF Scheme 2026 provides support for war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia through ECGC under the Export Promotion Mission.
n2afdf418cdf.tq: Link the risk described in the scenario with the specialised insurance-support scheme.
xs: **RELIEF Scheme 2026** covers **war-risk and logistics costs in West Asia** — option **(4)**.
It provides **₹497 crore** under the **EPM**, via **ECGC**.
xa: **Egypt and Jordan** were added in **April 2026**.
The **West Asia** conflict also led to procedural flexibility in export authorisations (TH, **3 Mar 2026**).
**ECGC** = export credit insurance.

nc6e44781d24.s: Which recent development was identified as having disrupted cargo movement and prompted procedural flexibility in export authorisations?
o: The merger of ODOP with DEH
A global shortage of software exports
The introduction of the LEADS index
nc6e44781d24.x: The West Asia conflict disrupted cargo movement, following which the Government allowed procedural flexibility in export authorisations.
nc6e44781d24.tq: Connect the external event with its direct trade-policy consequence.
xs: The **West Asia conflict** disrupted cargo, so the Govt allowed **procedural flexibility in export authorisations** (TH, **3 Mar 2026**) — option **(3)**.
**LEADS** is a logistics ranking, not a disruption.
xa: **RELIEF Scheme 2026** (**₹497 crore**, via **ECGC**) covers war-risk + logistics costs in West Asia.
**Egypt and Jordan** were added to RELIEF in **April 2026**.
**DGFT** issues FTP authorisations.

n695af169380.s: FDI in most manufacturing in SEZs is allowed under the automatic route up to:
n695af169380.x: 100 per cent FDI is allowed under the automatic route for most manufacturing; SEZs are governed by the SEZ Act, 2005.
xa: **Budget 2026-27**: measures to use **idle SEZ manufacturing capacity** hit by global trade.
⚠ SEZ = enclave (foreign territory); **EOU/EHTP/STP** = can be located anywhere.
EOU/EHTP/STP export all output and get **duty-free inputs**.

nc31654a8d3c.s: A bill of lading serves as:
o: A shipping company’s receipt and a document of title to the goods
An exporter’s application for a duty drawback
A customs order fixing the tariff rate
nc31654a8d3c.x: A bill of lading is the shipping company’s receipt and also functions as a document of title to the goods.
nc31654a8d3c.tq: Select the option that contains both parts of the document’s legal function.
xs: A **bill of lading** is the **shipping company's receipt** and a **document of title to the goods** — option **(1)**.
It is not a quota certificate, drawback claim or tariff order.
xa: ⚠ Bill of lading = document of title; **mate's receipt** = goods loaded on board.
**Shipping bill**: customs document for clearing export goods.
**Indent**: importer's order to buy goods.

n5598a5f2825.s: ICEGATE is best described as which of the following?
o: A postal export network of India Post
A logistics ranking index of NITI Aayog
A single-window system for foreign investment approvals
A customs e-filing portal of CBIC
n5598a5f2825.x: ICEGATE is the customs e-filing portal of the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC).
n5598a5f2825.tq: Identify the responsible authority behind the digital trade platform.
xs: **ICEGATE** is **CBIC**'s **customs e-filing portal** — option **(4)**.
**SWIFT** is the single window for import clearance; **LEADS** ranks States on logistics.
xa: **CBIC** also runs **RoDTEP** online.
**PM Gati Shakti** (**2021**) and **National Logistics Policy** (**2022**) aim to cut export logistics costs.
**Shipping bill**: customs document for clearing exports.

n358c926985a.s: The SWIFT system in the context of trade facilitation is associated with which function?
n358c926985a.x: SWIFT functions as a single window for import clearance.
n358c926985a.tq: Separate a clearance mechanism from portals, rankings and export-support institutions.
xs: **SWIFT** is the **single window for import clearance** — option **(1)**.
Export credit insurance is **ECGC**'s job; **LEADS** ranks States on logistics.
xa: **ICEGATE** = **CBIC**'s customs e-filing portal.
**PM Gati Shakti** + **National Logistics Policy** aim to cut export logistics costs.
**DGFT** runs **Districts as Export Hubs**.

n7c099e3306e.s: Which of the following best describes import substitution?
o: Increasing dependence on imported capital goods
Promoting only agricultural exports through export subsidies
Reducing import dependence by producing import substitutes at home
n7c099e3306e.x: Import substitution is an inward-looking strategy aimed at producing goods domestically in order to reduce import dependency.
n7c099e3306e.tq: Apply the inward-looking versus outward-looking distinction to a policy description.
xs: **Import substitution** means **reducing import dependence by producing import substitutes at home** — option **(4)** (PYQ).
It is an **inward-looking** strategy; **export promotion** is the outward-looking one.
xa: Import substitution ran in India for about **four decades**.
The **1991 Trade Policy** moved from **QRs** to a **price-based** regime.
An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction** on imports (PYQ 2019).

na515a4b9490.s: Which one of the following trade policy instruments is a quantitative restriction?
na515a4b9490.x: An import quota sets a ceiling on the quantity of a good that may be imported, so it is a quantitative restriction. An ad valorem tariff is a tax on the value of imports. Countervailing and anti-dumping duties are also price-based duties, not quantity limits.
na515a4b9490.tq: Quota limits quantity; duties and tariffs act on price.
xs: An **import quota** is a **quantitative restriction** on the amount of imports — option **(2)** (PYQ 2019).
A **tariff** is a **tax on imported goods**, a price measure, not a quantity limit.
xa: The **1991 Trade Policy** moved from **QRs** to a **price-based** regime.
**Import substitution** aimed at **reducing import dependency**.
**Rules of origin** fix a product's **national source**.

n188de8f286b.s: The principal purpose of rules of origin is to determine:
o: The international price of a product
The amount of countervailing duty payable
The national source of a product
n188de8f286b.x: Rules of origin establish the national source of a product and help determine eligibility for free-trade agreement concessions.
n188de8f286b.tq: Identify the administrative question answered by the rule rather than its possible trade consequence.
xs: **Rules of origin** are criteria that fix a product's **national source** — option **(4)**.
They tell customs **which duties and rules apply** (BPSC 2023 PYQ — all statements correct).
xa: Quantity limits are **import quotas**, a **quantitative restriction**.
**Bill of lading** is a **document of title** to goods.
**Letter of credit**: importer's bank guarantees payment.

nf4f7998d089.s: Under the Balance of Payments framework, which of the following best distinguishes the presentation followed by the IMF from that generally followed by the Reserve Bank of India?
o: The IMF uses only current and capital accounts, whereas the RBI uses current, capital and financial accounts separately.
The IMF uses only trade and services accounts, whereas the RBI uses current and financial accounts.
The IMF uses current, capital and financial accounts, whereas the RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts.
Both the IMF and the RBI invariably present the Balance of Payments through exactly three separate accounts.
nf4f7998d089.x: Under BPM6, the IMF distinguishes current, capital and financial accounts. The RBI generally combines the capital and financial accounts under the heading ‘capital account’.
nf4f7998d089.tq: Separate the IMF classification from the RBI presentation instead of treating the terms as identical.
xs: The **IMF (BPM6)** uses **three accounts — current, capital, financial**, while the **RBI combines** the last two as **"Capital Account"** — option **(3)**.
So the RBI does not keep them separate (option 1), and the two do not invariably use three accounts (option 4).
xa: **BoP** = systematic record of all transactions of residents with the rest of the world, on **double-entry** bookkeeping.
BoP has a **current account and a capital account** (PYQ 2025; APPSC-G2 2025 key).
Identity: Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = **0**.

n97d8f4d1830.s: Which of the following correctly represents the Balance of Payments identity?
o: Current balance + capital balance + financial balance + errors and omissions = zero
Current balance + merchandise exports = financial balance
Current balance − capital balance = trade balance
n97d8f4d1830.x: The Balance of Payments identity is current balance plus capital balance plus financial balance plus errors and omissions equal to zero.
n97d8f4d1830.tq: Recall the complete identity rather than restricting the BoP to the trade balance.
xs: BoP identity: **Current + Capital + Financial + Net Errors & Omissions = 0** — option **(2)**.
BoP always **balances in accounting terms**; a surplus in one account = a deficit in another.
xa: BoP uses **double-entry** bookkeeping.
IMF **BPM6** has three accounts; RBI merges capital and financial into **"Capital Account"**.
**Overall BoP** positive → adds to reserves; negative → draws them down.

n3ca5eff9964.s: What is the usual effect of the overall balance of payments position on foreign exchange reserves?
o: The overall balance has no relationship with reserve movements.
A positive overall balance reduces reserves, while a negative balance increases them.
A positive overall balance adds to reserves, while a negative balance draws them down.
Both positive and negative balances increase reserves because the BoP always balances in accounting terms.
n3ca5eff9964.x: A positive overall balance adds to foreign exchange reserves, whereas a negative overall balance draws them down. If reserves become insufficient, a balance of payments crisis may result.
n3ca5eff9964.tq: Use the direction of reserve movement to identify the correct surplus-deficit relationship.
xs: A **positive overall BoP adds to reserves**; a **negative** one **draws them down** — option **(3)**.
If reserves run short → **BoP crisis**.
xa: **July 2026**: overall BoP **$20.8 bn surplus**; capital account **$27.7 bn surplus**.
Forex reserves **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
Reserve components: **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs**, **Reserve Tranche Position**.

nb3c4003cbaa.s: The external-sector recovery in FY24 was mainly associated with:
o: A decline in remittances and a rise in primary-income outgo
A complete elimination of the merchandise deficit
Moderation in merchandise exports along with a sharp fall in imports
A sharp rise in merchandise imports and a fall in services exports
nb3c4003cbaa.x: The FY24 external-sector recovery came from moderation in merchandise exports accompanied by a sharp fall in imports.
nb3c4003cbaa.tq: Select the precise cause-effect combination and reject reversed trade trends.
xs: The **FY24 recovery** came from **moderation in merchandise exports** plus a **sharp fall in imports** — option **(3)** (APPSC-G1 2024 key).
The merchandise deficit was not eliminated; the **Q4 2023-24 surplus** came from services exports.
xa: Record **services surplus**: **$188.8 bn in FY25**.

nindian-economy-25-1.s: Which of the following best defines the Balance of Payments (BoP)?
o: A complete record of all economic transactions between residents of a country and the rest of the world during a specified period
A systematic record of only goods exported and imported during a year
A record of only services and transfer payments between countries
A record of only cross-border capital movements during a specified period
nindian-economy-25-1.x: The balance of payments is the full record of all economic transactions between a country's residents and the rest of the world over a period, usually a year. The 'only' options describe parts of it.
n: Balance of Payments is a systematic record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments is a complete record of all economic transactions between the residents of a country and the rest of the world. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments covers transactions during a specified period. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
The specified period for Balance of Payments is normally one year. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments covers all international economic transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xs: The **Balance of Payments** is a **complete record of all economic transactions** between **residents** of a country and the **rest of the world** during a **specified period** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It covers **goods**, **services**, **transfers** and **capital transactions**; the "only" options describe parts of it.
xa: The period is **normally one year**; BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping.
It has a **current account and a capital account** (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
IMF's **BPM6** uses three accounts; **RBI** combines capital and financial as "Capital Account".

nindian-economy-25-5.x: The balance of trade covers goods only; services and transfers belong to the wider current account.
n: Balance of Trade covers goods only. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Convertibility is the freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Current Account Convertibility applies to current international transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account Convertibility is the freedom to conduct investment transactions without capital controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account Convertibility is the freedom to conduct financial-asset transactions without capital controls. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Trade is visible trade. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments includes goods, services, transfers, and capital transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments is the broader external account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Balance of Payments includes Current Account transactions and Capital/financial Account transactions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
Capital Account includes international purchases and sales of assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #25 · pp 36-38]
xa: **Full current account convertibility** came in **August 1994** (IMF **Article VIII**).
**LERMS** (**1992-93 Budget**): **40%** official / **60%** market rate; unified **1 March 1993**.
⚠ **FEMA** enacted **1999**, in force **1 June 2000**.

n758201b166a.s: The balance of the current account is represented by which of the following expressions?
o: Exports minus imports of goods and services plus net primary and net secondary income
Capital inflows minus capital outflows plus errors and omissions
Exports and imports of goods only plus changes in foreign exchange reserves
Foreign direct investment plus portfolio investment minus external debt
n758201b166a.x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
n758201b166a.tq: Reconstruct the identity by adding goods, services, primary income and secondary income.
xs: **Current account balance** = (exports − imports of **goods and services**) + **net primary income** + **net secondary income** — option **(1)**.
Capital flows and reserve changes (options 2, 3) belong to the capital account.
xa: APPSC-GS 2019 key: exports minus imports of goods **and services** + net unilateral transfers.
⚠ **BoT** = goods only; current account balance = goods **and services** + transfers.
A **CAD** must be financed by a capital account surplus or by drawing down reserves.

na710b321cbe.s: Why are FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings viewed cautiously in discussions on India's external-sector sustainability?
o: They are domestic tax receipts and do not affect the balance of payments.
They are temporary inflows, whereas FDI is expected to support a self-sustaining capital surplus.
They are permanent grants and therefore cannot reverse suddenly.
They are components of merchandise exports and reduce the trade deficit directly.
na710b321cbe.x: FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are considered temporary sources of financing. The preferred long-term basis for a self-sustaining capital surplus is stronger FDI.
na710b321cbe.tq: Distinguish temporary financing flows from durable investment flows.
xs: **FCNR(B)** and **ECB** inflows are **temporary**; **FDI** must drive a **self-sustaining capital surplus** — option **(2)**.
They are capital account items (**NRI deposits**, **external commercial borrowings**), not tax receipts, grants or merchandise exports.
xa: RBI's special **FCNR(B)** scheme drew **$127 bn** in NRI deposits — a possible **one-time comfort**.
FY26 **net FDI** was only **$6.9 bn**, down from **$44.0 bn** in **2020-21**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, **remittances** create **no repayment obligation**.

naddefe5bab4.s: In the balance of payments, shipping, banking, tourism and software are classified as:
naddefe5bab4.x: These are non-factor services, part of invisibles along with primary (factor) income and transfers.
xa: Primary income = **interest, dividends, profits, wages**.
Secondary income = **remittances**, gifts, grants.
**Software services** are the largest part of the services surplus.

nabb08c0cc26.s: In the balance of payments, reserve changes and official borrowing are examples of:
nabb08c0cc26.x: Accommodating transactions such as reserve changes and official borrowing fill the gap left by autonomous transactions.
xa: The **monetary authority** is the ultimate financier of any BoP deficit.
**Overall BoP** negative → draws down reserves.
The **IMF** is the **last resort** when reserves cannot cover the deficit.

n05d0406337f.s: India recorded a current account surplus for three consecutive years during:
n05d0406337f.x: India had current account surpluses for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.
xa: **Q4 2023-24** also saw a **surplus**, due to a **surge in services exports**.
CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13** (taper tantrum).

n202c7164b3d.s: India's current account surplus in the fourth quarter of 2023-24 was driven by:
o: A sharp rise in gold imports
A rise in crude oil imports
n202c7164b3d.x: The Q4 2023-24 surplus came from a surge in services exports, not from gold imports.
xa: **FY24 recovery**: moderation in merchandise exports + **sharp fall in imports**.

n92ec1ca0ecc.s: Which of the following is a cyclical, not structural, cause of India's current account deficit?
o: Dependence on imported oil and gold
n92ec1ca0ecc.x: A temporary global slowdown is cyclical; oil and gold imports, weak export competitiveness and the savings-investment gap are structural.
xa: Cyclical causes: **commodity shocks**, global slowdown, **rupee volatility**.
**May 2026**: PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the Iran conflict raised prices.
**FY26** merchandise deficit: **$337.3 bn**.

n112756519ec.s: India's current account deficit reached its peak of about 4.8% of GDP in:
o: 1990-91, during the balance of payments crisis
FY24, after the fall in imports
H1 FY26, after the US tariffs
n112756519ec.x: The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period. In the 1990-91 crisis it was about 3.1-3.2% of GDP. FY24 saw a recovery, with a surplus in Q4, and H1 FY26 had a CAD of only 0.8% of GDP.
xs: India's CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13**, around the **taper tantrum** — option **(2)**.
The **1990-91** crisis CAD was **3.1-3.2%**; **FY24** saw a recovery; **H1 FY26** CAD was only **0.8%**.
xa: In the **2013** taper tantrum **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
**Rangarajan Committee**: sustainable CAD about **1.6% of GDP**.

n407ec89eef5.s: Which of the following increases a country's external vulnerability?
o: Adequate forex reserves for import cover
Reduced reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows
n407ec89eef5.x: Greater dependence on hot money increases vulnerability; adequate reserves, low short-term debt and less volatile flows are safeguards.
xa: Forex reserves **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
US Fed hikes push **"hot money"** out of emerging markets.
**2013**: India among the **"Fragile Five"**.

n01c92486674.s: During the 2013 taper tantrum, Morgan Stanley included India among the:
n01c92486674.x: Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘Fragile Five’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.
n01c92486674.tq: Recall the distinctive group label associated with the external shock.
xs: During the **2013 taper tantrum**, **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"** — option **(3)**.
The CAD then peaked at **4.8% of GDP** (**FY13**).
xa: In **May 2026** India's BoP was described as weak as the 2013 "Fragile Five" phase.
US Fed hikes → **hot money** exits → weaker rupee.
Safeguards: adequate reserves, low **short-term debt**.

nb8c2fca0099.s: Which of the following is an IMF lending window for balance of payments support?
nb8c2fca0099.x: The Extended Fund Facility (like the Stand-By Arrangement) is an IMF window; RBI's swap facilities and SRVAs are not IMF instruments.
xa: The IMF is the **last resort** for a BoP crisis.
India drew on the IMF in the **1991** crisis.
Reserves include **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF.

na70702d0476.s: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed approximately what proportion of the merchandise deficit?
na70702d0476.x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about two-thirds of the merchandise deficit. Remittances also acted as a cushion.
na70702d0476.tq: Identify the comparative proportion rather than treating the services surplus as full financing of the merchandise deficit.
xs: The record **services surplus** of **$188.8 bn** in **FY25** financed about **two-thirds** of the merchandise deficit — option **(4)**.
**Remittances** were the other **cushion**.
xa: **Software services** = largest part of the services surplus.
Net services in **Q1 FY27**: **$51.6 bn**.
Net **primary income** is an outflow — **$10.5 bn** in Q1 FY27.

n010c9f206eb.s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
n010c9f206eb.x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
n010c9f206eb.tq: Use the paired numerical figures and distinguish the annual estimate from other remittance measures.
xs: India, the **world's largest recipient**, got **$135.4 billion** (**3.5%** of GDP) in **FY25** — option **(1)**.
**$188.8 bn** is the **services surplus**; **$110.47 bn** and **$87.55 bn** are **workers' remittances** for FY26 and the year before.
xa: ⚠ **$135.4 bn** (FY25 total) vs **$110.47 bn** (FY26, workers' remittances — narrower measure).
Remittances exceed gross **FDI** inflows.

n02d5072080e.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of remittances in India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
n02d5072080e.x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.
n02d5072080e.tq: Apply the contrast between stable transfer inflows and debt-creating capital flows.
xs: Remittances are **counter-cyclical** and create **no debt burden / no repayment obligation** — option **(1)**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, they need no repayment; they are not FDI (they in fact **exceed gross FDI** inflows).
xa: Remittances = **$135.4 bn (3.5% of GDP)** in **FY25**.
Workers' remittances: **$110.47 bn** in **FY26**.
Critics warn of dependence on remittances + one-time deposit schemes instead of stable **FDI**.

n9a1a3441c4d.s: A capital-account transaction involving the purchase of foreign assets by residents is recorded as:
o: A current-account credit because assets are goods
A debit because foreign exchange flows out for acquiring the assets
A credit because foreign exchange enters the country
n9a1a3441c4d.x: Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit. Conversely, sale of Indian assets to foreigners is recorded as a credit.
n9a1a3441c4d.tq: Follow the direction of the financial flow to distinguish a debit from a credit.
xs: **Purchase of foreign assets** by residents is a capital-account **debit** — foreign exchange flows out — option **(3)**.
**Sale of Indian assets to foreigners** is a **credit**.
xa: BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping, so it always balances in accounting terms.
Capital account items: **FDI**, **FPI/FII**, ADRs/GDRs, **ECB**, NRI deposits.
Surplus in one account = **deficit** in another.

n12c6c4c83cf.s: How do increases in US Federal Reserve interest rates and a strong US dollar generally affect emerging markets such as India?
o: They automatically increase India’s net FDI
They raise US yields, attract hot money away from emerging markets and weaken the rupee
They reduce US yields and cause capital to flow into emerging markets
They eliminate exchange-rate volatility in emerging markets
n12c6c4c83cf.x: US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
n12c6c4c83cf.tq: Follow the capital-flow chain from interest-rate differential to exchange-rate pressure.
xs: **US Fed** rate hikes + a **strong dollar** → **higher US yields** → **"hot money" leaves emerging markets** → **weaker rupee** — option **(2)**.
So they do not lower US yields or raise India's FDI.
xa: **2013 taper tantrum**: India named one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
Safeguard: less reliance on volatile **FPI** and debt flows.
The rupee fell **~6.5%** against the dollar.

n1eb3d9fcd56.s: Which of the following is an expenditure-switching measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
n1eb3d9fcd56.x: Devaluation, like import tariffs and export incentives, switches demand from foreign to domestic goods; the others reduce expenditure.
xa: Other switching tools: **import quotas**, **import substitution**, **tourist incentives**.
Devaluation makes **home goods cheaper relative to foreign goods**.
⚠ Raising government spending is **NOT** a correction tool (PYQ 2025).

ne9184aff7be.s: Which of the following is an expenditure-reducing measure for correcting a BoP deficit?
o: Tight monetary policy through higher interest rates
ne9184aff7be.x: Tight monetary policy reduces aggregate expenditure and imports; devaluation, import substitution and export promotion are expenditure-switching.
xa: Other reducing tool: **tight fiscal policy** — cut government spending, raise taxes.
Financing tools: **foreign loans**, **IMF assistance**, encouraging FDI.
**Devaluation** = classic expenditure-switching policy.

n5abe885a1e9.s: A country whose reserves cannot cover its Balance of Payments deficit may approach which institution as lender of last resort?
n5abe885a1e9.x: The IMF assists a country that cannot cover its external deficit from its reserves and other sources.
xa: IMF lending windows: **Stand-By Arrangement** + **Extended Fund Facility**.
India drew on the IMF in the **1991** crisis.
**SDRs** and **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF are part of India's reserves.

n4e2b5d5324a.s: The increase in import duty on gold, when used to reduce external pressure, is best classified as:
n4e2b5d5324a.x: A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports. It is therefore an expenditure-switching measure.
n4e2b5d5324a.tq: Trace how an import duty changes the relative attractiveness of foreign goods.
xs: A **gold import duty hike** is an **expenditure-switching** step — option **(1)**.
Import tariffs/duties switch demand away from imports; it is not a monetary or transfer item.
xa: **May 2026**: the PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the **Iran** conflict raised prices.
Oil (**>80%** imported) and gold are **structural** causes of the CAD.
Other switching tools: **devaluation**, **export incentives**.

n90706ebff23.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the components of India’s foreign exchange reserves?
n90706ebff23.x: India’s foreign exchange reserves include Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF. Fiscal deficit deposits are not a reserve component.
n90706ebff23.tq: Find the non-member of a standard reserve-components list.
xs: **Fiscal deficit deposits** are not a reserve component — option **(2)**.
Reserves = **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF.
xa: Reserves of **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
A positive **overall BoP** adds to reserves.
**Reserve changes** are recorded in the capital account.

n93123dc7a4c.s: Which additional recommendation was associated with the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan?
o: A permanently fixed exchange rate determined by the IMF
Replacement of the current account by the capital account
n93123dc7a4c.x: Along with identifying a sustainable CAD of about 1.6% of GDP, the committee recommended a market-determined exchange rate.
n93123dc7a4c.tq: Pair the committee with its specific policy recommendation rather than its numerical threshold alone.
xs: The **Rangarajan Committee** recommended a **market-determined exchange rate** — option **(1)**.
It put a sustainable CAD at about **1.6% of GDP**.
xa: **LERMS** (**1992-93 Budget**): **40%** official / **60%** market.
Unified rate from **1 March 1993**.
Full **current account convertibility** in **August 1994**.

nae3300b8baf.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes FERA from FEMA?
o: FERA was a restrictive criminal law, whereas FEMA is a liberal civil law concerned with management and regulation
FERA followed a liberal approach, whereas FEMA imposed strict control over outflow
FERA was a civil law, whereas FEMA was a criminal law
Both FERA and FEMA were identical in nature and approach
nae3300b8baf.x: FERA 1973 was restrictive and criminal in nature, focusing on control of foreign exchange outflow. FEMA 1999 is a civil law based on management and regulation with a more liberal approach.
nae3300b8baf.tq: Compare the legal character and policy approach of the two paired statutes.
xs: **FERA 1973** was a **restrictive criminal law** (control of outflow); **FEMA 1999** is a **liberal civil law** (management and regulation) — option **(1)**.
Options (2) and (3) reverse the two.
xa: FEMA replacement proposed in the **1997-98 Budget**.
⚠ FEMA enacted **1999** but in force **1 June 2000**.
**Capital account convertibility** covers **FDI**, portfolio investment, borrowing.

ne548cdc3f7c.s: India achieved full current account convertibility in August 1994 by:
o: Setting up the second Tarapore Committee
Accepting Article VIII of the IMF
ne548cdc3f7c.x: Full current account convertibility was achieved in August 1994 when India accepted the obligations under Article VIII of the IMF.
ne548cdc3f7c.tq: Match the convertibility milestone with the specific IMF provision rather than with a domestic statute.
xs: India reached **full current account convertibility in August 1994** by **accepting Article VIII of the IMF** — option **(3)**.
**FEMA** came later (**1999**).
xa: Path: **LERMS** (**1992-93**) → unified rate **1 March 1993** → Article VIII (**1994**).
**Current account convertibility** = free conversion for trade, income and transfers.
Rupee delinked from **sterling** in **September 1975**.

n5a145455b88.s: Under a flexible exchange-rate system, the exchange rate is determined by:
n5a145455b88.x: Under a flexible system demand and supply set the rate; under a fixed system the government fixes it and the RBI intervenes.
xa: **Managed float** (India's system) = market-set with central-bank intervention.
Fixed regimes peg to a currency, basket or **gold**.
⚠ Devaluation/revaluation = fixed regime; depreciation/appreciation = floating.

nindian-economy-47-6.s: Under a flexible exchange rate, a change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹65 is:
nindian-economy-47-6.x: More rupees per dollar under a floating rate is depreciation; devaluation and revaluation apply to fixed rates.
n: A change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹58 represents rupee appreciation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
A change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹65 represents rupee depreciation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
Flexible exchange rates can involve depreciation or appreciation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
Fixed exchange rates can involve devaluation or revaluation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
xa: Appreciation = fewer rupees per dollar; depreciation = more rupees per dollar.
Rupee crossed **96.2/$** on **18-19 May 2026**.
**Bretton Woods (1944)** fixed rates on the dollar.

o: The annual percentage change in the exchange rate
Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
The number of months of import cover
Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency
nb3e03d6cb3f.x: A direct quote states the amount of domestic currency required for one unit of foreign currency, such as ₹95 = $1.
nb3e03d6cb3f.tq: Identify the domestic-currency side of the quotation.
xs: A **direct quote** gives **units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency** (e.g. **₹95 = $1**) — option **(4)**.
Option (2), foreign units per one domestic unit, is the **indirect quote**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the PYQ's "false" statement **swapped** the direct and indirect quote definitions.
**Import cover** = months of imports that reserves can pay for.
**Exchange rate** = price of one currency in terms of another.

n40448df61de.s: Buying a currency in a market where it is cheaper and simultaneously selling it in another market where it is dearer is known as:
n40448df61de.x: Arbitrage is the simultaneous purchase of a currency in a cheaper market and its sale in a dearer market (PYQ key). Hedging is covering exchange-rate risk, e.g. through forward contracts; speculation is taking an open position on expected future movements; devaluation is an official lowering of a currency's value under a fixed regime.
n40448df61de.tq: Arbitrage = same time, two markets, price gap.
xs: **Arbitrage** = buying a currency **cheap in one market** and **selling it dearer in another at the same time** — option **(2)** (PYQ key).
**Hedging** is covering exchange-rate risk (e.g. via forwards); **devaluation** is an official lowering of value under a fixed regime.
xa: **Spot rate** settles **within two days**; **forward rate** is agreed now for a future date.
**Hot currency** = temporary name for a hard currency.
⚠ Arbitrage needs **simultaneous** buying and selling.

n4cd864a427a.s: A rise in the rupee's Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) indicates:
n4cd864a427a.x: A rise in NEER means rupee appreciation, making imports cheaper and exports less competitive.
xa: **REER** = NEER adjusted for relative inflation.
**High REER = overvalued** rupee.
REER is the better competitiveness indicator.

n7c384674c7a.s: A high REER is generally interpreted as indicating that the rupee is:
o: Convertible only on the capital account
Fixed permanently to the US dollar
n7c384674c7a.x: A high REER generally indicates an overvalued rupee. Since REER incorporates relative inflation, it is a better indicator of competitiveness than NEER alone.
n7c384674c7a.tq: Apply the index interpretation to the policy meaning of an overvalued currency.
xs: A **high REER** means an **overvalued** rupee, which is **less competitive** — option **(1)**.
A **low** REER means an **undervalued** rupee, so option (4) is the reverse.
xa: REER = **NEER adjusted for relative inflation**.
REER is the **better indicator of competitiveness**.
⚠ Deliberate **undervaluation** (as alleged of **China**) = currency manipulation.

n1294bc2ddd7.s: A managed float is best described as a system in which the exchange rate is:
o: Fixed permanently by a constitutional provision
Determined only by the price of gold
Determined by the market, with central-bank intervention when necessary
Set exclusively by commercial banks without government influence
n1294bc2ddd7.x: In a managed float, market forces determine the rate, while the central bank may intervene directly through forex transactions or indirectly through interest rates.
n1294bc2ddd7.tq: Separate market determination from the degree of official intervention.
xs: A **managed float** is **market-set with central-bank intervention** — option **(3)**; it is **India's system**.
Intervention can be **direct** (buy/sell forex) or **indirect** (interest rates).
xa: **Fixed/pegged**: value fixed to a currency, basket or gold; RBI buys/sells to hold it.
**Floating**: market-determined by demand and supply.
India's dual rates were unified into a market-determined rate on **1 March 1993**.

n2e0313aa7c0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about exchange-rate terminology?
o: Depreciation under a floating regime means more domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.
Depreciation and appreciation are officially ordered changes under a fixed regime.
Appreciation under a floating regime means less domestic currency per unit of foreign currency.
Official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.
n2e0313aa7c0.x: Depreciation and appreciation are market-driven changes under a flexible regime; official changes under a fixed regime are devaluation and revaluation.
xa: Example: **Rs 80 → Rs 96** per $ = depreciation.
⚠ Depreciation/appreciation = market (floating); devaluation/revaluation = government (fixed).
**Devaluation** = government raises the Rs per $ rate, rupee cheaper.

nf42e0e05ec5.s: Which of the following can limit the improvement in the trade balance after a currency depreciation?
nf42e0e05ec5.x: Depreciation can cause imported inflation, makes inelastic oil imports costlier and raises ECB repayment costs.
xa: A **falling** rupee (vs a weak one) makes buyers **delay orders**.
**ES 2025-26**: net impact of a weaker currency is **positive**.
Devaluation makes **exports cheaper** in foreign currency.

nd6c852c2f6c.s: Purchasing Power Parity theory primarily links the long-run exchange rate to the:
o: Volume of domestic currency notes alone
Number of foreign banks in a country
Size of the stock market alone
nd6c852c2f6c.x: In the long run, the inflation differential between countries is a key exchange-rate anchor under Purchasing Power Parity theory.
nd6c852c2f6c.tq: Associate the named theory with its central determinant.
xs: **PPP** links the long-run exchange rate to the **inflation differential between countries** — option **(1)**.
PPP is the **long-run** theory among the exchange-rate determinants.
xa: **REER** also adjusts NEER for the **inflation differential**.
Other long-run determinants: **savings-investment balance**, **current account**.
Short-run drivers include **FPI** outflows and crude prices.

n6662fa7470d.s: Which one of the following combinations represents the three elements of the Impossible Trinity?
o: Flexible exchange rate, capital controls and fiscal surplus
Fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and independent monetary policy
Fixed exchange rate, trade surplus and gold convertibility
Independent monetary policy, zero inflation and balanced budget
n6662fa7470d.x: The Impossible Trinity states that a country cannot simultaneously maintain a fixed exchange rate, free capital flows and an independent monetary policy.
n6662fa7470d.tq: Recall the exact three-way policy combination in the Mundell–Fleming trilemma.
xs: **Impossible Trinity** (**Mundell-Fleming trilemma**): a country cannot at once have a **fixed exchange rate**, **free capital flows** and **independent monetary policy** — option **(2)**.
At most two of the three can be held together.
xa: It explains RBI's dilemma with volatile **FPI** flows.
Large inflows → **appreciation** (**Dutch disease**).
Sudden outflows → crashes (**1991**, **2013 Taper Tantrum**).

n6eabdc5c4d2.s: Large capital inflows tend to make a country's currency:
n6eabdc5c4d2.x: Inflows raise demand for the domestic currency and push its value up, an effect linked with Dutch disease.
xa: **Sudden outflows** → crashes (**1991**, **2013 Taper Tantrum**).
**Impossible Trinity**: no fixed rate + free capital flows + independent monetary policy together.
A **NEER** rise = rupee appreciation → exports less competitive.

n91a01965ede.s: A relatively hawkish monetary-policy stance or a repo-rate hike can support the rupee mainly by:
o: Eliminating the current account deficit automatically
n91a01965ede.x: A hawkish stance or higher repo rate can attract carry-trade capital by improving the relative return on rupee assets, thereby supporting the currency.
n91a01965ede.tq: Connect the interest-rate signal with the capital-flow mechanism rather than with trade restrictions.
xs: A **hawkish stance / repo hike** attracts **carry-trade capital**, supporting the rupee — option **(4)**.
It does not automatically end the CAD or cut gold reserves.
xa: **Repo 5.25%**, unchanged for the **4th** meeting (**Aug 2026**).
Monetary policy **signalling** is a core RBI tool.
**Managed float**: indirect action via **interest rates**.

n6735719573e.s: Deliberate undervaluation of a currency, as alleged in the case of China, is criticised as:
n6735719573e.x: Deliberate undervaluation of a currency to gain trade advantages is criticised as currency manipulation.
n6735719573e.tq: Match the policy criticism with the precise international-exchange term.
xs: **Deliberate undervaluation** (as alleged of **China**) is criticised as **currency manipulation** — option **(2)**.
An undervalued currency shows up as a **low REER**.
xa: **High REER** = overvalued rupee.
**China** holds the largest reserves — **$3.85 tn**.
⚠ RBI says it curbs **volatility**, not targets a level.

nindian-economy-47-1.s: What does the term 'exchange rate' refer to?
o: The price/value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency
The official reduction in currency value under a fixed exchange-rate system
The weighted average of real exchange rates against trading partners
The market-driven rise in the value of a currency
nindian-economy-47-1.x: The exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another. The other options describe devaluation, REER and appreciation.
nindian-economy-47-1.tq: Recall the definition of the exchange rate.
n: An exchange rate is the price or value of one currency expressed in terms of another currency. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
Devaluation is an official reduction in currency value under a fixed exchange-rate system. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) is a weighted average of bilateral nominal exchange rates. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The NEER is calculated against a basket of trading-partner currencies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is the NEER adjusted for relative price or inflation differentials. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
Appreciation is a market-driven rise in currency value. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
xs: The **exchange rate** is the **price or value of one currency expressed in terms of another** — so option **(1)** is correct.
An **official reduction** under a fixed system is **devaluation**; a weighted average against partners is **NEER/REER**; a **market-driven rise** is **appreciation**.
xa: **Direct quote** = domestic currency per unit of foreign currency; **indirect quote** = foreign per unit of domestic.
**Flexible / floating** rate: the **market determines** the currency value.
India follows a **managed float** since **1 March 1993**.

nindian-economy-47-5.s: The Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is the NEER adjusted for:
nindian-economy-47-5.x: REER is NEER adjusted for relative price or inflation differentials between domestic and foreign economies.
n: The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) is a weighted average of bilateral nominal exchange rates. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The NEER is calculated against a basket of trading-partner currencies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) is the NEER adjusted for relative price or inflation differentials. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
REER adjustment considers differences between domestic and foreign economies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
The World Bank does not determine the currency price. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
Demand and supply influence the exchange rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
xa: NEER base **2015-16 = 100**; RBI has **40-currency** and **6-currency** indices.
**High REER** = overvalued rupee.
**Inflation** and a **fiscal deficit** can also affect the exchange value.

nindian-economy-47-7.s: A rise in the Real Effective Exchange Rate (REER) tends to:
nindian-economy-47-7.x: A rising REER means real appreciation, which tends to reduce export competitiveness.
n: Devaluation makes imports relatively expensive. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
An increase in NEER does not indicate appreciation in the cited convention. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
An increase in REER does not automatically mean better competitiveness. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 69-71]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say an increase in NEER does not indicate appreciation in their convention.
**REER = NEER x (domestic prices / foreign prices)**.
**High REER** = overvalued rupee; low = undervalued.

n6a20d747661.s: An importer enters into a forward contract primarily for which purpose?
o: To increase the country's import cover automatically
To cover exchange-rate risk by fixing a rate for a future transaction
To convert a floating exchange-rate regime into a fixed regime
To obtain an official revaluation from the monetary authority
n6a20d747661.x: Hedging involves covering exchange-rate risk, and a forward contract can fix the exchange rate today for a transaction to be settled in the future.
n6a20d747661.tq: Apply the risk-management purpose of a forward contract to a trade transaction.
xs: An importer uses a forward contract for **hedging** — **covering exchange-rate risk** by fixing a rate for a future transaction — option **(2)**.
A forward rate is **agreed now for delivery at a future date**.
xa: **Spot rate** = immediate delivery, settled **within two days**.
RBI bore the full **hedging cost** on fresh **FCNR(B)** deposits till **30 Sep 2026**.
**Arbitrage** differs: simultaneous buy-cheap/sell-dear across markets.

n86455fa1884.s: The Bretton Woods system established in 1944 was primarily associated with:
o: Floating rates based entirely on private speculation
A universal currency managed by the WTO
Fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar
Independent floating of all national currencies
n86455fa1884.x: The Bretton Woods system of 1944 established fixed exchange rates centred on the dollar and was associated with the IMF and World Bank.
n86455fa1884.tq: Link the historical agreement with its defining exchange-rate principle.
xs: **Bretton Woods (1944)** set up **fixed rates on the dollar** — option **(3)**.
It also created the **IMF** and **World Bank**.
xa: India followed the **par value system** under the IMF in **1947-1971**.
**1971**: **Smithsonian Agreement** (**+/-2.5%** band).
**Sept 1975**: rupee delinked from the **pound sterling**, pegged to a basket.

nb3772d370ea.s: The Smithsonian Agreement was signed in:
nb3772d370ea.x: The Smithsonian Agreement was in 1971, after Bretton Woods (1944) and before India's 1991 devaluation and 1993 unification.
xa: Smithsonian band: **+/-2.5%**.
**LERMS** (Budget **1992-93**) preceded unification: **40%** official, **60%** market.
**August 1994**: current account convertibility (IMF **Article VIII**).

n36076634283.s: In September 1975, the Indian rupee was:
o: Made fully floating without any intervention
Pegged to gold under the Smithsonian Agreement
Delinked from pound sterling and pegged to a basket of currencies
Linked exclusively to the US dollar
n36076634283.x: In September 1975, the rupee was delinked from pound sterling and pegged to a basket of currencies.
n36076634283.tq: Test the exact sequence of delinking from one anchor and adopting another.
xs: In **September 1975** the rupee was **delinked from the pound sterling** and **pegged to a basket of currencies** — option **(3)**.
It was not floated or tied only to the dollar.
xa: **1947-1971**: par value system under the IMF.
**1971**: **Smithsonian Agreement**.
**1 March 1993**: market-determined (managed float) rate.

nf81b24d417d.s: India accepted IMF Article VIII and moved to current account convertibility in:
nf81b24d417d.x: India accepted Article VIII in August 1994, after the dual rates were unified on 1 March 1993.
xa: LERMS came with **Budget 1992-93**.
India has full current account but only **partial capital account** convertibility.
**Tarapore Committees** gave the roadmap to full capital account convertibility.

n8e59c4ebde8.s: The rupee was devalued from ₹4.76 to ₹7.50 per US dollar in:
n8e59c4ebde8.x: This devaluation was in June 1966; the others were September 1949 (with sterling) and July 1991 (two steps).
xa: 1949 devaluation went **alongside the pound sterling**.
1966 was **57.5%**, amid wars, drought and **36%** inflation.
⚠ **1991** = the **last formal devaluation**.
