⚠ **ES 2025-26**: **services** took **80.2%** of FDI in **FY23-FY25** — far above manufacturing.

n529d9223714.s: According to the Economic Survey 2025-26, services accounted for what share of FDI during FY 2023-FY 2025?
n529d9223714.x: Services accounted for 80.2% of FDI during FY 2023-FY 2025. Information and communication alone accounted for 25.8%.
n529d9223714.tq: Distinguish the aggregate services share from the narrower information-and-communication share.
xs: Per **ES 2025-26**, **services** took **80.2%** of FDI in **FY23-FY25** — option **(4)**.
**25.8%** is the share of **information and communication** alone.
xa: Global FDI fell **11%** in **2024**; India stayed the largest FDI recipient in **South Asia**.
**WIR 2026**: global FDI rose **6%** to **$1.6 trillion** in **2025**; **US** the largest recipient and source.
⚠ Manufacturing's share of effective inflows fell to **10.6%** (**2026**).

n0aa1301ad33.s: Under the General Route, the overall FPI limit in outstanding Central Government securities is:
n0aa1301ad33.x: The General Route limit is 6% of Central and 2% of State Government securities.
xa: **Security-wise and short-term limits** have been removed.
**VRR** (Voluntary Retention Route) and **FAR** (Fully Accessible Route) steadied debt flows.
The **JP Morgan EM bond index** inclusion (**10%** target weight) draws passive bond inflows.

n11703da8280.s: FPI flows into India are significantly influenced by:
o: US Federal Reserve interest rates and global risk appetite
n11703da8280.x: US interest rates and global risk sentiment strongly drive FPI flows; a flight to safety can cause outflows.
xa: FY26 FPI outflows: about **Rs 2.2 lakh crore**.
Outflows were a key cause of **rupee weakness** — past **96/$** in **May 2026**.
FPI is "**hot money**" — short-term and liquid.

na617e27e5a0.s: India opted out of the RCEP in 2019 mainly because of concerns over:
o: The exclusion of ASEAN countries from the bloc
China's market dominance and the widening trade deficit with China
A requirement to withdraw from the WTO
A ban on Indian exports to Australia
na617e27e5a0.x: India withdrew over China's market dominance, its rising trade deficit with China and risks to farm, dairy and small industries.
xa: The deficit with China rose from **$53.5 bn** (**2018-19**) to **$99.2 bn** (**2024-25**).
**Press Note 3** (**April 2020**) later required approval for FDI from land-border countries incl. **China**.
The **UK CETA** came into force on **15 Jul 2026**.

ncf90100d132.s: The headquarters of IRDAI is in:
ncf90100d132.x: IRDAI is headquartered in Hyderabad; Budget 2025-26 raised insurance FDI to 100%, and insurance is in the Union List.
xa: Enabled by amending the **FEMA (Non-Debt Instruments) Rules, 2019**.
⚠ CDI dates it to Budget **2026-27**, but the PYQ confirms **2025-26**.

n3ca6d86ae6f.s: Which one of the following sets consists entirely of instruments or markets associated with the organised financial system?
o: Artisans, farmers, small traders and nidhis
Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit
Indigenous bankers, chit funds, nidhis and moneylenders
Unregulated loan companies, repo, nidhis and moneylenders
n3ca6d86ae6f.x: Call money, Treasury bills, commercial bills and certificates of deposit are components of the organised financial system. The other sets include unorganised institutions or users.
n3ca6d86ae6f.tq: Classify each item before selecting the all-organised set.
xs: **Call money, T-bills, commercial bills and CDs** are all instruments of the **organised** (RBI-regulated) money market — option **(2)**.
**Indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated loan companies are **unorganised**; farmers, artisans and small traders are users, not instruments.
xa: Other organised instruments: **CPs**, **repo**, **MMMFs**.
Organised institutions: commercial banks, cooperative banks, foreign banks, **DFHI**, provident funds, **STCI**, mutual funds.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key: **finance companies** are **not** part of the organised money market.

n2ee39ddf035.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of indigenous bankers?
o: Chit funds, loan companies, moneylenders and RRBs
n2ee39ddf035.x: Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars are identified as indigenous bankers who accept deposits and deal in hundis.
n2ee39ddf035.tq: Identify the complete membership of a traditional financial-intermediary group.
xs: **Shroffs, Seths, Multanis and Chettiars** are indigenous bankers — option **(3)**.
**RRBs**, **DCCBs**, **StCBs**, **NABARD**, banks and **NBFCs** are all organised/regulated institutions.
xa: **Mahajans** are also indigenous bankers.
Indigenous bankers deal in **hundis** and combine banking with trade/commission business.
⚠ "Lends only in kind" does **not** describe an indigenous banker.

na5e53bfe826.s: Professional and agricultural moneylenders in India are governed by:
o: The Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934
na5e53bfe826.x: Moneylenders fall under state money-lending laws; the Chit Funds Act, 1982 relates to chit funds.
xa: Unregulated non-bank intermediaries: **indigenous bankers**, **moneylenders**, **loan companies**, **chit funds**.
**Nidhis** are also part of the unorganised market.

o: only illegal lending by unlicensed moneylenders
credit intermediation outside full bank regulation, including activity by NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds
the issue of currency by the central bank
n94b90e769c2.x: Shadow banking is bank-like credit intermediation outside full banking regulation; NBFCs and money-market or liquid funds are examples.
n94b90e769c2.tq: Apply the definition to distinguish broad shadow banking from illegal lending alone.
xs: **Shadow banking** is **bank-like credit intermediation** (**NBFCs**, **money-market/liquid funds**) **outside full bank regulation** — option **(2)**.
It is not just illegal moneylending, nor cooperative deposit-taking.
xa: **Liquid debt mutual funds** are NBFCs' main **short-term funding** source.
Criticism: **regulatory arbitrage** (shadow banking).
RBI's response to NBFC stress: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.
**IL&FS (Sep 2018)** defaults triggered a liquidity crisis.

n451fad1c41b.s: Which of the following belongs to the unorganised money market?
o: Certificates of Deposit and Commercial Paper
n451fad1c41b.x: Indigenous bankers and moneylenders form part of the unorganised money market. T-Bills, commercial bills, CDs, CPs and repos belong to the organised segment.
n451fad1c41b.tq: Classify the lender or instrument by the organised–unorganised divide.
xs: **Indigenous bankers and moneylenders** belong to the **unorganised** money market — option **(3)**.
**CDs, CPs, repos, call money, T-bills, commercial bills** are **organised** market instruments.
xa: Unorganised: also **chit funds**, **nidhis** and unregulated finance/loan companies.
The unorganised market serves **farmers, artisans, small traders**.
⚠ APPSC-G2 **2017** key placed **finance companies** outside the organised market.

nf053cafb3df.s: Urban Cooperative Banks traditionally operated under which form of dual control?
o: State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and RBI
nf053cafb3df.x: UCBs traditionally faced dual control by the State Registrar of Cooperative Societies and the RBI.
nf053cafb3df.tq: Identify the two authorities sharing cooperative and banking oversight.
xs: **UCBs** were under **dual control** of the **State RCS** and **RBI** — option **(3)**.
NABARD, IRDAI, SEBI have no such role over UCBs.
xa: **BR (Amendment) Act 2020** (after the **PMC Bank** crisis) put UCBs under RBI supervision like commercial banks.
**NUCFDC** is the UCB umbrella body.

n6cc92ceec15.s: Which institution was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks?
n6cc92ceec15.x: NUCFDC was set up as an umbrella body for Urban Cooperative Banks.
n6cc92ceec15.tq: Match the institutional acronym with its sector rather than with rural cooperative banking.
xs: **NUCFDC** is the **umbrella body** for **UCBs** — option **(1)**.
**NHB** is a housing DFI; **APCOB** is AP's apex cooperative bank.
xa: **Sahakar Sarathi** (NABARD) is a shared-services entity for **rural** cooperative banks.
RBI is resuming UCB licensing **on tap**.

n7751b5a488f.s: Which of the following institutions performs a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies?
n7751b5a488f.x: NHB plays a quasi-regulatory role in relation to Housing Finance Companies; NABARD and SIDBI have comparable roles in other sectors.
n7751b5a488f.tq: Match the quasi-regulator with the financial institution category it relates to.
xs: **NHB** is the **quasi-regulator** for **HFCs** — option **(1)**.
**NABARD** plays this role for **RRBs/cooperatives** and **SIDBI** for **SFCs**; **SEBI** is a full regulator.
xa: HFC **regulation** moved from NHB to the **RBI** (**Finance Act 2019**); NHB keeps **supervision and refinance**.
**90 HFCs** were registered (**June 2025**).
NHB: statutory, **1988** (**NHB Act 1987**).

n92094aaf21a.s: Which one of the following institutions was established on a World Bank initiative and later became a universal bank?
o: Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India
n92094aaf21a.x: ICICI was established in 1955 on a World Bank initiative and subsequently became a universal bank.
n92094aaf21a.tq: Identify the institution through its founding association and later transformation.
xs: **ICICI** (**1955**) was set up on a **World Bank initiative** and later became a **universal bank** — option **(4)**.
**IFCI** (**1948**) was the first DFI; **IDBI** (**1964**) the apex industrial DFI; **EXIM Bank** (**1982**) finances foreign trade.
xa: ICICI provided **industrial credit**.
Older AIFI class: **IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, SIDBI, IIBI**.
⚠ **IDBI** later became a **commercial bank**, reclassified **private** after **LIC** control (**2019**).

ne71beaf6463.s: After LIC acquired majority control in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a:
ne71beaf6463.x: Following LIC's majority acquisition in 2019, IDBI Bank was reclassified as a private sector bank.
xa: IDBI: **1964** under RBI; autonomous **1976**; reverse-merged **2004-05**.
Govt + LIC are offloading a combined **60.72%** stake (bidding under way).
**LIC** was set up in **1956**.

nd2dbac849cc.s: For regulatory purposes, which of the following are classified by the Reserve Bank of India as refinance institutions?
nd2dbac849cc.x: RBI classifies NABARD, NHB and SIDBI as refinance institutions. EXIM Bank is classified as a term-lending institution.
nd2dbac849cc.tq: Separate refinance institutions from term-lending institutions.
xs: RBI classes **NABARD, NHB and SIDBI** as **refinance institutions** — option **(4)**.
**EXIM Bank** is a **term-lending institution**; IFCI, IDBI, LIC and NaBFID are not refinance institutions.
xa: APPSC GS **2024** picked **NHB** against **IFCI, TFCI and EXIM**.
The **5** RBI-regulated AIFIs: **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI, NaBFID**.
NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs**; NHB refinances **HFCs and banks**.

n213f748dd42.s: Which of the following institutions are regulated and supervised by the Reserve Bank of India as All-India Financial Institutions?
o: IFCI, ICICI, IDBI, IIBI and LIC
EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID
NABARD, LIC, GIC, UTI and SIDCs
NHB, SIDBI, IFCI, TFCI and SFCs
n213f748dd42.x: The five RBI-regulated and supervised AIFIs are EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI and NaBFID.
n213f748dd42.tq: Start with the sure institutional names and eliminate older classifications.
xs: The **5** RBI-regulated and supervised **AIFIs** are **EXIM Bank, NABARD, NHB, SIDBI** and (since **2022**) **NaBFID** — option **(2)**.
**LIC, GIC, UTI** are investment institutions; **SFCs, SIDCs** are state-level FIs; **IFCI** is now an NBFC.
xa: Older notes list only the first **four**.
⚠ APPSC GS **2024** ("out of **17** AIFIs") keyed **9** — the notes do not explain that count.
**NaBFID** (**2021**) is the newest DFI.

ne505a3ba47b.s: Which development finance institution was the first DFI in India and was established for long-term industrial finance?
ne505a3ba47b.x: IFCI, established in 1948, was the first development finance institution and provided long-term industrial finance.
ne505a3ba47b.tq: Link the institutional first and its distinctive purpose.
xs: **IFCI** (**July 1948**, special Act) was **India's first DFI**, for long-term industrial credit — option **(1)**.
**IDBI** came in **1964**, **EXIM Bank** in **1982**, **SIDBI** in **1990**.
xa: Exam angle: IFCI's setting up **began the era of development financing** (APPSC GS **2018**).
It gave long-term project loans (**25 years+**).
Today IFCI is a **public sector NBFC-ND-SI** that manages **PLI** projects.
FIRST/LAST: IFCI first (**1948**); **NaBFID** newest (**2021**).

nc9ec4d54c89.s: Which of the following institutions was set up mainly to finance MSMEs?
nc9ec4d54c89.x: SIDBI focuses on MSME finance. IDBI was the apex industrial development bank, Exim Bank finances export-import activity and ICICI gave private-sector industrial credit.
xa: Years: **ICICI 1955**, **IDBI 1964**, **EXIM Bank January 1982**, **SIDBI 1990**.
ICICI was set up on a **World Bank** initiative.
SIDBI began as an **IDBI subsidiary**.

n93da1581db0.s: In which year was the Unit Trust of India (UTI) established?
n93da1581db0.x: UTI was set up in 1964. LIC dates to 1956, GIC to 1972 and CRISIL to 1987.
xa: **ICRA 1991**; **CARE Ratings 1993**.
LIC, UTI, GIC = public sector **investment institutions**.

n7ee0b4dc47f.s: LIC, UTI and GIC were collectively regarded as the:
n7ee0b4dc47f.x: LIC, UTI and GIC were the public-sector investment institutions.
n7ee0b4dc47f.tq: Identify the common classification shared by three institutions.
xs: **LIC, UTI and GIC** were the **public sector investment institutions** — option **(2)**.
Refinance institutions are **NABARD, NHB, SIDBI**; regulators include **SEBI, IRDAI**; credit-rating bodies are **CRISIL, ICRA, CARE**.
xa: Older classes: **specialised FIs** (**RCTC**, **TFCI**), **state-level FIs** (**SFCs**, **SIDCs**).

ndb1d59e3e07.s: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was subsequently merged into:
ndb1d59e3e07.x: The NBFC Ombudsman Scheme, 2018 was merged into the RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021.
ndb1d59e3e07.tq: Arrange the institutional schemes by identifying the later integrated framework.
xs: The **NBFC Ombudsman Scheme 2018** merged into the **RBI Integrated Ombudsman Scheme 2021** — option **(4)**.
**RB-IOS** is an RBI scheme, not a SEBI or other scheme.
xa: RB-IOS now also covers **state and central cooperative banks**.
**RBI** regulates **NBFCs** and **HFCs**.

n7029fd9606e.s: In September 2018, the default of which entity set off a liquidity crisis in India?
o: National Bank for Financing Infrastructure and Development
n7029fd9606e.x: Defaults by Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services Limited (IL&FS), an infrastructure NBFC, set off a liquidity crisis in September 2018.
n7029fd9606e.tq: Use the date-event association to distinguish the two major NBFC stress episodes.
xs: **IL&FS** (**Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services**) defaults in **Sep 2018** set off a **liquidity crisis** — option **(3)**.
**DHFL** was a **2019** episode; **Tata Sons** and **NaBFID** had no such default.
xa: IL&FS was an **infrastructure NBFC**.
Govt **superseded the board** (**NCLT** order); the new board handled asset sales.
Response: the **SBR framework** + closer supervision.

na81c5c76d18.s: The Andhra Pradesh Mutually Aided Cooperative Societies (MACS) Act was enacted in:
na81c5c76d18.x: The AP MACS Act dates from 1995; the AP Cooperative Societies Act dates from 1964.
xa: The **AP Cooperative Tribunal** (**Sec. 75**, 1964 Act) is **appellate** under the 1964 Act.
It has **original jurisdiction** under the **MACS Act**.
Cooperative societies are registered under **State Cooperative Societies Acts** + the **BR Act 1949**.

nindian-economy-2-9.s: In which year was NABARD established?
nindian-economy-2-9.x: NABARD was set up in 1982, on the Shivaraman Committee's advice. SIDBI followed in 1990.
nindian-economy-2-9.tq: Arrange the institutions in time order.
n: NABARD was established in 1982. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
xs: **NABARD** was established in **1982** (**12 July 1982**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
It was set up under the **NABARD Act 1981** on the **B. Sivaraman Committee / CRAFICARD** recommendation.
**1964** = IDBI and UTI; **1990** = SIDBI.
xa: NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs** and runs **RIDF**.
It launched the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** as a pilot in **1992**.
HQ: **Mumbai**.

nda1b851835e.s: The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) Act was enacted in:
nda1b851835e.x: The IFSCA Act dates to 2019. The PFRDA Act is of 2013, the IRDA Act of 1999, and SEBI became statutory in 1992.
xa: **PFRDA** regulates pension/**NPS**.
**HFC** regulation moved from **NHB** to **RBI** in **2019**.
**Chit fund companies** are regulated by the **State Government**.

nd5ca7c8299e.s: The International Financial Services Centres Authority (IFSCA) began functioning in April 2020 primarily as the regulator of:
o: all insurance companies and pension funds
International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City
nd5ca7c8299e.x: IFSCA is the unified regulator for International Financial Services Centres, including GIFT City, and began functioning in April 2020.
nd5ca7c8299e.tq: Distinguish the unified IFSC regulator from sector-specific regulators.
xs: **IFSCA** (**April 2020**) is the **unified regulator of IFSCs**, including **GIFT City** — option **(4)**.
FPIs come under **SEBI**, insurance under **IRDAI**, pensions under **PFRDA**; cooperative banks under **RBI/NABARD**.
xa: It was set up under the **IFSCA Act 2019**.
**PFRDA** is statutory under the **PFRDA Act, 2013**.
First meeting of RBI's **Payments Regulatory Board**: **Jan 2026**.

n4725625ec7f.s: Which of the following institutions was set up with the help of the Reserve Bank of India?
n4725625ec7f.x: The RBI helped set up IDBI, SIDBI, NABARD, NHB, Exim Bank and NEDB; SEBI is not among them.
xa: Their ownership has since **moved to the Government**.
**NHB** was wholly RBI-owned until **2019**.
SEBI regulates securities markets and became **statutory** in **1992**.

ne476f862410.s: The National Housing Bank, wholly owned by the RBI until then, was taken over by the Central Government in:
ne476f862410.x: NHB was set up in 1988 and stayed wholly RBI-owned until the Central Government took over its ownership in 2019.
xa: NHB Act **1987**; apex housing finance body; **C. Rangarajan** high-level group.
HFC **regulation** also moved to **RBI** in **2019**.
NHB launched **RESIDEX** in **2007**.

n0b7f6600d66.s: After the IL&FS defaults, the Government superseded the company's board through an order of the:
o: Securities and Exchange Board of India
n0b7f6600d66.x: Following the IL&FS defaults, the Government superseded its board through an NCLT order.
xa: IL&FS defaults (**Sep 2018**) caused a liquidity crisis.
The new board handled **asset sales**.
⚠ **DHFL (2019)** was the **first financial services company resolved under IBC**.

n715133c922f.s: Which one of the following is true of NBFCs in India?
o: They cannot issue cheques drawn on themselves
They have access to the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility
n715133c922f.x: An NBFC cannot issue cheques drawn on itself. NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits, their deposits have no insurance cover, and they have no LAF access.
xa: NBFCs are **not part of the payment and settlement system** (LENSD, **Aug 2026**).
NBFCs keep **no CRR**; deposit-taking NBFCs keep **liquid assets** instead.
NBFCs are registered under the **Companies Act**.

n4cb12082059.s: Which of the following about reserve requirements is NOT correct?
n4cb12082059.x: NBFCs do not maintain CRR; banks maintain CRR and SLR, while deposit-taking NBFCs maintain liquid assets instead.
xa: NBFCs have **no RBI LAF (repo)** access.
NBFCs are **not covered** by deposit insurance (**DICGC**).
All deposit-taking NBFCs fall in the SBR **Middle Layer**.

n33727d08e02.s: Under the principal business test for NBFCs, financial assets must exceed ____ of total assets (with financial income above the same share of gross income).
n33727d08e02.x: An NBFC meets the test when financial assets exceed 50% of total assets and financial income exceeds 50% of gross income.
xa: NBFCs are registered under the **Companies Act**.
**NBFC-MFI**: non-deposit-taking; at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans.
Microfinance loan (RBI, **March 2022**): household income up to **₹3 lakh**/yr; repayment **≤50%** of income.

n1de6aae180b.s: The minimum net owned fund required for a housing finance company (HFC) is:
n1de6aae180b.x: HFCs need a minimum NOF of ₹20 crore, against ₹10 crore for NBFC-MFIs and NBFC-ICCs.
xa: NBFC-ICC NOF was raised from **₹2 crore** under **SBR**, with a glide path to **Mar 2027**.
**NBFC-MFI**: at least **75%** of assets in microfinance loans.
HFC regulation moved from **NHB** to **RBI** in **2019**.

n157a9971976.s: Under the Scale-Based Regulation framework, which is the correct order of the four NBFC layers from lower to higher regulatory intensity?
n157a9971976.x: The four layers are Base Layer, Middle Layer, Upper Layer and Top Layer, with regulation increasing across the framework.
n157a9971976.tq: Arrange the regulatory layers in their stated progression from base to top.
xs: SBR layers in rising regulation: **Base (BL) → Middle (ML) → Upper (UL) → Top (TL)** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) gives the reverse order; options (1) and (2) mix up Middle and Upper.
xa: **Base**: small non-deposit NBFCs; **Middle**: all deposit-taking NBFCs, HFCs, IFCs, CICs.
**Upper**: identified by RBI; bank-like norms for at least **5 years**; **listing within 3 years**.
**Top**: kept empty — only for a sharp rise in **systemic risk**.

n562f20de925.s: The Top Layer under Scale-Based Regulation is intended to be used when:
o: there is a sharp rise in systemic risk
n562f20de925.x: The Top Layer is kept empty in normal circumstances and is intended for a sharp rise in systemic risk.
n562f20de925.tq: Apply the exceptional-use condition to identify when the otherwise empty layer becomes relevant.
xs: The **Top Layer** is kept **empty** — used only for a **sharp rise in systemic risk** — option **(1)**.
It has nothing to do with HFC supervision, the **50-50 test** or deposits.
xa: Layers: **Base → Middle → Upper → Top**.
**Upper Layer**: bank-like norms for at least **5 years**; listing within **3 years**.
NBFC-UL list **2026-27**: **17 companies**, incl. **Tata Sons**.

nedf5b2f5564.s: Under Scale-Based Regulation, an NBFC identified by the RBI for the Upper Layer must get listed within:
nedf5b2f5564.x: Upper Layer NBFCs are identified by the RBI, follow bank-like norms for at least five years and must list within three years.
xa: NBFC-UL list **2026-27**: **17 companies** (earlier **15** as of **Apr 2026**), incl. **Tata Sons**.
Proposed: a single **₹1 lakh crore** asset test for UL instead of the **parametric scoring model**.
RBI rejected **Tata Sons**' bid to surrender its licence and asked it to **list**.

n249a1f0699e.s: Which one of the following companies was specifically included in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27?
n249a1f0699e.x: Tata Sons was included among the 17 companies named in the NBFC-UL list for 2026–27.
n249a1f0699e.tq: Identify the company from the list while separating it from regulators and development institutions.
xs: **Tata Sons** is on the **NBFC-UL list 2026-27** (**17 companies**) — option **(1)**.
**NHB** and **NABARD** are AIFIs; **SEBI** is a regulator.
xa: The list grew from **15** (**Apr 2026**) to **17**.
RBI **rejected** Tata Sons' bid to surrender its NBFC licence and asked it to **list**.
UL entities must list **within 3 years**.

n4b3079455f9.s: Which of the following was NOT a major feature of the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis of 2010?
o: A rapid expansion of the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh
n4b3079455f9.x: The crisis involved multiple lending, over-indebtedness, coercive recovery and borrower suicides; the MFI loan book in Andhra Pradesh collapsed rather than rapidly expanding.
n4b3079455f9.tq: Identify the reversed trend among consequences of a financial crisis.
xs: A **rapid expansion** of AP's MFI loan book was **not** a feature — the loan book **collapsed** — option **(2)**.
The crisis did feature **multiple lending**, **over-indebtedness**, **coercive recovery** and **borrower suicides**.
xa: It led to the **AP MFI Ordinance (Oct 2010)**, later an **Act (2011)**.
RBI set up the **Malegam Committee** (**2010-11**).
This chain → today's **NBFC-MFI** regulation.

n7b844c3753c.s: The term ‘regulatory arbitrage’ in the context of shadow banking refers to:
o: The transfer of cooperative banks to the stock market
The allocation of all public debt to development finance institutions
The compulsory conversion of every NBFC into a bank
Using differences in regulatory treatment to conduct financial activities outside the stricter banking framework
n7b844c3753c.x: Regulatory arbitrage describes the use of differences in regulatory treatment to conduct activities through less strictly regulated financial entities, a criticism associated with shadow banking.
n7b844c3753c.tq: Translate the paired concept ‘shadow banking–regulatory arbitrage’ into its practical implication.
xs: **Regulatory arbitrage** = using differences in regulation to run bank-like activity **outside the stricter banking framework** — option **(4)**.
It is the main criticism of **shadow banking** (NBFCs, money-market/liquid funds).
xa: Shadow banking: **bank-like credit intermediation** outside full bank regulation.
NBFCs keep **no CRR**, have **no DICGC** cover and **no LAF** access.
RBI response: **SBR** — bank-like norms for **Upper Layer** NBFCs.

nedea9e435aa.s: In the cooperative credit structure, short-term credit at the village level is provided by the:
o: Primary Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Bank
nedea9e435aa.x: Village-level short-term credit comes from PACS; DCCBs work at the district level, StCBs at the state level, and PCARDBs give long-term credit at the village level.
xa: Long-term structure at state level: **State Cooperative Agriculture and Rural Development Bank**.
AP: apex **APCOB** (**18** branches), **13 DCCBs** (**436** branches), **2,024 PACS**.
⚠ **2,037** PACS in AP are computerised under the **CSS**.

n1d75f7dcb1b.s: State Cooperative Banks and DCCBs are licensed by the RBI and inspected by:
o: The State Registrar of Cooperative Societies
n1d75f7dcb1b.x: StCBs and DCCBs are licensed by the RBI and inspected by NABARD, while PACS fall under State Registrars.
xa: **NABARD** is the quasi-regulator for **RRBs/cooperatives**.
**RB-IOS** covers **state and central cooperative banks**.
RBI in-principle nod to NABARD's **Sahakar Sarathi** for rural cooperative banks.

n4f1fd24d786.s: The RBI granted a Certificate of Registration to the RMBS Development Company Limited (RDCL) in:
n4f1fd24d786.x: RDCL received its RBI Certificate of Registration in January 2025; NHB contributed equity and it aims to develop the residential mortgage-backed securities market.
xa: RMBS **PTCs** are listed on **NSE**.
APPSC GS **2024** PYQ: **both** statements on RDCL **correct**.
NHB launched **RESIDEX (2007)**.

ncb4454a205b.s: The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020 relating to UCBs was enacted after which event mentioned in the framework?
ncb4454a205b.x: The amendment strengthening RBI supervision over UCBs followed the PMC Bank crisis.
ncb4454a205b.tq: Link the legislative response with the specific banking event rather than a general financial crisis.
xs: The **BR (Amendment) Act 2020** came after the **PMC Bank crisis** — option **(1)**.
**IL&FS** was an NBFC episode (**2018**) and led to the **SBR** framework instead.
xa: It covers **UCBs and multi-state cooperative banks**.
RBI now supervises their **management, capital, audit and resolution**.
**NUCFDC** = UCB umbrella body.

n059b12750e7.s: What change in the licensing policy for Urban Cooperative Banks was indicated by the RBI?
o: Licensing restricted to multi-state cooperative banks only
Resumption of licensing on tap after a pause of more than two decades
Licensing transferred entirely to State Registrars
Permanent prohibition on new UCB licences
n059b12750e7.x: The RBI indicated that it would resume licensing UCBs on tap after a pause of more than two decades.
n059b12750e7.tq: Use the policy-action and time-duration combination to identify the correct statement.
xs: RBI is **resuming licensing UCBs "on tap"** after **more than two decades** (**20+** years) — option **(2)**.
Licensing is not banned or handed to State Registrars.
xa: There are **1,457 UCBs** (**TH, 6 Aug 2026**).
UCB licensing resumed in **Aug 2026**.
UCBs earlier faced **dual control** (State RCS + RBI).

n0f1b114ac16.s: The group-lending idea associated with the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme is derived from the model of:
o: Grameen Bank of Bangladesh founded by Muhammad Yunus
n0f1b114ac16.x: The group-lending idea is associated with Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank in Bangladesh.
n0f1b114ac16.tq: Identify the source institution and associated personality.
xs: The group-lending idea came from **Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank** (**Bangladesh**) — option **(2)**.
**Malegam**, **RIDF** and the **AP MFI Ordinance** came later and deal with regulation/funding, not the idea.
xa: **SHG-Bank Linkage**: NABARD pilot, **1992**.
**JLGs** (NABARD, **2006**): **4-10** members giving a mutual loan guarantee.
Microfinance borrowers: **95% women**, **80% rural**.

n2a4c657d17b.s: Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) in India were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by which law?
n2a4c657d17b.x: RRBs were set up in 1975-76 and are governed by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976. The BR Act 1949 is the general banking law, the NABARD Act 1981 created NABARD (which supervises RRBs), and the 1912 Act concerns cooperatives.
xs: **Regional Rural Banks** (set up **1975-76**) are governed by the **RRB Act 1976** — option **(3)**.
The **NABARD Act 1981** created **NABARD**, which **supervises** RRBs — it is not the RRBs' own law.
xa: Now **28 RRBs**, **22,000+** branches in **700** districts.
NABARD refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs**.
AP's four RRBs merged into **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank**.

nd377b7b8eaa.s: The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme, described as the world's largest microfinance movement, was launched as a pilot by NABARD in:
nd377b7b8eaa.x: NABARD launched the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme as a pilot in 1992. 1982 is NABARD's own establishment, 2006 is the JLG scheme, and 2010 is the AP microfinance crisis.
xs: **NABARD** launched the **SHG-Bank Linkage Programme** as a pilot in **1992** — option **(2)**.
**1982** is NABARD's founding; **2006** the **JLG** scheme; **2010** the **AP microfinance crisis**.
xa: It is the **world's largest microfinance movement**.
Banks lend directly to **SHGs** of mostly women members.
Idea from **Muhammad Yunus's Grameen Bank**.

n9a03b868e8c.s: The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF), funded by banks' priority-sector lending shortfalls, is managed by:
n9a03b868e8c.x: NABARD manages RIDF, which is funded by banks' PSL shortfalls; it also refinances StCBs, RRBs and land development banks.
xa: Refinance disbursed **2024-25**: **₹3,25,497.81 crore**.
NABARD also runs **LTIF** and **MIF**.

n3588ff92c70.s: Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank was formed through the merger of how many Regional Rural Banks?
n3588ff92c70.x: It was formed by merging four RRBs: Andhra Pragathi, Andhra Pradesh Grameena Vikas, Chaitanya Godavari and Saptagiri Grameena Banks.
xa: First-year (**2025-26**) business: **₹1,36,337 crore**.
Nationally, amalgamation left **28 RRBs** with **22,000+** branches.
RRBs date from **1975-76** (**RRB Act 1976**).

naf4cedf5709.s: The establishment of NABARD was based on the recommendations of which committee?
naf4cedf5709.x: NABARD was established on the basis of the B. Sivaraman Committee recommendations relating to CRAFICARD.
naf4cedf5709.tq: Use the committee–institution association rather than the sector alone.
xs: **NABARD** was based on the **B. Sivaraman Committee / CRAFICARD** — option **(1)**.
The **C. Rangarajan** high-level group is linked to **NHB**, not NABARD.
xa: NABARD: **12 July 1982**, **NABARD Act 1981**; HQ **Mumbai**.
It refinances **StCBs, RRBs, LDBs** and runs **RIDF** (funded by banks' **PSL** shortfalls).
It inspects **RRBs** and **cooperative banks**.

n4687dea2fe4.s: Which one of the following is NOT an NBFC category listed in the regulatory classification?
n4687dea2fe4.x: AFC, Loan Company, Investment Company, IFC, NBFC-MFI, CIC, HFC and IDF are listed NBFC categories. ‘Regional Rural Banking Company’ is not one of them.
n4687dea2fe4.tq: Find the invented-looking category that does not belong to the recognised list.
xs: "**Regional Rural Banking Company**" is not an NBFC category — option **(2)**.
Listed categories: AFC, Loan Co., Investment Co., **IFC**, **NBFC-MFI**, **CIC**, **HFC**, IDF — so **CIC**, **IFC** and **HFC** are valid.
xa: **RRBs** are banks under the **RRB Act 1976**, not NBFCs.
Minimum NOF: **NBFC-MFI ₹10 crore**; **HFC ₹20 crore**.
Under SBR, **HFCs, IFCs, CICs** sit in the **Middle Layer**.

na43d89458d9.s: Which of the following activities is NOT permitted to Payments Banks?
o: Accepting deposits within the permitted framework
na43d89458d9.x: Payments Banks cannot lend. Their role includes deposits and payment services, but not credit provision.
na43d89458d9.tq: Find the prohibited activity among functions of a specialised bank.
xs: **Payments banks cannot lend** — option **(4)**.
The notes list lending as their only bar, so the other activities are not ruled out.
xa: Other rural players: **11 Small Finance Banks**; **28 RRBs**.
SCB rural branches: **56,193** (**July 2025**).
First meeting of RBI's **Payments Regulatory Board**: **Jan 2026**.

n70756e4f791.s: The Andhra Pradesh MFI Ordinance, 2010 required microfinance institutions to register with:
n70756e4f791.x: The 2010 Ordinance required MFIs to register with district authorities; it also restricted doorstep recovery and capped interest.
xa: Issued **Oct 2010**; later an **Act, 2011**.
Cause: **multiple lending**, **over-indebtedness**, **coercive recovery** → borrower suicides.
**Malegam Committee**: no more than **2 MFIs per borrower**.

n6500a26372f.s: The Malegam Committee was constituted by the RBI primarily after the:
o: formation of the first RRB in 1975
launch of the SHG-Bank Linkage Programme in 1992
n6500a26372f.x: The RBI constituted the Malegam Committee in 2010–11 after the Andhra Pradesh microfinance crisis.
n6500a26372f.tq: Link a committee to the event that triggered its constitution.
xs: The **Malegam Committee** (RBI, **2010-11**) was set up after the **AP microfinance crisis (2010)** — option **(3)**.
**MFIN (2009)**, the **SHG-Bank Linkage pilot (1992)** and RRBs (**1975**) came earlier and did not prompt it.
xa: It proposed a separate **NBFC-MFI** category.
Margin and interest caps; loan-size and borrower-income limits.
No more than **2 MFIs per borrower**.

nfa896988231.s: Which of the following was NOT among the proposals associated with the Malegam Committee?
o: Unlimited lending by MFIs to every borrower
Limits on loan size and borrower income
nfa896988231.x: The committee proposed limits on lending, including no more than two MFIs per borrower; it did not support unlimited lending.
nfa896988231.tq: Reject an extreme statement that reverses a prudential recommendation.
xs: **Unlimited lending** was **not** proposed — Malegam capped it at **2 MFIs per borrower** — option **(1)**.
It did propose **margin and interest caps**, **loan-size and borrower-income limits** and a **separate NBFC-MFI category**.
xa: Set up by RBI in **2010-11** after the **AP crisis**.
**MFIN** (set up **2009**) and **Sa-Dhan** were recognised as **SROs** by RBI in **2014**.
NBFC-MFI: at least **75%** assets in microfinance loans.

n6d6a9fb7d8f.s: In March 2025, the largest share of the microfinance loan portfolio was held by:
n6d6a9fb7d8f.x: In March 2025, NBFC-MFIs accounted for the largest share at 39%, followed by banks at 32%, SFBs at 16% and other NBFCs at 12%.
n6d6a9fb7d8f.tq: Compare the listed sector shares and select the largest category.
xs: In **Mar 2025**, **NBFC-MFIs** held the largest share — **39%** — option **(2)**.
**Banks 32%**, **SFBs 16%**, other **NBFCs 12%**.
xa: Loans outstanding **fell 14%** in **FY25**.
Industry portfolio down **22%** YoY (**Dec 2025**).
Banks' MFI portfolio fell **40%** YoY to **₹65,687 crore** in **Q3 FY26** (Equifax-SIDBI).

n18b4bad8f5d.s: The Microfinance Industry Network (MFIN), the association of NBFC-MFIs, was set up in:
n18b4bad8f5d.x: MFIN was set up in 2009; the RBI recognised it as a self-regulatory organisation in 2014.
xa: MFIN is the association of **NBFC-MFIs**.
**Sa-Dhan** was recognised as an SRO alongside MFIN.
**NBFC-MFIs** held **39%** of microfinance loans in **Mar 2025**.

n73e1c2dd02e.s: Which was the first financial services company to be resolved under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC)?
n73e1c2dd02e.x: DHFL (2019) was the first financial services company resolved under the IBC; Piramal acquired it in 2021.
xa: IL&FS: Govt **superseded the board** (**NCLT** order).
The AP crisis → **Ordinance (Oct 2010)** → **Malegam Committee**.
Response to NBFC stress: **SBR framework**.

n8d52535f368.s: An indigenous banker is best described as one who:
o: Accepts deposits and lends, while also combining banking with trade or commission business
Provides only long-term loans to infrastructure companies
Operates exclusively under the supervision of the RBI
Only lends in kind and does not accept deposits
n8d52535f368.x: An indigenous banker accepts deposits and lends, while combining banking activities with trade or commission business. Shroffs and Mahajans are examples.
n8d52535f368.tq: Use the functional definition and reject the extreme ‘only’ statement.
xs: An **indigenous banker** **accepts deposits and lends**, combining banking with **trade/commission business** — option **(1)**.
⚠ One who "**lends only in kind**" is **not** an indigenous banker; they are part of the **unorganised** sector, not RBI-supervised.
xa: They deal in **hundis**.
Examples: **Shroffs, seths, Mahajans, Multanis, Chettiars**.
**Moneylenders** are a separate group under **state money-lending laws**.

nbff08bda4c1.s: As per the APPSC Group 2 (2017) answer key, which of the following lies outside India's organised money market?
o: Discount and Finance House of India (DFHI)
nbff08bda4c1.x: The 2017 key treated finance companies as outside the organised money market; commercial banks, DFHI and cooperative banks are RBI-regulated constituents of it.
xa: ⚠ The notes' general table does list finance companies under organised — follow the **key** for the PYQ.
Unregulated **finance/loan companies** sit in the **unorganised** column.
Organised also includes **STCI**, provident funds, mutual funds.

n623f2491025.s: Under the Finance Act, 2019, the regulation of housing finance companies was transferred from NHB to:
o: The Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
n623f2491025.x: The Finance Act, 2019 moved HFC regulation to the RBI; NHB retained supervision and refinance functions.
xa: ⚠ Older notes still list NHB as the regulator.
**90 HFCs** registered (**June 2025**).
HFC minimum **NOF**: **₹20 crore**.

n7db6700d97f.s: The Central Office of the Reserve Bank of India was shifted from Calcutta to Bombay in
n7db6700d97f.x: The RBI’s Central Office moved from Calcutta to Bombay in 1937.
n7db6700d97f.tq: Use a close-date chronology trap involving commencement, relocation and nationalisation.
xs: RBI's Central Office moved from **Calcutta to Bombay** in **1937** — option **(2)**.
**1935** is when RBI began (at Calcutta); **1949** is nationalisation.
xa: HQ today: **Mumbai** ("**Mint Street**"), with offices in **31** locations.
**1937** also ended **Sir Osborne Smith**'s term (**1935-37**).

The framework separates **realised equity** from **revaluation balances**.
Remaining net profit goes to the Centre under **Section 47**.

na8cd0178986.s: The Bimal Jalan Committee's Economic Capital Framework primarily sought to distinguish between which of the following?
na8cd0178986.x: The framework distinguished realised equity from revaluation balances and provided for a Contingent Risk Buffer.
na8cd0178986.tq: Identify the precise accounting distinction associated with the committee.
xs: The **Bimal Jalan Committee** framework separated **realised equity and revaluation balances** — option **(1)**.
It is the **Economic Capital Framework** (**2018**).
It also required a **Contingent Risk Buffer (CRB)**.
xa: CRB band: first **5.5-6.5%** of the balance sheet, widened to **4.5-7.5%** in **2025**.
**Tarapore** committee: roadmap to **capital account convertibility**.
Surplus left after provisions goes to the Centre under **Section 47**.

n9472f9be7ef.s: In Indian monetary statistics, M3 is also known as:
n9472f9be7ef.x: M3 is broad money and is described as aggregate monetary resources. It comprises M1 and time deposits with the banking system.
n9472f9be7ef.tq: Test the official descriptive label associated with the principal broad-money aggregate.
xs: **M3** is called **aggregate monetary resources** — option **(4)**.
It is **broad money**: **M1 + time deposits** with the banking system.
**Reserve money** is **M0**, not M3.
xa: M3 is the **main aggregate RBI tracks**.
M3 grew **12.1%** while M0 grew only **2.9%** (data to **31 Dec 2025**).
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0** = **6.21** (31 Dec 2025).

n338ad04328a.s: Which one of the following correctly describes M0 or reserve money?
o: M3 + all post office deposits excluding NSCs
Currency in circulation + bankers’ deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI
M1 + post office savings bank deposits
Currency with the public + demand deposits + time deposits
n338ad04328a.x: M0, or reserve money, consists of currency in circulation, bankers’ deposits with the RBI and other deposits with the RBI. It is the monetary base.
n338ad04328a.tq: Distinguish the monetary base M0 from the deposit-based aggregates M1 to M4.
xs: **M0 (reserve money)** = **currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) is **M4**; option (3) is **M2**.
Option (4) ignores M0's bankers' deposits and mixes in time deposits (the M3 idea).
xa: M0 is also called **monetary base**, **base money** and **high-powered money**.
It is the **basis of credit creation** and RBI's most important money indicator.
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0**.

n93fb904cc26.s: The present framework of monetary aggregates M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the:
o: Second Working Group on Money Supply
n93fb904cc26.x: The monetary aggregate framework from M1 to M4 was introduced on the recommendation of the Second Working Group on Money Supply in 1977.
n93fb904cc26.tq: Link the institutional recommendation with the year and monetary classification.
xs: M1-M4 came from the **Second Working Group on Money Supply** (**1977**) — option **(2)**.
The later **1998** group (the third) gave **NM0-NM3** and **L1-L3**.
xa: The **1998** group was chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**.
⚠ M2 = **M1** + PO savings; M3 = **M1** (not M2) + time deposits.
M4 = M3 + all post office deposits except **NSCs**.

o: the average number of times a unit of currency changes hands during a period
the total quantity of currency printed by the central bank in a year
the percentage of bank deposits kept as reserves
the rate at which coins are minted by the government
n3f80766f982.x: Velocity is the average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a given period. A ₹10 note used twice generates ₹20 of transactions.
n3f80766f982.tq: Choose the precise definition instead of related monetary terms.
xs: **Velocity** is **the average number of times a unit of currency changes hands during a period** — option **(1)**.
Example: a **₹10** note used twice = **₹20** of transactions.
xa: Velocity is **higher among low-income spenders** and **in booms**.
In Fisher's **MV = PT**, V is velocity; in Cambridge **M = kPY**, k = **1/V**.

nindian-economy-38-1.s: Which is the most commonly used measure of broad money supply in India?
nindian-economy-38-1.x: M3 (broad money) is the most used measure; M1 is narrow money and M0 is reserve money.
n: M3 is broad money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M3 is the most commonly used measure of broad aggregate money supply. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xa: **M3 minus M1** equals **time deposits with banks** — not "M1 minus M3".
**Liquidity order:** **M1 > M2 > M3 > M4** — M1 most liquid, M4 least liquid.
The M1–M4 aggregates come from the **Second Working Group on Money Supply (1977)**.
⚠ M2 = **M1** + PO savings; M3 = **M1** (not M2) + time deposits.

nindian-economy-38-4.s: Which of the following components of money supply is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Demand deposits with banks – locked for a fixed period; least liquid
Time deposits with banks – locked for a fixed period; least liquid
Currency with the public – immediate cash in hand
Other deposits with RBI – balances of foreign central banks and international bodies
nindian-economy-38-4.x: Demand deposits can be withdrawn instantly; it is time deposits that are locked for a fixed period and least liquid.
n: Currency with the public is immediate cash in hand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Demand deposits with banks can be withdrawn instantly on demand. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are locked for a fixed period. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are the least liquid deposits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are highly liquid balances. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
The liquidity order is currency, savings deposits, demand deposits, and time deposits. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Cash is the most liquid form of money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Fixed or time deposits are the least liquid form of money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xa: All four components are in **M3**; only **time deposits** are **excluded** from **M1**.
**Cash** is the **most liquid** form of money; **fixed or time deposits** the **least liquid**.
'Other' deposits with RBI also include **quasi-government and financial institutions**, including **primary dealers**.

n849ade3df2d.s: Which one of the following is classified as a contingent function of money?
n849ade3df2d.x: The contingent functions include acting as a basis of credit, distribution of national income and giving liquidity.
n849ade3df2d.tq: Recall the less commonly tested contingent-function group.
xs: **Giving liquidity** is a **contingent** function of money — option **(2)**.
Other contingent functions: **basis of credit** and **distribution of national income**.
**Unit of account** and **medium of exchange** are **primary**; **standard of deferred payments** is **secondary**.
xa: Secondary functions: **store of value**, standard of deferred payments, **transfer of value**.
⚠ **Production of goods** is NOT a function of money — asked in APPSC **2025**.

nbc9b9b94646.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the new monetary aggregates from the liquidity aggregates proposed by the RBI working group?
o: NM0–NM3 are residency-based, while L1–L3 add specified broader liquidity components.
NM0–NM3 measure fiscal deficits, while L1–L3 measure public expenditure.
NM0–NM3 are confined to equity shares, while L1–L3 cover government securities.
NM0–NM3 consist only of foreign-exchange reserves, while L1–L3 consist only of coins.
nbc9b9b94646.x: NM0–NM3 are residency-based aggregates that distinguish short-term from long-term deposits. L1–L3 broaden the coverage by adding specified post-office, financial-institution and NBFC liabilities.
nbc9b9b94646.tq: Separate the two families by their coverage and basis of compilation.
xs: **NM0-NM3 are residency-based**, while **L1-L3 add broader liquidity components** — option **(1)**.
NM aggregates **separate short-term from long-term deposits**.
L1-L3 add **post office deposits**, **term money/CDs of FIs** and **public deposits of NBFCs**.
xa: Both came from the **1998** RBI Working Group chaired by **Y. V. Reddy**.
The earlier **M1-M4** came from the **Second Working Group (1977)**.

ne8f7790c09f.s: Which of the following is a likely consequence of a high preference for cash in the economy?
o: An unlimited rise in the credit multiplier
A conversion of M3 into M0
A limitation on India’s credit multiplier
ne8f7790c09f.x: Weak banking habits and a high preference for cash raise the currency-deposit ratio, limiting the credit multiplier and the expansion of deposits.
ne8f7790c09f.tq: Connect the behavioural variable—cash preference—with the banking-system outcome.
xs: High cash preference results in **a limitation on India's credit multiplier** — option **(4)**.
It reflects **weak banking habits** and raises the **cdr**, which **lowers the multiplier**.
xa: A stronger **banking habit** raises the multiplier (UPSC **2019**).
**Cash withdrawal** raises cdr + reduces reserves → money supply contracts.
Higher **CRR/SLR** also lowers the multiplier.

nindian-economy-38-2.s: Which of the following about money supply measures is NOT correct?
o: M1 includes currency with the public
Time deposits with banks are part of M1
Other deposits with the RBI are part of both M1 and M3
M3 includes time deposits with banks
nindian-economy-38-2.x: Time deposits are not part of M1 (currency, demand deposits and other RBI deposits); they are included in M3.
n: Currency with the public is included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Other deposits with the RBI are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are not included in M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits with banks are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M1 consists of currency with the public. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M1 consists of other deposits with the RBI. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits are excluded from M1. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
Time deposits are included in M3. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xa: **M1** = currency with the public + **demand deposits** + other deposits with the RBI — **directly spendable transaction money**.
**Time deposits** are **locked** for a **fixed period** — the **least liquid deposits**.
**Liquidity order:** **currency**, **savings deposits**, **demand deposits**, **time deposits**.

nindian-economy-38-7.x: Since M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks, M3 − M1 equals time deposits.
n: M3 equals M1 plus time deposits with banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
M3 minus M1 equals time deposits with banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xa: **M3** is the **most commonly used measure** of **broad aggregate money supply**.
**M1** = **currency with the public** + **demand deposits** + **other deposits with the RBI** — narrow money, high liquidity.
⚠ M2 = **M1** + post office **savings bank** deposits; M3 is built on **M1**, not M2.
**M4** = M3 + all post office deposits (excluding **NSCs**) — broad, least liquid.

n6519956e3d8.s: With a reserve requirement of 10 per cent and no leakages assumed, ₹100 of reserve money can support deposits of approximately:
n6519956e3d8.x: With a 10 per cent reserve requirement, the simple deposit multiplier is 1/0.10, or 10. Thus, ₹100 of base money can support deposits approaching ₹1,000.
n6519956e3d8.tq: Convert the reserve ratio into its reciprocal before selecting the expansion value.
xs: With **10%** reserves, **₹100** of base can expand deposits towards **₹1,000** — option **(3)**.
Banks keep the required reserve and lend the rest; **each loan creates a new deposit**.
xa: The fuller formula is **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)** — leakages into cash lower it.
Actual Indian multiplier: **6.21** (**31 Dec 2025**).
Higher **CRR/SLR** = lower multiplier.

n1d7cbfa931f.s: Deposit money, created by lending beyond required reserves, is created mainly by:
n1d7cbfa931f.x: The RBI creates reserve money by issuing notes, while commercial banks create deposit money by lending beyond their required CRR and SLR reserves.
xa: Banks hold **CRR and SLR** and lend the rest; each loan creates a **new deposit**.
⚠ **Cash** = high-powered money; **bank money** = secondary money.

n43b507e8740.s: If cdr is the currency-deposit ratio and rdr the reserve-deposit ratio, the money multiplier (m) is given by:
n43b507e8740.x: The money multiplier is m = (1 + cdr)/(cdr + rdr), so a higher cdr or rdr (CRR, SLR) lowers it. The second option is its reciprocal, and the other two are not the standard formula.
xs: **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)** — option **(1)**.
**cdr** = currency-deposit ratio (preference for cash); **rdr** = reserve-deposit ratio (**CRR, SLR**-driven).
Option (2) is the reciprocal of the correct formula.
xa: In aggregate terms, the multiplier = **M3/M0**.
Higher **cdr** or **rdr** → **lower multiplier**.

n88134df43e8.s: Which one of the following correctly states the denominations covered by the 1978 demonetisation?
n88134df43e8.x: The High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act, 1978, under Morarji Desai, demonetised the ₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000 notes to curb black money. Option B (₹500, ₹1,000, ₹10,000) is how one source lists it, and option D is the 1946 episode.
n88134df43e8.tq: Use denomination discrimination to distinguish 1978 from 1946 and 2016.
xs: The **1978** demonetisation covered **₹1,000, ₹5,000 and ₹10,000** — option **(1)**.
It was done under the **High Denomination Bank Notes (Demonetisation) Act**, under **Morarji Desai**, to curb **black money**.
Option (4) is the **1946** episode.
xa: ⚠ One source (APP) lists **₹500, ₹1,000, ₹10,000** for 1978 — option (2) reflects that variant.
**2016**: **₹500, ₹1,000** withdrawn; legal basis **Section 26(2)** of the RBI Act.

n586f6872309.s: Which one of the following policy actions directly injects reserve money into the banking system?
o: RBI sells government securities in the open market
The public withdraws deposits as cash
RBI purchases government securities in the open market
n586f6872309.x: An RBI purchase of government securities credits reserves to the banking system and injects reserve money, supporting an expansion of money supply.
n586f6872309.tq: Ask whether the transaction adds or drains banking-system reserves.
xs: **RBI purchasing government securities** (**OMO purchase**) **injects reserve money** — option **(4)**.
**RBI selling G-secs** **reduces money supply** (UPSC **2012**) — option (1) is the opposite.
A higher reserve-deposit ratio and **cash withdrawal** both **lower the multiplier**.
xa: **Government borrowing from RBI** (monetisation) also injects reserve money.
OMO purchases: **₹2 lakh crore** (Dec 2025-Jan 2026); **₹1 lakh crore** (March 2026).

n3fc4f1a1d28.s: If money supply is fixed and the demand for money rises, the interest rate will:
n3fc4f1a1d28.x: With a fixed money supply, a rise in money demand raises the interest rate; a fall in demand lowers it.
xa: The **value of transactions** sets money demand.
At **higher interest rates, money demanded falls**.
Fisher: **MV = PT**; Cambridge: **M = kPY** (k = **1/V**).

nindian-economy-38-5.s: The money multiplier is represented as:
nindian-economy-38-5.x: The money multiplier is the ratio of total money supply to base money, i.e. M3 divided by M0.
n: The money multiplier equals total money supply divided by base money. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
The money multiplier is expressed as M3 divided by M0. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
An increase in banking habits increases the money multiplier. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
An increase in the cash reserve ratio decreases credit creation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xa: **Formula:** m = (1 + **cdr**) / (cdr + **rdr**) — cdr = currency-deposit ratio, rdr = reserve-deposit ratio.
**Weak banking habits** (high cash preference) limit India's credit multiplier.
**Data (31 Dec 2025):** money multiplier = **6.21** (**6.0** adjusted for reverse repo/SDF).
Example: **10%** reserves → **₹100** of base can expand deposits towards **₹1,000**.

nbbb9c03c18b.s: In the Cambridge cash-balance equation M = kPY, 'k' is:
o: The reciprocal of the velocity of money
nbbb9c03c18b.x: In M = kPY, k equals 1/V, the reciprocal of velocity; Fisher's version is MV = PT.
xa: ⚠ **MV = PT** = Fisher; **M = kPY** = Cambridge — a frequent matching trap.
**Velocity** = average number of times a currency unit changes hands in a period.
**Milton Friedman** gave the **modern quantity theory**.

nindian-economy-67-5.s: Monetarism and the role of money supply are associated with:
nindian-economy-67-5.x: Milton Friedman is associated with monetarism; Hayek with liberal, market-based economics.
n: Friedrich Hayek is associated with Liberal economics. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Friedrich Hayek is associated with market-oriented economics. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Milton Friedman is associated with Monetarism. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Milton Friedman is associated with Money supply. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
xa: Hayek is also linked to the **Austrian business-cycle approach**.
Friedman gave the **modern quantity theory** of money demand.
**R.G. Hawtrey** = **Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle**; **J.M. Keynes** = **Effective Demand**.

nindian-economy-67-16.s: The IS-LM model is associated with:
nindian-economy-67-16.x: Hicks gave the IS-LM model; Hawtrey gave the pure monetary trade-cycle theory and Hayek the Austrian cycle theory.
n: R.G. Hawtrey is associated with the Pure Monetary Theory of Trade Cycle. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
J.M. Keynes is associated with the Keynesian explanation of economic fluctuations. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
Friedrich Hayek is associated with the Austrian business-cycle approach. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
J.R. Hicks is associated with the IS-LM model. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #67 · pp 96-98]
xa: **Milton Friedman** → **monetarism**; **Joan Robinson** → **post-Keynesian economics**.
⚠ **MV = PT** = **Irving Fisher**; **M = kPY** = Cambridge (**Marshall, Pigou**).
**Baumol** (**1952**) and **Tobin** (**1956**) → inventory-theoretic transactions demand (**square-root rule**).

n64e26369dea.s: A ₹500 note costs approximately ₹4 to produce. The difference between its face value and production cost is known as:
n64e26369dea.x: Seigniorage is the difference between the face value of currency and its cost of production. It represents the issuer's profit and is a source of RBI surplus.
n64e26369dea.tq: Apply the definition to a numerical currency-production example.
xs: The gap between face value and production cost is **seigniorage** — option **(3)**.
A **₹500** note costs about **₹4** to print; the difference is the issuer's profit.
Seigniorage is a **source of RBI surplus** (profit to central bank/government).
xa: **Token coin**: face value above metal value — not the same as seigniorage.
**Fiat money**: notes and coins with **no intrinsic value**, money by government order.
**Legal tender**: money a creditor **is legally bound to accept** (UPSC **2018**).

n1d1b4ddee3e.s: Which one of the following is an example of near money?
o: Currency notes held by the public
n1d1b4ddee3e.x: Time deposits are highly liquid assets but cannot directly be used to pay for goods and services, making them near money. Other examples include Treasury bills, bills of exchange and savings certificates.
n1d1b4ddee3e.tq: Distinguish directly spendable money from highly liquid but non-payment assets.
xs: **Time deposits with banks** are **near money** — option **(3)**.
Near money = **highly liquid assets** that **cannot directly pay** for things.
Currency notes, the **Digital Rupee** and rupee coins are legal tender, i.e. money itself, not near money.
xa: Other near money: **T-bills**, **bills of exchange**, bonds near redemption, **savings certificates**.
**M3** = M1 + **time deposits** with the banking system (**broad money**).
**Plastic money** (debit/credit cards) is **not legal tender**.

n328ef64f0e4.s: A rupee coin is called a token coin because:
o: Its metal value is higher than its face value.
It can be used only for token payments.
Its face value is higher than the value of the metal contained in it.
It is not issued under government authority.
n328ef64f0e4.x: A rupee coin is a token coin because its face value exceeds the value of the metal contained in it.
n328ef64f0e4.tq: Use the direction of the value comparison to distinguish token coin from intrinsic-value coin.
xs: A rupee coin is a **token coin** because its **face value is higher than the value of the metal** in it — option **(3)**.
Option (1) reverses the relation.
Coins are issued by the **Government**, so option (4) is wrong.
xa: Coins are **limited legal tender**; RBI notes are **unlimited**.
**Seigniorage** = face value − cost of production (e.g. **₹500** note costs about **₹4**).
The **Government** creates **coins and the ₹1 note**; RBI creates reserve money (notes).

neb8798ea5a4.s: 'Store of value' is classified as which type of function of money?
neb8798ea5a4.x: Store of value is a secondary function; medium of exchange is primary and basis of credit is contingent.
xa: Primary functions: **medium of exchange** and **measure of value** (unit of account).
Secondary: store of value, **standard of deferred payments**, **transfer of value**.
Contingent: basis of credit, **distribution of national income**, gives **liquidity**.

n7375eb25187.s: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, placed India on which monetary standard?
n7375eb25187.x: The Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899, associated with Curzon, put India on the gold standard.
n7375eb25187.tq: Match the enactment with the monetary standard it established.
xs: The **Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899** (**Curzon**) put India on the **gold standard** — option **(3)**.
It was passed in **1899**, after the **Paper Currency Act, 1861** had given the Government the note-issue monopoly.
xa: Note issue passed to the **RBI** in **1935**.
**Decimal coinage** came from **1 April 1957** under the **Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955**.

n9b58b77ae9f.s: The General Bank of Bengal and Bihar was established in:
n9b58b77ae9f.x: It was set up in 1773, before the Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act (1899), transfer of note issue to the RBI (1935) and decimal coinage (1957).
xa: **Bank of Hindostan** (**1770-1832**) was even earlier than the General Bank.
**Paper Currency Act, 1861** sits between A and B: monopoly of note issue to the Government.
Under decimal coinage, **₹1 = 100 naye paise**; "naya" was dropped in **1964**.

nd1c6cc58604.s: The monopoly of note issue was given to the Government by which enactment?
o: Indian Coinage and Paper Currency Act, 1899
nd1c6cc58604.x: The Paper Currency Act, 1861, gave the Government the monopoly of note issue, replacing the earlier private and presidency-bank pattern of issuance.
nd1c6cc58604.tq: Distinguish the enactment granting note-issue monopoly from later coinage and RBI legislation.
xs: The **Paper Currency Act, 1861** gave the Government the **monopoly of note issue** — option **(2)**.
The **1899** Act put India on the **gold standard**; the **1955** amendment brought **decimal coinage**.
The **RBI Act, 1934** later led to note issue being handed to RBI in **1935**.
xa: Earlier issuers: **Bank of Hindostan** (**1770**) and **General Bank of Bengal and Bihar** (**1773**).
Before 1861, the **Presidency Banks** and currency circles issued paper currency.

n1709c4ce34b.s: Decimal coinage was introduced in India from:
n1709c4ce34b.x: Decimal coinage began on 1 April 1957 under the Indian Coinage (Amendment) Act, 1955, with ₹1 = 100 naye paise; 'naya' was dropped in 1964.
xa: The **1899** Act (Curzon) put India on the **gold standard**.
A rupee coin is a **token coin**: its face value is above its metal value.
Coins are only **limited legal tender**.

n8e5a32879cd.s: 'Hard money' refers to money backed by:
n8e5a32879cd.x: Hard money is backed by gold or credible assets; soft money is paper money backed by government bonds.
xa: **Bank money vs cash**: bank money = **secondary money**; cash = **high-powered money**.
**Fiat money** has **no intrinsic value**; it is money by government order.
**Digital Rupee** is legal tender under the RBI Act, amended by the **Finance Act 2022**.

n8366a8c7709.s: Currency in circulation includes which one of the following combinations?
o: Notes, foreign exchange assets and bankers' deposits
Notes, demand deposits and time deposits
Rupee coins, government securities and small coins
Notes, rupee coins and small coins
n8366a8c7709.x: Currency in circulation comprises notes, rupee coins and small coins. It is held partly by the public and partly as cash in hand with banks.
n8366a8c7709.tq: Split the aggregate into its physical currency components.
xs: Currency in circulation = **notes, rupee coins and small coins** — option **(4)**.
It equals **currency with the public + cash in hand with banks**.
Demand/time deposits and bankers' deposits are not currency; they belong to **M1/M3** or **M0** separately.
xa: **M0** = currency in circulation + **bankers' deposits with RBI** + **'other' deposits with RBI**.
Notes in circulation (May **2026**): **174 billion** notes worth over **₹42.12 lakh crore**.
That is up **~137%** from **₹17.74 lakh crore** (Nov **2016**).

nfc944cdb1cc.s: High-powered money is also known as:
nfc944cdb1cc.x: High-powered money is also called reserve money, monetary base and central bank money; bank money is secondary money.
xa: M0 is the **most important money indicator for RBI**.
Formula (PYQ): **H = currency held by the public + cash reserves of banks + other deposits with RBI** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**Money multiplier** = **M3/M0**.

nb7036887bc3.s: On the uses side, high-powered money comprises currency held by the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with the RBI and:
nb7036887bc3.x: The uses-side composition of high-powered money is currency with the public, banks' cash in hand, banks' deposits with RBI and other deposits with RBI.
xa: This formula was the APPSC-G2 **2025** answer.
High-powered money is also called **reserve money, base money, monetary base, central bank money**.
It is the **basis of credit creation**.

n15d007779c4.s: M2 is obtained by adding ____ to M1.
o: all post office deposits except NSCs
n15d007779c4.x: M2 = M1 + post office savings bank deposits; M3 = M1 + time deposits with banks.
xa: ⚠ M3 is built on **M1**, not on M2.
**M1** = **narrow money**, most liquid; **M3** = **broad money**, the main aggregate RBI tracks.
The M1-M4 scheme comes from the **Second Working Group on Money Supply (1977)**.

n209c6a2c2bd.s: The RBI Working Group on Money Supply: Analytics and Methodology of Compilation (1998) was chaired by:
n209c6a2c2bd.x: The 1998 (third) working group was chaired by Y. V. Reddy and proposed the residency-based NM0–NM3 and L1–L3.
xa: It also proposed liquidity aggregates **L1, L2, L3**.
NM aggregates **separate short-term from long-term deposits**.
L1-L3 add **post office deposits**, **term money/CDs** of FIs, and **public deposits of NBFCs**.

naaa7eac8379.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the additions made in the broader liquidity aggregates L1–L3?
o: Term money and certificates of deposit of financial institutions
Gold reserves held by the RBI
naaa7eac8379.x: L1–L3 add post-office deposits, term money and CDs of financial institutions, and NBFC public deposits; RBI gold reserves are not among them.
xa: They were proposed by the **1998** Working Group (**Y. V. Reddy**).
The same group gave the residency-based **NM0-NM3**.
⚠ **M4** = M3 + post office deposits except **NSCs** — different series from L1-L3.

n0fd338e7a90.s: Other things remaining unchanged, which of the following would RAISE the money multiplier?
n0fd338e7a90.x: A stronger banking habit raises the money multiplier, while higher CRR, SLR or currency-deposit ratio lowers it.
xa: Formula: **m = (1 + cdr) / (cdr + rdr)**; rdr is driven by **CRR and SLR**.
**Cash withdrawal** raises cdr and cuts bank reserves → money supply contracts.
**Weak banking habits** (high cash preference) limit India's credit multiplier.

n37457824745.s: The Cash Reserve Ratio was reduced by 100 basis points to what level of Net Demand and Time Liabilities, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore?
n37457824745.x: The CRR was reduced by 100 basis points to 3.0 per cent of NDTL, releasing approximately ₹2.5 lakh crore by December 2025.
n37457824745.tq: Combine the basis-point change, final ratio and liquidity-release figure without confusing percentage points.
xs: The **CRR** was cut **100 bps to 3.0 per cent** of **NDTL** — option **(2)**.
It released about **₹2.5 lakh crore** by **Dec 2025**.
xa: A lower CRR lowers rdr and so **raises the multiplier** (to **6.21**).
Recent **OMO purchases**: **₹2 lakh crore** (Dec 2025-Jan 2026).
March **2026**: ₹50,000 crore and **₹1 lakh crore** amid the **West Asia war**.

nfcd5358112d.s: According to Keynes, the demand for money arises from the transactions, precautionary and ____ motives.
nfcd5358112d.x: Keynes's liquidity-preference theory names three motives: transactions, precautionary and speculative.
xa: **Speculative demand** varies **inversely with the interest rate**.
Some notes name only the **transaction** and **speculative** motives.
⚠ **MV = PT** = **Fisher**; **M = kPY** = Cambridge (**Marshall, Pigou**).
Inventory-theoretic demand: **Baumol** (**1952**), **Tobin** (**1956**).

nd162a9a4970.s: The retail pilot of the e-Rupee (CBDC) began in:
nd162a9a4970.x: The wholesale pilot began in November 2022 and the retail pilot in December 2022.
xa: e-Rupee had **7 million** retail users (Jan **2026**).
Features: offline payments, **programmable money for DBT**, cross-border pilot with **UAE**.
**Digital Rupee** is legal tender under the RBI Act, amended by the **Finance Act 2022**.

n3f437b7ade4.s: Which of the following is NOT an identified feature or use of the e-Rupee?
o: Mandatory replacement of all bank deposits
Programmable money for direct benefit transfer
A cross-border pilot with the UAE
n3f437b7ade4.x: Offline payments, programmability for DBT and a UAE cross-border pilot are identified uses; mandatory replacement of bank deposits is not.
xa: **Digital Food Currency** pilot in **Puducherry** (**2026**): usable only for nutritional food.
Pilots: **wholesale Nov 2022**; **retail Dec 2022**.
e-Rupee = **direct liability of RBI**.

n04dee69114b.s: The demonetisation announced on 8 November 2016 primarily withdrew which notes from circulation?
n04dee69114b.x: The 2016 announcement withdrew ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes, effective from midnight. New ₹500 and ₹2,000 notes were subsequently issued.
n04dee69114b.tq: Distinguish the withdrawn denominations from the newly issued denominations.
xs: The **8 November 2016** move withdrew **₹500 and ₹1,000** notes — option **(3)**.
New **₹500** and **₹2,000** notes were then issued.
It was effective from midnight, so some keys say **9 Nov 2016**.
xa: Objectives: **black money**, **counterfeit currency (FICN)**, corruption, **terror financing**.
**₹2,000** was withdrawn from circulation in **May 2023** but stays legal tender.
SC upheld the move **4:1** (**2023**).

n7d992915bc9.s: The paramount objective of monetary policy formulated by the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934 is:
n7d992915bc9.x: Price stability is paramount; growth, financial stability and external balance are also pursued.
xa: The RBI-as-authority point was asked in APPSC-GS **2023**.
Since **2016** India follows **flexible inflation targeting**.
The **MPC** sets the **policy repo rate** to hit the inflation target.

n6bc5b50799d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about fiscal and monetary policy?
o: Fiscal policy generally affects aggregate demand directly
Fiscal policy is free from legislative lags
Monetary policy generally affects demand indirectly through interest rates
Monetary policy is more flexible because the MPC meets every two months
n6bc5b50799d.x: Fiscal policy can face legislative and implementation lags, so it is not free from them.
xa: Fiscal tools: spending, taxes, subsidies, borrowing; monetary tools: **repo, OMO, CRR/SLR, LAF**.
Monetary tools are **demand-side tools only** — they cannot fix supply-driven food inflation.

nb59657ed186.s: The upper end of the liquidity adjustment facility (LAF) corridor is the:
nb59657ed186.x: The MSF rate forms the upper end of the corridor; the repo rate is the overnight lending rate against approved collateral.
xa: Corridor order: **SDF (floor) < repo < MSF = bank rate (ceiling)**.
MSF = repo + **25 bps**; SDF = repo − **25 bps** → corridor **50 bps** wide (**5.00-5.50%**).

nd181de1d1c8.s: The correct order of the principal LAF corridor rates from the floor to the ceiling is:
o: Repo rate < SDF < MSF < Bank rate
SDF < MSF < Repo rate = Bank rate
SDF < Repo rate < MSF = Bank rate
Reverse repo < SDF < Repo rate < MSF
nd181de1d1c8.x: The SDF is the floor, the repo rate lies above it, and the MSF and bank rate are aligned at the ceiling.
nd181de1d1c8.tq: Arrange the instruments by their position in the interest-rate corridor.
xs: Floor to ceiling: **SDF < Repo rate < MSF = Bank rate** — option **(3)**.
Rates: **SDF 5.00%** < **repo 5.25%** < **MSF = bank rate 5.50%**.
xa: The corridor is **50 bps** wide.
The **fixed-rate reverse repo** (**3.35%**) is used only at RBI's discretion since SDF.
**LAF** = repo + reverse repo/SDF windows → main short-term liquidity tool.

nbc68fe661be.s: The fixed-rate reverse repo is different from the SDF in that it:
o: Permits banks to borrow by dipping into SLR
Absorbs funds against Government securities and is used at RBI's discretion
Requires banks to maintain cash with RBI without interest
Lends funds to banks without collateral
nbc68fe661be.x: The fixed-rate reverse repo absorbs funds against Government securities and is now used at the RBI's discretion, while the SDF absorbs funds without collateral.
nbc68fe661be.tq: Distinguish two liquidity-absorption windows by the collateral requirement and operational use.
xs: The fixed-rate reverse repo **absorbs funds against Government securities and is used at RBI's discretion** — option **(2)**.
The **SDF** absorbs funds **without collateral**.
Option (1) is the **MSF**; option (3) is the **CRR**.
xa: Fixed-rate reverse repo is at **3.35%** (May **2026**).
**VRRR** absorbs liquidity for longer maturities than the overnight SDF.

n1dcab2bcd1d.s: Banks may maintain their SLR in cash, gold, other approved securities and:
o: Unencumbered Government securities and Treasury Bills
n1dcab2bcd1d.x: SLR is held by banks themselves in cash, gold, unencumbered government securities (including T-Bills and SDLs) and approved securities.
xa: **MSS** securities also count towards SLR.
SLR is **not deposited with RBI** — that is CRR.
SLR earns **interest** on G-secs; CRR earns none.

neb6f4406613.s: Which ratio is maintained by banks as a cash balance with the RBI and earns no interest?
neb6f4406613.x: CRR is kept as a cash balance with the RBI and earns no interest; SLR is held by the bank itself in cash, gold and eligible securities.
xa: ⚠ **Sec 42 RBI Act** = CRR; **Sec 24 BR Act** = SLR.
CRR has **no floor or ceiling** since **2006**; SLR ceiling **40%**.

n92a7075dc5e.s: The statutory range of the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) is:
n92a7075dc5e.x: SLR can be set between 0% and 40% of NDTL; the earlier 25% floor was removed by the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2007.
xa: SLR shortfall penalty: **bank rate + 3%** → **bank rate + 5%** if continued.

n2866f6b60d1.s: Which one of the following combinations represents a contractionary monetary policy intended to control inflation?
o: Raise CRR, cut SLR, cut repo rate and sell Government securities
Cut CRR, cut SLR, cut repo rate and buy Government securities
Raise CRR, raise SLR, raise repo rate and sell Government securities
Cut CRR, raise SLR, cut repo rate and buy Government securities
n2866f6b60d1.x: A contractionary policy raises CRR, SLR and policy rates and sells Government securities through OMO, thereby reducing liquidity and demand.
n2866f6b60d1.tq: Match every instrument with its direction under the same policy stance.
xs: Contractionary (dear money): **raise CRR, raise SLR, raise repo rate and sell G-secs** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) is the **cheap money** (expansionary) set.
Options (1) and (4) mix contractionary and expansionary moves.
xa: **OMO sale absorbs** liquidity; purchase injects.
Raising CRR = **less money in circulation** + **lower demand** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).

n09f4b6999a2.s: If the RBI cuts the CRR and SLR, which of the following is the most likely immediate effect?
o: Absorption of surplus liquidity through SDF
Reduction in lendable funds and the money multiplier
Increase in lendable funds and the money multiplier
A compulsory fall in bank deposits
n09f4b6999a2.x: A CRR or SLR cut releases funds for lending and raises the money multiplier, subject to the banking system's willingness and ability to lend.
n09f4b6999a2.tq: Identify whether the reserve release expands or restricts banks' lendable resources.
xs: A CRR/SLR cut leads to an **increase in lendable funds and the money multiplier** — option **(3)**.
Option (2) is the effect of a **raise**, not a cut.
xa: The **100 bps** CRR cut to **3%** released about **₹2.5 lakh crore**.
CRR/SLR cuts are part of **cheap money** (expansionary) policy.

nf8524f9dd0c.s: The MCLR framework was intended mainly to achieve:
o: A single lending rate fixed by the RBI for all banks
Faster transmission of policy-rate changes to borrowers
Higher statutory reserves with the RBI
nf8524f9dd0c.x: MCLR aimed at transparency and faster transmission; it remained an internal benchmark calculated by each bank.
xa: MCLR introduced **1 April 2016**.
Example: **HDFC Bank** raised MCLR by up to **10 bps** on **8 Jun 2026** → 1-year MCLR **8.40%**.
Weak MCLR transmission led to **EBLR** (**1 Oct 2019**).

nb7149d8ce87.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about how a repo-rate cut can influence aggregate demand?
o: It works only through the interest-rate channel
It can work through the credit channel
It can work through the exchange-rate and asset-price channels
It can work through inflation expectations
nb7149d8ce87.x: A repo cut works through five recognised channels: interest-rate, credit, exchange-rate, asset-price and expectations, not the interest-rate channel alone.
xa: A rate cut **increases investment expenditure** (UPSC **2014**).
Mechanism: repo → **money-market rates** → **aggregate demand** → **inflation**.

n128a5da6d76.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about obstacles to monetary transmission in India?
o: Dependence on deposits may make banks reprice only new deposits
Administered small-savings rates can keep deposit rates elevated
Heavy government borrowing can keep yields high
