Informal credit markets are fully within the reach of RBI policy
n128a5da6d76.x: Informal credit markets remain outside the full reach of RBI policy, which is itself an obstacle to transmission.
xa: Other obstacles: **NPAs**, **structural rigidities**, **liquidity mismatches**.
GNPA is at a **multi-decadal low** of **2.2%** (Sep **2025**).

n2823605cfa3.s: Which of the following influence Indian government-security yields?
o: US Federal Reserve actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term rates
n2823605cfa3.x: G-sec yields are influenced by all three: US Fed actions, RBI actions, and domestic inflation and short-term interest rates.
xa: **OMO purchases** (**₹1 lakh crore**, Dec **2025**) were meant to **stabilise bond yields**.
A narrower **sovereign spread** over US bonds → lower borrowing costs.
**S&P** upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB** (**2025-26**).

nbc63e0f6c93.s: If the repo rate is 5.25 per cent, the MSF rate under the current corridor would be:
nbc63e0f6c93.x: The MSF rate is 25 basis points above repo (5.50%), and the SDF rate 25 basis points below it (5.00%).
xa: The corridor is **50 bps** wide (**5.00-5.50%**).
The **bank rate** equals the MSF.
⚠ MSF began in **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**.

nindian-economy-38-9.s: Central bank policy rates directly regulate which of the following?
o: The order of liquidity among deposits
The difference between M3 and M1
The composition of narrow money only
nindian-economy-38-9.x: Policy rates directly control how much credit banks can create. The other options are definitions of money measures.
nindian-economy-38-9.tq: Recall what policy rates act on.
n: Central bank policy rates directly regulate the capacity for credit creation. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #38 · pp 56-58]
xs: Central bank policy rates **directly regulate** **the capacity for credit creation** — option **(3)**.
A **lower bank rate** **expands liquidity**; a **higher bank rate** **contracts liquidity**.
The other options describe money measures: the **liquidity order** of deposits and **M3 minus M1** (= **time deposits**) are not set by policy rates.
xa: **Lower bank rate** = **expansionary stance**; **higher bank rate** = **tight stance**.
**MSF** began **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**; now **25 bps above repo**.
⚠ MSF borrowing limit: **1%** of NDTL (2011) vs **2%** now.

nindian-economy-40-2.s: Which of the following about the Reverse Repo is NOT correct?
o: Under it, banks borrow from the RBI
It is used to absorb surplus liquidity
It is a monetary policy tool
Under it, the RBI borrows from banks
nindian-economy-40-2.x: Under reverse repo the RBI borrows from banks to absorb surplus liquidity; banks borrowing from the RBI is repo.
n: The Reverse Repo Rate is the rate at which the RBI borrows from banks. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
A bank parks money with the RBI under the Reverse Repo Rate mechanism. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Reverse Repo Rate is used to absorb surplus liquidity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Reverse Repo Rate is associated with monetary policy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
xa: Under **repo**, a **bank borrows** from the RBI — **liquidity injection**.
**Reverse repo rate** = **3.35%** (May 2026); used at RBI's discretion since **SDF**.
**SDF** absorbs surplus **without collateral** — floor of the LAF corridor at **5.00%**.

nindian-economy-42-4.s: The RBI's principal policy lending rate is the:
nindian-economy-42-4.x: Repo is the main policy lending rate and the tool for regular liquidity; MSF is for emergency, marginal needs.
n: Repo is the principal policy lending rate in the source framework. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is used for marginal or short-term liquidity needs. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: MSF is an **overnight borrowing facility** that can involve **dipping** into the **SLR portfolio**.
**MSF** traditionally costs **more** than repo; now repo + **25 bps**.
The **policy repo rate** is the **main instrument** — the single operating policy rate under **FIT**.

nindian-economy-51-11.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) are associated with which of the following?
nindian-economy-51-11.x: Open market operations, the RBI buying and selling government securities, are a monetary-policy tool. Public revenue belongs to fiscal policy.
n: OMO is a monetary policy instrument. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #51 · pp 75-77]
xs: **Open Market Operations** are associated with **monetary policy** — option **(1)**.
OMO means the **RBI buying or selling government securities**; a **sale absorbs** and a **purchase injects** liquidity.
⚠ **Public revenue** is associated with **fiscal policy**, which uses **spending, taxes, subsidies and borrowing**.
xa: **OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity — e.g. **₹1 lakh crore** of purchases in **Dec 2025**.
FY26 OMO purchases: **₹2.39 lakh crore** (**Apr-May 2025**).
A **decrease** in the **Bank Rate** **increases liquidity**; an increase is **contractionary**.
To control inflation (**dear money**), the RBI **sells G-secs**; to boost growth, it **buys G-secs**.

n3bd0f5c5e9c.s: The gradual reduction in the SLR from its 1991-92 level was undertaken on the advice of the
n3bd0f5c5e9c.x: The SLR was gradually reduced after the recommendations of the Narasimham Committee on financial-sector reforms.
n3bd0f5c5e9c.tq: Use the committee-recommendation trap by matching the reform with the correct committee.
xs: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham Committee**'s advice — option **(2)**.
It fell from **38.5%** of NDTL (**1991-92**) to **18%** now.
xa: SLR statutory range: **0-40%**; the **25%** floor went in **2007**.
SLR is governed by **Sec 24** of the **BR Act, 1949**.

n078a4fb08eb.s: The Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is governed by which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
n078a4fb08eb.x: CRR is governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act; SLR by Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.
xa: CRR now **3%** of NDTL; SLR **18%**.
"Required reserve ratio" = **CRR** (APPSC **2023**).

n15c8a60fe21.s: The SLR, which was 38.5 per cent in 1991–92, stood at what level in September 2023?
n15c8a60fe21.x: The SLR was 18 per cent in September 2023, down from 38.5 per cent in 1991–92.
xa: SLR was cut gradually on the **Narasimham** Committee's advice.
SLR statutory range **0-40%**; **25%** floor removed in **2007**.
CRR was **4%** before the **2025** cuts → **3%** now.

n8c6c34d64d2.s: A bank is allowed to lend ₹70 against a security valued at ₹100. If the margin requirement is raised, the immediate effect will generally be to
o: increase the value of the security automatically
convert the loan into an equity investment
reduce the loan available against the same security
increase the loan available against the same security
n8c6c34d64d2.x: The margin is the gap between the value of the security and the loan. Raising the margin reduces the amount that can be borrowed against the same security.
n8c6c34d64d2.tq: Apply the inverse relationship between margin requirements and credit availability.
xs: Raising the margin will **reduce the loan available against the same security** — option **(3)**.
**Margin** = gap between the **value of the security** and the **loan**.
Higher margin = **smaller loan** → cuts credit against that security.
xa: Margin requirement is a **qualitative (selective)** tool.
⚠ **Moral suasion**, **margin requirements**, **direct action** = qualitative; **CRR, SLR, OMO** = quantitative.

nd80b30e8fce.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the monetary policy framework followed in India during 1985–1998?
nd80b30e8fce.x: During 1985–1998, India followed monetary targeting with feedback, with M3 as the principal monetary aggregate.
nd80b30e8fce.tq: Directly identify the framework associated with the given period.
xs: During **1985-1998** India followed **monetary targeting with feedback** (using **M3**) — option **(3)**.
The **multiple indicator approach** came in **1998-2016**; **flexible inflation targeting** from **2016**.
xa: Landmarks of that phase: **Chakravarty Committee 1985**, **Vaghul Committee 1987** (money market).
Multiple-indicator landmarks: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **Base Rate 2010**, **MSF 2011**, **MCLR 2016**.
**Shaktikanta Das** traced these phases in "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" (**24 Jan 2020**).

naaff5f965d5.s: The Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) was introduced in:
naaff5f965d5.x: MSF came in 2011, after LAF (2000) and MSS (2004), and before MCLR (2016).
xa: **Base Rate** came in **2010**, between MSS and MSF.
**SDF** began in **April 2022**, under the FIT phase.
All four belong to the **1998-2016** multiple indicator era (MCLR at its end).

na9d1bd31b97.s: India's flexible inflation-targeting framework is based on the recommendations of which committee?
na9d1bd31b97.x: The Urjit Patel Committee reported in 2014, the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement followed in 2015 and the RBI Act was amended in 2016.
xa: **SDF** (**2022**) is a later landmark of the FIT phase.
Under FIT, the **repo rate** is the **single operating policy rate**.
**Price stability** is the paramount objective.

n927552bef2b.s: India adopted the flexible inflation-targeting framework in:
n927552bef2b.x: Flexible inflation targeting began in 2016, after the multiple indicator approach of 1998–2016.
xa: **Money supply (M3)** targeting was the **1985-1998** framework.
The approach was dropped for being **opaque**.
Landmarks of the era: **LAF 2000**, **MSS 2004**, **MSF 2011**.

nd18fbf57c4a.s: Which of the following rates is correctly classified as a rate fixed by the RBI or the Monetary Policy Committee rather than by an individual bank or the market?
o: Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate
nd18fbf57c4a.x: The MSF rate is fixed by the RBI/MPC. MCLR is computed by each bank, EBLR is linked to an external benchmark, and the call money rate is market-determined.
nd18fbf57c4a.tq: Separate official policy rates from bank-specific benchmarks and market-determined rates.
xs: The **Marginal Standing Facility rate** is fixed by **RBI/MPC** — option **(3)**.
**MCLR** is set by **each bank**; **EBLR** is a bank's spread over an external benchmark.
The **call money rate** (WACR) is **market-determined**.
xa: RBI/MPC also fix **repo, SDF, bank rate, reverse repo, CRR, SLR**.
⚠ **SLR** and **CRR** are set by RBI, not by banks.

n97fec358c6f.s: The Base Rate system of bank lending was introduced on:
n97fec358c6f.x: The Base Rate came on 1 July 2010 and was based on the average cost of funds; MCLR (2016) uses the marginal cost of funds.
xa: Base Rate gave **slow transmission**.
**EBLR** from **1 October 2019**.

nc368e156b61.x: The Marginal Cost of Funds-based Lending Rate system was introduced on 1 April 2016.
nc368e156b61.tq: Test the close dates of successive lending-rate benchmark reforms.
xs: **MCLR** was introduced on **1 April 2016** — option **(2)**.
**1 July 2010** is the **Base Rate**; **1 October 2019** is **EBLR**.
xa: MCLR is based on the **marginal cost of funds** + CRR/SLR carry + operating cost + **tenor premium**.
**Janak Raj** group (**2017**) found MCLR transmission weak.
MCLR came at the end of the **1998-2016** multiple-indicator phase.

n1cdf1797e09.s: From 1 October 2019, new floating-rate personal, retail and micro, small and medium enterprise loans were required to be linked to
o: an external benchmark such as the repo rate or specified Treasury-bill yield
the BPLR fixed by the RBI
the average call money rate of the preceding financial year
an internal benchmark selected by the borrowing customer
n1cdf1797e09.x: From 1 October 2019, such loans had to be linked to an external benchmark, including the repo rate, the three- or six-month Treasury-bill yield, or an FBIL-published rate.
n1cdf1797e09.tq: Apply the external-benchmark rule to the specified category of floating-rate loans.
xs: From **1 October 2019**, such loans must link to **an external benchmark such as the repo rate or T-bill yield** — option **(1)**.
Benchmarks: **repo rate**, **3-month** or **6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL**-published rate.
**BPLR** was an old bank-set benchmark; the choice is not the borrower's internal pick.
xa: Loans linked directly to repo are the **fastest route** of transmission.
The mandate followed the **Janak Raj** Internal Study Group (**2017**).

nd2def7f6e7d.s: Which of the following best distinguishes the Base Rate system from the MCLR system?
o: Base Rate used average cost of funds, whereas MCLR uses marginal cost of funds
Base Rate used marginal cost of funds, whereas MCLR used average cost of funds
Base Rate is applicable only to government securities, whereas MCLR applies only to deposits
Both Base Rate and MCLR are directly linked to the repo rate
nd2def7f6e7d.x: The Base Rate was based on the average cost of funds and therefore transmitted policy changes slowly. MCLR uses marginal cost components, including marginal deposit costs, CRR/SLR carry, operating cost and tenor premium.
nd2def7f6e7d.tq: Discriminate between two closely related benchmark-rate systems by their cost-of-funds basis.
xs: **Base Rate used average cost of funds**, whereas **MCLR uses marginal cost of funds** — option **(1)**.
Option (2) reverses them.
Neither is directly linked to repo; that is **EBLR** — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Base Rate: **1 July 2010**; MCLR: **1 April 2016**.
MCLR adds **CRR/SLR carry**, **operating cost** and **tenor premium**.

n5ef9c2df651.s: Which one of the following represents the fastest route of monetary-policy transmission to lending rates?
o: Loans linked to fixed small-savings rates
Loans linked to the Base Rate
n5ef9c2df651.x: EBLR links lending rates directly to an external benchmark such as the repo rate, allowing loans to reprice more quickly than Base Rate or MCLR loans.
n5ef9c2df651.tq: Identify the institutional mechanism that transmits a policy-rate change most directly.
xs: **Loans linked to EBLR** are the fastest transmission route — option **(1)**.
EBLR loans linked directly to **repo** **reprice quickly**.
**MCLR** and deposit rates adjust **slowly**; **Base Rate** was slow too.
xa: **Administered small-savings rates** hold deposit rates up — an obstacle to transmission.
Outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lags fresh loans (**8.5%**) because MCLR loans reset periodically.

n55193bd9931.s: The Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system, constituted by the RBI in 2017, was chaired by whom?
n55193bd9931.x: The RBI’s Internal Study Group on the working of the MCLR system was chaired by Janak Raj in 2017.
n55193bd9931.tq: Use the committee-chairperson association to identify the correct answer.
xs: The **2017** Internal Study Group on MCLR was chaired by **Janak Raj** — option **(2)**.
It found **MCLR transmission weak** and recommended an **external benchmark**.
xa: Outcome: **EBLR mandate from 1 Oct 2019**.
⚠ **Urjit Patel Committee** (**2014**) led to **flexible inflation targeting**, not EBLR.

n524b0fb9361.s: Following the RBI's Internal Study Group on MCLR, the external benchmark-based lending rate (EBLR) became mandatory from:
n524b0fb9361.x: The study group found weak MCLR transmission and recommended an external benchmark, leading to the EBLR mandate from 1 October 2019.
xa: EBLR benchmarks: **repo**, **3-month**/**6-month** T-bill yield, or an **FBIL** rate.
EBLR covers new floating **personal/retail and MSME** loans.

n999458ae1ad.s: Why do interest rates on outstanding MCLR-linked loans generally respond more slowly than rates on EBLR-linked loans?
o: MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically, whereas EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly
MCLR-linked loans are unrelated to bank funding costs
Outstanding loans are excluded from monetary transmission
EBLR-linked loans are reset only once a year by law
n999458ae1ad.x: MCLR-linked loans reset at periodic intervals, creating a lag. EBLR-linked loans are directly linked to an external benchmark and reprice more quickly.
n999458ae1ad.tq: Discriminate between periodic reset behaviour and rapid external-benchmark repricing.
xs: **MCLR-linked loans reset only periodically**, whereas **EBLR-linked loans reprice quickly** — option **(1)**.
That is why outstanding-loan WALR (**9.26%**) lagged fresh-loan WALR (**8.5%**) in Sep **2025**.
xa: **Deposit rates** and **MCLR** adjust slowly.
WALR on fresh loans fell **64 bps** in **FY26** (ES **2025-26**).

nindian-economy-42-2.s: Which of the following about the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is NOT correct?
o: It is an overnight borrowing facility
Banks borrow from the RBI under it
Its rate is usually repo plus 0.25%
Its rate is lower than the repo rate
nindian-economy-42-2.x: MSF costs more than repo, usually repo plus 0.25%; it is an overnight emergency window, while repo is for regular liquidity.
n: Marginal Standing Facility (MSF) is an overnight borrowing facility. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Banks borrow from the RBI through the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF). [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
The MSF rate traditionally carries a higher cost than the repo rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
Repo is used for regular liquidity management. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 62-63]
xa: Under MSF banks can **dip into** their **SLR portfolio** up to **2%** of NDTL.
MSF began **May 2011** at repo + **100 bps**, up to **1%** of NDTL.
Corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.

n876b9475e84.s: The policy repo rate is regarded as the main monetary-policy instrument because the Monetary Policy Committee sets it primarily to
o: achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates
determine the annual SLR ceiling of 40 per cent
fix the exchange rate of the Indian rupee permanently
n876b9475e84.x: The MPC sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target, while liquidity operations help keep money-market rates close to that rate.
n876b9475e84.tq: Connect the policy instrument with the objective it is designed to achieve.
xs: The MPC sets the repo rate to **achieve the inflation target and guide money-market rates** — option **(1)**.
Liquidity is managed so **money-market rates stay near** the repo rate.
The **SLR ceiling of 40%** is statutory, not set via the repo rate.
xa: The repo is the **single operating policy rate** under **FIT** and the **most-watched signal**.
**OMOs** are the main tool for **durable** liquidity.

n5b098d598c8.s: When the RBI raises the repo rate, the first effect in the transmission sequence is:
n5b098d598c8.x: The sequence is higher money-market rates, then costlier credit, then lower consumption and investment, and finally lower aggregate demand.
xa: A rate cut **increases investment expenditure** (UPSC **2014**).
⚠ A rate cut does not raise savings or tax collection.
Transmission channels: **interest rate, credit, exchange rate, asset price, expectations**.

n092d270b877.s: Surplus liquidity in the banking system generally pulls market rates:
o: Below the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, speeding up transmission
Above the repo rate, weakening transmission
Below the repo rate, weakening transmission
n092d270b877.x: Surplus liquidity can lower market rates below the repo rate and aid transmission; deficit liquidity tends to weaken it.
xa: By **3 Sep 2026** surplus of about **₹10.32 lakh crore** had pushed the **call rate below repo**.
RBI drained it via **VRRR**.
Governor (Feb **2026**): RBI to keep "**sufficient liquidity**" for transmission.

n6e5d2f68813.s: The RBI may sterilise the liquidity effects of capital flows through MSS, OMO and:
n6e5d2f68813.x: Under an open capital account, flows alter liquidity and the rupee, and the RBI can sterilise them through MSS, OMO and VRRR.
xa: Example: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn** (Sep **2026**).
**MSS** (April **2004**) proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

n8054b3f25fa.s: Which of the following monetary-policy stances is INCORRECTLY described?
o: Neutral – rates can move either way, depending on the data
Accommodative – supports growth with ample liquidity; rate cuts likely
Calibrated tightening – no cuts; hikes measured, not at every meeting
Hawkish – worried about growth, with a bias towards easing
n8054b3f25fa.x: A hawkish stance worries about inflation and tightens; concern for growth with an easing bias is dovish.
xa: Stance path: neutral → **accommodative** (Apr **2025**) → **neutral** (**June 2025**) → retained through Aug **2026**.
**Hawkish** stance tightens: **raises rates** and **drains liquidity**.

n86e4ece16ad.s: A rise in the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) generally:
o: Raises demand for goods and services
n86e4ece16ad.x: A higher CRR withdraws lendable funds, reducing money in circulation and demand.
xa: CRR = share of **NDTL** kept as **cash with RBI**, earning **no interest**.
CRR is now **3%** of NDTL after a **100 bps** cut.
To control inflation (dear money): **raise** CRR, SLR, repo; **sell** G-secs.

nfe191d11103.s: The RBI's primary window for managing day-to-day liquidity through repo, reverse repo and SDF operations is the:
nfe191d11103.x: LAF is the framework through which the RBI injects liquidity via repo and absorbs it via reverse repo and SDF on a day-to-day basis.
xa: LAF was introduced in **2000**.
The LAF corridor: **SDF (5.00%)** floor, **MSF (5.50%)** ceiling — **50 bps** wide.
**VRR/VRRR** are auction-based LAF tools.

n9feeaeadd9e.s: Which LAF instrument absorbs surplus liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF?
n9feeaeadd9e.x: VRRR is an auction-based tool that absorbs liquidity for maturities longer than the overnight SDF, while VRR injects liquidity.
xa: They keep **short rates near repo**.
By **4 Sep 2026** RBI absorbed about **₹6.02 lakh crore** through two **3-day** VRRRs.

n8669a757d3c.s: Fine-tuning operations of the Reserve Bank of India are primarily conducted to
o: keep system liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance
determine the annual financial statements of banks
fix the statutory floor for the SLR
replace all permanent open market operations
n8669a757d3c.x: Fine-tuning operations, generally involving short-term VRR or VRRR auctions, are conducted to align liquidity conditions with the prevailing monetary policy stance.
n8669a757d3c.tq: Match a specialised operational tool with its precise policy objective.
xs: Fine-tuning operations aim to **keep liquidity in line with the monetary policy stance** — option **(1)**.
They are **short VRR/VRRR auctions**.
xa: RBI ran **49** fine-tuning operations in **FY2024** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
**OMOs** remain the main tool for **durable** liquidity — fine-tuning does not replace them.
Stance was **neutral** through Aug **2026**.

n5ba9e5c76c6.s: The temporary incremental CRR (I-CRR) announced by the RBI on 10 August 2023 was:
n5ba9e5c76c6.x: The temporary I-CRR was 10%, announced on 10 August 2023; it impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore.
xa: In APPSC-G2 **2025**, both I-CRR statements asked were correct.
Regular **CRR** is now **3%** of NDTL.
**Fine-tuning operations**: **49** in **FY2024**.

n71212d292b5.s: Open Market Operations (OMO) of the RBI involve outright purchase or sale of:
n71212d292b5.x: OMO is the outright purchase or sale of government securities to manage durable liquidity, conducted through banks.
xa: FY26 injections: **₹2.39 lakh crore** OMO purchases (Apr-May **2025**).
OMO **sale absorbs**; **purchase injects**.
**₹1 lakh crore** of purchases in Dec **2025** to **stabilise bond yields**.

n1ae31222ee7.s: A USD/INR buy-sell swap conducted by the RBI, such as a 3-year swap of $5 billion in December 2025, primarily:
o: Directly fixes the yield on all government securities
Injects rupee liquidity without changing the size of the RBI's balance sheet
Raises the CRR without affecting market liquidity
Absorbs rupee liquidity and permanently reduces foreign-exchange reserves
n1ae31222ee7.x: The specified buy-sell swap injects rupee liquidity while not changing the size of the RBI's balance sheet.
n1ae31222ee7.tq: Identify the liquidity and balance-sheet effect of a central-bank foreign-exchange swap.
xs: The buy-sell swap **injects rupee liquidity without changing the size of RBI's balance sheet** — option **(2)**.
Example: **$5 bn**, **3-year**, **Dec 2025**.
xa: In Dec **2025** RBI paired it with **₹1 lakh crore** of OMO purchases.
Dec **2025** tightness came from **currency leakage, tax outflows, reserve needs**.
**LTRO (2020)**: **1-3 year** funds at the repo rate.

n471bf2d1fcb.s: The Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS), introduced in April 2004, was meant to:
o: Sterilise excess liquidity created by foreign-exchange purchases
Replace the repo for daily liquidity adjustment
n471bf2d1fcb.x: Under the MSS the RBI issues Treasury Bills and securities to absorb rupees created by forex purchases; the proceeds sit in a separate account the Government cannot spend.
xa: **MSS** securities count towards banks' **SLR**.
Sterilisation tools: **OMO/MSS** sales and **VRRRs**.

n7b74f5aff3a.s: Sterilisation by the Reserve Bank of India refers to:
o: Increasing currency circulation after a fall in exports
Absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by foreign-exchange inflows
Replacing open market operations with fiscal expenditure
Converting all foreign-exchange reserves into gold
n7b74f5aff3a.x: When foreign-exchange inflows increase rupee liquidity, the RBI may sell government securities or conduct liquidity-absorption operations to offset the impact. This process is called sterilisation.
n7b74f5aff3a.tq: Identify the policy operation by linking foreign-exchange inflows with offsetting domestic liquidity action.
xs: **Sterilisation** = **absorbing or offsetting excess rupee liquidity created by forex inflows** — option **(2)**.
RBI sells G-secs (**OMO/MSS**) or runs **VRRRs** to offset it.
xa: Sep **2026** case: **FCNR(B)** inflows of **$127.23 bn**.
**MSS** began in **April 2004**.
Under an **open capital account**, flows move liquidity and the rupee.

n2f2e97e9647.s: Which of the following measures is most appropriate for a supply-driven food or fuel inflation shock rather than a purely demand-driven inflationary situation?
o: Buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms
Reducing the money multiplier through higher CRR
n2f2e97e9647.x: Supply-driven food and fuel inflation may require buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms, whereas CRR, SLR and policy rates primarily influence aggregate demand.
n2f2e97e9647.tq: Apply the demand-side versus supply-side distinction to select the suitable response.
xs: For supply-driven shocks, **buffer stocks, duty cuts and farm reforms** are needed — option **(2)**.
**Monetary tools are demand-side tools only** — rate hikes cannot add onions or tomatoes to the market.
So raising the **repo**, **CRR** or **SLR** alone (options 1, 3, 4) does not fix a supply shock.
xa: **Food inflation** is mostly **supply-driven**; RBI has little reach over it.
**Fiscal policy** acts on demand **directly**; monetary policy **indirectly** through interest rates.

n5037bd19c3c.s: Automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills was discontinued in 1997 and replaced by
n5037bd19c3c.x: The system of automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills ended in 1997 and was replaced by Ways and Means Advances.
n5037bd19c3c.tq: Test the reform by distinguishing the replacement mechanism from other liquidity instruments.
xs: Automatic monetisation through **ad hoc T-bills** ended in **1997** and was replaced by **Ways and Means Advances** — option **(1)**.
This was a response to **fiscal dominance** (large Government borrowing).
**MSS** (**2004**) is for **sterilisation**; **EBLR** (**2019**) is a lending benchmark; **MSF** (**2011**) is a penal window.
xa: **Heavy Government borrowing** keeps yields high (**crowding out**) and weakens transmission.
Other post-1991 challenges: **exchange-rate volatility** (main one), **external shocks**, weak transmission.

nf704cbc9325.s: Which one of the following was the main post-1991 challenge to monetary policy identified in India?
o: Exchange-rate volatility arising from capital flows
nf704cbc9325.x: Exchange-rate volatility caused by capital inflows and outflows was a major post-1991 challenge. The other conditions were not identified as the principal challenge.
nf704cbc9325.tq: Use elimination of reversed or exaggerated macroeconomic conditions to identify the principal challenge.
xs: The main post-1991 challenge was **exchange-rate volatility arising from capital flows** — option **(2)**.
This was asked in APPSC-GS **2023**.
⚠ Forex reserves were NOT a problem, inflation was not low, revenue was not in surplus — so options (1), (3), (4) are traps.
xa: Under an **open capital account**, RBI sterilises flows via **MSS, OMO, VRRR**.
Other challenges: **external shocks** (oil, global rate cycles, wars), **fiscal dominance**, weak transmission.

na575f3deebf.s: Fiscal dominance in the monetary-policy context is most closely associated with
o: exclusive reliance on foreign capital for infrastructure
large government borrowing exerting pressure on money supply and inflation
the RBI losing authority over the call money market
banks independently fixing the CRR and SLR
na575f3deebf.x: Large government borrowing, and earlier automatic monetisation through ad hoc Treasury Bills, could increase money supply and inflation, producing fiscal dominance.
na575f3deebf.tq: Translate the institutional term into its cause-and-effect relationship with borrowing, money supply and inflation.
xs: **Fiscal dominance** = **large government borrowing** pressuring money supply and inflation — option **(2)**.
Earlier it worked through **automatic monetisation via ad hoc T-bills**, ended in **1997**.
**CRR and SLR** are set by **RBI**, not banks — option (4) is wrong.
xa: Ad hoc T-bills were replaced by **Ways and Means Advances**.
**Heavy Government borrowing** keeps yields high (**crowding out**), an obstacle to transmission.

n067a5a526ab.s: A narrowing spread between Indian sovereign yields and US bond yields:
o: Ends the need for domestic bond issuance
n067a5a526ab.x: A narrower spread reduces the relative cost of borrowing for India.
xa: **S&P** upgraded India from **BBB- to BBB** (**2025-26**).
G-sec yields are driven by the **US Fed**, **RBI** and **inflation/short-term rates**.

n682c433c420.s: Who traced the phases of India's monetary-policy evolution in the lecture titled “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy”?
n682c433c420.x: Governor Shaktikanta Das traced these phases in “Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy” on 24 January 2020 at St. Stephen's College.
n682c433c420.tq: Test the speaker, title and date as a linked current-affairs fact.
xs: **Shaktikanta Das** gave "**Seven Ages of India's Monetary Policy**" — option **(2)**.
It was delivered on **24 Jan 2020** at **St. Stephen's College** (APPSC-GS **2024** statement).
xa: Phases: **1985-1998** monetary targeting; **1998-2016** multiple indicators; **2016** onwards FIT.
FIT came via **Urjit Patel Committee 2014**, **MPFA 2015**, RBI Act amended **2016**.

nf38687f7e94.s: In the context of RBI's monetary policy instruments, the term 'required reserve ratio' refers to which one of the following?
nf38687f7e94.x: The required reserve ratio is the CRR: the share of NDTL banks must keep as a cash balance with the RBI (Sec 42, RBI Act), earning no interest. SLR is a liquidity ratio held by banks themselves in cash, gold and approved securities, not a reserve with the RBI. CRAR and LCR are Basel prudential ratios on capital and liquidity, not reserve requirements.
nf38687f7e94.tq: Required reserve = cash parked with RBI = CRR (APPSC 2023 trap).
xs: The **required reserve ratio** is the **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR)** — option **(1)** (APPSC **2023** trap).
CRR is the share of **NDTL** kept as **cash with RBI**, earning **no interest** (**Sec 42**, RBI Act).
**SLR** is held by banks themselves in liquid assets, not a reserve with RBI.
xa: CRR = **3%** of NDTL after a **100 bps** cut.
Raising CRR means **less money in circulation** and **lower demand** (APPSC-G1 **2022**).
⚠ Raising CRR does NOT raise purchasing power or banks' lending capacity.

n9cc9dc596d9.s: A cut in the policy repo rate by the RBI is most likely to:
n9cc9dc596d9.x: Through the interest-rate channel, a rate cut makes loans cheaper, raising consumption and investment expenditure (UPSC 2014). It does not raise savings - lower rates reduce the reward for saving - nor does it raise tax collection, which is a fiscal matter. Cheaper funds increase, not reduce, bank credit.
n9cc9dc596d9.tq: Rate cut -> cheaper loans -> more investment; not more savings or taxes.
xs: A repo cut is most likely to **increase investment expenditure** — option **(1)** (UPSC **2014**).
Cheaper loans raise **consumption and investment** through the **interest-rate channel**.
⚠ It does not raise **savings** or **tax collection**; cheaper funds raise, not reduce, bank credit.
xa: **Credit channel**: banks have more funds and **lend more**.
**Asset price** channel: bond and equity prices rise — a wealth effect.

nindian-economy-40-5.s: Which of the following is used by the RBI to absorb surplus liquidity?
nindian-economy-40-5.x: Absorbing surplus liquidity is the role of reverse repo; the Bank Rate is the RBI's long-term rediscount rate on bills of exchange and commercial paper.
n: The Reverse Repo Rate is used to absorb surplus liquidity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
The Bank Rate is a traditional rate associated with RBI lending or rediscounting. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
Bank Rate transactions involve bills of exchange or commercial paper. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
Bank lending or rediscounting is associated with the Bank Rate. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 60-61]
xa: **Bank Rate** = **5.50%**, aligned with **MSF**; penal rates for **CRR/SLR shortfalls** are linked to it.
**SLR shortfall penalty:** **bank rate + 3%** a year → **bank rate + 5%** if it continues.
**Repo** is lending **against eligible securities** for **liquidity management**.

n5022f2532df.s: Which committee recommended monetary targeting with feedback and was associated with the organised money market in India?
n5022f2532df.x: The Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee, constituted in 1985, recommended monetary targeting with feedback and dealt with the organised money market.
n5022f2532df.tq: Use the committee–recommendation association to distinguish closely related monetary-policy committees.
xs: The **Sukhamoy Chakravarty Committee** (**1985**) recommended **monetary targeting with feedback** — option **(1)**.
It dealt with the **organised money market** (UPSC), with money supply growth as the anchor.
**Vaghul** (**1987**) gave the money-market blueprint; **Tarapore** dealt with capital account convertibility; **Urjit Patel** (**2014**) with FIT.
xa: ⚠ Order: **1985** Chakravarty – **1987** Vaghul – **1997** Tarapore – **2014** Urjit Patel.
Monetary targeting was the framework of **1985-1998**.

n767c6d85768.s: The blueprint for the money market that subsequently led to the introduction of Commercial Paper in 1990 was associated with which committee?
n767c6d85768.x: N. Vaghul headed the 1987 committee that prepared a blueprint for the money market and contributed to the introduction of Commercial Paper in 1990.
n767c6d85768.tq: Match the named committee with its distinctive market-reform contribution.
xs: The **N. Vaghul** Committee (**1987**) gave the **money-market blueprint** that led to **Commercial Paper** (**1990**) — option **(2)**.
**Chakravarty** (**1985**) gave monetary targeting; **Tarapore** (**1997**) the convertibility roadmap.
xa: **Urjit Patel** Committee (**2014**): **CPI** as nominal anchor, **4% ±2%** target, an MPC.
⚠ **1985** Chakravarty – **1987** Vaghul – **1997** Tarapore – **2014** Urjit Patel.

n21d52042035.s: Which one of the following was NOT a feature of the Urjit Patel Committee’s recommendations?
o: Creation of a committee to decide policy rates
Adoption of CPI as the nominal anchor
A 4 per cent inflation target with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points
Continuation of the multiple-indicator approach as the sole framework
n21d52042035.x: The Urjit Patel Committee recommended dropping the multiple-indicator approach, adopting CPI as the nominal anchor and establishing an MPC-based rate-setting framework.
n21d52042035.tq: Find the option that reverses the committee’s recommendation rather than merely changing a date or name.
xs: **Continuation of the multiple-indicator approach** was NOT recommended — option **(4)**; the Committee said **drop** it for **FIT**.
It did recommend **CPI as nominal anchor** (CPI-C), a **4% ±2%** target and a committee (**MPC**) to decide rates.
xa: Full name: **Expert Committee to Revise and Strengthen the Monetary Policy Framework**, set up by **RBI** in **2014**.
APPSC-G2 **2017** key: committee headed by **Urjit Patel**.
It was followed by the **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement** (**2015**).

n2d5f7cf1845.s: The RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted which range of sections into the RBI Act, 1934 in connection with the monetary policy framework?
n2d5f7cf1845.x: The 2016 amendment inserted Sections 45Z to 45ZO into the RBI Act, 1934, providing the statutory framework for the MPC and inflation-targeting provisions.
n2d5f7cf1845.tq: Test the exact statutory range, a common Article-or-section number trap.
xs: The **RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016** inserted **Sections 45Z to 45ZO** — option **(4)**.
These sections gave **statutory backing** to **flexible inflation targeting** and the **MPC**.
xa: **45ZA**: Centre (with RBI) sets the **inflation target** every five years.
**45ZB**: **MPC** constituted as a statutory body.
**45ZN**: failure = CPI **above 6% or below 2%** for **three consecutive quarters**.
APPSC-GS **2022** key: Act amended in **2016**.

n0552b18ea1d.s: In which year was the RBI Act, 1934 amended to give statutory backing to flexible inflation targeting and the Monetary Policy Committee?
n0552b18ea1d.x: The RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016 inserted Sections 45Z to 45ZO and gave FIT statutory backing. 2014 is the year of the Urjit Patel Committee report, and 2015 is the year of the Monetary Policy Framework Agreement, which was not a statute. 2018 has no link to this amendment.
xs: The RBI Act was amended for FIT in **2016** — option **(3)** (APPSC-GS **2022** key).
The **RBI (Amendment) Act, 2016** inserted **Sections 45Z to 45ZO**.
**2014** = **Urjit Patel** Committee; **2015** = **Monetary Policy Framework Agreement** (not a statute).
xa: The **MPC** held its first meeting in **October 2016**.
The first target notification came in **August 2016**.

n971c011763f.s: The decisions of the Monetary Policy Committee are:
o: Advisory and not binding on the RBI
Subject to approval by the RBI Central Board
n971c011763f.x: MPC decisions are binding on the RBI; the inflation target itself is set by the Central Government in consultation with the RBI.
xa: The MPC **fixes the policy repo rate** needed to reach the target.
Before the MPC, the **Governor decided alone**.

nf5020ee97bc.s: The inflation target is set by the Central Government, in consultation with the RBI, under which section of the RBI Act, 1934?
nf5020ee97bc.x: Section 45ZA covers the inflation target (set every five years and notified in the Gazette); Section 45ZB constitutes the MPC.
xa: ⚠ Many books wrongly print **45ZB** for the target.
**45ZN** = failure clause.

n062eae556e9.s: Under Section 45ZN of the RBI Act, failure to meet the inflation target is deemed to occur when the average CPI inflation remains
o: above 4 per cent or below 2 per cent for four consecutive quarters
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters
above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive months
above 5 per cent or below 3 per cent for two consecutive quarters
n062eae556e9.x: Failure is defined as average CPI inflation remaining above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent for three consecutive quarters. The statutory wording refers to quarters, not months.
n062eae556e9.tq: Trap the month-versus-quarter confusion while retaining the correct inflation bands.
xs: Failure = average CPI **above 6 per cent or below 2 per cent** for **three consecutive quarters** — option **(2)**.
The Act says **quarters**, not months — option (3) is the common error.
xa: RBI must report the **reasons**, **remedial action** and **time to return** to target.
First invoked in **2022**, after CPI stayed above **6%** from **January 2022**.

n78914247747.s: When the inflation target is missed in the statutory manner, the Reserve Bank of India is required to report to the Government the
o: exchange-rate level it will maintain for the next financial year
reasons for failure, remedial actions and estimated time to return to the target
names of all MPC members and their individual salaries
future Union Budget allocations and tax rates
n78914247747.x: The RBI must report the reasons for the failure, the remedial actions proposed and the period within which inflation is expected to return to the target.
n78914247747.tq: Ask what the responsible institution must do after a statutory failure.
xs: RBI must report the **reasons for failure, remedial actions and estimated time to return to the target** — option **(2)**.
This is under **Section 45ZN** of the RBI Act.
xa: Failure: CPI **above 6% or below 2%** for **three consecutive quarters**.
First invoked in **2022**.
Under the **2015** Agreement, RBI is **answerable to the Government** when it misses.

nccdcc26690f.s: The Monetary Policy Committee is constituted under which provision of the RBI Act, 1934?
nccdcc26690f.x: Section 45ZB provides for the constitution of the Monetary Policy Committee. Section 45ZA concerns the inflation target, while Section 45ZN deals with failure to meet the target.
nccdcc26690f.tq: Separate the similar statutory provisions by matching each section with its specific function.
xs: The MPC is constituted under **Section 45ZB** — option **(4)**.
**45ZA** = inflation target; **45ZN** = failure clause.
xa: The MPC is a **statutory body** created by the **2016** amendment.
Its **first meeting** was in **October 2016**.

nf62bd2ca64d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the composition of the Monetary Policy Committee?
o: The RBI Governor is its Chairperson ex officio
The three external members are appointed by the RBI Central Board
The Deputy Governor in charge of monetary policy is an ex officio member
One RBI officer is nominated by the RBI Central Board
nf62bd2ca64d.x: The three external members are appointed by the Central Government (for four years), not by the RBI Central Board.
xa: External members serve a **4-year** term and are **not eligible for reappointment**.
**6** members = 3 from RBI + 3 from Government.

n56200d16a14.s: The external members of the Monetary Policy Committee are appointed for a term of
o: Four years and are not eligible for reappointment
Two years and are eligible for unlimited reappointment
Five years and are appointed by the RBI Central Board
Three years and are eligible for one reappointment
n56200d16a14.x: The three external members are appointed by the Central Government for four years and are not eligible for reappointment.
n56200d16a14.tq: Test the term and reappointment condition together as a paired fact.
xs: External members serve **four years and are not eligible for reappointment** — option **(1)**.
They are appointed by the **Central Government**, not the RBI Board — option (3) is wrong.
xa: The **RBI officer** member is nominated by the **RBI Central Board**.
⚠ **6** members – quorum **4** – at least **4** meetings – **4**-year term.

n2c66dfc7b1e.s: Which one of the following is the primary objective of monetary policy under the flexible inflation-targeting framework?
o: Maintaining price stability while keeping growth in mind
n2c66dfc7b1e.x: Price stability is the primary objective, with growth kept in mind. Financial stability is also a recognised objective, whereas the other functions listed are not primary monetary-policy objectives.
n2c66dfc7b1e.tq: Find the valid objective by separating monetary functions from fiscal and regulatory functions.
xs: The primary objective is **price stability**, with **growth kept in mind** — option **(3)**.
Growth comes second, "**keeping in mind**" the target (RBI Act); **financial stability** is also a goal.
Not objectives: **maximising Government revenue**, **fixing the rupee-dollar rate**, regulating **mutual funds** (**SEBI**).
xa: Target: **4% CPI-Combined**, band **2-6%**.
The **MPC** fixes the **repo rate** needed to reach the target.

n1ed25f04dde.s: By law, the Monetary Policy Committee must meet at least ____ times a year.
n1ed25f04dde.x: The law requires at least four meetings a year; meeting six times (bi-monthly) is only the practice.
xa: Decisions by **majority vote** (UPSC).
External members: **4-year** term, no reappointment.

nac70a059ed8.s: The inflation target notified for the period from 1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031 was:
o: 5 per cent with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points
4 per cent with a tolerance band of 2 percentage points
2 per cent with a tolerance band of 1 percentage point
6 per cent with a tolerance band of 1 percentage point
nac70a059ed8.x: The 25 March 2026 notification retained the 4 per cent CPI target with a 2 percentage point tolerance band for 2026–2031.
nac70a059ed8.tq: Read the target and tolerance band together rather than treating the upper limit as the target.
xs: The target for **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031** is **4 per cent** with a **2 percentage point** band — option **(2)**.
It was notified on **25 March 2026** — the **second retention** of the original target.
xa: Upper tolerance **6%**, lower **2%**.
Anchor: **CPI-Combined** compiled by **NSO (MoSPI)**.

ncbb92d86191.s: During the period from May 2022 to February 2023, the policy repo rate was raised from
ncbb92d86191.x: The repo rate was increased from 4 per cent to 6.5 per cent during May 2022–February 2023, reflecting a tightening phase.
ncbb92d86191.tq: Match the policy period with its exact rate range.
xs: During **May 2022 - Feb 2023**, repo was raised from **4.00 per cent to 6.50 per cent** — option **(1)**.
It was then **held till early 2025** — a tightening phase.
xa: CPI stayed above **6%** from **January 2022** → failure clause first invoked in **2022**.
Cuts since **Feb 2025** total **125 bps** (to **5.25%**).

n61bc54a06e7.s: In April 2025, when the repo rate was cut to 6 per cent, the RBI's monetary-policy stance moved from neutral to:
n61bc54a06e7.x: The stance moved from neutral to accommodative in April 2025 with the cut to 6 per cent; it was neutral in 2026 when the repo rate was held at 5.25 per cent.
xa: The **Apr 2025** cut of **25 bps** was the **2nd cut of 2025**.
Governor **Malhotra**: hardening inflation "may suggest a **recalibration**".

n753b7a0039b.s: The new CPI-Combined series released by the NSO (MoSPI) in February 2026 has the base year:
n753b7a0039b.x: CPI-Combined, the nominal anchor for the inflation target, is compiled by the NSO under MoSPI; the new series of 12 February 2026 has base year 2024 (earlier 2012).
xa: New-series retail inflation: **2.75%** (Jan **2026**); **3.4%** (Mar **2026**).
⚠ Some July **2026** notes still print base **2012**.

n1161b4729ba.s: Global monetary tightening can affect India through capital outflows, pressure on the rupee and:
n1161b4729ba.x: Tightening abroad can cause capital outflows, rupee pressure and imported inflation through exchange-rate and import-cost channels.
xa: In **June 2026** major central banks were **gearing up to tighten**.
RBI's special **FCNR(B)** and forex measures drew about **$32 bn** after the June policy.

n8396e51401e.s: The failure clause under India's flexible inflation-targeting framework was first invoked in:
n8396e51401e.x: The failure clause was first invoked in 2022; March 2026 marked the second retention of the original target.
xa: First retention: **March 2021** (April 2021 to March 2026).
The original target was notified in **August 2016**.

n9d3866cf5af.s: Critics of flexible inflation targeting in India argue that the headline inflation target should be replaced by:
n9d3866cf5af.x: Critics argue for a core-inflation target because food and supply shocks, which drive headline inflation, are outside the MPC's direct control.
xa: Target **4% +/- 2%** retained to **March 2031**.
The failure clause was first invoked in **2022**.

ncedfe31bd57.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the first bank in India?
ncedfe31bd57.x: Bank of Hindustan is regarded as the first bank in India. The Presidency Bank of Bengal was the first bank of the East India Company.
ncedfe31bd57.tq: Use the direct first-in-the-list recall approach.
xs: The first bank in India was the **Bank of Hindustan** (**1770**) — option **(4)**.
**1770** is the standard date (one APP note says **1779**).

The **Presidency Bank of Bengal** (**1806**) was the first bank of the **East India Company**; **Oudh (Awadh) Commercial Bank** (**1881**) the first run by Indians; **PNB** the first with wholly Indian capital.
xa: First credit card: **Central Bank of India** (**1980**).
First ATM: **HSBC**, Mumbai, **1987**.

nfdf02445a42.s: Equitas Small Finance Bank has its head office at:
nfdf02445a42.x: Equitas SFB is headquartered in Chennai; Capital SFB was established at Jalandhar.
xa: SFBs: **11** operational (Jul **2026**).
SFB licences have been **on tap since 2019**.

n54553015e1d.s: The first bank with wholly Indian capital and management was:
n54553015e1d.x: Punjab National Bank is described as the first bank with wholly Indian capital and management. Awadh Commercial Bank was the first bank run by Indians with limited liability and an all-Indian board.
n54553015e1d.tq: Distinguish the broader ownership-and-management distinction from the first Indian-run bank.
xs: **Punjab National Bank** (Lahore, **1894**/95) was the first bank with **wholly Indian capital and management** — option **(1)**.
**Oudh (Awadh) Commercial Bank** (**1881**) was the first run by Indians; PNB was the **second** bank established by Indians.
⚠ **Allahabad Bank (1865)** = oldest joint-stock bank, not the standard answer.
xa: **Lala Lajpat Rai** was among PNB's founders; HQ now **New Delhi**.
**United Bank of India** and **Oriental Bank of Commerce** are now part of **PNB**.

n8f7d7ee4355.s: Which of the following institutions was NOT founded by Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya?
n8f7d7ee4355.x: Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya founded Andhra Insurance Company, Bharat Lakshmi Bank and the Krishna District Co-operative Bank. Punjab National Bank was established separately in 1894.
n8f7d7ee4355.tq: Find the one institution outside the founder’s associated group.
xs: **Punjab National Bank** was NOT founded by Pattabhi Sitaramayya — option **(2)**; PNB was founded at Lahore (**1894**/95), with **Lala Lajpat Rai** among its founders.
Pattabhi founded **Andhra Insurance Co. (1925)**, **Bharat Lakshmi Bank** and **Krishna District Co-operative Bank**.
xa: He founded **Andhra Bank** (**20 Nov 1923**, **Machilipatnam**).
He was **INC President (1948-49)**.

ne82660c2a65.s: Dr. Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was also the President of the Indian National Congress during:
ne82660c2a65.x: Dr. Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was also INC President in 1948–49.
ne82660c2a65.tq: Use the precise year range rather than the bank’s year of establishment.
xs: Pattabhi Sitaramaiah was **INC President** in **1948-49** — option **(2)**.
**1923** is the year he founded **Andhra Bank**, not his Congress presidency.
xa: His ventures: **Andhra Insurance Co. (1925)**, **Bharat Lakshmi Bank**, **Krishna District Co-operative Bank**.
Andhra Bank merged into **Union Bank of India** in **2020**.

n58c79bbf809.s: Andhra Bank, founded at Machilipatnam in 1923 by Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya, was merged in 2020 into:
n58c79bbf809.x: Andhra Bank merged into Union Bank of India in 2020; Indian Bank absorbed Allahabad Bank.
xa: **Corporation Bank** (also 1980 batch) merged into **Union Bank** too.
In AP, **Union Bank of India** is the **lead bank / SLBC convener**.

n2a030ef7915.s: Dena Bank, nationalised in 1969, was later merged with:
n2a030ef7915.x: Dena Bank was merged with Bank of Baroda, not Bank of India.
xa: Other 1969 banks: **BoB, BoI, BoM, Central, IOB, UCO, Union**.
The 1969 nationalisation took **14** banks holding about **85%** of deposits.

nd1674d49cf0.s: The associate banks of the State Bank of India and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI on
nd1674d49cf0.x: The associate banks of SBI and Bharatiya Mahila Bank were merged into SBI with effect from 1 April 2017.
nd1674d49cf0.tq: Use the year-specific merger date to distinguish closely spaced alternatives.
xs: SBI's **associate banks** and **Bharatiya Mahila Bank** merged into SBI on **1 April 2017** — option **(2)**.
The merger took effect at the start of the financial year **2017** — not **2015**, **2016** or **2018**.
xa: SBI was created from the **Imperial Bank** in **1955**.
**SBI subsidiaries** were formed in **1959**.
SBI's first **overseas banking unit** is in **Mumbai** (APPSC-GS **2025**).

n5abeb278aaf.s: Which one of the following is a liability of a commercial bank?
n5abeb278aaf.x: Customer deposits are liabilities because the bank owes these amounts to depositors. Loans, investments and cash reserves are assets of the bank.
n5abeb278aaf.tq: Apply the ownership-and-obligation test to distinguish assets from liabilities.
xs: **Deposits accepted from customers** are a **liability** of a bank — so option **(4)** is correct.
The bank owes deposits back to depositors.
**Cash in hand**, **SLR investments** and **loans and advances** are **assets**.
xa: Liabilities: **capital and reserves**, **deposits** (current, savings, term), **borrowings**.
Assets: cash in hand, **balances with RBI (CRR)**, investments, loans and advances, fixed assets.
⚠ Deposits = liabilities vs loans = assets — the commonest balance-sheet trap.

nindian-economy-2-2.s: Which of the following about SBI and Regional Rural Banks is NOT correct?
o: SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank of India
The first RRB was set up on 2 October 1974
Prathama Grameen Bank was the first RRB
nindian-economy-2-2.x: The first RRB, Prathama Grameen Bank, opened on 2 October 1975, not 1974.
n: The SBI was established on 1 July 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The SBI was formed from the Imperial Bank of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
Prathama Grameen Bank was the first Regional Rural Bank. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
The first Regional Rural Bank was established on 2 October 1975. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 3-4]
xa: **Five RRBs** were set up in **1975**; the **RRB Act, 1976** followed an ordinance.
RRB ownership: **Centre 50% : sponsor bank 35% : State 15%**.
RRBs were recommended by the **M. Narasimham Working Group on Rural Banks** (**1975**).

nindian-economy-30-6.s: The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act was passed in:
nindian-economy-30-6.x: The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act came in 1959, after SBI (1955) and LIC (1956), and before the 1969 nationalisation.
n: SBI was established in 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC was nationalised in 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
The SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act was passed in 1959. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
14 major commercial banks were nationalised in 1969. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
SBI was established on July 1, 1955. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
The 14 major commercial banks were nationalised on July 19, 1969. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xa: Exact dates: SBI **1 July 1955**; LIC **1 September 1956**; first nationalisation **19 July 1969**.
Before all these: **RBI** nationalised on **1 January 1949**.
After: **second nationalisation** of **6 banks** on **15 April 1980**.

ne67b8847450.s: In which year was the Reserve Bank of India nationalised?
ne67b8847450.x: The RBI was nationalised in 1949, followed by SBI's formation (1955), 14 banks' nationalisation (1969) and six more (1980).
xa: **SBI subsidiaries** came in **1959**.
The **Lead Bank Scheme** also began in **1969**.

na0c825f08eb.s: The six banks nationalised on 15 April 1980 each had deposits of over:
na0c825f08eb.x: The 1980 round covered banks with deposits above ₹200 crore; the 1969 round covered 14 banks with deposits above ₹50 crore.
xa: The 1969 banks held about **85%** of deposits.
The **50th anniversary** fell on **19 July 2019**.

n620246b10d9.s: Which principle is associated with the governance of co-operative banks?
n620246b10d9.x: Co-operative banks follow the principle of one member, one vote.
n620246b10d9.tq: Distinguish the co-operative voting principle from share-based corporate voting.
xs: Co-operative banks follow **one member, one vote** — option **(4)**.
They are registered under **State Co-operative Societies Acts** and regulated by RBI (**BR Act**).
xa: India has **1,457** urban co-op banks (Aug **2026**).
RBI is resuming **on-tap UCB licences** (Aug **2026**).
AP rural co-op credit: **APCOB** (**18** branches), **13 DCCBs**, **2,024 PACS**.

nindian-economy-30-2.s: The Life Insurance Corporation of India was formed under the LIC Act, 1956 on:
nindian-economy-30-2.x: LIC was formed on 1 September 1956 by merging over 240 insurers and societies; 19 July 1969 is when 14 banks were nationalised.
n: LIC was nationalised on September 1, 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC was nationalised through the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
LIC nationalisation merged over 240 private insurers and societies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xa: **SBI** was established on **1 July 1955**; the **SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act** came in **1959**.
The **1959** Act brought **8 princely state-associated banks** under SBI — the **SBI Associate Banks**.
The **RBI** was nationalised on **1 January 1949**.

nindian-economy-30-10.s: Which of the following banks was NOT among those nationalised in 1980?
nindian-economy-30-10.x: The 1980 round covered Andhra, Corporation, New Bank of India, OBC, Punjab & Sind and Vijaya Banks; Syndicate Bank was among those nationalised in 1969.
n: Andhra Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Corporation Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
New Bank of India was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Oriental Bank of Commerce was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Punjab & Sind Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
Vijaya Bank was one of the six commercial banks nationalised in 1980. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xa: Fate: **Andhra Bank** and **Corporation Bank** → **Union Bank**; **OBC** → **PNB**; **Vijaya Bank** → **BoB**.
⚠ **Trap:** Some notes print "Oriental Bank of India"; the correct name is Oriental Bank of **Commerce**.
**Andhra Bank** was founded by **Dr Bhogaraju Pattabhi Sitaramayya** at **Machilipatnam** (**1923**).

n374cc1acb5d.s: Which of the following was a significant result associated with bank nationalisation?
o: Exclusive lending to large industrial houses
Expansion of bank branches and growth of priority-sector lending
Withdrawal of institutional credit from agriculture
Reduction in branch expansion and contraction of rural banking
n374cc1acb5d.x: Bank nationalisation was associated with expansion of branches and increased lending to priority sectors, including agriculture and small units.
n374cc1acb5d.tq: Choose the outcome consistent with the stated social-control objective.
xs: Nationalisation brought **expansion of bank branches** and **priority-sector lending** — option **(2)**.
Before it, **agriculture and small units were neglected** while industrial houses controlled banks.
xa: Motive: **social control of credit**.
The **Lead Bank Scheme** (**1969**) assigned each district a lead bank for credit planning.

nb858f2ded26.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks?
o: A Payments Bank can undertake lending
A Small Finance Bank can undertake lending
A Payments Bank can accept only demand deposits, within a per-customer limit
A Small Finance Bank must direct 75% of its ANBC to the priority sector
nb858f2ded26.x: Payments Banks cannot lend; they accept only demand deposits, while Small Finance Banks lend and must give 75% of ANBC to priority sectors.
xa: SFB purpose: credit to **small units**, **small/marginal farmers**, unorganised sector.
Payments bank purpose: **payments and remittances** for migrants, low-income households.

n4905ae544b3.s: The maximum deposit that a Payments Bank may accept from an individual customer is presently
n4905ae544b3.x: The present maximum deposit limit for a customer of a Payments Bank is ₹2 lakh; the earlier limit was ₹1 lakh.
n4905ae544b3.tq: Use the updated figure and distinguish it from the earlier regulatory limit.
xs: A payments bank may take up to **₹2 lakh** per customer — option **(2)**.
The **earlier** limit was **₹1 lakh** — option (1) is outdated.
xa: Payments banks take **demand deposits only** and **cannot lend**.
**75%** of demand deposits must be in **SLR G-secs/T-bills** of up to **1** year; CRAR **15%**.
RBI **cancelled Paytm Payments Bank's licence**.

nb7cb231540c.s: The Nachiket Mor Committee, linked to differentiated banking licences, was constituted in:
nb7cb231540c.x: The Nachiket Mor Committee was set up in 2013; Small Finance Banks and Payments Banks arose from such niche licences.
xa: Licence types: **universal** and **differentiated** (niche).
SFB licences **on tap since 2019**.
nb7cb231540c.fixed: Nachiket Mor Committee was set up in Sept 2013 but submitted its report in Jan 2014; reworded so key (all three) stays true

ncb0b673ba38.s: Allahabad Bank, later merged into Indian Bank, was established in:
ncb0b673ba38.x: Allahabad Bank dates from 1865 and was merged into Indian Bank.
xa: Allahabad Bank is the **oldest joint-stock bank**.
Both Allahabad and Syndicate were among the **14 banks** nationalised in **1969**.

nc2954590716.s: The setting up of Regional Rural Banks in 1975 was recommended by the:
nc2954590716.x: The Narasimham Working Group recommended RRBs in 1975; Prathama Grameen Bank was the first RRB.
xa: RRBs were created by **ordinance**, then the **RRB Act, 1976**.
Ownership: **Centre 50% : sponsor bank 35% : State 15%**.

n727da463764.s: The shareholding of a Regional Rural Bank among the Centre, the State Government and the sponsor bank is:
n727da463764.x: RRBs follow a 50:15:35 shareholding among the Central Government, State Government and sponsor bank.
xa: RRBs are **regulated by RBI**, **supervised by NABARD**.
RRB **PSL** target: **75%**.

na90ab4539ef.s: The Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance before being placed under which legislation?
na90ab4539ef.x: Regional Rural Banks were initially created through an ordinance and were subsequently governed by the Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976.
na90ab4539ef.tq: Test the legislative sequence rather than recalling only the year of establishment.
xs: RRBs were created by **ordinance**, then placed under the **Regional Rural Banks Act, 1976** — option **(3)**.
They followed the **Narasimham Working Group** (**1975**).
xa: First RRB: **Prathama Grameen Bank** (**2 Oct 1975**).
RRBs were allowed **commercial interest rates** from the late 1990s.

n908a4bc6efc.s: Regional Rural Banks are regulated by the RBI and supervised by:
n908a4bc6efc.x: RRBs are regulated by the Reserve Bank of India and supervised by NABARD.
xa: **One State-One RRB**: **15** RRBs amalgamated from **1 May 2025** → **28** today.
AP: **Andhra Pradesh Grameena Bank** merged the four AP RRBs (May **2026**).

n33517b9785f.s: Under the Service Area Approach (1989), each rural bank branch prepares credit plans for:
n33517b9785f.x: Under the Service Area Approach, each rural branch plans credit for a specified set of villages.
xa: The **Lead Bank Scheme** began in **1969**, the same year **14 banks** were nationalised.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district-level forum; the **SLBC** works at State level.
RBI issued a **draft revision of the Lead Bank Scheme** in **Feb 2026** to strengthen SLBCs and LDM offices.
⚠ **1969** = Lead Bank Scheme; **1989** = Service Area Approach.

nindian-economy-30-1.s: RBI was nationalised on which date under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948?
nindian-economy-30-1.x: The RBI was nationalised on 1 January 1949 under the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. 1 July 1955 is SBI, and 19 July 1969 the bank nationalisation.
nindian-economy-30-1.tq: Match each date to its event.
n: RBI was nationalised on January 1, 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
RBI was nationalised through the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
RBI was nationalised in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xs: The RBI was nationalised on **January 1, 1949** — option **(1)**.
It was done through the **RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948**.
**July 1, 1955** = **SBI** established; **July 19, 1969** = **14 banks** nationalised; **September 1, 1956** = **LIC** nationalised.
xa: The **Banking Regulation Act** was enacted in the same year, **1949**.
**C.D. Deshmukh** was the **first Indian Governor** of the RBI.
**SBI** was the **first public sector bank**; RBI bought **92%** of its shares.

nindian-economy-30-8.s: In which year was the Banking Regulation Act enacted?
nindian-economy-30-8.x: The Banking Regulation Act was passed in 1949, the same year the RBI was nationalised.
n: The Banking Regulation Act was enacted in 1949. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xs: The **Banking Regulation Act** was enacted in **1949** — option **(1)**.
It came in the same year the **RBI** was nationalised (**1 January 1949**).
**1948** is the RBI (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act; **1955** the **SBI Act**; **1959** the **SBI (Subsidiary Banks) Act**.
xa: Payments banks are licensed under **Section 22 of the BR Act, 1949**.
The **RRB Act, 1976** created RRBs after an ordinance.
**Co-operative banks** are regulated by RBI under the **BR Act**.

nbf9884b7a13.s: The Imperial Bank of India was formed by merging:
o: Punjab National Bank, Allahabad Bank and Canara Bank
Awadh Commercial Bank and Punjab National Bank
nbf9884b7a13.x: The Imperial Bank of India was formed by merging the three Presidency banks.
xa: Under the **SBI Act, 1955**, RBI bought **92%** of its shares.
SBI was the **first public sector bank**.

nd60e28d9e25.s: Scheduled banks are those listed in which Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934?
nd60e28d9e25.x: Scheduled banks are in the Second Schedule; they need paid-up capital and reserves of at least ₹5 lakh and can borrow from the RBI.
xa: Five ownership groups: **SBI, nationalised banks, RRBs, foreign banks, private banks**.
Also **SFBs**, **payments banks** and **local area banks**.

n170c1b17106.s: Payments banks in India are licensed under which provision?
o: Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949
n170c1b17106.x: Payments banks are licensed under Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and are public limited companies under the Companies Act, 2013. Section 42 of the RBI Act governs CRR, Section 45ZB constitutes the MPC, and Section 24 of the BR Act governs SLR.
n170c1b17106.tq: Bank licence = Sec 22 BR Act; Sec 24 = SLR; Sec 42 RBI Act = CRR.
xs: Payments banks are licensed under **Section 22 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** — option **(1)**.
They are public limited companies under the **Companies Act, 2013** ("2019" in some notes is a slip).
xa: Payments banks: **no lending, no credit cards**; deposits up to **₹2 lakh**.
Paid-up voting equity of at least **₹100 crore**.

n1a4958f62dc.s: Which bank acts as the Lead Bank and SLBC convener in Andhra Pradesh?
n1a4958f62dc.x: Union Bank of India acts as the Lead Bank and the convener of the State Level Bankers’ Committee in Andhra Pradesh.
n1a4958f62dc.tq: Test the specific State-level institutional assignment rather than the general Lead Bank concept.
xs: **Union Bank of India** is the lead bank and **SLBC convener** in Andhra Pradesh — so option **(1)** is correct.
**NABARD** supervises RRBs; **AP Grameena Bank** is AP's merged RRB — neither convenes the SLBC.
xa: The **236th SLBC** met on **16 Sep 2026**: CM **Naidu** asked banks to lend more to MSMEs, tenant farmers and **PM Surya Ghar**.
**Andhra Bank (1923)** was absorbed into **Union Bank** in **2020**.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district-level forum under the **Lead Bank Scheme (1969)**.

n188c9f98600.s: The Lead Bank Scheme, under which each district is assigned a lead bank to coordinate credit planning, began in:
n188c9f98600.x: The Lead Bank Scheme began in 1969, the same year 14 banks were nationalised. 1975 is the year the first RRB was set up, 1980 is the second round of nationalisation, and 1989 is when the Service Area Approach was introduced.
n188c9f98600.tq: Lead Bank 1969 (same year as nationalisation); Service Area Approach 1989.
xs: The **Lead Bank Scheme** began in **1969** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**1969** was also the year **14 banks** were nationalised (**19 July 1969**).
**1975** = first RRB, **1980** = second nationalisation round (**6 banks**), **1989** = **Service Area Approach**.
xa: Each district is assigned a lead bank to coordinate credit planning, with branch expansion district by district.
The **Lead District Manager** runs the district forum; the **SLBC** is the State-level forum.
RBI issued a **draft revision** of the scheme in **Feb 2026**.

nindian-economy-30-12.s: The 14 major commercial banks were nationalised under which legislation in 1969?
o: Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969
nindian-economy-30-12.x: The 14 banks were nationalised under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969.
nindian-economy-30-12.tq: Match each event to its Act.
n: The 14 major commercial banks were nationalised under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 44-46]
xs: The 14 banks were nationalised under the **Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1969** — option **(2)**.
They were **14 major commercial banks** with deposits of at least **₹50 crore**, nationalised on **19 July 1969** under **Indira Gandhi**.
The **SBI Act, 1955** created SBI; the **LIC Act, 1956** nationalised life insurance.
xa: The 14 banks held about **85%** of deposits.
Indira Gandhi's note: "**Stray Thoughts on Bank Nationalisation**"; **50th anniversary** on **19 July 2019**.
Motives: **social control of credit** and a shift of credit to **agriculture and small industry**.

n22bf9d66c66.s: The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation was formed in 1978 by merging which two institutions?
n22bf9d66c66.x: DICGC was formed in 1978 through the merger of the Deposit Insurance Corporation and the Credit Guarantee Corporation of India.
n22bf9d66c66.tq: Match the institution with its constituent predecessor organisations.
xs: **DICGC** was formed in **1978** by merging the **DIC** and **CGCI** — option **(2)**.
The DIC dated from **1962**.
xa: **NBFC** deposits are **not DICGC-insured**.
**NABARD** and **Exim** are **DFIs** in the organised sector.

n385cf141bcb.s: Which of the following activities is an example of para-banking?
o: Distributing mutual funds and providing insurance services
n385cf141bcb.x: Para-banking refers to services beyond the traditional acceptance of deposits and provision of loans, including credit cards, insurance, factoring and mutual fund distribution. Credit to paramilitary personnel is not para-banking merely because of the category of borrower.
n385cf141bcb.tq: Apply the definition by separating ancillary financial services from ordinary banking or lending.
xs: **Distributing mutual funds and providing insurance** is para-banking — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Para-banking** = services beyond deposits and loans: **credit cards, insurance, factoring**, mutual fund distribution.
**Credit to paramilitary personnel** is not para-banking — a known trap; plain deposits or term loans are core banking.
xa: The **APPSC-G1 2022** key on para-banking was **I, II and IV**, excluding the paramilitary option.
**SFBs** can distribute **MFs and insurance**; **payments banks** cannot lend or issue credit cards.
**Cheque validity** is **3 months** from date of issue (since **1 April 2012**).

n8a8c0d2ce0b.s: Bank loans to micro and small enterprises must be given without collateral up to:
n8a8c0d2ce0b.x: MSE loans up to ₹20 lakh and all PMEGP units must be collateral-free; banks may raise this limit to ₹25 lakh.
xa: **Para-banking**: credit cards, insurance, factoring, mutual fund distribution.
**SFBs**: **50%** of loans must be **≤ ₹25 lakh**; **75%** of ANBC to PSL.
ATM cash-out penalty: **₹10,000** per ATM empty more than **10 hours in a month** (from **1 Oct 2021**).

n342886a345a.s: Since 1 April 2012, a cheque in India is valid for how long from its date of issue?
n342886a345a.x: Since 1 April 2012, cheques have been valid for 3 months from the date of issue. The earlier validity was 6 months. 1 month and 12 months were never the general rule.
xs: Since **1 April 2012**, a cheque is valid for **3 months** from its date of issue — so option **(1)** is correct.
The other durations are not the rule given in the notes.
xa: **Aadhaar** can be used for KYC verification **with the customer's consent** (APPSC-GS 2019).
ATM penalty from **1 Oct 2021**: **₹10,000** per ATM out of cash beyond **10 hours in a month**.
**Para-banking** covers **credit cards, insurance, factoring** and MF distribution.

n42202a8590e.s: A major motive behind bank nationalisation in India was to shift credit towards:
n42202a8590e.x: Nationalisation aimed at social control of credit and a shift towards agriculture and small units, reducing industrial houses' control.
xa: Results: **branch expansion** + **priority-sector lending**.
Intent: Indira Gandhi's note "**Stray Thoughts on Bank Nationalisation**".

n944ab670351.s: Andhra Pradesh's credit-deposit ratio in December 2025 stood at:
n944ab670351.x: The ratio fell from 162% (Dec 2024) to 157.40% (Dec 2025), still well above the RBI norm of 60%.
xa: AP Dec 2025: deposits **₹6,08,834 crore**, credit **₹9,58,277 crore**, **8,555** branches.
District CD ratios (Dec 2024): **Konaseema 213%**, **Nandyal 202%**; lowest **Tirupati 85%**.
AP's CD ratio (**157%**) is among the highest in India.

n82a06d0e199.s: Gross NPAs of banks in September 2025, a multi-decadal low, stood at:
n82a06d0e199.x: GNPA was 2.2% in September 2025, alongside the 4R strategy for public sector banks.
xa: The **UFBU** PSB strike on **12 Sep 2026** sought a **5-day week**.
AP's CD ratio (**157%**) is among the highest.
First RRB = **Prathama Grameen Bank**; first SFB = **Capital SFB**.

n6670d129aab.s: Which one of the following was the first private bank established after the 1994 liberalisation of banking in India?
o: UTI Bank, now known as Axis Bank
n6670d129aab.x: UTI Bank was the first private bank established after the 1994 liberalisation of banking. It is now known as Axis Bank.
n6670d129aab.tq: Match the historical first with its former and present identity.
xs: **UTI Bank** (now **Axis Bank**) was the first private bank after the **1994** liberalisation — option **(3)**.
**Capital SFB** and **Equitas** are small finance banks; **Andhra Bank** dates from **1923**.
xa: First SFB: **Capital Small Finance Bank**, Jalandhar (**2016**).
Commercial banks are now licensed "**on tap**".

n272443ecd55.s: A major change in the regulatory structure after financial-sector reforms was that:
o: SEBI assumed direct control over all public sector banks
The Finance Ministry’s Banking Division became the sole regulator of banks
The Banks Board Bureau replaced the RBI as the monetary authority
The RBI became the primary regulator and dual control with the Finance Ministry’s Banking Division ended
n272443ecd55.x: The RBI became the primary regulator, ending dual control with the Finance Ministry’s Banking Division. The reforms also promoted greater autonomy for public sector banks.
n272443ecd55.tq: Identify the correct authority and reject swapped institutional powers.
xs: **RBI became the primary regulator**, ending **dual control** with the Finance Ministry's **Banking Division** — so option **(4)** is correct.
RBI also moved from regulator towards **facilitator**; PSBs got more **autonomy**.
The **Banks Board Bureau** (from **2016**) selects PSB heads; it never became a monetary authority.
xa: Ending dual control was a **Narasimham-I** recommendation (APPSC-G1 2022 key).
**SEBI** became statutory in **1992**.
The **Banking Ombudsman** was introduced in **1995**.

n2f1b971cef2.s: Which committee recommended a three-tier banking structure and closure of weak and unviable banks?
n2f1b971cef2.x: Narasimham-II emphasised consolidation, a three-tier structure and resolution of weak banks; Narasimham-I recommended cutting SLR and CRR.
xa: Narasimham-I = **Committee on the Financial System (1991)**; Narasimham-II = **Committee on Banking Sector Reforms (1998)**.
Narasimham-II also recommended **CRAR 10%** and **universal banking**.
The merger idea ("fewer, stronger banks") fed the **2020** "ten into four" PSB merger.

n0a837ae01f2.s: The Narasimham-II Committee (report April 1998) recommended raising CRAR to:
n0a837ae01f2.x: Narasimham-II, the Committee on Banking Sector Reforms, recommended CRAR of 10%.
xa: ⚠ APPSC GS 2019 key called the 1991 body "Committee on Banking Sector Reforms" — the official title is **Committee on the Financial System**.
Narasimham-II's **3-tier structure**: 2-3 international, 8-10 national, many local banks.

na4c0d0c91df.s: The three-tier banking structure suggested by Narasimham-II envisaged how many international banks?
na4c0d0c91df.x: It proposed two or three international banks, eight to ten national banks and many local banks.
xa: Narasimham-II also recommended merging strong banks and DFIs and closing weak ones.
It raised the **CRAR** target to **10%** and backed **universal banking**.
PSB count fell from **27 (2017) to 12 (2020)** through mergers.

n7307d055c68.s: The Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms is associated with the report titled:
n7307d055c68.x: The Raghuram Rajan Committee’s report was titled “A Hundred Small Steps.”
n7307d055c68.tq: Identify a committee through its distinctive report title.
xs: The **Raghuram Rajan Committee on Financial Sector Reforms (2008)** wrote "**A Hundred Small Steps**" — so option **(3)** is correct.
"**7 parameters** for weak banks" belongs to the **M.S. Verma** Committee.
xa: Some notes date the Rajan report **2009**.
