n883d434da8c.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission linked CSS to measurable outcomes and proposed a high-powered committee to close inefficient schemes.
n883d434da8c.tq: Identify the policy reform from its stated objective and institutional mechanism.
xs: The 16th FC linked CSS to **measurable outcomes** and to **reviewing inefficient schemes** — option **(1)** is correct.
It proposed a **high-powered committee** to close inefficient schemes.
CSS are not Art. 275 grants; they keep a **matching share** from States.
xa: The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance**.
States' deficit capped at **3% of GSDP**; off-budget borrowing to be ended.

n4fa30480cce.s: What was the principal effect attributed to SASCI in the Economic Survey analysis?
o: It restricted capital expenditure to higher-income States.
It reduced State capital expenditure by replacing grants with revenue loans.
It converted all State borrowings into tax devolution.
It helped prevent pro-cyclical compression of State capital expenditure through 50-year interest-free capex loans.
n4fa30480cce.x: SASCI provides 50-year interest-free capital expenditure loans and helped prevent pro-cyclical compression of State capital expenditure.
n4fa30480cce.tq: Connect the policy instrument with its stated macroeconomic effect.
xs: **SASCI** gave **50-year interest-free capex loans** that kept State capex from **pro-cyclical compression** — option **(4)** is correct.
It did not restrict capex to richer States: **lower-income States** relied on it more, aiding **convergence**.
These are **capex loans**, not revenue loans, and do not replace tax devolution.
xa: States' capital outlay rose from **2.17% of GDP (FY22) to 2.37% (FY25)**.
⚠ Excluding SASCI, capital outlay **fell from 2.11% to 1.92%**.
Interest-free capex loans in Budget 2026-27: **₹1,85,000 crore**.

nddd5294c3c9.s: According to the Sixteenth Finance Commission framework, the fiscal deficit of a State should be capped at
nddd5294c3c9.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission recommended capping State fiscal deficits at 3% of GSDP.
nddd5294c3c9.tq: Distinguish the State fiscal-deficit cap from the Union’s corresponding GDP figure.
xs: The 16th FC caps States' deficit at **3% of GSDP** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is part of the shift from **entitlement to performance**.
The same framework says **off-budget borrowing** is to be ended.
xa: The 16th FC also introduced a **GDP criterion** and **conditional grants**.
Extra borrowing: **0.5% of GSDP** for power-sector reforms.
AP: RD grant loss pushes revenue deficit to **1.1%** (Budget 2026-27).

n81e4f2e0067.s: Which of the following correctly shows the States’ share of central taxes recommended by the 10th to 13th Finance Commissions?
n81e4f2e0067.x: The respective shares were 29% under the 10th, 29.5% under the 11th, 30.5% under the 12th and 32% under the 13th Finance Commission.
n81e4f2e0067.tq: Read the sequence across the comparison table without reversing adjacent percentages.
xs: 10th to 13th FCs: **29%, 29.5%, 30.5% and 32%** respectively — option **(2)** is correct.
**12th (C. Rangarajan)** 30.5%; **13th (Vijay Kelkar)** 32%.
xa: **14th (Y.V. Reddy)** jumped to **42%** — the largest-ever jump (+10 points).
**15th (N.K. Singh)** **41%**; **16th (Arvind Panagariya)** **41%** retained.
The 10th FC's 29% was of **gross proceeds** under the **"Alternative Scheme of Devolution"**.

nd1a80cc51d3.s: The reduction in the States’ share from 42% under the 14th Finance Commission to 41% under the 15th Finance Commission was attributed to:
o: The abolition of the divisible pool
The introduction of the GDP criterion
Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory
nd1a80cc51d3.x: The reduction was attributed to Jammu and Kashmir becoming a Union Territory.
nd1a80cc51d3.tq: Link the change in percentage to the specific institutional change responsible for it.
xs: The cut from **42% to 41%** was due to **Jammu & Kashmir becoming a Union Territory** — option **(4)** is correct.
J&K and **Ladakh** became UTs, so they dropped out of the States' share at the **15th FC (N.K. Singh)**.
The **divisible pool** was not abolished, and the **GDP criterion** belongs to the **16th FC**.
xa: The **16th FC** retained **41%** unchanged.
The **14th FC** (**42%**) was the largest-ever jump (+**10** points).
Shift from tax effort (**2.5%**) to GDP contribution (**10%**) criticised as rewarding size, not need.

n804ad45b650.s: Which of the following Centre-to-State transfers is untied?
n804ad45b650.x: Tax devolution under Article 270 is untied; Article 282 grants are discretionary and CSS generally need a matching State share.
xa: Art. 275 grants are **charged on the CFI**; Art. 282 grants are not.
CSS examples: **MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, PMAY, NHM**.

n8964f10fc86.s: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are best described as schemes which are
o: recommended only by the Finance Commission and funded only from Article 275 grants
designed by States and financed entirely by local bodies
designed by the Centre and require a matching State share
implemented without any State financial contribution
n8964f10fc86.x: Centrally Sponsored Schemes are Centre-designed schemes requiring a matching contribution from the States.
n8964f10fc86.tq: Apply the funding and design features to identify the scheme category.
xs: **CSS** are schemes **designed by the Centre** that need a **matching State share** — option **(3)** is correct.
Examples: **MGNREGA/VB-G RAM G, PMAY, NHM**.
They are not FC/Art. 275 funded: CSS mostly flow through **Art. 282** grants.
xa: **16th FC**: CSS linked to **measurable outcomes**; **high-powered committee** to close inefficient schemes.
CSS spending routed to States is one reason the share stayed at **41%**.

n94a979f10d4.s: Which of the following grants were discontinued by the 16th Finance Commission?
o: Revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and State-specific grants
All grants to rural local bodies
n94a979f10d4.x: The 16th Finance Commission discontinued revenue-deficit grants, sector-specific grants and State-specific grants.
n94a979f10d4.tq: Identify the complete set of discontinued grants without overextending the word “all”.
xs: The 16th FC dropped **revenue-deficit, sector-specific and State-specific grants** — option **(1)** is correct.
These were **15th FC** grants (total **₹10.1 lakh crore**).
The 16th FC kept **only local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) and **disaster** grants, so options 2–4 are wrong.
xa: 16th FC total grants **₹9.47 lakh crore**; share in FC transfers **19.4% → 8.3%**.
AP angle: **RD grant loss** → AP revenue deficit **1.1%** (Budget 2026-27).
AP's 16th FC local-body grants: **₹16,627 crore** (rural), **₹12,158 crore** (urban).

n4418adf3211.s: The expression “41% illusion” in discussions on tax devolution refers principally to the fact that:
o: cesses and surcharges are outside the divisible pool
the Finance Commission fixes all tax rates at 41%
States receive 41% of total public expenditure
41% of the divisible pool is transferred only through grants
n4418adf3211.x: The expression highlights that the stated share can overstate actual resources available to States because growing cesses and surcharges remain outside the divisible pool.
n4418adf3211.tq: Decode a debate-related phrase by identifying the fiscal mechanism behind it.
xs: The **"41% illusion"**: **cesses and surcharges** lie **outside the divisible pool** — option **(1)** is correct.
As cess/surcharge grows, the States' real share of gross tax revenue shrinks below the headline **41%**.
41% is a share of the **divisible pool**, not a tax rate or a share of expenditure.
xa: Divisible pool fell **89.2% (FC-13) → 82.1% (FC-14) → 78.3% (FC-15)** of gross tax revenue.
Capping cess/surcharge was called "**neither permissible nor desirable**".
16th FC asks for annual **CAG-certified** disclosure of net tax proceeds.

nf323c55b0d5.s: Which of the following best reflects the equity-efficiency issue in the design of fiscal devolution?
o: All States possess identical fiscal capacity, so devolution automatically equalises them.
Most Finance Commissions relied on income distance and population, while critics argue that fiscal capacity is not uniform.
Efficiency requires replacing all tax devolution with discretionary grants.
Equity is achieved only when every State receives an identical absolute amount.
nf323c55b0d5.x: Most Finance Commissions relied on income distance and population to pursue equity. Critics argue that fiscal capacity is not uniform, so devolution is not automatically self-equalising.
nf323c55b0d5.tq: Separate the equity objective from the criticism concerning unequal fiscal capacity.
xs: Most FCs relied on **income distance and population**, while critics say **fiscal capacity is not uniform** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **16th FC view** assumes fiscal discipline suffices.
Critics reply that, as fiscal capacity varies, devolution is **not self-equalising** — so option 1 is the very assumption criticised.
xa: Shift from tax effort (**2.5%**) to GDP contribution (**10%**) is criticised as rewarding **size, not need**.
**Horizontal devolution** = distribution of States' share among States.
The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance**.

n65eca4c8f81.s: Recommendations of the Finance Commission are:
o: Binding on the Union and the States
Advisory and not binding on the Government
n65eca4c8f81.x: FC recommendations are not binding on the Government; it may also deal with matters referred by the President.
xa: ⚠ GST revenue sharing is handled by the **GST Council**, not the Finance Commission.
Maintaining **income and expenditure accounts** of Centre and States is not its job (**APPSC-G2 2017** key).
Example of a Presidential reference: **disaster-management financing** under the **Disaster Management Act, 2005**.

n25d658858d5.s: Which of the following is excluded from the divisible pool of Union taxes?
n25d658858d5.x: Cesses and surcharges are excluded from the divisible pool, as is the cost of collection; pool taxes are shared under Article 270.
xa: Divisible pool fell from **89.2% (FC-13)** to **82.1% (FC-14)** to **78.3% (FC-15)** of gross tax revenue.
**80th Amendment, 2000** made all central taxes shareable.

n85f7f0dbb0b.s: The largest-ever increase in the States' share of Union taxes occurred under the
n85f7f0dbb0b.x: The Fourteenth Finance Commission increased the States' share from 32 per cent to 42 per cent, a rise of 10 percentage points, the largest-ever jump.
n85f7f0dbb0b.tq: Use the size of the change, not merely the final percentage, to identify the Commission.
xs: The **Fourteenth Finance Commission** gave the largest-ever jump — option **(2)** is correct.
It raised the States' share from **32%** (13th FC) to **42%**: **+10 points**.
The **15th** cut it to **41%** and the **16th** retained **41%**; the **13th** moved it only from **30.5%** to **32%**.
xa: 14th FC chairman: **Y.V. Reddy**; award period **2015-20**.
Its 42% award was **accepted 24 Feb 2015**.
The notes do not list the 14th FC's own vertical-devolution considerations (asked in **APPSC 2017**).

n306a94a0560.s: The 16th Finance Commission retained the States' share in the divisible pool at:
n306a94a0560.x: It retained 41 per cent; the demand of 18 of 28 States for 50 per cent was not accepted.
xa: Reasons: **CSS** spending routed to States anyway; Union needs funds for **defence and infrastructure**.
Capping cess/surcharge was called "**neither permissible nor desirable**".
⚠ The one-point cut (**42 → 41**) came at the **15th FC**, not the 16th.

n924f6134ba4.s: Which one of the following is NOT a channel of Centre-to-State transfers identified in the Economic Survey analysis?
o: Centrally Sponsored Schemes and other transfers under Article 282
n924f6134ba4.x: Tax devolution, Finance Commission grants, and CSS and other transfers are recognised channels. Article 123 concerns the President's ordinance-making power and is not a channel of Centre-to-State transfers.
n924f6134ba4.tq: Find the option that belongs to a different constitutional subject rather than fiscal transfers.
xs: **"Monetary policy transfers under Article 123"** is not a transfer channel — option **(4)** is correct.
The real channels: **tax devolution (Art. 270)**, untied.
**Finance Commission grants** = **Art. 275** statutory grants.
**CSS** and other transfers = **Art. 282** discretionary grants, with matching share.
xa: Budget 2026-27 total transfers: **₹26,20,769 crore** (+**12.2%**).
Tax devolution 2026-27: **₹15,26,255 crore**.
Interest-free capex loans 2026-27: **₹1,85,000 crore**.

o: Statutory grants recommended by the Finance Commission
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Discretionary, mostly tied and routed through Union ministries
Untied transfers from the divisible pool
nb07dfc3d075.x: Article 282 grants are discretionary, mostly tied and scheme-based; Article 275 grants are statutory and charged on the CFI.
xa: Art. 275 grants go to States in need of assistance, as **Parliament** determines; Art. 282 grants for **any public purpose**.
Art. 282 is the route for most **CSS**.
⚠ Exam trap: "Art. 282 needs FC recommendation" is **false**.

n8f0bd9146be.s: The 15th Finance Commission's revenue-deficit, sector-specific and State-specific grants totalled about:
n8f0bd9146be.x: The 15th FC's grants totalled about ₹10.1 lakh crore, against ₹9.47 lakh crore under the 16th FC.
xa: 16th FC grants: only **local body** (**₹7.91 lakh crore**) + **disaster** grants.
Budget **2026-27**: **₹1.4 lakh crore** FC grants for FY27.
15th FC gave **RD**, **sector-specific** and **State-specific** grants.

n26b79bfde3c.s: Which two phenomena were recommended to be notified as disasters under the disaster-grant framework?
n26b79bfde3c.x: Heatwave and lightning were recommended to be notified as disasters.
n26b79bfde3c.tq: Test the specific pair of newly proposed disaster categories.
xs: **Heatwave and lightning** were recommended as notified disasters — option **(3)** is correct.
This is part of the **16th FC** disaster-grant framework.
The other pairs are not the new additions the notes record.
xa: **SDRF/SDMF** corpus: **₹2,04,401 crore** (Union share about **₹1.55 lakh crore**).
Cost-sharing: NE/Himalayan **90:10**; others **75:25**.
Disaster financing under the **Disaster Management Act, 2005** came into FC terms of reference.

nb371fb17553.s: The 15th Finance Commission recommended Rs 4,800 crore for 2022-23 to 2025-26 to incentivise States on:
nb371fb17553.x: The 15th FC set aside Rs 4,800 crore (2022-23 to 2025-26) to reward States for better educational outcomes (UPSC 2025). Property tax was an entry condition for local-body grants, power-sector reform was tied to extra borrowing, and disaster funds come through SDRF/SDMF.
xs: The **₹4,800 crore** (**2022-23 to 2025-26**) was to reward better **educational outcomes** — option **(2)** is correct (**UPSC 2025**).
It was part of the **15th FC**'s sector-specific grants.
**Power-sector reforms** were linked instead to extra borrowing of **0.5% of GSDP**.
xa: 15th FC grants totalled **₹10.1 lakh crore** (RD, sector-specific, State-specific).
15th FC chairman **N.K. Singh**; award period **2020-26**.
NPS/UPS-linked extra borrowing since **2022-23** (**₹62,778 crore** in 2024-25).

n694fff9f899.s: The Gadgil formula was introduced in:
n694fff9f899.x: The Gadgil formula dates to 1969; formula-based plan transfers lapsed when NITI Aayog replaced the Planning Commission on 1 January 2015.
xa: **Gadgil-Mukherjee** revised the formula in **1991**.
Plan grants ran alongside **Finance Commission** transfers until abolition.
Formula was endorsed by the **National Development Council** in **1968-69**.

n5b1664525e3.s: Which of the following was among the initial Special Category States under the Gadgil formula?
n5b1664525e3.x: The initial Special Category States were Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, and Nagaland.
xa: ⚠ General-category States got **30% grant and 70% loan**.
The Gadgil formula gave **population** a **60%** weight.
Used from the **4th Plan (1969)**; revised as **Gadgil-Mukherjee (1991)**.

n657fd7b3f3f.s: Under the Gadgil formula, central plan assistance to Special Category States and to general-category States was given in which grant-loan proportions, respectively?
n657fd7b3f3f.x: Special Category States received assistance as 90% grant and 10% loan; general-category States received 30% grant and 70% loan. D reverses the two, and B and C are not the Gadgil proportions.
xs: **Special Category: 90% grant-10% loan**; **general category: 30% grant-70% loan** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option **(4)** reverses the two ratios — the classic trap.
The **70:30** and **50:50** splits in the other options are not Gadgil ratios.
xa: ⚠ Special Category **90:10** grant-loan vs general **30:70**.
Initial Special Category States: **Assam, J&K, Nagaland** — with **first claim** on assistance.
Gadgil formula: **1969**, Fourth Plan; revised as **Gadgil-Mukherjee (1991)**.

ncb167f0315e.s: Which one of the following best describes the principal shift associated with the Sixteenth Finance Commission in intergovernmental transfers?
o: From performance-based transfers to unconditional entitlement
From tax devolution to complete abolition of grants
From State transfers to exclusive Central expenditure
From entitlement-based transfers to performance-oriented transfers
ncb167f0315e.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission is associated with a shift from entitlement-based transfers towards performance-oriented transfers.
ncb167f0315e.tq: Identify the reversed comparison by focusing on the direction of the policy shift.
xs: The 16th FC shifts transfers from **entitlement to performance** — option **(4)** is correct.
Tools: **GDP criterion** + **conditional grants**; deficit capped at **3% of GSDP**.
Option 1 states the reverse; grants were not abolished — **local body** and **disaster** grants remain.
xa: 16th FC: CSS linked to **measurable outcomes**.
Grants' share in FC transfers fell **19.4% → 8.3%**.
Critics: fiscal capacity is not uniform → devolution **not self-equalising**.

nafd45b843d8.s: In Article 243H, the word ‘may’ indicates that:
o: The State Legislature has an enabling power and is not compelled to impose the taxes
Only the Union Parliament can authorise local taxation
Panchayats can impose taxes without State authorisation
The State Legislature is constitutionally compelled to impose every listed tax
nafd45b843d8.x: The use of ‘may’ makes the provision enabling rather than compulsory; the State Legislature may authorise the levy, collection and appropriation of the listed revenues.
nafd45b843d8.tq: Interpret the legal effect of the precise constitutional word.
xs: **"May"** makes Art. 243H an **enabling power** — the State Legislature is **not compelled** — option **(1)** is correct.
It is the **State Legislature**, not Parliament, that authorises the levy, collection and appropriation.
Panchayats cannot tax on their own: gram panchayats levy only **State-authorised** taxes.
xa: Under 243H the State may also **assign State taxes** and **give grants**.
**Art. 243X** gives the same enabling power for municipalities.
Panchayats constrained from taxing → **grant-dependent**.

n478379fa7ff.s: Under Article 280(3)(bb) and (c), the Central Finance Commission suggests measures to augment the State Consolidated Fund for local bodies on the basis of recommendations made by:
n478379fa7ff.x: The Central Finance Commission makes such recommendations on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations.
n478379fa7ff.tq: Identify the correct recommending body in a constitutional relationship.
xs: The Central FC acts **on the basis of State Finance Commission recommendations** — option **(3)** is correct.
This is **Art. 280(3)(bb), (c)** — augmenting the State **Consolidated Fund** for local bodies.
The SFC is set up by the **Governor** under **Art. 243I**.
xa: The same SFC reviews **municipal** finances under **Art. 243Y**.
**16th FC** entry condition: **timely constitution of SFCs**.
SFCs are not constituted regularly; regular SFCs are needed for **three-tier fiscal federalism**.

n75e618e1c9b.s: Which of the following is NOT an entry condition for local bodies under the 16th Finance Commission framework?
o: Timely constitution of the State Finance Commission
Properly constituted and elected local body
n75e618e1c9b.x: The entry conditions are elected bodies, online audited accounts and timely SFCs; municipal-bond issuance is not one.
xa: Municipal bonds exist **only in a few large cities**; **AMRUT 2.0** incentivises them.
AP's ULBs/panchayats under **Special Officers** → grants at risk.
Critics call the conditions a **re-engineering of fiscal federalism**.

nbfc209fce27.s: The National Commission on Urbanisation, constituted for the period 1985-88, was chaired by:
nbfc209fce27.x: The National Commission on Urbanisation functioned during 1985-88 under the chairmanship of Charles Correa.
nbfc209fce27.tq: Link the distinctive period with the corresponding committee chairperson.
xs: The **National Commission on Urbanisation** (**1985-88**) was chaired by **Charles Correa** — option **(2)** is correct.
**John Matthai** chaired the **Taxation Enquiry Commission (1953-54)**.
**A.P. Jain** chaired the **Rural-Urban Relationship Committee**; **P.K. Wattal** the **Local Finance Enquiry Committee**.
xa: Local Finance Enquiry Committee: **1949-51**.
Rural-Urban Relationship Committee: **1963-66**.
**K. Santhanam**: Committee on Panchayati Raj Finances (**1963**).

n815ace0f60f.s: The weak revenue position of municipalities is mainly due to chronic under-assessment and under-collection of:
n815ace0f60f.x: Municipal finances are weakened particularly by chronic under-assessment and under-collection of property tax.
xa: **Economic Survey 2016-17** measured actual vs potential property tax of **Bengaluru** and **Jaipur** using **satellite imagery**.
**AMRUT 2.0** incentivises property tax reform + **municipal bonds**.
**SVAMITVA** drone maps give a panchayat property-tax baseline.

na5ca68e3cd8.s: Which of the following is a non-tax revenue source of urban local bodies?
na5ca68e3cd8.x: Rents, fees and fines are non-tax revenues; professional and advertisement taxes are tax revenues.
xa: ULB grants: **Central and State grants** for schemes and reforms.
Devolution: **State funds** to municipalities on **SFC** recommendation.
No **accrual accounting** + weak balance sheets → no **bond-market** access.

na62359237e6.s: Gram panchayats may levy which of the following, subject to authorisation by the State?
na62359237e6.x: Gram panchayats levy only State-authorised taxes, including taxes on local fairs, house or property tax, fees and tolls. Sales tax and land revenue are State levies.
na62359237e6.tq: Distinguish panchayat levies from State-level taxes.
xs: Gram panchayats can levy a **tax on local fairs** with State authorisation — option **(2)** is correct.
They levy **only State-authorised** taxes: local fairs, house/property tax, **fees and tolls**.
⚠ **Sales tax** and **land revenue** are **State levies** (**UPPSC 2018** key); corporation tax is a Union tax in the **divisible pool**.
xa: **Art. 243H** — the State Legislature **may** authorise Panchayat taxes.
Gram sabhas spend only **4%** of time on revenue generation vs **13%** on local issues.
Panchayats are constrained from taxing → **grant-dependent**.

nf60390dc4a8.s: Under the 16th Finance Commission's local-body grants, the basic grant forms:
nf60390dc4a8.x: The basic grant is 80% (half tied, half untied); the 20% performance grant is fully untied.
xa: 16th FC local-body grants: **₹7,91,493 crore** — rural **₹4.35 lakh crore**, urban **₹3.56 lakh crore**.
Urban share up **36% → 45%**; **Urbanisation Premium** **₹10,000 crore**.
Conditions: **elected local bodies**, **audited accounts online**, **timely SFCs**.
⚠ SFCs are constituted by the **Governor** under **Art. 243I**.

nee95eddd965.s: The one-time Urbanisation Premium is associated with:
o: Merging peri-urban villages under a Rural-to-Urban Transition Policy
nee95eddd965.x: The premium is tied to merging peri-urban villages and adopting a Rural-to-Urban Transition Policy.
xa: It is a **one-time** grant of **₹10,000 crore**.
Urbanisation projected at **41% by 2031**.
Urban share of local body grants up **36% → 45%**.

nce1681c34ca.s: According to the IIHS study covering 80 urban local bodies during 2012–17, intergovernmental transfers accounted for approximately what share of ULB revenue?
nce1681c34ca.x: The IIHS study reported that intergovernmental transfers constituted about 40 percent of ULB revenue.
nce1681c34ca.tq: Identify the reported percentage and distinguish it from nearby round-number distractors.
xs: IGTs were about **40 percent** of ULB revenue — option **(3)** is correct.
Source: **IIHS** study of **80 ULBs**, **2012-17**.
This is the **grant dependence** problem of ULBs.
xa: India's IGTs ≈ **0.5% of GDP** vs global norm **2-5%**.
**Class I-A cities (50 lakh+)** cut IGT dependence **27% → 15%**.
Smaller cities stayed **grant-dependent**.

n3a0b76920fc.s: The urban share in the Sixteenth Finance Commission’s local-body grants increased from 36% to
n3a0b76920fc.x: The urban share increased from 36% to 45%. The projected urbanisation level by 2031 was 41%, which is a separate figure.
n3a0b76920fc.tq: Separate the grant share from the projected urbanisation percentage.
xs: The urban share rose from **36% to 45%** — option **(2)** is correct.
It reflects urbanisation projected at **41% by 2031** — a separate figure, so option 1 is a trap.
16th FC urban grants: **₹3.56 lakh crore** (some notes say **₹3.6 lakh crore**).
xa: Rural grants: **₹4.35 lakh crore** (or **₹4.4 lakh crore**).
Total 16th FC local body grant: **₹7,91,493 crore** for **2026-31**.
**Urbanisation Premium**: **₹10,000 crore**, one-time.

nd45ab17e411.s: Which was an entry condition for urban local bodies to receive the relevant Fifteenth Finance Commission grants?
o: Publication of audited accounts and notification of baseline property-tax rates
Transfer of land-revenue powers to municipalities
Issue of municipal bonds by every town
Levy of professional tax at the maximum permitted rate
nd45ab17e411.x: ULBs had to publish audited accounts and notify baseline property-tax rates to become eligible for the grants.
xa: **16th FC** conditions: **elected** local bodies, **audited accounts online**, **timely SFCs**.
15th FC local body grants: about **₹4.36 lakh crore**.
Property tax is ULBs' **single most important own-source revenue**.

ndb1b0f602e4.s: Delayed local-body elections in Andhra Pradesh put Finance Commission grants at risk because the grants are linked to:
o: Access of municipalities to the bond market
Appointment of Special Officers to run the bodies
Elected bodies, audited accounts and compliance with State Finance Commission requirements
ndb1b0f602e4.x: The grants are tied to the existence of elected bodies, audited accounts and SFC compliance, so delayed elections jeopardise eligibility and release.
xa: AP **ULB** terms expired **15 March 2026**; **panchayats** **4 April 2026**.
16th FC conditions: **properly constituted (elected)** bodies, **accounts online**, **timely SFCs**.
Critics call the conditions a **re-engineering of fiscal federalism**.

nf378db617c2.s: Drone maps under which scheme can give panchayats a property-tax baseline?
nf378db617c2.x: SVAMITVA drone maps provide a property-tax baseline; AMRUT 2.0 incentivises property-tax reform and municipal bonds.
xa: Property tax is ULBs' **single most important own-source revenue**.
ES 2016-17 used **satellite imagery** for **Bengaluru** and **Jaipur**.
Earlier FC condition: ULBs had to notify **baseline property tax rates**.

n6f712e933b0.s: Panchayats, being constrained in their power to tax, depend substantially on:
n6f712e933b0.x: Panchayats depend substantially on grants; gram sabhas spend only about 4% of their time on revenue generation.
xa: Panchayat sources: **FC local body grants**, **Central Cooperative Banks**, **CSS**, **SFC** allocations.
⚠ **NABARD** is not a direct source.
**SVAMITVA** drone maps provide a panchayat **property-tax baseline**.

n29cccb42682.s: India's intergovernmental transfers are about ____ of GDP, against a global norm of about ____.
n29cccb42682.x: India's intergovernmental transfers are about 0.5% of GDP, compared with a global norm of roughly 2–5% of GDP.
xa: **Class I-A cities** cut dependence **27% → 15%**.
No **accrual accounting** → no **bond-market** access.

ne4b6ad4096b.s: Which of the following is identified as a barrier to local bodies’ access to the bond market?
o: Excessive accrual accounting and strong balance sheets
Absence of accrual accounting and weak balance sheets
Complete dependence on property tax surpluses
Excessive control over State line-department staff
ne4b6ad4096b.x: The absence of accrual accounting and weak balance sheets restrict local bodies’ access to the bond market.
ne4b6ad4096b.tq: Match the institutional weakness with its stated financial-market consequence.
xs: **No accrual accounting** and **weak balance sheets** block bond-market access — option **(2)** is correct.
Option 1 states the opposite of the problem.
Hence **municipal bonds** exist only in a few large cities.
xa: **AMRUT 2.0** incentivises **municipal bonds**.
Other challenges: **grant dependence**, **delayed SFCs**.
16th FC needs **audited accounts published online**.

n2d4f7e1a6a9.s: The Economic Survey 2016-17 used satellite imagery to estimate the gap between actual and potential property tax in:
n2d4f7e1a6a9.x: The Economic Survey 2016-17 measured the actual-potential property-tax gap in Bengaluru and Jaipur using satellite imagery.
n2d4f7e1a6a9.tq: Test the precise city pair associated with a quantitative assessment method.
xs: **ES 2016-17** studied **Bengaluru and Jaipur** — option **(1)** is correct.
It used **satellite imagery** to measure **actual vs potential** property tax (**APPSC-G1 2017** key).
The gap reflects chronic **under-assessment and under-collection**.
xa: Property tax = **single most important own-source revenue** of ULBs.
**SVAMITVA** drone maps → panchayat property-tax baseline.
**AMRUT 2.0** incentivises property tax reform.

nf2d5fc17a92.s: Government expenditure that creates an asset or reduces a liability is classified as:
nf2d5fc17a92.x: Capital expenditure either creates assets or reduces liabilities; revenue expenditure generally does neither.
xa: Thumb rule: **Revenue = running the government; Capital = creating assets**.
Revenue spending is **recurring**; capital spending is mostly **non-recurring**.
Purchase of **defence equipment** is **capital outlay**.

n0c098895c86.x: Subsidies are revenue expenditure; grants to States are also revenue expenditure, while defence equipment purchase can be capital outlay.
xa: Exam angle: food and fertiliser subsidies are revenue expenditure (**APPSC-G2 2008**).
**Loans and advances to States** = capital.
**Interest payments**, salaries and pensions = revenue.

n99ee3403c73.s: Which of the following correctly defines effective capital expenditure?
o: Capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Revenue expenditure plus loans to State Governments
Capital expenditure minus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Capital outlay plus interest payments on public debt
n99ee3403c73.x: Effective capital expenditure is calculated as capital expenditure plus grants-in-aid for the creation of capital assets.
n99ee3403c73.tq: Test the exact formula by distinguishing additions from deductions.
xs: **Effective capex** = **capital expenditure + grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option **(3)** subtracts the grants instead of adding them.
Revenue expenditure and interest payments are not part of it.
xa: BE 2026-27 effective capex: **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**.
Of this, grants: **₹4.93 lakh crore**.
Effective capex / fiscal deficit = **101.1%**.

n4a99b9ee35f.s: The Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) provides States with:
n4a99b9ee35f.x: SASCI provides 50-year interest-free loans to States for capital expenditure.
n4a99b9ee35f.tq: Use the application-purpose and loan-terms pair to distinguish the scheme from ordinary grants.
xs: **SASCI** gives States **50-year interest-free loans** for **capex** — option **(1)** is correct.
They are **loans**, not grants, and for **capital** not revenue spending.
Allocation **₹1.85 lakh crore** in **2026-27**.
xa: Effective capex includes **grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets**.
**Golden Rule**: borrowing only for assets.

ncbb32be28a7.s: The Union capital expenditure of ₹12,21,821 crore in Budget 2026-27 is made up of:
o: Capital outlay plus loans and advances
Capital outlay plus grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
Revenue expenditure plus loans and advances
ncbb32be28a7.x: Capex 2026-27 (₹12,21,821 crore, +11.5%) = capital outlay ₹9,43,042 crore + loans ₹2,78,780 crore. Adding grants-in-aid for capital assets gives effective capex, not capex. Revenue expenditure and interest payments are not part of capital expenditure.
ncbb32be28a7.tq: Capex = outlay + loans; effective capex adds capital grants.
xs: Capex **₹12,21,821 crore** = **capital outlay + loans and advances** — option **(1)** is correct.
Capital outlay **₹9,43,042 crore** + loans **₹2,78,780 crore**.
Adding grants for capital assets gives **effective capex**, not capex (option 2).
xa: Effective capex **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**.
⚠ Loans and advances to States are **capital**; grants to States are **revenue**.

n34e04d0afb6.s: The 'Golden Rule' of public finance says government borrowing should ordinarily be used for:
o: Creation of assets through capital expenditure
n34e04d0afb6.x: The Golden Rule allows borrowing only for asset creation, so the quality and composition of spending matter more than its size.
xa: Effective capex / fiscal deficit = **101.1%** in BE 2026-27.
Revenue expenditure share fell **88% → about 77%**.
**9 of 18** large States budget revenue deficits for 2026-27.

nindian-economy-46-4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct?
o: Capital expenditure – directed toward creation or acquisition of assets
Non-plan expenditure – included subsidies, interest payments and defence
Revenue expenditure – involves no creation of assets
Revenue deficit – revenue receipts minus revenue expenditure
nindian-economy-46-4.x: Revenue deficit is revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts, not the reverse.
n: Capital expenditure strengthens long-term productive capacity. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Revenue expenditure does not create assets. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Capital expenditure involves asset creation or acquisition. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes subsidies. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes interest payments. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Non-plan expenditure includes defence services. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
Infrastructure or asset creation is an example of capital expenditure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #46 · pp 68-69]
xa: Thumb rule: **Revenue = running the government; Capital = creating assets**.
**Repayment of loans** is capital expenditure — it **reduces liability**.
Food and fertiliser **subsidies** are **revenue expenditure** (APPSC-G2 2008).

nbafbc0c20f3.s: Wagner’s law states that, as an economy industrialises:
o: Public expenditure rises faster than national income
Public expenditure falls faster than national income
Public expenditure rises only during wars and crises
Public expenditure remains constant irrespective of national income
nbafbc0c20f3.x: Wagner’s law, also called the law of increasing state activity, holds that public expenditure rises faster than national income as an economy industrialises.
nbafbc0c20f3.tq: Match the law with its distinctive continuous income-related trend.
xs: **Wagner's law**: public expenditure rises **faster than national income** as the economy industrialises — option **(1)** is correct.
It is also called the **law of increasing state activity**.
Rises only during **wars and crises** describes **Peacock-Wiseman**, not Wagner.
xa: Peacock-Wiseman (**1961**, UK data): spending rises in **steps** — the **displacement effect**.
After a crisis spending **does not fall back**.
Exam angle: "continuous rise with income" = **Wagner**.

n647755d0530.s: The displacement effect in public expenditure theory is associated with:
o: The fiscal multiplier of capital expenditure
n647755d0530.x: The displacement effect is associated with the Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis. Wars and crises raise the tolerable tax burden and displace public spending to a higher level.
n647755d0530.tq: Discriminate between the two theories using their signature concepts.
xs: The **displacement effect** belongs to the **Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis** — option **(3)** is correct.
Wars/crises raise the **tolerable tax burden**; spending rises in **steps** and **does not fall back**.
**Wagner's law** is about a **continuous** rise with income.
xa: Peacock-Wiseman used **UK data** (**1961**).
Wagner's law = **law of increasing state activity**.
The **Golden Rule** concerns borrowing only for **assets**.

n800210c7c13.s: Stepwise increases in public expenditure caused by wars and crises (the displacement effect) are explained by:
n800210c7c13.x: Peacock-Wiseman explains discontinuous rises through crises; Wagner's law links continuous growth of spending to industrialisation.
xa: Wagner: spending rises **faster than national income**.
Peacock-Wiseman: crises raise the **tolerable tax burden** — **displacement effect**.
Peacock-Wiseman hypothesis: **1961**, UK data.

n8832eea9540.s: Interest payments in Union Budget Estimates 2026-27 were approximately what proportion of total expenditure and revenue receipts, respectively?
n8832eea9540.x: Interest payments of ₹14,03,972 crore represented 26 per cent of total expenditure and 40 per cent of revenue receipts.
n8832eea9540.tq: Do not reverse the two denominators when comparing the percentages.
xs: Interest payments were **26%** of total expenditure and **40%** of revenue receipts — option **(3)** is correct.
Option **(1)** reverses the two figures.
Interest = **₹14,03,972 crore** in BE 2026-27.
xa: Interest/revenue receipts: **37%** in **2013-14**; **42%** in **2020-21**.
Interest takes **20%** in the rupee-goes-to breakup.
**Committed expenditure** = **65.3%** of revenue receipts.

n2c30e25992a.s: Committed expenditure consisting of salaries, pensions and interest payments accounted for what proportion of revenue receipts?
n2c30e25992a.x: Committed expenditure, comprising salaries, pensions and interest payments, was 65.3 per cent of revenue receipts.
n2c30e25992a.tq: Associate the exact percentage with the complete committed-expenditure group.
xs: **Committed expenditure** (salaries, pensions, interest) = **65.3%** of revenue receipts — option **(3)** is correct.
It leaves **little room** for discretionary spending.
Interest alone is **40%** of revenue receipts.
xa: States: committed expenditure + subsidies = **51.76%** of revenue expenditure in **FY24**.
**CAG** flags AP's rising committed expenditure + weak capex.
Interest = **26%** of total Union expenditure.

na99132d182e.s: For Indian States during 2014-24, revenue expenditure formed approximately what share of their total expenditure?
na99132d182e.x: States' revenue expenditure was 80-87% of their total expenditure, while total State spending was 16.15-17.49% of GSDP in 2014-24. 50-55% and 60-65% understate the share; 92-97% overstates it.
na99132d182e.tq: States spend mostly on revenue account: 80-87%.
xs: States' revenue expenditure was **80-87%** of total — option **(3)** is correct.
State spending was **16.15-17.49%** of GSDP over **2014-24**.
The other ranges understate or overstate the share.
xa: Committed expenditure + subsidies = **51.76%** of States' revenue expenditure (**FY24**).
States' total expenditure: **15.7%** of GDP (**FY19**) → **15.4%** (**FY24**).
**9 of 18** large States budget revenue deficits for 2026-27.

n41a138632c5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about effective capital expenditure in BE 2026-27?
o: Grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets account for ₹4.93 lakh crore of it
It is estimated at 101.1 per cent of the fiscal deficit
Grants to States are revenue expenditure even when used to create assets
It excludes grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets
n41a138632c5.x: Effective capital expenditure includes grants-in-aid for creation of capital assets.
xa: Effective capex BE 2026-27: **₹17.15 lakh crore (4.4% of GDP)**.
Capex growth **23.7%** in Q1 2026-27.

n32b561cd74d.s: The Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme was introduced from:
n32b561cd74d.x: The Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme commenced on 1 April 2010.
n32b561cd74d.tq: Discriminate the notified commencement date from adjacent years.
xs: **NBS** began on **1 April 2010** — option **(2)** is correct.
It fixes subsidy **per kg of nutrient** (**N, P, K, S**).
It applies to decontrolled **P&K fertilisers** — **22 grades** incl. **DAP, MOP, SSP**.
xa: ⚠ **Urea is outside NBS**.
**Oil Pool Account** (APM) dismantled **April 2002**.
Fertiliser subsidy 2026-27: **₹1,70,799 crore**.

n6030b0b965b.s: Which fertiliser remains outside the Nutrient Based Subsidy scheme?
n6030b0b965b.x: NBS covers 22 grades of decontrolled P&K fertilisers including DAP, MOP and SSP, with subsidy fixed per kg of nutrient; urea is outside the scheme.
xa: NBS started **1 April 2010**.
Food + fertiliser = **87%** of the subsidy bill.
Under later petroleum pricing, under-recoveries were compensated through **oil bonds**.

n210b7bb88f4.s: The Oil Pool Account under the Administered Price Mechanism was dismantled in:
n210b7bb88f4.x: It was dismantled in April 2002; later OMC under-recoveries were compensated through oil bonds.
xa: NBS (**1 April 2010**) covers **22 grades** of P&K fertilisers.
Major subsidies up **37.4%** in Q1 2026-27 on crude prices (**West Asia** crisis).
LPG subsidy 2026-27: **₹12,085 crore**.

nfac63eb62b5.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission's approach to subsidies favoured:
o: Well-targeted subsidies with exclusion criteria and sunset clauses
nfac63eb62b5.x: It supported well-targeted subsidies with exclusion criteria and sunset clauses, not unrestricted off-budget financing.
xa: Major subsidies: **₹4.11 lakh crore = 1.0% of GDP**.
Likely overshoot ≈ **₹50,000 crore** on crude prices.

n15b9a5f99b6.s: Which of the following is an example of an implicit or hidden subsidy?
o: A fertiliser subsidy shown in the Budget
An export incentive shown as a Budget provision
A food subsidy shown as a separate Budget line item
Under-pricing of higher education in a public university
n15b9a5f99b6.x: Under-pricing of publicly provided services, such as higher education in public universities, is an implicit or hidden subsidy. Food, fertiliser and export incentives shown in the Budget are explicit subsidies.
n15b9a5f99b6.tq: Distinguish a visible Budget line item from under-pricing of a publicly provided service.
xs: **Under-pricing of higher education in a public university** is a hidden subsidy — option **(4)** is correct (**APPSC 2018**).
Food and fertiliser subsidies and **export incentives** shown in the Budget are **explicit** subsidies.
Implicit subsidy = **under-pricing of publicly provided goods**.
xa: Other hidden subsidies: **public health**, **irrigation water**, **power**.
Other explicit subsidies: **LPG**, **interest subvention**.
Budget 2026-27 subsidy bill: **₹4,54,773 crore**.

na951f5498f3.s: In the Andhra Pradesh Budget Estimates for 2026-27, revenue expenditure constituted approximately what share of total expenditure?
na951f5498f3.x: Revenue expenditure constituted approximately 83% of Andhra Pradesh’s total expenditure in the 2026-27 Budget Estimates.
na951f5498f3.tq: Select the stated approximate share while rejecting nearby percentage distractors.
xs: AP's revenue expenditure was about **83 percent** of the **2026-27 BE** total — option **(3)** is correct.
It is AP's largest component: **Revenue Expenditure > Capital Outlay > Loans and Advances**.
For comparison, States generally spend **80-87%** on revenue.
xa: AP revenue spending: **rice subsidy, power subsidy, welfare pensions, housing**.
AP 2026-27 BE revenue expenditure: **₹2,56,143 crore**.
Union revenue expenditure share: about **77%** (**2026-27 BE**).

n3852ec9ef0e.s: Who chaired the Expenditure Management Commission of 2014?
n3852ec9ef0e.x: Bimal Jalan chaired the 2014 Expenditure Management Commission and also, separately, the RBI Economic Capital Framework committee (2018-19).
xa: ⚠ Spelling trap: **"K.R."** vs correct **K.P.** Geethakrishnan.
**Committed expenditure** = **65.3%** of revenue receipts.
Interest = **26%** of total Union expenditure.

n8d9aabdb36e.s: Internal debt constitutes what share of India's public debt?
n8d9aabdb36e.x: Internal debt is 96.7% of public debt; G-Secs are over 90% of Central Government debt.
xa: Gross market borrowing 2026-27: **₹17.20 lakh crore**; net **₹11.73 lakh crore**.
Weighted average maturity **19.03 years**; yield **6.65%**.
Total borrowing requirement 2026-27: **₹16,95,768 crore**.

nindian-economy-62-9.s: Public debt is classified into internal and external debt on the basis of the:
nindian-economy-62-9.x: Internal and external debt are distinguished by where the government borrows from.
n: Internal debt is government debt raised within the domestic economy. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
External debt is government debt raised from external or foreign sources. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Public debt is classified into internal debt and external debt. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xa: **Public Debt (Art. 292)** = borrowings against the **Consolidated Fund of India**.
**Internal debt** = **96.7%** of public debt.
**External liabilities** = only **3.3%** of the Centre's total liabilities.

nindian-economy-62-13.s: Short-term government debt instruments are called:
nindian-economy-62-13.x: Treasury Bills are short-term; G-Secs are long-term and SDLs are issued by States.
n: Government dated securities, or G-Secs, are long-term government securities. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Treasury bills are short-term government debt instruments. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
Market-based securities are issued through auctions. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
The major conceptual instruments of external debt are external assistance and foreign borrowings. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xa: T-Bills are of **91, 182, 364-day** tenors.
**Small savings**, **provident funds** and **reserve funds** are "**other liabilities**" in the Public Account.
⚠ Not all external debt is in **US dollars** (UPSC 2019).

nindian-economy-62-17.s: Which pair consists only of instruments of internal debt?
nindian-economy-62-17.x: G-Secs and Treasury Bills are internal-debt instruments; external assistance and foreign borrowings are external debt.
n: The major conceptual instruments of internal debt are G-Secs, T-Bills, and others. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
The major conceptual instruments of external debt are external assistance and foreign borrowings. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #62 · pp 91-92]
xa: Non-marketable internal debt includes **special securities to NSSF** and **14-day Intermediate T-Bills**.
**Market borrowings** = biggest source of **capital receipts** (APPSC-G2 2008).
2026-27 gross market borrowing: **₹17.20 lakh crore**; net **₹11.73 lakh crore**.

n054772542e4.s: Special securities issued to the National Small Savings Fund form part of the Centre's:
n054772542e4.x: NSSF securities, like saving and compensation bonds and 14-day intermediate T-Bills, are non-marketable internal debt.
xa: ⚠ Marketable part: **market loans**, **Treasury Bills**, **Cash Management Bills**.
**Small savings** and **provident funds** are **other liabilities**, not internal debt.
Household savings reach government borrowing via **small savings/NSSF**.

n67ca165f9a7.s: Household bank deposits reach government borrowing mainly through banks':
n67ca165f9a7.x: Bank deposits flow to government borrowing through SLR holdings, alongside small savings/NSSF and insurance and provident funds.
xa: **Dated securities** issued at market-related rates in auctions = large part of internal debt (**UPSC 2022**, both true).
NSSF gets **special securities** — non-marketable internal debt.
FCI once borrowed from the **NSSF** — the classic off-budget case.

n1f90c55f984.s: India's external debt at the end of December 2024 was estimated at:
o: USD 635.177 billion, equivalent to 36.04% of GDP
USD 711.82 billion, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP
USD 718.2 billion, equivalent to 20.4% of GDP
USD 718.2 billion, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP
n1f90c55f984.x: India's external debt stood at USD 718.2 billion at end-December 2024, equivalent to 18.4% of GDP in the cited estimate.
n1f90c55f984.tq: Keep the external-debt amount and its GDP ratio together while rejecting figures from other debt categories.
xs: External debt: **USD 718.2 billion** at end-Dec 2024 = **18.4% of GDP** — option **(4)** is correct.
**20.4%** is a different estimate (RBI Annual Report), so option 3 mismatches the pair.
**₹6,35,177 crore** / **36.04%** is AP's total debt, not external debt.
xa: Forex reserves cover **90%** of external debt (**RBI Annual Report**).
Ranking: **21st** in the world; **11th** in the **G20**.
Government's external debt ≈ **2.6% of GDP**.

nc0d34023d62.s: Most of India's external debt is owed by:
o: Non-sovereign borrowers such as companies and banks
nc0d34023d62.x: Most external debt is non-sovereign; the Government's external debt is only about 2.6% of GDP.
xa: Government's external debt ≈ **2.6% of GDP**, under **5%** of its total debt.
Sovereign borrowing: mostly **multilateral, concessional, project-linked**.
Forex reserves cover **90%** of external debt.

n7856108a45a.s: The Centre’s new medium-term debt-GDP target is:
n7856108a45a.x: The new medium-term target is to bring the Centre’s debt-GDP ratio to 50 ± 1% by 31 March 2031.
n7856108a45a.tq: Pair the target range with its deadline.
xs: The Centre's new target is **50 ± 1% by 31 March 2031** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Budget 2026-27** made the **debt-GDP ratio the primary target** instead of fiscal deficit.
Current level: **55.6%** (BE 2026-27).
xa: Old FRBM (amended **2018**): Centre **40%**, general govt **60%** by **2024-25**.
General government projection (**FC-16**): **73.1%** by **2030-31**.

n1afcd7c7394.s: The FRBM Act, as amended in 2018, set the Centre's debt target for 2024-25 at:
n1afcd7c7394.x: General government debt was set at 60% with the Centre at 40%, as the N.K. Singh Committee recommended (States 20%).
xa: New anchor: **debt-GDP ratio** replaced fiscal deficit in **Budget 2026-27**.
New target: **50 ± 1% by 31 March 2031**.

n908a0b7f965.s: Market borrowings are the largest source of the government's:
n908a0b7f965.x: Market borrowings are the biggest source of the government's capital receipts.
xa: "Borrowings and other liabilities" = **24 paise** of every rupee in 2026-27 — the single largest receipt head.
Gross dated-securities borrowing 2026-27: **₹17.20 lakh crore**.
**Switches and buybacks** ease redemptions.

n70f6a135536.s: A zero primary deficit means that fresh government borrowing is needed only to meet:
n70f6a135536.x: Primary deficit excludes interest payments; when it is zero, fresh borrowing covers only interest.
xa: If **g > r**, debt-GDP can fall even with a small primary deficit.
If **r > g**, a **primary surplus** is needed.
Debt trap = borrowing to pay **interest on past debt**.

na59d32874de.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the interest-growth differential?
o: When r exceeds g, a primary surplus is needed
The differential is r − g, where g is nominal GDP growth
When g exceeds r, the debt-GDP ratio can fall even with a small primary deficit
When the effective interest rate exceeds nominal GDP growth, the debt-GDP ratio falls even with a primary deficit
na59d32874de.x: When r exceeds g, a primary surplus is needed to stabilise debt; the ratio does not fall with a primary deficit.
xa: Floating-rate debt only **4.1%** (end-**FY24**).
States' key ratios: **debt-GSDP** and **IP/RR**.

n42ff0015d46.s: Interest payments on Central debt are approximately what proportion of revenue receipts?
n42ff0015d46.x: Interest payments account for about 40% of revenue receipts, thereby limiting the fiscal space for other expenditure.
n42ff0015d46.tq: Use the closest exact share rather than an approximate distractor.
xs: Interest payments are about **40%** of revenue receipts — option **(3)** is correct.
High interest **squeezes** other spending.
This is why **debt, not deficit**, is the new anchor.
xa: Effective interest rate on Central debt: **7.12%**.
For States, **IP/RR** is a key sustainability ratio.
Centre's debt-GDP: **55.6%** (BE 2026-27).

nd6ece6a64a1.s: Which pair of indicators is especially relevant for assessing the debt sustainability of States?
o: Debt-GSDP ratio and interest payments-to-revenue receipts ratio
Current account deficit and foreign exchange reserves
Fiscal deficit-to-GDP ratio and export-import ratio
nd6ece6a64a1.x: For States, debt-GSDP and interest payments as a proportion of revenue receipts are the key sustainability ratios.
nd6ece6a64a1.tq: Match the level of government with its relevant sustainability indicators.
xs: States' key ratios: **debt-GSDP** and **interest payments / revenue receipts (IP/RR)** — option **(2)** is correct.
CAD and forex reserves are **external-sector** indicators, not State-debt ones.
Highest debt-GSDP: **Punjab** (**42.9%**, 2023-24).
xa: AP total debt: **36.04% of GSDP** (**2025-26 RE**).
16th FC caps States' fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP**.
Combined States' FD: **3.2% of GDP** in **FY25**.

n257de072aec.s: Public debt has become a fiscal anchor mainly because high interest payments:
o: Squeeze expenditure on other public purposes
Expand fiscal space for capital expenditure
n257de072aec.x: Interest payments of about 40% of revenue receipts constrain fiscal space and squeeze other spending.
xa: Centre's debt-GDP **55.8%** on the **new GDP series** after **Q1 2026-27**.
AP's debt crosses **₹7 lakh crore** in **BE 2026-27**.

n1cef88bdae9.s: The main concern about State off-budget borrowings and guarantees is that they:
o: Make consolidated public debt appear lower than it actually is
n1cef88bdae9.x: Off-budget borrowings and guarantees conceal the true consolidated debt burden and may weigh on sovereign ratings.
xa: 16th FC: stop off-budget borrowing; bring existing debt on-budget; widen definitions of **deficit and debt**.
The **Union deferred** accepting this.
FRBM caps new Central guarantees at **0.5% of GDP** a year.

nd2db6e36835.s: Which institution publishes ‘India's External Debt: A Status Report’?
o: Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance
nd2db6e36835.x: The report is published by the Department of Economic Affairs under the Ministry of Finance. The RBI compiles the quarterly external-debt data.
nd2db6e36835.tq: Distinguish the institution that publishes the report from the institution that compiles quarterly data.
xs: **"India's External Debt: A Status Report"** is published by the **Ministry of Finance (DEA)** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **RBI** compiles the **quarterly data** but is not the publisher.
DEA also sets **debt strategy** and handles **external borrowing**.
xa: External debt: **USD 718.2 billion** (end-Dec 2024), **18.4% of GDP**.
India ranks **21st** in the world, **11th** in **G20**.
Largest component historically: **commercial borrowings**.

n2c64195ff31.s: Since 2005-06, external loans to States have been:
n2c64195ff31.x: External loans reach States only through the Centre, on a back-to-back basis for general category States.
xa: States borrow only **within India** on the security of the State Consolidated Fund.
States issue **SDLs (State Development Loans)**.
States borrowed **₹5.23 trillion** up to **Oct 2025** (**62%** of FY26 plan).

n7625401e00c.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission has capped the fiscal deficit of States at what percentage of GSDP for 2026-31?
n7625401e00c.x: The fiscal deficit of States has been capped at 3% of GSDP for 2026-31 under the Sixteenth Finance Commission framework.
n7625401e00c.tq: Discriminate between the 2021-22 borrowing ceiling and the 2026-31 fiscal-deficit cap.
xs: The 16th FC caps States' fiscal deficit at **3% of GSDP** for **2026-31** — option **(2)** is correct.
Combined States' FD was **3.2% of GDP** in **FY25**.
**18 States** were above 3% in **FY24**.
xa: States borrow via **SDLs**.
16th FC: **stop off-budget borrowing**; bring existing debt on-budget.
Union **deferred** accepting the off-budget recommendation.

nbe3853c940b.s: Which State had the highest debt or outstanding liabilities as a percentage of GSDP among the following in 2023-24?
nbe3853c940b.x: Punjab had the highest ratio among the listed States at 42.9% of GSDP in 2023-24, followed by West Bengal at 38.3%, Rajasthan at 37.9% and Andhra Pradesh at 34.6%.
nbe3853c940b.tq: Compare the values in a ranking table and identify the maximum.
xs: **Punjab** had the highest debt-GSDP: **42.9%** (2023-24) — option **(3)** is correct.
**West Bengal 38.3%**, **Rajasthan 37.9%**, **Andhra Pradesh 34.6%** (2023-24).
⚠ Highest is **Punjab**, not Kerala or WB.
xa: Data basis: **FC-16** comparison; **RBI Study of State Budgets 2025**.

n39d6eb123c9.s: Under Article 293 of the Constitution, a State Government may borrow:
o: Only within the territory of India, upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of the State
From anywhere, including abroad, upon the security of the Consolidated Fund of India
Only from the Reserve Bank of India, without any security
Only from foreign governments, with the consent of Parliament
n39d6eb123c9.x: Article 293 allows States to borrow only within India on the security of the State's Consolidated Fund; they do so by issuing State Development Loans (SDLs). States cannot borrow abroad directly (external loans come through the Centre since 2005-06), are not restricted to the RBI, and do not borrow from foreign governments directly.
n39d6eb123c9.tq: Art. 293: States borrow only within India; Art. 292: Union.
xs: Under **Art. 293**, States borrow **only within India** on the security of the **State Consolidated Fund** — option **(1)** is correct.
External loans reach States **only through the Centre** since **2005-06**, so options 2 and 4 are wrong.
States are not limited to the RBI: they issue **SDLs** in the market.
xa: A State owing the Centre needs the **Centre's consent**.
General category States get external loans **back-to-back**.
16th FC: States' deficit capped at **3% of GSDP**.

n29f1474e948.s: According to the 2025-26 Revised Estimates, Andhra Pradesh's total debt was approximately:
n29f1474e948.x: AP's total debt in 2025-26 RE was ₹6,35,177 crore = 36.04% of GSDP (35.73% in 2024-25), with market borrowing (₹4,83,093 crore) the largest component. ₹5,64,488 crore/35.15% is the 2024-25 RE figure; ₹9,74,556 crore is total liabilities incl. PSUs (White Paper); 42.9% is Punjab's ratio and ₹4,83,093 crore is only the market-borrowing part.
n29f1474e948.tq: AP debt 2025-26 RE: ₹6.35 lakh crore, ~36% of GSDP.
xs: AP's total debt (**2025-26 RE**): **₹6,35,177 crore = 36.04% of GSDP** — option **(2)** is correct.
**₹9,74,556 crore** is total liabilities incl. PSUs (**White Paper**); **₹4,83,093 crore** is only market borrowing.
xa: Accounts-based 2024-25 figure: **₹5,68,623 crore**.
AP's debt crosses **₹7 lakh crore** in **BE 2026-27**.

n74b4473e571.s: Which change was made in Budget 2026-27 regarding the principal fiscal anchor?
o: Revenue deficit replaced the primary balance.
The current account deficit replaced public debt.
The fiscal deficit replaced the debt-GDP ratio.
The debt-GDP ratio replaced the fiscal deficit.
n74b4473e571.x: Budget 2026-27 made the debt-GDP ratio the primary target instead of the fiscal deficit.
n74b4473e571.tq: Test the policy shift by identifying what replaced what.
xs: **Budget 2026-27** made the **debt-GDP ratio** the primary target, replacing the **fiscal deficit** — option **(4)** is correct.
Option 3 reverses it.
So **debt, not deficit**, is now the fiscal anchor.
xa: Target: **50 ± 1% by 31 March 2031**.
High interest (**40%** of revenue receipts) squeezes spending.
Centre's debt-GDP: **55.6%** (BE 2026-27).

n52c73264e6c.s: The FRBM framework caps new Central government guarantees at ____ of GDP a year.
n52c73264e6c.x: New Central guarantees, treated as contingent liabilities, are capped at 0.5% of GDP a year.
xa: AP guarantees: **₹1,77,328 crore** (**10% of GSDP**).
AP total liabilities including PSUs: **₹9,74,556 crore** (**White Paper, 12 Jun 2024**).
The **16th FC** asked to widen definitions of **deficit and debt**.

n94d6152caec.s: The 16th Finance Commission recommended that off-budget borrowing should be:
o: Stopped, with existing off-budget debt brought on-budget
n94d6152caec.x: The 16th FC recommended stopping off-budget borrowing, bringing existing debt on-budget and widening the definitions of deficit and debt.
xa: Off-budget = loans by **PSUs, SPVs, corporations** serviced from the budget.
AP off-budget debt: **₹1,40,470 crore** as of **31 March 2024**.
The 16th FC caps States' deficit at **3% of GSDP**.

ndd755ee3d1b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about public debt management in India?
o: The PDMC was set up in 2016 in the Department of Economic Affairs
A statutory PDMA was first proposed in Budget 2015-16
The PDMC is headed by the Joint Secretary (Budget)
The statutory PDMA has been created and has taken over the RBI's Public Debt Office
ndd755ee3d1b.x: The statutory PDMA has not yet been created; the RBI still manages public debt.
xa: PDMC is a transition to an independent statutory **PDMA**.
RBI manages public debt under the **RBI Act, 1934**.
**Public Debt Office**: issue, servicing and records of **G-Secs**.

n4df2d7bab02.s: Under Article 292 of the Constitution, Public Debt of the Union comprises borrowings contracted against the:
n4df2d7bab02.x: Article 292 relates to borrowings by the Government of India against the security of the Consolidated Fund of India. Other liabilities are recorded in the Public Account.
n4df2d7bab02.tq: Recall the constitutional article associated with the borrowing authority.
xs: **Public Debt** under **Art. 292** = borrowings contracted against the **Consolidated Fund of India** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Other liabilities** sit in the **Public Account**, where the government acts as **banker/trustee** — so option 4 is wrong.
States borrow on the security of the **State Consolidated Fund** under **Art. 293**.
xa: Marketable internal debt: **market loans (G-Secs)**, **Treasury Bills** (91, 182, 364-day), **Cash Management Bills**.
Public Account items: **small savings**, **post-office deposits**, **provident funds**, **reserve funds and deposits**.
**Internal debt** = **96.7%** of public debt.

n1d11fae1c98.s: Historically, the largest component of India's external debt has been:
n1d11fae1c98.x: Commercial borrowings have historically been the largest component of India's external debt.
n1d11fae1c98.tq: Identify the principal historical component while excluding domestic-liability categories.
xs: **Commercial borrowings** have historically been the largest component — option **(3)** is correct (**UPPSC 2017** key).
**Small savings** and **provident funds** are **domestic** other liabilities, not external debt.
**Sovereign multilateral** loans are a small slice: most external debt is **non-sovereign**.
xa: Government's external debt ≈ **2.6% of GDP**; under **5%** of its total debt.
⚠ Not all external debt is in **US dollars** (**UPSC 2019**).
Status Report published by **Ministry of Finance (DEA)**.

nindian-economy-59-7.s: Which is the main account of the Government of India?
nindian-economy-59-7.x: The Consolidated Fund is the main account and receives loan recoveries; the Public Account holds trust money.
n: The Consolidated Fund of India is the main government account. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
Loan recoveries are credited to the Consolidated Fund of India. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The Contingency Fund of India is used for urgent expenditure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The Contingency Fund of India is used for unforeseen expenditure. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
The Public Account of India holds money in trust for the government. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #59 · pp 88-89]
xa: The Public Account is a **government-held trust** or **liability account**.
The **State Provident Fund** is part of the **Public Account**.
**Small savings**, **provident funds**, **reserve funds** sit in the Public Account.

n0eb48d797f9.s: In Indian usage, deficit financing means meeting the budget gap by:
o: Borrowing from the RBI, which creates new money
n0eb48d797f9.x: In India, deficit financing means borrowing from the RBI and creating new money; Western usage covers any financing of a deficit.
xa: Effect of deficit financing: **increase in money supply** (UPPSC 2016).
Purpose: raising resources for **economic development** — a "**pragmatic tool**" for **Five Year Plans**.
Heavy reliance began from the **1970s** (oil shocks, welfare spending).

ncdbd6a3ebd2.s: In India, deficit financing was used as a pragmatic tool mainly to finance:
ncdbd6a3ebd2.x: Deficit financing mobilised resources for economic development and financed the Five Year Plans.
xa: Weak **privately owned banking** sector after **1947**.
From the **1970s**, oil shocks + welfare spending widened deficits.
That led to **debt and inflation** worries.

n3f9152e5a89.s: India's reliance on deficit financing became heavier from which period onwards?
n3f9152e5a89.x: Deficit financing was used in a limited way until the late 1960s and relied on more heavily from the 1970s onwards.
xa: **September 1994**: RBI-Government agreement began phasing out **ad hoc T-bills**.
**FRBM Act, 2003** bars RBI primary subscription from **1 April 2006**.
Purpose throughout: financing **Five Year Plans**.

n73547215809.s: When the FRBM escape clause is invoked, the deviation from the fiscal target is capped at:
n73547215809.x: The escape-clause deviation is capped at 0.5% of GDP a year; since 2018 monetised borrowing is allowed only on escape-clause grounds.
xa: **Ad hoc T-bills** were phased out from **September 1994** and ended in **March 1997**.
**WMA** replaced ad hoc T-bills from **1 April 1997**.
Liquidity tool now: **OMOs** — sale absorbs, purchase injects.

n3169246d4ae.s: Ways and Means Advances (WMA) came into operation from:
n3169246d4ae.x: WMA began on 1 April 1997 after the March 1997 agreement ended ad hoc T-bills, whose phase-out began in September 1994.
xa: **FRBM Act, 2003**: no RBI primary subscription from **1 April 2006**.
**2018 amendment**: permitted only on **escape-clause** grounds.
**OMOs** are now the liquidity tool.

nad1d033cc41.s: Which method of deficit financing is the most inflationary?
nad1d033cc41.x: Creation of new money is most inflationary, followed by bank and then public borrowing; debt repayment withdraws money.
xa: RBI financing raises money supply → **demand-pull inflation**.
Inflation hurts the **poor** most.
Indian deficit financing = borrowing from the **RBI**.

n0cf0df1dd7c.s: Heavy government market borrowing that raises interest rates and squeezes private investment is called:
n0cf0df1dd7c.x: Absorbing loanable funds and squeezing private investment is crowding out; borrowing to pay interest is the debt trap.
xa: RBI financing raises money supply → **demand-pull inflation**, hurting the poor most.
**Creation of new money** is the **most inflationary** mode (UPSC 2021).
**Repayment of public debt** is **not inflationary** — it withdraws money.

n4ca5aa63eb9.s: Deficit financing is particularly likely to cause demand-pull inflation when it:
o: Uses existing savings without increasing aggregate demand
Raises money supply and demand without a corresponding increase in goods and services
Withdraws money through repayment of public debt
n4ca5aa63eb9.x: RBI financing can raise money supply and demand without a matching increase in goods and services, producing demand-pull inflation. The burden of such inflation tends to affect the poor most severely.
n4ca5aa63eb9.tq: Connect the monetary expansion with excess demand rather than merely identifying a budget deficit.
xs: **Demand-pull inflation** arises when money supply and demand rise **without more goods** — option **(3)** is correct.
This is the effect of **RBI financing**.
Borrowing from the public uses **existing savings**; **repayment** withdraws money — neither is demand-pull.
xa: Such inflation **hurts the poor most**.
**Creation of new money** = most inflationary (**UPSC 2021**).
Effect of deficit financing: **increase in money supply** (**UPPSC 2016**).

n077444164f7.s: Andhra Pradesh's fiscal deficit in 2024–25 was:
n077444164f7.x: AP's 2024–25 fiscal deficit of 5.05 per cent exceeded the 4 per cent ceiling; market loans form 75 per cent of its debt.
xa: Market borrowing is the **largest** component of AP's debt.
States borrowed **₹5.23 trillion** till **Oct 2025**.
RBI urges shifting from **subsidies to capex**.

n93d17df9d8b.s: Effective Revenue Deficit is calculated as:
o: Revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets
Revenue deficit plus grants for creation of capital assets
n93d17df9d8b.x: Effective Revenue Deficit equals Revenue Deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets. Such grants are excluded from the consumption component because they help create assets.
n93d17df9d8b.tq: Split the formula into the basic deficit and the qualifying deduction.
xs: **ERD = revenue deficit − grants for creation of capital assets** — option **(2)**.
It is a **Rangarajan Committee** concept: the "true" consumption deficit.
FD − interest payments is the **primary deficit**, not ERD.
xa: ERD was introduced in **Union Budget 2011-12** and written into FRBM by the **2012 amendment**.
Grants to States that build assets (e.g. **MGNREGA** roads/ponds) are not counted as consumption.
Hence **ERD <= RD**.

n37003dfac58.s: Which deficit indicates government borrowing for day-to-day consumption?
n37003dfac58.x: Revenue deficit shows borrowing for consumption; fiscal deficit shows the total borrowing requirement from all sources.
xa: RD **1.5** / FD **4.3** = roughly **one-third** of borrowing still goes to revenue spending.
**ERD <= RD**.

o: The portion of revenue deficit covered by grants
The portion of deficit financed through external commercial borrowing
The portion of deficit financed by borrowing from the public
The portion of deficit financed by the Reserve Bank of India through creation of high-powered money
n0e354e33469.x: Monetised Deficit is the part of the deficit financed by the RBI, involving an increase in RBI credit to the government and creation of high-powered money.
n0e354e33469.tq: Match the specialised deficit term with its financing source and monetary effect.
xs: **Monetised deficit** is the part financed by the **RBI** through creation of **high-powered money** — option **(4)**.
It means borrowing from RBI / increase in RBI credit to government / printing fresh currency.
It is **inflationary**; FRBM disallows it under normal conditions.
xa: RBI is barred from subscribing to **primary issues** of G-Secs from **2006-07**, except under the **escape clause**.
**Ad hoc Treasury Bills** — automatic monetisation — abolished from **1 April 1997**.
Money-printing is the **most inflationary route** of deficit financing.

n4e3bf107af3.s: A government has a fiscal deficit of ₹1,50,000 crore and interest payments of ₹1,20,000 crore. Its primary deficit is:
xa: In the notes' worked example FD = 4,60,000 − 3,10,000 = **1,50,000** (= borrowings).
⚠ FD always equals **borrowings and other liabilities**.
With positive interest, **FD > PD** always.

nd68326b4e05.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the relationship between deficits?
o: Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments
The effective revenue deficit is always greater than the revenue deficit
Fiscal deficit exceeds revenue deficit when capex exceeds non-debt capital receipts
Effective revenue deficit equals revenue deficit minus grants for creation of capital assets
nd68326b4e05.x: Since ERD = RD minus grants for creation of capital assets, ERD is less than or equal to RD.
xa: ⚠ "PD always higher than FD" is **false** (APPSC 2023).
**ERD** was introduced in **Union Budget 2011-12**; written into FRBM in **2012**.

n2576459cdba.s: In Indian public finance, deficit financing primarily means covering a government financing gap by:
o: Drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the RBI or issuing new currency
Transferring revenue receipts to the central bank
n2576459cdba.x: Deficit financing in the Indian context includes drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the RBI and issuing new currency to cover the financing gap.
n2576459cdba.tq: Identify the combination of recognised financing methods rather than an individual fiscal measure.
xs: Deficit financing (Indian usage) = **drawing down cash balances, borrowing from the RBI or issuing new currency** — option **(2)**.
RBI money creation raises money supply → **inflation**; money-printing is the **most inflationary route**.
xa: Borrowing from the public absorbs liquidity and can **slow private activity**.
External borrowing carries **currency risk**.
**Crowding out**: heavy govt borrowing pushes up interest rates → private investment falls.

nf260c21f9dd.s: A high ratio of revenue deficit to fiscal deficit indicates that government borrowing is being used mainly for
nf260c21f9dd.x: A high RD/FD ratio means a larger part of borrowing finances revenue or consumption expenditure rather than investment.
nf260c21f9dd.tq: Interpret the quality of borrowing by asking whether it finances consumption or investment.
xs: A high RD/FD ratio means borrowing is **financing consumption or revenue expenditure**, not investment — option **(1)**.
RD shows borrowing for day-to-day consumption (**dissaving**).
Creation of capital assets is the opposite case (low RD share).
xa: 2026-27 BE: RD **1.5** / FD **4.3** = roughly **one-third** of borrowing still goes to revenue spending.
**ERD** = RD − grants for creation of capital assets.
RD and ERD show whether borrowing funds **consumption or assets**.

nad0a0df0d1c.s: A higher fiscal deficit can widen the current account deficit because government dissaving:
o: Reduces national savings and widens the savings-investment gap
nad0a0df0d1c.x: Lower national savings widen the savings-investment gap, which may be met by foreign capital, widening the CAD.
xa: CAD financing: **FDI** is most desirable; **FPI** is volatile.
**Crowding out**: heavy govt borrowing pushes up interest rates → private investment falls.

n23516ca5af1.s: The fiscal multiplier is generally largest for:
n23516ca5af1.x: Capital expenditure has a larger multiplier than revenue spending or transfers because it creates productive capacity and draws in complementary investment.
xa: Fiscal multiplier = **change in GDP / change in govt spending** (or taxes).
Public expenditure on capex is called **"pump priming"**.
Capex BE 2026-27: **₹12.2 lakh crore**.

ne55213395a9.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the headline marker of fiscal health?
ne55213395a9.x: Fiscal deficit is the headline marker of fiscal health. Revenue deficit and effective revenue deficit provide additional information about the nature of government borrowing.
ne55213395a9.tq: Use the direct one-term recall approach for the principal fiscal-health indicator.
xs: **Fiscal deficit** is the **headline marker** of fiscal health — option **(2)**.
**RD and ERD** show whether borrowing funds consumption or assets; **PD** excludes interest on past debt.
xa: Consolidation from **9.2%** to **4.4%** brought **three sovereign rating upgrades in 2025**.

n9312c5979f5.x: AP still runs a primary deficit, so it has a fiscal deficit even after excluding interest payments.
xa: **10** States slipped from revenue surplus to deficit between **FY19** and **FY25**.

nindian-economy-21-4.s: Fiscal deficit minus interest payments gives the:
nindian-economy-21-4.x: Primary deficit = fiscal deficit − interest payments; revenue deficit = revenue expenditure − revenue receipts.
n: Revenue deficit equals revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
Fiscal deficit equals total expenditure minus total non-debt receipts. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
Primary deficit equals fiscal deficit minus interest payments. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
Debt management is an objective of the FRBM Act. [Indian Economy · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 30-32]
xa: **Fiscal deficit** = the government's **total borrowing requirement**.
**Monetised deficit** = the part financed by the **RBI** — inflationary.

n0ef3126ca7f.s: Fiscal policy refers primarily to the use of government revenue and expenditure to influence:
n0ef3126ca7f.x: Fiscal policy uses government revenue and expenditure to influence aggregate demand, resource allocation and income distribution.
n0ef3126ca7f.tq: Select the option covering the full scope of the policy definition.
xs: Fiscal policy uses government revenue and expenditure to influence **aggregate demand, allocation and distribution** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It covers the level of **purchases**, **transfers**, the **tax structure** and **borrowing** of the government.
Money supply is managed by **monetary policy** (RBI / MPC), not fiscal policy; exchange rate and balance of payments are not "only" what it targets.
xa: Fiscal policy is made by the **Ministry of Finance**, with legislative backing.
**J.M. Keynes** (General Theory, **1936**) first linked fiscal policy to economic performance → basis of **active demand management**.
Musgrave's three budget functions: **allocation**, **distribution** and **stabilisation**.

nd62d299ff9d.s: In Musgrave's budget functions, providing public goods and allocating resources is the:
nd62d299ff9d.x: Allocation means providing public goods; distribution reduces inequality and stabilisation controls inflation and unemployment.
xa: The three functions are from **Richard (R.A.) Musgrave**, who popularised **fiscal federalism** (**1959**).
**J.M. Keynes**' General Theory (**1936**) is the basis of active demand management.
Direct taxes = **58.8%** of total taxes in **FY25** — evidence of progressive taxation.

n27ba001c92f.s: Who popularised the term 'fiscal federalism' in 1959?
n27ba001c92f.x: Richard Musgrave popularised fiscal federalism in 1959 and identified allocation, distribution and stabilisation as budget functions.
xa: **Allocation** = providing **public goods**, the **primary purpose** of a budget (APPSC GS **2023**).
**Distribution** reduces inequality through **progressive taxation** (APPSC GS **2019**).
**J.M. Keynes** (General Theory, **1936**) first linked fiscal policy to economic performance.

n3ef1370b3c0.s: Which one of the following is NOT a usual source of financing fiscal deficit?
o: Market borrowings through dated government securities and Treasury Bills
Small savings and the National Small Savings Fund
