n39bdd5af21c.s: Which institution is responsible for funding node trunk infrastructure at Kopparthy, Krishnapatnam and Orvakal?
n39bdd5af21c.x: NICDIT funds node trunk infrastructure at the Kopparthy, Krishnapatnam and Orvakal nodes.
n39bdd5af21c.tq: Match the institution with its specific funding function and nodes.

**APIIC** is the nodal agency for the BHAVYA parks in AP.
NICDIT has **₹3,000 crore** in BE 2026-27.

nb79e7f1977b.s: Which one of the following is the nodal agency for industrial infrastructure in Andhra Pradesh, including IT, biotech and apparel parks and SEZs?

**APIIC** is one of the VCIC's **four PIUs**, with **APRDC, AP Transco** and **GVMC**.

n2742f266240.s: In Chittoor district, the Bengaluru–Chennai Expressway passes through the elephant corridor of:

n41b8333c1f6.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the seven high-speed rail corridors identified as “growth connectors” in the Union Budget 2026–27?

The seven: **Mumbai-Pune, Pune-Hyderabad, Hyderabad-Bengaluru, Hyderabad-Chennai, Chennai-Bengaluru, Delhi-Varanasi, Varanasi-Siliguri**.

**Hyderabad-Chennai** is to take **2 h 55 min**.
An **Amaravati-Hyderabad** bullet train is proposed at **70 minutes**.

n6d3205baa19.s: Special Category Status (SCS) was first introduced in India in 1969 on the recommendation of which body?
n6d3205baa19.x: Special Category Status was introduced in 1969 on the recommendation of the Fifth Finance Commission. The National Development Council endorsed the Gadgil Formula (1968-69) for distributing Plan funds, but it was not the body that recommended SCS.
n6d3205baa19.tq: Identify the recommending body rather than the institution that later endorsed the related formula.
xs: SCS was introduced in **1969** on the recommendation of the **Fifth Finance Commission** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **National Development Council** only endorsed the **Gadgil Formula** (1968-69) for Plan funds.
The **14th FC** (Y.V. Reddy) made **no distinction** between general and SCS states.
xa: SCS is **not** in the Constitution; it is an **executive/Planning Commission-era** classification.
First three SCS states: **Jammu & Kashmir, Assam, Nagaland**.
Plan transfers: **Gadgil formula** (1969) → **Gadgil-Mukherjee formula** (1991).

n2c6223cf66c.s: Which formula was introduced in 1991 as the later version of the Gadgil Formula for Plan transfers to States?
n2c6223cf66c.x: The Gadgil Formula was later modified and became the Gadgil-Mukherjee Formula in 1991.
n2c6223cf66c.tq: Distinguish the original formula from its later modified version by the year of modification.
xs: The Gadgil formula (1969) later became the **Gadgil-Mukherjee formula** in **1991** — option **(3)**.
It governed **Plan transfers** to States.
xa: The **Gadgil Formula** was endorsed by the **NDC** in **1968-69**.
SCS states got a **reserved first share** of **Normal Central Assistance**.
SCS began in **1969** (5th FC); first three: **J&K, Assam, Nagaland**.

n5d136e119c7.s: Which were the first three States to be given Special Category Status?
n5d136e119c7.x: The first three SCS States were Jammu & Kashmir, Assam and Nagaland (1969). Manipur, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Meghalaya and Uttarakhand got the status later; Uttarakhand was the last of the 11.
n5d136e119c7.tq: First SCS trio = J&K, Assam, Nagaland.
xs: The first three SCS states were **Jammu & Kashmir, Assam** and **Nagaland** — option **(1)**.
Manipur, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Mizoram, Meghalaya and Uttarakhand are among the **11** but came later.
xa: SCS began in **1969** on the **5th Finance Commission**'s recommendation.
**J&K** became a **Union Territory** in **2019**.
Never granted despite demands: **Bihar** (BPSC 2019 key), **Odisha**, **Andhra Pradesh**.

na98c2e543c0.s: Which of the following was NOT a criterion associated with Special Category Status?
o: High population density and advanced infrastructure
na98c2e543c0.x: High population density and advanced infrastructure were not criteria for Special Category Status. The criteria included difficult terrain, low population density or sizeable tribal population, border location, economic and infrastructural backwardness, and non-viable finances.
na98c2e543c0.tq: Find the option that reverses the stated backwardness and population criteria.
xs: **High population density and advanced infrastructure** is not an SCS criterion — so option **(3)** is correct.
The criteria are the opposite: **low population density** and/or sizeable **tribal population**, and **economic and infrastructural backwardness**.
**Non-viable state finances**, **border location** and **hilly terrain** are genuine criteria.
xa: Five criteria: **hilly terrain**, **low density/tribal population**, **international borders**, **backwardness**, **non-viable finances**.
Rationale: a **larger tax share** to cover the gap.
Benefits include **concessional-interest** central loans and **tax breaks** for industry.

nbfdc73da43a.s: What was the rationale behind granting Special Category Status to States?
o: To give them exclusive legislative powers over Union List subjects
To give them a larger share of central taxes to cover the gap caused by geographic disadvantage and backwardness
To exempt them from the jurisdiction of the Finance Commission
To allow them to borrow abroad without central consent
nbfdc73da43a.x: SCS was meant to give such States a larger tax share to cover the gap arising from geographic disadvantage and economic and infrastructural backwardness.
nbfdc73da43a.tq: SCS = bigger share to bridge the gap.
xs: SCS gave states a **larger share of central taxes** to **cover the gap** from geographic disadvantage and backwardness — option **(2)**.
The gap comes from **hilly terrain**, **low density/tribal population**, **border location**, **backwardness** and **non-viable finances**.
xa: SCS loans come at **concessional interest**; industries get **tax breaks**.
Unspent SCS funds **do not lapse**.
The Centre argued the **14th FC**'s higher devolution **subsumed** SCS benefits.

n771df975e0e.s: Central loans to Special Category States carried ____ interest.
n771df975e0e.x: SCS States got Central loans at concessional interest, while general States got normal terms.
xa: Unspent funds in SCS states **do not lapse**; in general states they lapse.
PMGSY covers habitations of **250+** in SCS states vs **500+** in plains.
GST exemption threshold is lower (**₹10 lakh**) for SCS.

n8522dd8138d.s: What was the treatment of unspent funds in a Special Category State?
o: They lapsed at the end of the financial year
They did not lapse and could be carried forward
They were converted into Central loans
They were transferred automatically to general States
n8522dd8138d.x: Unspent funds in Special Category States did not lapse and could be carried forward. In general States, such funds lapsed.
n8522dd8138d.tq: Test the distinction between lapse and carry-forward treatment.
xs: Unspent funds in SCS states **did not lapse** and were **carried forward** — option **(2)**.
In **general** states, unspent funds **lapse**.
xa: SCS central loans: **concessional interest**.
Consumer Welfare Fund seed money: **90:10** for SCS vs **75:25**.
SCS industries get **income tax/excise-type** tax breaks.

na1816e95986.s: Under PMGSY, habitations eligible for road connectivity in Special Category States have a population of:
o: 250 or more, against 500 or more in the plains
500 or more, against 1,000 or more in the plains
100 or more, against 250 or more in the plains
1,000 or more, against 500 or more in the plains
na1816e95986.x: The PMGSY threshold is 250+ in SCS States against 500+ in the plains. The other options give the wrong thresholds, and the last one reverses the concession. A similar concession applies to Consumer Welfare Fund seed money (90:10 for SCS against 75:25).
na1816e95986.tq: SCS concessions: PMGSY 250 vs 500; CWF 90:10 vs 75:25.
xs: Under **PMGSY**, SCS habitations of **250 or more** qualify, against **500 or more** in the plains — option **(1)**.
Option (4) reverses the concession; the SCS threshold is the **lower** one.
xa: ⚠ Consumer Welfare Fund seed money: **90:10** for SCS vs **75:25** (2026).
GST exemption threshold is **₹10 lakh** (lower) for SCS.
SCS central loans carry **concessional interest**.

n200446d2843.s: Who chaired the Fourteenth Finance Commission (award period 2015-20)?
n200446d2843.x: Y.V. Reddy chaired the Fourteenth Finance Commission, whose award covered 2015-20.

It made **no distinction** between general and special category states.

n277dcd30196.s: Which Finance Commission added a 10 per cent 'Contribution to GDP' criterion while retaining the 41 per cent share?
n277dcd30196.x: The Sixteenth FC kept 41 per cent and added a Contribution to GDP criterion; the Fourteenth gave 42 and the Fifteenth 41 per cent.
xa: 16th FC chair: **Arvind Panagariya**; award **1 Apr 2026-31 Mar 2031**.

The **5th FC** recommended SCS (**1969**).

nef91ec254e7.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission gave the 'Contribution to GDP' criterion a weight of:
nef91ec254e7.x: The Sixteenth Finance Commission added Contribution to GDP as a criterion with a 10 per cent weight.
xa: 16th FC chair: **Arvind Panagariya**; award **1 Apr 2026-31 Mar 2031**.

n9b0e7cadd6b.s: The Sixteenth Finance Commission was chaired by ____ and its award covers ____.
n9b0e7cadd6b.x: The 16th FC is chaired by Arvind Panagariya, and its award runs from 1 Apr 2026 to 31 Mar 2031; it keeps the share at 41%. Y.V. Reddy chaired the 14th FC (2015-20). 2021-26 was the 15th FC period, and N.K. Singh chaired the 15th FC, not the 16th.
xs: The **16th FC** is chaired by **Arvind Panagariya**, with an award from **1 April 2026 to 31 March 2031** — option **(1)**.
**Y.V. Reddy** chaired the **14th FC** (2015-20).
xa: The 16th FC keeps **41%** and adds **"Contribution to GDP"** (**10%** weight).
It also ends **revenue deficit grants**.
14th FC: **32% to 42%**, accepted **24 Feb 2015**.

n7e5f4326fd0.s: Why did Andhra Pradesh say the Fourteenth Finance Commission's 42 per cent devolution did not meet its SCS concerns?

n7e5f4326fd0.x: The 42 per cent devolution applied uniformly to all States, so it did not compensate AP for its asymmetric loss of Hyderabad.
xa: 14th FC (chair **Y.V. Reddy**): **32% to 42%**, the **largest increase ever**.

nc1b91dbc186.s: For how long was Special Category Status assured to Andhra Pradesh in the Rajya Sabha in 2014?

xs: SCS was assured to AP for **five years** — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2018 key).

xa: It was **not written into the Reorganisation Act**.
In **Sep 2016**, a **Special Assistance Package** was offered instead.
AP argued a commitment on the **floor of Parliament** carries constitutional weight.

n9534e50cb0d.s: In which year was the Special Assistance Package offered to Andhra Pradesh?
n9534e50cb0d.x: The package came in September 2016, after the 2014 Rajya Sabha assurance and the 2015 Fourteenth FC award, and before TDP left the NDA in 2018.
xa: In **2019**, SCS became an "**emotional referendum**"; YSRCP branded the package a "**betrayal**".
In **2026**, Manickam Tagore, Botcha Satyanarayana and Y.S. Sharmila revived the demand.
In **2018**, TDP moved a **no-confidence motion** in the **Lok Sabha** (July), which was defeated.

n4bf5bf366b8.s: Which political development took place in 2018 in the context of Andhra Pradesh’s Special Category Status demand?
o: TDP broke from the NDA and moved a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha
YSRCP joined the NDA and withdrew the demand
The Rajya Sabha enacted SCS through a constitutional amendment
The Centre granted SCS to Andhra Pradesh for ten years
n4bf5bf366b8.x: In 2018, the TDP broke from the NDA and moved a no-confidence motion in the Lok Sabha in July; the motion was defeated.
n4bf5bf366b8.tq: Match the year with both linked political actions and avoid replacing a motion with a constitutional amendment.
xs: In **2018**, the **TDP broke from the NDA** and moved a **no-confidence motion** in the **Lok Sabha** — option **(1)**.
The motion (July 2018) was **defeated**.
xa: ⚠ Assurance in the **Rajya Sabha** (2014); no-confidence motion in the **Lok Sabha** (2018).
In **2019**, SCS became an "**emotional referendum**".
In **2026**, the demand was revived during the **AP Reorganisation (Amendment) Bill** debate.

n243ee68c598.s: Which of the following States received Special Category Status?
n243ee68c598.x: Uttarakhand was among the SCS States; Bihar, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh were never granted it despite their demands.
xa: **Bihar** never getting SCS was a **BPSC 2019** key.
⚠ **Telangana** was never granted SCS, though some notes wrongly list it.
First three SCS states: **J&K, Assam, Nagaland**.

nd5643976e2f.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the 11 States listed as having been granted Special Category Status?
nd5643976e2f.x: Telangana has never been granted Special Category Status. Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh and Tripura are included among the 11 SCS States.
nd5643976e2f.tq: Find the State wrongly inserted into an otherwise genuine list of SCS recipients.
xs: **Telangana** has never been granted SCS — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh** and **Tripura** are among the **11** SCS states.
⚠ Some notes (UPSC Economy notes) wrongly list Telangana among SCS states.
xa: The **11**: Assam, Nagaland, J&K, Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Meghalaya, Tripura, Sikkim, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram, Uttarakhand.
Never granted (asked): **Bihar, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**.
**J&K** became a Union Territory in **2019**.

ncc4b12dd56f.s: The Special Assistance Package covered which period?
ncc4b12dd56f.x: The package covered five years, from 2015-16 to 2019-20, corresponding to the promised SCS period.
ncc4b12dd56f.tq: Test the exact five-year span rather than just the duration.
xs: The package covered **2015-16 to 2019-20** — so option **(4)** is correct.
These **five years** match the promised SCS period.
xa: It was announced in **September 2016** by FM **Arun Jaitley**.
PM **Manmohan Singh** had promised SCS for **five years** in **2014**.
⚠ **2016-17** is the year of the **₹4,058.04 crore** special assistance, not the start of the package.

nf0e9e24c484.s: Which of the following benefits was associated with SCS but not provided in the same strength under the Special Assistance Package?
nf0e9e24c484.x: SCS included tax concessions for industry, whereas the package offered only the weaker Section 94(1) incentives.
nf0e9e24c484.tq: Focus on the benefit that changes in character rather than merely in delivery route.
xs: **Tax concessions for industry** came with SCS but are weaker under the package — option **(4)**.
The package has **only Sec 94(1)** incentives; the promised **10-year tax holiday** was delayed, diluted or subsumed in **GST**.
Amaravati support, multilateral repayment and project-linked borrowing are features **of** the package itself.
xa: SCS industry benefits are **income tax/excise-type** tax breaks.
SCS = **recognised category**, automatic yearly flows; package = **executive**, no statutory permanence.
CSS funding: **90:10** automatic under SCS.

nc0f6de7b58f.s: Unlike SCS funds, funds under Andhra Pradesh's Special Assistance Package were tied to:
nc0f6de7b58f.x: SCS funds could be used across all schemes, while the executive package's funds were tied to approved externally aided projects.
xa: SCS duration: promised **5 years**; package: **2015-16 to 2019-20**.
Comparative note: SCS = status with **automatic 90:10** flows vs package = money tied to projects.

na411759380a.s: Which of the following about the Special Assistance Package for Andhra Pradesh is NOT correct?
o: It included a special development package for Rayalaseema and North Coastal districts.
It supported specified capital institutions and buildings.
A ten-year tax holiday was implemented fully without dilution.
The Centre was to bridge AP's resource gap for 2014-15.
na411759380a.x: The promised ten-year tax holiday was delayed, diluted or subsumed in the GST framework; it was not implemented fully.
xa: **₹2,500 crore** was promised for the **capital**.
The **7** backward districts = **4 Rayalaseema + 3 North Coastal**; releases stalled.
The **2014-15** revenue deficit grant was **₹3,979 crore**.

nf5b5f055ae4.s: Under the Externally Aided Projects route for Andhra Pradesh, the Centre repays loan and interest up to:
o: The full loan without any limit
nf5b5f055ae4.x: The State borrows from agencies like the World Bank and ADB, and the Centre repays loan and interest up to the SCS-equivalent amount.
xa: ⚠ Some notes say "Centre to bear **40%** cost for EAPs"; the fuller account gives **90%**.
AP complains of **long approval cycles** and **heavy compliance** — red tape and delays.
**₹15,000 crore** for **Amaravati** is raised via multilateral lenders.

nf04047f9bce.s: Why has Andhra Pradesh criticised the Externally Aided Projects route?
o: It excludes multilateral agencies from project financing.
It requires long approval cycles and heavy compliance, creating red tape and delays.
It provides automatic tax concessions to industries.
It prevents the use of all external finance.
nf04047f9bce.x: Andhra Pradesh has argued that long approval processes and extensive compliance requirements create red tape and delay project implementation.
nf04047f9bce.tq: Link the administrative process to the stated consequence instead of confusing it with financing restrictions.
xs: AP says the EAP route has **long approval cycles** and **heavy compliance**, causing **red tape and delays** — option **(2)**.
The route actually depends on multilateral agencies (**World Bank, ADB**) — so options (1) and (4) are wrong.
xa: The Centre repays **loan and interest** up to the SCS-equivalent amount.
Criticism: package = **loans-and-projects** in place of a status; **fund lapses** + slow EAP approvals.
The State wants **grants**; the Centre prefers **loans and guarantees**.

n330f706bc0a.s: The Centre cited which development as having already absorbed the benefits associated with Special Category Status?
o: The GST Council's abolition of all central assistance
The 13th Finance Commission's reduction of devolution to 32%
The 14th Finance Commission's removal of the general-special category distinction and increase of devolution to 42%
The 16th Finance Commission's restoration of revenue-deficit grants
n330f706bc0a.x: The Centre relied on the 14th Finance Commission's removal of the distinction and increase of devolution to 42% as having absorbed SCS-related benefits.
n330f706bc0a.tq: Use the institution, percentage and policy change as a combined identification test.
xs: The Centre cited the **14th Finance Commission**'s removal of the **general-special category distinction** and rise in devolution to **42%** — option **(3)**.
The Centre said this **absorbed** SCS benefits.
xa: Other reasons: "**constitutional and technical constraints**" and fear of demands from **Bihar and Odisha**.
Outcome: an "**equivalent**" monetary package instead of the status.
AP FM **Payyavula Keshav** (Aug 2026): AP lost up to **₹38,000 crore** after the **16th FC** dropped revenue deficit grants.

nf56563ce9c3.s: According to the Centre's stated position, extending Special Category Status to Andhra Pradesh was opposed because:
o: The 14th Finance Commission recommended tax concessions only for Andhra Pradesh.
The Constitution prohibited all assistance to newly formed States.
Constitutional and technical constraints prevented extending SCS to a new State and could trigger similar demands from Bihar and Odisha.
Andhra Pradesh had already received permanent statutory SCS.
nf56563ce9c3.x: The Centre referred to constitutional and technical constraints and feared that granting SCS to Andhra Pradesh would lead to similar demands from Bihar and Odisha.
nf56563ce9c3.tq: Identify the stated policy rationale and the likely precedent effect.
xs: The Centre cited **constitutional and technical constraints** for any new state and feared identical demands from **Bihar and Odisha** — option **(3)**.
It also said the **14th FC**'s **42%** devolution had absorbed SCS benefits.
xa: The result was an "**equivalent**" monetary package instead of the status.
The package was announced by **Arun Jaitley** in **September 2016**.
Opposition parties (**YSRCP, Congress**) still demand SCS.

nd5e1577a005.s: From 2024-25 onward, the amounts specified for Amaravati and Polavaram were respectively:
nd5e1577a005.x: The specified assistance was ₹15,000 crore for Amaravati and ₹12,157 crore for Polavaram.
nd5e1577a005.tq: Split the options by checking the correct project-to-amount pairing.
xs: From **2024-25** onward: **₹15,000 crore** for **Amaravati** and **₹12,157 crore** for **Polavaram** — option **(2)**.
Option (3) reverses the two figures.
⚠ **₹2,500 crore** was the old promise for the capital; **₹8,226 crore** is AP's 2026-27 SASCI ceiling; **₹7,900 crore** its 2024-25 SASCI loans.
xa: Amaravati's **₹15,000 crore** is raised via **multilateral lenders**.
~**₹4,000 crore** is to come from the **Urban Infrastructure Development Fund**.

n39ae3ea0360.s: The special assistance released to Andhra Pradesh for 2016-17 under the Special Assistance Measure was:
n39ae3ea0360.x: ₹4,058.04 crore was released as special assistance for 2016-17 (APPSC-G1 2017 key). ₹3,979 crore was the 2014-15 revenue deficit grant, ₹24,350 crore the total SAM package, and ₹2,500 crore the amount promised for the capital.
xs: **₹4,058.04 crore** was released as special assistance for **2016-17** (APPSC-G1 2017 key) — option **(1)**.
**₹3,979 crore** = **2014-15** revenue deficit grant; **₹24,350 crore** = SAM total; **₹2,500 crore** = promised for the capital.
xa: The rest of the **₹24,350 crore** after the deficit grant was for **infrastructure**.
The package was announced in **September 2016** by **Arun Jaitley**.
Package period: **2015-16 to 2019-20**.

n0b3dc316183.s: The Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) began in:
n0b3dc316183.x: SASCI, run by the Ministry of Finance with 50-year interest-free loans for capital works, began in October 2020.
xa: SASCI gives **50-year interest-free** loans, over and above the net borrowing ceiling.
It lies outside the 16th FC's **3% of GSDP** deficit ceiling and funds **capital works only**.
AP can get up to **₹8,226 crore** under 2026-27 SASCI.

n297a9ef2ad1.s: Loans under the Scheme for Special Assistance to States for Capital Investment (SASCI) are:
o: 50-year interest-free loans for capital works, over and above the net borrowing ceiling
10-year concessional loans for revenue expenditure within the borrowing ceiling
grants routed only through externally aided project repayments
loans counted within the 16th FC's 3% of GSDP deficit ceiling
n297a9ef2ad1.x: SASCI (Ministry of Finance, since Oct 2020) gives 50-year interest-free loans for capital works only, over and above the net borrowing ceiling and outside the 3% of GSDP deficit ceiling. They are not for revenue expenditure and not EAP repayments.
n297a9ef2ad1.tq: SASCI = 50-yr, interest-free, capex only, outside the ceiling.
xs: SASCI gives **50-year interest-free loans** for **capital works**, **over and above the net borrowing ceiling** — option **(1)**.
They are not for revenue spending, not EAP repayments, and sit **outside** the **3% of GSDP** deficit ceiling.
xa: SASCI is run by the **Ministry of Finance** and began in **Oct 2020**.
2026-27 reforms tied to SASCI include **AgriStack** (**₹1,450 crore**) and **mining** (**₹950 crore**).

n9ec4f6b6d37.s: In August 2026, AP Finance Minister Payyavula Keshav said the State lost up to ₹38,000 crore because:
o: the 16th Finance Commission dropped revenue deficit grants
the 14th Finance Commission raised devolution to 42%
SASCI loans to the State were withdrawn
the Special Assistance Package ended in 2019-20
n9ec4f6b6d37.x: The loss of up to ₹38,000 crore came from the 16th FC dropping revenue deficit grants, with the revenue deficit rising from ₹16,000 crore (2014-19) to a projected ₹48,000 crore (2025-26). The 42% devolution was the 14th FC's, SASCI continues, and the package period simply ended.
n9ec4f6b6d37.tq: ₹38,000 cr loss = 16th FC ending RD grants.
xs: The loss of up to **₹38,000 crore** came because the **16th Finance Commission dropped revenue deficit grants** — option **(1)**.
**Payyavula Keshav** (AP FM) said this in **Aug 2026**.
⚠ **42%** devolution was the **14th FC**'s; SASCI loans continue (~**₹3,430 crore** so far in 2026-27).
xa: AP revenue deficit: **₹16,000 crore (2014-19)** → projected **₹48,000 crore (2025-26)**.
The 2026-27 SASCI ceiling for AP is **₹8,226 crore**, with **₹3,486 crore** received by Sep 2026.
AP's memorandum sought **higher devolution** + **capital-city weightage**.

nb5db04fe058.s: The Special Assistance Package for Andhra Pradesh, in place of SCS, was announced in September 2016 by:
nb5db04fe058.x: Union Finance Minister Arun Jaitley announced the package (also called SAM) in September 2016; Manmohan Singh gave the 2014 Rajya Sabha assurance on SCS.
xa: The package covers **2015-16 to 2019-20**, matching the promised **five-year** SCS period.
SAM total: **₹24,350 crore**, including a **₹3,979 crore** revenue deficit grant.
The **2016-17** special assistance was **₹4,058.04 crore** (APPSC-G1 2017 key).

nd8eab016b8c.s: The total Special Assistance Measure announced for Andhra Pradesh was:
nd8eab016b8c.x: The measure totalled ₹24,350 crore, of which ₹3,979 crore was the revenue deficit grant and the rest for infrastructure.
xa: ⚠ **₹4,058.04 crore** = 2016-17 special assistance; **₹3,979 crore** = 2014-15 revenue deficit grant; **₹24,350 crore** = SAM total.
**₹2,500 crore** was promised for the capital.
AP revenue deficit: **₹16,000 crore (2014-19)** → projected **₹48,000 crore (2025-26)**.

n2f02a19e715.s: The age of the universe and the approximate age of the Earth–solar system are, respectively:
n2f02a19e715.x: The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old, whereas the Earth and the solar system are approximately 4.6 billion years old.
n2f02a19e715.tq: Read the paired figures in the correct order and avoid reversing them.
xs: The universe is **13.8 billion years** old and the Earth–solar system about **4.6 billion years** — option **(3)**.
Option (4) wrongly says **13.8 million**; options (1) and (2) misplace or invent the ages.
xa: The universe's age of **13.8 billion years** was asked in **APPSC 2019**.
**Cosmology** is the study of the origin, evolution and structure of the universe.
All planets formed from the **same spinning protoplanetary disc** as the Sun.

ne6ad42a0e54.s: After hydrogen, the second most abundant element in the universe is:
ne6ad42a0e54.x: Hydrogen is the most abundant element in the universe, followed by helium.
xa: The Sun's **core** fuses **hydrogen into helium**; it becomes a **red giant** after exhausting its hydrogen.
**Jupiter and Saturn** are also mostly **hydrogen and helium**.
Early Earth's **hydrogen-helium** atmosphere was lost to the **solar wind**.

nd5d97bdddf8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the present view of planet formation?
o: Volatile ices were retained mainly in the cool outer region
The planets formed from the same spinning protoplanetary disc as the Sun
The hot inner region retained metals and rocky minerals in solid form
The hot inner region of the disc mainly retained water, ammonia and methane ices
nd5d97bdddf8.x: Ices were retained in the cool outer disc (linked to giant planets); the hot inner disc kept only metals and rocky minerals.
xa: Inner planets are **rocky/terrestrial**; outer ones are **gas giants** (Jupiter, Saturn) and **ice giants** (Uranus, Neptune).
Age of the Earth and solar system: about **4.6 billion years**.
**Ceres** is the dwarf planet of the asteroid belt; **Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Eris** lie in the Kuiper belt.

nb57c76766e9.s: Which of the following is the largest unit of distance?
nb57c76766e9.x: A parsec is about 3.26 light-years, and a light-year is far larger than an AU.
xa: Light from the Sun takes ~**8 min 20 s** to reach Earth.
**Absolute magnitude** is a star's brightness at a standard **10 parsecs**.
**Pluto** lies about **39 AU** out; the **Kuiper belt** spans **30-50 AU**.

n195e7cc3905.s: Polaris, the star within about one degree of the north celestial pole, lies in the constellation:
n195e7cc3905.x: Polaris is in Ursa Minor and lies close to the north celestial pole.
xa: Due to the **wobble of the axis**, **Vega** will be the pole star in about **12,000 years**.
**Magnitude**: lower number = brighter star.
The **Milky Way** is our barred spiral galaxy.

n022f7beaf37.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the revolution of the planets?
o: All eight planets revolve counter-clockwise when viewed from above the Sun's north pole
The period of revolution generally increases with distance from the Sun
An outer planet has a shorter period of revolution than every inner planet
Mercury has the shortest period of revolution
n022f7beaf37.x: Planets farther from the Sun generally take longer to revolve, so an outer planet's period is longer, not shorter.
xa: **Venus and Uranus** show **retrograde** (east-to-west) rotation.
**Jupiter** spins fastest (~**10 h** day).
Order: Mercury → Venus → **Earth** → Mars | asteroid belt | Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus → Neptune.

n2ba189beb3b.s: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006 primarily because it:
o: Has not cleared its orbital path
n2ba189beb3b.x: Pluto satisfies the orbiting and nearly round conditions but has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood, so it was classified as a dwarf planet.
n2ba189beb3b.tq: Apply the IAU criteria to the specific status change of Pluto.
xs: Pluto **has not cleared its orbital neighbourhood** (orbital path) — option **(3)**.
The **IAU (2006)** rule: a planet must orbit the Sun + be nearly round + **clear its orbital neighbourhood**; Pluto fails only the last test.
Pluto does orbit the Sun and has a moon (**Charon**), so options (2) and (4) are wrong.
xa: The trigger for the change was the discovery of **Eris**.
Pluto: largest **Kuiper Belt** object (**39 AU**); found **1930** by **Clyde Tombaugh**.
Kuiper-belt dwarf planets: **Pluto, Haumea, Makemake, Eris**; asteroid belt: **Ceres**.

n9399e20ffd8.s: The discovery of which object helped prompt the change in Pluto's classification?
n9399e20ffd8.x: The discovery of Eris, along with the need for a clearer planetary definition, helped prompt Pluto's reclassification as a dwarf planet in 2006.
n9399e20ffd8.tq: Identify the trigger object associated with a change in astronomical classification.
xs: The **trigger** for Pluto's reclassification was **Eris** — option **(2)**.
**Charon** is Pluto's largest moon; **Europa** is Jupiter's moon; **Phobos** is Mars's moon.
xa: **IAU (2006)**: Pluto fails the "**cleared its orbital neighbourhood**" test → dwarf planet.
Eris, **Haumea, Makemake** and Pluto are Kuiper-belt dwarf planets.
Pluto was found in **1930** by **Clyde Tombaugh**.

na60b8e33624.s: Oxygen was added to the Earth's early atmosphere mainly through:
na60b8e33624.x: After the hydrogen-helium atmosphere was lost and degassing supplied water vapour, nitrogen and CO2, photosynthesis added oxygen.
xa: The atmosphere evolved in **three stages**.
The **hydrosphere** formed as degassed water vapour **condensed** and filled ocean basins.
**Lithosphere**: iron sank to the core, lighter material formed the crust (**differentiation**).

n7d0f40d30c6.s: A 2026 study found that some geomagnetic pole reversals lasted up to about:
n7d0f40d30c6.x: The 2026 study found some reversals lasted up to about 70,000 years, against the assumed 10,000 years.
xa: The magnetic field **shields Earth from the solar wind**.
The Sun's own magnetic poles **reverse at each peak** of the **~11-year** cycle.
Solar storms cause **geomagnetic storms** and **auroras**.

na134fc20908.s: A full Moon occurring at apogee is called a:
na134fc20908.x: At apogee the Moon is farthest from Earth; a full Moon then is a micromoon, about 6–7% smaller and 10–14% dimmer.
xa: **Apogee** = Moon farthest from Earth.
A **Blue Micromoon** is the second full moon of a month at apogee.
A perigee full moon brings **higher tides**.

n6a945fd9ea4.s: The Himalayan Chandra Telescope, which completed 25 years in 2026, is located at:
n6a945fd9ea4.x: The Himalayan Chandra Telescope is located at Hanle and completed 25 years in 2026.
xa: PRL found exoplanet **TOI-6038A b** via **PARAS-2**, Mount Abu.
**27** twin-sun planets were found via **TESS**.
The IAU added **15** moons in June **2026**.

ngeneral-geography-1-20.s: What provides the centripetal force that keeps the planets in closed orbits around the Sun?
ngeneral-geography-1-20.x: The Sun's gravity supplies the centripetal force; without it a planet would fly off in a straight line.
n: Gravity keeps bodies in orbit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: **Newton** formulated the **laws of gravity**; **Kepler** the **three laws of planetary motion**.
All **8** planets revolve **counter-clockwise** (seen from above the Sun's north pole).
**Period of revolution** **increases with distance** from the Sun.
All planets formed from the **same spinning protoplanetary disc** as the Sun.

ngeneral-geography-1-50.s: The Sun's diameter is about ____ times that of the Earth.
ngeneral-geography-1-50.x: The Sun is about 109 times Earth's diameter and holds 99.8% of the Solar System's mass.
n: The Sun contains 99.8% of the Solar System’s mass. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The Sun’s diameter is 109 times Earth’s diameter. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
An astronomical unit is the mean Earth–Sun distance. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
One astronomical unit equals 149.6 million km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say light takes ~**8 min 20 s**; others say the Sun has **over 99%** of the mass.
**Perihelion** (~**4 January**) ~**147 million km**; **aphelion** (~**4 July**) ~**152 million km**.
**Sun's core** is about **15 million°C**; **photosphere** about **5,500°C**.

ngeneral-geography-1-54.s: One astronomical unit, the mean Earth-Sun distance, is about:
ngeneral-geography-1-54.x: One AU is 149.6 million km (149.6 × 10⁹ m), which light crosses in about 8 min 19 s.
n: An astronomical unit is the mean Earth–Sun distance. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
One astronomical unit equals 149.6 million km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
One astronomical unit equals approximately 149.6 × 10⁹ m. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Sunlight takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to reach Earth. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Light takes 8 minutes 19 seconds to travel one astronomical unit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say light takes ~**8 min 20 s**.
**AU < light year < parsec**; a **light year** ~**9.46 trillion km**.
**Perihelion** ~**147 million km** (early **January**); **aphelion** ~**152 million km** (early **July**).

ngeneral-geography-1-9.x: William Herschel found Uranus; Tombaugh found Pluto, Kepler gave the three laws and Copernicus the heliocentric model.
n: Copernicus proposed the heliocentric model. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Kepler formulated the three laws of planetary motion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: **Johann Galle** is associated with **Neptune**.
**Galileo** studied the **Galilean moons** and **falling bodies**; **Newton** the **laws of gravity**.
**Edwin Hubble** showed expansion by the **red-shift** of galaxies (**1929**).
**Copernicus** gave the **first mathematically predictive heliocentric** model.

nedd01bb8239.s: The Steady State theory of the universe was formulated in:
nedd01bb8239.x: The Steady State theory dates to 1948, after the Nebular (1755), Planetesimal (1904) and Big Bang (1927) theories.
xa: **Edwin Hubble** showed the universe's expansion through the **red-shift** of receding galaxies in **1929**.
**Cosmic Microwave Background** radiation, the leftover Big Bang glow, confirms the Big Bang.
The **Standard Model of cosmology** = Big Bang + **dark matter** + **dark energy** + **CMB**.

nd5e27671dc6.s: Who among the following is associated with the Big Bang theory as its principal proponent?
nd5e27671dc6.x: Georges Lemaitre proposed the Big Bang theory, also described as the expanding universe theory. Hoyle, Bondi and Gold are associated with the Steady State theory.
nd5e27671dc6.tq: Use the proponent–theory association rather than confusing rival cosmological theories.
xs: The Big Bang (expanding universe) theory was proposed by **Georges Lemaitre** in **1927** — option **(1)**.
**H.N. Russell** gave the **Binary star** hypothesis; **Immanuel Kant** the **Nebular hypothesis** (**1755**).
**Fred Hoyle**, with Bondi and Gold, proposed the rival **Steady State** theory (**1948**).
xa: **Edwin Hubble** showed the expansion via **red-shift** of receding galaxies (**1929**).
**CMB radiation** (leftover Big Bang glow) is the other key evidence for the Big Bang.
**Age of the universe**: **13.8 billion years** (asked in **APPSC 2019**).

n13f63ab6a22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Big Bang theory?
o: Hubble's 1929 red-shift of receding galaxies indicates an expanding universe
Cosmic Microwave Background radiation is its leftover glow
It was first proposed by Hoyle, Bondi and Gold in 1948
It was proposed by Georges Lemaitre in 1927
n13f63ab6a22.x: Hoyle, Bondi and Gold (1948) proposed the Steady State theory; the Big Bang was proposed by Lemaitre (1927).
xa: ⚠ **Lemaitre** proposed the Big Bang (**1927**) → **Hubble** showed expansion (**1929**); do not swap them.
The **Standard Model of cosmology** = Big Bang + dark matter + dark energy + CMB.
**Hydrogen** is the most abundant element in the universe, then **helium**.

n6084f63ced8.s: The first mathematically predictive heliocentric model is associated with:
n6084f63ced8.x: That model is associated with Copernicus; Aryabhata held that the Earth rotates on its axis and explained eclipses.

**Aditya-L1** is India's first solar observatory.
**Chandrasekhar** gave the white-dwarf ceiling, **~1.44 solar masses**.

n0cc8b561aa5.s: Which sequence represents the principal evolution of a massive star after the main-sequence stage?
o: Red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
n0cc8b561aa5.x: A massive star evolves into a supergiant, undergoes a supernova explosion, and may end as a neutron star or black hole.
n0cc8b561aa5.tq: Separate the massive-star pathway from the low- and medium-mass white-dwarf pathway.
xs: A **massive** star goes **Supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) is the path of a **low/medium-mass** star (red giant → planetary nebula → **white dwarf**).
xa: Low/medium mass: **nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf**.
**Giants live short, dwarfs live long**.
A **pulsar** is a fast-spinning **neutron star**; a **black hole** lets not even light escape.

n5e1da666a85.s: Absolute magnitude is the brightness a star would have at a standard distance of:

**Cepheids**' period-luminosity relation measures distances.
Colour shows surface temperature: **blue hottest**, **red coolest**.

ncb2e896d58c.s: The Chandrasekhar limit, an upper mass limit for a white dwarf, is approximately:

xs: The **Chandrasekhar limit** is about **1.44 solar masses** — option **(2)**.
**3.26** is the number of light years in a **parsec**, not a mass limit.
xa: Low/medium-mass stars end as **white dwarfs**; massive stars go **supernova → neutron star or black hole**.
**Giants live short, dwarfs live long**.
A **pulsar** is a fast-spinning neutron star emitting beams.

n09917ef46c6.s: Sunspots are markers of a solar cycle of approximately:
n09917ef46c6.x: Sunspots, cooler dark magnetic patches, mark the ~11-year solar cycle, at whose peak the Sun's magnetic poles reverse.

**Solar flares** are classed **A, B, C, M, X** (X strongest).

n72ea465730d.s: The next evolutionary change expected for the Sun after it exhausts its hydrogen is that it will become a:

xs: After exhausting its hydrogen, the Sun becomes a **red giant** — option **(4)**.

**Chandrasekhar limit**: **~1.44 solar masses** for a white dwarf.

n542a5b860b0.s: Sunlight takes about how long to reach the Earth?

Sun's colour class: **yellow**.

n899c8338e9a.s: Because of its suitable distance from the Sun, the Earth lies in the Sun's:

**27** possible **circumbinary (twin-sun)** planets were found with **TESS** data.

n8618990fbbd.x: Launched by PSLV-C25 in November 2013, Mangalyaan reached Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first Asian nation to reach Mars.

n805579c7ab9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Aditya-L1?

Data batches were released in **Jan and Feb 2025**.

n20368068825.s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of the major solar layers from the centre outward?
o: Core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, chromosphere, corona
Core, photosphere, radiative zone, corona, chromosphere, convective zone
Photosphere, core, radiative zone, convective zone, corona, chromosphere
Core, convective zone, radiative zone, chromosphere, photosphere, corona
n20368068825.x: From the centre outward, the sequence is core, radiative zone, convective zone, photosphere, chromosphere and corona.
n20368068825.tq: Build the sequence from the centre outward and eliminate reversed layer orders.
xs: From the centre: **core → radiative zone → convective zone → photosphere → chromosphere → corona** — option **(1)**.
The radiative and convective zones sit **between the core and the photosphere**; the **corona** is outermost.
xa: **Photosphere**: visible surface, **5,500-6,000°C**; supergranule cells ~**30,000 km**.
**Chromosphere**: reddish, seen at eclipses; **corona**: faint halo seen in a **total eclipse**.
⚠ The **corona** (outer) is hotter than the **photosphere** (surface).

n2e819d2144b.s: The temperature of the Sun's photosphere is about:
n2e819d2144b.x: The photosphere is about 5,500–6,000°C, while the corona, though farther out, can exceed one million °C.
xa: ⚠ Corona (outer) is **hotter** than the photosphere (surface) — a favourite trap.
The **chromosphere** is the reddish lower atmosphere seen at eclipses.
**CMEs** are plasma clouds from the **corona** at **250-3,000 km/s**.

n12151b95be4.s: The magnetic field of Earth is generated mainly by the:

churning of the liquid-iron outer core
condensation of water vapour in the atmosphere
reflection of solar radiation by the oceans

n12151b95be4.tq: Match the protective planetary feature with its internal source.
xs: Earth's magnetic field comes from the **geodynamo** — the **churning liquid-iron outer core** — option **(2)**.
It **shields Earth from the solar wind**.
xa: A **2026** study found some **pole reversals lasted up to ~70,000 years**, not the assumed ~**10,000**.
Aditya-L1 showed the **Oct 2024** storm strongly **compressed** Earth's magnetic shield.
**SMILE** will image the solar wind hitting the magnetic shield in **X-ray and UV**.

ngeneral-geography-1-49.s: The source of the Sun's energy is:
o: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium

The Sun’s energy comes from nuclear fusion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]

xa: Sun = **~74% hydrogen** and **~24% helium**.
**Photosphere** (visible layer) about **5,500°C**; the **corona** is **over a million °C** — hotter than the surface.
The Sun will become a **red giant** after exhausting its hydrogen.
**Diameter** **109 times** Earth's; holds **99.8%** of the Solar System's mass.

ngeneral-geography-1-52.s: The southern aurora is known as:

n: The corona is visible during a solar eclipse. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]

Aurora Borealis occurs in the north. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Aurora Australis occurs in the south. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]

**Solar flares** are classed **A, B, C, M, X** (**X** strongest).
**CMEs** travel at **250-3,000 km/s** and reach Earth in **1-3 days**.
⚠ The **corona** (outer) is **hotter** than the **photosphere** (surface).

o: The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon
The Moon lies between the Sun and the Earth
The Moon's shadow falls on the Earth
ngeneral-geography-1-67.x: In a lunar eclipse Earth's shadow falls on the Moon; in a solar eclipse the Moon's shadow falls on Earth.

na7827ec6791.s: Which planet has recorded the lowest single temperature, about −224°C?

n2d8846b8e58.s: Which planet is the least dense, with a density less than that of water?
n2d8846b8e58.x: Saturn is the least dense planet; its density is less than that of water. Earth is the densest planet, Jupiter is the largest and most massive, and Neptune is the coldest on average.

xs: **Saturn** is the least dense planet — density **less than water** — option **(2)**.

n539e5b8432d.s: The sinking of heavy iron towards the centre of the early Earth and the formation of the crust from lighter material is known as:

Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]

xa: ⚠ Equatorial > polar diameter → **oblate spheroid**.
Surface area ~**510 million sq km**; ~**71%** water, ~**29%** land.
Equatorial circumference **~40,075 km**.

n7133d251209.s: Gerardus Mercator developed the Mercator projection in:
n7133d251209.x: The Mercator projection (1569) has right-angled graticule, straight rhumb lines and enlarged polar areas.
xa: The **Equal Earth** projection (**2018** design) is the proposed replacement.
**UNGA** adopted a **non-binding** resolution for Equal Earth.
The **"Correct the Map"** campaign was backed by the **African Union**.

nfa2801b4223.s: The 'Correct the Map' campaign against the Mercator projection was backed by:
nfa2801b4223.x: The African Union backed 'Correct the Map'; the resulting UNGA resolution was non-binding (India for, US against).
xa: **Mercator** (**1569**) enlarges polar areas and **shrinks Africa**.
**Equal Earth** projection: a **2018** design.
The UN resolution for the Equal Earth map came in **Sep 2026**.

n9624215d8b5.s: The Tropic of Cancer passes through how many Indian States?
n9624215d8b5.x: It crosses 8 States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram (not Odisha).
xa: Tropic of Cancer: **23½°N** (23°26' N), crossing **17 countries**.
**Bhopal** (~**23°N**) lies near the Tropic.
**AP** lies wholly between the **Equator** and the **Tropic of Cancer**.

ncc2d16fe793.x: India measures about 3,214 km north-south and 2,933 km east-west, with an area of about 32,87,263 sq km.
xa: Land frontier ~**15,200 km**; India lies entirely in the **Northern Hemisphere**.
⚠ India and AP are both **7th largest** (country / state).

n9a975f7aaf9.s: As of 2025, how many districts does Andhra Pradesh have?
n9a975f7aaf9.x: AP had 13 districts in 2014, 26 in 2022 and 28 in 2025.
xa: AP's coast is **974 km** (updated Jul **2026**).

nea375b494a5.s: Which State borders Andhra Pradesh on the south-west?
nea375b494a5.x: Karnataka lies to the south-west of AP; Tamil Nadu is to the south, Telangana to the west and north-west, and Chhattisgarh and Odisha to the north.
xa: East: **Bay of Bengal** (a PYQ).
AP's coastline is **974 km** long.
AP has **28** districts (**2025**).

n285255da357.s: The coastline of Andhra Pradesh is about:
n285255da357.x: AP has a coastline of about 974 km and an area of about 1,62,970 sq km (~4.96% of India).
xa: AP is the **7th largest** state.
AP lies wholly between the **Equator** and the **Tropic of Cancer**.

nff587fda7bf.s: EOS-05, India's first Earth-imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit, orbits about how high above the Earth?
nff587fda7bf.x: EOS-05 is in geosynchronous orbit about 36,000 km up, allowing frequent views of the same area.
xa: The **Survey of India** is building a **Geoid Model** for precise GPS/GNSS-based heights.
The UN resolution for the **Equal Earth** map came in **Sep 2026**.
Earth's mean radius is **6,371 km**.

n948552c0de3.s: Andhra Pradesh, lying wholly between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer, has a tropical climate of the type:
n948552c0de3.x: Andhra Pradesh is described as having a tropical Aw climate.
xa: AP's latitude: **12°41'N - 19°07'N**, well south of the Tropic (**23°26' N**).
The Tropic of Cancer crosses **8** Indian states — AP is not one of them.
**Kakinada** district hosts the **IST meridian**.

na9704a91143.s: Which two planets rotate in the direction opposite to Earth's west-to-east rotation?
na9704a91143.x: Earth rotates west to east, whereas Venus and Uranus spin in the opposite direction.
xa: Seen from above the **North Pole**, Earth's rotation is **anticlockwise**.
The Sun and stars therefore appear to move **east to west**.
One rotation = **23 h 56 m 4 s**.

ndbd7750db30.s: Approximately 12 hours of daylight throughout the year is experienced at the:
ndbd7750db30.x: The Equator has about 12-hour days all year; variation in day length increases with latitude.
xa: Unequal lengths come from the **tilted axis** (**23½°**) + revolution.
**Poles**: ~**6 months day + 6 months night**.
Northern **Norway** is the "Land of the Midnight Sun".

ngeneral-geography-1-3.s: The Earth rotates on its axis from:
ngeneral-geography-1-3.x: Earth spins west to east once in 24 hours, turning each place toward and away from the Sun to give day and night.
n: Earth rotates from west to east. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Earth’s rotation takes 24 hours. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Earth’s rotation produces day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
Earth’s rotation takes 24 hours. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: **Revolution** around the Sun takes **365.25 days** and gives a **year** and **seasons** (with **axial tilt**).
**Angular speed:** **15° per hour** — **1° every 4 minutes**.
**Sidereal day** = **23 h 56 m 4 s**; **solar day** = **24 h**.
**Aryabhatta** explained the Sun's apparent daily motion through Earth's rotation.

ngeneral-geography-2-16.s: Which of the following is NOT primarily associated with the Earth's rotation?
ngeneral-geography-2-16.x: Perihelion and aphelion belong to revolution; day and night, the Coriolis effect and time zones come from rotation.
n: Earth’s rotation causes day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The main result of Earth’s rotation is day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The Coriolis effect is caused by Earth’s rotation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Rotation’s main result is day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Rotation produces time zones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Revolution is associated with perihelion and aphelion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Rotation does not cause perihelion and aphelion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: Rotation also causes a **centrifugal effect**.
Revolution has **no primary role** in the Coriolis effect and does **not produce** time zones.
**Solstices and equinoxes** are caused by **revolution along with axial tilt**, not rotation.

ngeneral-geography-2-17.s: The spinning of the Earth on its own axis is called:
ngeneral-geography-2-17.x: Rotation is Earth's spin on its axis; revolution is its elliptical path around the Sun.
n: Earth has two primary motions: rotation and revolution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Rotation means that Earth spins on its own axis. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Revolution means that Earth moves around the Sun in an elliptical orbit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution is its movement around the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: Rotation takes **24 hours**; revolution **365.25 days** (**365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes**).
**Average orbital speed:** **29.78 km/s**.
The Sun sits at **one focus** of the slightly elliptical orbit.
**Sun's gravity** supplies the **centripetal force** for revolution.

ngeneral-geography-2-18.s: The linear speed of the Earth's rotation is maximum at the:
ngeneral-geography-2-18.x: Linear rotational speed is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles.
n: Earth’s axis is an imaginary line joining the North and South Poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
A longitude difference of 1° corresponds to 4 minutes of time. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s linear rotational speed is maximum at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s linear rotational speed is zero at the Poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s axis is an imaginary line through the North and South Poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: Linear speed is ~**1,670 km/h at the Equator** and falls with latitude.
A full rotation of **360°** takes **24 hours**.
⚠ **Coriolis** is the opposite: **zero at the Equator**, maximum at the poles.

ngeneral-geography-2-25.s: The Earth takes about how many days to complete one revolution around the Sun?
ngeneral-geography-2-25.x: Earth takes about 365¼ days to complete one revolution on its elliptical orbit.
n: Earth follows an elliptical orbit around the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution period is also given as 365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes, and 9.51 seconds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Revolution changes Earth’s position around the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution produces a year. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution is its movement around the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: **Average orbital speed:** **29.78 km/s** (~**1 lakh km/h**).
The extra **one-fourth of a day** accumulates to **one day in four years** → leap year.
Revolution's **major result** is the **year**; with **axial tilt** it gives **seasons**.

n593be1b14f1.s: The rotation of the Earth is generally not felt by people on its surface because:
o: The Sun's gravity cancels the rotational motion
The atmosphere and objects on Earth move along with it at a nearly uniform speed
The Earth's rotation is confined to the polar regions
The Earth's magnetic field absorbs the motion
n593be1b14f1.x: Earth's motion is nearly uniform with no perceptible change in velocity, and the atmosphere and objects on it move along with it.
xa: Speed: ~**1,670 km/h** at the Equator, **zero at the poles**.
The **Foucault pendulum** (**Paris, 1851**) proved rotation.
Day and night are caused by **rotation**.

n0e6375dbdd7.s: Climate-driven melting of ice is lengthening the Earth's day by about how much per century?
n0e6375dbdd7.x: Melting ice shifts mass towards the Equator, raising the moment of inertia and lengthening the day by about 1.33 ms per century.
xa: **UPSC 2025** tested that a **shift in Earth's rotation and axis** is under way.
A **sidereal day** lasts **23 h 56 m 4 s**; a **solar day** **24 h**.
Earth rotates **west to east** (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole).

n32bad90290d.s: A sidereal day, measured relative to a distant star, lasts about:
n32bad90290d.x: A sidereal day lasts 23 h 56 min 4 s, about four minutes shorter than the 24-hour solar day measured from noon to noon.
xa: ⚠ Sidereal day is **shorter** than the solar day.
One rotation takes **23 h 56 m 4 s**.
Climate change is lengthening days by ~**1.33 ms per century**.

ngeneral-geography-2-44.s: Shifts in the Earth's rotational axis are mainly driven by:
o: Redistribution of mass, such as melting ice and groundwater depletion
ngeneral-geography-2-44.x: Mass redistribution from melting ice and groundwater use shifts the axis; solar flares only disturb the upper atmosphere.
n: Ice-sheet melting redistributes mass and water toward lower latitudes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Redistribution of mass and water toward lower latitudes can influence Earth’s rotation and axis. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections affect the upper atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Solar flares and coronal mass ejections were not the primary explanation in the relevant question. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: **UPSC 2025** tested that a **shift in Earth's rotation and axis** is under way.
Climate change raises the moment of inertia and **slows rotation** — days longer by ~**1.33 ms per century**.
The **length of day** has changed by a **very small measurable amount**.

nf3c1c2c8959.s: The Foucault pendulum experiment conducted in Paris in 1851 demonstrated the Earth's rotation through:
o: A permanent change in the length of the pendulum
The direct measurement of the Earth's orbital speed
The slow turning of the plane of the pendulum's swing
The rise and fall of ocean tides
nf3c1c2c8959.x: In Foucault's 1851 experiment at Paris, the plane of swing of the pendulum slowly turned, providing visible evidence of Earth's rotation.
nf3c1c2c8959.tq: Match the experiment with its distinctive observable result and date.
xs: In the **Foucault pendulum** (**Paris, 1851**), the **plane of swing slowly turns** → proves rotation — option **(3)**.
Tides and orbital speed are not what Foucault showed.
xa: **Aryabhata** first proposed that Earth rotates.
Other evidences: **Coriolis deflection**, **equatorial bulge**, apparent **east-to-west motion** of stars and Sun.
**Ferrel's law**: deflection **right in the NH**, **left in the SH**.

n28417f6b920.s: The circle of illumination passes through both poles at the:
n28417f6b920.x: The circle of illumination (grey line) divides day from night and passes through both poles only at the equinoxes.
xa: Day and night are caused by **rotation**.
Unequal day lengths come from the **tilted axis** (**23½°**) + revolution.
**Twilight** is diffused light before sunrise/after sunset.

n3843dba38ae.s: The phenomenon in which the Sun remains above the horizon for 24 hours during summer beyond the Arctic or Antarctic Circle is known as:
n3843dba38ae.x: The midnight sun refers to continuous daylight for 24 hours or more in high-latitude regions during their summer.
n3843dba38ae.tq: Match the distinctive high-latitude phenomenon with its exact term.
xs: This is the **midnight sun** — option **(2)**.
Beyond the **Arctic/Antarctic Circles** the Sun stays up **24 h in summer**.
xa: Example: **northern Norway**, the "Land of the Midnight Sun".
The **poles** get ~**6 months** of day and **6 months** of night.
**Twilight** is longest at high latitudes — **weeks-long** near the poles.

n1401323b8f4.s: How does the duration of twilight generally vary with latitude?
o: It occurs only between the Tropics.
It is approximately the same at every latitude.
It is longest at the Equator and shortest at the poles.
It is shortest at the Equator and becomes longer towards the poles.
n1401323b8f4.x: Twilight is shortest at the Equator because the Sun rises and sets nearly vertically. It lasts longer at high latitudes because the Sun follows an oblique path, becoming weeks-long near the poles.
n1401323b8f4.tq: Compare the angle of the Sun's path at low and high latitudes.
xs: Twilight is **shortest at the Equator** and **longer towards the poles** — option **(4)**.
At the Equator the Sun **rises/sets vertically**; at high latitudes it follows an **oblique path**.
xa: Near the poles twilight can be **weeks-long**.
**Twilight** = diffused light before sunrise/after sunset.
The **circle of illumination** is also the **"grey line"**.

ngeneral-geography-2-19.s: Day and night on the Earth are caused by its:
ngeneral-geography-2-19.x: Rotation, not revolution or tilt, causes day and night; the circle of illumination divides the two halves.
n: Day is experienced by the part of Earth facing the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Night is experienced by the part of Earth turned away from the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The circle of illumination divides the illuminated and dark portions of Earth. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s rotation on its axis causes day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution does not cause day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Axial tilt alone does not cause day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: The circle of illumination is also called the **"grey line"** / **"twilight zone"** (APPSC **2019**).
It passes through both poles only at the **equinoxes**.
**Unequal day lengths** come from the **tilted axis** (**23½°**) plus revolution.
**Twilight** is shortest at the **Equator**, longest at high latitudes.

ngeneral-geography-3-17.s: The six-month polar day and night is caused by:
ngeneral-geography-3-17.x: Revolution with axial tilt causes seasons, solstices and equinoxes, opposite seasons in the hemispheres and six-month polar day and night.
n: Earth’s revolution combined with axial tilt causes seasons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Axial tilt combined with revolution causes solstices and equinoxes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Axial tilt combined with revolution causes opposite seasons in the hemispheres. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Axial tilt combined with revolution causes six-month polar day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **Rotation** is **not the direct cause** of solstices and equinoxes.
Revolution alone gives the **year** — the **annual cycle**.
**Poles:** ~**6 months** day + **6 months** night.

ngeneral-geography-3-15.s: At the Equator, seasons are marked mainly by:
ngeneral-geography-3-15.x: Day length hardly changes at the Equator, so it has wet and dry seasons rather than winter and summer.
n: Seasonal variation in day length is very small at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Equator has no distinct winter or summer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Equator generally experiences wet and dry seasons instead of distinct winter and summer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: The Sun is **overhead at the Equator** during an **equinox**.
Day-length variation **grows with latitude**; the **Poles** have ~**6 months** day and **6 months** night.
**Twilight** is **shortest at the Equator**, as the Sun rises and sets vertically.

o: North of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle
Between the Tropic of Cancer and the Arctic Circle
ngeneral-geography-3-39.x: The midnight sun occurs beyond the polar circles, peaking near each summer solstice, as in Norway.
n: The midnight Sun occurs north of the Arctic Circle and south of the Antarctic Circle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The midnight Sun is strongest around the respective summer solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The midnight Sun can produce 24-hour daylight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Norway is an example of a place experiencing the midnight Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **Poles:** ~**6 months** of day and **6 months** of night.
**Twilight** is **longest at high latitudes** — weeks-long near the poles.
The **circle of illumination** passes through both poles only at the **equinoxes**.

n399bb8c3efa.s: In the Northern Hemisphere, tropical cyclones generally rotate:
o: In a direction determined only by ocean salinity
From east to west without rotation
n399bb8c3efa.x: The Coriolis effect causes tropical cyclones in the Northern Hemisphere to rotate anticlockwise.
n399bb8c3efa.tq: Apply the hemisphere-based deflection rule to the circulation of cyclones.
xs: Under the Coriolis effect, cyclones spin **anticlockwise in the NH** — option **(3)**.
Winds are deflected **to the right in the NH** (**Ferrel's law**).
xa: Cyclones rarely form **within 5° of the Equator**, where Coriolis force is too weak.
Coriolis force **increases with wind velocity** (**UPSC 2024**).
Cyclone **Montha** (**2025**) was steered NNW toward the **Kakinada coast**.

n503b5a8e788.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the effects of the Earth's rotation?
o: The Coriolis force deflects winds and currents to the right in the Northern Hemisphere
The Coriolis force deflects winds and currents to the left in the Northern Hemisphere
The Coriolis force deflects winds and currents to the left in the Southern Hemisphere
Rotation contributes to the flattening of the Earth at the poles
n503b5a8e788.x: In the Northern Hemisphere the Coriolis deflection is to the right, not the left; deflection is to the left only in the Southern Hemisphere.
xa: Other effects: **ocean gyres** and **current deflection**.
Coriolis force is **zero at the Equator**.
The **equatorial bulge** is an evidence of rotation.

nc04267294b3.s: The Coriolis force is maximum at the:
nc04267294b3.x: The Coriolis force (2Ωv sin latitude) is zero at the Equator, maximum at the poles and grows with wind velocity.
xa: ⚠ Coriolis is **zero at the Equator** — the opposite of rotation speed (~**1,670 km/h** there).
Cyclones spin **anticlockwise in NH**.
Its cause is **Earth's rotation** (APPSC-G1 **2019**).

ngeneral-geography-2-23.s: The centrifugal effect of the Earth's rotation results in:
ngeneral-geography-2-23.x: Rotation's centrifugal effect is greatest at the Equator and zero at the poles, causing polar flattening.
n: The centrifugal effect is caused by Earth’s rotation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The centrifugal effect is maximum at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The centrifugal effect is minimum or zero at the Poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The centrifugal effect causes equatorial bulging and polar flattening. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s rotation produces a centrifugal effect. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: **Weight** is **minimum at the Equator** and **maximum at the Poles**.
Linear rotational speed is **maximum at the Equator** (~**1,670 km/h**).
⚠ **Coriolis** is **zero at the Equator** — opposite of the centrifugal effect.

ngeneral-geography-2-59.s: The weight of an object on the Earth is minimum at the:
ngeneral-geography-2-59.x: The centrifugal effect of rotation is greatest at the Equator, so effective gravity and weight are least there.
n: The centrifugal effect is maximum at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Weight is minimum at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s rotation produces a centrifugal effect. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Rotation makes weight minimum at the Equator and maximum at the Poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: The same force causes **equatorial bulging** and **polar flattening**.
Linear rotational speed is **maximum at the Equator** and **zero at the Poles**.
The resulting shape is an **oblate spheroid**.

n484f9566c61.s: Which of the following is NOT an evidence of the rotation of the Earth?
o: Coriolis deflection of winds and ocean currents
The apparent east-to-west motion of stars and the Sun
The constant distance between the Earth and the Sun throughout the year
n484f9566c61.x: The constant Earth-Sun distance is not an evidence of Earth's rotation; in fact, the distance varies slightly because Earth's orbit is elliptical. Coriolis deflection, equatorial bulge and apparent celestial motion are evidences of rotation.
n484f9566c61.tq: Identify the unrelated orbital-distance statement among recognised rotation evidences.
xs: A **constant Earth-Sun distance** is not evidence of rotation — option **(4)**; the orbit is in fact slightly **elliptical**.
Real evidences: **Coriolis deflection** of winds/currents, the **equatorial bulge**, and the apparent **east-to-west motion** of stars and Sun.
xa: The **Foucault pendulum** (**1851**) also proves rotation.
Perihelion/aphelion slightly alter **tidal ranges**.
**Aryabhata** first proposed that Earth rotates.

ne32b0c7fd54.s: As the Earth rotates, a coastal place passing through two tidal bulges in a day generally experiences:
o: One high tide and one low tide
Four high tides and no low tide
Two high tides and one low tide
Two high tides and two low tides
ne32b0c7fd54.x: Passing through two tidal bulges gives two high tides and two low tides, with similar tides about 12 hours 25 minutes apart.
xa: **Spring tides**: Sun-Earth-Moon **in line** (new and full moon).
**Neap tides**: Sun and Moon at **right angles** (~**7 days** later).
Each occurs **twice a month**.

n5e29daa19e4.s: Neap tides occur when the Sun and the Moon are:
o: Both at their farthest from Earth
At approximately right angles to each other
n5e29daa19e4.x: Neap tides occur when the Sun and Moon are at about right angles; spring tides occur at new and full Moon when they are aligned.
xa: A neap tide comes ~**7 days** after a spring tide.
**Perihelion/aphelion** only **slightly alter** tidal ranges.
A place gets **two high and two low tides** a day (~**12 h 25 min** apart).

n5c90f6964c7.s: The principal centripetal force that keeps the Earth in its orbit around the Sun is provided by:
o: The gravitational force of the Sun
The magnetic force of the Sun
The gravitational force of the Moon
n5c90f6964c7.x: The Sun's gravitational attraction acts as the centripetal force that keeps the Earth revolving around it.
n5c90f6964c7.tq: Identify the body supplying the centripetal force rather than the body in motion.
xs: The **Sun's gravity** supplies the **centripetal force** that keeps Earth revolving — option **(2)**.
Not radiation pressure, magnetism or the Moon's gravity.
xa: The orbit is slightly **elliptical**, Sun at one focus.
Period of revolution: **365 days 6 hours**.
Mean orbital speed ~**29.8 km/s**.

na430c1cfbad.s: Under the Gregorian rule, which of the following century years was a leap year?
na430c1cfbad.x: A century year is a leap year only if divisible by 400, so 2000 was a leap year and 1900 was not.
xa: Leap years add **29 February every 4 years**.
The extra ~**¼ day** comes from the **365 days 6 hours** year.
Mean orbital speed ~**29.8 km/s**.

ngeneral-geography-2-38.s: The extra fraction of a day in each calendar year, which adds up to a leap day in four years, is about:
ngeneral-geography-2-38.x: The extra quarter day accumulates to one day in four years, giving a 366-day leap year with 29 February.
n: A normal calendar year has 365 days. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The extra fraction in a year is one-fourth of a day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The extra fraction accumulates to one day in four years. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
A leap year has 366 days. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The extra day in a leap year is 29 February. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: **Century years** are leap years only if divisible by **400** (**2000** yes, **1900** no).
Revolution takes **365 days, 6 hours, 9 minutes** and **9.51 seconds**.

n9384d02647c.s: One minute of arc of longitude corresponds to:
n9384d02647c.x: 15° = 1 hour and 1° = 4 minutes, so one minute of arc equals 4 seconds of time.
xa: Place to the **east** → time **ahead** (add); **west** → **behind** (subtract).
Steps: longitude difference **x 4 min** = time difference.
IST: **82.5 x 4 min = 330 min** = **5 h 30 min** ahead of GMT.

nbe5f052963b.s: Compared with a given place, the local time of places to its east is:
o: Ahead only in the Northern Hemisphere
nbe5f052963b.x: The Earth rotates from west to east, so places to the east see the Sun earlier and their local time is ahead.
xa: Each **1°** of longitude = **4 minutes** of time.
Local time **2 h behind** Greenwich → **30°W**.
The Sun rises ~**2 h** earlier in **Arunachal Pradesh** than in western **Gujarat**.

n4c120fed181.s: The longitudes of two places are 25°E and 35°W. Their local-time difference is
n4c120fed181.x: The longitudes lie on opposite sides of Greenwich, so they are added: 25° + 35° = 60°. Sixty degrees correspond to four hours.
n4c120fed181.tq: Add opposite-side longitudes before converting degrees into time.
xs: On **opposite sides** (E and W) → **add**: **25 + 35 = 60°**; at **15° = 1 hour**, **60°** = **4 hours** — option **(2)**.
Subtracting (35 - 25 = 10° = 40 min) gives the wrong option (1).
xa: Same side → subtract the degrees.
APPSC-G1 **2019** used the same "add opposite sides" step (60°W and 90°E).

n28d574b3ec4.s: Which of the following cities has the same clock time as Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai?
n28d574b3ec4.x: Mumbai, Kolkata, Chennai and Colombo observe UTC+5:30. Nepal uses UTC+5:45 and therefore does not have the same clock time.
n28d574b3ec4.tq: Start with the sure UTC+5:30 pair and distinguish it from nearby quarter-hour offsets.
xs: **Colombo** shares IST's clock time (**UTC+5:30**) with Mumbai, Kolkata and Chennai — option **(2)**.
**Nepal** (Kathmandu) uses **UTC+5:45**, so it differs.
xa: **IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min**, based on **82°30'E**.
India **does not use DST**.
Kiribati's Line Islands (**UTC+14**) are first to see a new day.

n5235e58c520.s: The poles experience about how long a period of continuous daylight?
n5235e58c520.x: The poles have roughly six months of day and six months of night.
xa: The **Arctic Circle** gets a **24 h day** on 21 June and **24 h night** on 22 Dec.
The **North Pole** is lit from ~**21 March** to ~**23 September**.
At the Tropic of Cancer, 21 June brings ~**13½ h** of day.

n6eedc295452.s: Which of the following is NOT a consequence of the Earth's axial tilt?
o: Unequal length of day and night
Location of the polar circles at about 66½°
n6eedc295452.x: Day and night are caused by rotation; the tilt gives seasons, unequal day length and the positions of the tropics and polar circles.
xa: Axis tilt: **23½° from the perpendicular** = **66½° to the orbital plane**.
The axis **wobbles (precession)**, changing the pole star.
**Milankovitch cycles**: orbital and axial cycles that drive long-period climate change.

ndfd9b57ca64.s: Vega was the pole star about 14,000 years ago and will be again in about 12,000 years because of:
o: The slow wobble (precession) of Earth's axis
ndfd9b57ca64.x: Earth's axis slowly wobbles (axial precession), changing the direction of the celestial pole; Vega was the pole star about 14,000 years ago and will be again in about 12,000 years.
xa: **Milankovitch cycles**: orbital and axial cycles that drive **long-period climate change**.
Melting polar and glacier ice shifts mass away from the axis → **slows rotation**.
Tilt: **23½°** from the perpendicular = **66½°** to the orbital plane.

nb172d8bb055.s: When it is 10 a.m. at place A (60°W), what is the local time at place B (90°E)?
nb172d8bb055.x: The places are on opposite sides of Greenwich, so the degrees are added: 60° + 90° = 150°; 150 x 4 min = 600 min = 10 hours. B is east of A, so its time is ahead: 10 a.m. + 10 h = 8 p.m. 12 noon and 4 p.m. come from subtracting the longitudes, and 12 midnight from an error in the minutes.
nb172d8bb055.tq: Opposite sides: add degrees; east: add time.
xs: This was a worked PYQ in **APPSC-G1 2019**.
xa: Same-side longitudes are **subtracted**.
**East is ahead (add)**, **West is behind (subtract)**.
Local time **2 h behind** Greenwich → **30°W**.

ndb98c6f8461.s: The Prime Meridian, the reference for Greenwich Mean Time, was adopted at the International Meridian Conference in which year?
ndb98c6f8461.x: The Prime Meridian through the Royal Observatory, Greenwich was adopted at the International Meridian Conference of 1884. 1851 is the year of Foucault's pendulum, 1947 the year a single IST was adopted, and 1569 the year of the Mercator projection.
xs: The Prime Meridian was adopted at the **International Meridian Conference, 1884** — option **(2)**.
**1947** is when a single **IST** was adopted after Independence.
Separate **Bombay and Calcutta times** also date **from 1884**.
xa: The Prime Meridian runs through the **Royal Observatory, Greenwich**.
**GMT** = mean solar time at Greenwich.
**UTC** is kept by **atomic (caesium) clocks**.

ne49957c6056.s: Which country has the greatest number of time zones when its overseas territories are included?
ne49957c6056.x: France has 12 time zones when its overseas territories are included, while Russia has 11.
ne49957c6056.tq: Watch for the qualification ‘including overseas territories’ in country-comparison questions.
xs: **France** has the most time zones — **12**, with overseas territories — option **(1)**.
**Russia** has **11**; **China** uses only **one**.
xa: ⚠ Most zones = **France**, not Russia.
Theoretical zones: **24** of **15°** each.
**Colombo** shares IST's **UTC+5:30**.

n477c8d4905e.s: Daylight Saving Time is mainly intended to:
o: Align a country's time with GMT
Make more use of evening daylight in summer
n477c8d4905e.x: DST makes better use of evening daylight in summer; India does not use it.
xa: Clocks are **set back in autumn**.
**UTC** is adjusted with **leap seconds**.
The Prime Meridian was adopted in **1884**.

ndd4eb7d4922.x: NavIC (7 satellites: 3 GEO + 4 GSO) uses rubidium atomic clocks; the clock on IRNSS-1F failed.
xa: ⚠ UTC = **caesium**; NavIC = **rubidium**.
The **White Rabbit** network cuts dependence on **GPS**.
Synchronised IST guards against **GPS spoofing**.

n2d88479c721.s: The long-term orbital and axial variations that influence climate are collectively known as
n2d88479c721.x: Long-period variations in Earth's orbit and axial behaviour that influence climate are called Milankovitch cycles.
n2d88479c721.tq: Match the named climate mechanism with orbital and axial variations rather than atmospheric circulation.
xs: Orbital and axial variations that drive long-period climate change are the **Milankovitch cycles** — option **(4)**.
They include changes in the axis such as **precession** (the axis **wobble**).
xa: Precession: the celestial pole pointed to **Vega ~14,000 years ago**; it will again in **~12,000 years**.
Melting polar and glacier ice shifts mass away from the axis → **slows rotation**.
Axis tilt **23½°** from the perpendicular explains seasons and **unequal day length**.

n210ecf83b07.s: India's single time zone mainly costs which region daylight hours?
n210ecf83b07.x: India's wide east-west extent leaves the north-east at a daylight disadvantage; separate-zone proposals remain undecided.
xa: Proposals: advance IST by **30 minutes**, or a separate zone **~1 h ahead** for the North-East keeping **82.5° E** as reference.
**Assam tea gardens** keep an informal "**Bagan time**".
Arunachal vs Gujarat: span **≈ 29°**, gap **~1 h 57 min** (nearly **2 hours**).

ngeneral-geography-2-12.x: Local time advances eastward, so moving west it falls behind (15° = one hour).
n: Earth completes a full rotation of 360° in 24 hours. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Local time advances when moving eastward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Local time retards when moving westward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
There are 24 theoretical world time zones, each covering 15°. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
