Earth’s rotation is 360° in 24 hours. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Eastward movement makes time advance. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Westward movement makes time decrease. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: **East is ahead (add time)**; **West is behind (subtract)**.
**180°** of longitude = **12 hours**.
⚠ **France** (**12** zones with overseas territories) has the most zones, not **Russia** (**11**).

nbab7e2559ee.s: A place is situated 30° west of Greenwich. Its local time, in relation to Greenwich Mean Time, will be
nbab7e2559ee.x: Thirty degrees correspond to two hours, and a place west of Greenwich is behind Greenwich Mean Time.
nbab7e2559ee.tq: Combine the longitude-to-time conversion with the east–west direction rule.
xs: **30°** x **4 min** = **2 hours**; a place **west** of Greenwich is **behind** — so **2 hours behind**, option **(2)**.
"Ahead" applies only to places **east** of Greenwich.
xa: Worked example in the notes: local time **2 h behind Greenwich → 30°W**.
**East is ahead (add)**, **West is behind (subtract)**.
**IST** (**82°30'E**) is **5 h 30 min ahead** of GMT.

n4313a321a18.s: If a flight departs from a western location at 10:00 a.m. local time, travels for three hours, and reaches a location 15° east of the point of departure, its local arrival time will be
n4313a321a18.x: The journey takes three hours and the eastward movement adds one hour because 15° equals one hour. The arrival time is therefore 2:00 p.m.
n4313a321a18.tq: Add journey time and the eastward longitude correction separately.
xs: Arrival = **10 a.m. + 3 h journey + 1 h** (15° east = **1 hour**, add going east) = **2:00 p.m.** — option **(1)**.
Rule: local arrival = departure local time + journey time **+/-** longitude time difference (**add when flying east**).
xa: **East is ahead**, so eastward flights gain clock time.
**1° = 4 minutes** of time.
Theoretically the Earth has **24 zones** of **15°** each.

n5a0f46a7bf1.s: Which one of the following is the correct reference location associated with the Indian Standard Time meridian?
n5a0f46a7bf1.x: Mirzapur in Uttar Pradesh is the reference town associated with the Indian Standard Time meridian.
n5a0f46a7bf1.tq: Distinguish the reference town from institutions and other places lying along the meridian.
xs: The IST reference town is **Mirzapur** (Uttar Pradesh) — option **(1)**.
**Kakinada** is the AP district the meridian crosses; **New Delhi** hosts **NPL**; **Jakkur** hosts the **White Rabbit** network.
xa: It crosses **5 states**: UP, MP, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh.
⚠ Trap: **not West Bengal** (APPSC **2021**).

n211a02526f7.s: The Indian Standard Time meridian passes through which one of the following sequences of States from west to east?
o: Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal
Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Jharkhand, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh
Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal and Andhra Pradesh
n211a02526f7.x: The meridian crosses Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and Andhra Pradesh. West Bengal is not included in this sequence.
n211a02526f7.tq: Use the complete geographical sequence and reject the option containing the neighbouring but excluded State.
xs: The IST meridian crosses **Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh** — option **(1)**.
**West Bengal**, **Rajasthan** and **Jharkhand** are not on it.
xa: ⚠ Trap: **not West Bengal** (APPSC **2021**).
In AP it passes through **Kakinada district**.
⚠ **8** states on the Tropic vs **5** on the IST meridian; **Chhattisgarh** is on both.

ne958281fff1.s: A weather balloon launched at 0000 UTC goes up at what Indian Standard Time?
ne958281fff1.x: IST (82°30′E) is 5 h 30 min ahead of GMT, so 0000 UTC is 5:30 a.m. IST.
xa: Reference town: **Mirzapur** (UP).
IST is kept by **CSIR-NPL, New Delhi**.
Both facts were asked in **APPSC 2019**.

n83bde8d6483.s: Indian Standard Time is maintained by:
n83bde8d6483.x: IST is maintained by the CSIR-National Physical Laboratory, New Delhi.
xa: NPL was set up in **1947** and is the custodian of national standards.
The **White Rabbit** network is at **Jakkur (Bengaluru)**.
**IST = GMT + 5 h 30 min**.

nffddaa77c13.s: India extends approximately from 68°7'E to 97°25'E. The approximate difference in local time between its western and eastern extremities is
nffddaa77c13.x: The longitudinal span is approximately 29°, which corresponds to about 116 minutes, or nearly two hours.
nffddaa77c13.tq: Estimate the time difference from the longitudinal span instead of using exact minute calculations.
xs: The span **68°7'E - 97°25'E ≈ 29°** gives ~**1 h 57 min** — nearly **2 hours** — option **(3)**.
At **4 min** per degree, **29°** ≈ **116 minutes**.
xa: The Sun rises ~**2 h** earlier in **Arunachal Pradesh** than in western **Gujarat**.
Local time at **Kibithu** is about **2 hours** ahead of **Guhar Moti**.
This gap drives the **two-time-zone** debate.

n8bb2873c6f3.s: The Tropic of Cancer does NOT pass through which one of the following States?
n8bb2873c6f3.x: Odisha lies wholly south of the Tropic of Cancer. Jharkhand, Tripura and Rajasthan are among the 8 States it crosses (with Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal and Mizoram).
n8bb2873c6f3.tq: Common distractors: Odisha, UP, Bihar - none is crossed.
xs: **Odisha** is NOT on the Tropic of Cancer — option **(2)**.
**Jharkhand, Tripura, Rajasthan** are among the **8** states it crosses.
xa: Odisha, **UP** and **Bihar** are the common "NOT crossed" distractors.
⚠ Odisha **is** crossed by the **IST meridian**.
The Tropic lies at **23°26' N**.

nc894ea3a8a8.s: On 21 June, daylight at the Tropic of Cancer lasts about:
nc894ea3a8a8.x: On 21 June the Tropic of Cancer has about 13.5 h of daylight, the Arctic Circle 24 h and the Equator about 12 h.
xa: On **22 December** the Tropic of Cancer gets **~10½ h** and the Arctic Circle a **24 h night**.
On **21 Mar / 23 Sep** every latitude in the table has **12 h** of day.
The **poles** have **six months of day and six of night**.

nindian-geography-47-2.s: The westernmost longitude of India is:
nindian-geography-47-2.x: India's westernmost longitude is 68°7′ E in Kutch. 82°30′ E is the IST meridian and 97°25′ E the eastern limit.
n: The westernmost longitude of India is 68°7′ E. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
xs: India's **westernmost longitude** is **68°7′ E** — at **Guhar Moti**, **Kutch**, **Gujarat** — option **(2)**.
**82°30′ E** is the **IST meridian**; **97°25′ E** to **97°30′ E** is the **easternmost extent** in Arunachal Pradesh.
xa: Longitudinal span **68°7'E – 97°25'E ≈ 29°** → local-time gap ~**1 h 57 min**.
The Sun rises ~**2 h** earlier in **Arunachal Pradesh** than in western Gujarat.
**Hyderabad** lies at about **78° E**; **Bhopal** and **Bengaluru** at about **77° E**.

nindian-geography-47-18.s: Fifteen degrees of longitude correspond to how much time?
nindian-geography-47-18.x: 15° equals one hour and 1° equals 4 minutes; IST (82°30′E) is GMT + 5 h 30 min.
n: The Indian Standard Time Meridian is 82°30′ E. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
One degree of longitude equals 4 minutes of time difference. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
Fifteen degrees of longitude equal 1 hour of time difference. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
Indian Standard Time is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
xa: **180°** of longitude = **12 hours**; **1'** of arc = **4 seconds**.
**East is ahead (add)**; **West is behind (subtract)**.
**Nepal** keeps UTC+**5:45**.

nindian-geography-47-20.s: The easternmost extent of India is approximately located between which longitudes?
nindian-geography-47-20.x: India's eastern limit is at about 97°25′–97°30′ E in Arunachal Pradesh.
n: The easternmost extent of India is approximately 97°25′ E to 97°30′ E. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
xs: India's **easternmost extent** lies at approximately **97°25′ E to 97°30′ E** — in **Arunachal Pradesh** — option **(4)**.
**68°7′ E** is the **westernmost longitude** (Guhar Moti); **82°30′ E** is the **IST meridian**; **80°34′ E–81°12′ E** is **Lucknow**.
xa: Longitudinal span ≈ **29°** → local-time gap ~**1 h 57 min** (nearly **2 hours**).
Local time at **Kibithu** is about **2 hours** ahead of **Guhar Moti**.
Proposals include advancing IST by **30 minutes** or a separate north-east zone ~**1 h** ahead.

nad86eee7986.s: The International Date Line passes through the:
nad86eee7986.x: The Date Line passes through the Bering Strait and deviates around the Aleutians and Pacific island groups.
xa: It also bends around **Siberia (Chukotka)**.
It roughly follows the **180° meridian**.
Westward crossing → **skip a day**; eastward → **repeat a day**.

nb2e7739ef4f.s: Which Pacific country moved to the Asian side of the International Date Line in 2011?
nb2e7739ef4f.x: Samoa shifted to the Asian side of the Date Line in 2011, changing its calendar relation with neighbours.
xa: The IDL zigzags around the **Fiji-Tonga-Kiribati** islands.
**Kiribati's Line Islands** (**UTC+14**) see the new day first.
Westward crossing (America → Asia) **skips a day**.

n958888b4cb2.s: Which of the following locations is among the first to experience a new calendar day?
n958888b4cb2.x: Kiribati’s Line Islands use UTC+14 and are among the first inhabited places to enter a new day.
n958888b4cb2.tq: Recall the extreme positive UTC offset associated with the earliest new day.
xs: **Kiribati's Line Islands** (**UTC+14**) are **first to see a new day** — option **(2)**.
The **Aleutians** and **Little Diomede** lie on the American side, behind; **Greenwich** is at **0°**.
xa: **Big Diomede (Russia)** and **Little Diomede (USA)** are on different dates.
The IDL lies roughly along the **180° meridian**.
**Samoa** moved to the Asian side in **2011**.

nindian-geography-47-16.s: When crossing the International Date Line (about 180°) eastward, one must:
nindian-geography-47-16.x: Crossing the Date Line eastward means subtracting a day.
n: The International Date Line lies at approximately 180° longitude. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
Crossing the International Date Line eastward requires subtracting 1 day. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #47 · pp 118-121]
xa: The IDL passes through the **middle of the Pacific** (APPSC **2021**) and the **Bering Strait**.
It **zigzags to avoid land** — around **Kiribati**, **Fiji**, **Tonga**, **Samoa**.
**Samoa** moved to the Asian side in **2011**; **Kiribati's Line Islands** (UTC+**14**) see a new day first.
⚠ Going **west** → skip a day; going **east** → repeat a day.

n56224144119.s: The winter solstice in the Northern Hemisphere occurs around:
n56224144119.x: The northern winter solstice is around 22 December and the autumnal equinox around 22 or 23 September.
xa: **APPSC-G1 2019 match:** winter solstice - **22 Dec**; summer solstice - **21 June**; vernal equinox - **21 March**; autumnal equinox - **23 Sept**.
APPSC has also accepted "**20 or 21 March**" and "**22 or 23 September**" as equinox dates.
On **22 December** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn**.

n5b43f2eb25b.s: The International Day of Yoga is observed on which date, which also corresponds to the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
n5b43f2eb25b.x: The International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June, the date of the Northern Hemisphere’s summer solstice.
n5b43f2eb25b.tq: Use the date-event association rather than confusing it with an equinox date.
xs: The **International Day of Yoga** is observed on **21 June** — option **(2)**.
**21 June** is the **summer solstice**: the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**, giving the Northern Hemisphere its **longest day**.
**21 March** and **23 September** are the **equinoxes**; **22 December** is the **winter solstice**.
xa: The **2026** theme of the Day was "**Yoga for Healthy Ageing**".
On **21 June** the **Arctic Circle** has a **24 h day** and the **North Pole** continuous day.
The **Tropic of Cancer** gets about **13½ h** of daylight on 21 June.

n73555956d55.s: On 22 December, the North Pole experiences:
n73555956d55.x: The North Pole has continuous night at the December solstice, continuous day at the June solstice and sunrise or sunset at an equinox.
xa: The **Arctic Circle** gets a **24 h day** on 21 June and a **24 h night** on 22 December.
The **South Pole** is lit in the other half-year.
The **Equator** has about **12 h** of day on all these dates.

ngeneral-geography-1-5.s: On 23 September, the Sun is overhead at the:
ngeneral-geography-1-5.x: On 23 September (and 21 March) the Sun is overhead at the Equator.
n: The Sun is overhead at the equator on 21 March. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer on 21 June. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The Sun is overhead at the equator on 23 September. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn on 22 December. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xa: APPSC-G1 **2019** matched: **winter solstice – 22 Dec**, **summer solstice – 21 June**, **vernal equinox – 21 March**, **autumnal equinox – 23 Sept**.
After **21 March** the Sun **starts moving northward**; after **21 June** it **starts moving southward**.
**21 June** is also the **International Day of Yoga**.

ngeneral-geography-2-13.s: On 21/22 December, the Southern Hemisphere has its:
ngeneral-geography-2-13.x: On 21/22 December the Southern Hemisphere has its longest day; on 21 June the Northern Hemisphere does.
n: The Northern Hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night on 21 June. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The Southern Hemisphere has its shortest day and longest night on 21 June. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The Southern Hemisphere has its longest day and shortest night on 21 or 22 December. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Day and night are approximately equal throughout the year at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: On **21 June** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**; on **22 December** at the **Tropic of Capricorn**.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes put the winter solstice on **22 December**.
At the **June solstice** the **Arctic Circle** has a **24 h day**.

ngeneral-geography-2-27.s: During the March Equinox, which season begins in the Southern Hemisphere?
ngeneral-geography-2-27.x: At the March Equinox spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere and autumn in the Southern Hemisphere.
n: An equinox means approximately equal day and night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
An equinox occurs twice a year. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The March equinox occurs approximately on 20 or 21 March. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The September equinox occurs approximately on 22 or 23 September. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Spring begins in the Northern Hemisphere at the March equinox. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Autumn begins in the Southern Hemisphere at the March equinox. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Autumn begins in the Northern Hemisphere at the September equinox. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Day and night are approximately equal during an equinox. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: An equinox is a **transition point** between seasons.
The Sun's **direct rays** fall on the **Equator** at both equinoxes.
Dates: **20 or 21 March** and **22 or 23 September**.

ngeneral-geography-3-34.s: From 23 September to 21 December, days in the Northern Hemisphere:
ngeneral-geography-3-34.x: In this period northern days shorten while southern days lengthen; the reverse happens from December to March.
n: From 23 September to 21 December, Northern Hemisphere days progressively shorten. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
From 23 September to 21 December, Southern Hemisphere days progressively lengthen. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
From 21 December to 21 March, Northern Hemisphere days progressively lengthen. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
From 21 December to 21 March, Southern Hemisphere days progressively shorten. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **21 March to 21 June:** NH days lengthen; **21 June to 23 September:** NH days shorten.
NH **longest day** **21 June**, **shortest day** **21 December**.
**North Pole** is continuously lit from ~**21 March** to ~**23 September**.

ngeneral-geography-3-62.s: Day and night are approximately equal at:
ngeneral-geography-3-62.x: An equinox is a seasonal transition with about equal day and night; a solstice has unequal day and night and maximum seasonal contrast.
n: Seasonal contrast is maximum at a solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
An equinox is a transition point between seasons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Day and night are not equal at a solstice. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Day and night are approximately equal at an equinox. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: There are **two solstices** and **two equinoxes** each year.
Equinoxes fall in **March** and **September**.
**21 June** (summer solstice) is the **International Day of Yoga**.

nae87856f10a.s: With respect to the Tropic of Cancer, Andhra Pradesh lies:
o: Along it, on its northern boundary
Crossed by it in its northern part
nae87856f10a.x: Andhra Pradesh lies wholly south of the Tropic of Cancer.
xa: States **wholly north**: UP, Bihar, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal, Uttarakhand, Sikkim, Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal, Nagaland, Manipur.
AP is on the **IST meridian** (via **Kakinada**).
On **21 June** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**.

n39c2f345f1d.s: Through how many Indian States does the Tropic of Cancer pass?
n39c2f345f1d.x: The Tropic of Cancer passes through 8 States: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram. 6, 7 and 9 are wrong counts.
xs: The Tropic of Cancer crosses **8 states** — option **(3)** (**APPSC 2025** answer: 8).
They are **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura, Mizoram**.
xa: ⚠ **8** states on the Tropic vs **5** on the IST meridian.
Common "NOT crossed" distractors: **Odisha, UP and Bihar**.
It cuts the **Mahi river twice**.

n76695dd1c5f.s: During the summer season in the Southern Hemisphere, which pole is tilted towards the Sun?
n76695dd1c5f.x: During southern summer, the South Pole is tilted towards the Sun, producing longer days and summer conditions in the Southern Hemisphere.
n76695dd1c5f.tq: Relate the hemisphere experiencing summer to the direction of axial tilt.
xs: During the Southern Hemisphere's summer, the **South Pole** is tilted towards the Sun — option **(1)**.
Seasons come from the **tilted axis** plus **revolution**: the hemisphere tilted toward the Sun gets summer.
The **North Pole** tilts toward the Sun in the Northern summer (**21 June** solstice), so it cannot be the answer.
xa: On **22 December** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn** — the **Southern Hemisphere's longest day** and summer.
The North Pole is **continuously lit from ~21 March to ~23 September**; the **South Pole** in the other half-year.
Earth's orbit is **elliptical**; revolution takes **365¼ days**, so every 4th year is a **leap year** (29 Feb).

ngeneral-geography-2-6.s: Seasons occur because of the Earth's revolution combined with its:
ngeneral-geography-2-6.x: The axial tilt changes the Sun's angle and day length as Earth revolves, producing seasons.
n: Earth’s revolution causes seasons along with axial tilt. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution produces seasons with axial tilt. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s axial tilt of 23.5° changes the angle and duration of solar illumination. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s revolution and axial tilt produce the seasonal cycle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: Axial inclination: **23.5°** from the **perpendicular** = **66.5°** to the **orbital plane**.
**Parallelism** of the axis produces **opposite seasons** in the two hemispheres.
Tilt also fixes the **tropics** (**23½°**) and **polar circles** (**66½°**).
**Milankovitch cycles** drive long-period climate change.

ngeneral-geography-2-8.s: The Earth's axis keeps approximately the same orientation during its revolution because of:
ngeneral-geography-2-8.x: Angular momentum keeps the axis parallel to itself; opposite seasons are a result of this, not its cause.
n: Earth’s axis remains approximately parallel during revolution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Earth’s axis maintains approximate parallelism during revolution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Parallelism of Earth’s axis produces opposite seasons in the two hemispheres. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Parallelism means that Earth’s axis maintains approximately the same orientation as Earth revolves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
Parallelism of Earth’s axis produces seasonal reversal between the hemispheres. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The correct statement is that there is parallelism of Earth’s axis. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: Axial inclination: **23½°** from the perpendicular = **66½°** to the orbital plane.
**Precession:** the axis **wobbles**, changing the pole star; it pointed to **Vega ~14,000 years ago**.
⚠ The correct statement is that **there is parallelism** of Earth's axis.

ngeneral-geography-3-18.s: The Earth's axis is inclined to the plane of its orbit at:
ngeneral-geography-3-18.x: The axis makes 66½° with the orbital plane, which is a 23½° tilt from the perpendicular.
n: Earth’s axis is inclined 66½° to its orbital plane. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Earth is tilted by 23½° as it revolves around the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: Tilt is a **major factor in seasons**, changing the **angle** and **duration** of sunlight.
It fixes the **tropics** (**23½°**) and **polar circles** (**66½°**).
**Parallelism** of the axis gives **opposite seasons** in the hemispheres.

ngeneral-geography-2-32.s: When the North Pole has six months of continuous daylight, the South Pole has:
ngeneral-geography-2-32.x: Axial inclination and revolution give the poles opposite six-month patterns of day and night.
n: The North Pole has six months of continuous daylight. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The North Pole has six months of darkness. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The South Pole has the opposite daylight and darkness pattern to the North Pole. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
The main reason for polar six-month day and night is axial inclination combined with revolution. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #2 · pp 11-19]
xa: North Pole is continuously lit from ~**21 March** to ~**23 September**.
**Arctic Circle:** **24 h day** on **21 June**, **24 h night** on **22 Dec**.
Continuous daylight occurs **beyond the Antarctic Circle** during **Southern Hemisphere summer**.

nindian-geography-45-4.s: Of the States crossed by the Tropic of Cancer, which is first in the west-to-east order?
nindian-geography-45-4.x: West to east, Gujarat is first, Madhya Pradesh third, Jharkhand fifth and Tripura seventh.
n: Gujarat is the first state crossed by the Tropic of Cancer from west to east. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
Madhya Pradesh is the third state crossed by the Tropic of Cancer from west to east. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
Jharkhand is the fifth state crossed by the Tropic of Cancer from west to east. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
Tripura is the seventh state crossed by the Tropic of Cancer from west to east. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
xa: It crosses **eight Indian states** (APPSC **2025** answer: **8**).
⚠ **8** states on the Tropic vs **5** on the IST meridian; **Chhattisgarh** is on both.
Common "not crossed" distractors: **Odisha**, **UP** and **Bihar**.
**Andhra Pradesh** lies **wholly south** of the Tropic.

nindian-geography-45-20.s: The Mahi river, which crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice, drains into the:
nindian-geography-45-20.x: The Mahi rises in Madhya Pradesh, flows through Rajasthan and Gujarat and drains into the Gulf of Khambhat.
n: The Mahi River crosses the Tropic of Cancer twice. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
The Mahi River originates in Madhya Pradesh. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
The Mahi River flows through Rajasthan. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
The Mahi River flows through Gujarat. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
The Mahi River drains into the Gulf of Khambhat. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #45 · pp 116-117]
xa: The Tropic of Cancer crosses **eight** Indian states, from **Gujarat** to **Mizoram**.
Tropic of Cancer: **23°30′ N** (other notes **23°26' N**).
The Tropic crosses **17 countries**, India among them.

n33cfa11fd3c.s: Separate Bombay and Calcutta times were introduced in:
n33cfa11fd3c.x: Bombay and Calcutta times date from 1884; a single IST was adopted after 1947.
xa: The Rules make IST the **single mandatory reference**, in force **180 days** after gazette publication.
White Rabbit gives **sub-nanosecond sync** over fibre, independent of GPS.
**NPL** (**1947**) is the custodian of national standards.

nc56457d52c3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026?
o: They were notified by the Ministry of Consumer Affairs
They make IST the single mandatory reference for legal, administrative, commercial and official purposes
They came into force immediately on notification
nc56457d52c3.x: The Rules come into force 180 days after Gazette publication, not immediately.
xa: IST is kept by **CSIR-NPL, New Delhi**.
Synchronised IST protects banking, railways, power grids and telecom against **GPS spoofing**.
The **White Rabbit** network was inaugurated in **Jul 2026**.

na93abcd69b1.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the White Rabbit-based IST Distribution Demonstration Network?
o: It was inaugurated at RRSL, Jakkur (Bengaluru)
It gives sub-nanosecond synchronisation over fibre
Its White Rabbit protocol was developed by ISRO
na93abcd69b1.x: The White Rabbit protocol was developed by CERN, not ISRO.
xa: Slogan: **"One Nation, One Time"**.
**NPL-ISRO** collaboration disseminates high-precision IST.
⚠ UTC = **caesium** clocks; NavIC = **rubidium** clocks.

n0b70d26f000.s: Which combination most accurately explains the seasonal variation in the angle of incidence of solar rays and the length of day?
o: Rotation alone and changing distance from the Sun
Ocean currents, tides and the changing speed of winds
Axial inclination, parallelism of the axis, revolution and the spherical shape of the Earth
The elliptical orbit alone and the rotation of the Moon
n0b70d26f000.x: Seasonal variation results from the Earth’s axial inclination, the parallelism of its axis, its revolution around the Sun and its spherical shape. These alter the Sun’s angle and the duration of daylight received by different regions.
n0b70d26f000.tq: Identify the complete causal combination instead of accepting the distance-from-Sun misconception.
xs: Seasonal change in Sun angle and day length comes from **axial inclination, parallelism of the axis, revolution and the spherical shape** — option **(3)**.
The **parallel axis** always points to the **Pole Star**, so tilt plus revolution changes the Sun's angle through the year.
**Distance from the Sun** does not cause seasons — option (1) is wrong.
xa: Key reason (APPSC **2018**): axis inclined **23½°** from the perpendicular (**66½°** to the orbital plane).
The hemisphere tilted **toward** the Sun has summer; the other has winter.
⚠ **Trap:** distance does **not** cause seasons; **tilt** does.

n2c049add9e8.s: Which of the following is NOT a factor affecting the distribution of insolation?
o: Angle of incidence of solar rays
n2c049add9e8.x: The major factors listed are the angle of incidence, duration of day, atmospheric transparency and land configuration. Direction of ocean tides is not one of them.
n2c049add9e8.tq: Find the unrelated factor among the components of insolation distribution.
xs: **Direction of ocean tides** is not a factor of insolation — option **(1)**.
The factors are **angle of incidence**, **duration of day**, **transparency of the atmosphere** and **land configuration**.
Options (2), (3) and (4) are all listed factors.
xa: Vertical rays heat a **smaller area**, so they are more intense.
Insolation **falls from the tropics to the poles**.
⚠ Maximum insolation is over **subtropical deserts**, not the Equator.

n027312953b2.s: When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, it experiences:
n027312953b2.x: The hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets more direct rays and longer days, producing summer.
xa: The Southern Hemisphere is the **exact opposite** of the North.
NH longest day **21 June**; SH longest day **22 December**.
⚠ **Trap:** distance does **not** cause seasons; **tilt** does.

ngeneral-geography-3-8.s: The summer hemisphere receives greater heating than the winter hemisphere because:
o: It is nearer to the Sun
Its solar rays are more direct and its days are longer
Its solar rays are more oblique
ngeneral-geography-3-8.x: Direct rays and longer days give the summer hemisphere more heating.
n: Summer solar rays are more direct. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Summer days are longer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Heating is greater in summer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The summer hemisphere receives more direct rays and longer days. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: The **winter hemisphere** gets **more oblique rays** and **shorter days**.
**Seasonal temperature** depends on **insolation** and **day length**.
Insolation factors: **angle of incidence**, **duration of day**, **transparency of the atmosphere**, land configuration.

ngeneral-geography-3-22.s: The summer hemisphere is the one that is:
ngeneral-geography-3-22.x: The summer hemisphere tilts towards the Sun, getting concentrated energy, a higher Sun and longer days.
n: During summer, the hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
During winter, the hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Winter solar rays are more oblique. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Summer solar energy has greater concentration. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Winter solar energy has lower concentration. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Summer days are longer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Winter days are shorter. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Sun’s apparent altitude is higher in summer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The Sun’s apparent altitude is lower in winter. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **Oblique rays spread energy over a larger area** — lower heating.
Seasons in **opposite hemispheres** are **opposite**.
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).

ngeneral-geography-3-45.s: More oblique solar rays produce lower heating because they:
o: Spread the same energy over a larger area
ngeneral-geography-3-45.x: Oblique rays spread the same energy over a larger area, so heating per unit area is lower.
n: More oblique or slanting solar rays spread energy over a larger area and produce lower heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: The **winter hemisphere** receives **more oblique rays** and **shorter days**.
⚠ Maximum insolation is over **subtropical deserts** (cloudless skies), not the **Equator**.
Insolation **falls from the tropics to the poles**.

n5e9919eac3e.s: The seasons on the Earth are caused mainly by:
n5e9919eac3e.x: Seasons come mainly from axial tilt affecting solar angle and day length; Earth is in fact nearest the Sun during northern winter.
xa: **Aphelion**: Earth **farthest** from the Sun **~4 July**, in NH summer.
Key reason for seasons: axis inclined **23½°** from the perpendicular (APPSC **2018**).
Other factors: **parallelism of the axis**, **revolution** and spherical shape.

n67a13603649.s: Which latitude zone experiences the greatest seasonal differences in day length and insolation?
n67a13603649.x: Seasonal differences are greatest in high latitudes because the annual swings in day length and insolation are very large there.
n67a13603649.tq: Use the latitude-based comparison and avoid reversing the trend.
xs: Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** — option **(1)**.
High latitudes see **huge swings in day length and insolation** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
**Low latitudes** have only a small temperature contrast; **mid-latitudes** have four distinct seasons.
xa: Low-latitude seasons are marked by **rain** (wet/dry).
**Subtropics**: hot summers, mild winters.
NH longest day **21 June**; SH longest day **22 December**.

n715a1cd23de.s: Four distinct seasons are generally experienced in:
n715a1cd23de.x: Mid-latitudes show four distinct seasons; low latitudes have wet and dry periods and subtropics hot summers and mild winters.
xa: Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
**Christmas in Australia** falls in **summer**.
NH longest day **21 June**; SH **22 December**.

n63350563f4b.s: The Southern Hemisphere has its longest day around:
n63350563f4b.x: The Southern Hemisphere's longest day is around 22 December, while the Northern Hemisphere's is around 21 June.
xa: **Christmas in Australia** falls in **summer**.
On **21 June** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Cancer**; on **22 December** at the **Tropic of Capricorn**.
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes**.

nb6cfd932118.s: Christmas in Australia generally falls during which season?
nb6cfd932118.x: Australia lies in the Southern Hemisphere, where December corresponds to summer.
nb6cfd932118.tq: Apply the hemisphere-season reversal to a familiar calendar event.
xs: **Christmas in Australia** falls in **summer** — option **(1)**.
Australia is in the **Southern Hemisphere**, whose longest day is **22 December**.
The Southern Hemisphere's seasons are the **exact opposite** of the North's.
xa: On **22 December** the Sun is overhead at the **Tropic of Capricorn**.
In SH summer the **South Pole tilts toward the Sun**.
NH longest day: **21 June**.

ne3fc432e663.s: Which one of the following places does NOT receive the overhead Sun at noon on any day of the year?
ne3fc432e663.x: Only places between the Tropic of Cancer and the Tropic of Capricorn can receive the overhead Sun. Delhi, being north of 23½°N, never does so.
ne3fc432e663.tq: Apply the tropical-latitude boundary to identify the exception.
xs: **Delhi**, north of **23½°N**, never gets the overhead Sun — option **(4)**.
The Sun is overhead **twice a year** only **between the Tropics** ("zero-shadow days").
**15°S**, **20°N** and the **Equator** all lie between the Tropics.
xa: **Srinagar** is also north of 23½°N and never gets an overhead Sun.
North of the Tropic, noon shadows are **shortest in June** and **longest in December**.
On **21 June** there is **no noon shadow** on the Tropic of Cancer.

n2b888797dd7.s: On 21 June, where is the noon shadow absent because the Sun is overhead?
n2b888797dd7.x: On 21 June, the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so an object there casts no shadow at local noon.
n2b888797dd7.tq: Link the solstice date with the corresponding overhead latitude.
xs: On **21 June** there is no noon shadow on the **Tropic of Cancer** — option **(1)**.
21 June is the **summer solstice**, when the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer.
**Delhi** lies north of **23½°N** and never gets an overhead Sun.
xa: Overhead Sun occurs **twice a year** only between the Tropics ("**zero-shadow days**").
North of the Tropic, noon shadows are **shortest in June**, **longest in December**.
**AP (12°41'N - 19°07'N)** gets the overhead Sun twice a year.

na5d18d6d37e.s: On 21 June, which of the following cities has the longest day?
na5d18d6d37e.x: On 21 June day length increases northward: Srinagar > Delhi > Hyderabad > Chennai > Kanyakumari.
xa: On **21 June** there is **no noon shadow** on the **Tropic of Cancer**.
**Srinagar** and **Delhi** lie north of **23½°N** and never get an overhead Sun.
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes**.

ne2bd14f1074.s: Lying between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer, Andhra Pradesh can receive the overhead noon Sun:
ne2bd14f1074.x: Andhra Pradesh (about 12°41′N to 19°07′N) lies between the Equator and the Tropic of Cancer, so the overhead Sun can occur there twice a year.
xa: AP lies **wholly south** of the Tropic of Cancer.
AP's seasons: summer (**Mar-May**), SW monsoon (**Jun-Sep**, ~**2/3** of rain), winter (**Oct-Feb**).
**Lambasingi** is AP's coldest place (~**2°C**).

n00837821c3e.s: In 1935, a temperature of about 50°C was recorded at:
n00837821c3e.x: About 50°C was recorded at Ganganagar in 1935, during the March-May hot weather season.
xa: Pre-monsoon showers in South India are called "**coffee blossom**" showers.
Heatwaves reach **AP, Telangana, Odisha**.
IMD's **pre-monsoon** season runs **Mar-May**.

n419243c65a3.s: Under the IMD's seasonal classification, which season follows the South-West monsoon?
n419243c65a3.x: IMD's four seasons run winter, pre-monsoon, South-West monsoon and post-monsoon.
xa: Traditional India counts **six ritus** (**Vasanta** to **Shishira**).
AP's winter runs **Oct-Feb**; its SW monsoon (**Jun-Sep**) brings **~2/3** of the rain.
India's hot weather season (**March-May**) brings heatwaves to **AP, Telangana, Odisha**.

ngeneral-geography-3-10.s: At the December solstice, the Sun is overhead at the:
ngeneral-geography-3-10.x: At the December solstice the Sun is over Capricorn; at the June solstice over Cancer; at the equinoxes over the Equator.
n: At an equinox, the Sun is overhead at the Equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The June solstice is associated with the Tropic of Cancer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The December solstice is associated with the Tropic of Capricorn. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
The equinoxes occur in March and September. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: At the **Equator**, the noon shadow is **absent** in **March** and **September**.
The overhead Sun occurs **twice a year** only between the Tropics ("**zero-shadow days**").
Places north of **23½°N** (Delhi, Srinagar) never get an overhead Sun.

nd746c471b5d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about sources of information on the Earth's interior?
o: Magma and lava from volcanic eruptions give direct evidence
Meteorites are used because they are made of material similar to the Earth's
Meteorites provide direct evidence of the interior
nd746c471b5d.x: Meteorites are an indirect source; only material such as magma and lava gives direct evidence.
xa: **Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.
Rise of **pressure and temperature with depth** is also indirect evidence.
Direct sources also include **deep drilling** and **surface rock from mining**.

n745167af499.s: The deepest hole, about 12 km deep, was drilled by the USSR in the 1970s on the:
n745167af499.x: The ~12 km hole was drilled on the Kola Peninsula; the Mponeng and TauTona mines (South Africa) reach only about 3.9 km.
xa: ⚠ Deepest hole = **Kola** (~12 km); deepest mines = **Mponeng, TauTona** (3.9 km).
India's scientific deep drilling: **Borehole Geophysics Research Laboratory, Karad**.
Direct sources: mining, drilling, **volcanic eruptions**.

n686566b75e0.s: Which one of the following is a direct source of information about the interior of the Earth?
n686566b75e0.x: Surface rocks obtained from mining areas are a direct source because the material itself is examined. Seismic waves, gravity anomalies and magnetic surveys are indirect sources that infer the interior from measurements.
n686566b75e0.tq: Mining, drilling, volcanoes = direct; seismic, gravity, magnetic, meteorites = indirect.
xs: **Surface rocks from mining areas** are a direct source — option **(3)**.
**Seismic waves**, **gravity** anomalies and **magnetic** surveys are all **indirect** sources.
This was the APPSC-G1 **2017** answer.
xa: Other direct sources: **deep drilling** and **volcanic eruptions** (magma, lava).
**Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.
Deepest mines: **Mponeng, TauTona** (South Africa), only **3.9 km**.

ngeneral-geography-4-26.s: Surface seismic waves are also called:
ngeneral-geography-4-26.x: Surface waves are L-waves; P-waves are primary and S-waves secondary waves.
n: P-waves are primary waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves are secondary waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves are also called compressional or longitudinal waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Surface waves are also called L-waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: P-waves **arrive first**; surface waves **arrive last**.
Surface waves do the **most damage**.
**National Centre for Seismology** (MoES): **160-observatory** network, detects Indian quakes of M **3.0+**.

ngeneral-geography-4-30.x: In P-waves particles vibrate parallel to propagation (push–pull); in S-waves they vibrate perpendicular (transverse).
n: P-wave particle vibration is parallel to the direction of propagation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-wave particle vibration is perpendicular to the direction of propagation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
P-waves are longitudinal push-pull waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves are transverse shake waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: P-waves travel through **solids, liquids and gases**; S-waves through **solids only**.
P-waves are the **fastest**; **surface waves** the **slowest**.
**Velocity changes** and **shadow zones** reveal internal boundaries.

n6b113f70cbc.s: S-waves are absent everywhere beyond about ____ from the epicentre.
n6b113f70cbc.x: S-waves are absent beyond 105°, so the S-wave shadow zone is larger than the P-wave shadow zone.
xa: CGPSC **2020** keyed the "own shadow zone" statement as true.
The S-wave shadow proves the **outer core is liquid**.
⚠ P = solids + liquids + gases; S = **solids only**.

ngeneral-geography-4-11.s: The P-wave shadow zone lies approximately between:
ngeneral-geography-4-11.x: The P-wave shadow zone is about 103°–142° from the epicentre.
n: P-waves are the fastest seismic waves. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves do not travel through liquids. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Surface waves have the highest destructive power. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The standard P-wave shadow zone is approximately 103°–142°. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
S-waves travel through solids only. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: shadow zone also given as **105°–140°** or **105°–145°**.
**Each earthquake has its own shadow zone**, set by its epicentre (CGPSC **2020**).
S-waves are **absent everywhere beyond 105°**.

n62c86d66647.s: Why do seismic waves help in identifying discontinuities inside the Earth?
o: Their speed remains constant in all materials.
They are produced only by volcanic eruptions.
They travel only through the crust and stop at the Moho.
Their speed changes with density, causing reflection and refraction at layer boundaries.
n62c86d66647.x: Changes in density alter seismic-wave velocity and produce reflection and refraction at boundaries, revealing internal discontinuities.
n62c86d66647.tq: Connect the observable wave effect with the inferred internal structure.
xs: Wave **speed changes with density**, so waves **reflect and refract** at layer boundaries — option **(4)**.
That is how the **discontinuities** were found; speed is not constant (option 1).
P-waves cross the core, so waves do not stop at the **Moho** (option 3).
xa: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**.
Downward order: **Conrad → Moho → Repetti → Gutenberg → Lehmann**.
**Seismic waves** are the **most important** indirect source.

nd8a6dc65129.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate thickness of oceanic and continental crust respectively?
nd8a6dc65129.x: Oceanic crust is approximately 5 km thick, whereas continental crust is approximately 30 km thick, though it may reach greater thickness beneath mountains.
nd8a6dc65129.tq: Use the direct numerical comparison and distinguish oceanic from continental crust.
xs: Oceanic crust is **~5 km**, continental crust **~30 km** — option **(2)**.
Continental crust reaches **~70 km** under **mountains**.
Some notes give a mean of **~20 km** — neither option (1) nor (4) matches the oceanic/continental pair.
xa: Continental crust is **granitic (SIAL)**; oceanic is **basaltic (SIMA)**.
Crust density: upper **2.8**, lower **3.0**.
The **Moho** lies **~30 km** under continents and **~5 km** under oceans.

n02a86152b65.s: The mantle accounts for approximately what percentage of the Earth's volume and mass respectively?
n02a86152b65.x: The mantle constitutes approximately 83% of Earth's volume and 68% of its mass.
n02a86152b65.tq: Distinguish the volume share from the mass share rather than reversing them.
xs: The mantle is **83%** of Earth's volume and **68%** of its mass — option **(1)**.
**16%** and **32%** are the **core's** volume and mass shares — option (2) is the trap.
xa: ⚠ Mantle = **83%** volume, **68%** mass; core = **16%** volume, **32%** mass.
Mantle extends from the Moho to **2,900 km**; mean density **4.6**.

ne5449845d5a.s: The Mohorovicic Discontinuity, separating the crust from the mantle, was discovered in:
ne5449845d5a.x: Andrija Mohorovicic identified it in 1909; it lies about 30 km below continents and 5 km below oceans.
xa: At the Moho, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**.
Rare **continental mantle earthquakes** occur **80+ km** below the Moho.
**Conrad** lies above it, within the crust.

n783124668f1.s: The Indian plate beneath Tibet has been reported to undergo which process?
o: Subduction of its entire crust into the outer core
Complete melting of its oceanic crust at the surface
Delamination of its dense lower layer into the mantle at about 100 km depth
Separation of its upper layer into the asthenosphere only
n783124668f1.x: The dense lower layer of the Indian plate is reported to be peeling away and delaminating into the mantle at roughly 100 km depth beneath Tibet.
n783124668f1.tq: Use the process-location-depth combination to distinguish delamination from subduction.
xs: The Indian plate beneath Tibet is **delaminating** — its dense lower layer peeling into the mantle **~100 km** down — option **(3)**.
Evidence: **94 seismic stations** and **helium isotopes**.
xa: The **lithosphere** (about **100 km**) moves over the **semi-fluid asthenosphere**.
The asthenosphere is the **main source of magma**.
Other recent findings: Stanford's first global map of **continental mantle earthquakes**; Swarm data on outer-core flow.

nacd0cec50a2.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Earth's core?
o: The outer core extends from about 2,900 km to 5,150 km
The inner core extends from about 5,150 km to the centre at 6,371 km
nacd0cec50a2.x: The inner core is solid; only the outer core is liquid.
xa: Inner-core density **13.3-13.6**; P-waves cross at **11.23 km/s**.
**Gutenberg** (~**2,900 km**) and **Lehmann** (~**5,150 km**) mark these boundaries.
Core = **16%** of volume, **32%** of mass.

n5cad1e9c6f2.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the approximate density progression from the crust through the mantle to the inner core?
n5cad1e9c6f2.x: Density increases downward from approximately 2.8–3.0 g/cm³ in the crust to 4.6 in the mantle and 13.3–13.6 in the inner core.
n5cad1e9c6f2.tq: Arrange the density values in increasing order with depth.
xs: Density goes **2.8-3.0 (crust) → 4.6 (mantle) → 13.3-13.6 (inner core)** — option **(2)**.
**5.5** is Earth's **average**, not the mantle's (options 1 and 4 wrong).
Option (3) reverses the order.
xa: Outer core density **~10-12**.
Upper crust **2.8**, lower crust **3.0**.
Density rises with depth, along with **temperature** and **pressure**.

ngeneral-geography-4-1.s: Which layer of the Earth is predominantly solid but behaves plastically over geological time?
ngeneral-geography-4-1.x: The mantle is mostly solid but flows slowly over geological time, which drives convection. The outer core is liquid and the crust and inner core are rigid.
ngeneral-geography-4-1.tq: Discriminate the state of each layer.
n: The mantle is predominantly solid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The mantle behaves plastically over geological time. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xs: The **mantle** is **predominantly solid** but **behaves plastically over geological time** — option **(1)**.
The **crust** is **solid**; the **outer core** is **liquid**; the **inner core** is **solid** (the **NIFE** or **solid core**).
The mantle is mainly **magnesium–iron silicates**, extending from the Moho to **2,900 km**.
xa: Mantle = **83%** of volume, **68%** of mass; mean density **4.6**.
**Mantle movement drives plate movement**; the mantle is the **major source region for magma**.

ngeneral-geography-4-5.x: Oceanic crust is basaltic, denser and richer in Fe–Mg, while continental crust is thicker and generally older.
n: Continental crust is thicker than oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is the main rock of oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oceanic crust has higher density than continental crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Continental crust is generally older than oceanic crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Oceanic crust contains more iron and magnesium. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Continental crust is **granitic (SIAL)**; oceanic **basaltic (SIMA)**.
Thickness: oceanic ~**5 km**, continental ~**30 km**, up to ~**70 km** under mountains.
Crust density: upper **2.8**, lower **3.0**.

ngeneral-geography-4-15.s: The layer lying directly below the mantle is the:
ngeneral-geography-4-15.x: The crust is outermost, then the mantle, then the outer core, with the inner core at the centre.
n: Earth’s crust is the outermost layer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The mantle lies below the crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The outer core lies below the mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The inner core is central. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: **Crust:** oxygen is the **most abundant** element.
**Outer core** is **liquid** (**2,900–5,150 km**); **inner core** **solid** (**5,150–6,371 km**).
**Moho** separates crust and mantle; **Lehmann** separates outer and inner core.

n0283946e11b.s: At the Mohorovicic Discontinuity, the velocity of P-waves rises approximately from:
n0283946e11b.x: A distinctive increase in P-wave velocity from about 6.9 to 8.1 km/s helped identify the Moho.
n0283946e11b.tq: Recall the paired numerical values associated with a seismic boundary.
xs: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9 to 8.1 km/s** — option **(4)**.
**11.23 km/s** is the P-wave speed at the **inner core**.
xa: The Moho separates **crust and mantle**; found **1909**.
Wave **speed changes with density**, so waves **reflect and refract** at boundaries.
Moho depth: **~30 km** under continents, **~5 km** under oceans.

ngeneral-geography-4-6.x: Gutenberg separates mantle and outer core; Moho, crust and mantle; Lehmann, outer and inner core; Conrad, upper and lower crust.
n: The Mohorovicic or Moho discontinuity separates the crust and mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Gutenberg discontinuity separates the mantle and outer core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core and inner core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The Conrad discontinuity separates the upper and lower continental crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: At the **Moho**, P-wave speed jumps from **6.9** to **8.1 km/s**; found by **Andrija Mohorovicic** in **1909**.
**Repetti** separates upper and lower mantle (~**700–1,000 km**).
**Gutenberg** ~**2,900 km**; **Lehmann** ~**5,150 km**.
⚠ The most confused trio: **Moho**, **Gutenberg**, **Lehmann**.

n8d2637ecc2d.s: The asthenosphere is located in the:
n8d2637ecc2d.x: The asthenosphere is a weak, partly molten upper-mantle zone at about 100–200 km and a major source of magma.
xa: Earthquake waves **slow down** in the asthenosphere; it extends to ~**400 km**.
Lithospheric plates **glide over** it.
**Lithosphere** = crust + rigid uppermost mantle, about **100 km** thick.

n810cfd3f92b.s: In the sequence Lithosphere – Asthenosphere – Mesosphere – Barysphere, the barysphere represents the:
n810cfd3f92b.x: From the surface inward the layers are lithosphere, asthenosphere, mesosphere and barysphere, the last being the core.
xa: **Lithosphere**: crust + rigid uppermost mantle, about **100 km**.
**Asthenosphere**: low-velocity zone at **~100-200 km**; **main source of magma**.
Suess's chemical zones: **SIAL, SIMA, NIFE**.

ngeneral-geography-4-8.s: Lithospheric plates are able to move because they glide over the weak:
ngeneral-geography-4-8.x: The weak asthenosphere lets lithospheric plates glide, so mantle movement below can drive them.
n: Mantle movement drives plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere allows plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Mantle movement drives plate movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The asthenosphere is the **main source of magma**.
It lies at ~**100–200 km** (extends to ~**400 km**); earthquake waves slow down there.
The lithosphere is the **earthquake-generating shell**.

ngeneral-geography-4-23.s: The lithosphere is made up of the:
ngeneral-geography-4-23.x: The rigid lithosphere is made of the crust and uppermost mantle, above the weak, ductile asthenosphere.
n: The lithosphere is the rigid upper zone associated with the mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The lithosphere is rigid. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere is weak and ductile. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The lithosphere consists of the crust and uppermost mantle. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The asthenosphere underlies the upper mantle portion below the lithosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The lithosphere is about **100 km** thick and **broken into tectonic plates**.
Asthenosphere = **low-velocity zone** at ~**100–200 km**.
Lithosphere is an **earthquake-generating shell**; asthenosphere is linked with **mantle flow**.

ngeneral-geography-1-7.s: What does the term ‘NIFE’ refer to?
ngeneral-geography-1-7.x: NIFE stands for nickel (Ni) and iron (Fe, ferrum), the main metals of Earth's core. N and F would wrongly suggest nitrogen and fluorine.
ngeneral-geography-1-7.tq: Read the chemical symbols in the acronym.
n: NIFE means nickel and ferrum, or iron. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #1 · pp 2-11]
xs: **NIFE** stands for **Nickel and Ferrum (iron)** — option **(3)**.
The term comes from **E. Suess**, whose chemical zones were **SIAL**, **SIMA** and **NIFE**; NIFE is the **core** (BPSC **2022**).
The other options wrongly read "N" as **nitrogen** or "F" as **fluorine**.
xa: **Iron** is the core's **main constituent**; **nickel** is **another major constituent**.
**SIAL** = silica + aluminium (granite, continents); **SIMA** = silica + magnesium (basalt, source of magma).
NIFE density ~**11**; it explains Earth's **magnetism**.
Lighter elements in the core: **silicon** (APPSC G2 **2017** answer), sulphur, oxygen.

ncad0db09683.s: Which is the second most abundant element by weight in the Earth's crust?
ncad0db09683.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element by weight in the crust, followed by silicon at about 27.72%.
xa: **Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal**; **iron** second.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates (iron-rich core).

n4b986208f57.s: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust by weight?
n4b986208f57.x: Aluminium (about 8.1%) is the most abundant metal in the crust, followed by iron (about 5%) and calcium (about 3.6%). Silicon (about 27.7%) is more abundant but is not a metal; oxygen is the most abundant element overall.
n4b986208f57.tq: Element order O > Si > Al > Fe; most abundant metal = Al.
xs: **Aluminium** (**8.13%**) is the most abundant **metal** in the crust — option **(2)**.
**Iron** (**5.00%**) is second; **calcium** (**3.63%**) next.
**Silicon** (**27.72%**) is more abundant but not a metal.
xa: **Oxygen** (**46.60%**) is the most abundant element overall.
⚠ JPSC **2011** keyed **Aluminium** for "second largest".
In the **whole Earth**, **iron** dominates.

n2b63da1a792.s: The magnetic axis of the Earth is inclined by approximately how much to its geographic axis?
n2b63da1a792.x: The Earth's magnetic axis is inclined approximately 11.5° to its geographic axis.
n2b63da1a792.tq: Distinguish magnetic-axis inclination from the better-known seasonal axial tilt.
xs: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis — option **(2)**.
The field is made by **convecting molten iron** in the **outer core** (geodynamo).
xa: Iron accounts for Earth's **magnetism and rigidity**.
Swarm (**ESA**): outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals last up to **~70,000 years**.

n134edeb35e3.s: The core constitutes approximately what percentage of the Earth's volume and mass respectively?
n134edeb35e3.x: The core accounts for approximately 16% of Earth's volume and 32% of its mass.
n134edeb35e3.tq: Distinguish the core's volume share from its greater mass share.
xs: The core is **16%** of Earth's volume and **32%** of its mass — option **(1)**.
**83%** and **68%** are the **mantle's** shares — option (4) is the trap.
xa: Core main elements: **iron and nickel (NIFE)**.
Core density **11-13.6** (inner core **13+**).
The core begins at **~2,900 km**.

n242801ab685.s: Besides iron and nickel, which one of the following is a lighter element present in the Earth's core?
n242801ab685.x: The core is mainly iron and nickel (NIFE), with lighter elements such as silicon, sulphur and oxygen. Aluminium, sodium and potassium are crustal elements and are not named as core constituents.
n242801ab685.tq: Core = Ni + Fe, plus silicon (and S, O).
xs: **Silicon** is a lighter element in the core — option **(2)** (APPSC G2 **2017** answer).
Other lighter core elements: **sulphur** and **oxygen**.
Main core elements: **iron and nickel (NIFE)**.
xa: "**Nickel and Ferrum**" keyed as the core's main elements (BPSC **2022**).
**Aluminium** is the crust's most abundant **metal**.
NIFE density **~11**.

n0cbae9be516.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the general variation of temperature, pressure and density inside the Earth?
o: Temperature increases, but pressure and density decrease with depth.
Temperature, pressure and density generally increase with depth.
n0cbae9be516.x: Temperature, pressure and density all generally rise with increasing depth inside the Earth.
n0cbae9be516.tq: Identify the common direction of the three internal gradients.
xs: **Temperature, pressure and density all rise with depth** — option **(2)**.
Pressure rises with the **weight of overlying rock**.
Density goes **2.8-3.0 (crust) → 4.6 (mantle) → 11-13.6 (core)**.
xa: Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust; the rate slows deeper.
Pressure keeps the **inner core solid**.
India's geothermal wells must reach **2-5 km**.

n6bf873e70ca.s: In the upper crust, the geothermal gradient is approximately:
n6bf873e70ca.x: Temperature rises by approximately 1°C for every 32 m of depth in the upper crust, although the rate slows at greater depths.
n6bf873e70ca.tq: Pay attention to the place value in the depth-temperature relationship.
xs: In the upper crust temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** — option **(1)**.
The rate **slows deeper**.
xa: **Temperature, pressure and density** all rise with depth.
Highest geothermal potential: **Puga Valley** (**Ladakh**).
Other sites: **Manikaran** (HP), **Tattapani** (Chhattisgarh), **Cambay** (Gujarat), **Bakreshwar** (WB).

n1314fe6aabb.s: Why does the inner core remain solid despite the very high temperature prevailing there?
o: Its temperature is lower than that of the crust.
The pressure exerted by the overlying rocks is immense.
It is located outside the mantle.
n1314fe6aabb.x: The immense pressure caused by the weight of overlying material keeps the inner core solid despite its extreme temperature.
n1314fe6aabb.tq: Link the physical condition to the controlling factor rather than to temperature alone.
xs: The **immense pressure** of overlying rock keeps the inner core solid — option **(2)**.
Pressure rises with the **weight of overlying rock**.
The inner core is not cooler than the crust — temperature **rises with depth**.
xa: ⚠ Outer core **liquid**, inner core **solid** (pressure).
Core main elements: **iron and nickel** — so option (4) is wrong.

n3f14a916162.s: The magnetic field generated by Earth's liquid outer core is important for life mainly because it:
o: Shields life from solar wind and cosmic radiation
n3f14a916162.x: The magnetic field generated by the liquid outer core helps shield life from the solar wind and cosmic radiation.
xa: The magnetic axis is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
Magnetic **reversals** can last up to **~70,000 years**.
**Swarm (ESA)**: outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from sluggish **westward** to strong **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.

ngeneral-geography-4-12.s: The Earth's magnetic field is generated by convection of conducting material in the:
ngeneral-geography-4-12.x: Convection in the liquid outer core generates the field, and changes in that flow are linked to field reversals.
n: Movement and convection of conducting material in the liquid outer core produce the geodynamo. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
The geodynamo generates Earth’s magnetic field. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Magnetic-field reversals are linked to changes in molten-core movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: The **magnetic axis** is inclined **~11.5°** to the geographic axis.
**Swarm (ESA):** outer-core flow under the Pacific switched from **westward** to **eastward**, weakening around **2020**.
Magnetic reversals have lasted up to ~**70,000 years**.

ngeneral-geography-4-36.s: The average density of the Earth is approximately:
ngeneral-geography-4-36.x: Earth averages about 5.5 g/cm³, the densest planet, with density increasing inward.
n: Earth’s average density is approximately 5.5 g/cm³. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth is the densest planet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Earth’s density generally increases inward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Heavier materials are concentrated in Earth’s core. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Density gradient: **2.8–3.0** (crust) → **4.6** (mantle) → **11–13.6** (core).
**Temperature, pressure and density** all **rise with depth**.
Temperature rises ~**1°C per 32 m** in the upper crust.

n6813cce5366.s: Diamonds reach the Earth's crust from the mantle mainly through:
n6813cce5366.x: Diamonds formed in the mantle are transported upward to the crust through kimberlite pipes.
n6813cce5366.tq: Match the resource with its geological transport pathway.
xs: Diamonds reach the crust through **kimberlite pipes** — option **(1)**.
They **form in the mantle**.
xa: **Madhya Pradesh** has **~90%** of India's reserves.
Mantle: Moho to **2,900 km**, silicates rich in **iron and magnesium**.
Mantle: **83%** of volume.

n1796b48f98b.s: Quartz, a major component of granite and sandstone, is chemically:
n1796b48f98b.x: Quartz is silicon dioxide (SiO2), hard and resistant to weathering, and a major component of granite and sandstone.
xa: Quartz is a **tectosilicate** (framework), like **albite** and **orthoclase**.
Quartz is the **most stable** mineral of Bowen's series; **olivine** forms first.

nfd23d6b10ad.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of sedimentary rocks?
nfd23d6b10ad.x: Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate are sedimentary rocks. The other groups contain igneous or metamorphic rocks.
nfd23d6b10ad.tq: Classify every option by identifying the rock type of each member.
xs: **Sandstone, limestone, shale and conglomerate** are all sedimentary — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) — **granite, basalt, gabbro, dolerite** — are all **igneous**.
Option (3) — **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss** — are all **metamorphic**.
Option (4) mixes igneous (granite, basalt), sedimentary (sandstone) and metamorphic (marble).
xa: Other sedimentary rocks: **coal** and **chalk**; **coal** is sedimentary (organic).
Igneous also includes **pegmatite**; metamorphic also includes **schist**.

n2f911f7ace2.s: Which one of the following is the odd one out?
n2f911f7ace2.x: Marble, slate and quartzite are metamorphic rocks, whereas limestone is a sedimentary rock and a parent rock of marble.
n2f911f7ace2.tq: Identify the common rock class and then locate the parent or non-metamorphic member.
xs: **Limestone** is the odd one out: it is **sedimentary** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Quartzite, marble and slate** are **metamorphic**.
Limestone is the **parent** of **marble**; shale → **slate**; sandstone → **quartzite**.
xa: ⚠ Odd-one-out trap: metamorphic rocks have non-metamorphic parents (**limestone, shale, sandstone, granite**).
**Granite → gneiss**; **coal → graphite** (via anthracite).

nea35322a33a.s: Sedimentary rocks are called ‘stratified rocks’ because they are generally formed as:
o: Successive layers of deposited, compacted and cemented sediments
Single layers of volcanic ash only
Metamorphosed rocks melted beneath the crust
nea35322a33a.x: Sediments are transported, deposited, compacted and cemented into successive layers called strata.
nea35322a33a.tq: Connect the descriptive term with its formation process.
xs: Sedimentary rocks form as **successive layers** of **deposited, compacted and cemented** sediments — option **(1)** is correct.
These layers are called **strata**, hence **"stratified rocks"**.
Unlayered crystallised magma (option 4) describes **igneous** rock.
xa: The hardening of sediments is called **lithification**.
Sedimentary rocks **may contain fossils** and host **coal, petroleum, natural gas**.

na4bdb041ba0.s: Which of the following is NOT a typical metamorphic mineral?
na4bdb041ba0.x: Garnet, kyanite and sillimanite are typical metamorphic minerals. Halite is associated with chemically formed sedimentary deposits.
na4bdb041ba0.tq: Find the odd mineral from a nearby sedimentary category.
xs: **Halite** is NOT a metamorphic mineral — option **(2)** is correct.
Halite is a **chemically formed sedimentary** deposit, like **rock salt** and **gypsum**.
**Garnet, kyanite, sillimanite** (and **staurolite**) are typical metamorphic minerals.
xa: Metamorphic rocks: **marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss, schist**.
Types of metamorphism: **thermal/contact** and **regional/dynamic**.

n0c1dcd3d30b.s: The important agents of metamorphism are:
n0c1dcd3d30b.x: Heat and pressure transform igneous and sedimentary rocks; complete melting is not required and would lead to magma.
xa: **Melting** in the rock cycle produces **magma**, which forms **igneous** rock.
Examples: **limestone → marble**, **sandstone → quartzite**, **granite → gneiss**.

ngeneral-geography-4-41.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about rocks?
o: Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma or lava
Granite is extrusive igneous and basalt is intrusive igneous
Metamorphic rocks are existing rocks altered by heat or pressure
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition
ngeneral-geography-4-41.x: It is the reverse: granite is intrusive igneous and basalt is extrusive igneous.
n: Igneous rocks form through cooling or solidification of magma or lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Sedimentary rocks form through surface deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Metamorphic rocks form when existing rock is altered by heat or pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Granite is an intrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Basalt is an extrusive igneous rock. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: Igneous rocks are "**primary**" rocks (APPSC **2019**) and hold **no fossils**.
**Sedimentary** examples: sandstone, limestone, shale, **coal**; **metamorphic**: marble, slate, quartzite, gneiss.
⚠ **Felsic** (granite) = silica-rich; **mafic** (gabbro) = rich in **iron, magnesium, calcium** (APPSC **2024** trap).
**Deccan Trap** basalt (~**65 million years**) gives **black cotton soil**.

n1872c002539.s: Which of the following is a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock?
n1872c002539.x: Intrusive rocks cool slowly at depth, forming coarse grains, as in granite and gabbro.
xa: **Extrusive (volcanic)** lava cools fast at the surface → **fine-grained**: **basalt, rhyolite, andesite**.
APPSC G2 **2024**: **granite = intrusive igneous**.
**Hypabyssal** rocks occur in **dykes and sills** — e.g. **dolerite**.

n47d893cb606.s: Which of the following is a felsic extrusive igneous rock?
n47d893cb606.x: Rhyolite is felsic extrusive; granite is felsic intrusive, diorite intermediate intrusive and basalt mafic extrusive.
xa: **Gabbro** is the **mafic intrusive** counterpart of basalt.
**Andesite** is another extrusive (volcanic) rock.
Volcanic rocks (**andesite, dacite, rhyolite, basalt**) need more energy to fracture than many sedimentary rocks.

n2540239dc98.s: Lithology primarily refers to the study of which of the following characteristics of a rock unit?
o: Its physical character, including texture, grain size and composition
Its magnetic field and seismic waves
n2540239dc98.x: Lithology describes the physical character of a rock unit, particularly its texture, grain size and composition.
n2540239dc98.tq: Test the precise meaning of a look-alike technical term rather than its broader subject area.
xs: **Lithology** = a rock unit's **physical character** — **texture, grain size, composition** — option **(3)** is correct.
It is not limited to **age** or **fossils**.
xa: **Petrology** is the study of rocks; **uranium dating** fixes the age of very old materials.
**Geological Survey of India**: set up **1851**, under the **Ministry of Mines**.

n4067c6229f5.x: Limestone becomes marble; shale becomes slate, sandstone quartzite and coal graphite.
xa: **Granite → Gneiss** is the fourth classic pair.
Metamorphism = recrystallisation under **heat and pressure**, without melting.

n7a80b5a264a.s: In the rock cycle, deposited sediments become sedimentary rock through:
n7a80b5a264a.x: After weathering, erosion and deposition, lithification forms sedimentary rocks; heat and pressure then form metamorphic rocks and melting forms magma.
xa: Full cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.
**Key rule:** any rock type can turn into any other.
Sedimentary rock forms through **burial, compaction, cementation**.

n4cea4234ca4.s: In the rock cycle, exposed metamorphic rocks can weather and become:
n4cea4234ca4.x: Exposed metamorphic rocks can weather into sediment; any rock type can be transformed into another.
xa: Mantle link: rock material comes up in **eruptions**; **subducted crust** melts back into the mantle.
Cycle: **Magma → igneous → sedimentary → metamorphic → magma**.

n16cfcbad369.s: Carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater contributes to weathering by forming:
n16cfcbad369.x: Carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which helps weather rocks.
n16cfcbad369.tq: Test the chemical agent involved in carbon cycling and weathering.
xs: CO2 in rain forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock — option **(1)** is correct.
The carbon ends up stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
xa: **Enhanced rock weathering**: crushed fast-weathering **basalt** on farmland locks up CO2 as **bicarbonate**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

ne0b2e7b2b85.s: Enhanced rock weathering, which locks up carbon dioxide as bicarbonate, involves spreading which crushed rock on farmland?
ne0b2e7b2b85.x: Enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed fast-weathering basalt on farmland, where weathering locks carbon dioxide as bicarbonate.
xa: Rain CO2 forms **carbonic acid**, which weathers rock; carbon is stored as **bicarbonate/limestone**.
Glacier-crushed **pyrite** in the upper **Indus** basin releases CO2 about **three times** faster than silicate weathering removes it.

n8dff58ebe2f.s: Which element constitutes the highest percentage by weight of the Earth's crust?
n8dff58ebe2f.x: Oxygen is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust, constituting approximately 46.6% by weight.
n8dff58ebe2f.tq: Use the direct-ranking approach for numerical abundance questions.
xs: **Oxygen** is the most abundant element in the Earth's crust at **46.6%** by weight — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Silicon** ranks second (**27.7%**), **Aluminium** third (**8.1%**) and **Iron** fourth (**5.0%**).
xa: **Aluminium** is the **most abundant metal** of the crust; **iron** is the **second-most abundant metal**.
⚠ For the **whole Earth (by mass)**, **iron (32.1%)** leads, ahead of oxygen (**30.1%**).
The "big eight" end with **Magnesium (1.5%)**, the least of them.

nf4d735d62e9.s: The second-most abundant element in the Earth's crust by weight is:
nf4d735d62e9.x: Silicon ranks second at about 27.7%; iron is the second-most abundant metal (~5.0%).
xa: Ranks 5–7: **Calcium 3.6**, **Sodium 2.8**, **Potassium 2.6**.
⚠ For the whole Earth, **magnesium (13.9%)** ranks fourth after iron, oxygen and silicon.

n1bd599b0885.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the order of major elements in the Earth as a whole by mass, from highest to lower proportion?
n1bd599b0885.x: For the Earth as a whole, the order is iron at 32.1%, oxygen at 30.1%, silicon at 15.1% and magnesium at 13.9%.
n1bd599b0885.tq: Separate whole-Earth composition from crustal composition and compare the first four positions.
xs: For the whole Earth by mass the order is **Iron, Oxygen, Silicon, Magnesium** — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (1) is the trap: oxygen leads only in the **crust** (**46.6%**), not in the whole Earth.
xa: After magnesium come **S, Ni, Ca, Al**.
The core is **NIFE** (nickel + iron), density ~**11** — which is why iron dominates the whole Earth.

nf843e3af39c.s: In Suess's classification, the granitic continental layer of silicon and aluminium is called:
nf843e3af39c.x: SIAL (silicon-aluminium) is granitic and continental; SIMA is basaltic and NIFE the nickel-iron core.
xa: These are **Suess's chemical layers** of the Earth.
The crust's most abundant element is **oxygen (46.6%)**; the whole Earth's is **iron (32.1%)**.

nbcecc8075be.s: Feldspar makes up approximately what proportion of the Earth's crust?
nbcecc8075be.x: Feldspar makes up approximately half of the Earth's crust; 'one-fourth' is incorrect.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024** used this exact trap: "one-fourth" is wrong — answer was **statement I only**.
Feldspars (**albite, orthoclase**) are **tectosilicates** (framework silicates).
**Quartz** (**SiO2**) is hard, resists weathering and forms a major part of **granite and sandstone**.

n467d5982bdd.s: Muscovite belongs to which silicate class?
n467d5982bdd.x: Muscovite is a phyllosilicate; albite is a tectosilicate, hornblende a double-chain and augite a single-chain inosilicate.
xa: **Olivine** is a **nesosilicate** (isolated tetrahedra).
Tectosilicates (framework) include **albite, orthoclase** and **quartz**.
⚠ "Mica = **phyllosilicate**" was asked in **APPSC 2024**.

nc8be25cdc8d.s: In Bowen's reaction series, which mineral crystallises last from cooling magma and is regarded as the most stable among the listed minerals?
nc8be25cdc8d.x: Quartz crystallises last in the stated sequence and is the most stable mineral among those listed in Bowen's reaction series.
nc8be25cdc8d.tq: Use the endpoint of the crystallisation sequence rather than its first high-temperature mineral.
xs: **Quartz** crystallises **last** in Bowen's reaction series and is the **most stable** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Olivine** crystallises **first**; **amphibole** comes in the middle of the discontinuous branch.
**Muscovite** comes just before quartz (K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz).
xa: **Bowen's reaction series** = the order in which minerals **crystallise from cooling magma** (APPSC **2024** answer).
Discontinuous branch: **olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite**.
Continuous branch: **Ca-plagioclase → Na-plagioclase**.
**Mafic** minerals form first, at the **highest temperature**.

n5b564545540.s: In the discontinuous branch of Bowen's reaction series, the first mineral to crystallise is:
n5b564545540.x: The discontinuous branch runs olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite; mafic minerals form first at the highest temperature.
xa: The series ends with **K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz**; **quartz is last** and most stable.
Bowen's series shows the order of **crystallisation from cooling magma** (APPSC **2024**).

n1d5595e02f3.s: Which mineral has a Mohs hardness of 7?
n1d5595e02f3.x: Quartz has a Mohs hardness of 7. Orthoclase is 6, topaz is 8 and apatite is 5.
n1d5595e02f3.tq: Use the central value in the hardness scale and distinguish neighbouring entries.
xs: **Quartz** has a Mohs hardness of **7** — option **(4)** is correct.
On the scale, **apatite** is 5, **orthoclase** 6 and **topaz** 8.
xa: The scale runs **1–10**: from **talc** (1) to **diamond (10)**; **corundum** sits just below diamond.
Quartz (**SiO2**) forms a major part of **granite and sandstone** and crystallises **last** in Bowen's series.

n7c70c7f44f7.s: The geological time scale was developed in 1760 by:
n7c70c7f44f7.x: Arduino developed it in 1760; the Standard scale was set in Italy in 1881 and the Indian scale was advocated by T.H. Holland.
xa: **J.D. Dana** coined **"Archaean"** in **1872** (some notes print 1782).
**GSI** was set up in **1851** under the **Ministry of Mines**.

n574542fa5e2.s: The principal repositories of fossils are:
