n574542fa5e2.x: Sedimentary rocks such as sandstone preserve fossils and hold coal, petroleum and natural gas.
xa: **Archaean** rocks are a **"no fossils"** zone, formed before life.
**Dravidian (Palaeozoic)** rocks are **fossil-rich**, with plenty of marine fossils.

n9c5a11e29d2.s: Which group of Indian rocks contains abundant marine fossils?
n9c5a11e29d2.x: Dravidian (Palaeozoic) rocks have abundant marine fossils, while Archaean rocks formed before life and are generally fossil-free.
xa: Dravidian age: **600–300 million years**; extra-peninsular.
**Everest** is made of **Upper Carboniferous limestone**; **coal formation** began in the Dravidian age.
Archaean = older than **2,500 million years**: granites, gneisses, schists.

nb3106835f96.s: Approximately what proportion of India’s coal is held by the Gondwana rocks?
nb3106835f96.x: Gondwana rocks hold nearly 98 percent of India’s coal.
nb3106835f96.tq: Test the distinctive percentage directly using close numerical distractors.
xs: **Gondwana** rocks hold **nearly 98%** of India's coal — option **(4)** is correct.
Gondwana coal lies in the **Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari** valleys.
xa: Gondwana = **freshwater sediments**, Upper Carboniferous–Jurassic.
⚠ **Dharwar** = iron ore, gold; **Deccan Trap** = regur; **Tertiary** = petroleum, **lignite (Neyveli)**.
In AP, Gondwana coal occurs in **East Godavari** and **ASR**.

nae297a15d87.s: Compared with Carboniferous coal, Gondwana coal is:
nae297a15d87.x: Gondwana coal is younger and has lower carbon content than Carboniferous coal, and is not confined to the Himalayas.
xa: Gondwana holds nearly **98%** of India's coal.
Younger coal and **lignite (Neyveli)** belong to the **Tertiary** system.

n161c5480d47.s: The Dharwar system is regarded as economically the most important mainly because it contains significant deposits of:
o: Coal, chalk and coral limestone only
Petroleum, natural gas and gypsum only
Iron ore, manganese, copper, lead and gold
n161c5480d47.x: The Dharwar system contains high-grade iron ore, manganese, copper, lead and gold and is economically the most important system.
n161c5480d47.tq: Use the economic-resource clue to identify the geological system.
xs: **Dharwar** rocks hold **high-grade iron ore, manganese, copper, lead, gold** — economically the most important — option **(4)** is correct.
**Barytes, asbestos, diamonds** = **Cuddapah**; **coal, chalk** = organic sediments; **petroleum** = **Tertiary**.
xa: Dharwar = **Archaean**; the **oldest metamorphosed sediments**; schists and gneisses.
In AP, **Ramagiri** gold belt (**Sri Sathya Sai**) is Dharwar.
⚠ **Dharwar** = iron ore, gold; **Gondwana** = **98%** coal.

n224f8d683ff.s: Which set contains only important coal-bearing valleys associated with the Gondwana system?
n224f8d683ff.x: Important Gondwana coal deposits occur in the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys.
n224f8d683ff.tq: Identify the resource-bearing valley group rather than an individual river.
xs: Gondwana coal lies in the **Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari** valleys — option **(1)** is correct.
The notes link none of the other river sets to Gondwana coal.
xa: These basins hold nearly **98%** of India's coal.
In AP, Gondwana coal occurs in **East Godavari** and **ASR**.
Younger coal and **lignite (Neyveli)** are **Tertiary**.

n0d4400ad046.s: The Deccan Trap is associated with which of the following combinations?
o: End-Cretaceous basalt from fissure eruptions and black cotton soil
Upper Carboniferous limestone and marine fossils
n0d4400ad046.x: The Deccan Trap formed from basaltic fissure eruptions near the end of the Cretaceous and is associated with black cotton or regur soil.
n0d4400ad046.tq: Match formation process, rock type and soil association.
xs: The **Deccan Trap** = **end-Cretaceous basalt** from **fissure eruptions**, giving **black cotton (regur) soil** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Upper Carboniferous limestone** = **Dravidian** (Everest); **Purana shale and diamonds** = Cuddapah/Vindhyan; **petroleum** = **Tertiary**.
xa: Deccan Trap age: ~**65 million years**.
AP's Deccan Trap patches: **Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur, East Godavari**.

ncc82a37f0c3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Tertiary rock system of India?
o: It spans roughly the Eocene to Pliocene
The Neyveli lignite belongs to the Gondwana system
The Himalayas were born during the Tertiary period
The petroleum of Assam and Gujarat is associated with it
ncc82a37f0c3.x: Neyveli lignite is Tertiary, not Gondwana; the other statements about the Tertiary system are correct.
xa: **Gondwana** holds the bulk — nearly **98%** — of India's coal.
Gondwana coal is **younger** and **lower in carbon** than Carboniferous coal.

nbf0f8c7255f.s: Which of the following Indian rock systems is the youngest?
nbf0f8c7255f.x: The broad order from older to younger is Archaean, Dharwar, Cuddapah, Gondwana, Deccan Trap and Tertiary.
xa: Dharwar = **Archaean**, the **oldest metamorphosed sediments**.
**Dravidian (Palaeozoic, 600–300 million years)** comes between the Purana and Gondwana.

nd7da1343e3b.s: The Cuddapah and Vindhyan systems belong to the:
nd7da1343e3b.x: Cuddapah and Vindhyan are Purana (Proterozoic) systems with a broadly similar age span; Cuddapah is not Archaean.
xa: Some notes label the Archaean "Purana"; **Purana = Cuddapah + Vindhyan**.
Cuddapah holds **barytes, asbestos, limestone, diamonds**; Vindhyan **building stone, limestone, diamonds**.

n9478ed2bf83.s: The Cuddapah system of rocks is mainly composed of which one of the following?
n9478ed2bf83.x: The Cuddapah system (Purana, ~1,400-600 million years) is sedimentary - shale, slate, quartzite and limestone; shales and slates are clay rocks, so the key was 'clay'. Basalt is the Deccan Trap rock, granite is typical of the Archaean, and coal belongs to the Gondwana system.
n9478ed2bf83.tq: Cuddapah = sedimentary Purana; shale and slate = clay rocks.
xs: APPSC **2021** keyed the Cuddapah system's composition as **"clay"** (shales and slates) — option **(2)** is correct.
Cuddapah is **sedimentary**: **shale, slate, quartzite, limestone**; **shales and slates are clay rocks**.
**Basalt** = **Deccan Trap**; **granite** = **Archaean**; **coal** = **Gondwana**.
xa: Cuddapah = **Purana (Proterozoic)**, ~**1,400–600 million years**.
**Shale / clay** metamorphoses into **slate**.
n9478ed2bf83.fixed: meta stem ('In APPSC 2021 ... keyed'); exam would ask directly

n81ffbdf7a76.s: Which one of the following is NOT associated with the Cuddapah basin?
n81ffbdf7a76.x: The Cuddapah basin contains barytes, limestone, asbestos, copper, nickel and cobalt. Coal is associated with the Gondwana formation.
n81ffbdf7a76.tq: Find the resource belonging to another formation rather than the basin named in the question.
xs: **Coal** is NOT a Cuddapah basin resource — option **(4)** is correct; coal is **Gondwana** (East Godavari, ASR).
The Cuddapah basin has **barytes (Mangampeta)**, **limestone**, asbestos, copper, nickel, **cobalt**.
xa: ⚠ **Mangampeta** = barytes (Cuddapah basin).
Kadapa–Kurnool limestone makes **Rayalaseema** a **cement hub**.

n4ad737a4597.s: The Ramagiri gold belt of Andhra Pradesh is associated with which formation?
n4ad737a4597.x: The Dharwar formation (schists and gneisses) occurs in Anantapuramu, Chittoor and YSR Kadapa and includes the Ramagiri gold belt.
xa: Gold mining is **reviving at Ramagiri** (Dharwar **greenstone belt**) (Jul **2026**).
⚠ **Mangampeta** = barytes; **Araku** = bauxite; **Ramagiri** = gold.

ndcc79aa1ea5.s: The Kurnool group is distinguished from the Cuddapah basin because it is associated with:
o: Cement-grade limestone and no metallic minerals
Gold and manganese in a greenstone belt
Bauxite and graphite in the Eastern Ghats
ndcc79aa1ea5.x: The Kurnool group contains cement-grade limestone, has no metallic minerals, and has petroleum potential.
ndcc79aa1ea5.tq: Compare neighbouring geological units by their distinctive resource combinations.
xs: The **Kurnool group** has **cement-grade limestone** and **no metallic minerals** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Coal** = **Gondwana**; **gold/manganese greenstone belt** = **Dharwar**; **bauxite, graphite** = **Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt**.
xa: Kurnool group: **Kurnool, Nandyal**; rocks **limestone, sandstone, shale**; also **petroleum potential**.
Kadapa–Kurnool limestone makes **Rayalaseema** a **cement hub**.

n04c7767a1c4.s: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt in Andhra Pradesh is associated with which one of the following resource combinations?
o: Copper, gold and cement-grade limestone only
n04c7767a1c4.x: The Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt contains bauxite, including at Araku, along with manganese and graphite.
n04c7767a1c4.tq: Use a resource-combination question to separate the Eastern Ghats from the Cuddapah and KG basins.
xs: The **Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt** holds **bauxite, manganese, graphite** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Cement-grade limestone** = **Kurnool group**; **oil and gas** = **KG basin**; **barytes, asbestos, cobalt** = **Cuddapah basin**.
xa: Rocks: **khondalite, charnockite**, quartzite, gneiss; districts **Srikakulam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, ASR**.
⚠ **Araku** = bauxite.
Mining must respect **tribal areas and biodiversity**.

n38303caad74.s: The khondalites and charnockites of Andhra Pradesh are associated with the:
n38303caad74.x: They are Archaean rocks, over 2.5 billion years old, associated with the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt.
xa: Khondalite is **not Vindhyan** (PYQ).
The Eastern Ghats belt holds **bauxite (Araku), manganese, graphite**.

neb944bcb0a0.s: Gold mining is reviving in Andhra Pradesh's Dharwar greenstone belt at:
neb944bcb0a0.x: Gold mining is reviving at Ramagiri; Kadapa-Kurnool limestone makes Rayalaseema a cement hub.
xa: The **Kurnool group** has **cement-grade limestone**, no metallic minerals.
Eastern Ghats hold **bauxite (Araku)**, manganese, graphite.

n4aa79e42deb.s: With respect to porosity and permeability, clay is:
n4aa79e42deb.x: Clay has pore spaces, but its very fine particles prevent easy passage of water, so it is porous but impermeable.
xa: **Chalk and sandstone** are both porous and permeable.
**Granite** is neither porous nor permeable.
**Shale / clay** metamorphoses into **slate**.

o: The Geological Survey of India in 1851
n23d37e41b1b.x: J.D. Dana coined the term ‘Archaean’ in 1872.
n23d37e41b1b.tq: Apply person-year matching and avoid confusing the term’s origin with the geological survey’s establishment.
xs: **J.D. Dana** coined **"Archaean"** in **1872** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Giovanni Arduino (1760)** developed the geological time scale; **Holland** advocated the Indian time scale; **GSI** was set up in **1851**.
xa: ⚠ Some notes print the year as **1782** — the correct year is **1872**.
**Archaean** rocks: older than **2,500 million years**; granites, gneisses, schists; **no fossils**.
The **Standard** time scale was set in **Italy (1881)**.

n5a89cad3577.s: The Geological Survey of India, under the Ministry of Mines, was set up in:
n5a89cad3577.x: The GSI was set up in 1851 under the Ministry of Mines.
xa: **Giovanni Arduino** developed the geological time scale; **Sir T.H. Holland** advocated the Indian time scale.
**Uranium dating** fixes the age of very old materials.

n9f753f7ab89.s: Who proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912?
n9f753f7ab89.x: Alfred Wegener proposed the theory of continental drift in 1912.
xs: **Alfred Wegener** proposed **continental drift** in **1912** — option **(1)** is correct (asked in APPSC **2018**).
**Arthur Holmes** gave the **convection current theory** (**1930s**); **Harry Hess** gave **sea-floor spreading** (**1961**).
xa: Wegener's driving forces: **pole-fleeing force** (Earth's rotation) and **tidal force** (Sun and Moon).
These forces were judged **too weak**, so the theory was not accepted.
⚠ Sequence: **1912** Wegener → **1930s** Holmes → **1961** Hess → **1967** plate tectonics.

o: The gravity of the Sun and the Moon
na3ba43088b0.x: The pole-fleeing force was linked to Earth's rotation and the tidal force to the Sun and Moon; both were too weak, so the theory was not accepted.
xa: **Arthur Holmes** (**1930s**) gave drift the driving force Wegener lacked — **convection currents**.
Wegener proposed continental drift in **1912**.

ndc415420f5e.s: The occurrence of Gondwana-type tillites in India and their counterparts in southern continents supports continental drift because tillites indicate:
ndc415420f5e.x: Tillites are glacial deposits. Their distribution across India and other southern continents indicates that these areas were formerly connected and experienced common glacial conditions.
ndc415420f5e.tq: Identify the process represented by a geological deposit.
xs: **Tillites** are **glacial deposits**, so they indicate **ancient glacial conditions** — option **(1)** is correct.
India's **Gondwana-type tillites** have counterparts in the **other southern continents**, showing they were once joined.
xa: Other evidences: **jig-saw fit**, **same-age rocks**, **placer deposits**, **fossils** (Mesosaurus, Glossopteris).
India belonged to **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia.

nee3738aa74a.s: Who proposed the convection current theory as an explanation for the movement of crustal plates?
nee3738aa74a.x: Arthur Holmes proposed the convection current theory in the 1930s.
nee3738aa74a.tq: Distinguish the proponent of the driving mechanism from proponents of continental drift and sea-floor spreading.
xs: **Arthur Holmes** proposed the **convection current theory** (**1930s**) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** gave continental drift (**1912**); **Harry Hess** sea-floor spreading (**1961**); **Vine** (with Matthews) explained magnetic stripes (**1963**).
xa: **Radioactive decay heat** in the mantle drives the convection currents.
Plate tectonics' driving force is **mantle convection** (Arthur Holmes).

n0ccf32808d3.s: In Holmes's convection-current theory, mantle convection is driven by heat from:
n0ccf32808d3.x: Radioactive heat drives convection; rising limbs split crust at ridges and sinking limbs drag plates at trenches.
xa: Holmes gave drift the **driving force Wegener lacked**.
**Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**; crust is destroyed at **trenches**.

n658079463d6.s: Who proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s?
n658079463d6.x: Harry Hess proposed the sea-floor spreading hypothesis in the early 1960s, including the creation of new crust at mid-ocean ridges and its destruction at trenches.
n658079463d6.tq: Use direct person–theory identification and distinguish the proponent from related plate-tectonic thinkers.
xs: **Harry Hess** proposed **sea-floor spreading** in **1961** (early 1960s) — option **(4)** is correct.
**Wegener** = continental drift (**1912**); **Arthur Holmes** = convection currents (**1930s**).
xa: Magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges**, new crust spreads sideways and is destroyed at **trenches**.
**Vine and Matthews (1963)** explained the **symmetrical magnetic bands** supporting it.

n8cc53f43595.s: Normal and reversed magnetic polarity bands on either side of a mid-ocean ridge occur:
n8cc53f43595.x: Ridge rocks preserve the field of their time, giving alternating normal and reversed bands symmetrically on both sides.
xa: The bands were explained by **Vine and Matthews, 1963**.
**Brunhes–Matuyama** reversal: **780,000** years ago.

n66336ba4b29.s: The theory of plate tectonics was put together in 1967 by McKenzie and Parker and independently by:
n66336ba4b29.x: McKenzie and Parker developed the theory in 1967, and Morgan proposed it independently.
n66336ba4b29.tq: Pair the principal proponents with the correct year and contribution.
xs: Plate tectonics was put together in **1967** by **McKenzie and Parker**, and independently by **Morgan** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Wegener** = drift (**1912**); **Holmes** = convection (**1930s**); **Bullard** = jig-saw computer fit (**1964**).
xa: The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates** floating on the semi-fluid **asthenosphere**.
Driving force: **mantle convection**.

n50ac5618d4b.s: The direct observation of sea-floor spreading in bursts was associated with which conclusion?
o: Sea-floor spreading occurs only at continental interiors.
Sea-floor spreading may take place in episodic bursts.
Sea-floor spreading always occurs at a constant rate.
Sea-floor spreading is unrelated to lava outpouring.
n50ac5618d4b.x: The observed rapid episode of sinking, spreading and lava emplacement suggested that sea-floor spreading can occur in bursts rather than at a uniform rate.
n50ac5618d4b.tq: Infer the process characteristic from the observed event rather than from a general definition.
xs: The first direct in-situ observation showed **sea-floor spreading happens in bursts** — option **(2)** is correct.
The seafloor sank **4 m**, spread over **1 m**, with **160 million cubic metres** of lava in **16 days**.
xa: **Harry Hess (1961)**: magma rises at **mid-oceanic ridges** and new crust spreads sideways.
Crust age, density and thickness **increase with distance from the ridge** (APPSC **2019**).

n5d00ac4f386.s: The mega-ocean that surrounded Pangaea was:
n5d00ac4f386.x: Panthalassa surrounded Pangaea; the Tethys Sea lay between northern Laurasia and southern Gondwanaland.
xa: Laurasia: **North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia (minus India)**.
Gondwanaland: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar, Arabia**.

n722ed59ae03.s: Which one of the following groups consists entirely of landmasses assigned to Gondwanaland?
o: South America, Africa, India, Australia and Antarctica
North America, Greenland, Europe and Asia
Europe, India, North America and Greenland
Asia, Africa, Europe and South America
n722ed59ae03.x: Gondwanaland included South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica, Madagascar and Arabia.
n722ed59ae03.tq: Classify a group by checking every member against the southern supercontinent.
xs: **South America, Africa, India, Australia, Antarctica** were all part of **Gondwanaland** — option **(1)** is correct.
**North America, Greenland, Europe, Asia** formed **Laurasia** (options 2–4 mix in Laurasian lands).
xa: Gondwanaland also included **Madagascar** and **Arabia**.
⚠ India = **Gondwanaland**, not Laurasia (APPSC **2018**: India is part of **Gondwana Land**).

n8a86a5461cf.s: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is bounded by which of the following fault systems?
o: Two thrust faults on both sides
A normal fault in the north and the Himalayan Frontal Fault in the south
The Himalayan Frontal Fault in the north and a normal fault in the south
Two strike-slip faults in the north and south
n8a86a5461cf.x: The Indo-Gangetic Plain is bounded by the Himalayan Frontal Fault to the north and a normal fault to the south.
n8a86a5461cf.tq: Test the location and type of the bounding structures together.
xs: The **Indo-Gangetic plain** is bounded by the **Himalayan Frontal Fault** (north) and a **normal fault** (south) — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (2) reverses the two.
xa: The **HFF** is one of the Himalayan **thrusts**, with **MCT** and **MBT**.
Plate collision explains the **Indo-Gangetic foreland basin**.

n2d309043495.s: The ancient rock belts of approximately 2,000 million years of age on the Brazil coast correspond to belts found in:
n2d309043495.x: Ancient rock belts on the Brazil coast match rock belts of the same age in Western Africa.
n2d309043495.tq: Connect the numerical age with the correct matching region.
xs: The **2,000-million-year** rock belts of the **Brazil coast** match those of **Western Africa** — option **(1)** is correct.
This is the "**rocks of the same age** across oceans" evidence (UPSC **2025**).
xa: **Placer gold** of the **Ghana coast** has its source in the **Brazil plateau** (UPSC **2025**).
UPSC **2025** counted rock belts, placer gold and a third evidence as **all correct**.
**Bullard's 1964** computer fit matched South America and Africa.

n0053e404763.s: Ghana's coastal placer gold supports continental drift because the source rock for that gold is found in:
n0053e404763.x: The Ghana coast has placer gold but lacks its source rock, which lies in the Brazil plateau, suggesting the two were once joined.
xa: Asked in UPSC **2025** along with the matching **Brazil–Western Africa** rock belts.
**Mesosaurus** fossils occur in **South Africa and Brazil**.

n36d2a2398ce.s: Moving away from a mid-ocean ridge, which one of the following trends is observed in oceanic crust and its sediment cover?
o: Age increases, while density and thickness decrease.
Only sediment thickness increases; crustal age and density remain unchanged.
Age, density and thickness decrease continuously.
n36d2a2398ce.x: The age, density and thickness of oceanic crust, along with the thickness of its sediment cover, increase with distance from the ridge.
n36d2a2398ce.tq: Apply the directional trend rule by comparing conditions near the ridge with those farther away.
xs: Away from the ridge, **age, density and thickness increase** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC **2019**).
The **sediment cover** also thickens with distance from the ridge.
xa: Ocean-floor rocks are **far younger** than continental rocks; the oldest are ~**200 million years**.
New crust forms at the **ridge** and is destroyed at **trenches**.

n7db9f63638b.s: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed primarily due to
o: northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate
southward subduction of the Indian Plate beneath the Arabian Plate
transform motion along the San Andreas Fault
divergence between the Nubian and Somalian plates
n7db9f63638b.x: The Ladakh Magmatic Arc formed through northward subduction of the Neo-Tethys Plate and lies between the Indus and Shyok suture zones.
n7db9f63638b.tq: Match the named magmatic arc with its subducting plate and direction of subduction.
xs: The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** formed by **northward subduction** of the **Neo-Tethys** plate — option **(1)** is correct.
It lies between the **Indus and Shyok suture zones**.
xa: Its **130-million-year** history laid the base for the Himalayas.
Delamination beneath **Tibet** is another new finding on the Indian plate.

nad435061d01.s: The Sagaing Fault in Myanmar is described as a transform boundary between the:
nad435061d01.x: The Sagaing Fault is a conservative or transform boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates.
nad435061d01.tq: Match a named fault with the plates on either side.
xs: The **Sagaing Fault** (Myanmar) is a transform boundary between the **Indian and Eurasian** plates — option **(2)** is correct.
Transform boundaries are **conservative**: plates slide past horizontally.
xa: The other classic transform fault is the **San Andreas Fault**.
Transform-boundary earthquakes come from **sudden slip**.

n02521cb6295.s: The Red Sea and the East African Rift are associated with
o: divergence of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates
collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
horizontal sliding of the Pacific and North American plates
subduction of the Nazca Plate beneath the South American Plate
n02521cb6295.x: The Red Sea and East African Rift are divergent settings associated with the separation of the Nubian, Somalian and Arabian plates near the Afar triple junction.
n02521cb6295.tq: Link a named regional feature with the specific plates and boundary process involved.
xs: The **Red Sea / East African Rift** mark **divergence** of the **Nubian, Somalian and Arabian** plates — option **(1)** is correct.
They meet at the **Afar triple junction**.
Indian–Eurasian **collision** = Himalayas; **Nazca subduction** = Andes.
xa: The **East African Rift** is a series of mostly **freshwater** lakes, with **Lake Malawi** at its southern end.
⚠ **Lake Victoria** is **not a rift lake** — it lies between the two branches (APPSC G1 **2024**).

n4d5c5a30e0d.s: The lithospheric plates float on the:
n4d5c5a30e0d.x: The rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that float on the semi-fluid asthenosphere.
n4d5c5a30e0d.tq: Distinguish the rigid layer from the underlying semi-fluid layer.
xs: Lithospheric plates float on the **semi-fluid asthenosphere** — option **(2)** is correct.
The lithosphere is broken into **rigid plates**.
xa: Plate tectonics: **1967**, **McKenzie and Parker**, independently **Morgan**.
There are **seven major plates** (APPSC **2018**).

n4b4c0660175.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the seven major plates listed in plate tectonics?
n4b4c0660175.x: The seven listed major plates are Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian and Antarctic. Nazca is a minor plate.
n4b4c0660175.tq: Separate a minor plate from the standard list of major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate is a **minor** plate, not one of the seven major — option **(1)** is correct.
The **7 major plates**: **Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Antarctic**.
xa: Minor plates: **Cocos, Nazca, Arabian, Philippine, Caroline, Fuji**.
Nazca lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate**.

nb79870105d5.s: The Nazca Plate lies between the:
nb79870105d5.x: The Nazca Plate is located between the South American Plate and the Pacific Plate.
nb79870105d5.tq: Test a minor plate by its bordering major plates.
xs: The **Nazca** plate lies between **South America** and the **Pacific plate** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Caroline** = between the Philippine and Indian plates; **Philippine** = between the Asiatic and Pacific plates; **Owen Fracture** separates African and Indian plates.
xa: ⚠ **Cocos** = Central America; **Nazca** = South America.
In the **Andes**, the **Nazca** plate subducts under the **South American** plate.

n2693c372c70.s: Which instrument-based method is used to monitor plate movement?
n2693c372c70.x: Plate movement is monitored using GPS data.
n2693c372c70.tq: Distinguish the modern monitoring technology from unrelated instruments.
xs: Plate movement is monitored using **GPS data** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC **2021**).
Tide gauges, barometers and rain gauges measure sea level, pressure and rain — not plate motion.
xa: **GSI** runs **34 GNSS stations** tracking crustal movement and building strain models.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

ncb654e89eeb.s: The Himalayas and the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin are mainly explained by:
o: Collision of the Indian and Eurasian plates
ncb654e89eeb.x: The India-Eurasia collision explains the Himalayas, the Indo-Gangetic foreland basin and India's earthquake risk.
xa: The collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago**.
The Indian plate **closed the Tethys**; the Himalayas are **still rising**.

nb7dc0f69ae8.s: Gondwanaland is estimated to have broken up approximately:
nb7dc0f69ae8.x: Gondwanaland broke up approximately 225 million years ago.
nb7dc0f69ae8.tq: Distinguish the geological breakup date from the later Himalayan uplift date.
xs: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago** — option **(3)** is correct.
**65 million years ago** is when the **Himalayas rose**, not the break-up.
xa: After the break-up, the **Indian craton** slid towards the **Eurasian craton**.
India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.

n66901b70dc0.s: The Deccan Traps were erupted while the Indian Plate was
o: crossing near the equator and passing over the Reunion hotspot
moving southward across the Tethys Sea
colliding with the Eurasian Plate in the Himalaya
n66901b70dc0.x: The Deccan Traps erupted as the northward-moving Indian Plate crossed near the equator and passed over the Reunion hotspot.
n66901b70dc0.tq: Connect a geological event with the plate’s position and hotspot passage at that time.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** erupted as India crossed **near the equator** over the **Reunion hotspot** — option **(2)** is correct.
India was moving **northward**, not southward; collision with Eurasia came later.
xa: ⚠ **Reunion hotspot** = Deccan Traps; **Owen Fracture** = African/Indian plates.
India was **far south** of the equator before the **Cretaceous**.

ne051043abb8.s: The collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates began approximately
ne051043abb8.x: The collision began approximately 4–5 crore years ago, equivalent to about 40–50 million years ago. Some older estimates place it at about 50–55 million years ago.
ne051043abb8.tq: Convert crore-based geological time into its equivalent million-year scale without changing the order of magnitude.
xs: The India–Eurasia collision began **~4–5 crore (40–50 million) years ago** — option **(1)** is correct.
⚠ Older notes say **50–55 million** years.
xa: The Indian plate **subducted** under Eurasia and **closed the Tethys**.
India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the **Tibetan Plateau**.

n0acd9998564.s: What does delamination in southern Tibet refer to in the context of the Indian Plate?
o: The melting of all continental crust at the surface of Tibet
The spreading apart of the Tibetan Plateau along a mid-ocean ridge
The peeling off and sinking of the denser lower layer of the plate into the mantle at about 100 km depth
The horizontal sliding of the entire Indian Plate along the Himalayan Frontal Fault
n0acd9998564.x: Delamination refers to the denser lower layer of the plate peeling away and sinking into the mantle at approximately 100 kilometres depth.
n0acd9998564.tq: Test the exact meaning of a specialised tectonic term through its mechanism and depth.
xs: **Delamination** = the denser lower layer **peeling off and sinking into the mantle** at ~**100 km** — option **(3)** is correct.
It was seen with **94 seismic stations** in southern Tibet (seismic imaging, **helium isotopes**).
xa: India **underthrust** Asia **45–20 million years ago**, lifting the Tibetan Plateau.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** lies between the **Indus and Shyok** suture zones.

n06315456683.s: The Indian Plate is moving northward at about:
n06315456683.x: The Indian Plate moves north at about 5 cm a year, so the young fold Himalayas are still rising.
xa: Uplift phases: **Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene**; began **~70 million years ago**.
The **Siwaliks** are the **youngest** range.

nfceb4d08ed4.s: An up-arched fold and a down-troughed fold are respectively called:
nfceb4d08ed4.x: An anticline is an up-arched fold, while a syncline is a down-troughed fold. Horst and graben are fault blocks, not folds.
nfceb4d08ed4.tq: Discriminate between the commonly confused anticline-syncline pair by their shapes.
xs: An up-arch is an **anticline** and a down-trough a **syncline** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Horst and graben** are **fault blocks** (block mountains), not folds.
**Nappe** and **overfold** are stages of folding under rising pressure.
xa: Folds are caused by **compression**.
Sequence: symmetrical → asymmetrical → **overfold** → recumbent → **nappe**.
The **Siwaliks** have simple anticline-syncline folds of the **"Jura" type**.

nf54641e8440.s: Which one of the following is an old fold mountain range?
nf54641e8440.x: The Aravallis are old, worn-down fold mountains and are among the oldest mountain systems in India.
nf54641e8440.tq: Use an odd-age association to distinguish an old fold range from the listed young fold ranges.
xs: The **Aravallis** are **old, worn-down** fold mountains — among India's oldest — option **(2)** is correct.
**Himalayas, Alps, Andes** are **young fold** mountains (Tertiary / **Alpine orogeny**).
xa: Other old folds: **Appalachians** (North America), **Urals** (Europe–Asia divide).
The **Rockies** (North America) are young fold mountains.
AP's **Eastern Ghats** are old, eroded hills of the **Gondwana shield**, not young folds.

n81b67aca29c.s: The Himalayan MCT, MBT and HFF are examples of which one of the following?
n81b67aca29c.x: The Himalayan Main Central Thrust, Main Boundary Thrust and Himalayan Frontal Fault are examples of thrust faults.
n81b67aca29c.tq: Test the association between named regional structures and the correct fault type.
xs: The Himalayan **MCT, MBT and HFF** are **thrust faults** — option **(3)** is correct.
A thrust is a **low-angle reverse fault** caused by **compression**.
**San Andreas** and **Sagaing** are **strike-slip**; **Rio Grande** and **East African Rift** are **normal** faults.
xa: The **Indo-Gangetic plain** is bounded by the **Himalayan Frontal Fault** (north) and a **normal fault** (south).
A **nappe** is a recumbent fold broken by a **thrust**.

nb69c16b281d.s: Which of the following is an example of a block mountain in India?
nb69c16b281d.x: The Satpura is a block mountain, flanked by the rift valleys of the Narmada and Tapi.
xa: Uplifted blocks = **horsts**; sunken blocks = **grabens**.
The **Red Sea** is also a rift.

n6c1e58da559.s: The Peninsular Plateau of India was part of the African landmass until the:
n6c1e58da559.x: The Peninsular Plateau, an old Gondwana shield, was part of the African landmass until the Cretaceous.
xa: **Gondwanaland broke up ~225 million years ago**.
AP's **Eastern Ghats** are old, eroded hills of the stable **Gondwana shield**, not young fold mountains.

na6e40bdf9b1.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Himalayas?
o: Their formation began about 70 million years ago and continues at present
They were formed from sediments of the Tethys Sea
Their uplift is associated with the Eocene, Miocene and Pliocene epochs
The Siwaliks are the oldest Himalayan range
na6e40bdf9b1.x: The Siwaliks are the youngest Himalayan range, not the oldest.
xa: India moves **north at ~5 cm/year** into the Eurasian plate.
The Himalayas are a **continent–continent** convergent boundary (**Indian vs Eurasian**).

nd12a3be8176.s: Which lake lies at the southern end of the East African Rift?
nd12a3be8176.x: The East African Rift holds a series of mostly freshwater lakes with Lake Malawi at its southern end; Lake Victoria lies between the two branches and is not a rift lake.
xa: ⚠ APPSC G1 **2024** keyed statements **I, II, III** on this rift.
The **Red Sea** is also a rift; with the East African Rift it meets at the **Afar triple junction**.

nd0a125e1f56.s: In plate-tectonic terms, the Eastern Ghats are best described as:
o: Old, highly eroded, discontinuous hills of the stable Gondwana shield
Block mountains of recently uplifted nappes
Young fold mountains formed by recent continental collision
Volcanic hills formed along a rift
nd0a125e1f56.x: The Eastern Ghats are old, highly eroded and discontinuous hills of the stable Gondwana shield, not young fold mountains.
xa: The Peninsular plateau is an old **Gondwana shield**, part of the African landmass until the **Cretaceous**.
Old fold example in India: the **Aravallis**.

n95620fa7193.s: The Himalaya were formed primarily through the uplift of Tethys sediments as a result of:
o: The vertical subsidence of the Eurasian Plate during the Palaeozoic
The southward movement of the Indian Plate during the Precambrian
The volcanic eruption of the Deccan Plateau during the Quaternary
The northward movement of the Indian Plate from the Eocene to the Pliocene
n95620fa7193.x: The Himalaya formed when Tethys sediments were pushed upward by the northward-moving Indian Plate. Uplift began about 70 million years ago and continues even today.
n95620fa7193.tq: Link the mountain range with its plate movement, sedimentary source and geological time span.
xs: Tethys sediments were pushed up by the **northward-moving Indian plate** from the **Eocene to the Pliocene** — option **(4)** is correct.
The movement was northward, not southward; Precambrian and Palaeozoic are wrong ages.
xa: Uplift began ~**70 million years ago** and **continues**.
It was the **Tethys geosyncline** uplift of the **Tertiary / Aryan era**.

n0ad90b26a84.s: Mountain-building movements caused mainly by horizontal (tangential) forces are called:
n0ad90b26a84.x: Orogenic movements build mountains through horizontal forces in narrow belts; epeirogenic movements are vertical uplift or subsidence of large areas.
xa: "Vertical (radial)" forces = epeirogenic was asked in UKPSC **2024**.
The **Peninsular block** escaped folding but had **vertical movements** → epeirogenic effect.

n728edd55105.s: The vertical movements of the Peninsular Block, including transgression and regression, are examples of which type of diastrophic effect?
n728edd55105.x: The Peninsular Block largely escaped folding but experienced vertical movements such as transgression and regression, representing an epeirogenic effect.
n728edd55105.tq: Apply the horizontal-versus-vertical movement distinction to a regional example.
xs: The Peninsular block's **vertical movements** (**transgression, regression**) are an **epeirogenic effect** — option **(3)** is correct.
It **escaped folding**, so it is not an **orogenic** effect.
xa: Epeirogeny = **continent building**: uplift or warping of large continental areas by **vertical (radial)** forces.
Orogeny = **mountain building** by severe folding in long narrow belts.

ngeneral-geography-5-11.s: A crescent-shaped sand dune is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-11.x: A barchan is a crescent-shaped dune; a seif is a long, narrow dune parallel to the wind.
n: Barchans are formed by wind deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Barchans are crescent-shaped dunes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Seif or longitudinal dunes are formed by wind deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Seif dunes are long, narrow ridges. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A barchan is crescent-shaped, whereas a seif dune is longitudinal. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: A **spit** projects from the coast; a **tombolo** connects an island to the mainland.
A **delta** is dominated by **deposition**; an **estuary** by **tidal or drowned-mouth** processes.
**V-shaped valleys** are formed by **rivers**; **U-shaped** by **glaciers**.

nc563d137e2d.s: The Black Forest is an example of a:
nc563d137e2d.x: The Black Forest is a block mountain; Fujiyama and Etna are volcanic and the Eastern Ghats are residual.
xa: **Kilimanjaro** (Africa) is also volcanic.
Fold mountains: **Himalaya, Alps, Andes**.

ncef9ac2d362.s: The world’s highest peaks are predominantly associated with which type of mountains?
ncef9ac2d362.x: The world’s highest peaks, including Mount Everest in the Himalaya, occur in young fold mountains.
ncef9ac2d362.tq: Connect the highest relief with the mountain type formed by recent folding.
xs: The **highest peaks** are in **young fold mountains** (Himalaya — **Everest**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Residual** mountains like the Aravalli are worn down (**300–900 m**).
xa: Young folds have **rugged relief** and **high conical peaks**.
Young (Tertiary / Alpine): **Himalaya, Alps, Andes, Rockies**.

ndd0f0dc8f77.s: Which one of the following is a young fold mountain range?
ndd0f0dc8f77.x: The Alps are young (Tertiary/Alpine) fold mountains. The Aravallis are very old Precambrian fold mountains, and the Appalachians and Urals are old Palaeozoic fold mountains.
ndd0f0dc8f77.tq: APPSC G2 2024: among Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals, only the Alps are young.
xs: The **Alps** are young (Tertiary / Alpine) fold mountains — option **(3)** is correct.
**Aravallis** = very old (**Precambrian**); **Appalachians** and **Urals** = old (**Palaeozoic**).
xa: APPSC G2 **2024**: of these four, only the **Alps** are young fold mountains.
Other young folds: **Himalaya, Andes, Rockies**.

n71a0b8596fc.s: Which one of the following is NOT a young fold mountain?
n71a0b8596fc.x: The Sierra Nevada is a block (fault) mountain, though it often appears in 'young folded' lists. The Andes, Rockies and Himalaya are young Tertiary fold mountains.
xs: The **Sierra Nevada** is a **block (fault) mountain** — option **(4)** is correct.
The **Andes, Rockies, Himalaya** are young (**Tertiary / Alpine**) fold mountains.
xa: ⚠ MPPSC **2021** trap: Sierra Nevada in "young folded" lists is a **block** mountain.
Other block mountains: **Vosges**, **Black Forest**.

ngeneral-geography-5-3.s: Young fold mountains, which are high, rugged and sharp-peaked, are formed mainly by:
ngeneral-geography-5-3.x: Recent compression folded the rocks, and erosion has not yet worn them down, so young fold mountains stay high and sharp.
n: Young fold mountains are formed by compression and folding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains are very high. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains have rugged terrain. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains have steep slopes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains have sharp peaks. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains are high and rugged, whereas old fold mountains are low and rounded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Old fold mountains** (**Aravallis**, **Appalachians**, **Urals**) are **lower**, **rounded**, **highly eroded**.
The **world's highest peaks** mostly lie in young fold mountains.
APPSC G2 **2024**: of Appalachians, Aravallis, Alps, Urals — only the **Alps** are young fold.

ngeneral-geography-5-28.s: Which of the following valleys is formed mainly by river (fluvial) erosion?
ngeneral-geography-5-28.x: The V-shaped valley is cut by vertical river erosion; U-shaped and hanging valleys are glacial and rift valleys are tectonic.
n: V-shaped valleys are river landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
U-shaped valleys are river landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Rift valleys are river landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Hanging valleys are river landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Blind valleys are river landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms V-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Rift valleys form when **divergence or tension** causes **faulting** and the **central block subsides**.
Rift examples: **Death Valley**, **Rhine Rift Valley**, **Narmada** and **Tapi** valleys.
A **delta** is dominated by **deposition**.

ngeneral-geography-5-17.s: The Vosges are an example of:
ngeneral-geography-5-17.x: The Vosges, like the Sierra Nevada and the Black Forest, are block mountains; Fuji is volcanic.
n: The Sierra Nevada are block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Vosges are block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Black Forest is a block mountain range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Fuji is a volcanic mountain. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: ⚠ **Sierra Nevada** in "young folded" lists is a **block (fault) mountain** (MPPSC **2021**).
Block mountains are associated with **horsts and grabens**.
Other volcanic mountains: **Kilimanjaro**, **Mount St. Helens**, **Cotopaxi**.

ngeneral-geography-5-41.s: Old fold mountains, formed by ancient folding and prolonged denudation, are generally:
o: Built from alternating layers of lava and ash
ngeneral-geography-5-41.x: Long denudation has made old fold mountains lower than young fold mountains, rounded and highly eroded.
n: Old fold mountains formed through ancient folding and prolonged denudation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are lower than young fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are rounded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Old fold mountains are highly eroded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Young fold mountains are high and rugged, whereas old fold mountains are low and rounded. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Examples: **Aravallis**, **Appalachians**, **Urals**, **Pennines**.
**Aravalli** — about **570 million years** old; highest peak **Guru Shikhar** (**1,722 m**).
Young fold mountains are **high and rugged**; old ones **low and rounded**.

ngeneral-geography-5-45.s: Mountains formed when magma pushes the crust upward without erupting are called:
ngeneral-geography-5-45.x: Dome mountains form when magma bulges the overlying crust upward without erupting; volcanic mountains build from erupted lava.
n: Residual mountains are remnants of older elevated surfaces. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Appalachians are residual mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Pennines are residual mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Dome mountains form when magma pushes upward without erupting through the crust. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Block examples: **Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**, **Black Forest**.
Volcanic examples: **Kilimanjaro**, **Fujiyama**, **Mount St. Helens**, **Cotopaxi**.
Volcanic mountains have **conical peaks** and **craters**.

ngeneral-geography-5-46.s: The Black Hills and the Bighorns are examples of:
ngeneral-geography-5-46.x: The Black Hills and Bighorns are dome mountains, formed by dome-shaped uplift.
n: Dome mountains have dome-shaped uplifts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Black Hills are dome mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Bighorns are dome mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Volcanic mountains** form by **accumulation of lava** — **Kilimanjaro**, **Fuji**.
**Residual mountains** are **remnants of older elevated surfaces**.
**Block mountains** form by **faulting** — **Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**.

ngeneral-geography-5-50.s: Block mountains are formed mainly by:
ngeneral-geography-5-50.x: Faulting is the main force for block mountains, while compression forms fold mountains and volcanism forms volcanic mountains.
n: Compression is the main force in fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Faulting is the main force in block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Volcanism is the main force in volcanic mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Block mountains are formed by faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Fold mountains result from compression, whereas block mountains result from faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Fold mountains: **rugged, parallel ranges** (**Himalaya**, **Alps**, **Andes**).
Block mountains: **fault scarps**, **horsts and grabens** (**Sierra Nevada**, **Vosges**).
Volcanic mountains: **cone shape**, **craters** (**Fuji**, **Kilimanjaro**).

nworld-geography-12-25.s: The Urals are an example of:
nworld-geography-12-25.x: The Urals are old fold mountains, unlike Fujiyama, Mount St. Helens and Cotopaxi, which are volcanic.
n: Fujiyama is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
Mount St. Helens is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
Cotopaxi is an example of a volcanic mountain. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 18-20]
xa: Other volcanic mountains: **Kilimanjaro** (Africa), **Etna** (Italy).
⚠ **Sierra Nevada** is a **block (fault) mountain**, not young fold.
**Dome mountains** form when magma pushes up **without erupting** — **Black Hills**, **Bighorns**.

n87535bec26c.s: Isostasy is best described as the:
o: Continuous erosion of mountains by running water
Horizontal movement of plates across ocean floors
Formation of folds exclusively by compression
Balance of crustal blocks floating on denser material below
n87535bec26c.x: Isostasy refers to the gravitational balance of crustal blocks floating on denser underlying material.
n87535bec26c.tq: Select the definition that expresses crustal buoyancy and balance.
xs: **Isostasy** is the **balance of crustal blocks "floating"** on denser material below — option **(4)** is correct.
Plate movement, erosion and compression folding are different processes.
xa: **Airy**: crust of **uniform density**, different thickness; mountains have deep **"roots"**.
**Pratt**: crust of **different density**, uniform **depth of compensation**; higher blocks are **lighter**.

n5d5651bac37.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Airy and Pratt concepts of isostasy?
o: Airy assumes uniform crustal density but varying crustal thickness.
In Pratt's concept, higher blocks are denser.
Pratt assumes varying crustal densities with a uniform depth of compensation.
In Airy's concept, mountains possess deep roots.
n5d5651bac37.x: In Pratt's concept higher blocks are lighter, not denser. The other three statements correctly describe Airy (uniform density, varying thickness, deep roots) and Pratt (varying density, common compensation depth).
xa: ⚠ Airy = same density, different thickness; Pratt = different density, same depth.
Isostasy = balance of crustal blocks **floating** on denser material.

nc612926f77d.s: Who proposed the geosynclinal theory associated with long, shallow sediment-filled troughs between rigid forelands?
nc612926f77d.x: Kober proposed the geosynclinal theory. It describes long, shallow sinking sea troughs between rigid forelands or kratogens, where sediments accumulate before being compressed into mountains.
nc612926f77d.tq: Identify the theorist from the central concept and its terminology.
xs: **Kober** proposed the **geosynclinal theory** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Geosynclines** (long, shallow, sinking sea troughs) collect sediments between rigid forelands (**kratogens**), which squeeze them into mountains.
**Airy** and **Pratt** gave isostasy models; **Wegener** gave continental drift.
xa: Stages: **lithogenesis → orogenesis → gliptogenesis**.
Indian example: the **Tethys geosyncline** uplifted into the **Himalaya**.

n0fc37e7328b.s: A recumbent fold that is broken and thrust far forward is called a/an:
n0fc37e7328b.x: A nappe is a strongly displaced recumbent fold that has been broken and thrust far forward.
xa: **Anticline** = up-arch; **syncline** = down-trough.
The **Siwaliks** are simple anticline-syncline folds, **Jura type**.

n8a6cab5a654.s: Which of the following is NOT a graben?
o: Great Rift Valley of East Africa
n8a6cab5a654.x: Sierra Nevada is a block mountain (horst), not a graben; the Great Rift Valley, Death Valley and Rhine Rift Valley are grabens.
xa: ⚠ UPSC **2024**: "Vosges – Central Asia – fold" and "Alps – block" were the **wrong** pairs.
Block mountains form when large areas **break and are displaced vertically**.

n5df2b7dd0a1.s: The westward-flowing Narmada river lies in a rift valley between:
o: The Satpuras to the north and the Vindhyas to the south
The Vindhyas to the north and the Satpuras to the south
The Aravallis to the north and the Vindhyas to the south
The Satpuras to the north and the Ajanta range to the south
n5df2b7dd0a1.x: The Narmada flows west through a rift valley situated between the Vindhyas in the north and the Satpuras in the south.
xa: A rift valley is a **graben** — a lowered block.
Other grabens: **Great Rift Valley**, **Death Valley**, **Rhine** valley.

ngeneral-geography-5-92.s: An uplifted fault block associated with block mountains is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-92.x: Horsts are uplifted fault blocks, while grabens are down-faulted blocks; together they are associated with block mountains.
n: Horsts and grabens are associated with block mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Vosges** (France) and **Black Forest** (Germany) are horsts flanking the **Rhine rift valley**.
**Death Valley** (USA) is a graben; **Lake Malawi** lies in the **Great Rift Valley**.
**Narmada** and **Tapi** flow west through **rift valleys**.

ngeneral-geography-5-15.s: An elongated depression formed when the central block subsides between faults as the crust pulls apart is a:
ngeneral-geography-5-15.x: A rift valley forms when the central block sinks between faults after divergence, producing a long depression.
n: A rift valley is an elongated depression associated with faulting. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Rift valleys form through divergence or tension. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Divergence or tension causes faulting in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Faulting causes the central block to subside in rift-valley formation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Tectonic faulting forms rift valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: A **graben** is a **down-faulted block** (rift valley); a **horst** an **uplifted** one.
Examples: **Death Valley** (USA), **Rhine Rift Valley**, **Narmada** and **Tapi** valleys.
⚠ A **rift valley** is **tectonic**; a **hanging valley** is **glacial**.

n5d6d6f3fbab.s: Processes that move, raise or build up the Earth's crust, including earthquakes and plate movements, are collectively called:
n5d6d6f3fbab.x: Diastrophism covers all crustal movements that move, raise or build up the crust, including earthquakes and plate movements, not just folding.
xa: ⚠ "**Heterogenic**" is NOT included (MPPSC **2023**).
Orogenic = **horizontal** forces; epeirogenic = **vertical** forces.

n318e16c6742.s: Which of the following is a Precambrian fold mountain?
n318e16c6742.x: The Aravallis are very old Precambrian fold mountains; the Appalachians are Palaeozoic, while the Himalaya and Alps are Tertiary.
xa: The Aravalli formed from **Dharwar sediments**; now residual (**300–900 m**).
Old Palaeozoic folds also include the **Urals** and **Pennines**.

nd145fc5bbb8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about recent measures concerning the Aravalli region?
o: The Supreme Court allowed fresh grants of new mining leases in the Aravalli region.
The Supreme Court accepted a uniform definition of an Aravalli hill and range in November 2025.
The MoEF&CC ordered a complete ban on new Aravalli mining leases on 24 December 2025.
The Supreme Court paused the grant of new mining leases in the Aravalli region.
nd145fc5bbb8.x: The Supreme Court paused, not allowed, the grant of new mining leases in November 2025. The other statements are correct.
xa: After protests, the SC **stayed its November directions** (Dec **2025**) and proposed a fresh review.
Definition: hill = **100 m** above local relief; range = two or more hills within **500 m**.

nec41c7472fd.s: In high-seismicity Himalayan zones, the collapse of hanging glaciers can trigger landslide-lake outburst floods and:
nec41c7472fd.x: Collapsing hanging glaciers in high-seismicity Himalayan zones can trigger GLOFs and landslide-lake outburst floods; coastal storm surges are not a consequence here.
xa: This happens in **high-seismicity** Himalayan zones.
The Himalaya is a **young fold** range whose uplift **continues**.

ngeneral-geography-5-102.s: A deposit that joins an island to the mainland is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-102.x: A tombolo, not a spit, joins an island to the mainland; spits are built by longshore drift.
n: Western Ghats rivers are short and swift. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Longshore drift forms spits. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: A **delta** is **dominated by deposition**; an **estuary** by **tidal** processes.
A **barchan** is **crescent-shaped**; a **seif dune** is **longitudinal**.
A **stalactite** hangs from a roof; a **stalagmite** rises from a floor.

nindian-geography-14-1.s: Which is the highest peak of the Aravalli Range?
nindian-geography-14-1.x: Guru Shikhar, 1,722 m at Mount Abu, is the highest Aravalli peak.
nindian-geography-14-1.tq: Recall the highest peak of each range.
n: Guru Shikhar is the highest peak of the Aravalli Range. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
Guru Shikhar is located in Sirohi district. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
Sirohi district is located in Rajasthan. [Indian Geography · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 41-46]
xs: **Guru Shikhar** (**1,722 metres**) is the **highest peak** of the Aravalli Range — option **(3)**.
It lies in **Sirohi district**, **Rajasthan**.
xa: The Aravalli lies in **Rajasthan**, **Haryana** and **Delhi**; its northern extension **reaches Delhi**.
Geological age about **570 million years**; a **residual mountain range** formed from **Dharwar** sediments.
SC (Nov **2025**) definition: an Aravalli hill rises **100 m** above local relief.
MoEF&CC banned new Aravalli mining leases on **24 Dec 2025**.

n91655ec0756.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the processes or phenomena associated with diastrophism?
n91655ec0756.x: Orogeny, epeirogeny, earthquakes and plate tectonics are included in the stated scope of diastrophism. Heterogenic movement is not included.
n91655ec0756.tq: Find the excluded term rather than selecting another crustal process.
xs: **Heterogenic movement** is NOT part of diastrophism — option **(4)** is correct (MPPSC **2023** trap).
Diastrophism includes **orogeny, epeirogeny, earthquakes** and **plate tectonics**.
xa: Diastrophism = processes that **move, raise or build up** the crust.
Orogenic forces are **horizontal**; epeirogenic forces are **vertical**.

n4b296367d3f.s: The old, heavily eroded residual hills of the Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh form part of the:
n4b296367d3f.x: The Eastern Ghats in Andhra Pradesh are old, heavily eroded residual hills and form part of the Eastern Ghats Mobile Belt.
xa: Rocks: **khondalite, charnockite**.
They are the state's **major mountain belt**.

ngeneral-geography-5-22.s: Which mountain range is identified as the longest major mountain range?
ngeneral-geography-5-22.x: The Andes, about 7,000 km long, are the longest mountain range. The Himalayas are the highest.
n: The Andes are the longest major mountain range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Andes are in South America. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: The **Andes** (**South America**) are the **longest major mountain range** — option **(3)**.
The **Andes** and **Himalayas** are **young fold mountains**; so are the **Alps** and **Rockies**.
xa: The **world's highest peaks** mostly lie in young fold mountains — **Himalaya**, **Everest**.
The **Himalaya** uplift began ~**70 million years ago** and continues.
**Aravalli** — one of the oldest fold mountains, now residual (**300–900 m**).

n519b61e6b9a.s: A cauldron-shaped depression formed when a large eruption empties the magma chamber and the summit collapses is a:
n519b61e6b9a.x: A caldera forms by summit collapse after the magma chamber empties; a crater is the funnel-shaped mouth at the top of a cone.
xa: **Magma** = molten rock below the surface; **lava** = magma at the surface.
Lava reaches the surface through the **vent**.
**Pyroclasts**: ash, **lapilli**, volcanic bombs.

nc0b117089c1.s: The most abundant volcanic gas is:
nc0b117089c1.x: Water vapour is the most abundant volcanic gas, followed by CO2 and SO2.
xa: Pyroclasts: **ash, lapilli, volcanic bombs**.
Mud volcanoes emit gases such as **methane, CO2, nitrogen**.
**Tiltmeter** monitors ground tilt over volcanoes.

ngeneral-geography-4-48.s: Molten material that reaches the Earth's surface is called:
ngeneral-geography-4-48.x: Molten rock below the surface is magma; once it reaches the surface it is lava.
n: Molten material below Earth’s surface is magma. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
Molten material that reaches Earth’s surface is lava. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #4 · pp 27-33]
xa: ⚠ Below surface = **magma**; at surface = **lava**.
**Acidic (felsic) lava** is silica-rich, viscous, explosive; **basic (mafic) lava** is fluid and flows far.
A **caldera** forms when the magma chamber empties and the summit collapses.

o: Silica-rich, viscous and associated with explosive eruptions
Silica-poor, fluid and forms broad shield volcanoes
nd6f6bb2dbc8.x: Acidic or felsic lava is silica-rich and viscous, making eruptions more explosive and producing steep cones and stratovolcanoes.
xa: Basic lava **flows far**, building **shield volcanoes and lava plateaus** (basalt).
⚠ **Shield** = fluid basalt, gentle; **composite** = lava + ash layers, steep, explosive.
Stratovolcanoes produce **pyroclastic flows** and **lahars**.

n05bb4aaa231.s: Pyroclastic flows and lahars are particularly associated with:
n05bb4aaa231.x: Pyroclastic flows and lahars (volcanic mudflows) are associated particularly with stratovolcanoes.
xa: Pyroclasts: **ash, lapilli, volcanic bombs**.
Examples: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.
Stratovolcanoes form from **andesitic magma**.

n38bca0d4dba.s: Basaltic lava plateaus such as the Deccan Plateau commonly weather into:
n38bca0d4dba.x: Basaltic lava plateaus such as the Deccan weather to form fertile black soil.
xa: In AP, **Deccan Trap basalts** (**Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**) give **black cotton soil**.
The Deccan Traps are **fissure (flood-basalt)** eruptions of the end-**Cretaceous** (about **65 million years**).
They are linked to the **Reunion hotspot**.

n9e3204f4c69.s: Hayli Gubbi, which erupted in November 2025 after remaining dormant for approximately 10,000–12,000 years, is an example of which type of volcano based on its form?
n9e3204f4c69.x: Hayli Gubbi in Ethiopia is identified as a shield volcano. Its eruption in November 2025 followed a dormant period of approximately 10,000–12,000 years.
n9e3204f4c69.tq: Combine the numerical time period with the volcano-type identification.
xs: **Hayli Gubbi** (Ethiopia) is a **shield volcano** — option **(3)**.
It erupted in **Nov 2025** after **10,000-12,000 years** dormant.
Shield volcanoes are **broad, gentle slopes** of **fluid basalt**.
xa: The other shield example: **Mauna Loa**.
**Complex volcanoes**: **Taal, Dukono**.
**Composite**: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.

nca02b86cf4f.s: Steep volcanic cones built from alternating layers of lava and ash, with explosive eruptions, are:
nca02b86cf4f.x: Composite or stratovolcanoes are steep, consist of alternating lava and ash layers and are associated with explosive eruptions.
xa: Examples: **Fuji, Vesuvius, St Helens, Fuego, Taftan**.
They come from **andesitic magma** and produce **pyroclastic flows and lahars**.
⚠ **Shield** = fluid basalt, gentle; **composite** = steep, explosive.

n24183562e77.s: Which belt is associated with the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes?
n24183562e77.x: The Pacific Ring of Fire has the greatest concentration of volcanic eruptions and earthquakes. It includes volcanoes such as Fuji and Mount St. Helens.
n24183562e77.tq: Identify the global belt from its combined volcanic and seismic activity.
xs: The **Pacific Ring of Fire** has the most eruptions and earthquakes — option **(3)**.
Its volcanoes: **Fuji, St Helens, Fuego, Mayon, Dukono, Popocatepetl**.
xa: **Mid-Atlantic belt**: Iceland - **Hekla**.
**Mediterranean belt**: **Vesuvius, Etna, Stromboli**.
**East African Rift**: **Kilimanjaro**; intraplate hotspot: **Hawaii**.

nfd143508583.s: A volcano that has been quiet for a long time but may erupt again is called:
nfd143508583.x: A dormant volcano has been quiet for long but may erupt again; an extinct volcano is one from which no eruption is expected.
xa: **Barren Island** is **India's only active volcano**.
**Narcondam** is **dormant**; **Dhinodhar** (Kutch) is **extinct**.
**Hayli Gubbi** erupted in **Nov 2025** after **10,000-12,000 years** dormant.

nedda2b479e1.x: Barren Island is India's only active volcano; Narcondam is dormant, Dhinodhar is an extinct volcanic hill and Baratang has mud volcanoes.
xa: Barren Island's last eruption in the notes: **2017**.
**Narcondam** is a wildlife sanctuary with the endemic **Narcondam Hornbill**.
⚠ APPSC GS **2021** key gave "Barren island" for mud volcanoes — the right answer is **Baratang**.

nfdbc10b065d.s: Baratang in the Andaman Islands is known for its:
nfdbc10b065d.x: Baratang is associated with mud volcanoes, which erupt mud, water and gases; Barren Island is India's only active magmatic volcano.
xa: ⚠ APPSC GS **2021** key gave "Barren island" for mud volcanoes — correct answer **Baratang**.
Fresh mud volcano eruption at **Diglipur** (North Andaman).
Mud volcanoes are **cool and shallow**.

n059815b5dab.s: The flood-basalt outpourings of the Deccan Traps occurred near the end of the:
n059815b5dab.x: The Deccan Traps are fissure flood-basalt outpourings on the Maharashtra Plateau at the end of the Cretaceous, linked to the Reunion hotspot.
xa: Linked to the **Reunion hotspot**.
In AP: **Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**.
They weather into **fertile black soil**.

n6c0a5ebc866.s: The Deccan Traps are linked in origin with the:
n6c0a5ebc866.x: The Deccan Traps are linked to activity of the Reunion hotspot near the end of the Cretaceous.
n6c0a5ebc866.tq: Discriminate among similarly named hotspot examples using the associated landform.
xs: The **Deccan Traps** are linked to the **Reunion hotspot** — option **(2)**.
They were flood-basalt eruptions at the end of the **Cretaceous** (about **65 million years**).
xa: They lie on the **Maharashtra plateau**; in AP in **Prakasam, Palnadu, Guntur**.
**Hawaii** is an **intraplate hotspot** volcano.
**Iceland** lies on the **Mid-Atlantic belt** (Hekla).

n678c14f512a.s: A mud volcano at Diglipur is distinguished from a lava volcano because it ejects:
n678c14f512a.x: The Diglipur mud volcano ejects mud, water and methane rather than lava. Its activity is driven by tectonic pressure on the active Andaman Arc subduction zone.
n678c14f512a.tq: Distinguish a process by its actual ejecta rather than by the word volcano.
xs: The **Diglipur** mud volcano ejects **mud, water and methane**, not lava — option **(4)**.
It is driven by tectonic pressure on the active **Andaman Arc** subduction zone.
xa: Mud volcanoes erupt gases such as **methane, CO2, nitrogen**; they are **cool and shallow**.
**Diglipur** is in **North Andaman**; **Baratang** (Middle Andaman) also has mud volcanoes.
⚠ **Baratang** = mud volcanoes; **Barren Island** = magmatic active volcano.

na7dbdc7f32c.s: The Tattapani hot spring is located in:
na7dbdc7f32c.x: Tattapani is in Chhattisgarh; Taptapani is in Odisha and Vajreshwari in Maharashtra.
xa: ⚠ **Tattapani** = Chhattisgarh; **Taptapani** = Odisha.
**Manikaran**: Himachal Pradesh (**Kullu valley**).
**Puga Valley, Chumathang**: **Ladakh**.

na8269451368.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about geothermal exploration at Puga Valley?
o: ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells there.
The wells were associated with a 1 MW pilot project.
The wells reached a depth of 1,000 metres.
Puga Valley is located in Himachal Pradesh.
na8269451368.x: Puga Valley is in Ladakh, not Himachal Pradesh. ONGC drilled India's first and deepest geothermal wells there to 1,000 m for a 1 MW pilot project.
xa: GSI has identified **340** geothermal sites.
**Chumathang** is another Ladakh geothermal site.
⚠ **Tattapani** = Chhattisgarh; **Taptapani** = Odisha.

n6ae408d7134.s: Which instrument measures slip along a fault?
n6ae408d7134.x: A creepmeter records fault slip; a tiltmeter records ground tilt over faults and volcanoes.
xa: These instrument matches were asked in APPSC **2018**.
⚠ **Trap:** anemometer = wind **speed**, not direction.
Most abundant volcanic gas: **water vapour**.

na765c45ca19.s: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake is the:
na765c45ca19.x: The epicentre lies on the surface directly above the focus, and shaking is generally strongest there; the focus is underground.
xa: Typical crustal quakes: **10-29 km** deep.
**Intensity** falls with **distance from the epicentre**.
**Seismic doublet**: two independent quakes of **similar magnitude**, in quick succession, close together.

nbafc5f3762c.s: A seismic doublet is best described as
o: two volcanic eruptions separated by a long interval
two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring close together in time and space
a main shock followed by aftershocks that gradually become weaker
two waves arriving at the epicentre at exactly the same time
nbafc5f3762c.x: A seismic doublet consists of two independent earthquakes of similar magnitude occurring in quick succession and close together. This differs from an aftershock sequence, which generally tapers off.
nbafc5f3762c.tq: Distinguish a doublet from the familiar mainshock–aftershock pattern by focusing on independence and similarity of magnitude.
xs: A **seismic doublet** is **two independent quakes of similar magnitude**, in quick succession, close together — option **(2)**.
An **aftershock sequence** tapers off — option (3) describes that, not a doublet.
xa: Example: **Venezuela (M 7.1 and 7.5)** on the Caribbean-South American **strike-slip** boundary.
Toll: **589 dead**.
**USGS** described it as a "seismic doublet" (**26 Jun 2026**).

ndisaster-management-10-1.s: Who is known as the Father of Modern Seismology?
ndisaster-management-10-1.x: John Milne, who built an early horizontal seismograph, is called the father of modern seismology. Richter devised the magnitude scale and Wegener proposed continental drift.
n: John Milne is the father of modern seismology. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Intensity** is measured on the **Mercalli Scale**; a **seismograph** measures earthquakes.
**Focus** = origin point inside Earth; **epicentre** = point directly above it on the surface.
India's **first observatory**: **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)**.
Each **+1** on the Richter scale = **10x** amplitude and about **31x** energy.

n6cba16e75b7.s: Earthquakes that occur when stress on a fault exceeds rock strength and the rock ruptures are called:
n6cba16e75b7.x: A tectonic earthquake is fault rupture when stress exceeds rock strength; it can occur at divergent as well as convergent boundaries.
xa: **Reservoir-induced**: weight of water — **Koyna 1967**.
**Intraplate**: old hidden faults — **Latur (Killari) 1993**, **Jabalpur**.
Induced (other): **mining**, **fracking** — usually low magnitude.

n0c0524827ea.s: The 1993 Latur earthquake is significant in the study of earthquake causes because it demonstrated that
o: earthquakes may occur in stable regions along hidden faults
earthquakes occur only at convergent plate boundaries
all intraplate earthquakes are caused by volcanic eruptions
stable continental regions cannot experience damaging earthquakes
n0c0524827ea.x: The Latur earthquake occurred far from a plate boundary and showed that stable continental regions can experience earthquakes along concealed or old faults.
n0c0524827ea.tq: Use the exception to the plate-boundary rule as the deciding clue.
xs: **Latur 1993** showed quakes strike **stable areas along hidden faults** — option **(1)**.
It lay **far from any plate boundary** (APPSC **2025**).
It struck a zone then rated low-risk (**Zone I**), with **M 6.2** and **~10,000 dead**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II**.
Latur is also called **Killari**.
⚠ **Koyna** = reservoir-induced; **Latur** = intraplate.

nc159ee4bb4f.s: Which one of the following is regarded as India's classic example of a reservoir-induced earthquake?
nc159ee4bb4f.x: The Koyna earthquake of 1967 is the classic Indian example of reservoir-induced seismicity, associated with the filling and weight of a large reservoir.
nc159ee4bb4f.tq: Link the named event and year with the specific earthquake mechanism.
xs: **Koyna 1967** (Maharashtra) is India's classic **reservoir-induced** quake — option **(1)**.
Cause: the **weight of water** when large reservoirs are filled.
**Latur 1993** was **intraplate**; **Bhuj 2001** tectonic.
xa: Reservoir-triggered tremors possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram**.
⚠ **Koyna** = reservoir-induced; **Latur** = hidden faults.
Koyna is also listed with intraplate quakes in the peninsula.

nb2e65c4bed2.s: The 2025 Myanmar (Mandalay) earthquake occurred along the:
nb2e65c4bed2.x: The 2025 Myanmar earthquake (M 7.7) was on the strike-slip Sagaing Fault between the Indian and Eurasian plates; Turkey-Syria 2023 was on the East Anatolian Fault.
xa: Tohoku: **M 9.0**; Turkey-Syria: **M 7.8**; Myanmar: **M 7.7**, **2,000+** dead.
**Seismic seiches** were reported during the **Myanmar** earthquake.
The **Sagaing Fault** is the **Indian-Eurasian** boundary.

n5b221e340cd.s: Which of the following regions is NOT identified as a prone area for significant earthquake activity in India?
n5b221e340cd.x: Kutch, the North-East and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands are earthquake-prone areas. Visakhapatnam is cited as an example of a low-risk stable-shield area.
n5b221e340cd.tq: Find the location that does not belong to the group of earthquake-prone regions.
xs: The **stable shield around Visakhapatnam** is not a prone area — option **(2)**.
**Visakhapatnam** lies in **Zone II** (low risk).
**Kutch**, the **North-East** and **Andaman & Nicobar** are prone areas, all in **Zone V**.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
AP is mostly in **Zones II and III**.
**Koraput-Jeypore quake (6 Apr 2026)**: **M 4.4**, shook **Araku** and **Paderu**.

nc0596f9ec54.s: Which gas is present in the greatest proportion among the principal gases released by volcanoes?
nc0596f9ec54.x: Volcanic gases consist mostly of water vapour, followed by carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and hydrogen sulphide.
nc0596f9ec54.tq: Recall the stated order of abundance rather than confusing gases with solid volcanic products.
xs: **Water vapour** is the most abundant volcanic gas — option **(3)**.
It is followed by **CO2**, **SO2** and **H2S**.
xa: Products: **pyroclastic debris, ash, volcanic bombs, lava**.
**Vulcanian** eruptions are **more explosive** than Strombolian.
**Shield** volcanoes have **fluid basaltic lava**.

n12fba8c25b5.s: Which one of the following is an extrusive volcanic landform?
n12fba8c25b5.x: Lava plateaus, cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas and lava flows are extrusive volcanic landforms. Batholiths, lopoliths and phacoliths are intrusive forms.
n12fba8c25b5.tq: Separate surface-formed extrusive features from underground intrusive bodies.
xs: A **lava plateau** is an **extrusive** landform — option **(2)**.
Other extrusive forms: **cinder and composite cones, craters, calderas, lava flows**.
**Lopolith**, **phacolith** and **batholith** are **intrusive** — magma cooled inside the crust.
xa: Example lava plateau: the **Deccan**.
**Dykes** fed the Deccan Traps.
⚠ **Sill** = horizontal; **dyke** = vertical.

nfceb7306ada.s: Love and Rayleigh waves are collectively classified as:
nfceb7306ada.x: Love and Rayleigh waves move along the Earth's surface and are classified as surface waves.
nfceb7306ada.tq: Test the exact classification of closely related seismic waves.
xs: **Love** and **Rayleigh** waves are **surface waves** — option **(1)**.
They **move along the surface** and arrive **last**.
xa: ⚠ **Love** = side to side; **Rayleigh** = rolling, like ocean waves.
Surface (L) waves **cause most damage**.
**P** (1st) and **S** (2nd) waves travel through the Earth's interior.

o: standing waves in rivers, reservoirs and ponds
waves generated only by volcanic ash
n56ab5f8eb0b.x: Seismic seiches are standing waves that may develop in enclosed or partly enclosed water bodies such as rivers, reservoirs and ponds. They were reported during the Myanmar earthquake.
n56ab5f8eb0b.tq: Distinguish a water-body phenomenon from earthquake source types and fault movements.
xs: **Seismic seiches** are **standing waves** in rivers, lakes, reservoirs, ponds — option **(3)**.
They were reported during the **Myanmar earthquake**.
Slow slip along a fault is **creep** — option (1) wrong.
xa: **Landslides**: fragile **Himalaya** and **North-East**.
**Liquefaction**: soft soils of the **Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Fires**: from **broken gas and power lines**.

n126e0ff71f0.s: The observed effects of an earthquake at a particular place, which vary with distance from the epicentre, are measured as its:
n126e0ff71f0.x: Intensity is the qualitative measure of observed effects at a place; magnitude measures energy released at the focus and has one value per earthquake.
xa: Magnitude: **Richter scale**, now **Moment Magnitude (Mw)**.
Intensity: **Modified Mercalli (MMI)** and **MSK**, both **I to XII**.
APPSC **2025**: magnitude = energy at focus; intensity = effect at a place.

nab852ecf3b1.s: Charles F. Richter developed the Richter scale in:
nab852ecf3b1.x: The Richter scale was developed by Charles F. Richter in 1935; it measures magnitude, not intensity.
xa: Mw has largely **replaced Richter** for strong quakes.
Intensity is measured on **MMI** and **MSK** scales.
⚠ APPSC **2022**: "Richter scale measures intensity" is wrong.

ndcfbeceb3e1.s: An increase of one unit on the Richter scale increases the energy released by approximately:
ndcfbeceb3e1.x: One magnitude unit means a tenfold increase in wave amplitude and about a 31-fold increase in energy released.
xa: **Mw** (Moment Magnitude) is based on **rupture area** and has largely replaced Richter.
Richter devised the scale in **1935**.
Magnitude has **one value per quake**.

n69f780bbf1d.s: Which of the following is NOT an induced cause of earthquakes?
o: Movement along the San Andreas Fault
n69f780bbf1d.x: San Andreas movement is tectonic; mining, hydraulic fracturing and reservoir filling induce earthquakes, usually of low magnitude.
xa: Intraplate quakes: **Latur 1993**, **Jabalpur**.
**Volcanic** quakes: rising magma fractures rock.
Tectonic quakes occur at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.

n7e08187aa5a.s: The absence of S-waves beyond about 105° from the epicentre shows that the Earth's outer core is:
n7e08187aa5a.x: S-waves are transverse and travel through solids only, so their absence beyond about 105° shows the outer core is liquid.
xa: **P-waves** arrive **1st**, push-pull, through solid, liquid, gas.
**Surface (L)** waves arrive **last** and **cause most damage**.
⚠ **Love** = side to side; **Rayleigh** = rolling.

n7c18b43cd0d.s: The 1993 Latur earthquake was significant because it occurred in an intraplate region that had earlier been rated as which risk zone?
n7c18b43cd0d.x: The Latur earthquake occurred in an intraplate region that was then classified as low-risk Zone I.
n7c18b43cd0d.tq: Use the numerical-zone clue to distinguish a low-risk intraplate event.
xs: **Latur 1993** struck a zone then rated **Zone I** (low-risk) — option **(3)**.
It was an **intraplate** quake, **M 6.2**, **~10,000 dead**.
xa: After Latur, **IS 1893: 2002** merged **Zone I into Zone II** → four zones.
⚠ **Bhuj 2001** → **DM Act 2005**; **Latur 1993** → Zone I merged into Zone II.
Latur showed quakes strike **stable areas along hidden faults** (APPSC **2025**).

n567a3863ced.s: The 2015 Gorkha earthquake in Nepal, along the Main Himalayan Thrust, had a magnitude of:
n567a3863ced.x: The 2015 Gorkha earthquake had a magnitude of 7.8 and caused liquefaction in Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal.
xa: Liquefaction hits the **soft soils of the Indo-Gangetic plain**.
**Uttarkashi** (**1991**, M ~**6.8**) also lay in the **Himalayan thrust zone**.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

nb43e6013edb.s: Earthquake-induced liquefaction is a particular concern in which region of India?
nb43e6013edb.x: Liquefaction is a particular concern in the alluvial Indo-Gangetic plain.
xa: **Kutch** is another prone area (**Zone V**).
**Jabalpur** is also an intraplate example.
Indian plate pushes north at about **5 cm/year**.

n38e503e02ff.s: Zone I was merged into which zone after the 1993 Latur earthquake?
