n38e503e02ff.x: After the 1993 Latur earthquake, Zone I was merged into Zone II, resulting in the four-zone classification under IS 1893:2002.
n38e503e02ff.tq: Link a classification change to the event that prompted it.
xs: After **Latur 1993**, **Zone I** was merged into **Zone II** — option **(3)**.
This came in **IS 1893: 2002**, giving **four zones**.
xa: **IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025** (BIS, **6 Nov 2025**) added **Zone VI** using a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** four-zone map is back in force.
The 2025 map put **over 60%** of India's land in moderate-to-high zones.

n34a36399ada.s: The National Centre for Seismology detects which combination of earthquakes through its monitoring network?
o: Only earthquakes capable of producing tsunamis
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 and above
Indian earthquakes of magnitude 1.0 and global earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
Only earthquakes occurring in the Himalayan region
n34a36399ada.x: The network detects every Indian earthquake of magnitude 3.0 or above and global earthquakes of magnitude 6.0 or above, including tsunami-capable events.
n34a36399ada.tq: Separate the two magnitude thresholds instead of treating them as identical.
xs: NCS detects every **Indian** quake of **M 3.0+** and **global** quakes of **M 6.0+** — option **(2)**.
Global coverage includes **tsunami-capable** quakes.
xa: NCS runs the **National Seismological Network** of **160 observatories**.
Public alerts: **IndiaQuake** app.
**Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

n5657503d44f.s: Composite or stratovolcanoes constitute approximately what share of the Earth's volcanoes?
n5657503d44f.x: Composite volcanoes, with viscous lava, steep cones and explosive eruptions, make up approximately 60% of Earth's volcanoes.
xa: Examples: **Etna, Mayon, Fuego**.
**Mayon** (Philippines) is a **symmetrical composite cone**.
**Fuego** gives **Strombolian** eruptions every **15-20 min**.

n32877bd0d26.s: A vertical wall of igneous rock cutting across the rock beds is called a:
n32877bd0d26.x: A dyke is a vertical wall cutting across beds; a sill is a horizontal sheet parallel to the beds. Dykes fed the Deccan Traps.
xa: **Phacolith**: wavy mass at the base of a **syncline** or top of an **anticline**.
Thin sills are called **sheets**.
⚠ APPSC G1 **2024**: domes are **laccoliths**, not phacoliths.

n45c926e2e08.s: Which volcano is known as the 'Lighthouse of the Mediterranean'?
n45c926e2e08.x: Stromboli is known as the Lighthouse of the Mediterranean; Hekla is in Iceland and Mauna Loa in Hawaii.
xa: Stromboli gives its name to **Strombolian** eruptions.
⚠ **Kilimanjaro** and **Fuji** = dormant; **Etna, Stromboli, Vesuvius** = active (all Italy).
**Ojos del Salado** (Chile) is the **world's highest active volcano** (**6,893 m**).

n2d8115f54ed.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about seismicity in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Most of Andhra Pradesh lies in Seismic Zones II and III.
Reservoir-triggered tremors cannot be ruled out near Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram.
Old faults in the Eastern Ghats are relevant to the possibility of tremors.
n2d8115f54ed.x: Visakhapatnam is in Zone II, not Zone V. The other three statements are correct.
xa: AP has **no area in Zone V** (APPSC **2024**).
**Koraput-Jeypore quake (6 Apr 2026)**: **M 4.4**, **5 km** deep, shook **Araku** and **Paderu** in ASR district.
⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.

ndisaster-management-10-3.s: Which earthquake, along with the 2004 tsunami, pushed India toward the Disaster Management Act, 2005?
ndisaster-management-10-3.x: The 2001 Bhuj earthquake was a turning point in disaster management and, with the 2004 tsunami, led to the DM Act, 2005.
n: The Bhuj earthquake occurred in Gujarat in 2001. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
The Bhuj earthquake was a major turning point that led to the Disaster Management Act of 2005. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
xa: Bhuj was an **intraplate** quake; **20,000+** dead.
**Latur (Killari) 1993** (M **6.2**) led to **Zone I** being merged into **Zone II**.
**Kutch** lies in **Zone V**.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra quake**.

n9a41d653381.s: Under IS 1893:2016, which sequence correctly represents the seismic zones from lower to higher risk?
o: Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V
Zone V, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone II
Zone III, Zone II, Zone V, Zone IV
Zone II, Zone IV, Zone III, Zone V
n9a41d653381.x: Under the four-zone map in force, Zone II represents low risk, Zone III moderate risk, Zone IV high risk and Zone V very high risk.
n9a41d653381.tq: Arrange the zones by increasing risk rather than by geographical location.
xs: Low to high risk: **Zone II, Zone III, Zone IV, Zone V** — option **(1)**.
The map in force (**IS 1893: 2016**) has **four zones**; **Zone II is the calmest**.
xa: **Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
**Zone VI** came in the **2025** code, **withdrawn on 3 Mar 2026**.
**Zone I** was merged into Zone II after **Latur 1993**.

nc374bdab96b.s: Which of the following areas is included in Zone V under the seismic zoning map in force?
nc374bdab96b.x: Kutch is included in Zone V, the very-high-risk zone. Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad are examples of Zone II, while Vijayawada is cited under Zone III.
nc374bdab96b.tq: Distinguish locations by their assigned seismic-risk zones.
xs: **Kutch** (Gujarat) is in **Zone V** — option **(3)**.
**Visakhapatnam** and **Hyderabad** are **Zone II**; **Vijayawada** is **Zone III**.
xa: Zone V also covers the **entire North-East**, **J&K, Ladakh, HP, Uttarakhand**, north **Bihar**, **Andaman & Nicobar**.
The withdrawn **2025** code placed parts of **Kutch** in **Zone VI**.

nab63c48b0ef.s: Under IS 1893:2016, Delhi lies in Seismic Zone:
nab63c48b0ef.x: Delhi, with the Himalayan foothills and the Indo-Gangetic belt, is in Zone IV (high); Vijayawada is Zone III and Visakhapatnam Zone II.
xa: ⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Zone III also includes **Chennai**, the **Latur-Koyna** belt and the **Amaravati** region.
AP has **no area in Zone V**.

ndisaster-management-10-2.s: Under IS 1893:2016, the zone factor for Seismic Zone III is:
ndisaster-management-10-2.x: Zone III (moderate, intensity VII) has a zone factor of 0.16; the factors are 0.10, 0.16, 0.24 and 0.36 for Zones II to V.
n: Seismic Zone V has very high risk. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone V has an expected intensity of IX and above on the MSK scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
The zone factor of Seismic Zone V is 0.36. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone IV has high risk. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone IV has an expected intensity of VIII on the MSK scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
The zone factor of Seismic Zone IV is 0.24. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone III has moderate risk. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone III has an expected intensity of VII on the MSK scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
The zone factor of Seismic Zone III is 0.16. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone II has low risk. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
Seismic Zone II has an expected intensity of VI or less on the MSK scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
The zone factor of Seismic Zone II is 0.10. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 25-27]
xa: **Zone V** covers the **entire North-East**, **J&K**, **Ladakh**, **HP**, **Uttarakhand**, **Kutch** and **A&N**.
**Andhra Pradesh** lies in **Zones II and III**; it has **no area in Zone V** (APPSC **2024**).
⚠ **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
IS 1893: **2025** (Zone VI) was **withdrawn on 3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** four-zone map is in force.

n1aa6ff0bc58.s: Which feature was introduced by the IS 1893 (Part 1): 2025 revision?
o: The abolition of all seismic zones in India
The exclusion of the North-East from the highest-risk category
The restoration of Zone I as the lowest zone
A new top Zone VI covering parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch
n1aa6ff0bc58.x: The 2025 revision introduced a new top Zone VI for parts of Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch, and placed more than 60% of India’s landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
n1aa6ff0bc58.tq: Identify the distinctive institutional change rather than a reversed zoning claim.
xs: The **2025** revision added a new top **Zone VI** for parts of **Kashmir, the North-East and Kutch** — option **(4)**.
It used a **probabilistic (PSHA)** model.
It put **over 60%** of India's landmass in moderate-to-high zones.
xa: The map was built by **IIT-Madras** for **NDMA**; **PGA 0.15-0.75 g** from Zone II to Zone VI.
Basis: **69,519 events** and **36 seismogenic zones**.
BIS **withdrew** it on **3 Mar 2026**.

nf661b67631a.s: The 2025 revision of IS 1893 was withdrawn on 3 March 2026 primarily after objections relating to which issue?
o: The inability to identify earthquakes of magnitude 3.0 and above
The absence of earthquake data from the North-East
The replacement of the National Seismological Network
The cost implications raised by MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA
nf661b67631a.x: The 2025 revision was withdrawn after MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA objected to the cost implications. The 2016 code was restored.
nf661b67631a.tq: Match the policy rollback with the specific administrative objection.
xs: The 2025 code was withdrawn after **cost objections** from **MoHUA, Metro Rail corporations and the NDSA** — option **(4)**.
BIS **withdrew it on 3 Mar 2026**; the **2016** code was restored.
xa: A **review panel** is to report to the **Cabinet Secretariat**.
Debate: safer **PSHA-based codes** vs **construction cost**.
Experts call the restored 2016 values **too low for the Himalaya**; NDMA called the new ones "**too high**".

nde21cbadac8.s: White Island (Whakaari), a volcano that erupted in December 2019, is located in which country?
nde21cbadac8.x: White Island (Whakaari) is in New Zealand and erupted in December 2019. Indonesia has Krakatoa and Dukono, Japan has Fujiyama and Mount Aso, and the Philippines has Taal and Mayon.
nde21cbadac8.tq: Whakaari = Maori name; New Zealand, Dec 2019 (APPSC PYQ).
xs: **White Island (Whakaari)** is in **New Zealand** — option **(3)**.
It erupted in **December 2019** (APPSC PYQ).
**Indonesia** has **Krakatoa** and **Dukono**; the **Philippines** has **Taal** and **Mayon**.
xa: **Krakatoa**'s **1883** eruption caused catastrophic tsunamis.
**Fujiyama** (Japan) last erupted in **1707**.
**Mount St. Helens** (USA, Cascades) erupted in **1980**.

nf1eefcc0abe.s: Which one of the following belts is associated with the greatest concentration of earthquakes in the world?
nf1eefcc0abe.x: The Circum-Pacific belt, also called the Ring of Fire, contains the world's greatest concentration of earthquakes and is associated largely with subduction around the Pacific basin.
nf1eefcc0abe.tq: Use the ranking of earthquake belts to select the most active belt.
xs: The **Circum-Pacific belt (Ring of Fire)** has the most earthquakes — option **(3)**.
The **Mid-Continental (Alpine-Himalayan)** belt comes next.
**Mid-oceanic ridges** give **shallow, milder** quakes.
xa: The Ring of Fire is driven by **subduction** around the Pacific basin.
Examples: **Japan, Philippines, Indonesia, Chile, Andes, Alaska**.
**2026** Ring of Fire quakes: **Flores M 7.7**, **Colombia M 7.4**, **Kyushu M 7.1**.

n30eb8b7d6ad.s: The Mediterranean-Himalayan seismic belt is associated mainly with:
o: A mantle plume beneath a moving plate
n30eb8b7d6ad.x: The Mediterranean-Himalayan belt is linked to continental collision; the Ring of Fire to subduction, the Mid-Atlantic belt to a divergent ridge and hotspots to mantle plumes.
xa: Hotspot examples: **Hawaii, Galapagos**, Reunion.
Mid-Atlantic example: **Iceland**.
Mediterranean-Himalayan: **Italy, Türkiye, Himalayas / India**.

n3d0e66c2d4c.s: India forms part of which major seismic belt?
n3d0e66c2d4c.x: India lies in the Alpine-Himalayan seismic belt, which extends eastward through the North-East into Myanmar.
n3d0e66c2d4c.tq: Recall the major global seismic belt associated with India.
xs: India lies in the **Alpine-Himalayan belt** — option **(1)**.
The **Indian plate** pushes north at about **5 cm/year** into the **Eurasian plate**.
The belt continues east through the **North-East** into **Myanmar**.
xa: **Sagaing Fault** = Indian-Eurasian boundary in Myanmar.
**Zone V** runs along the Himalayan front, where **magnitude-8** quakes have struck.
The **Circum-Pacific** belt has the most quakes; Alpine-Himalayan is **next**.

n3264e6f2d2c.s: The first seismological observatory in India was established at which place in 1898?
n3264e6f2d2c.x: India’s first seismological observatory was established at Alipore in Calcutta in 1898.
n3264e6f2d2c.tq: Recall the earliest observatory by combining its place and year.
xs: India's **first observatory** was at **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)** — option **(2)**.
**New Delhi** is the seat of the **National Centre for Seismology**, not the first observatory.
xa: NCS is attached to **MoES**.
The National Seismological Network has **160 observatories**.
MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**".

n57bb12d921d.s: RISEQ, the earthquake-related app of the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is now known by which name?
n57bb12d921d.x: The MoES app RISEQ is now called “Bhookamp.” IndiaQuake is the public-alert app of the National Centre for Seismology.
n57bb12d921d.tq: Discriminate between two similarly themed earthquake applications.
xs: The MoES app **RISEQ** is now "**Bhookamp**" — option **(1)**.
**IndiaQuake** is the separate **public alerts** app.
xa: NCS (New Delhi) is an attached office of **MoES**.
First observatory: **Alipore, Calcutta (1898)**.
NCS detects Indian quakes of **M 3.0+**.

n03e85bdbcab.s: India developed its Tsunami Early Warning System after which event?
n03e85bdbcab.x: India built its Tsunami Early Warning System after the 2004 Sumatra earthquake and tsunami.
n03e85bdbcab.tq: Match the warning-system initiative with the triggering disaster.
xs: India's **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra quake** — option **(3)**.
**Bhuj 2001** led to the **DM Act 2005** and **NDMA** instead.
xa: Tsunamis need **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
Over **80%** come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Tohoku (2011)**: tsunami and **Fukushima**.

naffdcc80c1f.s: Which combination of conditions is most conducive to the generation of a tsunami?
o: Magnitude below 5.0, deep focus and horizontal movement only
Magnitude above 6.5, shallow focus and vertical uplift of the sea floor
Volcanic ash fall without any displacement of water
Deep continental earthquake and subsidence of an inland basin
naffdcc80c1f.x: A tsunami generally requires an earthquake of magnitude greater than 6.5, a focus shallower than approximately 70 km and vertical uplift of the sea floor.
naffdcc80c1f.tq: Apply the necessary-condition test instead of relying on magnitude alone.
xs: A tsunami needs **M > 6.5**, a **shallow focus** and **vertical seafloor uplift** — option **(2)**.
The focus must be shallower than **~70 km**.
Horizontal movement or a deep focus will not do — option (1) wrong.
xa: Over **80%** of tsunamis come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
**Kamchatka (Aug 2025)**: **M 8.8** megathrust quake caused only a **limited tsunami**.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** was built after the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

n46457019ddd.s: Which of the following States or Union Territories has no area in Zone V?
n46457019ddd.x: Andhra Pradesh has no area in Zone V. Assam, Bihar and Jammu and Kashmir are identified as having areas in Zone V.
n46457019ddd.tq: Use the exception-based regional comparison to identify the outlier.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** has **no area in Zone V** — option **(3)** (APPSC **2024**).
**Assam, Bihar and J&K** do have Zone V areas.
AP lies mostly in **Zones II and III** (low to moderate risk).
xa: **Visakhapatnam** = Zone II; **Vijayawada** = Zone III.
Reservoir-triggered tremors possible near **Nagarjuna Sagar, Srisailam and Polavaram**.
Old **Eastern Ghats** faults can also trigger tremors.

n506d18ee73d.s: The M 8.8 megathrust earthquake off Kamchatka in August 2025 was notable because it:
o: Produced a tsunami that completely inundated the Pacific coast
Occurred on the Caracas strike-slip boundary
n506d18ee73d.x: Despite its M 8.8 megathrust magnitude, the Kamchatka earthquake caused only a limited tsunami.
n506d18ee73d.tq: Focus on the unusual consequence of the event rather than inferring impact solely from magnitude.
xs: The **M 8.8** Kamchatka megathrust quake (**Aug 2025**) caused only a **limited tsunami** — option **(1)**.
**M 4.4** was the **Koraput-Jeypore** quake; **Caracas** lies on a **strike-slip** boundary — options (3), (4) wrong.
xa: Tsunamis need **M > 6.5**, focus shallower than **~70 km**, **vertical seafloor uplift**.
Over **80%** come from **megathrust subduction** quakes.
The **Tsunami Early Warning System** followed the **2004 Sumatra** quake.

nbca76e0a2f2.s: The earthquakes associated with mid-oceanic ridges are generally:
nbca76e0a2f2.x: Mid-oceanic ridge earthquakes are generally shallow and milder, reflecting activity at divergent plate boundaries.
nbca76e0a2f2.tq: Use the depth-and-severity comparison among the major earthquake belts.
xs: Mid-oceanic ridge quakes are **shallow, milder** — option **(4)**.
The ridges are **divergent** settings, not collision zones.
xa: Ranking: **Circum-Pacific** (most) → **Alpine-Himalayan** → **mid-oceanic ridges**.
**Mid-Atlantic belt** example: **Iceland**.
Tsunamis need a focus shallower than **~70 km** and **vertical seafloor uplift**.

n0e3becf457d.s: A large, often dome-shaped mass of granite occurring at great depth and exposed after denudation is called:
n0e3becf457d.x: A batholith is a huge mass of granite emplaced at depth. It may become exposed after denudation removes the overlying rocks.
n0e3becf457d.tq: Identify the intrusive landform from its scale and depth.
xs: A huge dome-shaped **granite** mass cooled deep in the crust is a **batholith** — option **(3)**.
It forms **mountain cores** and is **exposed after denudation**.
**Sill** = horizontal sheet; **lopolith** = saucer; **phacolith** = wavy, lens-shaped mass.
xa: Intrusive bodies form from magma that **cools inside the crust**.
The **Ladakh Magmatic Arc** went through a **batholith phase**.
**Laccolith**: dome with a **flat base**, fed by a pipe.

n38b5eb5e6cd.s: The first stage in the process of denudation is:
n38b5eb5e6cd.x: Denudation proceeds through weathering, then mass wasting or erosion, transportation and finally deposition.
xa: Denudation agents: **water** (most powerful), **wind**, **ice**, **gravity**.
**Mass wasting** = downslope movement under **gravity** = landslide (**APPSC 2019**).
Weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.

n372dc901c39.s: Rainwater containing carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid. This process, which dissolves limestone and stores carbon as bicarbonate, is called
n372dc901c39.x: Carbonation occurs when carbon dioxide in rainwater forms carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone and converts carbon into bicarbonate.
n372dc901c39.tq: Link the chemical agent and the affected rock to identify the process.
xs: CO2 in rain forms **carbonic acid** that dissolves **limestone**, storing carbon as **bicarbonate** — this is **carbonation**, option **(3)**.
**Solution** is plain dissolving of soluble minerals (**rock salt**, **gypsum**), with no acid formed.
**Oxidation** is rusting of **iron minerals**; **hydration** is minerals absorbing water and **swelling**.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** (anhydrite → gypsum) vs **hydrolysis** (feldspar → clay) — a frequent trap pair.
**Hydrolysis**: muscovite → **vermiculite** (**APPSC 2024**).
Chemical weathering is **fastest in hot, wet climates**.
Oxidation gives **red and yellow soils**.

n7d11a5d18d2.s: Which one of the following correctly describes hydration in weathering?
o: Absorption of water by minerals causing them to swell
Dissolution of soluble minerals in water
Reaction of water with silicate minerals to form clay
n7d11a5d18d2.x: Hydration is the absorption of water by minerals, causing them to swell; conversion of anhydrite to gypsum is an example.
n7d11a5d18d2.tq: Separate hydration from hydrolysis by focusing on swelling rather than chemical replacement.
xs: **Hydration** = **absorption of water by minerals causing them to swell** — option **(1)** is correct.
Example: **anhydrite → gypsum**.
Dissolving soluble minerals is **solution**; rusting of iron minerals is **oxidation**; water reacting with silicates to form clay is **hydrolysis**.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** = swelling; **hydrolysis** = reaction (**feldspar → clay**, muscovite → **vermiculite**).
**Carbonation**: carbonic acid dissolves **limestone**, carbon stored as **bicarbonate**.
**Physical weathering** involves no chemical change: **frost wedging**, **exfoliation**, **salt crystal growth**.

n4b9a24c04c6.s: Muscovite changes into vermiculite when its potassium is replaced by hydronium. This is an example of
n4b9a24c04c6.x: The replacement of potassium in muscovite by hydronium is a hydrolysis reaction.
n4b9a24c04c6.tq: Use the specific mineral transformation as the identifying clue.
xs: Muscovite's potassium replaced by **hydronium** to form **vermiculite** is **hydrolysis** — option **(3)** is correct (**APPSC 2024**).
Hydrolysis is water **reacting** with silicate minerals; the other example is **feldspar → clay**.
**Hydration** is only absorption of water and swelling (**anhydrite → gypsum**); **solution** dissolves rock salt and gypsum.
**Biological weathering** is done by roots, burrowing animals, lichens and micro-organisms.
xa: ⚠ **Hydration** = swelling; **hydrolysis** = reaction — the classic confusable pair.
**Carbonation**: CO2 + rain → **carbonic acid** → dissolves limestone.
**Oxidation**: iron minerals rust → **red, yellow soils**.

n9205cb13ecd.x: Weathering is fastest in hot, wet climates.
xa: Physical weathering examples: **frost wedging**, heating and cooling (**exfoliation**), **salt crystal growth**.
Rainforest soils are poor because heavy rain **leaches** nutrients and dead matter decays fast.
Denudation: **weathering → mass wasting/erosion → transportation → deposition**.

nb233565736c.s: Exfoliation domes are commonly formed by
nb233565736c.x: Exfoliation domes develop through onion-like peeling of granite, commonly associated with weathering and pressure or temperature effects.
nb233565736c.tq: Identify the weathering landform from its distinctive surface appearance and rock type.
xs: **Exfoliation domes** form by **onion-like peeling of granite** — option **(1)** is correct.
Peeling comes from **heating and cooling** — a form of **physical weathering**.
**Rotational slipping of saturated soil** is a **slump**, a mass-wasting type, not a weathering landform.
xa: **Tors** = granite **block piles**.
**Block disintegration** = breaking along **joints** due to temperature change.
Other physical weathering: **frost wedging**, **salt crystal growth**.
Denudation agents: **water** (most powerful), wind, ice, gravity.

ncadc0ab139e.s: A very slow downslope movement of material, caused by repeated wetting-drying or heating-cooling, is called:
ncadc0ab139e.x: Creep is a very slow movement that may result from repeated wetting and drying or heating and cooling; rockfall is the free fall of rocks from cliffs.
xa: ⚠ **Slump** = rotational slip on a curved surface; **creep** = very slow.
**Debris flow / mudflow** is the fast type — water-soil-rock mix after heavy rain or snowmelt.
After rainfall, **earthquakes** are the next trigger.
Most at risk: **Himalaya and North-East**.

n0be165eb461.s: In India, the principal trigger of mass wasting is rainfall, followed next by earthquakes. The regions most at risk are the
o: Eastern coastal plain and Malwa plateau
n0be165eb461.x: The southwest monsoon makes rainfall the main trigger of mass wasting in India, while earthquakes are the next major trigger. The Himalaya and North-East are particularly vulnerable.
n0be165eb461.tq: Link the trigger sequence with the high-risk physiographic regions.
xs: The regions most at risk of mass wasting are the **Himalaya and North-East** — option **(3)** is correct.
The main trigger is **rainfall** from the **SW monsoon**, followed by **earthquakes**.
xa: Conditions: slopes above **30 degrees**, weak/fractured rock, bare slopes.
Types: **rockfall**, **slide**, **slump**, **debris flow/mudflow**, **creep**.
**Freeze-thaw** also breaks rocks in the **high Himalaya**.
Saturated **clay and silt** make slopes landslide-prone.

o: Residual island-hills of arid and semi-arid regions
Volcanic cones found only in humid regions
Submerged hills formed by coral growth
Glacial deposits arranged in elongated ridges
n908c72b4648.x: Inselbergs are residual island-hills characteristic of arid and semi-arid regions, formed through desert erosion by wind and sheet-wash.
n908c72b4648.tq: Match the landform with its climatic setting and erosional origin.
xs: **Inselbergs** are **residual island-hills of arid and semi-arid regions** — option **(1)** is correct.
They form by **desert erosion** — **wind + sheet-wash**.
xa: ⚠ **Monadnocks** = resistant residual hills on a **peneplain** (Davis cycle).
**Tors** = granite block piles.
**Wind erosion** dominates the **Thar**.

n6be1f318f8e.s: The Peninsular plateau of India is regarded as an old peneplain that has been
o: Converted entirely into a glacial landscape
n6be1f318f8e.x: India’s Peninsular plateau is an old peneplain, although parts of it have undergone rejuvenation.
n6be1f318f8e.tq: Test the precise qualification attached to the Peninsular plateau.
xs: India's **Peninsular plateau** is an old **peneplain**, **rejuvenated in places** — option **(4)** is correct.
A peneplain is the low, almost flat end-surface of the **Davis** cycle.
xa: Peneplains carry resistant residual hills = **monadnocks**.
Davis stages: **youth → maturity → old age** (**1899**).
Peninsular India is dominated by **residual (in-situ)** soils; North India by **transported** soils.

n41884e2ad26.s: Which of the following is associated with the end stage of Davis's geographical cycle?
o: A deeply incised youthful gorge only
A near-flat peneplain with residual monadnocks
A coastal lagoon formed by a bar
n41884e2ad26.x: The cycle is envisaged as ending in a nearly flat peneplain containing residual monadnocks.
n41884e2ad26.tq: Identify the characteristic end product of a geomorphic cycle.
xs: The Davis cycle ends in **a near-flat peneplain with residual monadnocks** — option **(2)** is correct.
Stages: **youth → maturity → old age**; the peneplain is the **old-age** end-surface.
xa: **W.M. Davis (1899)**: landscape = **structure + process + stage**.
**Penck**: uplift and erosion act together; **parallel slope retreat**.
India's **Peninsular plateau** = old peneplain, rejuvenated in places.

na816c835b28.s: Who stressed that uplift and erosion act simultaneously in landform development?
na816c835b28.x: Walther Penck stressed uplift and erosion acting together; Davis's cycle emphasised structure, process and time.
xa: ⚠ **Davis** = time-stages (**youth → maturity → old age**); **Penck** = uplift vs erosion, **parallel slope retreat**.
Davis cycle ends in a **peneplain** with **monadnocks**.
**Inselbergs** = residual island-hills of arid regions.

n9c985751589.s: Which soil is characteristically associated with cold taiga regions and is thin, acidic, leached and poor in humus?
n9c985751589.x: Podzol develops under cold taiga or boreal conifer forests and is generally thin, acidic, strongly leached and humus-poor.
n9c985751589.tq: Use the climate–vegetation setting to identify the soil.
xs: Thin, acidic, leached, humus-poor soil of the **cold taiga** is **podzol** — option **(4)** is correct.
Podzol forms under **boreal conifer forests**.
**Terra rossa** = Mediterranean, over limestone; **chernozem** = temperate grasslands, black and humus-rich; **laterite** = hot, heavy-rain tropics.
xa: ⚠ **Podzol** = cold taiga; **Chernozem** = temperate grassland; **Laterite** = hot heavy-rain tropics.
**Chernozem** belts: **steppes, prairies**.
**Oxisols** = long-stable equatorial-tropical surfaces (**APPSC 2019**).

n4b303e81dd3.s: Terra rossa soil is associated with:
n4b303e81dd3.x: Terra rossa develops in Mediterranean regions over limestone; chernozem is of temperate grasslands, laterite of hot wet tropics and oxisols of stable equatorial surfaces.
xa: **Podzol** = cold taiga (boreal conifer forests); thin, acidic, leached.
Laterite: leaching of **silica and lime** leaves **iron and aluminium oxides**; acidic.
Chernozem is **black and humus-rich**.

n42cfa17ac2e.s: Which of the following is an active factor in soil formation?
n42cfa17ac2e.x: Climate and biological activity are active factors in soil formation; parent material and topography are passive factors.
xa: Biological activity = **vegetation** and **micro-organisms**.
AP soil-forming factors (APSES line): **climate, altitude and bedrock composition**.
AP parent rocks: **granite, gneiss, basalt**, sedimentary rocks.

n1150d8c62fb.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about soil formation in Andhra Pradesh?
o: Bedrock composition has no influence on soil formation.
Climate and altitude influence soil formation.
Uneven rainfall and excessive heat contribute to the character of Andhra Pradesh soils.
River silt of the Godavari, Krishna and Pennar is among the parent materials of Andhra Pradesh soils.
n1150d8c62fb.x: Bedrock composition does influence soil formation, along with climate and altitude. The other statements are correct.
xa: AP soils are mainly a mix of **sand, silt and clay**.
Parent rocks: **granite, gneiss, basalt**, sedimentary rocks.
Climate contrast: **coastal rain** vs **Rayalaseema aridity**.
AP shares: **red ~60%**, **black ~25%**, deltaic alluvium **~6%**, laterite **~1%**.

ncf451dcb0c0.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the five classical factors of soil formation?
ncf451dcb0c0.x: The five classical factors are parent material, climate, relief or topography, organisms and time. Latitude is not included in this five-factor list.
ncf451dcb0c0.tq: Recall the standard five-factor framework and identify the extra term.
xs: **Latitude** is not one of the soil-forming factors — option **(1)** is correct.
The five factors: **parent rock**, **climate**, **relief**, **organisms** and **time**.
xa: **Active** factors = **climate** and **biological activity** (APPSC G1 2024).
**Passive** factors = parent material, **topography (relief)**, time.
AP line: **climate, altitude and bedrock composition**.

n0cc001f0f8b.s: Which soil particle has the highest water-holding capacity?
n0cc001f0f8b.x: Clay has the highest water-holding capacity, followed by silt and then sand, which drains readily.
xa: Clay and silt get **saturated** → landslide-prone; **sand drains well**.
Clay **binds organic carbon**; sandy soils lose it by **leaching**.

nc160989a170.x: Residual soils form where the parent rock weathered and are called sedentary soils (APPSC 2018).
xa: Transported (ex-situ) soils are moved by **rivers, wind, ice**.
**Alluvium** covers **45.6%** of India.
Peninsular plateau = old **peneplain**, rejuvenated in places.

n320a01d1b62.s: Transported alluvial soils, deposited mainly by rivers, cover approximately what share of India's area?
n320a01d1b62.x: Alluvium, a transported (ex-situ) soil found mainly in North India, covers about 45.6% of India. About 25% is the share of black soil in AP's cultivated land, about 66% is the older red-soil share for AP, and 10.5% is a distractor.
n320a01d1b62.tq: Alluvium = largest soil group of India, ~45.6%.
xs: **Alluvium** covers about **45.6%** of India — option **(1)** is correct.
It is a **transported (ex-situ)** soil, found mainly in **North India**.
**About 25%** is AP's black-soil share of cultivated land, and **66%** is the older red-soil figure for AP.
xa: Transported soils are moved by **rivers, wind, ice**.
**Residual (in-situ)** = **sedentary** soils (**APPSC 2018**), mainly in Peninsular India.
AP deltaic alluvium **~6%** (older notes: **5%**).

n6701da7b559.s: Which soil accounts for the largest share (about 60%) of cultivated land in Andhra Pradesh?
n6701da7b559.x: Red soil covers about 60% of cultivated land in Andhra Pradesh; black soil about one-fourth and laterite about 1%.
xa: Deltaic alluvium **~6%**; hill (skeletal) **~5%**.
⚠ Older notes: red **66%**, alluvium **5%**.
AP parent rocks: **granite, gneiss, basalt**, sedimentary rocks.

n5caeccc7f12.s: Which one of the following is the correct sequence of dominant river work from the upper course to the lower course?
o: Vertical erosion — lateral erosion and transport — deposition
Transport — vertical erosion — deposition and uplift
n5caeccc7f12.x: The upper course is dominated by vertical erosion, the middle course by lateral erosion and transport, and the lower course by deposition.
n5caeccc7f12.tq: Arrange river processes according to the downstream course sequence.
xs: From source to mouth the dominant work is **vertical erosion — lateral erosion and transport — deposition** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Upper (youth)**: vertical erosion, steep gradient; **middle (maturity)**: lateral erosion + transport; **lower (old age)**: deposition, gentle gradient.
xa: Upper-course features: **V-shaped valleys, gorges, canyons**, waterfalls, rapids, potholes.
Middle course: wider valleys, **meanders**, floodplains begin.
Lower course: broad floodplains, **levees**, **oxbow lakes**, braided channels, **deltas/estuaries**.
**APPSC 2022**: a **canyon** forms in the upper course.

n6ff19c7d9cf.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the middle course of a river?
o: Lateral erosion and transport are important processes.
Vertical erosion is the sole dominant work.
Valleys become wider than in the upper course.
n6ff19c7d9cf.x: Vertical erosion is not the sole dominant process in the middle course, which is marked by lateral erosion, transport, wider valleys and meanders.
xa: Floodplains **begin** in the middle course.
Meander: **outer bend** eroded (cliff, concave); **inner slip-off** side built up (convex).
Lower course = **deposition**, gentle gradient.

n9eeaf804150.s: A canyon is formed predominantly in which course of a river?
n9eeaf804150.x: A canyon is an upper-course feature produced by strong vertical erosion in a river's youthful stage.
n9eeaf804150.tq: Associate the landform with the river stage in which vertical erosion dominates.
xs: A **canyon** forms in the **upper course** — option **(3)** (**APPSC 2022**).
The upper (youth) course does **vertical erosion** on a steep gradient; floodplain, alluvial fan and delta do not form there.
xa: Canyon = **wider at the top**, step-like sides, in **horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks**.
**Gorge** = almost the same width top and bottom, forms in **hard rocks**.
Classic example: **Grand Canyon** (USA), cut by the **Colorado River**.

n66979abec82.s: A V-shaped valley develops through the sequence of:
o: Cirques, arêtes and horns produced by glacial plucking
Rills, gullies and valleys produced mainly by vertical erosion
Meanders, oxbow lakes and deltas produced only by lateral erosion
Dunes, beaches and spits produced mainly by marine deposition
n66979abec82.x: Rills enlarge into gullies and then valleys through predominantly vertical erosion, producing a V-shaped valley.
n66979abec82.tq: Recognise the erosional sequence leading to a named valley form.
xs: A V-shaped valley develops as **rills → gullies → valleys** by **vertical erosion** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a feature of the **upper (youth)** course with its steep gradient.
Meanders, oxbow lakes and deltas belong to the **middle and lower** courses.
xa: **Gorges and canyons** are forms of the V-shaped valley.
Dense gully network = **badland** topography.
**Potholes** and **waterfalls** also form in the upper course.

ngeneral-geography-5-23.s: Mountains are formed by which combination of processes?
o: River, glacier, tectonic and karst processes
ngeneral-geography-5-23.x: Mountains form by folding, faulting, volcanism and erosion. Deposition and marine processes form plains.
ngeneral-geography-5-23.tq: Recall the processes behind each landform.
n: Mountains are formed by folding, erosion, faulting, and volcanism. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: Mountains are formed by **folding, erosion, faulting and volcanism** — option **(1)**.
**Deposition, erosion and marine processes** form **plains**; **uplift, volcanism, erosion and deposition** form **plateaus**; **river, glacier, tectonic and karst** processes form **valleys**.
xa: Major mountains: **Himalayas**, **Andes**, **Alps**, **Rockies**, **Sierra Nevada**, **Aravallis**.
Major plateaus: **Tibetan**, **Deccan**, **Pamir**, **Patagonia**, the **Meseta**.
Major plains: **Indo-Gangetic Plain**, the **Great Plains**.

n969848c66c3.s: Coastal landforms such as cliffs, arches and stacks are formed by:
n969848c66c3.x: Cliffs, caves, arches, stacks and beaches are coastal landforms made by waves, currents and tides.
xa: Desert landforms: **dunes**, **yardangs**, **mushroom rocks**, **playas**, **loess**.
Coastal landforms also include **caves**, **beaches**, **spits**, **lagoons**.
Karst landforms form by **solution of limestone**.

ngeneral-geography-5-27.s: Valleys are formed by which combination of agents or processes?
o: River, glacier, tectonic and karst processes
Uplift, deposition, lava accumulation and denudation
Wind erosion, wave erosion, tides and currents
Folding, faulting, volcanism and marine processes
ngeneral-geography-5-27.x: Valleys are carved by rivers, glaciers, tectonic faulting and karst solution.
ngeneral-geography-5-27.tq: Recall the processes behind each landform.
n: Valleys are formed by rivers, glaciers, tectonic processes, and karst processes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: Valleys are formed by **river, glacier, tectonic and karst processes** — option **(1)**.
Valley types: **V-shaped**, **U-shaped**, **rift**, **hanging** and **blind** valleys.
**Wind erosion** forms **desert** landforms; **waves, currents and tides** form **coastal** landforms.
xa: A **canyon** forms in the **upper course** (APPSC **2022**).
**Sea level** is the **ultimate base level**; lakes and dams are local base levels.
**Gorges and canyons** are forms of the **V-shaped valley** (APPSC **2018** trap).

ngeneral-geography-5-31.s: Arêtes, horns, hanging valleys and moraines are formed by:
ngeneral-geography-5-31.x: Arêtes, horns, U-shaped and hanging valleys and moraines all come from glacial erosion and deposition.
n: Arêtes are glacial landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Horns are glacial landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
U-shaped valleys are formed by glacial erosion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is left above a main valley by a tributary glacier. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Moraine is a glacial landform. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glacial erosion forms cirques or corries. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glacial deposition forms moraines. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form U-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form arêtes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form horns. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form U-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form hanging valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Desert landforms** form by **wind erosion and deposition**.
**Karst landforms** form by the **solution of limestone**.
**Tectonic landforms** (rift valleys, horsts, grabens) form by **faulting, folding and crustal movement**.

ngeneral-geography-5-35.s: Sinkholes, dolines, stalactites, stalagmites and blind valleys are ____ landforms.
ngeneral-geography-5-35.x: Sinkholes, dolines, caves, stalactites, stalagmites and blind valleys are all karst landforms.
n: Sinkholes are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Dolines are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Caves are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Stalactites are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Stalagmites are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Blind valleys are karst landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Karst or groundwater forms sinkholes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Karst or groundwater forms stalactites. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Blind valleys** are also listed among **valley** types.
**Coastal** caves form by **waves**, not solution.
**Glacial** landforms: **cirques**, **arêtes**, **horns**, **moraine**.

n93ebfc7a393.s: Stream capture, also called river piracy, occurs when:
o: A tributary changes from a dendritic to an annular pattern
A lake drains through a newly formed coastal delta
A river deposits sediment until its mouth is completely blocked
A stream erodes headward, breaches a neighbouring basin and diverts its upper waters
n93ebfc7a393.x: In stream capture, headward erosion allows one stream to breach the divide of a neighbouring basin and divert the upper course of the captured stream.
n93ebfc7a393.tq: Test the process sequence: headward erosion, basin breach and diversion.
xs: Stream capture (**river piracy**): a **stream erodes headward**, breaks into a **neighbouring basin** and **diverts its upper waters** — option **(4)**.
Tributary pattern changes, sediment blocking a mouth or a lake draining through a delta are not capture — capture works by **headward erosion** across a **drainage divide**.
xa: **Drainage divide** = ridge separating basins; sharp in young relief (**Himalaya**), faint on old plateaus.
**Base level** = lowest level a river can erode to; **sea level** = ultimate base level.
**Graded profile** = smooth concave long profile; erosion = deposition.

naffcb333f8f.s: A graded river profile is one in which:
o: The river flows upward from its mouth to its source
The river consists entirely of waterfalls and rapids
The long profile is smoothly concave and erosion and deposition are broadly balanced
Deposition has completely stopped along the whole channel
naffcb333f8f.x: A graded profile is a smooth, generally concave long profile in which erosion and deposition are sufficiently balanced over time.
naffcb333f8f.tq: Distinguish the equilibrium profile from absolute absence of erosion or deposition.
xs: A **graded profile** is a **smooth concave** long profile where **erosion and deposition are balanced** — option **(3)**.
It is not a channel of only waterfalls and rapids (those are **upper-course** features), nor one where deposition has stopped — erosion **equals** deposition.
xa: **Base level**: lowest level a river can erode to; **sea level** is the ultimate base level.
**Lakes and dams** act as **local base levels**.
**Stream capture**: headward erosion diverts a neighbour's upper waters.

n2427126f262.s: Which one of the following represents the ultimate base level of a river?
o: The upper limit of the floodplain
The highest point of the river basin
n2427126f262.x: Base level is the lowest level to which a river can erode, and sea level is regarded as the ultimate base level.
n2427126f262.tq: Apply the definition of the lowest attainable erosional level.
xs: **Sea level** is the **ultimate base level** — option **(2)** is correct.
Base level = the **lowest level a river can erode to**.
**Lakes and dams** are only **local** base levels; a drainage divide is a ridge between basins.
xa: **Graded profile**: smooth concave long profile; erosion = deposition.
**Drainage divide**: sharp in the **Himalaya**, faint on old plateaus.
Lower course has a **gentle gradient** and deposits.

nc94e10772cc.s: An estuary is best described as:
o: A distributary network separated completely from the sea
A partly enclosed river mouth with a free connection to the sea
A river valley cut only by glacial erosion
A closed lake formed behind a sand bar
nc94e10772cc.x: An estuary is a partly enclosed river mouth that retains a free connection with the sea and functions as an ecotone.
nc94e10772cc.tq: Discriminate between the precise definitions of delta, lagoon and estuary.
xs: An estuary is **a partly enclosed river mouth with a free connection to the sea** — option **(2)**.
It is an **ecotone**, a drowned **funnel-shaped** mouth without a delta.
xa: Most estuaries formed in the **Holocene** sea-level rise.
Examples: **Narmada**, **Tapi**.
**Pulicat** is a **saltwater lagoon** on the AP-TN border.

ngeneral-geography-5-40.s: Which of the following combinations consists entirely of young fold mountains?
ngeneral-geography-5-40.x: The Alps, Andes and Rockies are all young fold mountains. The Appalachians, Urals, Pennines and Aravallis are old.
ngeneral-geography-5-40.tq: Discriminate young from old fold mountains.
n: The Alps are young fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Andes are young fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Rockies are young fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Aravallis are old fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Appalachians are old fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Urals are old fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Pennines are old fold mountains. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
The Salt Range is a block mountain range. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: The **Alps, Andes and Rockies** are all **young fold mountains** — option **(1)**.
Each other option mixes in an **older or non-fold** range — **Appalachians**, **Urals**, **Pennines**, **Aravallis** or the **Salt Range**.
Mountains form by **folding**, **erosion**, **faulting** and **volcanism**.
xa: Major mountains listed: **Himalayas**, **Andes**, **Alps**, **Rockies**, **Sierra Nevada**, **Aravallis**.
**Tectonic landforms** include **fold mountains**, **rift valleys**, **horsts** and **grabens**.

nf5bbe1887b1.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about gorges and canyons?
o: Gorges generally form in hard rocks.
A gorge is an extended form of a canyon.
A canyon is regarded as a variant of a gorge.
Canyons generally form in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks.
nf5bbe1887b1.x: The relationship is reversed: a canyon is a variant of a gorge, not the other way round.
xa: Both gorges and canyons are **V-shaped valleys**.
Canyon is **wider at the top**, with **step-like** sides; gorge has almost the same width at top and bottom.
**Dihang gorge** — the Brahmaputra enters India here.

n00640400ae8.s: The Brahmaputra enters India through the Dihang gorge, which is associated with the:
o: Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa
Colorado River canyon in the United States
n00640400ae8.x: The Dihang gorge is associated with the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa, where the Brahmaputra enters India.
n00640400ae8.tq: Separate similarly named Indian and international canyon or gorge features by river and location.
xs: The **Dihang gorge** is linked with the **Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon near Namcha Barwa** — option **(2)**.
The Brahmaputra enters **India** at the Dihang gorge in **Arunachal**; it is called the "**Grand Canyon of the Tsangpo**".
The **Colorado River** cut the **Grand Canyon** in the **USA**; the **Chambal** is a badland region.
xa: **Chambal valley ravines** = India's classic **badland** (**APPSC 2022**).
**Chos of Hoshiarpur** (Punjab) = gullied badland.
⚠ Canyon = **variant of a gorge** (**APPSC 2018**).

n39a54a97c97.s: A large pothole formed below a waterfall is called a:
n39a54a97c97.x: A large pothole below a waterfall is a plunge pool; potholes are drilled by rock fragments whirled by eddies.
xa: **Incised (entrenched) meanders**: cut deep into hard rock when **uplift rejuvenates** the river.
**V-shaped valley**: rills → gullies → valleys by vertical erosion.
Upper-course features also include **gorges, canyons** and **rapids**.

ncf785af7f38.s: Incised or entrenched meanders are most likely to form when:
o: A river is diverted into a newly formed coastal lagoon
Uplift rejuvenates a river and its meanders cut deeply into hard rock
A river loses all its gradient and deposits silt in a shallow sea
Strong tides reverse the direction of river flow
ncf785af7f38.x: When uplift rejuvenates a river, renewed vertical erosion may incise pre-existing meanders deeply into resistant bedrock.
ncf785af7f38.tq: Infer the landform from the interaction of rejuvenation, uplift and vertical erosion.
xs: **Incised (entrenched) meanders** form when **uplift rejuvenates a river** and its meanders **cut deep into hard rock** — option **(2)**.
Rejuvenation renews **vertical erosion**, so the old meander loops are entrenched.
xa: **River terraces** also form when a stream cuts **vertically into its own floodplain**.
**Unpaired terraces** occur in areas of **slow uplift**.
Peninsular plateau = old peneplain, **rejuvenated** in places.

n7d70b89252b.s: A dense network of gullies, formed from merging and deepening rills, produces ____ topography.
n7d70b89252b.x: Overland flow gathers into rills, the rills merge and deepen into gullies, and a dense gully network produces badland topography.
xa: **Gully** = water-worn channel of **semi-arid** areas.
**Chambal valley ravines** = India's classic badland.
**Chos of Hoshiarpur** (Punjab) = gullied badland.

nb5283cedec5.s: In a meandering river, which of the following correctly describes the two sides of a bend?
o: The outer bend is erosional and concave, while the inner slip-off side is depositional and convex.
The outer bend is depositional and convex, while the inner bend is erosional and concave.
The outer bend is depositional and straight, while the inner bend is erosional and steep.
Both bends are erosional and concave.
nb5283cedec5.x: The outer, concave bend experiences erosion and forms a cliff, whereas the inner, convex slip-off side receives deposition.
nb5283cedec5.tq: Use the reversed outer-bend and inner-bend comparison as the key distinction.
xs: The **outer bend is erosional and concave** (cliff); the **inner slip-off side is depositional and convex** — option **(1)**.
The other options reverse or confuse the two sides of the bend.
xa: Meanders develop in the **middle (maturity)** course with **lateral erosion**.
A cut-off meander loop leaves an **oxbow lake**.
**Incised meanders** cut deep into hard rock when uplift rejuvenates the river.

n9bffa0f3dc3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the conditions for delta formation?
o: The river must carry a heavy load of sediment.
The sea near the river mouth should preferably be shallow.
Strong tides and currents favour the accumulation of a delta.
The river flow should be slow and steady enough for silt to settle.
n9bffa0f3dc3.x: Strong tides and currents generally remove sediment and do not favour delta accumulation.
xa: Not all rivers form deltas.
West-flowing Deccan rivers form **estuaries** — mainly due to **steep gradient**.
Largest delta: **Ganga-Brahmaputra**.

nb0c8cfb9131.s: The Sundarbans are associated with which of the following?
o: The Narmada estuary and the world's largest freshwater lake
The Tiber delta and the world's largest coniferous forest
The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta and the world's largest mangrove forest
The Mississippi delta and the world's largest coral reef
nb0c8cfb9131.x: The Ganga-Brahmaputra delta includes the Sundarbans, recognised as the world's largest mangrove forest.
nb0c8cfb9131.tq: Connect the delta, regional name and ecological feature in one precise association.
xs: The **Sundarbans** are in the **Ganga-Brahmaputra delta** — the **world's largest mangrove forest** — option **(3)**.
The Ganga-Brahmaputra is the **largest delta**; it is an **arcuate** type.
**Narmada** forms an estuary; the **Tiber** delta is cuspate; the **Mississippi** delta is bird's foot.
xa: Seven major deltas incl. Ganga-Brahmaputra = about **57%** of the world's sinking delta area (Apr 2026).
Deltas cover **1%** of land but hold **~6%** of people.
Main causes of sinking: **groundwater extraction** + **reduced silt**.

ne8625710cac.s: Which one of the following drainage patterns develops over relatively uniform rock and has a tree-like appearance?
ne8625710cac.x: Dendritic drainage develops over relatively uniform rock and resembles the branching form of a tree; it is characteristic of the northern plains.
ne8625710cac.tq: Use the controlling rock condition and visual pattern together.
xs: Tree-like drainage over **uniform rock** is **dendritic** — option **(3)**.
Example: rivers of the **northern plains**.
**Radial** flows outward from a central high; **trellis** is on folded rocks; **annular** is on eroded domes.
xa: **Trellis**: tributaries parallel, joining at right angles — **Appalachians**.
**Rectangular**: right-angle bends along **joints and faults**.
**Centripetal**: inward to a depression — **Loktak**.

nf799cc707ff.s: The trellis drainage pattern is generally associated with:
o: A central depression into which all streams flow
Folded rocks, where tributaries join the main streams at right angles
An eroded dome with concentric rings of hard and soft rocks
A central high from which all streams flow outward
nf799cc707ff.x: Trellis drainage develops in folded terrain, with tributaries commonly joining the main streams at right angles; the Appalachians provide an example.
nf799cc707ff.tq: Distinguish drainage patterns by their structural control and tributary angle.
xs: **Trellis** drainage forms on **folded rocks**, with **tributaries joining at right angles** — option **(2)**.
Examples: **Appalachians**, old folded belts, old folded Himalaya, **Singhbhum**.
Central depression = **centripetal**; eroded dome = **annular**; central high = **radial**.
xa: ⚠ Trellis (folded rocks) vs **rectangular** (jointed/faulted hard rock) — both show right angles.
**Dendritic** = uniform rock, tree-like.
**Radial**: **Amarkantak** (Narmada, Son, Mahanadi).

nb87a156d769.s: Rectangular drainage is typically controlled by:
o: Joints and faults, producing right-angle bends
A single central volcanic cone only
Uniform unconsolidated alluvium without structural control
nb87a156d769.x: Rectangular drainage develops where joints and faults guide stream courses, producing frequent right-angle bends, especially on joint-controlled plateaus.
nb87a156d769.tq: Match the geometric pattern with the geological control responsible for it.
xs: Rectangular drainage is controlled by **joints and faults, producing right-angle bends** — option **(1)**.
It forms in **jointed/faulted hard rock** — joint-controlled plateaus, jointed **peninsular** rocks.
A drowned **funnel-shaped** mouth is an **estuary**; uniform rock gives **dendritic** drainage.
xa: ⚠ **Trellis** also meets at right angles but on **folded rocks**.
**Radial**: outward from a central high (**Amarkantak**).
**Annular**: eroded domes.

nfd8526eab4e.s: Kolleru is a freshwater lake situated between the:
nfd8526eab4e.x: Kolleru freshwater lake lies between the two major Andhra Pradesh deltas of the Godavari and Krishna.
nfd8526eab4e.tq: Locate the intervening feature between two neighbouring delta systems.
xs: **Kolleru** is a freshwater lake between the **Godavari and Krishna deltas** — option **(1)**.
These are the **two big deltas** that build the AP coastal plain; **Vamsadhara** and **Penna** form only minor deltas.
xa: Kolleru WLS = **308.55 sq km** (2024-25 annexure); older notes say **250 sq km**.
⚠ **Pulicat** = **saltwater lagoon** on the AP-TN border.
Godavari delta = **Konaseema**.

n3b4184a715f.s: Pulicat is best described as a:
o: Saltwater lagoon on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border
Cuspate delta on the Narmada estuary
River island in the Krishna delta
Freshwater lake between the Godavari and Krishna deltas
n3b4184a715f.x: Pulicat is a saltwater lagoon located on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border.
n3b4184a715f.tq: Distinguish the coastal lagoon from the inland freshwater lake and delta features.
xs: **Pulicat** is a **saltwater lagoon on the Andhra Pradesh–Tamil Nadu border** — option **(1)**.
The **freshwater** lake between the Godavari and Krishna deltas is **Kolleru**.
xa: Pulicat lies **well south of the Penna mouth** near Nellore (some notes place it at the Penna mouth).
Kolleru WLS = **308.55 sq km** (older notes: **250 sq km**).
AP coastal plain: **~950 km** long.

n08023ce3e18.s: Which region is classically associated with India's badland topography?
n08023ce3e18.x: The ravines of the Chambal valley in Central India form India's classic badland topography. The Chos of Hoshiarpur in Punjab are another example.
n08023ce3e18.tq: Use the region-specific association to distinguish badlands from coastal, deltaic and saline landscapes.
xs: India's classic **badland** is the **Chambal basin** (Chambal valley ravines) — option **(2)** (**APPSC 2022**).
The **Rann of Kutch**, **Godavari delta** and **western coastal plain** are the distractors usually set against it.
xa: **Chos of Hoshiarpur** (Punjab) = another gullied badland.
Badland = **dense gully network**; gullies form from rills by overland flow.
Gullies are typical of **semi-arid** areas.

ne514a89c51f.s: In the context of depositional activity by Himalayan rivers, which combination is appropriate?
o: Braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees
ne514a89c51f.x: Braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees are depositional features. Terraces are excluded in this classification because they result from vertical down-cutting.
ne514a89c51f.tq: Separate depositional features from erosional features before selecting the combination.
xs: Depositional work of Himalayan rivers: **braided channels, alluvial fans and natural levees** — option **(2)** (**APPSC 2023**).
Waterfalls, rapids, gorges, canyons and potholes are **erosional** upper-course features.
**Terraces** are excluded: they form by **down-cutting** into the floodplain.
xa: **Alluvial fan**: coarse load dropped at the **break of slope**.
**Braided channel**: sand deposits split the channel into many parallel threads.
**Natural levee**: raised banks of sand at channel edges.

nd1b1cf986ad.s: The west-flowing rivers of the Deccan generally form estuaries rather than deltas mainly because they:
o: carry no water during the monsoon season
are affected by exceptionally strong tides throughout their courses
have steep gradients, hard-rock courses and short courses
flow through extensive alluvial plains with very low gradients
nd1b1cf986ad.x: The west-flowing Deccan rivers commonly have steep gradients, hard-rock channels and short courses, conditions that favour estuaries rather than extensive deltas.
nd1b1cf986ad.tq: Link the landform outcome with the controlling relief and river-course conditions.
xs: West-flowing Deccan rivers form estuaries because they **have steep gradients, hard-rock courses and short courses** — option **(3)**.
Deltas need **slow, steady flow**, heavy sediment, a **shallow sea** and weak tides.
xa: Estuarine examples: **Narmada**, **Tapi**.
**Estuary** = partly enclosed river mouth with free connection to the sea (an **ecotone**).
Most estuaries formed in the **Holocene** sea-level rise.

nae132a76ea8.s: A river valley with step-like sides, wider at the top than at the bottom, is a:
nae132a76ea8.x: Step-like sides and greater width at the top describe a canyon, which forms in horizontally bedded sedimentary rocks; gorges form in hard rocks.
xa: Canyon is an **upper-course** feature (**APPSC 2022**).
Both form in the **youth** stage with V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids.
Braided channel: **Brahmaputra**, sandbars called **chars**.

n5195cb2a01e.s: Which of the following is a feature of the old (lower) course of a river?
n5195cb2a01e.x: Oxbow lakes and natural levees belong to the old (lower) course; waterfalls, potholes and rapids are youth (upper) course features.
xa: Old course also has **braided channels**, riverine islands and **deltas**.
Youth course also has **gorges** and **canyons**.
**Oxbow lake** = detached meander loop with stagnant water.

ne1cdbb36b9c.s: Badlands or ravines are characteristically associated with the:
ne1cdbb36b9c.x: The Chambal Valley is noted for badlands or ravines. Chos are the corresponding ravine features associated with Hoshiarpur in Punjab.
ne1cdbb36b9c.tq: Identify the regional landform from its well-known location.
xs: Badlands or ravines are associated with the **Chambal Valley** — option **(4)** (**APPSC 2022**).
Brahmaputra sandbars are **chars**; the **Kashmir Valley** has **Karewas** (lacustrine deposits).
xa: **Chos of Hoshiarpur** (Punjab) = ravines too.
Ganga-Yamuna **Doab** = westernmost Ganga plain.
**Bet land** = flood plain while floodwater stays on it.

neb3f4d3439a.s: Karst topography develops most characteristically in regions underlain by:
neb3f4d3439a.x: Karst landscapes are carved mainly by groundwater dissolving limestone or dolomite.
neb3f4d3439a.tq: Use the rock-type association to identify the landscape-forming process.
xs: Karst forms where groundwater dissolves **limestone or dolomite** — option **(3)**.
Granite/gneiss weather to **red soils** and basalt to **black soils**; they do not form karst.
xa: Named after the **Karst** region on the **Adriatic coast** (Slovenia).
Sequence: **sinkhole → doline → uvala → polje**.
Cave deposits = **speleothems** of **calcium carbonate**.

n9f9227f248b.s: Belum Caves are primarily characterised by:
o: Black limestone with stalactites and stalagmites
n9f9227f248b.x: Belum Caves are developed in black limestone and contain stalactites and stalagmites, reflecting their karst nature.
n9f9227f248b.tq: Identify the cave from its rock type and internal formations.
xs: Belum Caves are **black limestone with stalactites and stalagmites** — option **(4)** is correct.
That makes Belum a **karst** cave — carved by groundwater dissolving limestone.
**Sandstone** and **Buddhist stupas** fit Undavalli and Bojjannakonda, which are rock-cut, not karst.
xa: Belum: **2nd-longest** natural cave system in India.
First discovered **1884** by **Robert Bruce Foote**; mapped by **H.D. Gebauer** (1982-84).
Declared a **Geo-Heritage Site by GSI** (Jun 2025).

n43f560df4d3.s: The main agent of coastal erosion is:
n43f560df4d3.x: Waves are the main agents of coastal erosion, with tides, currents and wind also contributing; glacial ice is not the principal agent.
xa: Processes: **hydraulic action, abrasion (corrasion), attrition**, solution.
Sequence: sea cliff + **wave-cut platform** → sea cave → **arch** → **stack** → stump.
AP: severe erosion at **Uppada** (Kakinada) and the **Krishna coast**.

nc08b586047e.s: Structures built across longshore drift to trap sand are called:
nc08b586047e.x: Groynes are built across longshore drift to trap sand; they are hard defences, like seawalls and breakwaters.
xa: Soft defences: **beach nourishment**, **dune stabilisation**, **mangroves**.
Human causes of erosion: harbours, **sand mining**, dredging, dams.
Spit = sand ridge joined to land at one end.

ndc43a34860e.s: Which one of the following groups consists exclusively of landforms produced by running water?
o: Sand dune, yardang, mushroom rock and loess
Sea cliff, stack, spit and bar
ndc43a34860e.x: Delta, V-valley, gorge and canyon are formed by running water. The other groups represent glacial, marine and aeolian landforms respectively.
ndc43a34860e.tq: Classify the options by matching each landform with its geomorphic agent.
xs: **Delta, V-valley, gorge and canyon** are all made by **running water** — option **(1)**.
Sand dune, yardang, mushroom rock, loess = **wind**; cliff, stack, spit, bar = **waves and currents**; cirque, horn, U-valley, esker = **glacier**.
xa: Running water also makes **levees** and **peneplains**.
Groundwater (solution in limestone): **sinkhole, doline, stalactite, stalagmite**.
**APPSC-G2 2023**: Delta — running water; Cirque — glaciers; Cliffs — waves; Sand dunes — winds.

ngeneral-geography-5-68.s: A valley that ends abruptly where its stream sinks into limestone is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-68.x: A blind valley ends abruptly where its stream sinks underground into limestone.
n: V-shaped valleys occur in the upper and middle river courses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Rift valleys are formed by crustal faulting or divergence. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Blind valleys end abruptly. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Death Valley is a rift-valley example in the USA. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Death Valley is associated with a rift valley. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Tectonic faulting forms rift valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: V-shaped valleys are **narrow**, in **youthful rivers**.
Glaciers **widen and deepen** V-shaped valleys into **U-shaped** ones.
A **hanging valley** has a **waterfall** at its junction.

ngeneral-geography-5-9.s: Which of the following landforms is NOT formed by running water?
ngeneral-geography-5-9.x: A cirque is glacial; deltas, meanders and alluvial fans come from running water.
n: Deltas are formed by erosion, transportation, and deposition processes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Cirques are glacial landforms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Alluvial fans are formed by erosion, transportation, and deposition processes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms deltas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form cirques. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms alluvial fans. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms meanders. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Running water also forms **V-shaped valleys**, **gorges**, **canyon**, **levee**, **peneplain**.
APPSC-G2 **2023** matched: **Delta – running water**, **Cirque – glaciers**, **Cliffs – waves and currents**, **Sand dunes – winds**.
**Longshore drift** forms **spits**.

n88c08d0cf8b.s: Horns, eskers, U-valleys and moraines are associated with:
n88c08d0cf8b.x: Horn, esker, U-valley and moraine are all glacial landforms or deposits.
xa: Glacier landforms also include **cirque**, **hanging valley**, **till**.
⚠ **Moraine** = unsorted; **esker** = **stratified**.
**APPSC-G2 2023**: Cirque — glaciers; Delta — running water; Cliffs — waves and currents; Sand dunes — winds.

nc0270a2a3c5.s: A U-shaped valley is formed when:
o: A river cuts vertically into its bed
A central block subsides between faults
A glacier deepens and widens a river valley
nc0270a2a3c5.x: A U-shaped valley is a glacial landform made when a glacier deepens and widens a river valley; it is not aeolian.
xa: **Hanging valley**: tributary valley left high above the deepened main valley.
**Fjord** = glacially carved valley drowned by the sea.
V-shaped valley = **running water** (river).

n1a0780e9fea.s: A tributary valley that remains high above a deeply eroded main glacial valley and commonly enters it through a waterfall is called a
n1a0780e9fea.x: A hanging valley is a tributary valley left at a higher level than the deepened main valley, often producing a waterfall at its junction.
n1a0780e9fea.tq: Apply the relative-height description to identify the landform.
xs: This is a **hanging valley** — option **(4)**; its stream enters the main valley as a **waterfall** (agent = glacier, **UKPSC 2024**).
A **blind valley** ends where its stream vanishes underground (karst); a **playa** is a seasonal desert salt lake.
xa: **U-shaped valley**: glacier deepens and widens the main valley.
**Cirque** = armchair-shaped hollow at the valley head.
**Fjord** = glacial valley drowned by the sea.

nfd94b3ca77c.s: A long, winding ridge of stratified sediment marking a sub-glacial tunnel is called a/an:
nfd94b3ca77c.x: An esker is a winding ridge of stratified sediment from a sub-glacial tunnel; moraine is unsorted debris.
xa: Other moraines: **medial**, **ground**.
**Drumlin**: oval hill of till; long axis parallel to ice flow.
Also glacial: **kettle holes**, **outwash plain**.

n83d892d7155.s: A field of drumlins gives rise to which type of topography?
n83d892d7155.x: Drumlins are oval, egg-shaped hills of till, and a field of them gives 'basket of eggs' topography.
xa: Some notes attach "basket of eggs" to **boulder deposits**.
**Esker** = stratified ridge from a sub-glacial tunnel.
Till, moraine and boulder clay = **glacial activity** (**APPSC 2017**).

n804757ddbe7.s: A fjord is best described as a
o: ridge of rock parallel to wind direction
desert basin containing a seasonal salt lake
sand ridge joining an island to the mainland
glacially carved valley drowned by the sea
n804757ddbe7.x: A fjord is a glacially carved valley subsequently submerged by the sea. Norway, Greenland and New Zealand are associated with fjords.
n804757ddbe7.tq: Distinguish a drowned glacial valley from coastal depositional landforms.
xs: A **fjord** is a **glacially carved valley drowned by the sea** — option **(4)**.
Examples: **Norway**, **Greenland**, **New Zealand**.
A ridge parallel to the wind is a **yardang**; a seasonal desert salt lake is a **playa**; a bar joining an island to the mainland is a **tombolo**.
xa: Coast types: **Ria** = drowned river valley (NW Spain), ranges at **right angles** to the shore.
**Dalmatian** = ranges **parallel** to the coast (Adriatic, Croatia).
**U-shaped valley**: glacier deepens and widens a river valley.

ngeneral-geography-5-5.s: A blind valley is a ____ feature.
ngeneral-geography-5-5.x: A blind valley is a karst feature, not one of tectonic faulting.
n: V-shaped valleys are formed by river erosion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
U-shaped valleys are formed by glacial erosion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is left above a main valley by a tributary glacier. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Blind valleys occur in karst or limestone regions. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form U-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms V-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form U-shaped valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers form hanging valleys. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
V-shaped valleys are formed by rivers, whereas U-shaped valleys are formed by glaciers. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A hanging valley is glacial, whereas a rift valley is tectonic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Rift examples: **Death Valley**, **Narmada Valley**.
A **waterfall** occurs at the junction of a hanging valley.
**Fjord** = drowned glacial **U-shaped** valley.

ngeneral-geography-5-81.s: A deep, narrow sea inlet that is a drowned glacial U-shaped valley is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-81.x: A fjord is a deep, narrow inlet because it is a glacial U-valley drowned by the sea.
n: A fjord is a drowned glacial U-shaped valley. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A fjord is a deep, narrow sea inlet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Glaciers and marine submergence form fjords. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Glaciers with **marine submergence** produce fjords.
**Ria** coast = drowned **river** valley (NW Spain).
**Dalmatian** coast = drowned ranges **parallel** to the shore (Adriatic, Croatia).

n53096ed8c9d.s: The Peninsular Plateau is described as a:
o: Lacustrine plain formed entirely from lake deposits
Bhabar belt formed by Himalayan gravel
n53096ed8c9d.x: A peneplain is a nearly featureless surface produced by prolonged erosion, and the Peninsular Plateau is described as a rejuvenated peneplain.
n53096ed8c9d.tq: Identify the geomorphological term from the stated stage of erosion and rejuvenation.
xs: The Peninsular Plateau is a **rejuvenated peneplain** — option **(3)**.
A **peneplain** is a near-featureless surface left after **long erosion**, rejuvenated at places.
Lake deposits make a **lacustrine** plain; young floodplain = **khadar**; Himalayan gravel = **Bhabar**.
xa: Other plain types: **alluvial**, **flood plain**, **lacustrine**, **till plains**.
Plains are generally below **200 m**.
Alluvial plain = India's **youngest** physiographic division.

nc866c04504e.s: A mushroom rock develops mainly because
o: the base is abraded more intensively by wind than the top
the top is dissolved by rainfall while the base is protected
the rock is submerged by a rising sea
the rock is deposited by meltwater
nc866c04504e.x: Wind-driven sand is concentrated near the ground and abrades the base more than the upper part, producing an undercut mushroom rock.
nc866c04504e.tq: Infer the landform from the differential intensity of erosion.
xs: A mushroom rock forms because **the base is abraded more intensively by wind than the top** — option **(1)**.
The rock is **undercut at the base**.
xa: Other wind-erosion forms: **zeugen**, **yardang**.
⚠ A "table-like" ridge is a **zeugen**; a **yardang** is a ridge parallel to the wind.
**Inselberg**: isolated residual hill, e.g. **Uluru**.

n0f8d47d7809.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes a yardang from a zeugen?
o: A yardang is a ridge parallel to wind direction, whereas a zeugen is a table-like ridge with a hard cap over soft rock.
A yardang is an isolated residual hill, whereas a zeugen is a glacial ridge.
A yardang is a shallow lake, whereas a zeugen is a deflation hollow.
A yardang is a crescent dune, whereas a zeugen is a salt lake.
n0f8d47d7809.x: Yardangs are streamlined, steep-sided ridges parallel to wind direction. Zeugen are tabular ridges in which a hard cap protects softer rock beneath.
n0f8d47d7809.tq: Compare similar-looking aeolian features by structure and orientation.
xs: A **yardang** is a **ridge parallel to wind direction**; a **zeugen** is a **table-like ridge with a hard cap over soft rock** — option **(1)**.
An isolated residual hill is an **inselberg**; a crescent dune is a **barchan**; a shallow salt lake is a **playa**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: a "table-like" yardang description fits the **zeugen**.
Yardang ridges are of **soft rock**, long, steep-sided and streamlined.
**Mesa** → **butte** (smaller remnant).

nead8a4ccf1d.s: Long, narrow longitudinal dunes found in groups where sand is scarce are called:
nead8a4ccf1d.x: Seifs are long, narrow longitudinal dunes in groups where sand is scarce; barchans are crescent-shaped with horns pointing downwind.
xa: Wind transport: **deflation, saltation, surface creep**.
**Erra Matti Dibbalu** = late-Quaternary **red dunes**, Visakhapatnam (UNESCO Tentative List, Sep 2025).
**Playa** = seasonal salt lake in a desert basin.

n9fc9d8d1721.s: Uluru, an isolated residual hill, is an example of a/an:
n9fc9d8d1721.x: Uluru is an isolated residual hill, i.e. an inselberg.
xa: Largest loess example: **Loess Plateau of China**.
**Mesa** (wide flat-topped table hill) → **butte** (smaller remnant).
Wind-blown landforms: sand dunes, yardang, mushroom rock, loess.

nd559b8e0e6d.s: Which one of the following is NOT a hard-engineering measure for coastal protection?
nd559b8e0e6d.x: Beach nourishment is a soft coastal defence measure. Seawalls, groynes and offshore breakwaters are hard-engineering structures.
nd559b8e0e6d.tq: Find the option belonging to the opposite category.
xs: **Beach nourishment** is a **soft** defence, not hard engineering — option **(3)**.
Hard defences: **seawalls**, **groynes**, **offshore breakwaters**.
xa: Soft defences: beach nourishment, **dune stabilisation**, **mangroves**.
Groynes are built **across longshore drift** to trap sand.
Human causes of erosion: harbours, **beach sand mining**, offshore dredging, **dams**.

ngeneral-geography-5-14.s: A streamlined ridge formed by wind erosion is called a:
ngeneral-geography-5-14.x: A yardang is a streamlined wind-cut ridge; a mushroom rock is narrow below and wide above, a playa is a dry lake bed and loess is fine silt.
n: Yardangs are streamlined ridges. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Mushroom rocks have narrow bases and wider tops. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A playa is a dry lake bed. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Loess is a fine silt deposit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Wind erosion forms yardangs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Wind forms yardangs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: ⚠ A "table-like" ridge is a **zeugen**; a yardang lies **parallel to the wind**.
**Loess Plateau** of China; also **Plain of Normandy** and **Manchuria**.
**Barchans** are **crescent-shaped** dunes; **seifs** long, narrow ridges.

ngeneral-geography-5-96.s: A playa in a desert is formed by:
o: Evaporation of a temporary desert lake
ngeneral-geography-5-96.x: A playa is left when a temporary desert lake evaporates; mushroom rocks come from abrasion, dunes from deposition and deflation hollows from wind removal.
n: Wind abrasion forms mushroom rocks. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Evaporation or deposition forms playas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Wind transport: **deflation**, **saltation**, **surface creep**.
**Mesa** → **butte**; **inselberg** (e.g. **Uluru**) = isolated residual hill.
**Zeugen** = tabular ridge with a hard cap over soft rock.

ngeneral-geography-5-86.s: A large enclosed karst depression is called a/an:
ngeneral-geography-5-86.x: A polje is a large enclosed karst depression; an uvala is coalesced dolines and a swallow hole is where a stream sinks.
n: A uvala consists of coalesced dolines. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A polje is a large enclosed karst depression. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A blind valley terminates abruptly. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A swallow hole is a place where a stream disappears underground. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: **Lapiaz** (karren) = **grooved limestone**.
**Stalactites** hang from the roof (APPSC **2022**); **stalagmites** rise from the floor; joined → **pillars**.
Longest caves: India — **Krem Liat Prah** (Meghalaya); world — **Mammoth Cave** (USA).
**Belum** (Nandyal) is karst — APPSC-G1 **2017**.

nd734b46e2e4.s: Devprayag is significant in physical geography because it is the place where:
o: The Bhagirathi and Alaknanda meet and the Ganga begins
The Yamuna enters the Indo-Ganga plain
The Brahmaputra enters India through a gorge
nd734b46e2e4.x: Devprayag is the confluence of the Bhagirathi and Alaknanda; from this confluence the river is known as the Ganga.
