nd734b46e2e4.tq: Link the named confluence with the rivers meeting there and the resulting river.
xs: At **Devprayag** the **Bhagirathi and Alaknanda** meet and the **Ganga begins** — option **(1)**.
**Prayag** = confluence of rivers.
The **Chambal** valley is known for ravines; the **Brahmaputra** enters India through the **Dihang** gorge.
xa: **Doab** = land between two rivers; Ganga-Yamuna Doab = **westernmost** Ganga plain.
**Karewas (Vudr)** = lacustrine deposits of the Kashmir valley.
**Chos** of Hoshiarpur (Punjab) = ravines.

nf6b36fa5fd0.s: Cave deposits that hang from the roof of a limestone cave are called:
nf6b36fa5fd0.x: Stalactites hang from the roof, stalagmites rise from the floor, and where they meet they form pillars or columns.
xa: Speleothems are of **calcium carbonate**.
**Belum** (Nandyal) and **Borra** (ASR) caves have stalactites and stalagmites.
**Arwah** caves (Meghalaya, Sohra): limestone caves with fossils (**APPSC 2018**).

n74e415ebbca.s: Which one of the following correctly gives the longest natural cave systems mentioned?
o: India — Krem Liat Prah; World — Mammoth Cave
India — Mammoth Cave; World — Krem Liat Prah
India — Belum; World — Krem Liat Prah
n74e415ebbca.x: Krem Liat Prah in Meghalaya is identified as India’s longest natural cave, while Mammoth Cave in the USA is identified as the world’s longest natural cave.
n74e415ebbca.tq: Compare the national and global rankings without reversing the two levels.
xs: **India — Krem Liat Prah; World — Mammoth Cave** — option **(1)**.
**Krem Liat Prah** is in **Meghalaya**; **Mammoth Cave** is in the **USA**.
**Belum** is India's **2nd-longest** natural cave system; **Borra** is in the Ananthagiri hills.
xa: **Belum**: **Nandyal** district, black limestone; first discovered **1884** by **Robert Bruce Foote**.
Belum declared a **Geo-Heritage Site by GSI** (Jun 2025).
**APPSC-G1 2017**: karst among Bojjannakonda, Undavalli, Belum, Erravaram = **Belum**.

nda0a99666ff.s: Undavalli Caves are best described as:
o: Natural limestone caves through which the Gosthani flows
Buddhist rock-cut caves with a monolithic Buddha in Dhyana mudra
Rock-cut cave temples associated with the Vishnukundins and a reclining Vishnu image
nda0a99666ff.x: Undavalli consists of rock-cut cave temples associated with the Vishnukundins and contains a reclining Anantasayana Vishnu. It is not a karst cave.
nda0a99666ff.tq: Match the cave with its religious, architectural and dynastic features.
xs: Undavalli has **rock-cut cave temples** of the **Vishnukundins**, with a **reclining Anantasayana Vishnu** — option **(4)**.
The **Gosthani** flows through **Borra**; **Patalaganga** is in **Belum**; the **Dhyana mudra Buddha** is at **Bojjannakonda**.
xa: Undavalli: **four-storey**, **4th-5th c. CE**, near **Vijayawada**, **Guntur** district.
Carved from a **sandstone** hill (some notes say granite); **not karst**.
⚠ **Undavalli** and **Bojjannakonda** = rock-cut, not karst.

n4cd93d68307.s: Bojjannakonda at Sankaram is associated with:
n4cd93d68307.x: Bojjannakonda at Sankaram is a Buddhist rock-cut hilltop monastery complex with caves and stupas. It is not classified as a karst cave.
n4cd93d68307.tq: Identify the site from its religious and architectural association.
xs: Bojjannakonda at **Sankaram** has **Buddhist rock-cut caves and stupas** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is a **hilltop monastery** with a monolithic Buddha in **Dhyana mudra** (**Mahayana-Vajrayana**); **not karst**.
**Black-limestone karst** = **Belum**; fossil limestone caves of Meghalaya = **Arwah**; **Vishnukundin** temples = **Undavalli**.
xa: Bojjannakonda is in **Anakapalli** (Visakhapatnam region).
⚠ **Belum** and **Borra** = karst; **Undavalli** and **Bojjannakonda** = rock-cut.
**APPSC-G1 2017** karst answer = **Belum**.

na8e4f4c7635.s: The Borra Caves are associated with which combination of district and geological features?
o: ASR district; limestone formations with stalactites and stalagmites
Nandyal district; black limestone without mineral formations
Guntur district; a four-storey rock-cut monastery
Kurnool district; a Palaeolithic site with animal skeletal remains
na8e4f4c7635.x: Borra Caves are in the ASR district in the Ananthagiri hills near Araku. They are limestone caves containing stalactites and stalagmites.
na8e4f4c7635.tq: Start from the sure district–feature pair and reject combinations belonging to other caves.
xs: Borra Caves: **ASR district**; **limestone** formations with **stalactites and stalagmites** — option **(1)**.
They lie in the **Ananthagiri hills**, Araku.
Black limestone in **Nandyal** = **Belum**; four-storey rock-cut caves in **Guntur** = **Undavalli**; Palaeolithic site with animal remains = **Billa Surgam**.
xa: The **Gosthani** flows through Borra.
Discovered **1807** (William King George per some notes).
Borra has **Mesolithic paintings**.

n97c5ffd34fc.s: Which river passes through the Borra Caves?
n97c5ffd34fc.x: The Gosthani River passes through the Borra Caves. The caves are also associated with Mesolithic rock paintings.
n97c5ffd34fc.tq: Link the cave with its specifically associated river rather than a major regional river.
xs: The **Gosthani** flows through the Borra Caves — option **(4)** is correct.
Borra: limestone karst caves in the **Ananthagiri hills**, Araku, **Alluri Sitharama Raju** district.
xa: Borra was discovered in **1807** (William King George per some notes).
Borra has **Mesolithic paintings**.
⚠ **Patalaganga** belongs to **Belum**, not Borra.

nc58f84224b3.s: Belum Caves of Andhra Pradesh are notable as
o: The second-longest natural cave system in India
The longest natural cave system in the world
Rock-cut Buddhist caves of the Vishnukundin period
Sandstone caves through which the Gosthani flows
nc58f84224b3.x: Belum (Nandyal) is India's second-longest natural cave system after Krem Liat Prah in Meghalaya. Mammoth Cave (USA) is the world's longest, Undavalli is the Vishnukundin rock-cut site, and the Gosthani flows through the limestone Borra Caves.
nc58f84224b3.tq: Belum = 2nd-longest in India (after Krem Liat Prah); karst, black limestone.
xs: Belum is **the second-longest natural cave system in India** — option **(1)**.
The longest in India is **Krem Liat Prah** (Meghalaya); the world's longest is **Mammoth Cave** (USA).
Vishnukundin rock-cut caves = **Undavalli**; the Gosthani flows through **Borra**.
xa: Belum: **black limestone**, stalactites and stalagmites; **Nandyal** district.
First discovered **1884** by **Robert Bruce Foote**.
**Geo-Heritage Site by GSI** (Jun 2025).

ne1c0bf52dae.s: Which of the following is NOT a process of coastal erosion?
ne1c0bf52dae.x: Saltation, the bouncing of grains, is a mode of wind transport; hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition and solution are coastal erosion processes.
xa: Agents: **waves** (main), tides and currents, wind.
Erosional sequence ends: **arch → stack → stump**.
Hard defences: **seawalls, groynes, offshore breakwaters**.

n0394ae750e0.s: In the development of coastal erosional features, a sea cave becomes an arch, then a stack and finally a:
n0394ae750e0.x: The usual sequence is cliff and wave-cut platform, sea cave, arch, stack and finally stump.
xa: Main agent: **waves**.
Processes: **hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition**, solution.
Cliff and **stack** = waves and currents (**APPSC-G2 2023**: Cliffs — waves and currents).

ncd9a405f66a.s: Which of the following can reduce the supply of sediment to beaches and thereby intensify coastal erosion?
ncd9a405f66a.x: Dams, like harbours, beach sand mining and offshore dredging, can reduce the natural supply and movement of coastal sediment.
xa: **East coast** erodes more: soft, low-lying alluvial sand and silt, no rocky cliffs.
Soft defences: **beach nourishment**, dune stabilisation, mangroves.
AP: severe erosion at **Uppada** (Kakinada).

n887629368ff.s: Which pair of rivers forms estuaries rather than deltas?
n887629368ff.x: The west-flowing Narmada and Tapi form estuaries, river mouths freely open to the sea, rather than deltas.
xa: ⚠ **Lagoon** = shallow coastal water cut off by a bar/reef vs **estuary** = free connection to the sea.
Lagoons: **Chilika**, **Pulicat**.
Deltas: **Nile**, **Tiber**, **Mississippi**.

nd020af1fef0.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the east coast of India?
o: It is more vulnerable to erosion because it is soft and low-lying.
Its flat and wide plains allow the sea to move inland.
It consists largely of alluvial sand and silt.
Rocky cliffs are a dominant feature throughout the coast.
nd020af1fef0.x: Rocky cliffs are not dominant throughout the east coast, which is soft, low-lying and largely alluvial.
xa: AP: erosion severe at **Uppada** (Kakinada) and the **Krishna coast** (Jul 2026).
Human causes: harbours, sand mining, dredging, **dams cutting sediment supply**.
East-coast lagoons: **Chilika**, **Pulicat**.

n9822d6baa72.s: Shallow coastal water cut off from the sea by a bar, reef or sandbar is called a/an:
n9822d6baa72.x: A lagoon is shallow water cut off from the sea by a bar, reef or sandbar, whereas an estuary keeps a free connection with the sea.
xa: Lagoons: **Chilika**, **Pulicat**.
Estuaries: west-flowing **Narmada** and **Tapi**.
Estuary is an **ecotone**.

n8090df25449.s: Severe coastal erosion in Andhra Pradesh has been particularly reported at which of the following locations?
o: Uppada in Kakinada and the Krishna coast
n8090df25449.x: Severe coastal erosion has been reported at Uppada in Kakinada and along the Krishna coast. The other options refer to caves, lakes or deltaic features.
n8090df25449.tq: Use location-based elimination by distinguishing coastal erosion sites from inland landforms and water bodies.
xs: Severe coastal erosion is at **Uppada in Kakinada and the Krishna coast** — option **(3)** (Jul 2026).
Vamsadhara and Penna are **minor deltas**; Borra and Belum are **caves**; Kolleru and Pulicat are **lakes**.
xa: **East coast** erodes more: soft, low-lying **alluvial sand and silt**.
Human causes: harbours, beach sand mining, dredging, **dams**.
Soft defences: beach nourishment, dune stabilisation, **mangroves**.

n901547ec314.s: Pulicat in Andhra Pradesh is a ____ lake.
n901547ec314.x: Pulicat is a saltwater lake, whereas Kolleru is a freshwater lake.
xa: Pulicat is a **lagoon** formed by a bar closing a bay.
Minor deltas: **Vamsadhara** and **Penna**.
Coastal erosion: **Uppada** (Kakinada), Krishna coast.

o: A river cuts through rocks of differing hardness
A river erodes intensely over a long period
A glacier deepens a river valley
ngeneral-geography-5-72.x: An oxbow lake forms when a meander is cut off; waterfalls result from differential erosion and canyons from intense, prolonged erosion.
n: Intense prolonged erosion forms canyons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Differential erosion forms waterfalls. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Lateral erosion and deposition form meanders. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Meanders are sinuous river courses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
An oxbow lake forms through meander cut-off. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Meanders are formed by erosion, transportation, and deposition processes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Running water forms meanders. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xa: Meander: **outer bend** = erosion (concave cliff); **inner bend** = deposition (convex slip-off slope).
Canyon is an **upper-course** feature (APPSC **2022**).
**Old stage**: oxbow lakes, natural levees, braided channels, deltas.

ngeneral-geography-5-16.s: Which coastal landform connects an island to the mainland?
ngeneral-geography-5-16.x: A tombolo is a sand bar joining an island to the mainland. A spit is attached at only one end.
n: A tombolo is a bar connecting an island to the mainland. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Spits form through longshore deposition. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A lagoon is a water body separated by a bar or spit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
Bars are depositional ridges across bays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
A spit projects from the coast, whereas a tombolo connects an island to the mainland. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 33-42]
xs: A **tombolo** is a **bar connecting an island to the mainland** — option **(2)**.
A **spit** is a sand ridge **joined to land at one end**; a **bar** is a ridge **across a bay**; a **lagoon** is water **separated by a bar or spit**.
xa: A bar closing a bay forms a **lagoon** — e.g. **Chilika**, **Pulicat**.
**Longshore drift** moves sediment; **groynes** trap it.
⚠ **Ria** = ranges at right angles to the coast; **Dalmatian** = ranges **parallel**.

n7e847d0d55c.s: The belt of coarse gravel and pebbles deposited by Himalayan rivers where they enter the plains is called:
n7e847d0d55c.x: Bhabar is the coarse gravel and pebble belt at the foothills where Himalayan rivers enter the plains.
n7e847d0d55c.tq: Discriminate among the closely related Himalayan foothill and plain terms.
xs: The coarse gravel-pebble belt where Himalayan rivers enter the plains is the **Bhabar** — option **(1)**.
It is made of **alluvial fans**.
**Terai** is the marshy belt south of it; **Bhangar** is older alluvium with kankar; **Khadar** is new floodplain alluvium.
xa: ⚠ **Bhangar** = old, with **kankar**; **Khadar** = new, no kankar.
**Doab** = land between two rivers; Ganga-Yamuna Doab = westernmost Ganga plain.
Plains are generally below **200 m**.

n4e943507810.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Terai?
o: An older alluvial surface containing kankar
The active floodplain containing only coarse gravel
A marshy and forested belt south of the Bhabar where streams reappear
A confluence of two or more rivers
n4e943507810.x: The Terai lies south of the Bhabar and is a marshy, forested belt where streams that disappeared into the Bhabar come back to the surface.
n4e943507810.tq: Use the north-to-south relation and stream behaviour to separate Terai from Bhabar.
xs: The **Terai** is **a marshy and forested belt south of the Bhabar where streams reappear** — option **(3)**.
Older alluvium with kankar is **Bhangar**; a confluence is a **prayag**.
xa: **Bhabar** = coarse gravel-pebble belt (alluvial fans) where Himalayan rivers enter the plains.
**Khadar** = new alluvium, fine clay and sand, **no kankar**.
**Devprayag**: Bhagirathi + Alaknanda — the **Ganga** begins.

ne700716488e.s: The older alluvium lying above flood level and containing kankar (lime nodules) is called:
ne700716488e.x: Bhangar is older alluvium above flood level with kankar; khadar is the new alluvium of the active floodplain, of fine clay and sand without kankar.
xa: **Bhabar** = coarse gravel-pebble belt; **Terai** = marshy belt south of it.
**Bet land** = flood plain while floodwater stays on it.
Alluvial plain = India's **youngest** physiographic division.

n131d5c7c319.s: Land lying between two rivers is called a:
n131d5c7c319.x: Land between two rivers is a doab; bet land is a flood plain while floodwater stays on it, chos are ravines of Hoshiarpur and karewas are lacustrine deposits of Kashmir.
xa: **Chambal valley** badlands (**APPSC 2022**).
Lacustrine plains = **filled lake beds**.
**Prayag** = confluence (e.g. **Devprayag**).

nc8b5bdbc06b.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Dalmatian and ria coasts?
o: In a Dalmatian coast, mountain ranges run parallel to the coast.
Drowning of a Dalmatian coast produces long islands and channels parallel to the shore.
In a ria coast, mountain ranges run parallel to the shore.
Croatia on the Adriatic is associated with the Dalmatian coast.
nc8b5bdbc06b.x: In a ria coast the ranges generally lie at right angles to the shore; parallel ranges characterise the Dalmatian coast.
xa: **Ria** = drowned **river** valley — **NW Spain**.
**Fiord** = drowned **glacial** valley — **Norway**.
⚠ **Ria** = right angles; **Dalmatian** = parallel.

n8888130ce46.s: A bird-foot delta forms where the river's sediment is ____ sea water and is carried far.
n8888130ce46.x: Bird-foot deltas involve sediment lighter than sea water that is carried far out (sources differ on the equal-density case, so it is not asked here).
xa: ⚠ Rule: denser → **arcuate**; equal → **cuspate**; lighter → **bird-foot**.
Examples: arcuate — **Nile**, Sundarbans; cuspate — **Tiber**; bird-foot — **Mississippi**.
Arcuate is the **most common** type.

ne166645e280.s: The Mississippi delta is an example of a/an ____ delta.
ne166645e280.x: The Mississippi is a bird-foot delta; the Nile and Sundarbans are arcuate and the Tiber is cuspate.
xa: ⚠ Denser sediment → **arcuate**; equal → **cuspate**; lighter → **bird-foot**.
**Narmada** and **Tapi** form **estuaries**, not deltas.
AP: Godavari-Krishna delta plains = "**rice granary of South India**".

n0cefed2ea70.s: Hanging glaciers are stranded on steep slopes when the main glacier:
n0cefed2ea70.x: Hanging glaciers are left on steep slopes as the main glacier thins; their collapse can trigger ice-rock avalanches, LLOFs and GLOFs.
xa: CWC monitors **2,843** glacial lakes and water bodies (**2,485** glacial lakes) from **2025**, up from **902**.
Monitoring is under **NRSC's Glacial Lake Atlas**.
⚠ Hanging **glacier** vs hanging **valley** (tributary valley left high, stream enters as a waterfall).

nb0cf1da9f71.s: Erra Matti Dibbalu, a site of late-Quaternary red dunes, is located in:
nb0cf1da9f71.x: Erra Matti Dibbalu are late-Quaternary red dunes in Visakhapatnam; in September 2025 the site was added to UNESCO's Tentative List.
xa: Collector ordered **tourism upgrades** at Erra Matti Dibbalu (15 May 2026).
Belum = **Geo-Heritage Site by GSI** (Jun 2025).
Wind landforms include **sand dunes** and **loess**.

ndba91a84b71.s: Which of the following is NOT a physical weathering process?
ndba91a84b71.x: Carbonation is a chemical weathering process. Exfoliation, frost wedging and block disintegration are physical weathering processes without chemical change.
ndba91a84b71.tq: Find the chemical process embedded among physical weathering terms.
xs: **Carbonation** is not physical — it is a **chemical** weathering process — option **(3)** is correct.
**Exfoliation**, **frost wedging** and **block disintegration** are **physical** weathering — rock breaks with **no chemical change**.
xa: Chemical weathering: **solution, carbonation, oxidation, hydration, hydrolysis**.
Biological weathering: **roots, burrowing animals, humans**.
AP soils: granite/gneiss → **red soils**; basalt → **black soils**.

n9cde18d1e66.s: Weathering of granite and gneiss is associated with the formation of which soil in Andhra Pradesh?
n9cde18d1e66.x: In Andhra Pradesh, weathering of granite and gneiss gives rise to red soils. Weathering of basalt is associated with black soils.
n9cde18d1e66.tq: Match the parent rock with the resulting soil type.
xs: Weathering of **granite and gneiss** gives **red soil** in AP — option **(2)** is correct.
**Black soils** come from weathering of **basalt**.
xa: Physical weathering = **no chemical change** (exfoliation, frost wedging).
Chemical weathering: **solution, carbonation, oxidation, hydration, hydrolysis**.
AP deltas: Godavari-Krishna delta plains = "**rice granary of South India**".

nfcd83ed191a.s: Which of the following is NOT a form of mass wasting?
nfcd83ed191a.x: Oxidation is a chemical weathering process. Soil creep, landslide and rockfall are forms of mass wasting caused by gravity.
nfcd83ed191a.tq: Separate gravity-driven mass movements from chemical weathering processes.
xs: **Oxidation** is not mass wasting — it is a **chemical weathering** process — option **(1)** is correct.
**Soil creep**, **landslide** and **rockfall** are mass wasting — movement of material **under gravity**.
xa: Other mass-wasting forms: **slump**, **mudflow**.
Chemical weathering also includes **solution, carbonation, hydration, hydrolysis**.
Physical weathering: **exfoliation, frost wedging, block disintegration**.

na41540b5f96.s: In warm, wet tropical regions, water vapour may constitute up to ____ of the atmosphere.
na41540b5f96.x: Water vapour may reach 4 per cent in warm, wet tropics and is below 1 per cent in deserts and polar air; it decreases with altitude.
xa: It is the **most abundant greenhouse gas** and decides **air stability**.
It absorbs insolation and keeps in Earth's heat (**blanket effect**).
CO2 and water vapour reach only about **90 km**.

naf8d80df0e0.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the role of water vapour in the atmosphere?
o: It absorbs insolation but does not affect terrestrial heat.
It absorbs terrestrial heat but has no role in atmospheric stability.
It is a permanent constituent whose concentration is uniform at all heights.
It acts as a blanket by absorbing insolation and terrestrial heat and also influences air stability.
naf8d80df0e0.x: Water vapour is variable, absorbs insolation and terrestrial heat, produces a blanket effect and influences atmospheric stability. It is not uniformly distributed.
naf8d80df0e0.tq: Choose the option that combines the several stated functions without adding an absolute claim.
xs: Water vapour acts as a **blanket**, absorbing **insolation** and **Earth's heat**, and decides **air stability** — option **(4)**.
It is a **variable** constituent: up to **4%** in tropics, **under 1%** in deserts — not uniform (option 3).
xa: It is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**.
It **decreases with height** and from **equator to poles**.
**Dust** acts as **hygroscopic nuclei** for condensation.

n95bb252da4a.s: Atmospheric dust particles are generally more concentrated in the lower layers and are relatively more abundant in
n95bb252da4a.x: Dust is concentrated in the lower atmospheric layers and is more abundant in subtropical and temperate belts, where dry winds help raise and transport particles.
n95bb252da4a.tq: Use the distribution comparison rather than the extreme option involving only one belt.
xs: Dust is more abundant in **subtropical and temperate** belts — option **(3)**.
**Dry winds** there lift and carry it; **equatorial and polar** belts have less (option 2).
Dust is concentrated in the **lower layers**, not the thermosphere.
xa: Dust sources: **sea salt, soil, smoke, soot, ash, pollen, meteor dust**.
It acts as **hygroscopic nuclei** for condensation.
Water vapour is **under 1%** in deserts and polar air.

n8917ec7dd24.s: Oxygen in the atmosphere becomes negligible by a height of about:
n8917ec7dd24.x: Oxygen becomes negligible only by about 120 km, whereas CO2 and water vapour reach only about 90 km.
xa: The **homosphere** extends to **~80-90 km**.
CO2 rose to **423.9 ppm** in **2024**.
Greenhouse effect: atmosphere **transparent to incoming** solar radiation, **opaque to outgoing** terrestrial radiation.

n5cfde9ce619.s: Which one of the following gives the correct descending order of the following gases in dry air by volume?
n5cfde9ce619.x: Nitrogen (about 78.08%) > oxygen (20.95%) > argon (0.93%) > carbon dioxide (about 0.04%) (APPSC-G1 2023). Putting oxygen first, or CO2 above argon, or argon above oxygen are all wrong orders.
n5cfde9ce619.tq: N2 78 > O2 21 > Ar 0.93 > CO2 0.04 - argon beats CO2.
xs: **Nitrogen > Oxygen > Argon > Carbon dioxide** — option **(1)** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
⚠ Option (3) puts CO2 above argon — the common trap.
xa: Nitrogen ~**78%** was asked in APPSC-GS **2025**.
Trace gases: **neon 0.002**, **krypton 0.001**, **helium 0.0005**.
**Xenon** and **hydrogen** occur only in traces.
n5cfde9ce619.fixed: CO2 is a variable gas, not a permanent gas; stem was false (y4b6103a7175 asks plain order)

n6f3ab618c5a.s: Which one of the following sequences represents the principal gases of the heterosphere from lower to higher levels, according to molecular weight?
n6f3ab618c5a.x: The heterosphere is described as having nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium and hydrogen in upward order according to molecular weight.
n6f3ab618c5a.tq: Arrange the gases by the stated upward molecular-weight sequence.
xs: Upward order: **nitrogen, atomic oxygen, helium, hydrogen** — option **(2)**.
In the **heterosphere** gases are layered by **molecular weight**, heaviest lowest.
Option (1) is the reverse order.
xa: The heterosphere lies above **~80-90 km**.
It holds the **thermosphere and exosphere**.
The **homosphere** below has a **uniform** mix of gases.

n856af75e0bb.s: Excessive ultraviolet exposure due to ozone depletion is associated with which eye disorder?
n856af75e0bb.x: Increased UV exposure is associated with cataract, as well as skin cancer, immune suppression and lower crop yield.
xa: The ozone layer absorbs **UV-B and UV-C**.
Ozone depletion is driven by **halocarbons** (**CFCs, HCFCs**).
The **Montreal Protocol** (**1987**) controls nearly **100** ODS.

nb26e2ef8fe1.s: Which sequence correctly represents the ozone–oxygen or Chapman cycle?
o: O2 is split by UV, oxygen atoms combine with O2 to form O3, and O3 absorbs UV and dissociates
O3 combines with nitrogen to form O2, which is then converted into methane
O2 absorbs infrared radiation and directly forms carbon dioxide
Ozone is formed only by the action of pollutants in the troposphere
nb26e2ef8fe1.x: Ultraviolet radiation splits O2 into free oxygen atoms; these combine with O2 to form O3, which absorbs UV and can split back into oxygen molecules and atoms.
nb26e2ef8fe1.tq: Follow the chemical sequence from initiating radiation to the regenerated products.
xs: **Chapman cycle**: **O2 + UV → O + O**; **O + O2 → O3**; **O3 absorbs UV** and splits back — option **(1)**.
It is a **natural balance** of ozone forming and splitting.
Ground-level ozone from **pollutants** is a different thing — option (4).
xa: The cycle runs in the **stratosphere**, densest at **15-35 km**.
**Halocarbons** release **chlorine and bromine** that destroy ozone faster than it forms.
Unit: **Dobson Unit (DU)**.

n89c031a3473.s: Which one of the following best explains the greenhouse effect in relation to atmospheric radiation?
o: The atmosphere is transparent to incoming solar radiation but opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere is opaque to incoming solar radiation and transparent to outgoing terrestrial radiation.
The atmosphere absorbs both incoming solar radiation and outgoing terrestrial radiation completely.
The atmosphere reflects all incoming solar radiation and absorbs none of the terrestrial radiation.
n89c031a3473.x: The atmosphere is relatively transparent to incoming solar radiation but absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation, thereby contributing to the greenhouse effect.
n89c031a3473.tq: Apply the radiation-flow concept by distinguishing incoming solar radiation from outgoing terrestrial radiation.
xs: The atmosphere is **transparent to incoming solar radiation** but **opaque to outgoing terrestrial radiation** — that is the **greenhouse effect**, option **(1)**.
**CO2** is transparent to incoming sunlight but **absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation**; **water vapour** keeps in earth's heat (**blanket effect**).
The atmosphere neither absorbs all radiation nor reflects all incoming sunlight, so options **(2)-(4)** are wrong.
xa: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**; up to **4%** in warm, wet tropics.
CO2 rose **3.5 ppm** to **423.9 ppm** in **2024** — **152%** of pre-industrial (WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025).
**CFCs** are about **1,000 times** more heat-absorbent than CO2 and make up **15%** of the enhanced effect.

ngeneral-geography-6-2.s: What is the approximate proportion of argon in the atmosphere?
ngeneral-geography-6-2.x: Argon is about 0.93% of dry air, the third most abundant gas. 21% is oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide.
n: Argon (Ar) constitutes approximately 0.93% of the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Argon is a major inert gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xs: **Argon** makes up approximately **0.93%** of the atmosphere — option **(3)**.
It is a **permanent**, **inert** gas, **third** in dry air after **nitrogen** and **oxygen**.
**21%** is **oxygen**; **0.04%** is **carbon dioxide**; **0–4%** is the range of **water vapour**.
xa: Dry-air sequence: **N₂ > O₂ > Ar > CO₂** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
⚠ Third place = **Argon**, not CO2.
**Neon 0.002**, **krypton 0.001**, **helium 0.0005** (% by volume).

ngeneral-geography-6-10.s: Which atmospheric gas absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation?
ngeneral-geography-6-10.x: Ozone absorbs harmful UV radiation; carbon dioxide serves photosynthesis and the greenhouse effect, and oxygen supports respiration and combustion.
n: Nitrogen is an essential nutrient. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Nitrogen is a major atmospheric constituent. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Oxygen supports respiration. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Oxygen supports combustion. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Carbon dioxide contributes to the greenhouse effect. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Carbon dioxide supports photosynthesis. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: **Nitrogen**, **oxygen** and **argon** are **permanent** gases; **CO₂**, **water vapour** and **ozone** are **variable**.
Ozone is concentrated mainly in the **stratosphere**.
**CO₂** rose **3.5 ppm** to **423.9 ppm** in **2024** — **152%** of pre-industrial (WMO).

ngeneral-geography-6-12.s: Which of the following gases extends higher in the atmosphere than nitrogen and oxygen?
ngeneral-geography-6-12.x: Light hydrogen reaches higher than nitrogen and oxygen, while CO2 and water vapour occur only up to about 90 km.
n: Carbon dioxide is concentrated relatively low in the atmosphere, up to approximately 20 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Hydrogen extends higher than nitrogen and oxygen. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Water vapour is strongly concentrated near the surface or in the troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is concentrated mainly in the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: ⚠ The notes also say CO₂ is concentrated **relatively low** — **up to approximately 20 km**.
Water vapour is **more abundant in the tropics** than at the poles — up to **4%** in warm, wet tropics.
Oxygen is negligible by **120 km**.
**Dust** acts as **hygroscopic nuclei** for condensation.

ngeneral-geography-6-14.s: The Earth's early atmosphere was ____ in character, with little or no free oxygen.
ngeneral-geography-6-14.x: The early atmosphere was reducing with little free oxygen, whereas today's is dominated by nitrogen and oxygen.
n: The early atmosphere had a reducing character. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The early atmosphere contained little or no free oxygen. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The modern atmosphere contains significant oxygen. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Nitrogen and oxygen dominate the modern atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Early gases: **carbon dioxide**, **methane**, **ammonia** and **water vapour**.
**Biological evolution altered the atmosphere**; the biosphere and atmosphere **interact**.
Modern air is **oxygen-rich**, with **significant oxygen**.

ngeneral-geography-6-16.s: Which of the following is a permanent gas rather than a variable gas?
ngeneral-geography-6-16.x: Nitrogen is a permanent gas; water vapour, carbon dioxide and ozone are variable gases.
n: Nitrogen is a permanent gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Water vapour is a variable gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Carbon dioxide is a variable gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is a variable gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Carbon dioxide is a variable gas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Water vapour is **highly variable** — approximately **0–4%**.
CO₂ ~**0.04%**; ozone only in **trace quantities**.
Water vapour is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**.

ngeneral-geography-6-17.s: Carbon dioxide constitutes approximately ____ of the atmosphere.
ngeneral-geography-6-17.x: CO2 is about 0.04% of the atmosphere; oxygen is about 21%, water vapour 0–4% and ozone a trace.
n: Oxygen (O₂) constitutes approximately 21% of the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Carbon dioxide (CO₂) constitutes approximately 0.04% of the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Water vapour constitutes approximately 0–4% of the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone (O₃) occurs in trace quantities in the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Older notes give CO₂ as **0.036%**.
Water vapour: up to **4%** in tropics, **under 1%** in deserts and polar air.

ngeneral-geography-6-21.s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of trace minor atmospheric gases?
o: Oxygen, carbon dioxide, water vapour and ozone
Nitrogen, water vapour, methane and ozone
Nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide
Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton
ngeneral-geography-6-21.x: Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton are all trace gases. Every other group includes a major or variable gas.
n: Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton are minor trace gases. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xs: **Neon, helium, xenon, hydrogen and krypton** are all **minor trace gases** — option **(4)**.
Every other group includes a **permanent** gas (**nitrogen**, **oxygen**, **argon**) or a **variable** gas (**CO₂**, **water vapour**, **ozone**).
xa: Shares: **neon 0.002**, **krypton 0.001**, **helium 0.0005**; xenon and hydrogen in traces.
**Hydrogen extends higher** than nitrogen and oxygen.
**Methane** and **nitrous oxide** are greenhouse gases.

ngeneral-geography-6-23.s: Which of the following gases are identified as greenhouse gases?
ngeneral-geography-6-23.x: Methane and nitrous oxide are greenhouse gases that trap outgoing heat. Hydrogen, krypton, neon, helium and argon are not greenhouse gases.
ngeneral-geography-6-23.tq: Discriminate greenhouse gases from inert gases.
n: Methane and nitrous oxide (N₂O) are greenhouse gases. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xs: **Methane and nitrous oxide** (N₂O) are **greenhouse gases** — option **(4)**.
The other pairs — **hydrogen**, **krypton**, **neon**, **helium**, **argon** — are **trace** or **inert** gases.
xa: **CO₂** and **water vapour** also contribute to the **greenhouse effect**.
CO₂ is **transparent to incoming sunlight** but **absorbs outgoing terrestrial radiation**.
**CFCs** are potent GHGs — GWP **1,000–23,000**.

n7506920113c.s: The coldest layer of the atmosphere is generally the:
n7506920113c.x: The mesosphere is the coldest layer, with temperature falling to about −100°C near 80 km.
n7506920113c.tq: Use the extreme-value clue to identify the correct atmospheric layer.
xs: The **mesosphere** is the coldest layer — option **(4)**.
Temperature falls to about **-100°C** at **80 km**.
xa: Meteors **burn up** in the mesosphere (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
Its top is the **mesopause** (~**80 km**).
Tropopause temperature: **-80 °C** over the equator, **-45 °C** over the poles.

nd3d17125f0d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the thermosphere?
o: It is the coldest layer of the atmosphere.
It contains the ionosphere, where auroras occur.
Temperature rises rapidly with height in it.
The International Space Station orbits at about 400 km within it.
nd3d17125f0d.x: The mesosphere, not the thermosphere, is the coldest layer (about -100°C at 80 km).
xa: The **ionosphere reflects radio waves**.
The thermosphere's rise comes from **absorption of high-energy radiation**.
It extends to **~600 km**.

nbc2512c5c89.s: The outermost, extremely thin layer of the atmosphere that merges into outer space is the:
nbc2512c5c89.x: The exosphere is the outermost layer, extending roughly from 600 to 10,000 km and merging into space.
xa: Below it is the **thermosphere**, where temperature **rises rapidly**.
Exosphere and thermosphere make up the **heterosphere**.
The **ISS** orbits at **~400 km**, in the thermosphere.

n60f86745e4b.s: The primary basis for dividing the atmosphere into troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere is:
n60f86745e4b.x: These layers are identified mainly on the basis of how temperature changes with height. Composition provides the basis for the homosphere and heterosphere division.
n60f86745e4b.tq: Distinguish the basis of thermal layering from the basis of compositional layering.
xs: The five layers are based on **how temperature changes with height** — option **(3)**.
**Composition** gives the other division — **homosphere/heterosphere** (option 1).
xa: Trend: **falls → rises → falls → rises** (troposphere to thermosphere).
**99%** of the atmosphere's mass lies within **32 km**.
Reversal layers: **stratosphere and thermosphere**.

n10f8ab0e754.s: Which of the following sequences correctly represents the temperature trend with increasing altitude from the troposphere upward?
n10f8ab0e754.x: Temperature falls in the troposphere, rises in the stratosphere, falls in the mesosphere and rises again in the thermosphere.
n10f8ab0e754.tq: Track the alternating temperature reversals layer by layer.
xs: Temperature **falls, rises, falls, rises** — option **(1)**.
**Falls** in the troposphere; **rises** in the stratosphere (ozone absorbs UV).
**Falls** in the mesosphere; **rises** in the thermosphere (high-energy radiation).
xa: Reversal (inversion) layers: **stratosphere and thermosphere**.
Coldest point: about **-100°C** at **80 km**.
Normal lapse rate: **1 °C per 165 m**.

n3d515b90eed.s: Temperature rises with height in the stratosphere because:
o: Strong convection lifts warm air into it
n3d515b90eed.x: The stratospheric temperature rise is an inversion caused by ozone absorbing UV radiation.
xa: Reversal layers: **stratosphere and thermosphere**.
The mesosphere is the coldest layer (**-100°C**).
Troposphere lapse rate: **6.5°C/km**.

n2e7ccc76514.s: Meteorites generally burn up on entering the atmosphere in the:
n2e7ccc76514.x: Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere because of friction with atmospheric particles.
n2e7ccc76514.tq: Use the direct phenomenon–layer association and avoid confusing it with the ionosphere.
xs: Meteorites burn up in the **mesosphere** — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2025**).
The mesosphere runs from about **50** to **80 km**; temperature falls to about **-100°C** at 80 km, making it the **coldest layer**.
**Troposphere** = weather and clouds; **stratosphere** = ozone layer; **exosphere** = outermost, extremely rarefied layer merging into space.
xa: ⚠ Not the thermosphere/ionosphere — exam angle explicitly says **mesosphere**.
Top of the mesosphere = **mesopause** (~**80 km**).
Temperature trend: falls (troposphere) → rises (stratosphere) → **falls (mesosphere)** → rises (thermosphere).
**Auroras and airglow** occur in the **thermosphere** (ionosphere).

n8e68c7a90f2.s: Auroras and airglow are phenomena primarily associated with the:
n8e68c7a90f2.x: Auroras and airglow occur mainly in the thermosphere, particularly in the ionospheric region.
n8e68c7a90f2.tq: Distinguish upper-atmosphere light phenomena from lower-atmosphere weather phenomena.
xs: **Auroras and airglow** occur in the **thermosphere** (its **ionosphere**) — option **(3)**.
Solar **UV and X-rays** strip electrons from atoms; the resulting **charged particles** produce auroras and airglow.
**Stratosphere** holds the ozone layer, **troposphere** all weather, and **mesosphere** is where meteors burn up.
xa: The thermosphere begins above ~**80 km** and extends to ~**600 km**; temperature **rises rapidly** with height.
The **ISS** orbits at ~**400 km**, in the thermosphere.
Ionospheric layers: **D** (~60-90 km), **E / Kennelly-Heaviside** (~90-150 km), **F / Appleton** (~150-400 km).
The ionosphere **reflects radio waves** — key for long-distance communication.

ngeneral-geography-6-11.s: The Aurora Australis is seen in the:
ngeneral-geography-6-11.x: Aurora Australis is the southern aurora; Aurora Borealis is the northern one.
n: Ionisation is significant in the thermosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The ionosphere consists of electrically charged or ionised particles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Aurora Borealis occurs in the Northern Hemisphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Aurora Australis occurs in the Southern Hemisphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Ionosphere **reflects radio waves**, supporting **long-distance radio communication**.
⚠ **E** layer = **Kennelly-Heaviside**; **F** layer = **Appleton**.
**D layer** (~**60–90 km**) absorbs low-frequency waves and fades at night.
The ionosphere **expands by day** and **shrinks at night**.

ngeneral-geography-6-24.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the layers of the atmosphere?
o: The stratosphere extends from about 13–18 km to 50 km and holds the ozone.
In the mesosphere (50–80 km), temperature increases with height.
The thermosphere begins at about 80 km and its temperature rises sharply.
The exosphere is the outermost layer and transitions to space.
ngeneral-geography-6-24.x: Temperature decreases with height in the mesosphere, where meteors burn; it increases in the stratosphere and thermosphere.
n: The stratosphere extends from approximately 13 or 18 km to 50 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Temperature increases with height in the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is the major identity of the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The mesosphere extends from approximately 50 km to 80 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Temperature decreases with height in the mesosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Meteors burn in the mesosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The thermosphere begins at approximately 80 km and extends upward. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Temperature rises sharply with height in the thermosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ionisation and aurora are associated with the thermosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The exosphere is the outermost atmospheric layer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The exosphere has very high and rarefied conditions. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The exosphere transitions into space. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is the most important association of the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: **Inversion layers:** stratosphere and thermosphere.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes give the exosphere a height of ~**600–10,000 km**.
**ISS** orbits at ~**400 km** in the thermosphere.
**99%** of the atmosphere's mass lies within **32 km**.

ngeneral-geography-6-25.s: The lowest atmospheric layer, most important for biological activity, is the:
ngeneral-geography-6-25.x: The troposphere is the lowest layer and the one where life exists.
n: The troposphere is the lowest atmospheric layer. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The troposphere is the most important layer for biological activity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Average thickness **13 km** — **8 km** at the poles, **18 km** at the equator.
**Most atmospheric mass**, **water vapour** and **dust** are concentrated here.
**Almost all weather phenomena** occur in the troposphere.

ngeneral-geography-6-31.s: Which layer of the atmosphere, with very limited clouds and weather, is suitable for jet aircraft?
ngeneral-geography-6-31.x: The stratosphere, above the troposphere up to 50 km, has little weather and suits jet aircraft.
n: The stratosphere lies above the troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The stratosphere extends up to 50 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is present mainly in the lower stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Clouds and weather are very limited in the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The stratosphere is suitable for jet aircraft. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is the most important association of the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Temperature **increases with altitude** there, as **ozone absorbs UV**.
Ozone maximum roughly **15–35 km**.
Ozone layer = **Stratosphere** (APPSC **2025**).

ngeneral-geography-6-51.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the troposphere?
o: Temperature in it decreases with height.
It extends to about 18 km at the poles and 8 km at the equator.
Its upper boundary is the tropopause.
It is the layer where weather occurs.
ngeneral-geography-6-51.x: The heights are reversed: the troposphere extends to about 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator.
n: The troposphere extends from the surface to approximately 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Weather is the major identity of the troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The upper boundary of the troposphere is the tropopause. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Lapse rate **6.5°C/km** (about **1°C per 165 m**).
The **stratosphere** above has **ozone** as its identity.
Clouds, rainfall and storms result from **water vapour**, **dust**, **convection** and **condensation**.

ngeneral-geography-6-54.s: Long-distance radio communication is supported by the:
ngeneral-geography-6-54.x: The ionosphere, in the strongly ionised thermosphere, reflects radio waves for long-distance communication.
n: Ionisation is significant in the thermosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The ionosphere supports long-distance radio communication. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Ionosphere forms as solar **UV and X-rays** strip electrons from atoms.
**F (Appleton)** layer (~**150–400 km**) is the main reflector of **short-wave radio**.
**E (Kennelly-Heaviside)** layer (~**90–150 km**) reflects **medium-frequency** waves.
⚠ Sources differ: ionosphere about **60 km** to over **1,000 km**.

nf1ceea32dbe.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the homosphere and heterosphere?
o: The homosphere extends from the surface to about 80–90 km.
The gases of the homosphere are relatively evenly mixed.
The heterosphere lies above about 80–90 km.
In the heterosphere, gases are evenly mixed regardless of molecular weight.
nf1ceea32dbe.x: In the heterosphere gases are arranged in layers according to molecular weight; even mixing characterises the homosphere.
xa: Homosphere layers: **troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere**.
Heterosphere layers: **thermosphere and exosphere**.
Heterosphere gases upward: **N2 → O → He → H**.

nd62c55a3bfa.s: The average height of the troposphere is about:
nd62c55a3bfa.x: The troposphere averages about 13 km, being about 8 km over the poles and 18 km over the equator.
xa: The troposphere holds **all weather** — water vapour, dust, clouds.
Older notes give **0-10 km** for the troposphere.
It is thickest at the **equator** due to **convection currents**.

n21befe67ce6.s: Nearly 99% of the atmosphere's mass lies within about ____ of the Earth's surface.
n21befe67ce6.x: About 99% of the atmosphere's mass is concentrated within 32 km of the Earth's surface.
xa: The troposphere is **8 km** at the poles, **18 km** at the equator.
The stratosphere extends to **~50 km**.
The exosphere (**~600-10,000 km**) is extremely thin.

n08d78b7790e.s: The Kigali Amendment, adopted in 2016, entered into force in:
n08d78b7790e.x: The Kigali Amendment was adopted in 2016 and entered into force in 2019; it targets 80-85% HFC cuts.
xa: **HFCs** replaced CFCs; ozone-safe but **high GWP**, hence a climate-driven phase-down.
Parent treaty: **Montreal Protocol (1987)**, controlling nearly **100** ODS; framework: **Vienna Convention (1985)**.
India's **India Cooling Action Plan** (**Mar 2019**) runs to **2037-38**.

n45a67b819bb.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ozone?
o: Heatwaves can increase ground-level ozone concentrations.
North-west India and the Indo-Gangetic Plain are affected by heatwave-driven ground-level ozone.
Ground-level ozone is necessarily beneficial because all ozone protects against UV radiation.
The protective role against ultraviolet radiation is associated with stratospheric ozone.
n45a67b819bb.x: The beneficial UV-shielding role belongs to stratospheric ozone; ground-level ozone is not necessarily beneficial.
xa: Ground-level ozone forms from **NOx + VOCs in sunlight** and is part of **photochemical smog**.
⚠ Stratospheric ozone = **shield**; ground-level ozone = **pollutant**.
Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful **UV-B and UV-C**; it lies at **10-50 km** (about **90%** of ozone).
Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.

ngeneral-geography-6-6.s: The troposphere is thicker at the equator than at the poles because of:
o: Lower surface temperatures at the equator
ngeneral-geography-6-6.x: Strong equatorial convection lifts air higher, raising the tropopause to about 18 km against 8 km at the poles.
n: The troposphere is thicker at the equator than at the poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Strong convection transports heat upward at the equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Strong solar heating causes strong convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Strong convection causes air to rise higher. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Rising air causes the tropopause to rise. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
A higher tropopause produces a thicker troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The tropopause is higher at the equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The tropopause is lower at the poles. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Stronger convection at the equator causes the tropopause to be higher there. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: ⚠ The tropopause is higher **and** colder over the equator (**-80 °C**) than over the poles (**-45 °C**).
The tropopause is **higher in summer** than in winter.
**Almost all weather** occurs in the troposphere.

ngeneral-geography-6-26.s: The normal lapse rate of temperature in the troposphere is:
ngeneral-geography-6-26.x: Temperature falls with height in the troposphere at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per km, about 1°C per 165 m.
n: Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The normal lapse rate in the troposphere is 6.5°C per kilometre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The normal lapse rate is approximately 1°C per 165 metres. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Temperature is **very low near the tropopause**.
**Strong vertical convection** and **condensation** occur in the troposphere.
Older notes give the troposphere height as **0–10 km**.

ngeneral-geography-6-29.s: The boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere is the:
ngeneral-geography-6-29.x: The tropopause marks where temperature stops falling with height and the stratosphere's warming begins.
n: The tropopause is the boundary between the troposphere and the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The tropopause separates the weather-dominated troposphere from the relatively stable stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xa: Height: ~**8 km** at the poles, ~**18 km** at the equator.
Temperature: about **-80 °C** over the equator vs **-45 °C** over the poles.
Other upper limits: **stratopause** (~**50 km**), **mesopause** (~**80 km**).

o: expands during the day and contracts at night
remains unchanged between day and night
contracts during the day and expands at night
nd798d9a8629.x: Solar radiation causes the ionosphere to expand during the day, while it contracts at night.
nd798d9a8629.tq: Directly distinguish the day-night reversal in the behaviour of the ionosphere.
xs: The ionosphere **expands by day** and **shrinks at night** — option **(1)**.
It forms when solar **UV and X-rays** strip electrons from atoms.
xa: The **D layer** fades at night.
Within the thermosphere it lies at about **80-400 km**.
Topside ionosphere mapped over India up to **1,000 km** for **NavIC/GPS** accuracy.

n8d7315db050.s: The main reflector of short-wave radio in the ionosphere is the:
n8d7315db050.x: The F layer is the main reflector of short-wave radio; the D layer absorbs medium and long waves and the E layer reflects medium-frequency waves.
xa: ⚠ **E** = **Kennelly-Heaviside**; **F** = **Appleton**.
The **D layer** fades at night.
F splits into **F1, F2** by day.

n35caec6cdf5.s: About 90% of atmospheric ozone lies in the:
n35caec6cdf5.x: About 90% of ozone lies in the stratosphere between about 10 and 50 km, densest at about 15-35 km.
xa: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.
An unusually dense pocket was found at **21-23 km** over the North Bay of Bengal.
Ozone layer in the stratosphere: APPSC **2025**.

n03119e2b65f.s: The principal protective function of the ozone layer is to absorb:
n03119e2b65f.x: Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV-B and UV-C radiation and thereby acts as a shield for life on Earth.
n03119e2b65f.tq: Discriminate between ultraviolet radiation and other parts of the electromagnetic spectrum.
xs: The ozone layer absorbs harmful **ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation** (**UV-B and UV-C**) — option **(2)**.
It is **Earth's shield** (APPSC **2025**).
xa: **UV-B** causes **skin cancer, cataract, immune suppression, lower crop yield**.
Ozone absorbing UV is why stratospheric temperature **rises**.
⚠ Stratospheric ozone = shield; ground-level ozone = **pollutant**.

n877e20a0de8.s: The thickness or total column amount of ozone in the atmosphere is expressed in:
n877e20a0de8.x: Ozone concentration in an atmospheric column is measured in Dobson Units (DU).
n877e20a0de8.tq: Discriminate among scientific units by their measured quantity.
xs: Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)** — option **(2)**.
The DU expresses the ozone in the **stratospheric** shield, which absorbs **UV-B and UV-C**.
xa: About **90%** of ozone lies in the stratosphere, **10-50 km**.
Normal ozone peak: **25-30 km**.
Antarctic ozone hole **2025** peaked at just over **21 million sq km**.

n6d721a3821a.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes stratospheric ozone from ground-level ozone?
o: Ground-level ozone protects living organisms from UV-B, whereas stratospheric ozone is a pollutant
Stratospheric ozone is formed from NOx and VOCs near the surface, whereas ground-level ozone is formed naturally in the polar vortex
Stratospheric ozone absorbs harmful UV-B, whereas ground-level ozone is a pollutant formed from NOx and VOCs in sunlight
Both forms are produced only by volcanic eruptions
n6d721a3821a.x: Stratospheric ozone provides UV-B protection. Ground-level ozone is a pollutant produced through reactions involving nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds in sunlight.
n6d721a3821a.tq: Separate two similar terms by location, formation and environmental effect.
xs: **Stratospheric ozone** absorbs **UV-B**; **ground-level ozone** is a **pollutant** from **NOx + VOCs** in sunlight — option **(3)**.
Option (1) swaps the two roles.
Ground-level ozone is part of **photochemical smog**.
xa: ⚠ Stratospheric ozone = shield; ground-level ozone = pollutant.
Heatwaves push ground-level ozone up in **north-west India** and the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**.
Ground-level ozone is a **secondary** pollutant.

ngeneral-geography-6-4.s: The ozone layer is mainly concentrated at which approximate altitude range?
ngeneral-geography-6-4.x: The ozone layer lies mainly at about 15–35 km in the stratosphere.
ngeneral-geography-6-4.tq: Recall the height of each layer.
n: The troposphere extends from the surface to approximately 8 km at the poles and 18 km at the equator. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The mesosphere extends from approximately 50 km to 80 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The maximum concentration of ozone occurs roughly between 15 km and 35 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
The traditional approximate region of the ionosphere is 80–640 km. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
Ozone is the most important association of the stratosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 42-50]
xs: The **ozone layer** is mainly at about **15–35 km** — option **(1)**.
It lies mainly in the **lower stratosphere**, with **maximum concentration** roughly between **15 km and 35 km**.
**0–8 km** is the **troposphere** at the poles; **50–80 km** is the **mesosphere**; **80–640 km** is the **ionosphere**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: main ozone layer about **15–30 km**; normal peak **25–30 km**.
About **90%** of ozone is in the **stratosphere**, **10%** in the troposphere.
Ozone is measured in **Dobson Units (DU)**.

n6121ec771f9.s: Which of the following is the primary cause of stratospheric ozone depletion?
o: Oxygen combining with hydrogen in the mesosphere
Halocarbons releasing chlorine and bromine atoms
n6121ec771f9.x: Halocarbons such as CFCs and HCFCs release chlorine and bromine atoms that destroy ozone faster than it can form.
n6121ec771f9.tq: Identify the responsible chemical group and the destructive atoms released.
xs: **Halocarbons** releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms are the primary cause — option **(4)** (APPSC **2023**).
Examples: **CFCs, HCFCs**; they destroy ozone **faster than it forms**.
xa: **CFCs**: refrigeration, ACs, **aerosols**, foam blowing.
**Methyl bromide**: agricultural fumigant.
**Carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform**: solvents.

na0916c3ce59.s: The ozone hole refers to seasonal thinning of ozone mainly over Antarctica during:
na0916c3ce59.x: The Antarctic ozone hole develops mainly from August to November, during the Southern Hemisphere spring, aided by polar stratospheric clouds.
na0916c3ce59.tq: Use the seasonal and hemispheric clue to reject the opposite-season options.
xs: The ozone hole forms over **Antarctica** from **August to November** (**Aug-Nov**, southern spring) — option **(4)**.
It is helped by **polar stratospheric clouds**.
xa: It came into focus in **1985** (older notes: **1983**).
**2025** hole peaked at just over **21 million sq km** and closed early.
The **2006 record** was **29 million sq km**.

n2bc0db7bab1.s: The Antarctic ozone hole came into scientific focus in:
n2bc0db7bab1.x: The ozone hole came into focus in 1985; some older accounts cite 1983, but 1985 is the stated reference year here.
n2bc0db7bab1.tq: Distinguish the standard reference year from an older alternative date.
xs: The ozone hole came into focus in **1985** — option **(3)**.
⚠ Older notes give **1983** — option (2) is the trap.
xa: **Vienna Convention** was also **1985** (framework: research, monitoring).
**Montreal Protocol**: **1987**.

nac4f9ed9d78.s: Which one of the following correctly compares CFCs and HFCs?
o: CFCs spare ozone, whereas HFCs destroy ozone and have no warming effect.
CFCs destroy stratospheric ozone and are potent greenhouse gases; HFCs spare ozone but have high global-warming potential.
Both CFCs and HFCs destroy stratospheric ozone to the same extent.
Neither CFCs nor HFCs has any significant effect on the atmosphere.
nac4f9ed9d78.x: CFCs deplete stratospheric ozone and act as potent greenhouse gases. HFCs do not harm ozone but have high global-warming potential.
nac4f9ed9d78.tq: Use the contrasting ozone and warming effects to separate the two confusable groups.
xs: **CFCs** destroy **stratospheric ozone** and are potent GHGs; **HFCs** spare ozone but have **high GWP** — option **(2)**.
CFCs have a **GWP 1,000-23,000** and make up **15%** of the enhanced effect.
xa: HFCs **replaced CFCs**.
**Kigali Amendment** (**2016**, in force **2019**) cuts HFCs by **80-85%**.
It could avoid up to **0.5°C** of warming by **2100**.

n4598282f174.s: In 2025, the Antarctic ozone hole peaked at just over:
n4598282f174.x: The 2025 Antarctic ozone hole peaked at just over 21 million sq km and closed early, below the 2006 record of 29 million sq km.
xa: The ozone hole is a seasonal thinning over **Antarctica**, **Aug-Nov** (southern spring), helped by **polar stratospheric clouds**.
It came into focus in **1985** (older notes give **1983**).
Cause: **halocarbons** (CFCs, HCFCs) releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms.
An unusually dense **ozone pocket** was found at **21-23 km** over the **North Bay of Bengal** (16 Aug 2026).

nenvironment-27-9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ozone-depleting substances?
o: Methyl bromide is an ozone-depleting substance.
Carbon tetrachloride is an ozone-depleting substance.
nenvironment-27-9.x: HCFCs do deplete ozone, as do CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and methyl bromide.
n: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are ozone-depleting substances. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Halons are ozone-depleting substances. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Carbon tetrachloride is an ozone-depleting substance. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs) are ozone-depleting substances. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Methyl chloroform is an ozone-depleting substance. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
Methyl bromide is an ozone-depleting substance. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 47-50]
xa: Uses: **CFCs** — refrigeration, ACs, aerosols; **methyl bromide** — agricultural fumigant; **carbon tetrachloride**, **methyl chloroform** — solvents.
⚠ **1985** = **Vienna** (framework); **1987** = **Montreal** (ODS); **2016** = **Kigali** (HFCs).
**HFCs** replaced CFCs — ozone-safe but **high GWP**.
Antarctic ozone hole reported in **1985**, discovered by a **British team**.

n552b4086970.s: India's phase-out of HCFC-141b in rigid foam had which of the following outcomes?
o: It was the first such phase-out among developing countries, with a 44% cut against a 35% target by January 2020.
It concerned HFC-134a in refrigeration and achieved no measurable reduction.
It was the first phase-out among developed countries, with a 35% cut against a 44% target by January 2020.
It achieved a 15% cut against a 10% target by January 2015.
n552b4086970.x: India was the first developing country to phase out HCFC-141b in rigid foam and achieved a 44% reduction against a 35% target by January 2020.
n552b4086970.tq: Check the country status, chemical use, target and achieved percentage together.
xs: India was the **first developing country** to fully phase out **HCFC-141b** in **rigid foam**, cutting HCFCs **44%** against a **35%** target by **January 2020** — option **(1)**.
The phase-out concerned **HCFC-141b** (a transitional CFC substitute), not HFCs, and India was a **developing**, not developed, country.
xa: **HCFCs** were the **transitional substitute** for CFCs under the **Montreal Protocol (1987)**.
**India Cooling Action Plan**: **Mar 2019**, horizon **2037-38**.
**HFCs** (ozone-safe, high GWP) are being phased down under the **Kigali Amendment (2016)**.
The **Montreal Protocol** controls nearly **100** ODS and is universally ratified.

n477b93ce067.s: Which agreement, adopted in 1987, created legally binding measures to phase out ozone-depleting substances?
n477b93ce067.x: The 1987 Montreal Protocol is legally binding for phasing out ODS; the 1985 Vienna Convention set a framework for research, monitoring and cooperation.
xa: ⚠ **1985** = Vienna (framework); **1987** = Montreal (ODS); **2016** = Kigali (HFCs).
Montreal is **universally ratified** — the **most successful environmental treaty**; **197** UN member parties.
The **ozone hole** came into focus in **1985** (older notes give **1983**), the same year as Vienna.
Primary cause of depletion: **halocarbons** (CFCs, HCFCs) releasing **chlorine and bromine** atoms.

nbbdb3f4c7be.s: According to the WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide in 2024 was approximately
nbbdb3f4c7be.x: Per the WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin 2025, CO2 rose by 3.5 ppm to 423.9 ppm in 2024, the largest rise since 1957 and about 152% of the pre-industrial level.
nbbdb3f4c7be.tq: Test the precise current-affairs figure against nearby numerical distractors.
xs: CO2 reached **423.9 ppm** in **2024** — option **(1)** (WMO Greenhouse Gas Bulletin **2025**).
It rose **3.5 ppm** — the **largest rise since 1957**.
That is **152%** of the pre-industrial level.
xa: By volume CO2 is about **0.04%** (older notes: **0.036**).
CO2 absorbs **outgoing terrestrial radiation** — a greenhouse gas.
**Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas**.

n9b437a3148a.s: Which pair of atmospheric layers represents the principal temperature-inversion or reversal layers?
n9b437a3148a.x: The stratosphere and thermosphere are reversal layers in which temperature increases with height, unlike the normal decrease in the troposphere and mesosphere.
n9b437a3148a.tq: Distinguish layers with a temperature rise from those with the normal temperature fall.
xs: The reversal layers are the **stratosphere and thermosphere** — option **(1)**.
In both, temperature **rises with height**.
In the **troposphere** and **mesosphere** it falls.
xa: Stratosphere: **ozone absorbs UV**.
Thermosphere: **absorption of high-energy radiation**.
The thermosphere holds the **ionosphere**.

nd17b1b04391.s: Mission SANA, India's first indigenous stratospheric super-pressure balloon, was launched from:
nd17b1b04391.x: Mission SANA was launched from Vijayawada, with climate tracking among its objectives.
xa: AP angle: **World Ozone Day** (**16 Sep**) and Mission SANA from **Vijayawada**.
The **stratosphere** (tropopause to ~**50 km**) has calm, stable air — ideal for **high-altitude balloons**.
On World Ozone Day **2026**, Deputy CM **K. Pawan Kalyan** called for collective action to protect the ozone layer.

n03ae250431b.s: Which one of the following correctly describes insolation?
o: Vertical transfer of heat by rising air
Horizontal transfer of heat by moving air
Direct heating of the atmosphere by outgoing long-wave radiation
Direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation
n03ae250431b.x: Insolation is the direct heating received from incoming short-wave solar radiation.
n03ae250431b.tq: Use the precise mechanism rather than confusing insolation with atmospheric heat transfer.
xs: **Insolation** is **direct heating by incoming short-wave solar radiation** — option **(4)**.
**Vertical** transfer by rising air = **convection**; **horizontal** transfer by moving air = **advection**.
Outgoing long-wave heat is **terrestrial radiation**, the main source that heats the atmosphere.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** matched: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
The sun emits **short-wave** radiation; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**).
Planetary **albedo** is about **35%** of insolation.

n210206fe3fc.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the heating of the atmosphere?
o: Conduction heats the lowest air layers in contact with the warm ground.
Advection is the vertical transfer of heat by rising air currents.
Conduction works best in solids through particle-to-particle contact.
Convection is the vertical transfer of heat by rising warm air and is confined to the troposphere.
n210206fe3fc.x: Advection is the horizontal transfer of heat by wind; vertical transfer by rising warm air is convection.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** matched: **Advection – horizontal**, **Convection – vertical**, **Insolation – direct**, **Conduction – lower layers**.
**Terrestrial radiation** (long-wave) is the **main source heating the atmosphere**.
Normal lapse rate **6.5 °C/km**.

n179058dc0fd.s: The Loo, a hot wind of northern India, is an example of which of the following processes?
n179058dc0fd.x: The Loo transfers heat horizontally through moving air and is therefore an example of advection.
n179058dc0fd.tq: Identify the direction of movement in the example before naming the process.
xs: The **Loo** of north India is an example of **advection** — **horizontal** transfer of heat by wind — option **(2)**.
**Convection** is vertical transfer; **conduction** heats air in contact with the ground; **radiation** is via electromagnetic waves.
xa: APPSC-G2 **2023** match: **Advection - horizontal**, **Convection - vertical**, **Insolation - direct**, **Conduction - lower layers**.
Convection: heated air becomes **less dense and rises**, cooler air sinks.
**Terrestrial radiation** (long-wave) is the **main source** heating the atmosphere.

nd816845f1b0.s: The atmosphere is heated mainly by:
o: Direct absorption of incoming short-wave solar radiation
Outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation from below
nd816845f1b0.x: The atmosphere is largely transparent to incoming short-wave radiation but absorbs outgoing long-wave terrestrial radiation, so it is heated mainly from below.
xa: ⚠ Trap: "heated more by incoming solar radiation" is **wrong**; greenhouse gases absorb long waves is **right** (UPSC **2024**).
Earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

n617efcdebd2.s: Why does temperature normally decrease with increasing altitude?
o: Higher air receives more long-wave radiation from the Sun.
The ground heats the air from below, while higher air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust.
The Earth stops emitting radiation above the lower atmosphere.
The atmosphere is heated mainly from above by direct solar radiation.
n617efcdebd2.x: The ground heats the atmosphere from below. At higher levels the air is thinner and contains less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
n617efcdebd2.tq: Identify the heating source and the properties of higher air.
xs: The **ground heats the air from below**, while higher air is **thinner** with **less water vapour and dust** — option **(2)**.
So higher air absorbs less heat, and temperature falls at the normal lapse rate of **6.5 °C/km**.
The atmosphere is not heated mainly from above by direct sunlight, and the earth does not stop emitting radiation.
xa: The sun emits **short-wave**; earth re-emits **long-wave infra-red** (**8,000-25,000 nm**), absorbed by CO2 and water vapour.
**Temperature inversion** is when this reverses and temperature **rises** with height.
**Terrestrial radiation** is the main source heating the atmosphere.

ngeneral-geography-7-32.s: Which sky condition produces the greatest terrestrial cooling at night?
ngeneral-geography-7-32.x: Clear skies allow more daytime solar heating and more night-time terrestrial cooling, whereas clouds cut both.
n: Cloudy conditions reduce incoming solar radiation during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudy conditions produce cooler daytime temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies allow greater solar heating during the day. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Clear skies cause greater terrestrial cooling at night. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: **Cloudy nights** stay warmer.
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**; largest in high-latitude interiors (**Siberia**).
Seasonal differences are **maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).

ngeneral-geography-7-7.s: Which climatic control explains why the Himalayas are cooler despite their lower latitude?
ngeneral-geography-7-7.x: Altitude makes the Himalayas cool despite their low latitude, since temperature falls about 6.5°C per km.
ngeneral-geography-7-7.tq: Recall the effect of each climatic control.
n: Altitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Temperature generally decreases with increasing altitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The Himalayas are cooler despite having a lower latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Altitude** explains it — option **(1)**: temperature **decreases with increasing altitude**, so the **Himalayas** are **cooler despite a lower latitude**.
**Distance from sea** moderates range; **ocean currents** raise or lower coastal temperatures; **cloud cover** modifies day and night heating.
xa: Normal lapse rate **6.5 °C/km**.
Higher air is **thinner**, with **less water vapour and dust**, so it absorbs less heat.
Air is heated **from below** by terrestrial radiation.

ngeneral-geography-7-22.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about factors affecting temperature?
o: Cold ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
Continentality produces extreme interior climates with a large annual range.
Cloud cover reduces daytime heating and night-time cooling.
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.
ngeneral-geography-7-22.x: Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures and favour west-coast deserts; it is warm currents that raise them.
n: Distance from the sea or continentality is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Interior climates are extreme. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover modifies heating and cooling. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold ocean currents lower coastal temperatures. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relief alters temperature and air movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Mountain slopes and aspects affect temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloud cover affects day and night temperature. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Continental interiors have **large annual and daily ranges** — hot summers, cold winters.
**Cloudy nights** stay warmer; **clear nights** lose more heat.
**Relief** alters **temperature** and **air movement**.

n18587fd0a78.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the Earth's aphelion?
n18587fd0a78.x: Aphelion occurs around 4 July, when the Earth is approximately 152 million kilometres from the Sun.
n18587fd0a78.tq: Use the paired contrast between perihelion and aphelion.
xs: **Aphelion** (Earth farthest from the sun) falls around **4 July** at about **152 million km** — option **(1)**.
Option (2), ~**3 January** at **147 million km**, is **perihelion** (Earth nearest the sun).
xa: ⚠ Perihelion = **Jan**, nearer (**147**); aphelion = **Jul**, farther (**152**) — a common swap trap.
**Earth-sun distance** is one of the factors of insolation, along with **angle of rays** and **length of day**.
The equator receives the **most annual insolation**; the poles the least.

n27fe05dcf62.s: Which one of the following sequences correctly represents the surfaces in descending order of albedo?
o: Fresh snow, sand, grass, forest, water
Fresh snow, grass, sand, water, forest
Water, forest, grass, sand, fresh snow
Sand, fresh snow, forest, grass, water
n27fe05dcf62.x: The descending albedo sequence is fresh snow, sand, grass, forest and water, with fresh snow reflecting the most and water generally the least.
n27fe05dcf62.tq: Rank the surfaces from highest reflection to lowest reflection.
xs: Descending albedo: **fresh snow > sand > grass > forest > water** — option **(1)**.
**Fresh snow** reflects most (**80-90%**); **water** with sun high reflects least (**below 10%**).
Dry sand **20-40%** sits above grass **20-25%**, so options placing grass above sand are wrong.
xa: Fresh snow as highest albedo was asked in APPSC-G1 **2019**.
Crop land albedo: **15-25%**.
Clouds: **high, thin** = warming; **low, thick** = cooling.

n319a424c6a3.s: Which clouds tend to reflect incoming sunlight and produce cooling?
n319a424c6a3.x: Low, thick clouds reflect more sunlight and cause cooling, whereas high, thin clouds tend to trap outgoing heat.
xa: ⚠ **High thin = warming; low thick = cooling**.
Of 100 units of insolation, clouds reflect **27**; total reflected **35** (planetary albedo).
**Clear nights** lose more heat; **cloudy nights** stay warmer as clouds send heat back.

n40aec04c546.s: According to recent assessments (Apr 2025), the Arctic is warming at about what rate compared with the global average?
n40aec04c546.x: The Arctic has warmed by at least 2 deg C and is warming 3-4 times faster than the global average (older estimates said about twice), driven by the ice-albedo feedback in which melting ice exposes dark ocean. It is not slower, equal or ten times faster.
xs: The Arctic is warming about **3-4 times faster** than the global average (Apr **2025**) — option **(1)**.
It has warmed at least **2°C**; older notes said about **twice** as fast.
Driver: the **ice-albedo feedback** — melting ice exposes dark ocean that absorbs more heat.
xa: **Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo, adding to warming.
Global land temperature is up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).
India's annual mean is up **0.7 °C** since **1900**; slower partly because of **Arctic amplification** and aerosol masking.

nabf4dde5d48.s: A heat dome is best described as a situation in which:
o: A cold ocean current remains below a stationary cyclone
A low-pressure system forms over a rapidly moving jet stream
A monsoon trough shifts permanently towards the poles
A stalled high-pressure system remains under a slowed, meandering jet stream
nabf4dde5d48.x: A heat dome develops when a high-pressure system stalls beneath a slowed and meandering jet stream, producing persistent heat.
nabf4dde5d48.tq: Select the option that correctly links the pressure system with the jet-stream condition.
xs: A **heat dome** is a **stalled high-pressure system** under a **slowed, meandering jet stream** — option **(4)**.
It caused a record early heatwave in **Western Europe** (**27 May 2026**).
It involves high pressure, not a low-pressure system or cyclone.
xa: Oceans absorbed a record **+23 ZJ** of heat in **2025** (~**90%** of excess heat).
IMD heatwave thresholds: **40°C plains / 37°C coast / 30°C hills**.
AP 2026: **El Nino** intensified the heat (**22-23 May 2026**).

n7113fb6c4a8.s: Albedo of a surface refers to the
o: share of incoming radiation reflected by the surface
amount of heat stored below the surface
rate at which terrestrial radiation is emitted
amount of moisture absorbed by the surface
n7113fb6c4a8.x: Albedo is the proportion or share of incoming radiation that a surface reflects.
n7113fb6c4a8.tq: Use the exact definition and distinguish reflection from absorption and emission.
xs: **Albedo** is the **share of incoming radiation a surface reflects** — option **(1)**.
Heat storage, emission of terrestrial radiation and moisture absorption are not albedo.
xa: Ranking: **fresh snow** (highest, APPSC-G1 **2019**) > sand > grass > forest > water.
