Fresh snow **80-90%**; water (sun high) **below 10%**.
**Planetary albedo** ≈ **35%** (35 of 100 units).
**Black carbon** on snow cuts albedo; melting ice exposes dark ocean (**ice-albedo feedback**).

nb8f3b9f39f8.s: Melting of ice can intensify warming because it
o: converts long-wave radiation into short-wave radiation
increases the albedo of the exposed ocean
exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat
prevents the ocean from absorbing solar radiation
nb8f3b9f39f8.x: Melting ice exposes dark ocean water, which has a lower albedo and absorbs more heat, producing a positive ice-albedo feedback.
nb8f3b9f39f8.tq: Trace the cause-effect chain from surface change to albedo, absorption and warming.
xs: Melting ice **exposes a darker ocean surface that absorbs more heat** — option **(3)** — the **ice-albedo feedback**.
Dark water has **lower albedo** (**below 10%**) than ice and snow (**80-90%**), so it does not raise albedo or stop absorption.
xa: The Arctic has warmed at least **2°C** and warms **3-4 times** faster than the global average (Apr **2025**).
**Black carbon** on snow also cuts albedo.
Albedo ranking: **fresh snow** > sand > grass > forest > **water**.

ndb5f1e5e452.s: Of 100 units of insolation received at the top of the atmosphere, how many are absorbed by the Earth's surface?
ndb5f1e5e452.x: Of 100 units, 35 are reflected to space, 14 are absorbed by the atmosphere and 51 by the Earth's surface.
xa: Earth radiates **51** units: **17** straight to space, **34** absorbed by the atmosphere.
Of the 34: **6** direct, **9** convection/turbulence, **19** latent heat of condensation.
Atmosphere sends **48** (14 + 34) to space: **35 + 17 + 48 = 100** balanced.

n06b1c1202f6.s: Of the 35 units of insolation reflected back to space in the Earth's heat budget, how many are reflected by clouds?
n06b1c1202f6.x: Of the 35 reflected units, 27 are reflected by clouds, 6 by scattering and 2 by snow and ice.
xa: The atmosphere sends **48** (14 + 34) units to space.
Planetary albedo ≈ **35%**; the surface absorbs **51**, the atmosphere **14**.
Surplus in the **tropics**, deficit towards the **poles**; heat moves **poleward**.

n5819ae88978.s: Carbon dioxide contributes approximately what share of the greenhouse effect?
n5819ae88978.x: CO2 contributes about 60%, from fossil fuels, deforestation and cement; methane about 20%, CFCs about 15% and N2O about 5%.
xa: **Water vapour** is the most abundant greenhouse gas (a feedback).
Without the atmosphere the surface would be about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

n924229365ec.s: Which one of the following gases is the most abundant greenhouse gas and acts importantly as a feedback in the climate system?
n924229365ec.x: Water vapour is the most abundant greenhouse gas and functions importantly as a climate feedback.
n924229365ec.tq: Distinguish abundance from the percentage contribution estimates of the other gases.
xs: **Water vapour** is the **most abundant greenhouse gas** and acts as a **feedback** — option **(1)**.
**CO2** has the largest share (~**60%**) among listed gases; **methane** ~**20%**; **N2O** ~**5%**.
xa: Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** trap heat (APPSC **2025**).
Earth's long-wave radiation is absorbed by **CO2 and water vapour**.
Without the atmosphere: about **-18 °C** instead of **+15 °C**.

n9635aca7212.s: At the same latitude, insolation is generally higher over:
o: Polar seas than over tropical land
n9635aca7212.x: Insolation declines towards the poles and, at the same latitude, is higher over continents than over oceans.
xa: The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; maximum at the surface is over **subtropical deserts**.
Land heats and cools faster than water — hence the land-sea contrast.
Surplus heat in the **tropics**, deficit towards the **poles**; winds and currents carry heat **poleward**.

n8ebc405c016.s: In the Earth's heat budget, a heat surplus is found in the:
n8ebc405c016.x: The tropics have a heat surplus and the poles a deficit; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
xa: Overall the surface returns all **51** absorbed units, so earth neither warms nor cools.
Oceans took up a record **+23 zettajoules** of heat in **2025** (vs **+16 ZJ** in 2024) = ~**90%** of excess heat.
India's warming is slower partly because of **poleward heat transfer**.

n2f5bf5abd13.s: In January, isotherms in the Northern Hemisphere bend:
o: Equatorward over both land and oceans
Poleward over land and equatorward over oceans
Equatorward over land and poleward over oceans
n2f5bf5abd13.x: In January, Northern Hemisphere isotherms bend equatorward over colder landmasses and poleward over relatively warmer oceans.
xa: **Isotherms** join places of equal temperature, running roughly **east-west**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
**Thermal equator** lies mostly **north of the equator** (more land in the NH).

nb6d1cc9ef10.s: In winter, India's 20°C isotherm runs approximately from the mouth of the Tapi to the:
nb6d1cc9ef10.x: In winter the 20°C isotherm runs from the Tapi mouth to the Mahanadi delta; temperature rises from north to south.
xa: In **January**, isotherms bend **equatorward over land** and **poleward over oceans** (UPSC **2025**).
The **thermal equator** lies mostly **north of the equator** (more land in the NH).
India's winter **diurnal range** is highest in the north-west — **14–18°C**.

na09cdb227ef.s: The thermal equator is best defined as the
o: line joining places of highest mean temperature, generally lying north of the geographical Equator.
boundary between the tropical and polar zones, fixed at 23½° latitude.
line joining the coldest places in both hemispheres.
geographical Equator, which never shifts seasonally.
na09cdb227ef.x: The thermal equator is the line of highest mean temperature. It lies mostly north of the geographical Equator and shifts with the apparent movement of the Sun.
na09cdb227ef.tq: Distinguish the shifting thermal equator from the fixed geographical Equator.
xs: The **thermal equator** is the line of **highest mean temperature**, lying mostly **north of the geographical equator** — option **(1)**.
It lies north because the **NH has more land**, and it **shifts** with the sun's apparent movement — so it is not fixed.
xa: **Isotherms** run roughly east-west; in January they bend **equatorward over land**.
Southern Hemisphere isotherms are **more regular** (mostly ocean).
Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.

ne9e28d4312d.s: Which one of the following regions of India records the highest diurnal range of temperature in winter?
ne9e28d4312d.x: The diurnal range is highest in north-western India during winter, where it is about 14°–18°C.
ne9e28d4312d.tq: Identify the correct region before matching it with the associated numerical range.
xs: Winter diurnal range is highest in **north-western India** — **14-18°C** — option **(3)**.
Coasts and deltas have a **small range** due to sea moderation.
xa: **Continentality** gives large annual and daily ranges in northern interiors of India.
**Clear nights** lose more heat — cold nights and frost.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).

n3023b54f8a6.s: The normal lapse rate, at which temperature falls with increasing height in the troposphere, is about:
n3023b54f8a6.x: Temperature normally falls with height at about 6.5 °C per km, because the air is heated from below and higher air absorbs less heat.
n3023b54f8a6.tq: Normal lapse = 6.5 per km (about 1 °C per 165 m).
xs: The normal lapse rate is about **6.5 °C per km** — option **(3)**.
Air is heated **from below**; higher air is thinner with less water vapour and dust, so it absorbs less heat.
xa: **Convection** (vertical transfer by rising warm air) is **confined to the troposphere**.
In a **temperature inversion**, temperature **rises** with height instead.
The stratosphere is a **permanent inversion** layer.

nbbee96d0f59.s: An urban heat island is primarily produced because
o: cities receive no long-wave radiation at night.
rural vegetation reflects all incoming radiation toward cities.
urban areas are always located at lower latitudes than rural areas.
concrete and asphalt store heat and make cities warmer than surrounding rural areas.
nbbee96d0f59.x: Concrete and asphalt absorb and retain heat, causing urban areas to be warmer than their rural surroundings.
nbbee96d0f59.tq: Identify the physical surface property responsible for the urban-rural temperature contrast.
xs: **Concrete and asphalt** absorb and **store heat**, making cities **warmer than the surrounding rural** countryside — option **(4)**: the **urban heat island**.
It is not a matter of latitude, nor of cities receiving no long-wave radiation.
xa: **Hyderabad** UHI intensity: **5.74-6.82 °C**.
**Chennai**: vegetation fell **25% (2014) → 10% (2024)**; built-up area rose **36% → 67%**.
**Data centres** add ~**2 °C** to land-surface temperature within **10 km**.
**TRISHNA** (ISRO-CNES) will map **urban heat islands**; PSLV launch due **2027**.

ngeneral-geography-7-33.s: The equator experiences greater heating than the poles because it receives ____ rays of the Sun.
ngeneral-geography-7-33.x: Latitude sets the Sun's angle: the equator gets more direct rays and greater heating, while the poles get oblique rays and lower heating.
n: Latitude is a factor or control of climate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The equator receives more direct rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
More direct rays at the equator produce greater heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The poles receive oblique rays. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Oblique rays at the poles produce lower heating. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Seasonal variation increases with latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Annual temperature range is generally greater toward higher latitudes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Annual range is **minimum at the equator**.
The **equator** receives the **most annual insolation**; the **poles** the least.
**Perihelion** ~**3 Jan**, **147 million km**; **aphelion** ~**4 Jul**, **152 million km**.

ne80619ce523.s: The highest temperatures on Earth generally occur in the sub-tropical deserts rather than at the Equator because of:
o: The maximum annual rainfall of the deserts
The permanent presence of cold ocean currents
Persistent cloud cover and humid air
ne80619ce523.x: Sub-tropical deserts around 20°–30° N have clear skies and dry air, permitting very high temperatures; the Equator does not record the highest temperatures merely because it receives strong insolation.
ne80619ce523.tq: Apply the cause-effect relationship instead of choosing the latitude with the strongest general insolation.
xs: Sub-tropical deserts (about **20-30° N**) are hottest because of **clear skies and dry air** — option **(4)**.
Little cloud lets maximum insolation reach the surface; the **equator** has more cloud.
Deserts have scant rainfall, and **cloud cover and humid air** describe the equator, not deserts.
xa: World hottest: **Death Valley**, **56.7°C**; world coldest: **Vostok**, **-89.2°C**.
India coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi** — the "**Kashmir of AP**".

n9a5372bc8a1.s: In a valley inversion, the valley floor is colder than the slopes because
o: warm air flows downslope and accumulates at the valley floor.
the valley floor is always nearer to the Sun.
cold air drains downslope and settles in the valley.
the slopes receive no solar radiation in winter.
n9a5372bc8a1.x: Cold, dense air flows downslope and accumulates in valleys, producing frost pockets while the slopes remain relatively warmer.
n9a5372bc8a1.tq: Follow the movement of dense cold air to determine the colder location.
xs: In a **valley inversion**, **cold air drains downslope** and settles in the valley — option **(3)**.
This creates **frost pockets** on valley floors while **slopes stay warmer**.
xa: Hence **orchards/plantations** are placed on **upper slopes**.
It is also called **air-drainage inversion**.
Other types: **ground/radiation**, **frontal/advection**, **permanent** (polar areas).

ndisaster-management-33-5.s: Under IMD heatwave criteria, the minimum threshold temperature for coastal areas is:
ndisaster-management-33-5.x: A heatwave needs at least 37°C on the coast, 40°C in the plains and 30°C in the hills.
n: The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in plains is 40°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in coastal areas is 37°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
The minimum threshold temperature for declaring a heatwave in hilly regions is 30°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xa: Heatwave = departure of **4.5°C to 6.4°C**; severe = **more than 6.4°C**.
An actual maximum of **45°C** or more is a heatwave on its own.
**NDMA heat-wave guidelines:** **2019**; AP **Heat Wave Action Plan** since **2016**.

ndisaster-management-34-7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the criteria for declaring a cold wave?
o: In the plains, the minimum-temperature threshold is 10°C or below.
A severe cold wave is a negative departure greater than 6.4°C.
A cold wave is a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C from normal.
In hilly regions, the minimum-temperature threshold is 10°C or below.
ndisaster-management-34-7.x: The hilly-region threshold is 0°C or below; 10°C or below is the threshold for the plains.
n: The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in plains is 10°C or below. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In plains, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In plains, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
The minimum-temperature threshold for declaring a cold wave in hilly regions is 0°C or below. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In hilly regions, a cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure of 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
In hilly regions, a severe cold wave is declared when the minimum temperature has a negative departure greater than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 72-74]
xa: **Coastal stations:** threshold **15°C or below**; cold wave at **4.5°C or more** departure.
Plains by actual minimum: **cold wave** at **4°C or below**; **severe** at **2°C or below**.
India's coldest: **Dras** (Ladakh), **-45°C** (**1908**).

nb2e22754093.s: Lines joining places having equal temperature are called:
nb2e22754093.x: Isotherms join places of equal temperature; they generally run east-west and are more regular in the ocean-dominated Southern Hemisphere.
xa: January: isotherms bend **equatorward over land**, **poleward over oceans**; July reverses.
**Thermal equator** = line of highest mean temperature, mostly north of the equator.
India winter: **20°C isotherm** runs from the **Tapti** mouth to the **Mahanadi delta**.

n427c3521e76.s: The annual range of temperature is largest in:
o: High-latitude continental interiors such as Siberia
n427c3521e76.x: The annual range is largest in high-latitude continental interiors like Siberia and minimum at the equator; coasts have a small range.
xa: **Seasonal differences are maximum in high latitudes** (APPSC-G1 **2023**).
**Continentality** = large annual and daily ranges (northern interiors of India).
AP: coast low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** high.

n85835978403.s: In Andhra Pradesh, a high diurnal range of temperature is found in:
n85835978403.x: The coast has a low diurnal range moderated by the sea and sea breezes (as at Visakhapatnam and Kakinada), while interior Rayalaseema has a high range.
xa: Coasts are **equable/maritime**, moderated by the sea; interiors show **continentality**.
AP hottest: **Rentachintala** (Palnadu), above **47°C**; AP coldest: **Lambasingi**.
**48.1 °C** at **Piduguralla** (Palnadu) on **21 May 2026**.

n76dfb674516.s: A condition in which temperature rises with height instead of falling is called:
n76dfb674516.x: In a temperature inversion the normal lapse rate reverses; it is favoured by long winter nights, clear skies and calm dry air.
xa: Types: **ground/radiation**, **valley (air-drainage)**, **frontal/advection**, **permanent** (polar areas).
Effects: **fog**, **frost**, **smog**; pollutants trapped in the boundary layer.
Valley inversion makes **frost pockets** on valley floors — orchards go on **upper slopes**.

ne8824e7cded.s: Fog, frost, smog and the trapping of pollutants in the planetary boundary layer are effects of:
ne8824e7cded.x: Temperature inversions can produce fog, frost and smog and trap pollutants within the planetary boundary layer.
xa: Conditions: **long winter nights, clear skies, calm dry air, snow cover**.
**Valley inversion**: cold air drains downslope → **frost pockets** on valley floors; **orchards** on upper slopes.
Permanent inversion: **polar areas**; the **stratosphere** is a permanent inversion layer.

n6e9b3796531.s: Which is identified as the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh?
n6e9b3796531.x: Rentachintala in Palnadu is the hottest place in Andhra Pradesh, while Lambasingi is the coolest.
xa: 2026 peak: **48.1 °C at Piduguralla** (Palnadu), **21 May 2026**; **45 °C** crossed in **18** districts.
India coldest: **Dras** (**-45°C**, 1908); world hottest **Death Valley** (**56.7°C**).
AP coast has a low diurnal range; **Rayalaseema** high.

n448c3012ac9.s: TRISHNA, a thermal-infrared satellite mission, is a joint venture of ISRO and:
n448c3012ac9.x: TRISHNA is an Indo-French ISRO-CNES mission to map energy and water budgets, land surface temperature and urban heat islands; its PSLV launch is due in 2027.
xa: Urban heat island: **concrete and asphalt** store heat; Hyderabad UHI intensity **5.74-6.82 °C**.
Oceans took up a record **+23 zettajoules** of heat in **2025**.
A **heat dome** = stalled high pressure under a slowed, meandering **jet stream**.

n3f7ebc323a7.s: In the absence of the atmosphere, the average surface temperature of the Earth would be approximately
n3f7ebc323a7.x: Without the atmospheric heat-trapping effect, the average surface temperature would be about −18°C rather than approximately +15°C.
n3f7ebc323a7.tq: Distinguish the observed average from the estimated no-atmosphere value.
xs: Without the atmosphere, the surface would be about **-18 °C instead of +15 °C** — option **(3)**.
Trapped heat from **greenhouse gases** keeps the average temperature up (UPSC **2025**: all three statements correct).
Option (4) reverses the two figures.
xa: Atmosphere is **transparent to short-wave** sunlight, **opaque to long-wave** terrestrial radiation.
Greenhouse gases: **CO2, CH4, water vapour, N2O** (APPSC **2025**).
Global land temperature up **1.59 °C** since pre-industrial (UNEP Emissions Gap **2025**).

ndisaster-management-33-7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about heatwave criteria?
o: In the plains, a severe heatwave is declared at an actual maximum temperature of 45°C or more.
In the plains, a heatwave is a departure from normal of 4.5°C to 6.4°C.
In the plains, a severe heatwave is a departure from normal of more than 6.4°C.
In coastal areas, a departure of 4.5°C or more counts as a heatwave when the maximum is at least 37°C.
ndisaster-management-33-7.x: A severe heatwave by actual maximum temperature in the plains needs 47°C or more, not 45°C.
n: A heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A severe heatwave in plains is declared when the temperature departure from normal is more than 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A heatwave in coastal areas is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C or more. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A heatwave in hilly regions is declared when the temperature departure from normal is 4.5°C to 6.4°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xa: Plains heatwave by actual maximum: **at least 45°C**.
⚠ Sources differ: other notes apply **4.5 to 6.4 °C** to all regions, coast included.
AP **2026** peak: **48.1 °C** at **Piduguralla**; **45 °C** crossed in **18** districts.

ndisaster-management-33-9.s: In the plains, a severe heatwave is declared when the actual maximum temperature is at least:
ndisaster-management-33-9.x: In the plains an actual maximum of 45°C or more counts as a heatwave and 47°C or more as a severe heatwave.
n: A heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 45°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
A severe heatwave in plains is also identified when the actual maximum temperature is at least 47°C. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xa: Otherwise a heatwave needs a **40°C** threshold plus a departure of **4.5–6.4°C**.
Coastal threshold **37°C**; hilly **30°C**.
IMD criteria updated **Apr 2026**.

n7922412beb8.s: The subtropical high-pressure belt lies approximately between latitudes:
n7922412beb8.x: The subtropical high lies at about 30°–35°, the equatorial low at 0°–5° and the subpolar low at 60°–65° in both hemispheres.
xa: Equatorial low = **Doldrums / ITCZ**; subtropical high = **Horse latitudes**.
**Polar high** lies at the **poles (90°)**: cold, dense, sinking air.
Belts shift about **5-10° north in NH summer** and **south in winter**, following the overhead sun.

ndbdafbd7fb1.s: The term ‘horse latitudes’ refers to which one of the following?
o: The subpolar low-pressure belt between 60° and 65°
The equatorial low-pressure belt between 0° and 5°
The subtropical high-pressure belt between 30° and 35°
ndbdafbd7fb1.x: The subtropical high-pressure belts at approximately 30°–35° N and S are known as the horse latitudes.
ndbdafbd7fb1.tq: Match the alternate name with its precise latitude range.
xs: **Horse latitudes** = the **subtropical high-pressure belt between 30° and 35°** — option **(4)**.
It is a belt of **calm, weak winds** and **sinking dry air** that gives **hot deserts**.
The **equatorial low (0-5°)** is the **Doldrums**; the subpolar low (60-65°) is where westerlies meet polar easterlies.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2019** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
**Trade winds** blow from the subtropical high to the equatorial low; **westerlies** to the subpolar low.
**Hadley cell** air **sinks near 30°** and returns as trade winds.

n53164692b2b.s: Which pressure belt is associated with sinking dry air and hot deserts?
n53164692b2b.x: The subtropical high has sinking dry air and hot deserts; the equatorial low has calm rising air and the polar high cold sinking air.
xa: Latitudes: equatorial low **0-5°**, subtropical high **30-35°**, subpolar low **~60-65°**, polar high **90°**.
Other names: equatorial low = **Doldrums/ITCZ**; subtropical high = **Horse latitudes**.

n0d986b612eb.s: Following the overhead sun, the pressure belts shift seasonally by about:
n0d986b612eb.x: The belts shift about 5°–10° north in the NH summer and south in winter, not 25°–30°.
xa: In NH summer the **ITCZ** shifts north over the Indian plains (**monsoon trough**) — this drives the monsoon.
In winter the ITCZ migrates **south of India** → **north-east monsoon**.
Southward shift of the doldrums → heavy rain in **southern states** (**bimodal rainfall**).

n827c1185853.s: The polar vortex, a cold low-pressure region around the poles, is strongest during:
n827c1185853.x: The polar vortex exists year-round, is strongest in winter, and its anticlockwise flow keeps cold air near the poles.
xa: A **strong vortex** keeps the cold air up north and warm air to the south (**APPSC 2018**; **APPSC-GS 2018**).
Layers: tropospheric up to **15 km**; stratospheric **15-50 km** (seasonal).
**Sudden stratospheric warming** / **Rossby waves** weaken it → cold air spills into mid-latitudes.

nb9bdc8f39f1.s: Under El Niño conditions, the south-west monsoon rainfall in Andhra Pradesh was expected to be:
nb9bdc8f39f1.x: El Niño was expected to bring below-normal rainfall, partly offset by short, intense low-pressure spells.
xa: UK Met Office expects the **biggest El Nino in over a century** (peak **above 3 °C**) → **2027** possibly the hottest year.
A low over the **north Andaman Sea** brought heavy rain to AP from **19 Sep 2026**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** includes **ENSO**.

ngeneral-geography-7-3.s: When air is heated, it expands and its density decreases, producing:
ngeneral-geography-7-3.x: Heated air expands and becomes less dense, which lowers pressure, so rising temperature can lead to low pressure.
n: Increasing temperature causes air to expand. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Expansion of air decreases air density. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Decreased air density produces low pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: **Decreasing temperature** → air **contracts** → density increases → **high pressure**.
**Higher altitude** gives **lower atmospheric pressure**.
**Standard sea-level pressure** = **1013.25 mb (hPa)**.

nb6a9225a308.s: Which of the following correctly represents the direction of the trade winds?
o: From the subtropical high to the subpolar low; south-westerly in the NH and north-westerly in the SH
From the subtropical high to the equatorial low; north-easterly in the NH and south-easterly in the SH
From the equatorial low to the subtropical high; north-westerly in the NH and south-westerly in the SH
From the polar high to the subpolar low; north-easterly in the NH and south-easterly in the SH
nb6a9225a308.x: Trade winds blow from the subtropical high-pressure belts towards the equatorial low-pressure belt. They are north-easterlies in the Northern Hemisphere and south-easterlies in the Southern Hemisphere.
nb6a9225a308.tq: Separate the source-to-destination relationship from the hemispheric wind direction.
xs: **Trade winds** blow **from the subtropical high to the equatorial low**; **north-easterly in the NH**, **south-easterly in the SH** — option **(2)**.
Option (1) describes the **westerlies**; option (4) describes the **polar easterlies**.
xa: Trade winds are also called the **easterlies**.
⚠ **APPSC-G1 2024** trap: "NH trade winds blow from the north-west" is **wrong**.
Trade winds push tropical cyclones **westward** onto east coasts.
**Hadley cell**: air sinks near **30°** and returns as **trade winds**.

n0e864724cb1.s: In the Northern Hemisphere, the westerlies blow from the:
n0e864724cb1.x: Westerlies blow from the subtropical high to the subpolar low and are south-westerly in the Northern Hemisphere.
xa: **Trade winds** blow from the **subtropical high → equatorial low**: **north-east** in the NH, **south-east** in the SH.
**Hadley cell:** air rises near the **equator**, sinks near **30°**, returns as **trade winds**.
**Walker circulation** = east-west (zonal) **Pacific** cell.
Westerlies are **stronger and steadier in the Southern Hemisphere**.

n970d75bef19.s: Which planetary winds push tropical cyclones westward towards the east coasts of continents, and which winds later turn mature cyclones towards the north-east?
o: Westerlies push them westward; polar easterlies turn them north-east
Trade winds push them westward; westerlies turn them north-east
Polar easterlies push them westward; trade winds turn them north-east
Westerlies push them westward; trade winds turn them north-east
n970d75bef19.x: Trade winds (easterlies) steer tropical cyclones westward onto east coasts; on reaching higher latitudes the westerlies turn mature cyclones north-east. Westerlies do not push cyclones west, and polar easterlies do not act in the tropics, so the other options are wrong.
n970d75bef19.tq: Trades steer west; westerlies recurve north-east.
xs: **Trade winds push them westward; westerlies turn them north-east** — option **(2)**.
**Trade winds (easterlies)** steer tropical cyclones **westward to east coasts**; the **westerlies** then turn mature cyclones **north-east**.
xa: Example: **Cyclone Montha** (**Nov 2025**), **Kakinada** coast.
AP cyclones peak **October-December** (**Hudhud**, **Titli**, **Michaung**).
Cyclones form only beyond **5°** latitude, where the **Coriolis force** is enough.

n91f09f4464a.s: Closely spaced isobars on a weather map indicate:
o: A gentle pressure gradient and calm air
A steep pressure gradient and strong winds
Air moving from low to high pressure
n91f09f4464a.x: Closely spaced isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong winds; air moves from high to low pressure.
xa: **Isobars** join places of **equal pressure**, reduced to **sea level**.
**Standard sea-level pressure** = **1013.25 mb (hPa)**.
The pressure-gradient definition was asked in **APPSC-G2 2011**.

n9743db4fad4.s: The standard sea-level atmospheric pressure is about:
xa: **Pressure gradient** = fall of pressure per unit distance → sets **wind speed** (**APPSC-G2 2011**).
**Closely spaced isobars** = steep gradient = **strong wind**.
Barometer (**mercury**, **aneroid**) and **barograph** measure pressure in **millibar/hectopascal**.
⚠ **Anemometer** = wind **speed**; **wind vane** = wind **direction**.

nf0319405867.s: The Coriolis force is maximum at the:
nf0319405867.x: The Coriolis force is zero at the equator and maximum at the poles; it is proportional to wind speed.
xa: Because it is zero at the equator, **cyclones form only beyond 5°** latitude.
The deflection rule was asked in **APPSC-G1 2019**.
**Wind modifiers:** **Coriolis force** changes direction; **friction** changes speed.

o: Coriolis force is absent and air moves vertically
Friction alone drives air parallel to the equator
Pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance each other, with no frictional effect
Pressure gradient force becomes zero near the poles
n16662b3dae6.x: A geostrophic wind is an upper-air wind blowing parallel to isobars when the pressure gradient force and Coriolis force are balanced and friction is negligible.
n16662b3dae6.tq: Identify the force balance and the resulting direction of upper-air flow.
xs: A **geostrophic wind** forms when the **pressure gradient force and Coriolis force balance**, with **no friction** — option **(3)**.
It is an **upper-air wind** blowing **parallel to isobars**, since friction is negligible aloft.
The Coriolis force is not absent — it is one of the two balancing forces.
xa: **Coriolis force** is caused by the **rotation of the Earth**; deflects **right in NH, left in SH** (**Ferrel's law**).
Coriolis is **zero at the equator**, **maximum at the poles**.
**Friction** slows surface winds, more over **land**.

n90ac704025b.s: The Inter-Tropical Convergence Zone is best described as:
o: A high-pressure zone near the poles where polar easterlies diverge
A low-pressure zone at 60°–65° where polar highs converge
A high-pressure zone at 30°–35° where westerlies originate
A low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge
n90ac704025b.x: The ITCZ is the equatorial low-pressure zone formed where the trade winds from the two hemispheres converge.
n90ac704025b.tq: Distinguish the ITCZ from the subtropical and subpolar pressure belts by location and pressure type.
xs: The ITCZ is **a low-pressure zone near the Equator where the trade winds converge** — option **(4)**.
**ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone**, the **equatorial low** (doldrums).
**30-35°** is the subtropical high and **60-65°** the subpolar low — not the ITCZ.
xa: Asked in **APPSC 2019** and **APPSC-GS 2019**.
In NH summer the ITCZ shifts north over the Indian plains as the **monsoon trough**.
The **modern monsoon theory (1957)** is built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ**.

nffcd2148336.s: The east–west zonal circulation cell over the Pacific Ocean is called the:
nffcd2148336.x: The Walker circulation is the east–west zonal cell over the Pacific; the Hadley cell is meridional, between the Equator and the subtropics.
xa: Walker circulation was in the news in **Apr 2026**.
Hadley-cell sinking at about **30°** matches the **subtropical high / horse latitudes**.
The **modern monsoon theory** includes **ENSO**.

n6170ba53a9f.x: The Roaring Forties blow at 40–50° S and the Furious Fifties at 50–60° S; Southern Hemisphere westerlies are stronger because of little land friction.
xa: **Shrieking/Screaming Sixties** blow around **60° S**.
Westerlies blow from the **subtropical high → subpolar low** (**35-60°**).
Westerlies turn mature cyclones **north-east** (**Cyclone Montha**, **Kakinada** coast, Nov **2025**).

nc8e991556c8.s: Which one of the following correctly describes the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet over India?
o: It lies north of the Himalayas in winter and south of them in summer.
It remains north of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It remains south of the Himalayas throughout the year.
It lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
nc8e991556c8.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet lies south of the Himalayas in winter and shifts north of them in summer.
nc8e991556c8.tq: Test the seasonal reversal and location of a closely associated jet stream.
xs: The **STJ** lies **south of the Himalayas in winter** and shifts **north of them in summer** — option **(4)**.
Options (1), (2) and (3) reverse or freeze this seasonal shift.
xa: The STJ carries **western disturbances**; its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**.
It **returns in October** to end the monsoon.
The **TEJ** is the summer jet at **5-20°N**, June to early October.

n38565c39cd7.s: The return of the Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet over India, associated with the end of the monsoon, takes place in:
n38565c39cd7.x: The Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet withdraws before the monsoon burst and returns in October as the monsoon ends.
xa: STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Western disturbances come from the **Mediterranean**; they worsened extremes in the **2026** monsoon.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

nf177340bee5.s: The Tropical Easterly Jet, a summer jet of about 5°N–20°N, extends from the South China Sea to:
nf177340bee5.x: The TEJ extends from the South China Sea to East Africa from June to early October.
xa: The TEJ comes with and **strengthens the SW monsoon**.
**Somali (Findlater) Jet**: low-level, off the **East African coast**, intensifies monsoon winds.
⚠ **TEJ** = easterly, summer; **STJ** = westerly, winter.

o: Low-level jet off the East African coast
Upper-level easterly jet over the Indian plains
Sub-tropical westerly jet carrying western disturbances
n421ef9b1295.x: The Somali Jet is a low-level jet off East Africa that strengthens monsoon winds together with the Somali Current.
xa: The **TEJ** (**5-20°N**) runs from the South China Sea to **East Africa** and strengthens the SW monsoon.
The **STJ** carries **western disturbances**; its withdrawal lets the monsoon burst.
Jet streams in general blow at **10-12 km**.

n44a0c3548ad.s: Western disturbances are carried eastward from the Mediterranean region by the:
n44a0c3548ad.x: The Subtropical Westerly Jet carries western disturbances eastward; in 2026 they worsened monsoon weather extremes.
xa: The STJ lies **south of the Himalayas in winter**, **north** in summer.
Its **withdrawal** lets the monsoon **"burst"**; it **returns in October** to end it.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer, strengthens SW monsoon.

ngeneral-geography-7-14.s: During summer, what pressure condition over heated land helps monsoon circulation?
o: Low pressure over cooled land, reversing seasonal winds
Low pressure over heated land, drawing moisture-bearing winds
High pressure over heated land, drawing dry winds
High pressure over heated land, suppressing the pressure gradient
ngeneral-geography-7-14.x: In summer heated land develops low pressure, which draws moist winds in from the sea and drives the monsoon.
n: Summer heating produces low pressure over heated land. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
A pressure gradient draws moisture-bearing winds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The northward shift of the ITCZ helps monsoon circulation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xs: **Low pressure over heated land, drawing moisture-bearing winds** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Summer heating** produces **low pressure** over **heated land**; the **pressure gradient** draws **moisture-bearing winds**.
High pressure develops with **winter cooling**, not summer heating.
xa: The **ITCZ shifts northward** in summer, helping **monsoon circulation**.
**Winter cooling** reverses the pressure pattern → **seasonal wind reversal**.
In NH summer the ITCZ lies over the **Indian plains** as the **monsoon trough**.

n152eae2d573.s: Jet streams were first identified in the 1920s by:
n152eae2d573.x: Wasaburo Ooishi of Japan first identified jet streams in the 1920s; they became widely known during the Second World War.
xa: **Sub-Tropical Westerly Jet (STJ)** lies south of the Himalayas in **winter**, carries **western disturbances**; shifts **north of the Himalayas** in summer.
**Tropical Easterly Jet (TEJ)**: summer only, **5-20°N**, **strengthens the SW monsoon**.
**Somali (Findlater) Jet** is a **low-level** jet off the **East African coast**.
⚠ **STJ** = westerly, winter; **TEJ** = easterly, summer.

n0a716c84d81.s: What may happen when Rossby waves weaken the polar vortex?
o: The vortex becomes permanently stationary and cold air remains confined to the poles.
The tropical easterly jet disappears and the equator cools permanently.
The polar region changes into a high-pressure warm region throughout the year.
The winds may reverse, the vortex may split and cold air may spill into the mid-latitudes.
n0a716c84d81.x: Weakening by Rossby waves can reverse the winds, split the vortex and allow cold air to move into the mid-latitudes, producing cold spells.
n0a716c84d81.tq: Follow the cause–effect chain from weakened circulation to mid-latitude cold spells.
xs: **The winds may reverse, the vortex may split and cold air may spill into the mid-latitudes** — option **(4)**.
**Rossby waves** or **sudden stratospheric warming** weaken the vortex → **cold spells** in mid-latitudes.
A strong vortex, not a weakened one, keeps cold air confined to the poles.
xa: The vortex's **anticlockwise flow** locks cold air near the poles (**APPSC 2018**).
It is a **low-pressure, cold-air** reservoir, strongest in **winter**.
Tropospheric part to **15 km**; stratospheric part **15-50 km**.

n5229214a01e.s: Halley’s theory of 1686 regarded the Indian monsoon primarily as a:
n5229214a01e.x: Halley’s 1686 theory explained the monsoon as a giant land-sea breeze.
n5229214a01e.tq: Associate the earlier theory with its simple explanatory model and distinguish it from the modern theory.
xs: **Halley (1686)** saw the monsoon as a **giant land-sea breeze** — option **(1)**.
That is, the land-sea breeze on a large scale: seasonal heating of land and sea instead of daily heating.
xa: The **modern monsoon theory** dates from **1957**: **ITCZ** shift + jet streams + **Tibet** + **ENSO**.
**Sea breeze** blows by **day** (sea → land); **land breeze** by **night** (land → sea).
"Monsoon" is from Arabic **"mausim"** = season.

n2a7c2a89b30.s: The word ‘monsoon’ is derived from the Arabic word ‘mausim’, which means
n2a7c2a89b30.x: 'Monsoon' comes from the Arabic 'mausim', meaning season; the term refers to the seasonal reversal of winds, but the word itself means season, not reversal, storm or ocean.
n2a7c2a89b30.tq: Test the exact meaning of the terminology rather than its climatic effect.
xs: Arabic **"mausim"** means **season** — option **(3)**.
A **monsoon** is a **seasonal wind reversal**; the word itself means season, not reversal.
xa: **Halley's theory (1686)**: monsoon = giant land-sea breeze.
**Modern monsoon theory (1957)**: **ITCZ** northward shift + jet streams + **Tibet** + **ENSO**.
SW monsoon **2026** reached AP on **6 June** (normal **4 June**; **26 May** in 2025).

ngeneral-geography-3-9.s: Monsoon winds reverse their direction with the season mainly because of:
o: Differential heating and cooling of land and sea
Shifting of the jet streams alone
ngeneral-geography-3-9.x: Land and sea heat and cool differently, producing a seasonal pressure reversal and therefore the reversal of monsoon winds.
n: The main mechanism of monsoons is differential heating and cooling of land and sea. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Seasonal pressure reversal produces monsoons. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: **Monsoon** comes from the **Arabic** word **Mausim**, meaning **season**.
Summer monsoon winds blow **sea to land**; winter winds **land to sea**.
**Halley's theory** (**1686**): monsoon = **giant land-sea breeze**.
**Modern monsoon theory** (**1957**): built on the **northward shift of the ITCZ**, jet streams, **Tibet** heating and ENSO.

nde3a16facc5.s: Which of the following correctly describes mountain and valley breezes?
o: Valley breeze blows downhill during the day, while mountain breeze blows uphill at night.
Valley breeze blows uphill during the day, while mountain breeze blows downhill at night.
Both breezes blow uphill because slopes are heated throughout the day and night.
Both breezes blow downhill because cold air rises along mountain slopes.
nde3a16facc5.x: Valley or anabatic breeze rises uphill during the day. Mountain or katabatic breeze descends downhill at night.
nde3a16facc5.tq: Use the day–night reversal to separate anabatic and katabatic winds.
xs: **Valley breeze blows uphill by day; mountain breeze blows downhill at night** — option **(2)**.
**Valley (anabatic)** breeze flows **uphill by day**; **mountain (katabatic)** breeze flows **downhill at night**.
Option (1) reverses the two.
xa: ⚠ **Anabatic** = valley breeze, uphill; **katabatic** = mountain breeze, downhill.
At night cold air collects in valleys → **temperature inversion, frost**.
**Sea breeze** by day, **land breeze** by night.

n047363a7953.s: At night, cold air descending from mountain slopes collects in valleys. Which one of the following effects may result?
o: Permanent low pressure and intense convection
The formation of the equatorial low-pressure belt
n047363a7953.x: The nocturnal mountain or katabatic breeze carries cold air downhill, where it accumulates in valleys and may produce temperature inversion and frost.
n047363a7953.tq: Link the wind process with its immediate atmospheric effect.
xs: Cold air pooling in valleys causes **temperature inversion and frost** — option **(3)**.
This is the **mountain (katabatic) breeze**, flowing **downhill at night**.
xa: The **valley (anabatic) breeze** flows **uphill by day**.
⚠ Anabatic = uphill/day; katabatic = downhill/night.
**Land breeze** at night: cooler land → warmer sea.

nfdd91400b82.s: Which of the following is a significant climatic effect of sea and land breezes along the Andhra Pradesh coast?
o: They eliminate all seasonal variations in rainfall.
They create permanent westerlies over the coast.
They prevent the formation of any local pressure differences.
nfdd91400b82.x: The alternating sea and land breezes moderate temperatures along the coast, including the coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh.
nfdd91400b82.tq: Identify the practical coastal effect of periodic thermal winds.
xs: Sea and land breezes **moderate coastal temperatures** along AP's coast — option **(3)**.
**Sea breeze** by day (sea → hotter land) and **land breeze** by night (cooler land → warmer sea) alternate.
xa: Sea breeze cools coastal cities like **Mumbai** (**Mar 2026**).
AP coastline: **1,053.07 km**, **3rd longest** in India (AP Survey 2025-26); older figure **974 km**.
AP cyclones peak **October-December** (**Hudhud**, **Titli**, **Michaung**).

ngeneral-geography-3-14.s: Land and sea breezes are ____ phenomena.
ngeneral-geography-3-14.x: Land and sea breezes are daily, whereas monsoon winds reverse seasonally.
n: Monsoonal winds reverse direction according to the season. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
In summer, monsoonal winds blow from sea to land. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
In winter, monsoonal winds blow from land to sea. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
Land and sea breezes are daily or diurnal rather than annual. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 19-27]
xa: ⚠ **Mountain and valley breezes** are **periodic** winds.
**Sea breeze** blows by **day** (land heats faster); **land breeze** by **night**.
**Monsoonal climate** has **wet and dry seasons**.

n84560fbabe2.s: Which one of the following local winds is a hot, dry summer wind that affects North India as well as Rayalaseema?
n84560fbabe2.x: The Loo is a hot and dry summer wind affecting North India and also Rayalaseema.
n84560fbabe2.tq: Use the region–effect association to identify the local wind.
xs: The **Loo** is the hot, dry summer wind of **North India** and **Rayalaseema** — option **(4)**.
It is a hot, dry, dusty **summer afternoon** wind of the north and north-west plains; causes **heatstroke**.
**Mistral** is a cold northerly of the **Rhone valley**; **Harmattan** blows from the **Sahara to West Africa**; **Bora** is a cold wind of the **Adriatic**.
xa: **Harmattan** is called **"the doctor"** — relief from humidity.
East India's pre-monsoon storms: **Nor'westers / Kaal Baisakhi**; north-west dust storms: **"aandhi"**.
**Mango showers** in the south (Kerala, Karnataka, AP) aid mango ripening.

nab4ef32eaf0.s: The warm, dry wind of the Rockies popularly called the 'snow eater' is the:
nab4ef32eaf0.x: The Chinook of the Rockies is the 'snow eater'; the Foehn is its Alpine counterpart, and both can melt snow.
xa: ⚠ **Foehn** = Alps; **Chinook** = Rockies; **Harmattan** = "the doctor".
**Santa Ana** (Southern California): hot, dry, spreads **wildfires**.
**Sirocco** (Sahara → Italy) brings **"blood rain"**.

n5b0fd3f1235.s: Violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms of Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam are called:
n5b0fd3f1235.x: Nor'westers or Kaal Baisakhi are violent pre-monsoon thunderstorms in the east; Aandhi are dust storms of north-west India and mango showers occur in Kerala and Karnataka.
xa: **Kaal Baisakhi** benefits **tea, jute, rice**.
**Loo**: hot, dry, dusty summer wind of the north and north-west plains; also **Rayalaseema**; causes **heatstroke**.

n1bba002910a.s: In the Northern Hemisphere, the trade winds blow from the:
n1bba002910a.x: Northern Hemisphere trade winds are north-easterly; the doldrums near the equator are a belt of calm (APPSC-G1 2024).
xa: This was the **APPSC-G1 2024** question; answer = **neither**.
SH trade winds are **south-easterly**; NH **westerlies** are **south-westerly**.
Doldrums = **equatorial low** = **ITCZ**, where trade winds converge.

n5c7cdc7b00b.s: In the Northern Hemisphere winter, the southward migration of the ITCZ, with high-pressure cells over Tibet and Siberia, helps establish the:
n5c7cdc7b00b.x: In winter the ITCZ moves south of India and, with highs over Tibet and Siberia, sets up the north-east monsoon; the monsoon trough over the plains is a summer feature.
xa: **ITCZ** = **Inter Tropical Convergence Zone**, a low-pressure zone near the **equator** where **trade winds converge**.
Pressure belts shift about **5-10°** **north in NH summer** and **south in winter**, following the **overhead sun**.
The ITCZ's **northward shift** in summer **helps monsoon circulation**.
**Winter cooling** reverses the pressure pattern → **seasonal wind reversal**.

nb62577120e3.s: As per the AP Socio-Economic Survey 2025-26, Andhra Pradesh's coastline of about 1,053 km is the ____ longest in India.
nb62577120e3.x: The AP coastline is 1,053.07 km, the third longest in India.
xa: The earlier coastline figure **974 km** is still used in other chapters.
SW monsoon **2026** reached AP on **6 June 2026**, two days late, entering through **Rayalaseema**.
A **low-pressure area** over the **north Andaman Sea** brought heavy rain to AP from **19 Sep 2026**.

n6152bc66580.s: In 2026, the south-west monsoon entered Andhra Pradesh through:
n6152bc66580.x: The monsoon entered through Rayalaseema, reaching AP on 6 June 2026, two days after the normal date.
xa: In **2025** the monsoon had come on **26 May**.
IMD expected **below-normal** SW monsoon rain in AP under **El Nino** (**5 Jun 2026**).
UK Met Office expects the **biggest El Nino in over a century** (peak above **3 °C**).

ne5875a10ffd.s: Water vapour per unit weight of air (g/kg), which is unaffected by changes in air volume, is called:
ne5875a10ffd.x: Specific humidity (g/kg) is unaffected by volume changes; absolute humidity is vapour per unit volume (g/m³).
xa: ⚠ **Absolute** = per volume (g/m3); **specific** = per kg (g/kg).
RH = **100%** means **saturation**.
**Dew point**: temperature at which air becomes saturated and condensation begins.

ned990756d97.s: Air is said to be saturated when its relative humidity reaches:
ned990756d97.x: Saturation means relative humidity of 100 per cent; the dew point is the temperature at which this is reached and condensation begins.
xa: RH **falls when temperature rises** and rises on cooling (same vapour).
**Fog** forms when air is cooled **below its dew point**.
**Frost** forms when the dew point is **at or below 0 °C**; **dew** when it is above **0°C**.

n82a9a6c422b.s: If the actual amount of water vapour in the air remains unchanged and the air temperature rises, what happens to relative humidity?
o: It remains unchanged because the vapour content is constant
It falls because the moisture-holding capacity of air increases
It becomes 100 per cent in all cases
It rises because warm air contains more vapour
n82a9a6c422b.x: Warm air can hold more water vapour. Therefore, with the same actual vapour content, relative humidity falls as temperature rises and increases on cooling.
n82a9a6c422b.tq: Apply the same-vapour rule rather than confusing moisture content with relative humidity.
xs: RH **falls because the moisture-holding capacity of air increases** — option **(2)**.
**Warm air holds more vapour**, so with the same vapour RH **falls as temperature rises** and **rises on cooling**.
Option (4) is the trap: warm air can hold more vapour, but it does not contain more when the vapour is unchanged.
xa: RH = **100%** = **saturation**; reached at the **dew point**.
RH is **higher over oceans**, lower over continents.
AP: **Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%**; **Rayalaseema** often **below 30%** in peak summer.

n7cdab0fdf7e.s: Latent heat that helps power thunderstorms and cyclones is released during:
n7cdab0fdf7e.x: Evaporation absorbs latent heat and condensation releases it; this released energy powers thunderstorms and cyclones.
xa: **Dew point** marks where **condensation** begins.
**Cumulonimbus** clouds give **thunderstorms**, hail and **cloudbursts**.
**Evaporation + transpiration** = **evapotranspiration**.

n35822e2afd2.s: The amount of water vapour in the atmosphere ____ with altitude.
n35822e2afd2.x: Water vapour falls with altitude; it is up to about 4 per cent in the humid tropics and under 1 per cent in deserts and polar areas.
xa: RH **falls when temperature rises** (same vapour) — warm air holds more vapour.
**Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%** year-round → high **heat index**.
**Rayalaseema** RH is often **below 30%** in peak summer.

ngeneral-geography-7-6.s: The temperature at which air becomes saturated is called the:
ngeneral-geography-7-6.x: The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated; condensation then turns vapour into liquid or ice.
n: Absolute humidity is the actual mass of water vapour per unit volume. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Relative humidity is actual moisture divided by moisture-holding capacity, multiplied by 100. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The dew point is the temperature at which air becomes saturated. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Condensation changes water vapour into liquid or solid form. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: ⚠ **Absolute** = per volume (**g/m3**); **specific** humidity = per kg (**g/kg**).
**RH = 100%** means **saturation**; RH **falls when temperature rises**.
**Coastal Andhra** RH **70-90%**; **Rayalaseema** often **below 30%** in peak summer.
Water vapour is up to **4%** by volume in humid tropics.

nphysics-21-12.s: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is about:
nphysics-21-12.x: The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg or 540 cal/g; 80 cal/g is the latent heat of fusion of ice.
n: The latent heat of fusion of ice is 3.34 × 10⁵ J/kg. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
The latent heat of fusion of ice is 80 cal/g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
The melting point of ice is 0°C at 1 atmosphere pressure. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
The latent heat of vaporisation of water is 540 cal/g. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
The boiling point of water is 100°C at 1 atmosphere pressure. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
xa: **Temperature stays constant** during **melting** and **boiling**.
**Boiling point increases** with **pressure**.
**Steam** burns more severely than boiling water due to its **high latent heat of vaporisation**.

nphysics-21-13.s: What happens to the boiling point of water when pressure increases?
nphysics-21-13.x: Raising the pressure raises the boiling point, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster. Lower pressure at altitude lowers it.
nphysics-21-13.tq: Recall pressure cooker versus hill station.
n: The boiling point increases when pressure increases. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
xs: Boiling point **increases** with pressure — option **(4)** is correct.
The notes state the **boiling point increases with pressure**; it is **100°C** at **1 atmosphere**.
It is not constant: **temperature** stays constant only **during boiling** itself.
xa: **Latent heat of vaporisation** = **2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg** (**540 cal/g**).
**Melting point** of ice = **0°C** at **1 atmosphere**.
Steam burns **more severely** than boiling water.

nphysics-21-26.s: Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water mainly because of:
o: The latent heat it releases on condensing
nphysics-21-26.x: Steam releases extra heat (latent heat) when it condenses on the skin, so it burns more severely than boiling water.
n: Ice provides cooling because its high latent heat of fusion allows it to absorb a large amount of heat. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
Steam causes more severe burns than boiling water because of its high latent heat of vaporisation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
Evaporation of perspiration cools the body. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
Latent heat is released during condensation in the formation of clouds and rain. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
xa: **Refrigeration** uses **latent heat absorbed** during **evaporation**.
Latent heat of fusion = **80 cal/g**; vaporisation = **540 cal/g**.
Released latent heat **powers thunderstorms and cyclones**.

nphysics-21-46.s: During the operation of a refrigerator, the refrigerant:
o: Neither absorbs nor releases heat during the cycle
Releases heat during evaporation and absorbs it during condensation
Absorbs heat during evaporation and releases it during condensation
nphysics-21-46.x: The refrigerant absorbs heat inside the fridge as it evaporates and gives it out at the back as it condenses. Option B reverses this.
nphysics-21-46.tq: Recall evaporation absorbs and condensation releases heat.
n: A refrigerant absorbs heat during evaporation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
A refrigerant releases heat during condensation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 86-92]
xs: The refrigerant **absorbs heat during evaporation and releases it during condensation** — option **(4)** is correct.
**Refrigeration** uses the **latent heat absorbed** during **evaporation**.
**Latent heat** is **taken in during evaporation** and **released on condensation** — option (2) reverses this.
xa: **Perspiration** cools the body by the same **evaporation** principle.
Latent heat of vaporisation = **2.26 × 10⁶ J/kg** (**540 cal/g**).
**Ice** cools by absorbing heat through its **high latent heat of fusion**.

n2603d1e2a50.s: A corona around the Sun or Moon is formed mainly by
o: dispersion in raindrops when the Sun is behind the observer
diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds
refraction through large hexagonal ice crystals
n2603d1e2a50.x: A corona consists of coloured rings close to the Sun or Moon and is produced by diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds.
n2603d1e2a50.tq: Discriminate corona from halo by matching it with diffraction and water droplets.
xs: A **corona** is formed by **diffraction by small water droplets in thin clouds** — option **(3)**.
It appears as **coloured rings close to the sun/moon**.
Refraction through **ice crystals** makes a **halo**; dispersion in raindrops with the sun behind makes a **rainbow**.
xa: ⚠ **Halo** = refraction through ice crystals; **corona** = diffraction by water droplets.
Halo is about **22°** and forms in **cirrostratus**.

ngeneral-geography-8-16.s: The process by which water vapour changes into liquid or ice particles is called:
ngeneral-geography-8-16.x: Changing vapour into liquid or ice is condensation; precipitation is the fall of grown droplets as rain, snow or sleet.
n: Precipitation occurs when droplets grow and fall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Precipitation may produce rain, snow or sleet. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xa: **Uplift** of warm air → **adiabatic cooling** → condensation → clouds → precipitation.
**Rain** = drops over **0.5 mm**; **drizzle** = fine drops under **0.5 mm**, from **stratus**.
**Sleet** = rain freezing into **ice pellets** while falling through cold air.

n37cea77ef2d.s: The phenomenon known as ‘blood rain’ may occur when
o: sunlight is refracted through hexagonal ice crystals
raindrops freeze into transparent ice pellets
dust or spores become mixed with raindrops
sulphur dioxide dissolves in snow crystals
n37cea77ef2d.x: Coloured rain can result when dust or spores mix with raindrops. Sirocco dust over Italy and Kerala’s red rain of 2001 are examples associated with this phenomenon.
n37cea77ef2d.tq: Match the unusual colour of rain with its suspended material.
xs: 'Blood rain' occurs when **dust or spores become mixed with raindrops** — option **(3)**.
Example: **Sirocco** dust over **Italy**.
Refraction through **hexagonal ice crystals** makes a **halo**; freezing drops make **sleet**.
xa: **Kerala's red rain** of **2001** is another coloured rain.
The **Sirocco** blows hot and dusty from the **Sahara** towards Italy.
**Acid rain** (pH **below 5.6**) comes from **SO2** and **NOx**.

n91d1fcff241.s: Which cloud forms a thin, milky sheet that causes a halo?
n91d1fcff241.x: Cirrostratus is a thin milky sheet that produces a halo; cirrus is feathery, cirrocumulus forms ripples and cumulus has cauliflower tops.
xa: This match was asked in **APPSC-G1 2024**.
High clouds (cirrus family) lie above **~6 km** and are made of **ice crystals**.
**Nimbostratus** gives **steady, continuous rain**; **cumulonimbus** gives **thunderstorms** and **hail**.
**Cumulonimbus** towers can reach **15 km**.

nde9a48a022b.s: A low, dark, thick and shapeless cloud layer that gives steady, continuous rain is:
nde9a48a022b.x: Nimbostratus gives steady, continuous rain ('nimbus' means rain-bearing); cirrus is a high, fair-weather cloud.
xa: **Rain-bearing** clouds: **nimbostratus** and **cumulonimbus**.
**Cumulonimbus produces rainstorms** (**APPSC 2019**; APPSC-GS 2019).

nf5a994b497e.s: Clouds with heaped, cauliflower-like tops and flat bases, usually associated with fair weather, are:
nf5a994b497e.x: Cumulus clouds have heaped cauliflower tops and flat bases; they usually mean fair weather but can grow into cumulonimbus.
xa: Cumulus has vertical growth from **4,000-7,000 m**.
**Cumulonimbus** towers reach about **15 km** with an **anvil** top.
**APPSC-G1 2024**: cumulus = **cauliflower**.

n7d315671f36.s: A waterspout is best described as:
o: A horizontal ocean current generated by tides
A snowstorm occurring over high mountain ranges
A dust column formed over a dry desert surface
A funnel-shaped phenomenon extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over water
n7d315671f36.x: A waterspout is a funnel extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over a water body.
n7d315671f36.tq: Distinguish the water-based funnel phenomenon from land-based dust and snow events.
xs: A **waterspout** is **a funnel extending from a cumulus or cumulonimbus cloud over water** — option **(4)**.
It is not an ocean current, a snowstorm or a desert dust column.
xa: One was recorded over the **Brahmaputra** in **Barpeta, Assam** (**26 Aug 2026**).
**Cumulonimbus** also gives thunderstorms, hail and **cloudbursts**.
**Cumulus** (fair weather) can grow into cumulonimbus.

n699df071bd6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the hydrological cycle?
o: Sublimation can form part of the hydrological cycle.
Combustion is a normal stage of the hydrological cycle.
Groundwater flow is part of the movement of water through the cycle.
n699df071bd6.x: Combustion is not a stage of the hydrological cycle; evapotranspiration, sublimation and groundwater flow are components of it.
xa: Other cycle processes: **condensation**, **precipitation**, **infiltration/percolation**, **surface runoff**.
**Hydrometeorology** studies water and energy transfer between land surface and **lower atmosphere**.
**Lysimeter** measures **evapotranspiration** / water percolating through soil.

nb095cd5b700.s: In India, the approximate annual precipitation and utilisable water resources are respectively:
nb095cd5b700.x: India receives about 4,000 BCM of precipitation annually, of which approximately 1,139 BCM is utilisable, including 690 BCM of surface water and 449 BCM of groundwater.
nb095cd5b700.tq: Read the paired figures carefully and distinguish total precipitation from utilisable resources.
xs: About **4,000 BCM** precipitation and **1,139 BCM** utilisable — option **(3)**.
Utilisable **1,139 BCM** = **690 BCM surface** + **449 BCM groundwater** — so 690 or 449 alone is only a part.
xa: **Natural runoff** after evaporation: **1,999.20 BCM**.
These are India's **2026** water-budget figures.
Heavy rain bursts reduce **aquifer recharge** by exceeding **infiltration capacity**.

n2c136fce851.s: Frost differs from dew because frost
o: is a cloud at ground level with visibility below 1 km
forms only when the dew point is above 0°C
forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C
consists of rain drops larger than 0.5 mm
n2c136fce851.x: Frost forms as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C. Dew is liquid moisture condensed on cool surfaces with a dew point above 0°C.
n2c136fce851.tq: Use the temperature condition to distinguish two closely related forms of condensation.
xs: **Frost** forms **as ice crystals when the dew point is at or below 0°C** — option **(3)**.
**Dew** forms when moisture condenses on cool surfaces with the dew point **above 0°C**.
Ground-level cloud with visibility under **1 km** is **fog**; drops over **0.5 mm** are **rain**.
xa: **Lambasingi** ("**Kashmir of AP**") sees frost at about **2 °C**.
Ideal for dew/frost: **clear sky, calm air, high RH, cold long nights**.
**Snow** = condensation below **0 °C** as ice crystals.

nd7dcdcd8fe7.s: A cloud at ground level, with visibility under 1 km, formed when air cools below its dew point is:
nd7dcdcd8fe7.x: Fog is a ground-level cloud with visibility under 1 km; mist is thinner and wetter, with visibility over 1 km.
xa: **Smog** = fog + smoke/pollutants; ⚠ **London** smog = **sulphurous**, **Los Angeles** smog = **photochemical** (forms **PAN**).
**Frost** forms when the **dew point** is at or below **0 °C**.
Dew/frost need **clear sky, calm air, high RH, cold long nights**.

n9a348772e8c.s: Los Angeles smog, which requires sunlight and can produce PAN, is ____ in nature.
n9a348772e8c.x: Los Angeles smog is photochemical, needing sunlight and able to form PAN; London smog is sulphurous, cool and humid.
xa: **Smog** = **fog + smoke/pollutants**.
⚠ London = sulphurous; Los Angeles = photochemical.
**Acid rain** (pH **below 5.6**) comes from **SO2** and **NOx**.

n2bb0508b76b.s: Layered ice balls formed in cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts are called:
n2bb0508b76b.x: Hail forms in cumulonimbus clouds with strong updrafts; sleet is rain frozen into pellets and snow forms by condensation below 0°C.
xa: **Rain**: drops **over 0.5 mm**; **drizzle**: fine drops **under 0.5 mm**, from **stratus**.
**Nimbostratus** gives **steady, continuous rain**.

nc517a32dd60.s: Dew and frost are favoured by which combination of conditions?
o: Clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights
Continuous rainfall, turbulent winds and high atmospheric pressure
High daytime temperature, strong convection and dry air
Cloudy skies, strong winds, low humidity and short nights
nc517a32dd60.x: Clear and calm nights allow surfaces to cool efficiently, while high humidity and long cold nights favour dew or frost formation. Clouds and wind tend to prevent them.
nc517a32dd60.tq: Select the complete set of conditions favourable to surface condensation.
xs: Dew and frost need **clear skies, calm air, high relative humidity and long cold nights** — option **(1)**.
They are **prevented by cloudy skies, wind and low humidity** — option (4) lists exactly those.
xa: **Dew**: dew point **above 0°C**; **frost**: dew point **at or below 0 °C**.
**Lambasingi** ("Kashmir of AP") sees frost at about **2 °C**.
Fog forms when air is cooled **below dew point**, often under an **inversion**.

n16d5747a637.s: Above a wet-bulb temperature of about ____, the human body cannot cool itself by sweating.
n16d5747a637.x: Above a wet-bulb temperature of about 31.5°C, sweating can no longer cool the body; wet-bulb equals dry-bulb only at 100% relative humidity.
xa: The **sling psychrometer** reads **wet- and dry-bulb** temperatures to give humidity.
RH = **100%** = **saturation**.

n109c4203a5a.s: About two-thirds of Andhra Pradesh's average annual rainfall of about 966 mm comes from the:
n109c4203a5a.x: About two-thirds of AP's rainfall comes from the South-West monsoon and about one-third from the North-East monsoon.
xa: **2026 El Nino year**: **Sri Sathya Sai** district had a **57%** deficit (CDCA, Aug 2026).
**North Coastal AP** (Sileru, Sabari) gets the most (**140-152 cm**); **Hagari valley** the least (**< 51 cm**).

n252f1da801b.s: The eastern side of the Western Ghats receives scanty rainfall because it lies on the:
n252f1da801b.x: The eastern side is leeward, in the rain shadow, where descending air is warm and dry; peninsular rainfall decreases from west to east.
xa: Interiors of **Maharashtra, Karnataka, Telangana, AP and Tamil Nadu** lie in the rain shadow.
Wettest windward stations: **Agumbe**, **Hulikal**.

nab814e197aa.s: Pre-monsoon mango showers are an example of ____ precipitation.
nab814e197aa.x: Mango showers, like daily equatorial rain, are convectional precipitation; warm air lifted over cold air along a front gives frontal rain.
xa: Convection: strong heating → air rises, cools, condenses → **cumulonimbus**; **afternoon** downpours.
**Orographic** rain: moist wind forced up a barrier; heavy on the **windward** side.

nd40354897f1.s: The sun halo is generally observed as
o: a semicircular arc produced by reflection from raindrops
a ring of about 22° formed by refraction through ice crystals in high cirrostratus clouds
a coloured ring produced by diffraction near the Sun or Moon
a white ring caused by dust particles in the lower atmosphere
nd40354897f1.x: A sun halo is typically a ring of about 22° produced when sunlight is refracted through millions of hexagonal ice crystals in thin, high cirrostratus clouds.
nd40354897f1.tq: Use the distinctive combination of angle, cloud type and ice-crystal mechanism.
xs: A **halo** is **a ring of about 22°** from **refraction through ice crystals** in high **cirrostratus** — option **(2)**.
Sunlight refracts through **millions of hexagonal ice crystals** in thin, high cloud.
Coloured rings from **diffraction** close to the sun are a **corona**; raindrop arcs are a **rainbow**.
xa: ⚠ **Halo** = refraction through ice crystals; **corona** = diffraction by water droplets.
**APPSC-G1 2024** key on the halo: statements **I and II**.
A cirrostratus halo signals a **warm front** approaching.

ne08e955213b.s: Silver iodide is useful as a cloud-seeding agent because:
o: It can create clouds where none exist
Its crystal structure mimics that of ice
It removes supercooled water from clouds
ne08e955213b.x: Silver iodide resembles ice crystallographically; seeding needs suitable clouds already present and cannot work in their absence.
xa: Other agents: **potassium iodide**, **liquid propane** — they act as **condensation nuclei**.
**Kazakhstan** began seeding with **UAE** help for drought-hit **Turkestan** (**13 Aug 2026**).

na642e8acd00.s: Acid rain is precipitation with a pH below:
na642e8acd00.x: Acid rain has a pH below 5.6; the term was coined by Robert Angus Smith in 1872, and it comes mainly from SO2 and NOx.
xa: **London** smog is **sulphurous**; **Los Angeles** smog is **photochemical**.
Coloured rain: **Kerala's red rain** of **2001**.

nbc3ec2f3666.s: A cloudburst is generally defined as rainfall of about:
o: 10 mm per hour over 200-300 sq km
100 mm per hour or more over 20-30 sq km
100 mm per day over a whole district
50 mm per hour over 1,000 sq km
nbc3ec2f3666.x: A cloudburst is rainfall of about 100 mm per hour or more over a small area of 20-30 sq km, usually from cumulonimbus clouds. The other options give the wrong intensity, a daily rather than hourly rate, or far too large an area.
xs: A **cloudburst** is about **100 mm per hour or more over 20-30 sq km** — option **(2)**.
It comes from **cumulonimbus**; the other options give the wrong intensity, a daily rate, or too large an area.
xa: Himalayan cloudbursts: **June-August**, at **1,000-2,500 m**.
Example: **Dharali, Uttarkashi** (**Aug 2025**).
**16th Finance Commission** recommended adding **heatwaves and lightning** to notified disasters (**Apr 2026**).

o: The Sun is in front of the observer and water drops are behind
The Sun is behind the observer and water drops are in front
The Sun is directly overhead at noon
The Sun and water drops are both behind the observer
nphysics-18-82.x: The viewing condition for a rainbow is the Sun behind the observer and water drops in front; the rainbow itself comes from refraction, dispersion and internal reflection in the drops.
n: The main phenomena in a rainbow are dispersion, total internal reflection, and refraction. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
The Sun is behind the observer during rainbow formation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
Water drops are in front of the observer during rainbow formation. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A rainbow is caused by dispersion and total internal reflection in water drops. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
xa: Sunlight **enters** a drop and **disperses** → **TIR** at the **back** → **refracts out**.
**Primary rainbow:** **one** TIR; **secondary:** **two** TIRs, **reversed colours**, **fainter**.
⚠ **Halo** = refraction through **ice crystals**; **corona** = **diffraction** by water droplets.

nphysics-18-83.s: A secondary rainbow is formed by how many total internal reflections in each drop?
nphysics-18-83.x: A secondary rainbow uses two reflections in each drop (a primary uses one), so its colours are reversed and it is fainter.
n: A primary rainbow involves one total internal reflection. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A secondary rainbow involves two total internal reflections. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A secondary rainbow has reversed colours. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A secondary rainbow is fainter than a primary rainbow. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
xa: Primary rainbow: **red outermost**, **violet innermost**.
Rainbow phenomena: **dispersion**, **TIR** and **refraction** in water drops.
**Halo** is a ring of about **22°** radius from ice crystals in **cirrostratus**.

nphysics-18-84.s: In a primary rainbow, which colour appears on the outer side?
nphysics-18-84.x: Each wavelength refracts differently, so a primary rainbow has red on the outside and violet on the inside.
n: Dispersion occurs because different wavelengths have different refractive indices. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
In a primary rainbow, red is outermost. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
In a primary rainbow, violet is innermost. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A primary rainbow has red on the outer side. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
A primary rainbow has violet on the inner side. [Physics · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 64-76]
xa: **Secondary rainbow** has **two TIRs** and **reversed colours**; it is **fainter**.
The **Sun** is **behind** the observer; drops are **in front**.
⚠ **Corona** = **diffraction** by small water droplets — coloured rings close to the sun/moon.

nb9ba9b61ec8.s: Which instrument is used to determine the moisture or humidity present in the air?
nb9ba9b61ec8.x: A hygrometer measures moisture or humidity in the air. A hydrometer measures the density of a liquid.
nb9ba9b61ec8.tq: Separate the look-alike terms hygrometer and hydrometer by their measured quantities.
xs: The **hygrometer** measures **moisture (humidity)** in the air — option **(4)**.
⚠ The **hydrometer** measures **liquid density** — the classic distractor for hygrometer.
**Rain gauge** measures **rainfall depth**; **barometer** measures **pressure**.
xa: Asked in **APPSC-G1 2018**.
**Sling psychrometer** gives humidity from **wet- and dry-bulb** readings (**APPSC 2018**).
**Lysimeter** measures **evapotranspiration** / water percolating through soil.

ndc158e79b10.s: A sling psychrometer determines atmospheric humidity primarily by using
o: rainfall depth and wind speed readings
ndc158e79b10.x: A sling psychrometer estimates humidity from the difference between wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperatures.
ndc158e79b10.tq: Identify the instrument from the pair of observations required for its operation.
xs: The **sling psychrometer** uses **wet-bulb and dry-bulb temperature readings** — option **(3)**.
The gap between the two readings gives the **humidity** (**APPSC 2018**).
xa: **Wet-bulb temperature** = lowest temperature air can reach by **evaporation**.
Wet-bulb equals dry-bulb at **100% RH**.
Above **31.5°C** wet-bulb, the body **cannot cool itself by sweating**.

n652d52f7dba.s: Lines drawn on a map joining places having equal cloudiness are called:
n652d52f7dba.x: Isonephs join places of equal cloudiness (APPSC 2019). Isohyets join places of equal rainfall, isotherms equal temperature and isobars equal pressure.
xs: Lines of equal cloudiness are **isonephs** — option **(2)**.
**Isohyets** = equal rainfall; **isotherms** = equal temperature; **isobars** = equal pressure.
xa: Isoneph was asked in **APPSC 2019**.
⚠ **Isohyet** = rainfall; **Isoneph** = cloudiness.
**Hygrometer** measures humidity (**APPSC-G1 2018**).

na3196dae646.s: Which area records the lowest rainfall in Andhra Pradesh?
na3196dae646.x: The Hagari valley has the lowest rainfall in AP (below 51 cm), while the Sileru and Sabari valleys receive about 140–152 cm.
xa: AP average rainfall is **~966 mm** — about two-thirds from the **SW monsoon**, one-third from the **NE monsoon**.
**Sri Sathya Sai** district had a **57%** deficit in the **2026 El Nino** year.

n7f9cd3f6fc2.s: In the Bergeron classification of air masses, the first letter indicates the:
n7f9cd3f6fc2.x: The first letter denotes moisture: c means continental and dry, while m means maritime and moist.
n7f9cd3f6fc2.tq: Separate the two coding positions before interpreting the code.
xs: The first Bergeron letter shows the **moisture condition** — option **(4)**.
**c** = **continental** = dry; **m** = **maritime** = moist.
xa: Second letter = thermal source: **T** tropical, **P** polar, **A** arctic, **E** equatorial.
⚠ The first letter is **moisture, not temperature**.
⚠ **Bergeron** = air-mass classification; **Bjerknes** = polar front theory.

ngeneral-geography-7-17.s: The force exerted by air is called:
ngeneral-geography-7-17.x: Atmospheric pressure is the force of air; temperature is the degree of heat, humidity the water vapour and cloudiness the condensed particles.
n: Temperature measures the degree of heat. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Atmospheric pressure is the force exerted by air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Humidity is the water vapour present in the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cloudiness consists of condensed water or ice particles in the atmosphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: **Precipitation** = water falling as **rain, snow, sleet and hail**.
**Wind** = **horizontal movement of air** from high to low pressure.
**Sunshine/insolation** = incoming solar energy that **controls heating**.

ngeneral-geography-8-1.s: Which of the following best describes an air mass?
o: A narrow boundary zone between two contrasting air masses
A cloud formed when water vapour condenses
A weather system formed only over oceans
A large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity
ngeneral-geography-8-1.x: An air mass is a large body of air with fairly uniform temperature and humidity. A narrow boundary between air masses is a front.
n: An air mass is a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: An air mass is **a large body of air with relatively uniform temperature and humidity** — option **(4)**.
It forms over a **source region** with **uniform surface properties**, which may be **land or ocean** — so not "only over oceans".
A **narrow boundary zone** between two air masses is a **front**, not an air mass.
xa: Air masses are **classified** by the **temperature and moisture** of their **source regions**.
**Bergeron** code: first letter = moisture (**c** dry, **m** moist); second = thermal source (**T, P, A, E**).
Air masses control **temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation**.

ngeneral-geography-8-11.s: An air mass loses its original characteristics as it moves away from its source region because it:
o: Gains speed from the jet stream
Exchanges heat and moisture with the surfaces it passes over
Is deflected by the Coriolis force
ngeneral-geography-8-11.x: A moving air mass is warmed or cooled and gains or loses moisture over new surfaces, so it loses its source-region character.
n: An air mass loses its original characteristics as it moves away from its source region. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
Vertical mixing alters the temperature and humidity profile of an air mass. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
