xa: Over an **ocean** it **gains moisture**; over **land** it **becomes drier**.
Over a **warm surface** → **more unstable**; over a **cold surface** → **more stable**.
**Dust particles** act as **condensation nuclei** (hygroscopic nuclei).

ngeneral-geography-8-18.s: Air masses exert major control over which combination of atmospheric conditions?
o: Only wind direction and cloud colour
ngeneral-geography-8-18.x: Air masses control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation of the places they cross.
ngeneral-geography-8-18.tq: Recall the influence of air masses.
n: Air masses control temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: Air masses control **temperature, humidity, stability and precipitation** — option **(3)** is correct.
An air mass has **relatively uniform temperature and humidity** acquired over its **source region**.
The other options are partial lists; ocean currents and landforms are not air-mass controls in the notes.
xa: A **new air mass** can cause a **sudden rise or fall** in temperature.
**Seasonal shifts** in air masses give **seasonal climatic changes** — e.g. **monsoon winds**.
Persistent influence creates **maritime** and **continental climates**.

n2a10929340e.s: The very cold and very dry cA (continental Arctic) air mass originates over the:
n2a10929340e.x: cA originates over the Arctic basin and Greenland ice; cT comes from the Sahara and Arabia, mE from equatorial oceans and mP from high-latitude oceans.
xa: **cP**: snow-covered continents (**Siberia, Canada**) — cold, dry, stable.
⚠ **c** = dry, **m** = moist.

n0d9ac40b4e3.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about air-mass modification?
o: After leaving its source, an air mass is heated or cooled from below.
Warm air moving over a colder surface is heated from below, becomes unstable and gives cumulonimbus.
An air mass may gain or lose moisture after leaving its source.
Cold air moving over a warmer surface becomes unstable and gives convection, cumulus and showers.
n0d9ac40b4e3.x: Warm air over a colder surface is cooled from below, becomes stable and gives fog, stratus and drizzle.
xa: **Water vapour** controls the **stability/instability** of air.
**Dust and salt** particles act as **hygroscopic nuclei**.

n53cb0fb6be2.s: Which sequence of clouds is normally associated with the approach of a warm front?
n53cb0fb6be2.x: The usual sequence ahead of an approaching warm front is cirrus, cirrostratus, altostratus and nimbostratus.
n53cb0fb6be2.tq: Remember the cloud sequence from high, thin clouds to lower rain-bearing cloud.
xs: Ahead of a warm front: **cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus** — option **(2)**.
Clouds thicken and lower as the front nears; **pressure falls** and **steady, widespread rain** follows.
xa: **Warm sector**: clearing, some **stratus**; warmer, humid, rain eases.
**Cold front** passes with **cumulonimbus**, heavy showers, thunder; then **cold, clear air**.
**Cirrostratus** causes a **halo** — a sign of an approaching warm front.

n578ea111593.s: The passage of a cold front is followed by:
n578ea111593.x: A warm front brings falling pressure and steady rain, the warm sector warm humid air, and the cold front is followed by cold, clear air.
xa: Warm-front cloud order: **cirrus → cirrostratus → altostratus → nimbostratus**.
Cold front: **cumulonimbus**, heavy showers, thunder, **wind shift**.
⚠ Cold = steep, short heavy showers; warm = gentle, prolonged light rain.

ngeneral-geography-7-4.s: Wind is the horizontal movement of air from:
ngeneral-geography-7-4.x: Wind blows from high to low pressure, and a steeper pressure gradient makes it stronger.
n: Wind is the horizontal movement of air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Wind moves from high pressure toward low pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
A greater pressure gradient produces stronger winds. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: **Atmospheric pressure** = the **force exerted by air**; varies with **temperature** and **altitude**.
**Insolation** = **incoming solar energy**, which **controls heating**.
**Temperature range** = difference between **maximum** and **minimum** temperature.

n2fc442917a4.s: Arcus or shelf/roll clouds commonly form:
o: Behind every warm front after skies clear
At the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts
At the top of the stratosphere
Only at the centre of an anticyclone
n2fc442917a4.x: Arcus clouds form along the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts and mark the boundary between warm and cool air.
n2fc442917a4.tq: Associate the cloud form with its leading-edge boundary location.
xs: **Arcus (shelf/roll) clouds** form **at the leading edge of thunderstorm outflows or cold fronts** — option **(2)**.
They **mark the warm/cool air boundary** (**Jul 2025**).
xa: A **cold front** brings **cumulonimbus**, heavy short showers, **squalls**.
Polar anticyclones + polar fronts form **cold fronts** → storms and temperature drops.
The cold front's slope is **steep**.

n528575fa659.s: The weakening and dissolution of a front as its temperature contrast is lost is called:
n528575fa659.x: Frontolysis is the dissolution of a front as contrast is lost; frontogenesis is the formation or sharpening of a front.
xa: Frontogenesis happens where **contrasting air masses converge**.
A **front** is a sloping boundary between air masses of different **temperature and density**.
Occluded front: faster **cold front** overtakes the **warm front**.

nd2193178227.s: The Polar Front Theory of temperate cyclones was put forward by:
nd2193178227.x: Vilhelm and Jacob Bjerknes of the Bergen School, Norway, proposed that wave cyclones form on the polar front where cold polar air meets warm westerly air.
xa: **Life cycle:** wave on the front → warm and cold fronts → **occlusion** → dissipation.
⚠ **Bjerknes** = polar front theory; **Bergeron** = air-mass classification.
**Frontogenesis** = formation of a front; **frontolysis** = its weakening and dissolution.

ngeneral-geography-8-8.s: Along what feature do mid-latitude cyclones form?
ngeneral-geography-8-8.x: Mid-latitude cyclones form along fronts where warm and cold air masses meet.
n: Mid-latitude cyclones form along fronts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 55-58]
xs: Mid-latitude cyclones form along **fronts** — option **(4)** is correct.
A **front** is the **boundary zone** between **two contrasting air masses**.
**Bjerknes' polar front theory**: temperate (wave) cyclones form along the **polar front**.
xa: **Frontal uplift** produces **cyclonic or frontal rainfall**.
**Occluded front** is the **last stage** of a **temperate cyclone**.
Western disturbances reach north-west India at the **occluded-front stage**.

nd3cac5adb00.s: Dust and salt particles that act as nuclei for condensation are called ____ nuclei.
nd3cac5adb00.x: Dust and salt act as hygroscopic condensation nuclei.
xa: Cold air over a warmer surface becomes **unstable** (showers); warm air over a colder surface becomes **stable** (fog, drizzle).
A meandering jet carrying warm air into the Arctic → **Arctic amplification**.

ne3e986e4ad2.s: Because the Himalayas block cold, dry continental air from Central Asia, north India is approximately how much warmer than places on the same latitude during winter?
ne3e986e4ad2.x: The Himalayan barrier makes north India about 3–8°C warmer than places on the same latitude during winter.
ne3e986e4ad2.tq: Choose the correct numerical range by separating it from the rainfall and snowfall figures.
xs: North India is about **3–8°C warmer** in winter — option **(2)**.
The **Himalayas** block **cold, dry continental air from Central Asia** (UPSC Geo p.42; IYB).
xa: Winter **anticyclonic cell** over India: **clear skies**, light **northerly** winds, low humidity, **large daily range**.
Summer: moist maritime air from the **Indian Ocean**, fed by the **Somali Jet**.
**cP** air comes from snow-covered continents like **Siberia**.

nd662aa84b3b.s: The winter anticyclonic cell of sinking air over India is associated with:
o: Heavy convection, cumulonimbus and sudden temperature falls everywhere
Clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range
Persistent cloud and rain caused by a stationary front
Continuous south-westerly winds, high humidity and widespread monsoon rain
nd662aa84b3b.x: The winter anticyclonic cell produces clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range.
nd662aa84b3b.tq: Recognise the stable, sinking-air weather pattern of an anticyclone.
xs: **Clear skies, light northerly winds, low humidity and a large daily temperature range** — option **(2)**.
This comes from the winter **anticyclonic cell of sinking air** over India (IYB p.19; UPSC Geo p.41).
South-westerly winds and monsoon rain belong to **summer** maritime air.
xa: The **Himalayas** keep north India **3-8 degC warmer** than places on the same latitude.
Sinking-air highs give **clear skies, fog, frost**, sharp night cooling.

n4aff3329ccd.s: The south-west monsoon over India is primarily associated with:
o: Arctic air transported by the polar front
Cold dry continental air from Central Asia
Moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean fed by the low-level Somali Jet
Sinking air in the winter anticyclonic cell
n4aff3329ccd.x: The south-west monsoon is produced by moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean, supplied by the low-level Somali Jet.
n4aff3329ccd.tq: Identify the source and feeding current of the monsoon air mass.
xs: The SW monsoon comes from **moist maritime air from the Indian Ocean fed by the low-level Somali Jet** — option **(3)**.
**Cold, dry Central Asian** air and the **winter anticyclonic cell** belong to **winter**.
xa: AP has a **dual influence**: SW monsoon (summer maritime air) and **NE monsoon** (winter air returning over the **Bay of Bengal**).
Winter: Himalayas block **Central Asian** air → north India **3-8 degC** warmer.
**mT** air = warm, humid, from tropical/subtropical oceans.

ne61e316ab3d.s: Besides the south-west monsoon in summer, Andhra Pradesh receives rain from the ____ when winter air returns over the Bay of Bengal.
ne61e316ab3d.x: Andhra Pradesh is under the dual influence of the south-west monsoon and the north-east monsoon, the latter from winter air returning over the Bay of Bengal.
xa: SW monsoon = **summer maritime air** from the **Indian Ocean**, fed by the **Somali Jet**.
Source: **Block14 AP Climate**.
About **two-thirds** of AP rain is from the SW monsoon, **one-third** from the NE monsoon.

ngeneral-geography-7-10.s: The leeward slope of a mountain range is associated with:
ngeneral-geography-7-10.x: Windward slopes get orographic rain, while leeward slopes lie in the rain shadow, as across the Western Ghats.
n: Mountains block or redirect air masses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Windward slopes receive orographic rainfall. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Leeward slopes form rain shadows. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
The Western Ghats produce a strong rainfall contrast across their slopes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: The **Himalayas** **block cold continental winds** and influence the **monsoon**.
Blocked winter air keeps north India **3-8 degC warmer** than places on the same latitude.
Summer moist maritime air from the **Indian Ocean** is fed by the low-level **Somali Jet**.

n3f2c945eaeb.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the climatic effects of air masses?
o: Persistent air-mass influence creates maritime and continental climates.
A new air mass changes the temperature of a place only gradually, never suddenly.
Monsoon winds are an example of seasonal shifts in air masses.
Air masses and fronts can produce cold waves, heat waves, thunderstorms and blizzards.
n3f2c945eaeb.x: A new air mass can cause a sudden rise or fall in temperature; the other statements are correct.
xa: A stalled **heat dome** caused a record early heatwave in **Western Europe** (**27 May 2026**).
**AP angle:** **SW monsoon** = summer maritime air; **NE monsoon** = winter air returning over the **Bay of Bengal**.
Winter **anticyclonic** cell over India → **clear skies**, low humidity, large daily temperature range.

nea45b976521.s: Polar anticyclones such as the Siberian High and the Canadian High are built by:
o: Cold, dense cP and cA air
nea45b976521.x: Polar anticyclones are cold-core highs of cold, dense cP/cA air, strongest near the surface, giving clear skies, fog, frost and sharp night cooling.
xa: Examples: **Siberian High**, **Canadian High**, **Antarctic High**.
**cP** = **continental Polar** (cold, dry) from **Siberia, Canada**; **cA** = extremely cold and dry (**Arctic basin, Greenland ice**).
An **Antarctic high** reaching unusually far north brought snow to Chile's **Atacama Desert** (Jul **2025**).
⚠ **c** = dry (continental), **m** = moist (maritime).

n474db5dee04.s: A meandering jet stream carrying warm air masses into the Arctic is associated with:
o: The reversal of the Bergeron code
Formation of cP air over Arabia
n474db5dee04.x: The transport of warm air masses into the Arctic by a meandering jet stream drives Arctic amplification.
n474db5dee04.tq: Match the atmospheric process with its named climatic consequence.
xs: It drives **Arctic amplification** — option **(4)**.
A **meandering jet stream** carries **warm air masses into the Arctic** (UPSC Env p.220).
**cP** air forms over **Siberia/Canada**, not Arabia (Arabia gives **cT**).
xa: An air mass is **modified** when it leaves its source region.
**Frontolysis** = weakening of a front as temperature contrast is lost.

ne7a8b4db569.s: A cold front is characterised by which one of the following combinations?
o: Warm air riding gradually over retreating cold air and prolonged light rain
Cold air advancing and lifting warm air sharply, with heavy short showers and a sudden temperature fall
A faster warm front overtaking a cold front
Neither air mass advancing and rainfall persisting for several days
ne7a8b4db569.x: In a cold front, advancing cold air forms a steep wedge and lifts warm air sharply, producing cumulonimbus, heavy short showers, thunder, squalls and a sudden temperature fall.
ne7a8b4db569.tq: Use the movement of the advancing air mass as the key discriminator.
xs: A **cold front**: **cold air advancing and lifting warm air sharply**, with **heavy short showers and a sudden temperature fall** — option **(2)**.
It has a **steep** slope and brings **cumulonimbus**, thunder and **squalls**.
Option (1) is a **warm front**; option (4) a **stationary front**.
xa: After the cold front passes: **cold, clear air**, wind shift.
**Arcus (shelf/roll) clouds** form at the leading edge of cold fronts.
An **occluded** front forms when a faster cold front overtakes the warm front.

nddf3b12c99e.s: Which one of the following is the most essential oceanic condition for the formation of a tropical cyclone?
o: Sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C over a large area
Sea-surface temperature below 10°C over a narrow area
nddf3b12c99e.x: Tropical cyclones require a large warm ocean surface, generally with sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C. Moisture and low wind shear are also favourable conditions.
nddf3b12c99e.tq: Use the basic-condition recall method and reject reversed environmental requirements.
xs: The key oceanic condition is **sea-surface temperature above about 26.5–27°C** over a **large area** — option **(3)**.
Tropical cyclones form **only over warm oceans** and draw their energy from them.
They need **high humidity** and **low vertical wind shear** — so "no moisture" and "very high shear" are wrong; cold seas (below 10°C) cannot feed them.
xa: Other favourable conditions: enough **Coriolis force**, a **pre-existing weak low**, and **upper-level divergence**.
Belt: roughly **5-30° N and S**, western parts of tropical oceans.
They do not form within about **5°** of the equator, nor in the **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific**.

nb08a09afbac.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the formation of tropical cyclones?
o: A pre-existing weak low-pressure system is favourable for their formation.
A low-level cyclonic circulation is favourable for their formation.
Large vertical variation in wind speed is essential for their formation.
nb08a09afbac.x: Tropical cyclones need low vertical wind shear, not large variation of wind speed with height.
xa: Also needed: **SST above 26.5 °C** (some notes: above **27**), **high humidity** in lower and middle troposphere, enough **Coriolis force**.
**Marine heatwaves** raise TC winds by up to **20%** and rain by up to **12%**.
The **South Atlantic** has no cyclones partly because of **strong shear** and cold water.

nd98b9f1c60c.s: Tropical cyclones generally originate in which belt of the tropical oceans?
o: Between 30° and 60° latitudes in both hemispheres
Within 5° of the equator over all ocean basins
Roughly between 5° and 30° latitudes in both hemispheres, especially over the western parts of tropical oceans
nd98b9f1c60c.x: The usual belt of origin is approximately 5°–30° north and south, particularly in the western parts of tropical oceans.
nd98b9f1c60c.tq: Distinguish the broad confinement belt from the narrower practical genesis belt.
xs: They form roughly between **5° and 30°** latitudes in both hemispheres, especially over the **western parts of tropical oceans** — option **(4)**.
Within **5°** of the equator the **Coriolis force is negligible**, so option (2) is wrong; **30-60°** is the temperate cyclone zone.
xa: The APPSC **2022** key gave the belt as **between 30° N and 30° S**.
Temperate cyclones occur at **35-65°**, along the **polar front**.
Trade winds push tropical cyclones west onto **eastern coasts**.

ne7f902cda5c.s: Which pair of oceanic regions is noted for the absence of tropical cyclone formation?
o: Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea
South-west Indian Ocean and western Pacific
ne7f902cda5c.x: Tropical cyclones do not normally form in the South Atlantic and south-east Pacific, where cool waters and strong vertical wind shear are unfavourable.
ne7f902cda5c.tq: Use region-pair discrimination rather than assuming every tropical ocean basin produces cyclones.
xs: Tropical cyclones do not form in the **South Atlantic** and **south-east Pacific** — option **(4)**.
Reason: **cold waters** and **strong wind shear** there.
The **Bay of Bengal**, Arabian Sea, **North Atlantic** (hurricanes) and **NW Pacific** (typhoons) all produce cyclones.
xa: Regional names: **Hurricane** — North Atlantic, NE Pacific; **Typhoon** — NW Pacific, South China Sea.
**Willy-willy** — Western Australia; **Baguio** — Philippines.
Cyclone **Idai** (**2019**) formed in the **SW Indian Ocean**, hitting Mozambique, Zimbabwe, Malawi.

n629e086a0d2.s: A tropical cyclone weakens after landfall primarily because it:
o: Receives excessive moisture from the land surface
Enters a region of stronger Coriolis force
Is cut off from its warm, moist oceanic energy source
n629e086a0d2.x: Landfall cuts the cyclone off from the warm ocean and its moisture supply, causing the system to lose energy and weaken.
n629e086a0d2.tq: Identify the causal link between landfall and loss of the oceanic energy source.
xs: After landfall a cyclone is **cut off from its warm, moist oceanic energy source** — option **(4)**.
Cyclones form **only over warm oceans** and draw energy from them, so on land they lose energy.
Land does not supply excess moisture, and the system does not turn into an anticyclone.
xa: Tropical cyclones **die on land** in days; temperate cyclones live longer and **cross continents**.
**Storm surge** — sea water pushed ashore by winds and low pressure — is the **biggest killer**.
AP landfall: **Montha** (**Oct 2025**) on the **Kakinada coast**.

n843a5c7af2b.s: Tropical cyclones originate and intensify over which of the following?
n843a5c7af2b.x: Tropical cyclones form only over warm oceans (SST above about 26.5 °C over a large area) and draw their energy from them (APPSC-GS 2025). They do not form over rivers or lakes, and cold currents suppress them, so the other options are wrong.
n843a5c7af2b.tq: Cyclone fuel = warm ocean, never rivers/lakes.
xs: Tropical cyclones form and intensify only over **warm oceans** — option **(2)** (APPSC-GS **2025**).
They do **not** form over **rivers or lakes**; they need **SST above 26.5 °C** over a large sea surface.
Cold waters (as in the **South Atlantic**) prevent them.
xa: ⚠ Temperate cyclones can **originate over land and sea**; tropical ones **only over the sea**.
The **Bay of Bengal** produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India (warmer SSTs, funnel shape).
**Marine heatwaves** raise TC winds by up to **20%** and rain by up to **12%**.

na059b9ebca7.s: In which direction do tropical cyclones rotate in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres respectively?
na059b9ebca7.x: Because of Coriolis deflection, tropical cyclones rotate anticlockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
na059b9ebca7.tq: Use the hemisphere pair to avoid reversing the Coriolis-based circulation.
xs: Tropical cyclones rotate **anticlockwise** in the NH and **clockwise** in the SH — option **(1)**.
This is due to **Coriolis deflection** around a **low-pressure centre**.
xa: ⚠ **Anticyclones** do the reverse: **clockwise in the NH**, anticlockwise in the SH.
Anticyclones have **high pressure** at the centre with **outward, sinking** winds.
No cyclones within about **5°** of the equator — Coriolis negligible.

ngeneral-geography-9-2.s: The region of lowest pressure in a tropical cyclone is the:
ngeneral-geography-9-2.x: The centre of a cyclone has the lowest pressure; the eyewall has the strongest winds and the spiral rainbands bring rain and wind.
n: The eye of a tropical cyclone is the central region of comparatively light winds and fair weather. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The eyewall is the most intense zone of a tropical cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The eyewall has strong winds, heavy rainfall, and thunderstorms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Spiral rainbands are curved cloud bands that produce rain and wind. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The centre of a tropical cyclone is the region of lowest pressure. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A cyclone has a low-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: Eye: calm, clear, **sinking air**, **20-50 km** across.
⚠ **Eye** = calm, lowest pressure; **eyewall** = **strongest winds and heaviest rain**.
Rotation: **anticlockwise in the NH**, **clockwise in the SH**.

ngeneral-geography-9-18.x: In a cyclone (as a tropical cyclone is simply called in India), air flows inward and rises.
n: A tropical cyclone is called a cyclone in India. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air moves inward in a cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air rises in a cyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: Anticyclone air moves **outward** and **descends**.
Cyclones are **cloudier and stormier**; anticyclones generally **clearer**.
⚠ India does **not** get **hurricanes**.

n8b98e215c02.s: Over the oceans, tropical cyclones are generally pushed westward by the:
n8b98e215c02.x: Trade winds steer tropical cyclones westward; in mature systems the westerlies may recurve them towards the north-east.
xa: Tropical cyclones move **east to west** (trade winds); temperate ones **west to east** (westerlies).
**10 of 14** recent storms in the notes were **Bay of Bengal** storms striking India's **east coast**.
Arabian Sea storms (**Ockhi, Tauktae, Biparjoy**) hit the west.

n132d0bfa6bf.s: Which one of the following is a characteristic feature of temperate cyclones?
o: A clear frontal system involving warm and cold fronts
Movement exclusively from east to west
n132d0bfa6bf.x: Temperate cyclones possess a clear frontal system, including warm and cold fronts; an occluded front may also develop.
n132d0bfa6bf.tq: Identify the precise positive feature while rejecting the familiar but reversed statement.
xs: Temperate cyclones have a **clear frontal system** with **warm and cold fronts** — option **(1)**.
⚠ "They do not have a clear frontal system" was the **incorrect** statement in APPSC **2024**.
They form over **land and sea** (not only warm seas) and move **west to east**, not east to west.
xa: Fronts: **warm, cold, occluded**.
They cover a **larger area** with **gentler winds** than tropical cyclones.
Rain is spread over a **wide area and longer period**.

n2b4ebc279ff.s: Compared with temperate cyclones, tropical cyclones are:
n2b4ebc279ff.x: Tropical cyclones are smaller and more intense, while temperate cyclones cover larger areas and generally have gentler winds.
xa: Tropical: **5-30°**; temperate: **35-65°**.
Tropical cyclones live **days** and **die on land**; temperate ones **cross continents**.
Temperate fronts: **warm, cold, occluded**.

ngeneral-geography-9-4.s: Under the influence of the westerlies, temperate cyclones generally move from:
ngeneral-geography-9-4.x: Temperate cyclones form where contrasting air masses meet and are carried by the westerlies from west to east.
n: Temperate or extratropical cyclones generally move from west to east. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The key mechanism of temperate or extratropical cyclones is the interaction of contrasting air masses. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A temperate or extratropical cyclone is a mid-latitude cyclone associated with air-mass interaction. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Westerlies are the main wind influence on temperate or extratropical cyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
The major mechanism of temperate cyclones is air-mass interaction and fronts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: They occur at about **35°–65°** in both hemispheres.
Tropical cyclones move **east to west** with the **trade winds**.
Indian example: the **Western Disturbance**.

ndisaster-management-14-12.s: Which coast of India is more vulnerable to cyclones?
ndisaster-management-14-12.x: The east coast, including Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal and Tamil Nadu, is more cyclone-prone than the west coast.
n: The East Coast is more vulnerable to cyclones than the West Coast. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
The vulnerable East Coast includes Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, West Bengal, and Tamil Nadu. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
xa: **Bay of Bengal** produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India — warmer SSTs, enclosed funnel shape.
**Arabian Sea:** fewer but more intense (**Tauktae**, **Biparjoy**).
Nearly **5,900 km** of coast is directly exposed to cyclones.
Season is **bimodal**: main peak **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)**, secondary **pre-monsoon (Apr-May)**.

n302ff89deda.s: The IMD classifies a system as a cyclonic storm when its winds reach:
n302ff89deda.x: The IMD cyclonic-storm threshold is 62 km/h (34 knots); a hurricane begins at about 119 km/h.
xa: Cyclones are **named from the Cyclonic Storm** category (**62-88 km/h**).
**Super Cyclonic Storm**: **222 km/h and above**.
**Saffir-Simpson** scale rates hurricanes in **categories 1-5**.

n57da0733600.s: Under the IMD scale, cyclones are given names from which category onwards?
n57da0733600.x: Names are given from the Cyclonic Storm category (62–88 km/h) onwards; a Super Cyclonic Storm has winds of 222 km/h and above.
xa: **Depression 31-49**, **Deep Depression 50-61**, **Extremely Severe 167-221** km/h.
Names come from **IMD (RSMC New Delhi)** using lists from member countries.
IMD cyclonic storm = **62 km/h (34 knots)**.

nf17d03919af.s: Under the IMD classification, a Deep Depression has wind speeds of:
nf17d03919af.x: A Depression is 31–49 km/h, a Deep Depression 50–61 km/h, a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm 118–166 km/h and an Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm 167–221 km/h.
xa: **Cyclonic Storm 62-88** (named from here); **Severe CS 89-117**.
**Super Cyclonic Storm**: **222** km/h and above.
⚠ A **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h** — close to the Very Severe CS lower bound (**118**).

ndisaster-management-9-5.s: Which scale is used by the IMD to classify cyclones?
ndisaster-management-9-5.x: The IMD uses the Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale, from Depression up to Super Cyclonic Storm; Saffir-Simpson rates hurricanes in Categories 1–5.
n: The Saffir-Simpson Hurricane Wind Scale has categories from Category 1 to Category 5. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used for cyclones in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale measures wind speed. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]

The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale categories progress from Depression to Cyclonic Storm to Severe Cyclonic Storm to Very Severe Cyclonic Storm to Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm to Super Cyclonic Storm. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Indian Cyclone Intensity Scale is used by the IMD. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale is used for earthquakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale measures earthquake intensity. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The MSK-64 Scale ranges from I to XII. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xa: IMD classifies by **maximum sustained wind**, a **3-minute average**.
**Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm** was **introduced in 2015**.
Naming begins at **Cyclonic Storm** (**62 km/h**, **34 knots**).

ndisaster-management-14-6.s: Under the IMD classification, an Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm has wind speeds of:
ndisaster-management-14-6.x: An Extremely Severe Cyclonic Storm is 167–221 km/h; 118–166 km/h is Very Severe and 222 km/h or more is a Super Cyclonic Storm.
n: An IMD depression has wind speed of 31–49 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD cyclonic storm has wind speed of 62–88 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD very severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 118–166 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD extremely severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 167–221 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD super cyclonic storm has wind speed of at least 222 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD depression has wind speed of 17–27 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD cyclonic storm has wind speed of 34–47 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD very severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 64–89 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD extremely severe cyclonic storm has wind speed of 90–119 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
An IMD super cyclonic storm has wind speed of at least 120 knots. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #14 · pp 34-37]
xa: **Low Pressure Area** = less than **31 km/h** (weakest).
**Deep Depression** = **50–61 km/h**; **Severe Cyclonic Storm** = **89–117 km/h**.
Naming begins at **Cyclonic Storm** (**34 knots**).

ndisaster-management-30-5.s: The highest category in the IMD classification of low-pressure systems is:
ndisaster-management-30-5.x: The Super Cyclonic Storm is the top IMD category; the IMD scale covers the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea and differs from Saffir-Simpson.
n: The India Meteorological Department (IMD) officially classifies low-pressure systems over the North Indian Ocean. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
The North Indian Ocean region includes the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
A Super Cyclonic Storm is the highest category. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
The IMD classification differs from the Saffir–Simpson Scale. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
The Saffir–Simpson Scale is used for hurricanes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
The highest category is the Super Cyclonic Storm category, which has a wind speed of 222 km/h or more. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #30 · pp 65-66]
xa: Basis: **maximum sustained wind speed**, **3-minute average**.
**Extremely Severe** category **introduced 2015**.
IMD (**RSMC New Delhi**) names cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.

ne4c5f8d897c.s: The Beaufort scale measures wind force on a scale of:
ne4c5f8d897c.x: The Beaufort scale rates wind force from 0 to 12 by observed effects at sea and on land; a gale is force 8.
xa: ⚠ **Saffir-Simpson** = hurricanes; **Fujita** = tornadoes; **Beaufort** = wind force.
Saffir-Simpson grades hurricanes **1-5** by **sustained wind speed** (PYQ **2025**).
**Storm surge** is the biggest killer in a cyclone.

n23c0d36f4eb.s: The biggest killer in a cyclone is usually the:
n23c0d36f4eb.x: Storm surge, the abnormal rise of sea water pushed ashore by cyclone winds and low pressure, is the biggest killer.
xa: ⚠ **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita** = tornadoes (EF0-EF5 by damage); **Beaufort** = wind force (0-12).
A **hurricane** begins at **119 km/h**.
**"Zero casualty"** approach since **Phailin** (**2013**).

ndisaster-management-9-6.s: Which scale ranges from F0/EF0 to F5/EF5?
ndisaster-management-9-6.x: The Fujita/Enhanced Fujita scale runs from F0/EF0 to F5/EF5; moment magnitude is written Mw and Modified Mercalli is MMI.
n: The Fujita/Enhanced Fujita (F/EF) Scale ranges from F0/EF0 to F5/EF5. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
Charles Richter developed the Richter Scale in 1935. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Moment Magnitude Scale is denoted by Mw. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is abbreviated MMI. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xa: Richter and Mw measure **magnitude**; MMI measures **intensity** (**I to XII**).
**Mw** is preferred for **large earthquakes**.
**MSK-64** is used in **India** and many **European** countries.

ndisaster-management-9-8.s: The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale rates an earthquake on the basis of:
ndisaster-management-9-8.x: Intensity describes how strongly shaking is felt at a place, so the Mercalli scale rates it from observed effects and damage; magnitude measures energy at the source.
n: Earthquake intensity on the Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on observed effects and damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
The Modified Mercalli Intensity Scale is based on human observation and damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xa: MMI range: **I to XII**.
**MSK-64** is the other intensity scale, used in **India**.
**Richter** is **logarithmic**, developed in **1935**.

ndisaster-management-9-9.s: Which of the following scales is used in India and many European countries?
ndisaster-management-9-9.x: The MSK-64 intensity scale is used in India and much of Europe. MMI is used mainly in the USA.
n: The MSK-64 Scale is used in India and many European countries. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 24-25]
xs: **MSK-64 Scale** is used in India and many European countries — option **(2)** is correct.
**MSK-64** measures **earthquake intensity**, **I to XII**.
**MMI** is based on **human observation and damage**; **Mw** measures **magnitude**; **Fujita** rates **tornadoes**.
xa: **Mw** is the **modern standard**, preferred for **large earthquakes**.
**Beaufort Scale** measures **wind force** **0 to 12**.
**INES** rates nuclear events **Level 0 to Level 7**.

ndisaster-management-6-5.s: On the Saffir–Simpson Scale, Category 1 has wind speeds of:
ndisaster-management-6-5.x: Category 1 is 119–153 km/h (minimal damage); Category 3 is 178–208 km/h, Category 4 is 209–251 km/h and Category 5 starts at 252 km/h.
n: Category 1 hurricanes have wind speeds of 119–153 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 1 hurricanes cause minimal damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 3 hurricanes have wind speeds of 178–208 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 3 hurricanes cause extensive damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 4 hurricanes have wind speeds of 209–251 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 4 hurricanes cause extreme damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 5 hurricanes have wind speeds of at least 252 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
Category 5 hurricanes cause catastrophic damage. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xa: **Category 2** = **154–177 km/h**, **moderate** damage.
⚠ IMD classification **differs** from **Saffir–Simpson**.
**Super typhoon:** **240 km/h** (**150 mph**) = strong category 4 or 5.

ndisaster-management-5-6.s: How many categories are included in the Enhanced Fujita (EF) Scale?
ndisaster-management-5-6.x: The Enhanced Fujita scale has six categories, EF0 to EF5.
n: The Enhanced Fujita Scale has 6 categories. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
xs: The Enhanced Fujita Scale has **6** categories — option **(3)** is correct.
It runs **F0/EF0 to F5/EF5**, measuring **tornado** **wind speed and damage**.
**Saffir-Simpson** has **Category 1 to 5** — a common confusion.
xa: **Beaufort Scale** runs **0 to 12** (wind force).
Tornado winds: **105 to 322 km/h**.
**INES** has **Level 0 to Level 7**.

ngeneral-geography-9-7.s: A tropical cyclone affecting northern and north-west Australia is called a:
ngeneral-geography-9-7.x: Willy-willies strike north-west Australia, hurricanes the USA and Atlantic, and typhoons China and the western Pacific.
n: A tropical cyclone is called a hurricane in the USA and the Atlantic region. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tropical cyclone is called a typhoon in China and the western Pacific. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tropical cyclone is called a Willy-Willy in northern and northwestern Australia. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Nargis is an example of a tropical cyclone in Myanmar. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tropical cyclone is called a typhoon in the South China Sea. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: ⚠ Other notes say willy-willy = **Western Australia**.
**Baguio** = **Philippines**.
**Cyclones** = **Indian Ocean**, **Bay of Bengal**, **Arabian Sea**, **South Pacific**.

ndisaster-management-6-6.s: The minimum sustained wind speed for a storm to be classified as a hurricane, typhoon or cyclone is:
ndisaster-management-6-6.x: A hurricane has sustained winds of at least 119 km/h, which equals 74 mph, the same threshold used for typhoons and cyclones.
n: A hurricane is a large, rotating tropical storm system. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
A hurricane has sustained winds of at least 119 km/h (74 mph). [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
A wind speed of 119 km/h (74 mph) is the minimum for classification as a hurricane, typhoon, or cyclone. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xa: Hurricanes are **measured** on the **Saffir–Simpson Wind Scale**.
**North Atlantic** cyclones are called **hurricanes**.
Rotation: **counter-clockwise** in the **NH**, **clockwise** in the **SH**.

ndisaster-management-6-13.s: The Northwest Pacific region associated with typhoons includes:
o: The North Atlantic, South Atlantic and Indian Ocean
The Caribbean Sea, Gulf of Mexico and Northeast Pacific
East Asia, the Philippines and Japan
The Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea and South Pacific
ndisaster-management-6-13.x: The north-west Pacific, home of typhoons, covers East Asia, the Philippines and Japan.
ndisaster-management-6-13.tq: Match each storm name to its region.
n: The Northwest Pacific includes East Asia, the Philippines, and Japan. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 16-19]
xs: Typhoon region covers **East Asia, the Philippines and Japan** — option **(3)** is correct.
**Typhoons** = **Northwest Pacific**; also **China**, **western Pacific**, **South China Sea**.
**Caribbean, Gulf of Mexico, Northeast Pacific** = **hurricanes**; **Bay of Bengal, Arabian Sea, South Pacific** = **cyclones**.
xa: **Baguio** = **Philippines** name.
Example: **Typhoon Noul**, **Guangdong** (**27 Jul 2026**).
**Super Typhoon Bavi** = 3rd category-5 storm of **2026**.

n826716c8ca2.s: The strongest winds and heaviest rain in a tropical cyclone occur in the:
n826716c8ca2.x: The eyewall, a ring of towering cumulonimbus around the calm eye, has the strongest winds and heaviest rain.
xa: ⚠ **Eye** = calm, lowest pressure; **eyewall** = strongest winds.
The eye is about **20-50 km** across.
Cyclones are steered by **mid/upper-troposphere winds**.

nd3cc8a8aadd.s: A small, short-lived funnel cloud associated with a thunderstorm is a:
nd3cc8a8aadd.x: A tornado is a small, short-lived funnel tied to a thunderstorm, whereas a hurricane is hundreds of kilometres wide and may last for days.
xa: USA's **"tornado alley"** is the classic tornado region.
Tornadoes are rated on the **Enhanced Fujita** scale (**EF0-EF5**, by damage).
**Waterspout** = tornado-like funnel over water (Brahmaputra, **Barpeta**, Assam).

n2ec99dcd2dc.s: A tornado-like funnel that forms over a water body is known as a:
n2ec99dcd2dc.x: A waterspout is a tornado-like funnel over water. A waterspout was observed over the Brahmaputra in Barpeta, Assam, on 26 August 2026.
n2ec99dcd2dc.tq: Discriminate between land-based tornadoes and their water-based counterpart.
xs: A tornado-like funnel over water is a **waterspout** — option **(1)**.

**Nor'westers** are pre-monsoon storms of eastern India; **storm surge** is a sea-water rise; a **gale** is a Beaufort **8** wind.
xa: **Tornadoes** = land-based; **hurricanes, typhoons, cyclones** = ocean-born.
Tornado: small, **minutes-long** funnel from a thunderstorm.
Tornado scale: **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita** (by damage).

n4fabb5e1c4c.s: Western Disturbances affect north-western India mainly during:
n4fabb5e1c4c.x: Western Disturbances from the Mediterranean affect NW India mainly in winter, bringing rain for Rabi crops and snow on the mountains.
xa: They bring **winter rainfall** and **snowfall** to mountains — important for **Rabi crops**.
They reach NW India in winter at the **occluded stage**.
Temperate cyclones occur at about **35°–65°** in both hemispheres and move **west to east**.

n90bd6819df1.s: A farmer in north-western India receives moderate winter rainfall of about 10–15 cm that benefits rabi crops. This rainfall is most likely associated with:
n90bd6819df1.x: Western disturbances bring winter rainfall of about 10–15 cm to north-western India, which is beneficial for rabi cultivation.
n90bd6819df1.tq: Identify the weather system from its season, region and agricultural effect.
xs: Winter rain of **10–15 cm** that helps **rabi** crops in NW India comes from **western disturbances** — option **(4)**.
They originate in the **Mediterranean** and are carried by the **sub-tropical westerly jet**, reaching NW India in **winter**.
**Kaal Baisakhi** is a **pre-monsoon** storm of **Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal, Assam**, not a winter rain of the north-west.
xa: They arrive at the **occluded stage** of the temperate cyclone.
**Aandhi** = summer dust storm of the dry north-west plains.
Temperate cyclones give rain over a **wide area and longer period**, with weaker winds.

n0c0783da55c.s: Which of the following weather conditions is generally associated with the sinking air of an anticyclone?
o: Strong inward convergence and cloud development
Persistent uplift, heavy rain and thunderstorms
n0c0783da55c.x: Sinking and diverging air in a high-pressure system generally produces clear, dry, calm and settled weather.
n0c0783da55c.tq: Infer surface weather from the vertical movement of air in a high-pressure system.
xs: Sinking air of an anticyclone gives **clear, dry, calm (settled)** weather — option **(1)**.
Air sinks and **diverges** outward, so there is no uplift, convergence or cloud building.
xa: **Cold-core polar highs** (**Siberian, Canadian, Antarctic**) bring **fog and frost**.
**Heat dome**: stalled warm high traps hot air.
Anticyclone rotation: **clockwise in the NH**.

nac74c26308e.s: Kaal Baisakhi or Nor'westers are local storms associated with which group of regions?
o: Jammu and Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand
The dry plains of north-western India only
Bihar, Odisha, West Bengal and Assam

o: Air expanding explosively after being heated by lightning

**Kaal Baisakhi** and hailstorms are pre-monsoon convective storms.

n8e4f4f9153a.s: The 'Damini' mobile application in India is used to provide alerts about:

xs: The **Damini App** gives **lightning** alerts — option **(2)**.
Alerts come in **15** languages, backed by **104** lightning detection locations.
xa: Thunderstorms grow from **cumulonimbus** clouds up to **15 km** tall.
**Thunder** = air expanding explosively after a lightning stroke.
IMD warning colours: **Green** no warning, **Yellow** be aware, **Orange** be prepared, **Red** take action.

ngeneral-geography-9-10.s: Which of the following is a very local atmospheric disturbance?
ngeneral-geography-9-10.x: Cloudbursts, like thunderstorms, tornadoes and local squalls, are local disturbances; cyclones and anticyclones are large-scale systems.
n: A thunderstorm is local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A tornado or twister is very local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A cloudburst is local in scale. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
A local squall or local storm involves sudden, violent, gusty wind associated with a storm. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]

Tornado clouds: **cumulonimbus supercell**.

ngeneral-geography-9-11.s: Because of the Coriolis force, an anticyclone in the Northern Hemisphere rotates:
ngeneral-geography-9-11.x: The Coriolis force makes Northern Hemisphere anticyclones, high-pressure centres with outflow, rotate clockwise.
n: An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Air moves outward in an anticyclone. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Anticyclones rotate clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has a high-pressure centre. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
An anticyclone has outward-moving air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: Cyclones rotate **anticlockwise in the NH**; deflection comes from the **Coriolis** force.
Anticyclone air **descends**; weather is generally **clearer**.
**Cold-core polar highs:** **Siberian, Canadian, Antarctic** → fog and frost.

ngeneral-geography-9-24.x: Fronts belong to temperate cyclones; tropical cyclones, anticyclones, thunderstorms and tornadoes have none.
n: Fronts are not characteristic of tropical cyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of anticyclones. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of thunderstorms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
Fronts are not characteristic of tornadoes. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #9 · pp 58-62]
xa: ⚠ "Temperate cyclones **do not have a clear frontal system**" was the incorrect statement (**APPSC 2024**).
Temperate cyclones can originate over **land and sea**; tropical ones **only over the sea**.
Temperate cyclones cover a **larger area** than tropical cyclones.

ndisaster-management-5-4.s: The wind speed in a tornado ranges from about:
ndisaster-management-5-4.x: A tornado is a funnel cloud lasting a few minutes, moving at up to about 90–100 km/h, with winds of 105–322 km/h.
n: Tornado wind speeds range from 105 to 322 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado has a funnel-shaped cloud appearance. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado usually lasts for a few minutes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado rarely lasts more than 15–20 minutes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado can remain stationary. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
A tornado can travel at speeds of up to approximately 90–100 km/h. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 14-16]
xa: Wind can **exceed 300 km/h** in severe cases.
Measured on the **Fujita / Enhanced Fujita Scale** — **6 categories**.
Tornado: small, minutes-long; hurricane: **hundreds of km** wide, lasts days.

ndisaster-management-16-7.s: Western Disturbances and wind discontinuity lines are ____ factors associated with hailstorms.
ndisaster-management-16-7.x: Western Disturbances and wind discontinuity lines are synoptic factors; instability, moisture and updrafts are atmospheric factors, and plateaus and hills boost convection.
n: Strong convective instability is an atmospheric factor associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Abundant moisture is an atmospheric factor associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Strong updrafts are an atmospheric factor associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Western Disturbances are synoptic factors associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Wind discontinuity lines are synoptic factors associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Plateaus enhance convection associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
Hilly regions enhance convection associated with hailstorms. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #16 · pp 39-41]
xa: **Climate change:** increasing **frequency and intensity** of extreme convective events.
Hailstorms are part of **pre-monsoon convective weather**.
Cumulonimbus towers reach **15 km** in unstable, moist air.

ndb537de8451.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the agency that names cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and the Arabian Sea?
ndb537de8451.x: The India Meteorological Department, functioning as RSMC New Delhi, names storms over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.
ndb537de8451.tq: Apply the who-does-this-job method to distinguish the naming authority from supporting agencies.
xs: **IMD**, as **RSMC New Delhi**, names cyclones over the **Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea** — option **(3)**.
Names come from a list proposed by **member countries**.
**INCOIS** (Hyderabad) is a research body (El Nino study), not the naming agency.
xa: WMO set up **6 RSMCs** and **5 TCWCs** to name cyclones worldwide.
**WMO/ESCAP Panel**: **13** members; list of **169** names (**2020**).
"**Shakti**" was proposed by **Sri Lanka**.

na3297f5f87e.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the WMO/ESCAP Panel on Tropical Cyclones?
o: The name 'Shakti' was proposed by India.
Each member contributes names used in rotation.
na3297f5f87e.x: The name 'Shakti' was proposed by Sri Lanka, not India.
xa: **IMD (RSMC New Delhi)** names cyclones over the Bay of Bengal and Arabian Sea.
WMO: **6 RSMCs** and **5 TCWCs** worldwide.
**Shakti** (**2025**, Arabian Sea) brought alerts for Maharashtra and TN.

ncb8b79ba407.s: A cyclone warning issued in the colour red indicates:
ncb8b79ba407.x: The Indian cyclone warning colour codes are green—no warning, yellow—be aware, orange—be prepared and red—take action.
ncb8b79ba407.tq: Use the escalation sequence from awareness to immediate action.
xs: **Red** means **take action** — option **(3)**.
**Green** = no warning; **Yellow** = be aware; **Orange** = be prepared.
xa: Naming body: **IMD (RSMC New Delhi)**.
AP's **AWARE 2.0** auto-triggered evacuations during **Montha** with **423** drones.
Montha caused only **15** deaths.

n3c5c4c5afd4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cyclones affecting India?
o: The Bay of Bengal produces about 75–80% of them.
Remnants of Pacific typhoons can regenerate in the Bay of Bengal.
Arabian Sea cyclones are becoming less intense.
Arabian Sea cyclones are fewer than Bay of Bengal cyclones.
n3c5c4c5afd4.x: Arabian Sea cyclones are fewer but are becoming more intense (Tauktae, Biparjoy).
xa: **Biparjoy** (**2023**) = **longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone**.
INCOIS: **El Nino** may reduce post-monsoon Bay cyclones — El Nino **9** years gave only **15**; La Nina **11** years gave **33** (1995-2019).
Season is **bimodal**: main peak **Oct-Dec**, secondary **Apr-May**.

ncfe21bd2efb.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about cyclones in the North Indian Ocean?
o: Their frequency has a bimodal pattern.
They are most frequent in the peak monsoon months of July–August.
The secondary peak occurs during April–May.
The main peak occurs during October–December.
ncfe21bd2efb.x: During the monsoon, cyclones occur mainly at onset (June) and withdrawal (September); the main peak is October–December and the secondary peak April–May.
xa: AP is hit mostly in **Oct-Dec** (**Hudhud, Titli, Michaung, Montha**).
The **Bay of Bengal** produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India.
An **Andaman Sea** low (**19-21 Sep 2026**) may become the first cyclone of the SW monsoon season.

nb831182d366.s: According to an INCOIS study of 1995-2019, how does El Nino affect post-monsoon cyclones in the Bay of Bengal?
o: El Nino has no effect on them
El Nino shifts all of them to the Arabian Sea
nb831182d366.x: INCOIS (Hyderabad) found only 15 post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones in 9 El Nino years against 33 in 11 La Nina years, so El Nino may reduce them. It does not increase them, the data show a clear effect, and the study says nothing about moving them to the Arabian Sea.
nb831182d366.tq: El Nino → fewer BoB post-monsoon cyclones; La Nina → more.
xs: The **INCOIS** (Hyderabad) study says **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones — option **(2)**.
In **1995-2019**, **9 El Nino** years gave only **15** such cyclones vs **33** in **11 La Nina** years.
So El Nino does not raise them, the data show a clear effect, and nothing is said about a shift to the Arabian Sea.
xa: North Indian Ocean season is **bimodal**: main peak **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)**, secondary **pre-monsoon (Apr-May)**.
Bay of Bengal: **warmer SSTs** + **enclosed, funnel shape**; remnants of **Pacific typhoons** regenerate there.
The **Arabian Sea** has fewer cyclones but they are becoming **more intense** (Tauktae, Biparjoy).

n88751941d42.s: Compared with tropical cyclones, temperate cyclones generally:
o: Cover a smaller area with more intense winds
Cover a larger area with gentler winds
n88751941d42.x: Temperate cyclones originate over land and sea, cover a larger area and have gentler winds than tropical cyclones.
xa: They move **west to east** with the westerlies and **cross continents**.
Latitude: **35-65°** vs **5-30°** for tropical cyclones.
They have a **clear frontal system** (APPSC **2024** trap).

n7b8d505876a.s: The Odisha Super Cyclone of 1999 made landfall in which region?
n7b8d505876a.x: The 1999 Odisha Super Cyclone was a Bay of Bengal storm that struck Odisha, including the Paradip region.
n7b8d505876a.tq: Link the historical cyclone with its year and principal landfall region.
xs: The **1999 Odisha Super Cyclone** struck **Odisha**, including **Paradip** — option **(4)** (PYQ **2025**).
It was a **Bay of Bengal** storm; the **Kakinada coast** was hit by **Montha** (**Oct 2025**) and **Gujarat** by Arabian Sea storms.
xa: **Phailin** (**2013**) hit Odisha and AP; over **1 million** evacuated — start of the **"zero casualty"** approach.
**Fani** (**2019**) hit Odisha; **1.2 million** evacuated, praised by the **UN**.
Kerala/TN fishermen were hit by **Ockhi** (**2017**, Arabian Sea).

nad20892109d.s: Which cyclone of 2013 affected Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, with more than one million people evacuated?
nad20892109d.x: Cyclone Phailin occurred in 2013 in the Bay of Bengal, affected Odisha and Andhra Pradesh, and led to the evacuation of over one million people.
nad20892109d.tq: Use the distinctive evacuation figure to identify the cyclone.
xs: **Phailin** (**2013**, Bay of Bengal) hit **Odisha and AP**, with over **1 million** evacuated — option **(3)**.
**Tauktae** (**2021**) hit Gujarat; **Titli** (**2018**) Odisha and Srikakulam; **Amphan** (**2020**) caused Kolkata urban floods.
xa: India's **"zero casualty"** approach dates from **Phailin**.
**Fani** (**2019**): **1.2 million** evacuated, praised by the UN.
**Hudhud** (**2014**) hit **Visakhapatnam**.

nffd3e51e5e2.s: Cyclone Ockhi, which occurred in 2017, was associated with which basin and affected group or region?
o: Arabian Sea near Lakshadweep; fishermen of Kerala and Tamil Nadu
South-west Indian Ocean; Mozambique urban population
nffd3e51e5e2.x: Ockhi developed in the Arabian Sea near Lakshadweep in 2017 and affected fishermen in Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
nffd3e51e5e2.tq: Combine the basin location with the specifically affected coastal group.
xs: **Ockhi** (**2017**) formed in the **Arabian Sea near Lakshadweep** and hit **Kerala and Tamil Nadu fishermen** — option **(2)**.
It **exposed marine-warning gaps**.
**Idai** hit Mozambique (SW Indian Ocean); **Amphan** hit Kolkata (Bay of Bengal).
xa: Arabian Sea storms (**Ockhi, Tauktae, Biparjoy**) hit the **west** coast.
**Biparjoy** (**2023**) = **longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone**.
**Shakti** (**2025**, Arabian Sea): Maharashtra and TN alerts; name by **Sri Lanka**.

n891e7f1f0c9.s: Cyclone Amphan (2020), a super cyclonic storm, hit:
n891e7f1f0c9.x: Amphan (2020) hit West Bengal; Michaung (2023) hit the AP coast and Fengal (2024) the Tamil Nadu-Puducherry coast.
xa: **Biparjoy** = **longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone**.
⚠ AP hits: **Hudhud** = Visakhapatnam; **Titli** = Srikakulam; **Montha** = Kakinada.
**Ditwah** (Nov **2025**) hit **Sri Lanka** — India's **Operation Sagar Bandhu**.

ncbe3d4574ef.s: Cyclone Tauktae (2021), which hit Gujarat and its offshore infrastructure, formed in the:
ncbe3d4574ef.x: Tauktae was an Arabian Sea cyclone; Michaung (Chennai floods) and Fengal were Bay of Bengal cyclones.
xa: Arabian Sea cyclones are **fewer** but becoming **more intense** (Tauktae, Biparjoy).
**Ockhi** (**2017**) near **Lakshadweep** hit Kerala and TN fishermen.
The Bay of Bengal produces **75-80%** of cyclones affecting India.

n43a58f7c2da.s: Which cyclone was described as the longest-lived cyclone of the Arabian Sea?
n43a58f7c2da.x: Biparjoy, which affected Gujarat in 2023, was described as the longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone.
n43a58f7c2da.tq: Identify the superlative associated with the correct named event.
xs: **Biparjoy** (**2023**, Arabian Sea, Gujarat) is the **longest-lived Arabian Sea cyclone** — option **(4)**.
**Shakti** (**2025**), **Ockhi** (**2017**) and **Tauktae** (**2021**) were other Arabian Sea storms.
xa: The Arabian Sea has fewer cyclones but they are becoming **more intense**.
**Tauktae** hit Gujarat's **offshore infrastructure**.
**Shakti**'s name was proposed by **Sri Lanka**.

nff6b6bc883a.s: Which cyclone made landfall on the Kakinada coast of Andhra Pradesh in October 2025?
nff6b6bc883a.x: Cyclone Montha occurred in October 2025 in the Bay of Bengal and made landfall on the Kakinada coast of Andhra Pradesh.
nff6b6bc883a.tq: Use the precise landfall location to discriminate among similarly dated cyclones.
xs: **Montha** (**Oct 2025**, Bay of Bengal) made landfall on the **Kakinada coast, AP** — option **(4)**.
**Fani** hit Odisha (**2019**); **Shakti** was an Arabian Sea storm (**2025**); **Ditwah** hit **Sri Lanka** (**Nov 2025**).
xa: Montha caused only **15** deaths; **RTGS AWARE 2.0** auto-triggered evacuations with **423** drones.
Alerts reached **3.60 crore** people; the Centre gave **₹341.48 crore** extra NDRF aid.
⚠ AP hits: **Hudhud** = Visakhapatnam; **Titli** = Srikakulam; **Montha** = Kakinada.

nbb6de3c774f.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Andhra Pradesh and cyclones?
o: North coastal districts and Nellore/Bapatla suffer the most.
Its coastline is about 1,053 km long.
Its coastline is described as the third-longest among Indian States.
Cyclone impacts occur mostly during July–September.
nbb6de3c774f.x: Cyclone impacts in AP occur mostly during October–December (post-monsoon), not July–September.
xa: AP's Oct-Dec cyclones: **Hudhud, Titli, Michaung, Montha**.
**Montha** (**Oct 2025**): only **15** deaths; **AWARE 2.0** with **423** drones.
India's remeasured coastline: **11,098.81 km** (2023-24).

n826887fb962.s: Which group consists only of cyclones that affected Andhra Pradesh, mainly in October–December?
n826887fb962.x: Hudhud, Titli, Michaung and Montha are the cyclones cited for Andhra Pradesh's mainly October–December impacts.
xa: AP coastline: **1,053 km** (**3rd longest**).
Worst hit: **north coastal** and **Nellore/Bapatla** districts.
**Phailin** (**2013**) hit Odisha and AP.

n25ab871448f.s: India's “zero casualty” approach to cyclones has been followed since which cyclone?
n25ab871448f.x: The zero-casualty approach to cyclones in India is stated to have been followed since Phailin.
n25ab871448f.tq: Match the disaster-management approach with its stated starting event.
xs: India's **"zero casualty"** approach dates from **Phailin** — option **(4)**.
Phailin (**2013**, Bay of Bengal) hit **Odisha and AP**, with over **1 million** evacuated.
**Montha** (**2025**), **Hudhud** (**2014**) and **Tauktae** (**2021**) came later.
xa: **Fani** (**2019**): **1.2 million** evacuated, **praised by UN**.
**Montha**: only **15** deaths, with **AWARE 2.0** auto-triggered evacuations.
The **1999 Odisha Super Cyclone** hit **Paradip**.

n8f1cc1e4448.s: India is exposed to about what share of the world's tropical cyclones?
n8f1cc1e4448.x: India is exposed to about 10 per cent of the world's tropical cyclones; its coastline was remeasured in 2023–24 as 11,098.81 km.
xa: About **5,900 km** of the coast is directly exposed to cyclones.
AP coastline: **1,053 km** (**3rd longest**).
AP's worst-hit areas: **north coastal** and **Nellore/Bapatla** districts.

n4053cce099c.s: During Cyclone Montha (October 2025), Andhra Pradesh auto-triggered evacuations and alerts using which RTGS system?
n4053cce099c.x: RTGS AWARE 2.0 auto-triggered evacuations using 423 drones and sent alerts to 3.60 crore people, keeping deaths to only 15. Damini is the lightning-alert app, Sagar Bandhu was India's operation for Cyclone Ditwah in Sri Lanka, and 'Mausam 2.0' is not the system that did this.
xs: **RTGS AWARE 2.0** auto-triggered evacuations during **Montha** — option **(2)**.
It used **423** drones and sent alerts to **3.60 crore** people; only **15** deaths.
**Damini** is the **lightning-alert** app; **Sagar Bandhu** was India's operation for **Ditwah** in Sri Lanka.
xa: The Centre gave **₹341.48 crore** extra **NDRF** aid (**14 Mar 2026**).
Montha made landfall on the **Kakinada coast** in **Oct 2025**.
IMD warning colours: **Red** = take action; **Orange** = be prepared.

n0730eb710ac.s: Which of the following is an element of climate rather than a factor (control) of climate?
n0730eb710ac.x: Cloudiness is a measured condition, i.e. an element of climate; ocean currents, jet streams and altitude are factors that control climate.
xa: Other controls: **latitude**, **altitude**, **distance from the sea**, **relief**, **vegetation**.
⚠ **Distance from a river** is **not** a control of climate (**APPSC GS 2025**).
**Climate** = average weather over **30 years** (WMO); **weather** = one place and time.

nf08d9610777.s: The current IMD rainfall normal for the southwest monsoon season, based on the 1971–2020 period, is:
nf08d9610777.x: The IMD normal rainfall for June–September, based on the 1971–2020 base period, is 868.6 mm.
nf08d9610777.tq: Separate the precise normal value from nearby numerical distractors.
xs: IMD's SW monsoon (**Jun-Sep**) normal (LPA) is **868.6 mm** — option **(2)**.
It is based on the **1971-2020** period.
xa: WMO standard climate period: **30 years**.
Elements of climate: temperature, pressure, winds, humidity, **precipitation**, cloudiness.
About **40** coastal districts may warm by over **1** degC by **2040**; **AP and Tamil Nadu** to get excess SW-monsoon rain.

n2477340cfe3.s: Which one of the following is NOT regarded as a control of climate?
n2477340cfe3.x: Distance from a river is not a recognised control of climate. Latitude, altitude and distance from the sea influence climatic conditions.
n2477340cfe3.tq: Find the factor that does not belong to the standard climatic controls.
xs: **Distance from a river** is **not** a control of climate — option **(3)** (APPSC GS **2025**).
**Latitude** (angle of rays, insolation), **altitude** (lapse rate) and **distance from the sea** (equable vs continental) are true controls.
xa: Other controls: **mountain barriers/relief**, **ocean currents**, **winds and pressure belts**.
**Himalayas** keep north India **3-8 deg C** warmer in winter.
**Shimla** is far cooler than **Amritsar** at a similar latitude — altitude.

na1655468841.s: The mainland of India lies approximately between which latitudes?
na1655468841.x: India’s mainland extends approximately from 8°N to 37°N. Insolation generally decreases towards the poles.
na1655468841.tq: Recall the precise geographical range rather than the broader regional location.
xs: India's mainland lies between about **8°N and 37°N** — option **(3)**.
**Latitude** controls climate through the angle of the sun's rays; areas south of the **Tropic of Cancer** are tropical.
xa: The **Tropic of Cancer** crosses **8 states** and crosses the **Mahi twice**.
AP lies between **12 deg 41' N** and **19 deg 07' N**.
Insolation **falls poleward**.

n93027d13153.s: The normal rate at which temperature decreases with increase in altitude is approximately
n93027d13153.x: Temperature falls at approximately 6.5°C for every 1,000 metres of ascent under the normal lapse rate.
n93027d13153.tq: Use the standard numerical value associated with altitude and temperature.
xs: The normal lapse rate is about **6.5°C per 1,000 m** — option **(1)**.
That is the same as about **6.5 degC per km**.
xa: Example: **Shimla** is far cooler than **Amritsar** at a similar latitude.
Koeppen's **H** (highland) group is **cold due to altitude**.
The **tree line** marks the altitude beyond which trees cannot grow — **alpine tundra** lies above.

n3e430c92cd0.s: The Tropic of Cancer crosses how many Indian states?
n3e430c92cd0.x: The Tropic of Cancer crosses eight Indian states: Gujarat, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, West Bengal, Tripura and Mizoram.
n3e430c92cd0.tq: Test a fixed geographical count and its associated list.
xs: The **Tropic of Cancer** crosses **8** states — option **(3)**.
They are **Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, WB, Tripura, Mizoram**.
xa: It crosses the **Mahi river twice**.
Areas south of the Tropic of Cancer are **tropical**; **Aw** covers most of the Peninsula south of it.
India's mainland: **8 deg N-37 deg N**.

nf6d615b1a3b.s: What would be the most significant climatic consequence for northern India if the Himalayas did not exist?
o: The southwest monsoon would reverse permanently into a north-easterly wind.
The region would receive heavier monsoon rainfall because cold air would enter freely.
Northern India would tend to become a desert because the Himalayas would no longer block cold Central Asian air or trap the monsoon.
The Tibetan Plateau would become a permanent oceanic low-pressure centre.
nf6d615b1a3b.x: The Himalayas block cold Central Asian air and help trap the monsoon over the subcontinent. Without them, northern India would tend to become a desert.
nf6d615b1a3b.tq: Apply the barrier and trapping functions of a major relief feature to a hypothetical situation.
xs: Without the **Himalayas**, northern India would tend to become a **desert**, as nothing would **block cold Central Asian air** or **trap the monsoon** — option **(3)**.
The Himalayas **block cold Central Asian winds** and **trap the monsoon**.
xa: They keep north India **3-8 deg C** warmer in winter than places on the same latitude.
**Relief**: windward slopes wet, leeward slopes in **rain-shadow**.
**Mawsynram** (mean **1,187 cm**) is wettest due to **funnelling + orographic lifting**.

na3ba3ac8796.s: The Koeppen code 'Aw' represents which climatic type and area in India?
o: Monsoon with dry summer; Coromandel coast
Tropical savanna; most of the Peninsular Plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer
na3ba3ac8796.x: Aw denotes tropical savanna and covers most of the Peninsular Plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer.
na3ba3ac8796.tq: Pair the code with both its exact climate meaning and area.
xs: **Aw** = **tropical savanna**, covering **most of the Peninsular plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer** — option **(4)**.
Hot desert of western Rajasthan is **BWhw**; dry-summer Coromandel is **As**; polar is **E**.
xa: **AP** is predominantly **Aw** (tropical wet and dry).
⚠ **As** = Coromandel; **Amw** = west coast south of Goa.
Savanna: **wet summer, dry winter**; tall grass with scattered trees.

nworld-geography-19-1.s: Which biome is characterised by the highest biodiversity?
nworld-geography-19-1.x: Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity of any biome.
nworld-geography-19-1.tq: Recall the record each biome holds.
n: Tropical rainforests have the highest biodiversity. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
xs: **Tropical Rainforest** has the highest biodiversity — option **(3)** is correct.
Rainforests of the **Amazon**, **Congo** and **SE Asia** have the **highest biodiversity**.
Wildlife: **monkeys, apes, gorillas, orangutans, jaguars, parrots, macaws**, countless insects.
xa: Rainforests hold **over half** of all known species.
**Africa's tropical grasslands** have the **richest large mammal diversity**.
**Madagascar** has **high endemism** (**lemurs, tenrecs**).

nworld-geography-10-37.s: Which of the following characteristics is associated with the Yakuts?
nworld-geography-10-37.x: The Yakuts (Sakha) are known for cold adaptation, breeding horses and cattle in the permafrost of eastern Siberia, one of the coldest inhabited regions.
nworld-geography-10-37.tq: Recall the feature of each people.
n: Yakuts have cold adaptation. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
xs: **Cold adaptation** is the Yakuts' hallmark — option **(4)** is correct.
**Yakuts (Sakha)** adapted **horse and cattle breeding** to **extremely cold permafrost**.
Habitat: **Lena** and **Verkhoyansk** region — **Siberian tundra and taiga**, eastern Siberia.
**Maritime hunting** = **Chukchi**; **forest foraging** = **Aeta**.
xa: Cold pole: **Verkhoyansk / Oymyakon**, Siberia.
**Oymyakon** = **coldest inhabited place**.
**Nenets** = reindeer herders using **chums**.

na18ada4e6a2.s: Who proposed the empirical climatic classification scheme based on mean temperature, precipitation and natural vegetation?
na18ada4e6a2.x: Wladimir Koeppen proposed an empirical climatic classification based on mean temperature and precipitation, with climate types linked to natural vegetation.
na18ada4e6a2.tq: Use the direct name-and-contribution recall method.
xs: **Wladimir Koeppen** proposed the empirical scheme based on **temperature, precipitation and natural vegetation** — option **(4)**.
**Thornthwaite** (**1931**, revised **1948**) used **precipitation effectiveness** and **thermal efficiency**.
xa: Koeppen groups: **A** tropical humid, **B** dry, **C** warm temperate, **D** cold snow-forest, **E** polar, **H** highland.
Second letters: **f** no dry season, **m** monsoon, **w** dry winter, **s** dry summer.
AP is predominantly **Aw**.

n7c84b2fab5b.s: In Koeppen’s classification, the letter ‘H’ denotes:
n7c84b2fab5b.x: H denotes a highland climate in which low temperatures are controlled mainly by altitude.
n7c84b2fab5b.tq: Discriminate the exact classification letter from similar-sounding alternatives.
xs: Koeppen's **H** is a **highland** climate, **cold due to altitude** — option **(1)**.
Hot desert is **BW**; **E** is polar.
xa: **E** = warmest month below **10 degC** (ET tundra, EF ice cap).
Lapse rate: ~**6.5°C per 1,000 m**.
**Alpine tundra** lies above the tree line in the **Himalayas, Andes, Alps**.

na328bfb416a.s: Which of the following is NOT one of the four climatic regions identified in Andhra Pradesh?
na328bfb416a.x: The four regions are humid coastal, deltaic, semi-arid Rayalaseema and hill micro-climates. Ladakh is not an Andhra Pradesh climatic region.
na328bfb416a.tq: Find the geographically misplaced regional description.
xs: A **cold snow-forest region of Ladakh** is not one of AP's climatic regions — option **(2)**.
AP's four: **humid coastal**, **deltaic**, **semi-arid Rayalaseema**, **hill micro-climates** (Araku, Lambasingi, Horsley Hills).
"Cold snow-forest" is Koeppen group **D** (coldest month below **-3 degC**).
xa: AP extent: **12 deg 41' N** to **19 deg 07' N**.
AP is predominantly **Aw**.
**Six** agro-climatic zones in AP (older books say seven).

nworld-geography-18-23.s: Tropical deciduous trees shed their leaves during which period?
nworld-geography-18-23.x: Tropical deciduous trees shed leaves in the dry season to save water. Temperate deciduous trees shed in autumn.
n: Tropical deciduous trees shed their leaves during the dry season. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 29-31]
xs: Tropical deciduous trees shed leaves in **the dry season** — option **(4)** is correct.
Tropical deciduous (**monsoon**) forests get **seasonal rainfall** of **100–200 cm** and shed leaves in the **dry season**.
⚠ **Temperate deciduous** trees shed leaves in **autumn**.
xa: Tropical monsoon: **seasonal wind reversal**, **summer rain**.
Trees: **teak, sal**.
Tropical rainforests are **evergreen** (more than **200 cm** rain).

nworld-geography-19-17.s: Which of the following group consists entirely of wildlife of polar or tundra regions?
nworld-geography-19-17.x: Krill, seals and walruses are all polar animals. Jackals and scorpions are desert animals, and beavers and lynxes live in forests.
nworld-geography-19-17.tq: Recall the habitat of each animal.
n: Krill are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Seals are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Walruses are wildlife of polar or tundra regions. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Badgers are wildlife of temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Raccoons are wildlife of temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Koalas are wildlife of Australia's temperate forests and grasslands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
Lynxes are wildlife of boreal or taiga forests. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 31-33]
xs: **Krill, Seals and Walruses** are all polar/tundra wildlife — option **(4)** is correct.
**Jackals, lizards, scorpions** = **deserts/arid lands**.
**Badgers, raccoons, koalas** = **temperate**; **beavers, lynxes, wolverines** = **boreal/taiga**.
xa: Polar list also: **polar bears, penguins, musk oxen**.
**Mountains:** **snow leopards, yaks, pandas**, **condors**.
Tundra: **permafrost**, no trees; mosses, **lichens**.

nworld-geography-10-10.s: Pygmy groups such as the Mbuti, Baka and Twa inhabit the:
nworld-geography-10-10.x: The Pygmies (Mbuti, Baka, Twa) are short-statured hunter-gatherers of the Congo rainforest.
n: Pygmy is also represented by the Mbuti, Baka, and Twa. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
Pygmy groups have short stature. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
Pygmy groups are hunters and gatherers. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
xa: Countries: **DR Congo, Cameroon, Gabon** (Central Africa).
The **Sahara** is home of the **Tuareg** and **Bedouin**.
**Bushman (San)** = hunter-gatherers of the **Kalahari**.

nworld-geography-10-35.x: The Maasai (also spelled Masai) live in East Africa, in Kenya and Tanzania, not West Africa.
n: Masai is also spelled Maasai. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
Masai groups are not associated with West Africa. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
xa: They are **pastoralists** associated with **cattle**.
Habitat: **East African plateaus and grasslands** (savanna).
**West Africa:** **Hausa** and **Fulani** of the Sahel.

nworld-geography-10-8.s: The Semang, a Negrito group, are associated with:
nworld-geography-10-8.x: The Semang are a Negrito group associated with Malaysia.
n: Semang groups are found in Malaysia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
Semang belong to the Negrito group. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
Semang groups inhabit the tropical forests of the Malay Peninsula. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
xa: **Aeta** of the **Philippines** are also **Negrito**.
**Sakai (Senoi)** = **Orang Asli** of Malaysia's central highlands.
**Ainu** = **Hokkaido** and **Sakhalin**.

nworld-geography-10-32.s: The Aeta are identified as which of the following?
o: A widespread linguistic group of Africa
nworld-geography-10-32.x: The Aeta are an indigenous Negrito group of the Philippines.
nworld-geography-10-32.tq: Recall the identity of each people.
n: Aeta are an Indigenous Negrito group. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 13-16]
xs: The Aeta are **an Indigenous Negrito group** — option **(2)** is correct.
They live in the **mountainous rainforest interiors** of **Luzon**, **Philippines**.
They are **traditionally forest foragers and hunters**.
**Pashtun** = **Afridi**; **widespread linguistic group of Africa** = **Bantu**.
xa: **Semang** of Malaysia also belong to the **Negrito** group.
**Baguio** is the Philippine name for a tropical cyclone.
**Sakai** = **Orang Asli** of Malaysia.

n4faa40af914.s: Under Koeppen's scheme, the BWhw climate type in India occurs in:
n4faa40af914.x: BWhw (hot desert) occurs in extreme western Rajasthan; Amw is on the west coast south of Goa, As on the Coromandel coast and Dfc in Arunachal Pradesh.
xa: **Aw** — most of the Peninsular plateau south of the Tropic of Cancer.
**Cwg** — Ganga plain, eastern Rajasthan, northern MP, most of NE India.
APPSC-G1 **2024** asked a similar code-area match.

naa87c2aaa28.s: Under Koeppen's classification, Andhra Pradesh is predominantly classified as:
naa87c2aaa28.x: Andhra Pradesh is predominantly Aw, a tropical wet-and-dry (tropical savanna) climate.
xa: AP extent: **12 deg 41' N** to **19 deg 07' N**.
**Four climatic regions**: humid coastal, deltaic, **semi-arid Rayalaseema**, hill micro-climates (Araku, Lambasingi, Horsley Hills).
AP has **six agro-climatic zones** (older books say seven); India has **15**.

n16193c6ea2c.s: How many agro-climatic zones does Andhra Pradesh have?
n16193c6ea2c.x: Andhra Pradesh has six agro-climatic zones, while India has fifteen.
xa: AP's six zones are listed against the **13 pre-2022 districts**.
Four climatic regions: humid coastal, deltaic, semi-arid **Rayalaseema**, hill micro-climates.
AP is Koeppen **Aw**.
