n1a7970bd004.s: The mild climate of north-western Europe and the ice-free condition of ports such as those in Norway and Murmansk are associated with the
n1a7970bd004.x: The North Atlantic Drift, an extension of the Gulf Stream, carries warm water towards north-western Europe and helps keep its coasts mild and ports ice-free in winter.
n1a7970bd004.tq: Match a climatic effect and location with the responsible warm current.
xs: The **North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports ice-free in winter, e.g. **Murmansk** — option **(1)**.
It is the warm extension of the **Gulf Stream**, which runs off the **USA east coast → NW Europe**.
**California**, **Oyashio** and **Benguela** are all **cold** currents — they cannot warm Europe.
xa: The **Norwegian** current is also a **warm** North Atlantic current.
The North Atlantic Drift forms the **northern** boundary of the **Sargasso Sea**.
North Atlantic gyre: **N. Equatorial - Gulf Stream - N. Atlantic Drift - Canary**.

n2f6f667222b.s: Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich tracked which phenomenon regarded as an early signal of El Nino?
o: An eastward Kelvin wave carrying warm water along the equatorial Pacific
A southward-moving polar air mass over the Pacific
A westward cold-water surge across the Indian Ocean
A stationary cold eddy in the North Atlantic
n2f6f667222b.x: The satellite tracked an eastward Kelvin wave, meaning warm water moving east along the equatorial Pacific, an early El Nino signal.
n2f6f667222b.tq: Identify the signal by combining direction, water temperature and ocean basin.
xs: **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** tracked an **eastward warm Kelvin wave** along the equatorial Pacific — option **(1)**.
It is an **early El Nino signal**: in El Nino, warm western-Pacific water **slides east**.
xa: **Bjerknes feedback**: weaker easterlies → warm water east → trades weaken further.
**IMD** warned in **May 2026** of a developing **super El Nino**.
**Super El Nino** = SST anomaly above **+2.0 deg C** in the central Pacific.

n7e226e3f521.s: Which one of the following ocean currents is correctly classified as a cold current of the Indian Ocean?
n7e226e3f521.x: The West Australian Current is a cold current of the Indian Ocean. Agulhas and Mozambique are warm Indian Ocean currents, while Brazil is a warm South Atlantic current.
n7e226e3f521.tq: Use current type and ocean together to eliminate reversed classifications.
xs: The **West Australian Current** is a **cold** current of the **Indian Ocean** — option **(4)**.
**Agulhas** (SE Africa) and **Mozambique** (Mozambique Channel) are **warm** Indian Ocean currents.
The **Brazil Current** is a **warm** current of the **South Atlantic**.
xa: South Indian Ocean gyre: **South Equatorial → Agulhas → West Wind Drift → West Australian** (anticlockwise).
**Agulhas and Brazil** are NOT cold — the non-cold pair (**UPPSC 2025**).
**Humboldt** is not warm among Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio (**APPSC G1 2019**).

nd9475b963be.s: Which one of the following is the correct classification of the Agulhas, Brazil and Humboldt currents respectively?
nd9475b963be.x: The Agulhas and Brazil currents are warm currents, whereas the Humboldt or Peruvian Current is a cold current.
nd9475b963be.tq: Separate the two warm-current examples from the South Pacific cold-current exception.
xs: **Agulhas warm, Brazil warm, Humboldt cold** — option **(1)**.
**Agulhas** is a warm Indian Ocean current (SE Africa); **Brazil** a warm South Atlantic current.
**Humboldt (Peruvian)** is a **cold** South Pacific current off Peru-Chile.
xa: "**Humboldt** is not warm (among Agulhas, Brazil, Kuroshio)" — **APPSC G1 2019**.
"**Agulhas and Brazil** are NOT cold" — **UPPSC 2025**.
Humboldt causes the **Atacama** desert and **Peru** upwelling fisheries.

ngeneral-geography-12-7.s: Which of the following is a warm ocean current?
ngeneral-geography-12-7.x: The Agulhas is warm (like the Brazil and Gulf Stream); the Benguela, Canary and Labrador are cold.
n: The Agulhas Current is a warm current associated with the Indian Ocean and southeastern Africa or the South Indian Ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
The Benguela Current is a cold current in the South Atlantic Ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
The Brazil Current is a warm current in the South Atlantic Ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
The Canary Current is a cold current in the North Atlantic Ocean. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
The Gulf Stream is a warm current in the North Atlantic. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Warm currents move relatively warmer water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Cold currents move relatively colder water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xa: Other warm currents: **North Atlantic Drift**, **Norwegian**, **Kuroshio**, **Mozambique**.
Other cold currents: **Falkland**, **California**, **Oyashio**, **West Australian**.
**Gulf Stream + Labrador** meet at the **Grand Banks** — fishing ground and fog.

ngeneral-geography-12-17.s: Coastal areas next to warm ocean currents are generally:
ngeneral-geography-12-17.x: Warm currents warm adjacent coastal areas, while cold currents cool them.
n: Warm currents can warm adjacent coastal areas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Cold currents can cool adjacent coastal areas. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xa: Warm currents are often from **lower latitudes**, moving **toward higher latitudes**.
Cold currents come from **higher-latitude** or cold-water regions.
Currents **redistribute heat** and **influence climate**.

ne0ad7b50525.s: During November–February, the West India Coastal Current flows:
ne0ad7b50525.x: The WICC flows northward (poleward) in November–February and southward during the southwest monsoon.
xa: This WICC fact was the **APPSC GS 2018** key.
The **EICC** also reverses: **northward Feb-Sep**, **southward Oct-Dec**.
North Indian Ocean: SW monsoon **clockwise**, NE monsoon **anticlockwise**.

n583f0e67b2b.s: The Findlater Current, tied to the Somali Jet, flows in the:
n583f0e67b2b.x: The Findlater Current is an Arabian Sea current that reverses with the monsoon and causes upwelling off the Horn of Africa.
xa: **Somalia/Findlater** upwelling and **Peru/Humboldt** upwelling both support fisheries.
Upwelling brings **cold, nutrient-rich** water to the surface.
**NIOT** OMNI buoys feed **IOD** monitoring.

nf346d9f7898.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the meeting of warm and cold ocean currents?
o: The Gulf Stream meets the Labrador Current at the Grand Banks near Newfoundland.
Fog forms frequently near Newfoundland where warm and cold currents meet.
The rich fishing grounds off Japan form where the Kuroshio meets the Benguela.
The Benguela is a South Atlantic current.
nf346d9f7898.x: Off Japan the Kuroshio meets the Oyashio; the Benguela is a South Atlantic current.
xa: Where warm + cold currents meet, **plankton flourishes** → fishing grounds.
**Upwelling** fisheries: **Peru** (Humboldt), **Somalia** (Findlater).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.

n3245104f55b.s: The Namib and Kalahari deserts are associated with which ocean current?
n3245104f55b.x: The Namib and Kalahari are associated with the Benguela; the Atacama goes with the Humboldt and the Sonoran with the California Current.
xa: Cold currents along **west coasts** chill and dry coastal lands → **deserts**.
**Somalia** fishery — **Findlater** upwelling.
**El Nino**: warm water replaces the cold Peruvian current, **suppressing upwelling** → **fewer phytoplankton**.

ngeneral-geography-7-11.s: Arid west-coast desert climates are helped mainly by:
ngeneral-geography-7-11.x: Cold currents cool the coast and suppress convection, helping make west-coast deserts.
n: Warm currents warm adjoining coastal air. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents cool adjoining coasts. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents can suppress convection. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
Cold currents combined with subtropical highs are often associated with arid west-coast climates. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #7 · pp 50-55]
xa: Desert examples: **Atacama** (Humboldt), **Namib/Kalahari** (Benguela), **Sonoran** (California).
**North Atlantic Drift** keeps **NW Europe** mild and ports like **Murmansk** ice-free.
Warm currents **increase moisture availability**.

ngeneral-geography-12-1.s: Which ocean-water phenomenon involves horizontal movement and has major impacts on climate, fisheries and navigation?
ngeneral-geography-12-1.x: Ocean currents are horizontal movements that affect climate, fisheries and navigation. Tides are vertical changes in level.
n: Ocean currents involve horizontal movement of water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents produce horizontal water movement. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
Ocean currents affect climate, fisheries, and navigation. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 72-74]
xs: **Ocean currents** — option **(2)** is correct.
Currents are **continuous directed**, **horizontal movement** of water affecting **climate, fisheries and navigation**.
**Tides** are **vertical, periodic** changes in water level; **waves** are **oscillatory** movements.
xa: Current drivers: **winds**, **density differences**, **Coriolis force**, **pressure differences**.
Currents are **relatively continuous**; tides **highly periodic**; waves **variable**.
**Tsunamis** have **different causes** from wind-driven waves.

nd27a95fb139.s: Which planetary winds primarily drive the equatorial ocean currents westward?
nd27a95fb139.x: Trade winds push surface water westward and drive the equatorial currents. Westerlies generally drive oceanic drifts eastward.
nd27a95fb139.tq: Use the wind-direction relationship to distinguish trade winds from westerlies.
xs: **Trade winds** push the equatorial currents **westward** — option **(2)**.
**Westerlies** drive the oceanic **drifts eastward**, the opposite direction.
**Monsoon winds** reverse the **North Indian Ocean** currents seasonally; they are not the planetary driver of equatorial currents.
xa: Water piled up on the **western side** by trades flows back east as the **Equatorial Counter Current** through the **doldrums**.
**Wind friction** pushes surface water — the basis of wind-driven currents.
ENSO: during **La Nina** trade winds **strengthen**; during **El Nino** they **weaken or reverse**.

ndbdfd680c32.s: Upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water is particularly important for fisheries along the coasts of:
ndbdfd680c32.x: Cold, nutrient-rich upwelling supports fisheries along Peru and near Somalia, where the Somali (Findlater) current system is involved.
xa: Where warm and cold currents meet, **plankton flourishes** → fishing grounds (Grand Banks; off **Japan**, Kuroshio + Oyashio).
The Findlater upwelling zone is **small**, so its effect on the Indian monsoon is **limited** (unlike the **IOD**).
During **El Nino** upwelling off Peru is **suppressed** → **fewer phytoplankton**; **La Nina** brings strong upwelling.

nb77af77fab1.s: During La Nina, the trade winds are:
nb77af77fab1.x: Trade winds are stronger than usual during La Nina, with strong eastern Pacific upwelling and usually good rain over India.
xa: **Positive SOI** = La Nina; sustained **negative SOI** = El Nino.
El Nino: eastern Pacific warmer, **upwelling suppressed**, **fewer phytoplankton**.
El Nino weakens and delays the Indian monsoon (**drought risk**).

ne04df52be87.s: The Bjerknes feedback during El Nino involves:
o: Sinking of cold polar water that reverses the monsoon
Weaker easterlies allowing warm water to move eastward, which weakens the trade winds further
Cooling of the eastern Pacific causing stronger upwelling
Strengthening easterlies that push warm water westward
ne04df52be87.x: Weaker easterlies allow warm western-Pacific water to slide eastward. This further weakens the trades, forming a positive feedback known as the Bjerknes feedback.
ne04df52be87.tq: Identify the reinforcing feedback rather than a simple one-way ocean-current change.
xs: **Bjerknes feedback**: **weaker easterlies** let warm water move **east**, which **weakens the trades further** — option **(2)**.
The chain: warm **western-Pacific** water slides east → **Walker circulation** disrupted → sinking air over the **Indian Ocean** = high pressure.
Stronger easterlies and eastern-Pacific cooling with strong upwelling describe **La Nina**, not this El Nino feedback.
xa: El Nino: trade winds **weaken or reverse**; Indian monsoon **delayed, weakened**.
**Kelvin wave**: an eastward warm wave tracked by **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** — an early El Nino signal.
**Super El Nino**: SST anomaly above **+2.0 deg C** in the central Pacific.

n5c42993799f.s: The usual effect of El Nino on the Indian summer monsoon is that it:
o: Brings the monsoon early with normal rainfall
Has no relationship with the monsoon
n5c42993799f.x: El Nino is generally associated with a delayed and weakened Indian monsoon and a higher risk of deficient rainfall.
xa: Mechanism: Walker circulation disrupted → **sinking air over the Indian Ocean** = high pressure.
**IMD** warned in **May 2026** that a developing **super El Nino** could weaken the **2026** SW monsoon.
INCOIS study: **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon (Oct-Dec) cyclones in the **Bay of Bengal**.

n4fc76f925e9.s: The Southern Oscillation Index is the pressure difference between:
n4fc76f925e9.x: The SOI is Tahiti minus Darwin; a sustained negative SOI indicates El Nino.
xa: Described by **Sir Gilbert Walker** in **1920**.
ENSO: El Nino/La Nina = **oceanic**; Southern Oscillation = **atmospheric**.
High pressure over the equatorial South Pacific ↔ low pressure over the South Indian Ocean, and vice versa.

n8279f8c1710.s: In May 2026, the IMD warned that a developing super El Nino could have what effect on the 2026 South-West Monsoon?
o: It could strengthen it throughout India.
It could reverse it into a winter monsoon.
It would have no possible effect.
n8279f8c1710.x: The IMD warned that a developing super El Nino could weaken the 2026 South-West Monsoon.
n8279f8c1710.tq: Trace the climate-driver and monsoon-effect relationship without assuming every El Nino impact is strengthening.
xs: A developing **super El Nino** could **weaken** the **2026 SW monsoon** — option **(4)**.
**IMD** gave this warning in **May 2026**; El Nino usually **delays and weakens** the monsoon (drought risk).
xa: **Super El Nino** = SST anomaly above **+2.0 deg C** in the central Pacific.
**6 of 10** El Nino years brought **deficient** Indian rainfall.
INCOIS study: El Nino **may reduce** post-monsoon (Oct-Dec) **Bay of Bengal** cyclones.

n291f3bb16d6.s: According to the IMD criterion, El Nino is identified when the central equatorial Pacific is at least:
o: 0.2°C warmer than average for three consecutive months
2.0°C warmer than average for one season
1.0°C warmer than average for ten consecutive months
0.5°C warmer than average for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods
n291f3bb16d6.x: The stated IMD criterion is a warming of at least 0.5°C above average for five consecutive overlapping three-month periods in the central equatorial Pacific.
n291f3bb16d6.tq: Retain the threshold, duration and overlapping-period conditions together.
xs: IMD identifies El Nino when the central equatorial Pacific is at least **0.5°C warmer** for **five consecutive overlapping three-month periods** — option **(4)**.
A **Super El Nino** is a different threshold: anomaly above **+2.0°C**.
xa: **Nino 3.4 region**: **5°N-5°S, 120°W-170°W** in the central equatorial Pacific.
NASA's **Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** tracks **Kelvin waves** — an early El Nino signal.
Last global El Nino: **2023-24**.

n6f7c0219c98.s: Who described the Southern Oscillation in 1920?
n6f7c0219c98.x: Sir Gilbert Walker described the Southern Oscillation in 1920.
n6f7c0219c98.tq: Match the scientific concept with its associated investigator and year.
xs: **Sir Gilbert Walker** described the **Southern Oscillation** in **1920** — option **(1)**.
The Southern Oscillation is the atmospheric pressure seesaw between **Tahiti** and **Port Darwin**.
xa: ⚠ **Walker** = Southern Oscillation; El Nino mechanism disrupts the **Walker circulation**.
**Bjerknes feedback**: weaker easterlies → warm water slides east → trades weaken further.
ENSO: **El Nino/La Nina** = oceanic component; **Southern Oscillation** = atmospheric counterpart.

n9d364fe3271.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about El Nino off the Peru coast?
o: A warm current replaces the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current.
Phytoplankton decline and the fish catch collapses.
Upwelling of cold, nutrient-rich water intensifies.
n9d364fe3271.x: During El Nino the upwelling of cold nutrient-rich water off Peru stops, which is why fisheries collapse.
xa: In **La Nina** the opposite happens: **cold water upwells** in the eastern Pacific.
El Nino recurs every **3-7 years**; name = **"little boy / Christ child"**.
El Nino is a **climate pattern, not a storm**.

n6345893787e.s: The name ‘El Nino’ literally refers to which of the following?
o: The little boy or Christ child
n6345893787e.x: El Nino means ‘the little boy’ or ‘Christ child’ and is associated with its appearance around Christmas.
n6345893787e.tq: Test the meaning of a distinctive geographical term.
xs: **El Nino** means **"the little boy / Christ child"** — option **(4)**.
The name comes from its appearance around **Christmas** off the **Peru** coast.
xa: El Nino = abnormal warming of the **central and eastern equatorial Pacific**.
Recurrence: every **3-7 years**; some notes say **2-7 years**.
**Modoki** is a different Japanese term meaning **"similar but different"**.

nd84bd4b3bc7.s: El Nino is most accurately defined as:
o: A permanent warm current along the eastern coast of India
Abnormal warming of the central and eastern tropical Pacific
Abnormal cooling of the western Pacific only
A periodic reversal of the Atlantic Ocean currents
nd84bd4b3bc7.x: El Nino is the abnormal warming of the central and eastern Pacific. It is an oceanic component of the broader ENSO phenomenon.
nd84bd4b3bc7.tq: Use the exact region and temperature anomaly to distinguish El Nino from La Nina.
xs: **El Nino** = **abnormal warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific** — option **(2)**.
It is in the **Pacific Ocean**, off **Peru**, not India's east coast or the Atlantic; and it is **not permanent** (every **3-7 years**).
Warm water piled in the **western Pacific** shifts **east**; the west does not merely cool.
xa: A warm current flows **southwards along the Peru coast**, replacing the cold **Humboldt** current.
⚠ **Canonical** El Nino = max warming in the **eastern** Pacific; **Modoki** = **central** Pacific.
El Nino is the **warm phase**, La Nina the **cold phase** of ENSO.

n704223e86c0.s: El Nino generally recurs about every:
n704223e86c0.x: El Nino recurs about every 3-7 years; its name comes from its appearance around Christmas, but it does not occur every year.
xa: Name = **"the little boy / Christ child"**.
Last global El Nino: **2023-24**.
El Nino impacts in India: **drought**, lower **rice, sugarcane** yields, **food inflation**.

n8956937cc78.s: El Nino ____ the Walker circulation and shifts it eastward.
n8956937cc78.x: El Nino weakens the Walker circulation and moves it east, reducing convection over India; La Nina strengthens it.
xa: Normal Walker cell: rising air over **western Pacific/Indonesia**, sinking over the cool **eastern Pacific**, closed by **easterly trades**.
**Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich** tracks **Kelvin waves** — early El Nino signal.
**Positive IOD** brings more rain and can **offset El Nino** (e.g. **1997**).

n4e4f0e4dd89.s: Convection associated with the Madden-Julian Oscillation can rise up to about:
n4e4f0e4dd89.x: MJO convection rises up to about 10 km and shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward.
xa: The shift produces **active/break spells** of the monsoon.
Periodicity: every **30-60 days**.
Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.

n9b017c750b9.s: During the onset of El Nino, the easterly trade winds:
n9b017c750b9.x: In El Nino the trade winds weaken or reverse, warm western Pacific water shifts east, and the warming weakens the winds further.
xa: **El Nino weakens and shifts the Walker circulation eastward** → less convection over India.
**La Nina**: trade winds **strengthen**, warm water pushed further **west towards Asia**.
⚠ El Nino **weakens**, La Nina **strengthens** the Walker circulation.

n94393a770e7.s: During El Nino, rising air shifts eastward and air descends over the Indian Ocean. This generally produces:
o: No change in Indian monsoon conditions
High pressure and a delayed or weak Indian monsoon
Low pressure and a stronger Indian monsoon
High pressure and exceptionally heavy monsoon rainfall
n94393a770e7.x: Descending air over the Indian Ocean produces high pressure, which is associated with a delayed or weak Indian monsoon.
n94393a770e7.tq: Apply the pressure–vertical-motion relationship to a regional climate outcome.
xs: Descending air over the Indian Ocean gives **high pressure** and a **delayed or weak Indian monsoon** — option **(2)**.
Impacts: **drought**, lower summer-crop (**rice, sugarcane**) yields, **food inflation**, harsher heat.
A stronger or normal-to-above-normal monsoon is the **La Nina** pattern, not El Nino.
xa: **6 of 10** El Nino years brought depressed Indian rainfall.
A **positive IOD** can **offset** El Nino (as in **1997**).
IMD's **April 2026** forecast: below-normal monsoon, **92% of LPA**, due to a developing El Nino.

na13e758c412.s: Which inference regarding El Nino and Bay of Bengal cyclones is supported by the INCOIS study?
o: El Nino may reduce post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino always increases post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
El Nino shifts all Bay of Bengal cyclones to the Arabian Sea.
El Nino has no relationship with Bay of Bengal cyclones.
na13e758c412.x: The study indicated that El Nino may reduce the number of post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones.
na13e758c412.tq: Use the cautious wording ‘may’ and distinguish a possible tendency from an absolute rule.
xs: The **INCOIS** study says **El Nino may reduce** post-monsoon Bay of Bengal cyclones — option **(1)**.
ENSO governs the number of **post-monsoon (Oct-Dec)** Bay of Bengal cyclones.
**La Nina** goes the other way: **more floods and severe cyclones** in the Bay of Bengal.
xa: INCOIS is in **Hyderabad**.
Fewer/more Bay of Bengal cyclones affect **coastal AP**.
El Nino weakens the **Walker circulation** and shifts it eastward.

na60753f2e38.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about types of El Nino?
o: 'Modoki' is a Japanese word meaning 'returning child'.
In a canonical El Nino, maximum warming occurs in the eastern Pacific near Peru.
In El Nino Modoki, maximum warming occurs in the central Pacific.
El Nino Modoki has cooler waters on both the eastern and western sides.
xa: El Nino name = **"the little boy / Christ child"**, appearing around **Christmas**.
Recurrence: every **3-7 years** (some notes **2-7 years**).
**Bjerknes feedback:** trade winds weaken → warm water shifts east → winds weaken further.
Last global El Nino = **2023-24**.

na364074976f.s: In the normal Walker circulation over the tropical Pacific, air rises over the:
na364074976f.x: Normally air rises over the warm western Pacific and Indonesia, sinks over the cool eastern Pacific, with easterly trades at the surface.
xa: **El Nino weakens** it and **shifts it eastward** → less convection over India.
**La Nina strengthens** it.
**Walker** (**1920s**) first described the **Southern Oscillation**.

n77de5073097.s: In the positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole, which of the following conditions generally occurs?
o: The Arabian Sea is warmer and the region south of Indonesia is cooler.
The Arabian Sea and the region south of Indonesia become equally cool.
The Arabian Sea is cooler and the region south of Indonesia is warmer.
Both poles of the Indian Ocean become equally warm.
n77de5073097.x: During a positive IOD, the western pole near the Arabian Sea is warmer while the eastern pole south of Indonesia is cooler.
n77de5073097.tq: Compare the west and east poles before considering the monsoon consequence.
xs: In a **positive IOD**, the **Arabian Sea (western pole) is warmer** and the region **south of Indonesia (eastern pole)** cooler — option **(1)**.
Winds blow **east to west** (Bay of Bengal to Arabian Sea), giving **more rain** over India.
The reverse pattern — western cooler, eastern warmer — is a **negative IOD** (reduced rain).
xa: A positive IOD can **offset El Nino**; in **1997** it saved India from drought despite a **Super El Nino**.
IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
IOD discovered in **1999**; measured by the **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)**.

nd2fe4aff3db.s: Which condition is characteristic of a negative Indian Ocean Dipole?
o: Warmer western Arabian Sea and increased rainfall over India
Warmer eastern Pacific and stronger Peru upwelling
Cooler western Arabian Sea and warmer eastern pole, with reduced Indian rainfall
Cooler western and eastern poles with no monsoon effect
nd2fe4aff3db.x: In a negative IOD, the western Arabian Sea is cooler and the eastern pole is warmer, resulting in reduced rainfall over India.
nd2fe4aff3db.tq: Identify the reversed SST pattern and its linked rainfall effect.
xs: **Negative IOD** = **cooler western (Arabian Sea)**, **warmer eastern pole**, **reduced Indian rainfall** — option **(3)**.
A warmer western Arabian Sea with more rain is the **positive IOD**.
Eastern-Pacific warming and Peru upwelling belong to **ENSO**, not the IOD.
xa: IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
Some notes link **negative IOD** with **El Nino**.
**NIOT OMNI buoys** off **Nellore** support IOD monitoring.

n02bbc1a0352.s: The Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) is measured by the:
n02bbc1a0352.x: The IOD is measured by the Dipole Mode Index (DMI); the SOI measures the Southern Oscillation.
xa: Late **May 2026** DMI value **-0.34 °C** = **neutral**.
IOD = SST difference between the **Arabian Sea** (west) and **eastern Indian Ocean south of Indonesia** (east).

n97a99796507.s: In 1997, the effects of El Nino on India were offset by a:
n97a99796507.x: The IOD runs independently of ENSO, and a positive IOD offset El Nino in 1997.
xa: Some notes link **positive IOD with La Nina** and **negative IOD with El Nino**.
⚠ **Positive IOD** = more rain over India; **negative IOD** = reduced rain.
Measured by the **Dipole Mode Index (DMI)**.

n71c366f090a.s: The strong positive IOD in 1997 is significant because it:
o: Caused drought in India despite a weak La Nina
Saved India from drought despite a Super El Nino
Produced the first recorded Madden-Julian Oscillation
n71c366f090a.x: The strong positive IOD in 1997 helped save India from drought even though a Super El Nino was present.
n71c366f090a.tq: Use an exceptional case to test interaction between climate drivers.
xs: In **1997** a strong **positive IOD** **saved India from drought despite a Super El Nino** — option **(2)**.
A positive IOD brings **more rain** over India and **can offset El Nino**.
xa: IOD develops **April-May**, peaks in **October**.
The IOD **runs independently of ENSO**.
Positive IOD: winds blow **east to west** (Bay of Bengal to Arabian Sea).

ne44d0c8eeb5.s: The Madden–Julian Oscillation recurs about every:
ne44d0c8eeb5.x: The MJO is an eastward-moving belt of clouds and rain from the tropical Indian Ocean that recurs every 30–60 days.
xa: Identified by **Madden and Julian, 1971-72**.
Convection rises up to **10 km**; it fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.
It shifts the heavy-rain zone eastward → **active/break spells** of the monsoon.

n13d764208b5.s: The Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) contributes to which feature of the Indian monsoon?
n13d764208b5.x: By shifting the zone of heavy rain eastward, the MJO contributes to active and break spells of the monsoon.
xa: MJO recurs every **30-60 days** and moves **eastward**.
It begins as a warm pool in the tropical **Indian Ocean**.
Convection up to **10 km**; fades in the **eastern Pacific** but circles the globe aloft.

ndd4037c7e78.s: Which one of the following is a marine ecosystem associated with chemosynthetic life?
ndd4037c7e78.x: Hydrothermal vents are marine ecosystems that support chemosynthetic life, unlike rivers and freshwater lakes.
ndd4037c7e78.tq: Use the distinctive biological process to identify the ecosystem.
xs: **Hydrothermal vents** are marine ecosystems with **chemosynthetic** life — option **(3)**.
**Rivers** and **freshwater lakes** are freshwater (lotic/lentic) ecosystems, **not marine**; a glacial pond is freshwater too.
xa: Other marine ecosystems: **coral reefs, intertidal zone, estuaries, salt marshes, mangroves, seagrass beds, kelp forests**.
Ocean **primary producers** are **phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria).
The **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.

nb9919260f8c.s: The littoral or intertidal zone lies between the
o: sunlit and dark zones of the ocean
sea floor and the deepest ocean trench
continental shelf and the open ocean
nb9919260f8c.x: The littoral or intertidal zone is the area between the high-tide and low-tide marks.
nb9919260f8c.tq: Recall the physical boundaries of the intertidal zone.
xs: The **littoral / intertidal** zone lies between the **high-tide and low-tide marks** — option **(4)**.
Sunlit vs dark is the **photic/aphotic** divide; shelf vs open ocean is the **neritic/oceanic** divide.
xa: **Neritic** zone: from the **high-water line** over the continental shelf to about **200 m**.
**Benthic** = the **sea floor** and its organisms.
**Oceanic** = open ocean **beyond the shelf**.

n065b63b0496.s: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line over the continental shelf to approximately
n065b63b0496.x: The neritic zone extends from the high-water line across the continental shelf to about 200 metres depth.
n065b63b0496.tq: Associate the neritic zone with the continental shelf and its approximate depth.
xs: The **neritic zone** reaches about **200 m** depth over the **continental shelf** — option **(4)**.
It starts at the **high-water line**.
xa: The neritic shelf zone is the **richest fishing zone**.
The **photic (euphotic)** zone is the sunlit upper layer (~**200 m**) where photosynthesis occurs.
Corals grow in **clear, shallow, sunlit** water, usually < ~**50 m**.

n77c5220f745.s: The richest fishing zone among the following is generally the
n77c5220f745.x: The neritic zone over the continental shelf is generally the richest fishing zone.
n77c5220f745.tq: Link shallow continental-shelf waters with high fisheries productivity.
xs: The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone — option **(3)**.
It extends from the **high-water line** over the **continental shelf** to about **200 m**.
The **aphotic** zone is dark with no photosynthesis, so it cannot be the richest.
xa: **Upwelling** zones (Peru-Chile, California, Namibia, Somalia, Kerala) are also rich fisheries.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the most marine habitats/life.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

ne6907a3e82d.s: Which ocean zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life?
ne6907a3e82d.x: The epipelagic (sunlit) zone holds the highest percentage of marine habitats and life, because light there allows photosynthesis. The aphotic zone is dark with no photosynthesis, and the abyssal and hadal zones on the deep sea floor and in trenches support far less life.
xs: The **epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage** of marine habitats/life — option **(1)**.
Light there allows **photosynthesis**; the **aphotic** zone is dark with **no photosynthesis**.
xa: The **photic (euphotic)** layer is about **200 m** deep.
**Phytoplankton** (diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria) are the main primary producers.
The **neritic shelf zone** is the richest fishing zone.

ncf944aca13e.s: Coral reefs are called the 'Rainforests of the Sea' mainly because of their:
o: Large share of the ocean floor
ncf944aca13e.x: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor but support more than 25 per cent of all marine species.
xa: With tropical rainforests, reefs have the **highest species richness**.
Roles: **break wave power during storms**, preventing **coastal erosion**.
**APPSC 2024** paired the epithet with "breaks wave power" — both true, but the second does not explain the first.

n27ade553b9b.s: Rivers and freshwater lakes are examples of:
n27ade553b9b.x: Rivers and lakes are freshwater (lotic and lentic) ecosystems; marine ecosystems cover about 71% of Earth's surface.
xa: Marine: **coral reefs**, **hydrothermal vents**, **estuaries**, **mangroves**, **seagrass beds**, **kelp forests**.
**Neritic** zone: over the **continental shelf** to about **200 m** — **richest fishing zone**.
**Epipelagic (sunlit)** zone holds the **highest percentage of marine life**.

n1c900b9dcd0.s: Approximately how much of Earth’s oxygen is produced by the oceans, mainly through phytoplankton?
n1c900b9dcd0.x: The oceans, mainly through phytoplankton, produce about half or more than half of Earth’s oxygen, exceeding the contribution of all rainforests combined.
n1c900b9dcd0.tq: Select the approximate share rather than confusing oceanic production with rainforest production.
xs: Oceans, mainly via **phytoplankton**, produce **about half (50%+)** of Earth's oxygen — option **(2)**.
That is **more than all rainforests combined**.
xa: Phytoplankton = **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria**.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → **fewer phytoplankton**, fishery collapse.
Marine ecosystems cover about **71%** of Earth's surface.

na4e09932e26.s: Coastal upwelling brings cold, nutrient-rich water to the surface when:
o: Winds pile surface water against the coast
Rivers add fresh water at the coast
Warm surface water sinks due to evaporation
na4e09932e26.x: Coastal upwelling occurs when winds drive surface water away from the coast, allowing cold, nutrient-rich subsurface water to rise.
xa: Upwelling zones: **Peru-Chile** (Humboldt), **California**, **Namibia** (Benguela), **Somalia** (Findlater), **Kerala**.
**El Nino** **suppresses** the Peru upwelling.
Kerala upwelling supports **oil sardine and mackerel**.

nccc4672e07f.s: Cold temperate seas are more vulnerable to ocean acidification mainly because cold water has:
nccc4672e07f.x: Carbon dioxide is more soluble in cold water, making cold temperate seas particularly vulnerable to acidification.
xa: Chemistry: **CO2 + water → carbonic acid → bicarbonate + hydronium**; **carbonate ions fall**.
Normal seawater **pH ~8.1** (alkaline).
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2.

ngeneral-geography-10-11.s: Ocean organisms that swim actively are called:
ngeneral-geography-10-11.x: Nekton swim actively, benthos live on the bottom, and plankton (phyto- and zoo-) drift.
n: Phytoplankton are primary producers. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Zooplankton are animal plankton. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Zooplankton are part of the food chain. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Nekton are actively swimming organisms. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Benthos are organisms associated with the ocean bottom. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xa: **Plankton** = organisms that **drift** with water.
Phytoplankton include **diatoms, dinoflagellates, cyanobacteria**.
Oceans, mainly phytoplankton, produce **about half** of Earth's **oxygen**.

ndb6577c245d.s: Upwelling off Namibia is associated with which current?
ndb6577c245d.x: Namibia's upwelling goes with the Benguela; Peru–Chile with the Humboldt and Somalia with the Findlater Current.
xa: **Kerala / SW India** upwelling: **SW monsoon** — **oil sardine and mackerel**.
Upwelling: winds push surface water offshore → cold, nutrient-rich water rises.
**El Nino** suppresses Peru upwelling → fishery collapse.

nd4c64f21f28.s: Monsoon upwelling off Kerala and south-west India supports which fisheries?
nd4c64f21f28.x: Southwest-monsoon upwelling off Kerala supports oil sardine and mackerel fisheries.
xa: **Somalia/Horn of Africa** upwelling: **Findlater** current, SW monsoon.
**Peru-Chile** upwelling: **Humboldt** (anchoveta fishery).
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, now threatened by **marine heatwaves**.

nef0672e8c48.s: El Nino can cause a collapse of the Peru fishery because it:
o: Suppresses the Peru upwelling, reducing phytoplankton
Increases nutrient supply to coastal waters
Cools the sea surface off Peru
nef0672e8c48.x: El Nino suppresses the Peru upwelling system, reducing phytoplankton and thereby fish food, which contributes to fishery collapse.
xa: The Peru-Chile upwelling is tied to the **Humboldt** current — the **anchoveta** fishery.
Since **1998** every strong El Nino has coincided with a **global bleaching event**.
Phytoplankton are the ocean's main **primary producers**.

nb024393fa7a.s: Reef-building corals live in symbiotic association with:
nb024393fa7a.x: Zooxanthellae live in symbiosis with corals, which grow between about 30°N and 30°S in water above about 20°C.
xa: Minimum about **20-21 °C**; optimum **23-25 °C**.
Water must be **clear, shallow, sunlit** (usually < ~**50 m**), sediment-free, normal salinity.
Reefs avoid **muddy river mouths**.

ne21e1a865c7.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about coral reef growth conditions?
o: Corals need a minimum water temperature of about 20–21°C.
Corals flourish in clear, shallow, sunlit water.
The optimum temperature for coral growth is about 23–25°C.
Heavy sediment at muddy river mouths favours coral growth.
ne21e1a865c7.x: Heavy sediment and freshwater at muddy river mouths inhibit coral reef growth.
xa: That is why most of India's **east coast** (West Bengal, Odisha, **Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs**.
Depth usually < ~**50 m**; normal salinity.
Location: mostly within **30°N-30°S**.

nfb9d3def42c.s: Which one of the following is NOT a role of coral reefs?
o: Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves
nfb9d3def42c.x: Coral reefs break storm waves and thereby help prevent coastal erosion. They also provide nursery grounds and support fisheries and tourism.
nfb9d3def42c.tq: Find the option that reverses a stated ecological function.
xs: **Increasing coastal erosion by amplifying storm waves** is **not** a reef role — option **(3)**.
Reefs do the opposite: they **break wave power during storms**, **preventing coastal erosion**.
They also provide **nursery/spawning grounds**, **fisheries**, **tourism** and biodiversity.
xa: Reefs protect coasts from **storm surges**.
NGT cleared the **₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project** (Feb 2026) — **coral loss** is the core objection.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.

n0d5ab50c3fd.s: Coral bleaching occurs when coral polyps expel their:
n0d5ab50c3fd.x: Bleaching is the expulsion of zooxanthellae with loss of pigments; a bleached coral is stressed but not necessarily dead.
xa: Primary cause: **rising SST / marine heatwaves**.
**INCOIS** issues **coral bleaching** and algal bloom alerts.
Zooxanthellae normally supply the coral's **food and colour**.

n8539de522a5.s: Which one of the following is NOT identified as a factor that can contribute to coral bleaching?
n8539de522a5.x: Pollution, extreme low tides and ocean acidification are recognised contributors to coral bleaching. Increased carbonate availability is not listed as a bleaching factor.
n8539de522a5.tq: Eliminate the three recognised stressors and identify the reversed carbonate claim.
xs: **Increase in carbonate availability** is **not** a bleaching factor — option **(3)**.
In fact **ocean acidification** **lowers** carbonate ions, which harms corals — and acidification **is** a trigger.
**Extremely low tides** and **pollution and runoff** are listed triggers.
xa: Other triggers: **high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, crown-of-thorns starfish, coral mining, tourism**.
Primary cause: **rising SST and marine heatwaves**.
**Harmful algal blooms** also block sunlight for corals and seagrass.

ngeneral-geography-10-39.s: Coral reefs typically lie within which latitudes?
ngeneral-geography-10-39.x: Coral reefs lie mainly in tropical and semi-tropical waters around 25°N–25°S, extending to about 30°.
n: Coral reefs are distributed mainly in tropical and semi-tropical waters. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are typically found around 25°N–25°S. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Some coral reefs extend to approximately 30° latitude. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Coral reefs are extremely rich marine habitats. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Australia is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
Indonesia is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
The Philippines is a major concentration of coral reefs. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #10 · pp 62-67]
xa: **Great Barrier Reef** (Queensland) is the **largest coral reef system**, ~**2,300 km** long; **UNESCO** site **1981**.
India: **Andaman & Nicobar** = **highest diversity**; **Lakshadweep** = only true **atolls**.
**Andhra Pradesh** has **no reefs** — heavy river sediment.
⚠ Other notes give **30 deg N-30 deg S**.

n6d57e5b810d.s: A ring-shaped reef enclosing a central lagoon is called a(n):
n6d57e5b810d.x: An atoll encloses a central lagoon; a fringing reef grows close to the shore and a barrier reef is separated from the coast by a lagoon.
xa: Fringing: **Gulf of Mannar**, **Gulf of Kutch**.
Barrier: **Great Barrier Reef** (Australia) — Queensland, Coral Sea.
Atoll: **Lakshadweep** — India's only true atolls.

nc93c0dfdfb5.s: The Great Barrier Reef is correctly described as a:
o: Fringing reef in the Gulf of Mannar
Barrier reef off Queensland in the Coral Sea
Fringing reef off the coast of Maharashtra
nc93c0dfdfb5.x: The Great Barrier Reef is a barrier reef located off Queensland in the Coral Sea and extends for about 2,300 km.
nc93c0dfdfb5.tq: Discriminate among reef types by matching the named example with its location.
xs: The **Great Barrier Reef** is a **barrier reef** off **Queensland** in the **Coral Sea** — option **(3)**.
**Lakshadweep** has **atolls**; the **Gulf of Mannar** has **fringing** reefs; **Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs.
xa: **UNESCO World Heritage Site 1981**.
World's **largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.

n93e9b470100.s: Which one of the following sets contains only recognised true coral reef areas in India?
o: Godavari Delta, Mahanadi Delta, Malvan and West Bengal
Sundarbans, Krishna Delta, Chilika and Gulf of Kutch
West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh and Lakshadweep
Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep and Andaman and Nicobar Islands
n93e9b470100.x: India’s recognised true reef areas include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep. Patchy reefs also occur at Malvan in Maharashtra.
n93e9b470100.tq: Select the complete valid geographical set while rejecting sediment-rich east-coast locations.
xs: **Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Lakshadweep, Andaman & Nicobar** are true reef areas — option **(4)**.
Most of the **east coast** (**West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**) has **no reefs** — heavy river sediment + freshwater.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has only **patchy reefs**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** = **highest diversity**; **Lakshadweep** = only true **atolls**.
**Gulf of Mannar** (TN), **Gulf of Kutch** (Gujarat) = true reefs.
⚠ **AP** has **no true coral reefs**.

n600138c00a5.s: Coral reefs are absent along most of India's east coast mainly because of:
o: Heavy river sediment and freshwater input
n600138c00a5.x: Most of the east coast (West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh) lacks reefs because heavy river sediment and freshwater inhibit coral growth.
xa: No-reef states: **West Bengal, Odisha, Andhra Pradesh**.
AP fisheries depend on **Bay of Bengal plankton** productivity, threatened by **marine heatwaves**.
The east coast exception: **Gulf of Mannar** (TN) has true reefs.

ne0c52f5d084.s: The Great Barrier Reef was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in:
ne0c52f5d084.x: The Great Barrier Reef, about 2,300 km long off north-eastern Australia, became a World Heritage Site in 1981.
xa: Area ~**344,400 sq km**; ~**1,500** fish + **400+** coral species.
It is the **world's largest** reef, followed by the **Mesoamerican Barrier Reef**.
Type: **barrier reef** — parallel to the coast, separated by a wide, deep lagoon.

n8927e27cc70.s: The Malvan coral-reef region is in:
n8927e27cc70.x: Malvan is a coral-reef region in Maharashtra; other Indian reef regions include the Gulf of Mannar, Gulf of Kutch, Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep.
xa: **Lakshadweep** = India's only true **atolls**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute**: **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.

nc1407bf68a5.s: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at:
nc1407bf68a5.x: India's first National Coral Reef Research Institute is located at Chidiyatapu in South Andaman.
xs: India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman** — option **(4)**.
**Malvan** (Maharashtra) has patchy reefs; **Lakshadweep** has India's only atolls; **Gulf of Mannar** has India's first **marine biosphere reserve**.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has the **highest reef diversity** in India.
**CMLRE Kochi** studies **EEZ** living resources.
Andaman mass bleaching: about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature (**UPPSC 2024** key).

n55770a90906.s: The NGT's clearance of the ₹92,000-crore Great Nicobar project directed the Environment Ministry to:
o: Suspend marine research in the Nicobar Islands
Hand coral protection to the Fisheries Ministry
Translocate all coral reefs before construction
n55770a90906.x: The NGT clearance directed the Environment Ministry to protect and regenerate coral reefs; coral loss was a central objection to the project.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C rise** in Indian Ocean temperature.
Reefs **break wave power**, preventing coastal erosion.

n00b180bc10f.s: Marine heatwaves threaten Andhra Pradesh's fisheries because they depend partly on:
o: Plankton productivity in the Bay of Bengal
n00b180bc10f.x: Andhra Pradesh has no true coral reefs; its fisheries rely on Bay of Bengal plankton productivity, which marine heatwaves threaten.
xa: Other east-coast states without reefs: **West Bengal, Odisha**.
**Phytoplankton** are the ocean's main **primary producers**.
⚠ Highest diversity = **Andaman & Nicobar**; only atolls = **Lakshadweep**; AP = **no reefs**.

n352fe4d3c63.s: Since 1998, every strong El Nino has coincided with:
n352fe4d3c63.x: Every strong El Nino since 1998 has coincided with a global coral bleaching event.
xa: Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.
El Nino also suppresses **Peru upwelling** → fishery collapse.

o: The evil twin of global warming
nb26b575ac93.x: Ocean acidification, the fall in seawater pH from CO2 uptake, is called the 'evil twin of global warming' or 'the other CO2 problem'.
xa: CO2 + water → **carbonic acid** → carbonate ions fall → **calcifiers** (corals, plankton, shellfish) struggle.
Oceans absorb about **30-40%** of anthropogenic CO2.
Acidity is up **30%** since the Industrial Revolution; may rise **150%** by **2100**.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** and the melting **Arctic**.

n760ed6097b4.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the chemistry of ocean acidification?
o: The concentration of carbonate ions declines.
Carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid.
Carbonic acid yields bicarbonate and hydronium ions.
Calcifying organisms find it easier to build calcium carbonate shells.
n760ed6097b4.x: Falling carbonate ions make shell building harder, not easier, for corals, plankton and shellfish.
xa: Calcifiers hit: **corals, plankton and shellfish**.
Seawater is **alkaline**, **pH ~8.1**; acidification = falling pH from **CO2** uptake.
Epithets: **"evil twin of global warming"** / **"the other CO2 problem"**.

nb39a57aec96.s: Approximately what proportion of anthropogenic carbon dioxide is absorbed by the oceans?
nb39a57aec96.x: The oceans absorb approximately 30–40% of anthropogenic carbon dioxide; another cited estimate places the uptake above 25%.
nb39a57aec96.tq: Use the middle numerical range carefully rather than confusing it with the alternative lower estimate.
xs: Oceans absorb about **30-40 percent** of anthropogenic **CO2** — option **(3)**.
Some notes put it at **>25%**.
xa: Ocean acidity is up **30%** since the **Industrial Revolution**.
Acidity may rise **150%** by **2100**.
Worst areas: **cold temperate seas** and the **melting Arctic**.

n1d471c603d8.s: The Gulf of Mexico dead zone is linked to runoff from the:
n1d471c603d8.x: Runoff from the Mississippi feeds algal blooms whose decay strips oxygen, creating the Gulf of Mexico dead zone.
xa: Another dead zone: **Chesapeake Bay**.
Cause: excess **nitrogen and phosphorus** (farm runoff, sewage) → **eutrophication**.
**INCOIS** issues **algal bloom** and coral bleaching alerts.

nec6081c1603.s: Red tides are toxic algal blooms mostly associated with:
nec6081c1603.x: Red tides mostly involve dinoflagellates; they can discolour water, kill fish and contaminate shellfish.
xa: Dinoflagellates are also among the ocean's **primary producers** (phytoplankton).
Harmful algal blooms → decomposition → **dead zones**.
**INCOIS** issues algal bloom alerts.

nd42b801b431.s: Which is regarded as the strongest global driver of coral loss through bleaching?
o: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves
nd42b801b431.x: Rising sea-surface temperature and marine heatwaves are currently the strongest global drivers of coral loss associated with bleaching.
xa: Other triggers: **pollution and runoff, high UV, disease, storms/cyclones, ocean acidification**.
Also: **crown-of-thorns starfish**, coral mining, tourism.
GCRMN 2026: in **2024**, **87%** of reefs faced unprecedented heat stress.

n9cedffb0eec.s: The mass coral bleaching in the Andaman region was linked to approximately what rise in Indian Ocean temperature?
n9cedffb0eec.x: The Andaman mass bleaching was linked to an approximately 2°C rise in Indian Ocean temperature.
n9cedffb0eec.tq: Use the specific temperature figure rather than the general marine-heatwave threshold.
xs: The **Andaman** mass bleaching was linked to about a **2°C** rise in Indian Ocean temperature — option **(3)**.
This was the **UPPSC 2024** key; rising SST is the **primary cause** of bleaching.
xa: **Andaman & Nicobar** has India's **highest reef diversity**.
**Feb 2025** bleaching also hit the **Gulf of Mannar, Palk Bay, Lakshadweep, Gulf of Kachchh**.
India's first **National Coral Reef Research Institute** is at **Chidiyatapu, South Andaman**.

n35b5e61ed6a.s: The Aichi Target 11 under the Convention on Biological Diversity envisaged protection of what proportion of coastal and marine areas by 2020?
n35b5e61ed6a.x: Aichi Target 11 set the goal of protecting 10 per cent of coastal and marine areas by 2020.
n35b5e61ed6a.tq: Distinguish the Aichi target from the later 30x30 framework.
xs: **Aichi Target 11** (CBD, **2011-2020**) aimed to protect **10 per cent** of coastal and marine areas by **2020** — option **(2)**.
**30%** belongs to the later **30x30** target (by **2030**).
xa: 30x30: **30%** of land + **30%** of oceans by 2030 — **Kunming-Montreal GBF**, **COP15**, **Dec 2022**, **Target 3**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs **recover**.
Recovery from large-scale bleaching takes **more than 15 years**.

n72bf35642a5.s: The 30x30 target under Target 3 of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework seeks to protect by 2030
n72bf35642a5.x: The 30x30 target seeks protection of 30 per cent of land and 30 per cent of oceans by 2030. It was adopted under the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework at COP15 in December 2022.
n72bf35642a5.tq: Use the numerical phrase itself to distinguish the target’s two components.
xs: **30x30** = protect **30% of land and 30% of oceans** by **2030** — option **(4)**.
It is **Target 3** of the **Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework**, adopted at **COP15**, **Dec 2022**.
xa: Earlier target: **Aichi Target 11** — **10%** of coastal and marine areas by **2020**.
**MPAs**, no-fishing zones and sanctuaries help reefs recover.
Since **2010** major reef disturbances recur every **4-6 years**.

na7f671479ea.s: About what share of India's landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk?
na7f671479ea.x: About 58.6% of the landmass faces moderate-to-very-high earthquake risk; about 12% of the area is flood-prone and 68% of cultivable area drought-vulnerable.
xa: About **5,700 km** of the old **7,516.6 km** coastline is exposed to **cyclones and tsunamis**.
**Assam** alone has **31.05 lakh ha** of flood-prone area.
⚠ The coastline was remeasured to **11,098.81 km** (MHA, **Dec 2024**) — older hazard shares still use the old base.
**World Risk Index 2025:** India is the **2nd most vulnerable** country, after the **Philippines**.

n9e45b45e2e3.s: The OMNI buoys that feed India's tsunami warning system are operated by:
n9e45b45e2e3.x: NIOT Nellore's OMNI buoys provide inputs to the tsunami warning system serving the Indian region.
xa: **ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries within **10 minutes**.
Tsunami warning signs: sudden **receding of sea water**, rapid sea-level rise, earthquake shaking.
AP is in the **high** tsunami risk zone, with TN, Puducherry and Odisha.

ndisaster-management-18-1.s: Which of the following best defines a landslide?
o: Accumulation of soil and vegetation on flat agricultural land
Gradual movement of ocean water towards the coastline
Mass movement of rocks, debris or earth down mountain slopes or riverbanks
Sudden upward movement of rocks under the influence of gravity
ndisaster-management-18-1.x: A landslide is the mass movement of rock, debris or earth down a slope or riverbank under gravity. Option D wrongly says the movement is upward.
ndisaster-management-18-1.tq: Recall the definition of a landslide.
n: A landslide is the mass movement of rocks, debris, or earth down mountain slopes or riverbanks. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
A landslide is a rapid downward movement of rock, soil, debris, or vegetation. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
Gravity influences the downward movement in a landslide. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
xs: A landslide is the **mass movement of rocks, debris or earth down mountain slopes or riverbanks** — option **(3)**.
It is a **rapid downward movement** under the influence of **gravity** — not upward, as option (4) claims.
xa: It may occur **gradually** or **suddenly without warning**, mostly in **hilly regions**.
It is both a **geological** and a **hydro-meteorological** hazard.
About **12.6%** of India's land (about **0.42 million sq km**) is landslide-prone.

ndisaster-management-18-11.s: In which year was the National Landslide Risk Management Strategy issued?
ndisaster-management-18-11.x: The National Landslide Risk Management Strategy was issued in 2019. NDMA's landslide guidelines came in 2009.
ndisaster-management-18-11.tq: Discriminate the 2009 guidelines from the 2019 strategy.
n: The National Landslide Risk Management Strategy was issued in 2019. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
xs: The **National Landslide Risk Management Strategy** was issued in **2019** — option **(3)**.
**2009** is the year of the **NDMA Guidelines on Management of Landslides and Snow Avalanches**.
**2024** is the **Wayanad** landslide year.
xa: **GSI** is the **nodal agency** for landslide studies.
Most vulnerable regions: the **Himalayas**, the **Northeast**, the **Western Ghats**.
Landslide-prone: about **12.6%** of land, about **0.42 million sq km**.

ndisaster-management-18-15.s: Which of the following is identified as a landslide-prone area of the Eastern Ghats?
ndisaster-management-18-15.x: The Araku region of Andhra Pradesh is the Eastern Ghats landslide area. The Nilgiris are Western Ghats.
ndisaster-management-18-15.tq: Sort the areas by landslide region.
n: The Araku region is a landslide-prone area of the Eastern Ghats. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
xs: The **Araku region** is the landslide-prone area of the **Eastern Ghats** — option **(3)**.
Its trigger is **localised heavy rainfall**.
**Uttarakhand** is in the **Northwest Himalayas**, the **Nilgiris** in the **Western Ghats**, and **Meghalaya** in the **Northeast Himalayas**.
xa: **Northwest Himalayas:** **earthquakes**, **heavy rainfall**, **road cutting**.
**Northeast Himalayas:** **heavy rainfall**, **Jhum cultivation**.
**Western Ghats and Konkan:** **intense monsoon rainfall**, **deforestation**.
Cloudbursts now hit **Eastern Ghats agency areas (AP)** — flash floods in narrow valleys.

ndisaster-management-18-18.s: Which facility was set up by the Geological Survey of India to issue regional landslide forecasts?
ndisaster-management-18-18.x: GSI set up the National Landslide Forecasting Centre to issue regional landslide forecasts. Susceptibility mapping and hazard zonation are mapping exercises, and the NRSC is an ISRO centre.
ndisaster-management-18-18.tq: Find the initiative among the options.
n: The National Landslide Forecasting Centre is a key landslide initiative. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
xs: The **National Landslide Forecasting Centre** issues landslide forecasts — option **(3)**.
The **GSI** is **associated with landslide forecasting**, and the Centre is a **key** landslide initiative.
The **National Landslide Susceptibility Mapping programme** is a separate GSI **mapping** programme, not a forecasting facility.
xa: **GSI** is the **nodal agency** for landslide studies.
**NDMA Guidelines** on landslides and snow avalanches — **2009**; **National Landslide Risk Management Strategy** — **2019**.
Landslide-prone: about **12.6%** of India's land, about **0.42 million sq km**.

ndisaster-management-31-15.s: NDMA's guidelines for avalanche management provide for:
ndisaster-management-31-15.x: NDMA's avalanche guidelines cover both structural and non-structural measures, along with zonation and early warning.
n: NDMA guidelines provide for avalanche risk zonation. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
NDMA guidelines provide for avalanche early warning. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
NDMA guidelines provide for structural avalanche mitigation measures. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
NDMA guidelines provide for non-structural avalanche mitigation measures. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 66-68]
xa: **Structural** avalanche measures: **snow bridges**, **snow nets**, **retaining walls**, **galleries**.
**Non-structural:** **hazard zonation mapping**, **restricted movement**, **training**, **awareness**.
**Nodal ministry:** **Ministry of Defence**.

ndisaster-management-11-9.s: Which state developed a unique flood hazard atlas based on satellite images of floods from 2000 to 2018?
ndisaster-management-11-9.x: Odisha made the flood hazard atlas from satellite images of past floods (2000–2018) for better flood management.
n: Odisha developed a unique flood hazard atlas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas is based on historical flood inundation captured through satellite imagery. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas covers the period from 2000 to 2018. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
The Odisha Flood Hazard Atlas is intended to help manage floods more efficiently. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xa: **GIS** deals with **spatial data** — can **model**, **analyse** and **display** community vulnerability.
**Hirakud (Odisha)** releases worsen **Krishna-Godavari delta** floods together with **Srisailam** and **Nagarjuna Sagar**.
Flood control is a **state subject**; Centre supports through **FMBAP**.

n7ce8a64c88e.s: In 2025, the heaviest toll from climate-induced disasters in India was reported in:
n7ce8a64c88e.x: More than 4,000 deaths were reported in India from climate-induced disasters in 2025, with the heaviest toll in Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
n7ce8a64c88e.tq: Link the national figure with the specifically identified regional concentration.
xs: The heaviest 2025 toll from climate-induced disasters was in **Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand** — so option **(2)** is correct.
In **2025**, India saw about **331 days** of climate impacts and **over 4,000 deaths** from climate-induced disasters.
xa: **2025 flash floods** at **Dharali and Harsil** (Uttarkashi) diverted the **Bhagirathi**.
**Mandi (HP)** got nearly **20 times** its normal rain in 2025.
The **Dharali flood (5 Aug 2025)** came from an **ice-patch collapse on the Srikanta glacier** (ISRO study).

nb2097ef0b5e.s: A glacial lake outburst flood begins when glacier retreat enlarges a(n):
nb2097ef0b5e.x: Glacier retreat enlarges a proglacial lake; when it bursts, the stored water produces a GLOF.
xa: **Nepal** saw catastrophic GLOF flash floods on **26 Aug 2026**; UNDP counts **26 GLOFs since the 1970s**.
The world has lost **9,500+ Gt** of glacier mass since **1975**.
**Central Himalaya** glacier area is down **>20%** in three decades.

n314e3003a95.s: The India Meteorological Department provides flash-flood guidance not only for India but also to which group of neighbouring countries?
n314e3003a95.x: IMD supplies flash-flood guidance for India and neighbouring Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal.
n314e3003a95.tq: Match the agency with the correct cross-border service recipients.
xs: **IMD** gives flash-flood guidance for India and its neighbours **Bangladesh, Bhutan and Nepal** — so option **(1)** is correct.
These neighbours share Himalayan and Bengal-delta river basins with India.
xa: **Cloudburst (IMD):** about **100 mm per hour** over a small area (**~20-30 sq km**).
**India-Bhutan JGE** on floods held its **11th meeting** in **May 2025**; **India-China ELM** its **16th** in **Apr 2025**.
**ITWS** warns **25** Indian Ocean countries of tsunamis within **10 minutes**.

n4d19cd2e0bb.s: The 'monsoon paradox' of the Hindu Kush-Himalaya refers to declining or erratic seasonal rainfall alongside an increase in:
n4d19cd2e0bb.x: The HKH monsoon paradox is declining or erratic seasonal rain together with more short, intense cloudbursts.
xa: **Cloudburst (IMD):** about **100 mm per hour** over ~**20-30 sq km**.
**GLOFs:** glacier retreat enlarges proglacial lakes that burst.
The world has lost **9,500+ Gt** of glacier mass since **1975**.

nb034c3aa45b.s: Cloudbursts in the Eastern Ghats agency areas of Andhra Pradesh are especially hazardous because they cause:
nb034c3aa45b.x: Cloudbursts in Andhra Pradesh's Eastern Ghats agency areas can rapidly generate flash floods in narrow valleys.
xa: AP's three hazards: **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.
**Vijayawada** floods are linked to the **Budameru** rivulet.
AP coast has seen **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.

n68b6bafe114.s: Which combination forms coastal defence against storm surges?
o: Check dams, contour bunds and farm ponds
Mangroves, shelter belts, dune stabilisation and seawalls
n68b6bafe114.x: Mangroves and shelter belts anchor sediment and buffer storm surges, while dune stabilisation and seawalls strengthen coastal defence.
xa: Storm surge = abnormal sea-level rise from **cyclone winds + low pressure**.
Very high tsunami risk zone: **Andaman & Nicobar**.
AP faces **coastal cyclones, delta floods and Rayalaseema drought**.

nb0817130e8d.s: In Andhra Pradesh's hydrological-disaster pattern, the Rayalaseema region is mainly associated with:
nb0817130e8d.x: AP's coastal belt goes with cyclones and storm surges, the deltaic plains with floods and Rayalaseema with droughts.
xa: AP is the **most cyclone-prone state** — **62+ cyclonic events** in four decades.
**Krishna-Godavari** delta floods are worst when **Srisailam, Nagarjuna Sagar** or **Hirakud** release water together.
**Rayalaseema**: deep borewells → **severe groundwater depletion**.

ngeneral-geography-11-6.s: A flood in which river discharge exceeds channel capacity is a:
ngeneral-geography-11-6.x: A river flood is discharge exceeding the channel; a flash flood is sudden intense runoff and an urban flood is rain with poor drainage.
n: A river flood occurs when river discharge exceeds channel capacity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A flash flood involves sudden high-intensity runoff or discharge. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
An urban flood results from rainfall combined with inadequate urban drainage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A drought is a prolonged water deficit. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: **Cloudburst:** extremely intense localized rainfall → **flash floods** and **landslides**.
**Dam failure:** sudden water release → **catastrophic downstream flooding**.
**Coastal flooding:** **storm surge**, tidal or wave action on a **low-lying coast** → inundation, **salinity**.
**Drought** is **slow-onset** — a **creeping emergency**.

ngeneral-geography-11-7.s: Salinity intrusion is a secondary hazard mainly associated with:
ngeneral-geography-11-7.x: Coastal floods bring salinity intrusion; cloudbursts trigger flash floods and river floods cause bank erosion.
n: A cloudburst causes a flash flood as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A flash flood causes a landslide as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A river flood causes bank erosion as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A coastal flood causes salinity intrusion as a secondary hazard. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
A cloudburst causes flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: **Flash flood → landslide**; **urban flood → traffic or infrastructure collapse**.
**Flood → water contamination**, **disease risk**, **crop or livelihood loss**.
**Rapid-onset:** cyclone, flood, tsunami; **slow-onset:** drought.

ngeneral-geography-11-2.s: Which of the following reduces urban flooding?
ngeneral-geography-11-2.x: Restoring wetlands reduces urban flooding because wetlands store water; wetland loss, paved surfaces and blocked drains add to it.
n: Encroachment of drains causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetland destruction causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Impervious surfaces cause urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetland protection preserves natural storage. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Wetlands store excess water. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: Other urban-flood causes: **poor storm-water drainage**, **unplanned urbanisation**, **floodplain construction**.
**Urban green infrastructure** increases **infiltration** and reduces **runoff**.
**Prep:** unplanned **concretisation**, blocked drains/canals, **encroached lakes**.
Urban-flood cities: **Mumbai**, **Chennai**, **Bengaluru**, **Hyderabad**, **Delhi**.

ngeneral-geography-11-10.s: Which areas are highly vulnerable to flash floods?
o: Arid areas with prolonged water deficit
Mountains, steep catchments and urban areas
ngeneral-geography-11-10.x: Flash floods threaten mountains, steep catchments and cities, where water gathers fast; prolonged deficit describes drought.
n: Mountains are vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Steep catchments are vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Urban areas are highly vulnerable to flash floods. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: Main dangers: **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
Cloudburst-prone: the **Himalayan region** and the windward **Western Ghats**.
Flash floods occur in **Himalayan regions** and **urban areas** (types-of-flood table).

ngeneral-geography-11-25.s: Which of the following can cause urban flooding?
ngeneral-geography-11-25.x: Floodplain construction, like poor storm drains, unplanned growth, low ground and high tides, causes urban flooding.
n: Poor storm-water drainage causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
High tides or storm surge cause urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Unplanned urbanisation causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Low-lying terrain causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Floodplain construction causes urban flooding. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: Other causes: **intense rainfall**, **cloudbursts**, **cyclone rainfall**, **encroachment of drains**, **wetland destruction**.
Major urban floods: **Mumbai 2005** (**944 mm** in **24 hours**), **Chennai 2015**.
**AP City Flood Alert:** **48-hour rainfall** forecasts + **6-hour flash-flood** warnings.

ndisaster-management-29-1.s: The nodal ministry for landslides in India is the:
o: Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs
ndisaster-management-29-1.x: Landslides come under the Ministry of Mines; GLOFs under Jal Shakti and urban floods under Housing and Urban Affairs.
n: The nodal ministry for urban floods is the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) is the Ministry of Jal Shakti. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for landslides is the Ministry of Mines. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
The nodal ministry for biological disasters and epidemics is the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 63-65]
xa: ⚠ Landslide nodal **ministry** is **Mines**; the nodal **agency** is the **GSI**.
**Avalanches** — **Ministry of Defence**.
**Earthquakes, cyclones, tsunamis** — **MoES** with **IMD**.

ndisaster-management-11-5.s: Coastal floods are caused mainly by:
o: Storm surge, cyclones and high tides
ndisaster-management-11-5.x: Coastal floods come from storm surge, cyclones and high tides; GLOFs come from bursting glacial lakes.
n: Riverine or fluvial floods result from the overflow of rivers due to heavy monsoon rainfall. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Urban floods result from poor drainage, heavy rain, and encroachment on wetlands. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Coastal floods result from storm surges, cyclones, and high tides. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Glacial Lake Outburst Floods result from the bursting of glacial lakes. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xa: GLOF-prone: **Himalayan states** — **Uttarakhand**, **Sikkim**.
Riverine floods hit the **Ganga**, **Brahmaputra**, **Kosi** and **Godavari** basins.
Flash floods: **sudden intense rainfall** or **cloudbursts** in **Himalayan regions** and **urban areas**.

ndisaster-management-11-12.x: Flash floods come from sudden heavy rain or cloudbursts and are common in the Himalaya and in cities.
n: Flash floods result from sudden intense rainfall or cloudbursts. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Himalayan regions commonly experience flash floods. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Urban areas commonly experience flash floods. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xa: Flash floods are **very rapid onset** with a **very short warning time**.
Main dangers: **high flow velocity** and **debris**.
Cloudbursts: at least **100 mm** in **one hour** (IMD).

ndisaster-management-19-3.s: Cloudbursts are extremely difficult to forecast mainly because they are:
ndisaster-management-19-3.x: Their highly localised nature makes cloudbursts very hard to forecast.
n: A cloudburst is a highly localised extreme weather event. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
Forecasting cloudbursts is extremely difficult because of their highly localised nature. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #19 · pp 45-47]
xa: Forecasting tools: **Doppler Weather Radar** and **nowcasting**.
**IMD** gives **flash-flood guidance** for India and **Bangladesh, Bhutan, Nepal**.
**GLOF:** glacier retreat enlarges **proglacial lakes** that burst.

n55e4bd152bb.s: Siltation, a recognised cause of floods in India, results mainly from:
n55e4bd152bb.x: Siltation from soil erosion is a cause of floods, along with heavy rain, poor drainage, deforestation and dam failure.
xa: **Assam:** **800 sq km** of upstream **Nagaland** forest was cleared in **2013-23**, causing faster runoff.
**Rashtriya Barh Ayog** assessed about **40 million ha** as flood-prone.
Flood types: **riverine, flash, coastal, urban**.

n8889cd0624c.s: The Rashtriya Barh Ayog (National Flood Commission) assessed about how much area of India as flood-prone?
n8889cd0624c.x: The Rashtriya Barh Ayog assessed about 40 million ha as flood-prone; flood control is a State subject.
xa: The **Expert Committee for Scientific Assessment of Flood-Prone Areas** was set up in **2012** by the **Ministry of Water Resources**.
**India-China ELM** on flood data held its **16th meeting** in **Apr 2025**.
**India-Bhutan JGE** held its **11th meeting** in **May 2025**.

nd7c3425a92b.s: Severe groundwater depletion in drought-prone Rayalaseema is aggravated by:
nd7c3425a92b.x: Rayalaseema faces monsoon failure, crop loss, distress migration and severe groundwater depletion, aggravated by deep borewells.
xa: **Rayalaseema drought** is one of AP's three hazards, with **coastal cyclones** and **delta floods**.
Other drought-prone regions: Western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka.
Hazard → region: **drought** → **Rajasthan + Deccan interior**.

nc08e3bb2773.s: Which of the following is NOT listed among the drought-prone regions of India?
nc08e3bb2773.x: Lower Assam is flood-prone (Brahmaputra plains), not drought-prone. The drought-prone regions listed are western Rajasthan, Kutch-Saurashtra, Marathwada-Vidarbha, interior Karnataka and Rayalaseema.
nc08e3bb2773.tq: Find the geographically misplaced region in a regional classification.
xs: **Lower Assam** is not a drought-prone region — so option **(2)** is correct.
Assam is **flood-prone**: **31.05 lakh ha** of flood-prone area, in the **Brahmaputra-Ganga plains** flood belt.
**Interior Karnataka, Western Rajasthan and Kutch-Saurashtra** are listed drought-prone regions.
xa: Others listed: **Marathwada-Vidarbha** and **Rayalaseema** (AP).
Hazard → region: **drought** → **Rajasthan + Deccan interior**.
About **68%** of cultivable area is drought-vulnerable.

ngeneral-geography-11-5.s: Siltation contributes to floods because it:
ngeneral-geography-11-5.x: Silt reduces channel depth and capacity, so rivers overflow more easily.
n: Siltation reduces channel depth or capacity. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Embankment failure allows water to escape the channel. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Deforestation increases runoff. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Poor drainage causes water to accumulate. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: **Urbanisation** increases runoff through **impervious surfaces**.
**Floodplain encroachment** increases **human exposure**; **snowmelt** causes a **sudden increase in river flow**.
**APPSC 2025 key causes:** **heavy/prolonged rainfall, poor drainage, deforestation, dam failure**.
**Dam failure** causes a **sudden downstream discharge**.

ngeneral-geography-11-22.s: Compared with ordinary heavy rainfall, a cloudburst is:
ngeneral-geography-11-22.x: Cloudbursts are sudden and very local, while ordinary heavy rain can cover wider areas and last longer.
n: Cloudbursts are highly localized. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Ordinary heavy rainfall may cover a larger area. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Cloudbursts are sudden. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
Ordinary heavy rainfall can be prolonged. [General Geography · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 67-72]
xa: Intensity: cloudburst **extremely intense**; ordinary rain has **varying intensity**.
Flood potential: cloudburst has **strong flash-flood potential**; ordinary rain **depends on basin conditions**.
**HKH "monsoon paradox":** seasonal rain erratic while short, intense cloudbursts rise.

n4b707c09006.s: When water exceeds the crest of a dam, the condition is called:
n4b707c09006.x: Overtopping means water exceeds the dam crest; weak foundation, material and design failure are structural causes.
xa: **Natural causes:** an **extreme flood exceeding design capacity**, **landslides**, **earthquakes**, **extreme rainfall**.
**Management causes:** **improper reservoir management**, **poor inspection**, **poor maintenance**.
Dam failure → **catastrophic downstream flooding**.

ndisaster-management-11-10.s: The most frequent natural disaster in India is:
ndisaster-management-11-10.x: Floods are India's most frequent disaster, causing large yearly losses of money, lives and crops.
n: Floods are the most frequent natural disaster in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause damage worth thousands of crores annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause significant loss of life annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
Floods cause significant loss of crops annually. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #11 · pp 27-30]
xa: Flood-affected area: about **10%** of India.
Flood-prone area: about **40 million hectares** (Rashtriya Barh Ayog); recent estimates up to **49 million hectares**.
India loses about **0.4% of GDP** a year to disasters; drivers are **floods and storms**.

ndisaster-management-18-4.s: Landslides in the North-east Himalayas are linked mainly to heavy rainfall and:
ndisaster-management-18-4.x: North-east Himalayan landslides come from heavy rain and jhum farming; road cutting and quakes drive those of the north-west Himalaya.
n: Earthquakes are a trigger for landslides in the Northwest Himalayas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
Heavy rainfall is a trigger for landslides in the Northwest Himalayas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
Road cutting is a trigger for landslides in the Northwest Himalayas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
Heavy rainfall is a trigger for landslides in the Northeast Himalayas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
Jhum cultivation is a trigger for landslides in the Northeast Himalayas. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #18 · pp 43-45]
