AP has its own **State Minorities Commission**.

ne5385bacc76.s: A community had a population of approximately 27.8 million in 2011, after rising from 10.7 million in 1961. Which community does this describe?
ne5385bacc76.x: The figures describe the Christian population: about 10.7 million in 1961 and 27.8 million in 2011.
ne5385bacc76.tq: Use the beginning and ending values as identifying anchors in a population-series question.
xs: The series **10.7 million (1961)** → **27.8 million (2011)** is the **Christians** — option **(2)** is correct (UPSC **2001**).
**Sikhs 20.8**, **Buddhists 8.4**, **Jains 4.5** million in 2011.
xa: Christians = **2.3%** of India.
Christians have the highest sex ratio (**1,023**).

n06dd17986bb.s: The Dardic branch, including Kashmiri, belongs to which language family?
n06dd17986bb.x: Kashmiri belongs to the Dardic branch of the Indo-Aryan family. Dardic is not a Sino-Tibetan branch.
n06dd17986bb.tq: Discriminate between the closely confused Dardic and Sino-Tibetan classifications.
xs: **Dardic** (incl. **Kashmiri**) is **Indo-Aryan** — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ "**Dardi is Sino-Tibetan**" was the false statement in the APPSC-G1 **2024** PYQ.
xa: Dardic is spoken in **J&K**.
Other Indo-Aryan: Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Assamese, **Sindhi, Kachchhi**.
Sino-Tibetan includes **Manipuri, Bodo, Bhotia, Garo**.

nae653808663.s: Telugu is classified under which branch of the Dravidian language family?
nae653808663.x: Telugu is South-Central Dravidian; Tamil, Kannada and Malayalam are southern, while Kui, Gondi and Kurukh are Central or North Dravidian.
xa: ⚠ An older table puts AP under "**Central Dravidian**".
Dravidian share: about **20%** (older), **19.6%** in **2011**.
North Dravidian areas: **Bihar, Odisha, WB**.

n899ef459d89.s: The Austro-Asiatic language family in India is represented by which of the following branches?
n899ef459d89.x: The Austro-Asiatic family includes the Munda branch, with languages such as Santhali and Mundari, and the Mon-Khmer branch, including Khasi.
n899ef459d89.tq: Recall the two-branch structure of the Austro-Asiatic family.
xs: Austro-Asiatic has the **Munda** and **Mon-Khmer** branches — option **(4)** is correct.
**Tibeto-Burman** is Sino-Tibetan; **Dardic** is Indo-Aryan; the others are Dravidian branches.
xa: Munda: **Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Savara**; Mon-Khmer: **Khasi, Nicobarese**.
Areas: **Jharkhand-Odisha-WB** tribal belt, **Meghalaya**, **Nicobar Islands**.
Share about **1.1-1.4%**.

nf1ceaa6e801.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's language-family shares?
o: The older estimate for Indo-Aryan was about 73 per cent
The 2011 estimate for Dravidian was about 19.64 per cent
The 2011 estimate for Indo-Aryan was about 78.05 per cent
The older estimate for Tibeto-Burman was about 20 per cent
nf1ceaa6e801.x: The older Tibeto-Burman estimate was about 0.85 per cent, not 20 per cent (20 per cent was the older Dravidian figure).
xa: Census **2011**: Austro-Asiatic **1.11**, Tibeto-Burman **1.01**.
Older Austric figure: **1.38%**.
Indo-Aryan is the **largest** family.

n4703209d05e.s: Most of the tribal languages of central and eastern India belong to which language family?
n4703209d05e.x: Most tribal languages of central and eastern India (Jharkhand-Odisha-West Bengal belt: Santhali, Mundari, Ho) are Austric. Dravidian covers only some central tribal pockets (Gondi, Kui, Kurukh); Sino-Tibetan is the language family of the North-East and Himalaya; Indo-Aryan is the family of the north, west and east plains.
xs: Most tribal languages of central and eastern India are **Austric (Austro-Asiatic)** — option **(2)** is correct (APPSC **2007**).
Austric is spoken by the tribes of **Jharkhand**.
xa: Munda languages: **Santhali, Mundari, Ho, Savara**.
⚠ Some central tribal tongues — **Kui, Gondi, Kurukh** — are Dravidian.
Share about **1.1-1.4%**.
n4703209d05e.fixed: stem cites 'an APPSC (2007) question' - exam would not word it so

n84a26b82797.s: Which group consists of the scheduled languages with the smallest number of speakers as per Census 2011?
n84a26b82797.x: Sanskrit, Bodo and Manipuri are the smallest scheduled languages. Hindi, Bengali and Marathi are the three largest; Telugu, Tamil and Kannada are large Dravidian languages; Kashmiri is not among the smallest, and Punjabi and Odia have many speakers.
n84a26b82797.tq: Smallest scheduled: Sanskrit, Bodo, Manipuri (not Kashmiri).
xs: The smallest scheduled languages are **Sanskrit, Bodo, Manipuri** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Telugu, Tamil** are the top languages.
xa: ⚠ Some notes list **Kashmiri** among the smallest — it is not.
**Bodo** joined via the **92nd** Amendment; **Manipuri** via the **71st**.
**Sanskrit** was in the original **14**.

na5d346d0543.s: According to Census 2011, which language had the second largest share of speakers in India after Hindi?
na5d346d0543.x: Hindi (43.6%) was followed by Bengali (8.0%); Telugu had 6.7% and Tamil 5.7%.
xa: **Marathi** (**6.9%**) is third.
Telugu slipped **3rd (2001) → 4th (2011)**.
Hindi = most spoken first language.

na75a53f6c82.s: Gor Boli (Lambadi), spoken by the Banjaras, belongs to which language family?
na75a53f6c82.x: Gor Boli or Lambadi is an Indo-Aryan language spoken by Banjaras across several States and has no script of its own.
xa: Banjaras live in **AP, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Rajasthan**.
Demand for Eighth Schedule inclusion continues (**23 Jul 2026**).
**Halbi** is also Indo-Aryan.

n8f7e507a4d7.s: Which of the following languages are declared official languages of Meghalaya along with English?
n8f7e507a4d7.x: Meghalaya has English as an official language, with Khasi and Garo also declared official languages.
n8f7e507a4d7.tq: Distinguish the paired regional languages of Meghalaya from those associated with Sikkim and Goa.
xs: Meghalaya declared **Khasi and Garo** official languages along with **English** — so option **(2)** is correct.
A **2026 ordinance** gives them **associate official status** alongside English under **Art. 345**.
**Bhoti and Purgi** are Ladakh's; **Konkani/Marathi** are Goa's; **Nepali/Lepcha** are Sikkim's.
xa: ⚠ **Khasi** = **Austro-Asiatic (Mon-Khmer)**; **Garo** = **Sino-Tibetan (Bodo group)**.
**Khasi and Garo** are among the languages still **pending** for the Eighth Schedule.
Khasi's Mon-Khmer link is evidence the **Meghalaya plateau** was once part of peninsular India.

n2c37d1f9125.s: Telugu is popularly known as the:
n2c37d1f9125.x: Telugu is popularly called the ‘Italian of the East’.
n2c37d1f9125.tq: Test a well-known sobriquet using close but incorrect cultural comparisons as distractors.
xs: Telugu is called the **"Italian of the East"** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The notes give no such epithet as "Sanskrit of the South", "Latin" or "Greek of the East" for Telugu.
xa: Earliest Telugu word: **"Nagabu"** (**Amaravati** inscription).
First fully Telugu inscription: **Kalamalla (575 CE)**, Renati Cholas, Kadapa.
Telugu is the **4th** most spoken language (Census 2011), behind Hindi, Bengali and Marathi.

n84b1eb8c9e8.s: Which Telugu dialect region is regarded as the base of standard Telugu?
o: Coastal Andhra, particularly the Krishna-Godavari region
n84b1eb8c9e8.x: The Coastal dialect region, especially the Krishna-Godavari area, is regarded as the base of standard Telugu.
n84b1eb8c9e8.tq: Match the dialect region with its linguistic significance.
xs: The **Coastal (Krishna-Godavari)** region is the base of **standard Telugu** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Rayalaseema**, **Kalinga/Uttarandhra** and **Telangana** are the other dialect regions.
xa: **Kalinga/Uttarandhra** covers **Srikakulam-Vizianagaram-Visakhapatnam**.
Telugu = **"Italian of the East"**.
Earliest Telugu word **"Nagabu"** is in the **Amaravati** inscription.

nworld-geography-28-1.s: Which language family is the largest by speakers, accounting for approximately 46% of the world population?
nworld-geography-28-1.x: Indo-European is the largest family by speakers, about 46% of humanity. Niger-Congo has the most languages.
nworld-geography-28-1.tq: Discriminate speakers from number of languages.
n: The Indo-European language family is the largest language family by number of speakers. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Indo-European language family accounts for approximately 46% of the world population. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
xs: **Indo-European** is the largest family by speakers — about **46%** of the world — option **(3)**.
**Sino-Tibetan** is the **second largest** by speakers.
**Niger-Congo** is the largest by **number of languages**; **Dravidian** is mainly Indian.
xa: Indo-European languages: **English, Spanish, Hindi, Russian, Portuguese, French, German, Bengali, Persian**.
In India, Indo-Aryan is the largest family: about **78%** in 2011.
**Austronesian** is second by number of languages.

nworld-geography-28-2.s: Which of the following about language families is INCORRECT?
o: Sino-Tibetan spreads across China, Tibet, Myanmar and the Himalayas.
Dravidian languages are mainly found in North India.
Austronesian spreads across South-East Asia, the Pacific Islands and Madagascar.
Niger-Congo has the largest number of languages.
nworld-geography-28-2.x: Dravidian languages are mainly in South India, not North India; the other statements are correct.
n: The Sino-Tibetan language family is distributed across China. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Sino-Tibetan language family is distributed across Tibet. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Sino-Tibetan language family is distributed across Myanmar. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Sino-Tibetan language family is distributed across parts of Southeast Asia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Sino-Tibetan language family is distributed across the Himalayas. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Austronesian language family is distributed across Southeast Asia. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Austronesian language family is distributed across the Pacific Islands. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Austronesian language family is distributed across Madagascar. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Niger-Congo language family is the largest language family by number of languages. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Dravidian language family is mainly associated with India. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Dravidian language family is distributed across South India. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Dravidian language family is distributed across parts of Sri Lanka. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Dravidian language family is distributed across parts of Pakistan. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
xa: Dravidian languages: **Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam**.
Dravidian share in India: about **19.6%** (2011).
**Telugu** is **South-Central Dravidian**.

nworld-geography-28-9.s: The Bantu languages belong to which language family?
nworld-geography-28-9.x: The Niger-Congo family, spread across Sub-Saharan Africa, includes the Bantu languages.
n: The Niger-Congo language family is distributed across Sub-Saharan Africa. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
The Niger-Congo language family includes Bantu languages. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
xa: Niger-Congo is the **largest** family by **number of languages**.
Its languages: **Swahili, Yoruba, Zulu, Igbo**.
**Austronesian** is second by number of languages.

nworld-geography-28-14.s: Which language family is the second largest by number of languages, after Niger-Congo?
nworld-geography-28-14.x: Austronesian has the second-largest number of languages, after Niger-Congo. Sino-Tibetan ranks second by number of speakers, not languages.
nworld-geography-28-14.tq: Discriminate speakers from number of languages.
n: The Austronesian language family contains a large number of languages. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
xs: **Austronesian** is the second largest by number of languages, after Niger-Congo — option **(2)**.
**Sino-Tibetan** is second by **number of speakers**, not languages.
**Austro-Asiatic** has a **smaller number** of languages; **Afro-Asiatic** is noted for **significant numbers of speakers**.
xa: Austronesian spans **Southeast Asia**, the **Pacific Islands**, **Madagascar**.
**Trans-New Guinea** is **highly diverse**, with **many small languages**.
**Indo-European** is largest by speakers — about **46%**.

nworld-geography-29-4.s: Romani, the language originally spoken by the Gypsies (Roma), is related to which languages?
nworld-geography-29-4.x: Romani is related to the Indo-Aryan languages of India.
n: English is the official language of the largest number of countries. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
Gypsies, or Roma, originally spoke a language related to Indian Indo-Aryan languages. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
xa: **Mandarin Chinese** is the most spoken single language.
World ranking: **Hindi 2nd**, **Bengali 7th**, Punjabi 10th.
⚠ **English has never been in the Eighth Schedule**.

nworld-geography-29-5.s: In India, Austro-Asiatic (Austric) languages are mainly spoken in:
o: Central and East India and Meghalaya
nworld-geography-29-5.x: Austro-Asiatic is spoken in central-east India and Meghalaya; Dravidian in the south, Indo-European in the north, west and east, and Sino-Tibetan in the north-east and Himalayas.
n: The Indo-European (Indo-Aryan) language family is found mainly in North, West and East India. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
The Dravidian language family is found mainly in South India. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
The Austro-Asiatic (Austric) language family is found mainly in Central and East India and Meghalaya. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
The Sino-Tibetan (Tibeto-Burman) language family is found mainly in Northeast India and the Himalayas. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 46-47]
xa: Census 2011 shares: Indo-Aryan **78.05**, Dravidian **19.64**, Austro-Asiatic **1.11**, Tibeto-Burman **1.01**.
⚠ **Khasi** = Austro-Asiatic (Mon-Khmer); **Garo** = Sino-Tibetan (Bodo group).
⚠ **Dardi** is **Indo-Aryan**, not Sino-Tibetan (APPSC-G1 2024).

n5baa929f86b.s: Which one of the following is the correct present list of languages added by the 92nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003?
n5baa929f86b.x: The 92nd Amendment Act, 2003 added Bodo, Dogri, Maithili and Santhali to the Eighth Schedule.
n5baa929f86b.tq: Discriminate between the language groups added by the 71st and 92nd Amendments.
xs: The **92nd Amendment** (**2003**) added **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, Santhali** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali** = **71st** (**1992**); **Sindhi** = **21st** (**1967**); **Urdu** was original.
xa: ⚠ **21 – 71 – 92** = **Sindhi – Konkani/Manipuri/Nepali – Bodo/Dogri/Maithili/Santhali**.
Total now **22** (from **14**).
Last addition: **92nd Amendment** (**2003**).

n1103a539bbe.s: The 96th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011 changed the name of which language in the Eighth Schedule?
n1103a539bbe.x: The 96th Amendment changed the constitutional name of the language from Oriya to Odia. It did not add a new language to the Eighth Schedule.
n1103a539bbe.tq: Distinguish a change in nomenclature from the addition of a language.
xs: The **96th Amendment** (**2011**) changed "**Oriya**" to "**Odia**" — option **(3)** is correct.
It renamed a language already in the Schedule; it did not add one.
xa: Odia became **classical** in **2014**.
Odia was in the original **14** (**1950**).
Eighth Schedule: **14** originally, **22** now.

n679f7f86e82.s: Which community is associated with the demand for the inclusion of Gor Boli in the Eighth Schedule?
o: Koya community of the North-Eastern region
Banjara or Sugali community of Andhra Pradesh
n679f7f86e82.x: The Gor Boli demand is associated with Andhra Pradesh's Banjara, or Sugali, community.
n679f7f86e82.tq: Match the language demand with the concerned community and region.
xs: The **Gor Boli** demand concerns AP's **Banjara/Sugali** community — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Gor Boli (Lambadi)** is **Indo-Aryan**, spoken by **Banjaras** with **no native script**.
xa: It is written in **Telugu, Devanagari, Kannada** scripts.
The **Tribal Affairs Ministry** told Parliament the demand continues (**23 Jul 2026**).
Other pending demands: **Bhojpuri**, **Kokborok**, **Khasi and Garo**.

na144e4e9da5.s: According to the 1961 Census, how many mother tongues were listed?
na144e4e9da5.tq: Direct numerical recall of a census figure.
xs: Census **1961** listed **1,652 mother tongues** — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G1 **2024**, true statement).
xa: Census **2011**: about **19,500** raw → **1,369** mother tongues → **121** languages.
**Grierson** (**1903-1928**): **179** languages, **544** dialects.
**Ethnologue**: **455** living languages.

nd4880f796af.s: In Census 2011, the 1,369 rationalised mother tongues were grouped into how many languages?
nd4880f796af.x: The 1,369 mother tongues were grouped into 121 languages: 22 scheduled and 99 non-scheduled.
xa: ⚠ "**123** major languages" for **2011** is wrong.
A Census "language" needs **10,000+** speakers.
About **56** languages are counted as subsets of **Hindi**.

nd1211bd1469.s: Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India, conducted during 1903–1928, recorded:
nd1211bd1469.x: Grierson's Linguistic Survey of India recorded 179 languages and 544 dialects between 1903 and 1928.
nd1211bd1469.tq: Keep the language count and dialect count in their correct order.
xs: **Grierson**'s **Linguistic Survey of India** (**1903-1928**) recorded **179 languages, 544 dialects** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) swaps them; **121** and **1,369** are Census **2011** figures.
xa: **G.N. Devy**'s People's Linguistic Survey: **780+** languages.
Census **1961**: **1,652** mother tongues.
**Ethnologue**: **455**.

n2eb9391cfd6.s: The 22 languages in the Eighth Schedule cover approximately what percentage of the population's mother tongues?
n2eb9391cfd6.x: The 22 scheduled languages cover the mother tongues of approximately 96.71 percent of the population.
n2eb9391cfd6.tq: Distinguish the current coverage figure from the earlier 91 percent figure.
xs: The **22** scheduled languages cover **96.71 percent** (**96.71%**) of mother tongues — option **(3)** is correct.
Earlier, **18** languages covered **91%** (before **2003**).
xa: **99 languages** remain outside (**Jul 2025**).
Hindi alone = **43.6%**.
Census **2011**: **121** languages.

nde3efc8e81d.s: About how many Indian languages are listed in UNESCO's Atlas of Endangered Languages?
nde3efc8e81d.x: India has about 197 languages in UNESCO's Atlas, the highest for any country.
xa: **SPPEL (2013)** protects languages with **fewer than 10,000 speakers**; run by **CIIL, Mysuru**.
Threats: **globalisation + English**, **migration/nuclear families**, **no mother-tongue schooling**, **lack of scripts**.
**Kerala** published dictionaries of endangered **Mavila** and **Malaveduvan** (Kannur-Kasaragod).

n6ea4ab10149.s: In Census 2011, which language overtook Telugu for third place among India's languages?
n6ea4ab10149.x: Telugu was third in 2001, but Marathi overtook it in 2011, pushing Telugu to fourth.
xa: Marathi **6.9%**; Telugu **6.7%**.
Telugu is **classical** since **2008**.
**Telugu Language Day** = **29 August**.

n4f927cf57d5.s: According to Census 2011, about what percentage of Indians were bilingual?
n4f927cf57d5.x: About 26% were bilingual and only about 7% trilingual in Census 2011.
xa: The three-language formula remains a live dispute (**Jun 2026**).
**Art. 350A**: instruction in the **mother tongue at primary stage**.
Critics say the Census **understates English bilingualism**.

n54f2c5d9cff.s: For Census language classification, a language generally needs at least how many speakers?
n54f2c5d9cff.x: The Census counts a language when it has 10,000 or more speakers.
xa: Critics say the **10,000-speaker cutoff** helps Hindi "erase" **Maithili, Braj, Awadhi**.
**SPPEL** covers languages with **fewer than 10,000** speakers.
**121** Census languages in **2011**.

n24d024e8e2b.s: Under the Constitution, the official language(s) of a State are adopted by the:
n24d024e8e2b.x: Each State may choose its own official language(s) through its Legislature; a State is not required to adopt Hindi as its only official language.
xa: AP: **Telugu and Urdu** (**2019** PYQ).
Meghalaya: **English** + **Khasi and Garo**.
**Official Languages Act, 1963** kept English after **1965**.

n5a272683b46.s: Under the Munshi-Ayyangar formula (adopted 14 September 1949), Hindi in Devanagari was to become the Union's official language after a transition of:
n5a272683b46.x: The formula provided a 15-year transition; its adoption date, 14 September, is observed as Hindi Diwas.
xa: The formula recognised **14** languages in the Eighth Schedule.
**Official Languages Act, 1963** kept English in use after **1965**.
**Art. 343**: official language of the Union — Hindi in Devanagari.
**Art. 351**: Union's duty to develop Hindi.

n219088ab2c8.s: The Sitakant Mohapatra Committee on inclusion of languages in the Eighth Schedule was constituted in:
n219088ab2c8.x: The Sitakant Mohapatra Committee was constituted in 2003 and the Ashok Pahwa Committee in 1996; there are no fixed criteria for inclusion.
xa: Pending demands: **Bhojpuri, Kokborok, Khasi and Garo, Gor Boli**.
**99 languages** remain outside (**Jul 2025**).
Benefits: Sahitya Akademi recognition, **Art. 394A** translation, UPSC option.

n16fde836ea7.s: Which language was the first to be recognised as a classical language of India?
n16fde836ea7.x: Tamil was recognised in 2004, Sanskrit in 2005, Kannada in 2008 and Odia in 2014.
xa: **Telugu** was recognised in **2008** together with Kannada; **Malayalam** in **2013**.
India now has **11** classical languages; **Pali and Prakrit** are the only ones **outside** the Eighth Schedule.
⚠ Trap: "Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and Odia were all recognised in 2008" is **wrong**.
Classical status is granted by the **Government of India**.

n6274fe13b99.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the revised (2024) criteria for classical languages?
o: Knowledge texts were added to the scope of eligible literature
The requirement that the tradition be 'original, not borrowed' was retained
Both prose and poetry were recognised
Epigraphic evidence was added as a consideration
n6274fe13b99.x: The 2024 revision dropped the 'original, not borrowed' requirement.
xa: Core criterion: **high antiquity** — early texts **1,500-2,000 years** old.
Another criterion: a **rich ancient literary tradition** regarded as heritage.
India has **11** classical languages; status is granted by the **Government of India**.
**Granth Kutir** at Rashtrapati Bhavan holds books in all **11** classical languages.

n93dfa5feaf4.s: The status of a classical language is granted by:
n93dfa5feaf4.x: Classical-language status is granted by the Government of India, not by an individual State Government or an academic institution.
n93dfa5feaf4.tq: Apply the ‘who grants or authorises this?’ authority test.
xs: Classical-language status is granted by the **Government of India** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is not a power of a **State Government**, the **UGC** or the **Sahitya Akademi**.
⚠ Trap in the notes: "the **Government of Uttar Pradesh** granted it" is **wrong**.
xa: **Tamil** was the first classical language (**2004**); **Sanskrit** followed in **2005**.
**Pali and Prakrit** are the only classical languages outside the **Eighth Schedule**.

n6c5a1cfea17.s: How many classical languages does India have?
n6c5a1cfea17.x: India has 11 classical languages; Pali and Prakrit are the only ones outside the Eighth Schedule.
xa: **Telugu** became classical in **2008** along with **Kannada**.
**Tamil** (**2004**) was the first; **Sanskrit** (**2005**) the second.
**Granth Kutir** at Rashtrapati Bhavan holds about **2,300 books and 50 manuscripts** in all 11 classical languages.

nc6247b1883a.s: The Scheme for Protection and Preservation of Endangered Languages (SPPEL) is run by:
o: Central Institute of Indian Languages, Mysuru
nc6247b1883a.x: SPPEL, a Union Education Ministry scheme of 2013, is run by CIIL, Mysuru and covers languages with fewer than 10,000 speakers.
xa: India has about **197** endangered languages in the UNESCO Atlas — the most of any country.
The Census also treats **10,000+ speakers** as the cut-off for counting a "language".
**CESCT**, a wing of **CIIL Mysuru**, was moved to **Nellore**.

ne03883fab21.s: Telugu was recognised as a classical language in:
ne03883fab21.x: Telugu, a Dravidian language and one of the 22 scheduled languages, became a classical language in 2008.
xa: Telugu slipped from **3rd (2001)** to **4th (2011)** among India's most spoken languages, overtaken by **Marathi**.
**Telugu Language Day** is **29 August** (Gidugu's birth anniversary).
**CESCT**, a wing of **CIIL Mysuru**, was moved to **Nellore**.
⚠ An older table puts AP under "**Central Dravidian**".

n05aacf07049.s: In which year was Sindhi added to the Eighth Schedule?
n05aacf07049.x: Sindhi was added in 1967 (21st Amendment); the Telugu Language Act was 1966, Tamil became the first classical language in 2004 and Telugu in 2008.
xa: Sindhi was the **first addition** to the Schedule; the **last** addition was the **92nd Amendment (2003)**.
**Sanskrit** became classical in **2005**; **Kannada** alongside Telugu in **2008**.
**71st Amendment (1992)** added **Konkani, Manipuri, Nepali**.

nec418b9c373.s: Which Article of the Constitution provides for instruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage?
nec418b9c373.x: Article 350A deals with mother-tongue instruction at the primary stage; Article 350 covers representations for redress in any language.
xa: **350B** = Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities (**1957**, HQ **Allahabad**).
**351** = Union's duty to develop Hindi.
**344** = Official Language Commission.

n269a3216909.s: The Eighth Schedule is constitutionally linked with which of the following Articles?
n269a3216909.x: The Eighth Schedule is linked to Article 344(1), concerning the Commission and Committee on official language, and Article 351, concerning promotion of Hindi.
n269a3216909.tq: Use the constitutional-provision trap by separating linked Articles from other language provisions.
xs: The Eighth Schedule is linked with **Articles 344(1) and 351** — option **(1)** is correct.
**344** = Official Language Commission; **351** = Union's duty to develop Hindi drawing on **Eighth Schedule languages**.
xa: **Art. 394A**: authoritative translation — a benefit of inclusion.
**Art. 343**: Union language; **Art. 345**: State language.
Eighth Schedule: **14** originally, **22** now.

n20b2caf0143.s: The Official Languages Act, 1963 is significant because it:
o: Required every State to adopt the three-language formula
Continued the use of English alongside Hindi after 1965
Removed Hindi from the Union’s official-language framework
Made Sanskrit the sole official language of the Union
n20b2caf0143.x: The Official Languages Act, 1963 continued English in use alongside Hindi after 1965.
n20b2caf0143.tq: Identify the legal effect of the Act rather than confusing it with the original constitutional transition plan.
xs: The **Official Languages Act, 1963** kept **English** in use **after 1965**, alongside **Hindi** — option **(2)** is correct.
The three-language formula came from the **NPE 1968**, not this Act.
xa: **Munshi-Ayyangar** formula gave a **15-year** transition.
Union: **Hindi + English**.
**Art. 344**: Official Language Commission.

n188f44cad12.s: The Ladakh Official Languages Regulation, 2025 lists which languages?
o: English, Urdu, Bhoti and Purgi only
English, Hindi, Urdu, Bhoti and Purgi
n188f44cad12.x: The Ladakh Official Languages Regulation, 2025 lists English, Hindi, Urdu, Bhoti and Purgi.
xa: **Kerala's Malayalam Language Bill 2025** lets Tamil/Kannada minorities in notified areas correspond in their own languages.
**Sikkim** has Nepali, Sikkimese (Bhutia), Lepcha and English.
**Art. 345**: State Legislature adopts the State official language(s).

nc3bf87e9cd2.s: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language (Amendment) Act, 2022 is associated with which development?
o: Making Urdu the second official language statewide
Recognition of Telugu as a classical language
Creation of the Telugu Language Commission
Moving the Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu to Nellore
nc3bf87e9cd2.x: The 2022 amendment made Urdu the second official language of Andhra Pradesh throughout the State.
nc3bf87e9cd2.tq: Separate the original enactment from the later amendment and its specific effect.
xs: The **AP Official Languages (Amendment) Act, 2022** extended **Urdu's** status as **second official language** to the **whole state** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Telugu's classical status** came in **2008**, and the move of **CESCT to Nellore** is a separate step.
xa: The CM **confirmed** Urdu as the second official language (17 Mar 2026).
**AP State Urdu Academy**: free computer training in **36 centres** (2024-25).
**P. Trivikram Rao** heads the **Mandali Venkata Krishna Rao Official Language Commission**.

nf0aec492eb4.s: The Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu, a wing of CIIL, was moved to:
nf0aec492eb4.x: The Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Telugu was moved to Nellore.
nf0aec492eb4.tq: Test the headquarters or relocation site directly.
xs: **CESCT** was moved to **Nellore** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is a wing of **CIIL Mysuru** for studies in **Classical Telugu**.
xa: Telugu has been a **classical language since 2008**.
AP made **Telugu Mahotsavam** an **annual event** (announced at **Undavalli Caves**).
First fully Telugu inscription: **Kalamalla (575 CE, Renati Cholas, Kadapa)**.

nef323f1d124.s: Telugu Language Day (29 August) marks the birth anniversary of:
nef323f1d124.x: 29 August is Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy's birth anniversary; he led the Vyavaharika (colloquial) Telugu movement and designed a script for Savara.
xa: **Savara (Sora)** is an **Austro-Asiatic, Munda** language of the Srikakulam-Vizianagaram hills.
Telugu became a **classical language in 2008**; **CESCT** moved to **Nellore**.
First fully Telugu inscription: **Kalamalla (575 CE, Renati Cholas, Kadapa)**.
Earliest Telugu word: **"Nagabu"** (Amaravati inscription).

n6340280e493.s: The Kalamalla inscription (575 CE), regarded as the first fully Telugu inscription, was issued by the:
n6340280e493.x: The Kalamalla inscription of 575 CE, in Kadapa, was issued by the Renati Cholas; the earliest Telugu word 'Nagabu' is in the Amaravati inscription.
xa: Telugu is called the **"Italian of the East"**.
The **Coastal (Krishna-Godavari)** dialect is the base of **standard Telugu**.
Telugu has been **classical since 2008**.

n0a76766cd4d.s: Deccani Urdu developed during the rule of the Qutb Shahis in a context where:
o: Telugu was the official language and Persian was spoken by the people
Urdu was the official language and Sanskrit was spoken by the people
Persian was the official language and Telugu was spoken by the people
Kannada was the official language and Marathi was spoken by the people
n0a76766cd4d.x: Deccani Urdu dates to the Qutb Shahi period, when Persian was the official language and Telugu was spoken by the people.
n0a76766cd4d.tq: Test the reversed relationship between official and popular languages.
xs: Under the Qutb Shahis **Persian** was the official language and **Telugu** was spoken by the people — so option **(3)** is correct.
Option 1 reverses the roles of Telugu and Persian.
xa: Today **Urdu** is AP's **second official language**, statewide since the **2022** amendment Act.
**AP State Urdu Academy** gives free computer training in **36 centres**.
AP's official languages: **Telugu and Urdu** (2019 PYQ answer).

nb52e46055ce.s: The Koya tribal language of Andhra Pradesh is mainly spoken in the:
nb52e46055ce.x: Koya is spoken in the Godavari agency; Savara in the Srikakulam-Vizianagaram hills, Kui/Kuvi on the AP-Odisha border hills and Gadaba in the Visakhapatnam-Vizianagaram agency.
xa: ⚠ **Koya** and **Kui** = **Dravidian**; **Savara** = **Munda**.
**Gadaba** has **Munda (Gutob)** and **Dravidian (Ollari)** varieties.
Kui/Kuvi is spoken by the **Kandhas of Odisha** (Dongria Kondh).

ncdb74bc070d.s: Which law made Telugu the official language of Andhra Pradesh?
o: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966
The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1956
ncdb74bc070d.x: The Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966 made Telugu the official language of the State.
ncdb74bc070d.tq: Match the language policy with its exact Act and year.
xs: The **Andhra Pradesh Official Language Act, 1966** made Telugu the official language — so option **(1)** is correct.
The notes link Telugu to the **1966 Act**; **2008** is the year Telugu became **classical**, not of any Act.
xa: **Urdu** is the **second official language**; the **AP Official Languages (Amendment) Act, 2022** extended it to the whole state.
The Union's **Official Languages Act, 1963** kept English in use after 1965 alongside Hindi.
**CESCT** (Classical Telugu) is at **Nellore**.

n59ef85e342f.s: Ol Chiki, the script of Santhali, was created in 1925 by:
n59ef85e342f.x: Raghunath Murmu created Ol Chiki in 1925; Santhali entered the Eighth Schedule through the 92nd Amendment, 2003.
xa: The **92nd Amendment** also added **Bodo, Dogri, Maithili**.
Santhali is **Austroasiatic** (Munda).
The President released a **digital Constitution** in Santhali (**2026**).

nfedfb7d71da.s: Which of the following languages is NOT included in the Eighth Schedule?
nfedfb7d71da.x: Bhojpuri, like Kokborok and Gor Boli (Lambadi), is not in the Eighth Schedule; Konkani and Nepali were added by the 71st Amendment.
xa: PYQ: **Bhojpuri is NOT** in the Schedule, but **Nepali, Dogri, Bodo** are (UPPSC **2025**).
**English** has never been in the Schedule.
**Khasi and Garo** are also pending.

n5c595f3fd96.s: With regard to the Eighth Schedule, English has:
n5c595f3fd96.x: English has never been included in the Eighth Schedule.
xa: "**NOT** in the Eighth Schedule" PYQs: **Bhojpuri**, **English**.
**Official Languages Act, 1963** kept English after **1965**.
Meghalaya and **Nagaland** use **English** officially.

ne41bc29354d.s: A language community seeks authoritative translation of the Constitution under Article 394A, interpretation in Parliament and central development funds. These are principally associated with:
o: Recognition as a non-scheduled Census language
Classification as a dialect under Hindi
Recognition by the People's Linguistic Survey alone
ne41bc29354d.x: Interpretation in Parliament, authoritative constitutional translation under Article 394A and central development funds are stated benefits associated with Eighth Schedule inclusion.
ne41bc29354d.tq: Apply the listed benefits to identify the relevant constitutional status.
xs: **Art. 394A** translation, Parliament interpretation and central funds come with **inclusion in the Eighth Schedule** — option **(3)** is correct.
Non-scheduled Census languages and PLSI listing give no such benefits.
xa: Other benefits: **Sahitya Akademi** recognition, option in the **UPSC** Indian-language paper.
**No fixed criteria** for inclusion.
**22** scheduled languages now.

na4affb59edf.s: Which State published a comprehensive bilingual tribal dictionary series for preserving vanishing tribal languages?
na4affb59edf.x: Odisha published a comprehensive bilingual tribal dictionary series for preserving vanishing tribal languages.
na4affb59edf.tq: Use the location-based trap by matching the preservation measure with the correct State.
xs: **Odisha** published a comprehensive **bilingual tribal dictionary** series — so option **(4)** is correct (APPSC 2019 PYQ).
Odisha also runs multilingual education in **21 tribal languages** in **1,483 schools** across 17 districts.
**Kerala** produced dictionaries only of **Mavila** and **Malaveduvan**.
xa: **Gidugu Venkata Ramamurthy** prepared **Savara-Telugu dictionaries** — the **AP precedent**.
**Kui/Kuvi** is spoken by the **Kandhas of Odisha** (Dongria Kondh).
**SPPEL (2013)** is run by **CIIL, Mysuru**.

n747fdd0d7c2.s: Which of the following is NOT identified as a threat to endangered tribal languages?
o: Availability of scripts for tribal languages
Dominance of English on the internet
Absence of schooling in the mother tongue
n747fdd0d7c2.x: Availability of scripts is not a threat; rather, the lack of scripts for tribal languages is identified as a threat. Migration, nuclear families, English dominance and lack of mother-tongue schooling are threats.
n747fdd0d7c2.tq: Find the single reversed or negative formulation among otherwise valid threats.
xs: **Availability of scripts** is not a threat — the threat is the **lack of scripts** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Listed threats: **globalisation + English** (incl. **internet dominance of English**), **migration, nuclear families**, **no mother-tongue schooling**.
xa: **SPPEL (2013)** protects languages with fewer than **10,000** speakers.
**Adi Vaani** (2026): India's first **AI translation platform** for tribal languages.
The Centre is pushing **Devanagari** for NE tribal languages **without scripts**; Tripura's CPI(M) opposed it.

ndd6b3060340.s: Which script is the Centre encouraging for North-Eastern tribal languages that have no script of their own?
ndd6b3060340.x: The Centre has been pushing Devanagari for script-less North-Eastern tribal languages; Tripura's CPI(M) opposed the move.
xa: **Lack of scripts** is listed as a threat to tribal languages.
The Constitution was released in **Sindhi** (Devanagari + Persian scripts) and digital **Santhali (Ol Chiki)**, **Kokborok**, **Kashmiri** editions.
**Kokborok** is still a **pending** Eighth Schedule demand.

nworld-geography-28-8.s: Which language family is the second largest by number of speakers?
nworld-geography-28-8.x: Sino-Tibetan is the second largest family by speakers; Cantonese, Tibetan and Burmese are among its major languages.
n: The Sino-Tibetan language family is the second largest language family by number of speakers. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
Cantonese is a major Sino-Tibetan language. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
Tibetan is a major Sino-Tibetan language. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
Burmese is a major Sino-Tibetan language. [World Geography · ROCKET SHEET #28 · pp 45-46]
xa: Sino-Tibetan spans **China, Tibet, Myanmar**, parts of **Southeast Asia**, the **Himalayas**.
**Mandarin Chinese** is the **most spoken single language**.
In India, **Sino-Tibetan (Tibeto-Burman)**: **Bodo, Manipuri, Naga languages, Ladakhi**.

n56e3ca6d910.s: A person who leaves a place because of persecution based on race, religion, nationality or membership of a social or political group, and cannot return safely, is called a:
n56e3ca6d910.x: A refugee is forced to leave and cannot return because of fear of persecution based on race, religion, nationality or social or political group.
n56e3ca6d910.tq: Identify the precise legal-social definition from its cause and inability to return.
xs: Such a person is a **Refugee** — so option **(4)** is correct.
A refugee is **forced to leave** and **cannot return** for fear of **persecution** (race, religion, nationality, social/political group).
A **voluntary migrant** weighs push and pull factors; a **return migrant** goes back once the cause is over.
xa: Refugees are a part of **international** migration with legal and illegal immigrants.
**World Migration Report 2026** (**IOM**): forced displacement of more than **120 million**.
Disasters caused **65.8 million** internal displacements.

n76bb82f6be7.s: Which one of the following is the largest stream of internal migration in India?
n76bb82f6be7.x: Rural-to-rural migration is the largest stream of internal migration in India. It was also the stream contributing most to migration in 2011.
n76bb82f6be7.tq: Use the direct largest-share recall method and distinguish the dominant stream from urbanisation-linked migration.
xs: **Rural to rural** is the **largest stream** in India — so option **(1)** is correct.
It contributed most in **2011** (CGPSC 2018 PYQ) and is **female-dominated because of marriage**.
**Urban to rural** is the **smallest**; **rural to urban** is male, job-led.
xa: ⚠ UPPSC 2017: "rural-urban is the largest share" = **false**; "rural-rural is mainly female (marriage)" = **true**.
Historically rural-rural moved from **low- to higher-potential** farm areas.
**Urban to urban** is typical of **developed** countries (**USA, Japan**).

na4a57c4c3b8.s: Rural-to-urban migration in India is dominated by:
na4a57c4c3b8.x: Rural-to-urban migration is dominated by males moving for employment and is a key force driving urbanisation.
xa: BPSC 2024: causes = **high labour demand in cities**, **unbalanced rural-urban development**, few rural jobs.
About **26%** of the population is aged 10-24 — job search drives rural-urban migration.
Migration is the main component of the **rural vs urban growth difference**.

n464a2b257c6.s: India's record remittances of US$135 billion in FY 2024–25 increasingly came from:
n464a2b257c6.x: Remittances in FY 2024–25 came increasingly from skilled professionals in developed countries rather than mainly from West Asia.
xa: In **2024**, India received **USD 137 billion** — top recipient (WMR 2026).
**India-US** corridor (**6th**) is mostly **skilled workers + students**.
Global remittances: **USD 905 billion** (2024).

n0f83d89b69a.s: The Pre-Departure Orientation Training (PDOT), launched in January 2018, is run by which ministry and for whom?
o: Ministry of External Affairs, for emigrants going to ECR countries
Ministry of Labour and Employment, for inter-State migrant workers
Ministry of Education, for Indian students going abroad
Ministry of Home Affairs, for refugees entering India
n0f83d89b69a.x: PDOT is the MEA's programme (Jan 2018) for emigrant workers going to Emigration Check Required (ECR) countries; about 1,72,220 were trained by 31 Dec 2024. It is not a Labour Ministry scheme for inter-State migrants, not meant for students, and has nothing to do with refugees coming into India.
xs: **PDOT** is run by the **Ministry of External Affairs** for **emigrants to ECR countries** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It began in **Jan 2018**; **1,72,220** emigrant workers were trained by 31 Dec 2024.
It is not a Labour Ministry scheme for inter-state migrants, nor for students or refugees.
xa: **e-Shram** (**2021**) is the portal for **unorganised workers**.
**APNRT** is AP's **diaspora agency**; it ran a help desk for Telugus stranded in the Gulf.
**Konaseema** sent about **15,000** workers to the **GCC** by Dec 2025.

n9df73e56d98.s: Migration is regarded as the main component of the difference between rural and urban growth because:
o: natural increase differs little between rural and urban areas
all rural migrants move only to metropolitan cities
natural increase is absent in rural areas but very high in urban areas
urban areas have no migration-related population increase
n9df73e56d98.x: Migration is the main component of the rural-urban growth difference because natural increase differs little between rural and urban areas.
n9df73e56d98.tq: Link the cause with the demographic comparison instead of choosing absolute statements about rural or urban growth.
xs: **Natural increase differs little** between rural and urban areas — so option **(1)** is correct.
Hence **migration** is the main component of the **rural vs urban growth difference**.
xa: **Rural to urban** migration **drives urbanisation**.
Population **grows at the destination** and **falls at the source**.
Workers move from **high-fertility** to ageing **low-fertility** states.

n63f4e911406.s: Seasonal labour migration from Andhra Pradesh is mainly from:
o: The urban districts of coastal Andhra
n63f4e911406.x: Seasonal labour leaves drought-prone Rayalaseema and the north-coastal districts of Andhra Pradesh.
xa: **Srikakulam fishermen** migrate to the **Gujarat coast**.
Rayalaseema + north coastal AP see **distress migration** to Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai.
The CM said the **Bhogapuram airport** would end migration from **Uttarandhra**.

ne49aff3b413.s: Srikakulam fishermen are specifically reported to migrate seasonally to which destination?
ne49aff3b413.x: Srikakulam fishermen migrate seasonally to the Gujarat coast.
ne49aff3b413.tq: Test the migrant-origin and destination pair directly; the location is the key discriminator.
xs: **Srikakulam fishermen** migrate to the **Gujarat coast** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Srikakulam lies in the **Kalinga/Uttarandhra** north-coastal region.
xa: **Seasonal labour** also leaves **drought-prone Rayalaseema** and north-coastal districts.
**Rayalaseema** (Anantapur, Kadapa, Chittoor) sends Gulf domestic and unskilled workers.
About **25 lakh** AP migrant workers were reportedly affected by the **SIR** of electoral rolls.

nb4c96095161.s: The Chief Minister stated that migration from Uttarandhra would 'become a thing of the past' with the construction of which infrastructure project?
nb4c96095161.x: The statement linked the expected reduction in migration from Uttarandhra to the new Bhogapuram airport.
nb4c96095161.tq: Match the policy statement with the specific infrastructure project named in it.
xs: The CM linked it to the new **Bhogapuram airport** — so option **(2)** is correct.
He said migration from **Uttarandhra** "will become a thing of the past" (2 Aug 2026).
xa: **Uttarandhra/north coastal AP** sees **distress** and **seasonal** migration.
**Srikakulam fishermen** go to the **Gujarat coast**.
New **industrial nodes** aim to slow distress migration to **Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai**.

n456c2f9a8e1.s: PLFS/NSO treat a place as the Usual Place of Residence if a person has lived there for at least:
n456c2f9a8e1.x: The PLFS/NSO rule is at least 6 months; the Census uses both place of birth (lifetime migrants) and place of last residence.
xa: Census 2011: **455.8 million** migrants by **place of last residence** (about **37.6%**).
The **MoSPI** survey also uses the **6-month** UPR rule.
**Census 2027** will also record migration.

ndd2191a175f.s: Intra-state rural-to-rural migration in India is dominated by:
ndd2191a175f.x: Women dominate intra-state rural-to-rural movements linked to marriage, while men dominate inter-state rural-to-urban movements for work.
xa: PLFS 2020-21: about **86.8%** of female migrants moved for **marriage**.
About **22.8%** of male migrants moved for **employment**.
JPSC 2023: inter-state **female** migrants (2011) – key begins with **Urban-to-Urban**.

n668a63d17a4.s: According to PLFS 2020-21, India's overall migration rate was:
n668a63d17a4.x: The overall rate was 28.9%; the female rate was 47.9% and the male rate 10.7%.
xa: About **22.8%** of male migrants moved for **employment**.
**Economic Survey 2025-26**: **26.8%** of rural Indians were migrants in 2020-21.
⚠ Women → **marriage**; men → **employment**.

n0078eec6905.s: Which of the following can encourage rural-to-urban migration?
n0078eec6905.x: Rural-urban migration is encouraged by high urban labour demand, unbalanced rural-urban development and lack of rural employment.
xa: Rural-to-urban migration is **male**-dominated, for **employment**, and **drives urbanisation**.
About **26%** of the population is aged 10-24; job search drives rural-urban moves.
Distress migration from **Rayalaseema** and north coastal AP goes to **Hyderabad, Bengaluru, Chennai**.

n4101360c58c.s: The Nationwide Migration Survey conducted by MoSPI for July 2026–June 2027 is significant because it is:
o: The first international migration survey since 1951
The first full migration survey since 2007–08
The first survey limited to seasonal agricultural labour
The first Census survey based only on place of birth
n4101360c58c.x: The MoSPI Nationwide Migration Survey for July 2026–June 2027 is the first full migration survey since 2007–08.
n4101360c58c.tq: Link the survey period with its historical significance and avoid confusing it with Census methods.
xs: It is the **first full migration survey since 2007-08** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The **MoSPI Nationwide Migration Survey (NSO)** runs **July 2026-June 2027**.
xa: It redefines **short-term migration** as **15 days-6 months** (earlier 1-6 months).
A **migrant** = **Usual Place of Residence** differs; **6-month** rule.
**Census 2027** will also record migration.

n42238513931.s: Under the revised MoSPI definition, short-term migration covers a stay away of:
n42238513931.x: The revised definition covers 15 days–6 months; the earlier one covered 1–6 months.
xa: The **MoSPI** survey runs **July 2026-June 2027**, first full survey since **2007-08**.
Migrant = **Usual Place of Residence** differs, using the **6-month** rule.
**PLFS 2020-21** overall migration rate: **28.9%**.

n604d1b0256d.s: By place of last residence, about what share of India's population were migrants in Census 2011?
n604d1b0256d.x: 455.8 million people, about 37.6% of the population, were migrants by place of last residence; 141.2 million had moved during 2001-11.
xa: **Rural to rural** was the **largest stream** in **2011**.
**PLFS 2020-21**: overall migration rate **28.9%**.
**Census 2027** will give fresh migration data.

n127a317b6bc.s: Which one of the following groups consists of major in-migration (destination) States of India?
o: Delhi, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala
Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh
Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal and Punjab
n127a317b6bc.x: The listed leading in-migration destinations include Delhi, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala.
n127a317b6bc.tq: Recall the destination-state cluster and avoid mixing it with the source-state cluster.
xs: **Delhi, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh and Kerala** are destination states — so option **(1)** is correct.
**UP, Bihar, Odisha, Rajasthan, MP, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, West Bengal** are **source** states.
xa: **Delhi** and **Maharashtra** lead in-migration; **Haryana, Karnataka, Punjab** are also destinations.
**UP** and **Bihar** lead out-migration.
World: highest migrant share – **UAE**; largest number – **Europe**; highest percentage – **Oceania**.
n127a317b6bc.fixed: stem oddly tied to 'the migration data'

n538e991ef7d.s: One Nation One Ration Card (ONORC) is operational in how many States/UTs?
n538e991ef7d.x: ONORC, giving NFSA ration portability, works in all 36 States/UTs.
xa: Aadhaar seeding is **99.9%**.
**e-Shram portal** (**2021**) is a **"One-Stop-Solution"** for unorganised workers.
Migrant portability (**ONORC, EPF**) remains **patchy**.

nf1f7135b72b.s: The e-Shram portal is available in 22 languages through:
nf1f7135b72b.x: e-Shram's 22-language support comes through BHASHINI; it is a One-Stop-Solution linked to 15 central schemes.
xa: e-Shram has a **gig and platform worker** module.
**ONORC** works in **all 36 States/UTs** with **99.9%** Aadhaar seeding.
**PDOT** (MEA, **Jan 2018**) trained **1,72,220** emigrant workers by 31 Dec 2024.

n4f7639af1eb.s: The Global Compact for Safe, Orderly and Regular Migration was endorsed by the:
n4f7639af1eb.x: The UN General Assembly endorsed the Compact; it is non-binding and covers international migration, not internal displacement.
xa: Adopted at **Marrakech in December 2018**.
**Not all** UN members adopted it — the **US** stayed out.
Exam traps test **"all countries"**, **"legally binding"** and **"internal migration"** — all false.

n006bc871817.s: Which one of the following is NOT a form of forced migration identified in the classification of migration by will?
n006bc871817.x: Weighing push and pull factors is associated with voluntary migration. Persecution, development-induced displacement and exploitation are causes of forced migration.
n006bc871817.tq: Find the one item belonging to voluntary rather than forced migration.
xs: **Weighing push and pull factors** is **voluntary**, not forced, migration — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Forced** migration = **persecution**, **development-induced displacement**, **exploitation**.
xa: Push factors at origin: **low farm productivity**, **monsoon failure**, drought, rural unemployment.
Pull factors at destination: **jobs, higher wages**, education, health care.
**Push-pull theory** – **Everett S. Lee** ("A Theory of Migration", **1966**).

n19c59602b3f.s: Who propounded the Push-Pull Theory of migration in “A Theory of Migration” published in 1966?
n19c59602b3f.x: Everett S. Lee propounded the push-pull theory in his 1966 work, “A Theory of Migration”.
n19c59602b3f.tq: Link the theory, title and year with its proponent.
xs: **Everett S. Lee** gave the **push-pull theory** in "A Theory of Migration" (**1966**) — so option **(1)** is correct.
**E.G. Ravenstein** gave the **laws of migration** (**1885, 1889**).

n8aeb4293f38.s: As a demographic consequence of out-migration, the source area is often left with:

an ageing population and more men
a younger population and more women
an ageing population and more women

nc6dd0be0e90.s: The expression “son of the soil” hostility is associated with:

Transfer of skills from destination to source
Cultural exchange between migrants and local people

n41d170ff5d9.s: The Inter-State Migrant Workmen (RECS) Act, 1979 has been subsumed in the:

Portability of PDS and social security across States
