n6c2193d98c2.s: Gross primary productivity minus producer respiration is called:
n6c2193d98c2.x: NPP is GPP minus producer respiration; secondary productivity is new organic matter formed by consumers.
xa: **Tropical rainforests** have the highest NPP on land.
**Deserts** and **open ocean** have the lowest NPP per unit area.

n249e5dc4846.s: Which one of the following ecosystems is generally the most productive in terms of net primary productivity per unit area?
n249e5dc4846.x: Tropical rainforests are the standard highest-productivity ecosystem among the alternatives. Estuaries, coral reefs and swamps also have high productivity.
n249e5dc4846.tq: Identify the standard high-yield answer while distinguishing productivity per unit area from total output.
xs: **Tropical rainforests** are the most productive (**NPP**) on land — option **(4)** (**PYQ 2025**).
**Deserts** and the **open ocean** are the lowest; tundra is a simple, low-stability system.
xa: Also high: **estuaries, coral reefs, swamps**.
Rainforests have the **highest species richness** on land.

n675c94dfb73.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about oceanic productivity?
o: Open oceans have low net primary productivity per unit area
The total output of oceans is large because of their extensive area
Tropical rainforests are more productive per unit area than open oceans
Oceans are the most productive ecosystems per unit area
n675c94dfb73.x: Per unit area, open oceans are low in productivity; tropical rainforests and some aquatic ecosystems are more productive.
xa: High-NPP aquatic systems: **estuaries, coral reefs, swamps**.
**Deserts** share the lowest NPP with the open ocean.

ncfb3278b97b.s: Lichens are commonly used as indicators of
ncfb3278b97b.x: Lichens can indicate environmental health and are particularly used as indicators of sulphur dioxide pollution.
ncfb3278b97b.tq: Match the indicator organism with the environmental condition it signals.
xs: **Lichens** indicate **SO2 (sulphur dioxide) pollution** — option **(1)**.
They are **indicator species**, signalling environmental health.
xa: **Amphibians** are another indicator group.
A lichen itself is **mutualism** (alga + fungus).

na9393d07a54.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem stability?
o: Resistance is the ability of an ecosystem to recover after a disturbance
Returning to the earlier condition after a forest fire shows resilience
Homeostasis is self-regulation through feedback up to a limit
Resistance is the ability to withstand a disturbance without change
na9393d07a54.x: Recovering after a disturbance is resilience; resistance is withstanding it without change.
xa: ⚠ Resistance = **withstand**; resilience = **recover** (APPSC **2024**).
**Stability** rises with **diversity** and web complexity: **rainforest** and **coral reef** are more stable than **tundra**, desert or monoculture.
A **food web** is a network of interlinked food chains; more alternative pathways make an ecosystem more **stable**.

nfdd8c20df76.s: Which one of the following ecosystems is generally the most stable?
nfdd8c20df76.x: Diverse and complex systems such as rainforests are generally more stable than simple systems such as tundra, deserts and monoculture croplands.
nfdd8c20df76.tq: Use diversity and structural complexity as the basis of comparison.
xs: The **rainforest** is the most stable — diverse, complex systems are more stable — option **(2)**.
**Tundra, desert, monoculture cropland** are simple and less stable.
xa: **Coral reefs** are also diverse and stable.
Rainforests have the **highest species richness** on land.

nc03cf70411f.s: Which forest ecosystem generally has the highest species richness on land?
nc03cf70411f.x: Tropical rainforests have the highest species richness among terrestrial ecosystems.
nc03cf70411f.tq: Use the characteristic feature directly associated with the ecosystem type.
xs: **Tropical rainforest** has the **highest species richness on land** — option **(2)**.
**Taiga** has slow decay and acidic soil; temperate deciduous forests are less rich.
xa: Rainforests also lead in **NPP** on land.
Coral reefs match rainforests in species richness.

nfdc552dc15b.s: Which of the following is NOT a climate-resilience function of mangroves?
o: Increasing the salinity of all freshwater lakes
nfdc552dc15b.x: Mangroves buffer cyclones and storm surges, reduce coastal erosion and store carbon. They do not increase the salinity of all freshwater lakes.
nfdc552dc15b.tq: Find the option that falls outside the stated group of ecosystem services.
xs: Mangroves do **not increase the salinity of freshwater lakes** — option **(4)**.
Their real roles: **buffer cyclones and storm surges**, **protect coasts from erosion**, **store carbon**.
xa: Mangroves are a **marine-terrestrial** ecotone.
AP has India's **second-largest mangrove ecosystem**, in the Godavari and Krishna estuaries.
Mangrove plants are **halophytes** with **pneumatophores** and **vivipary**.

nenvironment-34-8.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about ecosystem productivity?
o: Primary productivity is at the autotroph level
Mangroves are among the most productive ecosystems
Secondary productivity is at the autotroph level
Open oceans are among the least productive ecosystems
nenvironment-34-8.x: Secondary productivity is at the consumer (heterotroph) level.
n: Primary productivity occurs at the autotroph level. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Secondary productivity occurs at the heterotroph level. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Mangroves have the highest productivity among the listed ecosystems. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Oceans have the lowest productivity among the listed ecosystems. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
xa: ⚠ Other notes say **tropical rainforests** are the most productive — the APPSC key answer.
**NPP** = **GPP minus respiration losses (R)** — energy available to consumers.
Plants fix only about **2-10% of PAR**; total primary production efficiency is about **1-2%**.
Also highly productive: **estuaries**, **coral reefs**, **swamps**.

nenvironment-29-4.s: Which biogeochemical cycle begins with rock weathering?
nenvironment-29-4.x: The phosphorus cycle starts with rock weathering; the water cycle is driven by solar energy.
n: A nutritional cycle is another term for a biogeochemical cycle. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
The carbon cycle involves CO₂ exchange through biological processes. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
The water cycle is driven by solar energy. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
The phosphorus cycle involves rock weathering. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
A nutritional cycle is a biogeochemical cycle. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
xa: CO₂ is **taken up** by **photosynthesis** and **released** by **respiration**, **decay** and **fossil-fuel combustion**.
A biogeochemical cycle is the **movement** of **chemical elements** through **biotic** and **abiotic** components.
⚠ **Nutrients cycle**, while **energy flows one way**.

n80a47023be1.s: An inverted pyramid of numbers may also occur in
o: a forest floor litter chain only
n80a47023be1.x: Parasitic food chains can have fewer hosts supporting numerous parasites, resulting in an inverted pyramid of numbers.
n80a47023be1.tq: Recognise the host–parasite pattern as a standard exception to an upright number pyramid.
xs: A **parasitic** food chain can give an **inverted pyramid of numbers** — option **(3)**.
Number pyramids are **upright** in grassland and pond.
xa: Another inverted number case: **tree ecosystem** — one tree, many insects.
⚠ "Which can never be inverted" = **energy pyramid**.

n5fb7c3a79c7.s: The Veld grassland is found in:
n5fb7c3a79c7.x: Veld is in South Africa; Prairie is North America, Pampas Argentina and Downs Australia.
xa: **Steppe** = **Eurasia** (temperate grassland).
**Savanna** = tropical wet-and-dry grassland, e.g. **Africa**.
Indian grasslands: **Shola**, **Terai**, **Banni**.

n275e34dc11c.s: Who wrote the book *Animal Ecology* and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers?
n275e34dc11c.x: Charles Elton wrote *Animal Ecology* in 1927 and is associated with food chains and the pyramid of numbers.
n275e34dc11c.tq: Match the publication and contribution with the ecologist.
xs: **Charles Elton** wrote **Animal Ecology (1927)** and worked on **food chains** and the **pyramid of numbers** — option **(4)**.
**Ramdeo Misra** = father of Indian ecology; **Cowles** = succession; **Odum** = Fundamentals of Ecology.
xa: Elton proposed the **functional niche** (**1927**).
**Grinnell** = habitat niche (**1917**); **Hutchinson** = n-dimensional niche (**1957**).

na371c4bdf4d.s: Ocean acidification poses a direct threat to marine ecosystems primarily because it:
o: Weakens calcifying plankton and corals, thereby affecting marine food webs
Increases the salinity of freshwater ecosystems
Stops all forms of photosynthesis in the oceans
Strengthens the shells of calcifying plankton and corals
na371c4bdf4d.x: Ocean acidification weakens calcifying plankton and corals. Since these organisms occupy important positions in marine food webs, the effects can cascade through the ecosystem.
na371c4bdf4d.tq: Apply the cause-and-effect chain from environmental change to ecosystem impact.
xs: **Ocean acidification** weakens **calcifying plankton and corals**, cascading through **marine food webs** — option **(1)**.
It weakens, not strengthens, shells; it does not stop all photosynthesis.
xa: Warming and acidification disrupt chains through **coral bleaching**.
New ocean-carbon models add **zooplankton grazing** to the biological pump (May **2025**).

nbiology-53-8.x: Cuscuta is a parasitic flowering plant; the pitcher plant is insectivorous.
n: Pitcher plants are insectivorous. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Cuscuta is a parasitic angiosperm. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Pea has tendrils. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
Sugarcane has nodes and internodes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #53 · pp 92-95]
xa: Cuscuta grows on **host plants** as a **stem parasite**.
**Nepenthes** is the **tropical pitcher plant**; pitcher plants grow in **nitrogen-poor soil**.
**Cactus**: **leaves modified into spines**; **stores water**.

nenvironment-31-1.s: Which ecological pyramid is always upright?
nenvironment-31-1.x: The pyramid of energy is always upright, because energy falls at each trophic level. Pyramids of numbers and biomass can be inverted.
nenvironment-31-1.tq: Discriminate pyramids that can invert from the one that cannot.
n: A pyramid of energy is always upright. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 55-56]
A pyramid of numbers may be upright or inverted. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 55-56]
A pyramid of biomass may be upright or inverted. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 55-56]
A pyramid of energy represents the energy at each trophic level. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #31 · pp 55-56]
xs: The **pyramid of energy** is **always upright** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Energy is **lost as heat** at every step, so it can **never** be inverted.
The pyramid of **numbers** is inverted in a **tree** ecosystem or **parasitic** chain; the pyramid of **biomass** is inverted in a **pond** and **marine** ecosystem.
xa: There are **three** types of ecological pyramid: **numbers**, **biomass**, **energy**.
Base = **producers** (always); apex = **top carnivore**.
Limitation: **saprophytes / decomposers** get no place in the pyramid.

nc802063c569.s: In the sequence ‘tiger, grass, snake, frog’, which trophic level is missing?
nc802063c569.x: Grass represents the first trophic level and the remaining animals are consumers. The second trophic level, occupied by herbivores or primary consumers, is absent.
nc802063c569.tq: Locate the producer first and identify the absent feeding group between producer and carnivore.
xs: "Tiger, grass, snake, frog" has **no herbivore**, so the **second trophic level** is missing — option **(2)** (**PYQ 2025**).
**Grass** is T1 (producer); the rest are carnivores.
xa: **T2** = **primary consumers** (herbivores, zooplankton).
A "correct grazing chain" starts with a **producer** and moves up in order.
Chains rarely exceed **4-5 trophic levels**.

n88f09548629.s: Which one of the following represents a grassland food chain mentioned in ecological examples?
o: Grass → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk
n88f09548629.x: A grassland chain begins with grass, followed by herbivores such as grasshoppers or rabbits, and then predators such as snakes or hawks.
n88f09548629.tq: Read the chain from producer to herbivore and then to predator.
xs: Grassland chain: **grass → grasshopper or rabbit → snake or hawk** — option **(2)**.
A chain must start with the **producer** (grass) and move up in order.
xa: Grazing chain (**PYQ 2025**): **grass → goat → human**.
Rabbit is a **primary consumer**.

n9484eae4df2.s: Which one of the following correctly distinguishes bioaccumulation from biomagnification?
o: Bioaccumulation is the rise of concentration across trophic levels, whereas biomagnification is accumulation within one organism
Bioaccumulation occurs only in apex predators, whereas biomagnification occurs only in producers
Bioaccumulation is the build-up of a pollutant within one organism over its life, whereas biomagnification is the rise in concentration at successive higher trophic levels
Both terms refer only to the accumulation of biodegradable pollutants in soil
n9484eae4df2.x: Bioaccumulation is the lifetime build-up of a pollutant inside one organism. Biomagnification refers to increasing concentration at each higher trophic level.
n9484eae4df2.tq: Discriminate between two closely related environmental terms by focusing on organism-level and food-chain-level accumulation.
xs: **Bioaccumulation** = build-up **inside one organism** over its life; **biomagnification** = concentration **rising at each higher trophic level** — option **(3)**.
Option (1) swaps the two terms.
xa: Biomagnification peaks in **top predators**.
Only **persistent, fat-soluble, non-biodegradable** pollutants biomagnify.

n7863e401309.s: Minamata disease, first reported in Japan, was caused by biomagnification of which pollutant?
n7863e401309.x: Methylmercury concentrated up the marine food chain and caused Minamata disease in Japan. DDT is linked to eggshell thinning in fish-eating birds; PCBs are another persistent biomagnifying pollutant but not the cause of Minamata disease; cadmium is not the cause either (it is associated with itai-itai disease).
xs: **Methylmercury** caused **Minamata disease** in Japan — option **(2)**.
**DDT** is linked to **eggshell thinning**; **PCBs** are another biomagnifying pollutant, not the Minamata cause.
xa: Methylmercury peaks in **dolphins and orcas**.
Only **persistent, fat-soluble, non-biodegradable** pollutants biomagnify.

nenvironment-34-4.s: When energy passes from one trophic level to the next, only about ____ is transferred.
nenvironment-34-4.x: Only about 10% of energy passes upward, so energy decreases at each level and flows one way.
n: Producers occupy the first trophic level. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Herbivores occupy the second trophic level. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Energy transfer upward in a food chain decreases. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
Lindeman's 10% law concerns energy transfer between trophic levels. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #34 · pp 59-61]
xa: The **primary source** of energy is the **Sun**.
Energy flow obeys the **laws of thermodynamics**: the first law — transformed, not created or destroyed.
Nutrients **cycle**; energy is **not cycled**.

nenvironment-36-15.s: Which of the following pollutants undergoes biomagnification along food chains?
nenvironment-36-15.x: Mercury builds up along food chains (biomagnification).
n: DDT is a non-biodegradable pollutant. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
Plastic is a non-biodegradable pollutant. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
Asbestos is a non-biodegradable pollutant. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
Mercury undergoes biomagnification. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
xa: **Sewage** is **biodegradable**.
Only **persistent, fat-soluble, non-biodegradable** pollutants (DDT, mercury, PCBs) biomagnify.
**Methylmercury** concentrates in apex predators and caused **Minamata disease** in Japan.
⚠ **Bioaccumulation** = build-up inside one organism; **biomagnification** = rise across trophic levels.

nenvironment-29-1.s: A biogeochemical cycle refers to the movement of which of the following?
nenvironment-29-1.x: A biogeochemical cycle moves chemical elements (carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus) between living things and the environment. Energy flows one way and does not cycle.
nenvironment-29-1.tq: Discriminate nutrient cycling from energy flow.
n: A biogeochemical cycle involves the movement of chemical elements. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #29 · pp 52-53]
xs: A biogeochemical cycle is the **movement** of **chemical elements** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It moves **nutrients** through **biotic** and **abiotic** components; also called the **nutritional cycle**.
**Solar energy** **flows one way** and is **not cycled**; **CO₂** is only part of the **carbon cycle**.
xa: **Carbon cycle**: **CO₂ exchange** through biological processes.
**Water cycle**: **driven** by **solar energy**.
**Phosphorus cycle**: involves **rock weathering**.

n7eedd208814.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes macroconsumers from microconsumers?
o: Macroconsumers are phagotrophs, whereas microconsumers are saprotrophs.
Macroconsumers are abiotic, whereas microconsumers are biotic.
Macroconsumers manufacture inorganic nutrients, whereas microconsumers consume sunlight.
Macroconsumers are decomposers, whereas microconsumers are herbivores.
n7eedd208814.x: Macroconsumers, or phagotrophs, ingest food particles or organisms. Microconsumers, or saprotrophs, obtain nutrients by decomposing organic matter.
n7eedd208814.tq: Use the feeding mode—ingestion versus saprotrophic absorption—to distinguish the two groups.
xs: **Macroconsumers = phagotrophs**; **microconsumers = saprotrophs** — option **(1)**.
Both are **biotic**; decomposers are **microconsumers**, not macro.
xa: Saprotrophs also called **osmotrophs** — **bacteria and fungi**.
Decomposers are the **link between biotic and abiotic** parts.

n92d7b8de9ff.s: Which one of the following is the most appropriate set of characteristics of a pollutant that biomagnifies?
o: Radioactive, gaseous and readily converted into oxygen
Highly soluble in water, biodegradable and short-lived
n92d7b8de9ff.x: Only persistent, fat-soluble and non-biodegradable pollutants are identified as biomagnifying pollutants in this context.
n92d7b8de9ff.tq: Identify the exact qualifying characteristics rather than selecting a broad pollution-related description.
xs: Biomagnifying pollutants are **persistent, fat-soluble and non-biodegradable** — option **(3)**.
Water-soluble, biodegradable or short-lived pollutants do not build up.
xa: Examples: **DDT, mercury, PCBs**.
Concentration rises at each **higher trophic level**, peaking in **top predators**.

nenvironment-36-18.s: Which of the following pair consists entirely of secondary pollutants?
nenvironment-36-18.x: PAN and smog are both secondary pollutants, formed in the air. CO, SO₂ and NOx are primary.
n: Peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) is a secondary pollutant. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
Smog is a secondary pollutant. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #36 · pp 62-64]
xs: **PAN and smog** are both **secondary pollutants** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Secondary pollutants: **O₃**, **PAN** (**peroxyacetyl nitrate**) and **smog**.
**CO**, **SO₂** and **NOx** are **primary pollutants**, so options (1), (2) and (3) each contain a primary pollutant.
xa: **Anthropogenic pollution** is **human-made**.
**Non-biodegradable** pollutants: **DDT**, **plastic**, **asbestos**; **biodegradable**: **sewage**.
**DDT** causes **thinning of bird eggshells** in fish-eating birds.

na5129e603b6.s: Which one of the following correctly represents the usual salinity gradient in an estuary?
o: 35 ppt upstream and nearly zero at the mouth
Uniformly zero salinity throughout the estuary
Nearly freshwater upstream and about 35 ppt at the mouth
na5129e603b6.x: Salinity generally increases from near-freshwater conditions upstream to approximately 35 ppt near the sea-facing mouth.
na5129e603b6.tq: Track the direction of the gradient and place the numerical value at the correct end.
xs: Salinity rises from **near-fresh upstream** to **35 ppt at the mouth** — option **(4)**.
Option (1) reverses the gradient.
xa: Brackish range: **5-35 ppt**; marine **35 ppt or more**.
AP's **Coringa** is a mangrove-estuary in the **Godavari** delta.

n5e7deaa1b7e.s: Wetlands in India are specifically protected under which of the following?
n5e7deaa1b7e.x: The Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017 provide the specific legal framework for wetland protection in India.
n5e7deaa1b7e.tq: Match the subject with the exact legal instrument and year.
xs: India protects wetlands under the **Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017** — option **(4)**.
The notes link no other rule or notification to wetland protection.
xa: India joined **Ramsar** in **1982**; it has **96 Ramsar sites**.
ZSI documented **8,213** faunal species in India's Ramsar sites.
AP's **Kolleru** is a **Ramsar site**.

nenvironment-3-5.s: World Wetlands Day, marking the signing of the Ramsar Convention, is observed on:
nenvironment-3-5.x: The Ramsar Convention was signed on 2 February 1971, which is observed as World Wetlands Day.
n: The Ramsar Convention was signed on 2 February 1971. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]
The Ramsar Convention concerns wetlands. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]
World Wetlands Day is observed on 2 February. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]
The principle of the Ramsar Convention is conservation. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]
The principle of the Ramsar Convention is wise or sustainable use. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #3 · pp 6-8]
xa: India joined Ramsar in **1982**; it has **96 Ramsar sites**.
Threatened Ramsar sites go on the **Montreux Record**.
India's **Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017**.
Wetland functions: **flood moderation**, **water purification**, biodiversity conservation, **carbon storage**.

n36aab81b733.s: Which of the following is a coastal wetland rather than an inland wetland?
n36aab81b733.x: Lagoons, estuaries and mangroves are coastal wetlands. Lakes, marshes and floodplains are inland wetlands.
n36aab81b733.tq: Distinguish coastal and inland members of a classification.
xs: A **lagoon** is a **coastal** wetland — option **(1)**.
**Lakes, marshes, floodplains** are **inland** wetlands.
xa: Coastal wetlands also include **estuaries** and **mangroves**.
AP's **Pulicat** is a **brackish-water lagoon** on the AP-Tamil Nadu border.
Wetland functions: **flood moderation, water purification, biodiversity conservation, carbon storage**.

n937f4b0f6a5.s: The AP State Biodiversity Board is planning Other Effective Area-based Conservation Measures (OECMs) primarily:
o: Inside all urban municipal limits only
n937f4b0f6a5.x: The AP State Biodiversity Board is planning OECMs outside protected areas as part of broader conservation efforts.
n937f4b0f6a5.tq: Distinguish area-based conservation outside the conventional protected-area network.
xs: OECMs are conservation **outside protected areas** — option **(1)**.
They are not limited to tiger reserves, cities or only wetlands.
xa: Partner: **CMFRI**; includes **estuarine fish-breeding grounds**.
AP's **Nallamala** and **Seshachalam** forests host tigers, leopards, sloth bears, elephants.

nb62e346ba04.s: Which of the following has a gaseous nutrient cycle?
nb62e346ba04.x: Carbon and nitrogen have gaseous cycles, while phosphorus, sulphur and potassium have sedimentary cycles.
xa: Other gaseous cycles: **oxygen** and **water**; another sedimentary cycle: **calcium**.
Gaseous reservoir = **atmosphere / ocean**; sedimentary reservoir = **soil and rocks**.
**Phosphorus** is released by **weathering of rocks** and ends in ocean sediments.

n7398d2cc1af.s: Which biogeochemical cycle has the atmosphere, rather than soil, as its principal reservoir?
n7398d2cc1af.x: The nitrogen cycle has the atmosphere as its principal reservoir; nitrogen gas makes up about 78% of the atmosphere.
xa: This was asked in **APPSC-G2 2025** as the cycle whose main reservoir is NOT the soil.
**Denitrification** (Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus) returns N2 to air.
Biological fixation uses the enzyme **nitrogenase**; **lightning** causes atmospheric fixation.

neef268abae6.s: Which of the following nutrient cycles has no atmospheric phase?
neef268abae6.x: The phosphorus cycle has no atmospheric phase; weathering releases phosphorus from rocks and much of it ends in ocean sediments.
xa: Other sedimentary cycles: **sulphur, calcium**, potassium.
**Fertiliser runoff** of **N and P** → **algal blooms / eutrophication**.
**PSB** (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) **solubilise phosphate**; **VAM** aids P uptake.

n96a9b984503.s: Which ecosystem acts as a sponge by storing floodwater, recharging aquifers and sustaining lean-season flow?
n96a9b984503.x: Wetlands store floodwater, recharge aquifers and sustain lean-season flow.
xa: Water carries elements through the ecosystem; cycles **would stop if water did not cycle**.
AP has the **second-largest mangrove** ecosystem in India (**Godavari and Krishna** estuaries).
Forests are vital **carbon sinks**.

ned41ff769dd.s: Which one of the following combinations contains only processes that add carbon dioxide to the carbon cycle?
o: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity
Photosynthesis, ocean dissolution, carbonate sedimentation and silicate weathering
Photosynthesis, respiration, carbonate sedimentation and deforestation
Ocean dissolution, decomposition, silicate weathering and photosynthesis
ned41ff769dd.x: Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity all add CO2. Each other option includes a process that removes CO2: photosynthesis, dissolution in oceans, carbonate sedimentation or silicate weathering.
ned41ff769dd.tq: Separate source processes from sink processes before evaluating the combination.
xs: **Respiration, decomposition, fossil-fuel combustion and volcanic activity** all add CO2 — so option **(1)** is correct.
Every other option includes a CO2-removing process: **photosynthesis**, **ocean dissolution**, **carbonate sedimentation** or **silicate weathering**.
xa: **Deforestation** also adds CO2.
Reservoirs: atmosphere, **oceans**, forests, soils; long-term: **carbonate rocks and fossil fuels**.
Burning fossil fuels + deforestation raise CO2 → **climate change**.

n018fb935eac.s: Which of the following is NOT a correct consequence of human disruption of biogeochemical cycles?
o: Fossil-fuel burning increases atmospheric carbon dioxide
Chemical pesticides invariably increase ecosystem resilience
Fertiliser runoff can cause algal blooms and eutrophication
Chemical pesticides can alter soils and microbial networks
n018fb935eac.x: Pesticides may alter soils and microbial networks and weaken resilience; they do not invariably increase it.
xa: All cycles are linked to the **water cycle**.
Removing decomposers would **block mineral movement** (**APPSC 2025**).
Long-term carbon stores: **carbonate rocks and fossil fuels**.

ndfef35fefb1.s: Prosopis juliflora has been described as an ‘ecological first responder’ primarily because it:
o: Forms the final climax community in every ecosystem
Spreads when hydrology and soil chemistry have changed
Prevents all invasive species from establishing
Fixes nitrogen exclusively in rice fields
ndfef35fefb1.x: The invasive Prosopis juliflora spreads in response to changes in hydrology and soil chemistry, leading to its description as an ecological first responder.
ndfef35fefb1.tq: Apply the ecological meaning of the descriptive phrase to the stated environmental changes.
xs: **Prosopis juliflora** is an "ecological first responder" because it **spreads when hydrology and soil chemistry have changed** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It acts as a **pioneer species** spreading in altered conditions, not as a climax community.
xa: Source: **TH, 7 May 2026**.
**Pioneer species** = first hardy colonisers.
Climax community = **last stage**, in equilibrium with climate.

n26d6e9d67d8.s: Which of the following processes directly converts organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia?
n26d6e9d67d8.x: Ammonification is the conversion of organic nitrogen in dead matter into ammonia by decomposer bacteria and fungi.
n26d6e9d67d8.tq: Separate the nitrogen-cycle processes by identifying the substance being transformed.
xs: **Ammonification** turns organic N in dead matter into ammonia — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is done by **decomposer bacteria and fungi**.
**Fixation** turns N2 into ammonia/nitrate; **nitrification** turns ammonia into nitrite then nitrate; **denitrification** returns N2 to air.
xa: Fixation, ammonification and nitrification **add** usable N to soil; denitrification **removes** it.
Nitrification = **Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter**.
Denitrification = **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.

ncf687465ffc.s: Which microorganisms are associated with the two stages of nitrification respectively?
ncf687465ffc.x: Nitrosomonas converts ammonia into nitrite, while Nitrobacter converts nitrite into nitrate.
ncf687465ffc.tq: Match each microorganism with its specific step rather than with nitrogen fixation generally.
xs: The two nitrification stages are done by **Nitrosomonas and Nitrobacter** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Nitrosomonas**: ammonia → nitrite; **Nitrobacter**: nitrite → nitrate.
**Pseudomonas** and **Thiobacillus** are denitrifiers; **Rhizobium**, **Frankia** and **Anabaena** are N-fixers.
xa: ⚠ Nitrification = **Nitrosomonas → Nitrobacter**; denitrification = **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.
Ammonification = **decomposer bacteria and fungi**.
Fixation agents include **Azotobacter** and the **Haber process**.

nbfd96a571f2.s: Which process removes nitrogen from the soil by returning it to the atmosphere as N₂ gas?
nbfd96a571f2.x: Denitrification returns nitrogen to the atmosphere as N₂; fixation, ammonification and nitrification add usable nitrogen to soil.
xa: Other N inputs: **lightning** (atmospheric fixation) and **industrial fixation** (fertilisers).
Biological fixation uses the enzyme **nitrogenase**.
Fertiliser runoff (**N and P**) → **algal blooms / eutrophication**.

n3db25154b1f.s: Frankia, a symbiotic actinomycete, fixes nitrogen in association with:
o: Non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina
n3db25154b1f.x: Frankia forms symbiotic associations with non-legumes such as Alnus and Casuarina.
xa: Denitrifiers: **Pseudomonas, Thiobacillus**.
**Rhizobium** = symbiotic, in **root nodules of legumes**.
Phosphate solubilisers: **Bacillus megaterium**, **Pseudomonas striata**.

n10f8861344c.s: Mycorrhiza, particularly VAM, primarily helps plants in the uptake of:
n10f8861344c.x: VAM is a fungus-root association that improves phosphorus and water uptake by plants.
n10f8861344c.tq: Distinguish nutrient- and water-uptake functions from nitrogen fixation.
xs: **VAM** helps plants take up **phosphorus and water** — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Mycorrhiza** is a **fungus-root association**.
xa: **PSB** (Bacillus, Pseudomonas) **solubilise phosphate**.
**Azolla** with **Anabaena** supplies N for paddy.
Phosphorus has **no atmospheric phase**; it is released by weathering of rocks.

nbiology-68-13.s: In rice fields, the cyanobacterium Anabaena lives in association with:
nbiology-68-13.x: Anabaena lives in the aquatic fern Azolla; the Azolla-Anabaena pair is used in rice fields.
n: Rhizobium is associated with legume root nodules for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Cyanobacteria, also called blue-green algae, are associated with paddy for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
Anabaena is associated with Azolla for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
The Azolla–Anabaena association fixes nitrogen in rice fields. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #68 · pp 128-131]
xa: **Azotobacter** and **Azospirillum** serve cereals, millets and vegetables.
**Leg-haemoglobin** (red or pink) in **legume root nodules** is linked with **Rhizobium symbiosis**.
**Frankia** is a symbiotic actinomycete in **non-legumes**.

nbiology-57-14.s: Which biofertiliser fixes nitrogen as a free-living organism?
nbiology-57-14.x: Azotobacter fixes nitrogen free-living, whereas Rhizobium fixes it symbiotically in legume root nodules.
n: Rhizobium performs nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Azotobacter performs free-living nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza improves nutrient acquisition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza improves water acquisition. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Phosphate-solubilizing microbes solubilize phosphorus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Mycorrhiza especially improves **phosphorus uptake** and gives **better plant growth**.
**PSB** include **Bacillus** and **Pseudomonas**.
**Cyanobacteria** are biofertilizers for **paddy**.

nbiology-57-15.s: The red or pink substance found in legume root nodules is:
nbiology-57-15.x: Leghaemoglobin is the pink pigment in legume root nodules, where symbiotic Rhizobium fixes nitrogen.
n: Rhizobium is a symbiotic bacterium. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Azolla is an aquatic fern. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Mycorrhiza is a fungus–plant-root association. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Leg-haemoglobin is red or pink. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Leg-haemoglobin **maintains suitable oxygen conditions** for **nitrogen fixation**.
**Azolla** is **associated** with **Anabaena** — nitrogen fixation in **rice fields**.
Mycorrhiza is also called **VAM**.

n9dc14da2163.s: In Frederic Clements' scheme of succession, which phase immediately follows nudation?
n9dc14da2163.x: Clements' sequence is nudation, invasion, competition and co-action, reaction and stabilisation.
xa: **Reaction** — organisms modify soil, water, light, temperature — is the **most important** stage.
Invasion includes **ecesis** (successful establishment) and **aggregation**.
Nudation causes: erosion, landslide, volcanic activity, fire.

nd8c50db337e.s: The term ‘ecesis’ in ecological succession refers to
o: the final stabilisation of a climax community
the successful establishment of invading organisms
the seasonal disappearance of a community
the elimination of unfit species through competition
nd8c50db337e.x: Ecesis is the successful establishment of organisms that have migrated into an area during the invasion phase.
nd8c50db337e.tq: Discriminate between closely related terms belonging to the invasion and stabilisation phases.
xs: **Ecesis** is the **successful establishment** of invading organisms — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is part of the **invasion** phase: migration of seeds/spores, ecesis, **aggregation**.
Elimination of unfit species is **competition and co-action**; the climax is **stabilisation**.
xa: **Reaction** is the **most important** stage.
**Pioneer species** = first hardy colonisers, e.g. **lichens** on bare rock.
**Climax community** = final stable community, in equilibrium with climate.

n8e302b56c48.s: In Clements' phases of succession, organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature during:
n8e302b56c48.x: Reaction, the most important phase, is when organisms modify soil, water, light and temperature, making the site suitable for later species.
xa: Clements' order: **Nudation → Invasion → Competition and co-action → Reaction → Stabilisation**.
Phases proposed by **Frederic Clements (1916)**.
**Competition and co-action**: intra- and inter-specific competition; unfit eliminated.

nf604f7141e4.s: Seasonal succession differs from succession caused by a disturbance because seasonal succession is
o: caused exclusively by the removal of soil
a permanent replacement ending only in a forest climax
a cyclic change driven by environmental rhythms
nf604f7141e4.x: Seasonal succession is cyclical and is driven by environmental rhythms; it is not caused by a disaster or disturbance.
nf604f7141e4.tq: Separate cyclic seasonal change from directional succession caused by disturbance.
xs: Seasonal succession is **a cyclic change driven by environmental rhythms** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is **not** caused by a disturbance (disaster), unlike primary or secondary succession.
xa: **Succession** = orderly, sequential replacement of one community by another, with change in species composition.
**Odum (1971)**: succession = an orderly process of community change within a unit area.
**Nudation** (bare area) results from erosion, landslide, volcanic activity, fire.

n6e0f9a5d350.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about primary and secondary succession?
o: Secondary succession is generally slower than primary succession
Primary succession begins where no soil is present
Secondary succession follows destruction of an existing community
Seeds and roots may already be present in secondary succession
n6e0f9a5d350.x: Secondary succession is generally faster, not slower, because soil, seeds or roots may remain.
xa: Primary begins on areas that never had life: **lava, bare rock, volcanic island**.
Primary: **lichens and mosses** first; slower, low biomass.
**Grasslands** do not turn into forest because of **water limits and fire**.

n3a1d34dfa28.s: Who proposed the monoclimax theory of ecological succession?
n3a1d34dfa28.x: Clements proposed the monoclimax theory; Tansley proposed polyclimax and Whittaker the climax-pattern theory.
xa: Monoclimax = **one climax per climatic region**.
Climax community = final stable community **set by climate** (forest, grassland, coral reef).
**Grasslands** do not turn into forest because of **water limits and fire**.

n04e2d5c3229.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about xerosere succession on bare rock?
o: Crustose lichens are the pioneers on bare rock
n04e2d5c3229.x: The sequence is crustose lichens, foliose lichens, mosses, herbs, shrubs and forest, so mosses come after foliose lichens, not before.
xa: **Lichens** = symbiotic association of **algae and fungi** — the bare-rock pioneers.
Scrub attracts **birds** whose droppings and seeds speed colonisation.
Pioneer trees (**birch, oak**) need high light; **shade-tolerant** species form the climax.

n83892e9e6d2.s: In a hydrosere, which stage comes immediately after the reed-swamp stage?
n83892e9e6d2.x: Hydrosere proceeds phytoplankton - submerged rooted plants - floating plants - reed-swamp - sedge-meadow - woodland - forest.
xa: Floating stage: duckweed **Lemna**, **Pistia** and the alga **Chara**.
Sedge peat above water is invaded by **alders and willows**; ends in wet woodland = **fen carr**.
Lake sediments keep a **permanent record** → hydroseres better studied than xeroseres.

n8c215a5795d.s: Ecological succession beginning on sand is known as:
n8c215a5795d.x: Psammosere begins on sand and, like lithosere (bare rock), is a sub-type of xerosere; halosere begins on saline soil or water.
xa: **Hydrosere** begins in water (pond, lake).
Xerosere: **crustose lichens → foliose lichens → mosses → herbs and grasses → shrubs → forest**.
Whole sequence of stages = **sere**; each step = **seral stage**.

n2bc1399fe1f.s: Biodegradation contributes to the functioning of an ecosystem primarily by
o: removing biodiversity from the food chain
converting organic waste into nutrients through microorganisms
n2bc1399fe1f.x: Biodegradation recycles waste when microorganisms break down organic material and release nutrients. This makes nutrients available for reuse in the ecosystem.
n2bc1399fe1f.tq: Apply the process to its practical ecological outcome: microbial breakdown and nutrient release.
xs: Biodegradation works by **converting organic waste into nutrients through microorganisms** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **biodegradation function** = recycling waste: microorganisms break organic material into nutrients by **biological action** (**APPSC 2023**).
It does not prevent decomposition or remove biodiversity; it is itself decomposition that returns nutrients for reuse.
xa: **Waste decomposition** is classed as a **regulating** service under the **MEA 2005**.
Removing **decomposers** would **block mineral movement** — nutrients locked in dead matter never return to the soil (**APPSC 2025**).
Other environment functions: **supplies resources**, **sustains life**, **aesthetic services**.

nc8f2cfb3a31.s: The ecosystem function of maintaining ecological balance is known as:
nc8f2cfb3a31.x: Homeostasis is the maintenance of ecological balance; succession, nutrient cycling and energy flow are other ecosystem functions.
xa: Forest **economic** functions: timber, bamboo, fuelwood, fodder, **NTFPs**.
Forest **ecological** functions: **carbon sequestration**, soil and water conservation, groundwater recharge, flood moderation, air purification.
The **MEA 2005** grouped ecosystem services into **provisioning, regulating, cultural, supporting**.

na975bb671b0.s: Under the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment, soil formation is classified as a ____ service.
na975bb671b0.x: Soil formation is a supporting service; food and water are provisioning, climate regulation is regulating and recreation is cultural.
xa: The four categories come from the **Millennium Ecosystem Assessment (2005, UN)**.
⚠ **Pollination** and **waste decomposition** = **regulating**; **nutrient cycling** and **soil formation** = **supporting**.
Supporting services also include **primary production**.

nfca3895f92f.s: Which one of the following is NOT a provisioning ecosystem service under the Millennium Ecosystem Assessment classification?
nfca3895f92f.x: Pollination is a regulating service. Timber, medicinal resources and fresh water are provisioning services.
nfca3895f92f.tq: Use category discrimination: identify the service that performs regulation rather than material supply.
xs: **Pollination** is NOT a provisioning service — so option **(2)** is correct.
Under the **MEA**, pollination is a **regulating** service, along with climate, flood and disease regulation and water purification.
**Fresh water**, **timber** and **medicinal resources** are all **provisioning** services.
xa: Provisioning also covers **food** and **fibre**.
⚠ Waste decomposition = **regulating**; nutrient cycling = **supporting**.
**Cultural** services: recreation, aesthetics, cultural heritage, spiritual value.

n5b63c8cffe5.s: Which of the following forest benefits is an ecological service rather than an economic product?
n5b63c8cffe5.x: Groundwater recharge and flood moderation are ecological services; timber and bamboo are economic products from forests.
xa: Forests are vital **carbon sinks**.
**Wetlands** act as sponges — store floodwater, recharge aquifers, sustain lean-season flow.
AP's forests regulate water flow and conserve soil and moisture → **intangible ecosystem services**.

ne65bde08a57.s: Which category of ecosystem services is most difficult to express in monetary terms, causing their value to be underestimated?
ne65bde08a57.x: Cultural services such as spiritual value, heritage and aesthetics are hard to price, so monetary estimates understate total value.
xa: Criticism: pricing nature (**Costanza**, **TEEB**) aids decisions but **undervalues cultural and spiritual services**.
**Costanza et al. (1997)**: about **US$33 trillion a year**.
Coral reefs valued at **$375 billion-$9.9 trillion** a year.

ncbbf51ee099.s: Nutrients in an ecosystem differ from energy in that nutrients
o: flow only through the atmosphere and never through organisms
are consumed permanently and cannot return to the ecosystem
are recycled indefinitely, whereas energy is not
ncbbf51ee099.x: Nutrients are recycled through ecosystems, while energy flows through the system and is not recycled indefinitely.
ncbbf51ee099.tq: Discriminate between the cycling of matter and the one-way flow of energy.
xs: Nutrients **are recycled indefinitely, whereas energy is not** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Nutrients cycle between **living organisms, air and the Earth's crust**; energy flows through and is lost.
They are not consumed permanently, nor generated by decomposers; decomposers only release them from dead matter.
xa: **Energy flow** drives the cycles; all cycles are linked to the **water cycle**.
**C, H, O, N and P** make up about **97%** of body mass.
Common components of all cycles: **inputs, internal cycling, outputs**.

nf7aa8dbaeca.s: In ecological succession, the stable terminal community in equilibrium with the climate is called the:
nf7aa8dbaeca.x: The climax community is the stable terminal community related to the prevailing climate; pioneers colonise first and seral communities are intermediate.
xa: Climax examples: **forest, grassland, coral reef**.
FIRST/LAST: **lichens** first on bare rock; **climax community** = last stage.
**Succession** = gradual, orderly, sequential replacement of one community by another over time.

n9137aee37ce.s: Which of the following is an intangible ecosystem service provided by forests in Andhra Pradesh?
n9137aee37ce.x: AP forests act as carbon sinks, regulate water flow and conserve soil and moisture - intangible services beyond market-priced goods.
xa: Forest **economic** products: timber, bamboo, fuelwood, fodder, **NTFPs**.
Pricing nature (**Costanza, TEEB**) undervalues cultural and spiritual services.
AP has the **second-largest mangrove** ecosystem in India (**Godavari and Krishna** estuaries).

nbiology-57-10.s: Phosphate-solubilising microbes act as biofertilisers mainly by:
nbiology-57-10.x: Phosphate-solubilising microbes release bound phosphorus, adding nutrients and promoting growth.
n: Phosphate-solubilizing microbes solubilize phosphorus. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Biofertilizers add nutrients. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Biofertilizers promote growth. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xa: Phosphate solubilisers: **Bacillus megaterium**, **Pseudomonas striata**.
**Mycorrhiza (VAM)**: a fungus–root association improving **phosphorus uptake**.
**Azolla–Anabaena** is a **biofertilizer** and **green-manure** association for **rice**.

nenvironment-22-7.s: Which one of the following is a function of wetlands?
nenvironment-22-7.x: Wetlands control erosion, retain sediment, support nutrient cycling and support biodiversity.
n: Wetlands control erosion. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands retain sediment. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands support nutrient cycling. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
Wetlands support biodiversity. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #22 · pp 38-39]
xa: They also act as **flood buffers**, store water and **purify water**.
They **recharge aquifers** and regulate the **microclimate**.
**Fertiliser runoff** of **N and P** causes **algal blooms / eutrophication**.

nbbee123ebb8.s: Protection from UV radiation by the ozone layer falls under which function of the environment?
nbbee123ebb8.x: Sustaining life includes genetic diversity, biodiversity and ozone's protection from UV radiation.
xa: Supplying resources is the **first function** of the environment.
**Assimilating waste** = the **biodegradation function**.
Recreation, aesthetics, cultural heritage and spiritual value are **cultural** services under the **MEA 2005**.

n9461042a366.s: Costanza and his associates first valued global ecosystem services in 1997 at approximately
n9461042a366.x: Costanza et al. estimated the annual value of global ecosystem services at approximately US$33 trillion in 1997.
n9461042a366.tq: Handle the figure by checking the order of magnitude and the decimal placement.
xs: **Costanza et al. (1997)** valued global ecosystem services at about **US$33 trillion a year** — so option **(1)** is correct.
It was the **first** attempt to value global ecosystem services.
xa: Later values: coral reefs **$375 billion-$9.9 trillion** a year; Amazon **$2.2-3.4 trillion** a year.
True values are higher — **cultural services** are hard to price.
**TEEB** (launched **2007**, G8+5, Potsdam; hosted by **UNEP**) makes nature's values visible in decisions.

nbbbd9fe8270.s: TEEB (The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity), launched in 2007 in the G8+5 context, is hosted by:
nbbbd9fe8270.x: TEEB was launched in 2007 at Potsdam in the G8+5 context and is hosted by UNEP; it seeks to make nature's values visible in decisions.
xa: TEEB = **The Economics of Ecosystems and Biodiversity**.
The **MEA (2005, UN)** gave the four service categories.
Pricing nature aids decisions but **undervalues cultural and spiritual services**.

nbiology-57-5.s: What is the principal function of leg-haemoglobin in legume root nodules?
o: Maintaining suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation
nbiology-57-5.x: Leghaemoglobin binds oxygen to keep its level low in nodules, because nitrogenase is destroyed by oxygen.
n: Leg-haemoglobin is located in legume root nodules. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
Leg-haemoglobin helps maintain suitable oxygen conditions for nitrogen fixation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #57 · pp 102-105]
xs: **Leg-haemoglobin** helps **maintain suitable oxygen conditions** for **nitrogen fixation** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is **located** in **legume root nodules**, is **red or pink**, and is linked with **Rhizobium symbiosis**.
It supports an **efficient nitrogen-fixing environment**; it does not solubilise **phosphorus** (that is phosphate-solubilising microbes).
xa: A **legume root nodule** has a **symbiotic relationship** with **Rhizobium**.
**Free-living** nitrogen fixation is done by **Azotobacter**.
Biological fixation needs the enzyme **nitrogenase**.

n1fdaa3bfb25.s: Deforestation contributes to the greenhouse effect primarily because it
o: raises soil fertility in all regions
reduces the carbon sink capacity of forests
n1fdaa3bfb25.x: Deforestation removes vegetation that acts as a carbon sink. The resulting loss of carbon absorption adds to the greenhouse effect.
n1fdaa3bfb25.tq: Link the environmental impact directly to the underlying ecological function.
xs: Deforestation adds to the greenhouse effect because it **reduces the carbon sink capacity of forests** — so option **(4)** is correct.
Notes: **loss of CO2 sink** adds to the greenhouse effect.
It does not raise fertility or prevent erosion — it causes **faster erosion** and **falling fertility**.
xa: Drivers: agriculture, urbanisation, industry, **mining**.
**Forest Declaration Assessment 2025**: forest loss **8.1 Mha in 2024**.
About **94%** of loss is in **tropical** forests.

o: the conversion of all forests into agricultural land
the spread of existing deserts alone into neighbouring regions
the natural formation of sand dunes only
land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas resulting from climatic variations and human activities
n627277011af.x: Desertification involves land degradation in arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid areas due to climatic variation and human activity; it is not merely the spread of existing deserts.
n627277011af.tq: Discriminate between the broad process of desertification and the narrower idea of desert expansion.
xs: Desertification is **the spread of desert-like conditions into non-arid areas through climatic and human factors** — so option **(4)** is correct.
In the **UNCCD** sense it is land degradation in **arid, semi-arid and dry sub-humid** areas from climatic variation and human activity.
⚠ It is **not** the spread of existing deserts alone — so option (2) is wrong.
xa: Main cause in semi-arid regions: **overgrazing and deforestation** (**APPSC 2025**).
**LDN** = no net loss of land health; target year **2030** (SDG 15.3).
**Rajasthan** has over **23%** of India's desertified land.
n627277011af.fixed: UNCCD definition is degradation of drylands, not of 'non-arid areas' (notes 0#0, 8#1)

n7c4f0d07399.s: In semi-arid regions, the principal causes of desertification are
o: low population pressure and regular rainfall
n7c4f0d07399.x: Overgrazing and deforestation are identified as the main causes of desertification in semi-arid regions.
n7c4f0d07399.tq: Select the primary cause rather than a secondary contributing factor.
xs: **Overgrazing and deforestation** are the main causes in semi-arid regions — so option **(3)** is correct (**APPSC 2025**).
Afforestation, water harvesting and improved drainage are remedies, not causes.
xa: Other causes: **improper irrigation**, excess chemicals, **erratic rainfall**, droughts, **population pressure**.
**Overgrazing** strips vegetation cover; **deforestation** exposes soil to wind and water erosion.
**Tragedy of the Commons** (Garrett Hardin, **1968**): overgrazing of shared pasture lowers land quality.

ndc3e0dffbcb.s: The concept used to describe degradation caused by over-use of a shared pasture is
ndc3e0dffbcb.x: Over-use of a commonly shared pasture is described as the Tragedy of the Commons, a concept associated with Garrett Hardin in 1968.
ndc3e0dffbcb.tq: Match the exact conceptual term with the common-resource situation.
xs: Over-use of a shared pasture is the **Tragedy of the Commons** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The concept is of **Garrett Hardin, 1968**; overgrazing lowers land quality (**APPSC 2018**).
xa: **Overgrazing** strips vegetation cover — a main cause of desertification in semi-arid regions.
**LDN** = no net loss of land health by **2030**.
Over-use of shared land drives the degradation that the UNCCD targets.

ndea5fd68fdd.s: Which of the following is the most conspicuous set of effects associated with modern agriculture?
o: Reduced irrigation, increased soil carbon and forest expansion
Declining crop production without any environmental effect
Soil formation, afforestation and ecological stability
Soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance
ndea5fd68fdd.x: The most conspicuous effects of modern agriculture are soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance.
ndea5fd68fdd.tq: Recognise the complete three-part consequence set rather than selecting one component.
xs: Modern agriculture's main effects are **soil degradation, pollution and ecological imbalance** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The answer "**all of these**" was keyed in **APPSC 2018**.
xa: Excess **urea** skewed the **NPK ratio** in Punjab and Haryana.
Over-irrigation + poor drainage → **waterlogging and salinity**.
**Soil organic carbon** reportedly fell from **1% to 0.3%** over 70 years.

n49f89649676.s: At UNCCD COP14 in New Delhi (2019), India raised its land-restoration target to how much by 2030?
n49f89649676.x: At COP14 India raised its target to 26 Mha by 2030, up from the 21 Mha pledged at Paris in 2015.
xa: LDN = **no net loss of land health** (SDG **15.3**).
**COP17**: **Ulaanbaatar, Mongolia (2026)**.
MoEFCC-IUCN report: India restored **~21.76 Mha** during 2011-2020.

nf90b90e1af9.s: Under the Watershed Development Component of PMKSY, watershed development in India follows which approach?
nf90b90e1af9.x: Watershed development under the PMKSY Watershed Development Component follows the 'ridge to valley' approach, treating the upper catchment first and moving downstream. The other options are not the stated approach.
xs: PMKSY watershed development follows **'ridge to valley'** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is the approach of the **PMKSY Watershed Development Component**.
xa: Other soil-conservation support: **MGNREGA**, state watershed projects, **participatory forest management**.
**Soil Health Cards** + village-wise soil nutrient mapping.
Water erosion causes **loss of topsoil** and sedimentation of rivers and reservoirs.

n3aff63a75c4.s: Salinisation and waterlogging are particularly associated with
n3aff63a75c4.x: Poor drainage and over-irrigation cause salinisation and waterlogging, including in delta regions.
n3aff63a75c4.tq: Link the land-management practice to its characteristic degradation outcome.
xs: Salinisation and waterlogging come from **poor drainage and over-irrigation** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Brick production** depletes **topsoil**; **wind erosion** blows topsoil away in dry areas — different processes.
xa: In AP, **delta areas** suffer salinity + waterlogging.
By **2050, 50%** of world arable land could be affected by waterlogging and salinity.
**Mitti Bachao Abhiyan** (MP, **1977**) opposed waterlogging and salinity.

nf685db321b7.s: In the context of intensive agriculture, excess urea is reported to have skewed the NPK ratio particularly in
nf685db321b7.x: Excess use of urea has skewed the nitrogen-phosphorus-potassium balance in the soils of Punjab and Haryana.
nf685db321b7.tq: Use the location-specific agriculture trap and distinguish it from other state pairs.
xs: Excess **urea** has skewed the **NPK ratio** in **Punjab and Haryana** (CSE) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Synthetic fertilisers and pesticides **contaminate soil and water**.
xa: Effects of intensive agriculture: soil degradation, pollution, ecological imbalance — **all of these** (**APPSC 2018**).
Indian **soil organic carbon** reportedly fell from **1% to 0.3%** over 70 years.
⚠ **Punjab** has the best (lowest) degraded-land share, **3.15%**.

n70f6d481c53.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the extent of land degradation?
o: The 2021 Atlas reports about 97.85 Mha of India as degraded
About 29.77% of India's area is degraded as per the 2021 Atlas
According to FAO, about one-half of the world's soils are degraded
Water erosion and chemical degradation are major contributors in India
n70f6d481c53.x: FAO says about one-third, not one-half, of the world's soils are degraded.
xa: The Atlas is by **ISRO's Space Applications Centre (SAC), Ahmedabad**.
India is adding **2.2 lakh ha** of degraded land a year.
UNCCD: degradation costs over **10% of global GDP**.

n6b0465fc39d.s: The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas was published by which organisation and centre?
o: Indian Council of Forestry Research and Education, Dehradun
National Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation, Kolkata
n6b0465fc39d.x: The Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas was published by ISRO's Space Applications Centre located at Ahmedabad.
xs: The Atlas was published by **ISRO's Space Applications Centre, Ahmedabad** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It is the **Desertification and Land Degradation Atlas of India 2021** (ISRO-SAC).
xa: It reports **97.85 Mha = 29.77%** of India degraded.
Major contributors: **water erosion + chemical degradation**.

n2b766fd6ef2.s: According to the AP SDG 15-related figures, the percentage of degraded land in Andhra Pradesh is:
n2b766fd6ef2.x: Under SDG 15 (SDG India Index 2023-24), degraded land is 33.81% of AP, about ten times Punjab's 3.15%. 18.28% is AP's forest cover and 21.26% its fallow-land share.
n2b766fd6ef2.tq: Distinguish the degradation percentage from forest cover and fallow-land figures.
xs: Degraded land is **33.81%** of AP (SDG 15, **SDG India Index 2023-24**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**18.28%** is AP's **forest cover** and **21.26%** its **fallow-land** share.
xa: The best state is **Punjab** at **3.15%** — AP's share is about ten times Punjab's.
AP's desertification area went up **3.45%** (Rajasthan **-1.34%**).
AP fallow land: **34.65 lakh ha** — more than its forest area.
AP tree cover: **2.87%**.

n35fa84dcf9a.s: Approximately what proportion of the Earth's land is covered by forests?
n35fa84dcf9a.x: FAO FRA 2025 puts forests at about 32% of Earth's land. 54% is the share of forests held by five countries (Russia, Brazil, Canada, USA, China), and 21.76 (Mha) is the land India restored in 2011-2020.
n35fa84dcf9a.tq: Use the numerical-value option set and distinguish a global figure from India-specific figures.
xs: Forests cover about **32%** of Earth's land (**FAO FRA 2025**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**54%** is the share of forests held by five countries; **21.76** Mha is what India restored during 2011-2020.
xa: Five countries with over **54%** of forests: **Russia, Brazil, Canada, USA, China**.
Net forest loss fell from **10.7 Mha/yr (1990s)** to **4.12 Mha/yr (2015-2025)**.
India rose to **9th** in total forest area (**10th in 2020**).

n8b6017ea616.s: Which one of the following correctly identifies the five countries that together contain more than half of the world's forests?
o: Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States and China
India, Brazil, Canada, Australia and China
Brazil, Canada, Australia, India and the United States
Russia, India, the United States, Indonesia and China
n8b6017ea616.x: More than 54% of the world's forests are found in Russia, Brazil, Canada, the United States and China.
n8b6017ea616.tq: Test a named-list fact; distinguish the exact membership of the group.
xs: **Russia, Brazil, Canada, the USA and China** hold over **54%** of forests — so option **(1)** is correct.
**India**, **Australia** and **Indonesia** are not in the FRA 2025 list of five.
xa: Forests cover about **32%** of Earth's land (**FAO FRA 2025**, Oct 2025).
**Asia** = only region with net gain 1990-2025, led by **China and India**.
India stays **3rd** in annual forest gain.

na90306c2cb3.s: As per older FAO FRA figures, annual net forest loss fell from 8.3 million ha in the 1990s to:
na90306c2cb3.x: The older FRA figures record a decline from 8.3 million ha per year in the 1990s to 5.2 million ha per year during 2000–2010.
xa: This FRA 2010-basis figure was asked in **APPSC 2018**.
Forests cover about **32%** of Earth's land.

n28551f3392b.s: The zones identified as having the highest forest loss are mainly the
o: coniferous forests of Russia and Canada alone
tropical forests of the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia
temperate forests of Europe and North America
mangrove forests of the Indian coastline alone
n28551f3392b.x: The highest forest loss is concentrated in tropical forests, especially in the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia.
n28551f3392b.tq: Use the geographic-cluster clue to identify the correct region rather than a single country.
xs: Highest forest loss is in **tropical forests of the Amazon, Congo Basin and Southeast Asia** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The Forest Declaration Assessment 2025 puts about **94%** of loss in **tropical** forests.
xa: Drivers: clearing for **agriculture**, urbanisation, industry, mining.
Impact: loss of the **CO2 sink** adds to the greenhouse effect.
⚠ **Asia** was the only region with net forest gain 1990-2025.

n5a9bdb6f152.s: About what share of India's degraded land faces desertification?
n5a9bdb6f152.x: About one-fourth of degraded land faces desertification; Rajasthan accounts for more than 23% of India's desertified land.
xa: ⚠ Desertification is land degradation in **drylands**, not the spread of existing deserts alone.
**Aravalli Green Wall** aims to check the **Thar's eastward spread**.
AP's desertification area went up **3.45%** (Rajasthan **-1.34%**).

n63f2799fde3.s: The Namo Van–Nagar Van Scheme primarily seeks to achieve which of the following?
o: Replacement of all rural forests with plantations
Expansion of mining areas around cities
Reduction of the urban heat island effect through urban forests
n63f2799fde3.x: The Namo Van–Nagar Van Scheme promotes urban forests with the aim of reducing the urban heat island effect.
n63f2799fde3.tq: Match the scheme with its specific environmental purpose.
xs: The **Namo Van - Nagar Van Scheme** aims at **reduction of the urban heat island effect through urban forests** — so option **(4)** is correct.
It was noted in **Jul 2026**.
xa: **Loss of vegetation** is one cause of UHI.
**AP Cool Surface Policy 2023**: affordable solutions against urban heat.
**NDMA** heat-wave action plan guidelines: **2016** (revised later).

n56179158b55.s: The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on:
n56179158b55.x: The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is observed on 17 June, following a 1994 UNGA decision.
n56179158b55.tq: Distinguish the environmental observance from other internationally known dates.
xs: The World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought is on **17 June** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was set by the **UNGA** in **1994**.
xa: **2026** host: **Kenya**; theme "**Rangelands: Recognise. Respect. Restore.**"
⚠ Sand and dust storms day = **12 July**.
UNCCD adopted **1994**, in force **1996**.

n14aaf8f457c.s: The Bonn Challenge was launched in 2011 by which of the following?
n14aaf8f457c.x: The Bonn Challenge was launched in 2011 by Germany and the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
n14aaf8f457c.tq: Test the launch-year and institutional partnership as a single factual pair.
xs: The Bonn Challenge was launched in **2011** by **Germany and IUCN** — so option **(3)** is correct.
The **African Union** leads the **Great Green Wall** in Africa, not the Bonn Challenge.
xa: Targets: **150 Mha by 2020**, **350 Mha by 2030** (extended **2014**, New York Declaration on Forests).
India joined at **Paris 2015** (21 Mha pledge) → raised to **26 Mha** (COP14, 2019).
Telangana led restoration 2011-2020 (**4.18 Mha**).

nf2c6947a0a9.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India and the Bonn Challenge?
o: India joined at Paris in 2015 with a pledge of 21 million hectares
Telangana led the States with about 4.18 million hectares restored
India restored about 21.76 million hectares during 2011-2020
Andhra Pradesh led all States in land restored during 2011-2020
nf2c6947a0a9.x: Per the MoEFCC-IUCN report Telangana led (4.18 Mha), followed by MP, Odisha, Gujarat and then Andhra Pradesh.
xa: India raised its target to **26 Mha by 2030** at **COP14 (2019)**.
⚠ Bonn Challenge = **Germany + IUCN, 2011**.
AP's degraded land is **33.81%**, about ten times Punjab's.

n348db123a9a.s: Which two regions are identified as the worst-hit continents or zones in terms of desertification?
o: Africa, particularly the Sahel, and Asia
n348db123a9a.x: Africa, especially the Sahel region, and Asia are identified as the worst-hit regions in relation to desertification.
n348db123a9a.tq: Use geographical pairing to distinguish the most affected regions from unrelated continents.
xs: The worst-hit regions are **Africa (Sahel) and Asia** — so option **(1)** is correct.
The notes name these two as the **worst-hit continents**; Europe, North America and Australia are not listed.
xa: The **Great Green Wall** (Africa) is an **African Union** belt across the Sahel, Senegal to Djibouti, to restore **100 Mha by 2030**.
Dust storms hit drylands of **NW India (Rajasthan)** and **West Asia/Sahel**.
UNCCD = treaty on **desertification, land degradation and drought**.

nedcd22af2f6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about land-restoration initiatives?
o: The Aravalli Green Wall aims to check the eastward spread of the Thar
The Great Green Wall is an African Union-led belt across the Sahel
The Bonn Challenge targets 150 Mha by 2020 and 350 Mha by 2030
The Bonn Challenge is an African Union-led belt across the Sahel
nedcd22af2f6.x: The Sahelian belt is the Great Green Wall of Africa; the Bonn Challenge is defined by its 150 Mha (2020) and 350 Mha (2030) restoration targets.
xa: Aravalli Green Wall: **41,410 ha** planted in 2024-25.
⚠ Bonn Challenge = **Germany + IUCN, 2011**.
**Great Green Wall of AP**: **SPSR Nellore** targets **50% green cover by 2047**.

n2854430aae0.s: On 24 December 2025, MoEFCC announced which measure for the Aravallis?
o: Declaration of the range as a tiger reserve
A ban on all construction activity
Cancellation of all existing mining leases
A ban on granting any new mining leases
n2854430aae0.x: On 24 December 2025, MoEFCC banned the grant of any new mining leases in the Aravallis.
xa: The **Aravalli Green Wall** restores Aravallis across **Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, Delhi**.
It acts as a barrier to the **Thar's eastward spread**; **41,410 ha** planted in 2024-25.
MoEFCC gets only **0.07%** of the Union budget (TH, 5 Jun 2026).

nc404686bcd5.s: The international day linked to the UN Decade on Combating Sand and Dust Storms (2025–2034) is observed on:
nc404686bcd5.x: The related day is observed on 12 July; the UNGA declared 2025–2034 the UN Decade on Combating Sand and Dust Storms.
xa: ⚠ **World Day to Combat Desertification and Drought** = **17 June** (UNGA, **1994**).
**2026 host Kenya**; theme "**Rangelands: Recognise. Respect. Restore.**"
Dust storms hit **Rajasthan** and West Asia/Sahel.

nf7737ce79b7.s: Which of the following best describes a cool roof?
o: A roof designed to store solar heat for night-time use
A roof made only of metallic sheets
A roof treated with a high-reflectance coating to reduce heat absorption
A roof covered entirely with vegetation
nf7737ce79b7.x: Cool roofs use white or reflective, high-reflectance coatings that reduce heat absorption and lower the indoor cooling load.
nf7737ce79b7.tq: Identify the precise functional definition instead of selecting a merely related roofing technology.
xs: A cool roof is **treated with a high-reflectance coating to reduce heat absorption** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Cool roofs use **white/reflective** coatings and cut the **indoor cooling load**.
xa: The **AP Cool Surface Policy 2023** promotes **reflective materials**.
UHI causes: **concrete/asphalt** (low albedo), loss of vegetation, waste heat, dense built canyons.
**NDMA** issued national heat-wave action plan guidelines in **2016**.

n2bdb5b925c6.s: Which one of the following is NOT an objective of the Andhra Pradesh Cool Surface Policy, 2023?
o: Promoting the use of reflective materials
Promoting rural heat as a separate policy objective
Providing affordable solutions against urban heat
n2bdb5b925c6.x: The policy objectives include affordable urban heat solutions, reduction of heat and energy demand, and promotion of reflective materials. Rural heat is not identified as an objective.
n2bdb5b925c6.tq: Find the option that falls outside the stated policy objectives.
xs: **Rural heat** is NOT an objective of the AP Cool Surface Policy 2023 — so option **(2)** is correct.
Its objectives: affordable solutions against **urban** heat, tackle **heat and energy demand**, promote **reflective materials**.
xa: ⚠ The **"rural heat"** trap was asked in **APPSC 2023**.
**Cool roofs** = high-reflectance roof coatings.
**71%** of Indians surveyed had faced heat waves (Yale survey, TH 5 Jun 2026).

n8a9831c79e9.s: Which Act made Central approval necessary for diversion of forest land?
n8a9831c79e9.x: The Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 made Central approval necessary for diverting forest land.
xa: Chronology: **Water 1974 → Water Cess 1977 → Forest 1980 → Air 1981 → EPA 1986 → NGT 2010**.
**Green Credit** afforestation can be swapped for compensatory afforestation under **Van (S&S) Rules 2023**.
The **Wildlife (Protection) Act** dates from **1972**.

na2fb546e8d7.s: The National Green Tribunal Act was enacted in:
na2fb546e8d7.x: The order is Air Act 1981, EPA 1986, Public Liability Insurance Act 1991 and NGT Act 2010.
xa: The **PLI Act 1991** was amended by the **Jan Vishwas Act, 2023**.
**Biological Diversity Act 2002** falls between PLI and NGT.
⚠ Water (**1974**) always precedes Air (**1981**) and EPA (**1986**).

n1f4e391aa78.s: Which body was renamed the Central Pollution Control Board by the 1988 amendment to the Water Act?
o: Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution
n1f4e391aa78.x: The Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution, created in 1974, was renamed the CPCB by the 1988 amendment.
n1f4e391aa78.tq: Use the predecessor-to-present-name relationship to avoid confusing neighbouring water institutions.
xs: The **Central Board for the Prevention and Control of Water Pollution** was renamed **CPCB** by the **1988 amendment** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It was created by the **Water Act** in **1974**.
xa: CPCB is a **statutory body** under **MoEFCC**; its chair is nominated by the **Central Government**.
CPCB **co-ordinates SPCBs**; it is the enforcement body under the EPA framework.
**CPCB (1974)** came before the Air Act, which gave it air functions.

n4f6fc26de9e.s: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) is:
o: A constitutional body under the Ministry of Finance
A judicial body under the National Green Tribunal Act
n4f6fc26de9e.x: The CPCB is a statutory body under MoEFCC and provides technical services to the Ministry under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
xa: Chairperson nominated by the **Central Government**.
Functions: **co-ordinates SPCBs**; technical assistance, research, training, national monitoring.
NAMP network: **1,646 stations in 603 cities (March 2026)**.

n1af2e11306d.s: For the purpose of environmental enforcement under the Environment (Protection) Act framework, which body is identified as the enforcement body?
n1af2e11306d.x: The Central Pollution Control Board is identified as the enforcement body under the Environment (Protection) Act framework.
n1af2e11306d.tq: Distinguish the pollution enforcement agency from other environment-related attached bodies.
xs: The enforcement body under the EPA framework is the **CPCB** — so option **(4)** is correct.
The **Central Zoo Authority** (1992) and **FSI** are bodies under MoEFCC with other roles.
xa: CPCB is a **statutory body** giving technical services to MoEFCC under **EPA 1986**.
CPCB **co-ordinates SPCBs**.
**National AQI** launched **2015**.

ncd5a444e733.s: The Central Zoo Authority, a body under MoEFCC, was established in 1992 under the:
ncd5a444e733.x: The Central Zoo Authority was set up in 1992 under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972.
xa: MoEF became **MoEFCC in 2014**.
Department of Environment: **1980**; Ministry of Environment and Forests: **1985**.

n812e3257a3b.s: Which of the following is a common requirement under both the Water Act, 1974 and the Air Act, 1981?
o: Compulsory registration under the Water Cess Act
Declaration of every industrial site as an air pollution control area
Prior consent of the concerned Board to establish and operate a polluting unit
Prior approval of the National Green Tribunal for every industrial unit
n812e3257a3b.x: Both Acts require prior consent of the Pollution Control Board for establishing and operating a unit that may cause pollution.
n812e3257a3b.tq: Find the common legal mechanism rather than a feature belonging exclusively to one Act.
xs: Both Acts require **prior consent of the Board to establish and operate a polluting unit** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Industries need this consent **before discharging effluent**.
**Air pollution control areas** are declared by the State Government under the Air Act only; no NGT approval is required for each unit.
xa: Two-stage consent from SPCB: **Consent to Establish (CTE)** before setting up; **Consent to Operate (CTO)** before production.
**Jan 2026** amendment: single integrated application for Air and Water consents + waste authorisations.
**CTO valid until cancelled** (**29 Jan 2026**), instead of periodic renewal.

nd3a3084b7d9.s: Which of the following best describes the statutory role of the AP Pollution Control Board?
o: It implements the Water, Air and Environment Protection Acts and specified waste-management rules in Andhra Pradesh.
It administers only the Wildlife Protection Act in Andhra Pradesh.
It functions exclusively as an appellate judicial tribunal for environmental disputes.
It regulates only municipal drinking-water supply and not industrial pollution.
nd3a3084b7d9.x: The APPCB implements the Water Act, Air Act and Environment (Protection) Act, along with rules relating to hazardous, biomedical, plastic and solid waste.
nd3a3084b7d9.tq: Select the comprehensive but precise description and reject the exclusive-function distractors.
xs: **APPCB implements the Water, Air and EP Acts and waste rules** in AP — so option **(1)** is correct.
Waste rules: **Hazardous, Bio-medical, Plastic, Solid**.
It is a regulator, not a judicial tribunal or a wildlife body.
xa: APPCB was set up in **1976** under the Water Act.
It issues **siting guidelines** for industries and SOPs for **marine outfall monitoring** and hazardous waste.
**Computerised inspection allocation** — high-risk industries inspected more often (APSES 2025-26).

n44facc2eb31.s: Which of the following is an additional regulatory activity of the AP Pollution Control Board?
o: Granting forest clearance for diversion of forest land
n44facc2eb31.x: The APPCB issues siting guidelines for industries and also prepares SOPs for marine outfall monitoring and hazardous waste.
xa: APPCB implements **Water, Air and EP Acts** + waste rules.
Ease of Doing Business: **computerised inspection allocation**.
APPCB set up in **1976** (APSES 2024-25).

na1e79dd8fcf.s: The Supreme Court in M.K. Ranjitsinh v. Union of India recognised environmental protection as inherently included in:
na1e79dd8fcf.x: The Court held that environmental protection is inherently included within Corporate Social Responsibility.
na1e79dd8fcf.tq: Associate the case with the precise legal principle rather than a neighbouring constitutional concept.
xs: In **M.K. Ranjitsinh v UoI**, environmental protection was held inherent in **Corporate Social Responsibility** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The notes record that **CSR inherently includes environmental protection**.
xa: **Vanashakti v UoI**: no retrospective ECs via the **2021 Office Memorandum**.
SC (**Aug 2025**) upheld PCBs' power to impose environmental compensation.
**NGT suo motu** notice to **Rajasthan, MP, UP** over sewage in drinking water.

n04c4ac70a5b.s: Which is regarded as India's first pollution-control law?
o: Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Cess Act, 1977
Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
n04c4ac70a5b.x: The Water Act, 1974 is India's first pollution-control law; the NGT Act, 2010 is the latest in the chain.
xa: The Water Act was India's **first pollution law**, passed under **Article 252**.
The NGT is a **specialised environmental tribunal**.
**CPCB (1974)** came before the Air Act.

n9097d7fa004.s: The Andhra Pradesh Pollution Control Board was established in which year?
n9097d7fa004.x: The APPCB was set up in 1976 under the Water Act.
n9097d7fa004.tq: Discriminate between closely related years associated with environmental institutions and laws.
xs: **APPCB** was set up in **1976** under the Water Act — so option **(2)** is correct.
**1974** is the Water Act/CPCB year; **1981** the Air Act; **1986** the EPA.
xa: APPCB enforces **Water, Air, EP Acts** and waste rules (APSES 2024-25).
It issues **siting guidelines** for industries.
**Computerised inspection allocation**: high-risk industries inspected more often.

nenvironment-21-6.s: The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) deals with which of the following types of pollution?
nenvironment-21-6.x: The CPCB deals with water pollution (under the 1974 Act) and air pollution (under the 1981 Act).
n: The CPCB deals with water and air pollution. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #21 · pp 37-38]
xs: The **CPCB** deals with **water and air pollution** — so option **(4)** is correct.
