**RDF** is used in **cement kilns**.

n137b58e14aa.s: Which pair of Andhra Pradesh cities is associated with WtE plants?
n137b58e14aa.x: The cited Andhra Pradesh WtE plants are located at Guntur and Visakhapatnam.
n137b58e14aa.tq: Recall a location pair without substituting nearby urban centres.
xs: AP's **WtE plants** are at **Guntur** and **Visakhapatnam** — option **(1)** is correct.
**Ongole** is linked with biomining; **Nellore** with a CHWTSDF.
xa: India: **21 operational WtE plants**, **170+ MW** (Feb 2026).
**Anantapur** is setting up a **170 TPD** waste-processing plant.

nafc6ccde64f.s: In Andhra Pradesh, the ban on single-use plastic and carry bags applies to carry bags having thickness below:
nafc6ccde64f.x: Andhra Pradesh bans single-use plastic and carry bags below 120 microns, with enforcement involving the Revenue Department, Police and Pollution Control Board.
nafc6ccde64f.tq: Distinguish the precise statutory threshold from nearby thickness values.
xs: AP bans SUP and carry bags **under 120 microns** — option **(4)** is correct.
Enforcement involves **Revenue, Police, PCB**.
xa: National carry-bag limit is also **120 microns** from **31 Dec 2022**.
AP seizures: **5,505.06 kg** carry bags + **3,571.40 kg** SUP (SES 2025-26).
**100 microns** is the limit for banned **PVC banners**.

n0b286a645e6.s: Which State is identified as the highest solid-waste-generating State in India?
n0b286a645e6.x: Maharashtra is identified as the highest solid-waste-generating State.
n0b286a645e6.tq: Test the precise State association rather than the general urban-waste trend.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the highest solid-waste-generating State — option **(3)** is correct (APPSC-G2 2025 key).
The notes name no other State for this record, so the remaining options are not the answer.
xa: **Indore (MP)** keeps ranking **#1** as the cleanest city.
First **Swachh Survekshan**: **2016** — world's largest annual urban cleanliness survey.
India = **3rd largest** e-waste generator, after **China** and **USA**.

n8ed6d3188ea.s: Which method of solid-waste disposal is described as not viable in urban India?
n8ed6d3188ea.x: Composting, incineration and landfilling are all used in urban India; only uncontrolled dumping is described as not viable.
xa: **Composting** = aerobic, for biodegradable organic/wet waste; **incineration** suits hazardous, biomedical, combustible waste.
**Sanitary landfill** is the most common and economic method, for **residual** waste only.
Incineration cuts volume **up to 90%** but causes air pollution and ash disposal problems.

n9f50cf76f05.s: Which of the following correctly describes the SATAT–GOBARdhan linkage?
o: It establishes 500 new MRFs exclusively for e-waste.
It provides 500 MW from existing WtE plants only.
It targets 500 new waste-to-wealth CBG plants.
n9f50cf76f05.x: The SATAT and GOBARdhan linkage targets 500 new waste-to-wealth compressed biogas plants.
n9f50cf76f05.tq: Link two initiatives with their stated numerical target and output.
xs: The **SATAT + GOBARdhan** linkage targets **500 new waste-to-wealth (CBG) plants** — option **(4)** is correct.
**CBG plants** turn municipal **wet waste** into green fuel.
xa: **GOBARdhan (2018, under SBM-G):** cattle dung, agri and solid waste → **biogas + bio-slurry**; unified GOBARdhan portal.
**Circular Bioenergy Scheme (MoPNG)** supports **100%** scientific processing.
SBM-U 2.0 also targets **10,000 TPD** additional WtE capacity.

o: Secondary microplastics formed only by tyre wear
Primary microplastic pellets generally measuring 1–5 mm
Biodegradable plastic fibres used in clothing
naecae49fc05.x: Nurdles are primary microplastic pellets, generally 1–5 mm in size.
naecae49fc05.tq: Distinguish a specific microplastic form from its sources and effects.
xs: **Nurdles** are **primary microplastic pellets** of **1-5 mm** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Tyre-wear** microplastics come from **synthetic rubber** — a different source.
xa: India's **first major nurdle landing**: **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck (LDPE, HDPE).
Microplastics = particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS 2023).

n5e02cb767f3.s: India's first major nurdle landing was reported in:
o: Kerala, from the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck
West Bengal, from a fishing vessel
n5e02cb767f3.x: The first major nurdle landing in India occurred in Kerala following the MSC Elsa 3 shipwreck. The nurdles included LDPE and HDPE.
n5e02cb767f3.tq: Combine location, event and source-vessel clues.
xs: India's first major nurdle landing was in **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck — option **(1)** is correct.
The nurdles were **LDPE and HDPE**.
xa: Nurdles = primary microplastic pellets (**1-5 mm**).
**National Action Plan for Marine Litter** (Dec 2025).

n69d1fae4bef.s: Microplastics are generally defined as plastic particles of size:
n69d1fae4bef.x: Microplastics are particles up to 5 mm (APPSC-GS 2023). 'Up to 5 micrometres only' is far too narrow, while 5-50 cm and above 5 mm describe larger debris.
n69d1fae4bef.tq: Micro = up to 5 mm; nurdles 1-5 mm.
xs: Microplastics are particles **up to 5 mm** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2023).
"**Above 5 mm**" and **5-50 cm** describe larger debris; "5 micrometres only" is far too narrow.
xa: **Nurdles** = primary microplastic pellets, **1-5 mm**.
Hidden sources: **tea bags, chewing gum, wet wipes, glitter, cigarette filters, polyester clothing**.

n3d98d3aebed.s: Which was the first country to ban thin plastic bags, in 2002?
n3d98d3aebed.x: Bangladesh banned thin plastic bags in 2002; New Zealand's supermarket produce-bag ban came in July 2023.
xa: ⚠ **Bangladesh** = first country (thin bags); **New Zealand** = first, thin produce bags in supermarkets.
India's **first major nurdle landing** was in **Kerala**, from the **MSC Elsa 3** shipwreck.
**Maharashtra** is the highest solid-waste-generating State (APPSC-G2 **2025** key).

nb8de0505d1c.s: According to MeitY, approximately how much e-waste was collected and processed in India in FY 2021?
nb8de0505d1c.x: MeitY put e-waste collected and processed in FY 2021 at about 3.54 lakh tonnes (APPSC-GS 2021 key). 2.2 MT (2025) and 1.75 MT are generation figures, and 35.4 lakh tonnes is ten times the stated value.
nb8de0505d1c.tq: Processed FY21 = 3.54 lakh t; generated 2025 = 2.2 MT.
xs: **MeitY**: about **3.54 lakh tonnes** of e-waste collected and processed in **FY 2021** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2021 key).
**2.2 MT** (2025) and **1.75 MT** are **generation** figures; **35.4 lakh tonnes** is ten times the stated value.
xa: Only **10-20%** of materials are recovered in informal processing.
**468 authorised recyclers** (CPCB 2024).

nchemistry-8-43.s: Which of the following is an impact of non-biodegradable plastics?
nchemistry-8-43.x: Non-biodegradable plastics persist, pollute, break into microplastics, create landfill problems and harm wildlife.
n: Non-biodegradable plastics persist in the environment. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics cause pollution. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics produce microplastics. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics create landfill issues. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
Non-biodegradable plastics harm wildlife. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #8 · pp 30-33]
xa: **Most synthetic plastics** are non-biodegradable — **polythene**, **PVC**, **polystyrene**, **Teflon**.
**Microplastics** are particles **up to 5 mm** (APPSC-GS **2023**).
FSSAI found microplastics in **all tested sugar and salt samples**.

nenvironment-26-1.s: Which of the following is compost?
o: Disposal of solid waste in a designated land area
Decomposed organic waste that becomes nutrient-rich material
nenvironment-26-1.x: Compost is organic waste that has broken down into nutrient-rich material. The other options describe landfill, recycling and incineration.
nenvironment-26-1.tq: Match each waste term to its meaning.
n: Compost is decomposed organic waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost is a nutrient-rich material. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
A landfill is the disposal of solid waste in a designated land area. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Incineration is the controlled burning of waste. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Recycling is the processing of waste into usable material. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost contains organic matter. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
Compost contains nutrients. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #26 · pp 45-47]
xs: **Compost** is **decomposed** organic waste that becomes **nutrient-rich material** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Disposal in a designated land area** is a **landfill**; **processing waste into usable material** is **recycling**.
**Controlled burning** of waste is **incineration**.
xa: **Indore method** = aerobic composting with turning at intervals.
⚠ **Bangalore method** = anaerobic pit composting, **4-6 months**.
**Vermicompost** is produced using **earthworms**.

ne8b19050690.s: Which one of the following is biodegradable?
ne8b19050690.x: Wool is a natural fibre and is biodegradable. Aluminium foil, glass and synthetic rubber are non-biodegradable.
ne8b19050690.tq: Use the material-property distinction to identify the biodegradable item.
xs: **Wool** is a natural fibre and is **biodegradable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Biodegradable matter is decomposed by microorganisms, mainly **bacteria**, into simpler substances.
**Glass bottles**, metals such as **aluminium foil**, and **synthetic rubber / tyres** are all **non-biodegradable**.
xa: Other biodegradable items: food/kitchen waste, **vegetable peels**, **cow-dung**, **paddy husk**, **paper**, **sewage**, **cotton**.
**DDT** and **heavy metals** are non-biodegradable and accumulate in the environment.
⚠ Exam angle: "which is NOT biodegradable" → **tin/metal/glass/plastic**; "which IS biodegradable" → **wool, peels**.

nb5f6919394a.s: Which one of the following is NOT biodegradable?
nb5f6919394a.x: Tin scrap is a metal and cannot normally be decomposed by microorganisms. Paddy husk, vegetable peels and cow-dung are biodegradable.
nb5f6919394a.tq: Find the non-biodegradable item by separating metals from organic wastes.
xs: **Tin scrap** is a metal and is **non-biodegradable** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Metals (**tin**, aluminium foil, metal scrap) are not broken down by microbes and accumulate in the environment.
**Vegetable peels**, **paddy husk** and **cow-dung** are biodegradable — decomposed by bacteria.
xa: Non-biodegradable waste is mainly **inorganic**: plastics, **glass bottles**, DDT, heavy metals, synthetic rubber tyres.
Natural fibres — **wool** and **cotton** — are biodegradable, as are **paper** and **sewage**.
Aerobic decomposition of biodegradable waste gives **compost**; anaerobic gives **methane (CH4)**/biogas.

nfdea976f1f3.s: Which footprint measures freshwater use as blue, green and grey water?
nfdea976f1f3.x: The water footprint counts freshwater use as blue, green and grey water; the ecological footprint is the land and water needed to support consumption and absorb waste.
xa: ⚠ **Carbon** = GHGs; **Ecological** = land and water; **Water** = blue, green, grey.
**1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e** avoided or removed.
**Scope 2** = emissions from purchased electricity or heat.

n302d7788859.s: A company's diesel generator emits greenhouse gases, its purchased electricity causes indirect emissions, and emissions occur in the manufacture and transport of its purchased inputs. These are respectively classified as:
n302d7788859.x: Direct emissions from owned sources are Scope 1, emissions from purchased electricity or heat are Scope 2, and the remaining value-chain emissions are Scope 3.
n302d7788859.tq: Classify the emissions by asking whether they are owned, purchased-energy or value-chain emissions.
xs: They are **Scope 1, Scope 2 and Scope 3** respectively — option **(1)** is correct.
Own **diesel generator** = **Scope 1** (direct, owned source); **purchased electricity** = **Scope 2**; **purchased inputs** = **Scope 3** (rest of value chain).
xa: **Net Zero Portal (MoEFCC, Sep 2026)**: **Scope 1 and 2 reporting encouraged; Scope 3 voluntary**.
**NAPCC Dashboard** launched with it (**17 Sep 2026**).

nde83b7412f0.s: REDD+ stands for Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and ____.
nde83b7412f0.x: REDD+ is Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation; India takes part and forest conservation can earn tradable credits.
xa: **1 carbon credit = 1 tonne CO2e**.

ncf531248edc.s: NET Power's Allam-Fetvedt cycle plant burns natural gas in oxygen and uses ____ as the working fluid.
ncf531248edc.x: The La Porte, Texas plant burns gas in oxygen with supercritical CO2 as the working fluid and captures nearly all its CO2.
xa: **Nuclear** supplies close to **one-third** of the world's low-carbon electricity.
**CCS** = store only; **CCUS** = use or store.

n5d7759178ec.s: Under which Article of the EU CBAM Regulation can a carbon price already paid, such as under India's CCTS, be deducted?
n5d7759178ec.x: Article 9 allows deduction of a carbon price already paid; CBAM revenue stays in Europe.
xa: ⚠ **EU** CBAM definitive phase = **1 Jan 2026**; **UK** CBAM = **1 Jan 2027**.
CBAM covers **iron and steel, aluminium, cement, fertilisers, hydrogen, electricity**.
Importers buy **CBAM certificates** priced on the **EU ETS**.

nenvironment-39-8.s: The Common Carbon Metric is associated with which of the following?
nenvironment-39-8.x: The Common Carbon Metric measures carbon emissions from running buildings.
nenvironment-39-8.tq: Recall what the Common Carbon Metric covers.
n: The Common Carbon Metric is associated with building operations. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
The key provision of the SWM Rules 2016 concerns landfill and waste-processing site criteria. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 68-70]
xs: The **Common Carbon Metric** relates to **building operations** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Electronics recycling** is **R2**; **wastewater** and **electricity** is the **MFC**.
**Landfill and waste-processing site criteria** come from the **SWM Rules, 2016**.
xa: **Carbon footprint** = **total GHGs emitted by human activities**, tonnes CO2e per year.
**Scope 1** = direct emissions from owned sources; **Scope 3** = rest of the value chain.
**Bhutan** is **carbon-negative**.

ne97db99e28a.s: Which terrestrial ecosystem stores more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem?
ne97db99e28a.x: Tropical peatlands store more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem.
ne97db99e28a.tq: Identify the superlative comparison and avoid substituting a generally forested ecosystem.
xs: **Tropical peatlands** store **more carbon per hectare** than any other terrestrial ecosystem — option **(1)** is correct.
Grasslands, savannas and alpine forests are not given this record in the notes.
xa: **Blue carbon**: mangroves, seagrass, salt marshes.
**CO2 fertilisation** = **70%** of Earth's recent greening.

n77c2d76560b.s: The National Carbon Project is implemented under:
o: National Action Plan on Climate Change
n77c2d76560b.x: The National Carbon Project is under the ISRO Geosphere-Biosphere Programme and assesses carbon pools, fluxes and net carbon balance of India's terrestrial biomes.
xa: CO2-observing satellites: **OCO-2** (NASA), **GOSAT** (Japan).
**Green India Mission** raises carbon stock.

nb6b21dc4742.s: Which one of the following is NOT included among the five IPCC carbon pools?
nb6b21dc4742.x: The five pools are above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter and soil organic carbon. Atmospheric oxygen is not one of them.
nb6b21dc4742.tq: Recall the five-member list and identify the item outside the classification.
xs: **Atmospheric oxygen** is not an IPCC carbon pool — option **(2)** is the answer.
The **five pools**: **above-ground biomass, below-ground biomass, dead wood, litter, soil organic carbon**.
xa: **National Carbon Project** assesses carbon pools and fluxes under **ISRO**.
**Green India Mission** raises carbon stock.

nb62b64d8619.s: The process of capturing carbon dioxide from industrial processes and storing it so that it does not enter the atmosphere is called:
nb62b64d8619.x: Capturing and storing CO2 from industrial processes is carbon sequestration (APPSC-GS 2024 key; carbon capture was also accepted). CO2 fertilisation is plant greening from higher CO2, carbon leakage is emissions shifting abroad (the CBAM concern), and offsetting means using credits to balance emissions.
xs: Capturing and storing CO2 from industrial processes = **carbon sequestration** — option **(1)** is correct (APPSC-GS 2024 key; carbon capture also allowed).
**CO2 fertilisation** = greening from higher CO2; **carbon leakage** = what **CBAM** tries to stop.
xa: Sequestration types: **geological**, **ocean**, **terrestrial**.
**CCS** stores CO2 from **stationary sources** such as power plants.

n6a4c9e9cf25.s: Which technology combines bioenergy with carbon capture and storage to give net-negative emissions?
n6a4c9e9cf25.x: BECCS (Bioenergy with Carbon Capture and Storage) gives net-negative emissions.
xa: **Direct Air Capture** pulls CO2 straight from ambient air.
DST set up **five CCU testbeds** in the **cement sector**.
NET Power's **Allam cycle** plant burns gas in oxygen, capturing nearly all CO2.

n2cb420e446a.s: The carbon-removal method that pulls CO2 straight from ambient air is:
n2cb420e446a.x: Direct Air Capture pulls CO2 from ambient air; enhanced rock weathering spreads crushed silicate rock on land.
xa: **BECCS** → net-negative emissions.
**CCS** stores CO2 in geological or ocean formations.

n459e15de81d.s: Gold Standard, a voluntary carbon standard, was founded by which organisation?
n459e15de81d.x: Gold Standard was founded by WWF, the World Wide Fund for Nature.
n459e15de81d.tq: Identify the founding organisation rather than the administrator of a different carbon market.
xs: **Gold Standard** was founded by **WWF (World Wide Fund for Nature)** — option **(1)** is correct.
**BEE** administers India's CCTS — not a voluntary standard founder.
xa: **Verified Carbon Standard** is run by **Verra**.
Carbon credits began with the **Kyoto Protocol (1997)** → **CDM** → **CERs**.

n8fc5ffd69e9.s: Which pair correctly identifies the first country to propose and the first country to actually levy a livestock carbon tax?
n8fc5ffd69e9.x: New Zealand was the first country to propose a tax on agricultural emissions, while Denmark is to become the first to actually levy a livestock carbon tax from 2030.
n8fc5ffd69e9.tq: Distinguish a proposal from actual implementation and keep the countries in the correct order.
xs: **New Zealand** was first to **propose** an agri-emissions tax; **Denmark** first to **levy** a livestock carbon tax (from **2030**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Option (4) reverses them; the UK is not named.
xa: New Zealand fact = **APPSC-G1 2024** key.
⚠ **New Zealand** = propose; **Denmark** = levy (from 2030).

need2812edac.s: Palli village in Samba district was declared India’s first carbon-neutral panchayat in which year?
need2812edac.x: Palli in Samba, Jammu and Kashmir, was declared India’s first carbon-neutral panchayat in 2022.
need2812edac.tq: Combine the first-in-India claim with its exact year and location.
xs: **Palli** (Samba, J&K) became India's **first carbon-neutral panchayat** in **2022** — option **(3)** is correct.
2018, 2020 and 2024 are not the stated year.
xa: **Ladakh** is working to be a **carbon-neutral UT** (2026).
**CCTS** = India's **first mandatory compliance carbon market**.

n494b0f9b871.s: NITI Aayog's decarbonisation roadmaps for the cement, aluminium and MSME sectors rely on which combination of measures?
o: Round-the-clock renewable-energy power, nuclear power and CCUS
Hydropower, biofuels and ocean alkalinity enhancement only
Natural gas, nuclear disarmament and direct air capture only
Coal expansion, diesel generation and afforestation only
n494b0f9b871.x: The roadmaps rely on renewable energy available round the clock, nuclear power and carbon capture, utilisation and storage.
n494b0f9b871.tq: Identify the complete policy package rather than selecting a single decarbonisation measure.
xs: **NITI Aayog** roadmaps rely on **RE round-the-clock power, nuclear and CCUS** — option **(1)** is correct.
They cover **cement, aluminium and MSMEs**.
xa: **CCUS** captures CO2 and **uses** it or **stores** it permanently; supports **coal gasification and hydrogen**.
**Nuclear** supplies close to **one-third** of the world's low-carbon electricity.

n97c56147884.s: Which of the following is NOT a natural carbon sink identified in the context of carbon sequestration?
n97c56147884.x: Forests, soil and oceans are natural carbon sinks. Chlor-alkali plants are industrial entities covered by emission-intensity targets, not natural sinks.
n97c56147884.tq: Find the odd category by separating natural systems from an industrial sector.
xs: **Chlor-alkali plants** are not a natural sink — option **(1)** is the answer.
**Natural sinks** are **forests, soil, oceans**; chlor-alkali is a **CCTS-covered industry**.
xa: **Blue carbon** is stored by **mangroves, seagrass and salt marshes**.
**Tropical peatlands** store more carbon per hectare than any other terrestrial ecosystem.

na3a40d443b0.s: The Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) under the Kyoto Protocol issues:
na3a40d443b0.x: The CDM issues Certified Emission Reductions (CERs); the VCS is run by Verra. One carbon credit equals one tonne CO2e.
xa: **Gold Standard** was founded by **WWF**.
India's **CCTS** trades **Indian Carbon Credits (ICCs)**.

na0bce08e879.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS)?
o: It is India's first mandatory compliance carbon market.
It was notified under Section 14AA of the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986.
It is administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency under the Ministry of Power.
na0bce08e879.x: Section 14AA belongs to the Energy Conservation Act, 2001, not the Environment (Protection) Act.
xa: **Oct 2025:** targets for **aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp & paper**; **282 obligated entities**.
The offset mechanism has **9 methodologies**.
⚠ The **UK** recognised CCTS as a qualifying carbon price (**Sep 2026**).

nf2931b3d4d7.s: Emission-intensity targets for aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali and pulp and paper were notified in October 2025 under:
nf2931b3d4d7.x: These sectoral emission-intensity targets were notified under India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS).
xa: Only **China, EU and South Korea** cover more than India's CCTS (World Bank 2026).
Cement **~6%**, aluminium **~2.8%** of India's GHG emissions.

n6ee827fffc8.s: The definitive phase of the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) started on:
n6ee827fffc8.x: CBAM had a transitional phase from 2023 and its definitive phase began on 1 January 2026; certificates are priced on the EU ETS.
xa: CBAM aims to stop **carbon leakage**; also covers some downstream goods (**screws, bolts**).
⚠ **UK** CBAM starts **1 Jan 2027**.

ncd9f5984078.s: From FY 2025-26, coal-based power plants must co-fire what share of biomass?
ncd9f5984078.x: The co-firing requirement is 5% in FY 2024-25 and 7% from FY 2025-26, monitored by the SAMARTH mission.
xa: **BECCS** (bioenergy + CCS) → **net-negative** emissions.
**2035 NDC**: **60%** non-fossil power capacity.

n59bfbb8de5f.s: The Gevra coal mine, listed among India's 'carbon bombs', is in:
n59bfbb8de5f.x: Gevra is in Chhattisgarh and Rajmahal in Jharkhand; a carbon bomb is a fossil project that could emit over 1 Gt CO2 in its lifetime.
xa: India's **2035 NDC**: **47%** emission-intensity cut vs 2005.
Coal plants must co-fire **biomass** (5% → 7%).

n01d1f4b4a6f.s: India's 2035 NDC targets what cut in emission intensity compared with 2005?
n01d1f4b4a6f.x: The 2035 NDC targets a 47% cut in emission intensity vs 2005 and 60% non-fossil power capacity.
xa: Earlier pledge: **33-35%** intensity cut by **2030**.
Indian carbon bombs: **Gevra** and **Rajmahal** coal mines.

n2887aae1e63.s: The DST's cement-sector initiative concerning carbon capture and utilisation consists of:
o: three CCU testbeds forming a regional demonstration network
seven DAC testbeds for urban transport
five CCU testbeds forming a first-of-its-kind research cluster
five CCS testbeds located only in coal mines
n2887aae1e63.x: DST has established five Carbon Capture and Utilisation testbeds in the cement sector as a first-of-its-kind research cluster.
n2887aae1e63.tq: Check both the number of testbeds and the technology abbreviation.
xs: **DST** set up **five CCU testbeds** in the **cement sector** — a **first-of-its-kind research cluster** — option **(3)** is correct.
They are **CCU** (utilisation), not CCS or DAC testbeds.
xa: Cement = **~6%** of India's GHG emissions.
**CCUS** supports coal gasification and hydrogen.

n29d31d4b3fd.s: Which of the following correctly characterises the Budget 2026–27 carbon credit programme?
o: It follows the DST roadmap and is industrial in orientation, rather than being a farmer-only scheme.
It is a panchayat-level programme focused only on blue carbon.
It follows the Kyoto Protocol and is administered exclusively by WWF.
It is a voluntary scheme restricted to 282 agricultural entities.
n29d31d4b3fd.x: The programme follows the DST roadmap and concerns industrial carbon credits; it is not a farmer-only scheme.
n29d31d4b3fd.tq: Distinguish the policy’s target and institutional roadmap from attractive but incorrect sectoral labels.
xs: The **Budget 2026-27 carbon credit programme** follows the **DST roadmap** and is **industrial, not a farmer scheme** — option **(1)** is correct (Mar 2026).
**282** is the number of CCTS obligated entities, not agricultural entities.
xa: India could earn **$20-40 bn** from voluntary credits by 2030.
Agricultural credits face **measurement and credibility gaps** (Dec 2025).

n7f700b3ac8a.s: Which Union Territory's carbon-neutral effort includes solar water lifting, passive solar buildings, geothermal heating and electric vehicles?
n7f700b3ac8a.x: These measures are part of Ladakh's effort to become a carbon-neutral Union Territory.
xa: **Palli (Samba, J&K)** = first **carbon-neutral panchayat** (**2022**).
**Maruti Suzuki** railway siding = world's first **modal-shift** project under VCS.

n22e9f175ab2.s: Portland limestone cement is also known as:
n22e9f175ab2.x: Portland limestone cement is green cement, an example of green technology in the cement industry.
xa: Green tech also uses **alternative fuels** — biomass, waste-derived fuel.
Other end-of-pipe tools: **scrubbers**, **selective catalytic reduction** (UPSC).

n1b9d4375503.s: Incineration of waste is best classified as:
o: A conventional method of waste treatment
n1b9d4375503.x: Incineration is a conventional waste-treatment method and is not classified as an alternative pollution-control approach in this context.
n1b9d4375503.tq: Discriminate between a conventional pollution-control method and alternatives to it.
xs: **Incineration** is a **conventional** method of waste treatment, **NOT an alternative** (PYQ) — option **(2)** is correct.
It is not carbon storage, green cement or bioremediation.
xa: ⚠ Trap: incineration = conventional; **green tech, CCS, bioremediation** = alternatives.
**Green cement** = **Portland limestone cement**.

n9183e44f9f6.s: The regulatory approach associated with the Jan Vishwas reforms is described as a shift from:
o: Trust-based regulation to manual command-and-control regulation
Technology-enabled regulation to prohibition of digital systems
Command-and-control regulation to trust-based, technology-enabled regulation
Judicial regulation to complete self-regulation without technology
n9183e44f9f6.x: The reforms are described as moving regulation from a command-and-control model to trust-based, technology-enabled regulation.
n9183e44f9f6.tq: Identify the correctly oriented before-and-after comparison.
xs: The shift is from **command-and-control** to **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation (2025-26) — option **(3)** is correct.
Option (1) reverses the direction; technology is used, not prohibited.
xa: **Jan Vishwas Act 2023** turned jail into **monetary penalties** for minor offences.
**CTO** now valid **till cancelled** (Jan 2026).
**PARIVESH 3.0**: single-window clearances + **compliance monitoring**.

n4e4e52c8f37.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Jan Vishwas reforms to pollution laws?
o: The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act was passed in 2023.
It decriminalised minor offences under the Air Act and the Environment (Protection) Act.
The Water Act was amended likewise in 2024.
The reforms replaced monetary penalties with imprisonment for minor offences.
n4e4e52c8f37.x: The reforms replaced jail with monetary penalties for minor offences, not the reverse.
xa: Shift: "**command and control**" → **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation.
Penalties go to the **Environmental (Protection) Fund** under **Sec 16 EPA**.

nfaa0c0f6a4a.s: Under the 2026 Rules, the Environmental (Protection) Fund is shared between States/UTs and the Centre in the ratio:
nfaa0c0f6a4a.x: The Fund (Section 16, EP Act; audited by the CAG) is shared 75% States/UTs and 25% Centre.
xa: Uses: monitoring, **remediation of contaminated sites**, labs, clean-tech R&D.
**Jan Vishwas Act, 2023** decriminalised minor offences under the **Air Act** and **EP Act**.
⚠ Water Act = **Sec 33A**; Air Act = **Sec 31A**; EPA Fund = **Sec 16**.

n813eef43ecb.s: In August 2025, the Supreme Court upheld the power of Pollution Control Boards to impose environmental compensation under:
o: Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act
Section 16 of the Environment (Protection) Act alone
Section 33A of the Air Act and Section 31A of the Water Act
n813eef43ecb.x: The Supreme Court upheld PCB power under Section 33A of the Water Act and Section 31A of the Air Act.
n813eef43ecb.tq: Match each statutory section with the correct Act instead of swapping the pair.
xs: The SC (**Aug 2025**) upheld PCB power to impose **environmental compensation** under **Sec 33A Water Act** and **Sec 31A Air Act** — option **(1)** is correct.
Option (4) swaps the Acts; **Sec 16 EPA** is the **Environmental (Protection) Fund**, not compensation.
xa: ⚠ Water Act = **Sec 33A**; Air Act = **Sec 31A**; EPA Fund = **Sec 16**.
**Jan Vishwas Act, 2023** decriminalised minor offences under the **Air Act** + **EP Act**; the Water Act followed in **2024**.
**CTO** (**Jan 2026**): valid till cancelled.
Shift: "command and control" → **trust-based, technology-enabled** regulation (2025-26).

n981494b741a.s: Carbon capture and storage (CCS) captures CO2 from:
o: Point sources such as cement plants
n981494b741a.x: CCS captures CO2 from point sources such as cement plants; it remains largely at the research stage.
xa: **NITI Aayog** issued a report on a **CCUS policy framework (2022)**.
⚠ Trap: **incineration** = conventional; green tech, CCS, bioremediation = alternatives.

ne14a60015ee.s: Compared with conventional methods, bioremediation is:
ne14a60015ee.x: Bioremediation is eco-friendly and cost-effective but slower, and its results vary with local conditions.
xa: Bioremediation is **eco-friendly** — an alternative to conventional tools.
Conventional end-of-pipe tools: **ESPs, scrubbers, SCR**.

n719711a778f.s: PARIVESH 3.0 is primarily designed as a:
o: single-window portal for clearances and compliance monitoring
grant scheme for strengthening Pollution Control Boards
programme for replacing BS-IV vehicles with BS-VI vehicles
mobile application for publishing air-quality readings
n719711a778f.x: PARIVESH 3.0 functions as a single-window portal for environmental clearances and compliance monitoring.
n719711a778f.tq: Identify the precise institutional function rather than the associated environmental programme.
xs: **PARIVESH 3.0** is a **single-window portal for clearances** + **compliance monitoring** (2025-26) — option **(1)** is correct.
PCB grants come under **SAAP (1992)**; **BS-VI** is a vehicle norm.
xa: **CETPs** serve clusters of small industries.
AP's **BRAP** also streamlined clearances via **digitisation + single-window** systems.

n7436a894375.s: Common Effluent Treatment Plants (CETPs) are meant to serve:
n7436a894375.x: CETPs serve clusters of small industries; SAAP (1992) gives grants to strengthen Pollution Control Boards.
xa: **PARIVESH 3.0** is the single-window portal for clearances + **compliance monitoring**.
**BS-VI** came from **1 April 2020**; NAAQS cover **12 pollutants**.
New **Blue** industry category (e.g. Compressed Biogas).

n1678a92be40.s: India's National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) cover how many pollutants?
xa: Other air programmes: **NCAP**, **CAQM**, **GRAP**.
Jan Vishwas Act 2023 decriminalised minor **Air Act** offences.

n2ce8bc56587.s: PM E-DRIVE (2024) is the successor to which scheme for electric mobility?
n2ce8bc56587.x: PM E-DRIVE (2024) gives EV and charging incentives, succeeding FAME; PM-KUSUM is for farm solar pumps.
xa: UNEP-CCAC "**Hidden Assets**" cites **PMUY** as a model clean-cooking programme.
Every **$1** in integrated action yields about **$15**.
Clean cooking/heating = South Asia's leading solution to **2035**.

o: Certification of electric vehicle charging stations
Voluntary third-party certification for sustainable forestry and agroforestry
Certification of indoor air quality in hospitals
nc2ea05fa4a2.x: PRAMAAN is a voluntary third-party forest and wood certification initiative for sustainable forestry and agroforestry.
nc2ea05fa4a2.tq: Discriminate between similarly themed environmental labels by their certified subject.
xs: **PRAMAAN** = **voluntary third-party forest and wood certification** for **sustainable forestry and agroforestry** — option **(3)** is correct.
CCS for cement and EV charging are unrelated.
xa: **Ecomark** (**1991**) — environment-friendly consumer products.
**Blue Flag** — beaches, by **FEE, Denmark**.

n145d085adc1.s: How many Indian beaches were recommended for Blue Flag certification in 2020?
n145d085adc1.x: Eight Indian beaches were recommended for Blue Flag certification in 2020.
n145d085adc1.tq: Recall the specific count and year rather than substituting a later status figure.
xs: **8 Indian beaches** were recommended for **Blue Flag** in **2020** (PYQ) — option **(2)** is correct.
6, 10 and 12 are not the stated number.
xa: Blue Flag is awarded by the **Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), Denmark**.
**Ecomark** is India's product eco-label (**1991**).

nf9140361fa5.s: The 'Blue Flag' eco-label for beaches is awarded by:
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
International Union for Conservation of Nature
nf9140361fa5.x: Blue Flag is an international beach eco-label of the Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), Denmark. UNEP, MoEFCC and IUCN do not award it; MoEFCC ran Ecomark (1991).
nf9140361fa5.tq: Blue Flag = FEE Denmark; 8 Indian beaches in 2020.
xs: **Blue Flag** is awarded by the **Foundation for Environmental Education (FEE), Denmark** — option **(1)** is correct.
**MoEFCC** ran **Ecomark (1991)**, not Blue Flag.
xa: **8 Indian beaches** recommended in **2020**.
**PRAMAAN** — forest and wood certification.

n8e16c256865.s: APPCB allocates industrial inspections through a computerised system based on:
n8e16c256865.x: APPCB uses computerised, risk-based inspection allocation and has SOPs for effluents, marine outfalls and hazardous waste.
xa: APPCB was established in **1976**.
AP imposed a **green tax** on industries (**September 2019**).

n971e653498f.s: In September 2019, the Andhra Pradesh government decided to check industrial pollution by:
o: Imposing and collecting a green tax from industrial houses
Banning all industries near water bodies
Launching the Blue Flag programme for beaches
n971e653498f.x: In September 2019 AP decided to impose and collect a green tax from industrial houses (PYQ). Siting near water bodies is handled by APPCB guidelines, not a blanket ban; APPCB (est. 1976) continues; Blue Flag is an FEE eco-label.
xs: In **September 2019**, AP decided to **impose and collect a green tax** from industrial houses (PYQ) — option **(1)** is correct.
**APPCB** (est. **1976**) continues; **Blue Flag** is an **FEE** eco-label.
xa: APPCB issues **siting guidelines** — not a blanket ban near water bodies.
AP angle also includes **BRAP single window**.

nae991f5731f.s: In Andhra Pradesh's environmental initiatives, BRAP is associated with:
nae991f5731f.x: BRAP is associated with a single-window system, while APPCB is associated with siting guidelines.
xa: AP **green tax** on industries (**Sept 2019**).
APPCB uses **computerised inspection allocation** by risk.

n66de18faea9.s: Which of the following supports the management of all hazards through a GIS database and satellite-based disaster management capabilities?
n66de18faea9.x: ISRO's Disaster Management Support programme and the National Database for Emergency Management support all hazards, with NDEM functioning as a GIS database.
n66de18faea9.tq: Match the technological system with its stated cross-hazard function.
xs: **ISRO's DMS programme and NDEM** (a **GIS database**) support all hazards — option **(4)**.
**SACHET** is NDMA's alert system and **NPDRR** a multi-stakeholder body; **Aapda Mitra** trains volunteers; **NTRB** handles tsunami readiness.
xa: **SACHET** was developed by **C-DOT** on the **Common Alerting Protocol**.
**NPDRR** is chaired by the **Union Home Minister**.
**Tsunami Ready**: **24 Odisha villages**, target **100**.

n2cd4fb51693.s: Under the Disaster Management Act, Panchayati Raj Institutions and Urban Local Bodies have:
o: A legal role in local plans, relief and capacity building
No legal role in disaster management
Only an advisory role to the NDRF
n2cd4fb51693.x: The DM Act gives PRIs and ULBs a legal role in local plans, relief and capacity building.
xa: **National Project for Community-Based DRR in PRIs**: **Rs 507.37 crore**, MoPR + NDMA.
It builds **20 Model GPs** on **6 hazard themes**.
**Aapda Mitra**: NDMA scheme training **community volunteers** as **first responders**.

nf3a6a750d84.s: Which one of the following best distinguishes a hazard from a disaster?
o: A hazard and a disaster are identical terms used in disaster management
A hazard refers only to economic loss, whereas a disaster refers only to physical damage
A hazard is always caused by human activity, whereas a disaster is always natural
A hazard is a potentially damaging event, whereas a disaster results when hazard interacts with vulnerability and causes serious harm
nf3a6a750d84.x: A hazard is a potentially damaging event. It becomes a disaster when it interacts with vulnerability and produces serious adverse consequences.
nf3a6a750d84.tq: Discriminate between closely related technical terms instead of treating them as synonyms.
xs: A **hazard** is a **potentially damaging event**; it becomes a **disaster** when it **interacts with vulnerability** and causes serious harm — so option **(4)** is correct.
The two terms are not identical: **risk** is the probability of harm from the **hazard-vulnerability interaction**.
A hazard need not be human-made: **natural** hazards arise from **environmental or geological processes**, **man-made** ones from human activity.
xa: **Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity** — capacity reduces risk.
**Vulnerability** = susceptibility (**physical, social, economic, environmental**).
**Resilience** = ability to **resist, absorb and recover quickly**.
**DRR** works best when it **addresses underlying causes of vulnerability** (**APPSC 2024**).

ndb973f16192.s: The ability of a community to resist, absorb and recover quickly from a hazard is called:
ndb973f16192.x: Resilience is the ability to resist, absorb and recover quickly; susceptibility to damage is vulnerability.
xa: **Hazard** = a potentially damaging event.
**Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity**.
**DRR** works best when it **addresses underlying causes of vulnerability** (APPSC **2024**).

ncd63d5d696f.s: In disaster management, disaster risk is commonly expressed by which relationship?
ncd63d5d696f.x: Risk rises with hazard and vulnerability and falls as coping capacity rises, so Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity. Putting capacity in the numerator (B) or adding/subtracting terms (C) reverses or breaks this logic, and D drops vulnerability entirely.
ncd63d5d696f.tq: Capacity divides risk; vulnerability multiplies it.
xs: Disaster risk is expressed as **Risk = Hazard x Vulnerability / Capacity** — option **(1)**.
Risk rises with **hazard** and **vulnerability** and falls as **capacity** (strengths/resources to cope) rises, so capacity belongs in the **denominator**.
The other formulas put capacity in the numerator or drop vulnerability, reversing this logic.
xa: **Risk** = probability of harm from the **hazard-vulnerability interaction**.
**Vulnerability** dimensions: **physical, social, economic, environmental**.
**DRR** works best when it **addresses underlying causes of vulnerability** (**APPSC 2024**).

ndisaster-management-20-8.s: Which one of the following is an example of a geophysical natural hazard?
ndisaster-management-20-8.x: A volcanic eruption is geophysical. Epidemics are biological, thunderstorms meteorological, and forest fires climatological.
n: Volcanic eruption is an example of a geophysical natural hazard. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Epidemics are examples of biological natural hazards. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xs: A **volcanic eruption** is a **geophysical** hazard — so option **(1)** is correct.
**Epidemic** is **biological**; **thunderstorm** is **meteorological**; **forest fire** is **climatological**.
xa: Other geophysical hazards: **earthquake**, **tsunami**, **landslide**.
**Hydrological** hazards: **flood**, **flash flood**, **avalanche**.
**Climatological**: **drought**, **heat wave**, **cold wave**.

n27ce22b4a81.s: Which one of the following is correctly classified as a biological disaster?
n27ce22b4a81.x: Epidemics, pandemics and pest attacks are biological disasters, so pest attack is correct. Earthquakes are geological, cyclones are weather-related (hydro-meteorological), and nuclear incidents are man-made/industrial disasters.
n27ce22b4a81.tq: Classify the example rather than the general term.
xs: **Pest attack** is a **biological** disaster — option **(1)**.
**Earthquakes** are **geological**; **nuclear incidents** are **man-made / industrial**.
xa: Biological also includes **epidemics** and **pandemics (COVID-19)**.
Geological: **earthquakes, landslides, volcanic eruptions, tsunamis**.
Climatological: **extreme temperatures, droughts**.
Emerging: **cyber attacks, space weather, AI failures**.

n6631d77f68d.s: Which of the following is an emerging hazard identified in addition to conventional natural and technological hazards?
n6631d77f68d.x: Cyber attacks, space weather and AI failures are identified as emerging hazards.
n6631d77f68d.tq: Pick the item belonging to the emerging-hazard category.
xs: **Cyber attack** is listed as an **emerging** hazard — option **(2)**.
Emerging hazards also include **space weather** and **AI failures**, beyond conventional natural and man-made types.
xa: Man-made / industrial: **chemical and industrial accidents, fires, nuclear incidents**.
Biological: **epidemics, pandemics (COVID-19), pest attacks**.
**Man-made** disasters arise from **human activity, negligence or technological failure** (**APPSC 2025** key).

nbc80e5cc38b.s: After August 2026, how many notified disasters are eligible for SDRF/NDRF assistance?
nbc80e5cc38b.x: The number rose to 14 after heatwave and lightning were added on the Sixteenth Finance Commission's advice; no man-made calamity is notified.
xa: **Heat wave**: max temp **>=40 C** in plains — now notified.
**Drought** is administered by the Ministry of **Agriculture** (with hailstorm, frost, pest attack).
AP funds (Jul 2026): SDRF/NDRF released **Rs 479.01 crore** in **2026-27** (Rs **277.63 crore** in **2025-26**).

nfc55d579130.s: A fire caused by careless handling of gas cylinders in a residential building is best classified as a:
nfc55d579130.x: Man-made disasters arise from human activity, negligence or technological failure (APPSC 2025 key), so a fire from careless gas-cylinder handling is man-made. It is not natural (no environmental or geological process), not biological (no pathogen or pest) and not hydrological (no water-related event).
xs: A fire from **careless handling of gas cylinders** is a **man-made disaster** — option **(4)** (**APPSC 2025** key).
**Man-made** disasters arise from **human activity, negligence or technological failure**; the notes rule out **natural, biological and hydrological**.
**Natural** disasters arise from **environmental or geological processes**; **biological** ones are epidemics and pest attacks.
xa: Man-made / industrial: **chemical and industrial accidents, fires, nuclear incidents**.
**Bhopal Gas Tragedy, 1984** — a chemical leak, an **anthropogenic** hazard.
⚠ **No man-made calamity is notified** for SDRF/NDRF.

n8f43e23893d.s: Which Ministry administers drought-related disaster management along with hailstorm, frost and pest attack?
o: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
n8f43e23893d.x: The Ministry of Agriculture administers drought-related matters along with hailstorm, frost and pest attack.
n8f43e23893d.tq: Apply the 'who administers this subject?' authority-identification method.
xs: **Drought** is administered by the **Ministry of Agriculture**, along with **hailstorm, frost and pest attack** — option **(4)**.
**Overall coordination** of DM rests with the **Ministry of Home Affairs**' DM division.
xa: **NTRB** was set up by **MoES**.
Climatological disasters: **extreme temperatures, droughts**.
**Pest attacks** are **biological** disasters.

ndisaster-management-20-7.s: Industrial, chemical and nuclear disasters are classed as:
ndisaster-management-20-7.x: They are man-made (human-induced) because they arise from human activity, technology or negligence, not natural processes.
n: Industrial or chemical disasters are man-made or human-induced hazards. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Nuclear disasters are man-made or human-induced hazards. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
Biological disasters are man-made or human-induced hazards. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xa: A **nuclear explosion** is **not** a **natural disaster** — it is in the **CBRN** category.
**Natural** disasters **arise from environmental or geological processes**.
⚠ Some notes list **biological** hazards as natural, not man-made.

ndisaster-management-20-12.s: Which subtype is included under man-made or anthropogenic hazards along with technological and transport hazards?
ndisaster-management-20-12.x: Man-made hazards have three subtypes: technological, transport, and social or complex. The other options are natural hazard types.
ndisaster-management-20-12.tq: Discriminate natural from man-made hazard types.
n: Man-made or anthropogenic hazards include the social or complex subtype. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #20 · pp 47-49]
xs: The third man-made subtype is **social** / **complex** — so option **(2)** is correct.
**Social or complex** hazards: **terrorism**, **riots**, **war**, **civil strife**.
**Geophysical**, **hydrological** and **climatological** are **natural** hazard subtypes.
xa: **Technological**: **industrial accidents**, **chemical leaks**, **nuclear accidents**, **dam failure**.
**Transport**: **air**, **rail**, **road** and **ship** accidents.
**Emerging** hazards: cyber attacks, space weather, AI failures.

ndisaster-management-33-1.s: Which agency is responsible for forecasting heatwaves in India?
ndisaster-management-33-1.x: The IMD forecasts heatwaves. NDMA sets guidelines, and NDRF responds.
n: The India Meteorological Department is the nodal agency for forecasting heatwaves. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #33 · pp 70-72]
xs: The **India Meteorological Department** is the **nodal agency** for **forecasting heatwaves** — so option **(1)** is correct.
IMD gives **early warning** through **colour-coded alerts**.
**NDMA** issues guidelines; the **NDRF** is a response force — neither forecasts.
xa: Heatwave season: mainly **March to June**, **sometimes extends** to **July**.
Heatwave is now a **notified disaster** eligible for **SDRF** and **NDRF** assistance.
IMD is also the nodal agency for **cold-wave** forecasting.

n4e236005dfa.s: Building embankments, planting mangroves and land-use zoning belong to which phase of the disaster management cycle?
n4e236005dfa.x: Embankments, mangroves and zoning are pre-disaster mitigation measures. Response covers rescue and relief during or just after the event; recovery covers restoration and rebuilding after it.
n4e236005dfa.tq: Mitigation = before; response = during; recovery = after.
xs: **Embankments, mangroves and zoning** are **pre-disaster** measures of **mitigation** — option **(3)**.
**Response** (during/after) covers **rescue and relief**.
**Recovery** (post-disaster) covers **restoration and rebuilding**.
xa: **DRR** works best when it **addresses underlying causes of vulnerability** (**APPSC 2024**).
Cyclone mitigation uses **mangroves (Coringa, Krishna)** and **shelter belts**.
Flood mitigation: **embankments, reservoir regulation, flood forecasting**.

ndisaster-management-12-11.s: Which of the following is a structural disaster-mitigation measure?
ndisaster-management-12-11.x: Retrofitting is structural mitigation, like earthquake-resistant buildings and sea walls; awareness and building codes are non-structural.
n: Earthquake-resistant buildings are structural mitigation measures in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
Retrofitting is a structural mitigation measure in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
Sea walls are structural mitigation measures in India. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
xa: Other structural examples: **embankments**, **dams**, **cyclone shelters**, **check dams**.
**Non-structural**: **building codes**, **Flood Plain Zoning**, **insurance**, **early warning systems**.
⚠ **Building codes** (**IS 1893**) are **non-structural**.

ndisaster-management-12-15.s: Indian Standard IS 1893 is associated with:
ndisaster-management-12-15.x: IS 1893 governs earthquake-resistant design, a structural earthquake-mitigation measure.
n: Earthquake-resistant design is a structural earthquake-mitigation measure. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
IS 1893 is associated with earthquake-resistant design. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
Building codes are non-structural earthquake-mitigation measures. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
Awareness is a non-structural earthquake-mitigation measure. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #12 · pp 30-32]
xa: Non-structural also covers **land-use planning**, **insurance**, **training**.
**Earthquake** mitigation: **seismic zoning**, **safe construction**.
**Retrofitting** and **sea walls** are structural.

n12ec2ec5700.s: Which one of the following is NOT one of the four priorities of the Sendai Framework?
o: Investing in disaster-risk reduction for resilience
Replacing all community-based systems with centralised response agencies
n12ec2ec5700.x: The four priorities include understanding risk, strengthening risk governance, investing in risk reduction, and enhancing preparedness for effective response and Build Back Better. Replacing community systems is not a Sendai priority.
n12ec2ec5700.tq: Find the option that does not belong to the recognised priority set.
xs: **Replacing community-based systems with centralised agencies** is NOT a Sendai priority — option **(4)**.
The **4 priorities**: **understanding risk**, **strengthening risk governance**, **investing in DRR** for resilience, **enhancing preparedness** + **Build Back Better**.
xa: Sendai also has **7 global targets** (cut mortality, economic loss, etc.).
Sendai covers **2015-2030** and **succeeds Hyogo**.
Community role: the **DM Act** gives **PRIs and ULBs** a legal role.

n19c65ed7255.s: The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) is best described as:
o: A predecessor framework to the Hyogo Framework for Action
A UN treaty body headquartered in Geneva
An India-led infrastructure-resilience coalition with its secretariat in New Delhi
A State-level fund administered by the Ministry of Home Affairs
n19c65ed7255.x: CDRI is an India-led coalition focused on infrastructure resilience, and its secretariat is located in New Delhi.
n19c65ed7255.tq: Combine the organisation’s identity, leadership and headquarters.
xs: **CDRI** is an **India-led infrastructure-resilience coalition**, secretariat in **New Delhi** — option **(3)**.
It was launched in **2019** — well after **Hyogo** (**2005-2015**), so it is no predecessor.
xa: **Sendai Framework**: **2015-2030**.
**IDNDR** (**1990-1999**) was the first concerted UN effort.
**Yokohama Strategy**: **1994**.

ne6e2749c868.s: The Yokohama Strategy is best described as the:
o: blueprint that emerged from the IDNDR process
ne6e2749c868.x: The Yokohama Strategy, adopted in 1994, was the blueprint developed from the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction.
ne6e2749c868.tq: Identify the framework’s relationship with IDNDR rather than its date alone.
xs: The **Yokohama Strategy** (**1994**) was the **blueprint from IDNDR** — option **(1)**.
It came long before **Sendai** (**2015-2030**), so it is no successor.
xa: **IDNDR** (**1990-1999**): first concerted UN effort; prompted India's **DM Cell**.
**Hyogo Framework**: **2005-2015**, Hyogo, Japan.
**CDRI**: launched **2019**, secretariat **New Delhi**.

nfabb5f3743e.s: Which set contains the three post-2015 frameworks identified as shaping India’s disaster-risk reduction approach?
o: Sendai Framework, Sustainable Development Goals and Paris Agreement
Hyogo Framework, Kyoto Protocol and Montreal Protocol
Yokohama Strategy, SDGs and Convention on Biological Diversity
IDNDR, Paris Agreement and Ramsar Convention
nfabb5f3743e.x: The three post-2015 frameworks are the Sendai Framework, the Sustainable Development Goals for 2015–2030 and the Paris Agreement.
nfabb5f3743e.tq: Use the post-2015 time filter to eliminate the earlier IDNDR, Yokohama and Hyogo instruments.
xs: The three post-2015 frameworks are **Sendai**, the **SDGs (2015-2030)** and the **Paris Agreement** — option **(1)**.
⚠ **Hyogo** is NOT one — it covered **2005-2015**.
xa: **Sendai** succeeds Hyogo: **4** priorities, **7** targets.
**CDRI** launched **2019**, India-led.

n3778c082756.s: The first concerted UN effort on disaster reduction, which prompted India to set up a Disaster Management Cell, was the:
o: Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction
International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction (IDNDR)
n3778c082756.x: The IDNDR (1990-1999) was the first concerted UN effort and prompted India's DM Cell. Hyogo (2005-15) and Sendai (2015-30) came later, and CDRI is an India-led coalition launched in 2019.
xs: The first concerted UN effort, which prompted India's **DM Cell**, was the **IDNDR** — option **(3)**.
**Hyogo** (**2005-2015**) and **Sendai** (**2015-2030**) came later; **CDRI** is an India-led coalition launched in **2019**.
xa: **Yokohama Strategy** (**1994**) = blueprint from IDNDR.
Hyogo stressed **resilience of nations and communities**.

ndisaster-management-27-4.s: The UN office for disaster risk reduction was rebranded as UNDRR in:
ndisaster-management-27-4.x: The rename to UNDRR came in 2019; 1989–1999 was the International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction.
n: The International Decade for Natural Disaster Reduction lasted from 1989 to 1999. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 59-61]
UNISDR supported the Hyogo Framework for Action from 2005 to 2015. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 59-61]
UNISDR supported the adoption of the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction in 2015. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 59-61]
UNISDR was rebranded as UNDRR in 2019. [Disaster Management · ROCKET SHEET #27 · pp 59-61]
xa: **UNISDR** was **established 1999**.
UNDRR headquarters: **Geneva, Switzerland**.
⚠ Some notes give IDNDR as **1990 to 2000**.

ndisaster-management-27-8.s: Which institution convenes the Global Platform for Disaster Risk Reduction?
o: The Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction

ndisaster-management-33-10.x: States and cities prepare heat action plans with help from NDMA and the IMD.
