neecf0b99bad.x: Kisan drones are used for crop assessment, soil health analysis and spraying, and can reduce human exposure to chemicals. They do not eliminate the need for all irrigation water.
neecf0b99bad.tq: Find the option that overstates the technology’s benefit.
xs: Kisan drones do **not** eliminate the need for all irrigation water — so option **(4)** is correct.
Their uses: **crop assessment**, **soil health analysis**, **spraying**; they cut **human exposure to chemicals**.
xa: They save water **up to 30%**.
Regulated by **DGCA** under **Drone Rules 2021**.
APDC drone spraying covers **all 26 districts**.

ndb63e26a2f9.s: Which authority regulates agricultural drones under the Drone Rules, 2021?
o: Soil and Land Use Survey of India
ndb63e26a2f9.x: Agricultural drones are regulated by the Directorate General of Civil Aviation under the Drone Rules, 2021.
ndb63e26a2f9.tq: Apply the ‘who regulates this activity?’ institutional test.
xs: Drones are regulated by **DGCA** under the **Drone Rules 2021** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**ISRO** handles crop forecasting via satellites; **MNRE** runs **PM-KUSUM**.
xa: Drone categories: **nano, micro, small, medium, large**.
**Drone Shakti** supports **Remote Pilot Certificate** training.

o: an Aadhaar-like digital public good built through a federated Centre-State approach
a satellite used for crop forecasting
a centralised crop insurance claim portal managed only by States
n270908788d0.x: AgriStack is described as an Aadhaar-like digital public good developed through a federated Centre-State build.
n270908788d0.tq: Combine the analogy with the governance model to identify the correct description.
xs: **AgriStack** is an "**Aadhaar-like**" **digital public good** with a **federated Centre-State** build — so option **(1)** is correct.
It is not a satellite (that is ISRO's crop forecasting) or a drone-licensing system (**DGCA**).
xa: Registries: **Farmers' Registry**, **geo-referenced village maps**, **Crop Sown Registry**.
Part of the **Digital Agriculture Mission** (**September 2024**, **₹2,817 crore**).
Karnataka's **FRUITS** (**2020**) is a unified farmer database.

n71564519745.s: The gross irrigated area as a percentage of gross cropped area increased from approximately 41.7% in 2001-02 to:
n71564519745.x: The gross irrigated area increased from 41.7% in 2001-02 to 55.8% in 2022-23.
n71564519745.tq: Track both endpoints of a trend and avoid substituting an unsupported intermediate year.
xs: Gross irrigated area rose from **41.7% (2001-02)** to **55.8%** of GCA in **2022-23** — so option **(2)** is correct.
The other percentages and years do not match the reported figure.
xa: Skew: **rice ~67%** irrigated vs **pulses ~26%**, millets **<15%**.
Criticism: irrigation is **still skewed to rice**.
PDMC brought **102 lakh ha** under micro-irrigation (**2015-16** to **2025-26**).

n1c01ac3c0d8.s: Which areas receive priority under Per Drop More Crop?
o: Rainfed areas, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks
Only command areas with assured canal irrigation
n1c01ac3c0d8.x: The priority areas are rainfed regions, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks.
n1c01ac3c0d8.tq: Match the intervention’s resource-conservation objective with the areas facing water stress.
xs: PDMC prioritises **rainfed areas, water-stressed districts and critical groundwater blocks** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It is not limited to saline soils, peri-urban clusters or canal commands.
xa: PDMC was launched in **2015-16**; under **RKVY** from **2022-23**.
It brought **102 lakh ha** under micro-irrigation.
**NMSA** gives up to **55%** subsidy, capped at **5 ha**.

nb6c0bfc6e2c.s: Which State ranked first in India in micro-irrigation implementation in 2024–25?
nb6c0bfc6e2c.x: Andhra Pradesh ranked first in India in micro-irrigation implementation in 2024–25.
nb6c0bfc6e2c.tq: Use the year-specific ranking rather than a general leading-state assumption.
xs: **Andhra Pradesh** ranked **1st** in India in micro-irrigation implementation in **2024-25** — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Six AP districts** were in the national **top 10**, led by **Ananthapuramu**.
xa: AP's micro-irrigation is implemented State-wide under **PMKSY**.
APMIP reports **30-40% higher productivity**.
Automation-based micro-irrigation facility at **Governorpet, Vijayawada**.

na83ad8ce400.s: Which irrigation technology is most suitable for water-scarce regions?
na83ad8ce400.x: Drip irrigation applies water directly to the root zone, reaching about 90% efficiency and cutting evaporation and runoff, so it suits water-scarce areas (APPSC-G2 2025). Flood, furrow and basin irrigation are surface methods with only about 30-50% efficiency.
xs: **Drip irrigation** suits **water-scarce regions** (APPSC-G2 **2025**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
Drip reaches ~**90%** efficiency; **flood/furrow** reaches only ~**30-50%**.
xa: Drip applies water **directly to the root zone**, minimising **evaporation and runoff**.
Micro-irrigation saves **water, labour, power and fertiliser**.
AP ranked **1st** in micro-irrigation implementation (**2024-25**).

n8cf43988305.s: Which one of the following is NOT a stated feature of zero tillage?
o: Wheat can be sown without burning the previous crop residue.
It can contribute to soil carbon sequestration.
It necessarily requires complete removal of all crop residue before sowing.
Paddy seed can be planted directly without raising a nursery.
n8cf43988305.x: Zero tillage is associated with sowing wheat without burning previous residue, direct planting of paddy without a nursery, and soil carbon sequestration. Complete removal of residue is not a stated feature.
n8cf43988305.tq: Identify the extreme and reversed residue-management statement.
xs: Zero tillage does **not** require **complete removal of all crop residue** — so option **(3)** is correct.
Its stated features (UPSC **2020**, all three): wheat sown **without burning residue**, **paddy without nursery**, **soil carbon sequestration**.
xa: **Reduced/zero tillage + leaving crop residue** conserves water (UPSC **2017**).
**Direct-seeded rice** is promoted with **zero-till wheat** under **NICRA**.

n7e088f682b2.s: Which of the following practices helps conserve water in agriculture?
o: Repeated deep ploughing after every irrigation
Reduced or zero tillage with crop residue left on the field
n7e088f682b2.x: Reduced or zero tillage combined with leaving crop residue helps conserve water. Gypsum application before irrigation is not identified as the water-conserving practice in this comparison.
n7e088f682b2.tq: Separate the positive resource-conservation practice from the deliberately inserted non-example.
xs: **Reduced or zero tillage with crop residue left on the field** conserves water (UPSC **2017**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Gypsum before irrigation** does NOT; flood irrigation and residue burning waste resources.
xa: **Laser land levelling** spreads water evenly and saves irrigation water.
Zero tillage also gives **soil carbon sequestration**.
Drip irrigation efficiency ~**90%**.
n7e088f682b2.fixed: drop odd meta phrase about gypsum 'in the stated comparison' (yeb13c4efdcd)

nbiology-42-5.s: Copying or amplifying a desired gene or DNA fragment is called:
nbiology-42-5.x: Gene cloning copies a desired gene; whole-animal cloning copies a complete organism.
n: Gene cloning is the copying of a desired gene or DNA fragment. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Gene cloning is the amplification of a desired gene or DNA fragment. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Bacteria in a bacterial cloning system rapidly copy recombinant DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Whole-animal cloning produces a complete organism. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Bacteria act as factories to copy recombinant DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
xa: **Plasmid cloning** inserts a gene into a **plasmid vector**.
**Stem cells** can **differentiate** into other cell types.
Cloning is a **genetic** and **biotechnological technique**.

nbiology-42-9.s: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is a technique for:
o: Copying small quantities of DNA for analysis
nbiology-42-9.x: PCR copies small amounts of DNA for molecular analysis, diagnostic testing and research.
n: PCR is used for molecular and genetic analysis. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR is used for detection and diagnostic testing. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR is used in DNA-based research. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
PCR supports analysis of small quantities of DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
xa: PCR = **Polymerase Chain Reaction**; core purpose: **amplification** of DNA.
In rDNA, PCR amplifies the desired fragment (**step 3**).
**Genetic testing** identifies relevant variants in personalised medicine.

n3dd48952027.s: In plant genetic engineering, Agrobacterium tumefaciens is commonly used because:
o: Its ribosomes replace the plant cell nucleus.
Its disarmed Ti plasmid transfers T-DNA into the plant nucleus.
It destroys all plant viruses without transferring DNA.
It produces human insulin directly in plant leaves.
n3dd48952027.x: Agrobacterium tumefaciens is called nature's genetic engineer because T-DNA from its disarmed Ti plasmid can carry the desired gene into the plant nucleus.
n3dd48952027.tq: Ask which biological mechanism explains the organism's use as a vector.
xs: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** carries the gene in a **disarmed Ti plasmid**, and **T-DNA** takes it into the **plant nucleus** — so option **(2)** is correct.
It is called "**nature's genetic engineer**"; it does not make insulin or replace the nucleus.
xa: Other vectors: **plasmids**, **BACs**, **YACs**.
First human hormone by rDNA: **insulin**.
Common bacterial host: **E. coli**.

n4933d1c93e0.s: Which of the following is a distinctive concern associated with gene-drive mosquitoes?
o: The released trait can be recalled easily by stopping pesticide application.
The trait may spread through wild populations and there is no simple recall mechanism.
The technology is incapable of affecting mosquito populations.
The trait remains confined to the laboratory by definition.
n4933d1c93e0.x: Gene drives may spread a trait through wild populations, potentially causing population collapse or producing malaria-resistant mosquitoes. Unlike pesticide use, there is no simple recall mechanism.
n4933d1c93e0.tq: Test the practical implication of an irreversible or difficult-to-recall intervention.
xs: A gene-drive trait **spreads through wild populations** with **no simple recall** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Unlike pesticides, it cannot be stopped by ceasing application (14 Jul **2026**).
xa: Inheritance: **over 90%** of offspring (normal **50%**).
Types: **population suppression** (sterile females) vs **population modification**.
Tanzania-led **"Transmission Zero"** project.

nc49064da39c.s: A soybean variety containing a Brazil-nut gene was not released commercially primarily because of concern regarding:
nc49064da39c.x: The Brazil-nut gene was intended to improve methionine content, but the resulting soybean raised allergy concerns and was therefore never released.
nc49064da39c.tq: Identify the risk that explains why a genetically modified product was withheld from release.
xs: The Brazil-nut-gene soybean was **never released** because of **allergenicity** — it triggered allergy in Brazil-nut-allergic people — option **(1)**.
The gene was added for **methionine**, so failure to produce methionine was not the issue.
xa: **Horizontal gene transfer**: genes moving between **unrelated organisms**.
**Antibiotic-resistance marker genes** raise fears of spreading resistance.
**Mon 863**: Monsanto's **pest-resistant maize** (against **corn rootworm**), in news over feeding-study safety.

nf9939c1778c.s: Horizontal gene transfer in the biosafety context refers to:
o: Replacement of nuclear DNA by mitochondrial DNA in every cell
Movement of genes between unrelated organisms
Transmission of genes only from parent to offspring
Movement of pollen only within one flower
nf9939c1778c.x: Horizontal gene transfer is the movement of genes between unrelated organisms. Antibiotic-resistance genes may potentially pass from environmental bacteria to human pathogens.
nf9939c1778c.tq: Distinguish horizontal transfer from ordinary vertical inheritance.
xs: **Horizontal gene transfer** is the **movement of genes between unrelated organisms** — option **(2)** is correct.
Example: **antibiotic-resistance genes** can pass from soil/environment bacteria to **human pathogens**.
Parent-to-offspring transmission is vertical inheritance, not horizontal transfer.
xa: **Allergenicity**: **Brazil-nut** gene soybean caused allergy → **never released**.
**Mon 863** = GM **pest-resistant maize** (Monsanto; corn rootworm).
**Gene drives** spread a trait in a wild population — **over 90%** of offspring inherit it (normal **50%**).

nbiology-39-3.s: Microbial production of useful products is an application of biotechnology in which field?
nbiology-39-3.x: In industry biotechnology gives microbial products; in agriculture GM crops, in medicine drugs and vaccines, and in research biochips.
n: Biotechnology is used in agriculture to produce improved crops. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in agriculture to produce transgenic or genetically modified crops. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in medicine to produce drugs. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in medicine to produce vaccines. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in medicine for diagnostics. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in medicine for gene therapy. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in industry for the microbial production of useful products. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
DNA-based biochips are used in basic research. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
RNA-based biochips are used in basic research. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Protein-based biochips are used in basic research. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology produces transgenic organisms carrying introduced genes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
xa: Biochips are used in **drug discovery**.
**Human insulin** is made by **recombinant bacteria** carrying the human insulin gene.
**Genetic diagnostics** identify **genetic diseases**.

nbiology-39-4.s: A recombinant plasmid is introduced into a bacterium through:
nbiology-39-4.x: The recombinant plasmid enters the bacterium by transformation, and rapid bacterial multiplication then yields large quantities of DNA or product.
n: A recombinant plasmid contains a desired DNA fragment or gene inserted into a plasmid. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
A recombinant plasmid is introduced into a bacterium through transformation. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Rapid multiplication of bacteria produces large quantities of DNA or product. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Bacteria multiply rapidly. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
xa: **Gene cloning** amplifies or copies a desired gene.
rDNA steps begin with **isolation of DNA** and cutting by **restriction endonucleases**; rDNA is joined by **DNA ligase**.
First GMO: **1973**; first human hormone by rDNA: **insulin**.

nbiology-39-6.s: In biotechnology, the creation of a collection of genetic material is called a:
nbiology-39-6.x: A genetic library is a collection of genetic material; gene cloning copies a gene and biochips aid drug discovery.
n: Biotechnology in genetics includes the creation of genetic libraries. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biotechnology is used in diagnosis through genetic diagnostics. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Biochips have applications in drug discovery. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
Gene cloning amplifies or copies a desired gene. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #39 · pp 61-63]
xa: Biochips are **DNA-**, **RNA-** and **protein-based**, used in **basic research**.
Medicine uses: **drugs**, **vaccines**, **diagnostics**, **gene therapy**.
Industry: **microbial production** of useful products.

nbiology-42-6.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about plasmids?
o: Plasmids are usually linear, single-stranded DNA
Some natural plasmid genes confer antibiotic resistance
Experimental plasmids are used as vectors
Plasmids are used to clone, transfer and manipulate genes
nbiology-42-6.x: Plasmids are usually circular, double-stranded DNA, not linear single-stranded DNA.
n: A common plasmid form is circular, double-stranded DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Natural plasmid genes may confer advantages such as antibiotic resistance. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Plasmids are used in biotechnology to clone genes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Plasmids are used in biotechnology to transfer genes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
Plasmids are used in biotechnology to manipulate genes. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
An experimental plasmid is a vector. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #42 · pp 68-71]
xa: A plasmid is a **small DNA molecule** separate from chromosomal DNA that **replicates independently**.
**pBR322**: early **E. coli** cloning vector — **p** = plasmid, **BR** = **Bolivar and Rodriguez**.
Plants: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** with a disarmed **Ti plasmid**.

n47b2f4220d7.s: Human insulin was first marketed as Humulin in:
n47b2f4220d7.x: Humulin was marketed in 1982, after the first GMO in 1973; CRISPR-Cas9 was demonstrated in 2012.
xa: First commercially sold GM food: **Flavr Savr tomato**, **1994**.
First transgenic cow: **Rosie (1997)**.
First GM crop in India: **Bt cotton**, **2002**.

n781f51007b4.s: The first human hormone produced using recombinant DNA technology was:
n781f51007b4.x: Insulin was the first human hormone produced by rDNA technology; human insulin was marketed in 1982 as Humulin. Growth hormone, thyroxine and oxytocin are not the answer to this 'first'.
xs: The first human hormone made by rDNA was **insulin** (UKPSC **2024**) — so option **(2)** is correct.
Human insulin was marketed in **1982** as **Humulin**.
xa: Synthetic biology also makes **artemisinin** by microbes and **semaglutide** in baker's yeast.
First GMO: **1973**.
Recombinant vaccines: **Hepatitis B, HPV, COVID-19**.

n24515f06288.s: The Flavr Savr tomato, developed by Calgene in the United States in 1994, was notable because it was the first commercially sold GM food and had which characteristic?
o: Resistance to the fruit and shoot borer
Delayed ripening and a longer shelf life
n24515f06288.x: Flavr Savr was the first commercially sold genetically modified food. Its delayed ripening provided a longer shelf life.
n24515f06288.tq: Combine the product's historical identity with its distinctive intended trait.
xs: **Flavr Savr** had **delayed ripening and a longer shelf life** — so option **(4)** is correct.
**Beta-carotene** is Golden Rice; **fruit and shoot borer** resistance is Bt brinjal.
xa: It was made by **Calgene, USA**, in **1994** — the first commercially sold GM food.
First GMO: **1973**.
First transgenic cow: **Rosie (1997)**.

nbiology-43-1.s: Which of the following correctly represents a classic GMO application pathway?
nbiology-43-1.x: The human insulin gene is put into bacteria, which then make insulin, the classic GMO application.
n: A human insulin gene can be transferred to bacteria to produce insulin. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
GMO applications produce desired traits or products. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
xs: The classic GMO pathway is **human insulin gene → bacteria → insulin** — option **(3)**.
**Human insulin** is produced using **recombinant bacteria** carrying a transferred **human insulin gene**.
xa: **Insulin** was the **first human hormone by rDNA**; human insulin marketed **1982** (**Humulin**).
First GMO: **1973**.
First commercially sold GM food: **Flavr Savr tomato** (**1994**).

nbiology-41-1.s: What is the full form of CRISPR?
o: Clustered Regularly Interspaced Small Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Repeatedly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats
Clustered Regularly Integrated Short Palindromic Repeats
nbiology-41-1.x: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. The other options change one word.
nbiology-41-1.tq: Check each word of the expansion.
n: CRISPR stands for Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
xs: CRISPR = **Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats** — option **(3)**.
The other options change one word (**Small**, **Repeatedly**, **Integrated**).
xa: CRISPR originated as a **natural defence mechanism** of **bacteria and archaea**.
**Jennifer Doudna** and **Emmanuelle Charpentier** demonstrated it in **2012** → **Nobel Prize in Chemistry 2020**.
**Cas9** = **molecular scissors**; **guide RNA** = the **navigator**.

nbiology-41-3.s: In CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, which component guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location?
nbiology-41-3.x: Guide RNA leads the Cas9 enzyme to the target site; CRISPR itself is specialised stretches of DNA.
n: CRISPR consists of specialized stretches of DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Cas9 is an enzyme. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Guide RNA guides Cas9 to the desired genomic location. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
A restriction enzyme cleaves DNA into fragments. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
Restriction enzymes have a role in genetic engineering by cutting DNA. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #41 · pp 66-68]
xa: CRISPR is simpler, cheaper, more accurate than **ZFNs and TALENs**.
**TnpB (ICAR)**: indigenous, **smaller alternative to CRISPR-Cas9**.
**Base editing** converts one base to another **without double-strand breaks**.

nebf05f31f8d.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Bt brinjal?
o: The GEAC recommended its release in 2009
It was developed through collaboration among Mahyco, UAS Dharwad and TNAU
Its principal target was the fruit and shoot borer
The moratorium on it was imposed in 2012
nebf05f31f8d.x: The moratorium on Bt brinjal was imposed in 2010 by Jairam Ramesh, not 2012; the other statements are correct.
xa: India is a **centre of diversity of brinjal** — key argument against Bt brinjal.
Exam angle: Bt brinjal was "developed for" **insect resistance**.
Gene flow into **wild relatives** is the primary environmental concern (PYQ).

nc83067e8461.s: GM mustard DMH-11 (Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11) was developed by:
o: Delhi University (Centre for Genetic Manipulation of Crop Plants)
nc83067e8461.x: DMH-11 was developed at Delhi University's CGMCP (Deepak Pental). MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad and TNAU developed Bt brinjal; ICAR-IARI developed genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1.
nc83067e8461.tq: DMH-11 = Delhi University; Bt brinjal = Mahyco.
xs: **DMH-11** was developed by **Delhi University** (**CGMCP**, Deepak Pental) — so option **(2)** is correct.
**MAHYCO with UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU** developed **Bt brinjal**, not GM mustard.
xa: DMH-11 = **Dhara Mustard Hybrid-11**.
GEAC approved its environmental release in **Oct 2022**.
It is **under Supreme Court consideration**.

n66c022f84dd.s: Which one of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern about the cultivation of GM crops?
o: Transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives
n66c022f84dd.x: Gene flow, the movement of transgenes by pollen into non-GM crops and wild relatives, is the primary environmental concern (PYQ). It can create superweeds and alter native gene pools. The other options are not GM-crop concerns.
n66c022f84dd.tq: GM crop main worry = gene flow by pollen.
xs: The primary environmental concern of GM crops is **gene flow**: **transgenes moving by cross-pollination into non-GM crops and wild relatives** — option **(1)** (PYQ).
Soil evaporation, ozone depletion and canal salinisation are not GM-crop concerns.
xa: Gene flow effects: invasive **superweeds**, raised **weediness**, altered **native gene pools**.
Risk is highest at a crop's **centre of origin/diversity**; India = centre of diversity of **brinjal**.
**Non-target harm**: pollinators, natural enemies, **soil nematodes/microbes**, aquatic organisms.

n27cc8122ee0.s: The inactive Bt protoxin is activated in the gut of the insect larva because of its:
n27cc8122ee0.x: The protoxin is activated in the alkaline gut of the larva; the active toxin then binds midgut cells and creates pores.
xa: **Bollgard I (2002)** = **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard II (2006)** = **Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab**.
Target trait of Bt: **insect resistance**.
Bt proteins **degrade in soil**, despite fears of persistence.

ndb0cd1bfe0b.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes Bollgard I from Bollgard II?
o: Bollgard I is herbicide-tolerant, whereas Bollgard II is drought-tolerant.
Bollgard I contains Cry1Ac, whereas Bollgard II contains Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.
Bollgard I contains Cry2Ab, whereas Bollgard II contains only Cry1Ac.
Both contain only Cry2Ab but differ in the host plant.
ndb0cd1bfe0b.x: Bollgard I, introduced in 2002, contains Cry1Ac. Bollgard II, introduced in 2006, combines Cry1Ac and Cry2Ab.
ndb0cd1bfe0b.tq: Compare the versions by separating their gene composition and introduction years.
xs: **Bollgard I** has **Cry1Ac**; **Bollgard II** has **Cry1Ac + Cry2Ab** — so option **(2)** is correct.
Both are **insect-resistance** traits, not herbicide or drought tolerance.
xa: Bollgard I came in **2002**, Bollgard II in **2006**.
⚠ Trap: Bt cotton approval year is **2002**, not 2006.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.

n552ab795a49.s: In recombinant DNA technology, which enzyme joins DNA fragments?
n552ab795a49.x: DNA ligase joins the fragments; restriction endonucleases cut DNA.
xa: Plant vector: **Agrobacterium tumefaciens** ("nature's genetic engineer").
⚠ Antibiotic-resistance **marker genes** raise fears of spreading resistance.

n3d613be8e6b.s: Bt cotton was approved for commercial cultivation in India in:
n3d613be8e6b.x: Bt cotton was approved in March 2002 (three MAHYCO hybrids); 2006 is when Bollgard II came.
xa: ⚠ **2006** is the year of **Bollgard II**, a common trap for the approval year.
Bt cotton covers ~**10.8 million ha**, ~**90%** of cotton area.
Largest Bt cotton producer: **Maharashtra** (APPSC-G2 2017).

n8d454272a04.s: Bt cotton, which covers about 90% of India's cotton area, has cut pesticide use by about:
n8d454272a04.x: The cut in pesticide use is about 40-50%, not 70-80%; Bt cotton covers about 90% of the cotton area (~10.8 million ha).
xa: Benefits **varied by region**.
Problems: **pink bollworm** resistance, **secondary pests**, **seed dependency**.

n6770d1d9c82.s: HTBt cotton combines the Bt trait with tolerance to which herbicide?
n6770d1d9c82.x: HTBt cotton combines glyphosate tolerance with the Bt trait; its approval in India is pending over weed-management and socio-economic concerns.
xa: HT crops encourage heavy **glyphosate** use.
**Punjab banned glyphosate sale in 2018**.

n853d62562af.s: Which pest has developed resistance to the Bt toxins of Bt cotton?
n853d62562af.x: The pink bollworm has overcome Bt toxins; whitefly and mealybug are sucking pests whose numbers rose, a separate problem.
xa: Another problem: non-adoption of **refuge** practices.
Yield rose from **190 kg/ha (2002)** to **480 kg/ha (2023)**.
Pesticide use was cut by **40-50%**.

n79f7cd5991b.s: The genome-edited Pusa Rice DST1 is tolerant to:
n79f7cd5991b.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is genome-edited for drought and salinity tolerance, giving about 10-30% higher yield under stress without foreign DNA.
xa: India is set to commercially launch it as its **first genome-edited rice** (1 Sep **2026**).
AP angle: it is an edited version of **MTU1010**, AP-bred at **Maruteru**.
**SDN-1** and **SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

n326afd134d0.s: Biofortification usually raises the nutrient level of crops through:
n326afd134d0.x: Biofortification generally raises nutritional value through conventional breeding, whereas GM technology inserts foreign genes.
xa: Biofortification examples: **Dhanshakti** iron-rich pearl millet (**ICRISAT**); **high-lysine maize**.
ICAR released **524 varieties**, incl. **34 biofortified**.
**Golden Rice** is a GM route to more nutrients (beta-carotene).

nd720ee33e68.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about gene-drive mosquitoes?
o: Population suppression aims to make the mosquito unable to support parasite development
Over 90% of offspring inherit the drive instead of the normal 50%
A CRISPR-Cas9 gene drive copies itself onto the partner chromosome
'Transmission Zero' is a Tanzania-led project on GM mosquitoes
nd720ee33e68.x: This reverses the two types: population suppression uses sterile females, while population modification stops the parasite developing.
xa: Gene drives give "**super-Mendelian**" inheritance.
Unlike pesticides, there is **no simple recall** (14 Jul **2026**).

n78e2f188039.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about site-directed nuclease (SDN) gene editing categories in India?
o: SDN-1 makes a small change without a template or foreign DNA
SDN-3 inserts foreign DNA and is regulated as GM
SDN-1 is exempt from GM rules under the 2022 guidelines
SDN-2 uses a template and inserts foreign DNA
n78e2f188039.x: SDN-2 uses a template but introduces no foreign DNA, and it is also exempt under the 2022 guidelines.
xa: Criticism: **GE crops bypass GMO rules**.
**Pusa Rice DST1** is genome-edited without transgenes.

nf5ea6975a40.s: Base editing differs from conventional double-strand-break editing because it:
o: Changes proteins without altering DNA bases
Converts one DNA base into another without creating double-strand breaks
Works exclusively by destroying the host cell
nf5ea6975a40.x: Base editing converts one DNA base into another without producing double-strand breaks in the DNA.
nf5ea6975a40.tq: Focus on the defining molecular distinction rather than the general purpose of gene editing.
xs: **Base editing** converts one DNA base into another **without double-strand breaks** — so option **(3)** is correct.
It does change DNA bases, so (1) is wrong; it does not insert chromosomes or destroy cells.
xa: Risk: a **6-year-old** in China died (March **2025**) after a first-of-its-kind **brain base-editing therapy**.
**ContactSeek** (27 Jul **2026**) cuts off-target edits.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

n217548e9997.s: The Centre of Excellence for CRISPR Innovation and Translation (CoE-CIT) is to be set up in:
n217548e9997.x: The CoE-CIT is to be set up in Bengaluru.
xa: CRISPR was demonstrated in **2012** by **Doudna and Charpentier**.
**SDN-1/SDN-2** edits are **exempt** from GM rules (**2022**).

nafeeb28155c.s: In genetic medicine, engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles serve as:
o: Carriers to deliver the medicine into cells
Probes that detect pathogens in blood
Enzymes that cut DNA at specific sites
nafeeb28155c.x: Genetic medicines, which correct or compensate for faulty genes, are delivered by engineered viruses and lipid nanoparticles.
xa: **Mitochondrial replacement therapy** = "**three-parent baby**" technique.
**Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.

n11d941fc75d.s: Mitochondrial Replacement Therapy is popularly known as the ____ technique, and its main ethical concern relates to ____.
o: three-parent baby; germline editing and designer babies
three-parent baby; pollen sterility in crops
synthetic-embryo; germline editing and designer babies
n11d941fc75d.x: MRT is the 'three-parent baby' technique and raises ethical issues of germline editing and designer babies (A). B has the wrong name and concern; C has the right name but a crop issue; D has the right concern but the wrong name.
n11d941fc75d.tq: Three parents = nuclear DNA of two parents + donor mitochondria.
xs: **Mitochondrial replacement therapy** is the **"three-parent baby"** technique, and its ethical issue is **germline editing and designer babies** — so option **(1)** is correct.
Option (2) has the wrong name and concern; option (3) has the right name but a crop issue (pollen sterility); option (4) has the right concern but the wrong name.
xa: Genetic medicines aim to **correct/compensate for faulty genes**, carried by **engineered viruses** and **lipid nanoparticles**.
Gene therapy in India is regulated by the **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
⚠ **Sterile seeds** (crop issue) belong to **V-GURT (Terminator)** technology, not to human therapy.

nda5605c1a39.s: In synthetic biology, semaglutide has been grown in:
nda5605c1a39.x: Semaglutide was grown in baker's yeast; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes.
xa: **Recombinant vaccines**: **Hepatitis B**, **HPV**, **COVID-19**.
First human hormone by rDNA = **insulin** (UKPSC **2024**); **Humulin** marketed **1982**.
**Genetic medicines** correct or compensate for faulty genes (carriers: **engineered viruses**, **lipid nanoparticles**).

n72ad08b5445.s:
Which of the following may be adversely affected by Bt toxins or other engineered traits?
1. Pollinators and natural enemies of pests
2. Soil nematodes and microbes
3. Aquatic organisms
n72ad08b5445.x: Bt toxins or other engineered traits may affect pollinators and natural enemies, soil nematodes and microbes, and aquatic organisms.
xa: Bt gene source: **Bacillus thuringiensis**; protoxin activated in the **alkaline gut** of larvae, creates pores in midgut.
Bt proteins were feared to persist, but experiments show they **degrade in soil**.
**Pink bollworm** developed resistance to Bt toxins — resistance build-up is also a listed risk.

n1a5b68d59d9.s: V-GURT (terminator technology) is banned in India under which Act?
n1a5b68d59d9.x: V-GURT, which makes plants produce sterile seeds, is banned in India under the Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001.
xa: T-GURT is still at **research stage**.
GURT ends **seed saving/replanting** and forces annual seed purchase.
**National Genebank** holds **4,70,513 accessions** (2026).

n9f40fc558b3.s: Golden Rice produces which precursor of Vitamin A?
n9f40fc558b3.x: Golden Rice produces beta-carotene, using daffodil phytoene synthase and Erwinia crtI, to target Vitamin A deficiency.
xa: Golden Rice targets **Vitamin A deficiency/blindness** (APPSC 2025).
**Biofortification** usually uses **conventional breeding**, e.g. **Dhanshakti** iron-rich pearl millet.
**Edible vaccines**: transgenic potato/banana with cholera or hepatitis B antigens.

na711883989a.s: A key gene-flow argument against Bt brinjal was that India is a centre of diversity of:
na711883989a.x: Transgene escape risk is highest in a crop's centre of diversity, and India is a centre of diversity of brinjal itself.
xa: **Bt brinjal**: GEAC recommended release **2009**; **moratorium 2010** (**Jairam Ramesh**).
Bt brinjal was developed by **Mahyco + UAS Dharwad + TNAU** against **fruit and shoot borer**.
Gene flow can create **superweeds** and alter native gene pools.

n95e0ed5e062.s: The principal concern of farmers regarding terminator technology is that it:
o: Allows farmers to reuse seed indefinitely without purchase
Increases the nutritional value of every seed
Makes all crops resistant to every insect
Prevents plants from forming viable seeds, ending normal seed saving and replanting
n95e0ed5e062.x: Terminator technology makes the next generation of seeds non-viable, preventing seed saving and replanting and potentially forcing annual purchases.
n95e0ed5e062.tq: Apply the mechanism to the farmer’s seed-saving decision.
xs: Terminator technology **prevents plants from forming viable seeds**, **ending seed saving and replanting** — option **(4)** is correct.
Farmers are forced into **annual purchase** of seed; it does not add nutrition or universal insect resistance.
xa: Terminator = **V-GURT**; **banned in India under the PPV&FR Act (2001)**; not commercialised anywhere.
**T-GURT (Traitor)**: trait controlled by a **proprietary chemical**; research stage.
Wider concerns: **seed sovereignty** and **corporate dependency**.

nad76b5a962b.s: Which State is the largest producer of Bt cotton in India?
nad76b5a962b.x: Maharashtra is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 2017 key). Gujarat, Punjab and Andhra Pradesh grow Bt cotton but are not the largest producer.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the largest Bt cotton producer (APPSC-G2 **2017**) — so option **(3)** is correct.
**Punjab** is known for banning **glyphosate** sale in **2018**.
xa: Bt cotton covers ~**90%** of India's cotton area.
Bt cotton targets the **American bollworm**.
AP angle: **Pusa DST1** is an edited version of AP-bred **MTU1010**.

na3f0fa1c477.s: Mon 863, which was in the news over the safety of feeding studies, was a genetically modified:
o: Vitamin-A enriched rice targeting night blindness
na3f0fa1c477.x: Mon 863 was a Monsanto genetically modified pest-resistant maize variety directed against corn rootworm and was discussed in connection with feeding-study safety.
na3f0fa1c477.tq: Use the crop-pest association to identify the correct GM variety.
xs: **Mon 863** was a **genetically modified pest-resistant maize** (Monsanto) **against corn rootworm** — option **(2)** is correct.
It was in the news over the **safety of feeding studies** (PYQ).
**Vitamin-A rice** is **Golden Rice**, not Mon 863.
xa: **Golden Rice** makes **beta-carotene**; genes: **phytoene synthase** from daffodil + **crtI** from **Erwinia uredovora**.
GEAC cleared confined trials of Bayer's **HT + insect-resistant GM maize** at **PAU**, Kharif **2025**.
**Brazil-nut** soybean → never released (allergenicity).

n76db0a1934c.s: Which one of the following best explains genetic homogenisation in agriculture?
o: Cultivation of many locally adapted landraces in small farms
Increase in the number of unrelated crop species in a field
Exchange of seeds among farmers without commercial restrictions
Use of uniform engineered varieties over large areas, reducing agro-biodiversity
n76db0a1934c.x: Genetic homogenisation results when uniform varieties are widely cultivated, reducing agro-biodiversity and increasing vulnerability to new pathogens and climate shocks.
n76db0a1934c.tq: Choose the option that contains both the process and its defining consequence.
xs: **Genetic homogenisation** = **uniform engineered varieties over large areas**, **reducing agro-biodiversity** — option **(4)** is correct.
It raises vulnerability to **new pathogens** and **climate shocks**; growing many landraces is the opposite.
xa: **Monoculture** and a few patented seed firms displace **landraces** and farmer varieties.
Safeguards: **National Genebank** (**4,70,513** accessions, **2026**), **PPV&FR Act**, **National Gene Fund**.
PYQ: **genetic modification** is the technology flagged for impact on **biodiversity**.

n633a00a3426.s: Which technological development has been specifically flagged for its impact on biodiversity?
n633a00a3426.x: Genetic modification has been identified as the technology among these options that was flagged for its potential impact on biodiversity.
n633a00a3426.tq: Use the exclusion pattern to distinguish the biodiversity concern from unrelated technologies.
xs: **Genetic modification** is the technology flagged for its impact on **biodiversity** (PYQ) — option **(4)** is correct.
⚠ Trap: **solar panels**, **wind turbines** and **rainwater harvesting** are not the answer.
xa: GM risks to biodiversity: **gene flow**, **superweeds**, **genetic homogenisation**.
**Monoculture** displaces **landraces** and farmer varieties.
**National Genebank** holds **4,70,513** accessions (**2026**).

nbiology-40-5.s: The basic idea of gene therapy is to:
o: Change the environmental conditions of the patient
Alter, replace or correct defective genetic function
Replace damaged tissue with artificial implants
nbiology-40-5.x: Gene therapy is a genetic-engineering application that alters, replaces or corrects defective genes; it does not change the environment.
n: Gene therapy is a biotechnology and genetic-engineering application. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
Gene therapy targets genetic abnormalities or diseases. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to alter defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to replace defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
The basic idea of gene therapy is to correct defective genetic function. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
Genetic engineering is used in gene therapy. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #40 · pp 63-66]
xa: **CRISPR** has the potential to **correct genetic defects**.
Regulation: **CDSCO gene therapy rules 2023**.
A child in China died (**March 2025**) after a first **brain base-editing therapy**.

nbiology-44-4.s: The field that relates an individual's genetics to drug response is:
nbiology-44-4.x: Pharmacogenomics links genes to drug response and supports personalised or precision medicine.
n: Personalised or precision medicine adapts treatment using individual biological or genetic information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
Genome sequencing provides genomic information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
Pharmacogenomics links genetics to drug response. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
DNA sequencing detects sequence or variant information. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
The goal of personalised medicine is more individually tailored prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #44 · pp 73-75]
xa: **DNA sequencing** gives sequence or **variant information**.
**Genetic testing** identifies relevant variants.
Personalised medicine built on genetic make-up = **CRISPR** (UKPSC 2025).

nbiology-43-2.s: In producing a GMO, genetic engineering transfers genes in ways that:
nbiology-43-2.x: Genetic engineering changes the genome by moving genes, often from another organism, in ways that would not happen naturally.
n: GMO changes the genome or genetic makeup. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
GMO production uses genetic engineering. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
GMO production transfers a gene from one organism to another. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
Genetic transfer in GMO production occurs in ways that would not naturally occur. [Biology · ROCKET SHEET #43 · pp 71-73]
xa: GMO is approximately **synonymous** with **transgenic organism**.
A **transgenic organism** carries a **foreign gene** for a desired characteristic or product.
Purpose: to produce **desired traits or products**.

n7d6af761a4c.s: Experiments on Bt proteins in agricultural soil have shown that they:
o: Can be removed only by burning crop residue
n7d6af761a4c.x: Although persistence of Bt proteins in soil was feared, experiments have shown that they degrade.
xa: Bt gene source: soil bacterium **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
Bt toxins may harm **non-target** organisms such as soil nematodes/microbes.
Bt cotton cut pesticide use by **40-50%**.

n16e339e4c97.s: Which one of the following is the apex statutory body regulating genetically modified organisms in India?
o: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
n16e339e4c97.x: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC) is the apex statutory body regulating GMOs in India. FSSAI, CPCB and ICAR are not the apex GMO regulator.
n16e339e4c97.tq: Distinguish the correct regulatory authority from closely related bodies.
xs: The **Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee (GEAC)** is the **apex statutory body** that regulates GMOs in India — option **(2)** (APPSC-G2 **2023**).
⚠ Trap (PYQ): **FSSAI**, **CPCB** and **ICAR** are not the GMO regulator.
xa: GEAC is constituted in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** of the **Environment (Protection) Act 1986**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
Renamed from "**Approval**" to "**Appraisal**" Committee in **2010**.

nd60c46400a7.s: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee is chaired by:
o: The Special or Additional Secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
The Chairperson of the Central Pollution Control Board
The Director-General of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research
nd60c46400a7.x: GEAC is chaired by a Special or Additional Secretary of MoEFCC. A senior officer from the Department of Biotechnology serves as co-chair.
nd60c46400a7.tq: Apply the 'who would do this job?' method to identify the correct chairing authority.
xs: GEAC is chaired by the **Special/Additional Secretary of MoEFCC** — option **(1)** is correct.
The **Department of Biotechnology** provides only the **co-chair**, not the chair; CPCB and ICAR have no such role.
xa: GEAC sits in **MoEFCC** under the **Rules, 1989** (EPA **1986**).
It approves **field trials** and **commercial release** of GM crops.
**RCGM** (under **DBT**) monitors ongoing research and recommends to GEAC.

n00d986e6c59.s: Which one of the following is NOT a function of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee?
o: Approving field trials of genetically modified crops
Approving commercial release and cultivation of GM organisms
Approving large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants
Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds
n00d986e6c59.x: GEAC deals with field trials, environmental release, commercial cultivation and large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms and recombinants. Fixing the maximum retail price of all commercial seeds is not its function.
n00d986e6c59.tq: Find the one unrelated function among powers of the same regulatory body.
xs: **Fixing the maximum retail price of commercial seeds** is not a GEAC function — option **(4)** is the answer.
GEAC approves **field trials and commercial release** of GM crops — option (1) is a function.
It approves **large-scale use, environmental release and commercial cultivation** of GMOs, and **large-scale use of hazardous microorganisms** and recombinants — options (2), (3).
xa: GEAC = **apex/statutory** GMO regulator, in **MoEFCC**.
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair: **DBT**.
⚠ Genome-edited **SDN-1/SDN-2** crops **skip GEAC** and need only **IBC** approval.

n9ae46ae6cdd.s: Which one of the following technologies has been flagged for raising concerns about biodiversity?
n9ae46ae6cdd.x: Genetic modification is the technology flagged for biodiversity concerns (APPSC-GS 2023), through gene flow, monoculture and loss of diversity. Drip irrigation, solar panels and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xs: **Genetic modification of crops** is flagged for **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**) — option **(2)** is correct.
Drip irrigation, rooftop solar and rainwater harvesting are not flagged this way.
xa: Concerns: gene flow, **monoculture**, loss of diversity, **genetic homogenisation**.
Primary environmental concern: **cross-pollination** to non-GM crops.
Resistance also stems from control by **big seed companies** holding patents.

n94baf119840.s: The expression “designer babies” is most directly associated with which ethical debate?
o: Use of adult stem cells for tissue repair
Inspection of laboratories handling moderate-risk agents
Protection of traditional knowledge from patent claims
Use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits
n94baf119840.x: “Designer babies” refers to the ethical concern that genetic technologies could be used to select or modify desired traits in human offspring.
n94baf119840.tq: Translate the ethical term into its underlying biotechnology application.
xs: **"Designer babies"** refers to the **use of genetic technologies to select or modify desired human traits** — option **(4)** is correct.
It is tied to **germline editing**, an ethical issue in bioethics.
xa: Other ethical issues: **three-parent baby** technique, **animal cloning welfare**, **informed consent**.
**He Jiankui** (China, **2018**): human embryo editing — **"CRISPR babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** monitors genome-editing ethics.

nenvironment-5-8.s: The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in:
nenvironment-5-8.x: GEAC, constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, was renamed from 'Approval' to 'Appraisal' in 2010.
n: The Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee was constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The earlier name of the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee was the Genetic Engineering Approval Committee. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Genetic Engineering Approval Committee was renamed the Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee in 2010. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
The Environment (Protection) Act was enacted in 1986. [Environment · ROCKET SHEET #5 · pp 10-12]
xa: GEAC is the **apex/statutory body** regulating GMOs (APPSC-G2 2023).
Chair: **Special/Additional Secretary, MoEFCC**; co-chair from **DBT**.
It approves **field trials and commercial release** of GM crops.

ndf05d4df4c1.s: Which body forms the first, institutional-level tier of India's biosafety system?
ndf05d4df4c1.x: The sequence begins with IBSC at institutional level, followed by RCGM, GEAC, SBCC, DLC and expert committees.
xa: **IBSC** = institution level, first tier; **RCGM** = **DBT**; **GEAC** = **MoEFCC**, apex.
**SBCC** = State (punitive action); **DLC** = District (field monitoring).
**RDAC** (DBT) is **advisory**, recommending safety regulations.

nff4cbdc2dd4.s: The initial commercial approval of Bt cotton in India covered how many MAHYCO hybrids?
nff4cbdc2dd4.x: Three MAHYCO hybrids were initially approved for three years; Bt cotton remains the only GM crop commercially cultivated in India.
xa: Leading State: **Maharashtra** (PYQ).
**Bollgard** = GM technology (PYQ); genes from **Bacillus thuringiensis**.
**DMH-11**'s commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.

n97a61da527c.s: Which of the following correctly distinguishes SDN-1 and SDN-2 genome editing from SDN-3 editing?
o: All three categories are treated as conventional crops
SDN-1 alone is transgenic, while SDN-2 and SDN-3 are exempted
SDN-1 and SDN-2 introduce foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 does not
SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA, whereas SDN-3 is transgenic
n97a61da527c.x: SDN-1 and SDN-2 involve small edits without foreign DNA and are exempted from GMO rules under the 2022 guidelines. SDN-3 is transgenic and remains under full regulatory control.
n97a61da527c.tq: Discriminate the paired categories by checking the presence or absence of foreign DNA.
xs: **SDN-1 and SDN-2** are **small edits without foreign DNA**, while **SDN-3 is transgenic** — option **(4)** is correct.
SDN-1/2 are **exempted** from GMO rules (**2022 guidelines**); SDN-3 stays under **full GM control** — so options (1)-(3) are wrong.
xa: Exempt GE crops **skip GEAC**; need only **IBC** approval.
Comparison: GMO = foreign gene, full **GEAC** route; SDN-1/2 = treated like **conventional crops**.
⚠ Criticism: the GE exemption is called a **"back door"**.

n0290ae83005.s: Which of the following is NOT listed as an environmental or health risk of GM crops?
n0290ae83005.x: Insect resistance, harm to non-target organisms, weediness, genetic homogenisation, toxicity, allergenicity and antibiotic resistance are listed risks; ozone depletion is not a GM-crop risk.
xa: Primary environmental concern: **gene flow/cross-pollination**.
Reasons for resistance: **monoculture**, loss of diversity, control by **patent-holding seed companies**.
Herbicide-tolerance fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

n270be4621c9.s: In which year did the GEAC clear field trials of 11 crops and 21 varieties?
n270be4621c9.x: GEAC cleared these trials in 2014, after Bt cotton (2002), the PIL (2006) and the Bt brinjal moratorium (2010).
xa: **2009**: GEAC recommends **Bt brinjal** release.
**2012**: Parliamentary Standing Committee (**37th report**) — end all GM field trials.
**2022**: GEAC clears **DMH-11** environmental release.

n0ba9e866c3f.s: The 2010 decision relating to Bt brinjal included which of the following additional measures?
o: A requirement that all GM seeds be branded by the State
A transfer of field-trial approval exclusively to FSSAI
A mandatory State no-objection certificate for field trials
A permanent ban on every GM crop in India
n0ba9e866c3f.x: In 2010, a State NOC was made mandatory for field trials. The decision was not a permanent ban on every GM crop or a transfer of approval to FSSAI.
n0ba9e866c3f.tq: Separate the specific administrative condition from exaggerated consequences.
xs: In **2010**, along with the **Bt brinjal moratorium**, a **State NOC was made mandatory** for field trials — option **(3)** is correct.
It was not a permanent ban on all GM crops (**Bt cotton** continued), nor a shift of approvals to FSSAI.
xa: Moratorium by Minister **Jairam Ramesh**: no scientific consensus, opposition of brinjal-growing States.
Bt brinjal targets **fruit and shoot borer**; by **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended its release in **2009**.

n545731dceb3.s: In July 2024, the Supreme Court's ruling on GM mustard DMH-11 was a:
o: Dismissal of the case as withdrawn
n545731dceb3.x: The July 2024 verdict was split, though both judges directed the Centre to frame a national GM crop policy; GEAC had cleared its environmental release in 2022.
xa: **DMH-11** = hybrid seed system (**barnase-barstar**), **25-30%** higher yield; **Delhi University**.
Its commercial use is held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: **DMH-11** carries the **bar gene**.

n382e4508f30.s: The Biotechnology Regulatory Authority of India (BRAI) Bill, 2013 proposed:
o: A ban on all GM crops
A separate patent office for seeds
A GM approval committee in every State
n382e4508f30.x: The BRAI Bill proposed a single biotechnology regulator but lapsed with the 15th Lok Sabha.
xa: **BioE3 Policy 2024** now proposes **single-window clearance** + **regulatory sandboxes**.
Overlapping regulators: **DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI, NBA**.
GM approval takes **7-10 years** vs **3-5** globally.

n6479eb3856e.s: Which policy proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes in the biotechnology sector?
n6479eb3856e.x: The BioE3 Policy, 2024 proposes single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes.
n6479eb3856e.tq: Identify the policy by pairing its year with its distinctive regulatory features.
xs: The **BioE3 Policy, 2024** proposes **single-window clearance and regulatory sandboxes** — option **(3)** is correct.
**BRAI** was a **Bill (2013)** that **lapsed**, not an Act.
xa: **FSSAI GM food framework** is also of **2024**.
Delays from overlapping mandates: **7-10 years** for approval.
⚠ India has **no biosafety liability law**.

na77208af2a0.s: Lethal agents with no cure, such as Ebola, require which biosafety level?
na77208af2a0.x: Such agents need BSL-4; BSL-2 is for moderate-risk agents and BSL-3 for serious airborne agents such as TB.
xa: **BSL-4**: lethal agents with no cure (e.g. **Ebola**); India: **NIV Pune**.
**DBT** handles **biocontainment**; **NCDC** handles surveillance.
**Cartagena Protocol**: adopted **2000**, in force **2003**.

n652f78f22a6.s: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance against the:
n652f78f22a6.x: Bt brinjal was developed for resistance to the fruit and shoot borer insect.
n652f78f22a6.tq: Match the crop with its target pest rather than with another Bt crop’s pest.
xs: **Bt brinjal** was developed for resistance to the **fruit and shoot borer** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Bollworm** resistance is **Bt cotton**'s trait; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr**.
xa: Developer: **Mahyco** with **UAS Dharwad** and **TNAU**.
GEAC recommended release **2009**; **Jairam Ramesh**'s moratorium **2010**.
Gene: **Cry1Ac** from Bt.

ne82c1443f70.s: The barnase-barstar genes used in GM mustard DMH-11 come from:
ne82c1443f70.x: Barnase-barstar comes from Bacillus amyloliquefaciens; Bacillus thuringiensis is the source of Bt genes. DMH-11 was developed by Delhi University.
xa: Higher yield **25-30%**.
GEAC cleared environmental release in **2022**; held up under **Supreme Court** review.
Herbicide fears: DMH-11 carries the **bar gene**.

neb9c3f7c2dd.s: Pusa Rice DST1 is associated with which of the following traits and editing features?
o: Insect resistance; insertion of a Bt toxin gene by SDN-2
Drought and salinity tolerance; DST gene knockout by SDN-1
Higher phosphate uptake; insertion of a foreign bacterial gene
Vitamin A enrichment; mitochondrial gene replacement
neb9c3f7c2dd.x: Pusa Rice DST1 is an edited form of MTU1010, designed for drought and salinity tolerance through DST gene knockout using SDN-1.
neb9c3f7c2dd.tq: Combine the crop, trait and technical method instead of relying on the variety name alone.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1** gives **drought and salinity tolerance** by **DST gene knockout via SDN-1** — option **(2)** is correct.
It is a **CRISPR-Cas9** edit of **MTU1010**, with **no foreign DNA** — so not Bt insertion, foreign bacterial gene or vitamin A.
xa: Yield **10-30%** higher under stress; set for commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
Developer: **ICAR-IARI, Delhi**.
**Phosphate uptake** rice is **NIPGR**'s; **vitamin A** rice is **Golden Rice**.

n51ef0d58725.s: For genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption, which approval route is indicated?
o: IBC approval without the GEAC route
Only approval from the State Pollution Control Board
Approval from the Supreme Court after public consultation
n51ef0d58725.x: Genome-edited crops covered by the SDN-1 and SDN-2 exemption can skip the GEAC route and require IBC approval.
n51ef0d58725.tq: Ask which authority performs the relevant regulatory function instead of assuming every biotechnology product follows the GEAC route.
xs: Genome-edited crops under the SDN-1/SDN-2 exemption need only **IBC approval** and **skip the GEAC** route — option **(1)** is correct.
No State Pollution Board or Supreme Court route is involved.
xa: **IBSC** now clears **genome-edited crops** (Dec **2025**).
**2022 guidelines** exempt **SDN-1/SDN-2** (no foreign DNA).
**SDN-3** (transgenic) remains under full GM control.

n0423a11203c.s: Golden Rice is designed to enhance the biosynthesis of:
o: Beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A
n0423a11203c.x: Golden Rice is designed for beta-carotene biosynthesis, linked to Vitamin A nutrition.
n0423a11203c.tq: Match the product’s popular name with its intended nutritional trait.
xs: **Golden Rice** enhances **beta-carotene, a precursor of Vitamin A** (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
**Cry toxins** = **Bt cotton**; **barnase** = **DMH-11**; **polygalacturonase** relates to **Flavr Savr** tomato.
xa: Genes from **daffodil** and a **soil bacterium**.
**Flavr Savr**: first commercial GM food (USA, **1994**).
Bt cotton genes: **Cry1Ac**, **Cry2Ab**.

n6445909c7b3.s: Pusa Rice DST1 was set for commercial launch as India’s first genome-edited rice and was to be regulated like:
n6445909c7b3.x: Pusa Rice DST1 was described as India’s first genome-edited rice for commercial launch and was to be regulated like a conventional crop.
n6445909c7b3.tq: Test the regulatory classification rather than the biological trait.
xs: **Pusa Rice DST1**, an **SDN-1** edit with no foreign DNA, is treated like **a conventional crop** — option **(1)** is correct.
SDN-1/SDN-2 crops are **exempt** from GMO rules (**2022** guidelines) and **skip GEAC**.
xa: Developer: **ICAR-IARI**; edit of **DST gene** in **MTU1010**.
**Pusa DST1/Kamala** = first genome-edited rice; commercial launch (**1 Sep 2026**).
⚠ GE exemption criticised as a **back door**.

nad2c806d2d2.s: Regulation of genetically modified food, including its import, in India rests on which law?
o: Protection of Plant Varieties and Farmers' Rights Act, 2001
nad2c806d2d2.x: GM food is governed by the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, with the FSSAI GM food framework of 2024; import of GM food without approval of the competent authority is prohibited. The EPA governs GMO release, the PPVFR Act plant varieties, and the Patents Act patents.
xs: GM food, including imports, rests on the **Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006** — option **(2)** is correct.
The **EPA 1986** governs GMO release (GEAC), the **PPVFR Act 2001** plant varieties, and the **Patents Act** patents.
xa: The law **prohibits GM food import without approval**.
**FSSAI GM food framework 2024**: approval of the **competent authority**.
July **2024**: SC **split verdict** on GM mustard; Centre told to frame a **national policy on GM crops**.

n06eae1600dc.s: Which provision of the Patents Act excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability while permitting patenting of microbial processes?
n06eae1600dc.x: Section 3(j) excludes plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes from patentability, while microbial processes can be patented.
n06eae1600dc.tq: Distinguish closely numbered statutory provisions by their subject matter.
xs: **Section 3(j)** excludes **plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes**, but **microbial processes** can be patented — option **(1)**.
**Section 3(d)** is the anti-**evergreening** clause (new form of a known substance).
xa: UPSC **2019**: a biological process to create a seed **cannot** be patented; plant varieties **not eligible**.
**IPAB** existed then; abolished **2021**.
Plant varieties are protected instead by the **PPVFR Act 2001**.

nbc01a6650e5.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about Section 3(d) of the Patents Act?
o: It bars a patent for a new form of a known substance unless it shows enhanced efficacy
It is meant to block evergreening
In Novartis v Union of India (2013), the Glivec rejection was upheld under Section 3(j), not 3(d)
Section 3(j), a different clause, excludes plants, animals and seeds
nbc01a6650e5.x: The Supreme Court upheld the Glivec (imatinib) rejection under Section 3(d); Section 3(j) deals with plants, animals, seeds and essentially biological processes.
xa: **Section 3(j)**: plants, animals, seeds and **essentially biological processes** are not patentable; **microbial processes** can be.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)** over **FL-2027 (FC5)**; registration revoked in **2021**.

n7f239314b0f.s: Under the PPV&FR Act, 2001, farmers are NOT allowed to sell:
n7f239314b0f.x: Farmers may save, use, sow, resow, exchange, share and sell farm produce including seed, but not branded seed of protected varieties.
xa: The Act **bars registration** of varieties carrying **GURT**.
**PepsiCo potato case (2019)**: **FL-2027 (FC5)**; PPVFR Authority revoked its registration (**2021**).
⚠ Plant varieties are **not eligible** for patents under **Section 3(j)** — the PPVFR Act protects them instead.

n8ec5fa205bb.s: In the FL-2027 (FC5) potato variety case, PepsiCo sued farmers of which State?
n8ec5fa205bb.x: PepsiCo sued Gujarat farmers, later withdrew the suits, and the PPVFR Authority revoked the variety's registration in 2021.
xa: Farmers may save, resow, exchange and sell seed — but **not branded seed**.
**PPVFR Act 2001** protects plant varieties and **farmers' rights**.
**IPAB** was abolished in **2021**.

nbd0da3d9d5e.s: Which of the following is NOT an objection raised by farmers against GURT or terminator seeds?
o: Guaranteed improvement in farmers' autonomy over seed supply
Higher recurring costs of purchasing seed
nbd0da3d9d5e.x: Farmers' objections include dependency on companies, recurring costs and loss of seed-saving. Guaranteed improvement in seed autonomy is contrary to these objections.
nbd0da3d9d5e.tq: Find the option that reverses the direction of the stated social and economic concerns.
xs: **Guaranteed improvement in farmers' autonomy over seed supply** is not an objection — it is the opposite — option **(3)**.
Real objections: **seed dependency** on companies, **costs**, and **loss of seed-saving** — options (1), (2), (4).
xa: Terminator seeds yield **sterile seeds** → farmers buy fresh seed each season.
The **PPVFR Act** bars registration of GURT varieties.
Debate also flags **farmer seed dependency**, **public mistrust**, **labelling** debates.

n4d701804137.s: Which of the following is NOT correct about the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety?
o: It is named after a city in Brazil
It was adopted in 2000 and entered into force in 2003
It has an Advance Informed Agreement procedure for transboundary movement of LMOs
It is supplementary to the Convention on Biological Diversity
n4d701804137.x: Cartagena is in Colombia, not Brazil.
xa: **173 parties**, including **India**.
Also covers **liability and redress**.
India's **National Biosafety Framework**: **2009**.

n8296e253283.s: Which Indian law criminalises biological weapons?
n8296e253283.x: The WMD Act, 2005 criminalises biological weapons in India; India is also a Party to the BWC (opened 1972, in force 1975).
xa: **DBT** = biocontainment; **NCDC** = surveillance.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
Gap: **no unified national biosecurity framework**.

n2db928ecbec.s: Which of the following is identified as a gap in India’s biosecurity system?
o: Non-membership in the Biological Weapons Convention
Absence of any institution concerned with disease surveillance
Complete prohibition of all genetic engineering research
Absence of a unified national biosecurity framework
n2db928ecbec.x: The stated gap is the absence of a unified national biosecurity framework, with laws also lagging behind synthetic biology and gene editing. India is a party to the BWC.
n2db928ecbec.tq: Identify the stated institutional gap while rejecting absolute distractors.
xs: The gap is the **absence of a unified national biosecurity framework** — option **(4)** is correct.
India **is a Party** to the **BWC**, and **NCDC** does surveillance — so options (1), (2) are wrong; research is not prohibited.
xa: Laws also **lag synthetic biology and gene editing**.
**Global Health Security Index (2023)**: India **66th**.
**BWC**: opened **1972**, in force **1975**.

n7698d270a7d.s: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued jointly by which organisations?
n7698d270a7d.x: The National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017 were issued through the ICMR-DBT framework and provide ethical and regulatory guidance.
n7698d270a7d.tq: Identify the institutions directly associated with the named guidelines.
xs: The **National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** were issued jointly by **ICMR and DBT** — option **(3)** is correct.
They provide an **ethical + regulatory framework**.
xa: Stem cell sources: **embryonic**, **adult**, **umbilical cord blood**, **iPSC**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** is the **global monitor** of genome-editing ethics.
**rDNA Guidelines** are also of **2017**.

n63e0cdf4d78.s: Human embryo editing associated with the birth of the so-called “CRISPR babies” was carried out by He Jiankui in:
n63e0cdf4d78.x: He Jiankui’s human embryo-editing experiment in China became widely associated with the “CRISPR babies” controversy in 2018.
n63e0cdf4d78.tq: Discriminate between closely placed country-year combinations.
xs: **He Jiankui** carried out **human embryo editing** ("CRISPR babies") in **China in 2018** — option **(1)** is correct.
**2000** (Colombia) is the **Cartagena Protocol**; **1994** (USA) the **Flavr Savr** tomato; **2017** India's **stem cell guidelines**.
xa: Ethical issues: **germline editing**, **"designer babies"**.
**UNESCO's International Bioethics Committee** = global monitor.
**National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017** (**ICMR-DBT**).

nfb714185de6.s: Which State is recognised as the leading Bt cotton-growing State in India?
nfb714185de6.x: Maharashtra is identified as the leading Bt cotton State.
nfb714185de6.tq: Test the crop-State association directly using a nearby cotton-growing State as the distractor.
xs: **Maharashtra** is the leading Bt cotton State (PYQ) — option **(3)** is correct.
Punjab, Gujarat and Telangana are not named as the leader in the notes.
xa: Bt cotton approved **March 2002**: three **MAHYCO** hybrids.
Area **12.5 million ha**, **over 90%** of cotton area.
Trait: **bollworm** resistance via **Cry1Ac**/**Cry2Ab**.

n8c9f8de2c5b.s: Which of the following is regarded as the primary environmental concern associated with genetically modified crops?
o: Cross-pollination and gene flow to non-GM crops
Reduction in soil mineral content in every cultivated field
Increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide from all crops
n8c9f8de2c5b.x: The primary environmental concern is cross-pollination or gene flow from GM crops to non-GM crops. The other effects are not identified as the primary concern.
n8c9f8de2c5b.tq: Select the precise environmental impact rather than a general ecological claim.
xs: The primary environmental concern is **cross-pollination/gene flow to non-GM crops** (APPSC-G2 **2023**) — option **(1)** is correct.
Groundwater, soil minerals and CO2 are not named concerns.
xa: Other environmental risks: **insect resistance build-up**, harm to **non-target organisms**, weediness in wild relatives, **genetic homogenisation**.
Health risks: **toxicity**, **allergenicity**, **antibiotic resistance**.
**Genetic modification** = technology raising **biodiversity concerns** (APPSC-GS **2023**).

na9afc97561b.s: Approval of a GM product in India may take about 7–10 years, compared with about ____ globally.
na9afc97561b.x: Overlapping mandates of DBT, GEAC, CDSCO, FSSAI and NBA and the lack of a biosafety liability law mean 7–10 years in India against 3–5 years globally.
xa: ⚠ Criticism: multi-layered regulation **delays approvals yet lacks a liability law**.
**BioE3 Policy 2024**: **single-window clearance** + regulatory sandboxes.
**BRAI Bill 2013** (single regulator) **lapsed**.

n6950545e4b0.s: Besides quantum effects, the unusual properties of nanomaterials arise mainly from their:
n6950545e4b0.x: Quantum effects and a very high surface-area-to-volume ratio give nanomaterials enhanced reactivity and unusual optical and electrical behaviour.
xa: They also show different **optical/electrical** behaviour.
Nanoparticle size: **1-100 nm** (APPSC **2018**).
**1 nm** = one billionth (**10^-9**) of a metre.

n6ed10801b27.s: A particle is generally classed as a nanoparticle when its size lies in the range of:
n6ed10801b27.x: Nanoparticles are 1-100 nm in size (APPSC 2018 key); one nanometre is one billionth (10^-9) of a metre. 0.1-1 nm is atomic scale, while 100-1,000 nm and micrometre ranges are too large.
xs: A nanoparticle is **1-100 nm** in size (APPSC **2018**) — option **(2)** is correct.
**1 nm** = one billionth (**10^-9**) of a metre; the larger ranges fall outside the nanoscale.
xa: New properties arise from **quantum effects** and high **surface-area-to-volume ratio**.
**Nano Urea** particles are **~20-50 nm**.
Natural nanoparticles: **volcanic ash**, **sea spray**, **smoke**.

nc2f0fb1201e.s: The Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) is used to image atoms on:
nc2f0fb1201e.x: STM images atoms on conducting surfaces, whereas the AFM can work on non-conducting materials as well.
xa: **STM**: **Binnig and Rohrer** (**1981**), Nobel Physics **1986**.
**AFM** = Atomic Force Microscope (**1986**).
**Sol-gel** is a **bottom-up** synthesis method, not an imaging tool.

ne09aa007ad0.s: Which of the following is a bottom-up method of nanomaterial synthesis?
ne09aa007ad0.x: Self-assembly builds structures from atoms and molecules (bottom-up); lithography, milling and etching cut bulk material down (top-down).
xa: **AFM** = Atomic Force Microscope; works on **non-conductors** too.
Wells / wires / dots = confinement in **1 / 2 / 3** dimensions (**2D / 1D / 0D**).
**Quantum dots**: semiconductor nanostructures with **size-tunable colour**.
Nanoparticle size: **1-100 nm** (APPSC 2018).

n84a6418c2f2.s: Bawendi, Brus and Ekimov received the 2023 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for work on:
n84a6418c2f2.x: The 2023 Chemistry Nobel was for quantum dots, which show size-tunable colour and are used in displays and solar cells.
xa: **Wires** = confinement in **2** dimensions (**1D** structure).
**Nanocrystals**: **LEDs**, imaging.
**Graphene** Nobel: Physics **2010**.

n97f3a39467c.s: The term 'nanotechnology' was coined in 1974 by:
n97f3a39467c.x: Norio Taniguchi coined the term in 1974; Feynman's 1959 lecture gave the idea, and Iijima discovered carbon nanotubes.
xa: **Binnig and Rohrer (1981)**: **STM**, Nobel Physics **1986**.
**Geim and Novoselov**: **graphene**, Nobel Physics **2010**.
**Quantum dots**: Bawendi, Brus, Ekimov — Nobel Chemistry **2023**.
⚠ **STM** works on conductors only; **AFM** (**1986**) works on non-conductors too.

n5fc9b29218a.s: The Scanning Tunnelling Microscope (STM) is correctly associated with:
o: Binnig and Rohrer; 1986; Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1981
Binnig and Rohrer; 1981; Nobel Prize in Chemistry, 1986
Binnig and Rohrer; 1981; Nobel Prize in Physics, 1986
Kroto and Smalley; 1981; Nobel Prize in Physics, 1986
n5fc9b29218a.x: The STM is associated with Binnig and Rohrer in 1981; they received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986 for related work.
xa: ⚠ **STM** images atoms on **conductors only**; **AFM** works on **non-conductors** too.
**Fullerene (C60)**: Kroto, Curl, Smalley (**1985**); Nobel Chemistry **1996**.
**Graphene**: **Geim and Novoselov**; Nobel Physics **2010**.

nchemistry-6-5.s: Graphene is a single atom-thick, sp²-hybridised layer of:
nchemistry-6-5.x: Graphene is a one-atom-thick sp² layer of graphite; rolled graphene sheets form carbon nanotubes.
n: Diamond has sp³ hybridisation. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Graphene has sp² hybridisation. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Fullerene has a hollow cage structure resembling a soccer ball. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Graphene is a single-atom-thick layer of graphite. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Carbon nanotubes consist of cylindrical rolled graphene sheets. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Graphene is a single-layer, two-dimensional allotrope of carbon. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Carbon nanotubes are tubular allotropes of carbon. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Fullerene has a hollow cage structure. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
xa: C₆₀ has **12 pentagons**, **20 hexagons**, **60 carbon atoms**.
**Graphite** forms **planar sheets** of hexagonal rings.
**Amorphous carbon** (coal, charcoal, coke, lampblack) is **non-crystalline**, mixed hybridisation.

nchemistry-6-11.s: In diamond's tetrahedral network, each carbon atom is bonded to how many other carbon atoms?
nchemistry-6-11.x: Each carbon in diamond bonds to four others at the corners of a tetrahedron, giving a rigid 3D network.
n: Diamond has a three-dimensional tetrahedral network structure. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Each carbon atom in diamond is bonded to four other carbon atoms. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
Diamond has a rigid lattice. [Chemistry · ROCKET SHEET #6 · pp 23-26]
xa: Diamond is **sp³** hybridised.
It is the **hardest natural substance** — **Mohs hardness 10**.
Graphite, in contrast, is **sp²** in layered sheets.

nd8c1427455a.s: The third generation of nanoproducts consists of:
nd8c1427455a.x: The third generation is systems of nanosystems, including complex devices such as nanoelectronics and nanomedicine.
xa: 3rd-gen examples: **nanoelectronics**, **nanomedicine**, **energy storage**, **robotics**.
2nd-gen: **sensors**, **actuators**, **targeted drug delivery**.
Classification after **M.C. Roco**.

n85ce98fb048.s: The classification of nanotechnology products into four generations is associated with:
n85ce98fb048.x: The four-generation classification of nanoproducts is associated with M. C. Roco.
n85ce98fb048.tq: Use the author-association approach for a named classification.
xs: The four generations of nanoproducts are classified after **M.C. Roco** — option **(2)** is correct.
**Feynman** gave the idea (**1959**); **Taniguchi** coined the term (**1974**); **Iijima** found nanotubes (**1991**).
xa: **1st** passive → **2nd** active → **3rd** systems of nanosystems → **4th** molecular nanosystems.
2nd gen includes **biosensors** and **targeted drug delivery**.
3rd gen includes **3D networking** and **robotics**.

n7992fa96182.s: In public health, gold nanoparticles are used for:
o: Rapid lateral-flow diagnosis of malaria, dengue and typhoid
n7992fa96182.x: Gold-nanoparticle lateral-flow kits rapidly diagnose malaria, dengue and typhoid; graphene enables bendable wearable sensors.
xa: **CSIR-CGCRI**: **silver-nanoparticle** dressings cut infections ~**60%**.
**CNT membranes** (IIT Kanpur) are for **desalination**.
**Nano-cellulose**: packaging, filters.

n1f5a43a6ce1.s: The nanogenerator developed by the National Chemical Laboratory, Pune, produces electricity when pressure is applied. This is based on the:
n1f5a43a6ce1.x: The NCL nanogenerator converts mechanical pressure into electricity through the piezoelectric effect.
n1f5a43a6ce1.tq: Discriminate between closely related physical effects by linking the input stimulus to the output.
xs: The **NCL (Pune)** nanogenerator makes electricity from **pressure** — the **piezoelectric effect** (APPSC **2018**, **2019**) — option **(4)**.
⚠ Trap: it is **not photoelectric or thermoelectric**.
xa: **IIT Bombay**: perovskite-silicon tandem cells, **27.3%** efficiency.
**Internet of Nano Things**: nanodevices networked over the internet.
**IIT Roorkee**: Uttarakhand's **first nano-fabrication facility**.

nae305cfc651.s: The smart, biodegradable, natural-polymer nanoparticles developed by IIT Mandi were designed for treatment of:
nae305cfc651.x: IIT Mandi developed renewable-resource-based natural-polymer nanoparticles for colorectal cancer applications.
nae305cfc651.tq: Identify the disease associated with the named research institution and product.
xs: **IIT Mandi**'s biodegradable **natural-polymer nanoparticles** target **colorectal cancer** (APPSC-G1 **2024**) — option **(1)** is correct.
**Parkinson's** and **rheumatoid arthritis** work is **INST Mohali**'s; **malaria** is detected by **gold-nanoparticle** kits.
xa: Made from **renewable resources**.
**INST Mohali** (**2026**): **nano-cups** for heat-based cancer therapy.
**Liposomal nanoparticles** = targeted delivery.

nff6f49f6f52.s: Nano-zero-valent iron is used in water-related applications mainly for:
nff6f49f6f52.x: Nano-zero-valent iron is used to remove contaminants from water.
nff6f49f6f52.tq: Match the nanomaterial with its environmental remediation function.
xs: **Nano-zero-valent iron** is used for **removing contaminants** from water — option **(2)** is correct.
N-use efficiency is the job of **Nano Urea**, not nZVI.
xa: **CNT membranes** (IIT Kanpur) for **desalination**.
**Nanoporous materials**: separation, catalysis.
**Nanofibres**: **filtration**, smart clothing, scaffolds.

nd4b4a63554a.s: The first nano-fabrication facility of Uttarakhand was established by IIT Roorkee. It is intended to complement which missions?
o: National Health Mission, Jal Jeevan Mission and Swachh Bharat Mission
Nano Urea, Nano DAP and Nano-cellulose missions
nd4b4a63554a.x: IIT Roorkee’s facility complements the Semiconductor, Nano and Quantum missions; it is not associated with Samudrayaan.
